Thus, O Lakṣmī, having understood these gifts according to their true nature and how they are to be kept secret, both women and men should bestow them with a desire for liberation. 98.
The gift of a woman should always be given with great devotion;
for "woman" (yoṣā) is declared to be "illusion" (māyā), she who is the dawn (uṣā) at the beginning of night.
For that [māyā] which binds living beings must be surrendered to the Supreme Self;
being himself free from māyā, he proceeds to the supreme state.
The gift of a maiden should be bestowed upon the youth, which bestows happiness;
for that maiden is thirst, she is the hope for pleasure, and she belongs to the youth who is the Supreme Self. 101.
Having offered oneself to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is devoid of Māra, one should proceed to his abode;
and the gift of a cow should be bestowed, for the auspicious knowledge of Śrī Hari is contained within the cow.
"Having given, both the giver and the receiver go to the imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, having thus understood my majesty in this world, those who— || 103 ||
They perform their duties in the land of action and wander for the sake of liberation; by taking refuge in my state, they become enjoyers of eternal bliss. 104.
Thus has this majesty of mine, born of yoga, been recounted to you here;
by reading or even hearing it further, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Attaining Brahminhood and Sainthood, the Means for Going to the Abode, the Means for the Stainless Path, Divine Gifts and the Like, and the Yoga of Hari," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī-Śrī said: O Mādhava, you ought indeed to explain all the duties of virtuous women;
for all virtuous women are born from your body, yet they are indeed subject to *māyā*.
How indeed should they conduct themselves constantly in this world?
For those who have abandoned their husbands are followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. || 2 ||
All those women were beloved by Hari, for they were indeed the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa; they were of the nature of Brahman, great devotees of the Lord, and truly Sāttvatas.
By what path could they exist as those who offer themselves entirely?
How could their devotion to their husbands (pātivratya) endure without a husband who has taken them in marriage? (4)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; for women who are consecrated by renunciation, the initiation is indeed the marriage itself, as it has been joined with me.
With this mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," that virtuous woman was married in the presence of the sacred fire.
Having performed the fire sacrifice, she, being initiated, then reached me who am identical with my own form;
and having worshipped me, she arrived at the sacrificial pavilion where the fire had been offered.
That virtuous woman accepted my saffron robes,
and by my preceptor’s command, from the very moment of her initiation, she became my wife.
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is her husband, and I am Nārāyaṇa;
she remains truly married, and her devotion to her husband is always fixed upon me.
This virtuous and purifying wife of mine must be protected by you;
for others might travel upon my path, and they might also live upon my path.
They shall live with divine devotion on the path of liberation, the true path; and they shall perform service to the virtuous, for the virtuous are my very forms.
They should live with a desireless disposition and likewise serve [Me];
in every way, they should offer themselves to My forms.
These virtuous duties of women were established by the sages at the time of marriage;
they become partners in the practice of dharma and other duties with their husbands upon being wedded.
Therefore, just as my wife Lagnavatī was obedient to her husband’s command,
so too is my virtuous wife Tyāgavatī obedient to my command.
Having invoked Agni as witness, as well as the preceptor, the parents, Gaṇeśa, and likewise myself and my virtuous wife—both of whom are indeed equal—[she spoke]. 15.
That bull, who upholds the supreme dharma of devotion to his wife, is equal [to me];
likewise, the devotion of my husband to his wife is equal to that of Hari and myself. || 16 ||

In the presence of the fire and other witnesses, she becomes the partner in dharma for her husband; in the presence of the fire and other witnesses, he becomes the partner in dharma for his wife. (17)
She who is always devoted, of excellent character, gentle speech, virtuous conduct, and pleasing appearance, should constantly remember her beloved partner in dharma. (18)

With a mind focused on no other, pleasant-faced, and a companion in the practice of dharma with her husband, she should be devoted to the true dharma and become a partaker of the true dharma. || 19 ||
The virtuous woman should constantly gaze upon her husband, the god of gods;
endowed with divine conduct, she should perform service and attendance upon him.
For she who is not of another mind, who is free from distraction, pure in nature, and a giver of happiness, should gaze repeatedly upon her husband’s face as if it were the face of her own son. (21)
And Namadā, rich in self-restraint and a practitioner of dharma, bowed to her husband,
having understood the duties of a married couple and the religious obligations shared between them.
Realizing this, she should be devoted to dharma and share the same vows as her husband;
indeed, with a tranquil mind, she should serve her husband as the God of gods.
Even if she has been instructed, she should always have a very serene face toward her husband; even when struck or addressed with harsh words, she should remain submissive at all times. (24)
A virtuous woman should not touch another man, nor should she look at him with desire;
she should not even engage in joking or other such behavior with another.
For her, there is nothing dear except her husband; even his leftovers are dear to her.
When joined with her husband, everything is dear, and that is indeed a great favor.
The husband’s command is the Lord’s own command; the husband is the venerable Supreme Lord.
She who ascends to her husband shall indeed be a follower of dharma. ||27||
She who attends upon her husband—whether he be poor, diseased, wretched, suffering, exhausted, or humble—is one who partakes of the fruits of righteousness. (28)
A mother who has daughters is one who possesses children; one who is childless is fruitless. She who is dear to her husband and whose life is her husband shall be a partaker of dharma.
She who performs service, even the state of a servant or menial labor,
and who practices attendance and personal care, is a partaker of merit.
Disciplined, of gentle conduct, affectionate toward her husband, and firm in resolve—she who has dedicated her entire being to her husband shall be a partaker of dharma. (3.1)
She who has no longing for sensual pleasures, nor for wealth, nor for powers, nor for delights, as she has for her beloved—she is a virtuous woman, a partaker of Dharma. //32//
She who delights in rising early, is devoted to attending to the household in the morning, and is always intent on purification through sweeping, smearing, and other such tasks; (33)
She who is devoted to the fire-ritual, likewise devoted to the rites for the gods,
and intent upon her duties— she shall be a partaker of dharma.
She who, having first given water and other offerings according to their needs to the deities, guests, dependents, her husband, and elderly people, satisfies them; 35.
She who eats only the remaining food after having fed all of them,
and whose family is satisfied and well-nourished, shall be a partaker of dharma.
Constantly bowing and serving the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and always devoted to her own mother and father, she shall be a partaker of dharma. (37)
She who supports the virtuous, the poor, and the helpless with food and other necessities according to her ability fulfills her duty as a wife and shall partake in the merit of righteousness. (38)
Like those most devoted to Brahman, she who stands in the position of a wife does not look upon any other man anywhere—
even one situated at the four crossroads— provided her eyes are bound.
Such a person is rare in the world without Lakṣmī abiding in the heart,
and without Satī, who dwells in the heart of Śambhu and has assumed an invisible state.
She who observes the difficult vow commanded by her husband, being devoted to her husband and intent on his welfare, shall be a partaker of dharma. ||41||
This is merit, this is heaven, this is austerity, and this is the vow—for her whose husband is indeed the supreme deity, Nārāyaṇa himself. (42)
For a husband is indeed the god of women; the husband is the teacher, the husband is the refuge;
the husband is the kinsman, the husband is fortune, the husband is life, and the husband is the ultimate goal. (43)
Reconciliation brings heaven; displeasing one's master leads to hell.
It may result in an improper act, unrighteousness, or even the loss of life.
The husband should speak thus, and she should act accordingly; devotion to her husband is the supreme virtue.
Poverty, disease, calamity, enmity, or being consumed by a curse—[these do not affect her]. (45)
She should perform every action in accordance with her husband's disposition;
considering all this to be his good fortune, she should indeed serve her husband. (46)
Thus, the dedication of all one's possessions that proceeds toward the husband, having disregarded the duties for times of distress, is the practice of a devoted wife. 47.
"And as I am always married to a virtuous wife in this world, so may that virtuous woman remain devoted to me alone here, having me as her supreme goal. (48)
Her purity is for my sake, her stainlessness is for my sake;
she has assumed her attire for my sake, and she is endowed with beauty for my sake. (49)
She who has renounced all conditioned things for my sake is indeed a virtuous wife devoted to her husband;
for my sake she wears red garments, and for my sake she wears saffron robes, seeking only me.
Adorned with the Puṇḍra mark, the moon, and other ornaments, she is a practitioner of perfumes for my sake;
she wears flower garlands for my sake and bears wreaths for my sake. (51)
For my sake, that virtuous and devoted wife adorned her neck and hands;
for my sake she took her food and drink, and for my sake she partook of wine.
She who has prepared her ornaments for my sake, she who has prepared enjoyments and vehicles for my sake, and she who has adorned herself for my sake—she is a virtuous woman, my devoted wife. 53.
She has assumed the dress of Keśava for my sake; she has put on the bodice for my sake;
she has donned the upper garment for my sake; and she has wrapped the loincloth for my sake. (14)
For my sake she has hands and feet, for my sake her head is formed;
for my sake she possesses a torso, and for my sake she moves within.
She who considers my welfare her own primary concern, who showers the rain of bliss upon me, and who is immersed in my name and virtues—that virtuous woman is my devoted wife. 56.
She who is eternally established in sattva for my sake, eternally characterized by rajas for my sake, joined with obstruction for my sake, and protected by affection for my sake. ||57||
She whose heart is always fixed on me, who acts for my sake and fulfills my desires—
she who conducts herself thus is truly my virtuous wife, Harivratā.

Even while performing meritorious deeds, righteous actions, and auspicious conduct, or whatever else [is prescribed], a virtuous woman who possesses the excellence of character and good fortune [attains her goal]. (59)
She should be devoted to Me, resting in Me, her life-breath centered on Me, and endowed with devotion to Me;
she should exist as My very form—that virtuous woman who observes the vow of Hari.
She whose duty is renunciation for my sake, who is adorned with truth for my sake, who has gone to sleep for my sake, and who remains awake for my sake. (6.1)
She is occupied for my sake and has withdrawn from everything for my sake;
thus she finds contentment in my sake and observes the vow of non-violence for my sake. (62)
They have renounced sacrifice for my sake; they perform the ritual of oblation for my sake;
they abide in celibacy for my sake; and they observe non-possession for my sake.
She whose conduct and purity were for my sake, who was established in austerity for my sake,
who was devoted to Vedic study for my sake, and who was intent on worship for my sake— (64)
The activity of my senses is for my sake; my mind is always for my sake;
my thought is for my sake, and it is endowed with resolutions directed toward me. (65)
Exertion for the sake of sentient beings is for my sake; the cultivation [of the path] is based on my sake;
the accomplishment of sovereignty is for my sake; and abiding in meditative concentration is for my sake. ||66||
Abiding on the pure path for my sake, honoring guests for my sake,
performing the work of cooking for my sake, and having food as her domain for my sake— (67)
Her house and halls are for my sake; she sings and recites songs for my sake;
she remains in the state of dance and emotion for my sake, and she listens to stories for my sake. (68)
She possesses great zeal for my sake; she wanders to sacred fords for my sake;
she has undertaken her pilgrimage for my sake; and she is a garden of flowers for my sake. (69)
She performs her activities for my sake; she engages in buying and selling for my sake;
she is rich in the effort of agriculture for my sake; and she protects the kingdom for my sake. (3.77.70)
Her service is for my sake; she is endowed with servitude for my sake;
she has entered into slavery for my sake; every arrangement is for my sake. (7.1)
Because she went for my sake and brought [the gift] for my sake, and was possessed of thoughts for my sake—in this way that virtuous woman, devoted to Hari, has become dedicated to me. (72)
For my sake she observes the Kārttika vow; for my sake she is an ascetic in Pauṣa;
for my sake she is rich in the merit of Caitra; and for my sake she remains steadfast in Śrāvaṇa. ||73||
She gave lamps for my sake, she ate in rows for my sake;
she attained the status of a disciple for my sake, and she became a teacher for my sake. (74)
For my sake, even though she was accompanied by all her female disciples, that servant became heavy; yet that virtuous woman attained the status of a Guru and became an embodiment of me.
She is virtuous, her conduct is that of a virtuous woman; she is my virtuous wife, devoted to Hari.
Such is Lakṣmī, my chaste wife, whose dharma is renunciation. (76)
Likewise, there were the friends of Rādhā, the friends of Lakṣmī, and also the friends of Śrī; there were also the friends of Māṇikī and those auspicious friends of Satī. (77)
Those who are friends of Sāvitrī, as well as those who are friends of Sītā, those who are friends through devotion, and all those who are considered Nārāyaṇīs; ||78||
Likewise, there are those belonging to Vāsudeva, those belonging to Kṛṣṇa, those dear to Brahmā,
those belonging to Viṣṇu, the divine ones, those belonging to Brahmā, and those who are liberated.
Likewise, those who possess supreme sovereignty, as well as the women of the Īśāna quarter—
all those sovereign ladies are indeed virtuous wives devoted to their husbands.
"For whomsoever and for whatever purpose my entire being exists, all of that is solely for the sake of my beloved.
Thus, this mutual state of being a virtuous husband and wife—I am the Supreme Lord.
Without me those virtuous women do not exist, and without them I do not exist;
established in mutual dependence, we bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. 82.
We are the bestowers of enjoyment and liberation for the gods, the lords, the perfected ones, the exponents of Brahman, and indeed for all embodied beings. (83)
Understand, O Lakṣmī, the majesty of yourself, of your friends, and also of me;
likewise, take heed of the majesty of my liberated ones. (84)
I am the truly existent Blessed One, the manifest Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Lord;
you are the virtuous Consciousness, the foremost among chaste women, the beloved of Brahmā and the beloved of Hari. 85.
Through union with that, there is constant bliss and great bliss for us both;
there is indeed eternal bliss, and its enjoyer is truly liberated. (86)
I am indeed the virtuous Sādhu; Ramā is the virtuous Lakṣmī, ever Satī;
Śrī is prosperity, and Māṇikī is happiness—these five are the supreme deities. (87)
A virtuous man bestows and brings about every kind of happiness;
a virtuous woman also bestows and brings about every kind of happiness. ||88||
Being virtuous, one abides in truth; from this, supreme prosperity and goodness arise.
Thereby, one indeed protects happiness, and eternal well-being prevails. (89)
"O Lakṣmī, she who is always equal to liberation, who has become the Great Supreme Brahman, and who is thus ever-virtuous, is my Satī, the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. (3.77.90)
Filled with all bliss, she rejoices with me, her Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. 91.
This body—whether man or woman—is not the self; nor is it the self whether it be woman or man.
Likewise, there are sages who delight in the Self, as well as virtuous men and virtuous women.
Those men and women who are established in Brahman and the Self, who are united with me, whose nature is mine, and who take refuge in me—they are my remaining beings; among them, I am Nārāyaṇa. (93)
The woman who takes refuge in a man is herself dependent on him; likewise, all men are dependent on women by virtue of their nature as dependents. (94)
"I am the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master and Sovereign, the very foundation of man.
Having thus understood this truth here, the virtuous woman became endowed with good fortune. 95.
Knowing her to be his own beloved, he should always practice devotion to his wife;
for that virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, is the beloved of the world and the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. 96.
In the world, a youth becomes beloved through union with the body of a young woman; but I am always beloved—in the womb, in childhood, and in youth. (97)
In old age and even at death, in the state of being a ghost or in another world, in saṃsāra or in the heavenly realms and so forth, and even in liberation—He alone is truly beloved. (98)
I indeed exist as the self of all beings, for I am eternal;
I am always present within the self as the inner controller. (99)
Likewise, even there, I am eternally indeed beloved, and the state of being beloved resides within me;
for through my yoga, the quality of being beloved exists truly within the self alone.
Thus, as the eternal beloved, I manifest within all;
indeed, through my splendor, all those who are liberated likewise become possessed of splendor and become lords.
The gods and humans and so forth, as well as animals and even trees; the insentient and the sentient, as well as Māyā and its products (māyika). 102.
Those who possess luster through my luster are my beloveds by nature;
thus, everything consists of the beloved, and widowhood truly does not exist anywhere.
Therefore, virtuous women, endowed with good fortune, should worship me as their beloved;
thus, O Lakṣmī, this secret of virtuous women has indeed been declared by me.
The conduct of all souls is hidden and filled with the essence of reality;
therefore, one should never give way to the intoxication of thinking, "I am a person."
Having made the thought "He is my very self," one should worship the Lord, the Master;
for I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme husband.
O virtuous ones, having truly understood this secret, those people and women who reflect upon it and act accordingly shall attain the supreme goal.
They shall likewise attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as happiness and bliss,
and my eternal yoga and the supreme state of Nirvana.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Limit of Devotion to the Husband and the Knowledge of Satī-Sādhvīs," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this most excellent narrative of a virtuous woman.
In the city of Jālakapura in Saurāṣṭra, there was a cowherd girl named Sucandrikā.
Her husband, Gopa, also worships Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
he has always been a devotee, intent on ritual bathing, and a follower of the cowherds.
Gopāla and Gopavāsa always serve me, as well as Bālakṛṣṇa, with forest produce and other offerings in the forest. || 3 ||
He worships me with milk-porridges, boiled milk preparations, milk, curds, ghee and the like, as well as with fresh butter, flowers, and water.
And he, my devotee who possessed the characteristic of longing, having indeed abandoned his own body due to fever during the rainy season, went to heaven with his desires fulfilled.
Having abandoned his wife Gopī when half of his lifespan had expired,
Gopāla indeed, out of compassion for me, ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Accompanied by Apsarases and cows, he shines resplendent,
together with all [his attendants] provided with every requisite, including various kinds of food and edibles.
And his wife on the earth is devoted to me;
though pregnant with a child, she desires to die following her own husband.
The devoted wife, unable to endure the suffering of being apart from her husband,
was then prevented by the people from ascending the funeral pyre of her lord.
O Gopī, by destroying the embryo, your sin has become manifold;
yet for your husband, heaven has been attained, along with a celestial chariot.
"Protect the fetus; you shall become a mother within a year. Furthermore, if she dies on her husband's back, there is indeed great merit for the wife of a husband. (11)
For one who is not pregnant, this is indeed possible; but for one who is pregnant, it is a source of affliction.
Therefore, do not commit this slaughter; dwell happily in Govraja.
Although she was thus being restrained, she fell along with her husband;
at that very moment, this husband of hers ascended to a celestial chariot from the funeral pyre.
He saw her on the path of the sky; "Do not do this, O cowherd girl! Do not! he cried, and with his own hand he restrained her and lifted up his beloved.
Having consoled her while she was still unburnt and having instantly extinguished the fire,
he took her onto his celestial chariot and instructed her on the protection of the fetus.
"Having provided for your son's protection and having married him off, come to my heaven thereafter; do not make me your follower."
Thus addressed, she became tranquil and happy, her mind fixed on her husband's words;
freed from grief, she was brought by her husband down from the celestial chariot to the earth.
Having bowed to the funeral pyre and having bowed to her husband, the cowherd woman indeed went home;
she then worshipped me, saying, "O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! (18)
The cowherd woman Gopikā indeed maintained her religious duties, devotion, vows, and virtuous conduct;
and that cowherd woman Sucandrikā gave birth to a son with a beautiful face.
The boy grew up, and having become a youth, he was married;
then the cowherd woman informed her son of his former birth.
Then the son also rejoiced at all that had occurred regarding his own father;
he said, "Now I must go to heaven toward my father."

Having spoken thus, she smeared the ground with cow dung and sat down for a moment; then, after meditating, she abandoned that body. At that moment, her husband’s celestial chariot appeared, accompanied by the Goddess of the Gods.
And as she arrived from the sky, they indeed caused her to ascend [the chariot]. ||23||
While the excellent apsarases increased the beautiful moonlight with cries of "Victory!",
the cowherd’s son, accompanied by his bride, beheld them in the sky.
Then, having mentally perceived his father as a divine form and likewise his mother as the vital breath,
the celestial chariot ascended in a mere moment to the heights of the sky.
Seated in her celestial chariot, Mañjughoṣā, the foremost of the Apsarases, questioned Gopikā and Sucandrikā right in the presence of her husband.
By what vow, O auspicious lady, and by what conduct was she raised, that the cowherd woman, having shaken off her sins, has arrived in the world of the gods? (27)
Wearing garments as radiant as fire, beautiful with golden campaka flowers, and blazing with splendors, how has this divine being come here of her own accord? (28)
"O cowherd girl, you have reached the heavenly world not through slight austerity, nor through charity, nor through religious observances; tell me, how did you come to be there? (29)
Having heard this, the cowherd girl Sucandrikā spoke to Mañjughoṣā:
"How indeed is heaven attained? Tell me the cause for that. (3.78.30)
Then Mañjughoṣā spoke: "O Gopī, listen to the reason:
she who wears saffron robes and is devoted to the path of renunciation. (3.1)
Whether she be shaven-headed or wearing matted locks, likewise clad in bark garments, such an ascetic woman who is devoted to giving and is highly meritorious [attains this state]. (22)
That virtuous woman who is devoted to her husband, who gives to all guests and to the noble-souled saint, shall go to heaven. 33.
The husband is the god; the husband is Kṛṣṇa; the husband alone is the supreme bull.
The husband’s command is the highest Veda; the husband’s satisfaction is the bull for the woman. (34)
"In this way, the virtuous woman who conducts herself thus attains the imperishable heaven.
Having heard this, the cowherd woman then said: "Listen, O rider of the celestial chariot! (25)
I am not one clad in saffron robes, nor am I devoted to renunciation; I am neither shaven-headed nor do I wear matted locks, nor do I wear garments of bark.
I am not a female ascetic wearing garments of wool and such, nor am I one who dwells in the forest, milks cows, or even recognizes a guest. (37)
I was a cowherd woman devoted to serving the virtuous and appointed by the cowherds; I was intent on serving my husband, and by that [merit], I have attained the state of a goddess. (38)
I never spoke harsh or cruel words to my husband;
rather, I remained devoted to the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, and the saints. (39)
I am a servant of my husband’s cattle and remain devoted to my mother-in-law and father-in-law;
I do not engage in backbiting, nor do I harbor any deceit in my mind. (3.78.40)
I do not stand in an improper place, nor do I utter vulgar speech, nor do I speak what is false, or laugh improperly, or say anything harmful that is filled with evil. (41)
Whether it be a secret or not a secret, I shall certainly not do so in any way;
for my husband has come home after having gone out for the sake of the cows. ||42||
I always serve as her follower by offering water, food, a seat, and other such things;
yet there is no food that pleases her, nor is there any edible thing that she finds to her liking. (43)
I renounce all that is to be chewed, licked, and drunk;
indeed, I always perform every task for the sake of my family.
May all kinds of auspicious things be for the sake of my lord:
collyrium, yellow pigment, bathing, garlands, ointments, and so forth. (45)
I do not delight in adorning myself when my husband has gone out, nor do I ever wake my husband while he is sleeping soundly. (46)
I perform even the domestic duties while endowed with happiness;
I do not weary my husband, and therefore my mind is satisfied. (47)
I am always one whose secrets are well-guarded and who remains under the control of his command;
having thus served my husband, I shall follow him in death upon his funeral pyre.
Though she had settled there, was forbidden [to stay], and uprooted—yet for the sake of her son's life, she brought her son along with his wife to the earth and then departed for heaven. (49)
"O Mañjughoṣa, it was indeed for this purpose that I came here during the day;
I have found a husband here, and my son exists upon the earth. (3.78.50)
Such various kinds of gopīs indeed exist upon the earth;
and those who were the gopīs of Kṛṣṇa have been born again in every single kalpa and at the end of every kalpa.
Having worshipped Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as my husband, and having likewise worshipped my divine husband in this manner, I have come here. (52)
Upon hearing this, Mañjughoṣā was delighted and praised her;
the other apsarases also praised that devoted wife.
Having dwelt there for a long time and enjoyed various pleasures many times over,
the virtuous Sucandrikā went to Satyaloka together with her husband.
And there Sāvitrī asked: "The gods indeed go from heaven to the mortal world; how is it that you remain here to experience what remains? (55)
"O virtuous lady, you have come here for a true purpose; tell me the reason for it.
Then Sucandrikā, with a joyful heart, spoke to Sāvitrī.
In heaven, I have seen every supreme pleasure consisting of enjoyment; however, that indeed lacks restraint and is devoid of virtuous conduct and vows. (57)
The gods indeed possess no moral discipline, nor does the discipline belong to the celestial women;
even sexual intercourse is found among the Apsarases in the highest heaven. (58)
Even among the gods, O Sāvitrī, such a custom generally exists even for the goddesses; what more can I say?
The gods and goddesses, likewise possessing the power to assume any form at will,
roam about exactly as they please, indeed devoid of all restraint.
Such devotion to a husband is not found among goddesses, nor is such a vow of a wife found among celestial beings;
those who have enjoyed the remnants of such [merit] go to the abode of mortals.
Among the principal gods, even the vow of a wife is not found;
what then can be said of the minor deities? When they die, they go to the realm of mortals.
Saṃjñā, daughter of Candra; Rohiṇī, daughter of Puloman; and the wives of the sages—these and others of few number are indeed devoted to their husbands.
In heaven, within my husband’s celestial chariot, I have always observed the vow of devotion to my husband in every way, just as I did on earth.
Because of my past merit, I have performed the worship of Hari daily and have also protected the bull; thus, I have become one who cannot be touched by any other man. (65)
O Sāvitrī, it was solely by the grace of Śrī Hari and through His power that I have come to Satyaloka with my husband; there is no other cause.
Having dwelt here, I shall depart by the grace of my Lord, to Vaikuṇṭha, which is above the waters, through the vow of my husband Hari. (67)
Thus spoke that virtuous woman; they both indeed dwelt there for a long time, and then they both went to Vaikuṇṭha, to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu.
Having gone there, the great virtuous woman bowed to Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari;
the cowherd bowed to Viṣṇu, and they both honored them with joy.
Questioned by Lakṣmī, "O virtuous lady, how have you come from Satyaloka?
Sucandrikā said to Śrī, "I have come through devotion to my beloved. (3.78.70)
"This cowherd is indeed my beloved, and he is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord. I worship my beloved eternally—the eternal Beloved of the Beloved. (71)
A virtuous woman who has fully embraced dharma and is devoted to her husband—by the power of my husband's dharma, I have arrived at Vaikuṇṭha. (72)
Then, having dwelt there for a long time together with her husband,
that gopī, graced by the gopa, went even to Goloka.
Some of these gopīs bowed to Rādhikā, and the cowherd bowed to Kṛṣṇa;
they both remained there in that world among the hosts of gopīs and cowherds.
Rādhā said to Sucandrikā: "How did she come here?
Tell me the reason, O Gopī; by what merit has she arrived? (75)
Sucandrikā said to Rādhā: "By serving Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved;
by serving the Beloved; and by serving even the Beloved of the Beloved. (76)
O Rādhikā, through the dharma of devotion to my husband, the dharma of Kṛṣṇa, and the dharma of a virtuous wife, I have come here to the house of the cowherds. 77.
Devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma, the highest among all dharmas;
devotion to Kṛṣṇa is the supreme dharma, the highest among the dharmas of virtuous women.
By me, my beloved, the best of cowherds, has been constantly worshipped;
and Kṛṣṇa, the protector of even the cowherds, has always been fully honored. (79)
By that merit, O Rādhikā, I have come here to this world;
having dwelt for a long time, I shall afterwards indeed go to the imperishable abode.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous woman, having dwelt for a long time with her beloved and having maintained her devotion to her husband, then departed for the imperishable abode. ||8 1||
Taking refuge in the Supreme beyond the supreme, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, she bathed in the Brahma-lake and became a great female liberated soul (mahāmuktānikā). 82.
Then the husband also became liberated and endowed with the state of Brahman;
indeed, all the effects of Māyā were then dissolved within both of them.
Then the principles became of a single nature for both;
indeed, the entire principle of the Self was beautiful, supreme, and embodied. (84)
Then, it was manifested in the form of the Supreme Person; having attained the states of male and female there, they entered into a divine condition. (85)
There, they attained sārūpya, sālokya, and sārṣṭitā with Śrī Hari;
there also sāmīpya was attained, and they both bowed to Puruṣottama. (86)
And they dwelt in the imperishable abode, chanting the names of Puruṣottama:
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Parameśvara. (87)
"O Supreme Brahman, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama!"—by thus [calling out], O Lakṣmī, those two then became liberated in my imperishable realm. (88)
Previously, on the surface of the earth, those two received my mantras from Lomaśa;
by their power, my devotion toward them both increased over a long time. (89)
The devotion to her husband, the devotion to Hari, and the auspicious devotion to her husband were constantly increasing for the cowherd woman, as well as for the cowherd, more and more.
Indeed, by serving the virtuous, by my character in every respect, and likewise through my devotion throughout all the worlds, they have obtained me as their husband. (9.1)
Māṇikyā, my beloved Dhāmni, Jayā, and Lalitā likewise questioned that gopī: "How indeed have you come here? (92)
Sucandrikā said to Māṇikyā, "O Śrī Parameśvarī, O auspicious one, [you have attained this] through service to your husband and by following the virtuous conduct of a chaste woman. (93)
"Through devotion to the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa and her wifely fidelity, she has come here;
this husband of mine is a great liberated soul who was immersed in the lake of Brahman."
I myself was also born, and I am in every way dear to Brahmā;
the virtuous Muktānikā was born, for Māṇikī is indeed liberated in form. (95)
Supreme liberation is obtainable through compassion; of this there is no doubt whatsoever.
For service to the virtuous is true association with the good, and through such service, one acquires a treasure of merit. (96)
Through heaps of merit, discrimination between one's own self and the Self of others arises;
from that discrimination, an engagement in the welfare of the Self is born. (97)
From those two, the destruction of evil and purification arise, and through them, devotion is born;
and by means of devotion, there comes the remembrance of the Name, the Abode, and so forth, filled with affection. (98)
Through the offering of affection, all kinds of desired success arise;
the Supreme Self is indeed the beloved one, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (99)
Thus, this very accomplished Lord Kṛṣṇa, my most beloved, has been attained;
in this manner, Hari, my consort, was reached by me here in the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara-dhāman).
Thus addressed, Māṇikī was pleased and praised Sucandrikā;
having obtained the virtuous friend, she became filled with joy. (101)
Sucandrikā, ever liberated, dwelt there like another Śrī;
O Lakṣmī, she was my beloved devotee in that abode consisting of the syllables of Hari’s name. 10.2.
Thus has the supreme greatness of a virtuous woman been shown to you here;
for my devoted and virtuous mistress is indeed the ultimate bestower of liberation.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Miracles of the Virtuous Woman," concerning how the gopī named Sucandrikā—possessing conjugal fidelity and devotion to the Lord’s own wife—along with her husband, attained the celestial realms of Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Imperishable Abode (Akṣaradhāma), in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Kṛṣṇa, if a virtuous and devoted wife abides in the life of a householder, what must she do to attain prosperity? Tell me, O Beloved who bestows happiness.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having entered the householder’s life as a virtuous wife, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama should be constantly propitiated; He indeed bestows prosperity.
Sages, ancestors, gods, virtuous men, twice-born ones, the elderly, guests, and noble women are especially worthy of worship. (3)
One should worship the gods with offerings and sacrifice, humans with constant hospitality,
the sages and ancestors with funeral cakes and *śrāddha* rites, and [the sacrificial fire] by making oblations into the fire.
One should perform the śrāddha with water, roots, and fruits, and feed the virtuous;
one should also honor the twice-born with gifts such as food and clothing.

A virtuous woman should feed guests; she should also feed virtuous and chaste women, as well as the officiating priest, one who has completed his Vedic studies, a holy man, her teacher, and her father-in-law.
She should honor her husband, the master of the household, with sweet offerings of madhuparka;
she should also scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcastes, and birds.
One should give [an offering] here to Nārāyaṇa accompanied by the utterance "svāhā";
one should give bundles of grass to the cows and sugar and other sweets to the children.
One should give water to the trees and chickpeas and other grains to the fish; one should give grain-particles to the flocks of birds and the remains of offerings (prasāda) to those standing nearby.
One should give in this manner according to one's capacity, attend to the hearing of sacred stories, perform the spinning of rosaries, and behold the deity.
One should perform the offering of water, as well as bathing, meditation, worship, and so forth;
one should likewise engage in the chanting of the Name, devotion, and remembrance.
One should practice the purification of the body, the purification of righteousness, and the purification of the mind.
One should perform service to the virtuous and service to the holy according to one's ability and as is appropriate.
One should offer flowers, incense, and lamps according to the prescribed rite.
Herbs, which are portions of the moon, are always endowed with nectar.
Various species of flowers remove fierce poison born of heat;
they also instantly bestow the nectar of mental joy and complete satisfaction.
Indeed, through their fragrance, flowers remove the poison from embodied beings.
They truly gladden the mind, bestow prosperity, and bring joy to the heart.
The gods and others are pleased by flowers, and being pleased, they bestow prosperity as well.
Contemplate that flowers with desirable fragrances are dear to the gods. Indeed, white flowers from thornless plants are truly beloved by the gods.
Water-born lotuses and garlands belong to the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and serpents;
flowers with pungent thorns and red blossoms are for those seeking malevolent rites; and sharp-potent flowers and black thorny ones belong to the spirits (bhūtas). || 17–18 ||
O beloved, flowers from impure grounds, though they may delight the minds and eyes of men and are indeed dear to them, must be avoided in every way.
The gods are satisfied by their fragrance, while the yakṣas and rākṣasas are pleased by the sight of them.
Through their very enjoyment, serpents and humans likewise [satisfy the gods] by means of these three alone.
Scents from flowers and sandalwood immediately gratify the gods;
and being gratified, they in turn bless these mortals with perfections and prosperity.
Incense in the form of resin is indeed considered excellent, namely guggulu;
the gods are pleased by this incense, which bestows prosperity upon the life of a householder.
Agallochum (agaru) is likewise the best for yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhogins.
Artificial incenses for the Daityas, as well as those made from sallakī resin of that same kind, are used;
through the offering of incense made from turmeric, the bhūtas become satisfied and depart.
Furthermore, incenses such as sarjarasa and others are indeed desired by human beings.
The gift of a lamp always produces beloved increase of splendor; having overcome blinding darkness, gloom, and even the southern solstice,
the offered lamp grants the northern path.
A lamp is the giver of upward movement; it is the medicine for the destruction of darkness.
Indeed, by the gift of lamps, the gods became radiant and illuminators;
they were born in the heavenly world as luminous beings. Therefore, one should offer a lamp.
By the gift of light, one becomes possessed of keen vision and endowed with the illumination of intelligence.

One who steals a lamp becomes blind, destined for darkness, with his light extinguished. Indeed, those who give lamps become like the full moon through offerings of clarified butter, medicinal herbs, juices, and resins. (28–29)
For as many years as there are twinklings of the eye during which the lamps burn, for that long shall the giver of lamps possess keen vision, beauty, and power. (3.79.30)
Therefore, lamps should be offered by a virtuous woman devoted to the life of a householder;
furthermore, she should by all means perform ascetic penance during the final stage of her life.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe that unsurpassed dharma of virtuous women, by which austerity one may attain the state of the imperishable abode of Brahman. (32)
Having performed that by which one may attain liberation, there was in a former kalpa a personage whose story is told;
in a former kalpa, there was a Manu named Haripratha.
His wife was Brahmaprathā, a virtuous woman endowed with consecration;
she was the daughter of the great sage Kaṇḍāyana and was devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
And she was born in the house of Kaṇḍāyana as Mānasī;
she was full of knowledge, full of austerity, and free from all mental fluctuations. (35)
Though young, she lived as a forest-dweller; while remaining in her father’s house, that virtuous woman undertook the initiation of consecration.
Abiding in celibacy, she became an ascetic even within the home.
With her body uninjured and untouched by any man, that virtuous woman sat on the bank of a river in the forest of Viṣṇu, radiant as the moon. (37)
Having gone with her father to bathe, she returned wearing wet clothes after her bath;
she was a well-nourished young woman, established in virtuous conduct, and endowed with the quality of generosity.
For as he was traveling through the sky, Manu Haripratha beheld the beautiful and auspicious abode of Brahmā,
pervaded by the splendor of Brahmā’s ascetic penance.
The goddess was divine, worthy of her station, and a virtuous bringer of splendor to the home; her body was pervaded by luster, and her beauty surpassed even the radiance of the sun.
She is endowed with all splendors, the abode of the fortune of all sovereignty; among all women, she is the foremost as Nārāyaṇī in beauty, majesty, and other qualities. 41.
Having merely looked and reflected, the king quickly descended from his celestial chariot onto the riverbank and joyfully prostrated before that sage.
He honored him like a father and gave his own introduction;
having heard this, the sage Kāṇḍāyana then rejoiced at Manu.
Seeing the king, the son of Vaidhasa, she honored him;
the maiden also, having quickly approached, performed a respectful reception for Manu. (44)
Having inquired after one another's welfare, they indeed praised the sight of each other;
and Manu, having bowed to the Brāhmaṇa, remained silent for a moment.
The sage said quickly, "O Manu, what indeed may I do for you?
Manu replied, "O Guru, there is a desire residing in my heart. (46)
If you are capable in this matter, you ought to fulfill it;
for the sage, through meditation, has fully discerned the mind of Manu.
The daughter questioned that virtuous woman who was renouncing her for the sake of giving away [the child]:
"Speak, daughter; Manu desires you—what shall I do? (48)
The daughter said: "The dharma of my father’s command shall be fulfilled;
nevertheless, I always delight in virtuous conduct (*śīla*), for it is through that that one attains the state of a chaste woman (*sādhvī*). (49)
Nevertheless, a maiden who remains under the authority of her father should follow her father’s word; for once she has come under her father’s command, a maiden indeed becomes subject to her husband.
Wives indeed become virtuous and faithful to their husbands;
act as you wish in this matter, for I am pleased with your request.
Kāṇḍāyana became pleased and gave his daughter to Manu;
through this connection with Manu, he became honored throughout the three worlds.
Having wedded Brahmaprathā, Manu led her to his own abode;
he then granted Brahmaprathā the oversight of the kingdom over the three worlds.
Manu’s wife, Manu, ruled an excellent kingdom;
devoted to the sanctity of the home, she always served the virtuous.
This virtuous woman served him well and accepted his words of blessing;
during the time of Manu, she performed all kinds of sacrifices.
She performed various excellent and meritorious vows of giving,
as well as all kinds of beautiful acts of hospitality.
She attended upon virtuous men and women, as well as great sages; she served female renunciants and ascetics, and attended upon those practicing austerities. (57)
When the period of Manu’s authority was complete, that virtuous woman, together with Manu, went by celestial chariot to my imperishable abode of Hari. (58)
There, having honored that virtuous woman with ten million coins, I asked her:
"O beautiful one, tell me, by what merit have you come to this imperishable state? (59)

And she said: "O Blessed One, I am a great devotee, a follower of the Sātvatas, and a servant of the virtuous; O Lord, O Beloved, O Master of the Beloved, I worship you and I bow down to you. (3.79.60)
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, you are omniscient; nevertheless, I am your servant, acting according to the command given by my beloved husband, the Supreme Soul. (61)
Indeed, I shall report everything to you accordingly; listen to me:
[I have made] a gift of one hundred thousand gold coins to a twice-born man. (62)
I gave gifts of jewels, silver, millions, and thousands;
I observed the vow of Brahmā, yet because of the fruit of that, I did not come here. (63)
He performed fifteen-night sacrifices, ten-night and one-night rites, and a hundred Jyotiṣṭomas; yet he did not even attain the status of a Nāga through the fruit of those deeds.
Having performed most severe penance for a hundred years on the banks of the Gaṅgā and having given away a hundred thousand horses, I did not indeed attain the fruit thereof.
I gave ten times ten thousand horses and twenty times ten thousand milch cows;
yet, because I gave them away as a gift to women, I did not attain the fruit thereof. (66)
Likewise, I gave away a thousand maidens adorned with golden crescents,
as well as sixty-three thousand women decorated with every kind of ornament.
I gave away ten arbudas of cows with their calves during Gosava sacrifices, along with gifts of gold, bronze, and other items; yet, indeed, I did not attain the fruit thereof.
In the Āptoryāma sacrifices, ten cows are invariably given to a twice-born;
indeed, I gave a hundred thousand cows multiplied by ten, for that is the fruit of those [sacrifices].
I gave ten times ten thousand beautiful horses born in Bāhlīka, richly adorned with golden garlands and trappings; yet, I did not attain [the desired fruit] as a result of that.
I gave eighteen million gold coins every day;
yet, even for each individual sacrifice, I did not attain the fruit thereof. (71)
O Supreme Lord, O Kṛṣṇa, I gave fifteen crores of green horses with black ears, adorned with golden garlands. (72)
I gave fifteen thousand other Padminas— tall, large-bodied, with long tusks and golden ornaments.
I gave ten times ten thousand well-adorned golden chariots,
yoked with horses and embellished with golden ornaments, at the sacrifice.
I also gave away the southern limbs as well as other parts prescribed by the Vedas,
complete with all their constituent members, in ten Vājapeya sacrifices.

I gave ten great male slaves with necklaces around their necks, female slaves, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) during the ten Rājasūya sacrifices; indeed, it was by the fruit of that [merit] that I obtained the Nāgas.
The stream of the Brahmaputrā was covered by gifts of gold, gems, and elephants from the south and other regions; for indeed, that was the fruit of his [meritorious] deeds. (77)

I gave away a hundred million villages to the Brahmins throughout the seven continents, and I worshipped the gods with sacrifices performed at the distance of a throw of a yoke-pin, involving hundreds of thousands of Sādyaska rites.
"Even though I was present at the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice through thirteen and twelve-day rites, as well as with the flowers used therein, I have not come here. (79)
In that sacrifice, I gave eight thousand humped bulls to the twice-born,
as well as white oxen and white cows adorned with gold.
I gave heaps of gold and jewels, trees of pearls, and gardens of grain and crops; likewise, I gave gifts of sugar-candy.
I performed sacrifices lasting eleven days and repeatedly those lasting twelve days,
along with horse-sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, as well as sixteen Ārkāyaṇa rites.
I gave a forest a hundred yojanas long, filled with mountains,
adorned with fresh golden neck-ornaments, and provided with magnificent gardens.
Nevertheless, it was not by virtue of the merit accumulated from that [previous life] that I came here; I also performed daily and occasional religious observances (vratas). ||84||
I performed thirty Agni sacrifices, as well as eight Soma sacrifices,
seven Sarvamedhas, and ten Naramedhas.
Nor have I come here, O Blessed One, by means of the merits of a hundred and eight Viśvajit sacrifices or likewise Aśvamedha sacrifices. (86)
Furthermore, in the Gaṅgā, the Brahmaputrā, and the Irāvatī, as well as in the great river Menakāṅgā and the Bālakṛṣṇa lake. ||87||
Furthermore, at Śvetavārdhi, Śītavārdhi, and likewise at Nārāyaṇī,
I performed austerities, being entirely devoted to the service of the virtuous.
In various places, he indeed served the virtuous who have Kṛṣṇa as their ornament;
and he served the virtuous women, satisfying them with all kinds of gifts. (89)
They were fed, honored, seen, touched, and their bodies massaged; they were massaged at the feet, bowed down to, and served. || 3.79.90 ||
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama! (91)
Thus, the virtuous singers of my glories and the saintly women who have followed them—those holy men are pleased with me, and those saintly women are always pleased with me. (92)
The Brahmins, the sages, and the devoted guests, as well as the Sāttvatas, the female devotees of the Lord, and the Yoginīs, were all thoroughly gratified.
And my father was indeed highly pleased by their compliance with his words;
having received great blessings from them,
both men and women, I instantly became perfected, virtuous, purifying, and divine.
Possessing a divine body through sacrifices to Hari, she was born as a companion to the beloved of Brahmā.
Together with my beloved husband, I have reached the further shore of Māyā;
I was told by holy men and women, "Go to the imperishable abode of Hari. (96)
I am that very one, O Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the imperishable abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. 97.
Having come to this world for the sake of serving you and obtaining your favor, O Kṛṣṇa, take my hand and dwell with me here forever. 98.
"Make me, your peerless friend Māṇikyā, your own servant.
Having been addressed thus by me, O Lakṣmī, she was then made your friend. (99)
There is indeed no higher duty than service to the virtuous;
it bestows prosperity, liberation, heaven, and likewise peace.
Thus has this been told to you here: namely, that service indeed follows upon giving.
Furthermore, through reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Virtuous Woman, including Worship and Charity; the Residence of the Virtuous Sādhvī—the Wife of Brahmā, the First Manu of Hari—in Heaven; and the Attainment of the Imperishable Abode as the Fruit of Serving Saints and Holy Women," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the supreme fruit of serving the virtuous—
the constant service of saintly men and women which bestows a full lifespan.
Dharma is characterized by conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by their behavior; whatever is the actual way of life of the perfected ones (sādhus), that is the characteristic of conduct.
Even when he is out of sight, people who have traveled far away remember the righteous man who practices the true Dharma and performs acts of devotion simply by hearing of him. (3)
One who desires his own welfare should indeed protect the dharma of the virtuous;
for the bull among the virtuous destroys the sin even of one whose body is sinful.
Through virtuous conduct, a full lifespan is attained:
ten thousand years in the Kṛta age, ten thousand years in the Tretā age, and one thousand years in the Dvāpara age.
One who always lives a full hundred years is born under the asterism Tiṣya;
through constant right conduct, prosperity always abides, and the Goddess Śrī dwells permanently in his home.
Fame arises from virtuous conduct both in this world and the next;
it is my view that it is the cause of the favor of the wise and of long life. (7)
Everything else is indeed subject to sublation, but the word of the virtuous is not sublated;
they are endowed with devotion to me, observant of moral conduct and vows, and possessed of peaceful forms.
And those virtuous ones, adorned with goodness, who perform the task of propitiating me,
rescue even the dead and purify those still living.
For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world; because living beings tremble before him, and that very trembling is the destroyer of life. 3.80.10.
Those who are revilers of the virtuous, cruel, transgressors of the commands of their gurus and the scriptures, established in unrighteousness, and of evil conduct—they become short-lived. (11)
Those who have transgressed the bounds of propriety, who are cruel and addicted to sensual pleasures, as well as those devoid of devotion and shameless, will indeed become short-lived. || 12 ||
For even a person who is devoid of all auspicious marks, if they possess noble conduct, are endowed with faith and devotion, and are virtuous, lives for a full hundred years. 1.3.
Free from malice, truthful in speech, and devoid of anger, deceit, and the like; straightforward and non-violent, he lives for a full hundred years.
One who crushes clods of earth, one who cuts grass, one who bites their nails, one covered in filth, and one whose mind is unstable—such a person does not attain a long life in this world. 15.
One who is unfaithful and promiscuous does not live long at all;
indeed, nothing else in this world is so detrimental to longevity. (16)

Just as there is no atonement for a man here in this world who consorts with another's wife, so too one who betrays his guru, betrays his father, or betrays a virtuous person does not live [in peace].
One who betrays his wife, one who betrays his mother, and one who betrays the gods do not live [long].
One who is attached to women, one who crosses rivers [frequently], and one who practices with weapons do not live [long]. 18.
One who drinks liquor and eats meat does not live for long;
one whose mouth is like an arrow of speech that pierces the vital organs suffers from extreme disease.

One cursed by a spell, one who acts with rashness, a practitioner of malevolent magic, a murderer, and one who neglects the worship of those worthy of honor—none of these indeed live for long. (3.80.20)
One who kills those who have sought refuge, one who kills those under his protection, one who betrays trust, and one who slays children—such a person certainly does not live for long. ||21||
One who destroys the testicles, one who destroys the penis, one who binds the vulva, one who causes abortion,
one who destroys the menstrual cycle, one who destroys living beings, and one who kills bees— such a person does not live.

One who performs the work of a hunter, as well as a wheel-maker, a butcher, one afflicted by poison, one possessed by spirits, one with wind-diseases, one suffering from consumption, one with urinary disorders, and one with phlegm disorders do not live long. (23)
One who suffers from asthma, one who has blood in the urine, one with slow digestion, and one who causes distress does not live long;
likewise, one who seizes property by force, an arsonist, and one who travels through the sky do not live long. (24)
One who is constantly away from home, one who is a habitual deceiver, one who consumes intoxicants, and one who is addicted to opium do not live for long at all. (25)
He who, having risen first, salutes his mother, father, teacher, preceptor, the virtuous, a faithful wife, her husband, a deity, and the elderly; || 26 ||
One who constantly eats wholesome food lives for a long time;
indeed, through the clarity of ghee, one attains a long lifespan. (27)
Eating while facing the east indeed brings about great longevity;
one who eats food mixed with ghee that is wholesome shall certainly become long-lived. (28)
One who eats with wet feet certainly lives a full lifespan;
one who is still impure from eating should never touch the four luminaries.
By honoring the fire, the cow, and a virtuous Brahmin, one's life-force does not perish;
for the vital breaths of a youth indeed ascend when an elder approaches. (3.80.30)
One should again attend to them by rising to meet them and by saluting them.
One who is impure from eating should not touch another's head, for all the vital breaths (prāṇas) are dependent upon it. 3.1.
One should not bathe one's head frequently; thus one's lifespan will not be impaired. One should not eat food mixed with sesame seeds; thus one's lifespan will not be impaired. (32)
If one practices [recitation] on a forbidden day (anadhyāya), his lifespan is diminished;
likewise if he recites facing the sun, facing fire, facing a cow, or facing a woman. (33)
Those who urinate on the path have their life-span diminished;
there is no doubt that the reviling of one's guru burns away the lifespan of human beings. (34)
One who desires to live long should not cause pain to a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, or a serpent; nor should one revile a virtuous man, a chaste woman, a cow, a deity, or the sacred law.
One should not desire conversation with those who have fallen [from their status], one should avoid seeing them, and one should certainly not associate with them; thus, one attains a long life.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day, nor with an unmarried girl, nor with a prostitute, nor with a woman who has not bathed; by doing so, one attains a long life.
The elderly, the virtuous, virtuous women, the gods, and the highest gurus are worthy of worship; they should be invited to dwell in one's home, for that indeed brings merit and long life. (38)
Insulting great-souled beings always brings about the exhaustion of one's lifespan;
the most secret matters of great-souled beings must never be spoken. (39)
One should praise the virtuous and the good; thus one attains a long life.
One should never sleep during the twilight hours; by chanting prayers for a long time, one lives long.
One should have the work of shaving performed while facing either the east or the north;
one should not utter slander, for in this way one attains a long life.
Envy is detrimental to longevity, as is the disparagement of those worthy of honor;
likewise, sleeping during the day and adultery are similarly destructive to one's life-span. (42)
Proper conduct generates prosperity; proper conduct increases fame.
Indeed, through proper conduct life is prolonged, and proper conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Dharma originates from right conduct; through Dharma, life is increased.
Indeed, the benedictions of the virtuous bestow long life. (44)
The longevity of Mārkaṇḍeya, as attested by the words of the Seven Sages and also by the word of the Creator (Brahmā), is indeed the supreme illustration of this. 45.
Likewise, Nāciketa met his death through his father’s anger;
and those monkeys who were slain in battle were restored to life by Rāmacandra.
O Rame, the body is of two kinds: that composed of the elements and that which is the form of glory.
The elemental body depends upon life-span, while glory is bound by conduct.
Through blessings, the auspicious lifespan of a material being increases here;
through virtuous conduct and service, however, auspicious fame increases. (48)
Through virtuous deeds, a mass of merit increases along with fame;
through devotion, both arise and increase eternally. (49)
If there should be someone virtuous in the family, or a virtuous woman who is a yoginī of Brahman, that family will certainly attain fame and secure renown in the world. (3.80.50)
For in a virtuous family, men indeed possess renowned conduct;
but in a sinful family, they are surely born as sinners in many ways. (51)
In whatever family sinful men are born, all manner of misfortunes arise;
they surely produce infamy and even destroy one's reputation. (52)
A single son who is wise and devoted brings glory;
he alone, being of virtuous conduct, truly delivers his kinsmen in this world. (53)
If a maiden or a bride should be virtuous and follow the conduct of the righteous, she certainly purifies her entire family and delivers it. (54)
In whosever heart the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa resides, he is surely the savior;
by him the worlds are saved, or she saves them. (55)
His lineage shall be long-lived, his fame shall endure for a long time, and liberation is certain for him; from her, auspicious offspring are born. (56)
In this world, the preceptor (upādhyāya) is said to be superior to ten teachers (ācārya);
and in every respect, the father is superior to ten preceptors. (57)
A mother is always superior and more venerable than ten fathers;
a virtuous, faithful, and devoted wife is as weighty as ten mothers.
For she is endowed with virtue, devoted to the holy life, and truly dear to Brahman;
that virtuous woman is always identical to my own nature—she is Vaiṣṇavī, she is Nārāyaṇī. (59)
She is the dark one, she is the daughter of Madhu, she is Lakṣmī, and she is indeed the power of the Supreme Person;
and I am always of virtuous form throughout all the cycles of creation.
The virtuous are indeed my own form, and the virtuous women are my powers;
they all bestow my abode and are purifiers, O beloved. (6.1)
In all creations, there is nothing more purifying than the virtuous;
there is no merit or austerity equal to the service of the virtuous in every respect. (62)
Those wealthy with riches serve embodied beings worthy of worship;
those poor, rich in service to the virtuous, attain the eternal Brahman.
The wealthy indeed go to heaven, and the poor go to the divine abode;
those without wealth serve the virtuous with their bodies and with devotion.
They perform fasts that bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
therefore, the sacrifice of service is superior to a sacrifice consisting of material wealth.
A holy place that liberates the self should always be resorted to with joy;
the gross holy place consists of earth, water, and so forth, while the subtle holy place is the service of the virtuous. (66)
The divine sacred ford is purity of mind; one should practice frequenting that ford.
One who is purified at the sacred ford of the mind is liberated at the sacred ford of the Self.
One should bathe in the mental sacred ford— a deep, stainless, and pure lake whose waters are truth— having taken hold of eternal goodness.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I proclaim the purification of sacred sites (tīrtha-śauca), which bestows liberation; by means of this, goodness arises and illusion is destroyed. (69)
Non-possessiveness, lack of desire, straightforwardness, and truthfulness;
as well as non-violence, gentleness, tranquility, compassion, self-restraint, and inner peace. || 3.80.70 ||
Freedom from possessiveness and egoism, freedom from dualities, lack of worldly attachment, and purity—these are the qualities by which the virtuous have indeed become sacred fords. (71)
The knowers of Brahman are the great sacred ford, the deliverer that destroys sin;
they delight in renouncing everything, possessing devotion and knowledge, and viewing all with equanimity. ||72||
Free from passions, tranquil, virtuous, and the ornaments of the sacred ford— therein, one who has bathed in the supreme purity of mind is liberated.
One whose limbs are merely moistened with water is not truly called bathed;
he who has bathed with self-restraint is the one who is pure both externally and internally.
Those who are always free from the sense of "mine" do not grieve for what has passed, even when it is before their eyes;
for those in whom no longing arises, their purity is indeed like that of a sacred bathing place.
Freedom from worldly attachments for the body, clarity of mind,
and purity of knowledge for the self— these indeed are the three sacred pilgrimage sites.
Purity of conduct pertains to the body, purity through vows pertains to the mind, and purity through sacred fords pertains to the self; indeed, these three bring about liberation.
Supreme purity arises from knowledge, consisting of the water of the realization of Brahman;
he who bathes there in the mental lake attains liberation, without a doubt. (78)
But a person who has established purity in reality, who is constantly endowed with devotion, and who is perfected in the virtues of service, is always a true sacred ford itself. (79)
By the glorification of this sacred ford, by bathing therein, and by the libations offered to the ancestors, all sins are consumed; thereafter, one goes to the imperishable state.
By accepting the virtuous, by the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s seizing their minds, and by the immersion in the river of devotion, they cross over the darkness of material nature. 8.1
The virtuous are indeed the best of sacred fords, and goodness is the most excellent of sacred fords;
he who bathes in both shall swiftly attain perfection.
Good conduct is the supreme dharma, and it is indeed the highest sacred ford;
by following the dharma of the virtuous, an individual attains the ultimate goal. (83)
Dharma alone is the companion for human beings in the world beyond;
if it is made divine in this life, that is through service to the virtuous. (84)
It is the supreme giver of liberation, the giver of the divine abode, and the giver of eternal bliss;
there is no dharma equal to the Dharma of Liberation (mokṣadharma) that is more preeminent within all creations. ||85||
The Dharma consisting of all holy places is the Dharma of liberation found among the virtuous;
he by whom the virtuous have been protected, served, and propitiated [possesses it]. (86)
By him every duty has been performed and the Supreme Self has been propitiated—by him who has become the self of all beings and who beholds all beings as himself. ||87||
For one intent upon serving the virtuous, the supreme state of liberation shall come to pass;
just as other footprints are indeed contained within the footprint of an elephant.
In that way, all virtues enter into the service of the virtuous;
for those who serve the virtuous, the world of Brahmā is ordained. (89)
By Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa, Gaya, Citraketu, Āyu, Anaraṇya, and King Dilīpa; ||3.80.90||
By Śibi, Mucukunda, Māndhātṛ, and Bharata;
likewise by Janaka, Rukmāṅgada, and King Alarka. (91)
By Pṛthu, by Sāgara, by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,
and by these kings as well, the virtuous have always been served.
The virtuous women are truthful and honored; I, the Supreme Self, am worshipped by them.
Having performed their ablutions in the sacred ford of the Self, they are further strengthened by the auspicious blessings of the virtuous.
Having become devoted to the dharma of the virtuous, they have gone to the supreme state,
as long as peace has not arisen in the functions of all the senses.
As long as there is activity, there exists this cycle of existence that creates the stream of birth and death;
for when activity ceases, there is goodness, and in goodness, supreme liberation.
Indeed, all the messengers of Nārāyaṇa who are here are virtuous;
having caused [the devotees] to perform kīrtanas, they lead them to the imperishable abode. 96.
These virtuous women are indeed the saving powers (śaktis) of Nārāyaṇa;
having caused [others] to perform service to Hari, they lead them to the imperishable abode. 97.
All those who are dear to Brahmā, virtuous, devoted to their husbands, followers of the Bhāgavata, and followers of the Sātvata path, exist by his playful power in various lands. 98.
They have arisen by my own will for the sake of the excellence of the land, and solely for the purpose of instilling devotion toward me among the people. (99)
"All of you have indeed been born as my virtuous wives; may you, remaining steadfast in your husband Śrī Kṛṣṇa, uphold the duties of virtuous women."
In me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, you shall always remain eternal, possessing the enjoyment of everlasting life, and forever equal to me. 101.
Dwelling in my abode, you truly remain by my side;
yet, in a second form, you reside here upon the earth together with me.

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Attaining Longevity, the Means for Liberation, and Service to the Virtuous," etc., in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasahitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the true fruit of association with the virtuous.
Once, I went to the bank of the Bhadrāvatī river for the purpose of recreation. || 1 ||
There, on the bank of that field, there were a hundred vultures, eaters of flesh;
having taken up a water-pot for the sake of purification, I went into the middle of the field. || 2 ||
Making my way through the midst of the vultures, I proceeded forward;
seeing me, those vultures spoke these words in sweet voices. (3)
"Wherever we stay, there we are confident, fearless, and happy;
oh, what great fortune has come upon us on this earth! (4)
This Nārāyaṇa has arrived here in our midst in person;
he is of virtuous form and virtuous character, the giver of liberation and likewise the bestower of final release.
Let them take the dust from his feet upon their wings, and let them place upon their heads and faces the purifying water from his pitcher.
The water from Brahmā’s water-pot is not equal to even a thousandth part of this;
liberation will surely be ours, for we shall touch both its feet.
Fanning the beloved of Śrī, Puruṣottama, with both their wings, they praised him with melodious voices, saying, "Nārāyaṇa! Nārāyaṇa! (8)
Bowing their heads to this Hari, the burner of sins,
let them approach him on foot and circumambulate him again and again.
With their eyes, let them behold Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa,
the true Lord, the virtuous one, the Lord of the virtuous, the protector of saintly women, the Lord of birds, and the Sovereign.
Uttering these words, they approached me from all sides;
they bowed, touched my feet, and gazed upon me again and again.
They prayed most intensely for liberation from their state as birds, and they said: "We were indeed human beings who were Śūdras and hunters. (1.2)
Those who are unrighteous, cruel, miserly, living by sinful means, plunderers, thieves, and likewise haters of embodied beings; ||| 13 ||

They engage in wrongful conduct and infidelity, delight in seizing the property of others, and are haters of sacrifices to the gods and ancestors; indeed, they are a source of terror to embodied beings.
Having seen the abundance of wealth, grain, and other possessions belonging to another, we became envious;
by that sin, we have been born as birds of the vulture species. (15)
Among birds, we are all outcastes, devourers of foul-smelling corpses;
degraded by our own sins, have mercy on us and deliver us! 16.
Even in their state as hunters, having seen holy men in the forest and offered them fruits,
they received blessings and thereby acquired great merit.
"O Lord Hari, by that merit, may memory not forsake us.
Thus entreated, I then spoke to them by the power of our association: || 18 ||
This recollection of former births is indeed the fruit of serving the virtuous;
likewise, even my sight here serves to ward off rebirth as an animal.
Then you shall become kings;
after that, you will become Brahmins, then gods, and finally auspicious celestial sages (brahmarṣis).
Having dwelt for a long time in Satyaloka, you shall go to my imperishable realm;
for in each of those places, there will be a meeting with the virtuous.
O Lakṣmī, having been addressed thus by me, all those vultures met their death;
they were all born as Kṣatriyas, and after dying from that state, they subsequently became Brāhmaṇas.
Then the gods and the sages went from there to the imperishable abode;
thus have I described to you the fruit of association with the virtuous.
For even for me, who am among the animals, the vision of Him has become easily attained, by which the vultures reached the eternal, perfect state of Brahman. (24)
Therefore, even a sinner should repeatedly seek the company of the virtuous; for by this, the washing away of sin occurs, as well as merit and liberation. 25.
Once, Lomaśa, accompanied by hundreds of virtuous men, wandered upon the earth for the welfare of the worlds and with a desire for their purification.
Hearing the sounds of the footsteps on the path, Jīvaṭa-kīṭaka indeed ran from the garden area with great haste to go outside. ||27||
Seeing Jīvaṭa the insect, Lomaśa questioned him: "Why are you so hurried and terrified? Tell me, where are you going? (28)
Having heard this, Jīvaṭa-kīṭa said: "I too, having beheld the circle of the virtuous in great numbers and likewise having heard the sound of their footsteps," (29)
Having encountered the fear born of death from the crushing of my feet,
I run swiftly along the path so that I may indeed go outside.
I possess a home nearby, filled with the happiness of wife, children, and so forth;
may untimely death not befall me or my family members in this empty place. (3.1)
My death alone in a desolate place, deprived of my family, would surely lead to an evil rebirth;
my kinsmen would surely grieve for me. (32)
Therefore, I speak quickly of the supreme misery of death; I urge you on for the sake of life, for the happiness of one who lives is the highest good. (33)
Lomaśa, having heard this, said to Jīvaṭa: "From where do you come? Tell me, how can there be happiness here in this womb of insects, which is a source of suffering? (34)
Death would be better for you here than this birth from suffering;
indeed, you do not recognize the most excellent and supreme pleasures of touch and enjoyment.
And you do not enjoy desired flavors, nor vehicles, mounts, or festivals;
therefore, O sinful one, death would indeed be better for you in this body.
Having heard this from the far-sighted Lomaśa, Jīvaṭa said:
"A living being is truly happy wherever it functions within a body. (37)
I see a diverse forest with various things arising from what is visible;
and I see my family, enriched by wife and sons, filled with festive joy. (38)
On this earth, I touch a woman, a son, or a daughter of a householder;
and in the forest, accompanied by my own kinsmen and others, I hear various songs. (39)
I consume sweet juices produced from trees and creepers;
I smell many kinds of fragrances and enjoy numerous sensory objects. ||3.81.40||
Just as my body exists, so do the most excellent objects of sense abide for me;
I dwell here with my family, and my family is most excellent.
Having heard this, the sage said: "Listen, O insect, I shall tell you;
though you have exerted yourself in every way, you appear here to be short-lived. (42)
For death stands near you, holding his noose;
therefore, do not harbor desire for the sake of living or for the sake of pleasure. (43)
O worm, association with the virtuous leads to great merit;
yet death is certain for you, even this very moment—of this there is no doubt. (44)
"O worm, if through my sight you desire an excellent birth, tell me what it is;
by the power of the virtuous, I shall grant you that auspicious birth here. (45)
Having paid homage to these virtuous ones, go then toward death; I shall bring you auspiciousness. Tell me, what is your mind’s inclination in this matter?
Then Jīvaṭa said: "If it must be so, let my death occur in the presence of my family, by my side. (47)
And may a human body then arise here on this earth, through which various forms of spiritual welfare shall come to me by association with the virtuous. (48)
Having spoken thus, he quickly approached the side of the enclosure and saw the family members who had made their dwelling at the base of a grass clump and were living in holes.
Kīṭa quickly summoned them, and having closed his eyes, he passed away;
he then established that soul within the womb of Kṣattrā in Surāṣṭra.
Born into a royal family of citizens, he was a king who governed his subjects;
then Lomaśa proceeded further toward the shore of the ocean with joy.
Remembering his former birth, he beheld the king once again while honoring the sage;
with devotion, he grasped the king's feet and related everything that had occurred.
O Sage, by your grace I emerged from the state of a worm and became a king;
likewise, women, elephants, horses, camels, vehicles, and all manner of riches [were restored]. (53)
O Guru, by your grace, they are always my objects of enjoyment here;
this is the fruit of the saint’s compassion, which I partake of as something sweet and supreme. (54)
I sleep upon an excellent couch attended by queens, yet I remain awake when saluted by bards and others, like the god Hari. (55)
"I have indeed innumerable female and male servants, as well as auspicious ministers who carry out my commands.
Homage be to you, O virtuous Guru; tell me, what shall I do here? (56)
Having heard this, Lomaśa was delighted and said to King Jīvacandraka:
"O King, you must indeed depart from this royal body."
"O King, you have enjoyed various pleasures through my grace;
now, indeed, become a Brahmin and receive an excellent birth. (58)
