The sight of you has been granted to me; that alone is my merit once again. Become a Vaiṣṇava, take up the mantra, and it will lead to your welfare. (59)
Abandon delusion regarding family, kingdom, and women;
take up true compassion here, and do not be heedless in this matter.
Thus addressed, that king quickly took up the supreme mantra:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (6.1)
Then the illustrious Lomaśa meditated upon Nārāyaṇa within his heart;
at that moment, the king cast off his body in the presence of everyone.
And in Saurāṣṭra, there was a Brahmin in this excellent Akṣarakṣetra,
at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
That great seer was a path for yoga, possessed of the memory of his former births, and exceedingly devoted;
from birth he was perfected, righteous, most established in Brahman, and supremely purifying.
Then Śrī Lomaśa addressed that youth:
"O high-minded one, worship Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
Through my yoga and through the yoga of the sacred field (kṣetra), auspicious liberation shall be yours;
and from devotion to the Supreme Lord, you shall obtain a most excellent fruit.
That boy, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, received all the mantras from the mouth of the sage; thereafter, he went to his own mother, Kalāvatī.
Then he bowed with devotion to his father, named Āryaśīla;
having received his permission, he quickly performed the excellent worship at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having approached me and cast off his own body, he ascended a celestial chariot and attained the same world as mine— the eternal abode of Brahman.
He attained my supreme, imperishable abode, O Lakṣmī;
for in this way, the state of liberation is obtained simply through association with a virtuous person.
The virtuous who resort to my feet grant inner vision;
they shake off sins and even bring about the diminution of rebirths.
Out of compassion, they cause the exhaustion of karma and bestow a treasure of merit even upon their own followers who are devoted and self-controlled. (72)
Having shattered here the various and firm bonds that bind themselves, they bestow auspicious things.
The delightful pleasures of heaven, arising from the Kalpa of Truth,
consist of bodies equal to those of the gods, which are objects of enjoyment and possess the splendor of lords.
Having fashioned my eternal, divine form and my imperishable abode,
my holy devotees send them forth by means of their own splendor.
And virtuous women of auspicious conduct, devoted to me, send the souls that have come through their yoga to my own abode. (76)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious and purifying story of the brahmin woman Vinodinī, a devotee of mine who dwelt in Dhārāgrāma. 77.
The virtuous and devoted wife always served her husband, who was like a lord,
as well as the excellent Brahmin named Śatānanda, a devotee of the Lord.
Ten thousand years passed for those two devotees on the surface of the earth,
both of whom were solely devoted to Brahman and remained childless.
Once, Śatānanda, who was of virtuous intent, said to his wife:
"O auspicious lady, how is it that you, though having bathed after your menses and being approached according to dharma, [have not conceived]?"
Tell me here why you do not carry a son who will perpetuate the lineage in your womb; whether it be the cause, or a discernible obstacle, or even barrenness itself—if you know it. (8.1)
Is it my fault, or is it simply that my fortune does not exist? Why is it that even after such a long time, you are not seen as one who possesses a son? (82)
Having heard this, the wife said to her husband, "O King of Devotees, listen to the reason:
dwelling in the womb is a great suffering for the living being, as it is cooked by fire. (83)
The suffering of birth, the suffering of the body, and the suffering of death again and again;
impurity is yet another suffering, and the going to hell is yet another. (84)
Even the latent impression (vāsanā) is great suffering, and likewise the suffering born of affection;
having thus observed these sufferings, one finds supreme happiness in childlessness.
"Thinking it to be a deceptive illusion, I did not conceive this embryo.
Hearing her, her husband said, "O beloved, [this is] a debt incurred by your father. (86)
As long as he has not crossed over, there is suffering for the ancestors;
that suffering of theirs is my own suffering, arising from the hell named Put. (87)
O virtuous lady, you ought to conceive a child in order to refute the charge of barrenness and to dispel all talk of your lineage being extinct. (88)
Having heard this, the virtuous woman said: "If it be so, my dear, listen:
whichever sons there may be, they should all be sent toward Hari. (89)
"These devotees and holy men will grant me liberation"—
with such a verbal bond do I maintain my longing.
"So be it," the husband replied; and having been approached after her ritual bath at the end of her season, she conceived.
The fallen one entered her womb, and in due time she gave birth to a son.
And the boy gradually grew up, awakened like one who knows the Self; his son, possessed of discernment, was invested with the sacred thread by his mother. (92)
Having been presented to me for the sake of his perfection, he was offered up;
I made him, who was virtuous and dispassionate, my path to liberation by the name Sādhu.
Śatānanda became joyful upon beholding his virtuous son;
then, in due course of time, his wife conceived a second fetus.
She gave birth to him in due time and nurtured him with affection; she awakened him with higher knowledges and bestowed that son upon me. (95)
Having been initiated, he was given the name Brahmāyana by me;
he became a great and virtuous poet, devoted solely to the path of liberation.
And Śatānanda, seeing him, became joyful;
with a serene mind, he bestowed his third embryo upon his wife.
She gave birth to that son and instructed him in service;
she also bestowed upon me knowledge and song for the very purpose of the initiation of a holy man.
I initiated him and gave him the name Premāyana;
that virtuous man, skilled in singing songs, became intent upon liberation. (99)
In this way, five hundred sons were born to me after a long time;
they were all virtuous and devoted to my initiation.
They are divine, possessing celestial abodes and divine activities; indeed, they are virtuous, appearing as sacred fords (tīrtha), and entirely devoted to moral conduct and vows. || 10.1 ||
All these virtuous ones, who are adorned with goodness, are bestowers of liberation upon living beings; they are devoted to knowledge and meditation, gentle, and endowed with devotion to me.
Possessing knowledge and virtuous conduct, devoted to my own form, these yogis indeed dwell in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara. || 103 ||
These sons of Śatānanda are great devotees of the Lord; they abide as practitioners of devotion in my imperishable sacred field.
Then, at the end, Śrī Śatānanda said to his wife: "Give me one son who will be the perpetuator of my lineage; do not indeed make him a mere ascetic."
Having spoken thus, the delightful Brāhmaṇī gave her youngest son,
Viśvāyana, who was well-trained, to her beloved husband, the son of Padmā.
For he was always devoted to the duties of a householder;
thus, that great sage, having married in the hermitage of Lomaśa, became a perpetuator of his lineage.
He was a great devotee of the Lord, initiated and a master of the Vedāṅgas;
and this virtuous woman was likewise well-initiated in the initiatory rite that brings delight.
The one named Amṛtā, a friend of Brahman, dwells here relying on renunciation;
Śatānanda also abides in the state of a virtuous householder within my hermitage.
"O Lotus-born One, he shall always be devoted to my service and possess a divine state.
Thus has this story of Vinodinī been told to you here.
By reciting or hearing this account of the offering of all her sons by Samavartinī for the sake of liberation, the path to liberation shall become certain.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Vultures through Association with the Holy, the Liberation of the Jīvaṭa insect, the saintliness of Vinodinī and her five hundred sons," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, O All-pervading One! [Tell me] regarding even a woman who is self-willed, lustful, or unchaste.
Tell me, how can sins along with their latent impressions (vāsanās) be destroyed? What is the destiny of such a person, and by what means is purification achieved? (2)
Or how might there be a good rebirth? Out of compassion, please tell me;
for you are the protector of one who is protectorless, and you are the strength of one who is weak.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to these auspicious words you have asked;
for since you have asked out of compassion, I shall speak to you straightforwardly.

From association, from strength, from nourishment, from intoxication, from the [taste of] flavors, and from youth, intense latent impressions arise—namely, desires whose nature is that of worldly enjoyment. (5)
The seasons, the bodily constituents, the firmness of the sense organs, and the longing for pleasures—these are indeed the stimulators of desires and the increasers of the threads of craving. (6)
For the latent tendencies of desire generally increase from seeing the limbs [of others], from laughter, from frequenting solitary places, and from touch and other such stimuli. (7)
Even those who are unfit are indeed joined with two bodies by their own will,
having abandoned the conventions of worldly life and scripture.
From that, there arises in this world for women the state of being lustful, unchaste, and wanton,
due to their acting according to their own desires while remaining attached to the internal [senses].
The independence of men, the fickleness of women, and their state of being subject to desire— these indeed arise from excessive passion, craving, and even illusion.
O lotus-born one, for the sake of destroying their sins, there are many means of accomplishment, as well as expiatory rites and vows.
Likewise, there are many difficult tasks and torments of Yama,
as well as other punishments for the body and even punishments from kings.
The delightful hermitages of renunciation and the dwellings of ascetics,
as well as various sacred fords, exist for the sake of purification.
Therefore, for these [beings], taking refuge is what brings about the supreme good;
there is no other means here that is equal to this. (14)
In that regard, service to the virtuous is considered the destroyer of all evils, the bestower of all merits, and the cleanser of latent impressions. (15)
Association with the virtuous bestows knowledge therein and wards off delusion and attachment; indeed, compassion is considered by the wise to be the cause for attaining self-elevation. (16)
The food offered with devotion, water for the feet, and drinks such as nectar immediately purify even a person burdened by tens of millions of sins. (17)
The virtuous are the manifest sacred fords; the virtuous are the manifest fires;
the virtuous are the manifest rain; and the virtuous are the manifest nectar of immortality.
The virtuous are the very embodiments of Dharma; I myself am the Blessed One, manifest as the virtuous.
The virtuous are indeed the objects of sacrifice; the virtuous are the God above all gods.
The virtuous are all sacred vows; the virtuous are the boats in the ocean of existence.
All who are not Nārāyaṇa are the virtuous; the virtuous are the splendors of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The virtuous perform all austerities; the virtuous are indeed the purifying Brahman.
The virtuous should be understood as the wish-fulfilling cows; the virtuous are truly the trees of paradise.
The virtuous are wish-fulfilling creepers; the virtuous are sovereign wish-granting gems;
and the virtuous are inexhaustible vessels for meritorious deeds of dharma. (22)
The virtuous possess peaceful and imperishable treasuries; they are stars from the ocean of eternal bliss, sustainers [of others], and swift cleansers of sins. (23)
The virtuous are indeed the abodes of Hari; the saintly are my very forms.
Through association with them, even those who are oceans of great sins are swiftly purified.
Just as grass is reduced to ashes by fire at the mere touch, so too, for the sake of their own purification in this world, [even] those women who have committed great sins [are purified]. 25.
Indeed, the virtuous should be served with a spirit of total self-surrender;
and one should learn from the good the mantras that grant refuge and other protections. (26)
In the manner of one possessing great fortune, she should serve virtuous people through beholding them, touching them, bowing to them, attending to them, and honoring them. || 27 ||
One should perform eating, massaging, drinking, bathing, and listening to the glories of Hari for those virtuous ones with whom I am their master. (28)
Then, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous are considered by me to be like lords;
and indeed, servants who have sought refuge are truly like the virtuous themselves. (29)
And their female attendants likewise become truly divine and free from qualities;
all of them—Viṣṇu’s virtuous servants—are sinless and purifying. (3.82.30)
This, my dear, is my supreme secret, most hidden; it has been told for the sake of women—easily accessible, purifying, and supreme. (31)
By relying upon which, through the practice of yoga, women become like fire, they indeed become like Brahman, their bodies free from sin. (3.2)
Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you here a direct illustration for you:
the city of Vārāṇasī belongs to your father, Śiveśvara.
There, thousands of male and female attendants belonging to your father— both unmarried men and women— are present as members of his retinue.
And those who practice devotion to Śiva act according to their own desires; indeed, even wanton women, unchaste women, passionate women, and courtesans [attain this]. 3.5.
In the city of their father, there dwell such men as well:
groups of musicians, actors, dancers, singers, and even instrumentalists.
Naked are the Gaṇas, and likewise naked are the Yoginīs and the courtesans;
taking refuge in the Lord of Yogins, Śaṅkara, they act according to their desire. || 37 ||
Once, indeed, a gathering of those men and women took place upon boats in the waters of the Gaṅgā, accompanied by singing, chanting, and dancing.
At the onset of night, the dances of courtesans, the laughter of jesters, and the jests of buffoons proceeded.
That great festival, known by the name Pravṛddhamangala, takes place there;
indeed, even hundreds of thousands of men gather as spectators there at night.
In groups, they held festivals on boats in every direction for seven days, and then they ceased their celebrations for your father.
In the temple of Viśvanātha-svasūpa, through dances and other performances, the venerable Yogi Vātsyāyana, the great ṛṣi, [was present]. 42.
Living his life established in celibacy, devoted to the dharma of the virtuous, with vital energy drawn upward like that of Śambhu, he was the most excellent among the great lords of yogins. || 43 ||
The maker of the excellent ford arrived at that very place from Dharmāraṇya;
he was naked, devoid of luster, and his entire body was grey with dust. Though he was a youth free from physical change, he was adorned with the behavior of an old man.
And everything proceeds as having the nature of Brahman in whose vision it appears. ||45||
Free from the distinction between male and female, himself virtuous and most beautiful,
he beheld the god Śaṅkara and his attendants intent on worship.
And all the courtesans were likewise adorned as young women;
they were so decorated that they appeared like wanton women.
The unchaste women and the passionate maidens as well, endowed with every graceful gesture, exerted themselves diligently at the festival to win the favor of your father. (48)
As beautiful as daughters of fire, as radiant as goddesses, they were exquisitely lovely, adorned with jewels, diamonds, pearls, and other ornaments. (49)
Beholding them all, the virtuous sage Vātsyāyana bowed down;
likewise, seeing that all those female devotees of Hara stood there peacefully, the sage remained tranquil.
He is youthful and nourished by blood, naked and resembling Śaṅkara;
absorbed in meditation, devoid of physical luster, yet radiant as the sun.
And the form that produces delusion, which is the support for the mind of enjoyment, is a mass of merit that, by mere touch, burns away the mass of evil. (52)
Beholding such a boon-granting one and concluding him to be Śaṅkara himself arrived in embodied form, the groups of courtesans touched him. ||53||
Although some [women] were in the state of passion, some in the state of delusion, some in the state of divinity, and some in the state of saintliness; ||54||
They kissed the feet of the divine sage and touched his linga with their eyes; they felt an intense sense of fulfillment and considered themselves to have achieved their life's purpose.
O Lotus-born One, listen indeed to the wonder that arose among them there:
the sage remained motionless, like one who is insentient, absorbed in profound meditative concentration.
Those courtesans who had previously touched him all adopted the conduct of royalty;
yet, at the touch of the sage, they all vanished.
All of them became free from desire, filled with goodness and pure intentions;
indeed, devoid of the functioning of passion, they were [transformed] in an instant merely by touch. (58)
Restlessness was entirely destroyed among the courtesans on all sides; indeed, the disorders of the female organs and their violent urges reached a state of total tranquility. 59.
The minds of all became free from modification; their intentions, latent impressions, desires, passions, attachments, and longings ceased to exist. (3.82.60)
In an instant, all those women who had been overcome by the touch of the yogi became dissolved;
and divine visions arose for those wives of Śambhu.
Then they beheld a great marvel in the sky,
and from it there emerged hundreds of thousands of hunters with their faces turned downward.
Having traveled through the path of the sky along the Gaṅgā to the Himālaya,
they were all born there as courtesans, free from all obscurations.
Divine and possessing divine bodies, they were like the virtuous Rādhārāmā;
thereafter, they all attained purity and were freed from all sin.
Indeed, having perceived with his inner vision this Vātsyāyana as a yogi who is the very form of Brahman and who, through his touch, utterly destroys all sin; 65.
Having recognized that lord of sages as a virtuous one adorned with goodness,
they bowed to him, touched him, and again questioned the holy one with humility.
"O holy one, by the power of your merit, divine visions have appeared to us here;
moreover, our bodies too have become divine through the touch and sight [of you]. (67)
Desires of the heart have perished, for youthfulness is indeed fickle; everything has dissolved through union with you by the washing away of the dust from your feet. (68)
We have all been purified here; though we were formerly wanton women, courtesans, and unchaste lovers, we have indeed become virtuous.
"Today indeed we have obtained here in this world the fruit of our worship of Śaṅkara and of the great festival, since our hearts have become pure. (3.82.70)
O virtuous one, we shall simply ask others about this;
for those who were like hunters have flown up into the sky by the hundreds of thousands and departed from here.
What are they? How did they come? Where have they gone, and from where do they originate?
Tell us that truthfully, for you are the one who brings us purity.
Having heard this, Vātsyāyana said: "O virtuous ladies, listen to my words: by whatever means possible, you must avoid any physical contact with me. (73)
Therefore, O ladies, whatever dispositions have been formed here by any means whatsoever, as well as those latent tendencies of yours whose nature is the sin of lust; [74]
Thirsts that are evil in nature, as well as innumerable sins, and all those deeds performed by courtesans—[all these are destroyed]. (75)
By the touch of my feet, by the touch of my linga,
and even by bearing my dust, [the fetters] have indeed departed from their bodies.
And having observed the sanctity of your bodies, they were indeed unable to remain and have issued forth in every direction. (77)
All those sins, having taken the form of pills,
went together to Lake Mānasa in the Himalayas.
A lake will truly arise there; that liberation is dissolution.
By my yoga, indeed, the sins of all have departed.
"Then, all of you together, receive this supreme mantra.
Having said this, he gave my mantra to the courtesans. (3.82.80)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord, svāhā!
Having quickly taken this mantra, the goddesses Gaṇikās became four-armed. ||81||
Having become the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavī goddesses, possessing divine and most beautiful bodies, the Nārāyaṇīs went by means of celestial chariots to my imperishable abode. ||82||
From that, thousands of courtesans became dear to Hari;
they remain in my imperishable abode, devoted to my service.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even a wanton woman becomes instantly purified through association with the virtuous; she becomes rich in dharma and a divine servant. (84)
Therefore, the service of the virtuous is the purifier of even the most heinous sins;
for by whatever disposition they are served, they purify one. (85)
Then other courtesans, having heard of this, approached that sage;
and for their purification, he then taught them the science of love (kāmaśāstra).
Having caused them to hear [the teachings], having instructed them, and having bestowed his own service upon them, the great sage Vātsyāyana then brought about their liberation. (87)
And Śaṅkara himself, having become manifest in bodily form, became visible to him and said:
"O sage, you are blessed; you have brought about the liberation of a courtesan."
O virtuous one, you are the very embodiment of goodness; for even though you have fully indulged your desire as you willed, you remain entirely unstained by passion, O author of the treatise on love.
Just as I am both the consumer and the healer of desire,
so too is Kṛṣṇa the conqueror of desire even while he delights in it.
In that same way, even while describing it, you shall be the conqueror of desire;
O virtuous one, become the giver of liberation to women by destroying their sin. (91)
"The scripture shall become renowned in the world by your very name.
Having said this, Lord Śaṅkara, your father, vanished from sight. (92)
That virtuous man went to Kāśī and wandered upon the earth;
for Vātsyāyana was indeed a Vaiṣṇava who liberated all living beings.
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, or even practicing this, great sins are destroyed and the attainment of liberation becomes certain. (94)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told this secret concerning the service of the virtuous—a narrative that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants a divine state of being. (95)

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how even wanton women, lustful women, harlots, and courtesans attain liberation after the destruction of their sins through union with the holy Vātsyāyana at Kāśī," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: For what reason indeed is the virtuous one called Nārāyaṇa? Although there may be many reasons for this among those of firm vows, [please explain]. (1)
Nevertheless, please speak in such a way that I may understand either a simple cause, or one that is excellent and unsurpassed, or even one that is difficult to comprehend.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the many kinds of causes for greatness:
forgiveness, character, dispassion, tranquility, and non-possessiveness. (3)

Freedom from craving, being devoid of attachment to flavors, and self-abidance; likewise, lack of greed, freedom from hatred and other passions, and universal friendliness—[these constitute the qualities of the self]. (4)
The duty of self-realization is the total surrender unto me;
it is freedom from attachment, the absence of bondage, and the relinquishing of service performed with illusion.
The acquisition of only what is necessary for the maintenance of the body, senses, and so forth;
the patient waiting for the world of liberation; and likewise, the abandonment of the notions of "mine" and "I. (6)
The cessation of the onset of new impulses and stability within the self, and not elsewhere—character and purity of mind are indeed the causes for goodness. (7)
He who possesses the desire to assist others by showing them the path to liberation, and who observes vows and moral conduct for the sake of Nārāyaṇa as his supreme goal— (8)
He who possesses fierce austerity free from the bondage of illusion,
and whose mental functions are always within my domain— he indeed is such a one.
O Lakṣmī, this fourfold set is the primary cause of saintliness;
for neither saffron robes nor external marks [bring it about]. (3.83.10)
Neither initiation nor dress are the primary causes for saintliness;
rather, those who obstruct their own liberation and long for the liberation from illusion (māyā) and the like [are not true saints]. 1.11.
The ascetics, most excellent among the virtuous, were proficient in the Supreme Brahman;
and the virtuous women were likewise devoted to the duty of chastity and dedicated to moral conduct. 12.
Free from passion, full of devotion, virtuous, and adorned by their own goodness—
freedom from attachment to the body is the first step upon the ladder of the holy.
The emptiness of passion for the sense faculties is the second step; mastery over the internal organ is the third step. (14)
The offering of oneself to Kṛṣṇa is the fourth step;
and the abiding of my own form within one's knowledge is the fifth step. (15)
The effort toward the fruit of liberation is indeed the sixth step;
the constant abiding in the fourth state (turyāvasthā) is the final step.
A virtuous man who has ascended the seven steps is indeed the most excellent of the good;
likewise, virtuous women of such conduct are, in my view, considered the most excellent of the virtuous.
These virtuous women who have been described by me abide in the highest stage;
now listen as I show you those who belong to the middle stage.
They do not abide in attachment to the body, senses, and so forth, nor do they desire the pleasure produced by them;
rather, they offer everything to Kṛṣṇa and surrender their very selves to me.
O beloved, those virtuous men and virtuous women who stand at the highest level both in the secondary power of Māyā and in my own power are of this kind; they are the middling ones.
Now, O Lakṣmī, hear also of those situated even lower than that, who act for my sake,
yet are in every way possessed of passion and are joined with the body, senses, and so forth.

Even though they have received initiation, those who dwell in the stage of renunciation remain intent on their own self-interest; though they place me at their forefront, they rely solely upon me [as a means]. (22)
They do not perceive even the slightest trace of the fragrance of renunciation;
nevertheless, having encountered hardship, they appear as if established on the path of renunciation.
Those who exist with humble minds, covered by nets and bearing green banners—all these indeed become virtuous ones by name. (24)
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a tiger made of skin, so too is a virtuous man who is clothed in rags; these three possess no real power. (25)
These three betrayers of trust cause fear to the ignorant, yet to the wise they are like stones; they grant no desired benefit to those who have sought refuge with them. 26.
They destroy one's certain purpose and oppose one's advancement;
like glass beads, they bring about ruin through association. (27)
Austerity, sacred learning, and power—these are the characteristics of goodness;
indeed, forgiveness, devotion, and detachment are the causes of goodness. (28)
When such a virtuous person is indeed satisfied, the gods and others are satisfied as well;
for just as a farmer obtains fruit when the field is fertile. (29)
Having thus offered it to a virtuous person, the giver indeed enjoys the fruit;
but what is given to one who is not virtuous becomes futile—of this there is no doubt.
The one who is not virtuous destroys the food, and being consumed, he destroys that [eater];
but the virtuous one protects that food, and he who is not virtuous guards the food. (31)
That which is bestowed upon a worthy recipient provides protection even in the next world;
for the virtuous man who consumes the food is indeed the master who nourishes the donor as well.
Therefore, one should bestow food upon a worthy recipient through meritorious action;
for the merit that belongs to the giver is exactly the same as that which belongs to the receiver.
If both vessels were indeed auspicious in form and stainless, where indeed virtuous men exist who are endowed with learning and good conduct. (34)
In that regard, the fruit of giving indeed arises as merit a thousandfold for those who are constantly pure in Brahman, pure in conduct, and virtuous. (35)
Moreover, those devotees who are devoted to austerity are indeed most worthy of worship;
by those virtuous ones, a divine path has been established, without a doubt. (36)
Those who have traveled by it are not deluded in the realm of illusion or in the state of the Lord;
for the virtuous, whose vehicle is Brahman, reach the further shore. || 37 ||

That which is difficult to follow, difficult to overcome, difficult to attain, and difficult to transcend—all this comes to pass through the constant bestowing of blessings; there is no doubt in this. (38)
The drinker of spirituous liquor, the killer of an embryo, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—by means of a virtuous person, all these are delivered and are liberated from every sin. (39)
For the virtuous who possess knowledge are worthy of all worship and are rich in the wealth of merit;
those who practice austerity, delight in giving, and are full of devotion are indeed saviors.
Both this world of Brahmā and the unsurpassed state of liberation are attained by worldly people who perform good deeds and serve the virtuous. (4.1)
When honored, these virtuous ones honor in return; when respected, they likewise show respect.
Having kindled the fires that consume the sins of the wicked, they indeed deliver them across [to liberation]. 42.
Where there is such virtuous conduct—that the master is pleased with his servants and the servants are pleased with their master—there lie millions of blessings. (43)
Just as one removes dirt from the limbs with water, or darkness with the light of fire, so too does one cast off all evil through service to a virtuous person. 44.
It brings well-being to all and purifies embodied beings;
the virtuous person devoted to this practice is the creator of welfare throughout the three worlds. (45)
O Lakṣmī, for the liberation of living beings, I have composed this Sāman;
the virtuous sing this Sāman here to awaken the people.
They teach the mantras and so forth, and they glorify me repeatedly;
they describe my stories and my many deeds. (47)
"In every way, my virtues define my duties;
thus indeed do the virtuous proclaim through conciliatory words and songs. (48)
The learned constantly praise me through the portals of the scriptures; the poets compose verses about me, and those who accomplish their goals offer hymns of praise. 49.
In this way, men indeed purify me in many ways through conciliation;
having obtained me from the mouth of the Guru through conciliation, one should win me over with gifts.
Giving is the offering of oneself with one's entire being; this self-surrender is true giving, and by means of it, one should always win me over. (51)
The virtuous acquire [merit] through the practice of giving and they also bestow it:
namely, the gift of knowledge, the gift of mantra, and likewise the gift of the name of Hari. (52)
The gift of grace, the gift of garlands and such, the gift of imparting instruction, the gift of gain, the gift of happiness, and the gift of liberation, which is supreme among the supreme. (53)
The gift that bestows fearlessness is a gift of austerity and a source of auspiciousness;
such virtuous people, who are the ornaments of the righteous, perform this gift of merit.
The gift of compassion, as well as the bestowing of delightful blessings, the granting of one’s presence, and the gift of service bring about auspiciousness. (55)
For by bestowing various virtuous qualities, the holy ones indeed acquire me, Hari, and they also give them to their devotees. (56)
Having bestowed initiation and even the gift of their own selves, they deliver others;
having performed the auspicious gift of devotion, they deliver people from worldly existence.
Finally, by providing shelter, giving the nectar of their feet,
offering words of encouragement, and even acting as witnesses, they cause others to cross over.
The gift of the mind, the gift of affection, the gift that bestows purity and so forth, the gift of instruction in the practice of right conduct, and the gift that bestows mindfulness; ||59||
Having given gifts of necklaces and gifts of insignia, they deliver others;
having given gifts of images and gifts of vessels, they also deliver others.
Now they apply the method of division where neither gift nor conciliation is possible:
"This body is joined with impurities, it is defiled, and it is momentary and perishable. (6.1)
"The self is pure, a devotee of Hari, fit for liberation, and indeed eternal;
thus do the virtuous truly apply this discrimination regarding difference. (62)
Then they inflict punishment as an atonement upon the one who acts contrary to dharma; the virtuous restrain a person who has gone astray by means of their noble vows.
By means of expiatory rites such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, which consist of specific actions;
by great sacrifices involving the expenditure of wealth; and by festivals of pleasure. ||64||
They engage them in acts that produce merit for the sake of purification, such as food-offerings, meals, worship, gifts, and dedications, as well as other forms of exertion.
The virtuous either forcibly compel them to engage in righteous deeds and the like, or else they restrain them with severe punishment. (66)
Just as sins may be destroyed and liberation attained,
so indeed do the virtuous employ the rod of self-discipline for one's own benefit.
Indeed, the virtuous sometimes inflict a cruel punishment upon those who are most arrogant,
for the sake of their purification and also for the sake of their liberation.
Or they impel auspicious divine punishment, such as the recitation of prayers and the like,
by which, having attained freedom from blemish, they go to the supreme state.
Whether he be a sinner or a virtuous person, or one mixed with both; whether he be devoted or undevoted, an atheist or even a believer. (3.83.70)
Whosoever may be an embodied being, they lead him forward into refuge;
having refined him through various means, they purify him again and again.
Having constantly rendered it serene and having made it pure and eternal,
the virtuous then lead it to their own equal, imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the quality of being intent on helping others is always found among the virtuous;
it is indeed not to be obtained through any recompense, and by means of it, embodied beings are purified. (73)
Just as I am, so indeed are your gurus, the saviors of the world;
for they are my own pure forms, existing from the tips of their nails to the crown of their heads.
Just as a piece of sugar-candy possesses a sweet flavor in every respect and there is no part of it to be discarded, so too are you my saints. (75)
Or just as a lump of fresh butter is entirely composed of fat and there is no part of it that can be discarded, so too are you my virtuous ones. (76)
Just as a pure pearl, or a clear crystal, or likewise the Kaustubha gem, so too are those holy ones to me. (77)
Just as the wish-fulfilling cow is white, just as milk is devoid of water, and just as gold is pure, so too are those holy ones to me. (78)
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem is supreme, or as the desire-granting tree is, or as the excellent wish-granting creeper is, so are those holy ones to me. (79)
Just as my heart is supreme, just as my form is transcendent,
and just as the imperishable is the highest abode, so too are my virtuous ones to me.
Just as Viṣṇu is eternally pure, just as virtuous conduct is the highest vow,
and just as tranquility is the greatest wealth, so too are those holy ones mine.
Just as a field is enriched by grain, as a cow is ready for calving,
and as a sacrifice is complete with its sacrificial fee, so too are you, O virtuous ones, to me.
Just as trees are rich in fruit and creepers are rich in flowers, and just as a generous person is wondrous, so too are those holy ones to me. (83)

Just as the earth is composed of jewels, just as illusion consists of the three qualities (guṇas), and just as the Self is enriched by the three states of consciousness, so too are those holy ones to me. 84.
Just as I possess all power, just as Lakṣmī is indeed prosperity,
and just as everything has Kṛṣṇa as its essence, so too are the virtuous ones mine.
Just as the Sudarśana discus, just as the staff of Yama, and just as the grace of Viṣṇu, so are the virtuous ones to me. (86)
Just as was the devotion shown by Śambhu, just as was the service rendered by Satī, and just as was the affection displayed by Kāma—so too are those virtuous ones toward me. (87)
Just as forbearance is the ultimate goal of the virtuous, just as speech directed toward a devotee, and just as service rendered to a chaste wife—so too are you considered by the virtuous. (88)
Just as a vow directed toward one's wife, just as satisfaction free from craving, and just as the purifying water of the Gaṅgā—so too are those holy ones to me. (89)
Just as a lineage passes to one's son, as a gift goes to one's daughter,
and as worship is directed toward Gaṇeśa, so too are those virtuous ones mine.
"Just as I am indeed virtuous and you shine as a virtuous woman, and just as there is indeed a union between us, so too are those virtuous ones mine. (9.1)
What more need I say? No praise can be found here;
the venerable ones are my virtuous [gurus], and I am in every way a devotee of the holy.
He who, not having offered [food] to me or to the virtuous, eats only for the sake of filling his own belly,
is born in a desolate land as a wretched Brahmarākṣasa.
He who rejoices in his home without performing worship appropriate for the virtuous,
due to his own pride, is born as a Brahmarākṣasa at the end of his body.
Even one endowed with wealth and power who does not serve virtuous people, but instead reviles and disregards them, shall become a Brahmarākṣasa. ||95||
One who is bound by pride in his own virtues looks down upon those who are truly wise and virtuous, and treats the poor with contempt; such a person becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
He who treats even unconquerable and virtuous men with contempt and imputes false faults to them shall become a Brahmarākṣasa. ||97||
That lord who subjects virtuous people, who have committed no offense, to suffering, even if he be prosperous, dies and is subsequently reborn as a brahmarākṣasa. (98)
Even if he is learned, one who disregards and despises those who are virtuous and tranquil—
even if he is himself declining due to his wicked conduct— becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
But he who is a friend in appearance yet a foe, a killer by his very breath,
ignoble and a hater of the noble, is born as a Brahmarākṣasa.
One who acts wickedly even while living among the virtuous mocks the nature of the good;
by praising evil dispositions, he is reborn as a Brahmarākṣasa. 101.
But he who, being devoid of great virtues, yet desires everything great, and who treats the virtuous with contempt, becomes a Brahmarākṣasa upon being joined with that [state]. || 102 ||
He who treats with contempt by force an ascetic, one endowed with patience, a teacher, a man of realized knowledge, or a lord, is born as a Brahmarākṣasa.
He who, seeing virtuous forest-dwellers, does not rise before them,
and he who does not practice what is beneficial for his own soul— he, indeed, though living, is a Rākṣasa.
The Rākṣasa also, having bowed down, serves the virtuous devotees of Hari;
he propitiates them with his services and receives their blessings. (105)
O Lakṣmī, he who accepts the virtues that grant happiness from a virtuous person becomes truly a righteous man in this world, one whose conduct is indeed that of the good.
Neither birth, nor effort, nor outward appearance brings about goodness;
rather, service to the virtuous and association with the good are the causes for the attainment of goodness.
O Lakṣmī, by the mere sight or even the touch of those very stars,
and through their service and attendance, embodied beings cross over from worldly existence.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Various Causes and Conditions for Righteousness, as well as the Fruits of Praising and Not Praising the Righteous," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O ocean of mercy, O friend of living beings, O Lord of my own life-breath, O All-pervading One!
Now that this auspicious human body, the field of action, has been attained.
By one who seeks the highest good, though poor and entirely lacking in fortune,
where even the company of the virtuous is not to be found— (2)
Having performed the ritual there, what indeed would one obtain as one's own liberation?
How does one who desires their own welfare attain that welfare? (3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; you ask an excellent and auspicious question. This field of action exists for one who has obtained the supreme human state. || 4 ||
One should perform service to one's mother in every way, for she is the sacred site of the home;
in whatever manner one's own mother may become pleased, in that very manner [one attains merit]. || 5 ||
Having served them, one should indeed seek their blessings, which are highly meritorious,
destroyers of poverty, auspicious, and bestowers of all that is beneficial.
Through service to one's mother, the fortune of even the luckless increases;
for the mother is Nārāyaṇī and Brāhmī, and she brings about welfare through her blessing.
In this way, auspicious service should be rendered to one's father, who is like a sacred pilgrimage site;
for by receiving his blessings, one indeed attains welfare and merit.
One's fortune may become vast, prosperous, and filled with excellence; furthermore, through such service and the dawning of good fortune, a virtuous intellect shall arise.
Therefore, one should acquire knowledge by contemplating the meaning of the scriptures;
after knowledge comes discernment, and thereafter, one should meditate upon me, Hari.
One should always meditate upon and practice auspicious devotion toward me alone, wherein the mind may attain manifold purity and stability. (11)
One should perform the chanting of the Name: "Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Puruṣottama. (12)
Thus, indeed, while performing and causing others to perform the supreme worship through chanting, one should establish a companion and cause fellow devotees to flourish. || 13 ||
Thereafter, one should establish the circle of the assembly of the virtuous and worship Me;
one should always perform My kīrtana, and in the evening, the assembly should gather in one place.
Those devotees of Hari who are present in the assembly should then be understood as saintly persons (sādhus),
always by means of the benefit of hearing the scriptures or through the words of the elders.
Having obtained virtuous qualities and friends, one should then increase the company of the righteous;
having done so, one should indeed make one's own circle extensive.

Indeed, through the power of great merit from the circle of association with the virtuous, the highest desire for liberation arises; from that, through devotion characterized by a pure disposition, [the goal is attained]. 17.
Having worshipped me, he should perform what is for his own welfare; he is the king of devotees.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, he should always increase his own power along with its seed. 18.
That which nourishes association with the virtuous leads to both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
indeed, there is no practice so easily accessible as the chanting of the Name.
For one who has not attained the company of the virtuous, the chanting of the Name is supreme; one's own tongue should be understood as virtuous, and it should seek such association. 2.84.20
One’s own virtuous intellect should be awakened; by means of that, one should meditate upon Mādhava.
One’s own mind should be properly awakened; by means of that, one should always meditate upon Me.
Thinking, "The Lord is virtuous," one should serve Keśava;
having thus attained such association, one should worship me, the eternal. || 22 ||
The teachers and gurus, who bring about millions of auspicious things,
likewise crossed the ocean of existence by their own power alone.
And by the grace of Śrī Hari, they delivered others here as well;
for Hari assists his own striving devotee even when he is devoid of help from others. ||24||
Having descended there himself and dwelt even within the heart,
or having dwelt in the midst of the circle of devotees, he shall bestow the highest good.
O beloved, no one who performs kīrtana ever encounters anything undesirable;
indeed, by means of kīrtana, he alone becomes truly virtuous in that regard.

O Lakṣmī, even if he be an outcaste, one who chants my names within his home is indeed like a saint— provided he is pure-minded and affectionate toward the virtuous, for he is truly a saint, however far away he may be.
Even the leather-worker is rich in virtue and devoted to me; affectionate toward the holy, he is truly a saint who performs his own duties while chanting my praises. (28)
Even a barbarian, if he is endowed with virtuous conduct, devoted to me, affectionate toward the holy, non-violent, and glorifies me, is indeed a saint. (29)
Even a hunter who is a killer becomes truly virtuous by abandoning violence, being affectionate toward the good, and proclaiming me as one who practices non-violence. (2.84.30)
Whether bearing my banner or my discus, the virtuous one who is devoted to love for the saintly, who observes moral conduct and vows, who is non-violent, and who glorifies me day and night; ||3 1||
The courtesan and the libertine were both devoted to their affection for the virtuous; they possessed the character and vows of the righteous, spoke of me, and were free from desire. (32)
Even a fisherman who eats fish may be one who observes vows of conduct and practices non-violence;
such a virtuous person, devoted to love for the saintly, is truly good when he glorifies me as the Supreme Lord. (33)
The thief is a robber and a pilferer, while those devoted to the affection of the virtuous possess moral conduct and vows yet are empty of action; if such people proclaim me to be a saint! (34)
Or when a servant, or even a common person, is virtuous and devoted to moral conduct, affectionate toward the saintly, and glorifies me, Hari, the Supreme Person; ||35||
Merchants, actors, dancers, and virtuous bards, as well as those devoted to moral conduct and vows who are affectionate toward the saintly, shall glorify me, Hari. (36)
They assume many forms, act as jesters, carry corpses, and appear as holy men; they observe vows and ascetic practices, are affectionate toward the virtuous, and proclaim me, Hari.

Those who eat everything, those with hair like that of a harlot, those who eat iguanas, and those who feed on snakes—virtuous men, observers of vows, and those affectionate toward the good—are crying out to me. (38)
The fish-catchers and flesh-eaters have abandoned their cruel ways;
virtuous men, observant of moral vows and affectionate toward the good, cry out to me. (39)

"Those who set fires, those who administer poison, those who wield the spear, and even those who cast the noose—though they cry out against me, the virtuous are indeed kind and affectionate toward the righteous. (2.84.40)

If those who live by weapons, those who practice medicine, and those who maim living beings were to cry out to me, "We are of virtuous character! For the righteous are indeed kind toward the virtuous! (41)
The Bhārṣṭras, Bhaṭṭhīkaras, and those who do not destroy forests and groves—virtuous men, devoted to moral conduct and affectionate toward the good, indeed cry out to me. 42.
Mad, deranged, deceitful, and self-serving indeed are those who call me virtuous; they boast of their qualities while being merely affectionate toward the good and devoted to moral conduct. (43)
Even the Asuras, Rākṣasas, Daityas, Dānavas, and sinners, as well as those who are affectionate toward the virtuous, possessed of good character, and holy men, cry out to me. (44)
"Indeed, the virtuous beings—such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*—are crying out to me;
they are devoted to moral conduct, firm in their holy vows, and likewise affectionate toward me. (45)
The honey-gatherers, the fish-catchers, and the bird-hunters are indeed virtuous;
they are of good character, kind to the good, and free from worldly action, yet they cry out to me. (46)
They carry beasts of burden, wear cages, and are betrayers of trust;
yet they cry out to me, "We are virtuous in character, for the righteous are indeed affectionate toward the virtuous. (47)
Even those who act like animals, who sell their own wives and blood, cry out to me; for the virtuous are indeed kind to the good.
For those who possess mechanical devices, those who possess discuses, and those who possess weapons are indeed virtuous;
crying out for me, they are of good character, truly affectionate toward the virtuous, and possessed of the quality of goodness (sattva).
For the lords of royal officers, the judges of justice, and the kings are indeed virtuous;
crying out for me, they are of righteous character, affectionate toward the good, and possessed of the quality of goodness.

Those who castrate others, those who feed on teeth, and those who cut off the linga—these are the ones crying out at me; for those of virtuous conduct, those who are affectionate toward the righteous, are indeed of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

Those who are inactive, those who perform forbidden acts, and even the cruel—when they cry out to me, they become virtuous; for the virtuous are indeed gentle toward the good and possess a virtuous nature.
Destroying the cravings of the womb, consuming the elements, and devoid of ritual purity—yet crying out for me, they are indeed virtuous, gentle, and truly holy. (53)
Those for whom these five are perfected are always considered true practitioners:
freedom from desire, lack of greed, absence of pride, and lack of attachment to flavors. (54)
The virtuous possess freedom from attachment everywhere, as do those with the fivefold functions;
they are devoid of the latent impressions of desire, being free from longing according to their respective natures. (55)
Freedom from desire for anything beyond what is necessary, being devoid of greed, absence of pride, complete lack of conceit, and freedom from stubbornness. ||56||
Indeed, it is taught that the attainment of food for the sake of sustaining life is characterized by a lack of relish;
thus, the virtuous person is devoted to ethical discipline and intent upon the path of devotion. (57)
For he is a great devotee who crosses over [the ocean of existence] and causes others to cross;
or those for whom there is the other pentad, namely, the desire for liberation and the hearing of the sacred narrative. (58)
Association with a saintly devotee, the practice of service and devotion, and self-surrender—these five are considered the characteristics of a saintly person (sādhu). (59)
Or for those who daily perform at dawn the fivefold rite along with bathing and worship,
and at midday the offering of food to Hari.
Likewise, a twentieth part of one's earnings should be offered to Hari;
there should be the daily turning of the rosary, and at the end, the surrender of oneself.
These virtuous ones may dwell in a house, in a forest, or in a secluded place;
whether in society or otherwise, they are indeed the saviors of living beings.
He who abandons wicked qualities and acquires virtuous ones will become a saint in this world; he shall do so even more if he constantly worships Hari.
May those who possess deceit, sinful souls who are indeed full of guile, cast off the evil quality of deceit, attain virtuous qualities, and become devoted to me. (64)
In this world, the virtuous rely on the power of Dharma and are adorned by goodness;
however, all those living beings who wander in saṃsāra are filled with evil qualities.
Thereafter, having attained the most excellent qualities of the virtuous, they become holy men;
freed from the stain of illusion, those saints become stainless.
He who does not regard with even his heart the jewels, woolen blankets, garments, and all enjoyments of prosperity being offered to him; ||67||
He whose activity regarding the state of being the enjoyer and the enjoyed does not recur again and again—
he is to be known as a true ascetic of virtuous conduct, who scorches away all defects.
By that Great-Souled One, the sense of taste and the sense of touch were conquered; thus everything was conquered.
He who cannot hear is deaf, and he who cannot see is deprived of sight. (69)
Untouchable and deprived of skin, devoid of smell and lacking a nose; unfit for speech and bereft of a tongue, and unable to taste that which is inedible. || 2.84.70 ||

He is devoid of hands regarding that which is ungraspable, and devoid of feet regarding that which is inaccessible; he is devoid of the anus regarding that which should not be discarded, and devoid of desire regarding that which is unfit for it. ||71||
Though devoid of a physical body and free from all marks, he is entirely devoted to me;
this virtuous one, though bodiless, grants liberation even to others. (72)
He whose face is like that of a deer, whose posture for lying down is like that of a python, whose sleep is like water, and whose mental constructs are like flowers in the sky; //73//
For him whose body is like a shadow, for whom the multitude of objects is like a dream, for whom prosperity is like ashes, and for whom festivities are like a cremation ground; //74//
He for whom existence is equal to non-existence is a saint; he is the most excellent of the virtuous.
He in whom everything dwells as it does in me—that saint alone is equal to me. (75)
Just as water situated in the sky falls down through the force of lightning, so too does a devotee rain down with affection through association with a holy person. //76//
Just as clouds dissolve in the sky by the force of the wind, so too do millions of sins dissolve through association with a holy person. //77//
Just as a dream vanishes in an instant for one who is awake, so too,
O Rāma, do the impurities vanish in that very moment through the yoga of the saint.
Just as the destruction of darkness indeed occurs through the rays of the sun,
so too, O virtuous one, are all impurities dissolved by the wonders of the saintly.
Just as millions of sorrows dissolve through the birth of a son, so too do millions of sorrows dissolve through association with the virtuous. ||2.84.80||
Just as there are festive joys upon the occasion of a wedding, so too through association with the virtuous arise the festive joys of liberation. (8.1)
Just as happiness arises for a child upon seeing its mother, so too does happiness arise for a devotee upon seeing a holy person. ||82||
Just as young boys and girls rejoice upon obtaining sweet food,
so indeed do millions of devotees rejoice upon obtaining a holy man.
Just as peacocks utter their cries upon the arrival of the rainy season,
so do people proclaim the glories of Hari when they encounter a virtuous person.
Just as the loss of an only son brings about a state of bodilessness for aged parents, so too does separation from the virtuous bring a state of bodilessness for their devotees. (85)

Just as a barren woman becomes intoxicated with joy at the birth of a son, so too do those who have taken refuge in me become intoxicated with joy upon obtaining a gain in the house of a holy man. 86.
Just as the mind blossoms with the fragrance of the essence of sandalwood and other such things, so does the heart of the devotee blossom through Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the saintly, and the true dharma. 87.
Just as all joys indeed arise from the attainment of what is desired, so too do all joys truly arise upon the arrival of a virtuous person. 88.
Just as an actor on the stage brings great delight to the audience, so too does the servant of a holy man bring great delight to the holy ones. (89)
Just as a virtuous wife always serves her beloved husband with happiness,
so too does a devotee joyfully and happily serve the holy Hari.

Just as a hunter’s affection for his son and others always consists in providing them with sustenance, so too a devotee’s affection for virtuous beings and the like always consists in their liberation. 9.1
Just as a cow, having approached her calf, gives milk in a continuous stream,
so too a devotee, having approached the virtuous, bestows his very all upon them.
Just as trees, having drunk water, put forth blossoming new sprouts, so too do devotees, having attained the True Being, produce new sprouts of extensive surrender. 93.
Just as rivers, intoxicated by the swelling of their floods, rush to reach the ocean, so too do devotees, intoxicated by the increase of their devotion, seek to attain the Lord. 94.
Just as a barber rejoices upon obtaining service from a king, so does a devotee always rejoice upon obtaining the service of the virtuous. ||95||
Just as a youth, upon reaching a young woman, attains her very nature, so too does a devotee, having reached the virtuous Hari, attain His very nature. (96)

Just as servants conduct themselves according to the king’s command, following a humble path, so too do devotees conduct themselves according to the command of the virtuous, following the path of Dharma. ||97||
Just as a lamp shines by its own light when joined with the night, so too does the devotee shine with the radiance of Hari when joined with the virtuous. 98.
Just as a ripe fruit naturally falls from the tree in due time, so too does a devotee who has reached spiritual ripeness cast off that which is illusory. 99
Just as a wife of virtuous character follows her good husband,
so does the queen of devotion follow the virtuous one.
Just as one becomes like Nārāyaṇa by dwelling with Nārāyaṇa, so indeed does an individual become like a virtuous person by dwelling with the virtuous. (10.1)
Just as a human being becomes a devotee by dwelling in devotion,
O Lakṣmī, so does a human being become a virtuous person by dwelling in goodness.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means to Liberation Even for One Devoid of the Company of the Holy, the Attainment of the Holy, the Attainment of Holiness, and the Various Kinds thereof," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the eternal dharma of the virtuous;
that by which the worlds are sustained is the dharma of the good, which is Hari himself. (1)
The playful deeds and exploits of Hari should always be remembered by me;
the dharma of the saintly, which is Kṛṣṇa himself, should always be protected within my own heart.
It also yields the fruit of great renown, as well as the fruit of all forms of giving,
the fruit of cows, the fruit of sacred fords, and likewise the fruit of religious observances.
That person who possesses the virtuous dharma attains this fruit;
for the righteous one, the work of liberation is always accomplished through taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
The destruction of bondage is likewise proclaimed as the task of the virtuous alone—those who speak [of the truth], those who practice devotion, and whose minds are pure. (5)
It is evident that the worlds of those virtuous people who associate with the virtuous have been won;
they are liberated from evil and are not defiled by sin.
The embodied being who associates with the virtuous constantly attains righteousness,
and from that, through a drop of the grace of the virtuous Hari, he attains liberation.
But human beings, O Lakṣmī, are always like fools, deluded;
they revile the virtuous who are my very form, and they go to many hells.
In this world, men have become cruel, devoid of compassion, and murderous; regarding virtuous people as useless, they abandon them as if they were a burden.
Indeed, there can be no destination for them anywhere, because of their lack of accumulation of merit;
they are cruel revilers of the unrighteous, following their own ways characterized by tamas and other such qualities.
Deluded, they harm living beings born in the animal realm—worms, ants, snakes, scorpions, beasts, and birds. (11)
Moreover, if they indeed go for refuge to the virtuous for the removal of their sins,
they should serve the holy ones with both body and mind.
Then they are liberated from sins, provided they do not commit violence again;
through service to the virtuous, merit arises even more powerfully.

Through merit, one's intentions become auspicious and even one's virtuous actions proceed gradually; there is the abandonment of unwholesome deeds and great proficiency in the company of the virtuous. (14)
Repentance for one's own deeds is the supreme austerity and atonement;
it consists of fasting and the like, devotion, sacrifice, giving, and offering.

The worship of deities and others, the recitation of mantras, meditation, and virtuous praise; pilgrimage to sacred fords and the attainment of knowledge—these indeed come to the righteous person. (16)
From that, the path to heaven and subsequently the path to liberation may arise;
all this occurs swiftly and most excellently through the yoga of the virtuous. || 17 ||
All virtuous beings are Nārāyaṇas, destroyers of sin, and bestowers of liberation;
within them I always shine as the eternal Person, Hari. 18.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, marked with the Śrīvatsa, Hṛṣīkeśa, who is worshipped by the Lord of All and others. (19)
The omniscient one, united with all, omnipresent, facing every direction, the supreme self residing in the heart, the eternal pervader of all. (3.85.20)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed one, whose womb is Śrī and who dwells with Śrī, is the leader of all creations and of all abodes, as well as of those who inhabit those abodes. ||21||
Bearing the marks of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and other symbols, he was endowed with self-restraint, virtuous conduct, and tranquility; and by his prowess, supreme heroism, and sublime vision.
He was endowed with enthusiasm, authority, fortitude, and a wealth of straightforwardness, as well as compassion, affection, and devotion toward his own people. ||23||
He possesses all the senses through his yogic power, is devoted to Brahman, and is the refuge for all;
he removes the fear of those afflicted by fear and is intent on protecting the distressed.
He is learned, filled with all meanings, and the bestower of boons upon those who seek them;
he is the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of the earth, and the husband of the beloved of Brahmā. ||25||
All the deities are comfortably established within my body;
I am that very Supreme Lord, the manifest Śrī-Bhū-Līlā-Ramāpati.
For whoever indeed wishes to see me, both the one who descends and the one who causes descent,
by him my virtuous ones must be seen— those whose purpose is goodness and who are adorned with saintliness.
When these are seen, I am seen; there is no distinction between them and me here.
Know this, my beloved: all virtuous beings are Nārāyaṇas.
Thus, for whomsoever I, the illustrious Puṇḍarīkākṣa, am pleased,
the host of gods is pleased with him, and all his goals come into his hand.
And whatever man in the world of men shall take refuge in me,
for him there shall be fame, victory, and even heaven.
He will be a teacher of the dharmas, worthy of worship, and a partaker of the Dharma; he should be considered truly virtuous and always honored by people. (3.1)
That alone would be the supreme dharma in which I am honored;
for that reason, I have indeed created millions of virtuous beings for the sake of the welfare of my subjects.
[He saw] all [the sages] beginning with Brahmāyana, those starting with Saccidānanda,
including Sanatkumāra, as well as the earlier and even more ancient ones.
Thus, I am the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is perfect;
I am the Blessed One, the sustainer, creator, and destroyer of all forms. (34)
When I am saluted, I salute him; when I am honored, I honor him as well;
when I am treated with hospitality, I treat him with hospitality; and when I am worshipped, I worship him. (35)
"I see him whom I have seen; having taken refuge in him, I take refuge in him.
Thus, O beloved, for me who practices meditation, he is the object of meditation and I am the meditator at all times. (36)
Such is my constant vow: that such virtuous people as you are mine; for this vow of mine is the conduct practiced by the noble, not that of others here.
Therefore, the virtuous are my forms here on earth for embodied beings;
indeed, the righteous should be served through action, mind, and speech. (38)
Indeed, upon seeing the virtuous, the same vision has arisen for me as well;
for all the gods always dwell within the body of the virtuous. (39)
Sureśvara, as well as Viṣṇu and I myself, dwell in the virtuous;
I am Sarvārāma, Surāma, Rameśa, and the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
I dwell together with you in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, accompanied by the beloveds of Brahmā and attended by the beloveds of Hari. 41.
Wherever there is fame, fortune, fortitude, peace, nourishment, contentment, delight, Lakṣmī, enjoyment, liberation, Śrī, and Līlā—there I myself am present. (42)
O beloved, fame and the other virtues always abide in the virtuous; therefore, I always dwell within them, for the virtuous are my very form.
He who understands in every way the power of the assembly of the virtuous, having taken refuge together with them and attained me, goes to my state. ||44||
And indeed, all their desires are fulfilled exactly as wished,
O Lakṣmī, for those who here chant my name with concentrated minds.
The heart's desires of those devotees who engage in kīrtana are fully realized;
those devotees of kīrtana are worthy of my worship, and I too bow down before them. (46)
I bow to those who pay homage to Sārdhamukta, the virtuous and chaste Satī, the beloved of Brahmā and the beloved of Hari, as well as to the holy Aśvapaṭṭabhūmi. 47.
I bow to those who pay homage to Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Śrī, Māṇikyā, the bestower of happiness Śrī, Ramā, Padmāvatī, and Kṛṣṇā. (48)
I always bow down to those who pay homage to my incarnations, my manifestations, my devotees, and even my attendants—those who worship my forms. 49.
I bow to those who pay homage to Varuṇa, Bhāskara, Vāyu, Vahni, Candra, Balāhaka, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Aja, and the gods.
I bow to those who pay homage to Durgā, Sarasvatī, Bhūmi, Śāradā, Virajā, as well as Maṅgalā and Amṛtā. 5.1.
I bow to those who pay homage to Bṛhaspati, Nārada, Sanatkumāra, Acyuta, Nara, and Nārāyaṇa. (52)
I bow to those who pay homage to the great seers whose wealth is austerity, to the virtuous people whose wealth is devotion, and to the learned ones whose wealth is knowledge. (53)
I bow again and again to those virtuous ones who, dear to the Lord, perform their divine duties without seeking reward, remaining contented and forgiving. (54)
I bow to those dear friends who perform sacrifices and rituals with their senses subdued and their minds perfectly tranquil, and who devote themselves to the Lord both morning and evening. 55.
I bow to Dharma, devotion, my parents, cows, and my guru—to those who are indeed self-controlled, peaceful, and dwell in the forest subsisting on roots and fruits. (56)
I constantly bow to those virtuous ones who possess no accumulation, O beloved;
they nourish their dependents, provide refuge for guests, and eat only the remnants of offerings.
I always bow to those virtuous ones who speak the truth, who observe celibacy, whose hearts are serene toward all beings, and who possess discernment like mine. (58)
I bow to those virtuous people who are devoted to the study and meditation of the scriptures, who strive for the grace of the Guru and devotion to Me, and who are firm in their vows. (59)
I pay homage to those virtuous people who are eager to hear, free from malice,
firm in their vows, wise in conduct, devoted, most established in Brahman, and givers of the Veda.
I always bow to those virtuous ones who carry my favor—those devoted to the practice of begging for alms, humble, and dwelling in the preceptor’s household. (61)

I bow to those virtuous people who are free from cruelty, whose wealth is imperishable, who are devoid of the sense of "mine," who have transcended latent impressions, and who are speakers of Brahman and lords.
I bow to those virtuous people who are devoted to non-violence, firm in their vow of truth, self-controlled, free from craving, and who live like pigeons (content with whatever is obtained). 63.
Established in the four goals of life, peaceful, and practitioners of yoga free from desire, yet engaged in the conduct of the virtuous—I bow to them and always take delight in them. 64.
I always bow to those Brahmins who have the Veda as their body, who are devoted to worship, highly meritorious, who subsist on nectar, who are joined with vows, and who are my constant refuge. 65.

I perpetually bow to those virtuous ones who are not born from a womb, who are born from fire, who are born from Brahman, who have their origin in the eternal, and who belong to the lineage of Acyuta and the lineage of Śrī.
And those who desire to go to the imperishable Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the immortal state, and the unmanifest state of Īśvara; ||67||
O Lotus-born One, I indeed pay homage to all those virtuous ones who have attained the abode of Viṣṇu, as well as to those who desire to go to the excellent stages of life (āśramas).

I bow to the holy ones who are the elders of the world and the elders of their lineages, who destroy darkness, who are suns for the world, who bestow the abode of Kṛṣṇa, and who bring one to the further shore of worldly existence.
I bow to the virtuous and true people who are worthy of worship, who foster well-being, who bestow happiness, who nourish, and who protect against time, illusion, and other evils. (3.85.70)
In this world and the next, those virtuous devotees of Hari indeed bestow happiness;
they who are always guests to all—I bow to them forever and take delight in them. (71)
Those who follow and take delight in such devotees, holy men, and practitioners of Brahman-yoga, cross over all difficulties.
Those who are devoted to peace among them, who praise them, who serve them,
and who are free from envy and full of devotion— they cross over all difficulties.
By bowing down to all virtuous beings—gods, elders, and those who bring auspiciousness—one who possesses faith and devotion overcomes even the most difficult obstacles. (74)
Ascetics who are virtuous and have observed celibacy from their youth,
whose souls are empowered by devotion, rescue even those people who are sinners.
Those people who dwell with devotion toward their mother, father, and elders, being recipients of constant blessings, cross over all difficulties. (76)
O Lakṣmī, just as you conduct yourself, so do the virtuous;
and just as those dear to Brahmā conduct themselves, so do those dear to Hari.
Just as the men and women residing at Kuṅkumavāpī abide there, all are liberated and dwellers in Brahman; they are indeed virtuous and, in my opinion, truly saintly. (78)
In the fourteen worlds,
there are no such Ṛṣis, nor indeed Pitṛs, Munis, gods, or humans.
Other Brahmins are not purifiers in the same way as these, who are my very own forms;
this is the Kṣetra of Kukumavāpī, which is my imperishable abode.
Those residing there are all liberated, as are my other liberated Śaktis;
all the women here are beloveds of Brahman, and all the men here are likewise liberated.
Trees, egg-born beings, womb-born beings, and other creatures as well—whether born of sweat or otherwise—all those who dwell in the field of the syllable abide there. (82)
For all of them are indeed divine and liberated; they are worthy of worship by all.
They alone are all truly virtuous, bestowing liberation merely by their presence.
Indeed, all the limbs of the wish-fulfilling tree are purifying;
likewise, those who dwell in the land of the Imperishable are truly purifying to me. 84.
Those virtuous ones are indeed worthy of refuge and protectors of those who have come for shelter;
just as I am, so too are they full of compassion and bestowers of liberation.
Even by giving away their entire possessions, they protect those who have come for refuge.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of the virtuous Vṛṣāyana. (86)
For the virtuous Vṛṣāyana, having undergone initiation and dwelling in the forest, being free from dualities and without possessions, worships me, Hari Kṛṣṇa. (87)
O King, you are like Videha in your majesty, like the sun in your splendor; through compassion, you are a giver of fearlessness to living beings and remain established in their welfare. ||88||
She dwelt beneath a nimba tree in a tiger-infested forest;
there, on one occasion, she was being pounced upon by a hawk and became overcome with fear.
The sparrow sought refuge with the yogi named Vṛṣāyana;
seeing her there, helpless and having come to his lap out of fear, he [took her in].
He comforted her, saying, "O sparrow, let there be no fear for you here in my presence.
Having said this, he took the sparrow in the palm of his hand and placed her upon that seat. (9.1)
While he was guarding her at the front, a hawk said to him:
"O virtuous sage, let this female sparrow be given to me as my food. (92)
"Having obtained her with great effort, abandon the thought of eating her;
the flesh of her alone shall suffice for my satisfaction today. (93)
"O virtuous one, hunger afflicts me; let food be given to me quickly.
For this woman, whom I have pursued, has appeared before me in the form of my own prey. (94)
A virtuous person should not remain here as a mediator between two parties; for what benefit is there for you in this state of indifference, which is merely a form of aversion and attachment? (95)
A virtuous person should be impartial; partiality is not righteousness for you.
O holy one, I am extremely hungry; otherwise, my death would occur. (96)
"O compassionate one, give me this sparrow that I have struck down;
if you do not protect the sparrow, the sin of killing shall fall upon you. (97)
"But by granting me my life, you would incur the sin of destroying the sparrow;
therefore, remain indifferent in this matter. (98)
Having heard this, Vṛṣāyana fell into reflection for a moment;
then, considering the granting of safety to both, he spoke to him thus: (99)
"Speak, O hawk, for your own sake, so that your hunger may indeed be appeased;
I shall do exactly as you say, but I will not release the sparrow."
Seeking refuge for the sake of her life, she has come to me as her protector;
she does not leave my limbs—behold her, who desires protection. (10.1)
Even there, a woman must never be killed;
moreover, O twice-born one, if she is found to be pregnant, she must not be slain by you.
"I give you fruit, roots, and desired food obtained through alms;
indeed, I shall bring sweet food for your sake—please eat it."
The hawk said: "I have no need for fruits or roots, nor for alms;
that which has been ordained by fate as my prey is this sparrow."
Meat is the food of the hawk species; this is the ancient custom. O virtuous one, if you have such affection for the sparrow, let it be like a partiality for your own wing.
Therefore, give me today your own flesh, measured by the weight of a sparrow;
let it be weighed on a scale for me, sufficient and certainly no more.
Vṛṣāyana became delighted upon hearing this, and he quickly said to him:
"O bird, a great favor has been bestowed upon me by you."
Then, having prepared two leaf-cups and fashioned a balance according to the proper measure,
he repeatedly cut off his own flesh and weighed it against [the hawk's weight].
The son of Bāhu gave his own flesh, the weight of which was equal to that of a sparrow, to the hawk;
having obtained it, the hawk ate it, drank water, and went to the forest.
The sparrow became protected; she became serene and entirely fearless.
Then, having slowly bowed to the sage, she departed from his side into the forest. (3.85.110)
Having obtained the most excellent medicinal herb, Sandhinīpūraṇī, he returned;
he placed the leaf-juice into the hand of the virtuous man, and his arm was restored.
From that time forward, she too became free from disease as before;
that noble bird lived forever in attendance by the side of the holy man.
Taking fruits and leaves, she indeed offered them to the virtuous one;
then, in due time, she gave birth to five eggs.
By the fruit of their service, all those children became knowers of the elements and so forth; they all became perceivers of the three periods of time and took on the form of Śveta.
Indeed, those great seers have composed the Dīpotsavī and the Ghoṭaka;
these birds, who are knowers of omens, are honored by those who understand destiny.
Then, in the course of time, that sparrow reached death in her old age; she went to heaven by means of a celestial chariot and was born as an auspicious and excellent Apsaras.
Named Ālambuṣā, she was a servant of Indra;
thereafter, by the fruit of serving the virtuous one, she indeed attained liberation in the world of Brahmā.
Thus, virtuous ones who have given away all their possessions for the sake of helping others both protect embodied beings and send them toward liberation.
He who is the protector of devotees, of those who are devoted, and of those seeking refuge—he is the virtuous and compassionate one who bestows happiness; so they know.
In this world, people of virtuous conduct practice goodness;
what could he not have attained who has rained down the sacrifice of his own self for my sake?
For the Blessed One dwells at Aśvasarovara as Vṛṣāyana;
by taking refuge in him, many go to my imperishable abode.
"Behold, Lakṣmī, how this seeker of my favor stands on the shore of the ocean in meditation;
thus do the virtuous in this world become bestowers of blessings. (122)
