Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Primary Dharma of the Righteous Person, Nārāyaṇa, and How Righteousness is Attained Through Him; the Bowing to Nārāyaṇa by the Righteous; and how the Sparrow was Protected by the Righteous Vṛṣāyana after giving the weight of the sparrows' flesh to the hawk," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī-Śrī said: "By doing what here do kings, others who are intoxicated by wealth, and people arrogant in their strength indeed attain supreme happiness? (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: One who desires happiness should always perform service to those most established in Brahman;
one should also honor the virtuous, the devotees of Nārāyaṇa, and the elderly. (2)
And he should also honor the virtuous people of the city and the countryside, who are deeply learned, with devotion, gifts, service, and prostrations. || 3 ||
One should serve virtuous people just as one would oneself or one's own sons;
moreover, one should especially honor those among them who are most worthy of worship.
The virtuous are worthy of worship, salutation, and honor, just like the gods on earth;
when they are satisfied, there are always abundant riches such as sovereignty and great happiness.
One should constantly perform service and proclaim the glory of those virtuous ones who are devoted to meditation on Kṛṣṇa, who practice devotion to Brahman, and who possess knowledge of the Dharma.
For she is worshipped by the gods, the ancestors, the gandharvas, and likewise by the brahmins;
as well as by the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the Rudras.
They can make a non-god into a god, and they can also make a god into a non-god;
whoever they wish to be a god shall be a god, and whoever is ruined by them shall perish.
Those who engage in slander shall perish; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should indeed honor the virtuous, for they are the lords over both happiness and suffering.
These should be fed and honored by kings with whatever excellent things they desire, and they should be protected like fathers through salutations, offerings, and other such acts. (3.86.10)
Through the virtuous, the pacification of calamities and obstacles is brought about;
indeed, for those endowed with spiritual luster, the sacrifices themselves become manifest.

The king should always maintain in his home one who is most devoted to Brahman, endowed with devotion, possessed of the virtues of righteousness and character, virtuous, and a constant bestower of liberation.
The lords accept the oblation offered into the mouths of the virtuous;
likewise, the ancestors, the deities, and the liberated yogis are satisfied.
The Ṛṣis, Vasus, Siddhas, Manus, Bhāskaras, Śivas, Suras, Viṣṇus, Brahmās, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts. || 14 ||
The Vālakhilyas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the best of men—these incarnations of the existent (Sat)—having entered into food, enjoy it with happiness. || 15 ||
Whatever wealth and whatever joys our devotees of the Blessed One experience during a festival or a great festival are proclaimed to end at the cremation ground. (16)
Those festivals in which virtuous people of auspicious appearance are present bestow higher rebirths; they are meritorious and auspicious. (17)
Without the virtuous, even a great kingdom becomes a cremation ground that nourishes the realm of Yama;
yet even a forest inhabited by the virtuous is divine, bestowing Goloka and liberation. (18)
Wherever they behold a virtuous person—whether dwelling, wandering, or standing—the messengers of Yama do not approach that place. (19)
Upon merely beholding a virtuous person, obstacles depart to a great distance;
diseases, illusions, and the forces of time flee far away in terror.
Whatever offerings the virtuous here are repeatedly satiated with, and those who follow after the virtuous—their merit is infinite. (21)
Those who receive the virtuous words from the mouths of the righteous do not perish after death, nor do they suffer defeat.
Even those who are sinful do not suffer defeat;
for whatever is seen, heard, or read in this world [is overcome by it]. ||23||
All that arose from the words of blessing of the illustrious and meritorious ones;
indeed, the Earth formerly questioned the Lord Śvetavārāha.
"By what means are the evil deeds of householders destroyed at their very root?
Then Varāha, having meditated, spoke these most excellent words:
For those who serve the virtuous, all evil dissolves;
one should always serve the virtuous, the pure ones who uphold the world. (26)
From these, prosperity, fame, abundance, and wisdom are born;
through them, devotion arises and the purifying intellect is attained. (27)
One who performs the great sacrifice and is a devotee of Hari is indeed a saint; of this there is no doubt.
O Earth, one should constantly serve the saint for the sake of all prosperity.
Beyond the Brahmins, there are others who are teachers; and beyond those teachers who instruct, the Upādhyāyas are considered superior. (29)

Superior to them are always the teachers; superior to the teachers are those endowed with virtuous conduct; and superior to the students of sacred knowledge are those devoted to the glorious Supreme Soul. (3.86.30)
Among devotees, those who have always offered themselves to Me are the best;
superior even to those who have offered themselves are the saintly ones, who are My very forms. (3.1)
There are others who are superior to others, and even those who are superior to them; there are even those who are higher than I. Being such as these, I am a servant of the virtuous.
The man whom the virtuous praise shall become like Mādhava;
he who reviles the virtuous shall soon meet with defeat.
Just as salt thrown into the great ocean dissolves completely,
so too do sins, when cast upon a virtuous person, reach a state of dissolution.
He whom the virtuous praise is born here and prospers with fame, prosperity, abundance, nourishment, fortune, wife, and sons. (35)
The virtuous indeed know the path to heaven as well as that to liberation, and likewise the course of hell and the destiny of karmic actions.
Virtuous people also understand the course of fortunes;
they know both the present and the future through the births and actions [of beings]. (37)
The powerful splendors of all the classes of Kṣatriyas are pacified within the Brāhmaṇas, and those of the Brāhmaṇas themselves within the virtuous.
For those who serve the virtuous, all passion (rajas) is destroyed;
and they may desire fame, prosperity, and even the most excellent of worlds.

A king, a merchant, or anyone else should abide by the consent of the virtuous; yet he who is born with a natural brilliance and becomes most devoted to Brahman through his very birth [is beyond such dependence]. (3.86.40)
He, the son of Acyuta, is worthy of homage by all beings and is truly virtuous;
for the righteous are in every way friends who provide only what is beneficial.
When worshipped, they meditate upon the supreme welfare of those who have taken refuge in them, through recollections associated with Kṛṣṇa and through auspicious words and the like.
Prosperity, growth, splendor, and powerful majesty [attend them].
Indeed, all kinds of fortunes arise through the virtuous resolve [of others].
There are various types of holy men who are difficult to approach and who seek the welfare of others;
some possess the nature of Nārāyaṇa, while others possess the nature of Śīla.
Some have vows as their essence, some have austerity as their essence, and others likewise have meditation as their essence;
some have detachment as their essence, some have knowledge and so forth as their essence, while others have devotion as their strength.
Even those who are neutral toward sentient beings and so forth may be encountered;
yet, by one seeking liberation, all types [of persons] are to be served, but only the essence is to be grasped. ||46||
Some possess the nature of lions, while others possess the nature of deer; some possess the nature of serpents, and others likewise possess the nature of monkeys. (47)
Likewise, there are beings of the nature of fire, others of the nature of water, beings of the nature of earth, and beings of the nature of air; they are of such various kinds.
Indeed, some are like lions in their nature, unable to endure anything, while others are like deer, enduring everything.
Those whose poison is hatred are like serpents; those who steal are like monkeys. || 49 ||
Those whose nature is like fire destroy evil; those whose nature is like water grant peace;
those who are like the earth are patient; and those who are like the wind perceive virtues.
One should rely upon those who are like lions, serpents, or monkeys only as long as it serves one's purpose. (3.86.50)
For the sake of liberation, a wise person should rely upon all others. || 5.1 ||
For the virtuous are great-souled beings, the deities even of the gods;
one should always worship the virtuous with service and the attitude of a servant.
Once, Queen Mālatī questioned her husband, the king:
Having paid homage to Citraketu, who is worshipped by the three worlds, Satī asked:
"O King, by what conduct do you preside over the three worlds? Tell me truly, by what vow did you attain such preeminence?"
Citraketu, however, said to her: "Service to the virtuous is my vow;
not a single day of mine ever passes without the service of the virtuous. (55)
The virtuous are indeed before me; the virtuous are behind me here.
The virtuous are at my sides, and the virtuous are in my assembly.
The virtuous are with me on my journey, and in my eating, and in festivals and other such occasions.
"Indeed, virtuous men devoted to Brahman abide at my commencement;
I have the vow of service toward them, and by that great vow, I preside over the three worlds and I practice devotion to Hari. || 57–58 ||
"Listen, O wife, to other auspicious qualities chosen by me, by which one possesses honor in the world as well as invincibility. (59)
I do not find fault with the virtuous anywhere; I honor them according to their merit.
I do not despise those most devoted to Brahman, nor do I ever commit an offense against them.
Having worshipped him, I inquire after his well-being and constantly perform service;
having prostrated like a staff, I touch his feet and [drink] the water [from them]. (61)
Whatever command they assign to me, I carry it out and please them;
I always listen to the nectar-like discourse of those lords who delight in the truth.
This is indeed the supreme, divine nectar and the vision that transcends all;
it is the word from the mouth of one most devoted to Brahman, from which the scripture and its injunctions proceed.
Those who are most devoted to Brahman, possessing the strength of intellect, always attain perfection through austerity and devotion;
endowed with the power of the Self and my own powers, they even deliver others.
The sages who dwell in the abodes of Brahma, who possess equanimity of vision, abide in nirvana upon this earth; they are the bestowers of excellence and the bestowers of happiness.
The earth indeed swallows him who does not serve one most devoted to Brahman;
pride destroys the prosperity even of a wealthy man of little intelligence.
Then, having abandoned pride and likewise having abandoned the intoxication of royalty,
I indeed constantly and joyfully performed the massaging of their feet for those virtuous ones.
And having heard that I, Citraketu, am a devotee, virtuous people indeed come from every region— whether from the terrestrial world, the heavenly realms, the netherworld, or even from the ocean.
Indeed, the purifiers such as Nārada and others come from Satyaloka;
blessed is my fortune, for I am a king who is the husband of ten million women.
He was renowned as "Devoted to the Holy," for whom the holy ones had respect;
his home was filled with the holy, and his women were devoted servants of the holy. (3.86.70)
What king indeed could be more fortunate than I, who eats only the remains of offerings and grants whatever anyone asks of me at that very moment? (71)
I constantly gratify the virtuous, the Brahmins, and the yogis;
for I consider my kingdom to be of great value only when it serves the purpose of the virtuous, just as one’s own senses serve their respective objects.
"O beloved, my kingdom exists for the sake of the highest Brahman and for the sake of liberation;
without afflicting the circle of subjects, I would bestow all worldly enjoyments. (73)
Just as virtuous men are worthy of my worship, so too are the Brahmins—the officiating priests, domestic chaplains, teachers, disciples, kinsmen, and relatives. (74)
Women, boys, and girls who are unprotected and without refuge;
those who have come for shelter, as well as guests and mendicants. ||75||
Those who possess no worldly support are worthy of my worship, whether they be forest-dwellers or householders;
those who perform virtuous deeds, who are learned in the scriptures, and who are people of Hari are always to be honored.

Therefore, those who act otherwise shall indeed be punished according to the principles of the scriptures. Devotion, righteousness, virtuous conduct, knowledge, and self-discrimination—[these are the means]. (77)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, straightforwardness, self-control, mastery over the senses, freedom from anger, absence of pride, lack of malice, modesty, patience, and restraint. (78)
Forbearance, the destruction of latent impressions, the destruction of craving, and purity—O beloved, these are seen in him, and indeed no improper acts. (79)
Such a person shall be a worthy recipient in this world and always deserves honor, whether the gift be unprecedented or old, belonging to another or one's own. (3.86.80)
Whether it be specially distinguished, or even one who has just arrived,
whoever is most devoted to Brahman and established in the highest good— that person is a worthy recipient of honor.
In this world, there are many people burdened with excessive pride, who are full of envy and hatred, unable to tolerate others. (82)
They cannot endure the fame of others, nor the happiness of others, nor the prosperity of others; they cannot endure these things, they burn with envy, and therefore they revile the virtuous. (83)
Considering the Vedic words of the virtuous, which are esteemed by the world, to be invalid, they even transgress the bridges of dharma. (84)
And those who consider themselves wise create disorder on their own; by propounding arguments based on mere reasoning, they commit malice toward the virtuous. (85)
Abusers, as well as wicked men who speak in opposition to the scriptures, fools, those of harsh speech, and men devoted to sin—[these are the ones who suffer]. (86)
Having found dogs that are equal to themselves and well-fed, the wicked indeed honor them;
O Mālatī, such hypocrites are like dogs among men throughout the three worlds.
Those who do not perform what is wholesome, who destroy their own kin as well as others, and who invite their own ruin, must be punished by kings in every way. (88)
Just as a dog is intent on both barking and devouring,
so indeed do they blaze forth to destroy the boundaries of the world.

Therefore, O Queen, having observed the assembly of people, the law, what is beneficial for oneself, one's own welfare, the heart [of the people], the place, and the time, a person should carry out the royal command. (3.86.90)
Thus proceeding constantly, kings, wealthy men, or powerful people here increase for eternal years. (9.1)
If they continue to live in that very manner and are never overcome [by worldly attachments], those devotees of Hari, freed from debt, attain liberation at the end. ||92||
Thus Citraketu indeed spoke to Mālatī, and she too, having obtained the supreme power of Hari, served the virtuous one day and night. ||93||
She devoted herself to the Supreme Self through service, worship, and chanting;
she indeed performed her entire range of duties for the sake of the virtuous.
Indeed, by the king's command, he constantly attended upon virtuous and auspicious men with food, gifts, service, and the offering of water, clothing, and fruit. (95)
And she, her heart ascended with devotion, beheld me, the Supreme Lord,
in my divine form during the worship— four-armed and seated upon a celestial chariot.
Having obtained the king's permission, he also requested release;
then, quickly casting off his physical body, he ascended a celestial chariot.
Divine, four-armed, and fair-faced, she became the companion of Lakṣmī; Mālatī, the beloved of Brahmā and the consort of Nārāyaṇa, now dwells in that abode. (98)
Thus, through association with the virtuous, the king indeed became virtuous; and through association with her virtuous husband, she attained the path to liberation. (99)
O Lakṣmī, having attained the path of liberation, Mālatī, the companion of Ramā, became the beloved of Brahmā; for the company of the virtuous is fruitful only so long as it lasts.
Whether poor or wealthy, virtuous or even devoid of merit, by taking refuge in the virtuous one indeed becomes Narayana. || 101 ||
Through the force of devotion, a portion of myself is born as one possessing supreme fame—
the savior of all worlds and the sustainer of all who follow the path of dharma.
It leads one to the Imperishable and protects one in its own presence;
through reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of the Prowess of the Virtuous through the Example of Citraketu’s Attainment of the Supreme Good, Even for Kings such as Dhanamada and others who were proud of their strength," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Those Brāhmaṇas who are the sons of Brahmā are my very bodies;
for they are purifiers in every way in the world, being the highest among all castes.
Always enveloped by the snares of desire, anger, great delusion, and greed; possessed of women, devoted to the duties of householders, and shrouded by hope, thirst, and the like. || 2 ||
They are your most excellent ones—supportless, dispassionate, and virtuous;
they are empty of desire, anger, and the like, and are entirely free from craving and hope. || 3 ||
Free from the snares of greed and other such bonds, all these excellent stages of life are auspicious;
they follow the dharma of non-possession, are faultless, and are devoted solely to the path of liberation.
The peaceful ones are the best among the two; tell me, O Lord, where lies their excellence?
Do both of these indeed exist as bodies, or is there a difference between the two? (5)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which is beneficial, true, wholesome, and a matter of direct perception:
those who are free from desire are indeed far superior to those who possess desires. (6)
Ascetics are always most excellent and beloved compared to those who have wives;
indeed, desire, anger, and great delusion arise through association with women.
My bodies that delight in passion are excellent, yet they are not the most excellent;
the virtuous, who are entirely free from all illusion, are the most excellent to me.
Householders who are full of deceit are indeed constantly joined with hell;
like those destined for hell, they perpetually frequent cremation grounds.
The ascetics, ever empty of illusion and devoted to Mādhava,
those yogins of Hari, serve the eternal residents of Vaikuṇṭha.
The householder stage is always lower than the stage of renunciation;
among the social classes, Brāhmaṇas are superior, but not so in all respects when women are present.
Among those in the castes and stages of life, the virtuous are indeed most excellent to me;
celibacy is always supreme, and goodness is likewise supreme. (1)
The forest-dweller's stage of life is superior, yet not even slightly like that of the virtuous;
those who cherish sensual pleasure bear their pride in vain, just like denizens of hell. 1.3.
There is no place anywhere superior to the state of renunciation (saṃnyāsa);
by its very nature, illusion (māyā) and the actions born of illusion are base.
Indeed, virtuous people established in the vow of sincerity are superior to all;
even lords who possess wives honor such holy persons.
For indeed, the twice-born, kings, and even the gods worship the virtuous;
yet among those who follow the profession of service, farmers are always superior.
The protectors [should give] to the farmers, and the ascetics to the protectors; the ascetics are Brahmins, and from them come virtuous men, excluding women. (17)
For the virtuous are devoted to Brahman, devoted to the Self, and devoted to liberation;
indeed, the virtuous are free from fault, possess upward-directed vigor, and have Brahman as their very essence. || 18 ||
Among the castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the best; among Brāhmaṇas, those who are virtuous;
among the learned, those worthy of worship; and indeed, among the purifiers, the purifiers themselves.
My tamasic forms are the rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas;
my rajasic forms are the kṣatriyas and others who seek their own self-interest.
My bodies are of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), and the twice-born are possessed of knowledge;
the virtuous ones, free from the qualities (nirguṇa) and possessing divine forms, grant me liberation.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous are most excellent, and not the twice-born; for all the splendors of the kṣatriyas enter into the splendor of the brahmins.
Indeed, all the splendors of the virtuous merge into the splendor of the truly righteous;
and all the splendors of the truly righteous dissolve into me, Mādhava.
Those like me are always virtuous sages who serve as guides for the Brahmins on earth;
being sanctified, they are the extinguishers of sin and the bestowers of liberation upon those devoted to the yoga of giving.
Austerity, splendor, vows, truth, wonder, and good character—these virtues flow away from an embodied being through association with women. (25)
All those qualities increase for the virtuous who are devoted to moral conduct;
indeed, such good people are born as true Nārāyaṇas, like Nārāyaṇa himself.
Therefore, the Brahmins are the best and the most excellent of all beings at all times;
for in ancient times, Brahmā became enraged with the virtuous Sanatkumāra.
He indeed weighed the excellence of goodness against that of brahminhood;
and in the presence of the twice-born, goodness attained the state of being most excellent.
Thereafter, he again placed them within a single balance scale:
the state of being a Brahmin, the state of being a Kṣatriya, the state of being a Vaiśya, the state of being a Śūdra, and the state of being a religious student (brahmacārin).
Then Aja placed the captured woman with another man,
so that all embodied beings might perceive goodness to reside solely in truth.
Goodness has attained respectability from all seven [classes] in every way;
therefore, goodness is the most excellent in creation and even in matters of liberation.
Indeed, Brāhmaṇas are the best recipients, but the virtuous are the most excellent.
Among them, the householders are the most excellent great devotees of the Lord; among those, the virtuous are the best. || 32 ||
Those who are generous and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa are always the best;
those who merely carry burdens are certainly not the best, just as those who know the nature of perfumes are superior.
Likewise, those who merely carry wood are not the best; rather, the virtuous are the best. O Lakṣmī, I am a householder, and I honor righteous people.
All those liberated ones who dwell in the world of Brahmā are my virtuous [refuges];
I mutter their names and worship those Nārāyaṇas and Narāyaṇas.
He sent forth the most eminent of Brahmins, Brahmins who were practitioners of the yoga of Brahman,
those possessed of virtuous conduct, virtuous ones as well, and the supreme ascetics among ascetics.
I constantly honor those who are free from craving for the taste of flavors, who possess no sensual pleasures of the senses, and who are accompanied by the fragrance of heedfulness. 37.
"O Lakṣmī, this household life does not please me, for it is indeed defiled;
yet, at the desire of you devoted wives, I became a householder. (38)
In whatever manner people approach me, in that very same way do I favor them;
this is my eternal vow, for I am indeed the fulfiller of the desires of my devotees.
By granting the objects of desire to those who long for them, and by destroying the suffering of those who are afflicted, [I act].
I fulfill the desires of those seeking wealth by bestowing riches upon them.
O beloved, having become devoid of qualities for the sake of the wise, I effect their liberation;
the holy ones (sādhus) are indeed my incarnations, and in them I dwell eternally.
I dwell among those who are virtuous, both individually and collectively; elsewhere, however, I abide according to necessity, according to pleasure, and according to the fruit [of their actions].
Therefore, the virtuous who are disciplined in character are always the most excellent.
Then once, Viṣṇu himself, accompanied by Lakṣmī, went to the forest.
He performed various kinds of penance for many thousands of years;
while Lakṣmī remained engaged in service, the ascetic did not touch her.
Then Lakṣmī, with a humble disposition, questioned the Supreme Lord:
"O Viṣṇu, why do you not touch me? Pray, tell me the reason for this. (45)
Viṣṇu declared this most excellent vow, wherein there is no contact with women;
it is a vow of celibacy, a penance that bestows the perfection of the highest of the high. (46)
Contact with virtuous women is the highest excellence; excellence is the strength of austerities.
Through excellence, the unassailable perfection of austerities arises. (47)
Lakṣmī fell into doubt, thinking: "Even though he is Nārāyaṇa himself, though he is faultless, how is it that the Lord speaks like an ordinary living being? (48)
Then, indeed, after the successful completion of his penance, Viṣṇu went to Vaikuṇṭha itself for the purpose of dispelling Śrī’s doubt. 49.
There the divine Nārāyaṇa shines together with Lakṣmī;
he too constantly honors the virtuous and the yogis.
Having thus shown Lakṣmī this, he then departed for the supreme Goloka, the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, where Kṛṣṇa dwells together with Rādhikā. (51)
Having thus demonstrated that he constantly honors the virtuous,
Viṣṇu then departed for the supreme abode called Akṣara, the most excellent of all realms.
There, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Brahmapriyā,
honors the perfected saints and reveals his own splendor to them.
Then Lakṣmī’s doubt was indeed dispelled from its very root;
thereafter, Viṣṇu, having perceived Lakṣmī within his own form, [remained as he was].
He showed to Lakṣmī his eternal form as Lakṣmī;
that very Lakṣmī is indeed his character, which is the very nature of celibacy (brahmacarya). ||55||
A woman acts according to her own will, yet in reality she is the embodiment of virtuous conduct;
she is non-different from the Goddess herself—you, O Lakṣmī, are my beloved. (56)
"You abide in the form of virtue," "you are one whose form is that of a virtuous woman"—thus you are dear to me;
for the conduct of a Brahmin is exceedingly dear to me, and nothing else is so. (57)
You, being of that very nature, are my eternal beloved; nothing else is dear to me beyond that.
Furthermore, all those who possess your true nature are most beloved to me.
The virtuous are my heart, and Lakṣmī is likewise my heart;
the Kaustubha gem is in my heart, and the Śrīvatsa mark is also in my heart.
The virtuous Śrīvatsas indeed dwell within my heart;
for as I am the Lord of Śrī, so too am I the Lord of the virtuous.
I am always the Lord of Love, and I am always the Lord of Virtue;
I am always the Lord of the Holy, and I am always the Lord of Fortune.
The mark of Lakṣmī, which consists of love and is called virtuous conduct, resides within me;
wherever that exists, it is indeed proclaimed as "Lakṣmī. (62)
You possess that [nature], and you are my will; the virtuous are my very forms.
My character is my eternal quality; thus, I am one whose true nature is the virtuous.
Therefore, although they are the most excellent among all created beings, how many Brāhmaṇas there are who are joined with the taint of women! 64.
Neither the gods nor the lords, nor even those equal to the virtuous, nor the sages nor the attendants, have ever attained the yoga of women in any way whatsoever. (65)
O Lakṣmī, among those, the virtuous are the most excellent, higher than the highest;
austerity joined with good conduct is supreme, and such austerity resides in the virtuous. (66)
Therefore, O Rame, the virtuous are indeed the best and are always worthy of your worship.
Now, lest you have any doubt as to how the virtuous are truly superior— 67.
In the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, honor the holy men who have assembled there;
welcome your guests and those devoted to renunciation with respectful offerings.
Through their words of blessing, supreme welfare is attained;
indeed, the merit born of their favor shall be eternal. (69)
The fruit of serving them is equal to the bliss of ten million Golokas;
and from that, all the beloveds of Brahmā and the beloveds of Hari are attained.

Let them practice service to the virtuous and please holy people—the gurus who are free from worldly transformations, bestowers of liberation, and those who enable one to cross beyond the realm of illusion. 7.1
Having slain the great asuras, such as Mahiṣa and others, Durgā, Caṇḍī, Mahākātyāyanī, the Supreme Goddess, then questioned Śambhu.
"Non-violence is the supreme dharma; this you yourself have declared, O Śambhu.
Yet violence is destructive, and it was practiced by me in an exceedingly cruel manner. (73)
For many Kāśyapas have been struck down and torn asunder—those Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas who encountered him in battle. (74)
Their sin, as well as the weeping and so forth of those women, my own sin born of widowhood, and the wailing of the children who have lost their protector—[may all this be removed]. (75)
"How indeed should I avoid it? By what means of purification—by action, by a vow, or even by expiation? Tell me. (76)
Having heard this, Śambhu then said: "You are the manifest Pārameśvarī, the divine Brāhmī, the Great Power (Mahāśakti), in whom no sin exists. (77)
You are of an eternally pure nature; you are Lakṣmī, you are Ramā, and you are Rati.
You are Māyā, you are Mahālakṣmī; no sin exists in you at all. 78.
I am Rudra, the agent of dissolution; you are Rudrāṇī, the destroyer.
You are Mahākālī, the Great Power, the purifier, and the devourer of the worlds.
"You are indeed always of my own nature; I am Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
You are Nārāyaṇī, the sustainer of the world, the auspicious Śivā, composed of merit."
You are a virtuous and chaste woman, pure as fire and belonging to the Supreme Person;
nevertheless, for the sake of the peace of your mind and for the purpose of gathering the world [in dharma], [I shall perform this]. 81.
O Maheśvarī, I shall show you that reality; practice it accordingly.
Indeed, these three—a sacred ford, a vow, and austerity—are capable of washing away sins.
And among these, the service of the virtuous is the most powerful and supreme fortress;
the sight of the virtuous is meritorious, as is their touch and the act of pleasing them. (83)
Prostration, servitude, massaging the feet, and so forth—all that which produces [the Lord's] grace is an immediate destroyer of sin. (84)
Therefore, go to Viśālā, where the virtuous Hari himself—the son of Dharma, the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa—resides in splendor. (85)
He is always observant of vows, an ascetic, and a celibate student; he is my guru.
Through service to him, the destruction of great sins and other evils will come to pass. (86)
Therein dwell other holy beings, divine and highly devoted to the Lord, who are endowed with devotion and grant liberation through their very sight. ||87||
Purifying beings in the form of Brahman, such as Nārada and others, as well as Sanatkumāra and other virtuous ones, constantly come there. //88//
Through the sight and service of virtuous ones such as Lomaśa and others, and by residing at the hermitage of Badarī, there shall be the destruction of all impurities. (89)
Thus addressed, Satī said to Śambhu: "I shall go at your command;
if it pleases you, O Śambhu, you too must come, O Lord."
Saying "So be it," Hara, having resolved thus, went with the Goddess and his attendants to Badarī by way of the sky; he did not bow to Nārāyaṇa, his preceptor.
Then Satī, having offered all that to Nārāyaṇa, performed service consisting entirely of attendance upon the virtuous.
Likewise, every morning, the sweeping of the ground and the offering of water should be performed in the vicinity of Nārāyaṇa’s seat and the Badarī tree.
Durgā performed, as was appropriate, the offering of leaves and flowers, the offering of garlands, meditation, visualization, recitation of mantras, and so forth. (94)
Śambhu also performed services such as attending upon the great sages, and he offered greetings and hospitality to the virtuous according to their needs. || 95 ||
In this manner, Satī indeed performed service to her true guru, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, for just one month; the Lord Hari was pleased.
He said to her, "Speak, O Durgā; what do you require?
Durgā replied, "O ocean of compassion, I am indeed your daughter, Vaiṣṇavī."
I have received from Śambhu this purifying initiation, which is always accompanied by [his] grace;
nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world, it brings about the destruction of the Daityas. (98)
Because of that, I have become fearful of great sins such as the slaughter of a cow;
by the command of Hara, I have come to you for refuge in order to purify myself. 99.
O Lord, through the service of the virtuous Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Hari,
may all my sins be destroyed, for such is the desire that dwells within my heart.
Having heard this, Śrī Hari Nārāyaṇa said to you, O Śivā:
"There is not even a trace of sin in you; you are Brāhmī, the supreme sovereign."
You abide as Śiva-Śakti, the destroyer of great sins;
nevertheless, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you observe such a vow.
Indeed, all your sins consisting of the slaughter of Daityas have been pacified; you are truly purifying by the mere sight of me, a virtuous man. 103.
"O virtuous lady, because you have served the sages, those powers which were lost have now returned to you.
Having said this, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa then gave her water.
The virtuous Śivā drank the nectar-like water known as the grace of the *kamaṇḍalu*. Then Śiva, together with his own attendants, [approached] the Lord Hari.
Having worshipped him and received his command, they both departed for Kailāsa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the supreme majesty of the virtuous been described by Śambhu. 106.
And the fruit of service has been shown to be the destroyer of sins, as well as the bestower of heaven and liberation, and likewise the bestower of worldly enjoyment and ultimate release. || 107 ||
Service to the virtuous is the bestower of wealth and prosperity, the most excellent;
it grants progeny, acts as a savior, and destroys the suffering of poverty.
I delight in the service of the virtuous, which destroys the darkness of ignorance, brings about the attainment of Nārāyaṇa, and bestows both happiness and spiritual splendor.
From reciting this, from hearing it, from remembering it, or even from reading it,
there shall be enjoyment of worldly prosperity and heaven, and there shall also be liberation belonging to the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu as an Exemplar of the Saints Being in Every Way Superior to Brāhmaṇas and Householders, and the Exemplar of Durgā’s Service to the Saints," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Person, you are one of virtuous form;
knowing this, I rejoice especially from your own mouth. (1)
The virtuous are the saviors in the world, and the virtuous women are likewise the deliverers;
detached from worldly ties and established on the path of renunciation, they always grant the upliftment of living beings.
They, who are dear to Brahmā and always delighted by the blessings of the virtuous, are indeed constantly honored by us through even a fraction of our compassion. (3)
We exist through your various and most extraordinary yogic powers;
there is no end to our merits, since you, Hari, are our beloved.
Now, in this regard, I wish to know that vow which is known as *sahadharma*,
considered by the wise to belong to the husband and wife at all times from the moment of taking the hand in marriage onwards.
What kind of dharma is this? Is it momentary or eternal? Is it Vedic or imagined, or is it sensory or demonic? (6)
How could it be that for a husband and wife, [the same state] exists either in this very life or in another?
For, due to the difference in their karma, the death of husband and wife does not occur simultaneously.
Since there is no movement toward a single destination at all, how could there be a "partner in dharma"?
Whether that partnership in dharma is by choice, or fixed, or even by force. (8)
Tell me everything— what it is like and what its fruit is—
so that by hearing this, there may be the attainment of dharma for all here in this world.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the eternal, shared dharma:
that which the bridegroom takes in the hand when the marriage fire has been made the witness. (3.88.10)
She who, greatly delighted, gives her own hand into the hand of the groom—their dharma is *sahadharma* (the shared duty) indeed for as long as they live. (11)
Whether by one's own will in the union of two, or likewise by the desire of the parents, or by the desire of relatives, or even by force in some cases; || 12 ||
The duty of giving may consist of a previous union by force, or it may be a joint religious rite for both [the bridegroom and the groom], or likewise for the daughter or the young man. (13)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the joint religious duty of a husband and wife proceeds;
there is unity between the two in their minds, their bodies, and likewise in their actions. (14)
There is oneness of qualities, oneness of wealth, and oneness of home for both;
there is oneness of utensils and oneness of all objects of enjoyment.
Through food and recreation, through playful conversation and secret counsel, through vows, gifts, and pilgrimages—thus [he attained] unity with their hearts as well as with their senses. (16)
There is oneness through waking and sleeping; oneness through assistance and service;
oneness with my vital breaths; and oneness with me through the bonds of affection. ||17||
There is unity with internal states and with external dualities such as fruits and the like;
likewise, there is unity with merit and so forth, as well as with income, expenditure, and preservation. || 18 ||
By means of vehicles, mounts, ornaments, jewelry, gold, garments, and the like; as well as by abundance, prosperity, fields, gardens, kingdoms, marketplaces, and so forth. (19)

There is identity with one's young children and offspring, identity with suffering, pleasure, and the like, and identity with their respective specific qualities—namely, the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded. (3.88.20)
Through joys, delights, great festivals, and all auspicious activities, that which constitutes the very oneness of the couple [is established]. (21)
This dharma has been declared, preceded by devotion to the husband;
it shall be complete only if it is maintained together with fidelity to one's wife. || 22 ||
By the power of dharma, the husband and wife shall indeed travel together toward heaven at the same time, according to their desire. ||23||
O Lakṣmī, as much loss as there may be regarding one's shared dharma, so too shall there be death at different times for the two of us, and likewise our departure [from this world]. (24)
And it indeed becomes distinct in another womb, just as it is in heaven;
likewise, the destiny of those following different dharmas would be distinct in another world. (25)
If there is no injury, their shared dharma shall be eternal forever;
both shall go from here to heaven—therefore truth is supreme. (26)
He attains both Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, my supreme imperishable abode;
as a couple sharing the same dharma, they both obtain liberation together.
If dharma here were indeed maintained as a shared dharma accompanied by injury, then the separation of husband and wife would certainly occur; of this there is no doubt. (28)
Therefore, that dharma is momentary and not of an eternal nature;
this Vedic dharma conforms to place and time. (29)
And there is no imagined [object], O Lakṣmī, since imagination depends [on something else];
if dependence were to arise from a disparity in space, time, and so forth. (3.88.30)
At that time, the practice of dharma becomes secondary in certain calamities;
yet there is no loss thereby, for one is purified through expiation. ||3.1||
Even that which is purely sensory is not ultimate;
for in this world, the purpose of the self exists together with its dharma, though it is dependent upon the body. (32)
Established in the self regarding the next world, and firmly situated in liberation and freedom from bondage—
if there is a desire for the state of a married couple, that is declared to be purely voluntary.
That which is obtained by force is proclaimed as the Āsura [form of marriage]; that which is obtained by any other means whatsoever is the subsequent [Uttara] form.
That dharma, when preserved in its complete form, is eternal;
but when not preserved, it becomes impaired and is the very cause of separation. ||35||
Just as it is, so long as he is protected, will he indeed bestow fruit;
if the younger brother is protected, he will yield the fruit of the younger.
The middling [type] yields middling fruit, and the superior yields the most excellent fruit.
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, pairs were fashioned by Brahmā. (37)
Having produced pairs [of offspring], thereafter, by means of dharma,
they go together to the next world— whether to liberation or to heaven— after death.
By the power of devotion to her husband alone, and by the strength of her vows as a wife,
she remained firm even when time itself grew weak and her companion in dharma fell into decline.
There is weakness even in association, and there is weakness regarding the world beyond;
thus, when such decline has arisen, men and women follow divergent paths. (3.88.40)
Those of discordant birth experience the fruits of their own actions;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has this secret of the shared dharma been declared. (41)
Divine beings protect [their subjects], whereas others do not, being intent solely on their own self-interest;
for their paths are divided, and thus they wander in the ocean of existence.
Not bound to one another, not sharing with one another, and ignorant of one another's duties, they repeatedly resort to the cremation ground. (43)
Those equal to Lakṣmī and Rādhārāmā are never separated; those equal to Satī and Padmāvatī are never separated. (44)
Those whose splendor is equal to the luster of rubies are never separated;
those whose splendor is like cotton-wool or the fur of a female elephant are separated here and there. (45)

Servants are separated from those who are not their equals, yet they may sometimes be joined with others; however, one who resembles a stranger is never truly joined, and once departed, she is gone forever.
Thus does this wheel revolve here in the world, O Lakṣmī, which is difficult to restrain;
it is indeed the wheel of Dharma, the protector of yoga, as powerful as strength itself. ||47||
That very same weak enemy does not protect the union at all;
therefore, there is separation for all couples and for men and women. (48)
O Lakṣmī, unrighteousness and the burden of debt are the causes of separation;
some, having married quickly, are indeed separated from their spouses and even pass away.

Some are separated [from their loved ones] in their youth, some in middle age, and others at the end; they are parted according to the time when their debt remains unpaid, just like those who carry a debt. (3.88.50)
In that matter, I alone am the cause for both union and separation;
therefore, one should practice virtue, observing the unbroken common duty (*sahadharma*).
Having abandoned the common duty and having cast aside the scriptures and the words of the guru, [one falls].
But those who, having abandoned the bull of conventional practice, proceed by a wrong path.
Householders who merely fill their own bellies, performing neither rites for the gods nor for the ancestors, go to a terrible hell filled with suffering and poverty. (53)
Those who do not honor guests go to a terrible hell—those who are devoid of charity, devoid of purity, and bereft of auspicious conduct. ||54||
Those seized by the Kali age, fallen from the dust of purity, those who live by the livelihood of dogs, and those overwhelmed by weeping, affliction, and strife— these indeed go to a downward state.
Those who are empty of the name of the Blessed One, who eat the leavings of others, who are evil-minded and devoid of mantra, go to a most terrible hell. (56)
Those devoid of ritual action, devoid of ancestral rites, devoid of devotion, and devoid of the Lord, as well as those devoid of great festivals and the like, go to a most terrible hell. ||57||

Those who have fallen from their caste, the dull-witted, the insane, those afflicted with leprosy or vitiligo, the impotent, those stricken by consumption, and the sinful— these indeed go to a downward state.
Physicians, temple-priests who live off offerings, those who prescribe vows in vain, those who revile the sick, and those devoid of devotion—these indeed go to a downward state. || 59 ||
Singers, dancers, acrobats, musicians,
storytellers, and warriors who are devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state;
those fallen from dharma, fallen from their vows, and fallen from their lineage and family [follow the same path].
Those whose devotion is mixed with others and who lack faith go to a lowly state. || 61 ||
Those who neglect the fire-sacrifice, omit the ancestral rites, indulge in sexual misconduct,
teach with atheistic intent, and lack devotion, surely go to a downward state.
Those who sell the Veda, as well as those who sell women,
and those who sell their husbands— being devoid of devotion— they indeed go to a downward state.

Those who pride themselves on all their attachments, those who are preoccupied with the purification of corpses, thieves, and those who live off their daughters— all such sinners go indeed to a downward state.

Those who live off their daughters-in-law, those who live off their maternal relatives, those who live by begging without being known for it, those who are in debt, those who steal, and those devoid of devotion— these indeed go to a downward state.

Those who sell living beings, those who subsist on the trade of women and the like, those who have no master other than a prostitute, and those who do not recite the sacred prayers— all these sinners indeed go to a downward state.
Those people who are devoid of vows, who cause suffering to their own wives, who are like beasts,
and who perform improper deeds— these sinners indeed go to a downward state.
Those who disparage one another, those who deceive one another,
the dishonest, the deceitful, and those devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state.
Those who are devoid of the Sāvitrī, those devoted to false trade and the like, those whose speech is false, those whose actions are untrue, and the sinful—these indeed go to a downward state. (69)
The poor, those who live off the fortune of others, the violent, the deceitful, the wicked, the defiled, those who inflict stains upon others, and the sinful— all these indeed go to a downward state.

Gamblers, those who live without a means of subsistence, those who eat all kinds of food, those who wander about aimlessly, those who perform cruel deeds, and those devoid of devotion— these indeed go to a downward state.
Furthermore, those who take false oaths, meat-eaters, drinkers of liquor,
and those who do not observe Vedic vows or conduct— these sinners indeed go to a downward state.
Except for the sake of tasks such as protecting their guru from fear, those whose speech, actions, and thoughts are repeatedly devoted to falsehood are indeed destined for hell. (73)
Those people who destroy the wealth of others, those who abduct the wives of others,
and those sinful ones who speak slanderously— verily, they go to hell.
They establish water-stations, rest-houses, assembly halls, and shelters, providing shade and food for travelers;
they care for the helpless, women, children, the elderly, the frightened, and the deceived.
The hypocritical ascetic, the deceitful female ascetic, and the rogue are those who go to hell—those who destroy livelihoods, homes, friends, wives, trust, and dharma. ||76||
Those who violate boundaries, justice, virtuous deeds, charity, and sacrifice; those who are ungrateful and corrupters—such people go to hell. (77)
Heretics, those who lack discernment, people who sell poison, those who perform malevolent magic, arsonists, and poisoners—these sinners go to hell. (78)

Those who frustrate hopes, those who violate their promises, those who destroy devotion, those who render labor fruitless, those who sow discord, and those who destroy what is auspicious—such people go to hell. (79)
Those who employ weapons and arrows, those who kill cows, virgins, or women, and those who slaughter children, animals, and the like—such people go to hell. (3.88.80)
Those who obstruct paths with stakes, stones, and thorns, and those who abandon their servants, devotees, and wives, go to hell. (81)
Those who castrate bulls, those who pierce their noses, those who knock out their teeth, those who cause suffering to animals, and those who kill them, go to hell. (82)
Kings who do not protect their subjects, lords of wealth who are devoid of charity, and fools who abandon those who have sought refuge—such men are considered destined for hell. 83.
Those superior persons who consume [resources] without giving to their dependents and the destitute, being sinful rulers unfit for their office, are considered to go to hell. (84)
Devoid of worship, devoid of the gods, devoid of devotion, and lacking service;
devoid of affection and practicing deceit—such sinners indeed go to a downward state. 85.
Indeed, there is no commonality of dharma between those [men] and those [women] who follow a contrary dharma;
for the life of those unrighteous sinners is truly like that of beasts.
In this world there is no happiness, no Dharma, and no vow;
there is no giving, no merit, and no compassion—how can those who are like cattle be happy? (87)
In the next world as well, those hungry ghosts indeed become miserable;
they do not obtain water, food, or drink, and likewise, they do not see their families. (88)
Alone, yet caught in the snare of their offspring, they go to the abode of hell;
they do not know the true dharma, being consumed by the objects of craving. ||89||
Those who are dominated by darkness do not recognize the suffering of others for the sake of their own happiness;
like venomous serpents, they go to the abode of hell.
They do not know how to protect women, nor do they understand how to protect cows; they have no desire for the welfare of their male and female servants, and thus they go to a downward state. 91.
Those who seize wealth, those who violate vows, those who steal righteousness, and corrupters—who turn truth into falsehood—these sinners indeed go to a state of woe. 92.
Those who are not satisfied with righteous conduct but pursue unrighteousness, who do not perceive the welfare of others, and who are devoid of devotion, indeed go to a downward state. (93)
Those householders who behave like paramours or like courtesans, and those who regard the interests of others as their own, all indeed go downward.
Those who behave like a predator, a thief, a rogue, or a gambler, and likewise like Time or Death, indeed go downwards. (95)
Where there is mental distress for two people in a household over matters concerning the Dharma, that is hell manifest before one's eyes; it will be the same in the next world as well. (96)
Lack of affection, enmity, contempt, humiliation,
defeat, and severe censure— these are indeed manifest hells.
Severe illness, poverty, confinement in prison, and the lack of food, ornaments, and other necessities—these are indeed manifest hells. (98)
Childlessness, as well as having many enemies,
and a life of excessive toil— these are indeed manifest hells.
For him whose wife is the female demon of anxiety, equal to a male demon,
and who is possessed by the demon called poverty, his very home is the Raurava hell.
Therefore, having reflected, a wise man should practice his duties together with his partner;
abandoning all faults and being skillful, he shall become happy. 10.1

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Shared Dharma and the Demonstration that One Who Does Not Share Dharma Goes to Hell," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: "O Lord Hari, please describe to me here those hells which truly exist, causing anxiety and grief."
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to those things which indeed cause anxiety and grief,
as well as those which produce loss of luster, emaciation, and other diseases of wasting.
Indeed, all those hells that exist as mere suffering in their direct form become manifest for one who has been honored, even when there was no expectation [of such honor]. (3)
Without friends, without a wife, and without one's family—
such a state of being in a foreign land is indeed the realm of hell.
Furthermore, the failure to satisfy one's family members even when they have been properly cared for,
as well as reproach and humiliation— this is what constitutes hell in this world.
Enduring the insults inflicted by people superior in wealth, power, and so forth, as well as by one's own kinsmen—that is hell; such is the object of experience here.
When one's own virtues are superior, there arises great respect for those possessing other virtues;
yet, even in their very presence, hell becomes one's domain.
That hunger which arises during one's livelihood out of shame or fear regarding alms-begging constantly burns the impassioned mind; that is the domain of the "without-reproach" (nirapacāra).
Even in a dispute where one holds the superior position, one may be defeated by an inferior;
this defeat is constant, and hell is the destination for such a person in this world.
He whose friends are always afflicted people will experience suffering and fear; hell is his domain. (3.89.10)
A person who is honored for his wisdom yet treated with contempt by fools, and the humiliation suffered at the hands of the wicked—this is what constitutes "hell" in this world. (11)
The host of enemies has a friendly face and is intent on deceiving from all sides;
indeed, by that very deception, hell becomes one's sphere of experience here.
Even one who is skilled in secrets and understands the course of all matters is not honored by those who know the truth; for him, hell is his destination in this world.
When many wicked people are present at one's side, even one's own virtues appear as vices due to those wicked ones; moreover, hell becomes the sphere of experience in this case.
Even those devoid of wealth, intellect, and learning, upon seeing great men and being consumed by the fire of hope for greatness, find that hell itself becomes their domain in this world.
Relatives do not rejoice in one who has achieved his purpose, accomplished his success, and gained renown for his scholarship; for him, hell is the destination here.
Her neighbor was another man—strong, wealthy, and young—who behaved toward her own wife in a way she did not desire; moreover, hell was a constant presence there.
Indeed, for that statement which possesses no value even though it is factual, hell becomes one's destination even among those who know the truth. (18)
Constant residence among fools, dwelling among revilers,
and even living among people possessed of envy and malice— these, indeed, are hells in this very world.
Moreover, for that master who, having failed to engage someone in his work, constantly solicits wealth and other things from him later, there is indeed hell in this very world.
It is impossible to reveal one's inner intention due to dullness, fear, and laxity; moreover, hell is the destination in such cases. (21)
If one desires to conquer the possessor of qualities through envy even though he is devoid of qualities,
and cannot endure seeing those qualities, hell is his destination.
The ignorant man, timid and seeking little, who yet desires great fame, burns constantly with anxiety; hell is his inevitable destination.
For that suffering person who does not obtain what has been long desired,
and for whom what was obtained has been taken away by others, hell is the destination.
Cursed by his mother, by women, and indeed by virtuous brahmins, he who has fallen into this wretched state through his own fault becomes a denizen of hell in this very world. (25)
He who, upon seeing virtuous people who have attained liberation, utters insults and commits evil against them, is considered to have hell as his own abode in this world. (26)
He who, even upon seeing the suffering of others, is unable to remove it, will surely grieve and hell shall certainly be his domain. (27)
Sons who do not follow his commands, a woman who disregards his words,
and disciples of contrary conduct— for him, there is indeed hell even here in this world.
Having consumed what was given by the wicked, he lives even without his own home;
he who wanders through the forest is within the range of hell.
He whose evil increases and whose merit perishes, who is considered a vessel of reproach—for him, hell is the destined realm. (3.89.30)
He who has become a prey for his enemies and is separated from his friends, whose life is precarious and uncertain—he has entered the domain of hell. (3.1)
For one who is intent on ill-will toward enemies, who desires what is unattainable, and who covets the property of others, hell is his destined realm. (32)
For those possessing kingdoms and wealth, childlessness and illness, infamy and mental derangement—these are the hells experienced here in this very world. (33)
In this world, the desire for sensual enjoyment by a virtuous man or a virtuous woman is hell;
likewise, the reviling of teachers and elders is hell in this world. (34)
A weak digestive fire, chronic diseases, and hells in this world;
being deprived of women in youth, and likewise being bereft of a beloved—[these are the fruits]. (35)
Widowhood, separation from one's husband, and the experience of hells in this world;
even when sons exist, servitude and the maintenance of oneself under the control of others. (36)
Dependence on others in old age—these are hells in this world; likewise, a long life for one without sensory faculties, and poverty for one who possesses strength. (37)
In poverty, there is a multitude of offspring; indeed, these are the hells manifest in this world:
dwelling without a home and residing in the houses of others. (38)
Living off the fortune of others and always adopting the lifestyle of a beggar—
these are the hells manifest in this world for the householder, O Rame.
A wife’s lack of affection for her husband, sons wandering onto wrong paths, and even the pregnancy of daughters—these are the hells manifest here in this world. (3.89.40)
The imposition of shackles for the fault of the chief minister, the queen, the prince, or likewise the preceptor of the realm; 41.
Dwelling in prison for a king, for a brahmin, and for a woman; and for a learned man, the company of gods—these are the hells manifest here in this world. (42)
Obtaining food that is incomplete, as well as the acquisition of wealth that is incomplete;
food that is tasteless, dry, or leftover—this indeed is hell in this world. (43)

But when an elder exists, the destruction of one's offspring and even hell await [the offender] here; moreover, the entry of the deceased into the realm of ghosts and the like are the manifest torments of Yama. (44)
The suffering of royal punishment and the like is the manifest torment of Yama;
likewise, calamities and other miseries are the manifest torments of Yama. (45)
Rivalry with co-wives, constant beating, and dependence on others—this entire animal-like existence is the manifest torment of Yama. (46)
Being overtaken by famine, being struck down by fire, poison, nooses, and the like, and falling into water, pits, or precipices—these are the manifest torments of Yama. (47)
Blows from spears, weapons, and missiles; confinement in caves and similar places;
the pain of the womb and the agony of childbirth—these are the manifest torments of Yama. (48)

Furthermore, the unbearable indulgence in sensual pleasures and the consumption of unwholesome food result in the afflictions of the fever of the three humors and other such sufferings; these are the manifest torments of Yama. (49)
Digestive fires, bodily fluids, and excrement constantly fill this body; the continuous presence of phlegm, mucus, and other secretions is hell itself manifest right here. (3.89.50)
There is constant unrest in the mind, as well as exile from one's country;
for the one without a companion, there is untimely death, and hell is manifest right here in this world. (51)
To have only daughters, to be devoid of sons, to be a eunuch, or to be impotent—these are the hells manifest right here in this world. (52)
The state of being an outcaste, the carrying of filth, the presence of moisture and the like, and dwelling in a place of foul odor—this is hell manifest here in this very world. (53)
Agitation is always present in the mind, like a forest fire of the flames of craving;
for one who possesses neither peace nor happiness, hell is indeed manifest right here. (54)
Childhood, extreme old age, and likewise addiction to sexual intercourse—these cannot be purified by earth and water; indeed, the hells are manifest here in this world.
Wine, meat, sexual pleasure, and desire are here the hells manifest before one's eyes;
for these are hells during times of calamity, yet they are nectar at all times during prosperity.
Affection is heaven, while hatred is hell in this world, O Lotus-born One;
knowledge is heaven, discernment is the celestial realm, and the cow is dharma, which is one's own kingdom.
Contentment is eternal heaven, while liberation is the destruction of latent impressions;
having understood all this, the wise man should renounce that which is to be renounced. (58)
A discerning person whose heart is set on the highest good should acquire what is to be grasped with contentment;
for the virtuous, heaven is Hari, heaven is devotion, and indeed, heaven is eternal. (59)
The state of Brahman is the supreme heaven; the attainment of Brahman is the highest heaven.
Fearlessness is the great heaven; I rejoice in it always, even while living.
Listen: there was a certain man who toiled as a servant and was devoted to his daily labors;
indeed, he became a farmer by means of receiving a regular wage.
Known by the name Viśrāmagupta, he was a nourisher of crops and other plants in the field; every morning he would go forth and perform labor in the field. (62)
Having obtained in the evening wealth and food—both ethical and earned from the farmer—he goes to his own home, which is devoid of gates and walls. (63)
It was adorned with beds of leaves and grass, as well as beds made of earth;
it was beautified by two or three earthen pots and graced by a movable hearth.
Having placed [the grain] on a tripod of three unrefined stones and heating a frying pan with fire, he cooked the flatbread and ate it with salt water. || 65 ||
Having eaten it together with *marīcaka*, or with radish, or with a tuber, or having drunk the water brought from there, [one attains the desired result] at night. (66)
Having washed his earthen vessel while chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa,
he sleeps upon the ground, covered with a single worn-out rag.
Fearless and free from anxiety, he is well-nourished, healthy, and possessed of great strength;
neither cold afflicts him, nor even the heat of poison-tainted sunlight.
The one who lives in celibacy always sleeps free from all anxiety;
because he possesses nothing, he has no fear of theft.
For a servant who is humble, there is no fear of enemies;
indeed, being peaceful, he sleeps soundly even until the break of dawn, though he may have no desire for sleep himself.
That [state] indeed becomes profound, free from the thoughts of dreams;
then, at dawn, one suddenly awakens to the sounds of people.
Having quickly made a *roṭaka* (flat cake), he takes it with him and departs;
exhausted by the journey, he eats it at that place at the appropriate time. (72)
While he was living thus in happiness, a most excellent merchant named Somacandra lived in close proximity to him. (73)
With a mind devoted to helping others, he indeed considered him to be suffering;
overcome by compassion, he summoned a servant of a farmer and gave him wealth.
He also accepted the gift of two hundred silver coins as assistance;
then, anxiety arose regarding their protection within his own home. (75)
He concealed it in a corner so that no one else would know;
having dug in the dust at the spot where he had spat, he cast it into a pit. (76)
Having deposited it there, he then constantly goes for the sake of his business;
even when he has gone to the field, he remembers the wealth well-guarded at home.
Having come from there at midday, he departs after seeing [the ground];
having arrived in the evening and inspected the earth, he eats and sleeps as usual. (78)
At night he indeed sleeps, yet he wakes quickly at a sound;
reflecting on the need to protect what might be stolen by thieves, he remains vigilant.
Thus, her pleasant sleep gradually diminished day by day; moreover, indigestion arose and her strength also began to fail. (3.89.80)
Even the mind, though attached to material wealth, has become entirely unstable;
likewise, its connection to action, whether in worldly affairs or in the field of ritual work, has gradually faded away.
Day by day, the work of one who is distracted becomes deficient;
then indeed he was questioned by his high-souled master, the farmer. (82)
How is it that you behave thus—deluded, distraught, and possessed by spirits?
You do not perform even the work of farming at all, nor in any way whatsoever. (83)
"I shall give you wages and daily food, less than what is customary.
Thus addressed, that servant reflected for a moment upon the farmer.
He stated the reason for this: "There are two hundred silver coins; they were indeed offered by a merchant and remain right here in my leaf-hut. (85)
And because of that thought, though it was not intended, I have indeed become bewildered;
for wealth is truly hell itself, since it has caused the destruction of my sleep. (86)
Since the destruction of nourishment, the destruction of peace, and the destruction of ritual action have occurred, wealth itself exists as manifest danger; death resides within wealth.
Time shines within wealth, and decay shines within wealth;
wealth is a visible hell that increases the threads of craving. (88)
For grasping is hell; renunciation is considered the supreme heaven.
Tranquility is the internal heaven; renunciation is the external nectar of immortality. (89)
"Having obtained wealth, I ruined or exiled myself from heaven;
therefore, by renouncing it, I shall become happy once again as before. (3.89.90)
Having spoken thus, he took the farmer along and led him to that corner,
where he showed him the hell of sin before his very eyes.
Having extracted from the pit all that was painful, causing suffering, destroying peace, and consisting of two hundred [pieces], he gave it back to the merchant once again.
O merchant, material wealth that is devoid of direct perception does not please me at all; rather, you should grasp that which is truly hell in the form of wealth—the destruction of happiness. (93)
Having spoken thus and having bestowed [the teaching], he slept peacefully as he had come;
indeed, free from craving and without possessions, he became happy once again. (94)
He became enriched with all his duties fully accomplished, just as he was before;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, in this world, hells are indeed the givers of suffering. (95)
For all those possessions result in the hells of suffering here;
whereas for the virtuous person, heaven always remains, and they dwell there together in happiness. (96)
Likewise, Nārāyaṇa and I dwell in the minds of the virtuous;
they are gladdened by my bliss and delighted by their own innate bliss. (97)
They deliver other people and send them to the imperishable state;
they burn away sins and strike down the hells. 98.
They teach the principles and grant discernment;
having caused me to practice devotion and established divine contemplations, [they lead me]. 99.
Having caused images in the form of Nārāyaṇa to be made, they lead those who are well-devoted to the imperishable state; indeed, they are always bestowers of heaven.
Indeed, the virtuous who are adorned with goodness should be constantly served;
by reading about them, hearing of them, and even remembering them, one becomes a partaker of liberation. 101.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Manifest Hells, the Demonstration that Wealth and Other Such Things are Manifest Hells by Way of the Example of the Farmer and the Servant, and the Definition of Manifest Heaven," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to those for whom heaven is indeed eternal:
they are constantly endowed with the virtue of giving, devoted to the gods, and possessed of auspicious intentions. || 1 ||

Those who are devoted to austerity and truth, who are pure, who are radiant through service to their gurus, and who are beautifully adorned by learning and virtuous conduct, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who have no desire for the sin of accepting gifts go to the stainless heaven—
whether out of self-interest, for the sake of fame, out of fear, due to illness, or from the hardship of the blemish of poverty.
Through knowledge, through greed, through their refuge, through affection, through the formation of bonds, and through living together, those who possess devotion go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are rich in forgiveness, fortitude, and endurance; who are always diligent in performing virtuous deeds;
and who are perfected in conduct such as worship—go to the stainless heaven.
Those who abstain from intoxicants, meat, sexual intercourse, and the like, who avoid theft,
and who partake of food as a grace from the gods, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who construct Dharma-halls, those who perform the upliftment of the land and similar deeds, and those who protect trees, gardens, and hermitages, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who protect the people of villages, towns, and cities,
and who provide assistance in times of calamity— all such persons go to the stainless heaven.
Those who bestow ornaments and garments, as well as those who provide food and drink,
and all those who serve their families, go to the healthy heaven.
Those who refrain from violence, malice, and the like; who always endure calamities;
and who grant refuge to all—go to the heaven that is free from suffering.
Those who provide dwellings, as well as those who offer beds and couches for reclining, and those who give vehicles and mounts, go to the stainless heaven. (11)
Those who give villages, fields, and so forth, as well as houses, cows, and bulls,
and those who bestow worthy recipients and necessary implements, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who serve their elders, their preceptor, the gods, their beloved, their mother, their father, and Hari, as well as virtuous women, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are affectionate, who act for the benefit of their family members as is appropriate, who accomplish the welfare of others, and who possess true wisdom, go to the stainless heaven. (1.4)
Those who are rich in dharma, strong in self-control, having conquered thirst and subdued their desires, being steadfast and devoted to spiritual practice, go to the stainless heaven. (15)
Those who are compassionate toward offenders, affectionate, endowed with gentleness,
free from anger and punishment, and learned in the scriptures, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are hospitable, providers of refuge, givers of thousands, highly virtuous, and performers of manifold acts of protection, go to the stainless heaven. (17)
Givers of gold, silver, and gems, as well as givers of garments and pearls,
go to the stainless heaven.
Likewise, those who bestow wealth and goods during great festivals,
as well as those who give dowries and other such gifts, go to the healthy, painless heaven.
Those who bestow articles for marriage as well as those required for initiation,
and those who give male and female slaves, go to the healthy heaven.
Those who establish water-stations, pleasure groves, assembly halls, wells, and lakes,
and those who construct long ponds and sacrificial grounds, go to the healthy heaven.
Likewise, those who provide fields, dwellings, palaces, mountain caves, and rivers [attain the same].
The givers of reservoirs of water go to the heaven that is free from affliction. || 22 ||
Likewise, those who give grains, split pulses, and cereals,
as well as those who provide juices, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who give sweet foods, fruits, bulbous roots, leafy vegetables,
and likewise potherbs, go to the healthy heaven.
Those who remove sufferings and destroy the heat of afflictions,
O Lakṣmī, and who bring about the destruction of calamities, go to the stainless heaven—
even if they are born into any family whatsoever, provided they are by nature affectionate. || 25 ||
They possess an extensive lineage and are endowed with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. || 26 ||
Those who are compassionate, of virtuous character, established in shame and moral restraint, whose hearts are free from deceit, and who are peaceful, go to the stainless heaven. (27)
Those people who do not cause harm to others, who are untouched by blame or hatred, and who are rich in contentment and service to their gurus, go to the stainless heaven. (28)
Those who accept blessings, those who perform meritorious deeds, and those who provide assistance in meritorious works go to the stainless heaven. (29)
Those who are free from greed regarding their status, devoid of attachment to their own dignity, and humble in disposition like servants, go to the stainless heaven. (3.90.30)
Indifferent toward wealth and filled with great contentment,
those who possess nothing as their own go to the stainless heaven.
Those who always refrain from grasping [possessions], whose faces do not hang down with longing,
and who are free from plucking [plants] and eating forbidden food, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are free from all forms of violence and likewise avoid self-destruction,
and who are free from the killing of Brahmins and other such acts, go to the stainless heaven.
Householders who always abide by the Dharma, who perform righteous deeds, who are devoted to faith and charity, and who are pure, go to the stainless heaven. (34)

Those who observe the vow of moral conduct, those who constantly observe the vow of forest-dwelling, and those whose character is defined by the vow of renunciation, go to the stainless heaven. ||35||
Those who do not harm what has been done, those who do not betray trust, and those who do not destroy what is desired—these meritorious ones go to the stainless heaven. (36)
Those who perform acts that benefit the world, those who provide assistance toward liberation, and those who bring about beneficial aid, go to the stainless heaven. (37)
Those who provide assistance through sacred learning, those who provide assistance during times of calamity,
and those who provide assistance through diligent effort, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who possess new schemes that remove obstacles for the country and bring about the happiness of the subjects go to the stainless heaven. (39)
Those who are always free from malice, who observe the vow of non-violence, who take refuge in the gods, and who are self-contented, go to the stainless heaven. ||3.90.40||
Those people here who, though called "killers," do not actually commit killing, avoid association with such as those and go to the healthy, painless heaven. ||41||
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Hari, I wish to know those men who, though not having committed a killing themselves, are nonetheless killers; show them to me here."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe those men as well;
for even without harming others, people may become perpetrators of violence toward them. (43)
He who causes suffering like a killer is proclaimed a killer;
furthermore, he who yields fruit like a killer is also declared a killer. ||44||

He who, having personally summoned a mendicant at the proper time for the sake of alms—excluding those on their designated day—says "there is nothing," should know him to be a killer of a mendicant. (45)
But that king who, having determined someone to be deserving of punishment, subsequently seizes his livelihood from him, is a destroyer of life and a plunderer of one's means of subsistence. (46)
He who creates an obstacle for thirsty cows or for others, as well as one who steals water, a killer of cows, or even a killer of living beings, shall become such [a being] here in this world. (47)
And he who, being ignorant, destroys the scripture, the rules, the teaching, and the instruction, corrupts them; such a person is a destroyer of logic and a destroyer of the author of the scripture.
He who does not give his own daughter, though she is young, to a suitable bridegroom at the proper time, is a destroyer of his lineage and a transgressor of dharma in this world. 49.

And he who is most unrighteous, who causes piercing pain to virtuous persons, the twice-born, those worthy of worship, and other living beings, and who brings them grief— he shall be considered a destroyer of the venerable.
He becomes the plunderer of all possessions for the lame, the blind, the foolish, women, and those who are protectorless; likewise, he is the destroyer of life and the destroyer of everything. (51)
One who sets fire to villages, forests, groves, hermitages, sacred fields, houses, and so forth, is indeed a destroyer of all; he is considered a village-destroyer and a slayer of a Brahmin.

as he fell to the earth to die, Indra approached him.
And he, devoted to compassion through the granting of boons, took hold of him as he fell.
He said, "Choose a boon here; I shall grant it to you, O emaciated one."
With emaciated limbs, he chose a boon: "Grant me the status of a Brahmin forever."
