Indra said: "That is certainly not difficult for you to obtain; it is easily found somewhere."
It is not attained even through austerities lasting ten million years;
rather, by [giving] to Brahmins, the ancestors, the deities, and others are completely satisfied. (115)
There dwells a Brahmin who is a god on earth; such Brahminhood is difficult for you to attain.
Choose another boon, whether it be the state of being worshipful or preeminence.
The emaciated one said, "O Indra, you do not appear to be capable at all."
"Why do you pierce me, already so full of suffering? Why do you kill one who is already dead? (117)
The status of the twice-born is attained by the three castes through their qualities and actions;
furthermore, the status of the twice-born and the status of a Brahmin are identical in terms of those qualities and actions. (118)
A twice-born man is distinguished by the sacred thread and by higher knowledge;
it is proclaimed that his status as a Brahmin is established therein through union with Brahman. 119.
Through steadfastness in Brahman comes the state of being most devoted to Brahman, and through that, goodness in liberation;
thus, by the union of these qualities, everything is accomplished. (3.91.120)
Through the process of heating by fire, the earth becomes possessed of the most excellent and supreme jewels.
And through the ripening of merit, their bodies take on the form of Brahmins and holy men. ||121||
In this world, one is a beast by virtue of one's qualities, a yakṣa by qualities, and even a rākṣasa by qualities;
a brahmin becomes a kṣatriya or other caste by qualities, and a virtuous person becomes a sovereign of the liberated by qualities.
A man is born as Nārāyaṇa through the qualities of his actions;
you are to be pitied, for you do not recognize that Brahminhood is the supreme wealth. 123.
"Even having obtained it, you do not recognize it; you are but a human kṣatriya.
You are not worthy to grant a boon; go, Śakra, to your own abode! (124)
Having established myself in the virtues of a Brahmin, how am I not worthy of Brahminhood?
Through my asceticism, the defects of my mother and the defects of my father have been destroyed. (125)
"I am a Brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt; go, Śakra, to your own abode.
Thus addressed, Mahendra indeed granted an auspicious boon to Lakṣmī.
O you of emaciated limbs, you are purified by austerities and cleansed as well;
you are like the fire Kṛśānu—become the very essence of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.
May you be worthy of worship by all, always honored by the Brahmins, the best among the gods, the most excellent of the twice-born, and most devoted to Brahman even throughout other kalpas. 128.

By your virtues, the status of a Brahmin was earned here; furthermore, by those same virtues, you have always attained the state of being most devoted to Brahman, and indeed the nature of fire itself.
Having thus granted the boon, Śakra departed for heaven;
and Kṛśāṅga became Kṛśānu at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
The Kṛśānu-tīrtha is situated here; I delight in it, for it bestows the state of being most devoted to Brahman.
Indeed, in this place, one attains goodness, purity, and stainlessness.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Purification of Butchers through Association with Holy Places; Mobile Holy Places such as Virtuous People; and How, in Ancient Times at Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, the Son of a Brāhmaṇa Named Kṛśāṅga—though born of a Śūdra and being a Cāṇḍāla—Attained the State of a Fire-like Brāhmaṇa Supreme in Vedic Knowledge through Austerities and a Boon from Indra," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; even by my word, the status of a Brāhmaṇa shall belong to you, though you were previously born of another caste, and so it shall be in the world.
Divodāsa, the king of Vārāṇasī, was a great devotee;
once defeated in battle by the Haihayas, he went to Prayāgaka.
He bowed down to the sage Bharadvāja, the son of Bṛhaspati;
then the sage, out of compassion, had him disclose his sorrow.
And through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, a son was born to Divodāsa from his wife;
that Pratardana, having gone to the city of Vārāṇasī as a youth, [ruled there].
He fought together with the Haihayas, but the Haihayas were defeated;
intent on flight, they went for refuge to Bhṛgu’s hermitage. || 5 ||
Pratardana followed behind him and, having bowed to Bhṛgu, said:
"Give me back my enemy kings, Vītahavya and the other Haihayas."
"By slaying them, I shall be free of my debt to my father; please show me mercy.
Moved by compassion, Bhṛgu said, "Indeed, there are no Kṣatriyas here at all."
Pratardana replied: "O Bhṛgu, I have indeed accomplished my purpose;
by my valor, even kings have been made to abandon their own caste."
Having bowed to Bhṛgu, Pratardana [sought] the brahmin King Vītahavya for the sake of protecting his life, according to the word of Bhṛgu.
Then, at the mere word of Bhṛgu, Vītahavya the Haihaya abandoned [the kingdom] and went to his own capital, Vārāṇasī.
Out of fear, he completely renounced his status as a kṣatriya and attained the state of a brahmin seer.
His son was Gṛtsamada, a brahmin seer who became learned in the Vedas.
His son was Dvija; his son was Sutejas; his son was Vihavis; his son was Vitatya; his son was Satya; and his son was Śravas, who was a twice-born.
His son was Ṛṣi; his son was Prakāśa; his son was Vācika; his son was the brahmin Pramiti; and his son was the eminent brahmin Ruru.
His son was Śunaka, and his son was Śaunaka, the best of Brahmins; thus, by the word of that virtuous great ṛṣi, he likewise attained the status of a Brahmin.
Devotion to Brahman indeed arises through initiation as well;
by means of initiation, those born of the three castes become the most excellent Brāhmaṇas. (15)
All virtuous Vaiṣṇavas and Brāhmaṇas born of the lineage of Acyuta— thus, through such qualities, speech, and initiation, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is attained.
Even if he has remained in the house of a Brāhmaṇa since childhood and been refined there, he is born as a Brāhmaṇa; he is held in the lap by the twice-born.
A child who is nourished by breast milk and with food, water, and so forth, attains the status of that [nurturer]; thus, in the case of a Brahmin, he becomes a Brahmin.
O twice-born ones, through austerity, miraculous powers, and blessings, even Brāhmaṇas become resplendent with virtuous deeds and other such qualities.
Listen, Lakṣmī, and hear another thing as well; for the Capable One indeed explains it:
even though Nandin was a human being, he was made by Śaṅkara into his own attendant (gaṇa).
Rama made the daughter of the ocean his own as Narayani;
King Trishanku was made into a deity by Vishvamitra.
In Goloka, Kṛṣṇa made Harā and others into female gopīs;
and month after month, Sudyumna became a man and likewise a woman.
Śambhu is Ardhanārīśvara, and Viṣṇu likewise [became] Mohinī;
through the seed of man, both daughter and son are born in every creation.
The sons of gods, the young brahmins, and all the progeny of Kāśyapa—thus, even regarding the seed, there arises a turning back that brings about the cessation of birth. (24)
Indeed, all those of different species are born from sweat-born beings;
and from the dull-witted, the dull-witted of different species are also born. (25)
Therefore, birth is not fixed; it depends upon qualities and actions.
Excellence is the highest of all states, and it is to be attained through auspicious deeds. (26)
Listen, Lakṣmī: Nahuṣa became a serpent in that very body due to the curse of Agastya, who was being carried by that king.
Due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha, he suddenly became a Rākṣasa with the lower half of his body as a horse;
for twelve years, he roamed within the depths of the forest.
And Ahalyā, due to her husband’s curse, became stone once again;
and that Vṛndā became Tulasī, taking the form of a tree in an instant. (29)
Hari took the form of a Śālagrāma stone; Kālī likewise became Gaurī; Śanaiścara attained the state of a serpent, and Indra became a cat.
Hari, assuming forms such as the fish and others, and Vahni, bearing the form of gold;
likewise King Bhaṅgāsvana, having bathed in a lake in the forest. ||31||
Even Śataputrajana truly attained womanhood;
again, she became the wife of a seer in the forest, giving birth to a hundred sons.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O beloved Hari, how did King Bhaṅgāsvana become a man and likewise a woman? I desire to hear this; tell me that story."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
In ancient times, there was a virtuous and pure royal sage named Bhaṅgāsvana;
being childless, he performed the auspicious Putreṣṭi sacrifice.
Because his status as the preeminent lord was no longer existent, Indra blazed with rage and sought to create an obstacle; yet, he could find no opening whatsoever. (35)
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the king went to the forest for the sake of hunting;
Indra, seizing a supreme opportunity, arrived and entered the monarch's body.
He led that king, Aśvattha, who was wandering in delusion, far away into the forest;
and there, the thirsty king beheld an excellent lake.
He caused the horse to drink water and tied it to a tree;
having drunk the water himself, he afterwards performed his bath in the lake.
Merely by plunging into it, he quickly attained womanhood;
and seeing himself transformed into a woman, he became filled with shame.
He reflected: "What kind of face shall I show in my city?
I have a hundred sons; what indeed shall I say to them? (3.92.40)
Thus that distressed king, having mounted his horse with great difficulty and casting aside shame, departed for the city on that very horse.
Then his sons, wives, servants, citizens, and countryfolk, seeing this, were filled with wonder and amazement, exclaiming, "What indeed is this? ||42||
He said: "I had gone to a lake within the forest for the sake of hunting;
while I was bathing there, I indeed attained womanhood. (43)
"I shall entrust my kingdom to my sons and then depart for the forest";
having spoken thus and bestowed the kingdom, he went to the forest.
That wife of the sage Svarvaha indeed became female in form;
from her, the queen, a hundred sons were then born to Svarvaha.
Taking them with her, she went toward her own kingdom and her former sons;
she said, "In your case you are sons by virtue of being males, but these others are sons by virtue of being females."
"O dear sons, let the kingdom be enjoyed together in a spirit of brotherhood. Having heeded the words of their father and mother, they enjoyed the kingdom together. (47)
Then Indra, having arrived there, created dissension among the ancestors;
fathers and sons were fit for the kingdom, but mothers and sons never were.
"O Brahmins, you have wives and sons; indeed, you do not deserve the position of a king.
Therefore, he spoke to those born later: 'And you, sirs, are truly the best. (49)
The Kṣatriyas who were your ancestors are indeed considered your servants;
let them not rule your kingdom, for the Brahmins are truly fit for sovereignty.
Having thus caused mutual enmity, they were destroyed by war;
hearing this, their mother, a female ascetic, wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Indra, having approached her, said, "In what sorrow do you weep?
She, assuming the form of a brahmin, replied to him, "I have two hundred sons. (52)
"O best of Brahmins, because they were lost in battle, I grieve for them and weep for them.
Indra said: 'In former times, O King, a well-performed sacrifice was offered by you. (53)
"O Queen, disregarding me, you have brought about my suffering;
the enmity has been avenged by me, so do not weep. (54)
Upon hearing this, the queen fell at his feet and said, "Forgive me.
Indra granted her a boon, asking, "Which of your sons shall live? (55)
She said, "May my sons born of a woman live!
Indra said, "Tell me here, why did those born previously not live? (56)
He said: "A woman's affection for her offspring is indeed greater than a man's;
therefore, may all my sons born later live. (57)
Indra said: "Indeed, let all these two hundred sons of yours live;
out of compassion I shall restore them to life, and let them rule the kingdom together. (58)
Thus addressed by the speaker of truth, all those good sons were restored to life;
then Indra spoke again to the woman for the purpose of granting a boon. (59)
"Choose a boon—whether manhood or womanhood, whichever you desire.
The woman said, "May I always possess womanhood; let there never be manhood for me. (3.92.60)
Indra asked, "How can there be such an attachment to specific qualities in the state of womanhood?
She replied, "A woman always possesses a greater affection when united with a man. (51)
"I shall be satisfied with the tenfold pleasures of desire, appearing in the form of a woman.
Having granted this boon, Indra departed for heaven, and that virtuous lady remained there.
Assuming the form of a woman, Svarvaha enjoyed the lovely Bhaṅgāsvana;
she questioned him regarding the nature of women, and her lover spoke to her.
For women are the root of all faults, fickle-minded, and destructive;
thus spoke Pañcacūḍā, the best of Apsarases, to Nārada when he questioned her. (64)
"Nārada, the nature of women is fickle and dependent upon men; a weak woman desires a lover who is eager for dalliance. (65)
Women who are of noble birth, beautiful, and have protectors do not abide by the bounds of propriety; this is the inherent fault in womankind. (66)
Women always desire womanhood, which makes them dependent on men;
for the kingdom of the household is indeed dependent on women, and the man himself is likewise dependent on the woman.
Women always enjoy objects of pleasure without effort;
they are honored, they deserve respect, and they harbor delusion and pride. (68)
Free from anxiety regarding livelihood, effort, and so forth, they always desire the state of being enjoyed;
they desire womanhood and good fortune—this is the constant firm resolve of a woman. (69)

Having obtained those who are favorable, possessed of supernatural powers, handsome, and under their own control, they enjoy them after setting aside their own kin, having approached others immediately thereafter. (3.92.70)
This indeed is the great fault of women, for it lies beyond the scope of understanding:
that he who desires a woman gives her what she wishes again and again. (7.1)
She performs service for him with desire, for those shameless ones indeed enjoy him;
yet he who travels the wrong path does not truly unite with her at all. 72.
There is no fear for the family, nor is there any restraint for others; yet, if they have fear of royal punishment, then those women do not engage in sexual intercourse. (73)
There is no man who is unattainable for them, nor do they respect age; they do not consider firmness in beauty or other qualities, but enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Though they are protected by all manner of gifts and by the fulfillment of every desire, they nevertheless become entangled with the humpbacked, the blind, the dull-witted, and the dwarfs. (75)
The fault of desire is great for them; women interact with one another, being fickle by nature, difficult to satisfy, and hard for their own husbands to restrain. (76)
For women are indeed unrestrained; they do not take account of a husband who provides them with sensual pleasures, acts for their mental delight, and protects them. //77//
For women, the primary human goal that accomplishes their desired ends is the favor of sexual pleasure; dharma, artha, and mokṣa are considered secondary to that during their youth. (78)
Impetuosity, deceit, folly, greed, secrecy, obstinacy, falsehood, impurity, and cruelty—these are the faults found in women. (79)
Devotion to her, self-surrender, service, endurance, being her life-giver, gentleness, affection, and submissiveness—these indeed are the virtues found in a woman. (3.92.80)
To share in sorrow when there is sorrow, to share in joy when there is joy, unity of heart, oneness in wealth, self-surrender, and service—these are generally the virtues found in women. 8.1
Adherence to dharma, observance of vows, faith, worship of Hari, hospitality, and reputation among one's kin—these indeed are the most excellent qualities in a woman. (82)
Generosity, preeminence within the family, not hearing the censure of one's beloved, forbearance, and the capacity for protection—these qualities indeed exist in a woman. (83)
Indeed, the qualities of managing household affairs, the intellect for acquiring wealth, and even a fear of expenditure exist in a woman. (84)
The pleasure of touch, the taste of flavor, the massaging of limbs, and the pacification of an agitated mind—these indeed are the qualities found in a woman. (85)
The expansion of one's lineage, protection of children, the settling of a household, and a disposition toward altruism—these indeed are the virtues found in a woman. (86)
They laugh at him when he laughs, and they weep when he weeps;
and by means of their illusory power, they gratify him with pleasant words when he is distressed. (87)
The fickleness of female monkeys, the secrecy of female cats, the quarreling of female ruddy geese, and the conduct of female mice—[these are the traits of women]. (88)
The gathering of ants, the searching of vultures, and the manifestation of the rising sun—these are indeed the surges of bliss. (89)
The grief of one whose only son has died is like the stupidity of a camel;
likewise, the gentleness of a thief is like the sharpness of a razor.
These qualities indeed exist especially among women;
however, in a former creation, women here were virtuous and truthful.
The subjects themselves were equal to the gods and indeed went to heaven;
therefore, for the sake of deluding human beings, [the Lord created] unchaste women who delude the entire world.
Brahmā created those devoid of ritual action, devoted to desire and anger, [and addicted] to beds, seats, ornaments, food, drink, and ignoble conduct. 93.
The Lord of Creatures bestowed upon women a harsh disposition and a fierce passion; by those very traits, women can never be restrained in any way. ||94||
Nevertheless, O Lakṣmī, women are born pure and sanctifiers of the world through asceticism, vows, fasts, and service to the virtuous. 96.
Devoted to devotion to Kṛṣṇa, these virtuous women become [liberated] through yoga;
having burned away their defects like a forest with fire, they are indeed born as liberated souls.
Those twice-born women who are born in any family whatsoever but have taken refuge in a Brahmin,
and who are endowed with the initiation of a virtuous woman (sādhvī), are indeed virtuous and true twice-born ones.
Those Brahmins who are endowed with the initiation of Yoga are indeed Yoginīs and deities.
But those women of Brahmā, who were liberated and endowed with Sāṃkhya and Yoga, [were different]. ||98||
Having attained the status of wives of Hari, those Brahmanīs are dear to Hari;
having attained renunciation, they are considered always to be dear to Brahman. 99.
The cowherd girl, having approached Brahmā, became Gāyatrī;
she is the Brahmin woman worthy of worship and salutation, the consort of Brahmā, and the mother of the worlds.
Having obtained Vasiṣṭha as her husband, the auspicious daughter of a dog-cooker became a Brahmin woman;
known by the name Arundhatī, she was a venerable and devoted wife. || 101 ||
The maidens of many castes, having obtained Kṛṣṇa as their husband, became gopīs;
these women, dark-complexioned and possessing the form of Kṛṣṇa, are purified through yoga.
Having approached a god, Rākṣasīs invariably become goddesses;
indeed, Paulomī became a deity by approaching Mahendra.
The goddess Devayānī, having approached the human Kṣatriya and become the wife of Yayāti,
that daughter of Manu gave birth [to sons].
Some of the daughters of Dakṣa became divine goddesses in heaven;
others became wives of the gods, celestial beings, wives of Brahmins, and wives of sages.
The wives of Manu were Mānavyas, Kāśyapīs, and of many other lineages;
they were born from him, for there is no fixed caste-status for women anywhere.
What is the use of saying more in this matter? My wives are in the tens of millions—those born on all the earths, heavens, Satyaloka, Janaloka, Pātāla, and among embodied beings.
Through union with me, women born of all castes become of noble birth;
wearing the sacred thread, they are beloved by Brahman like goddesses Ramās. 108.
There are indeed Brāhmaṇa women here in this very field of syllables (akṣarakṣetra) along with me; they are worthy of all worship, divine, and bearers of my own form.
All these [women] are indeed supreme goddesses, possessing the highest human excellence and lordly power;
they are purifiers of all creations, as dear as Śrī, Bhū, and Gaṅgā.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, through my yoga, may you become Nārāyaṇī;
and by divine yoga, she shall indeed become Devī, and through the yoga of the virtuous, Sādhvī. || 111 ||

From separation she is Viprāṇī, and from union with Brahman she is Brāhmaṇī; from the yoga of Brahman she is Brahmayoginī, and from liberation through yoga she is Muktānī; she is Siddhi, the one who practices the yoga of the perfected ones.

She is a *gaṇikā* because of her connection with the *gaṇas*, a *yoginī* because of her connection with the *yogins*, an *īśvarāṇī* because of her connection with the *īśas*, and a *mānavī* because of her connection with Manu. (113)
And thus noble women are always born virtuous through the power of truth;
in all those places, I am the foremost, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person.

And by my yoga, the state of being Pauruṣottamī, which is higher than the highest, is to be attained; likewise, the state of being a virtuous wife is attained only by worshipping me and by service to the virtuous.
Since liberation alone is that which is eternal forever, one should abandon the non-eternal and take refuge in the eternal. 1.16
From reciting or hearing this, the state of being Brahmī arises here;
there shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and one attains the state of Nārāyaṇī.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Transformation of Various Castes and the Attainment of Brāhmaṇahood through the Yoga of Virtuous Vows, Conduct, Initiation, Boons, and Planetary Alignments—even for those of other castes," within the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, including examples such as the case of King Bhaṅgāsvana becoming a woman.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; in this world, that which is difficult to attain is easily obtained through vows, austerities, blessings, service, and self-surrender.
In the presence of the power of the yoga of Brahman, all other powers whatsoever sink away, just as everything sinks before the power of celibacy, O Lotus-born One.
I shall relate a story concerning a former birth that illustrates the protection of moral discipline:
how a disciple who was a yogin protected the moral discipline of his teacher’s wife.
In Surāṣṭra, there was a brahmin named Devaśarmā who was indeed a great sage;
his wife, named Ruci, was equal to Rādhikā in beauty.
Equal to Lakṣmī in her virtues, possessing divine youth, she was the most excellent of goddesses;
by her beauty, the gods, the Siddhas, and human beings were all rendered mad.
They were born in great numbers, and Mahendra fell into a state of delusion;
in a moment, he began to reflect upon how he might always overcome her.
Devasharman, knowing the nature of women, protected her in his own residence according to his ability; he never allowed her to remain in solitude anywhere.
Indra repeatedly approached the vicinity of the hermitage seeking her;
yet, for the sake of obtaining her alone, he did not succeed even at that moment.
Indeed, fearing the curse of the brahmins, he does not come within the range of vision;
remaining hidden, he departs in many different forms.
Through the power of his asceticism, Devaśarman knew that Indra was searching for him,
wandering about the edge of the forest as a lustful man seeking diversion.
Then once, O Lakṣmī, the sage, desiring to perform a vow,
summoned his own beloved disciple Vipula, a practitioner of Brahman-yoga.
He is capable of protection, established in dharma, and steadfast in his word; my livelihood consists in following my vow at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
"Endowed with vows, I shall go to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
having performed the Cāturmāsya vow, I will indeed return from there. (13)
"Mahendra desires to enjoy my beautiful wife Ruci;
protect her constantly so that there may be no violation of her virtue. (14)
May your devotion to your husband never perish;
remain vigilant, O Indrakā, for Indra comes here constantly, assuming many forms.
In one place he was the diadem-wearing wielder of the thunderbolt, and in another the archer bearing the staff;
in a mere moment he became a Cāṇḍāla, then a crested Brahmin with matted hair observing vows.
In some places he was clad in bark garments, and in others he was a guest who was either stout or lean;
sometimes he was an ascetic of fair complexion, and at other times a forest-dweller of dark hue.
Whether a child, an old man, or one who is insane; whether a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a servant; or even a parrot, a crow, a swan, a deer, or a tiger. (18)
Whether he becomes a king, a god, or a demon, or even a mouse—indeed, that yoga proceeds exactly according to how it is desired. 19.
Even a fly or a mosquito may become a flowering creeper;
such is Mahendra seen through the eye of yoga.
Therefore, you are the one fit for this; protect her with vigilance against him.
Be watchful toward Indra so that he may not taste Ruci.
And Vipula, considering the words of his guru, became lost in thought;
for Indra is a master of illusion, powerful, invincible, and capable of assuming many forms. (22)
"How should I protect her after establishing this great hermitage?
Having reflected thus in many ways, he considered the entry of his own body [into her] to be the best course. 23.
Since she cannot be protected by others through human effort,
I myself, remaining within her body, shall protect her by the power of yoga.
Having thus resolved, Vipula entered into meditative absorption;
concentrated, he dwelt within the body of his preceptor’s wife. (25)
He became unattached, like a drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf;
having fashioned his own subtle body all around the body of his guru. (26)
Having dissolved his pervasive body into the physical form through yoga, he indeed entered the entire body of the Guru by means of that very gross form. (27)
Having thus become vast and remained still, she did not even realize it;
he protected his mother for the entire duration of the four-month period.
Constantly exerting himself, he remained hidden like a shadow;
Indra, assuming a divine form, entered the hermitage of Yuvāśrama.
Becoming most alluring and adorned with every kind of ornament,
he [approached] Ruci, whose eyes were like lotus petals and whose splendor was equal to the luster of the moon.
Seeing a tender young woman before him, he fell into a state of infatuation;
he was deluded by the sight of her private parts through the edge of her exceedingly fine and delicate garment.
Astonished by his extraordinary beauty and wishing to ask "Who are you?",
she desired to rise up, but she was held fast by Vipula.
Restrained by meditative concentration, she was unable to rise at all;
Indra, laughing, spoke to that young woman who had surrendered her mind. (32)
"Mahendra, the lord of the deities, has come here for your sake;
grant him pleasure and come quickly with me upon my celestial chariot."
But she was unable to rise up or say anything;
Vipula, having understood everything regarding the conduct of the two there, [acted accordingly]. (35)
He bound all her senses with the bonds of yoga;
then, seeing her motionless and free from any change of expression, Indra was filled with shame.
Then Vipula indeed spoke again, "Come, come!
Abiding within the body, he replied, "O sir, what is the purpose of your coming? (37)
Then Purandara, having reflected,
became mindless toward the reply and gazed with divine vision upon the great sage Vipula residing within his own body.
Upon seeing that formidable ascetic, Purandara, fearing a curse, became trembling, paralyzed, and for a moment remained like one who is senseless. (39)
Then Vipula, quickly emerging from his body, addressed Indra:
"O evil-minded one! O wicked-souled one! O you of sinful intellect! O lowest of the gods!"
"Intending to cause this human Brahmin woman to fall from dharma, you have come here; you deserve punishment, yet I release you—go indeed! (41)
"Was it not forgotten by you that Gautama marked you with his sign?
I know you to be of wicked conduct; therefore, this [child] is protected from you. (42)
Go quickly so that my preceptor does not consume you with the fire of his wrath;
never again issue such an invitation to destruction.
Even for an immortal, death may indeed come suddenly through the power of asceticism;
neither a god nor a brahmin can stand before a virtuous man. 44.
I am a virtuous man, characterized by the nature of Brahman, a yogi taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
here I perform service to my guru and always protect my guru’s wife. (45)
"I shall indeed remain a celibate student until I am capable of subduing you.
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods, filled with terror, departed for heaven.
Thus that Vipula constantly protected his mother;
then one day, at twilight, the Rākṣasa Lomaśarṣaṇa [appeared].
Vipula arrived there intending to abduct that virtuous woman;
lifting her up quickly, he placed the heavy burden upon his shoulder and departed through the sky.
Suddenly beholding that vast [being], he leapt through the path of the sky and then seized the Rākṣasa Lomaśarṣaṇa by the throat.
Having fashioned a noose, she obstructed his vital breaths and protected Gaurī;
the terrifying Rākṣasa, becoming lifeless, fell upon the earth.
Then, lifting Gaurī up into the sky, he slowly descended to the ground.
Vipula prostrated himself and indeed protected his mother.
Then once, while wandering through the path of the sky, the great asura Kapardaka, situated upon the ocean, saw Ruci in his own hermitage.
While she was dwelling at the foot of a tree, watering it,
he suddenly descended from the sky and, overcome by delusion, approached her.
He forcibly seized Ruci and then ascended into the sky;
Vipula pursued him from behind with great speed along the path of the atmosphere.
Suddenly, he forcefully seized that wicked Kapardaka once again.
He struck him repeatedly on the head with blows of his fist. ||55||
He pierced the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in the forehead of this Kapardaka and entered his head through the sky; then the asura seized him by the throat. ||56||
Having quickly carried his own heavy corpse through the sky, he departed;
then Vipula returned to the leaf-hut and became peaceful.
In this manner, he protected that goddess repeatedly during the four-month period.
Once, for the sake of testing him, his guru [assumed] a beautiful form.
But the second one, having become Ruci, in a secluded place filled with darkness, embraced Vipula at the edge of the forest out of a desire for pleasure. (59)
Vipula, endowed with perfect virtue, perceiving the transformation of Ruci,
became himself a stone-like statue by means of his yogic power.
Nevertheless, that passion embraced the stone idol;
then, from the idol, fire indeed emerged, burning and terrifying.
Vipula quickly produced it and she burned him;
then the preceptor Ruci, in his true form, being eager, abandoned Vipula.
Thus, seeing his excellent disciple so vigilant in guarding his moral conduct, the sovereign guru was pleased and then vanished from sight.
Vipula did not know this; he always protected Ruci's wishes.
Thus, the four-month vow with his teacher was completed. (64)
Having arisen from his vow, he reported everything to his guru:
how the obstacles had arrived and how they had been dispelled.
Having heard the perfect preservation of his conduct, the king of teachers was satisfied and said:
"I am pleased with you, my disciple, because you have guarded your virtue. (66)
And by means of yoga, he even entered her female body and repeatedly provided protection from wicked gods and rākṣasas.
You do not touch it yourself, nor do you have any longing for such desire;
therefore, I am pleased with you—be forever liberated and happy.
O best of disciples, had I seen you acting wickedly, I would have cursed you for it; however, you are steadfast in righteousness. (69)
"You alone remain a true saint who has attained victory in every respect;
by serving those such as you, liberation will certainly be achieved. (3.93.70)
In this world, virtuous people like you, who are free from delusion, are rare; yet you, whose nature is like a stone, have abandoned Ruci when she came to you of her own accord. (7.1)
If one's own kinsmen or women should become a seducer of a man, then if he remains virtuous therein, he shall abide in the Dharma. (72)
Association with the virtuous makes one virtuous and protects one's character; association with the wicked destroys both chastity and virtue.
Association with the wicked destroys righteousness and bestows suffering; the company of the unrighteous kills the virtuous and honors the non-virtuous. (74)
When one's livelihood comes from unrighteousness, the intellect and mind engage in sinful actions;
consequently, the self is struck by defilement. (75)
Therefore, one should cultivate association with the virtuous and seek the company of holy men;
for association with the good is an eternal treasury, and association with the good is the supreme hoard.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and practicing this, as well as through devotion to Dharma, virtuous conduct, and so forth, humans shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (77)
Having spoken thus, Devaśarman ceased, O Lotus-born One;
and Vipula, free from desire, served his teacher and the teacher’s wife.

Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory of the Yogin named Vipula over Ruci Brāhmaṇī in the Preservation of Her Virtue through the Power of Brahmanical Yoga—which is superior to all other powers—along with Indra’s Defeat, the Destruction of the Rākṣasas Lomamarṣaṇa and Kapardaka, the Guru’s Grace and Blessing, and the Dignity of Sainthood," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 93 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; from always taking refuge in the great, greatness, auspiciousness, and the protection of dharma arise. (1)
Indeed, through association with the virtuous, all forms of supreme welfare arise.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient account that serves as a source of auspiciousness. (2)
This region, extending ten thousand yojanas from the navel of the earth,
reaches as far as the Sahya mountain to the west and the place called Mātrāgaskara.
In ancient times, the central region known as Siṃhāraṇya was a most excellent sacred site (tīrtha), abounding in the dwellings of great sages; it was a portion of the earth called Gokarṇa.
For that western part of the earth was indeed excavated by the sons of Sagara;
the southern part of the earth, extending for eight thousand yojanas, was likewise excavated.
Of this region, two thousand [yojanas] remain;
for a long time, the holy site of Gokarṇa has been situated beyond the Pṛthvīkhāta.
The ocean water that has entered [the land] becomes saline water buried in the earth;
there is also the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Gokarṇa, and likewise the Śārabha tīrtha.
The entire Siṃhāraṇya forest then became submerged in water;
indeed, the ground of Gokarṇa became half a yojana in extent.
This is the sacred field (kṣetra) of the sage known as Gokarṇa, who is an incarnation of Hara;
there are countless holy fords (tīrthas) there, as well as hermitages and temples of the gods.
And hosts of Siddhas and sages of rigid vows dwelt there,
having attained supreme Nirvāṇa from which there is no return.
O Lakṣmī, in that field Śaṅkara always dwells with affection along with hosts of spirits, the Goddess, and all the gods.
Certain sages desiring spiritual perfection resided there;
by its power, they attained that perfection in no time at all.
Seeing the earth, including the hermitages and other sites, submerged in the waters of the ocean, the virtuous ones— treasuries of asceticism— as well as the common people, [were filled with grief].
Having deliberated among themselves, those virtuous ones ascended Sahyādri, located in the eastern region, for the purpose of taking up residence; they remained there.
They set out to go to Rāma, who was performing austerities on Mount Mahendra and other peaks—the supreme means for deliverance and one who takes refuge in the virtuous. || 15 ||
The inhabitants of the Malaya mountains, as well as those dwelling on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri) and the residents of the countryside, set out to go to Rāma. || 16 ||
The sages Śuṣka, Sumitra, Dharmā, and others, firm in their vows,
went toward Mount Mahendra, desiring to see Rāma.
Having traversed very many countries, forests, valleys, and rivers,
they reached the best of mountains and beheld the region of Rāma.
Having entered the hermitage, which was enriched by all beings who were profoundly peaceful and adorned with trees of every season, they beheld the Lord Paraśurāma.

They paid homage to the Lord Hari, who sat comfortably upon a deer-skin, surrounded by his disciples, observing the great vow of silence; they worshipped him with offerings of water for the feet and other honors.
Having offered hospitality to the sages, Rāma spoke to them with a smile:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! I am purified by your auspicious arrival."
"May the sages show me the service that is worthy of me; indeed, I shall perform it.
Having heard this, the great seers said, "The region of the earth known as Gokarṇa."
While those born of the ocean were digging, it fell into the waters of the sea;
that sacred field, which dispelled the waters of the ocean, is the purifier of all. 23.
We desire to obtain [this knowledge]; therefore, show us your compassion.
You are an incarnation of Viṣṇu, a virtuous man who is the source of strength for the righteous. (24)
Jamadagni was the stainless son of Ṛcika, the son of Bhṛgu;
you are his [son], a knower of the Veda and dharma, capable and a great lord. ||25||
Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by you;
we have come to entreat you, the granter of all desired objects. (26)
By the power of your own self, having dispelled the waters of the ocean,
you [established] the sacred field known as Gokarṇa, submerged in the water within the Siṃha forest.
"O Blessed One, you ought to grant [this] to us, all the best of sages.
Having heard this, O ascetics, Rāma then spoke what was appropriate.
The duty of the virtuous must be performed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
However, having laid down my weapons, I have come here to practice asceticism. (29)
"Without a weapon, that cannot be accomplished; what should be done? Please instruct me. Having heard those words spoken by Rāma, the sages, Śuṣka and the others, replied: ||| 3.94.30 ||
The taking up of weapons for the sake of protecting the virtuous certainly nourishes one's vow, commitment, duty, and truth. (3.1)
He does not deviate from truth, nor from dharma, nor from his vows.
Therefore, O virtuous one, you should accept this weapon for the sake of his welfare.
"Penance alone is great, and that shall be accomplished by you here;
through it, the great Dharma itself shall be practiced by you. (33)
Thus addressed, he took up his axe and, having reflected upon the protection of the virtuous,
set out with his weapon to practice the supreme dharma of the Bhāgavatas.
Having abandoned his asceticism and undertaken the protection of the virtuous, he ascended into the sky and departed;
he then went to the Sahya mountain and subsequently arrived at the Malaya mountain.
He summoned Varuṇa with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"I have come together with the hosts of sages, desiring to see you. (36)
"Therefore, O Pracetas, you who maintain your own true form, grant me a vision of yourself.
Yet, though he was summoned again and again, he did not come. (37)
Enraged, Hari desired to turn the ocean into one devoid of water;
having sipped water for purification, he took up his bow, strung it, and made the twang of the bowstring resound.
And he fixed and discharged a most terrible arrow with golden feathers, belonging to Bhārgava and having fire as its presiding deity, together with its mantra and weapon-essence.
Then the earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
and all the worlds and the oceans fell into a state of supreme agitation.
The quarters of the sky became shrouded by clouds that blazed with fire;
then the waters, ignited by the fire of the weapon, went to their destruction. ||41||
Even though he was the god Varuṇa, he became exceedingly arrogant; yet, consumed by the fire of the arrow, he was quickly reduced to ashes, and the ocean indeed turned to dryness. 42.
Then Brahmā and the others arrived there and praised the Lord:
"Enough, enough, O Hari! O Supreme Lord, accept our peace-offering. (43)
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for you, O Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self;
Varuṇa has been reduced to ashes, and the water is being destroyed. (44)
The entire world, deprived of water, will go to destruction in an instant;
be gracious, O ocean of mercy, and restrain this fierce weapon! 45.
And revive Varuṇa, the god whose source is water, O Lord!
Salutations to you in the form of Rudra; salutations to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa! ||46||
Salutations to you whose nature is Mahākāla, whose form is Death;
salutations to you who effect the destruction of all, appearing in the form of the virtuous Kṛṣṇa. ||47||
Salutations again and again to the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas and to the benefactor of the gods;
salutations to you, Śrī Hari Rāma, for the welfare of the virtuous. ||48||
Then Hari, seeing the gods standing before him there,
attained a state of peace and restrained the fire-weapon for the sake of desisting.
Having withdrawn his weapon, Rāma stood still; Varuṇa had met his destruction.
Then the gods and others, including the two Aśvins, [appeared] for the sake of restoring him to life.
Having arrived swiftly at the command of Brahmā, they remembered the medicinal herbs and sprinkled the heap of Varuṇa’s ashes with them while reciting mantras.
There, Varuṇa, having regained life from the ashes, rose up;
trembling with fear, he fell at Rāma’s feet with palms joined in reverence.
He said, "O Rāma, protect me out of compassion, for I have come to you for refuge; disregarding this offense entirely, please grant me your grace. (53)
To Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who was speaking thus, Rāma said:
"Formerly, while digging for the earth in your waters, the sons of Sagara [discovered it]. (24)
"The holy site of Gokarṇa, frequented by sages, has been cast down below;
grant that auspicious field to them for their residence, just as before. (55)
Let no one go there, even within two hundred yojanas, nor ever at the sacred sites of Gokarṇa or Śūrpāraka. (56)
At Bhavatīrtha, Satītīrtha, and likewise at Śārabhatīrtha,
Varuṇa, having heard [these words], accepted them by saying "Om," and performed worship.
Having given back the earth and regained his life, he departed together with the gods;
and the sages were filled with wonder upon seeing Rāma’s prowess.
Having reached that place, the sages were exceedingly delighted and became serene;
feeling they had accomplished their purpose, they honored Rāma with blessings. (59)
Commanded by them, Rāma went toward Mount Mahendra;
there, in the sacred field issuing from its waters, the great sages dwelt with their subjects.
And those islands exist within the waters, appearing as sacred fords (tīrtha);
indeed, the sages who are yogis travel by way of the sky.
Thus, O lotus-born one, through virtuous application and through the union with Rāma,
your father bestowed the earth and life itself upon Varuṇa.
Hari granted that very place as a holy site (tīrtha) once again;
for a virtuous person indeed bestows everything—enjoyment, liberation, and exaltation.
Indeed, the virtuous are by nature intent on helping others and are never desisting.
Listen also to another beneficial story concerning virtuous people:
there was once a most excellent king named Ikṣvāku, who was the son of the Sun.
And in Ayodhyā, in that lineage, there was a king named Kuvalāśva;
he was righteous, a great hero, a performer of sacrifices, and a protector of the virtuous.
He lived near the Himalayas, close to the hermitage of Uttaṅka.
A fierce Rākṣasa named Dhundhu was the son of Madhu;
indeed, Uttaṅka himself appointed Kuvalāśva for the purpose of his destruction.
Enraged, Kuvalāśva prepared himself swiftly to destroy Dhundhu,
accompanied by his twenty-one thousand sons.
Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu entered him with his own splendor,
at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
And the gods scattered divine flowers over him from all sides.
And Dhundhu was indeed beneath the surface of the ground within the sands.
Having gone there, the king, together with his sons,
dug a vast trench into the earth where Dhundhu was located.
Dhundhu, for his part, indeed emitted a terrifying fire from his mouth.
By the fire, all the sons of Kuvalāśva were completely consumed.
Three remained there at a distance, accompanied by their vital breaths;
Kuvalāśva extinguished that fire with the water-weapon (jalāstra) and swiftly slew Dhundhu with the Śiva-weapon (śaivāstra).
The king showed him that dead Rākṣasa, Uttaṅka.
Uttaṅka was pleased and granted a boon to the monarch:
inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against enemies.
May they find constant delight in the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven;
and may those Rākṣasas who have been slain here attain imperishable worlds for their sons.
Then, by the grace of Uttaṅka, the deities arrived,
bringing their celestial chariots, as did his twenty-one sons.
Having assumed divine bodies and being seated in celestial chariots, thousands of them went to heaven while all the Jayanas and others looked on.
Thus, by the power of the sage, the king attained victory;
and by the power of that virtuous one, his sons obtained imperishable heaven.
Now, in this manner, Kuvalāśva’s son Dṛḍhāśva was restored to life;
in his lineage there arose a king named Satyavrata, who was possessed of great strength.
And that one of great strength went to the marriage pavilion of the King of Vidarbha at the very time of the taking of hands, having indeed waged war [there].
Out of desire, force, delusion, and through both excitement and power,
and by the force of destiny, he carried his wife away from the pavilion.
Having indeed committed a sin by showing contempt for the gods and the wise,
that unrighteous man was abandoned by his father, who was named Trayyāruṇa.
And although he was told by the outcaste dog-cookers that he must stay outside,
he went outside and stayed near their dwellings.
Then, for twelve years, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain;
at that time, Viśvāmitra performed severe austerities in that region.
And the wife of Viśvāmitra, accompanied by many sons, sold her middle son for the sake of maintaining her family. (86)
Having understood that, Satyavrata indeed liberated his son,
having given him many foods produced from the power of truth.
Thus, Satyavrata then undertook her maintenance both for the sake of pleasing Viśvāmitra and out of compassion. (88)
He who was the son of Viśvāmitra and was indeed liberated by Gālava became a heroic great seer (maharṣi), endowed with devotion to his vows. ||89||
By virtue of his vow, devotion, compassion, and promise,
Satyavrata indeed sustained Viśvāmitra’s wife and the others.
And Vasiṣṭha indeed became the king in the kingdom of King Trayyāruṇi at Ayodhyā, O observer of true vows, appearing as if entirely despondent.
For this reason, indeed, Vasiṣṭha had not even the slightest inclination toward Satyavrata; for there, by the power of what was destined to happen, [the outcome] was otherwise.
Then Satyavrata, out of anger, went to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage and, like a child, seized all the food and other provisions. 93.
He caused all of that to be fed to Viśvāmitra and his sons;
then Vasiṣṭha said to him, "You are indeed forever free from sin."
The abduction of a maiden and a woman, cohabiting with a Cāṇḍāla, and the theft of my food and other provisions—from these, you are considered by me to be Triśaṅku. (95)
But Viśvāmitra, having desisted from his asceticism, understood this;
he became pleased and granted a boon, saying, "Be as happy as a god. (96)
Then the meritorious Triśaṅku, though firm in his vows,
chose to go to heaven in his physical body after having enjoyed a kingdom free from all thorns.
When Trayyāruṇa had died, they consecrated Triśaṅku in the kingdom;
having ruled the kingdom, he went to heaven in that very body.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha were looking on, Viśvāmitra, the descendant of Kuśika, caused the king to ascend to heaven in his physical body. 99.
This occurrence of the impossible was like a marvel;
by the grace of Viśvāmitra, Triśaṅku shines in heaven.
This great majesty belongs to that virtuous and ascetic sage;
therefore, indeed, the righteous should be served, for they are the deliverers of sinners.
Satyarātā, his wife, gave birth to Haricandraka;
and Rohita was his son, who was the abode of Viśvāmitra’s grace.
The wise Viśvāmitra, enduring many hardships,
delivered his wife, son, and king, and thereby established eternal fame for them in the world.
This has been told to you, O Lakṣmī, regarding the constant taking of refuge in the virtuous;
indeed, various kinds of auspiciousness arise, as well as even liberation.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Prowess of the Virtuous," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how the inhabitants of Siṃhāraṇya regained access to the Gokarṇa Tīrtha which had been submerged in the ocean through the refuge of Paraśurāma; how Kuvalāśva attained the status of Dhundhumāra by the grace of Uttaṅka; and how Triśaṅku, known as Satyavrata, ascended to heaven in his own body through the grace of Viśvāmitra.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O Beloved, what should be chanted by beautiful women at all times for their own liberation?
Who is to be worshipped, and who is to be saluted? Tell me, you who are overcome with compassion for women. (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"The name 'Śrīkānta' (Beloved of Śrī), which bestows happiness, should always be chanted by women;
because of that, I indeed grant liberation through this supreme name of mine. (2)
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, O Master!"—thus should widows repeat my name again and again for their own liberation. || 3 ||
The name "Rādhāvara" (the husband of Rādhā) of mine should always be chanted by young maidens;
indeed, the name "Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa" should always be chanted by elderly women.
The recitation of "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa" is supreme;
it should be performed by all women for the attainment of all perfections.
"I am worthy of worship and salutation; Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my beloved husband.
And in an image made of gold or other materials, I am the supreme lord within that husband. (6)
Śrī Nārāyaṇī-Śrī said:
"Wherever men are always engaged— in a vow, a great festival, at home,
in a temple, during the worship of the gods, at a śrāddha ceremony, or likewise upon departing on a journey— "
Whether on a journey or an entrance, at a marriage or an auspicious rite, during the commencement of a house, in agricultural work, or in an enterprise seeking victory— (8)

Likewise, in times of prosperity, in health, or indeed in dejection and the occurrence of the undesirable—what should be recited regarding auspicious or inauspicious events and so forth for the sake of attaining one's desired fruits? (9)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: It bestows gain everywhere, grants peace and nourishment, destroys fear, provides protection, eliminates enemies and obstacles, and is approved by the virtuous. (3.95.10)
I shall proclaim the Brahma-śara mantra, which destroys all sins; by reciting it anywhere, an embodied being is liberated from all evils. (11)
The venerable one attains long life, and supreme prosperity comes to him;
he achieves equality with the Imperishable Brahman in that abode which is for my satisfaction. 12.
At that time, O Lotus-born One, when I entered into creation along with you, the entire body of speech was established together with the circles of liberated souls.
Salutation to the illustrious Supreme Lord; salutation to the Sovereign of the Imperishable;
salutation to the Lord of the Liberated; salutation to the one who delights in the beloved of Brahmā.
Salutations, salutations to the Lord of Haripriyā and others; salutations to the Incarnate One;
salutations to the Supreme Self, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Salutation to the Lord of Īśvaranātha, salutation to the Master of Īśvarīṇī;
salutation to the Overlord of the Vyūha, salutation to the Master of Vaiṣṇavī. || 16 ||
Salutations to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī; salutations to You, the Lord of Śrī Lakṣmī. Salutations to the Inner Controller, the treasure-house of the Vedas; salutations again and again to You.
Salutations to you who have a thousand heads and innumerable names;
salutations to you, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and the Unborn, who possess three forms. ||18||
Salutations also to the Ādityas, and salutations, salutations to the Vasus;
salutations to the two Aśvins, and salutations, salutations to all the gods. || 19 ||
Salutations indeed to the gods of sacrifice, and to Time and Death;
salutations again and again to the Viśvedevas and to the ancestors. ||3.95.20||
Repeated salutations to the Siddhas, the Munis, and the Sādhus;
repeated salutations to all the lords of the Gaṇas and to their attendants. ||21||
Salutations again and again to the virtuous women, the chaste ones, and the goddesses;
salutations again and again to mothers, fathers, and the elderly. ||22||
Salutations again and again to the Brahmins, to the groups worthy of worship, and to the sacred fords;
salutations again and again to Kambharā, the Great Lakṣmī, who is ever-contented. ||23||
Salutations again and again to Māṇikyā, Prabhāvatī, and Prajñā; salutations again and again to Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rādhikā, and Kamalā. ||24||
Salutations to the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa, to that Great Viṣṇu; repeated salutations to the seven Ṛṣis, the descendants of Manu, and the Brāhmaṇas. ||25||
Salutations again and again to the wondrous sages, the true gurus;
salutations again and again to Dharma, to Bhakti, to Kṛṣṇa, and to Hari. ||26||
Salutations again and again to Nara, to his elder brother, and to those born from the bull;
salutations to all the guardians of the quarters and to the protectors of the worlds. || 27 ||
Homage again and again to the gurus, the bestowers of liberation, and the bestowers of peace; homage again and again to the protectors, the pure ones, and the sanctifiers. ||28||
Salutations again and again to the fires, to the principles, and to the sovereign powers;
salutations again and again to all the Brahma-knowledges that grant liberation. ||29||
Repeated salutations, repeated salutations to the virtuous ones who are like weighty wish-fulfilling cows;
salutations, salutations to the ascetics who possess the dharma of good conduct and to the yogis. 3.95.30.
Salutations to You, the Soul of All, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the one whose nature is self-luminous, the treasury of all mantras. ||3 1||
One should proclaim these who are of the nature of Brahman, the increasers of fame;
likewise, one should proclaim the incarnations, the liberated ones, and the divine lords.
One should indeed glorify me as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, revealed by all the scriptures, the auspiciousness of all beings, and the purifier. (33)
One should always recite my Kalpa in the evening, at night, and incessantly during the day; it pacifies diseases, bestows spiritual accomplishments, and likewise grants nourishment.
These deities, when invoked, bestow the accomplishment of all undertakings for men;
they protect them, rain down their desires, and nourish them. (355)
All these leaders are also witnesses of one's actions;
when they are thus praised, being satisfied, they dispel the inauspiciousness of men. (36)
Having thus aroused the resolve, one should repeatedly perform prostrations;
for such a person there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor any obstruction on the path. (37)
For him there shall be no inauspiciousness; indeed, there shall be auspiciousness at every step.
For him there shall be no bad dreams; he shall be well-being personified at every moment.
All sins are destroyed and great merits arise;
diseases and ailments perish, and prosperity shall prevail within the family. 39.
May the arrow of Brahmā provide protection for oneself, for one's sons, for one's wives and family members, for wealth, and for medicinal herbs.
In battle, enemies perish and victory belongs to the reciter;
it should be recited during rites for the gods and ancestors, for then the ancestors and the deities are satisfied. 41.
Impurity shall be far removed and purity shall always prevail through the recitation of the *Brahmaśara* during travel or on the occasion of an auspicious rite. (42)
Supreme accomplishment shall come of one's desired undertakings; of this there is no doubt.
He shall have no fear of kings, nor any fear of wild beasts. 43.
He has no fear from enemies, nor from piśācas, serpents, or rākṣasas; he has no fear of fire, water, wind, or space, nor of earthquakes or malevolent planets. (44)
Where the hymn of Brahmaśara exists, there suffering dissolves;
there a child does not die, nor is one born with unfulfilled hopes. (45)
Wealth is his treasure-trove as he recites, and his cows have many calves;
such is this hymn of Brahmaśara, which protects like an arrow. 46.
O Lakṣmī, the eternal Brahman, the heart of all beings, has been truly declared to you; my hearing is the eternal Vāk. 47.
By reciting [the names of] Mahāviṣṇu and likewise those of the lords of the gods, they go to heaven;
by proclaiming them here, they go to the worlds and to his abode.
By glorifying me—Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, who am without beginning—they go to my imperishable state; by glorifying Lakṣmī, they obtain prosperity.
By chanting the names of Rādhā and likewise the two Aśvins, one attains the highest form;
by remembering Dharma, one becomes a bull (a virtuous man); and by remembering Brahman, one attains imperishable happiness. (3.95.50)
By remembering the virtuous, one always attains supreme merit and freedom from obstacles;
for the sake of accomplishing all tasks and goals, one should recite the *Brahmaśara-stotra*. (5.1)
The virtuous are to be honored for the pacification of all evil;
indeed, the humiliation of the virtuous would bring even the lords to ruin. (52)
Having fully propitiated virtuous people, one never comes to harm;
the holy ones are to be honored, saluted, and served like the Supreme Lord. (53)
One should always behave toward virtuous people as if they were miserable;
for compassionate saints sustain all these worlds. (54)
Endowed with devotion, the virtuous—those great bridges of dharma who are united with the Blessed One through their practice of worship—protect those who have come for refuge. (55)
Those who renounce the wealth of women, who are virtuous and disciplined in the restraint of speech,
are worthy of being beheld by all beings, for they are endowed with good conduct and firm in their vows.
They are the liberators of the worlds and likewise the protectors of the scriptures;
they are also scribes and commentators, devoted to the exertion of dharma.
For those who possess austerity, devotion, and wealth, for whom Lord Hari is their vast strength,
who are the refuge of all dharmas, and who are holy men possessing divine vision— (58)
Desiring liberation, they remain established in devotion and in dharma, as well as in the bridges of dharma,
relying upon which all subjects and embodied beings live.
The virtuous are the steps to Brahman and the paths for those traveling toward liberation;
they are the eternal givers of the merit of sacrifice for the sake of providing food.
They are the deliverers of the ancestors and the gods, partaking first of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings;
by means of their blessings, they protect the three worlds from the fear of illusion.
The Suns are the eyes for all the worlds and likewise for those who possess sight;
they are skilled in the wealth of hearing all narratives and are the bestowers of liberation.
Knowing the destinies of all sentient beings and contemplating their internal courses of rebirth, they understand the beginning and end of undertakings; they are those who go to the supreme goal.
Possessing knowledge of the higher and the lower, they are adorned by the awakening to the Self and other virtues;
liberated and free from evil, they have shaken off all sin and taken refuge in the abode [of the Absolute]. ||64||
Free from dualities, devoid of bonds, as sharp as the tips of spokes, and without possessions;
they are worthy of honor and are honored by the virtuous, the great-souled, and the true Vaiṣṇavas. (65)
They regard with equanimity mud and sandalwood paste, meat and the taste of vegetables, linen, deerskin, and silk; they are devoted to fasting. (66)
They may wither their limbs through austerities, knowledge, and vows;
they may turn that which is godless into one possessed of gods and endowed with wealth.
For by the power of their asceticism, the virtuous can indeed create other worlds;
they are the Brahmins even among Brahmins, and the deities even among deities.
The virtuous are the authorities among authorities and the ornaments of the scriptures;
for them, whether old or young, even the poor is endowed with wealth. (69)
Whether woman or man, one deserves equal honor;
however, through the excellence of austerity and knowledge, one deserves superior honor.
Whether ignorant or a knower of Brahman, a virtuous person is a great and supreme vessel;
a wise and virtuous person who knows the Supreme Brahman is a purifying and most excellent vessel. (71)
Whether ignorant or learned, a virtuous person is indeed a great divinity;
for even in a cremation ground, the radiant fire is never defiled.
Likewise, in the wheel of saṃsāra, the virtuous person is never defiled;
like the fire that licks the sacrificial oblation during a sacrifice, the virtuous one shines forth beautifully. ||73||
Even when thousands of Brahmins are feasting at a great sacrifice, if there is no virtuous person present, it would be in vain; for Nārāyaṇa is the truly virtuous one.
The virtuous are worthy of worship by the Moon, the Sun, and others; they are the lords of lords.
Indeed, through the worship of the virtuous, one gains longevity, renown, fame, and strength. (75)
Devotion, liberation, and divinity increase constantly day and night;
indeed, those who worship the virtuous become lords of the worlds and the world beyond.

For the sake of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; for fame, prosperity, and the pacification of disease; and for the worship of deities and ancestors—the stainless virtuous ones should be gratified. (77)
For those virtuous ones are indeed Mādhavas in this world and the next;
when satisfied, they would deliver the entire world just as the Lord of Śrī does.
In the house of Kaśyapa there was a virtuous Vaiṣṇava ascetic and renunciant named Praṇadbrahman, who was the mind-born son of the Creator.

He was devoted to vows and observances, wore matted hair, and was emaciated; he possessed great supernatural powers and other perfections, was deeply absorbed in reciting mantras with garlands, and was generally intent on maintaining silence. ||3.95.80||
Mārīca Kaśyapa, however, always attended upon him in the morning with services such as massaging his feet and by offering food, drink, and other necessities.
This virtuous man, worshipping Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and me, Hari, is devoted to my service and generally remains absorbed in meditation. (82)
He wanders at will through the divine worlds, among the Nāgas and humans,
and returns again to the abode of the high-souled Kaśyapa.
Once, Praṇad said to Kaśyapa, "Feed me";
Kaśyapa then fed him milk-porridge and cakes. ||84||
Then Praṇadbrahmā spoke to his servant, the sage Kaśyapa: "Anoint my limbs repeatedly with milk-rice pudding. (85)
Kaśyapa performed everything, including anointing with milk-rice; he bathed the great sage Praṇada with milk-rice. (86)
Then, having risen, he smeared the mouth and the head of Kaśyapa with the remnants of the *praṇadbrahma* milk-rice (*pāyasa*). ||87||
Then, seeing the young woman Aditi standing nearby,
he took hold of her hand and smeared her with the milk-rice porridge.
Then that lord of sages, chanting the sacred syllable *praṇava*, discharged her [the seed] upon his face, chest, waist, thighs, back, and hips. (89)
Then he spoke again to Aditi, whose body was covered with milk-rice:
"Carry me on your shoulder and place me outside, in the presence of everyone."
Having thus placed her upon his shoulder, Aditi then went outside;
meanwhile, the sage struck that girl, who was in the bloom of youth, with creepers.
She too, having placed virtuous people upon her shoulders, wandered everywhere;
and while all the world looked on, she returned toward her own home.
That sage, with [the child] upon his shoulder, returned home by way of the royal road;
neither Kaśyapa nor Aditi experienced even the slightest bit of sorrow.
Having entered the house, the king of sages quickly fell to the ground;
at that moment, Kaśyapa, Aditi, and the other women likewise fell from his shoulders. 94.
They performed services, saying, "Be gracious, O Blessed One!
Then that king of sages, having become composed, looked at Kaśyapa in that state.
With a gratified soul, he said to Aditi: "You shall become the mother of the gods;
because you have conquered anger, you are indeed Kaśyapa here. (96)
"You shall become the father of all beings, of this there is no doubt;
in your lineage there will indeed be millions and billions of virtuous ones such as myself. (97)
All will be upholders of their lineage, devoted to meditation on Brahman, and likewise possessed of wives and enriched with houses and other such things. (98)
All kinds of offspring shall indeed belong to you alone;
your meritorious fame shall be eternal, of this there is no doubt. ||99||
O Kaśyapa, your lineage and that of Hari shall indeed manifest again and again for the sake of uplifting the worlds.
Neither old age, nor disease, nor even death shall afflict you;
you shall become Aditi, the foremost among all women.
"May this very same disposition toward the virtuous always remain yours.
Having spoken thus, he ceased; having bathed, he became pure.
"O Aditi, those auspicious deities who consume the nectar (amṛta) shall always be your sons, partaking of the milk-rice and the fruits."
By the turn of fate, some other women may at some point become recipients of your favor; O Kaśyapa, be happy.
"May the houses of Kaśyapa indeed possess all prosperity," the sage said, and they became exactly so.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the benedictory words of the holy sage Praṇadbrahma and the services rendered by Kaśyapa, free from all doubt, have indeed borne fruit.
O virtuous one, even the service of Aditi bears fruit, for she is the mother of Hari; indeed, Aditi is born as the mother of the gods, and no other woman is so born again and again. 107.
O Lakṣmī, the fruit of serving a virtuous person bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it grants all prosperity and fulfills every desire. (108)
The virtuous are constantly worshipped by all— by deities and others,
as well as by humans, the lords of the world, the guardians of the directions, Īśvara, and the rest.

On one side is the service of all beings, and on the other is the service of the virtuous; in comparison to the fruit of serving the virtuous, all other things do not equal even a sixteenth part. (3.95.110)
By reading and hearing this, one obtains the fruit of serving the virtuous;
one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and become a partaker of eternal bliss. (111)

Thus, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the account of the greatness of virtuous people who are worthy of worship and salutation, this is the fifth chapter titled "The Description of how Kaśyapa and Aditi obtained the status of being the parents of the gods through the blessing and service of the sage Praṇad-Brahma."
The Ninety-fifth Chapter. || 95 ||

Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: "O beloved, regarding the statements that 'the virtuous are Hari,' 'you are Dharma,' 'the virtuous woman is liberation,' and 'devotion is the means,' what indeed are the authoritative proofs for these?"
For that which is not proclaimed by authoritative means is not firmly settled in the heart;
therefore, what is considered an authoritative means for you to establish their validity? (2)
Speak to me, O Lord of the World, you who are the treasure-trove of all sciences; [speak] so that there may be no doubt for me, truly for the benefit of the worlds. (3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī, Queen of Śiva; the primary authority is indeed direct perception—that object which has been observed by oneself again and again.
For that [knowledge] is indeed directly determinative through familiarity and the sense organs;
likewise, the virtuous are those possessed of good conduct and vows, endowed with devotion, and free from latent desires.
Even while sleeping on the bed, those who possess virtuous character must be examined through living together,
through devotion, through the giving of enjoyments, and through their conduct.
Those who are virtuous must indeed be examined directly and never otherwise;
for one whose nature undergoes no change whatsoever upon being embraced or when subjected to effort [to seduce]. (7)
Those great beings here are indeed Nārāyaṇas themselves who possess virtuous conduct;
for them, there is truly no fatigue at all in their constant and manifold devotion.
In dancing, singing, service, and so forth, shame does not restrain them;
they should be understood as truly devoted, auspicious, and saintly beings. (9)

Various kinds of enjoyments should be given to a virtuous person, even if they are fashioned [artificially]; yet he does not consume them and remains free from desire—this is the direct determination of his true virtue. (3.96.10)
Latent impressions (vāsanā), the tongue (rasanā), the subtle body (liṅga), and the objects of examination— among these,
direct perception (pratyakṣa) alone is the decisive factor that brings about one's welfare.
One should never utter speech that merely follows the crowd;
for there is no inference free from error without the constant presence of the cow of true knowledge.
That which is based on false reasons cannot be determinative;
for me, there is the direct perception of the marks upon Hari, Kṛṣṇa, who am I myself. (13)
The observation of marks and so forth on the hands, feet,
and body is proclaimed here as the direct evidence for the state of being the Blessed One.
The authoritative measure for these marks is indeed the scripture handed down through tradition;
it consists of the words of trustworthy authorities and is likewise rooted in the Veda. (15)
The Vedas are indeed authoritative, as are the forms and weapons that were seen and recorded by those with divine vision who stood by my side. (16)
He on whose hand or foot there is the mark of that weapon is indeed the Blessed One; he may assume the form of a human being or other such appearances.
Just as I am marked upon my hand with the fish, the trident, and other signs,
so too am I the Lord of Ramā, possessing a manifest divine form and the splendor of ten million lotuses.
I exist possessing the sixteen marks upon my feet and my body;
I am possessed of innumerable marks, manifestly bearing the discus, mace, and other symbols.
In this way, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is to be understood through the means of valid cognition;
the Dharma is honored by those who desire the happiness of worldly convention. 3.96.20
"This is the path to be followed"—thus he was indeed resolved;
[namely,] charity, service to others, marriage, and the protection of others. (21)
Purity, acquisition through righteous means, worship, and likewise exertion—these and other such paths [are to be practiced] according to place and time. (22)
For the sake of happiness and for the sake of being free from obstacles, that alone is the certain Dharma;
the word of the authoritative one and the action of the authoritative one shine forth as the very form of Dharma.
A virtuous and faithful wife should always be awakened by her husband through noble conduct such as devotion;
she, in turn, is constantly awakened by him through their living together. 24.
Indeed, those women for whom truthful sovereignties are recorded in the scriptures and who likewise display wonders are truly virtuous wives (satī). ||25||
Liberation is the state of emptiness within the self; it is realized here through the afflictions and so forth.
It is eternal peace, innate bliss, and likewise everlasting. ||26||
Thus [is the glory] of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who bestows eternal bliss upon the worlds of happiness, as well as of myself.
Furthermore, there is the attainment of the stages beginning with Akṣara as places of residence,
and liberation according to the method of the scriptures, even if only slightly perceived through direct experience.

O Lakṣmī, he should always be ascertained through devotion; indeed, he is considered attainable either by the path of knowledge or, upon the destruction of delusion, by the state consisting of realized wisdom. (29)
That which is to be known is the form of liberation; therein, the scripture is the authoritative means of knowledge.
O beloved, there exists no other measure equal to this wonder.
In the case of a miracle, there is a salutation [to that power], for therein everything—whether perception, inference, comparison, or even verbal testimony—is eclipsed. (3.1)
Presumption, perception, probability, tradition, gesture, silence, expression, dreaming, and mental intuition—these are the means of knowledge. (32)
Indeed, even the fourteen types of pride dissolve into wonder;
therefore, the nature of spiritual attainment is truly the most powerful authority.
Even that which is already established by direct perception is further subverted by [theoretical] proof;
what then can be said, O Lotus-born One, regarding the other means of valid cognition? (34)
O Lakṣmī, serve virtuous people with honor and respect; for among the virtuous, there is enjoyment as well as liberation, and in every way, a good state of existence is found among the virtuous. (35)
Hari, dharma, devotion, and liberation prevail among the virtuous; goodness, chastity, and everything else prevail among the virtuous. (36)
Knowledge, service, devotion to me, and likewise all forms of charity—these virtues are indeed the most preeminent and are accompanied by contentment. (37)
In them there is happiness, and in them supreme joy is considered to be delight;
in them, O beloved, there is liberation through union with Hari, which occurs only among the virtuous.
Pervaded by passion and ignorance, those nihilists who revile the virtuous and those who are envious of the dharma of the righteous fall into hell. (39)
But those who serve the virtuous and attend upon the righteous in accordance with the dharma of the good, being devoted to truth and uprightness, they, having become such, go to my abode. (3.96.40)
Devotion to the Dharma and their ultimate goal shall arise from service to and worship of Me;
for those virtuous ones who possess devotion indeed go to My abode. 41.
Householders who possess only a measure of merit go to the heavenly world—those lay followers who are virtuous, endowed with good character, and refined in their conduct. (42)
Having given food to these five—the cow, the deity, the sun, the virtuous man, the chaste woman, and the ascetic—the righteous eat what remains. (43)
Those who perform circumambulation around an elderly, virtuous Brahmin, as well as toward guests, servants, family members, and women; ||44||
Those who protect those who have come for refuge, those who are devoted to the service of their guru, and those who serve the elderly; ||45||
For they are always devoted to solitude, dwell at sacred fords, and are dear to Hari;
they possess knowledge, are contented, and are always filled with happiness.

Those who disregard the words of the elders, those devoted solely to Vedic recitation, and those whose senses have withdrawn from their objects—even they [do not attain liberation] without Śrī Puruṣottama. 47.
And toward all those who are afflicted by disease and who long for longevity and the like, the virtuous, who are adorned with goodness, refrain from using the address "thou. (48)
Just as salt submerged in water dissolves away, so too every sin offered to the virtuous perishes instantly. 49.
A Buddha does not conceal evil; for that which is concealed increases. Having committed it, one should confess it to the virtuous, for they indeed bring it to rest. (3.96.50)
One should practice dharma endowed with devotion; one should not be a hypocrite who makes a banner of dharma.
For those who trade in dharma, having enjoyed heaven, fall once again. (51)
One should worship the gods without hypocrisy and serve the virtuous without deceit;
one should follow one's gurus with devotion and practice charity for the sake of liberation. 52.
One should acquire fortune through devotion, service, austerity, and vows;
thereafter, one may obtain good luck even without effort or exertion.
When it is not the time for gain, one does not obtain it even when effort is exerted;
but when it is the time for gain, by serving the virtuous, one may attain that supreme state. //54//
For that which is performed at the proper time remains unsummoned, staying of its own accord;
service never becomes fruitless when accompanied by blessings. 55.
If one has studied the treatises on ethics but is not endowed with ethical conduct, that study is fruitless for him and leads to the hells. (56)
Having attained a human birth, my worship must be performed;
if it is not done here, then whatever else has been done is fruitless.
If one who possesses knowledge does not apply that knowledge for the sake of the self, then, being unpeaceful and full of craving, his knowledge is indeed fruitless. (58)
If a wise man, having abandoned peace and forsaken his own liberation,
acts according to worldly views, his life is fruitless.
Those of passionate nature (rājasa) and others do this, will do it, and are doing it;
if those of virtuous nature (sāttvika) were likewise to follow such paths, their livelihood would be fruitless.
He indeed demonstrates to the world his honored practice of helping others;
having taught those equal to himself, he causes them to recite [the scriptures] immediately, thereby establishing his own fame. ||61||
