The wicked, having attained identification with the body, do not follow the path of devotion;
they alone are destroyers of dharma, possessing outward vision but none within.
If a person attains peace by relying upon knowledge, that is his most excellent fruit; nothing greater than that has been accomplished.
A wise man should not, for the sake of his livelihood, depend upon one who is devoid of knowledge;
nor should a wise man, out of a petty desire, praise wealthy fools.
Base desires do not arise for the wise man, nor does ignorance for one of noble mind;
the wise man is ever-contented, virtuous, and possesses the joy of Brahman.
There is equality between the virtuous and the wise in contentment, in self-realization,
in truthful speech, in devotion, in being most established in Brahman, and in the Supreme Lord.
If he desires to undertake enterprises but does not find assistance, he should engage in fierce austerity; for that which is not sown does not sprout.
What has been given is obtained later, and service bestows prosperity; through non-malice one gains long life, and through devotion to the virtuous, the supreme state.
One should give abundantly to the virtuous, constantly serve the good, and do what is pleasing to embodied beings; having attained victory, one should go to the Imperishable.
One should not beg from those who wear fine garments, nor should one dwell among the poor;
one should certainly not cultivate friendship with the wicked, but should serve the virtuous for the sake of liberation. (3.96.70)
One should enjoy happiness established within the self and always be an heir of Hari; one should become a son obedient to the virtuous and desire liberation in the supreme Imperishable.
One should pay homage to virtuous and chaste women and worship me, Lord Hari;
being devoted to me alone, one should indeed offer everything belonging to oneself unto me. (72)
If it is not offered, it perishes; and what is acquired through labor becomes fruitless.
By offering it after performing it in that manner, one obtains eternal liberation.
Generosity should be practiced for the sake of attaining Dharma, peace, joy, celebration, bliss, and even immortality. //74//
One should perform the gift of service in every way, even with one's own wealth; and the gift of home and family should also be performed for the attainment of those respective goals. //75//

One should have confidence only in the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda), and never in the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist (asatkāryavāda). One should have confidence in the conception of Dharma and then proceed with it swiftly.
Dharma, when practiced swiftly, turns the mind toward devotion;
performing devotion, one attains me, the Supreme Lord, as a son. //77//
In this very way, the righteous indeed attain the Self through the self;
for the acquisition of the Supreme Self is dharma, and dharma is indeed the bestower of victory. //78//
Wherever dharma is constant and innate for all beings whose bodies are composed of the five elements and who possess similar natures, there I, Hari, am eternally present.
For all embodied beings who possess equal natures and follow the path of dharma, devotion and service toward the true guru, the father, and Lord Hari grant liberation. (3.96.80)
Service to the lineage of the virtuous is indeed said to be the supreme good; likewise, one becomes free from sin and attains happiness through such service. 8.1
Service to the virtuous is indeed auspicious and the destroyer of impurities;
it destroys the sin produced by the body, the senses, and likewise the internal organs. (82)
Whether done knowingly or unknowingly, all that is dissolved through service to the virtuous;
even what has occurred at night or during the twilight hours perishes for one who recites [the mantra]. 83.
Service to the virtuous and my own recitation of mantras bring well-being to the yogi;
indeed, rebirth as an animal, hell, and birth in mixed castes shall be destroyed. (84)
Through the service of the virtuous, there is neither fear nor sudden death;
I am the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Guru of all. (85)
O Lakṣmī, the Supreme Lord—the inner self of all living beings and the master of souls—is always to be remembered, as are the millions of his incarnations. (86)
Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and also the Creator of the Universe;
Viṣṇu, Śiva, Satī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Sūrya, and Candramas. ||87||
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as their attendants, are to be remembered;
likewise Yama together with Dhūmorṇā, and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) together with Gaurī.
Through his supernatural power, Dhaneśvara, the cow Surabhi, the host of Maruts, the Vālakhilya sages, and the great seers such as Nārada and others [were also present]. ||89||
Urvaśī, the daughter of Śrī Hari, should always be remembered at dawn;
as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, along with the Aśvins and the Pitṛs.
Dharma, Śruta, Tapas, Dīkṣā, and likewise Bhakti and Bṛhaspati;
also Aśvapaṭṭasara, Prabhāsa, and likewise Gomatī. ||9.1||
The Gaṅgā, Revā, Gaṇḍakī, Yamī, Sarayū, Gautamī, Nārāyaṇī, Indratoyā, Brahmaputrī, and Hiraṇvatī. ||92||
Puṣkara, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the lake Sarasvatī;
likewise Meru, Himālaya, Vindhya, Urala, and Raivata. (93)
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, and Gandhamādana—these, as well as the oceans and the principles (tattvas), should always be remembered. 94.
May all the divine deities protect me, whether they have been named or not;
may all the virtuous men and women protect me always.
May Kambharāśrī protect me always; may Gopālakṛṣṇa protect me.
May the goddess Pārvatī protect me, and may Prajñā Rādhikā protect me. 96.
May those dear to Brahmā always protect me, and may those dear to Hari protect me as well;
may the Blessed One, Śuka, and Vallabha also protect me.
May the Brahmin seer devoted to his wife, the self-luminous Lord, and the aged preceptor Lomaśa—may they all protect me forever. (98)
May the Goddess Kuṅkumavāpikā, the field known as Akṣara, and Sādhu, Lālāyana, and the others—those supreme lords—protect me. (99)
By reciting this very [hymn], one is liberated from all sins;
by praising and rejoicing [in it], one is released from every fear.
By remembering my divine sports, the virtuous ones who have taken refuge in me and whose selves are united with me through the recitation of the Saṃhitā indeed attain my supreme, imperishable state.
By remembering the divine wonders of virtuous women who have taken refuge in me—women who are the consorts of Brahmā—they attain the supreme state. 102.

Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Validity of Authorities Regarding Devotion and Other Means to Liberation for Śrī Hari, Holy Men, Dharma, and Chaste Women, as well as the Meeting with the Virtuous and the Power of Miracles," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:

What should be done by a human being who is engaged in the activities of the world? What dharma should he contemplate as truly virtuous for the sake of maintaining his physical life and his worldly course?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having abandoned malice, having renounced theft, and likewise having abandoned sexual misconduct, one should perform all that is most excellent, having cast off sins with the body. || 2 ||
Having abandoned these four [faults] of speech— village talk, harshness, slander, and falsehood— one should always utter what is true.
One should always maintain in one's mind a lack of desire for the property of others, friendliness toward all embodied beings, and faith in the fruits of actions and so forth.
One should not give rise to latent impressions and should abandon craving;
having left behind that which causes fear, one should by oneself take refuge in the virtuous.
Having offered all one's possessions and practiced the ninefold devotion,
one should attain Me through love and meditation, and thus proceed to the supreme state.
Thus one should always practice that which is excellent, auspicious, beneficial, and productive of good fruit;
one should never, however, practice that which is inauspicious or contrary.
One should perform service to one's mother, service to one's father, and likewise service to one's husband;
one should also perform service to one's teacher, service to cows, and attendance upon the elderly.
One should practice service to the gods, service to the virtuous, and service to chaste women;
one should always practice hospitality, assistance to others, and similar duties.
He should perform service for me and practice service to the poor;
he should practice service to the world, service to the nation, and service to the subjects.
One should practice the service of sacred fords (tīrtha), the service of Brahman, and the service of liberation.
Listen, Lakṣmī, how in former times, having served a sacred ford and a circle of virtuous men, [he attained his goal]. 11.
And the great seer known as Ālambāyana attained liberation at the great holy site of Gokarṇa in Siṃhāraṇya; he himself was a king among sages.
He lived happily for a hundred thousand years through his service to the virtuous;
when he reached the age of ten, a man born in the land of Saurāṣṭra arrived.
Having bowed to his own mother, Keśariṇī, that boy said:
"O Mother, if you have a desire for me to meet with the virtuous again and again," (14)
Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent, and human birth is likewise difficult to attain; devotion to Hari is difficult to find, and the company of the virtuous is rare. (15)
A home, a garden, a wife, kinsmen, wealth, cattle, and servants are all easily obtained; yet they are the ultimate causes of bondage. (16)
Sages are rare to find, as is devotion taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
even liberation, O Mother, is difficult to attain. Therefore, a wise man should strive to achieve these.
"Such is my resolve; instruct me as to how I should act.
The mother said to her son, "You are blessed; you truly behave like a deity. (18)
"O son, from your childhood these resolutions of yours have been nurtured by discernment;
blessed am I, your mother, and blessed too is your father, O son. (19)
O son, since you desire to practice devotion to the Lord and to serve Him,
and since your mind seeks to attain liberation through the virtuous, your intellect is a worthy vessel for blessings.
O son, having today heard this supreme discourse on the Supreme Lord from you,
who are desirous of liberation, I have become possessed of great merit.
O son, may your auspicious intentions regarding devotion to Hari and service to the virtuous always be fulfilled and free from obstacles.
Having abandoned childhood play and the like, having discarded the notions of youth, and disregarding passion and other such impulses, it is because your mind is set upon liberation. (23)
"I am pleased, my son; you are the savior of your family.
This human birth is for the sake of liberation; any other would lead to the ocean of worldly existence."
Now, having abandoned the ocean of existence, fulfill this human birth;
having informed your father and obtained his permission for crossing to the further shore. (25)

And by which [means] one attains the state from which there is no returning—the abode of the true path—where those wise and virtuous ones are heard to dwell, having reached the further shore of Brahman. (26)
O you who are beyond attributes, who possess the qualities of Brahman, and who bestow liberation—remember me there indeed;
do not remember me as a mother anywhere, nor father, nor kinsmen, nor home. (27)
Do not remember your various bonds, nor your birthplace, nor your friends; O son, do not long for sense-objects, and do not direct your meditation toward worldly matters.
Do not ever fall into the current of tastes and flavors; O son, let there never be for you attachment to sense objects anywhere. (29)
And may your path to liberation, O son, proceed to its conclusion without obstacles;
for the human body is intended to be dedicated to the service of the virtuous.
O son, always act in such a way that you may attain auspicious supreme welfare;
in the end, may you have the attainment of Nārāyaṇa and a residence in His abode.
"Having asked your father Brahmātāra, go and perform what is auspicious.
Having spoken thus, she, with a heart full of joy, smelled the head of her son.
The mother provided him with food and gave him firm resolve;
she sent him toward his father for the sake of entering the stage of renunciation.
The son went to his father, who was sitting comfortably, and bowed to him;
he then reported everything to the yogi Brahmatāra.
The Brahmin Brahmatāra also spoke to his auspicious-souled son:
"O, how blessed I am always, since such a son as this dwells in my house! (35)
Devoted to the Lord, with a mind intent on the company of holy and virtuous people, he is free from worldly enjoyment and devoid of desire for pleasures; thus, from childhood, he is auspicious. (36)
Indeed, by virtue of past merit, a son is born who is devoted, observant of vows, virtuous, dispassionate, steadfast, and possessed of superior conduct. (37)
"O son, worship Hari constantly and serve virtuous people;
having gone to the holy site of Gokarṇa, establish yourself in liberation. (38)
Make this human body fruitful and endowed with the highest fruit;
I am truly possessed of a son through a son such as you, a great yogi. (39)
When the merit accumulated over a hundred births arises,
then indeed there shall be a desire to know the path to liberation and the way of service to the virtuous.
But having severed the firm bond of servitude toward family and kin, some hero becomes one who is immersed in the battle for liberation. 41.
Whether among insects, moths, gods, demons, humans, birds, reptiles, animals, perfected beings (siddhas), or sages, enjoyments are indeed equal. (42)
Those very same things are the moisture-born (vārijāḥ), the elemental (bhautikāḥ), and those that are nourished by food (prabhojanāḥ);
the sense organs (indriyāṇi) are equal, and the vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) born of wind are likewise equal.
Likewise, the days pass away equally for all embodied beings;
yet those devoid of divine grace do not strive for the sake of liberation, being overcome by the sleep of negligence.
Those very objects that serve as the purpose of hell exist here and in the next world, yet they are merely constructed [fictions].
Liberation is the supreme human goal and the true goal of the self; other goals concern only the body and do not lead to liberation.
He who, having completely crossed over the three heaps, enters the fourth northern one—he indeed is the deity here, he is the Lord, and he is the sovereign of the liberated. 46.
He alone has accomplished all that was to be done; he alone is truly virtuous;
he alone is Nārāyaṇa; and he alone is the liberating Guru. ||47||
The mental resolve for sensual desire is difficult to conquer; women, wealth, and the like are difficult to comprehend;
one's own mind is difficult to understand, and likewise, latent tendencies (vāsanā) are difficult to overcome. (48)
Even craving, which is so difficult to conquer, has been overcome by you, the self-controlled one;
for he who has here conquered his organ of generation and restrained his tongue has truly triumphed.
He by whom the king of the mind is conquered has conquered all, for he has conquered his own self;
O son, quickly attain victory over this world which is as substantial as a mere illusion.
May you attain victory even over the supreme, eternal Brahman;
may there be welfare for you, may there be auspiciousness for you, may there be joy for you, and may there be great celebration. (51)
And being immersed in eternal bliss, become liberated in the state of Hari;
I shall behold you situated within the center of the circle of yogis in the imperishable abode.
"O son, you are indeed accompanied by your wife, for you are the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus addressed, the son, having applied the tilaka mark, was filled with affection.
Having bowed to the water at his parents' feet, having drunk it, and performed auspicious rites,
and likewise having bowed to his hundred brothers, he went to the Gokarṇa Tīrtha.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
Hare Rādhāpati, Lakṣmīpati, Hare Hare, O Lord! (55)
Performing worship in this manner while keeping time with his hands,
he then proceeded on foot from Jālikā to the excellent holy site of Somanātha.
Then he went to Bhavanātha, Śarabha, and Satītīrtha;
thereafter, at Gokarṇa Tīrtha, he worshipped Viṣṇu with great devotion.
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, who is named Divyakarṇa, he then went to the great holy site of Svargalakṣmī, and from there to the great river Brāhmī.
Then he went to Gokarṇa Śambhu and from there to the dwellings of the sages;
thereafter, he made his residence in a forest of coconut trees.
He performed the propitiation of Hari and served the virtuous;
he performed the chanting of my names, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (3.97.60)
Thus he performed his devotions, constantly remembering me;
by obtaining the food of alms from the virtuous, he sustained the journey of his body.
For nine times ten thousand years he sustained himself on alms-food;
thereafter, for a thousand years, he subsisted on roots and tubers.
Then, for five thousand years, he subsisted on dry leaves;
thereafter, he remained absorbed in meditative concentration, subsisting only on air.
Meditating on the self within the self, he united with the Supreme Self;
then, when a hundred thousand years had fully elapsed, [a voice] from the sky [spoke]. ||64||
Beholding that celestial chariot of Viṣṇu, accompanied by his divinely beautiful attendants, approaching, this noble lord Ālambāyana [stood there]. (65)
Quickly casting off his physical body, he then became possessed of a divine form,
four-armed and marked with the signs of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and other emblems.
And the sage, the foremost attendant of Viṣṇu, having bowed to the hosts of sages,
went to the abode of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, causing the people to marvel as he spoke.
Then, as he was departing, the sages praised that lord of munis:
"O great devotee, lead us to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha. (68)
And he said, "O all you sages, be ready quickly;
having gone to Vaikuṇṭha itself, I shall return by means of celestial chariots. (69)
Having asked Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa for permission to take him along with you,
and being told "Om" by the sages, he went quickly to the abode of Hari.
Honored by the attendants and brought down from the celestial chariot,
he entered that most excellent palace within the supreme divine mansion in Vaikuṇṭha.
Not seeing Śrī Hari in the palace, she quickly went outside;
she searched for that palace where Śrī Narāyaṇa resides.
Having gone there and performed prostration like a staff, he indeed offered worship from his heart;
he cried out again and again, "Victory to Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa!"
He shed tears from his eyes and was choked with emotion for a moment;
he fell at the feet of Viṣṇu and then drank the nectar of those feet.
Questioned with a welcome by Hari, he spoke what was in his heart:
"O Lord, by your grace, I have joyfully attained your eternal feet. (75)
And those sages dwelling at Gokarṇa, whose wealth is their austerity, said to me at the time of my departure: "Go to that abode together with us. (76)
I replied, "I am going; I shall come to you by all means. Having received the command of Hari, let everyone be prepared in every respect. (77)
Thus addressed, they awaited the arrival of Vaikuṇṭha, saying, "If you have the command, I shall go and bring him to your presence. (78)
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "O devotee, you have performed what is fitting;
however, understand from me something further, the most excellent among the excellent, the supreme. (79)
Without devotion to me, there shall be no dwelling for me in Vaikuṇṭha.
At Gokarṇa dwell sages whose wealth is austerity and who are fond of penance.
Those who possess control over the mind and likewise control over the senses, who always delight in the Self alone, and who are solely devoted to knowledge; ||81||
Many others are devoted solely to their vows and are free from passion; some are intent on the practice of yoga, while others abide in dry asceticism. ||82||
Devoid of devotion to me and lacking my worship, how could they be worthy of the meaning of the scriptures or of my abode? ||83||
Vaikuṇṭha is not for those who are devoid of devotion, even if they constantly perform austerities;
nor is Vaikuṇṭha for ritualists who do not know how to worship.
The cause for my coming to my abode is always love and devotion toward me;
indeed, the service of my devotee consists of the total surrender of the self unto me. (85)
Meditation upon Me, as well as constant devotion and chanting of My names, and the dedication of austerities, vows, and gifts unto Me—[these are the means]. (86)
The dedication of all actions and the undertaking of initiation from me, as well as the reception of my divine mantra, are likewise the causes. (87)
Since even the propitiation of Me leads to the arrival in Vaikuṇṭha,
those yogins who are unripe must practice austerities for a long time.
Some have lifespans equal to ten lakhs, some likewise equal to one lakh, and others are long-lived for many yugas by the thousands. (89)
"Give this mantra of mine, which bestows liberation, to them;
having granted initiation, perform the great sacrifice of the Name-sacrifice."
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge and husband.
Having granted this mantra, then bestow upon me the gracious initiation.
One should wear a tulasī necklace on the neck, as well as a garland and a rosary for recitation;
furthermore, one should apply the tilaka and the crescent mark (candraka), and likewise bear the marks of the discus and other emblems.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who are without beginning; O Śrī Puruṣottama; O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī; O all-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! ||93||
In this way, constantly promote the glorification of the virtuous;
day and night, let those who are consecrated remain there for the great sacrifice.
To those whose propitiation is complete and whose devotion shall be perfect, I shall always [convey] them by means of my own resplendent celestial chariot.
"I shall indeed lead you to Vaikuṇṭha; go and commence the sacrificial session.
Thus addressed, Alambāyana, the king of devotees and a personal attendant (pārṣada), bowed down.
He arrived at his ancient abode in Gokarṇa by means of a celestial body and a divine chariot;
at that time, it was instantly illuminated by his splendor. ||97||
The sages, filled with agitation, fled toward that retinue; having bowed to them as they stood ready, he delivered the message spoken by Viṣṇu.
"Let those who are well-initiated perform a sacrificial session here for the chanting of the Name.
The auspicious sages likewise performed it for the sake of attaining Vaikuṇṭha. (99)
And by the power of their austerity, they perceived the supreme greatness of devotion;
having become devotees and been initiated, they received their rosaries for recitation.
Indeed, for the sake of liberation, hundreds of thousands of sages as well as other people of the world chanted his glories day and night. || 10.1 ||
Having heard that narration, they gathered there and performed worship;
consequently, that sacred site became famous by the name Vaikuṇṭhasatra.
At the end of the month, for those who had become ripened through devotion,
the Lord Hari arrived in his own celestial chariot, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Śrī.
The Supreme Lord led a thousand virtuous ones to Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, at the end of each month and even at the end of three months, he led some others.
At the end of four, five, or more months, Hari led hundreds of thousands of people away;
having become fully ripened, those sages depart for his abode.
Those virtuous ones residing at Gokarṇa all departed for Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode, at the end of the year; indeed, that was a great wonder.
Beginning with the Nāmasatra sacrifice, the gods and others, as well as human beings,
go from the holy site of Gokarṇa to the Supreme Lord Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme majesty of devotion been described,
wherein the Blessed Lord, through association with the virtuous, causes the chanting of His glories to be performed.
Having caused the ascetics to be purified, he led them to his own supreme abode;
at the end of the year, having completed the sacrifice of names, this virtuous one departed.
Having assumed a divine body and traveling in a celestial chariot, he went to the abode of Hari;
thereafter, millions of perfected beings (sādhus) came to be there in Siṃhāraṇya.
That great Gokarṇa became a sacred abode equal to the abode of Viṣṇu;
thus, O Lakṣmī, the service of the virtuous indeed bears fruit, albeit after a long time.
Even for those born as humans, association with the virtuous bears fruit, though perhaps after a long time;
therefore, one should cultivate excellent association with the good, for it will be fruitful. (11.2)
O Lakṣmī, through its recitation, hearing, and even remembrance, this [work] bestows liberation;
it brings about association with the virtuous, which grants eternal emancipation.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how Liberation is Attained through the Company of the Virtuous even by those Engaged in Worldly Exertions, and likewise by Ascetics," concerning the attainment of liberation at Gokarṇa by hundreds of thousands of men through the association with the saint Ālambāyana, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Kṛṣṇakānta, for the benefit of the world, show me that way by which even one fallen into great calamity may be swiftly delivered. || 1 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
I always bow down to the virtuous ones, for whom Brahman is the supreme wealth;
in whose palm heaven resides, and even liberation abides in their speech.
I bow down to those— whether children, youths, or the elderly— who are virtuous and stainless,
and who bear the burden of devotion to Hari.
They were experts in the knowledge of Brahman, humble, with minds under control,
speakers of the language of Brahman, learned in the Vedas, observant of vows, and adorned by their virtuous conduct.
I bow to those virtuous people who, in assemblies, are speakers of Brahman and whose forms are the imperishable Brahman; they are auspicious in nature and radiant.
I long even more for those who are worthy of being served by them, who occupy the foremost seats in the assembly of Brahmā, and who are perfected in higher knowledge and meditative absorption.
When they listen with devotion, there is great happiness both in this world and after death;
they bring about the destruction of all calamities and are auspicious deliverers.
O Rame, well-prepared foods, cool waters,
and beautiful garments should always be given to them.
Blessed would he be who, being meritorious, obtains birth in a virtuous family;
and may he become, in a future time, the liberator of ten million beings.
"O Lakṣmī, there is no one on the surface of the earth dearer to me than you;
yet all those who are beloved of Brahmā, the virtuous ones, are most dear to me. (3.98.10)
O lotus-eyed ones, my parents are not as dear to me in this world as virtuous and peaceful people, who are always my most excellent and supreme beloveds.
Even for one fallen into great calamity, the virtuous in this world bring about auspiciousness;
they are to be revered and worshipped as deities even by the gods.
The worlds call me "Sāttvata," and I am pleased by that;
those who practice devotion call me the virtuous Lord through their union with the good. (13)
Just as the dharma of women is known to have its basis in their husband, so too is the dharma of all people considered to have its basis in the virtuous; such is the bull [of dharma]. 14.
Among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, virtuous men are considered gurus;
indeed, virtuous men are to be worshipped like gods and like Kṛṣṇa, and are truly to be served.
Those virtuous and stainless Brahmins should be served like fire;
through service to the virtuous, that Brahminhood which purifies all remains established. (16)
Just as a woman, in the absence of her husband, takes her brother-in-law as her husband, so too, in the absence of a virtuous ruler, the subjects make an image their lord. (17)
One should always attend upon the virtuous—those who are upright, truthful in character, devoted to the welfare of all living beings, and friends to all creatures. (18)
Just as a king protects his own kinsmen, so should he protect virtuous people;
and he should look after the hermitage, considering what sustenance is available for their livelihood.
The wealthy man should protect those most devoted to Brahman as well as the Veda itself in every way;
the wealthy man should obtain the blessings of the virtuous who are satisfied with alms.
Having given one's word, one must not fail to give; for that very act leads to a great hell—the sin of destroying hope, which destroys all merit. (21)
The oblation offered, the gift bestowed, and the austerity practiced—all these are frustrated for one who destroys hope;
yet the giving of hope indeed produces the merit of a horse-sacrifice. ||22||
The fulfillment of hope shall yield the fruit of a thousand Viṣṇu-sacrifices;
therefore, having granted this hope, one should fulfill it according to one's power.
Once, a dog-eater and a vulture met at a cremation ground;
then the dog-eater slowly questioned the vulture as it was devouring a corpse.
What sin indeed have you committed that you eat this putrid food—this loathsome corpse, exceedingly foul-smelling and soaked with moisture here? (25)
The vulture said: "In former times, I was a wealthy man possessed by greed;
even after making a promise, I gave nothing at all, or gave only an incomplete portion.
By that sin, I have been born here as a vulture dwelling in the cremation ground. (26)
Therefore, being hungry, I eat even such an extremely despicable thing as this;
tell me now, how did you come to be born in the womb of a dog-eater? (27)
The dog-cooker said: "Formerly, although I was possessed of wealth and grain, I was a reviler of the virtuous; though a Brahmin, I was full of contempt. (28)
Seeing virtuous people, I revile them and treat them with contempt; I mock them, I do not give alms to anyone, and I even obstruct others. (29)
"Because of that sin, my entire property—including my home, wife, children, and so forth—was destroyed by the fury of fire; I myself was consumed, and thus I am burnt. (3.98.30)
Having gone to the realm of Yama, they were cast there by the agents of Yama into the blinding darkness for many years, with their eyes and tongues extracted.
Then I became a female hunter with a snare;
after that, I was a snake, then an owl, and then a lizard. (3.2)
Consequently, I was indeed born as a caṇḍāla because of my reviling of the virtuous;
therefore, those who are dear to Hari, the virtuous, should never be treated with contempt.
Their alms are not to be obstructed, nor indeed should their gift ever be withheld; their property must not be seized, but rather given to them for their satisfaction. (34)
One should avoid disputes with those who are most devoted to Brahman, with virtuous men, and likewise with virtuous women; and what has been promised must be given.
One should never engage in censuring them, nor should one ever listen to such talk; furthermore, one must not harbor pride regarding one's status as a Brahmin in the presence of the virtuous. (36)
Those Brahmins who are householders frequent women and cemeteries;
though they follow a downward path compared to the virtuous, the virtuous are indeed worthy of worship by Brahmins.
Those who are drenched and stuck in urine are indeed destined for hell;
those virtuous ones who are disciplined in ethical conduct are capable of uplifting them. (38)
A thief cannot save a thief; he who is not a thief can save him.
One possessed by desire cannot save from desire; one free from desire can save the lover.
One must not take the property of the virtuous, and one should always be patient with them;
nor should children, the wretched, or those who are powerless be held in contempt. (3.98.40)
One should not constantly place expectations upon the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's own interests;
nor should one employ the virtuous like servants merely for the purpose of obtaining food. (41)
Likewise, for the sake of obtaining water, for the perception of the sky, the wind, the moon,
and so forth, and for the purpose of a seat, a dwelling, and a shelter in a house.
One should not cause a virtuous person to undergo hardship, for through such exertion his merit perishes;
indeed, householders should never dwell in the company of the virtuous. 43.

One should always go to the hermitage for the sake of the company of the virtuous, never for the sake of the afflictions, nor for the sake of sleep, nor for the sake of discharging excrement and urine. (44)
One should not go out at all to attend to one's own bodily needs;
for holy men, even the distraction or movement involved in such acts during a time of peace is a hindrance. (45)
One should never engage in improper conduct, nor should one ever sit upon a high seat in the presence of virtuous people. (46)
One should never engage in dispute—whether by word, wealth, action, knowledge for the sake of one's own livelihood, or through force—as a person driven by greed. (47)
One should not engage in debate with the wicked, nor with the virtuous; one should harbor no desire for their wealth, nor should the virtuous be brought under one's control. (48)
For the virtuous, the act of observation should never concern the physical body;
their own dispositions of passion and aversion must not be directed toward the virtuous. (49)
In the hermitage, one should not engage in talk of villages, talk of afflictions, false talk, or talk of sensual enjoyments; nor should one utter anything that causes dishonor. (3.98.50)
One should not employ pride, nor should one display strength or power toward the virtuous;
for the virtuous must never be humiliated, since by doing so, one's merit perishes. (51)
"I know what is good"—thinking thus, she became proud;
indeed, pride should never be indulged in anywhere, for it is the cause of one's downfall. (52)
Upon seeing a virtuous person, one should bow; for failing to bow is a destroyer of merit.
One should [recognize] one's own defects such as desire, as well as the defects inherent in women and those within one's own self. (53)
One should not inflict impurity upon the good regarding their own true nature;
one should indeed go to the abode of the virtuous solely for the sake of attaining excellence.
In this world, there are many people who are masters of wickedness, acting for the sake of satisfying their own sense-objects and even for the sake of satisfying their sense of touch. (55)
They go even to the grounds where throngs of women gather merely for the sake of visual gratification—
to temples, festivals, and sacred sites— where there is the crushing of womenfolk.
In the midst of a crowd, even while engaged in playful stories and the like, they seize upon faults right there in the case of virtuous men as well as women. (57)
By that sin, they are born blind from birth, afflicted with leprosy, or as eunuchs; likewise, they become long-suffering from disease, impoverished, and wretched. (58)
Women also become similarly afflicted by diseases, and they are deprived of children and the like, as well as destitute of wealth, grain, and other possessions. (59)
Therefore, one should not grasp at the faults of even virtuous and holy people;
rather, one should grasp only their virtues, which grant happiness, merit, and auspiciousness. (3.98.60)
Just as people, having set aside the fine thorns, the leaves, the bark, and the fibers from a stalk of sugarcane, extract its juice; ||61||
Just as when burnt asafoetida has been cast into vegetables within a meal, people discard the leaves and other parts and eat only the vegetables themselves. (62)
Just as embodied beings, having indeed discarded the seed-skin and other parts contained within the fruit,
consume only the embryo and suck its juices.
Just as people, having abandoned the defects inherent in a tree, take its fruit;
and just as they, having abandoned the defects inherent in a creeper, take its flower.
Likewise, having abandoned the faults found in the virtuous, one should acquire their virtues;
for one who conducts oneself in this manner, there is the attainment of merit at every step.
For those who possess the virtues of the virtuous, there shall arise an infinity of increase in lifespan, knowledge, and fame, as well as the perfection of wealth, grain, and prosperity. (66)
For when the virtuous are pleased and welcome their servant,
that house indeed becomes enriched with all kinds of jewels.
One who delights the virtuous should nourish sons, grandsons, cattle, kinsmen, and householders, as well as the village and the entire country. (68)
By giving to virtuous people, the unsurpassed heaven is certainly attained;
liberation can also be achieved, for service to the virtuous is the supreme practice. (69)
The deities and the ancestors live upon what is given to the virtuous;
when they are liberated, they are satisfied, for the Blessed One indeed partakes [of offerings] among the righteous people.
Therefore, gifts should be given to the virtuous by one who possesses discernment; for the virtuous person of pure consciousness is indeed a most divine sacred ford. 71.
The upholders of the Dharma are my virtuous embodiments;
they are the protectors of the helpless and the removers of suffering for those in pain. (72)
The virtuous are indeed the washers away of sins, the destroyers of the faults of offenders, and the providers of refuge for those who have been insulted. (73)
Listen, I shall relate an ancient tale: a twice-born man was rescued by holy men.
On the Himalayas there was a beautiful hermitage frequented by sages. (74)
The hermitage named Ṛṣidhāma was adorned by perfected sages and brahmins,
as well as by ascetics observing vows, those practicing restraints, and those who had been initiated.
It was likewise established by those of perfected selves,
virtuous ascetics, for the sake of the seer Dīrghatapas, the best of the twice-born and a yogin.
Then a certain Śabara, a forest-dweller,
arrived there and beheld the auspicious hosts of sages, who were like gods and devoted to asceticism.
Having resolved to practice austerities, he questioned Dīrghatapas:
"O Blessed One, you should tell me the Dharma and initiate me into the wandering life. (78)
“I am a Śūdra and I wish to perform service for you; be gracious to me.
Dīrghatapas then said, “Since you abide as a Śūdra... (79)
"It is not possible for you to go forth [into homelessness], for you have not relinquished your royal authority. Therefore, remain right here; if it pleases you, perform service [to me]."
"O forest-dweller, through service you shall attain the highest worlds.
Having been addressed thus, that Śabara also rejoiced in the vicinity of the hermitage. (81)
Having made his own dwelling at the foot of a tree, he indeed lived there;
he provided food such as fruits and flowers and performed service for the sage. ||82||
Once, by his own nature, he caught a wild hare;
having killed it, he made a meal near the hermitage of the sage. (83)
Then those sages abandoned that harmful Śūdra and cursed him:
"Become a Rākṣasa and remain miserable in the midst of the forest! (84)
Quickly assuming a deformed form as a Rākṣasa, he roamed through the forest;
then, overwhelmed by the extreme suffering of hunger and thirst, he went to the bank of the Gaṅgā. ||85||
There, he beheld a virtuous man named Nārāyaṇa-muni, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, who was immersed in austerity and devoted to bhakti. (86)
The Rākṣasa quickly went to the bank to devour the Sādhu;
seeing the Rākṣasa, the Sādhu likewise gazed back at him with his eyes. (87)
He sprinkled water upon the head and the body of the Rākṣasa, saying:
"Become pure, become righteous-souled, and be freed from suffering. (88)
"O sinner, you shall be released from the curse right here in the presence of me, the ascetic.
Thus addressed, the Śabara quickly touched water.
Having abandoned his demonic nature, the man became divine;
then he approached the holy Nārāyaṇa-muni, the deliverer.
The purifier of the worlds served her with supreme affection;
even though he was a Śūdra, through his association with the virtuous, he thereafter became full of devotion. (91)
Having received the command of the virtuous one, he departed toward another forest;
there he constantly worshipped Nārāyaṇa and performed rigorous austerities. (92)
At the end of his body, that Śabara indeed attained a supreme kingdom;
for he became King Vīravikrama of Ujjayinī.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of Hari and likewise performed supreme devotion,
he went to the imperishable abode and became liberated through the company of the virtuous.
That family, having performed service to the holy man (sādhu), attained the supreme state;
therefore, O vulture, holy men who are adorned by their saintliness should always be served. 95.
"Come; here nearby is a virtuous man named Kṛṣṇa.
By taking refuge in him, we two shall indeed become purified and cleansed of sin. (96)
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, Kṛṣṇa and [Balarāma] went toward your name; they bowed, they praised, and they indeed made their request. 97.
Then the virtuous one performed their liberation and made them drink water;
the purifier quickly offered them his grace and fed them. 98.
He caused their sin to be consumed by fire and made it heard;
he also quickly bestowed upon them both the name Nārāyaṇa. 99.
Then, having abandoned their physical bodies through the power of their virtuous conduct,
those two, freed from sin, went to heaven and became gods.
Having indeed enjoyed heaven as the fruit of their grace by virtue of that excellent refuge,
the two of them in due time went to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Supreme Self.
Thus, association with the virtuous, even if practiced for but a moment, truly purifies and swiftly bestows a mass of merit— this is indeed Lakṣmī herself.
Association with the true yogis of Kṛṣṇa bestows both sovereignty and heaven, grants even liberation, and bestows supreme bliss. (103)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How Even for One in Distress, Association with the Holy Brings Prosperity," concerning the liberation from heaven and other realms of the vulture, the outcaste, and the Śabara, in the section on the Dvāpara Age within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 98 ||
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe, that is true; wherever Your saints reside, there the accomplishments of the goals of human life are found. (1)
And those virtuous, stainless people who are most dear to my husband—I always carry the dust of their feet upon my head. (2)
I carry out their commands— whether they be beneficial or harmful—
with total fearlessness and by giving everything, solely for your sake.
The speech of the virtuous, purified by truth—however it may be—is indeed the supreme Veda;
for you reside within that speech.
The vow of silence always abides in the wise, for their speech is never obscured;
the virtuous speak only of the supreme reality and not of worldly matters.
It must be said that they possess a mouth; this is simply the natural state of the virtuous.
For the subtle course of truth is indeed difficult to be understood by those of undisciplined mind.
One should never speak according to the inclinations of the deluded;
since faults may be transferred through speech, silence is better for the virtuous.
Such men are born and exist in this world;
even a teacher or an instructor would speak according to his own opinion if he were to say so. (8)
Then that king of gurus is proclaimed as one who knows otherwise;
such indeed become the disciples, shrouded in most terrible darkness.
A teacher who does not oppose his own doctrine is indeed a teacher, and not otherwise;
therefore, they become hell-beings both in this world and in the next.

Therefore, whatever opinion is held here by the female disciples or by the male disciples—if that opinion is indeed contradictory and subverts the scriptures, the Dharma, and so forth—[it must be rejected]. || 1.1 ||
At that time, the teacher should not accept them; such disciples must be rejected, for generally many in the world possess a false pride in their learning. 12.
Indeed, disciples who consider themselves wise become subordinates who dictate to their teachers; wandering upon a wrong path, they surely fall further and further down. 13.
Evil speech is a great sin and must never be uttered;
the virtuous should not speak such things before anyone at all. (14)
O Kṛṣṇa, sages observe the excellent vow of silence during their initiation into self-restraint; out of fear of speaking ill, they do not utter idle or false words.
Righteous, endowed with virtues, and possessed of truth and devotion,
the sages lead others to the supreme state through instructions in truth.
Through the gift of the Veda, they indeed shatter the evil deeds of listeners and lead them to the ocean of bliss, bestowing the grace of the Supreme Lord. (17)
One who is an unfit vessel should seek refuge; such a person must be examined in every way. Instruction should not be given hastily without first ascertaining their disposition.
And because of teaching one who is unworthy, that sin transfers to the teacher;
therefore, the gift of knowledge must indeed be bestowed by one devoted to truth after careful deliberation.
For instruction given to one who is untruthful or unworthy indeed destroys one's own [virtue];
therefore, such knowledge should be imparted by which one may preserve the truth. (3.99.20)
By whom the eternal deity Nārāyaṇa is propitiated—such are those of truthful character who have taken refuge in Satyanārāyaṇa. (2.1)
The virtuous gurus are my devotees of truth and the eternal;
O Blessed One, I dwell wherever my stainless gurus reside.
Fortunate ones who know Brahman, who are bold, skilled in devotion, and intent upon the service of Śrī Hari, are honored by you together with [yourself]. (23)
Devoted to the gods, grateful, with senses conquered, and characterized by goodness; intent on the goals of human life, divine, and virtuous—there I dwell. (24)
Wherever my beloved Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, dwells, there you shall abide; I shall reside there by means of the gift of all my possessions.

I do not dwell with one who is devoid of the goals of human life, nor with an atheist, nor with an ungrateful person; I certainly do not dwell with one who causes the confusion of dharma, nor with one who has broken the boundaries of conduct.
I do not dwell at all—in any way—within one who is cruel, a slanderer, a wicked person, a thief, one who is envious of gurus, a hater of the virtuous, or one who is arrogant. (27)
I do not abide in one who has little splendor, who is devoid of being, who is bereft of strength, who is afflicted, who is angry, or who is unstable and lacking in steadfastness. (28)
I do not dwell forever in one who is by nature unseeking, who is ruined when thwarted, who is easily satisfied with little, who is profligate, or who is addicted to vice. (29)

I dwell in this great festival among those rich in Dharma, who know the Dharma, who are self-controlled, who serve their elders, who are devoted to forbearance, and who have accomplished all that was to be done. (3.99.30)
I dwell among women who are truthful in nature, self-controlled, and humble;
I dwell among those rich in uprightness, who serve the virtuous. (3.1)
And I dwell within those who honor their bodies, twice-born brahmins, gurus, masters, and deities;
yet I reside in one who is impure, fickle, indolent in her own duties, and antagonistic. (32)
I always avoid one who stands in opposition to her husband, who aids the side of his enemies, and who is shameless and intolerant.
I abandon her who is full of service to the wicked and the unvirtuous, who is angry, devoid of fortitude, deceitful, the root of quarrels, and excessively prone to sleep. (34)
I dwell among those women who are devoted to truth, divine, and endowed with virtue and good fortune; those who are faithful to their husbands, possessed of good character, and well-adorned. (35)
I dwell in well-yoked vehicles, in devoted young maidens, in sacrifices properly performed, and in temples. (36)
I dwell in flowers, in the bodies of grain, in elephants and stables, in cow-pens, at the feet of the virtuous, and in lotuses. (37)
In regions endowed with rivers, among ascetics, perfected ones, and yogis;
likewise in a bull, in a herd of cattle, in a king, and in a virtuous person. (38)
O Mādhava, I always dwell in a lofty seat, in one where offerings are made to the sacrificial fire, in a place that honors gods, cows, and Brahmins, and in a mansion beautiful with hospitality. (39)
I dwell eternally and powerfully within the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, in the saintly man who is His follower, in the virtuous woman, and also in the devotees. (3.99.40)
O Keśava, in this place where I dwell, beings have become serene and invisible;
by your command, I increase their virtue, fame, wealth, and desire.
O Blessed One, I shall tell you my secret here in every respect:
wherever virtuous people are served, there I always dwell. (42)
The virtuous are the forms of the Blessed One, the embodiments of my Lord; for the sake of attaining service to them and for the sake of obtaining your favor, [I pray]. (43)
I dwell eternally with the virtuous, with the female servant, and with the male servant;
wherever Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa is, and wherever the chaste Śrī-Kambharā is.
Wherever those who are contented dwell, wherever Śrī Harivallabha resides, and wherever there is worship of you and Hari, there indeed I dwell eternally. (45)
Those people who worship Hari with the disposition of offering their very selves, being devoid of any sense of self-interest—I never abandon them at any time. (46)

Where there are excellent food-offerings and sacrificial sessions, where there are always virtuous hermitages, and where there is auspicious service to the righteous—there I dwell, bestowing prosperity. (47)
Wherever the intellect of a servant remains free from guile, and wherever the mind is devoid of fault, there I dwell in every way. (48)
I dwell in every way in the house of that person for whom the virtuous are considered superior to home, wife, children, sons, and wealth. (49)
Where virtuous men honor women more than their husbands, fathers-in-law, and other elders, there I shall dwell in every way. (3.99.50)
Where there is the chanting of the virtuous, where there is the sight of the virtuous, and where there is always affection for the good—there I dwell in every way. (51)
Wherever the Blessed One, the Blessed Ones, Hari, and likewise the saints, as well as master and servants dwell, there I always reside. (52)
Where my Lord does not abide, nor do His devoted saints, there I shall set, having risen like the sun through the power of my merit. (53)
I shall surely abandon that house where a day passes without the chanting of your name, for I am tormented by fainting. (54)
That house where no food for virtuous men is found, I consider a dark abyss and abandon it like a cremation ground. (55)
That house where even in the rainy season the foot of a virtuous person is never seen—I indeed abandon that meritless dwelling as if it were a cemetery. (56)
I shall surely abandon that house which is devoid of your festivals, even if no festival of Kṛṣṇa occurs there during the entire year. (57)
Wherever your devotees do not exist and do not dwell anywhere,
there I have no desire at all for residence, even in an ocean of mud.
In whatever palace, mansion, house, or temple the Lord Nārāyaṇa is not present, there I do not dwell at all. (59)
Wherever there is no offering to Nārāyaṇa in the morning—whether in a golden palace, a golden treasury, or even upon a royal throne—I do not dwell there at all. (3.99.60)
Where there is no ghee lamp before the worship of Hari,
where there is no incense and no arati offering, there I do not dwell at all.
Where there is no food offering made for Viṣṇu, nor even water, and where a devotee of Viṣṇu never eats, there I do not dwell. (62)
Where there is no great festival for the eighth day of Jayantī and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, there I certainly do not dwell. (63)
Where the verses of descent are not heard, nor is there any worship or image of the Lord, there I do not dwell at all. (64)
Where the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth, as well as the tulasī plant, are not found at all, there I do not dwell. (65)
Where there is neither the story nor the physical form of the incarnations of Lakṣmī, nor even those of the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa, there I do not dwell. ||66||
Where there is no honoring of the virtuous, no service to the elderly, and no respect for cows, there I certainly do not dwell. (67)
Where there is no ancestral rite for the gods, the ancestors, or the living, and where there is no gift of merit, there I do not dwell at all. (68)
I do not dwell at all in that house where children are not protected with food and other necessities, nor where women are subjected to torment. (69)
I do not dwell at all in that place where there is a breach of social order within the household, where those who have sought refuge are oppressed, or where cattle are confined.
In the city gate there is an image of Nārāyaṇa;
even there I do not dwell for long. (7.1)
I dwell in that house where Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, garlanded with elephant-lotuses, shine upon the moon-chambers and other parts.
Where Gaṇeśa is not present, nor have the Śrī Mātṛs been established, and where there is no form of the Bindu, I do not dwell there for long at any time. 73.
Where there is mental distress between a man and a woman regarding their children and so forth, or indifference between a servant and a master, there I do not dwell. (74)
I do not dwell where the protector is a master who consumes [his subjects] and is devoid of dharma, nor where there is one who hates Nārāyaṇa; such a place is a den of thieves.
In that garden where divine trees do not exist at all, nor sacrificial creepers and trees, there I certainly do not dwell. //76//
In whatever field, though beautiful with crops, there is no wandering of the virtuous,
there I do not arise even as a single grain, for I am one who transcends such things.
Where the virtuous do not bathe—in a lake, a river, a stream, a small pond, or even a well—I do not dwell in that water, however pleasant its taste may be. //78//
Neither in a worldly assembly, nor likewise in an assembly of gods,
nor in an assembly of the learned do I dwell, if it is not virtuous.
Whether in an assembly of kings or an assembly of subjects, or likewise at a sacred pilgrimage site, there is no one whose soul is devoted [to me] there; therefore, I shall depart from that place.
I shall withdraw even from that assembly which is devoid of virtuous men, from that work which is not offered to Hari, and from that acquisition which is devoid of charity. 8.1.
Wherever Indra, victory, and prosperity reside—in the sacrificial post, the pillar, or the house—and wherever the Lord of Śrī himself dwells, there I dwell, O Keśava. (82)
Where there is no lamp at night and no offering by day, where there is no arrival of oil, from there I shall depart. (83)
Where poverty shines even in matters such as religious duties and hospitality, and where gifts are but worn-out remnants, from there I shall depart. (84)
Where Sītā and the bulls are not honored at the time of plowing, and where the earth is not honored, there I do not dwell at all. (85)
Where there is no mark of vermilion or sandalwood paste upon the forehead, and where the ornament of good fortune is absent—from there I shall depart. (86)
O Keśava, I dwell wherever there is the gift of fearlessness, the pointing out of the path to liberation, and the songs and life-stories of devotees. (87)
I always dwell with joy in the speech, the heart, and the feet of the virtuous, who are of the nature of ethical discipline and free from grasping. (88)
I dwell in all things—in the water, leaves, flowers, and grains remaining from the worship of Hari; in His grace, in food, in clothing, and in every material object. (89)
I dwell tirelessly within one who is initiated, within a devotee of Sāttvata, within a virtuous wife of a Brahmin, and within a woman who cooks for the sake of Hari.
Since you are indeed Nārāyaṇa, ever devoted to your wife, you shall never accept anything offered by another without my hand being between us. 91.
Therefore, I dwell perpetually and swiftly within the one who offers [the gift], whether he be the informant, one of my own nature, or even any servant whatsoever. 92.
Whosoever is your female servant is undoubtedly Lakṣmī herself;
indeed, your male servants are the virtuous ones who have surrendered their very selves in every way.
O Lord, I too always practice dwelling among them;
and so do those men and women who are devotees of Hari.
The gods, the ancestors, the great seers, and human beings;
the nāgas, daityas, rākṣasas, and dānavas—all who practice devotion. (95)
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the supreme Vasus;
as well as the Siddhas, Kinnaras, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins—[all these were present]. (96)
The Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases who are the consorts of the lords;
the Yoginīs, the Mothers, the Śaktis, and likewise the Sādhikās. ||97||
The courtesans and their groups, as well as maidens and young boys, the yakṣas, the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, and millions of holy fords; || 98 ||
Whether they be quadrupeds—whether characterized by light (taijasa) or darkness (tāmasa)—or even insects and birds, whatever beings there may be, whether insentient or sentient; || 99 ||
"These have been raised here and there solely for the sake of your devotion;
having gone there quickly, I shall dwell and purify them."
Therefore, O Nārāyaṇa, you accepted that which was given by me from my own hand;
such a vow of devotion to one's wife is not found elsewhere. (101)
Likewise, such devotion to her husband is found in Lakṣmī and nowhere else;
indeed, the virtuous are always endowed with truthfulness and devotion to their husbands. 10.2.
As is Lakṣmī, so are the virtuous; the virtuous are the objects of your sight and are dear to you.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, you are called the beloved of Lakṣmī and the lord of the virtuous.
Therefore, I always dwell undivided within the bodies of my co-wives; yet no one else knows this.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, to you;
salutations to the holy ones, to Lakṣmī, and also to those enriched by Lakṣmī.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eternal Abode of Lakṣmī Among Holy People, the Places Where Lakṣmī Resides, and Her Non-Residence Among Sinners and Others," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy,
Kṛṣṇa is the supreme wealth of the virtuous, the life of the liberated, and the highest deity of the gods.
Is it solely out of compassion that you, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, have come here to this earth, or is there perhaps some other reason? || 2 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O beloved of Śivārājñī, compassion is always the primary cause here;
indeed, my own will alone is the cause for my arrival in every respect regarding creation. (3)
Nevertheless, I shall manifest another certain cause:
whenever I arrive within another creation during a kalpa.
At first, having obtained some pretext from the great sage Bhṛgu in certain places,
I come repeatedly, and also by the desire of my devotees.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: "O Lord, what was the cause for Bhṛgu’s birth, for whose sake you indeed repeatedly assume manifestation here in human form? Please tell me."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the ancient account of the cause [of my birth] among humans due to the curse of Bhṛgu resulting from the killing of the renowned wife of Bhṛgu.
The manifestation of Viṣṇu,
who possesses divine sovereignty and wields the Śārṅga bow, occurs in many ways for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of the gods.
Then, when the dharma of the age has turned away and the bull [of righteousness] has become slack,
the imperishable Viṣṇu is born in order to establish the system of dharma.
In former times, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was the sovereign ruler over the kingdom of the three worlds for ten crores of years.
Furthermore, for seventy-two lakhs of years and likewise eighty thousand years,
the sovereign remained free from disease.
After that, King Prahlāda ruled the earth for ten yugas;
then King Bali likewise reigned for ten koṭis of years.
The earth was level for thirty-six million years;
at that time, three Indras of the Daityas became renowned.
This entire kingdom, extending through the three worlds, was occupied by the Daityas;
in the meantime, there occurred battles that brought about the destruction of both gods and asuras.
There were twelve fierce ones where Viṣṇu,
entreated by the gods, repeatedly joined them and destroyed the Daityas with his divine discus.
O beloved, hear now about all those battles in the Vārāha Kalpa:
first, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Nārasiṃha.
The second was also the Boar incarnation, wherein Hiraṇyākṣa was slain;
and the third was during the churning for the nectar, wherein Prahlāda was conquered.
And Virocana was indeed slain during the Tārakāmaya war;
that Tārakā was the wife of Bṛhaspati, who had been carried off by Candra.
On account of that, a hair-raising battle took place;
at that time, there was a great conflict when Bali was bound by Vāmana.
For in the sixth [kalpa], Āḍībaka and Jambha were slain by Śakra and Viṣṇu;
in the seventh, the Daityas of Tripura and others were destroyed by Śambhu.
In the eighth [chapter], Andhaka, along with the Daityas and Dānavas, was slain;
in the ninth, hundreds of thousands beginning with Vipracitti were destroyed by Śakra.
The asura Vṛtra was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt in the tenth [kalpa],
while in the eleventh, all the Daityas were destroyed by Raji.
And in the twelfth [war], Śaṇḍa, Marka, and the others were struck down by the gods;
these were indeed the twelve battles between the gods and the asuras.
And Viṣṇu was everywhere there a helper to the inhabitants of heaven; and in due course, the sovereignty over the three worlds came to the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
Then the gods indeed approached the sacrifice to receive their shares;
and Yajñanārāyaṇa also became a partisan of the gods.
When the gods had departed from the sacrifice, the Dānavas, the foremost Daityas and Asuras, being powerless and having fallen into terror, spoke to Śukra. || 26 ||
"We are unable to stand upon the earth; we shall enter the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Thus addressed, the preceptor of the asuras, being dejected, spoke these words of consolation.
"Do not fear; O Asuras, I shall sustain you with my own splendor—rain, herbs, foods, juices, nectars, and comforts."
"Having sustained it by my own splendor, I shall bestow it for your sake;
I shall go to Mahādeva for the purpose of the mantra and for victory. (29)
"I shall favor you again once I have returned here later;
for now, you must indeed perform penance in the forest, clothed in bark garments."
If the gods do not slay me until my return, then I shall obtain formidable great mantras from Maheśvara. (3.1)
"I am coming; then we shall fight and surely conquer them. O Dānavas, stay at the hermitage of our father Bhṛgu and wait! (32)
Having instructed the Asuras and having sought refuge in Mahādeva, Kāvya,
having received a welcome and offered worship, bowed down and spoke to Śaṅkara.
"O Śambhu, I desire those mantras which do not exist even in Bṛhaspati—mantras that bring about the defeat of the gods and grant fearlessness among the asuras. (34)
Having heard this, Maheśvara said: "For a full thousand years, indeed, I have observed the vow of conduct by drinking smoke from a pit while remaining with my head downward. (35)
"Living as a celibate student (brahmacārī), you shall drink it; from that, you will obtain the mantras.
Thus addressed by her, Śukra himself became a smoke-drinking ascetic (dhūmapa).
Constantly hanging head-downwards from a branch of a banyan tree on Mount Kailāsa,
the gods then rushed at the Daityas through that opening out of indignation.
Then the Dānavas, with weapons grasped and led by Bṛhaspati, quickly [resolved]: "We shall certainly not be able to conquer the gods. (38)
Having bowed down to Śukra’s mother, Khyāti, they then departed;
terrified with fear, they sought refuge and obtained safety from her.
The wife of Bhṛgu performed a protection-rite; however, the gods, filled with wrath, struck down the Asuras on all sides, and at that time, Khyāti became enraged.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, Satī restrained Indra and worshipped him;
thus restrained, Indra was quickly brought under her control and became motionless.
Upon seeing him, the gods fled in the ten directions;
then Viṣṇu said to Śakra, "Entrust him quickly to me."
"Having caused you to enter, I shall protect you; do not fear, O best of gods.
Viṣṇu, having caused Indra to enter his own body, indeed protected him.
Seeing that he was protected by Viṣṇu, the enraged Khyāti spoke these words:
"In a mere moment, I shall consume both Viṣṇu and Mahendra! (44)
Having heard this, Indra said to Hari, "O Supreme Lord, act quickly!
Slay her with the Sudarśana before Satī consumes us with her fire."
Viṣṇu, in great haste, released his discus for the sake of her life;
Khyāti severed her head, and having fallen, she died.
Upon hearing of the murder of his sister, Bhṛgu was immediately incensed and cursed him:
"May you be a slayer of women among human beings again and again. (47)
Having taken birth, experience extreme sufferings again and again; endure the miseries caused by women in this world over and over. (48)
Thus, through the power of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu, the Infallible One, is born here among men for the sake of the welfare of the world's affairs when dharma has perished. (49)
Then Bhṛgu, taking up the head, quickly joined it to the body:
"If the entire Dharma has been practiced by me, or even if it is known," [3.100.50]
I am devoted to my wife, and you are intent on devotion to your husband;
by that truth, live, live in the presence of Viṣṇu!
Having spoken thus and sprinkled her with water, Bhṛgu restored her to life;
Khyāti, having quickly awakened from her sleep, understood that at that very moment.
Viṣṇu, through his yogic power, destroyed that paralysis of Indra;
thereafter, Bhṛgu became pacified and praised the Supreme Lord.
He constantly begged for forgiveness and offered auspicious food and other gifts;
yet Viṣṇu would not accept them, for Mādhava spoke thus to Bhṛgu.
"When your daughter becomes my future wife, O Bhārgava, then I shall indeed come and take my meal together with her. (55)
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu then departed, leaving behind the Daityas and the others;
Indra, restored to his composure, went to heaven, and the gods returned to their own abodes.
The Daityas and others, established in their own places near the hermitage in the field of Bhṛgu,
perform austerities and await the arrival of Śukra.
Śukra, too, by the command of Śaṅkara, performs severe penance beneath a banyan tree with his head hanging downwards in the presence of Hara and Pārvatī. 58.
When a full thousand years had passed, Śaṅkara himself, having approached the banyan tree, became visible nearby in a divine form. (59)
And Śakra, even while hanging from the banyan tree, praised that Śambhu:
"Salutations be to the blue-throated one, to the one with matted hair, and to Śambhu! (3.100.60)
To you, the bountiful Rudra, the possessor of heroic power, the ruddy one, the Lord of the Mountains, whose eye is the sun, and who sports with Takṣaka. ||61||
Salutations to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the white-hued one, the formidable, and the fierce;
salutations to you, Mahādeva, Śarva, and the hunter of the deer. ||62||
Salutations to Sthāṇu, to the one of many forms, to the three-eyed one, and to Mṛtyu; salutations be to Tryambaka, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva.
Salutation to you, the meditator, the all-pervading, the Lord born in the beginning;
salutation to Vāmadeva, the wearer of animal skins, the sovereign source.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes;
salutations to you, the Lord of creatures (Paśupati), and to the slayer of Pūṣan. ||65||
Salutations to you who are the form of the sun, to the banyan tree, and to Time;
salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Rudra, to Fire, and to the Yogi.
Salutations to the one whose form consists of the eightfold nature beginning with earth, who is both with and without marks;
salutations again and again to you, the Lord of Pārvatī and the Lord of Light.
Salutations to you, the Great Lord, who sounds the hand-drum;
salutations again and again to you, who dwell on Kailāsa and are praised by the gods.
Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas, known by the name Mahāvaiṣṇava;
and repeated salutations to the father of Śukra, who is most established in Brahman. ||69||
Having spoken thus, Śukra ceased; then Śaṅkara said to him:
"O best of Brahmins, do not perform penance; your resolve is fraught with danger."
Nevertheless, O Śukra, at the end of the year I shall fulfill the request of you who are virtuous; to you, whose conduct is marked by vows, I will grant the mantras as you desire.
Having spoken thus, the god Śaṅkara vanished right there;
then Indrāṇī dispatched her own daughter, Jayantī.
"O daughter, it has been told that Śakra is indeed performing a severe penance for the sake of sleeplessness throughout the three worlds; therefore, go to him quickly. (73)
"Serve this Śukra quickly with the service of the bed and other such things, attending to him with various agreeable attentions, remaining ever vigilant. (74)
Having heard this, that beautiful maiden Jayantī went indeed to him;
she, being virtuous, acted according to the words spoken by her father regarding Śukra.
Śukra said to her, "O fair-hipped one, remain with me for ten years in invisible form, and grant me union. (76)
Thus commanded by Śukra, she remained with him for ten years;
like Śukra, she became an ascetic, always possessed of subtle yogic power.
Then, after ten years, Bṛhaspati assumed his own form consisting of Śukra’s appearance and instructed the Asuras at that time.
Then, after ten years had passed, Śukra approached the Daityas and said:
"I am Śukra, O lords of the Daityas; listen to my words. (79)
The Daityas said: "You are not our master; Śukra is certainly not true to his word.
For ten years, this Śukra alone has been our true master."
Thus insulted by the asuras, Śukra cursed them:
"O Daityas, you have not welcomed the truth as taught by me. (81)
"Therefore, with your vigor utterly destroyed, you shall meet with defeat.
Having been thus cursed, those Asuras and the deities both understood the curse. (82)
They fought with the Dānavas and others, and they slew many asuras;
yet, overcome by the curse of Kāvya and deprived of the support of Śukra, [they were defeated]. ||83||
Being struck down, those Asuras entered the netherworld (rasātala);
victory was achieved by the gods, with Viṣṇu as their ally.
O Lakṣmī, this cause of Viṣṇu’s births has been told to you;
taking Bhṛgu as the occasion, Viṣṇu is born again and again.
From Dharma, Nārāyaṇa was born; and during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, Hari appeared.
During the Vaivasvata Manvantara, Viṣṇu became Pṛthu and Vāmana, the son of Aditi. (86)
He became Dattātreya and also Pārśurāma;
likewise, he is always Viṣṇu Rāmāditya and Vyāsa.
Vāsudeva is Viṣṇu, and Kalki will be Viṣṇu;
likewise, other incarnations of Viṣṇu also become human beings.
For the sake of destroying the Daityas and for the purpose of protecting Dharma,
[he acted] sometimes by means of women and sometimes for the protection of the gods.
In some cases by means of a religious sign, and in others indeed through compassion—O Lakṣmī, all these are my incarnations and manifestations. (3.100.90)
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person;
by my will and through my grace, I come for the benefit of the virtuous. 9.1.
As a human sage, I protect virtuous brāhmaṇas, bulls, and cows;
the virtuous are my incarnations, and likewise, even my weapons are of such a nature.
The sovereign powers, the incarnations, and likewise the various energies—indeed, my incarnations and my devotees are also of such a nature. (93)
The gods as well are my incarnations for the protection of dharma in every way; by my command, they are born and dissolve within the worlds of creation.
Whatever divine forms of mine exist, all of them are indeed my incarnations, always accepting service and compassionate toward devotees. 95.
Those gods and asuras, daityas, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, men, and women who have obtained my yoga of descent— (96)
Domestic animals, beasts of burden, elephants, and horses, as well as camels, bulls, and others, have come into my power. (97)
"Those who have attained union with my auspicious yoga go, are going, and will go to the supreme state;
such is my compassion, and such is my very nature. (98)
For one who has fully attained my yoga, equality with me arises;
through the yoga of the virtuous one becomes virtuous, and through the yoga of the divine one becomes a deity. 99.
Through my yoga, one such as I indeed becomes a sovereign devotee in person;
by the yoga of Nārāyaṇa, a human being may become Nārāyaṇa himself.
O my beloved, just as Nārāyaṇī was Muktānikā and Ramā,
so too has Padmāvatī become two Nārāyaṇīs for me.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī-Śrī said:
"O Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my husband!
Since two Nārāyaṇīs have now arisen from the lotuses of Ramā, please fulfill my desire for knowledge."
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me clearly here: how and by what cause did this union between Padmāvatī and Ramā come about?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; for you are omniscient like me. Nevertheless, having assumed a human state, you wish to inquire about this.
I shall relate the ancient account of how and by what means this union of these two—
the descendants of Kakutstha and Sūrya— came to pass within the Kārava family.
Formerly, when the thousand-rayed Sun was born, the various high and low regions became like a fire capable of burning the entire universe. || 106 ||
Possessing unbearable brilliance and being exceedingly fierce, it blazed forth from the fissures;
having recognized the radiant Sun, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
That maiden named Saṃjñā also blazed with the splendor of the sun;
she abandoned her own husband and made her own shadow his wife.
Having mounted her own chariot, she departed from her own home;
with a distressed heart, concealing her true feelings, she went to the abode of Viśvakarman.
Although she had been instructed by her father to go to the house of the Sun, that virtuous woman did not go;
instead, having become a mare, she roamed the Himalayas.
Then the Sun-god came to the Snowy Mountain to seek her out;
having become a horse, he began his pursuit, but she did not yield to his desire.
Then the Sun gave him a face; he released [the seed] for the two nostrils, and from the two nostrils were born the two delicate sons of Aśvinī.
Then she set out together with Sūrya toward the solar orb;
however, she blazed with the splendors of the Sun as she had done before. (113)
Then the father Viśvakarman spoke to his father Sūrya for the purpose of dulling [his light], and he indeed ground the Lord of Day with a whetstone.
The exceedingly beautiful and utterly deluding Sūrya was cut down on all sides;
his splendor became subdued, and consciousness became stable within him.
Then, seeing that beautiful, pleasant, endurable, and divine youth who bestows enjoyments, the young maiden, having become the direction [the North], desired him. 116.

With gestures such as amorous glances, expressions, and playful charms, he desired her— she who was exceedingly beautiful, who had approached his side with passion, and who was longing for sexual union.
Seeing her there, the Sun said, "O Goddess of the Quarter, why have you come?
The Goddess of the Quarter said to him, "Grant me my desired wish, which shall provide complete satisfaction."
The Sun said: "My enjoyment must not be in vain; therefore, consider this.
If you desire the child, then accept union with me."
Then the goddess Diśā herself, though she had personally reflected that "the fetus is not desired," being utterly deluded, still craved enjoyment from the Lord of Day.
The Sun said: "O dear goddess, I shall grant you enjoyment accompanied by its fruit;
at some point, in a human state, you will be born as a maiden."
Then my yoga shall become fruitful for you, O noble lady of human birth, when Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, [is attained]. 1.22.
Wandering upon the earth in human form as the fulfiller of desires,
he will be the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd boy, the son of Kaṃbhārā.
"Then your birth will become fruitful in every respect.
Having spoken thus, the Sun ceased speaking and vanished from the direction of the maiden.
Then Sūrya, being pleased, spoke with joined palms to his own father-in-law:
"Choose a boon; I shall grant here whatever is dear and desired by your mind."
Then Viśvakarman said: "O Lord, if you are pleased, even though he is indeed my son-in-law appearing in the form of a son, I still desire a son."
"I request a beautiful boon: become my son, O Bhāskara.
Sūrya replied, "So be it," and spoke further to her who was intent upon that.
When Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shall appear on earth as the cowherd boy, the joyful son of Satī Kambharā; || 128 ||
Therefore, if I truly desire birth for the sake of attaining union with that [Brahman], whether today, or at the end of a Yuga, or even after ten thousand Yugas; || 1.29 ||
O Viśvakarman, at that time on the surface of the earth, I shall become an excellent man for the sake of attaining union with Śrī Hari.
Manifestation must be achieved in a human form for the sake of proving my fatherhood;
having obtained you as a father, your son shall be born from the womb of a fish. (13.1)
"I shall become your good son and fulfill your heart's desire"—having reached this agreement, when Hari himself [descended] upon the earth... (1.32)
The cowherd boy became the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
at that moment, Viśvakarman also entered the house of Śrī Kabharā.
In the house of Maṅkaṇaka Sukāru, Viśvakarman himself—the king of artisans and lord of Jaṭilā—was born as Bāluja. (1.34)
Having designated Bāluja, the supreme artisan and incarnation of Viśvakarman,
as his father, Sūrya then became his son.
Nakamicchilpirāṭ, the best among all artisans and a sovereign of great yogis—
Kakub became the wife of this very one in his full form.
The auspicious girl who was born, consisting of a portion of the quarters, being a human being,
was Ambā’s mother, the excellent daughter created by the mind of the preeminent artisan.
