On earth, she was married to Digaṃśa, who had conquered the Sun and the Moon;
to the couple were born five daughters, the eldest of whom was Abjikā.
She who is the very essence of a portion of the quarters, the elder sister of Ambā’s daughter, Padmāvatī, equal to a chaste woman, the beloved wife of Kṛṣṇakānta. 1.39
Sūryaprabhā herself was born from the Sun and was deeply infatuated with Hari;
that daughter of the Sun, though a human being, desired to make Hari her husband.
The daughter of Sūryamānava was indeed born with a beautiful form;
she was the second one, Ramā, born as the daughter of Nākajit through a portion of the Sun.
The daughter of the Sun, the most excellent Ramā, beloved of Hari and endowed with the beauty, fortune, and virtues of a *padminī*, was born of Sāmbādevī. (142)
Those two daughters of Brahmā from ancient times, named Ramā and Padmāvatī,
[attained their state] indeed through the vow on the thirteenth day of the month of Puruṣottama.
When they had attained the supreme imperishable abode, by the will of Śrī Hari,
she became the daughter of the Sun on earth in order to perform service to the Blessed Lord.
Then Ramā was born, and likewise Padmāvatī, the daughter of the quarters;
both were offered upon the earth as wives to Hari in his human form.
"Bhargas and Hemanta—these two attendants of mine who reside in my abode—I have brought them here along with myself, these two brothers, for the sake of service. (146)
When they were born, these two were in that house where the wife was born;
for the Lord Bharga became Hemanta, known as Hema. (147)
Those two, devoted to the Supreme Brahman, served me, Hari;
that son born in their midst was indeed an attendant of the Blessed Lord.
From him was born Hemanta as a younger brother, most excellent like gold;
then there were three daughters: Mālatī, Haṃsī, and Sadguṇā.
Those three friends of Vaikuṇṭha became the sons of Ambikā;
thus everything was endowed with devotion and took refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The family became like a deity, born as a supreme object of devotion;
they existed on earth solely for the purpose of serving Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 151.
Thus, O beloved of mine, this former history has been told to you here concerning Padmāvatī and myself, who have always been dear to one another. 152.
Just as Lakṣmī, Jayā, Rādhā, Māṇikyā, Lalitā, and Priyā [are dear], and just as you, Śrī, are so, even so is Padmāvatī, Ramā, my beloved here. (153)
This "Eight Verses Dear to Brahmā" is the most excellent among tens of billions of verses;
by reciting or hearing it, one shall likewise obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Compassion of the Lord toward the Creation and Arrival of His Incarnations in the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse, the twelve battles of the Daityas, and the prior history of the family of Padmāvatī and Ramā.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me that which is beneficial: how can the liberation of that deceased person be achieved who had no association with holy men in this world?"
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñīśrī; at the funeral rite (śrāddha) for the deceased, virtuous people should be fed by the relatives and honored with excellent gifts.
The virtuous and the Brahmins who know the Veda should be gratified with garments, ornaments, jewels, silver, gold, wealth, and vehicles.
Gifts of cows should indeed always be bestowed, for cows are eternal deliverers;
by the gift of a cow, the deceased who has arisen shall attain the eternal worlds.
A cow acquired through righteous means, when given as a gift, immediately delivers one's entire lineage;
listen to what Bṛhaspati said to Māndhātṛ in former times.
Having worshipped a peaceful Brahmin and likewise having worshipped his preceptor and a cow,
he should offer a cow to a high-souled worthy recipient, using the name of the deceased.
A cow is my mother and my father is pure; therein heaven is established.
At evening, remaining in the cow-pen as one observing a vow, he should be devoted to the service of cows and other such duties.
Having risen at dawn and remembered Paretaka, one should perform the gift of a cow;
the deceased swiftly goes to heaven, O Kamalā—of this there is no doubt.
He who dwells for a single night among cows, sharing their friendship and observing the same vows,
being endowed with the realization of oneness with them, is liberated from his impurities.
Milk-cows accompanied by their calves should be given at dawn upon the sight of the sun—
youthful, beautiful, containing nectar within, and yielding abundant growth.
May these cows drive [me] forward toward the path to heaven;
may they protect me like a mother and bestow their blessings upon me. (11)

May cows, being well-pleased, grant the rising of all auspicious things— whether for the destruction of disease, for supreme liberation, for heaven, for prosperity, for happiness, or for wealth— in that state which is the abode of all blessings.
O meritorious ones, the refuge of all the gods, grant us the supreme goal;
being united in soul and mind, bestow the fruit of self-surrender.
I offer arghya, clothing, a golden eagle, and as many vessels of food;
and I give a well-pleased, upward-faced cow, together with her calf, dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having recited [the mantra], the giver of a cow should bestow it and obtain the supreme fruit;
he who gives a cow, who is virtuous, who is a worshiper, and who is a giver and a servant of the *arghya* offering. || 15 ||
One who is devoted to the virtuous, devoted to his parents, devoted to his teachers, and respectful toward the gods;
one who is truthful in character and an ascetic—such persons shall never be miserable anywhere.
One who practices ritual bathing, one delighted by sacred stories, one devoted to the worship of Brahman, and one rich in service to cows— these four are Vaiṣṇavas, yogis of the abode.

One who observes the cow-vow, a donor of cows, one who eats cow-products, one who subsists by means of cows, a Vaiṣṇava, and the supreme knower should be understood as such; a mother of cows has Viṣṇu as her deity. (18)
One who observes the vow of the gods, the vow of the Vedas, the vow of the cows, and the excellent vows of the virtuous,
as well as the Gomedha and other such vows, attains the foremost abodes of radiant light.

The giver of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) here enjoys all desires and great festivals bestowed by her, as well as both earthly and celestial foods consisting of offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya). || 3.101.20 ||
One should drink barley mixed with cow's products, sleep on the ground, and reside in a cow-pen;
being disciplined, one should give a milch cow as a gift, and thus obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
For the sake of the initiation of a virtuous person, one should give a son who performs auspicious deeds;
by that merit performed by him, the embodied spirits of the deceased are uplifted. (22)
One should give a virtuous maiden who is chaste and full of dispassion, as well as a young woman endowed with knowledge and dedicated to the upliftment of the world, to a holy woman. ||23||
Devoted to moral discipline, free from attachment to the dharma of householders, possessing a disposition of renunciation, and beautiful in her station as a noble teacher—thus auspicious. (24)
The king should give a female slave to his preceptor and a male slave to a twice-born; he should give the son of a twice-born to a brahmin, and he should give land to a virtuous ruler.
One should indeed give a gift to a twice-born who is equal to a guru, who is a treasure-trove of knowledge and the company of the virtuous, and who possesses such character and disposition. ||26||
The gift of a Brahmin youth is considered equal to the gift of a cow;
the Brahmin who receives it shall always be a rescuer in this world and the next. (27)
One should indeed give much gold and wealth to the father of the Brahmin’s son;
having thus purchased the Brahmin’s son, one should bestow gifts upon the twice-born.
One who is childless may take [a wife] for the purpose of completing sacrificial rites, for the sake of a school, or for the sake of attaining the status of a royal preceptor. (29)
The gift of sacred knowledge, the gift of sacred knowledge, the gift of a cow, the gift of gold,
the gift of oneself, and the gift of liberation— these indeed are considered the gifts that bestow liberation.
Having approached a cow that is affectionate, endowed with vigor, young, and adorned,
and giving her as a gift, one becomes fully united with all merits.
By giving such a cow, one does not go to the worlds of those who suffer from misery and poverty:
one that is toothless, wrinkled, whose milk has dried up, and whose fertile season has passed. (32)
One that is aged, diseased, angry, or wicked should never be given;
among all cows, the tawny one (kapilā) is the best, and she should especially be given as a gift.
The gods and the sun indeed bring forth rain when gratified by sacrifice;
and sacrificial rites are performed with the milk and clarified butter derived from cows. (34)
In ancient times, Prajāpati himself attained satisfaction with clarified butter;
thereafter, he created the Mothers of the World from the cows residing in Goloka.
These cows, golden-hued and tawny, flowing with streams of milk,
pour forth milk and nectar— the sustenance for living beings.
Then that Prajāpati gave them to the sages and to the gods,
and he also gave them to human beings for the purpose of performing sacrifices and other rites involving milk.
He also gave them to the Brahmins for the successful accomplishment of his divine purpose;
indeed, the gift of Kapila cows is considered the most excellent of all. (38)
By giving cows—which grant milk, bestow merit, provide life, and secure liberation for the deceased—one becomes a granter of all desires both in this world and the next. (39)

The man who gives a cow obtains sacrificial offerings for the gods and ancestors, libations, peace, vehicles, as well as clothing, and the satisfaction of the elderly, children, and others. (3.101.40)
Cows possess a fragrant scent as well as the aroma of guggulu resin;
cows are the foundation of the worlds, and cows are a great means of securing well-being.
Neither the wind, nor fire, nor gold, nor the ocean is corrupted;
neither milk, nor nectar, nor sunlight, nor a cow, nor a virtuous man, nor the Lord is ever defiled. 42.
Cows are wealth that is eternally obtainable; cows are eternal nourishment. Cows are the supreme root of prosperity (lakṣmī), and they alone are the very root of all riches. ||43||
For food is the supreme cow-pen, and it is the supreme oblation for the gods;
indeed, what is given to cows is eternal, established in both the *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* calls.
Cows are the fruit of sacrifice, and sacrifices are established in cows;
from cows the vital essences increase, and children live upon milk-rice.
But those who give a cow for whatever sins they have committed, even if they are small or very slight, they indeed cross over [suffering] and attain liberation.
Those who bestow a tawny cow, together with her calf, a bronze milking vessel,
ornaments, and covered with cloth, conquer both worlds.
In ancient times, Kṛṣṇa presented a bull to Śaṅkara;
from that time forth, the gift of a bull indeed became established as the most excellent on earth. ||48||
Those who bestow a young, exalted, white bull, adorned with many horns, become endowed with sovereign power. (49)
Having remembered the cows and remembering the holy Hari, one should always sleep at night;
having risen, one should likewise remember them and offer salutations, and thus one shall attain prosperity.
Having observed an inauspicious dream, one should repeatedly recite the name of the Cow;
one should cook with cow-dung and perform purification with cow-mash.
One should offer oblations with cow's ghee and have blessings recited with ghee;
one should give ghee and consume ghee, and thus one attains the prosperity of cows.
May the cow always be before me, and may she always be behind me and at my sides; I give this cow, composed of all jewels, for the attainment of auspiciousness. (53)
May cows with golden horns, yielding milk, approach me;
may cows that are fragrant and of noble breed always look upon me. (54)
Cows, truthful ones, deities, virtuous women, auspicious fortunes, devoted wives, the saintly, the liberated, lords, teachers, the good, and heroes—[these are all worthy of honor]. (55)

Devotion, merit, virtue, service, what has been given, what has been practiced as austerity, and what has been done as a favor—these protect one in great dangers, both in times of equality and in times of adversity. (56)
Listen, Lakṣmī! Even the cows, having come to this earth, performed austerities in ancient times, thinking, "May we attain preeminence. (57)
"We are the most excellent even among all sacrificial gifts;
we destroy all sins and cannot be defiled by impurities. (58)
In that way, may all people indeed be purified by our cattle and other [products];
and by means of our dung and urine, may all embodied beings be purified. (59)
"O lotus-born one, may those who give cows go to Goloka";
thus Brahmā granted these supreme boons to the female ascetics and the cows.
"O Yoginīs, may you likewise deliver the worlds;
and may you be pure in every way and bestowers of liberation. ||6 1||
"May Lakṣmī dwell in cow dung; I grant those boons to you.
Having thus granted the boons, Brahmā departed for Satyaloka, and they [the cows] likewise followed him.
Worthy of morning salutations and worship, they were in every way auspicious bestowers of nourishment;
acting for the welfare of the world, they became saviors from worldly existence.
Having given away a tawny, milch cow with a calf of the same color,
adorned with ornaments and garments, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
By giving such a red cow, one is glorified in the world of the Sun;
by giving such a brindled cow, one is glorified in the world of the Moon. ||65||
By giving such a white cow, one is glorified in the world of Śakra;
and by giving such a black cow, one is glorified in the world of Vahni. ||66||
Having given such a smoky-colored cow, one is glorified in the world of Dharma;
having given such a pale-white cow, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
By giving a cow with the color of a speech-maker (a learned man), one is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
by giving one that is golden-colored and tawny-eyed, one attains the state of Kubera.
By giving such a yellow cow, one is glorified in the world of the ancestors;
by giving such a brindled cow, one is born as a Viśvadeva.
By giving away a cow as white as Gaurī, one attains the world of the Vasus;
by giving away a cow with the color of a pale woolen blanket, one becomes a Sādhyasura.
By giving a cow with a broad back, one attains the worlds of the Maruts;
by giving such a cow enriched with jewels, one may attain the state of a Gandharva.
Having given a young ox or a great bull adorned with all kinds of jewels, one is glorified in the world of Prajāpati.
The giver of a cow goes to the supreme heaven, Goloka,
by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot or by a vehicle drawn by a bull through the sky.
In heaven, thousands of celestial damsels constantly serve that giver of cows and awaken him each morning with auspicious hymns of praise.
For as many years as there are hairs on the cow's body, he rejoices;
thereafter, he becomes a donor of cows on earth and even a protector of cattle and land.
May cows that yield ghee and milk, whose bodies are ghee, and who originate from ghee—may these rivers of ghee with whirlpools of ghee be ever present in my home. (76)
May cows dwell eternally in my heart, in my navel, and likewise in my self;
may cows dwell everywhere in my body and within my mind. (77)
Ghee resides in their bodies, senses, and vital breaths;
may cows be before me, and may milch-cows be behind me. (78)
"May cows be everywhere for me, for I dwell in the midst of cows. For one who contemplates in this way, millions of sins are destroyed. (79)
Where there are golden palaces and the arrival of gold is indeed immeasurable;
where the goddesses are skilled in the Gandharva arts, and where nectar and prosperity abound.
Where there are streams of curd, streams of ghee, and streams of milk, and where there are streams of fresh butter—
there go those who give gifts of cows.
The giver of a thousand cows shall become a lord of the gods in heaven;
the one who performs the gift of a hundred thousand cows shall become an emperor of the three worlds, O Rame.
One who performs the gift of ten million cows attains Vaikuṇṭha and partakes in liberation;
one who gives a hundred million cows attains Goloka and partakes in liberation. (83)
The giver of a cow with her calf and a vessel of water indeed attains the imperishable abode;
by the gift of ten cows, a deceased person is liberated from the bondage of rebirth.
Recalling his mother, father, wife, and ancestors, the giver of a cow certainly delivers eleven generations of his lineage. (85)
By remembering the cow and by the offering of sesame seeds or even water, one indeed dispels the torments of the deceased in the world of Yama. (86)
"The mothers who give me milk are indeed divine cows;
may the cows attend upon me"—thus one should constantly recite. (87)
Since the gift of a cow is the supreme merit and its fruit is eternal, nothing further remains to be done by the giver of cows for the sake of attaining heaven. (88)
Indeed, those cows intended for a gift rescue that person;
they sustain their calves and nourish them with the nectar of their milk. (89)
Cows indeed exist in the world of Manu, in Svarga, and in Satyaloka; they also truly exist in the realm of Īśvara, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in Goloka. ||3.101.90||
In the Imperishable (Akṣara), the cows with many horns and the unwearied ones truly abide;
the cows constitute the sacrificial nature of sacrifice and are the deity even of those who dwell in heaven.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are the supreme merit and ultimate refuge.
In brief, cows are the sacrificial session itself for those desiring to accomplish it, as well as its very hooves.
And in the tenth month, the Creator then provided horns for them;
thus, horns were produced for those cows according to the specific forms they were intended to have.
The virtuous protect the great and divine splendor of the cows;
those who perform good deeds, partakers of merit, and devoted to the service of cows, are like gods. 94.
There the trees have sweet juices and are endowed with fruits that exude honey;
their flowers possess the fragrance of honey, and the ground is likewise composed of jewels.
Where there are regions of golden ground that grant happiness and fulfill desires, and where the reservoirs of water shine with every kind of lotus; ||96||
Where there are filaments rich in fragrance wafted by the wind, stalks bearing fruits of six tastes, vegetables, and honeys; (97)
There, the creepers are adorned with pearls, laden with fruit, and bestowing nectar; the mountains are made of gold and possess an eternally fresh splendor.
Women wearing nine garments serve him with their hair loose;
all desires, all pleasures, and all enjoyments are present. 99.
Where the sandalwood forests bloom, there dwell the givers of cows;
they are enriched by all their intentions fulfilled, free from sorrow, and increased in fortune.
The givers of cows travel in various celestial chariots and go to great gardens; they rejoice and sport in every way. (101)
They dwell together with women and are honored by the inhabitants of heaven;
they enjoy joy, delight, bliss, and pleasures every day.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Cows and Other Matters," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning how the gift of a cow is the cause for the liberation of virtuous people and for the deliverance of a ghost devoid of yoga. || 101 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said: For the sake of liberation, the descendants of the deceased, as well as his wife, sons, relatives, and kinsmen, should perform the vow known as Gavārādhana.
Dwelling in a cow-pen, likewise serving the cows, as well as providing fodder for the cows and even providing water for the cows. (2)
Likewise, there is the settling of the cattle at night, as well as their awakening at dawn;
the sweeping of the cow-pen and so forth, and the warding off of gadflies and other insects.
Providing grassy pastures for grazing, feeding them with cow-products, honoring them appropriately, protecting them in every way, and always keeping them in the cow-pen at all times. || 4 ||
One should never harbor malice even in thought toward cows, who are the constant bestowers of happiness;
one should honor them with the thought that they are Lakṣmī herself and worship them with prostrations.
For three days one should drink warm urine, for three days one should drink warm milk,
for three days one should drink warm ghee, and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
One should carry clarified butter on one's head, offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter,
give clarified butter as a gift, eat clarified butter, and have benedictions recited with clarified butter.
One who eats barley that has been left over from cows removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
likewise, the gods, when forcibly joined with Daityas and Dānavas at a meal, [attain the same].
Having eaten their own respective foods, they then performed for the sake of purification alone a vow lasting for one month known as the "Worship of the Cow."
Then the gods became pure again, fully accomplished in their own duties;
therefore, cows are sacred, purifying, and likewise bestowers of merit.
Having given that auspicious gift of a cow, one becomes purified and attains heaven;
even while dwelling in the midst of fire, in the midst of cows, or in the midst of the virtuous.
Even while dwelling among Brahmins, among virtuous women, in the midst of the Vedas,
in the midst of a sacrifice, or in the midst of a sacred pilgrimage site, one is purified from sin.
Cows, when satisfied, bestow sons, wealth, a husband, and a beloved wife.
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, for you were by nature Śrī in ancient times. (1.3)
Having fashioned a lovely body, you stood in the midst of the cows;
and the cows, filled with wonder, beheld the perfection of your form.
They asked you: "Who are you, O girl? From where have you come, O beautiful one? And how did you arrive here, O gentle lady? Tell us, if indeed you think it right to do so. (15)
Then, having been propitiated, you bowed down to the cows and said:
"I am the beloved of Viṣṇu; may it be well with you; I am Śrī, the dear consort of Hari. (16)
Seized by me, the gods and others rejoice for eternal years—the sun, the moon, Mahendra, the Vasus, and tens of millions of deities. (17)
Fire and water, when entered by me, indeed become prosperous and manifest their power;
but those cows which I do not enter perish in every way. 18.
That house in which dharma, artha, and kāma are pursued by me shall indeed be rich in joy,
delight, and tranquility, and filled with great bliss.
"And I also desire to dwell among you; may you be gracious to me.
A firm longing has indeed arisen in me to always reside within the circle of my women."
Having heard you, the cows said: "You are indeed fickle; we do not desire you who go everywhere. May it be well with you; please go elsewhere. (2.1)
Having heard this, you have requested it; why then do you not rejoice in me?
After performing great and formidable austerities, human beings serve me.
O Yakṣas, Asuras, Gandharvas, Īśvaras, Uragas, and Suras:
how can you accept me, for I am indeed difficult to obtain? 23.
Having heard this, the cows said: "You are indeed fickle-minded in every respect; what is the use of saying more? Therefore, we shall avoid you. (24)
Having heard this, you said, "I shall abandon my fickleness;
for your sake, O cows, grant me a place to dwell. ||25||
Then the cows spoke: "Dwell firmly in our dung and urine!
Om! You, Lakṣmī, have descended into the urine and dung of the cows. (26)
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, since I am the cow’s urine and the cow dung, this house is indeed yours;
wherever you dwell, there I also dwell—of this there is no doubt.
Knowing its greatness in this way, those people who bestow a cow are indeed eaters of the remnants of the oblation; they are performers of long sacrificial sessions and officiants of the sacrifice.
Without curd and ghee, no sacrifice whatsoever proceeds here;
therefore, the very nature of sacrifice is established as being rooted in the cow. (29)
The sons of the Earth constantly practice the application of agriculture in this world;
they produce grains, and by means of them, sacrifices proceed. (3.102.30)
Afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other such needs, they carry various loads;
moreover, they support holy men here upon their backs and even upon their carts.
When given as a gift, it leads one indeed to Goloka, even for the deceased;
therefore, the station of cows is above heaven, truth, and likewise the realm of Īśvara.
Goloka is indeed the abode of cows and my own temple, Kṛṣṇa’s;
the giver of a cow goes to Goloka, the dwelling place of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Listen to another thing, O Mahālakṣmī; indeed, in a former age of the gods, Aditi performed penance [thinking], "May Viṣṇu become my son. (34)
Then, seeing Tapati standing on one foot,
Dakṣa’s daughter named Surabhi also performed penance together with her.
Then Brahmā himself went there and granted a boon to Aditi:
"Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, shall become your son to accomplish the work of the gods. (36)
Then the Creator of the Universe granted a boon to Surabhi:
"O daughter of Dakṣa, O ascetic woman, you shall indeed attain immortality. (37)
"You shall attain the status of a sovereign goddess and the state of being a cowherd girl along with all those born in your lineage;
likewise, you shall become the one who leads others to liberation and the bestower of liberation. (38)
You shall dwell above, as the most worshipful one in the three worlds;
and by the grace of the Lord of Cows, you shall attain those Goloka realms for the givers of cows.
They shall obtain dwelling places wherever the cows reside;
likewise, the descendants of the lineage shall go wherever there are cows with many horns.

That supreme abode, the highest station of Kṛṣṇa, the wide-striding one, is reached through the merit of offering oblations and other such acts—[a state] which indeed belongs to those who are your daughters. 41.
They shall become performers of service to the gods and will dwell in their station;
all enjoyments conceived by your mind shall be attained as happiness for you. 42.
For those who give cows, there are supreme worlds endowed with all desires;
neither death, nor old age, nor fire prevails within them. (43)
Neither poverty nor anything inauspicious exists anywhere even in a cow’s footprint there;
rather, there are divine forests and divine palaces. (44)
There are most divine celestial chariots that travel according to one's will,
and there are also streams of clarified butter, streams of curd, and streams of milk.
There are lotus ponds filled with nectar, mountains of fresh butter,
and heaps of ambrosia that taste like sugar and honey.
O Saurabhi, those who give cows— wherein there are young cowherd girls adorned with divine ornaments— shall go to your supreme abode.
Through celibacy, austerity, service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, by means of gifts, meritorious deeds, self-restraint, truthfulness, and visits to sacred fords; ||48||
Through devotion to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and especially through devotion to Rādhā, it is possible to attain Goloka, which is adorned by Kṛṣṇa. (49)
The devotee of the Cow obtains everything auspicious that he desires;
and devoted women obtain every excellent thing they long for. (3.102.50)
One desiring a son obtains a son, and likewise one desiring a daughter obtains a daughter;
one desiring wealth obtains wealth, and one desiring dharma attains dharma. ||5 1||
One seeking liberation shall attain liberation; one seeking prosperity shall obtain prosperity;
one seeking knowledge shall acquire knowledge; and one seeking happiness shall find happiness. (52)
One seeking flavor obtains flavor; likewise, one seeking firmness obtains firmness;
one seeking a husband obtains an excellent husband; and one seeking a beloved obtains a beautiful and auspicious woman.
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; one seeking heaven attains heaven;
and a giver of cows indeed obtains even a great earthly kingdom.

The station of Indra, the station of Sūrya, the station of Candra, the station of Kubera, the station of Yama, likewise the righteous station of Dharmya, and also the station of Vahni and that of Īśa. 55.
One may attain Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, and even the station of Vairāja;
one may attain the supreme Goloka and the imperishable abode.
The giver of a cow indeed obtains health, as well as fame and renown;
moreover, the donor of a cow shall obtain elephants, horses, and cows. (57)
The giver of a cow indeed obtains forms, jewels, garments, rubies, and a treasure of gold; this is traditionally taught as the fruit of the time of giving a cow.
Untimely death shall perish, and the state of being a ghost shall depart far away;
all sins shall be utterly destroyed for both the giver of the cow and for one who remembers her. (59)
Thus indeed did Brahmā grant boons to the cow;
for O Lakṣmī, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to obtain in this world for one who is devoted to cows. (3.102.60)
The supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, all the riches of universal sovereignty and the like, and whatever wonders there may be, O Dhenude, they all arise from you.
The merit of the Vedas, the merit of sacrifices, the merit of giving a maiden in marriage, the merit of sacrificial fees,
the merit of land, and the merit of gold— all these are produced by the gift of a cow.
Gold, given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), is equal in merit to the gift of a cow;
for when a physical cow is unavailable, a golden cow should indeed be given.
Gold should always be given for the sake of land and cattle;
O Lotus-born One, gold, a cow, and earth—these three are the [supreme] gifts. (64)
They indeed become the means for the liberation of the deceased; there is no doubt in this matter.
By giving cows, land, and wealth, even a sinner is purified.
The goat is Agni, the ram is Varuṇa, and the horse was born in the east as Sūrya;
indeed, gifts of these various animals lead even the deceased to liberation.
Elephants, deer, serpents, buffaloes, and even asuras—
this supreme gift of elephants and other such beings is for the sake of liberation from the womb of asuras.
Cocks and boars are proclaimed to be rākṣasas; for the sake of liberation from the womb of a rākṣasa, the gift of those respective animals is praised. (68)
The *iḍā*, the cows, the milk, the *soma*, and the earth were indeed born [from that].
For the sake of the liberation of those who have passed away and others, the gift of cows and land is highly praised. (69)
For Agni is indeed the deity of gold; thus gold is praised as a divine substance.
Therefore, the gift of gold is declared to be supreme, a divine gift that bestows auspiciousness.
In the absence of fire, however, he performs [the rite] with gold in the places where the fire would normally stand;
he offers the oblation into a bundle of *kuśa* grass, and there, gold is placed.
In the absence of the fire, one offers oblations into the hand of a Brahmin, the hand of a virtuous person, a clump of Darbha grass, the ear of a goat, water, wood, or gold.
When the oblation has been performed, the Lord of Śrī bestows delightful supernatural power;
moreover, the practitioner constantly gives gold according to his capacity. (73)
He attains the same world as Brahmā, Vāyu, Agni, and Soma;
for the auspicious state of the householder consists of three aspects: mother, father, and son.
The gift of cows, gold, and land constitutes the threefold supreme gift;
likewise, faith, affection, and respect are the threefold means of pleasing a guest. (75)
Likewise, land, cattle, and gold indeed bestow the next world;
a dwelling, wealth, and a livelihood—these three are the means for accomplishing happiness.
In this way, cows, land, and gold indeed bestow happiness when given as gifts;
furthermore, knowledge, tranquility, and renunciation—these three are the causes of bliss. (77)
A cow, land, and gold indeed bestow great bliss;
devotion to Hari and liberation—these three are eternally interconnected. (78)
The virtuous man, moral conduct, and patience—these three are likewise interconnected;
and in the same way, they are eternally bound to the giving of gold, cows, and land. (79)
They bestow enjoyment and liberation, as well as the deliverance of the deceased;
they grant heaven, destroy heaps of sins, and bestow merit—these three.

Having performed the sacrifice of cows by the gift of cattle, the sacrifice to the ancestors by libations, and the sacrifice to the virtuous by providing food along with a golden sacrificial fee; ||81||
Having performed the Nārāyaṇabali and having caused the libation to be offered with the tail of a blue bull,
one should release the deceased by giving a gift to the person who was requested.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described the auspicious liberation of the deceased; and even the recitation performed according to the scriptures of liberation shall bring about deliverance. (83)
Indeed, the chanting of my names, uninterrupted devotion to me, and the water from the hands of the virtuous grant liberation from the state of being a ghost. (84)
The purificatory bath, the cleansing rite, the ceremonial bath, and the ancestral offering at an auspicious moment;
likewise, the sight of the virtuous, their touch, and following their instructions. (85)
Resorting to the waters of a sacred ford (tīrtha) grants liberation even from the state of a preta;
moreover, wherever one may go, one is liberated by devotion to Hari.
Whether it be a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a bhūta, a preta, or a piśāca;
whether it be a serpent, or even one with the body of a beast, or one belonging to Yama, or possessing the body of the wind. (87)
Whether it be a ḍākinī, a śākinī, a bhūtī, a piśācinī, a vetālinī, or a vetāla—wherever they may have gone. ||88||
Whether one obtains the sight of the virtuous, or the grace of Śrī Hari, or even the water [of the Ganges], one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. ||89||
For the virtuous are indeed the saviors in the world, as well as the destroyers of evils,
the removers of impurities, and the bestowers of divine liberation.
I always delight in the virtuous, who are superior to cows, gold, fire, and the gods;
indeed, association with the virtuous is my own yoga, which bestows all the goals of human life. 9.1
Once, a Puṣkasa named Bhāruṇḍa, who was a drinker of intoxicants,
a meat-eater, devoid of virtue, and a thief, died in the middle of a forest.
Led by the messengers of Yama to the city of Yama, he was cast into the hells;
however, his wife performed the gift of a cow at a sacred ford (tīrtha) and offered gold.
At that very moment, all the sins of the preta were cast far away;
the preta swiftly went to heaven, while his sins went to Surabhi. (94)
O Surabhi, you are able to destroy the sins of the Creator;
indeed, the sins of the Puṣkasa have attached themselves to me through this gift. (95)
"O Father, tell me where I must go so that these illusions may be destroyed.
Having heard this, Brahmā said to her, "Go to Sanatkumāra."
"Having heard this, Surabhi went to that virtuous one and requested him accordingly: 'He will quickly destroy your virtuous conduct and vows; [therefore,] he shall destroy your sins. (97)
For the very purpose of destroying her sins, the virtuous man gave her the water from his feet;
that fragrant cow drank it, and her sins were instantly destroyed.
Then Surabhi, having been consecrated by the virtuous, approached Brahmā;
bowing to her preceptor, the venerable Creator, she spoke these verses with great satisfaction. (99)
Blessed indeed are those virtuous ones in the world who possess moral conduct and are free from passion;
they are free from deceit and possess divine forms, for by taking refuge in them, one's sins are destroyed.
The sins of sacred fords, wish-fulfilling cows, virtuous women, ascetics, and Brahmins—all these perish when one associates with the righteous. (101)
The sins of ancestors, gods, great seers, women, and embodied beings— all these perish when [the merit] is bestowed upon the virtuous.
Indeed, the sins of kings, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, spirits, and inhabitants of the realm of Yama—even those destined for evil rebirths—are surely destroyed when they encounter the virtuous. 103.
Whatever sins belong to those who are lustful, wrathful, greedy, or deluded,
as well as to those who are murderous, they perish in the presence of the virtuous.
Indeed, the sins of those who commit murder, those who slaughter animals, the cruel, those who obstruct life, and those who betray trust, perish when they seek refuge among the virtuous. 105.
The sins of courtesans, unchaste women, those who carry banners, those who possess wheels, as well as those who bear weapons and physicians, perish when they seek refuge with the virtuous. 106.
The sins of those who harm guests, those who kill children, those who set fires, those who administer poison,
those who give poison, and those who destroy forests, perish when they encounter the virtuous.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, Surabhi, who is firm in her vows, departed for the cow-pen.
By reciting or hearing this, millions of sins shall be destroyed. (108)

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow Named *Gavārādhana*, the Abiding of Lakṣmī in Cow-Dung and Cow-Urine, the Various Fruits of Giving Cows, the Means for the Liberation of the Dead, the Refuge of the Virtuous, and the Savior of All," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Keśava, please enlighten me as to at what time the gift of gold, cows, and land yields fruit, and what kind of fruit they bestow.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Lotus-born One, by giving gifts accompanied by the performance of Śrāddha feasts on the first day of the bright fortnight,
one shall obtain fortunate and beloved wives.
By giving likewise on the second [lunar day], one obtains daughters and sons;
by giving likewise on the third, one obtains excellent horses.
By giving on the fourth day, one then obtains cattle and wealth;
likewise, by giving on the fifth day, one obtains sons endowed with excellent qualities.
By giving likewise on the sixth day, one obtains immediate fame and strength;
and by giving likewise on the seventh day, one obtains a field and a garden.
Likewise, by giving on the eighth day, one obtains excellent wealth;
and by giving on the ninth day, one obtains elephants, camels, horses, and so forth.
By giving likewise on the tenth day, one becomes possessed of a wish-fulfilling cow;
by giving likewise on the eleventh day, one becomes a possessor of a treasure of silver.
By giving gold, jewels, and other such things on the twelfth day, one shall become possessed of them;
likewise, by giving on the thirteenth day, one shall become a king of the world.
Likewise, by giving on the fourteenth day, one shall attain universal sovereignty;
and likewise, by giving on the full moon day, one shall become a person of wondrous power.
Likewise, by giving on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), one shall obtain all desires;
and likewise, by giving on the Jayantī day, one shall attain supreme liberation.
I shall also declare the specific fruit of giving according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
By making a gift under Kṛttikā, one indeed becomes free from all affliction.
By making gifts under Rohiṇī, a person shall obtain offspring;
by giving under Mṛgaśiras, a man shall become radiant with splendor.
By making a gift under Ārdrā, one shall always be victorious;
by making a gift under Punarvasu, one shall become wealthy and prosperous.
One who gives gifts under Puṣya will certainly be prosperous in every way;
by giving under Āśleṣā, one obtains wise sons.
By giving a gift under Maghā, one attains preeminence among offspring;
by giving under Pūrvāphālgunī, one becomes endowed with excellent fortune.
From a gift given under Uttarāphālgunī, a person shall have many offspring;
one who performs a gift under Hasta, however, shall obtain the fruits of his undertakings. (16)
By making a gift under Citrā, one obtains handsome sons;
by being a giver of gifts under Svāti, one becomes a possessor of trade and jewels.
One who gives under Viśākhā will have a virtuous son and many sons;
one who gives under Anurādhā will become a preeminent universal monarch (cakravartin). || 18 ||
One who bestows a gift under Jyeṣṭhā indeed attains sovereignty in this world;
one who performs an act of giving under Mūla shall obtain supreme health.
By the gift of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, a person shall possess glory;
by the gift of Uttarāṣāḍhā, one shall always be free from sorrow. (3.103.20)
One who performs a gift-giving ceremony under the constellation Abhijit shall attain success as a physician;
however, one who makes a gift under Śravaṇa shall obtain the most supreme goal.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā, one may become a donor, a teacher, a preceptor, or a king;
by the gift under Śatabhiṣā, one shall attain mastery over the elements.
The fruit of receiving [a gift] from Pūrvabhādrapadā consists of goats, sheep, and the like;
from Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, one shall possess cows, horses, and elephants. (23)
By making a gift under the asterism Revatī, one becomes possessed of gold, silver, and the like;
a person who performs a gift under Aśvinī shall possess buffaloes, horses, and so forth.
One who gives gifts under Bharaṇī becomes long-lived; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, a giver of cows, land, and gold shall obtain all fruits. (25)
One who knows the duty of giving should never examine the recipients of gifts;
in rites for the gods, for the ancestors, or for virtuous persons, one should never examine them at all. (26)

The twice-born Sāma-singers are possessed of knowledge, full of devotion, most established in Brahman, purifiers of all, devoted to virtuous conduct, and recipients of gifts for sacred learning. ||27||
Those who serve their parents and likewise those who serve the gods, those devoted to celibacy, the pure, and the ascetics—all these are purifiers of all. ||28||

They were devoted to truth, righteousness, vows, and moral conduct; they frequented sacred fords, performed sacrificial consecrations, and undertook the purificatory ablutions at the conclusion of rites.
They were reciters of the Pārāyaṇa, ascetics devoted to chanting, intent upon the path to liberation, narrators of sacred stories, and teachers of dharma. ||3.103.30||

Those who bestow the guru’s mantra, those who show respect to the elderly, those who serve cows, those who are virtuous, and those rich in service to the virtuous—these are worthy recipients who purify all. ||3 1||

They are foremost among those who write on the Dharma and leaders among those who write on liberation; taking refuge in knowledge, possessing the nature of wisdom, they are indeed peaceful and purifiers of the assembly. (32)
As soon as these behold [the assembly], they purify that very moment;
they are devoted to meditation and knowledge, devoted to devotion, and likewise devoted to austerity.
The virtuous who are endowed with disinterested action are purifiers of the assembly;
when fed, honored, and bowed to, these holy ones grant liberation to the departed spirits.
Devoted, ascetic, virtuous, and sanctifiers of the universe—of these, the supreme austerity is considered to be the restraint of the senses. (35)
The restraint of the mind, the constant meditation upon Śrī Hari, and the perfection of renunciation—this indeed is the highest austerity. (36)
Fasting, celibacy, silence, forbearance, supreme austerity, endurance, contentment, generosity, and patience are the highest forms of asceticism. (37)
Speaking the truth, as well as eating only the remains of offerings, and even eating only the nectar [of the gods], are said to be the highest austerity. (38)
He should indeed eat only once a day, always as if he were observing a fast; he should remain devoted to his one wife and always be like a celibate student. (39)
He who engages with a woman only during her season is indeed truly virtuous; he who is free from attachment to women in general is liberated on this earth—of this there is no doubt. (3.103.40)
The Supreme Lord is two-armed and free from the noose of a golden woman;
such a woman, endowed with righteousness, is considered to be Nārāyaṇī herself.
She is a virtuous wife, a worthy recipient of gifts, and likewise a most excellent vessel of purity.
A widow is a worthy recipient of gifts, and one who is destitute is also a worthy recipient of gifts. ||42||
A maiden is a worthy recipient of gifts, as is an elderly woman;
even one who is destitute is a worthy recipient of gifts, provided she is endowed with the strength of devotion.
The devoted giver of gifts indeed always becomes pure;
having distributed [the food] and then eating it himself, he truly becomes an eater of nectar. || 44 ||
Having offered [the food] to the gods, he should eat the remains;
for such a person, even supernatural powers remain invisible in his abode. (45)
Having attained that supreme embodied form,
the deities, ancestors, Siddhas, yogins, ascetics, holy men,
lords, and sovereign goddesses rejoice and cause him to rejoice in the abode of the Giver.
And the Apsarases, Gandharvas, gods, goddesses, and the virtuous ones. ||47||
Indeed, his sons, grandsons, daughters, and daughters-in-law, as well as his cows, become truthful, fortunate, and like wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu). 48.
In this way, the entire household of the donor indeed becomes a temple of the gods;
the livestock become divine cattle, and even the crops become deities. (49)
All gold, silver, and the like are forms of Lakṣmī and are auspicious deities; all fortunes as well as beauty and ornaments are deities. (3.103.50)
In this way, for the donor, there shall indeed arise a divine and celestial family;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, gold, cows, and auspicious earth should be given. || 51 ||
If one has the power of digestion, one may accept [gifts], but not otherwise;
for one of weak capacity, the merit is surely destroyed by accepting them.

Long ago, King Vṛṣādarbhi, being eager, displayed jewels to the Seven Sages to give them away; however, the sages did not accept them at that time. Then Vṛṣādarbhi himself said, "You are capable of accepting gifts."
Receiving gifts delivers one; choose this supreme wealth.
Gold, silver, pearls, and diamonds;
gems, white elephants, horses, and likewise white cows and bulls. ||55||
I shall bestow upon you first-calving cows, wish-fulfilling cows, villages, and fields;
I shall offer you kingdoms, queens, groups of male servants, female slaves, and great assemblies.
"I shall give palaces, rivers, mountains, and forests in every way;
let the Brahmins and my virtuous sages accept them from me today. (57)
"There is nothing that cannot be given by me, since I strive for the sake of liberation;
by giving to worthy recipients, I shall obtain here the eternal fruit. (58)
To him who was thus entreating and ready to give the gift, the sages—calm, wise, tranquil, and contented—spoke without agitation. (59)
O King, the acceptance of gifts from kings is like honey in taste but like poison;
once obtained, such royal acceptance may consume one like a forest fire.
Therefore, one who desires happiness both in this world and after death must not accept what is unfit to be accepted;
indeed, by accepting royal wealth, one attains the most sinful state.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth—all that is not enough for even one person; therefore, the wise man should dwell in tranquility.
As the body of one who has been born grows as he develops, so too does the desire of both man and woman always increase. (63)
There is no substance in this world that could completely satisfy the worlds;
a person whose thirst is like that of the ocean is never truly satiated.
When desire is indulged by one who longs for it, that desire increases excessively; being accompanied by thirst, it pierces [the heart] all the more.
Restraint in receiving gifts indeed certainly sustains austerity;
however, through the possession of property, all austerity is surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
In this world, the accumulation of austerity alone is superior to the accumulation of material wealth;
therefore, O King, let there be wealth for you, but do not sprinkle poison upon a brahmin.
We great sages, being peaceful, do not desire even the royal wealth of the forest;
may it be well with you, O Great King, we are returning to heaven once more.
Having spoken thus, all the sages departed without accepting any gifts;
Vṛṣādarbhi then thoroughly understood the terrible nature of receiving such offerings.
A gift bestowed upon an unworthy recipient is indeed most certainly unwholesome;
therefore, the twice-born are the worthy recipients of gifts and the locus of merit. (3.103.70)
To those who are saintly devotees of the Lord, one should give especially;
even to Brahmins who are devotees of Hari, one should give especially. (71)
To those who do not harbor greed at all and have abandoned the pursuit of their own self-interest—those worshippers of Śrī Hari—to them gifts should especially be given. (72)
A person who possesses a sacred vessel (pātra) should always avoid greed in every respect;
considering it as an offering to Hari, he should accept [gifts], and never otherwise.
Then, O Lakṣmī, Vṛṣādarbhi, being full of devotion, went to Prayāga during the Kumbha conjunction and gave gifts to the virtuous.
Then the celestial chariot arrived from Vaikuṇṭha at the bank of the Yamunā,
at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, adorned by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
The attendants, having taken the king, went indeed to the abode of Vikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Rame, liberation is attained by the service of virtuous people.
This indeed comes to pass; there is no doubt. Therefore, one should cultivate a worthy recipient and give to him with devotion, thinking, "May this be an offering to Hari."
Then one should give the gift of an umbrella and also the gift of sandals, as well as the gift of a turban and a tunic, and the offering of a helmet. (78)
By that [act], one becomes a lord of an umbrella and likewise a dweller in celestial palaces;
by giving the gift of a lion-throne, one thereafter becomes a sovereign of a kingdom.
One should give the gift of a chowrie and likewise offer the gift of a staff;
one should perform the gift of a banner and likewise carry out the gift of a chariot.
One should also perform the gift of a treasury, the gift of a collection of grain, the gift of a sugarcane field, and the gift of a crop-bearing field. ||8 1||
One should also diligently perform the dedication of a lake, the gift of a vegetable garden, and the donation of gardens, flower groves, and the like. (82)
One should indeed give gifts of fine garments, ornaments, and bodices;
likewise, one should provide gifts of couches and beds for the liberation of the deceased. (83)
One should give gifts of alms-bowls, water-pitchers, jars, and cooking pots, as well as articles of adornment, for the liberation of the deceased. (84)
The offering of water-jars, milk-jars, and curd-jars;
the presentation of water-tanks, jars of clarified butter, mortars, and so forth. ||85||
The gift of a pestle, the presentation of a broom, the gift of a fan and so forth, and the gift of a lamp-stand; ||86||
The gift of a bedstead and the gift of a bowl-stand;
the offering of a hearth and a grinding stone, and the presentation of a ladle and a winnowing basket. ||87||
One should cause the gift of tongs, the gift of *kāṅgakeśī*, the gift of a mirror, and the gifts of a girdle and a rope to be made for the liberation of the deceased. 88.
The gift of water, the gift of cooked food, the offering of fruits, the gift of milk, rice-porridge, and the like, and the bestowing of sweetmeats; ||89||
One should perform various gifts of wheat, rice, and sesame seeds,
as well as the offering of liquids, honey, and salts, for the liberation of the deceased.
One should perform the giving of great woolen blankets, the bestowing of great garments, and the giving of great ornaments for the liberation of the preta. 91.
On auspicious days such as Ekādaśī, one should diligently perform the giving of vows, the giving of austerity, the giving of devotion, and the offering of sacred narratives. (92)
One should perform the gift of recitation and the gift of Dharma for the liberation of the preta;
likewise, the gift of the vehicle of Vāyu and the gift of the vehicle of Agni. (93)
The gift of a water-vehicle, the bestowing of a land-vehicle, the gift of a human vehicle, and the gift of a mechanical vehicle. ||94||
One should perform the gift of a mansion, the gift of a temple, the gift of a palace, the gift of a village, and the gift of armor for the liberation of the deceased. (95)
Listen, Lakṣmī: formerly, while dwelling in his own hermitage, the sage Jamadagni discharged arrows while playing with his bow. (96)
Having brought those arrows, Renuka’s wife gave them back again and again;
meanwhile, at midday, the fierce heat of the sun became intense. ||97||
But with her feet burned, that wife approached her husband slowly;
the sage said, "O beloved, why does it take so long to fetch the arrows? (98)
The wife said, "I am indeed being scorched at my feet by the heat of the sun. Having heard this quickly, the sage discharged arrows toward the sun. 99.
Terrified of the sun, he approached the sage in the form of a brahmin and said: "O Ṛṣi, spare me! I implore you for grace; forgive me!"
The sage said: "O Sun, please arrange it so that the path for my wife may be easy to traverse and truly free from heat. (10.1)
Upon hearing this, Sūrya immediately gave him an umbrella and sandals,
as well as a small vehicle that travels at will, along with ornaments and garments.
He also gave an inexhaustible vessel, a canopy providing shade for an eon,
a necklace that removes all heat, and likewise nectar that grants satisfaction.
Sūrya gave her other requisites and comforts;
having bowed, the Sun went to heaven, and Reṇukā became the abode of happiness.
The sage, whose feet were scorched yet who was tender-hearted, attained a state of serenity;
thus indeed did the practice of giving umbrellas and other such gifts originate from Sūrya.
By the offering of various gifts for those living beings whose bodies have become ghosts, their suffering is surely pacified; through merit, there shall be liberation.
From reading or hearing this, the fruit of all giving shall accrue;
O Lakṣmī, the entire fruit of every gift returns once more to the giver.

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of How the Liberation of the Departed Soul Occurs Through Various Gifts, the Excellence of the Recipient of Gifts Being a Holy Person, and the Exemplification of Vṛṣādarbhi and Sūrya," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me the essence of the dharma of the householder's life;
by doing what does a householder, possessed of sons and wife, attain prosperity? (1)
What must necessarily be performed, and by doing what is it accomplished, such that the inclusion of all other duties arises? (2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Holy men, ancestors, gods, teachers, great sages,
virtuous women, and devotees are to be worshipped and honored daily according to one's wealth.
For the virtuous are to be gratified with offerings of food, flowers, prostrations, and the like;
the virtuous are to be propitiated through service and devoted attendance. (4)
Indeed, the ancestors are to be gratified by the offering of water, food, milk, roots, fruits, leaves,
and prepared foods accompanied by the six flavors.
One should cause the dedication [of offerings] to the gods, perform the worship of the gods,
conduct sacrifices regularly, and always satisfy the deities.
One should serve one's gurus and always carry out their commands;
one should offer oneself to the guru and dedicate oneself to one's mother and father.
One should offer what is desired to the elders and serve them with joy for their delight;
likewise, one should bow to the sages and the twice-born and offer [these things] to them.
One should also recite the Sāmaveda and cause the gift of knowledge to be bestowed;
one should give food, water, and other necessities to virtuous and faithful women.
One should provide shelter and clothing, and satisfy those who are without refuge;
one should constantly worship devotees and practice the company of the virtuous. (3.104.10)
One should cultivate the path to liberation and always accumulate merit,
acting in such a way that the embodied beings who come to one's home may indeed be happy.
Having provided a dwelling and rendered assistance, one should satisfy him;
for this Hari, Nārāyaṇa, has arrived as a guest who has come to one's home.
Nārāyaṇa resides therein; may this Janārdana be pleased. Thus one should offer a welcome, for everything becomes an offering unto Brahman. || 13 ||
The householder should give to mendicants and likewise give to cows; he should give to dogs and also offer food to crows. (14)
One should offer [food] even to aquatic creatures and present it to those who are helpless;
one should offer the bali-oblation at night to the night-roaming spirits (niśācara-bhūtas).
One should give food to living beings such as nagas and serpents, and even to insects;
namely, flour, grains, roasted food, grass, or leaves, as appropriate for each.
One should always announce: "This is in my house for the teacher, the father, the virtuous friend, the trusted relative, and the guest. (17)
A householder should always be one who eats only what remains after [offering to] Kamalākānta;
the wife, established in her husband’s place, is the mistress of the home and the protector of the household.
Always performing the protection of the Dharma, you should contemplate all phenomena; O auspicious one, always practice generosity and cultivate respect. (19)
By receiving blessings and other such favors, a woman becomes Nārāyaṇī;
a man becomes Nārāyaṇa; and the earthly world attains the state of Goloka. ||3.104.20||
This is declared to be the nectar of the household, by practicing which one becomes prosperous;
having heard this essence of Dharma, he who acts accordingly shall attain heaven.
Listen further in brief and contemplate that which resides in your heart:
I am Nārāyaṇa, always present in the home in the form of the husband.
You are Śrī herself in the form of a woman, always the wife in every householder's home;
my attendants indeed exist in the home in the form of sons and daughters.
"My guests are honorable, virtuous, and well-versed; thus indeed does my family conduct itself in the home," he thought with his divine vision. (24)
They served one another with the nature of offering everything to Kṛṣṇa; through devotion, there remained nothing further for him to do. ||25||
O beloved, those very same sense-objects, those very same senses, and those very same enjoyments,
when conceived within Me, Kṛṣṇa, become free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa) and grant liberation.

This essence of the Dharma has been declared; it is auspicious, yielding the fruit of immortality within the home, bestowing supernatural powers and merit, free from bondage, granting liberation, and bringing happiness. ||27||
Such a reality is known through the merit of a thousand births;
however, it is difficult for one who is unworthy, sensual, and defiled to grasp. (28)
O beloved, the virtuous must be gratified in every way by means of the body, senses, mind, intellect, and consciousness; established in that, I myself become satisfied. (29)
The virtuous should be gratified with houses, gardens, fields, horses, elephants, cows, buffaloes, and wealth, as well as with water, clothing, food, and service.
Perform various sacrifices with abundant food and golden sacrificial fees;
serve the virtuous and the virtuous women, and gratify the ancestors and the gods.
Delight those who love the Veda, serve the elderly,
and honor those who depend on you with auspicious hospitality as is appropriate for each.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in former times there was indeed a thief named Naraśāya;
accompanied by his wife and son, he always lived by means of theft. (33)
Dwelling constantly in the Siṃhāraṇya forest, he would indeed go to his dwelling at night after forcibly breaking into the palaces of the wealthy and carrying off their riches.
Taking food, clothing, and other such things, he would go back into the forest;
thus he constantly sustained himself by theft in that forest. (35)
A virtuous Vaiṣṇava named Śrīcakrabhāsa, while traveling on the road, met that thief, who was lying down like a man, near a lake. (36)
Having recognized that virtuous man as faultless, fearless, and auspicious, the thief approached him, bowed, and then sat before him for a moment. (37)
The saintly man, having drunk the water, gave him water born of his grace;
the thief, honoring his good fortune, quickly drank that nectar-like water. (38)
By the mere drinking [of it], his heart turned toward the auspicious refuge;
his mind was purified, his body became cleansed, and discernment arose within him. (39)
Considering him to be purifying, peaceful, and a bestower of happiness, he asked him:
"O holy man, how may there be the destruction of sin? Show me the true path. (3.104.40)
Having heard this, Śrī Cakrabhāsa said to him: "Abandon indeed that worldly theft; instead, practice the theft of the virtues of the virtuous and of Hari. (41)
"O noble-minded one, always practice the service of Hari, the Holy One.
Having heard this, the king questioned that holy man again and again. 42.
"O sage, tell me in what manner I should perform service. The holy man replied: "In the forest, serve with forest-grown offerings presented [to me]. (43)
Make your sustenance from fruits and roots, abandon theft, worship the form of Hari here, and perform his devotion constantly. (44)
"By thus serving Hari, all sins shall perish.
Having been addressed in this way, that thief spoke to the virtuous man near the lake.
"O virtuous one, my residence is here; please come to my home.
I shall serve you and Hari as revealed by you. (46)
Sins will perish and wives and sons shall become pure, simply by hearing this while chanting the name of Nārāyaṇa Hari, O Śrīcakrabhāsa. (47)
Clad in bark garments, with matted locks and joyfully holding a garland in his hand,
the old man went to that hut, which was occupied by his wife, sons, and others.
Having been offered a seat, he sat down, honoring Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
meanwhile, the thief, his wife, sons, daughters, and others considered the old man to be their father’s guru. (49)
At that very moment, they placed a water vessel, excellent fruits, and ripe mangoes near the saint, and then said, "Please eat."
Delighted and filled with joy, they massaged his feet again and again;
the virtuous one ate the fruits and drank the cool water. (51)
While eating, he gives to them again and again in the midst of his meal;
and his wife, sons, and others consider these gifts to be a supreme favor. (52)
They ate the most delicious foods; even the thief then partook of them, having remembered me, Nārāyaṇa, and offered them to Viṣṇu.
They eat and give to these [beings], and having eaten, they become freed from sin;
through service and through touch, they quickly become purifiers. (54)
Their hearts were turned toward him; in his presence, they all said, "O Blessed One, may what is truly auspicious for us come to pass. ||55||
"Act accordingly; while dwelling here in the forest in our hut," [the king said].
"So be it," the virtuous one replied, and he, possessing peace, dwelt there for a long time. (56)
He instructed me in the constant worship of Nārāyaṇa;
having gathered together at night, they performed the worship and chanted with melodic intonation.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O All-pervading One! (58)
Having thus recited [this] to me, they always sleep;
likewise, having risen in the morning, they perform worship together with virtuous people.
Having performed these, they go to the lake, bathe, and pay homage to the Sun;
then, having bowed to the virtuous man and the garland, and having recited the five [mantras], they proceed toward the forest.
They go out to gather fruits and return to their own hut;
at midday, they roast fruits, roots, and other foods over a fire. (61)
Having given that to their guru and offered it to Hari, and having fed [the guru], they eat; thereafter, they perform worship.
In the evening they perform worship and partake of the nectar of sacred discourse;
the sons serve the saintly person, and the wife serves him day and night. (63)

Even a thief, if he constantly serves the virtuous one whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, [is purified of] whatever past deeds consisting of theft were committed by him through his wife, sons, and others. (64)
He reported everything to him, including all the wealth he had gathered;
having accepted it all, the virtuous man departed for the Gokarṇa pilgrimage site.
Saying, "This is offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa," he cast all that wealth into the midst of the water; at that moment, the maiden who was the very form of Śrī Lakṣmī appeared.
Having become virtuous, she said to the saintly one: "I have been offered to Kṛṣṇa by you;
indeed, I have become purified, and my impurity has vanished. (67)
Moreover, having purified both the thieves as well as those who previously possessed wealth, I shall lead them to the feet of Kṛṣṇa; this indeed is my duty.
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī took that virtuous man and went to that forest where those thieves were;
they too were struck with wonder.
Seeing the maiden, they questioned her; the saintly man said to them, "Lakṣmī herself has arrived to lead her to the abode of Nārāyaṇa."
"Be ready quickly and go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa!
Having heard this, they were filled with joy; having become ready and bowed to that Guru, [they departed]. (71)
When the celestial chariot, rich in divine splendor, arrived, they ascended it;
by the command of the saintly one, they departed with their attendants and followers.
O Lakṣmī, Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord, is attained through association with a saintly person;
then that maiden, who was the very embodiment of Śrī, went forward together with the saintly man.
She went to the palaces of those wealthy men, and upon seeing her, even those wealthy men,
filled with agitation, honored the Queen of the Gods with welcomes and other marks of respect.
Having learned the account from the beginning, everyone honored the virtuous man;
for the fortune that had fallen into the hands of thieves was now restored through the hand of the virtuous one. (75)
Having attained divinity in Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of auspiciousness,
they too, understanding this, became ready at the command of the saintly one.
For the sake of liberation, even then, a great, radiant celestial chariot arrived from the sky,
accompanied by his attendants and others.
Lakṣmī, having taken all the guardians of wealth and boarded the celestial chariot, bowed to the virtuous Śrī Cakrabhāsura and departed, leading them away. 78.
O Lakṣmī, in this way you formerly [described] Goloka, the abode of Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Hari, which is higher than the highest, as belonging to the families of the best of thieves. (79)
Through the union with the virtuous one, auspiciousness was achieved by her who had been joined to Hari;
and the virtuous Śrī Cakrabhāsa went to the realm of Lomaśa.
For the sake of the sacred ford, he sat in meditative absorption for an age after age;
there he beheld the path to liberation, and how people proceed from here.
Having pierced through Svarga, Maharloka, Jana, Tapa, and Satyaloka,
they go above the waters to Vaikuṇṭha, there into the presence of Hari.
They obtain rest, happiness, and great honor through a welcome and other honors;
then, by the command of Hari, they go to the supreme Paravaikuṇṭha.
And those wise ones, possessing divine bodies and divine qualities, with solid forms, go to Goloka, the imperishable abode, the supreme abode. (84)
Having entered that celestial chariot called Praṇava, which is rich with rays of light, they proceed to the world of Brahmā, becoming indeed the body of Brahmā and free from the flow of rebirth. 85.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have gone to immortality;
in the world of Brahman is the imperishable Brahman, the priest indeed of all. ||86||
Placing Mukteśvara at their head, they enjoy the nectar of bliss;
without [the need for] sovereignty, they become equal to the Supreme Self. //87//
Equal in physical splendor, victory, sovereignty, and power—such is this eternal Brahmasattra known as Amṛta. 88.
They have gone to that place from which there is no returning to death, for the sake of immortality;
devoted to Brahman and disciplined in yoga, they abide in the supreme goal. 89.

Free from passion, having conquered their vital breaths, devoid of delusion, speakers of truth, peaceful, devoted to the welfare of living beings, compassionate, and masters of their senses. ||3.104.90||
Those heroes who, free from desire, have burned away their sins through austerities, are remembered as pure devotees who attain union with Brahman. (91)
For them, there are worlds that do not decline, auspicious and of immeasurable bliss;
this is my divine state of Brahmā, supreme and radiant in the sky.
Having attained this, the immortals, together with Brahmā, do not grieve;
for theirs is supreme vigor, supreme longevity, and supreme austerity.
She is the supreme power, the supreme dharma, the supreme knowledge, and the supreme fortitude;
she is the supreme Brahman, the supreme wisdom, and the supreme sovereignty. ||94||
Therefore, there exists no being higher than that;
for he, abiding in the Supreme, is the Supreme among all things, and beyond him there is nothing further. (95)
Having become the supreme Brahman, one perceives [it] and not otherwise;
thus, being established in knowledge, one perceives everything as Brahman. ||96||
O Lakṣmī, for those liberated in the field of the Imperishable, there exists an eternal abiding in the imperishable abode, which bestows eternal bliss. (97)
O Lakṣmī, the constant association with the virtuous bestows the world of Brahmā; it removes all sins and likewise purifies one's own fortune. 98.
It effects the purification of the self and likewise the purification of liberation;
it effects the purification of knowledge and likewise the purification of worship. ||99||
It bestows the purity of nirvāṇa, is auspicious, and purifies omniscience;
it is the purifier of self-offerings and the purifier of service.
He is the purifier of defects, as well as the purifier of illusion;
he is the purifier of discernment and the purifier of bonds. || 101 ||

Having studied this sacrificial session of nectar, which is indeed the sacrificial session of Brahman, one is born here with the nature of Brahman and in the hereafter as well; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Thief Naraśaya through his Association with the Holy Cakrabhāsa by Means of Divine Lakṣmī, as well as the Liberation of Former Wealthy Men and the Knowledge of the Brahma-sattra," in the *Gārhasthyadharmasāra* within the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "O Mādhava, tell me the root of both dharmas and karmas,
by resorting to which a human being attains full nourishment in virtue."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, to the eternal root of dharma,
just as Lakṣmī is to Nārāyaṇa and Rādhikā is to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, you shine within me,
just as Lakṣmī resides in Viṣṇu and as Kambharā resides in Gopāla.
Just as Sāvitrī is to Agni, Durgā to Śiva, and Siddhi to Vināyaka, so too is a wedded wife; for she is indeed the root of dharma for embodied beings.
The married wife is the root of the ancestors, the gods, and guests; of one's own kin, the household, the lineage, and the branches of that lineage. (5)
Having adorned her, he should give the maiden— youthful, of beautiful limbs, and an embodied dwelling for the god of love— to an auspicious bridegroom, preceded by the offering of water.
When a maiden is desired by someone and he too is desired by her,
their marriage should indeed be performed with joy, for it brings about mutual welfare.
This is indeed the rule for virtuous Brahmins who are characterized by sattva:
to purchase [the girl] with wealth in various ways, or to take her away by force.
One who desires happiness should never form an attachment to anyone;
for everything struck by the sighs of women is surely consumed by fire.
One who desires his own welfare should marry a wife who has manifested the female characteristics;
one who possesses full youth and vigor should marry a woman whose youth is blossoming and who is well-nourished.
One should never cause one's own wife to be deflowered unless she is in her menses;
however, if she is lustful, she may be touched out of affection, for that is natural.
If she approaches her husband of her own accord during dalliance, there is no fault at all;
however, one should not marry against the wife's wish, lest one become unfaithful to women.

One who is lustful and acts according to his own whims destroys the dharma based on the household; for such a person, even that which is performed out of affection is considered to be nothing but unrighteousness. || 13 ||
Listen, Lakṣmī! In Mahārāṣṭra there was a Kṣatriya named Jāṅgalāmukha;
he chose as his wife a beautiful girl of twelve years.

[She was] one whose state of youth had not yet arisen, whose heart was united with the Dharma, endowed with right discernment, and who, after her menses, [remained faithful] toward her husband. || 15 ||
Desiring the fulfillment of her husband's wishes and not otherwise,
that woman of steadfast virtue remained before him after performing his duties, always devoted to the service of her husband.
Her husband, being lustful, desired to touch her by force for the sake of satisfying his passion; she said to him, "O beloved, dharma stands in my way. (17)
"I am not fit for this without the dharma-season, O Lord;
I perform only the service of touch here, so abandon the pursuit of sensual desire. (18)
Although addressed in this way, the lustful man, disregarding the duty of a husband, forcibly seized his wife; the virtuous woman then heaved a deep sigh.
At that very moment, fire in embodied form emerged from his breath;
it set ablaze the master, the mansion, the prosperity, and the household furnishings.
When her husband was lost, the devoted Satī grieved in many ways;
she remembered Dharma, and at that moment, Dharma himself appeared before her with four arms.
He approached and said to the blameless girl, "Do not grieve;
O girl, for the sake of protecting dharma, I am pleased with you; I am Dharma."
Choose a boon—may it be well with you—but do not swerve from dharma, O beautiful lady;
for dharma, when protected, protects, and when destroyed, it destroys as well. (23)
Because of that, I caused his destruction, and thus his ruin occurred;
yet because you protected him, you continue to live free from harm.
"O child, the fire did not burn you here in my house by its power;
choose a boon as you desire, for I shall grant it to you today—do not delay. (25)
Having heard this, the young girl named Kundadharmā then chose as her boon a husband,
a family for that husband, and a home restored to life.
"Provided with all necessary articles and endowed with the knowledge of Dharma, may my husband be restored to life; so spoke Dharmadeva, and immediately the husband was revived. (27)
Together with his family and provided with all household requisites, he,
endowed with knowledge of dharma and filled with intense devotion, rejoiced exceedingly.
He praised the supreme dharma that prevents the violation of his wife's fertile season;
then Dharma departed after receiving worship, as did the sacrifice of the Jāṅgala forest.
She always fulfilled the duties of a wife as they were prescribed;
being virtuous and truthful, Satī recovered her own husband even though he had been consumed by fire.
Thus, there is always this boundary established by the wife's own wish;
by observing it, merit is produced, whereas otherwise, it is considered a sin. (3.1)
Listen, Lakṣmī, and hear another [duty]: the rule regarding young maidens.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years. (32)
But when the fourth [period] arrives, she may seek a husband for herself;
her offspring shall not fail, nor shall her pleasure fail. (33)
If she were to behave otherwise than this, she would be subject to public censure;
therefore, one should marry her while she is still under the observances of menstruation, and not protect her [from them]. ||34||
A man should follow this woman who is not a sapinda of his mother and who is not of the same gotra as his father; for this is the rule. (35)
People indeed repeatedly request [a boon] preceded by the taking of the hand;
if an excellent boon should be met, one should give it to him, setting aside anything else. (36)
One should certainly not give it to one who is undesirable, nor to one who is inferior, nor to one who is diseased;
one should not give it to an enemy, nor to one who is loathsome, nor to one of cruel deeds.
One should certainly not give [a daughter] to one who is unrighteous, nor likewise to one who is harmful;
for a wife must never be purchased, nor should she ever be sold under any circumstances.
Wherever she desires, there she should be given away, adorned and free of charge;
indeed, when her husband has died, a woman should be given away wherever she wishes. (39)
If she has been abandoned by one who was married, another wife must be given to him;
and if he has been abandoned by his wife, he may marry another wife. (3.105.40)
Even when his wife has died, he may marry another wife; or the brother-in-law may enter [the bed of] the widow, or the brother-in-law may enter the woman [of the deceased]. (41)
If there is harmony between the two, this is the eternal law:
one may marry a virtuous woman of human descent who has neither father nor mother [to oppose her union]. (42)
One should circumambulate the god Agni, a father, or a cow in every way;
or else, in the presence of elders, one should indeed exchange garlands with one another.
Or else, having joined their hands and bowed to one another, he should perform the marriage ceremony in front of the Guru, either in the pavilion or in the temple. ||44||
