Without causing discord among the people, their families, the king, and the subjects, one should undertake both the taking of a wife and the giving away in marriage. (45)
That mutual illumination which is a beautiful unity between the two without contradiction—that too is an ancient duty, wherein the heart serves as the witness. (46)
In the absence of light, she is like a fetus—condemned and deprived of her father; like the lineage of slave-girls, she does not merit any mention in the records of the righteous. 47.
Even through the practice of *niyoga*, sons are born who attain the world of their fathers;
they establish the lineage of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, for that too is an ancient dharma. (48)
Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is more important and is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Commanded by her father, she chose him for herself and entered into union with her husband. (49)
She was born with virtuous conduct, for she is indeed considered married;
for the relationship between husband and wife is auspicious and enduring until death.
This eternal dharma is common to all who take delight; for a connection between man and woman based merely on the pursuit of pleasure is not righteous.
Even in the matter of inheritance, a son is indeed reckoned as the heir to the lineage;
if there should be no son, then the daughter is the one entitled to the inheritance.
A son and a daughter should be understood as equal heirs when it comes to inheriting property;
even if one has many sons, or daughters who are likewise [many]. (53)
Upon his partition of inheritance, his sons and daughters shall be the entitled heirs;
they should be given equal shares—this is the eternal law. (54)
Those who, having married a girl, send her away without giving her her share of the inheritance, are indeed consumers of their daughter's portion and fall into hell. (55)
Having sold a son or a daughter for the sake of their livelihood, those who enjoy that wealth are in fact eating the flesh of those very children. (56)
Furthermore, even a single man should not be sold, much less one's own subjects;
no one should forcibly sell a submissive young girl.
With the thought that it is his duty (*dharma*), he should indeed bestow her along with her dowry upon his son-in-law;
whatever may be the mother’s dowry, that too is the portion belonging solely to the maiden.
The daughter's son alone shall take the inheritance of a father who has no son;
according to the law, there is no distinction between a son and a daughter's son. ||59||
By fathers, brothers, fathers-in-law, and brothers-in-law, she should be honored and adorned by those desiring abundant prosperity. (3.105.60)
Women who reside in the home should always be honored and cherished; where beautiful women are contented, there prosperity dwells. (61)
The *siddhis* rain down and bestow all desires;
yet where women hold men in contempt, there all ritual actions are fruitless.
Lineages devoid of prosperity neither shine nor flourish;
yet, the dharma rooted in women is always supreme, bestowing the celestial realms and the world of truth.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born, the pursuit of pleasure, and the maintenance of worldly life—all these depend upon women. (64)
There is indeed no sacrifice such as that, nor a funeral rite, nor a fast;
there is no other dharma equal to the affection between a couple that bestows both celestial splendor and liberation.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; such is the ancient law for the protection of women.
These women are indeed named Śrī (Fortune); they should be honored by one who desires the earth.
A woman who is protected and favored shines forth as Śrī herself.
Moreover, O Lakṣmī, it is agreed that even the share of inheritance should be given to a woman;
her wealth always consists of a portion equal to that of a son and a daughter. (68)
That wealth given by her husband she is entitled to enjoy as she pleases;
for the inheritance from a husband is considered by women to have enjoyment as its sole fruit. (69)
When one man has many wives, the Brāhmaṇī wife is in every way the most excellent;
she performs the husband's bathing, his adornment, his cleaning of the teeth, and the application of collyrium.
A Brāhmaṇī woman should perform the offering to the gods (havya), the offering to the ancestors (kavya), the worship of the deities, and the preparation of food;
she should also provide food, drink, garlands, garments, and ornaments. (71)
A Brahmin woman should give these to her own husband, for she is indeed most venerable;
or else, it should be done in such a way that there is harmony among women.
Whether they be Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or others, one should serve them with freedom from affliction, with joy, and with affectionate compliance. (73)
Having fully accepted her husband’s command, she must not act otherwise in any way;
and the purity of the womb is to be recognized by those who possess innate excellence of character and form. (74)
Offspring is indeed the reflection of either the father or the mother;
that offspring should be known as being of pure lineage, possessing the very nature of its progenitor.
In that regard, wherever there is a state of separation, that is considered indeed impurity of the womb;
through the mixing of the seed, deformity occurs in the child. (76)
In the presence of undesirable objects, a state of mental confusion arises;
that [confusion] transfers into the seed, and its manifestation occurs in the womb. (77)

Then, in a secret place that is invisible, free from obstacles, where sounds are hushed, the world is tranquil, and the cries of beasts and other animals are stilled, the rite of impregnation (garbhadāna) should be performed.
This should be performed when all principles (tattvas) are thoroughly pacified, and not otherwise;
she will be born of a pure lineage here—of this there is no doubt. (79)
The refutation of the intrinsic nature of other sounds, touches, forms, and tastes proceeds from the sowing of the seed as well as from the seeing of the image. (3.105.80)
Therefore, at that time, it is held that nothing other than the face before one is visible;
moreover, both should maintain a clear heart, free from anger or resentment. (81)
One should not dwell in a state of impurity, but rather be filled with fragrance;
one should dwell with a serene mind and cultivate the virtues of sentient beings. (82)
The donor and the nurse must both cultivate their minds with one-pointed concentration in every way;
thus that lineage shall remain pure, and nothing else should be kept in mind at that time. (83)
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest—He alone, and no other, should be remembered by the couple during the act of procreation. (84)
Whatever qualities exist in things proceed from their remembrance;
therefore, the divine Janārdana, the god of gods, is the supreme Lord. ||85||
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you an auspicious ancient tale: how Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, gave gifts according to the season. (86)
Then Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, remembered Nirṛti, the Rākṣasa;
by him, Rāvaṇa was born, from whom the nature of the Rākṣasas arose.
When, during her menses, she remembered Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari,
she became permeated by his nature and gave birth to a devoted son, Vibhīṣaṇa.
In the east, Pārvatī and Śaṅkara remembered their son, the commander-in-chief, who was endowed with strength, the destroyer of the Daityas, and the bestower of victory. 89.
Skanda became the Lord of the Gaṇas for the purpose of destroying obstacles;
and Vairāja, having recollected the three qualities (guṇas), indeed brought forth the triad.

The birth [of the deity] is according to tradition as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Maheśa; likewise [it applies] to the cooked offering (caru), the fruit, the grace (prasāda), the seed-syllable (bīja), and the words of blessing (āśīrvacana). ||91||
Whatever kind of remembrance arises, such indeed is the offspring that is born;
whatever be the contemplation and devotion, the fruit is permeated by that very state of being.
When there is a wish-fulfilling tree, an image of Hari, a guru, or a husband,
as well as when there is medicine, a mantra, or austerity, the fruit corresponds exactly to one's inner disposition.
In learning, in exertion, in battle, in agriculture, in the performance of service, in material prosperity, and in speed, the fruit is exactly in proportion to the effort applied. (94)
As there is grace when a king, a virtuous person, Hari, one's parents, a merchant, a master, a deity, or a father is satisfied, so too is the fruit [obtained]. (95)
Whether toward an enemy, a restrainer, a serpent, a brahmin, one bearing a weapon, or an ascetic;
whether in the context of a quarrel, an obstruction, or destruction—the fruit is exactly in proportion to the anger. (96)
In devotion, in yoga, in prayer, in service, in rites for the gods, in scripture, in objects of enjoyment, and in long-term undertakings, the fruit is exactly as the peace [of mind]. //97//

In religious duty, in battle, in giving, in speech, in removing obstacles, in theft, in liberation, and regarding place and time—the fruit is exactly according to the swiftness [with which these are performed]. //98//
In poetry, in logic, in instruction, in command, at the final moment, in dissolution, in adversity, and at the beginning—just as it was studied, so is its fruit. (99)
In the field, in heaven, in a wife, in a disciple, in a son, in an undertaking, in the acquisition of wealth,
in a mantra, in a scripture, and in composition— just as the seed is, so is the fruit.
In fame, in pleasure, in virtue, in lineage, in happiness, in exertion, in food,
in the treasury, in hospitality, in the home, and in heaven— the fruit is exactly as it is with one's wife.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, a wife who is ever devoted to her husband is in every way the root of all religious duties, especially so. 102.
For the four aims of human life, as well as their means and instruments, all activities proceed and reach fulfillment through one's own wife. (103)
A wife is indeed the field for all dharmas, the garden for the attainment of sons, the wish-fulfilling creeper of happiness, and the root of all blessings.
She is the stable for the horses of the mind, the nest for the birds of the vital breaths;
she is the ship for those wandering in saṃsāra, and likewise the vehicle for those bound for heaven.
In sacrifice, lineage, happiness, suffering, merit, great festivals, assemblies,
domestic affairs, wealth, and fame, one’s own wife is renowned as half of oneself.
O Lakṣmī, through recitation, hearing, and likewise by taking refuge in Dharma, both enjoyment and liberation shall accrue in every way to both woman and man. (107)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marital Wife as the Root of All Religious Duties and Rites," including the marvel of the Kṣatriya Jāṅgalāmakhya’s wife Kundadharma and Saradharma, as well as the eligibility for giving a daughter in marriage, the eligibility of a groom, the eligibility for inheritance, the purity of seed, and so forth, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle. 105.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Just as a wife, so too is a son considered by the father to be a refuge of dharma;
the father exists in the form of the son, and the father’s dharma resides in the son.
Whether hidden or manifest, a son is proclaimed to be his father;
[he inherits] nobility, a virtuous character, gentleness, and perseverance. (2)
Devotion and discernment manifest an excellent son;
whereas ignobility, lack of conduct, cruelty, and a state of inaction [manifest] the opposite.
Indeed, lack of devotion and lack of discernment manifest impurity;
he inherits either the character of his father, that of his mother, or both.
One born from a pure womb indeed does not incur the state of social confusion;
however, even one who is superior in age does not deserve honor if he is deficient in character.
Even a Śūdra who is rich in virtue and of good conduct is honored by people; for in this world, one proclaims oneself through one's own character, conduct, and deeds.
One's own biological son is said to be one's very self;
however, a son born to another through the rite of *niyoga* in one's own wife is the second [type]. (7)
The third is one born in secret from a woman of the same caste without formal authorization;
the fourth is one born of a wife who was already pregnant at the time of marriage. (8)
The fifth was given by someone from birth and reared [there];
the sixth was also taken as an adopted son in his youth. (9)
The seventh son is said to be one who arrives in the form of a disciple;
the eighth is called the purchased son, and the ninth son is born of an unmarried woman.
The tenth son is said to be Manojanya, the mind-born;
one who is abandoned on the road immediately after birth and then taken up is called a *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
The eleventh is to be known as the son of a daughter's son (dauhitra), and the twelfth is recorded as the daughter herself;
thus, those born of the lineage are to be understood as twelvefold.
For conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) arise as if they possessed a self, like a master;
indeed, a son born of an unmarried woman (kānīnaka) takes on the caste of his mother. (13)
The offspring of courtesans indeed possess the complexion of their mothers;
likewise, those who are the offspring of slave-women who have no husbands.

The initiates to be awakened are of the same caste as their mothers or likewise of the same caste as their masters; for those children obtained through the initiation of mendicancy belong to the lineage of Acyuta.
All virtuous women and virtuous men become members of the lineage of Acyuta;
indeed, the groups of renunciants, as well as sons and daughters, belong to Nārāyaṇa.

O Lotus-born one, such is indeed the established order in this world on the surface of the earth; however, in other worlds, it proceeds according to one's own will, and this same principle applies there as well.
O Lakṣmī, there are generally four kinds of wives that exist:
she who is called a wife by marriage, and she who is a maidservant who has come along with [the husband]. (18)
But she who, while still a student (upakurvāṇikā), remains in her father's house for some time and has entered into a secret union is called "protected" (rakṣitā). || 19 ||
O Lotus-born One, listen: the husbands of women also exist in four such ways;
he who is married is called a husband, and he who has been betrothed is indeed the best of them.
The second is proclaimed as the secondary lover (gauṇakānta), such as a brother-in-law and others;
the third is the one obtained through the rite of appointment (niyoga), for he is indeed the "benefactor" (upakurvāṇaka).
One who has entered into secret yoga is proclaimed as "protected" (rakṣita);
their offspring, according to the circumstances, belongs either to the woman or to the man. //22//
In a dispute, the offspring itself belongs here to whichever [father] one might desire;
for it is distinct due to differences of place, differences of time, and differences of custom. (23)
How is it not conceived that a daughter given away in the form of a gift is [the giver's] own?
She is conceived as being for the enjoyment [of another]; therefore, custom is indeed the cause. ||24||
Whatever the nature of one's cultivation, such is the worldly conduct;
whether having abandoned [the object] through anger after enjoying it, or likewise through dispassion. (25)
Even through renunciation and discernment, she is indeed abandoned, for she is like a mother;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, this flow of the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) consists of a state of intense infatuation.
They always lead embodied beings through various melodies (mūrchanās), according to the nature of the flow that exists at whatever time, place, and age. 27.
Dharma established according to such a method shall be the bestower of happiness and peace;
for the methods of the gods are one thing, and those of the yogis are another. (28)
The various customs of humans, as well as those of animals and other beings, are indeed dharma provided they do not lead to harm, according to their respective traditions. (29)
A path that leads to misfortune is not considered righteous even if it is of a virtuous nature;
there is no dharma that causes suffering, for dharma is in every way a bull that bestows happiness.
Wealth that is pursued in accordance with righteousness is beneficial; wealth joined with unrighteousness is harmful.
Desire that is conjoined with dharma and artha is [true desire]; devoid of those, it does not serve the purpose of man.
He who has reached the further shore of dharma, artha, and kāma attains the Imperishable;
whereas he who is unrighteous, seeks only what is harmful, and is addicted to sense-objects undergoes the torments of Yama.
Even the regulation of family life and so forth is directed toward the goals of human existence; a way of life devoid of these goals is bestial, not human. (33)
The scripture, which is indeed the teaching of the Dharma, functions among humans and other such beings; it certainly does not exist in the animal realm, for they are indeed devoid of knowledge.
Force, instinct, and delusion are the bonds of animals;
upon these are based the beasts, the aquatic creatures, and those born as insects. (35)
For those who proceed in this manner, there is no end to existence;
only by chance, through association with the virtuous, might the end of existence occur at some point. (36)
For the self cannot be slain; therefore, one should practice its upliftment.
One should practice beholding the virtuous with affection and dwelling with them through service. (37)
A person should serve a holy man who has initiated the practice of dwelling in Brahman, having subdued pride, sorrow, anger, joy, and latent desire. (38)
He is the vessel of trust for all beings, pure, having Śrī Kṛṣṇa as his deity, established in the supreme state of Brahman, peaceful, and pleasing to behold for everyone. || 3.9 ||
He had brought all worldly undertakings to an end, was established in meditation, and possessed mastery over his senses;
he was proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, endowed with the "equal eye," and supremely compassionate. (3.106.40)
One should likewise seek refuge in and pray to such virtuous people, saying:
"O Teacher of the World, wash away the sin committed through ignorance. (4.1)
O Teacher of the World, show the ladder to the path of liberation;
having burnt away the knot of latent tendencies, purify your own people, O Teacher of the World! 42.
"O Teacher of the World, having displayed supreme devotion, grant liberation!
One should indeed offer such a prayer so that [the Lord] may show compassion accordingly. (43)
And I must say before the virtuous again and again: "I am yours";
whatever command you may give, I shall perform it all, however difficult it may be. (44)
Whether it be a kingdom, wealth, cattle, one's own home, a sacrifice, a gift, a son, or a garden—tell me, and I shall give you everything. (45)
Thus one should properly entreat the holy man and satisfy him with offerings;
by offering everything without hesitation, he shall indeed become a partaker of liberation. 46.
Illusion is said to be doubt; there is no doubt regarding Brahman.
If there were doubt among the virtuous regarding yoga, service, speech, or action, [it would be illusion]. (47)
When will there be liberation? When will there be purity? How can service be performed here?
And when will there be steadfastness in one's own pure nature here? 48.
Therefore, having become free from doubt, one should serve the most excellent holy person—one capable of washing away evil, the giver of liberation, and whose conduct is divine. (49)
One should always serve my form—contented, a treasury of knowledge, the substratum of Brahman, without support, without dependence, and my own refuge. 3.106.50
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the supreme fruit of serving the virtuous, through which one’s own master, cattle, birds, kinsmen, and friends are all liberated. (51)
In the land of Karṇāṭaka, there was a devoted ascetic sage named Śambhalavāra, who by birth was born of the Sūta caste. ||52||
He indeed took up residence alone on the bank of a river;
though young, he maintained his composure, having no desire for the enjoyment of the god of love without a woman.
Having performed supreme and excellent austerity and having enjoyed pleasures in accordance with dharma,
I shall then go to heaven, the eternal and highest state.
Having reflected thus, he departed from his home to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred sites,
arriving at a beautiful and auspicious elevated spot on the bank of the Godāvarī.
Then, having observed a favorable terrain for performing penance, he established his own residence in a village named Satrāśaya.
Honored by men with food and other offerings, he set his mind [on penance] and thereafter sat amidst the five fires for six months.
The ascetic remained standing on one foot for a full year, performing supreme penance while worshipping Viṣṇu Narāyaṇa. (58)
At the end of the year, having bound his own feet with a creeper to a branch of a banyan tree, he hung there for an entire year with his head downward.
Having performed penance in this manner, at the end of the year he placed his head upon the ground and,
standing on his tiptoes, practiced severe austerity.
At the end of the year, with his hands raised and weighing only a thumb's breadth,
he performed severe penance, gazing at the sun with unblinking eyes.
After that, he dwelt within the waters of a river for six months;
then, in the fifth year, Viṣṇu assumed the form of a fish in the water.
He arrived, marked with the sign of the discus, and tore away the sage's skin;
he likewise devoured his flesh, yet the sage did not tremble.
Viṣṇu spoke to the fish with these words: "You dwell here in the water; who are you? How have you come to stay here? Tell me, what is your purpose here? (64)
Having heard that from Śambhalavāra, the fish said to him who possessed auspicious intentions:
"I shall perform penance for the sake of happiness, since happiness is the fruit of dharma. (65)
Kingdoms, homes, wealth, wives, sons, daughters, cows,
male servants, female servants, and vehicles are always obtained through austerity.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are obtained through the practice of household life;
having become a householder, I shall go to the supreme state after performing ascetic penance.
Thus addressed, the fish said: "Do you still have any attachment to worldly enjoyments?
Perform penance and enjoy the fruit thereof in the supreme state, the station of liberation. (68)
Indeed, enjoyments are impermanent, they bestow suffering, and are of the nature of bondage;
abandoning them, go to the eternal abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard this, Śambhalavāra then spoke again to Matsya:
"O Matsya, you are like a wise man even amidst the objects of the senses."
Even having known them thus, there is no turning back from enjoying sense objects;
for even after enjoying various sense objects and attaining complete satisfaction in every way, [the mind does not turn away].
"Having brought about the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), one may then go to the supreme state;
thus is the path easy to attain, while any other is fraught with doubt. (72)
There is no destination for one possessed by passion; therefore, one should pacify that passion.
Thus, having propitiated Viṣṇu and gratified Mādhava through austerity, [I shall proceed].
"Having enjoyed these pleasures and having ruled over them, I shall go to that state through devotion.
Having heard this, the Fish then said: "Behold my divine form! (74)
"I am pleased with your austerity; I, Nārāyaṇa, have come before you.
Choose whatever you desire, and I shall grant it to you entirely and for all time. (75)
The sage chose wealth, kingdom, women, sons, cattle, daughters,
elephants, horses, bulls, cows, and the four aims of human existence.
"So be it," Hari said, and having granted the boon, he vanished;
then Śambhalavāra also emerged from the water.
Repeating the garland of names of Nārāyaṇa, indeed of Hari,
he dwelt on the delightful bank of the river at its highest point.
Then the village of Satrāśaya, consisting of ten thousand people,
was completely surrounded on all sides by the floods of the river during the rainy season.
The king also became submerged in the water and met his death;
many others as well—men, women, people, and subjects—perished.
Five thousand perished by means of a flood;
thereafter, others went to other regions for the sake of dwelling there. (81)
A thousand men dwelt there, sustained by fortitude;
they were all devotees and ascetics, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Now, Śambhalavāra was also a supreme and auspicious object of veneration for the inhabitants of that village, because there lived an ascetic. (83)
Thereupon, honored by the subjects, he ruled over the kingdom;
thus he became the king there, worshipped by thousands of men. (84)
The people of the village gave him twenty-one maidens,
as well as cows, livestock, male servants, female servants, and their subjects.
From that, goats, sheep, horses, and bulls all came into being for him.
Thus, through his ascetic penance, he obtained a kingdom, enjoyments, women, sons, and so forth.
He attained devotion to Nārāyaṇa and performed service to the virtuous;
through his devotion, the subjects, who were the bearers of dharma, flourished once again.
There were ten thousand upright sacrificial posts (satranāgara) there;
all of them were indeed rendered Vaiṣṇava by this sage.
He also performed the chanting of the names and the worship of Śrī Hari as was appropriate, and he likewise had a temple constructed.
Thousands of saintly persons always resided in his house, and he constantly practiced the ninefold devotion within that beautiful mansion.
Then, when that time had passed, the discerning one spoke to his subjects:
"By fate, my hundred sons and likewise five daughters remain. (91)
I have twenty-one daughters and two hundred more;
I possess thousands of cows, as well as bulls and horses;
I also have parrots and sarika birds, elephants, and dogs.
In this world, you subjects have become masters and mistresses; thus you are happy.
Likewise, dharma has been performed, as well as artha and kāma, and now liberation is seen. || 93 ||

"I wish to bestow my kingdom upon my eldest son immediately and then depart for the imperishable state of Nārāyaṇa. "So be it," the subjects replied, and they spoke further words that were a source of auspiciousness.
We shall all go together to the supreme state. ||95||
Having established each of his sons in their respective duties according to their authority,
the king, after deliberating thus, attained union in meditative absorption.
Having entrusted everything to his son and established himself in the state of liberation,
he then placed all the queens and all the subjects under Śrī Hari at that very spot.
Having yoked their senses and vital breaths, they remained absorbed in their own selves, worshipping the Lord of Śrī, Nārāyaṇa, their beloved Master and Lord. 98.
Then Viṣṇu indeed arrived there with his attendants in celestial chariots,
illuminating all directions and making the quarters of the sky resound with thunder.
He said to that devotee Śambhala, "Come to the celestial chariot.
Having bowed to and worshipped the Blessed One, the protector of Śambhala spoke to him.
O Blessed One, out of compassion, please lead away all those subjects who are eager and ready to come here for the sake of liberation itself. 101.
Cows, horses, bulls, goats, sheep, cattle, parrots, and others—whatever beings there may be here, they are purified by your grace. 102.
"Bring my sons and daughters, as well as the queens and their attendants—whosoever among them are ready here—to your own abode. (103)
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, fulfill this desire of mine; show me your grace. Hari said, "So be it; by your devotion, I shall do so."
Your sons are of diverse castes, born of women of different origins;
they are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, others who are Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras.
The sons born of queens of different castes, as well as their followers, male servants, attendants, female servants, and others who follow the path of devotion; || 106 ||
"Ascend my celestial chariot; I shall lead you all to my own abode. Thus addressed were all those who had become seekers of liberation.
Then, by the grace of Śrī Hari, all those nine thousand animals and birds ascended the celestial chariot.
Then, possessing divine bodies and four arms, they ascended that celestial chariot;
and the women, having become Śarvas, likewise possessed four arms and held lotuses.
All the subjects, radiant with divine splendor, ascended the celestial chariot,
each leaving behind a single son as the seed of their lineage, according to their respective status.
All the subjects, as well as the king together with his royal family,
all went by means of a celestial chariot to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode.
Thus, indeed, the practitioner of the Śambhala rite, even while remaining at home,
may enjoy the pleasures of the earth like an ascetic, having worshipped Keśava.
Taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa with devotion, he went to the supreme state,
even though he was the husband of wives of different castes and was accompanied by his sons and others.
Thus, through association with the virtuous, the family prospers in every way;
it attains the supreme abode, for there indeed no distinction is made between the worthy and the unworthy.
By reading and hearing this, one becomes possessed of detachment from worldly enjoyments;
having attained enjoyment through devotion, one shall by the power of Hari attain liberation.
Through virtuous conduct one may attain liberation, and by it one may lead thousands to liberation—
by which that very Śambhalavāra attained liberation along with ten thousand subjects.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Sons, Various Wives, and Various Lords in the Third Section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; [and] Liberation through the Yoga of the Holy (Sādhu); and how a person of the Sūta caste, a devotee of Śambhalavāra who was devoted to the Holy, after attaining a kingdom, sons, cattle, birds, and so forth by means of devotion and austerity, attained liberation along with his progeny. || 106 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of the virtuous Śrīcihnayogin, a resident of Saurāṣṭra; I shall tell it here to you, for it bestows both prosperity and liberation.
There was a virtuous man devoted to me, residing in Kīśādana-pura;
he was accomplished in the yoga of the Śrīcihna-samādhi, possessed of divine deeds, and established in meditative absorption.
He worshipped me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; I exist sometimes in an invisible form and sometimes in a visible form.
In some places he dwells in water, in a forest, under a tree, or on a mountain;
in some places in rain or heat, and in others on the shore of the ocean or at Lake Aśva.
Sometimes in fire and sometimes in wind, and sometimes he enters into a deep abyss;
though capable of such things, he constantly resorts to me.
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Parameśvara, O Lord of Akṣara, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Śrī Puruṣottama! (6)
Thus he constantly calls out to me and worships me again and again;
he perpetually makes a garland with the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He performs my bathing, meditation, and worship constantly;
indeed, he always beholds me in embodied form within his mental heart.
Thousands and hundreds of thousands of men worship him;
seeing him as equal to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), they imagine him to be such.
All that bears fruit for them by mere thought in His presence;
there is no need for benedictions, nor is there any need for service.
Once, such a virtuous man, wearing nothing but a loincloth,
happened by chance to come before King Devānīka.
The King of Saurāṣṭra, having recognized him as a holy man, bowed to and honored him;
then, after offering a welcome and a seat, he presented him with the *madhuparka*.
Having obtained the water that was the nectar of his feet, the king, together with his family, drank it;
as did Kalyāṇadevā, Anīkastrī, and the queen Sahajāśrī.
He gave him that food, sweet fruit, water, and ghee;
the sage accepted it with devotion, drank the water, and was satisfied.
Having honored the sage in many ways, the king spoke to him again:
"O Blessed One, we two are at your disposal; tell us, what shall we do? (15)
Whether it be a kingdom, whether wealth, whether cows, whether a beautiful woman, a vehicle, a daughter, a son, or a palace—tell me, I shall give you all of it. (16)
"This house, this kingdom, and this seat of dharma are yours;
O King, you are the one who must rule the earth, for our enemies have been slain by you. (17)
Having heard this, the yogi Śrīcihna said to that devoted king, the twice-born:
"O King, I do not desire sovereignty, nor wealth, nor even a beautiful woman. (18)
“O King, I do not desire cattle, drink, wine, a palace, or even a son;
however, I have undertaken a vow, and it is for its fulfillment. (1.9)
"I am at your service; I shall attend upon you both without hesitation.
Upon hearing this, the king was delighted and said to that sage, "So be it."
He led him into the interior of the house and showed him its beautiful features, saying:
"This is the bedchamber of the Blessed One; please stay here as you wish."
"Enjoy this palace and these pleasures; make use of your own wealth. Perform your vows perfectly and accept everything for the sake of spiritual merit."
"What food, what water, or what else do you require?
I shall strive to bring you joy; what may I provide for you? (23)
Having heard that the food was excellent and as it had been prepared, the sage said, "Serve the milk-rice and other delicacies," and the king brought them forth.
Having drunk water and eaten, the illustrious Yogirāja said with a voice marked by grace:
"I wish to sleep upon my bed; I am not to be awakened under any circumstances. (25)
"Your feet must be massaged for me, and you must remain awake during the night";
having said this, he fell asleep for seventy-one days.
Then the two queens and the king became intent on service, abstaining from food; thereafter, the virtuous one arose, established in his vow.
He then said, "An oil massage now pleases me.
The queen and the king then performed an oil massage rich with fragrant scents.
They caused him to bathe and likewise adorned him;
they also fed the virtuous man with various kinds of sweet foods.
All kinds of sweet dishes, *laḍḍukas* of every variety, special preparations of minced meat (*veśavāra*), *polikās*, *pūrikās*, and so forth. ||3.107.30||
Various kinds of savory foods, diverse vegetables, liquids of every sort, and likewise parched grains. ||3.1||
Alkaline and sour substances, sweet powders, various fruits, delightful fermented gruels, and all kinds of foods fit for a king's meal. (32)
There they both fed him, and the great seer ate with ease.
He said to the auspicious king and queen, "Carry me to the forest."
Placing the Sage upon a palanquin adorned with gold, silver, and other precious materials, the King and Queen were filled with joy. (34)
They searched both in the city, at the edge of the city, and likewise in the forest;
indeed, the two servants were serene in mind and free from agitation.
The serene yogi, marked with the signs of Śrī, descended from the palanquin;
having released those two excellent boons, he said to them, "Speak what you desire, and I shall grant it. (36)
And when those two, who were so delicate, were pierced in their feet and shoulders,
the King of Yogins touched them with his hands, which were like nectar.
Both were perfectly formed and free from fatigue, like two divine deities; they possessed fresh forms and were likewise in the bloom of youth. (38)
The sage said to them both, "You two may go to your own city, Kiśādana;
I shall dwell here in the forest and observe my vow. (39)
"Whatever you two desire shall all indeed come to pass. When this was said, the king and queen spoke to that lord of sages: [3.107.40]
O Lord of Sages, if any offenses have occurred during our service, all of these should be forgiven by you, whose great soul is an ocean of compassion. (41)
"O Sage, we always desire your affection and grace," [they said].
But the yogi Śrīcihna spoke while they were beholding his divine form:
I am gracious, I am Hari, and I am he whose heart bears the mark of Śrī;
my name is Śrīvatsavakṣas, and I am Lakṣmīpati. 43.
Appearing in the form of a holy man, I have come here to your house out of compassion;
my descent is always for the sake of the welfare of my devotees.
Therefore, O Janārdana, I truly move about as a virtuous one with a divine body;
I am pleased with the host of gods and I delight in innate prosperity.
"Choose excellent boons that you desire; I shall grant you the fruit of your service.
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, the host of gods then bowed down to him.
Having worshipped the Supreme Self and considering it his own meritorious deed,
he then addressed me, the Blessed One, with words full of affection.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, everything has been attained by me through your arrival; together with my wife, I have crossed over [the ocean of existence] by means of complete service—this is great indeed. 48.
O Hari Kṛṣṇa, since you are pleased, my family has been protected and delivered;
this is my grace, and it is the fruit of my living being in service to you. 49.
"This is indeed the fruit of sovereignty and also the fruit of my devotion;
moreover, you appear pleased—dispel my doubt."
"What was his vow, of what nature was it, and for what reason was all this performed?
Having heard this, Śrīcihnayogin spoke to Devānīka.
Listen, O devotee, to that which has been determined by me of my own accord in its entirety:
I, the Lord who is dear to his devotees, shall appear in your lineage. (52)
I have come here for the sake of purifying you and your queen;
therefore, I shall indeed descend into this lineage of devotees who are worthy of purification.
My form in the guise of a virtuous man purifies human beings;
having first purified you as a seed through that virtuous form, [I shall act] thereafter. (54)
I am indeed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself; I am the glorious Gopāla-bāla, Hari, the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā. (55)
Thinking, "I shall become [the bestower of results]," I have indeed come here in every way to cause [you] to perform service for the very purpose of granting the fruit of that service. (56)
Indeed, you and this woman have performed the service of me as described:
massaging my feet, bathing me, feeding me, and carrying my palanquin. (57)
"Everything has indeed been accomplished by me for you; therefore, all those born in your lineage shall likewise be endowed with happiness both in this world and in the next. (58)
And you too, in the course of time, shall go to Goloka;
together with your wife, you shall attain the great bliss of my own abode.
The Brahminhood of you, a Brahmin devoted to his wife, remains intact;
under your control lies both royal prosperity and the sovereignty of royalty, as well as the state of Brahmanhood once again.
By my dwelling here, the status of a Brahmin will certainly be yours forever;
likewise, the state of being most devoted to Brahman, the rank of a great seer, asceticism, and goodness shall be yours. (61)
Liberation, divinity, and blackness, the bestowing of liberation, being worshipful by all, and being an ocean of all jewels. (62)
She is the mine of all good fortune, likewise enriched with all sovereignty,
and the eternal refuge of the prosperity and wealth of Śrī Lakṣmī, Śāradā, and Bhūti.
"All this shall come to pass in my lineage through my dwelling," having said this, that Blessed One, I myself, gave him a golden necklace.
Having likewise given a garland of jewels, he gave the supreme mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ. (65)
Having repeatedly given the inexhaustible vessel and the Sudarśana discus,
I vanished from sight, and Devānīka returned home.
Having seen his own [city], golden-hued and very pleasing, with a rampart likewise made of gold, surrounded by the Kalpa gardens and filled with Apsarases; 67.
And likewise, he gave a temple beautifully adorned with a divine celestial chariot,
along with groups of divine male and female servants marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, and other emblems.
On all sides were wish-fulfilling cows, Gaurīs, Lakṣmīs, and maidens;
subjects equal to those of Vaikuṇṭha, and elephants with eight tusks.
White horses with black ears like swans, and white birds;
chariots traveling through the sky, resplendent as the multitude of suns and moons.
Devānīka rejoiced in the presence of the attendants who were forms of Viṣṇu,
as well as the sacrificial pits, the pavilions, the great sages, and the assembly of virtuous men.
The king of devotees indeed beheld hundreds of thousands of virtuous people and all the gods;
he also saw the celestial river flowing along his side.
By the grace of Śrī Hari, O Lakṣmī, the king became like Mahendra, the lord of the gods, and his queen became like Ramā. ||73||
Through my yoga, by my grace, the imperishable abode (dhāman) was manifested;
that city, Kīśādana, became Śrīśāyana.
The host of gods went toward that great wonder and toward me, the Lord;
remembering Him in His virtuous form, they worshipped Him with supreme devotion.
Then, with the passage of time, I was born as Śrī Puruṣottama, the Lord of millions of billions of lotus-eyed wives, who is affectionate toward His devotees.
Thus, through repeated association with a saintly person and likewise with Hari, the entire family of a servant indeed becomes the family of Hari. (77)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "You are the beloved, you are the lord of all, the Supreme Lord, Hari himself.
For you, the illustrious Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, there is no lineage, for you are beyond lineage. (78)
Nevertheless, O Kṛṣṇa, in the world of men, lineage-based tradition proceeds; therefore, I desire to have that explained to me. (79)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, in ancient times before creation I was Nārāyaṇa; from my limbs were born Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the gods, and others.
And at the beginning of creation, from the mouth-mass of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul, the Brāhmaṇa, devoted to his illustrious wife, came into being. 81.
His wife, known as Pativratā, formed a pair with him; for that couple possessed a lifespan equal to that of Parameṣṭhin and was indeed of the nature of the form of Vṛṣa.
O Lakṣmī, understand from me this first [progenitor] known as Pūrvapitāmaha;
he was the mind-born son of Brahmavrata, who was himself the son of Patnīvrata. (83)
Śīlavrata was his wife, and she was Mānasī;
both were equal in lifespan to Parameṣṭhin and were born from ten million cosmic arrays (vyūha).
Vāsudeva and Vāsudevī—both of them became [his disciples];
even their disciples numbered in the hundreds of thousands, through that self-luminous yogin. (85)
And they were gazed upon from every direction in Saurāṣṭra;
there was a Brāhmaṇa, a lord of the earth, who was indeed the son of one devoted to the vow of Brahman. ||86||
He was named Kalyāṇadevānīka, the lord of Kīśādāna;
he lived as a couple with his wife, who was known by the name Sahajāśrī.
Those two became equal in lifespan to the first half of the *vedha* period;
they were Bhūmānārāyaṇa, who was endowed with the splendor of the earthly *nikī*.
Indeed, by my command, these two have manifested here in this universe;
and by them, I, who am the true reality, have been made manifest in the form of the Śrīcihnayoginī. 89.
A blessing was indeed granted for the sake of manifestation within my lineage;
then there was also the mind-born son of Kalyāṇadevānīka.
He whose soul was the crest-jewel of Kṛṣṇa, who was honored by the king of Ānarta, whose name was Picudevānīka, and who possessed the very form of Nārāyaṇa. (91)
Here, indeed, was born a son to Miṣṭādevī by Mukuṭakalpa; both of them possessed a lifespan equal to half the duration of the current age of Brahmā. (92)
The glorious Mahāviṣṇu himself, the Lord known as Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the son of Picu and Devānīka, shall indeed have a lifespan of ten kalpas.
He was indeed accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, the goddess Kaṃbharāśrī;
they had both arrived for the sake of granting a boon to King Khaṭvāṅgada.
Recognizing these two as my parents, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, I, Śrī Puruṣottama, became his mind-born son. 95.
He is the Lord and Master of the devotees who number ten million times a hundred billion times a hundred million;
He is the Sovereign of the Imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, the Avatāra, and the one higher than the highest. (96)
I am Śivarājñīśrī, and Kṛṣṇamādhava is your beloved;
I am his father, his father’s father, and likewise his father’s father. (97)
His father, his father’s father, and all those ancestors of his were Nārāyaṇas; they were portions of Nārāyaṇa and possessed my own nature. (98)
All the mothers, the Nārāyaṇīs, are indeed identical with my own self; what need is there for much speaking? O Lakṣmī, you know this in every way. (99)
Having become the soul of all, I manifest that divine play;
from hearing and reciting this lineage, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of the Service of the Devotee Kalyāṇadevānīka and the Instruction on the Lineage of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me that which is to be chanted here for embodied beings who are immersed in the principles of the world when some affliction has arisen."

Who is the refuge for the helpless, what is the deity, and who is the protector? What is the supreme source of strength, the bestower of auspiciousness, and that which is of the nature of virtue (vṛṣa)? || 2 ||
It destroys calamities, washes away sins, and is the supreme bestower of liberation;
it annihilates latent impressions and severs the bonds of the knot of Māyā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Chanting the thousand names of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, known as the *Puruṣottama-sāma*, and bowing to Hari and to me, [he attained his goal]. (4)
Always worshipping me with devotion, reciting [my name], reflecting upon me,
and meditating on me as abiding well within the self of all, one shall overcome all obstacles.
The refuge of all merits, a treasury of dharma, the Lord who is the locus of righteousness,
the manifestor of the three worlds, unassailable by the three periods of time, and the infallible one.
One should indeed glorify me with devotion as one whose form is like the celestial tree of plenty (kalpavṛkṣa), who is filled with wonders and the like, and who possesses all sovereign powers.
[He worshipped] the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, who bestows the ocean of splendor when served with divine syllables and the like,
and who is the means of attaining the eternal, ancient, and full-blown bliss.
He is the purifier of all purifiers, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest;
he is the very form of fortune for the liberated and the sovereign self of all lords.
It bestows divinity upon the gods, possesses the quality of seerhood among the sages,
and consists of the nature of truth, virtue, sincerity, affection, service, and vows.
He who fulfills all desires, bestows divine power, capability, and strength, and is a friend at the time of death who accompanies one during the departure from the body. || 11 ||
One should constantly chant my name, Śrī Hari, the support of all and the true friend;
one should bow to me, the beloved and peaceful one, who shines within hearts and stands before one.
I delight in Hari, the bestower of security, well-being, and other blessings;
[I delight] in that thousand divine names which destroy all sins and fear.

I shall speak that which bestows perfection, which is manifested through divine play, sovereignty, qualities, actions, and its essential nature, and which is sung by liberated beings, lords, seers, gods, and others.
O Lakṣmī, for this hymn of praise consisting of the names of the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the seer is the Lord of All; and I am Śrī Puruṣottama. (15)
The meter is Anuṣṭubh; the supreme deity is the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He is indeed the one called Akṣara, the Great Liberated One, the Lord of the liberated, and the Seed-syllable (Bīja).
Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, Ramā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī are his consorts.
The Śaktis, the Hṛdaya, and the venerable Puruṣottama Sāman. || 17 ||
To Gopālakambharābāla, to Kīlaka, to the infallible Astra, to Padmāvatī, to Ramāpadma, and to the Lord, Vaṣaṭ! Namaḥ! || 18 ||
"Omnipotent weapon! O you who bear the trident, the fish-banner, the bow, and the arrow! Phaṭ svāhā!
This mantra is to be employed during recitation for the purpose of removing all afflictions. (19)
I meditate upon Him who shines in the world of Brahmā, who is cherished by the circles of those most devoted to Brahman, the Lord beloved of the friends of Brahman, abiding within all. 3.108.20.
I meditate upon the beloved Kṛṣṇa, who sports in the divine Lomaśa-kṣetra, who is enchanting, whose smile is gentle, and whose desires are fulfilled. (21)

I remember the Lord who bestows nourishment, is beloved, grants desires, removes suffering, and bestows happiness—the one who grants liberation, whose name ends with the four hundred and fortieth [syllable]. 22.
I worship Lord Hari, the bestower of enjoyment, liberation, desired objects, and everything;
I worship my Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
who is adorned with the ornaments of a crown and earrings and is beautiful in form.
I bow to the attractor, white in color, who is a dark child. || 24 ||
I serve with self-surrender the Lord of the powers of ten million billion universes, the sovereign Master of the Self,
the yellow-robed one, the most excellent among the virtuous.
Homage to the one whose essential nature is infinite, who abides in every foot and eye,
who is awakened by the knowledge of his thousand names, and whose self is the lord of desire and illusion.
Oṃ! You are the self of valid knowledge, the supreme self, the supreme Brahman, the supreme Lord;
the highest person, the Lord of lords, the sovereign of the imperishable, the Master. || 27 ||
The Lord of the Liberated, the Lord of Incarnations, the Lord of the Liberated Women, the Great Master, the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Son of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 28 ||
The external form is the self-existent activity; he is the omniscient, glorious Hari, the all-pervading Lord, the imperishable Brahman, the Blessed One Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa. || 29 ||
Nārāyaṇa, the self-luminous Bālakṛṣṇa, the ether of consciousness, the Lord of the Abode, eternal bliss, the incarnate Supreme Lord. (3.108.30)
He is the possessor of the earth, the abode of divine qualities, the dark and beautiful one within;
he is the truly eternal bliss, the conscious self endowed with the insentient. || 31 ||

The king who possesses supernatural power and prosperity, Saṃkarṣaṇa, the restrainer; the cowherd who has gone to the Ganges, the sustainer of the earth, the lord of the gopīs, and the master of the cows. || 3.2 ||
He is the attendant, the one honored by the assembly, the assembly itself, and the lord of the attendants;
he is divine, peaceful, the bestower of peace, the being, and the possessor of the excellence of being.
He is praise, verse, tradition, sound, the poet, the Veda, the injunction, and supreme wisdom;
he is the seat, the locus, fortitude, steadfastness, forgiveness, and self-restraint. || 34 ||
Pradyumna, the radiant one; Dyaus, the beloved; the Lord of Kamalā; Aniruddha, the infallible Acyuta; the Infinite (Bhūmā); Mahākāla; and Maheśvara. || 35 ||
Mahāviṣṇu, Madhyaviṣṇu, Viṣṇu, the Pervasive One, the Upward-Gazer; Vairāja, the Cause, the Agent, the Action, the Effect, the King, and the Recitation. || 36 ||
The monkey, the sky-goer, the object of the senses, the lord of the senses, the one possessed of meditative concentration;
the yogi, the yoga, the universal emperor, the wielder of the discus, the conch-bearer, the mace-bearer, and the banner-bearer.

The charioteer, the kṣatriya, the one who knows the stars, livelihood and non-livelihood, the victorious, the unmanifest, the thread-self (sūtrātman), and the fourth state which is the abode of bliss. (38)
He is Sadāśiva and the Divine; he is Śiva, possessing the nature of dissolution;
he is the Creator, the Nourisher, the Ordainer, the Father, the Mother, the Well-wisher, and the Friend. (3.9)

The lord of life, the companion, the master, the support, the possessor of wealth, the friend, the treasury, the universe, the great element, existence, and the sovereign of all possibility. ||3.108.40||

He is the goal, the splendor, and the purifier; He is the reflection of consciousness, the fruit, and the fructifier; He is the inner controller, the Supreme Person, the knower of the field, the field itself, and the destroyer of suffering. 41.
The witness, the Supreme Person, the Lord of Prakṛti, the Sovereign of the Guṇas;
the Lord of Goloka, whose abode is nectar, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, the Consort of Ramā. ||42||
The Lord of Rādhā, Śrīnivāsa, Dāmodara, Vibhāvasu, Prabhājāpa, Vāmana, Trikrama, and Bhūrivikrama. ||43||
Keśava, Kapila, Kāśī, Nṛsiṃha, Māpati, Nidhi, Śrīśa, Sthāṇu, Satīśa, Śaśī, Vidyud-dhruva, and Ravi. ||44||
Brahmā, Aryamā, Viṣṇurāta, Hara, Vaiṣṇava, Sāttvata, Sādhu, Yati, Brahmacārī, Bhartṛ, Dhartṛ, Amara, and Amṛta. ||45||
He is dissolution and manifestation; he is the earth and the abundant bestower of much;
he is the musical note, the melody, and the scale; he is the instrumental playing, the vocal discourse, and the festival. ||46||
Sava, Satra, Makha, Yajvan, Yajña, Vahni, Prahavyabhuj, Dattātreya, Mahāmatsya, Padmanābha, and Abjanetraka. ||47||
He whose palms are like lotuses, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the architect of the universe, the lord of the gods;
he who has a white boar as his emblem, the bull, he who was born from the bull, and Vṛṣākapi. ||48||
Sūta is the speaker, the Guru is the scripture, Manu is the great teacher, and Madhu is the Lord;
he is the instructor, the ruler, the logician, the leader, and the possessor of statesmanship. ||49||
He is logic and final determination, the eldest, the sovereign, and the ancient one;
he is the eternal, the renunciant, the sage, the observer of vows, and the ascetic.
He is Hiraṇyagarbha, the lover of the golden-hued one, whose palms are like lotus petals;
he is the learned, the master of knowledge, the eloquent, the lord of speech, and the bearer of the virtues of an ascetic.
He is the householder, the master of the home, the protector, the sower, and he who bears the Śrīvatsa mark;
he is Vyāsa, the one of beginningless excellence, the seer, and the illustrious Kṛṣṇacandra.
The wise Kāmbhareya, Prajāpati, Lord of Heaven, Lord of the Quarters, Lord of Śrī, Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Brahmā, and the one who bows. || 53 ||
Kṛtajña, Śaraṇa, Vipra, Vivāha, Vararūpavān,
Varahāra, Saṃvarta, Maṇḍapa, and Anaṅga are the most excellent.
He is the womb of all, the man of valor, the self of progeny, the year, and the flow;
he is the sun in heaven, the desired and the beloved, the junction, the staff, happiness, and tranquility. || 55 ||
Dāna, Dātā, Svatvarūpa, Tyāga, Sneha, Sumaṅgala, Śakuna, Śakunī, Pattrī, Haṃsa, Śuka, Kaṇa, and Kṛṣi. || 56 ||
Sphuraṇa, Prama, Kūrma, Rāma, Raivata, and Ātmavid;
Pṛthu, Parśudhara, Khaḍgī, Dhanvī, Raṇī, Rathī, and Iṣudhi. || 57 ||
He is the object of perception, the sequence, and the cognition; he is the perfected, the unborn, the eternal, and the auspicious.
He is self-luminous, the possessor of all wealth, the truth, the seer of equality, and the one whose path is equanimity.
Bhogī, Śukla, Arjuna, Dakṣa, Pratyaya, Pratyagātmavān, Āmaugha, Sarvayoni, Paramahaṃsa, and Ārthika—[these are the names]. ||59||
The foundation of Nirvana, the hollow one, pervaded by veins, the one of wide renown;
the gentle, the fierce, the one whose nature is restraint, the one of noble ascent, the all-pervading, the radiant.
He is consciousness, the nature of the object of knowledge, the knower, the treasury of the Vedas, and the Ordainer;
he is Viśvaksena, of perfect form, the presiding overseer, and the one whose sphere is direct perception.
He is the created and the uncreated, the three ages, the world and the beyond-the-world, and the path to the Goddess Ramā.
The manifestations are the Vyūha, the Aṃśa, and the Vibhava; these consist of the arcā-form, the svarūpa, and the ūrjita. || 62 ||
The patient one, the steadfast, the enjoyer, the bestower of fruit, the diligent creator,
the unerring, the destroyer of pain, the tiger, the lord of the mountain, and the upholder of the mountain.
He is the inexpressible and the well-expressed, the mountain, and the bearer of the ruby;
he is the embodiment of existence, Pārśvatikeśa, Govinda, and the one whose banner bears Garuḍa.
Ṛṣabha, Garuḍa, Kalki, Kumāra, Buddhisarjana, Hayaśīrṣa, Svarṇavarṇa, Surarṣi, and Padmajāpati. (65)
Muktāpati, Bhūpati, Muktapati, Ramāvasu, Viśvāvasu, Siṃharūpa, Nimiṣa, and Bṛhaspati. ||66||
He is the forest of the Maruts, the mind, the splendor, the sky, and the one clad in the directions;
he is the Veda, the three-footed, the foot, the protector from all sins, the one who has descended, and whose course is gentle.

He is the sweet one, the agitator, the remainder, the welcome arrival, and the possessor of true news; he has innumerable eyes, possesses the dharma of the learned, is clad in the armor of dharma, and is renowned.
The multitude of Nārāyaṇīs, the husband of Śivarājñī and Satī, Mādhavīśa, Bhārgavīśa, and the great Tulasīnāyaka. 69.

The embodied one, the lord of bodies, the jewel, the sectarian mark (puṇḍra), the person who bears the mark, the sustainer, the bridge of all, the heaven, the waters, the fire, and memory. ||3.108.70||
He is formative action, gravity, pride, the universal, the granter of boons, the bearer, establishment, the state of being spilled, the leader of the yoke, the vehicle, and the foremost guide. ||71||
Deva, Meru, Garuḍa, Prājña, Ārṣa, Caturmukha, Kṛpa, Tīrtha, Sāvana, Megha, Vārdhi, Rasa, and Śaya. ||72||
Bhadra, Suta, Śūravīra, Tāraka, Sthavira, Yuvan, Arka, Plakṣa, Śarabha, Gaja, Gajānana, and Mṛga. (73)
The occasion, the cause, the belly, fortune, the star, darkness, the digit, the possession, the *praṇava*, the seed, the purpose, wealth, and the capable one. (74)
Ṛtu, Yūpa, Vatsala, Dhaneśa, Somapa, Puru, Sthūla, Sūkṣma, Liṅga, Suparṇa, Anaśana, and Mṛdha. (75)
Kīśa, Jaya, Bhāgavata, Sāttvata, Yantracetana, Mantra, Mukunda, Viśvāsa, Patnīvrata, and Pradakṣiṇa. ||76||

The living soul, the infinite, and the end-maker; the Arhat, joy, the giver, the cave, and the house; the water-pot, the sacred fig tree, the Vṛndā tree, and the abode of the wish-fulfilling creeper. ||77||
Stambha, Vāstu, Mahākuṇḍa, Āyudha, Kambala, Kara, Kāru, Śilpī, Vātsya, Āpta, Tvaṣṭṛ, Stara, and Prarocana. ||78||
Aśoka, khadira, bilva, vaṭa, palāśa, āmala, udumbara, kadalīśa, pūga, rājeśvara, and rati. ||79||
The couple, Kumuda, Moda, Nandana, Śrīdhara, Smara,
Śṛṅgāra, Dāsyada, Nemi, Bindu, Bhasma, Bhrami, and Mahas.
Keśava, Kāmakṛt, Jiṣṇu, Brahmaṇya, Vāsuki, Priya, Lekha, Bimba, Pratibimba, Nirodha, Dīrghikā, and Payas. (81)
Prapā, Pāna, Piśaṅga, Piṅgākṣa, Gāyaka, Gaya, Nartaka, Naṭaka, Māyī, Mantrī, Tantrī, and Jitendriya. ||82||
He is the wish-fulfilling gem, possessed of great heroism, the great dust, and the supreme person;
he is the assembly of virtuous men, the assembly of women, and the imperishable one consisting of the wives. ||83||
Stanyapa, Sādhyadeva, Dharmajanya, Vṛṣāsuta, Ṛtambhara, Camatkāra, Svāhākāra, and Karmaṭha. ||84||
The nightly lamp-offering, the consecration, the crown, the necklace, and the beloved sindūraka;
saffron, dūrvā grass, rice, barley, and sesame seeds. ||85||
He is the betel vine, the sugarcane stalk, the bilva fruit, and the increaser of devotion;
he is the nature of the areca nut, the fragrant one, the auspicious, and the pleasure grove. (86)
He is composed of splendor, he has assumed a splendid form, his limbs are splendor itself, and he bestows the bliss of splendor.
He is the tilaka of splendor, his thighs are made of splendor, he rests upon splendor, and he is the refuge of the stories of splendor. ||87||
He is the service of Śrī, the assembly of Śrī, the food of Śrī, and possessed of the samādhi of Śrī;
he is marked by Lakṣmī, the source of Mahālakṣmī, and the creator of prosperity. ||88||
He has Lakṣmī by his side; he is the womb of Mahālakṣmī; he is the supporter of Lakṣmīdhara.
He is the knower of Brahman, the one for whom Brahman is supreme, the reciter of Brahman, free from debt, and a jewel. ||89||
He is the guest, the full moon, the path of the gods, and the one who moves through the sky;
he is the teacher of the world, the Lord of Victory, the beloved of Lalitā, and the solitary one.
Praise, recitation, stability, steadfastness, existence, prosperity, the possessor of power, joy—the fivefold witness, the essence, affection, and the one of perfect fortune. (91)
Clad in saffron robes, radiant in spirit, he is a mountain-like ascetic practicing the penance of the five fires;
he is a serpent, free from desire, a grandson, and a youth who grants the fruit of all wishes.
He is the Svastika, the nature of creative intuition, the essence of the proposition, and the means of valid cognition;
he is the innate, the intrinsic nature, the stake, the Kuśa grass, the Śāla tree, the stone, and Śiva. ||93||
The Caitya, the Garta, the Huṃkāra, the Jaghana, the Vīthi, the Ajvara, the Udgītha, the Upaniṣad, the Purāṇapuruṣa, and the Śanī. (94)
Satpara, Sannivāsa, Śrīdruma, Asuranāśaka, Kuñcikātmā, Brahmarandhra, Brahmahrada, and Mahādhruva. ||95||
Paridhi, Kiraṇa, Keśa, Pañcaśikha, Parāsana, Pravargya, Mahopāya, Viśiṣṭa, Vidruma, and Vaśa. ||96||
Modaka, taṇḍula, apāmārga, devādhidaivata, devānīkatilaka, and mahāśvapaṭṭasārasa. ||97||
The son-in-law, the increase of dharma, resolve, the honey-mixture offering, the form of the Sarvatobhadra diagram, the pedestal, the altar, the sacrificial oblation, and the water. 98.
Sthaṇḍila, Maṇikṣetreśa, Pādmakṣetramaheśvara, Lomaśānandada, and Patnīvratavaṃśaprabhākara. ||99||
The protector of Indradyumna’s site, the Lord of the Narasiṃha forest,
the dweller in the tiger-forest, and the bestower of desired boons upon Rukmāṅgada.
Prābhāsikaprabhānu, the nourisher of the lunar region (Somakṣetra), the lord of the night-lotuses of the Sāman chants, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, and Prajāpati. || 101 ||
Vasanta, Kiśora, Mahendra, Śamprada, Saha, Maṅgaleśa, Manaseśa, Reveśa, and Virajāpati. || 102 ||
Ratīśa, Gomatīśa, the incomparable Kāmadugheśvara,
Ekādaśīpati, Svarṇarekhākānta, and indeed Amūrtaka.
Nandinīśa, Doleśa, Puṣpa, the husband of Kalāvatī, Badarīśa, Pampeśa, Darpahā, Bāndhava, and Dhava. || 104 ||
Affectionate toward his devotees, the leader, the creator of honor, the sustainer of the world, the upholder;
the blessed one, the four-armed, the inaccessible, the creator of the thread, the doer of good deeds, the virtuous one. 105.
Sundara, Aśvamedha, Parjanya, Amṛtāpati,
Sulabha, Adurlabha, Aśvattha, Rakṣoha, and Daityanāśana.
He who has seven horses and seven tongues, the eastern hall, the dawn, the hermitage, Yama, he whose eyes are the sun and moon, and the three-eyed one. 107.
He whose navel is the sky, whose feet move upon the earth, whose breath is the wind, whose life-force is the sun, whose ears are the quarters of space, who dwells in heaven;
he whose mouth is turned elsewhere, whose bladder is the ocean, whose body is the universe, who is the essence, yet free from passion.
He is dark as a rain-cloud, beneficial, truthful, the abode of Brahman, and possessed of His own glory;
He is eternal, conscious, the inner controller, and endowed with specific knowledge.

He is the nature of cause and effect, the uniter, the steadfast, the one who bestows rank; he is the trusted witness, accessible through sacred revelation, the author of the Vedic verses, the reckoned, and the imperishable.
Bestower of well-being, creator of well-being, the embodiment of well-being, and possessed of praise;
the lofty substratum of creation, the sphere, Ka, Kha, and Khaga. (11.1)
The middle state, the middle abode, the twilight portion consisting of Abhijit;
it is nectar, auspicious, a gain, the bringer of security, and the leader of success. (1.12)
Dhanvantari, Nala, Nāla, Pravāha, Dadhimaṇḍapa, Puttra, Svarga, Āśīrātmā, and Pralaya, who is worshipped by the Vaiṣṇavas. || 113 ||
It is fresh butter, liberation, the lamp of the heart, and the bestower of the supreme goal;
it removes the fear of time, illusion, evil karma, and the messengers of Yama.
The door, the doorkeeper, the moon-chamber, the consumer of ghee, and the peerless one;
the one with many offspring, the childless, the wakeful, the progenitor, and the innermost self. (1.15)
It is without knots, it is noble, it is the limit of the boundary yet devoid of boundaries; it is unobstructed, undivided, immutable, and subject to no transformation.
The delimiting factor is sovereignty; the definition is the Lord; the defined is the Ruler;
"iti" is the food; and the most eternal one is the eater. (1.17)

The flute-player, the cluster of Kadamba trees, the stake, the assembly, the caravan, and the respectful one; the noble one, the dual-natured, the merchant-leader, the three ages, and the one whose nature is the pair. || 1.18 ||
The lord of women, one's own husband, attainment, identity, creation, action, reality, ownership, intention, the origin of effort, and the creative imagination; || 1.19 ||
Udaya, Pramada, Suṣumṇā, Mūrtidarśana; Dāna, Dama, Dayā, Diṣṭa, Diti, Darvī, and Dohana.
He is the speaker, the reciter, the one who causes [the text] to be written, and the teacher; he possesses intuitive wisdom (*ūha*).
He is beyond the range of speech and mind, the meritorious one, worthy of being chanted by those of pure hearing.
Life is gentle laughter; conduct on the true path is the wager; battle is the stake;
he is the son of Āgama and Naigameya, indeed the unobstructed one. || 122 ||
He is the innumerable and the singular, the fearless one who destroys fear;
he is the sacrificial rite, the one from whom oblations are offered, the one who bestows existence, and the remover of worldly rebirth.
He is one whose vigor is upward-turned, who does not stumble, and who destroys obstacles; he is the best of men, the destroyer of evil dreams, the bestower of peace, and the creator of joy. (124)
The attractor, the inexhaustible vessel, the ultimate end, the legitimate son, the utterance, the worldly transaction, the manifestation, and the monosyllabic sound. (125)
The giver of enjoyment, the giver of liberation, the washer away of sins, the bestower of merit, the famous, the one whose self is renown, Sarvasena, Dik, Tāra, Nāda, and Īpati. 1.26.
He is the explosion, the boat, the fruit, the flower, the flour, and the nature of both existence and non-existence;
he is the sacred thread, the bracelet, the true cause, and the wielder of all weapons.
He is the root, the primary and the secondary, the beginning of the root, and he who abides at the end of all.
He is the repository, the foundation, the belly of all, and the body of all.

Oṃ, salutations! You are the positive concomitance and the negative concomitance, eternally joined with the Name; you are the perfected one, the blossoming state, the true being of the universe—Oṃ, salutations!
Thus, this thousand names of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is purifying, meritorious, and the destroyer of all afflictions. (3.108.1) [30]
O Lakṣmī, this hymn called *Puruṣottamasāma* has been uttered by me;
indeed, the sins of the listener, the speaker, and the reciter are destroyed. 1.31.
In this world and the next, there shall be no affliction; obstacles shall be swiftly destroyed.
A Brahmin shall become learned and a knower of Brahman, and a Kṣatriya shall become a hero and victorious. (1.32)
He shall become a wealthy merchant of the Vaiśya caste, or a happy Śūdra; as a celibate student he will be wondrous, and as a householder he will be endowed with wives and riches. (133)
A merchant who possesses the prosperity of the forest-dweller shall become a virtuous and tranquil man;
one who delights in dharma shall find dharma, and one who desires wealth shall become wealthy. || 134 ||
One who desires sensual pleasures attains the fulfillment of those desires; one who seeks liberation attains liberation;
one who seeks a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom, and one who seeks subjects shall obtain subjects. (135)
One desiring a son shall indeed obtain a son; one desiring a wife shall obtain a new bride;
one desiring a daughter shall obtain a daughter; and one desiring a husband shall obtain a husband. (136)
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
one seeking a livelihood shall possess a livelihood; and one seeking enjoyments shall become possessed of enjoyments.

One who desires a desired object shall obtain that desired object, and one who desires a house shall attain a house—provided he recites this daily in the morning with devotion, his inner self being purified. (138)
He attains preeminence, fame, renown, prosperity, and the highest good;
no fear whatsoever comes upon him, and his splendor and valor increase. (1.39)
From reciting this, one becomes free from disease; through its recitation, one becomes nourished, strong, and virtuous;
one becomes handsome, delightful, and desirable. (3.108.140)
The bonds of the speaker are shattered, fear perishes in every way;
transgressions are destroyed, and even enemies perish. (141)
For one who praises Him, even difficult passages indeed become easy to traverse—provided he has taken refuge in Puruṣottama and possesses devotion to Puruṣottama. 142.
One whose self is free from the ointment of illusion attains the Supreme Person;
for my devotee there is no inauspiciousness, nor any fear of saṃsāra.
For my devotee, misfortune, birth, death, disease, old age, infirmity, futility, and oppression never arise. (144)
From the recitation of this, there shall arise the bliss of the Self, peace, excellent prosperity, success, fortune, fame, magnanimity, preeminence, nourishment, and lordship. (145)
The liberated lords, the ancestors, the perfected ones, the gods, and the great seers attained supreme accomplishment solely through the recitation of this hymn. (146)
Having heard it, the venerable one becomes free from sin; by reciting it, he becomes so.
The speaker, endowed with faith and devotion, rejoices both in this world and after death. (147)
This Lakṣmī-stotra, which is devoted to me, has been spoken by me, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; by reciting it, one shall become devoted to me. 148.
"Even by reciting a single verse, the recitation of this entire work will be accomplished.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you a verse full of wonder. (149)
I bow to the ordainer of the three worlds; I worship the one endowed with millions upon millions of powers;
and I meditate upon the one who resides within the inner self.
I bestow all-encompassing sovereignty upon the knower of the Self.
Homage to the one whose essential nature is infinite; homage to the one of innumerable forms;
homage to the one whose form is a couple; homage to the glorious Supreme Self.
Salutations to the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
salutations to the one born as Śrī Kambharā, Lakṣmī, and Gopāla. || 152 ||
Homage to the Lord of the helpless; homage to You who are compassionate toward Your beloved;
homage to You, the protector of the Dharma; homage to You, Bālakṛṣṇa.
Salutations to you, the Lord Śivarājñīsvāmin, and to you, Nārāyaṇīśvara; salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā and Padmāvatī. || 154 ||
Salutations to You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved lord of Brahmā;
salutations to You, the Lord of Teachers, the omniscient master of all guides. || 155 ||
This hymn has been recited and offered unto you for the attainment of its fruit;
O Giver of All, protect me, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, salutations, salutations! (156)
One should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) by reciting this one thousand times;
great calamities will perish and great happiness will certainly arise. || 157 ||
Through the recitation of this [work], his consciousness of all principles increases;
and by a single drop of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion, he shall attain a state equivalent to omniscience. (158)
The king is preeminent; he is preeminent on earth, preeminent in heaven, and preeminent as a giver of wealth. He is preeminent in knowledge and preeminent in worthiness of honor.
May the person who performs the excellent recitation of this hymn become [one who attains such merit]. ||159||
O Lakṣmī, by the mere recitation of a single chapter daily, one becomes possessed of the fulfillment of all desires through a fraction of my compassion; therefore, dwell in that person's home.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand-Name Hymn of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Known as the Śrī Puruṣottama Sāman," which destroys all obstacles and grants all desires, in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:

"O Blessed One, this supreme hymn of yours has been obtained; it leads to the further shore of existence, destroys all afflictions, is most excellent, and is the highest bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
O Lord, those who are diligent in performing their duties attain the fruit of their actions through the recitation of hymns;
they proceed either to enjoy that fruit or, without enjoying it, they attain liberation.
If they indeed depart after having eaten, where do they go and what kind of fruit do they enjoy?
Or, as a result of what action, having enjoyed what kind of fruit, do they depart? (3)
But as for those worlds belonging to the performers of good deeds, tell me what they are like, once one has enjoyed them and departs, such that delusion does not arise again.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivārājñī, for I shall speak of the excellent fruits [of these deeds];
once known, they do not lead to further delusion.
For austerity is always the foremost among all actions;
indeed, heaven, filled with glory, is attained through austerity as the highest goal.
Through the power of austerity, long life, excellent enjoyments, prosperity, beauty, health, learning, and supreme discernment are obtained. (7)
Supreme sovereignty, great wealth, good fortune, and the expansion of one's lineage are obtained through austerity; even the state of a most excellent deity is attained through austerity.
Having indeed enjoyed all this— the fruit of long asceticism—
the ascetic subsequently enjoys the fruit of his hymn of praise in the eternal world of Brahmā.
The vow of silence is declared to be a form of austerity; for him by whom it is observed, mastery over speech arises, as well as the power to issue commands.
He may become the instructor of many, a guru, or even an ācārya; he may also become a royal preceptor or a commander-in-chief. || 11 ||
He shall become a teacher of the Dharma and likewise a guide;
having enjoyed the fruit of this hymn in this world and in the heavenly realm. (12)
To enjoy the fruit [of his merit], he indeed proceeds to Hari’s supreme, imperishable abode;
the giver of gifts shall become a lord of gods in heaven and a wealthy man on earth. (13)
Having enjoyed worldly pleasures, the king shall obtain the fruit of praise;
indeed, in that which is known as the Supreme Imperishable, he shines, partaking in all happiness.
The vow of celibacy is the highest austerity, which excludes worldly pleasure;
such a person shall be long-lived in this world, powerful, nourished, firm, and youthful. (15)
He shall become invincible, incapable of being defeated, and a lord equal to Brahmā;
having enjoyed the fruit for many years, he thereafter obtains the full fruit of the hymn of praise.
He surely goes to the world of Brahmā and rejoices with those who know Brahman;
non-violence is also declared to be the highest austerity, known as restraint (niyama). || 17 ||
One who does not harm living beings attains a state of mere happiness free from suffering;
having enjoyed supreme bliss there, he shall thereafter obtain the fruit of the hymn of praise. || 18 ||
He goes to the supreme, imperishable abode and rejoices with those who discourse on Brahman.
Initiation endowed with righteousness and joined with austerity—such austerity is considered the highest. (19)
Initiated and endowed with devotion, he shall attain the station of Parameṣṭhin;
he shall also attain the station of Bṛhaspati and the station of a Great Teacher (Mahācārya). ||3.109.20||

Having been initiated there, he attains birth in a family worthy of worship, in the family of the virtuous, or in the abode of Acyuta; thereafter, having enjoyed worldly pleasures, he proceeds further.
One enjoys the fruit of praise as happiness in my supreme imperishable abode;
even subsisting on fruits and roots is declared to be the highest austerity.
Having attained the fruit of that, which is sovereignty, one finds the supreme heaven;
those who subsist on leaves or consume only water go to the heaven that bestows prosperity.
Having enjoyed the fruit thereof, they then attain the imperishable fruit of praise;
even through the gift of gold, they obtain sovereignty and the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Wherever in the world he may obtain it, from that he goes to the Imperishable;
there he enjoys the fruit of the hymn, which is a treasure-trove of eternal bliss. (25)
Service and attendance upon the guru are declared to be the supreme austerity;
through service, one obtains knowledge, as well as the guru’s favor and auspicious blessings. (26)
Merit is supreme; indeed, whatever is desired, such as heaven, is obtained through it.
[This applies] toward one's mother and father, the elderly, the husband, the wife, and family members. (27)
Serving cows, the virtuous, the gods, guests, those living abroad, the sick, the helpless, and the wretched is auspicious. (28)
Austerity is indeed declared to be supreme; its fruit is the highest happiness.
Whatever is most desired in the world, one obtains all of it through service.
Having attained omniscience through service, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
having enjoyed the fruit in heaven and in truth, they experience the fruit of the hymn of praise. ||3.109.30||
One shall become a servant of those who possess the bliss of eternal, perfect joy;
one shall forever be a great liberated soul in the supreme, imperishable abode. 3.1
Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony here and offers the most excellent kavya and havya to the ancestors, as well as food, sacrificial fees, and other gifts to the twice-born; ||32||
Having enjoyed the fruit of heaven for a long time, he goes to the world of the ancestors;
having enjoyed the fruit there for a long time, he shall thereafter obtain the fruit of the hymn of praise. ||33||
