Leaving Satyaloka behind, he proceeds to the imperishable world (akṣara-loka); moreover, in this world, the progeny of the one who performs the śrāddha becomes abundant.
That family shall be Vaiṣṇava, having worshipped the Supreme Lord and having offered the food offering (naivedya) while constantly worshipping with devotion. ||35||
O Rame, by the power of this hymn, one attains the imperishable abode;
thus, indeed, the progeny of the giver of the śrāddha shall flourish through their lineage.
They go to the imperishable abode, and the speaker of the hymn rejoices;
his descendants and those who dwell with him likewise rejoice eternally in the Imperishable.
By the merit of serving cows, one goes to heaven;
beyond that, by the merit of this hymn of praise, one goes to the supreme, imperishable Goloka. (38)
By bathing at the three periods of the day, women obtain excellent boons; and through this imperishable hymn, they attain the state of being led by Brahmins and the status of goddesses. (39)
Subsisting on air and performing austerities, one obtains the fruit of sacrifice and reaches heaven;
and by means of this hymn, one thereafter attains the supreme, unsurpassed, imperishable state.
One who bathes daily becomes wise, intelligent, and radiant;
one devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) goes to heaven, and through this hymn, one attains the Imperishable.
One who is richly devoted to sleeping on the bare ground indeed obtains palaces worthy of kings in heaven; and by means of this hymn, one goes to the Imperishable.
Clad in rags, bark, and fine garments, he proceeds;
thereafter, he obtains beautiful beds and seats.
By means of this hymn, he goes to my imperishable abode and finds great joy;
having been purified by fire, he indeed proceeds to the world of the Sun, and from there, to that which is beyond.
Then, by the power of praise, one goes to the world of fire and reaches the imperishable state;
through the restraint of the tastes, one attains good fortune and the highest heaven. 45.
One who eats without attachment goes to heaven and is born there with long life;
thereafter, through hymn of praise, one indeed reaches the imperishable abode, the source of happiness.
The king shall become a dweller in water and a lord of the ocean;
having become Varuṇa through the power of this hymn, he then attains the imperishable abode.
One who is devoted to the vow of truth surely goes to heaven by means of a hymn of praise;
by the mere gift of water, one becomes an eater of nectar in heaven. (48)
Even the giver of food goes indeed to the highest heaven, rich in enjoyments;
having enjoyed desires and pleasures as a lord, he goes to the imperishable state by means of this hymn. 49.
One who bestows consolation upon all beings goes to the auspicious state of Truth;
through service to the gods, one goes to the world of the Siddhas established by Brahmā.
And by means of this hymn, one then goes to the imperishable state, the supreme goal beyond me.
A giver of lamps becomes possessed of divine vision and attains perfect accomplishment.
Having remained for a long time in the world of truth (satyaloka), one goes to the imperishable state by means of this hymn;
and the giver of mirrors and other such gifts attains the excellent station of Vairāja.

Through the gift of perfumes, garlands, and so forth, one attains the Gāndharva marriage, which is of the nature of passion (rājasa); by performing the rite of shaving five locks of hair, one becomes a progenitor who expands his lineage.
But he who performs the rite of giving away a daughter in marriage attains heaven, the excellent station of Vairāja,
the state of Īśvara, and a thousand male and female servants.
Through ornaments, great enjoyments, divine and most excellent palaces,
as well as through sacrifices, fasting, and other such practices, one attains heaven and likewise the abode of the ancestors.
By the gift of fruits, flowers, and the like, one becomes the master of gardens and such;
but the giver of sesame seeds and a cow indeed goes to the world of the Vasus.
The giver of land goes to the unmanifest abode, a place of happiness;
and by the gift of a draft animal, one goes to the world of the Vasus, a refuge of bliss. ||57||
By the gift of an umbrella, a person attains lordship on Kailāsa;
by the gift of sandals, one comes to possess vehicles and celestial chariots.
By the gift of fragrance, one becomes fragrant and attains the state of ten million lords;
the giver of a tree bearing flowers and fruit shall go to the state of immortality. (59)
By giving nectar-like juice, one attains the abode of the Immortal and becomes like ten million lords;
by the gift of garlands, incense, and ointments, one obtains the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
The king of devotees who indeed performs the rite of giving a bed goes to Goloka;
having enjoyed great blisses here and there, he attains the imperishable state through this hymn.
O Lakṣmī, by my power, the donor of a pond indeed proceeds to the most excellent of abodes; he truly goes to the immortal realm. (62)
Having enjoyed supreme enjoyments there, one goes to the Imperishable through this hymn;
it is the bestowal of a lake that grants virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (63)
By means of a pond, the splendors of the region reach full bloom;
creatures dwelling in the fourteen worlds take refuge in that reservoir of water. (64)
The fruit of the Agnihotra, as well as the fruit of gifting a cow that leads to heaven, the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma, and likewise the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice; ||65||
Furthermore, the giver of a lake obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
cows, virtuous people, and the best of birds—all living beings—[are benefited].
Beasts, trees, and living beings alike drink the water;
they wander upon its banks, bathe therein, and cleanse themselves.
Thus, the fruit for the giver of a pond shall indeed be infinite;
among all gifts, water is the most excellent and the supreme bestower of peace. (68)
Having become a consumer of nectar from the clouds, he is born in the station of Īśvara;
and, remaining on the bank of the Virajā for a long time, he goes to Goloka.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he then, through my hymn of praise, attains the Imperishable; for one who is devoted to me, the fruit of the hymn is the Supreme Imperishable.
Then the giver of trees attains auspicious divine Vṛndāvana,
as do the giver of shrubs and the giver of creepers, who reach Goloka itself.
The giver of a creeper, the giver of a bamboo pole, and the giver of grass go to that same state;
having enjoyed the auspicious world of the gods, he proceeds to the world of the ancestors.
Trees indeed worship the hosts of gods with flowers, the ancestors with fruits, guests with sap and other juices, and living beings with shade and leaves.
Species of trees provide an excellent refuge for embodied beings;
moreover, those who give trees are saved in the next world by the trees as if they were their own sons. (74)
One who plants trees, performs sacrifices through ritual action, speaks the truth, and has conquered the senses [attains] heaven,
truth, the Vairāja world, immortality, and the unmanifested abode.
O Lakṣmī, even those who are highly exalted and filled with great joy in Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka attain the supreme imperishable state solely through this hymn of praise.

Having granted fearlessness to all beings and having found fearlessness in the supreme, immutable [Reality], one surely attains it even through this hymn alone and shall become a partaker of eternal bliss. (77)
Even in times of adversity, showing favor to people is the supreme virtue;
one who removes suffering and dispels calamity goes to heaven, the abode of happiness. (78)
Whatever desired object one might give to a thirsty person who asks for it, if that gift is given quickly and utilized, the recipient shall attain satisfaction. (79)
Among these, that gift alone which is most excellent returns to the giver;
namely, the gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and the supreme gift of land.
The gift of a palace, the gift of a maiden, the bestowing of knowledge, the giving of food and water, and the giving of ornaments and garments. ||81||
The gift of household utensils is the gift of adornment;
the gift of vehicles and mounts, and especially the gift of fearlessness. ||82||
The gift of trust, the gift of goods, and the gift of a son;
the gift of bulls, elephants, and horses is supreme. (83)
The gift of an umbrella, a seat, and so forth, as well as the gift of a staff, is considered supreme;
likewise, the gift of a lion-throne and the gift of an elephant-throne. (84)
The gift of knowledge, the gift of devotion, and the gift that bestows the goals of human existence—these are the gifts of desire, pure and supreme. (85)
O Lotus-born One, these [gifts] given to virtuous persons who are like deities indeed constantly liberate the giver from sin. (86)
They endow beings with heaps of merit and lead them to the highest heaven;
indeed, they lead them to Satyaloka and the worlds of the Vairājas.
They lead them indeed to the worlds of Viṣṇu and the worlds of Sadāśiva;
they cause them to reach the worlds of Māyā, the worlds of Īśa, and Goloka.
They lead them to the worlds of Lakṣmī, the worlds of the Liberated, and the worlds of Śrī;
and they lead them to the specific abodes of the unmanifest nectar.
They lead the attendants to the great worlds and to the worlds of women;
they lead the virtuous wives and the faithful to the worlds of givers.
They lead them to the worlds of fire, the worlds of dharma, and the worlds of the moon;
whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is cherished and dear.
That should be given to a worthy recipient, for it yields imperishable fruit;
one who does what is pleasing always obtains what is pleasing, and thus becomes a giver of what is dear.
One becomes dear to all living beings both in this world and in the next, even if one is an enemy, provided that person has come to one in a state of misery seeking refuge. (93)
He who bestows favor upon one in distress is indeed considered Nārāyaṇa;
[he who helps] the emaciated, the learned, the one whose livelihood has failed, and the suffering. (94)
He who bestows [wealth] and destroys suffering—indeed, he is considered Nārāyaṇa—who [supports] virtuous people devoted to good deeds, along with their sons, wives, and families. ||95||
One should give even to those who do not ask, using every means to satisfy them;
they do not harbor any longing for enjoyments, even in the heavenly realms.
Those who are eternally content, free from desire, and dwell in their own homes, being devoted to Brahman, should be honored with all prosperity and with great respect. 97.
If they should accept what has been offered, purified by faith, then that gift shall bestow ten million merits and become a giver of liberation. (98)
Those who are righteous, devoted, learned, and observant of vows; ascetics endowed with good conduct and yoga, self-controlled, and virtuous—these are the worthy recipients. ||99||
A gift given to them is a great sacrifice; it is eternally a sacrifice to Brahman, distinguished above all other sacrifices, and it always grants freedom from debt.
They do not become angry even when they receive nothing, nor are they greedy even for blades of grass;
seeing others happy, they are satisfied, they rejoice, and they cause [others] to prosper. || 10.1 ||
The virtuous, the Brahmins, those who uphold the Veda, and the pure officiating priests always and constantly remember me as Nārāyaṇa through their hymns of praise.
Likewise, the domestic priests, the teachers, such virtuous women, mothers who bring about the welfare of their sons, and those who are most worthy of worship; || 103 ||

They should always be honored with wealth and other offerings, and saluted according to their rank; they should be constantly provided with prosperity, for they are considered to be gods and goddesses. 104.
Just as in this world the eternal dharma of women is to have recourse to a master,
so too the dharma consisting of giving has recourse to a master and takes refuge in the deities.
One should repeatedly give auspicious gifts first to virtuous people who know Brahman;
thereafter, one should give to the destitute, and after that, to mendicants.
Then one should give to the brahmins, and after that to women;
then one should give to other brahmins, and after that to others.
Then he should give [the merit] to his servants and others; thus the donor rejoices.
Having enjoyed the fruit of his gift in the worlds, he subsequently attains Brahman.
By means of the hymn known as *Puruṣottamasāma*, one attains the imperishable state,
the fruit of all gifts, and the bliss of joy, delight, and festival.
Established in union with Brahman, he attains an eternal form;
by reading or hearing this, one shall partake in union with Brahman.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Donor Experiences the Fruit of Chanting the Puruṣottama Sāman—Consisting of Eternal Bliss Residing in the Imperishable Abode—Following the Enjoyment of the Fruits of Giving," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Lakṣmī, learning, conduct, noble birth, initiation, and a virtuous refuge—wherever these qualities are found, that person is the most excellent recipient for gifts. || 1 ||
That which is given to one who asks is declared to be truly meritorious;
however, a gift given to one who does not ask is a mere relinquishing of one's own ownership.
One who is most devoted to Brahman is indeed a worthy recipient of gifts, for a virtuous person is the ornament of such a recipient;
having obtained [the gift], the virtuous and wise man gladdens the deities and his teachers.
O Lakṣmī, begging is in every respect a source of the most base distress;
for one who begs becomes a thief in broad daylight, indeed a doer of evil.
Begging is indeed death, and death is indeed begging;
it bestows suffering, therefore one should not give to a beggar.
The state of being a giver is declared to be life itself; if one gives when asked, that life is truly auspicious, and the giver attains prosperity as well. (6)
The receiver indeed becomes endowed with excellence, and likewise the non-dharma [is avoided];
the giver indeed becomes supreme—therefore, giving is praised.
When one asks for something, compassion is manifested by the act of giving;
but when one does not ask, the fruit of heaven is manifested through the gift.
For those people who are endowed with knowledge, wisdom, austerity, and devotion are indeed worthy of worship;
yogis and holy men are worthy of worship, and everything should be given to them.
That which is given to a learned guest who is virtuous and in need produces inexhaustible fruit; he attains the eternal heaven.
Those whose disciples, sons, and wives await food and water—
by eating what is given by them, they please the three sacrificial fires.
They indeed enjoy what has been given to virtuous celibates;
they gratify the Brahman-fire, for that is the supreme sacrifice.
The midday libation (madhyandina-savana) is always the offering to mendicants;
likewise, the offering to the gods and the ancestors is indeed the Vaiśvadeva rite.
That third pressing was indeed the three sacrifices that bestow heaven;
for that which was given to me, Nārāyaṇa, was truly a divine sacrifice.
O Lakṣmī, this [dharma] consisting of self-surrender should be practiced by one who possesses discernment;
it consists of non-malice toward all beings and sharing with one's followers. (15)
Service, contentment, self-control, renunciation, and sacrifices become characterized by goodness (sāttvika);
these, when purified by faith and accompanied by sacrificial fees, serve as the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice.
The virtuous do not accept [offerings] from people who have committed evil;
therefore, in a sacrifice consisting of material wealth, that which destroys sin should be given.
If the virtuous accept the gift of this sinner, it indeed becomes a purifier;
through the power of the recipient, it becomes capable of washing away sins. (18)
He should gratify the Brahmins with various desired gifts,
those who are friendly, virtuous, knowers of the Vedas, and devoted to good conduct, vows, and austerity.

One who possesses progeny should satisfy devoted people who themselves have progeny with various gifts, sweet foods, sacrificial fees, and so forth; for indeed, how could one who lacks progeny be born [with it]? 3.110.20.
Indeed, for as many virtuous qualities as the righteous truly cultivate, those who bring about the welfare of living beings should be supported with abundant gifts. 21.
Cows, bulls, ornaments, garments, and wealth; clarified butter, food, vehicles, umbrellas, clothing, and sandals. (22)
Vehicles drawn by horses, houses, and beds—
these should be given to virtuous and noble persons, for they indeed bestow heaven and liberation.
The donor, liberated from sins and purified, indeed goes to heaven;
whether in secret or openly, he should protect the virtuous through his conduct. (24)
He will certainly partake in the fruits of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
he attains security and well-being, as well as the eternal, imperishable state.
One should never do that which the virtuous do not praise;
for one might indeed bestow great enjoyments, yet fail to dispel the fear of hunger for the good. (26)
In whatever land children see delicious foods yet see them only and do not eat, that land is of a sinful and impure nature.
In whatever land virtuous men, the helpless, women, and children suffer from hunger, that land will utterly perish. (28)
In whatever region women are forcibly held while crying out, and likewise cows and subjects as well, that region is on the verge of death. (29)
Therefore, the gift known as the gift of fearlessness is considered the supreme gift;
indeed, the giver of fearlessness attains the imperishable state of fearlessness.
The Udgātṛ priest attains the imperishable syllable of the Puruṣottama-sāman;
O Lakṣmī, one who gives land attains the earth whose nature is the imperishable.
Having been given here, she assumes a divine form and rises up in the imperishable state;
she is immovable, inexhaustible, a milch-cow, and the fulfiller of divine desires and more.
The giver of land obtains in the imperishable realm garments of jewels, delightful things, nectar, rice, barley, and every kind of ambrosia.
The giver of land prospers eternally in all worlds for as many years as there are atoms of dust upon that land; for as long as life exists here on earth, so long does the giver of land flourish.
Those who give land as a gift enjoy the highest land;
land is prosperity and great fortune, and she makes the giver beloved. (35)
As is the gift, so is the enjoyment; giving is considered the supreme prosperity—even in one who is of sinful conduct, a slayer of a Brahmin, and devoid of devotion. (36)
If the earth is thrown away by the virtuous, it is indeed purified;
for it considers itself fortunate and blessed when it has come into the hands of the righteous. (37)
Just as a mother makes her own child pure, she makes the donor pure;
thus the name of the earth, "Priyadattā" (She who gives what is dear), is truly meaningful in its connection to Dharma.
By giving land to a virtuous person, one obtains celestial land;
but he who takes the land of a virtuous person does not obtain land at all. (39)
The ground of the virtuous is praised here; it is considered to belong to Nārāyaṇa.
Even a sinner is purified by the gift of land measuring a single *gocarma*. (3.110.40)
Whoever should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice or should give land to a virtuous person—the gift of land is praised, as it bestows the fruit of eternal bliss. (41)
He who gives the earth has given all of this: gold, silver, clothing, jewels, pearls, and wealth. (42)
Austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, service to the guru, worship of cows, and the honoring of holy beings and deities—these, O dweller of the earth, are yours. (43)
Engaged in the supreme welfare of the giver, she bestows the highest good upon him, just as a mother daily nourishes her own son with her milk. (44)
In that same way, the earth nourishes the donor with all fragrances and flavors;
yet death, time, the staff of Yama, illusion, fire, and fever are indeed his enemies. (45)
Fetters, afflictions, obstacles, fear, and even calamities—these misfortunes do not approach the giver of land without cause. (46)
The giver of land fully satisfies the ancestors, the gods, the great seers, the perfected ones, practitioners of yoga, virtuous women, chaste wives, and those devoted to Brahman. (47)
By giving land that provides a livelihood to one who is emaciated, destitute of means, helpless, and suffering,
a person becomes a performer of all sacrificial sessions (sarvasatrin).
Just as a cow, out of affection for her calf, yields milk and nourishes him, even so does the earth exceedingly nourish the donor. 49.
He who bestows a house that is filled with grain, or contains seed, or even has a single grain of millet,
and offers it as a superior dwelling, becomes a Brahmā through that act of giving.
Just as the moon increases day by day during the bright fortnight,
so does the king attain supreme growth in every crop.
The Earth, personified, said: "O lords of the earth, you shall obtain me only by taking me away and giving me away; having given me, you will regain me. (52)
The gift of land serves as an atonement and purifies ten generations on both sides;
he is truly well-born, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, for he is a doer of merit.
He is a true donor, he is a sacrificer, he is a virtuous man, who bestows the earth;
for as crops grow, so do the desires of such a giver of land.
The earth is the mother, the father, fortune, and food is life itself;
beings flourish upon the earth and indeed attain their final end upon the earth. (55)
The Ādityas, Varuṇas, Rudras, Brahmās, Viṣṇus, Anals,
Vasus, and Śaśins— the gods became divine after having given away the earth.
By giving gifts of gold, gifts of cows, gifts of land, and the offering of houses here to a virtuous person, one is liberated from all sins. (57)
A devoted wife, who is half the body of her husband and intent upon his supreme welfare, should perform the gift of land;
by that act, her husband attains the imperishable state.
One who gives land strewn with jewels and endowed with all desirable qualities shall become a sovereign king of kings; meritorious, he is glorified in heaven.
By giving a cow that milks all desires, the earth that rains down every wish,
or a virtuous maiden who perpetuates the lineage, one is glorified in heaven.
Rivers flowing with honey and clarified butter, as well as those carrying milk and curd, provide satisfaction here; yet others bestow the very earth.
Having given away the earth conquered by weapons, one dispels the sin of battle;
his worlds in heaven are never exhausted, and he indeed rejoices there.
Desiring prosperity, one should give land that is holy and endowed with the essence of wealth,
along with oceans, rivers, mountains, and forests in their entirety.
By giving land, one gives ponds, wells, streams, and lakes, as well as all kinds of oils and savory juices. (64)
He [beheld] medicinal herbs endowed with potency, trees laden with flowers and fruits,
forests, stones, mountains, minerals in every way, and mines.
By giving land covered with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice, one who gives the earth provides a livelihood for all living beings. (66)
He who gives a treasure-chest filled with cattle, horses, and vehicles, along with its contents and implements,
attains great happiness in imperishable worlds.
For him, there shall be a land-sacrifice that destroys all impurities;
in this world and in the divine world beyond, the giver is honored by the virtuous.
A hundred celestial women adorned with divine garlands,
as well as all forms of prosperity, attend upon the giver of earth in the world of Brahmā.
The conch, the auspicious throne, the parasol, excellent horses and superior mounts,
flowers that are the merits of dharma, and likewise heaps of gold.
He bestowed upon him an ever-unimpeded command, shouts of victory, and riches;
as well as golden flowers, medicinal herbs, kusha grass, gold, and lush meadows.
The donor of land attains prosperity, which is a ground that yields the fruit of immortality;
there is no gift equal to land, and there is no teacher equal to a mother. (72)
There is no dharma equal to truth; there is no treasure equal to generosity; there is no worthy recipient equal to the virtuous; there is no happiness equal to liberation. //73//
There is no hymn that bestows liberation like the Puruṣottama-sāman;
both the one who performs the gift and the one who recites the hymn go to my imperishable abode.

Having fully enjoyed the supreme fruit of his charity in heaven, in Satyaloka, and likewise in Īśvaraloka, he then goes from that divine world to my imperishable abode through this hymn of praise. (75)
Just as with the land, so too is food praised as a form of gift; the course of worldly life depends on food, for the vital breaths are established in food. (76)
That food is the primordial Brahman; it is always life-sustaining and fulfilling.
Food is the source of vitality, the bestower of power, and indeed the sustainer.
Ascetics and monks exist depending on the food provided by householders;
indeed, one who gives food to the hungry is certain to possess a treasure in the next world. (78)
A householder should quickly honor a guest who has arrived with water and food;
the giver of food attains the highest nectar both in heaven and here on earth.
Food given to an outcaste or even to a dog is not lost;
one should give to such a person who has never been seen before, for he shall attain great merit.
He who gratifies the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the learned brahmins, virtuous men, helpless women, and guests with food, his merit is infinite. 8.1
The gift of food is praised for all social classes, for it bestows merit;
one should not inquire about [the recipient's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or even their native land. (82)
If one should indeed give excellent food when asked by a mendicant,
the grains of that food-giver will always yield fruit.
For indeed, there are fruits here and even in the next world that are as sweet as nectar;
the ancestors also await, thinking, "May there be one among us in the family who gives food. (84)
The virtuous, the learned, the helpless, the maimed, and those who beg for food—having honored these as deities and bestowed gifts upon them, they return with merit. (85)
One who constantly gives sweet food dwells in heaven, highly honored;
the giver of food possesses cattle, sons, wealth, and enjoyments as well. (86)
One who possesses vital breath and physical form is born and honored by the gods;
the field is endowed with hunger, and the vessel sown therein sprouts.
Visible, producing joy, and like nectar, it is the meritorious fruit of good deeds;
it truly becomes the sprout of life for both the enjoyer and the giver. (88)
The source of the elements is desire; the source of desire is the womb; and the source of the womb is constant food.
Furthermore, procreation, as well as dharma and artha, and the destruction of disease, are considered to arise from food. (89)
O lotus-born one, the worlds of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Satyaloka all abide in food;
in the absence of food, the five elements in the body fall apart.
Strength, beauty, prowess, and other qualities perish from the cessation of food;
for indeed, festivals, marriages, and sacrifices exist by means of food. (9.1)
Whatever is stationary and whatever is moving, all is established in food; both the insentient and the sentient likewise depend upon the principle of nourishment. (92)
Even mechanical devices require oil; what then need be said of the Self?
The palaces of those who give food shine even in heaven. (93)
They arise in the form of stars, or they are as white as the moon;
they have the color of the rising sun and are adorned with networks of small bells.
They have many hundreds of stories, contain water-dwelling creatures within them,
possess the brilliance of lapis lazuli and the sun, and are composed of silver and gold.
Even there, the creepers and trees grant the fruits of all desires;
and in those places, there are ponds, pathways, assembly halls, wells, and oblong lakes.
Resounding celestial mansions are obtained even in the [lower] abodes;
there are mountains consisting of edible foods, as well as garments and ornaments. (97)
There are rivers of milk, rivers of curd, and rivers of clarified butter here;
as well as divine, lovely palaces and splendid couches shining with gold. (98)
In that temple, charming and worthy goddesses are obtained;
through the giving of food, Lakṣmī, showering nectar, increases forever. (99)
Rivers of nectar and oceans of ambrosia flow forth;
having thus enjoyed auspicious worlds according to their merit, they proceed beyond this.
O Lakṣmī, by means of the Puruṣottama Sāman, one indeed goes to my abode;
he enjoys the imperishable, supreme realm along with me, together with all his desires.
One should indeed gratify virtuous Brahmins with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa),
and one should satisfy them with kṛsara, polikās and other such foods, as well as with soup and boiled rice.
With sesame-based cooked foods, snacks, molasses, auspicious milk-rice, vegetables, fruits, roots, tubers, leaves, and roasted flour-grits; || 103 ||
One should satisfy the virtuous with black gram, sweet foods, and sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas);
likewise, one should offer gold and silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having enjoyed the heavens through the recitation of the Sāman, he proceeds even to the imperishable;
O Lakṣmī, he enjoys eternal supreme bliss together with me. 105.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Giving to a Worthy Recipient, the Fruit of Giving Land, the Fruit of Giving Food, the Fruit of the Puruṣottama Sāman, and so forth," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; water is indeed eternal life.
The gift of water is proclaimed to be the gift of life, having the nature of nectar. || 1 ||
Having made the water cool, sweet, delicious, and fragrant,
she should give sugar-cane juice to the virtuous Brahmins and others who are afflicted by thirst.

One should construct water-stalls and cause them to be built, and indeed cause good waters to be drunk; one should have wells, step-wells, and tanks constructed, which bestow satisfaction upon the world.
The gift of water and the gift of juice attain fruition in the other world;
water given, which bestows perfect satisfaction, removes half of one's sin. (4)
Water is the very nature of the witness and shines forth as the essence of Varuṇa;
it is the conscious Brahman, worthy of being sought, and the most meritorious water to be offered.
The cows, the learned brahmins, the virtuous women,
and all other embodied beings who drink the water from one's excavation rescue their entire lineages.
Just as water, so too should one give ghee for consumption;
by giving it even to virtuous twice-born ones and guests, one shall become handsome and possessed of excellent flavor.
The giver of ghee obtains fruit, nourishment, fame, affection, and nectar in heaven;
he also obtains strength, cows, and female buffaloes.
One should give milk-rice as a gift, and especially one should give clarified butter;
the houses of the giver of ghee are not assailed by Rākṣasas, Yamas, and other such beings.
One who gives water from a water-jar does not die of thirst;
and for one who gives a cart, there shall indeed be vehicles.
Beautiful celestial chariots for traveling to heaven and auspicious palaces belong to the one who gives sandals; moreover, thorns are forever destroyed for him. (11)
Indeed, a cart yoked with draft animals is given to him;
furthermore, an offering of sesame seeds should be made, for sesame seeds are auspicious and fit for the ancestors' meal.
He who bestows sesame seeds performs all sacrifices—
those that grant prosperity, those that bestow beauty, and likewise those that destroy evil.
Where there is no ghee, rice, fruits, or milk-rice, there one should offer oblations with sesame seeds; thus the ancestors and the gods are satisfied.
For the giver of sesame seeds, ambrosia and heaven always attend;
the giver of sesame is declared to be a giver of food and is also said to be a giver of fruit. (15)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the giver of land obtains a sixth part of the merit of a sacrifice;
he does not perish in times of distress, nor does he encounter difficulties. (1.6)
He who gives a beautifully adorned house-site that endures cold, wind, and heat,
rejoices in heaven and is not displaced even when his merit is exhausted.
The giver of shelter indeed goes to heaven and rejoices;
and the builder of a rest-house for the Dharma rejoices in the world of heaven. (18)
He whose palace contains a school, a hall for the virtuous, and a herd of cows— that donor shall attain his own Vairāja abode, the foremost of dwellings.
The one who provides shelter saves hundreds of families; the giver of land bestows eternal prosperity, and the giver of jewels brings about the expansion of the lineage.
The giver of a garden attains the essence of fruits; the giver of a sacred ford attains supreme liberation;
the giver of a cow goes to Goloka; and the giver of a Brahmin attains the imperishable Brahman.
The giver of a young boy attains the world of the earth; the giver of a maiden, the auspicious Śrīsthalī;
the giver of a female servant, the world of the Apsarases; and the giver of a lamp, the proximity of the Sun.
The giver of ghee attains the world of Soma; the giver of milk, the abode of nectar; the giver of jewels, the unmanifest abode; and the giver of a woman, the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
The giver of a house goes to Satyaloka; the giver of prosperity goes to the ordinary realm;
and the giver of ornaments goes to the abode of Viṣṇu for eternal years. ||24||
The giver of a cow is declared to be a bestower of life, as is the giver of refuge;
he who gives ten thousand cows attains the status of Indra. (25)
Kaṇāda attains the great abode of Svāyambhuva;
and the teacher Lomaśa has declared that the gift of life is considered supreme.
That by which the vital breaths are protected is considered the gift of life;
this may be accomplished through food, water, or sometimes through medicines and the like. (27)
O Lotus-like One, those gifts which provide refuge, fearlessness, and shelter, as well as the protection of life, are always considered gifts of life itself. (28)
These gifts should be given, for they yield the fruit of long life and bestow heaven;
for water given here becomes nectar for the gods. (29)
To the Nāgas, that water takes the form of nectar (sudhā); to the ancestors (pitṛs), it consists of the svadhā offering; and even to calves and children, it becomes milk.
One who desires his own prosperity should always give the gift of water;
these gifts are auspicious, conducive to long life, and bring happiness.
These gifts indeed bestow all desires and grant joy after death;
having given these gifts here and enjoyed pleasures in the third heaven, [one attains such results].
Having dwelt there for many eons, one proceeds from the hymn of praise to the Imperishable;
indeed, the fruit of the Puruṣottama-sāman is the abode of the Imperishable.
A householder should give his own auspicious gift to a renunciant;
having renounced everything, he should offer himself to the virtuous one for the sake of the imperishable state. (34)
The devotee who knows Brahman rejoices, having become liberated and free from all limits;
likewise, O Brāhmaṇas, the kings of old [rejoiced]—I delight in the self-surrender of the renunciant.
They offered their own selves to the Guru for the sake of the renunciant order (tyāgāśrama).
Having thus become forest-dwellers and then renunciants (nyāsī), they shall indeed go to the supreme state.
Indeed, by means of the Puruṣottama Sāman, one may attain the abode of the Imperishable;
listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the Brāhmaṇa Dīrghaśīla. 37.
On the bank of the river Śatruñjayā, in the village of Virāmaṇa,
there lived a Brahmin named Dīrghaśīla, as did other Brahmins.
Then Yama spoke to one of his own terrifying messengers:
"Go and bring Virāmaṇa, who possesses long-standing virtue. (39)
He was of the Bhāradvāja lineage, devoid of ritual bathing and worship,
an atheist, a reviler of the scriptures, and indeed a speaker of falsehoods.
And do not bring another who is similar to him in name and lineage—one who is generous in character, long-established in virtue, and residing indeed at Viramaṇa. ||41||
Having gone, the messenger brought back Dānaśīlin, even though he had been forbidden;
a great clamor arose in the village, for the virtuous Dīrghaśīlavān was indeed dead.
Relatives and friends arrived at the houses of both [brothers];
having wandered about and seeing that only one was alive, they turned back.
Some said, "We have seen the terrifying messenger of Yama, traveling through the sky with great speed, his long shadow appearing as if he were walking. (44)
Upon hearing this, even the atheist was struck with terror at his own approaching death;
yet the messenger, having come so near, forgot me entirely. (45)
"I have indeed taken away the wealth of a believer; therefore, I shall now perform an act of charity.
He then immediately gave away cows, sesame seeds, garments, and ornaments. (46)
He repeatedly muttered the *Gṛha*, *Ghṛta*, *Subhojyānna*,
and *Puruṣottama-sāman* mantras, while filled with fear of death.
That merit, having arisen in manifold ways and destroying all sins, awaits the messenger of Yama as he repeatedly approaches from every direction. (48)
Then, having gone to the city of Saṃyaminī, that virtuous brāhmaṇa was seen by Yama Dharma; he bowed down, and rising up, he was honored.
Having been properly honored with the madhuparka offering and other rites, as well as saluted,
fed with food that was like nectar, he was then requested for forgiveness.
Then King Dharma said to the messenger: "This man does not deserve punishment;
let him be honored and sent away, and let that other one be brought here. (51)
When these words had been spoken, Āstika said to the son of Dharma:
"I am weary; I would remain for all the time that remains. (52)
"O Yama, I do not wish to dwell in this body, which is so full of suffering.
May you be blessed; proclaim to me those dharmas by practicing which one attains happiness. (53)
Then the King of Dharma said: "Listen to the truth, O Brahmin!
The gift of land is equal to all gifts and bestows all happiness. (54)
O Brahmin, the gift of a house, augmented by all necessary implements and furnishings, is considered supreme; it bestows happiness, merit, and the attainment of heaven. (55)
The gift of a garden grove is considered the supreme gift of flavor;
one obtains all flavors as well as fruits, flowers, and the like. (56)
The gift of tanks and rivers is considered the best, providing satisfaction;
O Brahmin, the gift of cows is supreme, considered to bestow both heaven and liberation. (57)
The offering of a cow indeed delivers one from the Vaitaraṇī river, destroys the bonds of illusion, rescues one from the ocean of existence, and washes away all sins. (58)

The gift of heaven is considered supreme when it involves the offering of ornaments and the like; likewise, the gift of fine garments and jewelry is regarded as the highest bestower of prosperity. (59)
The gift of a daughter in marriage is the most excellent, bestowing a husband and wife and granting heaven;
likewise, the gift of male and female servants and the gift of wealth are auspicious.
Indeed, the gift of coin is the provider of all household enjoyments;
likewise, the gift of sesame, the gift of ghee, and the gift of lamps are supreme. (61)
The gift of sugar and molasses, the gift of barley and wheat, and the gift of an umbrella and sandals are considered bestowers of the kingdom of heaven. (62)
All those things should be given, as well as the gift of fearlessness;
however, the gift of liberation is supreme and indeed excels all others.
O Brahmin, you have bestowed all these many things in every way;
you are truly meritorious, so act for the ultimate welfare of embodied beings.
Chant repeatedly the hymn known as the *Puruṣottama-sāma*, which bestows liberation, grants eternal bliss, and provides the joy of emancipation. (65)
It bestows eternal happiness, destroys sin, and grants the imperishable state;
it [purifies] even a former sinner who recites the Puruṣottama Sāman.
I do not inflict punishment here; rather, he is proclaimed as a purifier.
O Brahmin, even if he be a great sinner, the reciter shall be exempt from my punishment.
"O Brahmin, you must endure even the King of Dharma with ease";
having been addressed thus by the messenger, Dīrghaśīla quickly departed together with him.
Having bowed to Dharma, he indeed returned to his own body and perished;
his kinsmen became joyful, and the Brahmin gave gifts.
At the end, having recited my beloved hymn known as the Puruṣottama-sāman, which removes all obstacles, he went to the imperishable abode.
The messenger of Yama led that atheist away and went toward Yama;
then the King of Dharma informed Daṇḍa and Citragupta.
Having seen this, Citragupta said: "Indeed, his merit increases;
all those sins and wicked deeds that were committed are [now purified]."
All [impurities] are completely dissolved through the grace of the Supreme Person;
meanwhile, heaps of merit increase here through all forms of giving and other virtuous acts. (73)
"Therefore, he is certainly not to be punished; rather, he is to be honored in every way.
Having heard this, the illustrious Dharmarāja also paid homage to Dīrghaśīlin.
Out of fear, he offered water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and water for washing the feet to the performer of meritorious deeds, who was reciting the hymn of praise.
He offered a welcome, hospitality, food, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and other offerings; having entered into an agreement with him, he then indeed dismissed him.
He questioned that Dharmarāja: "How is it that my merit (kṛta) has been destroyed?
I have become an atheist, a reviler, unrighteous, and a sinner. (77)
Nevertheless, there is no punishment for me; this is a great marvel to me.
Tell me, O Dharmarāja, how it is indeed that there is no punishment for me? (78)
Having heard this, the King of Dharma said to him: "That which has been done is always experienced;
there is a constant law in the world that what is blazing cannot be consumed. (79)
Food, clothing, a house, a vehicle, a bed, and even a wicked bull—these are not enjoyed when they are ablaze; O twice-born one, sin is likewise ablaze. (3.111.80)
O Brahmin, by the recitation of the hymn known as the *Puruṣottama-sāma*, the supreme merit arising from all forms of charity has been produced for you in every way. (81)
Enjoy the merit on earth after dwelling there for a long time;
thereafter, [attain] well-being, and then Satyaloka, Vairājyaloka, and beyond that, Vaikuṇṭha.
Therefore, go to the imperishable and eternal, and enjoy great bliss;
for those who are devoted to the Supreme Person, no inauspiciousness exists at all. 83.
The fears of Time, Illusion, and evil karma are destroyed in every way;
even I have no power over those who are devoted to the Supreme Person. (84)
Then that former atheist Brahmin went there and questioned Yama:
"Tell me now what must be done by me in this matter."
"I shall do as much as I am able, and I shall cause this auspicious work to be performed.
Having heard this, King Yama spoke to the Brahmin regarding the bull composed of dharma.
Listen, O Brahmin, a temple for the Supreme Soul must be constructed;
Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, should be installed there. (87)
All kinds of service should be rendered to him whenever the opportunity arises; likewise, virtuous people should be honored and served continuously. (88)
By massaging their feet and so forth, and by gifts of all kinds of objects, the virtuous should always be served; they are the givers of liberation and the saviors from saṃsāra. (89)
The offering of lamps in the temple, the dedication of water fountains, as well as the offering of Vedic knowledge and the offering of materials for worship; || 3.111.90 ||
The gift of vehicles and carriages, the dedication of gardens and groves, the offering of banners, the offering of water-pots, and the offering of alms-bowls. ||91||
The offering of a bed, the offering of juices, the offering of perfumes, as well as the offering of golden ornaments and the offering of divine garments and the like. ||92||
The offering of leafy vegetables, as well as the offering of betel leaves and the like;
likewise, the offering of fans and the like, and the offering of woolen blankets and the like. ||93||
Likewise, the offering of substances for the continuous flow of worship, the auspicious gift of musical instruments, and the presentation of garments; ||94||
The gift of large vessels and so forth, as well as the gift of water-pitchers;
the gift of couches and the like, and the offering of great seats. ||95||
The gift of cows, horses, and elephants, as well as the offering of bulls and the giving of jewels, gems, and so forth, should always be performed in the temple. (96)
Everything should indeed be given to the guru as an offering worthy of one's chosen deity;
likewise, the gift of male and female slaves and the gift of assembly halls and pavilions.
The gift of wells, step-wells, tanks, and so forth should be made at the temple;
likewise, the gift of umbrellas, chowries, and the offering of thrones and the like [should be performed]. (98)
The offering of books, as well as the offering of chests and the like, the offering of grains, and also the offering of wheat and rice; ||99||
Such gifts, indeed accompanied by water and food,
should especially be given by a householder who is a devotee of the Brahmins.
One should perform bathing, the twilight prayers with recitation, devotion, and the chanting of hymns;
likewise, one should study the knowledge of Brahman and the realization of the Self, which bestows liberation.
One should serve one's parents and likewise perform service for others;
one should be of a nature devoted to the Brahman and likewise be of a nature devoted to [one's teacher]. (102)
He should be free from passion and always avoid hatred;
he should perform the worship of Viṣṇu and be devoted to the scriptures of liberation. || 103 ||
One should constantly glorify Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
one should meditate upon Him, Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of the liberated.
One who chants the Puruṣottama-sāman should worship the illustrious Supreme Lord;
having thus performed these virtuous deeds which grant merit and liberation.
"Having conquered illusion as well as time, and having conquered death, one shall go to the Imperishable;
thus, O Brahmin, having gone there, always perform the worship of the gods."
Always perform the worship of the ancestors and the honoring of the virtuous as you would yourself;
thus, victory shall always be yours in heaven, in truth, and likewise in the imperishable.
Thus addressed by the Lotus-born One, the brahmin went home and performed that [rite];
in the end, having enjoyed many heavens, he went to the imperishable abode.
Having heard, remembered, recited, or even performed the worship of the deity,
a living being who has become my refuge attains my imperishable state, O Rame.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Instruction and Liberation at the Gate of Yama for Dīrghaśīla the Astika and Dīrghaśīla the Nastika, as well as the Description of the Giver of Water, Land, and Various Other Gifts, and the Reciter of the Puruṣottama Sāman," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; a cow should always be given according to the prescribed rite.
A cow is to be understood as being of three kinds, and the earth-cow is the most excellent: the cow, the earth, and Sarasvatī. (1)
The knowledge of Brahman should be given to a disciple who seeks liberation;
the knowledge of the arts to a craftsman; and material science to one who understands the nature of tastes.

Knowledge of one's own self should not be given even to a group of calculators, nor should knowledge of cooking be given to a noble woman; and knowledge of the scriptures should be given to a learned man, for that is indeed equal to [giving] cows and land.
The gift of a cow should be bestowed; cows are always the mothers.
By one who constantly desires prosperity, cows should be circumambulated.
Divine and auspicious goddesses must not be struck with the foot;
those who ride cows and those who seize cows are Rākṣasas destined for hell.
Thirsty and hungry cows might destroy people along with their kinsmen,
as well as ancestral dwellings, palaces, and temples of the gods.
Those whose dung is purified by fire—what could be more pure than them?
He who gives a handful of fodder or a handful of food to a cow for even a year [attains great merit]. (7)
By personally refraining from food, one observes that vow which fulfills all desires;
he attains the fruit of sons, fame, wealth, and even prosperity.
His inauspiciousness perishes and no evil dream ever arises for him;
a cow should not be given to one who is wicked, nor to one who is greedy, nor to an atheist.
O child, she must never be given to one who is devoid of compassion, to a cruel man, to a killer, or to one who lacks the service of providing fodder.
It should never be given to one who is devoid of the householder’s life, nor to one who lacks grass and other such necessities, nor to one who is bereft of devotion and righteousness.
A cow should be given to a virtuous person who has many sons, to a mendicant seeking a deity, to one who possesses a field, and to one who performs service with grass. || 12 ||
Service to cows, service to gurus, and service to parents always bring me joy;
they destroy heaps of sins and deliver those who offer themselves. 13.
O Lakṣmī, association with the virtuous certainly delivers one in such a manner;
however, in the absence of cows, one should give a cow made of ghee, which brings auspiciousness.
For him, these [streams] flow like affectionate mothers carrying ghee;
in the absence of ghee, one should give a milk-cow with enthusiasm and faith. || 15 ||
He is rescued from hardship by the cow and rejoices in a river of milk;
if milk is unavailable, one should give a sesame-cow, and he rejoices through the sesame seeds.
In the absence of sesame seeds, one should give a fruit-cow; one rejoices through fruits. In the absence of fruits, one should give a grain-cow; one rejoices through food.

In the absence of food, one should give a "hidden cow" (gūḍhadhenu), for one rejoices through sweet things; in the absence of a hidden cow, one should give a "clothing cow" (ambaradhenu), for one rejoices through garments.
In the absence of all [other gifts], one should give a water-cow; such a person rejoices in the rivers.
Even a single tawny cow, when given, becomes for him a river of nectar.
Even a single offering given to a virtuous person, when employed for the worship of the Divine,
surely leads my donor to the imperishable, eternal abode.
To whatever worlds the giver of a cow goes, those are eternally joyful;
there Time does not prevail, nor old age, nor fire.
Therein exists neither impurity, nor disease, nor indeed exhaustion;
whatever they desire comes to them by the power of the merit of cows.
Cows that go at will and move according to their desire frequent that place;
likewise, there are ponds, lakes, and rivers consisting of clarified butter and milk.
They go to houses, mountains, wildernesses, and forests;
they obtain that which is pleasing, desirable, sweet, and endowed with flavor. (24)
In that place, those who endure all things, those patient ones, go indeed as givers of cows;
likewise, those who serve their teachers, the generous, and those who honor guests go there. ||25||
Indeed, those wicked ones who steal cows do not go to the world of merit;
rather, one should purchase a cow with one's own wealth and give it away for the sake of spiritual welfare.
Having purchased [the image] with counterfeit coins, one should offer it specifically for the sake of liberation;
having won wealth at dice, one should purchase [the image] with that and give it for the attainment of heaven.
One should give a cow as a portion of inheritance, or one that has come through a gift; for the giver of such a cow who is devoted to truth, the fruit is equal to that of giving a thousand cows.
He who daily bows to a cow at dawn and likewise offers her mouthfuls of grass,
and causes her to drink water, shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He who, observing the cow-vow (govrata), gives the first portion of his meal to a cow while remaining without food himself,
obtains through that service the fruit of giving a thousand cows for a year.
Indeed, he who, having eaten but one meal a day, purchases a cow and gives it to his guru, shall obtain the fruit of as many cows as there are hairs upon that cow. ||3 1||
But he who, having sold himself, buys a cow and bestows it as a gift—
for every single hair of that cow-giver, inexhaustible worlds come into being.
He who protects a cow, a Brahmin, or a virtuous person in the forest obtains a fruit equal to that of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and rejoices.
Whatever divine splendor he may desire at the time of death, the Protector grants all of that through his protection. (34)
Gold is the supreme gift, and it should indeed be given according to one's ability along with a cow; it bestows prosperity and is always purifying. (35)
He who is poor, destitute, and without possessions may perform the vow;
indeed, by performing the vows, he shall attain the supreme state. ||36||
O Rame, the restraint of the senses is indeed the most excellent vow;
one who has conquered the senses and is devoted to Brahman rejoices in the world of Brahman.
Self-control bestows happiness; those who are self-controlled turn away from the multitude of sense objects.
Having withdrawn the impulse of the mind, they, being purified, proceed toward Brahman. (38)
Through valor, austerity, sacrifices, gifts, service, devotion, tranquility, and knowledge, there exist eternal worlds. (39)

Those devoted to moral conduct and vows indeed go to the worlds of the ṛṣis, the worlds of the gods, the worlds of the Siddhas, the abodes of cows, the worlds of the liberated, and the worlds of the lords. (3.112.40)
One who is a teacher, a performer of fire-sacrifices, devoted to the service of the guru, and a worshiper of chaste and virtuous women, goes to my imperishable abode. (41)
They were heroes in devotion, in dharma, and in their vows; in giving, in the act of study, in sacrifice, in battle, in service, and even in the acquisition of wealth. ||42||
O heroes, even in the absence of knowledge, you are heroes in the forest; you are heroes in renunciation, even in the home;
and you are performers of heroic deeds in self-restraint, discipline, tranquility, and uprightness. (43)
Likewise, others are heroes in the service of their guru, mother, father, or husband; and some are heroes in mendicancy, in hospitality toward guests, or in asceticism. (44)
All go to the worlds of the lords, which bear the fruits of their respective actions;
but those who are devoted and firm in the vow of truth go to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. 45.
He who remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) in this world from birth until death—for him there is nothing unattainable, just as there is none for Nārāyaṇa. ||46||
Celibacy burns away defects and all sins when practiced;
indeed, the celibate student, strengthened by his powers, shall attain the abode of Brahman. 47.
He who serves his mother, father, guru, or the infallible teacher, attains my abode, the imperishable and eternal state. 48.
Nothing is born without a seed, nor is there fruit without a seed;
whatever kind of seed one sows, such is the fruit one reaps. (49)
The seed is indeed human effort, consisting of service and characterized by virtue;
the field is the true guru, the mother, the father, and the Lord of the deity Gaudeśvara. ||3.112.50||
Just as a farmer sows and reaps accordingly, so too does one obtain happiness through virtuous action and suffering through sinful action. (51)
One obtains the fruits of one's deeds everywhere: heaven and the pleasures of heaven, beauty, fortune, great charm, and various kinds of jewels. (52)
The Tārakas, the Tridaśas, the Siddhas, the Yakṣas, the Moon, the Sun, and the Winds—
all these deities attained their divine status from the human state through the practice of dharma.
Wealth does not attend one who does not give, nor does it attend one who is inactive;
wealth does not attend one who lacks merit, but it attends one who accomplishes its purpose.
He who, without making human effort, waits for fate alone, will find no success;
like a eunuch’s wife, O Lotus-born One, he possesses neither.
For him who possesses heroism in service and whose strength consists of virtuous conduct, and for whom effort is his destiny, success rests in the palm of his hand. (56)
Destiny alone does not merely delight, nourish, sustain, and protect;
destiny flourishes well when joined with one's own effort. //57//
Indeed, a lamp without oil extinguishes by itself;
likewise, fortune without merit and without effort extinguishes by itself. (58)
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, one who desires prosperity must always exert effort in austerity, religious observance, merit, charity, acquisition, devotion, and service. (59)
One devoid of merit is never able to enjoy vast wealth, pleasures, women, or food at any time. (3.112.60)
Vast wealth comes to one who is disposed toward expenditure and charity;
and in some cases, O beloved, it arrives without effort through what was given in the past.
One should give everything in every way that which is most dear to oneself;
for this world, bound by its karma, experiences only the fruit of its giving. (62)
Fortune is not obtained without giving; a beloved woman is not obtained without giving;
a cow is not obtained without giving; and the earth is not obtained without giving. (63)
Wisdom is not obtained without being given; prosperity is not attained without being given. Service is not achieved without being performed; happiness is not obtained without being earned.
A lifespan is not obtained without having performed [meritorious deeds], nor is a kingdom attained without it being given;
likewise, great sensory pleasure and prosperity are not acquired without having been earned.
Therefore, gifts should be given—ornaments, garments, houses, foods, beloved things, and all those objects of enjoyment that are indeed most dear to oneself. (66)
Having created the various manifestations and propitiated the presiding deities of the incarnations with gifts of daughters, the fruit thereof is indeed as vast as a hundred million lotuses.
"Even though I am capable and Hari is the eternal refuge of merit, hundreds of millions of beings are born from my left side alone. (68)
I have no expectation for the fruit of my giving, for I am capable of protecting myself and others; nevertheless, this example has been displayed for the sake of protecting the world.
The entire world is my body; men and women are my half-forms.
Men are half of Nārāyaṇa, and likewise women are my half-womanhood.
In this way, the fruit that sustains one through saṃsāra is attained through generosity;
for the virtuous, endowed with austerity and self-restraint, are firm in their vows. (71)
Having attained the fruit, they indeed become lords equal to Nārāyaṇa,
by whom the three worlds were created in the past by me, the Lord of Śrī.
Thus, I perform penance in the Ocean of Milk and take delight for a long time in Badarī;
having manifested myself, I show it to you—perform supreme austerity.
Having attained the earth as Vāmana, as well as Paraśurāma and Pṛthu,
Rāmāditya also indeed performed the gift of the earth in ancient times.
Even though I am Yajñanārāyaṇa, the Blessed One, having become the supreme giver, instructed the subjects through sacrificial rites and sacrifices.
Indeed, by me Rādhā was given to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is my own self;
likewise, Nārāyaṇī was given by me to Nārāyaṇa, who is my own self.
In ancient times, the Earth was given to Varāha, Śrī was given to Viṣṇu,
Lakṣmī was given to Mahāviṣṇu, and Sāvitrī was offered to Brahmā.
That primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the fundamental form, was offered to Puruṣa in the beginning;
having thus performed this synthesis, the system of giving was set in motion. //78//
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, all joys are indeed the fruit of giving;
for with whatever body a person performs whatever gift, [that very body experiences its reward]. (79)
In whatever state one performs a good or evil deed, one reaps that very fruit with that same body. (3.112.80)
In each respective state, the agent indeed experiences that fruit:
one should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give speech that bears truth. (81)
One should indeed offer oneself and constantly serve the guru;
such is declared to be the supreme gift—one should give one's body as is appropriate. (82)
Even by such giving, one indeed crosses the ocean of karma;
listen, for I shall now describe the supreme gift of knowledge. (83)
That fruit which was called the world of Brahmā, which Brahmasatī attained in the past—she was a yoginī, that Brahman-woman, that young maiden. (84)
At the auspicious holy site of Somanātha, she worshipped Śaṅkara;
she was young, beautiful, endowed with virtuous character, and rich in ascetic merit. (85)
She performs her recitations and other rites three times a day at the Sarasvatī;
those who follow other holy places see her as equal to the Sun and fall into delusion. (86)
She did not cast her gaze anywhere at all in any manner whatsoever;
however, on one occasion, the Daitya Sthaṇḍilaghoṣaka beheld her.
By sheer force, he lifted his own palace from the sky into the ocean;
indeed, having violently seized her, he enjoyed the wife of Brahmā.
She too was protectorless and despondent, knowing [the truth] and detached from the body;
yet, being established in the Self, she regarded both sorrow and the absence of sorrow as equal. (89)
Virtue and religious vows must always be protected; their violation is indeed sorrow itself.
If they are not protected during times of calamity, one should remain free from grief, thinking, "I am not this body. (3.112.90)
Through discernment, she indeed considered the Self as distinct from the body;
having likewise understood the body to be separate, she abandoned her grief by taking refuge in the Supreme. 91.
Seeing her in such a state, the Daitya questioned her repeatedly:
"O beautiful woman, why do you not grieve, even though you have been violated? (92)
She replied: "This body is indeed impure and has been violated by you;
I myself have not been violated, O Daitya, for I am pure and consist of consciousness. (93)
Nārāyaṇa, who is Brahman, the supreme Lord, resides within you; the body is not conscious, for it is experienced as such only through being presided over by Him.
O Daitya, you remain ignorant, yet I am not situated in ignorance;
how can I, being helpless, grieve for that body which is always to be pitied? (95)
The self is neither female nor male, nor is it of the nature of earth or stone; the body alone bears such designations—what cause for lamentation is there in that? (96)
Upon hearing this, Sthaṇḍilaghoṣa was filled with supreme wonder;
having attained knowledge, he then requested forgiveness for his past actions.
Placing her upon his own shoulder, he brought Somanātha;
even the Daitya performed penance and devotion through the yoga of knowledge.
Having become purified through yoga and austerity, he attained the status of a Gaṇa of Hara over time and went to the supreme Kailāsa.
Even though I was a chaste wife of Brahmā, I grieved there where I was subject to another's will;
then, having fallen into the hands of the Daitya, I became dependent upon the ocean.
"The sin has been consumed by me with the fire of knowledge, yet it was worldly; therefore, an expiation must be performed so that my virtue is not lost. (101)
She went to a peaceful yogin who wore a crown and was devoted to Hara;
she asked him about the purity of character, and the wearer of the crown then spoke to her.
"O virtuous lady, you possess a form that can even delude Śaṅkara;
therefore, obstacles will arise for you again and again during your youth. (103)
Therefore, seek out a beloved refuge—a person who knows Brahman and is dear to you—by whom the destruction of obstacles may occur and through whom your sin shall be pacified. (104)
Through the purification of the body, as well as by marriage according to the prescribed rite,
your very expiation shall be accomplished, and the menstrual impurity shall likewise be cleansed.
Thus addressed, that Jñānakośā, being devoted, chose that very yogi named Kirīṭin as her husband; she made him her teacher and her husband.
In the presence of Śaṅkara, she received the initiation that adorns the life of a householder;
her forehead was marked with the *tilaka* by Pārvatī, and the moonlight of good fortune was bestowed upon her.
By the auspicious blessing of Śambhu, she became a capable and divine Yoginī;
thus, with her body offered [to him], she became the wife of Gaṇa, a most excellent Yoginī.
Endowed with divine power, that eternal Satī indeed departed;
once, she went to the world of Viṣṇu together with Śambhu.
Having assumed the form of a maidservant, she took that chaste Brahmin woman with her;
and upon seeing me as Nārāyaṇa, that beautiful woman was infatuated with me.
When Satī was offered to me, she indeed became Muktā;
eternal and in a divine form, she shines together with Ramā.
Thereupon, she became my wife by the very name of Brāhmīsatī;
moreover, that beautiful woman was also the wife of Kirīṭin.
She dwells eternally on Kailāsa and rejoices as a servant of Śambhu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this secret been told to you regarding the rite of offering.
If Nārāyaṇa is obtained, one should perform the gift of one's own body;
and if the Lord who bestows liberation, the giver of Nārāyaṇa, is obtained. || 1.14 ||
The gift of one's body should be performed at all times for the sake of liberation;
let this body, which is otherwise enjoyed by others, be enjoyed by the Supreme Self.
O Lakṣmī, by offering that [merit] to Him, the virtuous woman attains the state of Lakṣmī;
and from reading and hearing this, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and the supreme goal.
This supreme secret was told to you in the past;
thereafter, other beautiful women also offered themselves.
In Nārāyaṇa, there were indeed millions of virtuous and auspicious women;
having crossed over saṃsāra through my yoga, they went to the abode of Brahmā.
And all those beloved of Brahmā abide here before you;
among these beloved of Brahmā are the Yoginīs, who are liberated and possess divine forms.
O Narayani, this knowledge must not be given to those who are unworthy vessels;
nor should it ever be given to those who, upon hearing it, speak in disparagement.

This auspicious [teaching] must indeed be given to those who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of liberation, by attaining which my divine state is reached by those who have taken refuge in me. (121)

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of the Body and Liberation by the Yoginī Satyā, along with the Description of the Fruits of Bestowing the Gift of Cows, the Kalpa-gift of Cows, and Various Vows and Practices," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the various types of austerities; I shall describe to you both those that are performed alone and those joined with devotion.
By that very same action through which heaven, merit, and stainless prosperity are attained,
when performed with devotion, my imperishable abode is reached.
Supreme magnanimity is declared to be austerity that is ever characterized by self-sacrifice;
one should give wealth, one should give a grove, and one should give a house as a virtuous refuge.
One established in generosity should give a whole family, or one should give even a mere grain;
for the world belongs to the noble, and among givers, the giver of wealth is preeminent.
Devotion accompanied by great generosity shall grant me my abode;
sleeping perpetually on the bare ground is considered the supreme austerity.
The fruit of that is great: in heaven there arise palaces resplendent with gold, as well as delightful couches that bestow the nectar of immortality.
Wearing rags and bark garments is proclaimed as the highest austerity;
its fruit shall be beautiful clothes and ornaments.
The mind of yoga is the supreme austerity; its fruits are indeed celestial palaces, divine vehicles, and the supernatural powers that lead to dwelling in heaven.
Austerity involving the heat of fire is excellent, and its fruit may be sovereignty or heaven;
the renunciation of flavors is excellent, and its auspicious fruit is austerity itself.
A woman shall possess good fortune, and her home shall be filled with flavors;
this vow, free from meat, is supreme, and its fruit consists of progeny, sons, and so forth.
He who dwells with his head downward attains the supreme station of Indra;
and he who dwells in water, the world of the Moon is his true reward.
He who becomes a celibate student (brahmacārī) indeed goes to the world of Brahmā;
[he should offer] water for the feet, a seat, food, water, and even shelter. || 1-2 ||
One should give to a guest; this sacrifice has five limbs, and austerity is supreme.
These, when performed with devotion, truly bestow my imperishable state upon me.

For the sake of the gods, for the sake of cows, or for the sake of one's guru, lying down as a hero (vīraśāyana) is a supreme austerity that bestows life; it grants liberation and is the highest giver of heaven.
Silence is declared the supreme vow, and non-malice is the highest austerity;
freedom from censure and freedom from cavil are considered the ultimate austerity.
Therefore, one who possesses uninterrupted movement shall become a commander in heaven;
fasting is considered the best austerity, and its fruit is held to be enjoyments.
Through self-restraint and virtuous conduct, one becomes long-lived and strong;
non-violence and austerity are supreme, bestowing sovereignty, health, and beauty.

Even subsisting on fruits and roots is considered an austerity that bestows a kingdom; by eating only leaves one may attain heaven, and by eating the remnants of a meal (vighasa), one goes to Hari. 18.
For one who sits in the vow of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśa), there shall indeed be supreme happiness everywhere;
he becomes a giver of vegetables, possessed of vegetables, and endowed with great gardens.
One who gives a cow becomes possessed of cattle; one who eats grass becomes a partaker of nectar.
Bathing at the three periods of the day is most excellent; it is the supreme fruit of austerity.
It is said that celestial women attend upon him who bathes at the three times of day;
subsisting on air is the highest austerity, and its fruit shall be the fruit of sacrifice.
Truthfulness is the highest austerity; through it, one attains heaven endowed with jewels.
Initiation is the most excellent austerity; through it, one's lineage becomes most excellent. (22)
Subsisting on water is the best austerity, and its fruit is always the consumption of nectar;
the Agnihotra sacrifice is the best austerity, and its fruit shall be the world of fire.
Recitation of mantras, austerity, sovereignty, heaven, and liberation—the vow of eating but one meal is considered the most excellent, yielding the highest fruit of heaven. (24)
Fasting as part of initiation (dīkṣopavāsa) is considered penance that bestows heaven;
indeed, ritual consecration (abhiṣeka) is the most excellent penance, for it brings about the status of a guru.
The acquisition of knowledge is the highest austerity; he attains that which belongs to Bṛhaspati.
But by practicing mental dharma, he enjoys the world of dharma. ||26||
The destruction of craving is the highest austerity; happiness is like that of Vaikuṇṭha.
Through constant worship and austerity, he shall go to the abode of Goloka. 27.
The father is Brahmā, the mother is the Earth, and the preceptor is the eternal Brahman;
by him who has satisfied these three, all austerity has been performed. ||28||
By him all dharmas have been performed, and the vows as well; endowed with devotion, these indeed bestow my imperishable state upon me. (29)
All duties have been performed by that woman who has propitiated her husband; likewise, all duties have been performed by that man who has fully satisfied his wife. (3.113.30)
The king performed all righteous deeds by which his subjects were fully satisfied;
and the subjects performed righteous deeds by which Nārāyaṇa was worshipped. ||3.1||
The mantra of a violent person is in vain; a sacrifice without a priestly fee is indeed in vain;
an oblation without a mantra is in vain; and a vow devoid of truth is false. (32)
Service is in vain without devotion; worship is in vain without Hari;
dharma is in vain without virtuous conduct; and existence is in vain without happiness. (33)
Without a virtuous person, charity is in vain; without devotion, birth is in vain;
without wealth, a home is in vain; and without liberation, death is in vain. (34)
Knowledge is in vain without a worthy vessel; battles are in vain without victory;
everything is in vain without affection; and the acquisition of wealth is in vain without Kṛṣṇa. (35)
Dwelling is in vain without peace; nourishment is false without a mother;
sight is in vain without the Divine; and the ear is in vain without sacred discourse. (36)
The skin is indeed in vain, even if it possesses beauty, without the touch of Śrī Hari;
the tongue is in vain without tasting the nectar situated in the grace of Kṛṣṇa. (37)
Likewise, speaking of the qualities of Kṛṣṇa at other times is useless speech;
smelling the fragrance of Hari without [recollection] is useless smelling; and the intellect without remembrance is useless. (38)
All the essential constituents of the body are useless without me;
strength is in vain, fortitude is in vain, and fame is in vain without me. (39)
Knowledge, eloquence, logical reasoning, intellect, and discernment—all these are useless without the propitiation of the Supreme Soul. (3.113.40)
Just as a woman, even if she be young, is fruitless when with a eunuch, so indeed everything is fruitless when I, the eunuch, have been rejected. (41)
And likewise, O Lakṣmī, without me—that is, without my virtuous presence—a prosperous kingdom, a noble lineage, and honor become as fruitless as the end of one's life. 42.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to this ancient story of King Vaivarta, concerning how, through his former ascetic penance, he obtained a kingdom extending as far as the ocean. 43.
Indeed, his entire dominion was prosperous and governed as a single wheel;
even the messengers who traveled through the sky were conscious beings within his kingdom.
The rulers and the scriptures became natural [to them], and the suns always became excellent streams of splendor. (45)
In his kingdom, there were messengers of the sky appearing everywhere;
likewise, there were water-messengers who traveled by water-vehicles and moved through the depths below. (46)
By the power of his merit, even celestial chariots belonging to other worlds became available to him—everything, whether human or divine. (47)
At that time, his kingdom became as if it had attained identity with him;
though insentient, it was rich in the form of consciousness and was always engaged in the performance of action. (48)
Memory and the god of love became rain; nectar became memory and the god of love; crops became memories and gods of love; and prosperities became memories and gods of love. ||49||
Women who remember their past lives, male and female servants who remember their past lives,
and indeed all objects of enjoyment that he remembers, attend upon him.
Such was the perfected king named Vaivarta.
Once, his virtuous queen, Kālindharā by name, spoke to him. (51)
O King, as the Lord dwells upon the earth today, so are you without equal;
for everything has been acquired by you on this earth through austerity, just as it was by Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, its essence remains within, shining like white milk;
for this is just like milk from which the butter has been extracted. (53)
Without Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, without the virtuous bull,
without sacrifice, without charity, and without the hospitable honoring of guests.
Without devotion even to Hari, everything appears to me as essence-less;
therefore, worship Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa and serve his devotees. (55)
"Having made the bull of self-liberation your vehicle, you shall thus go to the supreme state.
Though addressed in this way, that lord of the earth did not at all accept the words spoken by his beloved.
He repeatedly refuted all of that through his atheism, saying:
"Kṛṣṇa is neither a god nor a human; he is not a saint who bestows anything upon anyone. (57)
Everything is obtained through austerity; everything else is of the nature of falsehood.
Through austerity alone shall I go again to heaven, the most excellent of heavens.
"This second heaven, consisting of stars, resides upon the earth;
I shall obtain it through asceticism alone, so do not worry, O beautiful lady. (59)
Thus, deluded by the glare of pride, he no longer took account of his beloved;
as a ruler of the kingdom, he spent a long time in atheistic indifference.
Then, upon the exhaustion of his lifespan and when the merit of his performed deeds was entirely spent,
he was indeed driven forth from his own body by the noose of Time.
In time, no one remained to protect him;
his subjects, queens, principal ministers, sons, and daughters by the thousands [perished]. (62)
They stood there, merely looking on and weeping, overwhelmed with grief;
at that moment, neither the gods nor the teachers were present for this atheist.
Even the virtuous did not come to lead the deceased to the next world;
neither dharma nor merit, neither the goddesses nor the state of the righteous followed him. (64)
They could not lead him away, for he was dead both in his kingdom and in his body;
without merit, his path was blocked upon reaching the other shore.
The subtle [body], presided over by the senses, was not then capable of departing;
nor were the mind, the ego, the intellect, and the vital breath able to go forth. ||66||
Having emerged from his body like an inanimate object, he stood upon the roof of the palace;
he awaited the merit arising from the deceased's virtuous deeds for the sake of his own spiritual welfare.
For the nihilist, there is indeed neither heaven nor this world, much less the next;
for him, there is no path of the gods, nor is there the path of smoke.
