Having fainted and died, he found himself in a state of suffering and lamented:
"I did not give water or food, nor did I perform a sacrifice. (69)

I have never rendered assistance anywhere, nor have I served the virtuous; neither the worship of the gods, nor the offering of oblations, nor hymns of praise and the like have been performed by me. (3.113.70)
The helpless were not protected, nor were mendicants satisfied;
guests were not honored, and virtuous women were not treated with respect. ||71||
I have not performed the gift of cows, the gift of gold, nor the gift of land;
yet, endowed with all prosperity, I have acted without having engaged in false reasoning.
Today, for me who am destitute of merit, there is no way out whatsoever; indeed, even my celestial vehicles and aerial chariots do not appear before me.
Those weapons which were formerly mine do not remain in their transformed state; they no longer present themselves as conscious entities as they once did.
That supreme sovereign power, which is existence itself, is as if vanished and is no longer seen;
that yogin has departed along with the gross elements and the physical body. (75)
What is done through subtle yoga does not at all provide assistance;
indeed, everything that is performed is obtained [in its own time], while my asceticism has gone to waste.
The gross is considered non-existent; there remains only the subtle cause, which today exists as powerless. What purpose, then, is there for me, and what is my course? (77)
The Fourth Lord has not been worshipped; what state awaits me today?
Yet even the messengers of Yama do not fall within the range of my vision.
By which I am impelled to go to the city of the King of Dharma;
there is no destination for the nihilist, and none at all for one who has not performed [meritorious] deeds. (79)
Whether fortunate or unfortunate, there is no other state for me;
alas, even this body of a preta that was to be mine does not exist at all.
The form of wind is complete, yet it does not consist of spirits or ghosts;
my eye is not complete here, nor are my ears or my tongue.
Neither my feet nor my hands have power; indeed, I am devoid of strength.
Today I am merely mind, stripped of all capability.
Just as the state of the embryo in the womb proceeds, so too is my manifestation; it appears without conceptual construction and is likewise free from the act of cultivation. 83.
He is not even able to grant me a vision in a dream or speak to me, by whom I might tell my wife for the sake of her going to bestow merit. (84)
"Alas! Today there is no refuge for me, the sovereign lord of the earth;
everything has been lost, as nothing was accomplished by that deceiver who robbed me. (85)
"My wife told me previously: 'Remember Hari, Nārāyaṇa.
I remember that Lord today; may He deliver me, the lowest of men. (86)
Reflecting thus in her mind, she held me—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama—within her non-conceptual state. 87.
Just as he meditated upon me, so too did inner illumination arise within him;
at that moment, I spoke to him there.
Just as by means of an invisible form or through the voice from the sky, you have not performed any merit, nor indeed has any other been performed. (89)
Therefore, that [heavenly] path has been blocked for you, yet the path of Yama is certainly not yours;
such sin was never committed by you that there should be a destination in the realm of Yama.
Therefore, O Devarāta, you must go again to your brother's wife;
let your younger brother touch the queen, and you shall become her son. (91)
"By the touch of the hand, the birth of a son occurs according to the age; such indeed it shall be. Therefore, O Anuja, become a son to him. (92)
Then, having performed worship in his own field preceded by acts of charity, and having performed sacrifices, honored the virtuous, and rendered supreme service to others; ||93||
Having given the gift of a cow, the gift of land, and the unsurpassed gift of gold, and having performed religious vows, he indeed became a rememberer of his past births for a long time. (94)
Having enjoyed pleasures and worshipped me, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
Go now to the dream of your wife as well as that of your younger brother. (95)
Then the voice from the womb in the sky spoke thus: "O fisherman, become so [as your son]," and having said this, it ceased. 96.
Having become possessed of power, Vaivarta went to his younger brother and the queen in a dream at night; he then informed them of the truth.
Touched even by the hand of the fisherman, the queen named Kālindharā, who was in her fertile season, became pregnant. (98)
And in due time she gave birth to a son who remembered his former births;
even from childhood, he too practiced devotion toward the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow within the lotus.
He bestowed all kinds of gifts for his own liberation,
and he had sacrifices performed and constructed ponds everywhere.
He caused delightful food-distributions to be established everywhere, as well as water-stations,
dharma-halls, and Vedic schools in all directions.
He gave gifts of cattle, land, and gold, as well as gifts of maidens;
he bestowed gifts of houses and constructed temples for the gods.
O Lakṣmī, he constructed palaces for me there, and having caused dwellings for the virtuous to be built, he served me with his own person.
Having thus established the entire kingdom as pure and full of devotion,
and having exercised lordship over it, he enjoyed manifold pleasures and comforts.
Having been a royal sage named Saṃvarta, he cast off his own body and,
at the end, went through devotion to me to the imperishable abode, the supreme state.
Therefore, gifts should be given, the virtuous should be served, the deities should be honored, and sacrifices should be performed according to one's wealth. 106.
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, and likewise practicing this, one attains worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the divine state; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Various Austerities, and how those same austerities grant liberation when joined with devotion; [the account of] King Vaivarta’s lack of faith resulting in a state of no higher destination and his rebirth through his wife as Devarāta, followed by his attainment of liberation through the performance of faithful rites and devotion," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Queen of Śiva, to liberation through the refuge of a virtuous woman;
indeed, through the refuge of a virtuous woman comes protection, life, and likewise auspiciousness.
There was a cowherd named Romapada in an excellent forest,
in a region on the banks of the Ojasvatī in Saurāṣṭra, which was frequented by lions.
Romapāda, devoid of righteousness, behaves like a mere beast;
though he possesses a household, he does not perform bathing, worship, or giving of gifts.
He maintains his livelihood with milk, curd, wild grains, and other forest products;
he even kills wild animals and consumes their meat.
Having gone far away at the onset of night, he repeatedly commits theft by bringing back food and other items belonging to others from fields and such places.
Thus Vṛṣaṅgama became the son of Adharmamārga;
having been born, he grew up as a youth and became a protector of buffalo herds.
Once, while observing the vow of a herdsman, he went to the forest with his father;
there, his father encountered a deer wandering in the woods.
A black deer was struck down by his father’s dogs in the vicinity of the forest;
Vṛṣagamana, joined by his father, also went quickly toward the deer.
As the deer was being torn apart by dogs while dying,
he cried out in agony, his feet striking the ground.
Seeing this, he became overcome with compassion; he fell into a state of great terror and even trembled violently, and so he released that deer.
Afflicted by natural compassion, he did not seize the deer there, thinking:
"I shall not eat meat, nor shall I kill anything at any time."
Who would commit such an evil act—forcibly depriving one of life—for the sake of a belly, like a man devoid of compassion? (1.2)
Thus, endowed with compassion, he abandoned the harming of living beings;
thereafter, Vṛṣaṅgama himself departed for some place during the month of Kārtika.
For the sake of the sacred ford at Somanātha, he bathed and beheld Śaṅkara;
he then confessed to Hara the sin committed by himself. ||14||
His sin was destroyed and purity arose in his heart;
the holy men arrived there, were seen by him, and then he bowed down to them.
They have been worshipped and served by me, and likewise I have cultivated the company of the virtuous; thus I have obtained the mantra "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, my refuge. (16)
A garland of tulasī has been obtained, and auspicious devotion has been attained;
one should never eat without first offering it to Śrī Hari. (17)
Milk, curd, and likewise ghee should be given to virtuous men and chaste women; the holy ones (sādhus) should be served, and Janārdana should be worshipped. 18.
Having thus obtained these observances, she returned to her own home;
yet she continued to practice them in that very same manner, worshipping Śrī Narāyaṇa.
The virtuous come there once a year into the midst of the forest;
having received service, they indeed depart for another village or another forest.
Vṛṣaṅgama also then indeed makes offerings of food, of flat cakes,
and gifts of milk and curd.
In this way, the merit resulting from his gift increased exceedingly.
Then, as his time had come, his father met his death. (22)
The terrifying messengers of Yama arrived with weapons in their hands;
terrified, he cried out in many ways, repeatedly exclaiming, "They are killing me! (23)
May some kinsmen of mine release me from the messengers of Yama;
they are severing my veins and striking me with mallets. (24)
"O people, protect me indeed! O housewife, protect me well!
O son, protect me, a wretched man being beaten by the followers of Yama. (25)
To him who was thus crying out, the son said: "O father, remember the Lord Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa; he will provide protection. (26)
"Recite the mantra: *Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇaḥ gatirmama* (Oṃ, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my refuge).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that son gave the mantra to his father. (27)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Svāmin, O Consort of Śrī, Supreme Person! 28.
Thus he proclaimed; meanwhile, the messengers were struck with fear.
They left their father behind, stood at a distance, and spoke among themselves. (29)
For this cowherd, who was our portion, has been liberated by his son;
he has been purified by the giving of Hari’s mantra and by his devotion.
When the messengers of Yama were speaking in this manner,
a circle of virtuous men happened to arrive there by chance.
The son quickly offered him a welcome reception;
seeing that the time was right, the saint gave him water born of his grace.
While the father was drinking, Hari arrived mounted upon an elephant;
he himself was indeed Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having expelled Romapāda from his body, he led him to the supreme state;
for the virtuous, the vision of the Lord at the time of death occurs through union with their sons.
The liberation of his father and the fruit of his gift were attained through devotion;
thus, O Lakṣmī, by the yoga of devotion, in a mere moment, [all was achieved] through the yoga of devotion. (35)
Therefore, association with the virtuous must be cultivated, for even sinners may attain liberation;
indeed, even Vṛṣaṅgama went to my abode after the end of his body.
Listen to another story, O Lakṣmī, concerning protection through association with the virtuous.
There was once a certain great thief, Nagra-bhaṅga by name, who was exceedingly cruel. (37)
At night, a group of twenty thieves would plunder the houses of those whose great wealth they had heard of, and then they would consider their weak points. (38)
When a favorable opportunity arises, he commits terrible theft;
having killed, beaten, and crushed people, he takes their wealth. (39)
He carries away objects made of gold, silver, and jewels, and he rejoices;
thus it is for one who acts in this manner, once upon a time, on account of some business during the day.
At that time, a goldsmith who fashioned golden ornaments in the royal palace was seen on the royal road as a long-standing friend coming within his sight. 41.
Nagrabhaṅga, too, seeing him on the road, met him with joy;
he inquired after his welfare and then indeed asked about his undertaking.
The goldsmith related his entire personal history to him, saying,
"Today, for one month, I have been performing the work of crafting ornaments for the king."
I am going to the royal palace where ten million gold pieces reside,
as well as thousands of pearls and even tens of thousands of gems.
In that very treasury, within an auspicious chamber by its side,
the goldsmiths— those artisans of gold— indeed fashion the ornaments.
Then Nagrabhaṅga said: "If my words please you, tell me the path through the deserted night for entering the interior. (46)
"I shall steal gold and other wealth, and I will give you a share as well.
Thus addressed, the goldsmith indeed showed him the way.
He showed him the strategic positions, the exits, the guarded gates, and the various weapons that had been prepared, as well as the firm missiles.
Displaying his departure in such a way that he appeared to be carrying away [the goods] while remaining concealed,
he then entered that city at night with his own caravan so as not to break the king's vigilance.
Having stolen wealth from the palace— gold, silver, excellent gems, and pearls— he fled well-concealed, unobserved by people.
Having given everything to his companions, he sent them away into the depths of the forest;
he then swiftly commanded his own men to cast him into a pit in the earth.
But he, eager for the sake of dispelling his fatigue and for a drink from the tavern,
slowly went outside the city of Śrīnagara during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Having gone to where those virtuous Śaiva practitioners— the *gañjā*-drinkers and fire-ascetics—
were seated, he indeed begged for a drink of that *tāmalagāñjika*.
Some did not prostrate themselves like staffs with feigned devotion;
they sat down nearby and presented a seal-ring as a gift. (54)
The virtuous ones also, considering him to be a devotee and a follower according to his devotion,
and having received him at the ritual, gave him a *tamālaka* flower for worship.
He drank [the water] and slept until sunrise in the morning;
then he woke up and remained there until midday.
He indeed provided food and the like, and likewise dispelled their fatigue;
then all those caravan robbers, having cast that wealth into a pit, [departed]. (57)
They traveled by way of the forest for a distance of one yojana toward their own village;
meanwhile, it became evident that the theft of that wealth had occurred within the king's palace.
Having placed the foot-doctors at their head, the soldiers,
bearing weapons, set out in the morning to search for the thieves before the king.
From Śrīnagara, horsemen, together with foot-doctors,
went into the forest and seized those who were going to their own village.
They beat them excessively and even brought them there;
likewise, they confined those fierce men in prison against the king.
Then, by means of associating with the virtuous, he protected the city from destruction; and though he was a secret lover of the king, he was not detected by the royal guards.
Other thieves were cast into fetters, punished, and killed;
but having heard of this foremost breach [of the law], he who was associated with the virtuous attained life itself. (63)
Considering himself truly unimpeded, he joyfully entreated the holy men:
"The dharma of the virtuous must be observed by me, and the initiation of the virtuous must be received. (64)
Service to the virtuous must be performed, and from this day forward I shall become a virtuous person;
I speak my sincere resolve in the presence of holy men. (65)
"O sinless ones, I have indeed repeatedly committed many kinds of theft;
please act so that I may be freed from the faults thereof. (66)
The virtuous are always intent on protecting those who have come for refuge;
it is through association with them that I live, while others are indeed as if dead.
Therefore, having attained dispassion, I shall worship the Supreme Lord;
and having become a saint myself, I shall also constantly serve the virtuous.
Thus entreated, those virtuous ones, headed by Cidambarāyana and others,
caused him to perform penance and washed away his accumulation of sins.
Having caused Nagra-bhaṅga to be purified, they underwent the Bhāgavata initiation;
he too, being liberated from sin, was named Bhāgavatāyana.
He was always devoted and a virtuous man who worshipped Me, the Supreme Lord; having performed supreme service to the saintly, he went to the imperishable realm for the sake of visiting holy places.
He came to Kuṅkumavāpī and attained liberation on the shore of the lake;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described protection through association with the virtuous. ||72||
Indeed, by means of his self-surrender, I have here granted him liberation.
Now I shall relate to you another narrative concerning the past.
In former times, there was a great saint named Śukāyana, who was exceedingly righteous;
he always worshipped me, the Supreme Lord, day and night. (74)
Possessing nothing as his own property, clothed only by the directions, and devoted solely to me, he dwells at the foot of a mango tree and subsists on fruits. (75)
She subsists on wild leaves, petals, tubers, and flowers,
and dwells forever in the forest to the east of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He endures cold and heat, and he endures rain, hunger, and thirst;
having bathed in the morning, he constantly circumambulates the lake. (77)
In this way, he takes his single midday meal at noon;
and having performed my divine glorification in the evening, he goes to sleep. (78)
He always worships my image made of variegated materials upon the trunk of a mango tree, and day after day he meditates upon it within his heart. (79)
A mango grove was always most excellent and dear to him;
he, too, would repeatedly offer me nothing but mango fruits.
While he was thus occupied with nurturing the mango tree, by the turn of fate, a fire broke out one day in the forest. (81)
Heaps of grass, heaps of stalks, heaps of leaves, and likewise medicinal herbs—
all were ablaze with flames, and at that time, all the trees were also set on fire.
Then even the mango tree at its own place blazed up;
thereafter, the fire indeed flared up with great force on all sides.
Driven by the wind, sharp, terrifying, and most cruel, he stood there in meditation, thinking of me, Hari, at that time. (84)
Indeed, I awakened him again and again with a voice from the sky:
"Go far away, leaving these trees; do not be consumed here. (85)
And he said: "I shall not go, abandoning my speech, my supports, my own place, my life, and my home, in every respect. (86)
I obtain a body, pleasure, and food, yet I do not abandon them;
"All these are my kinsmen, or my fathers, or my children. (87)
How indeed can I abandon all these mothers, my sisters?
For I am not ungrateful, nor do I become a sinner through my own self-interest. (88)
Having abandoned those by whose fruits I live well, in whose shade I dwell,
and through whose juices I obtain nourishment— where shall I go?
"These are not my bondsmen, nor are they dull-witted or of a different caste; they are not my family members, but rather these are those who have rendered service to me. (3.114.90)
Such servants, always characterized by altruism, who remain as my own refuge, assisting me day and night. ||9 1 ||
"How can I depart after burning these forest-dwellers who possess excellent virtues?
I shall be consumed right here; I will not go elsewhere. (92)
I am virtuous and patient, and these trees are also patient; they are virtuous and adorned with virtue. Therefore, I will not depart from them, having abandoned them.
Whether it be ashes or life itself in this world, one must indeed exist together with a virtuous person who is worthy of being nourished along with oneself. (94)
Having spoken thus, that treasury of fortitude neither moved nor rose;
as one meditating on Brahman, he sat down and remained exactly as he was.
Compassion and affection for the virtuous shall always be the great dharma;
having relied upon this capable one, I shall indeed cast off my own body today.
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Person!
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, protect these trees! 97.
Thus making this speech heard, the virtuous one meditated upon me with a mind single-pointed in conviction through his devotion. (98)
Then the fire began to burn the sides of the yogin,
as well as his feet, hands, matted hair, shoulders, body hair, and skin on all sides.
Nevertheless, even while worshipping me, he did not stir from that spot at all.
Knowing him to be my devotee, one who disregards the body and other such things, who is devoted solely to abiding in the Self, and who is now bodiless (videha), I said to him, "Choose a boon."
I am pleased with you because of your dispassion, your endowment with the virtuous dharma,
your abundance of the dharma of compassion, and because devotion abides in my mind.
"Choose a boon; I am capable, for I am Narayana himself, whom you, O wise one, meditate upon and for whose sake you have made this petition."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
was deeply gratified upon seeing your account of compassion.
"Choose a boon, O virtuous one; I shall grant you everything you desire.
The virtuous one then mentally chose [the power] over trees and forests.
Knowing that he was born with a perfect sense of taste and possessed such power as before,
and recognizing his firm devotion to that virtuous man which bestows supreme happiness, I [acted].
Delighted, I sprinkled the supreme mango tree with the nectar of my gaze,
as well as all the trees, creepers, fields, and the entire forest.
He sprinkled that excellent forest, reviving it with showers of nectar;
thereafter, fruits, leaves, branches, and flowers appeared everywhere.
Furthermore, the riches that had previously existed in the forest were restored once more;
the fire was entirely extinguished, and not even its ashes remained there.
All the work performed by Agni has dissolved, and my own creative power has emerged;
thus, a divine grove of mango trees has arisen near the lake.
Just as all success in every aim came to that forest which had taken refuge in the virtuous Bhāgavatāyana, who was full of devotion, so it is for one who takes refuge in the righteous. || 11.1 ||
Relying upon him, one shall attain the auspicious perfection fashioned by the virtuous;
this very virtuous one, whose path is the Bhāgavata, shines in my abode.
For by my grace and through devotion, one attains liberation in due time;
likewise, through reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Cowherd Romapāda through His Refuge in a Holy Man, the Protection of the Thief named Nagrabhaṅga from Royal Fear by Meeting with a Saint, and the Rejuvenation of Mango Trees and Other Plants Burnt by Fire through Association with the Holy Bhāgavata Āyana," in the Third Section on the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Nārāyaṇī-Śrī said:
"I have been born many times in this creation along with you—Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī, Śrī, Bhārgavī, Mādhavī, and Ramā. (1)
Vṛndā, Tulasī, Śivarājñī, Śrī, Kamalā, Pramā,
Padmā, Vidyāparā, Padmāvatī, and so forth, by the hundreds of thousands.
"O Lord Śrī Hari, Your forms exist here in this world;
a desire to know has arisen in me as to when and how Mahālakṣmī [appeared]."
And once she was born on earth, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, what was her name?
Even though I know that she is your mother-in-law and my own mother. (4)
And then Mahālakṣmī, as well as Gajānanā, who was born in Surāṣṭra;
she who was born in Camatkārapura and emerged from the Ocean of Milk.
I recognize that second one as being likewise made of great gold;
I recognize that third one as well, or whatever other [image] may be situated on the earth.
If she exists as the accomplisher of great deeds, proclaim her to me;
having heard of her, I shall rejoice, as well as her power and her wondrous nature.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe Mahālakṣmī, who is currently on the surface of the earth in the south; she is worshipful and a source of wonder.
In the city of Kāñcanī, that virtuous mother indeed shone resplendent.
Formerly, Kāmadeva arrived there for the purpose of deluding Śambhu.
On Mount Kailāsa, for the sake of a divine purpose, he was reduced to ashes by Śaṅkara; the Gaṇa Citrakarman, having taken some of that ash, fashioned it into an effigy.
He fashioned it right there and infused it with life;
that boy also became conscious and exceedingly full of wrath.
Having recited the Śatarudrīya in the presence of Śaṅkara, he became Śambhu himself;
then, being pleased, he spoke to him for the sake of a boon.
He chose this boon for me: "May my sovereignty over the three worlds be free of all thorns;
may the missiles and weapons of those who oppose me be rendered utterly futile. (1.3)
"May my missiles, weapons, and mantras never be in vain anywhere.
Śambhu then said, "So be it," and likewise granted him sovereignty.
"May your kingdom be free of thorns for sixty thousand years.
Then Brahmā himself, seeing him, spoke [to him] by the name Bhaṇḍāsura.
Thinking, "This has indeed become a smashing of the vessel," he spoke;
for now, this [being] was scorched by the fire of wrath from the forehead of Rudra. (16)
Born again from those ashes, he became a Dānava born of Rudra;
he grew up very quickly and summoned his preceptor, Śukra.
Then Maya again offered worship to those two; thereafter, Maya spoke to that architect: "As for that ancient city..."
"Make that city of the lords of the Daityas, which has been destroyed, new again.
Having heard that, Maya went and indeed built that city anew.
Having been consecrated there by Śukra and the mighty Daityas, he formerly ruled over the three worlds from that very place.
He shone with supreme opulence, splendors, strength, and other such qualities—
that very crown which Hiraṇyakaśipu had formerly worn.
Bhaṇḍa bore that crown, which was living, indestructible, and worn by Śukra; he also bore two living chowries, resplendent with their power.
No diseases nor sufferings arise from serving him, whose parasol was held aloft so that millions of weapons stood as if in its shade. (23)
Neither destruction, nor defeat, nor birth afflicts him;
[he possesses] the bow named Vijaya, the enemy-slaying conch, and his ornaments. (24)
The sage gave him a fiery lion-throne and inexhaustible valor;
thus the king was restored, along with his eight mighty sons.
They were preeminent, honored by the army, and traveled through the three worlds:
Indraśatru, Amitraghna, Vidyunmālī, and Vibhīṣaṇa. ||26||
Ugrakarman, Ugradhanvan, and Vijaya, who had mastered the Vedas—all were indeed knowers of the Vedic scriptures and devoted to the ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa). ||27||
Skilled in battle, experts in illusion, and full of prowess,
he then dispatched the Daitya Viśukra with his right shoulder.
With his left shoulder, he cast forth Viṣāṅga, whose crest was wicked;
and from his throat, Bhaṇḍaka also cast forth his sister Dhūminī.
Sumohinī, Kumudvatī, Citrāṅgī, and Sundarī—
these four daughters of Daityas were then offered as his wives.
Chariots, horses, elephants, and thousands of celestial palaces appeared for those who had conquered the worlds and followed the doctrine of the preceptor Śukra.
That Bhaṇḍa, along with all the Daityas, became a devotee of Śaṅkara;
at that time, sacrifices to Rudra were being performed everywhere, in house after house.
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the ritual manuals and the formulas for receiving gifts,
proceeded even among the hosts of Daityas at that sacrifice.
Then, at the sacrifices of the Daityas, those who consume the sacrificial offerings feasted together with the two brothers of fierce valor and with their principal forces.
He conquered all the quarters and then shone like the great Indra;
exalted by his heroism and prowess, he shattered the cosmic egg.
Many times the gods and others, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, were defeated by him at the front of the battle; yet upon seeing his blazing splendor, they [were overcome]. (36)
Intent on flight, they all took up residence in their respective abodes:
some within the depths of the netherworld (pātāla), and others in the waters of the ocean.
Some, utterly terrified, wandered in disguise, hidden in the remote corners of the directions or within the groves of mountains.
The ancestors, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the gods, the Nāgas, the sacrifices, the lords of the directions, as well as Brahmā, Padmanābha, Rudra, and the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra). ||39||
Considering all the worlds as mere straw, Bhaṇḍa indeed ruled;
such was the reign of Bhaṇḍa, who appeared victorious.
After sixty thousand years had passed beyond that,
the Lord of Kamalā, beholding the gods whose strength was waning, [acted].
In order to slay the fierce demon Bhaṇḍāsura and to protect the three worlds,
he suddenly manifested an illusion in his own form that was utterly bewildering.
That Lalitā, the supreme deity who is Mahālakṣmī herself, became my mother Kambharā in her own form. 43.
Adorned with four arms holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, she is the Mother, the Supreme Power, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman. 44.
Hari spoke to that Māyā, the Great Vaiṣṇavī who causes the destruction of the hosts of Daityas: "Slay the Daitya Bhaṇḍa!"
Having thus received this command, she made a request to the host of apsarases;
Hari granted her the apsarases, and she [chose] them along with Viśvācikā and the others.
She went to the Himalaya mountain where the demon Bhaṇḍaka resides;
there, that Mahālakṣmī was at the foot of a campaka tree.
He made his dwelling in that delightful place; and hearing her singing with a sweet voice, the Daitya, afflicted by love, approached and entreated her. (48)
She too, by employing amorous gestures, emotional expressions, graceful movements, and charming conversation,
captivated the minds of the Daityas and of Bhaṇḍaka.
Then Bhaṇḍa and the Daityas forgot their evening prayers to Lord Śiva,
as well as the twilight rituals, hymns of praise, worship, and service to the elders.
They abandoned all their auspicious sacrificial activities,
and likewise, they ceased honoring their own preceptor, Śukra.
Having deluded them, this goddess besieged the foremost of the Daityas;
then Śukra, struck by humiliation, became repeatedly incensed with anger.
He said to the Daityas: "Truly, you are not fit for the prosperity of a kingdom;
fall indeed from another's kingdom, and let your pride go to its destruction. (53)
But seeing the demons created by Māyā rendered inert, Indra and the others donned their armor and went to the Yamunā for the sake of performing penance. ||54||
The gods indeed commenced an auspicious sacrifice that bestows strength upon Viṣṇu;
they performed the worship of Nārāyaṇī, the Great Lakṣmī. 55.
Established in fierce austerity, devoted to recitation and meditation, Lakṣmī remained vigilant with her mind fixed on no other. 56.
After many years had passed, the priest Śukra himself said to the Daityas: "The gods and others are indeed intent upon your destruction. (57)
"O gods and others, even as you perform sacrifices, meditation, and austerities on the banks of the Yamunā, mere birth alone shall destroy you. (58)
Hari will surely slay all those on your side before long;
for by him alone was created this illusion in the form of Mahālakṣmī.
"Seeing you there among the bewildered ones, Indra and the other gods are indeed performing penance;
go there quickly and create obstacles for them immediately."
Having heard this, the Daityas, skilled in battle, joined by the demon Bhaṇḍa,
reached the bank of the Yamunā and created an obstacle by engaging in a great war.
Seeing the Daityas who were creating obstacles to her penance, Mahālakṣmī, acting for the sake of her devotees,
constructed a magnificent and radiant great wall.
Seeing that firm city named Indraprastha, which was impenetrable by the Dānavas and Daityas,
Bhaṇḍaka became despondent and returned to his own city.
O King, Śrutavarman, his friend, said to Bhaṇḍa: "Listen to these words:
your kingdom, for sixty thousand years, has been offered to Śiva. (64)
Therefore, this time for the end of your kingdom has been ordained by Śiva;
it is impossible to counteract, so pass the time.
"Enjoyment should be practiced in its proper time, and withdrawal at the proper time is supreme.
Having heard this instruction, Bhaṇḍakāsura desisted.
The deity, having fashioned a sacrificial pit of suitable dimensions in the vast expanse of the forest at Indraprastha, and having established the sacred fire there— ||67||
Having made a firm vow and having worshipped Mahālakṣmī,
they performed oblations all around for the sake of pleasing Hari with Śrī.
"We shall become one with Brahman, or we shall enjoy the celestial realm"—
thinking thus, they performed the oblation, when suddenly [the deity] appeared.
A great splendor in the form of a wheel; in its center is the Supreme Goddess, the Mother of the World, the Bestower of Life, Nārāyaṇī, the Sovereign of the Highest.
She consists of the splendor of the divine array, she rejoices in Brahman, and she is beautiful as Hari;
her radiant hands hold a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and a lotus garland. (71)
Upon seeing her, the gods were bewildered; their afflictions vanished, they bowed down, and they praised Śrī Mahālakṣmī—the graceful mother of Viṣṇu. (72)
Victory, O Lakṣmī, Mother of the World! Victory, O Lakṣmī, higher than the highest!
Victory, O Abode of Auspiciousness! Victory, O You whose essence is all the arts! ||73||
Victory to you, O Brāhmī, O Mahālakṣmī, O you whose self is Brahman, O Supreme Self!
Victory to you, O Nārāyaṇī, O Peaceful One! Victory to you, O Śrī Lalitā, O Rāmā! (74)
Victory, O Śrī Vijayā, Sovereign Goddess, O Śrīde, O bestower of prosperity! Salutations to her who has a thousand heads, a thousand faces, and a thousand eyes. (75)
Salutations to you, O Lakṣmī, who are beautified by the lotus-like feet with their thousand lotus-hands;
you who are subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest. (76)
Aṭala is considered your two feet in memory, Vitala your knees,
Rasātala your hips, and the Earth is regarded as your belly.
May the heart of the earth be yours; may truth be considered your face and your head;
may the moon, sun, and fire be your eyes; the quarters of space your ears; and the gods your arms. (78)
The Maruts are your breaths, your words are considered the Vedas, the creation of the worlds is your play, and the Supreme Lord is your friend. (79)
Sadānanda is your food, and your dwelling is in the heart of Hari;
the visible and invisible forms and the worlds are yours.
Your thick locks of hair are indeed the stars, and those flowers are you;
Dharma and the others are your arms, and Kāla and the others are your weapons.
The *yamas* and *niyamas* are also your nails on the hands and feet;
your two breasts are the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā*, yielding the milk that sustains all living beings. (82)
Your breath is *prāṇāyāma*, your tongue is Sarasvatī;
the trees are the hairs upon your body, and the dawn is your garment. (83)
In the beginning, Compassion, the lawful wife of Dharma, created all beings;
you are she who dwells in the heart, the pervasive Lakṣmī, the Enchantress, and likewise the Supreme One.
Now you are seen as Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, and Priyaṃkarī;
salutations to that Mahālakṣmī, salutations again and again to the one with the face of a preeminent elephant. ||85||
Salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, the possessor of all powers, the sustainer of all,
who created Virāj, and from him, the unborn Viṣṇu and Īśvara.
Salutations again and again to that Lakṣmī, who is Rudra as well as the foremost of the gods;
salutations again and again to you, Hariṇī, who possesses the three qualities and yet is beyond all qualities. ||87||
Salutations again and again to you, the Mother of the World, whose nature consists of the Yantras and Tantras;
salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, the embodiment of the Guru, the sovereign power of speech. ||88||
Salutations again and again to you, Kambharā, the bearer of all knowledge;
salutations again and again to Jayā, Lalitā, Pāñcālī, and Ramā, who manifest themselves. ||89||
"Obeisance to Padmāvatī, the consort of Rāma, who is endowed with excellent qualities, wisdom, and glory!
Obeisance! Thus praised, she became pleased and granted him excellent boons.
The gods, being pleased, said: "If you are satisfied, destroy Bhaṇḍāsura! Grant long life and happiness to us who seek your refuge. (91)
Mahālakṣmī said: "Let all be joyful and fearless;
I, Lalitā, the great chaste lady, shall destroy the demon Bhaṇḍāsura."
They will be my praisers, endowed with glory, fame, and virtue;
they will be perfected in knowledge and discipline, free from disease, and long-lived. (93)
"Rich with sons, friends, and wives, they shall possess great prosperity.
Having thus obtained this boon, the gods performed a sacrificial session (*satra*) until it was complete.
Then that Lalitā Lakṣmī took the bridegroom’s garland, which was held in her hand,
and offered it to the Supreme Self, who is the very nature of the beginningless Śrī Mahāviṣṇu.
While all the gods were watching right there, he placed it around [his] neck;
then the divine drums resounded and shouts of "Victory! arose.
There, songs were sung by the celestial nymphs and the wives of the gods;
the Apsarases danced and the best of the Gandharvas sang.
The sages offered hymns of praise, intent on bestowing blessings;
the virtuous prostrated themselves, and the attendants performed service. (98)
Lakṣmī and the others performed the worship of the couple at Indraprastha,
and they also gave them wedding gifts, ornaments, and wealth.
At the conclusion of the wedding there, the gods and others provided various kinds of jewels as well as foods for the couple. 3.115.100.
Then Brahmā spoke for the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura,
[addressing] Mahālakṣmī, known as Lalitā, who is likewise the Supreme Brahman and Hari.
Then, for the sake of protecting the Dharma and for the protection of the gods,
Mahālakṣmī immediately [appeared] by the command of Nārāyaṇa.
He remembered his divine weapons, such as the discus and others, which possessed celestial forms;
they arrived in embodied form and stood before Hari.
The virtuous Mahālakṣmī, who fulfills all desires, accepted them by the command of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of all desires.
Having taken all the gods along with their allies, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa,
she set out, her victory increasing, to destroy the Daityas.
The armies of the attendants, the hosts, and likewise the celestial beings,
as well as the goddesses and the Siddhas, set forth with their weapons ready.
By the thousands there were cows and horses, lions, tigers, and birds;
as well as bulls, śarabhas, swans, and likewise garuḍas.
Then thousands of celestial chariots, as well as vehicles and chariots equipped with weapons, all fashioned for the occasion, set forth from Indraprastha.
The great army of Mahālakṣmī, accompanied by Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Kamalā,
and joined by ten million goddesses including Durgā, Satī, and Mahācaṇḍī.
And that divine chariot, moving with unimpeded course, emerged into the sky;
it was likewise augmented and protected by divine missiles, weapons, mantras, and other means.
The sky, as far as the realm of Satyaloka, was filled with the roar of the army;
hearing this, all the lords who are Nārāyaṇas quickly arrived.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arraying of the Armies of Lalitā and Mahālakṣmī, Who Manifested at the Sacrifice of the Gods Arrived at Indraprastha for the Purpose of Destroying the Asura Bhaṇḍa, Born from the Ashes of Kāmadeva," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Mahākṣmī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Śāradā, Durgā, Gaṅgā, Yamī, Revā, Rādhā, Ramā, and Padminī. || 2 ||
Kamalā, Śrī, Pāśavatī, Ramā, Māṇikī, Mañjulā, Sukhadā, Kambharā, Lakṣmī, Santuṣṭā, Vijayā, and Jayā. (3)
Suparṇā, Mādhavī, Haṃsī, Bhārgavī, Suguṇā, Satī, Nārāyaṇī, Vāsudevī, Hariṇī, and Hiraṇmayī. || 4 ||
Śārdūlavāhanā, Mattā, Gajānanā, Haṃsinī, Viśvā, Bhūti, Piṅgalākṣī, Kāmākṣī, Vallabhā, and Dayā. (5)
Kārṣṇī, Vṛndā, Vaiṣṇavī, Jyoṣṭrī, Kāmadughā, Anaghā, Bhūḥ, Dyauḥ, Dhariṇī, Dhātrī, Bhāratī, Karīṇī, and Kṛti. || 6 ||

Māyā, Rati, Maṅgalā, Amṛtā, and Mānasā as the sixth; Śānti is the eleventh, followed by Haimī, Urjaskā, and Puruṣottamī.
All these were indeed Vaiṣṇavī weapons, with Mūrdhanī at their head and Yoddhṛnāśikā; likewise, other Śāṅkarī weapons issued forth in the battle, O coward.
Śāṃkarī, Mālinī, Caṇḍī, Vāyavyā, Dūtikā, Khagā, Cāmuṇḍā, Śatānandā, Calacchikhā, and Supicchalā. || 12 ||
Balā, Cātibalā, Mātṛnandā, Nandā, Aparājitā, Mahākālī, Bhairavī, Karālī, and likewise Gaṇī. || 13 ||
Mṛtyu, Mārī, Mahāmārī, Diti, Ghaṭodarī, Danu, Ulūkī, Karṇamoṭī, Vajrahastā, and Kapālikā. || 14 ||
Piśācī, Rākṣasī, Kheṭā, Bhṛśuṇḍī, Lāṅgalī, as well as Dhūmrā, Karālinī, Ekavīrā, Udumbarī, and Kukkuṭī. (15)
Kekarī, Pretayānā, Krauñcī, Śailamukhī, Sakhī, Kapardinī, Kāmarūpā, Rocanā, and likewise Keśinī. || 16 ||

Mahādevī, Rudrasaṭā, Kātyāyanī, Karālinī, Gaurī, Sāṃkarṣiṇī, Devī, Prāleyī, and Bhūtaḍāmarī. || 19 ||
Sṛṣṭigarbhā, Mahāmāyā, Khaṭīyārī, and Pāśinī—
these and other Rudrāṇīs, adorned with darkness, emerged for the battle.
Then all the Pārameṣṭhyīs and the Brahmāṇīs also went forth—
the Saṃkrāntis, the Susiddhānyas, the Siddhis, and those who have the essence of Brahman.
Daṇḍanāthā, Mantranāthā, Dhūmorṇā, Mantranāyikā, Śyāmalā, Yantriṇī, Ghanaśyāmā, and Saṃgītayoginī. (22)
She is Tripurā, the mistress of the cakras, the sovereign empress, the universal ruler;
she is the mistress of the tradition of the Great Vidyās, the Vedic one, and likewise the supreme goddess.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Caṇḍikā of the crimson form. ||24||
Kṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Vaśaṃkarī, as well as Unmādinī, Khecarā, Yaṣṭi, and Mahāṅkuśā. ||25||
And other powers of reality and so forth, dwelling within all seeds, numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions, went forth, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle. (26)
The goddesses who attract the elements, as well as those who attract the mind, those who attract the self, and likewise those who attract the body. ||27||
Anaṅgalekhā, Sarvajṛmbhaṇā, Mṛtyupradāyinī, Sarvavyādhiharā, and the one named Rakṣā—these are the secret Yoginīs. 28.
Vaśinī, Jīvanī, Vahnivāsinī, Kulasundarī, Śoṣiṇī, Rati, Prīti, Kānti, Śānti, and Tuṣṭikā. ||29||
Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Bhū, Pramāthinī, Nāgavīthikā, Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī, Durgāmbā, and likewise Potriṇī. ||3.116.30||
The Yakṣiṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Lākinī, and likewise Hākinī;
Śākinī, Ḍākinī, Dhātunāthā, Vārtālikā, and Āndhinī. (3.1)
These other Śaktis, born from the Arbudābja, emerged in the battle;
then Indra, the Apsarases, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas [also came forth]. (32)
Viśvakarman, Maya, and Agni; the Rudras and the Piśācas;
as well as the Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Mitrās, and Kinnaras. ||33||
The Vidyādharas, and also Govinda, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Kamalā;
Brahmā, the two sons of the Aśvins, the Gaṇakas, Dhanvantari, and Vāsuki. (34)
The Nāgas, the Brahmins, and the family priests also went forth;
at that time, there were mṛdaṅgas, murajas, paṭahas, and groups of atukulī drums.
There were *selukās*, *jhallarīs*, *rāndyās*, *huḍukās*, *huḍḍukās*, and *gharas*;
as well as *ānakas*, *paṇavas*, *gomukhas*, and *ardhacandrikās*. (36)
There were also the yavamadhyas, mardalas, ḍiṇḍimas, and jharjharas;
likewise the varītās, uddhakas, tuhuṇḍas, and barbaras.
During the exertion for battle, the sounds of "hum" and kettledrums resounded,
along with all manner of missiles, weapons, arms, and millions of mantras.
Accompanied by all the warriors on chariots, horses, elephants, and the like,
as well as great vehicles and celestial chariots, they arrived at the abode of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura.
Seeing the sky pervaded by the army and filled with the clamor of battle,
the asuras then trembled with agitation at the onset of the graceful [divine] movement.
Then, for the Asuras, there were misfortunes at every step;
it was as if the walls of the Daityas' city had been shattered out of season.
Great meteors fell, whirling from the expanse of the sky;
then, earthquakes and heart-tremblings occurred again and again. (42)
Kanka birds, vultures, cranes, and other birds perched upon the tops of the banners;
moreover, a wheel appeared within the solar disc as a portent of destruction. (43)
The left limbs of men and the right limbs of women throbbed there, and banners were seen in the sky. (44)
And the ornaments and garlands of the Daitya women fell out of place prematurely;
so too did their mirrors, armor, banners, and excellent swords.
At that time, there was a soiling of the jewels and the garments;
drops of bloody water fell into the centers of the sacrificial altars.
Seeing the portents, the terrified Daityas spoke to Bhaṇḍaka;
Bhaṇḍa, overcome with anger, then summoned his two ministers.
In the assembly hall, he quickly held a consultation regarding the undertaking of war;
Viśukra and Viṣaṅga were the ministers who provided him with counsel.
Likewise, the lords of the Daityas, having assembled for the purpose of receiving his command,
Viśukra then spoke while they all listened.
Surā and the others, having obtained their opportunity, created a woman proud of her strength;
and the gods, having prepared her, came together with her.
"Alas, what a tragedy ordained by fate! They have come to conquer us;
if these women should defeat us, it would be a cause for mockery. (51)
Today the female sex is rushing toward us for our victory;
even if she be a woman, she must be slain by those who desire conquest. (52)
Having dragged her by the hair, that wicked Sadāsikā must be brought here; she will surely submit to the status of your very own maidservant.
Having spoken thus, he increased Bhaṇḍa’s anger there;
then Viṣaṅga spoke words that were wise and conducive to happiness.
Everything should be done after thorough deliberation; discernment is the supreme recourse.
An action performed without discernment leads to destruction. (55)
By means of spies, strength and weakness must be known by those desiring victory and success; for even a person of low birth, a woman, or one of humble status may [prove decisive] for kings. (56)
One should not show contempt toward enemies, for power exists everywhere;
indeed, power alone is the cause of the glory of victory in all circumstances. (57)
