Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Giving Away of a Daughter, the Giving of Lakṣmī, the Vow for a Daughter, and so forth, for the Purpose of Obtaining a Daughter," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my beloved, O Teacher of the World!
[Tell me of that vow] which is the foremost of all vows and the bestower of all supreme spiritual welfare.
It is the door to all security, the warder-off of all obstacles, the remover of all distress, and the destroyer of all diseases. || 2 ||
This vow, which brings about all fortune and leads to the highest state, is the performer of all prosperity;
indeed, by its single observance, all vows are fulfilled in every respect.
Tell me that supreme vow which, when performed, truly causes all sins to perish. (4)
All expiations exist for the sake of that by which [this is performed];
it bestows all goals, is the highest of all dharmas, and is supreme beyond the supreme.
Tell me that [vow] at the beginning of which all other multitudes of vows seem as mere blades of grass,
and into which all meritorious acts such as sacrifices enter once it has been performed.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which is higher than the highest, for the sake of attaining that which cannot be accomplished even by performing all religious duties, gifts, pilgrimages, rituals, and vows.
The vow thus performed will certainly grant success; I tell you this as a certainty.
Although I have already explained it to you in many ways, I shall state it clearly once more. (8)
This excellent vow, consisting of service to the servant, accomplishes all goals;
it is the foremost of all vows and brings about every auspiciousness. || 9 ||
It removes all suffering, removes all obstacles, and is the abode of happiness; it dispels mental anguish, external conditions, and physical disease, and bestows the arising of all good fortune.
It bestows all supernatural powers, removes all sins, and destroys all impurities;
it is the essence of all dharmas, meritorious, and indeed the essence of all sacrifices.
One should constantly worship the virtuous, for that is indeed the vow of honoring the virtuous; one should satisfy the lords of sages with whatever offerings are obtained. 1-2.
One should always perform the auspicious act of seeing them in the morning;
that vow of beholding the virtuous is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
The massaging of the feet of the virtuous should always be performed in the evening;
it is auspicious, bestows merit, and grants prosperity—such is the vow of massaging the feet. (14)
Milk drawn at dawn and other such drinks, as sweet as nectar, should indeed be given daily to the virtuous according to one's ability; this is the vow of offering wholesome drink to the righteous.
One who desires their own welfare should give fruits and other such items to holy men in the morning;
ripe fruits of desirable flavors should be given—this is the vow of offering fruits to the virtuous.
Grains and other foods ripened by the sun, ripened by fire, or ripened by the seasons should always be given to the virtuous; that is the vow of the offering of excellent grains.
Leafy vegetables should be given, as well as various kinds of edible foods, sugarcane, tubers, sprouts, and so forth; this is the vow of offering excellent greens.
Raw substances, ghee, flour, and milk should be given;
likewise, sweet items, alkaline substances, and fermented gruel—this is the virtuous vow of offering uncooked food.
One should always offer with devotion various kinds of cooked foods that are sweet and delightful; this is the vow of offering wholesome food. 3.123.20.
Cool water should be offered for the purposes of bathing and drinking;
this is the vow of offering pure water that is sweet, fragrant, and fit for consumption. (21)
Betel nuts and leaves suitable for mouth-freshening, along with seeds and other ingredients, should be offered; this is the vow of providing excellent fragrance.
Or, in the evening, whatever foodstuffs and drinks there may be [should be offered].
One should give gifts according to one's ability; for that is indeed the virtuous vow of the evening.
One should perform the massaging of the body to alleviate fatigue; likewise, one should apply oil and other unguents, which effectively bring about the exhaustion of wholesome exertion. (24)
The gift of clothing should be bestowed, as well as the giving of blankets and the like; the vow of offering fine garments includes the giving of beds, seats, and so forth. (25)
The daily offering of cooking pots, gourds, bowls, leaf-plates, and baskets— these constitute the vow of bestowing vessels upon worthy recipients.
Flowers, flower garlands, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like should be offered; this is the vow of offering excellent perfumes. (27)

Wood, sacrificial fuel, and what is to be offered—mats, cloth strips, fine plaids, cushions, four-legged stools, couches, and so forth; indeed, that is the vow of the virtuous regarding sacrificial fuel. (28)
The gift of books of knowledge, the gift of a hall, the offering of a house, the gift of a residence for the study of the Veda, and the vow of imparting noble learning; ||29||
The offering of a viewing instrument, a water-wheel, letters, and a pen;
and the offering of ink, paper, and so forth—this is the vow of offering virtuous instruments. (3.123.30)
The giving of thread and needles, the giving of footwear, and the giving of garments such as tunics—this indeed is the vow of protecting the virtuous. (3.1)
Having constructed a hermitage adorned with trees and other features, its dedication constitutes this excellent vow of the hermitage, which bestows both heaven and liberation. (32)

If one possesses wealth, a well, a pond, a lake, a large oblong pool, or a canal should be constructed within a virtuous hermitage; this is the auspicious vow of providing pure water for the righteous.
A gateway, a hall of Dharma, a moon-chamber, a balcony, a sacrificial mound, a water-shed, and a hut for providing shade should be constructed. (34)
A fire-sanctuary should be constructed, as well as a kitchen for the sake of the virtuous;
there should also be a hall for bathing, meditation, and recitation—this indeed is the vow of the holy ones. (35)
Cows that yield milk and are accompanied by their calves should be given to virtuous men, as well as bulls for the purpose of transport; this indeed is the "Virtuous Cow Vow" (sādhudhenuvrata).
Elephants, camels, horses, lions, tigers, deer, and other such animals should be given; indeed, one should observe the excellent vow of giving suitable vehicles to a capable and virtuous person. (37)
The wind-vehicle, the celestial chariot, the swan-vehicle, the boat on the water, the cart, the man-borne vehicle, the palanquin, and the guarded carriage—these are under one's control. (38)
A carriage, sandals, a lion-throne, an elephant-throne, and even a plank-seat should be given; this indeed is the vow of the virtuous vehicle (sādhuyāna-vrata). //39//
A garden, a grove, a field, a livelihood, and the seasonal occupation; the share of income to be given—this indeed is the vow of righteous conduct. (3.123.40)
Musical instruments include bronze cymbals, the jhallarī, the paṭaha drum, the auspicious tantrikā lute, the flute, the vīṇā, the mṛdaṅga and other drums, the mūraja, and the tāratumbikā. ||41||
The water-instrument, the vocal instrument, the hand-clap, and the drum;
the lightning-instrument is also to be offered—this indeed is the vow of the virtuous instruments. (42)
The skin of a lion, an elephant, a tiger, and a deer—this pure hide should be given; this indeed is the vow of the virtuous regarding skins. (43)
Pearl, diamond, gem, jewel, glass, and the finest stone;
the mardalī drum and the pestle—these should be given as a true vow for the successful practice of the virtuous. 44.
A small box, a granary, a basket, a gourd, a pitcher, as well as a binding rope—these should be given; this indeed is the Sādhujolī vow. 42.
Alms should be given in the manner of a honey-gatherer (mādhukarī), and a garland of tulasī beads should be worn;
the materials for worship should also be offered—this indeed is the vow of the worship of the holy ones.
A fan, a fly-whisk, a water-vessel, and an upper garment should be given;
a cloth and a water-dipper should also be provided—this indeed is the vow of the virtuous twilight (sandhyā).
Medicines, powders, pills, and likewise boluses, as well as decoctions and electuaries should be administered; this indeed is the vow for the restoration of health. (48)
An umbrella, a sickle, a helmet, sandals, a garment, a loincloth, and a cloth should be given; this indeed is the vow of protecting the virtuous. (49)
Holy ashes, a tooth-stick, a sacred thread,
a waist-band, and a neck-ornament should be given to the virtuous one who observes the vow of the bull.
Giving what is required by the virtuous is good; observing the vows required by the virtuous is good.
The words of the virtuous are to be accepted; obeying the commands of the virtuous is a vow. (5.1)
The grace of the virtuous is to be enjoyed; the vow is the nectar of the merit of the virtuous.
The water from the feet of the virtuous is to be drunk; the vow is the nectar of the speech of the virtuous. (52)
The favor of the virtuous is to be obtained; this is the vow of the virtuous' grace.
The gracious object of the virtuous is to be accepted; this is the vow of taking refuge in the virtuous. (53)
O Lakṣmī, thus have the vows of the virtuous been described to you in truth;
now I shall describe other vows as well, which consist of service.

But for those embodied beings for whom success is truly achieved in their practice, there is that sense of pride which arises when they encounter suffering, intended for the purpose of serving the virtuous. (55)
Service should be performed in the form of a servant or in the form of a slave;
it may consist of the offering of one's entire being or the offering of material wealth.

That which consists of the offering of a lamp, that which takes the form of the offering of food, that which consists of the offering of oil, or that which consists of the offering of ornaments; ||57||

That which consists of the offering of clothing, that which consists of the offering of a daughter or a son, and that which consists of service—such honor is appropriate for a virtuous woman and a virtuous man. (58)
That auspicious vow of devotion to a virtuous woman, which consists of service to a chaste wife, destroys all suffering and poverty; it must be practiced by a woman with humility. 59.
A person should perform that auspicious service consisting of attending upon the virtuous, so that there may be protection of dharma and merit may increase, bestowing happiness. (3.123.60)
Just as a woman or a man may attain supreme merit from a guru or a guru’s wife, so too may they attain it from a virtuous man or a virtuous woman. ||6.1||
One should indeed perform service with faith, by means of a path free from doubt;
one should serve the true guru with that same reverence which was previously cultivated.
For that is declared to be service to the virtuous, the supreme and auspicious vow of the righteous;
when an evil dream has occurred, this auspicious practice of honor should be performed.
I shall behold the virtuous and serve them for even a moment;
may the fruit born of evil sleep never befall me at any time. (64)
Even when an inauspicious omen occurs, one should perform auspicious acts of veneration;
having beheld holy men, one should offer them words of auspicious blessing. (65)
Thinking, "I shall obtain the fruit of this ill omen; may it not come to pass," one should maintain a virtuous composure when fear of an enemy has arisen. (66)
"Having stayed in the hermitage for two auspicious days, I shall perform the sight, worship, and service of the virtuous; thus, I shall have no fear of the enemy. (67)
But when fear of the king has arrived, auspicious humility should be practiced:
"I shall perform the sight and service of the virtuous for five days. (68)
"I shall feed the virtuous and give abundant wealth to the worthy;
I shall perform service to the gods and the gift of Dharma; let there be no fear of the king. (69)
When fear has arisen among the subjects, auspicious honor should be shown;
for the sake of the virtuous, I shall provide a means of livelihood and beautiful fields, groves, and so forth.
"I shall serve the virtuous for only a month; there is no fear for my subjects from me.
When the danger of malevolent magic arises, auspicious respect must be shown. (71)
"If my magical rites for possession by spirits and the like should perish, then I shall serve the virtuous for five days and likewise perform worship. (72)
When a foul affliction arises that is equal to the destruction of life, then one must maintain respect day and night toward the virtuous hermitage and the monastery. (73)
Having dwelt there for the duration of a month, I shall serve holy people;
I shall practice devotion and indeed become free from all affliction.
While nature and its transformations are arising, one should maintain a pure state of mind;
one should practice the company of the virtuous and serve the righteous side. (75)
When my constitution is restored to its natural state, I shall feed virtuous people;
in cases of wind-disease (vāyu-roga), one should practice humility and seek the company of the wise. //76//
I shall perform [this] for ten days, and my madness will perish;
when bitten by a venomous creature, this supreme observance must be performed.
"May the poison be destroyed and may my life become firm for that purpose;
I shall constantly serve the virtuous day and night for one month. (78)
When suffering arises from such things as the stroke of a weapon, it is auspicious to maintain the pride [of thinking]:
"For the sake of destroying this pain, I shall perform worship for the virtuous. (79)
I shall dwell for just one month in the residence of the virtuous, eager to serve him, offering gifts of wealth and likewise gifts of food and other enjoyments. (3.123.80)

In cases of heart pain, fainting, the three humors (tridoṣa), or the cessation of vital functions, the excellent practice of *mānatā* (pride) should be employed, thinking: "I shall live even if I am struck down. (8.1)
Having become a virtuous person, I shall dwell in a virtuous monastery for the sake of attaining devotion; or else, I shall perform auspicious service to the holy ones day and night for a year. (82)
I shall perform [this] with my mind, with material offerings, and with my body whose self is absorbed in that;
for the sake of destroying diseases such as fever, auspicious veneration must be performed. 83.
For two days, I shall perform service while staying with the virtuous for the sake of dispelling disease;
likewise, I shall have a great worship performed and a Sarvatobhadra mandala drawn.
"I shall have a mandala constructed for the removal of cruel diseases;
I shall give various kinds of food to the virtuous for the alleviation of suffering. (85)
In the event of suffering from a broken limb or similar ailment, a vow (mānatā) should be undertaken for the sake of auspiciousness:
"If my limbs attain health, I shall perform a silver offering. (86)
The surrendering of one's home, the surrendering of one's livelihood, and service to holy men;
when medical treatment with surgical instruments has been performed upon the body by the best of physicians; ||87||
If I am to be restored to life and freed from disease, I shall remain for six months in the service of holy men, providing them with food and wealth. (88)
Whether in a flowing stream, in the middle of a lake, in a hole, or even in mud—in such places as these, a measurement made while submerged is auspicious. (89)
"If I were wealthy enough to live, then I would offer my entire property and even my old age to the temple of the God, as an offering against this unavoidable calamity. (3.123.90)
For six months, day and night, I shall serve the virtuous in the monastery with my food, wealth, clothing, body, mind, and all my powers. (91)
For the sake of attaining victory in battle, auspicious pride should be maintained;
[one should seek] villages, countries, riches, and gold, silver, diamonds, and so forth. (92)
Vehicles, mounts, ornaments, umbrellas, chowries, and silk bands—
I shall offer these to Śrī Hari and to the virtuous ones as well, each according to its proper place.
I shall serve the virtuous like a servant for five months;
I shall feed the holy men at the sacrifice and cause a temple to be built. (94)
"Bound by a noose and standing in fetters, I must practice humility;
if I am released from this, I shall serve the virtuous. (95)
Having stayed in the monastery for two months and having provided food according to his ability, one who is surrounded by enmity should indeed practice humility for the sake of survival. (96)
"If I were alive, I would give you a body weighing a load of gold, or my own body weighing a load of silver, or even a load of sugar. (97)
Furthermore, for the sake of recovering wealth stolen by theft and the like, a superior ordeal must indeed be performed, provided that such wealth can actually be recovered. (98)
"I shall give half to the Supreme Lord, who is virtuous and performs righteous deeds;
and with that wealth, I shall then perform sacrifices, acts of charity, and other such rites. (99)
When the theft of a wife, son, daughter, father, mother, sister, or a family member has been committed by enemies, the highest atonement must be performed. (3.123.10)
If, moreover, they should return here alive and unhurt,
then for the duration of a year I shall practice the service of the virtuous.
I shall give wealth, provide food and other offerings, and perform auspicious worship;
I shall effect the supreme pacification of misfortune, which is protective in nature. (102)
Thus have these vows of service to the virtuous, known as Lakṣmī, been described to you; they should indeed be performed by men and women alike, for they truly remove all suffering.
Moreover, I shall also briefly describe all other [rites], by the performance of which obstacles and afflictions go far away. (104)
In this creation, there is no vow superior to the service of the virtuous;
by their blessing, even incurable suffering is swiftly destroyed.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Vow among All Vows, Consisting of Service to the Holy and Humility," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 123 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, beloved of Śiva’s queen, listen; I shall describe to you the multitude of vows for the service of the virtuous, which are exceedingly auspicious. (1)

If the milking of cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, or camels is obstructed by another person, or if malevolent magic (abhicāra) is performed against them, one should take recourse in the vow of the virtuous.

Having obtained the dust from the feet of a virtuous person and having uttered the words "May [the disease] be destroyed," one should place it upon the back of the afflicted animal; by that means, the malevolent spell is certainly destroyed.
A woman who is like a beast suddenly gives milk to be milked,
or else she provides all the milk for a single day in the virtuous hermitage.
One should offer service and perform acts of devotion for the virtuous; one should entrust them with the milking of cows.
When cattle are afflicted by disease, one must then show them great respect.
"I shall perform animal sacrifice if my disease is destroyed;
otherwise, I will serve the virtuous day and night like a servant in the monastery."
When there is affliction to the mounts— the elephant, horse, and Garuḍa, as well as the swan, bull, and bird— an auspicious propitiatory rite (mānatā) must be performed.
Once their suffering has been destroyed, I shall indeed have a vehicle prepared for those virtuous ones and,
with devotion day and night, I will offer that vehicle to them.
I shall serve the virtuous people at the monastery of the holy ones at my pleasure; having seated the saints upon my vehicle, I will lead them toward the garden.
Having brought him to my own home as well, I shall honor him with the offering of garments;
I shall bestow wealth and grain if there is to be protection for the cattle.
In the corner of my house, in the courtyard, and on the street, there is the wandering of spirits; for their destruction, an auspicious propitiatory rite must be performed. 1.1.11.
Here, I shall cause the virtuous to eat, perform their worship, and chant the praises of Hari; I shall sprinkle them with water and shower upon them the nectar of divine grace.
When there is a blockage of the urinary organ and so forth, one should perform the auspicious *mānatā* penance;
having stayed in a monastery for a month, I shall serve the most excellent of holy men. (13)
"I shall feed them, I shall honor them, and I shall abide by their word; yet, if disease arises among living beings even when there is an abundance of grain and ears of corn," 14.
In that regard, respect must be shown for the sake of removing diseases of living beings;
a tenth part of the grain should be offered in the temple of the deity.
I must provide food for the virtuous, as well as gifts of food to guests and the destitute;
likewise, O best of men, the festival of the mountain of grain (annakūṭa) must be performed by me.
I must perform [this rite] so that my field may become well-ripened and prosperous, and so that diseases may be eliminated from the fruit-bearing trees and other plants in the gardens. (17)
If the disease is destroyed, excellent honor should be bestowed;
indeed, I shall offer the very fruits of my merit to the virtuous, according to a tenth part. || 18 ||

If a loss is observed during the cooking of roots, tubers, and the like, yet there is auspiciousness during the cooking of leaves, flowers, and so forth, as well as during the cooking of vegetables; || 19 ||
"I must maintain my dignity; if my prosperity should increase, I shall always give roots, tubers, leaves, and so forth first to the virtuous. (3.124.20)
I shall cause a virtuous dwelling to be established within this auspicious field;
for in a place where sugarcane ripens, there is indeed destruction caused by jackals, rats, and the like.
One should observe a vow of penance there for the pacification of those afflictions;
indeed, every day I shall give excellent pieces of sugarcane to the virtuous.
Five, ten, or eleven [parts] should be given daily, or likewise on the eleventh day;
and from the fruit that has arisen, a tenth part should be secretly given to a virtuous person for their welfare.
I shall offer sugar and other gifts, and I shall organize a great festival; if there is indeed a superior and abundant share of profit in my business, [then so be it].
Then I shall certainly give a tenth part to virtuous people or to the God;
if my profit from the holding [of the capital] should indeed be greater, [I shall do so]. (25)
At that time, even if it be only half a share, I shall give it to the glorious Lord Hari;
for at the moment of total destruction, all forms of pride must always be abandoned.
When the fear of death has arisen, one should cultivate auspicious humility:
"I shall offer myself to the virtuous or to Lord Hari. (27)
If I should be saved here from the force of time while still living, even when my leprosy has withered, I have become numb, blood is flowing, and there is a splitting pain; (28)

In cases of derangement of the bodily humors, skin eruptions, digestive disorders, dropsy, fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, blood-related and heat-related afflictions, and menorrhagia, I offer my salutation. (29)
In the case of urinary disorders (prameha) or emaciation, the highest penance (mānattottama) should be performed, provided that I am indeed freed from these diseases. (3.124.30)
Then, staying in the monastery during the four months of the rainy season, I shall serve the virtuous,
providing them with bodily service in the form of devoted attendance that bestows upon them joy.
Resorting to the state of servitude through all possible means, I shall act as a debtor; indeed, one who is freed from debt may truly maintain his honor. (22)
I shall bestow upon the virtuous a tenth, a twentieth, or even a fifth part of my wealth, or of my grain and other possessions, acquired through righteous means.
For two days in the month, I shall serve those who are virtuous as well as those who give;
likewise, staying in the monastery, I shall perform service for five days. (34)

For one who is without lineage and childless, however, the prescribed penance must be performed for the sake of obtaining a daughter or other offspring; furthermore, for the purpose of securing conception, one should perform the gift of a cow and serve virtuous people. 35.
Sweeping the monastery and sweeping the temple,
plastering the dwelling of the virtuous, and likewise fetching water— (36)
The constant offering of cooked food, the regular sight of the virtuous, the massaging of their feet, and always receiving their blessings; 37.
When this has been done, the impregnation indeed takes place;
thereafter, one must observe the prescribed observances for the sake of protecting the embryo. (38)
For one full year, I shall constantly offer lamps with ghee and present offerings of raw rice to the eternal Hari. (39)
During the complications of childbirth, for the sake of a comfortable delivery, one should perform the *mānatā* rite;
[the mother should carry] a weight of gold, silver, or sugar representing the burden of the son.
I shall distribute excellent food to the virtuous and to the children, as well as gifts of wealth to Hari and the bestowal of riches upon the young girls. (41)
"I shall cause the child to perform the coming and going of the virtuous, the vision of the gods, the acquisition of necklaces, and likewise the seizing of Manu."
Dwelling in his monastery for five days, I shall serve and attend upon the holy men for the sake of my son's advancement. (43)
"May there be no miscarriage for me, and may there be no death of my son;
for that purpose, indeed, I must perform an act of homage worthy of the deities. (44)
I shall perform a great worship and offer food as an act of reverence to the virtuous;
I shall undertake a pilgrimage and serve the virtuous for ten days.
I shall also perform service in the temple for the buffaloes and cows,
and I shall attend upon the devotees while engaged in recitation and praise.
I shall indeed bestow gifts of grain and gold at the monastery of the virtuous;
and even though I have many sons, I shall practice the devotion of a son toward them.
If there were no disease, no loss of life, and no obstacle whatsoever, I would indeed perform the act of surrendering my son. (48)
"In this excellent dwelling, I shall cause a good well and other such works to be made, as well as a water-shed;
I shall provide shaded resting places and likewise an excellent hall for peace. (49)
I shall have a leaf-hut built as a dwelling for the virtuous, providing a constant refuge; I shall also have an assembly hall constructed and an excellent throne for exposition established.
I shall offer that which is pleasing to him to my virtuous guru,
and I shall cause the blessing "May you live long" to be bestowed upon my son.
If an obstacle is perceived in the course of performing the rite for donning the sacred thread, one should maintain confidence therein, thinking: "I shall perform the most excellent sacrifice. (52)
The food of the virtuous, the offering to one's own chosen deity, various objects of knowledge, as well as water, fruit, leaves, and so forth—[these are the offerings]. (53)
I shall bring happiness to this virtuous woman, who is devoted to the gods, by bestowing upon her gifts of garments, ornaments, and articles of adornment through the offering of wealth. (54)
If an obstacle is perceived at the giving of the bride in marriage, at the engagement ceremony, during the wedding festival, or upon the second visit,
then an auspicious expiation (mānatā) must be performed.
"If the giving of the word, the engagement, and the marriage ceremony can be performed here without obstacles, I shall perform the offering in this temple. (56)
The offering of gold and silver weighing a thousand [units] and so forth, or alternatively, the constant service of virtuous people for a period of six months. (57)

Likewise, I shall perform service for the temple arising from my own body, and I shall maintain myself by the most excellent livelihood of offering food (naivedya) for the sake of my chosen deity. 58.
Either my first son shall be Devārpita, or that virtuous daughter of mine shall be Sādhvikādevyarpitā. ||59||
I shall perform many gifts of cows to a virtuous person, or I shall make the offering of land, elephants, and horses.
Or even the offering of male and female servants, or the offering of a village, to the Supreme Self, to the existing temple, to the Guru, and to the twice-born. 61.
I shall likewise provide means of livelihood to the helpless and the destitute, and I shall give food,
wealth, and ornaments to women and young maidens.
When children are defeated by malevolent spells or wrong views, and when other calamities arise, one should perform auspicious rites of propitiation. (63)
"If my child becomes healthy, I shall give him a load of sugar;
I will perform a great worship and likewise provide a feast for the virtuous. (64)
Or else, I shall perform service for two days in the monastery of the virtuous;
or else, I shall give wheat, rice, and barley to the holy man.
In cases of discord between father and son, or when the family is afflicted by distress,
or when kinsmen fail to assemble, one should likewise observe the practice of Mānatā.
If there should be mutual goodwill and affection among them,
then I shall perform [this] for the virtuous Hari.
I shall perform, as is appropriate, the offering of wealth and food, the auspicious reunion with kinsmen, and the service of the gods and other such rites.
In the event of a dispute between a husband and wife, or in cases of dejection or separation, one should practice respect toward them for the sake of supreme goodwill. (69)
I shall cause a great worship to be performed for the virtuous, providing them with service for three days,
including food, the offering of garlands, and attendance in the temple.
Even if she has been cast out by her husband, or treated with contempt and insult, she should indeed manifest her affection there by showing herself as humble. (71)

I shall cause a great worship to be performed; I shall practice the service of the virtuous; and I shall perform the service of the gods with wealth and other means, as well as through gifts of food and other necessities.
"I shall perform the recitation of mantras, the turning of the rosary, the offering of flower petals, and the total surrender of all; my husband will look after me. (73)

If some man of a house, wandering through various directions due to confusion of the quarters, goes astray onto a wrong path and becomes lost, he has gone to a state from which there is no return. (74)
One should maintain a sense of reverence toward him, for he is the cause of one's arrival;
when he has come to my house, I shall perform the gift of a cow in the temple of the God. (75)
For two days, one should perform service to a virtuous person and honor them with sweet food and other offerings,
in the case of abducting a maiden as well as in the case of abducting a human being.
Even in the case of abducting a woman, one who seeks the sacred tradition must maintain her honor;
likewise, when she has arrived at my home, I shall perform a great worship for the virtuous.
Providing food for five days, service in the monastery and the temple, the offering of wealth such as gold and jewels, and the chanting of Hari’s praises. ||78||
But if there is an obstruction to one's livelihood, an auspicious *mānata* penance must be performed, [thinking]:
"If the flow of my livelihood should be obstructed... (79)
Or rather, when another means of livelihood shall be found,
then I shall perform service to the virtuous for five days and offer my first-earned wealth.
I shall perform a great worship, including food and other offerings for the virtuous; at the commencement of business, such honor should be rendered as it bestows profit. (8.1)
Whatever profit there may be, I shall indeed give one-tenth of it to Nārāyaṇa;
and for the sake of Dharma, I shall properly carry out expenditure and service to the virtuous.
In a royal court, in legal proceedings, and in a dispute with five witnesses, one should practice the service of the virtuous for the sake of one's own benefit. (83)
For the sake of profit, I shall give food and other offerings to Hari and to the virtuous;
but upon victory, having given auspicious wealth, I shall provide a new and beautiful mansion. (84)
"I shall cause a virtuous hermitage to be built, as well as an excellent sattra of food;
I shall cause a divine garden to be made for the great festival, with abundant offerings. (85)
Upon the sudden attainment of a desired object, one should perform a great festival by offering a chariot, giving away cows, giving a house, or offering a plot of land. (86)

Adorned with the chanting of the Name, musical instruments, and other such things, the festivals of worship consisting of feasts should be performed, as well as the offering and dedication of banners. (87)
The offering of coconuts and the like, the offering of oil, the offering of ghee, the offering of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍūkas), and likewise the offering of saṃyāva and other such foods. ||88||
Likewise, there is the offering of clusters of Karṇikāra flowers when a sudden danger has arisen, solely for the purpose of destroying that fear. (89)
The highest form of honor should be rendered, consisting of service to the guru; likewise, service to Hari and service to the virtuous, characterized by the offering of wealth and grain. (3.124.90)
But when attachment and other such qualities arise in people toward worldly objects, one must perform the practice of offering garlands and prostrations in order to destroy them. (9.1)
During the calamity of famine, there was respect for the chanting of the name of Kṛṣṇa;
there was respect for the performance of sacrifices and for the giving of food to the Brahmins. 92.
Welcoming the virtuous and generating joy in them, honoring a devoted wife, and offering morsels of food to cows—[these are meritorious acts]. (93)
During calamities such as great pestilence, as well as during the affliction of a country, for the sake of protecting all the gods, the planets, and likewise Śrī Hari; (94)
And for the sake of their very lives, women and men alike must perform service, worship, and devotion with humility toward the goddesses and the virtuous day and night. (95)
In the event of a shipwreck at sea, the observance of the vow of silence for protection is auspicious; likewise, in the event of a shipwreck in the sky, constant devotion to Hari is required. (96)
Remaining in the temple for six months, I shall serve the virtuous Guru; furthermore, reverence must be shown even when calamities are unavoidable. (97)
Upon the destruction of these portents, I shall perform a supreme sacrifice, as well as provide food for the virtuous and the worship of the gods. (98)
The offering to the deities should indeed be made as is appropriate and according to one's wealth;
for it is through such honor that there is the cessation of sufferings such as imprisonment and confinement. (99)
Everything should be offered to the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
one should provide food for the holy sages and worship the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa. (3.124.10)
Service to me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
is considered to be the great honor appropriate for the attainment of sovereignty.
Upon the attainment of life, that [devotion] consisting of total self-surrender is considered appropriate;
indeed, upon the attainment of prosperity or the attainment of a lineage, it is considered appropriate according to the circumstances.
Everywhere, the service and attendance of virtuous men and women, as well as supreme honor, bestow swift accomplishment through their nature of grace. (103)
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
one should bear the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and svastika.
Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord.
May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (1.05)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times;
may the saintly ones be my protectors and the removers of my suffering. (1.06)
Having thus gone to me for refuge, one should seek protection in whatever place— whether on land or in water, in the sky, in a pit, or in fire or wind.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Guru, the Holy One, the God, and the eternal Dharma,
and having also meditated upon the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), one should remain bowed for the sake of protection.
In loss or gain, in pleasure or pain, one should maintain composure;
well-cultivated devotion to the True Teacher, the Divine, and so forth, indeed protects one. (10.9)
As the inner controller within the Virāj, I hear what has reached the heart;
indeed, through the act of surrender, I immediately provide protection for the distressed devotees and others.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of Serving Virtuous Devas and Others, as well as Reverence and Other Matters Concerning Happiness and Suffering," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
O Kṛṣṇa, by your grace I have heard this auspicious, excellent, and virtuous vow, which bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; nothing remains for me to hear. || 1 ||
Nevertheless, for householders who follow the path of dharma, there is an inquiry characterized by the practice of giving for the sake of accomplishing worldly aims and the like. (2)
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, for the benefit of householders, there exists that great gift which is the most excellent among all gifts. (3)
If such a one exists, or if there are indeed such as these,
O beloved Kṛṣṇa, inform me for the benefit of the world.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī; I shall describe that very same thing to you.
That unsurpassed great gift exists in many forms.
It causes the destruction of all sins, destroys all evil dreams, is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, auspicious, and removes every form of evil. (6)
That which has been declared as the sixteenfold bestowal upon a worthy recipient—that gift of wealth acquired through righteous means is the supreme gift. (7)
The first among all gifts is that known as the Tulāpuruṣa;
the Hiraṇyagarbha gift is proclaimed as the second.
The gift of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa) is the third unsurpassed great gift;
the gift of the Kalpa-tree is recorded as the fourth supreme one.
The fifth is the unsurpassed gift of offering a thousand cows and so forth;
the sixth is the excellent gift of offering gold and wish-fulfilling cows.
The gift of a golden horse is considered the most excellent gift;
likewise, the gift of a chariot drawn by golden horses is the eighth and likewise excellent.
The gift of a golden elephant-chariot is declared the ninth and most excellent;
the gift of five ploughs is considered the tenth and supreme.
The gift of land is considered the eleventh, the most excellent and greatest;
however, the gift of the universal wheel (viśvacakra) is a great gift, unsurpassed. (13)
The gift of the Kalpalatā is the thirteenth, unsurpassed;
and the gift of the seven oceans is declared as the fourteenth.
The gift of a jewel-cow is indeed the fifteenth and unsurpassed;
the sixteenth, however, is the gift of the great elemental jar, which is supremely auspicious.
All these gifts are in every way protectors;
they indeed bestow heaven, grant liberation, and fulfill all desires.
Indeed, on this earth, even each single one of these great gifts, appearing in the form of a deity, protects [the donor] in every way from thousands of obstacles. (17)
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, one should perform any one of these;
having honored virtuous Brahmins and others, one should perform a great gift-sacrifice (mahādāna-makha).
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall again tell you those [gifts] in brief according to the rule— how, where, and indeed what they are to be given.
The gift of the tulāpuruṣa should be given during the equinoxes and solstices,
on the day of dinakṣaya, during the vyatīpāta yoga, on auspicious days, and on the sacred day of a vow.

On the day marking the beginning of a Yuga, during a lunar eclipse, on the days marking the beginning of a Manvantara, at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), during the Vaidhṛti yoga, on the fifteenth day (amāvāsyā), and on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī). ||21||
On the eighth, the twelfth, and the eleventh lunar days; on festival days; during sacrifices, celebrations, and weddings; and upon seeing an evil dream or a portentous marvel—(22)
Upon obtaining material wealth, Brahmins, or deities; upon meeting virtuous people;
and at sacred fords, temples, cow-pens, wells, groves, and rivers—23.
In a new house, at a pond, and toward a purifying vessel of faith; toward a virtuous person, a wretched person, an orphan, a child, and a young widow. (24)
In the supportless one, in the great devotee, in the ascetic free from possessions, in the divine one, in the capable person, and in the radiant Nārāyaṇa. ||25||
In the pure portion of Nārāyaṇa, in a yoginī, in an attendant of Hari, in a virtuous woman, in Satyā, in a female yoginī, in a goddess, in a woman, or in one who is weak. (26)
In this manner, those great gifts should be bestowed during the initial [stages];
having bathed at an auspicious moment and performed the meritorious rite of reciting by the Brahmins.
One should have a pavilion constructed there measuring sixteen *aratnis*, or ten or twelve *karas*, and within it, a beautiful and auspicious four-legged throne.
Having constructed an altar seven cubits in extent, with a central area of five cubits, and having erected in the center an auspicious archway made of solid wood; || 29 ||
One should indeed construct four auspicious sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the four directions, provided with girdles and yonis; one should cause full water-pots to be placed therein.
The sacred seats, auspicious mats, all the sacrificial vessels, as well as two copper bowls; ||31||
One should place offerings of sesame seeds, clarified butter, incense, flowers, and other beautiful articles in close proximity, specifically in the north-eastern area.
For the purpose of worshipping the planets and other deities, one should prepare an altar measuring one cubit;
there, my worship as the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) is to be performed.

The worship of those such as Kṛṣṇa, who possess forms like Vāsudeva and others, as well as the worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa with fruits, garlands, garments, and so forth [yields great merit]. (34)
Banners together with flags should be offered in the pavilion that resounds with the tinkling of small bells;
indeed, beautiful archways should be constructed at the entrances.
At each gate, there should be two jars made from the wood of milk-exuding trees, provided with garlands, perfumes, unbroken rice, incense, water offerings, garments, jewels, and fruits. (36)
Likewise, two pillars were fashioned from śāla, iṅgudī, devadāru, śrīparṇī, bilva, candana, priyaka, and kāñcanaka wood.
Having dug a pit two cubits deep with both hands and having made it firm,
[the altar] should be five cubits high, with the middle ground being four cubits.
Having firmly attached a beam to the pillar so that it supports a good load,
one should place the wood known as the "middle-load" and make it stable.
In the middle of that, a balance-beam four cubits long should be suspended;
the two pans should be ten finger-breadths wide, with beautiful chains made of gold bands.
It was also provided with iron chains and adorned with garlands of jewels;
it was furnished with flower garlands and unguents, and worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings. ||4 1 ||
In the middle space between the two vessels, one should draw saffron lotuses;
there, one should scatter flowers upon the two scales of the balance.
And one should suspend a beautiful fruit in the middle of the scale-beam.
Then, the officiating priests—learned in the Vedas, virtuous, and adorned with goodness—[should perform the rite]. (43)
The best of the twice-born, the gurus, the virtuous, and the preceptor who imparts the mantras—
my devotee clad in white garments— shall reside on the ground near the Tulā tree.
In the east, two were knowers of the Ṛgveda; likewise, in the south, two were knowers of the Yajurveda;
in the west, two were knowers of the Sāmaveda; and in the north, two were then knowers of the Atharvaveda. ||45||
Thereafter, the recitation of the hymn (sūkta) should be performed, as well as an oblation (homa) in the fire with clarified butter and other substances.
[One should worship] Gaṇeśa, the planets, the world-protectors (lokeśas), the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are to be gratified with oblations and other offerings;
likewise Parameśa, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Narāyaṇa.
Vāsudeva, his incarnations, Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭ, and Hari,
as well as all the goddesses Lakṣmīs and Samastikās, are to be propitiated with oblations.
After the fire sacrifice, the preceptor should invoke the deities with the sounds of musical instruments;
having offered the oblation, flowers, and incense, he should likewise recite the mantras.
Come, come, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt; protect the sacrifice, homage be to you!
Come, come, O Agni, bearer of oblations; abide at the sacrifice, homage be to you!
Come, come, O Dharmarāja; protect the sacrifice, homage be to you! Come, come, O god Nirṛti; protect the sacrifice, homage be to you! ||5 1||
Come, come, O God Varuṇa! Protect us; let there be salutation unto you!
Come, come, O Lord of Life, Vāyu! Salutation unto you in this sacrifice! 52.
Come, come, O Kubera; here, salutations to you, the holder of wealth!
Come, come, O Maheśāna; accept [this], for you are worthy; salutations be to you! 52.
Come, come, O King of Serpents, protect my sacrifice!
Come, come, O Ordainer, Soul of the Universe; homage be unto you here at this rite! 54.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving, may they, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, provide protection for me. 55.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas; sages, Manus, cows, and even the divine mothers (devamātṛs). ||56||
May all goddesses—Ramā, Lakṣmī, the beloveds of Brahmā, the beloveds of Hari, the liberated ones, and the sovereigns of lords—grant protection for my sacrifice. 57.
May they indeed accept the bali offering, the sweet food, and the excellent oblation presented by me;
may they also accept the worship, the ārārtika rite, and the sacrificial fees.
Having thus invoked the gods and worshipped them, following the rite of *nīrājana*,
one should give the sacrificial fees, ornaments, and other gifts to the officiating priests.
And golden earrings, threads, bracelets, rings, sacred threads, garments, and beds. (3.125.60)
One should give double [the usual fee] to the preceptor, as well as ornaments and garments;
and the reciters should chant peace-mantras in every direction.
Having performed the ritual consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should have the Brahmins recite the benedictions;
then, having bathed with auspicious waters, one should perform three circumambulations.
Holding a handful of flowers on the scale and wearing white garments, one should pray:
"Salutations to you, O power of Dharma, whose form is truth and who is rich in ascetic merit. (62)
Obeisance to you, the witness of the world-mother, who are equal to Ramā;
you were created by Brahmā in ancient times for the purpose of examining dharma and adharma.
You are the standard for all beings in regard to ultimate giving;
lifting me up from saṃsāra while weighing me [in the balance], homage be to you! (65)
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, who is indeed presided over by the Inner Controller, the Supreme Lord, and by the individual soul, which is His very body.
Lūtā is Māyā, which is Prakṛti; its web is the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Since the tulā destroys that [web] and sends one forth to the supreme world, it is so called. 67.
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Tauleya, salutations to you! You, who are the embodiment of the Tulāpuruṣa sacrifice, deliver us from the cycle of worldly existence. 68.
Having thus paid homage to the balance, worshipped it, and performed a circumambulation,
the donor himself should mount the balance within the vessel.
Fully endowed with his own attire and equipped with all ornaments and weapons,
he should likewise gaze upon Dharmadeva, Sūrya, and Śrī Hari.
One should behold the virtuous, chaste lady, who is the very embodiment of the Divine; then, with both hands joined in a clenched fist, one should bow down to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||7 1||
Householders may place their own burden— whether it be gold, silver, or other materials, even such things as sugar and the like— as mere wealth.
To remove all sins, they should place gold, silver, wealth, or even sugar, equal to or exceeding [the weight of the sin]. ||73||
One desiring prosperity should fashion an image of the Earth upon the ground in the form of a balance;
having weighed herself there for a moment, she should then worship the Supreme Goddess.
Salutations to you, O Mahālakṣmī, the righteous one, the witness of dharma, the eternal one, the destroyer of all sins, and the bestower of merit. ||75||

O Mother Lakṣmī, salutations to you, O Tula, who are the bestower of liberation in the form of a load of gold, a load of camphor, and a load of silver; O Goddess, who are rich in essence and the giver of rasa.
"O bestower of the fruits of all gifts, by whom the entire world is sustained;
O beloved of Hari, being offered to me, bring about my purification. (77)
Having spoken thus, he should then descend and offer half [of the merit] to the preceptor;
he should indeed give the other half to the officiating priests, preceded by the pouring of water.
Likewise, he should present village-jewels to the preceptor and to the officiating priests;
by their command, he may also bestow gold and other riches upon others.
Having honored the poor, the helpless, and the destitute; virtuous, chaste, and noble women; as well as children, girls, and holy, righteous men. (3.125.80)

The Brahmins, mendicants, learned men, those most devoted to Brahman, the attendants, and the lords—whosoever there may be who are worthy recipients of gifts, they [should be honored] thereafter. (81)
Having worshipped with devotion, one should offer gold, silver, sugar, and so forth;
wealth weighed out for the purpose of giving should not be kept in the house for long. (82)
For gold, silver, or wealth, even if consecrated or prepared for sacrifice, remains a source of fear, as it brings about grief and disease. (83)
By quickly taking possession of the property of others, one attains prosperity from the givers;
for whatever wealth of the gods or Brahmin’s coinage has been purified by the gift in one's own home [is thus secured]. (84)
Virtue, chastity, and widowhood are stolen away;
whatever wealth is one's own property, it perishes as soon as it has been enjoyed. (85)
That which has been enjoyed does not lead to happiness; indeed, it attaches one to disease. It results in the ruin of one's lineage and brings about the extinction of the family line. (86)
Therefore, the wealth of the gods, the wealth of the virtuous, the wealth of Brahmins, as well as the wealth of Dharma and the wealth of helpless women, must certainly not be consumed. ||87||
Nor should it be deposited in one's own wealth, since that results in total ruin;
formerly there was a Brahmin named Śuktaka who was a devoted worshipper of the gods and the virtuous. (88)
While the deity’s image and other objects are being worshipped by virtuous people, he eats the wealth offered by devotees, such as sweets, sugar, and the like. (89)
Out of partiality, he constantly ate without giving anything, merely filling his own belly;
by that sin, his merit was entirely exhausted on all sides.
On the contrary, he became a sinner, afflicted by the suffering of poverty;
the fortune of his home perished, and his wife, sons, and others were lost. (9.1)
His fields and gardens were lost, and he became a debtor;
overcome by hunger and exceedingly wretched, he became a beggar. ||92||
Deprived of sight and devoid of dharma, hungry at every step, he became one of sinful conduct and entered the jaws of death. ||93||
Having experienced the sufferings of Yama, he then fell into the state of a dog-cooker;
after some time, he was again born among the animal realms and other such states.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, wealth should not be kept in the house by a virtuous woman, a goddess, or a yogi; for it brings loss and causes total destruction from the very root. 95.

Indeed, that man who, according to the prescribed rite, gives away his own weight in wealth and other goods through the tulādāna ceremony, shall attain the station of Mahendra and other such realms. (96)
He shall become a sovereign lord of the world-protectors and attain eternal heaven,
traveling in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, garlanded with networks of tiny bells.
Honored by the deities and having enjoyed heaven for a very long time, he shall go to Satyaloka, the world of Mahālakṣmī, and Śrīnagara. ||98||
He shall go to Viṣṇupura, the world of Hari, and likewise to Goloka;
the devotee goes to Vaikuṇṭha and attains the imperishable, eternal state. 99.
He beholds the great gift being given, praises it, announces it to the worlds, and even remembers it at a later time. (3.125.10)
Whether it be a person, a woman, a king, a queen, a male friend, or a female friend, whoever listens to or recites this with a spirit of devotion shall be endowed with devotion. (101)
Whether it be a Brahmin, a female Brahmin, another woman, a slave, or even another servant,
one who praises that gift obtains a tenth part of its fruit there.
Having enjoyed the fruit of his gift in heaven, he shall go to my abode through devotion;
indeed, the fruit of the gift of the scales (tulādāna) is thus distinguished above all else.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa Gift," within the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*) in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the great gift known as Hiraṇyagarbha;
it removes all sins, bestows merit, and should be given for the attainment of auspiciousness. (1)
Having observed an auspicious day, as in the case of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa,
[he should provide] the officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, vessels, and garments.
Having gathered [the materials] and observed the fast, he should perform the invocation of the deities in the morning;
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), he should have the Brahmins recite the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
One should place an image of the supreme deity Dharmadeva made of gold,
and likewise a golden pitcher or one made of silver, within the pavilion.
It should be seventy-two finger-breadths in height, with a golden lotus at its center;
its width should be reduced by one-third [of its height], and it should be filled with ghee, milk, and other substances.
Adorned with jewels, sprouts, rice, cloth, and fruits,
one should place near it the donor, a needle, and a golden stalk.
A seat, the outer sun-disc, a garment, and likewise a sacred thread;
a golden staff, a cover, and a beautiful, new water-pot.
One should place a pearl necklace and rubies near the water jar;
one should also place a vessel containing a drona measure of sesame seeds upon the jar.
Having placed the jar in the center of the altar within the pavilion,
one should worship it with auspicious Vedic mantras, the chanting of the Vedas, and auspicious hymns.
The patron of the sacrifice, having been respectfully sprinkled and bathed with water infused with all medicinal herbs,
shall wear white garlands and garments and be adorned with ornaments.
Having bound this *kusumāñjali* (handful of flowers), one should recite the hymn of praise: "Obeisance!
Obeisance to You, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord of the syllables. (1.1)
Salutations to the eternally golden one, to the one of golden hue;
salutations to the one with golden hair, whose essence is the golden *praṇava*.
Salutation to the protector of the golden ones; salutation to the lord of the tawny deer;
salutation to the golden-embryoned one and to him whose armor is gold. || 1.3 ||
Homage to the one of golden complexion, who is beautifully adorned with a golden beard;
homage to you, the lord of Mahā-Mahā-Nārāyaṇī; homage to you! 14.
Salutations to the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations also to You, the god of dharma, and to You, the Creator. || 15 ||
Salutations to you, the sovereign lord of the three worlds and the sustainer of the universe;
all worlds abide within the womb of you, the all-pervading one. (16)
All the gods are established within your body, O Mādhava;
all the goddesses are situated within your body, which is of the nature of Lakṣmī. || 17 ||
Salutations to you whose form is the universe, salutations to the body of the Supreme Lord;
salutations to you who have the world as your form, salutations to you, the support of the world. || 18 ||
O refuge of the worlds, O Soul of all, salutations to You who exist in the form of the embryo;
salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, salutations to You who are the womb of Brahman.
Salutations to You whose essential nature is the womb of all perfections, salutations to You who are the womb of merit;
salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the womb of liberation, salutations to You who are the womb of heaven. ||3.126.20||
Salutations to that God in whose womb the three gods reside;
you are indeed Śrī Hari, the soul of all, established within every living being. 21.
"O Soul who has become the self of all beings, lift me up from the ocean of existence!
Having thus performed the salutation, he then offered this golden hymn of praise.
Having grasped both Dharmarāja and Caturmukha with his two fists and placing his head between his knees, he should remain there for five breaths.
Then the twice-born man should perform there the auspicious Vedic sacraments:
the conception rite (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
There, [he saw] the god Hiraṇyagarbha, Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
and Dharmadeva, who was situated within a jar-vessel.
Then the Guru should cause [the child] to rise with auspicious songs, mantras, and so forth;
furthermore, the sixteen sacraments, beginning with the birth rite (jātakarman), should be performed.
Then one should bow to Śuddha, Pūrṇamūrti, Vedhas, and Vṛṣa;
and one should indeed give the needle and other items to the Guru or to a virtuous person.
While performing prostrations, one should indeed offer this auspicious hymn of praise:
"Obeisance to Hiraṇyagarbha; obeisance to the Lord of Sāvitrī. (28)
Salutations to the supreme lord of Mahālakṣmī, to the husband of Hariṇī;
salutations to you, the womb of the universe, and salutations to you, whose womb is golden. ||29||
Salutations to you, who have become the abode of the world of moving and non-moving beings;
salutations to you, the divine witness, whose nature is Brahman. ||3.126.30||
Just as I was previously born subject to the nature of mortals, so too, through being born from your womb, I shall become possessed of a divine body. (31)
O twice-born ones, thus entreating him, they should bathe the patron with four jars, being intent upon the mantras and benedictions.
We shall gaze upon your limbs as you are born for the first time;
with this divine body, live long and be happy.
Free from sin, a treasury of merit, and possessing the right to heaven, may you become one who possesses devotion and liberation at the end, partaking in eternal bliss. (34)
And one should bestow sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins consisting of gold and silver, as well as those made of jewels, wealth, clothing, food, and drink. (35)
Then one should give the excellent Hiranyagarbha to the venerable Guru;
one should give Dharma to the virtuous, and one should give water-pots to the mendicant.
One should give to the Brahmins gold coins, silver jars,
vessels, garments, and also excellent foods.
Brahmins and virtuous men should be honored by those devoted to giving abundant gifts;
or else, one should offer all the equipment used therein to the preceptor.
Shoes, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, seats, and vessels;
or a village, a district, a hall, a house, or an auspicious palace.
Thus, by the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one becomes a giver of Hiraṇyagarbha; always being a giver of special merit, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
For as many as a hundred koṭis of kalpas he is honored in the world of Brahmā;
he shall dwell in the cities of the World-Protectors throughout each Manvantara.
Having established the supreme sovereignty of Indra, and likewise the sovereignty of the Sun;
then having established the sovereignty of the Moon, and after that the sovereignty of Dhruva.
Having enjoyed the station of Parameṣṭhin, one becomes a possessor of the sovereignty of Vairāja;
having attained the eternal kingdom of Mahālakṣmī known as Śrīpura. (43)
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of Bhūma and the sovereignty of Vāsudeva thereafter,
he indeed goes to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self, who is without beginning.
Having become a devotee at the lotus feet of Lalitāśrī Mahālakṣmī Nārāyaṇī, [worship] me, the Lord Śrīśa Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||45||
Having attained it, he enjoys all desires together with Nārāyaṇa;
O Rame, that gift of Hiraṇyagarbha bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 46.
It is the savior of the ancestors, the bestower of lineage, and the giver of sons and grandsons;
it is the deliverer of those in hell and the destroyer of all obstacles. ||47||
It is the destroyer of misfortunes and likewise the destroyer of ill fortune;
it is also the destroyer of afflictions and the bestower of accomplishment, wisdom, and happiness. ||48||
For the reciter as well as for the listener, and likewise for one who is reading, it yields fruit equal to honey and equal to nectar, granting success and joy. (49)
One should indeed give the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha with a focused mind;
for that embodied soul, becoming a leader, is honored by gods and celestial nymphs.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another unsurpassed great gift, known as the Brahmāṇḍa-dāna, which destroys all sins. (51)
It bestows all prosperity, as well as the glory of universal sovereignty;
it grants the state of Brahman, and likewise bestows heaven and happiness. ||52||
Having reached an auspicious day, one should then have a pavilion constructed;
one should then summon the officiating priests and prepare the necessary materials.
One should place there ornaments, garments, wealth, gems, gold, silver, and diamonds for the purpose of giving, as well as pitchers made of gold and other materials. (54)
One should place there in the pavilion fruits, water, a golden garland, whatever materials for giving there may be, and all sacrificial offerings.
One should cause various kinds of foods and likewise various flavors to be offered,
and perform the invocation of Śrī Hari and Mahālakṣmī.
One should invoke the world-protectors, the hosts of gods,
and the avatāras with perfumes, nectar-water, flowers, unbroken rice grains, sandalwood, and saffron.
One should worship all [the deities] according to the prescribed rite with golden images;
then, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the glorious gods.
Alternatively, having fashioned a Brahmāṇḍa out of gold or silver weighing more than twenty palas, one should place that auspicious object within the pavilion.
It is joined with two pitchers, adorned by the serpent Śeṣa and the tortoise, endowed with the eight elephants of the quarters, and accompanied by the six Vedāṅgas. || 3.126.60 ||
It was endowed with the eight guardians of the world, with the four-faced one (Brahmā) situated in the center,
and it was resplendent with the abodes of deities such as Śiva, Acyuta, Arka, and Candra.
Accompanied by Umā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Brāhmī, Sāvitrī, and Māṇikī;
joined by Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Kṛṣṇā, Rādhā, Śrī, and Bhū. (62)
It is the abode of the Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, Rudras, the treasures (Nidhis), and the Siddhis; it contains within its womb the fourteen worlds and is adorned by the central axis of Mount Meru.
And it should be made from the finest king of jewel-mines, endowed with great precious substances,
measuring one hundred finger-breadths in length and breadth, up to the span of a cubit.
One should place [the image] wrapped in silk cloth upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds;
likewise, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around it.
To the east, one should place Anantaśayana Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa;
in the southeast, one should place Pradyumna, the supreme lord and god of gods.
In the south, one should place Prakṛti, Māyā, Mahālakṣmī, and Kambharā;
and in the southwest (Nirṛti), one should install the lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Great King Śrī.
In the west, one should place the four Vedas together with the Vedāṅgas;
and in the northwest, one should install the Lord Aniruddha, the husband of Śrī.
One should place the golden deity Vahni in the north, served by Śrī; and in the southeast, one should place the illustrious Vāsudeva, accompanied by Vāsudevī.
In the center is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā;
on all sides is the Beloved of Śrī Rādhikā, the Consort of Śrī, accompanied by His male attendants.
One should place images of Vāsudeva made of gold,
and one should set ten water-pots all around upon pedestals of jaggery.
Richly adorned with fivefold sprouts and jewels, provided with fruits and unbroken grains, joined with coconut fruits, wrapped in cloth, and filled with water.

One should establish ten cows made of gold, silver, or sugar; or, according to one's capacity, they may be fashioned with images [of deities], accompanied by their calves, and excellent givers of milk.
They were endowed with golden horns, possessed silver hooves, covered in cloths,
equipped with copper backs, and provided with bronze milking vessels.
Provided with mouthfuls of fodder and other offerings,
they were adorned and worshipped with sandals, wooden shoes, umbrellas, chowries, seats, and mirrors.
One should worship all the gods with various kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as water, lamps, sugarcane, fruits, garlands, and ointments; one should also honor cows and Brahmins.
One should honor virtuous men and virtuous women with all articles of worship— such as sandalwood paste fit for kings, garlands, food, clothing, and so forth.
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering and circumambulate the Brahmāṇḍa;
one should offer salutations to the gods, virtuous men, chaste women, and the twice-born.

Having performed one hundred and more oblations of rice grains enriched with sesame flowers smeared with ghee, and then, at the conclusion of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), accompanied by mantras; ||79||
O Brahmins, the bathing of the patron with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) destroys sin;
they should properly perform it with the waters of the jars, which bestows great merit. (3.126.80)
The patron of the sacrifice should perform circumambulation three times;
thereafter, he should pray to the Lord Narayana, known as the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
Homage to you, O Ananta, who contain the great creation within; you who dwell as the soul of the universe, the abode of all, the field of the world, and the cosmic egg—homage, homage to you! 82.
The upper half of you is the Supreme Brahman, and the lower half of you is Śrī Narāyaṇī;
between these two is the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma), which contains all creation.
All abodes of incarnation, all manifestations of the Lord of All, all dwellings of the gods, and all human forms. ||84||
All those who dwell within the interior of the cosmic egg reside in her midst;
the Supreme Goddess Nārāyaṇī is the embodiment of the entire creation. 89.
O Brahmāṇḍa, you shine here; I bestow this gift upon you.
May all my sins be destroyed, and may meritorious deeds be mine. (86)
"By this gift, my ancestors will certainly be liberated;
may those who are suffering become happy, and may poverty come to an end. (87)
May all diseases perish; may there be prosperity in my home. May there always be success, and may there be constant well-being in my house. (88)
"May gold, silver, great jewels, and diamonds be in my home;
may I also become one who expands your lineage through your gift. (89)
May the faults of sin perish for my family members and for me as well;
and may there always be good fortune for the women in my household.
"Salutation be to you who have the form of Brahmā; Svāhā to you, O Nārāyaṇa!
Having spoken thus, one should prostrate like a staff with a golden or silver [image]. 91.
One should give to the Guru, to a virtuous person, to a worthy recipient, or to a twice-born;
likewise, one should give other articles of utility to the venerable Guru.
One should give various jewels and gold coins to the twice-born,
and one should also give silver coins to mendicants according to one's wealth.
Alternatively, having divided the cosmic egg into ten parts thereafter,
one should offer two portions to the venerable Guru and the remaining portions to a twice-born Brahmin.
And one should bestow further wealth upon the Brahmins and other mendicants;
having thus performed the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one should indeed feed the virtuous.
One should feed virtuous men and women, as well as boys and girls;
one should also feed the poor, the helpless, widows, and female mendicants. (96)
One should feed female students and also feed male students;
one should feed those most devoted to Brahman, and likewise feed one's own devotees.
Thus, by the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one obtains the merit born of the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa:
the kingdom of heaven, great sovereignty, and the supreme station of Parameṣṭhin. 98.
Having attained the sovereignty over many celestial palaces endowed with the bliss of divine perfections, or having reached the station of Vairāja, one attains the eternal Goloka. ||99||
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme world filled with liberated female souls, or the eternal Nitya-Kailāsa world, or Goloka; ||3.126.1||
There, having caused his ancestors, the lineages of his mother’s family, and thousands of householders to attain the infinite state, he— ||101||
Having delivered others, the person who performs this act of giving proceeds to the imperishable abode;
so too does he who hears, recites, or even remembers this ritual procedure.
Indeed, the merit of that gift arises for him who gives the highest heaven;
and also for him who directs the mind toward the act of giving to another.
In the end, he shall attain heaven through his share of merit and a share of sovereignty;
by giving further supreme gifts, he indeed goes to the highest state.
Thus, O illustrious Queen of Śiva, this supreme gift of the Cosmic Egg has been described to you; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants the highest state. 105.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Gift of Hiraṇyagarbha and the Gift of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa) among the Great Gifts," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to another great gift known as the gift of the Kalpa-tree, which destroys all sins.

Having reached the sacred day of purification, one should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed, well-adorned with water-jars and other ornaments, just as in the rite of the gift of one's weight in gold (tulāpuruṣadāna).
It was adorned with flowers and cloths, with pillars of plantain trees and archways;
it was beautiful, provided with sacrificial pits and altars, and graced by the seats of the Brahmins.
It was provided with all kinds of requisites, including jars of water from sacred fords,
and was complete with the materials for the ritual of worship, as well as a banner.
[He should worship] the deities at the gateway and the archway, the guardians of the quarters (dikpāla-devatās),
the gods of the door-posts, the God of gods, and the incarnations of the Supreme Lord.
One should invoke all the goddesses of fortune, beginning with Mahālakṣmī, each in their proper place, preceded by the proclamation of a meritorious day (puṇyāha).
A beautiful golden tree, endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
made splendid by flocks of birds, and adorned with clusters of blossoms and sprouts.
Equipped with garments, ornaments, coverings, and so forth, along with threads and creepers,
it should be made according to one's capacity, weighing from more than three palas up to a thousand palas.
Having thus performed the excellent planting of that wish-fulfilling tree upon a prastha of jaggery,
one should offer an excellent pair of white garments upon its branches.
Upon a tree that was beautifully adorned by the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—
a radiant tree with five main branches and many secondary branches, white and red in hue— (10)
It is rich with green-colored leaves, possessed of red sprouts, white at its root, and endowed with a trunk section that is tawny and so forth. || 11 ||
Having adorned [the deity], he should place Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the fulfiller of all intentions, upon a beautiful, great golden seat below.
"May you establish me as Kamaleśa, together with my wife, made of gold;
and all my incarnations, as well as my father and my mother. (13)

One should install all forms of prosperity (Lakṣmī) and Kāmadeva together with his wife; one should also install the eight supernatural powers (Aṣṭasiddhi) and fashion the wish-fulfilling creepers (Kalpavallī).
One should arrange new sprouts all around the clusters of the ritual structure,
and one should adorn them all with saffron, barley, and sandalwood.
One should fashion small, beautifully adorned trees called "sons" around the great tree; these, representing its progeny, should be one-fourth the size [of the main tree]. || 16 ||
Having placed a lump of ghee and a broad vessel of ghee in the eastern part,
one should place a small, auspicious wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
One should place [the vessel] upon ghee, adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers;
one should also place the Mandāra tree on the right side together with Śrī.
In the assembly of wheat-grains, adorned with the Kalpastamba pillar and other features,
there was then, on the western side as well, the auspicious Pārijāta tree.
One should place a golden vessel, adorned with creepers rich in seasonal flowers,
upon a heap of rice that is beautified by sprouts of grass and other ornaments.
One should place it together with a cluster of cumin seeds accompanied by the Sāvitrī mantra;
then, to the north, one should place a beautifully adorned [image] rich in fragrance upon a cluster of sesame seeds.
One should place excellent yellow sandalwood together with clusters of *kunda* flowers,
adorned with heaps of rice and provided with all the requisites for worship,
in the corner regions; and the *bakula* tree belonging to the northeast direction.
But in the southeast, a beautiful campaka flower; in the southwest, one produced from a coconut. ||23||
In the northwest, having created a most beautiful garden containing betel-nut trees together with betel vines, and joined with cardamom and other stalks; ||24||
One should plant stalks of sugarcane provided with fruits, garlands, and garments,
and having likewise made the roots of silken cloth, one should thus create an auspicious grove.
Indeed, its edges were lined with mango trees frequented by peacocks and cuckoos, and it was provided with cattle, cowherds, bulls, and water-pools. ||26||
Having beautified that place, one should place there eight auspicious full jars,
enriched with jewels, sprouts, and cloths, and provided with fruits and water.
One should place the sandals, the fly-whisks, the parasol, the staff, the canopy, the chariot,
as well as the celestial vehicle (vimāna) and the mount, in close proximity there.
One should place near the foot of the tree a vessel for the offering of food, a pot for eating, and a water-pot for drinking. (29)
One should offer lamps and incense, and place sweet fruits and flavorful juices;
likewise, one should indeed provide all types of grains, numbering eighteen varieties.
According to one's capacity, one should place there, at the foot of the tree within the pavilion,
wheat, rice, millet, *jvārikā*, and likewise *barjara*.
Baṇṭikā, śīṇikā, mung beans, chickpeas, rājamāṣa beans, kulattha, vaṭāṇa, masha beans, and likewise kodrava; ||32||
One should place sixteen varieties of grain before [the deity], such as barley, tuvarī,
nivāra, rājaguruka, śṛṅgāṭaka, and cirbhaṭa.
Mangoes, sugarcane, coconuts, immortals (amṛtā), and likewise wood-apples; jackfruits, rose-apples, licikās, and kaliṅgaras. ||3||
One should place sixteen pieces of sugar, watermelons, and cucumbers;
then, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations in the fire of the sacrificial pit.
One should worship Gaṇeśa together with his consort with milk-rice, various fruits, and foods prepared with savory juices, as well as with gold.
One should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of my image and of the tree;
one should bathe the tree and me, and perform three circumambulations. ||37||
One should offer salutation, perform praise, and then make a prayer:
"Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, who are the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree. (38)
Salutations to the sovereign of the wish-fulfilling vine, who bestows whatever is desired, whose form is the very source of the splendor of all tastes, fragrances, and forms. (39)
Salutations to you, the divine Sustainer of the universe; salutations to you, whose form is fulfillment.
Salutations to you, the god who is full of all food, the embodiment of all nectar.
Salutations to the abode of all nectar, who is the very form of ambrosia;
you alone are the Supreme Lord, you are Nārāyaṇa, you are Mādhava. (41)
You are Saṃkarṣaṇa, you are Aniruddha, and you shine as Pradyumna;
you are the sun, the moon, fire, and Indra; you are the eternal digestive fire within all beings.
You are the Lord of the mental garden of Brahmā and you are the lord of the forest;
though possessing a manifest form, you are also formless, and you consist of both the seed and the tree.
You possess the nature of both man and woman, and you are endowed with Mahālakṣmī;
you are the eternal essence, the performer of creation, preservation, and destruction.
