Protected by the creepers and trees of the lineage, protect us from all sides;
grant us heaven, bestow prosperities, and grant auspicious riches. ||45||
Grant me supernatural powers and celestial chariots; likewise, bring about the upliftment of my lineage.
You are indeed the bestower of liberation upon the ancestors; therefore, provide for their satisfaction.
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, grant me the state of supreme bliss before [death].
Having thus entreated Him, one should give the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) to the guru. 47.
Then, one should present the lineage offerings and so forth to the four officiating priests;
all other gifts, however, should be given to virtuous twice-born men.
One should provide delicious food and cause it to be given to the monks and yogins;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, but should give money as is appropriate. 49.
One should give fruits, roots, and grains only to those who are worthy;
having offered salutations and shown favor, one should then personally bid them farewell.
In this manner, the man who bestows gifts should provide food as an act of grace;
thus liberated from all sins, he attains the merit arising from ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
The righteous-souled one, together with his wife and kinsmen, and along with his family, obtains merit;
having enjoyed great sovereignty here on earth, he shall then go to heaven.
Having indeed enjoyed the great heaven, he shall then go to Satyaloka;
having enjoyed the station of Vairāja, he shall go to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
For he shall deliver men of a hundred lineages— those who have been,
those yet to be, and their fathers, sons, and grandsons— as they are being praised upon the heights of heaven.

By means of celestial chariots equal to the sun, he sends them to the world of Viṣṇu, which is higher than the highest; and by those merits, they then proceed to the imperishable abode that is beyond even that.
Endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, intent upon the stories of Nārāyaṇa, and a servant of Nārāyaṇa. ||56||
The sacrificer shall go to the abode of Anādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
and his listener, speaker, and rememberer will certainly be born as Mahendra.
Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī, to another great gift, the great gift of a thousand cows, which bestows all merit. (58)
Having reached an auspicious lunar day marking the beginning of a Yuga or Manvantara,
as well as the Jayantī of the gods and goddesses, and likewise that of Nārāyaṇa, me.
Having constructed a beautiful pavilion and then an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should gather the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and thereafter invoke the deities.
One should worship me, Hari, as well as my incarnations and the goddesses;
one should also worship all forms of Lakṣmī and an image of the cow fashioned from gold.
The patron, observing a vow of milk, should worship her for three days, or for one day;
thereafter, he should have the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions.
And one should perform an oblation in the fire with ghee, rice, fruits, and so forth;
having performed the oblation one thousand times, [one shall obtain] a thousand cows.
One should worship and circumambulate [the cow] standing outside,
honoring it with garments, garlands, fine clothes, ornaments, and by providing excellent horns, hooves, and milk-yielding capacity.
Then one should worship her with chains and coverings for the back made of saffron;
she has golden horns and ornaments, and is provided with silver hooves. 65.
They were equipped with golden bells and provided with bronze milking vessels;
they were adorned with golden tilakas and decorated with gold bands and other ornaments.
Clad in silken garments, honored with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings,
provided with mouthfuls of fodder, and adorned with staffs and chowries.
They are provided with sandals, shoes, umbrellas, vessels, and seats;
they are accompanied by Nandikeśvara, as well as by a calf and a heifer.
Alternatively, Nandika may also be made of gold in the midst of ten golden cows; he is adorned with garments, ornaments, and the like.
On the peak of Lavaṇadroṇa, it is composed of garlands, sugarcane, and fruits;
it is made of gold weighing either fifty palas or three hundred palas.
Alternatively, it may be fashioned from three thousand palas according to one's capacity;
it should be installed and worshipped, as well as ten auspicious cows.
One should indeed worship the golden image, or perhaps worship it with a tenth part [of the materials];
having bathed it with nectar-like waters accompanied by the auspicious sounds of songs.
Having circumambulated them three times and holding a handful of flowers,
he should worship the herd of cows, pay homage, and then make his request.
Homage be to those who possess the form of Brahmā; salutations to the Mothers of the Universe! And repeated salutations to the Rohiṇīs who dwell in the worlds! ||74||
The three creations indeed abide within the limbs of cows;
likewise, the fourteen worlds are also said to be the creation of Brahmā.
There are twenty-eight levels of the earth belonging to Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva as well;
and fifty-six worlds of Māyā reside within the cows.
May the Rohiṇīs, the unfriendly ones, the sovereigns, and the Mothers protect me always!
May cows be before me, and may cows be behind me. (77)
The cows are always upon my head; I dwell in the midst of the cows.
This bull is the embodiment of Dharma, and he is indeed eternal. (78)
Dwelling within the form of Hari, may He always protect me along with my family—
[the realms of] heaven, truth, the cosmic egg (vairāja), the earth, and the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
May Śrīpura, Amṛta, the Unmanifest, Goloka, the Imperishable, the Abode of Brahman, Vṛṣa, and the Cows likewise grant me auspiciousness. (3.127.80)
Having thus prayed, one should offer a golden cow to the venerable Guru;
likewise, one should present Nandīśvara, the embodiment of Dharma, to the virtuous one.
One should give a single auspicious cow, adorned with ornaments, to each of the officiating priests (ṛtvij),
and one should also give other cows to the Brahmins as is appropriate.
One [remedy] should not be given to many, for it would indeed cause affliction;
rather, many should be given to one by the wise for the increase of health. (83)
Beautiful women adorned with all ornaments should be given to the Guru;
many may be given to the illustrious Guru if no obstacle exists. (84)
Various kinds of wealth, as well as grains, garments, gold, silver, and other precious metals, should be given to beggars and others. 85.

Observing the milk-vow, remaining celibate, and being solely devoted to the worship of Hari, one should cause the story of Dhenuka to be heard or listen to it oneself, and perform the chanting (japa) of Hari’s name. (86)
He attains vast prosperity and likewise becomes free from sin;
possessing great merit, he travels by means of a celestial chariot as resplendent as a thousand suns.
At the end of his body, having gone to the vault of heaven, he shall thereafter attain the Absolute Truth;
honored by the world-protectors, he will be adorned by the expansion of his lineage.
Having enjoyed divine pleasures while residing in the world of Vairāja,
he resorts to Vaiṣṇava yoga and thereafter goes to the imperishable state.
This wise man shall deliver one hundred and one ancestors;
likewise, he shall deliver his maternal grandfathers and those born of his hundred lineages.
The ancestors rejoice at a son who bestows a thousand cows;
"May there be such a son, or even a daughter's son, in our lineage! (91)
Having become a giver of a thousand cows, he will deliver [others] from hell;
this applies even to his servant, or one who merely witnesses or approves [the act]. (92)
He too shall deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra;
for even when one has died and is traveling on the path to the world of Yama, cows go before him.
They cause [beings] to cross the Vaitaraṇī river and [to dwell] even in the abode of Dharmarāja;
or in heaven, or in Satyaloka, or in the residence of Maheśvara. (94)
Likewise, in the abode of Viṣṇu, in the abode of Īśānī, in Śrīpura, in the residence of Mahālakṣmī, and in the dwelling place of the incarnations; ||95||
Cows that carry burdens, nourish others, and are auspicious go everywhere;
wherever there is a cow, there indeed are the gods and my own attendants. 96.
There dwell all the goddesses of fortune, the wives of Brahmā, where the cows truly reside;
there also exists the imperishable Brahman, and there Goloka is situated.
Through the union with cows, Goloka was born to me and Kṛṣṇa;
where there are cows, there am I, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and Māṇikī. (98)
She is Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Śrī, Mahālakṣmī, and the Supreme Sovereign;
there is the divine city Amṛtā, the auspicious Śrīpurī, the abode of light. (019)
It is eternal, rich with all enjoyments, endowed with divine implements,
crowded with hosts of divine powers, and resplendent with divine majesty.
It is filled with an abundance of eternal bliss, provided with divine food and excellent vessels, and furnished with celestial garments, garden groves, beds, and places for recreation. || 101 ||
One who gives a thousand cows attains such a glorious city,
and he also attains Goloka as well as the imperishable state.
O Queen of Śivā, he obtains my entire sovereignty;
O Nārāyaṇī, he obtains all the essences—of this there is no doubt.
One obtains various powers that are filled with happiness even amidst suffering,
and one enjoys all desires together with Brahmā in his abode.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, teaching, and inspiring others to this [text], the patron obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 105.
Whether a man, a woman, a virtuous wife, a holy person, a deity, a teacher, or a lord—
whosoever is a donor of the gift of a cow goes to my eternal state, the Absolute Brahman.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Great Gift of the Kalpavṛkṣa and the Great Gift of a Thousand Cows," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivārājñīśrī, to that kind of great gift—
the golden wish-fulfilling cow— which fulfills all one's desires.
One should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed, adorned with sacrificial pits and archways,
and provided with seats, ritual implements, oblations, fire, and other necessities.
Having likewise invoked the world-protectors, the deities, the Supreme Lord, and the Consort of Ramā,
Lakṣmī should cause the worship and the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed.
Then the sacrificer should perform the consecration ceremony there;
and virtuous Brahmins should chant the sounds of the sacred Vedas and hymns of praise.
One should have a cow and a calf fashioned from exceedingly pure gold;
the best [cow] should weigh a thousand palas, while the middling one should weigh half of that.
Having had her made half that size, or even three palas larger than that,
he should have her brought into the pavilion upon a deer-skin.
Having placed [the cow] upon the altar over molasses, one should adorn it with auspicious great jewels and the like,
as well as golden ornaments for its horns, hooves, back, and hump.
One should worship her, together with the calf, on the forehead using saffron and other substances;
and [one should prepare] eight jars adorned with jewels, leaves, water, and rice.
One should place all eighteen kinds of grains there in the pavilion,
as well as eight stalks of sugarcane and various fruits.
One should likewise place in the pavilion the vessels, the milking bowl, the rope, the beautiful chain, the food vessel, and the delicious fodder.
A pair of silken garments, ornaments, an umbrella, and lamps;
likewise earrings, chowries, bells, golden horns, and so forth.
One should place ornaments, silver knives, all auspicious flavors,
turmeric, fruits, flowers, musk, and likewise sandalwood.
Camphor, sugar, the moonstone, a canopy, and likewise a garment—all these auspicious and divine materials, as well as the water of sacred fords (tīrtha). 13.
Having placed darbha grass, unbroken grains of rice, and tulasī leaves there in the pavilion, the sacrificer himself, being pure, [should proceed]. (14)
With flowers in hand, the Brahmin should worship the cow and recite the Vedas;
joined with auspicious hymns of praise, he should perform three circumambulations.
Then, standing in the presence of the cow, he should indeed perform this hymn of praise:
"O Mother, you are the abode of all the gods and the sanctuary of all yogis. (16)
You are indeed the savior of embodied beings, the auspicious refuge of all powers; you bestow the path to heaven, you grant liberation, and you are the giver of prosperity.
O Mother, who destroys sin, bestows happiness, grants desired fruits, and eliminates the torment of suffering—I bow to you. (18)
O wish-fulfilling cow, O bestower of great bliss, O Supreme Goddess! O eternal giver of liberation to Hari, O source of delight—salutations be unto you! (19)
You are Kānakī, you are Hariṇī, and you are Hiraṇyā; you are Candrikā, you are Śrī, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Kamalā, and the beloved of Hari.
You are Nārāyaṇī, the giver of aesthetic delight, the fulfiller of intentions, and Ramā;
you are Padmā, the power of the abode, you are Jayā, and you are Laliteśvarī. 21.
You are Śāradā, you are Māṇikī, you are Prabhā, you are the Supreme Goddess;
you are the destroyer of suffering, you are Pāśavatī, you are Padmajā, and you are Tulasī. 22.
You are Mādhavī and you are Gāyatrī; you are Kārṣṇī and you are the virtuous Śāṅkarī.
You are Vaikuṇṭhā and you are Akṣarī; you are Brāhmī and you are Kanakeśvarī. ||23||
You are the celestial one, you are the ascetic, you are the truth, and you are the beloved of Viṣṇu;
you are the earth, you are the progenitor, and you are indeed the eternal garden.
She is indeed the protector and the bringer of eternal merit;
she is the liberator from sins, the giver of liberation, and the purifier. (25)
O Cow, having rendered me sinless along with my family,
and having granted us the prosperous heaven forever, you shall thereafter bestow liberation.
By your grace, my ancient ancestors have gone to heaven;
other departed spirits shall also go to heaven and attain liberation through this gift.
"You, lady, have been given to the Guru, to the Brāhmaṇa, to the divine and virtuous Sādhu, and also to Hari. (28)
Having spoken thus and offered water, he should then give a cow to the preceptor,
as well as gems, jewels, seals, silver coins, and grains.
One should respectfully give grains and various kinds of clothing to others, as well as diverse foods and the finest sweetmeats. (3.128.30)
One should feed those separated from their loved ones fragrant milk-rice;
one should also well-feed the poor, the helpless, virtuous wives, holy women, and children. (3.1)
One should give many other gifts as well according to one's wealth;
thus, the giver of a golden cow goes to the eternal Brahman.
He who is capable of giving a golden cow should give a silver one along with its calf; if he is unable even for that, he should give a young female calf.
But that person who, being unable even to give a single calf, praises giving, enlightens others, and encourages them [to give], [attains merit]. (34)
One who hears it, causes it to be heard, or recites it shall attain that fruit.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you another unsurpassed gift.
The great gift of gold and horses bestows the kingdom of heaven;
it grants liberation and the celestial chariot that travels through the sky for those who possess white steeds.
Having reached an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
or else, one should have an altar or an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made there for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).
Likewise, he should keep all necessary implements nearby, as well as all materials for giving, such as gold, silver, and diamonds. (38)
Those desiring to perform worship should set out food, clothing, and vessels, as well as all necessary materials, including sandalwood, unbroken rice, and garlands. (39)
Then, one should place the items for the food offering (naivedya) and the waving of lights (ārātrika) nearby;
furthermore, one should place a pitcher filled with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) within the pavilion.

There, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) performed by the most excellent brahmins, and one should cause the invocation of the world-protectors and other deities to be carried out. (41)
[This belongs] to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, as well as to all the female powers (śaktis) who have been released from his incarnations.
One should perform the invocation and worship according to the prescribed ritual;
one should establish [the deity] in the center of the altar upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds.
A golden, excellent horse, clothed in silk garments, weighing from three palas up to one thousand palas; 44.
With a saddle-cloth of gold upon its back, adorned with golden necklaces and beautiful trappings, equipped with a golden girth, and beautified by golden bands. ||45||
It had a golden eyelid, was adorned with diamonds for its lashes, possessed a parasol, excellent fetlocks, and beautiful hooves, and was exceedingly charming. 46.
Alternatively, one should place a golden image of Aśvinī, adorned with ornaments and having the color of the moon, upon sesame seeds in the pavilion for the purpose of giving.
One should place sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and vessels there in the pavilion, as well as stalks of sugarcane and eight water-pots.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, filled with water and containing garlands, rice, leaves, and the like, together with jewels and bilva fruits. (49)
Other objects suitable for giving, though they be auspicious—diamonds, rubies, gems, and various kinds of grain. (3.128.50)
One should place there garments, ornaments, and vessels for the purpose of giving, as well as a bed equipped with a couch and provided with a headrest and other accessories. (51)
One should place [the image] adorned with side-pillars, cushions, utensils, and so forth; one should also place a beautiful cooking pot, a water-pot, and a small garden.
One should also place sweet foods and drinks such as milk,
and one should likewise place many kinds of desirable, well-ripened fruits.
One should place bulbs, root-bulbs, and leaf-vegetables [within the altar];
in such a pavilion, the patron, pure and auspicious, [should perform the rite]. (54)
Having been bathed with all medicinal herbs by the Brahmins, he should offer a handful of flowers,
circumambulate three times the fire, the horse, and then the preceptor.
One should pray to the Supreme Self, who is resplendent with all horses:
"Salutations to you, O Lord enriched by all horses, O Soul of All, who have entered the heart of the horse. (56)
O you who brought forth the Vedas, O son of the Aśvins, salutations to you!
O you whose form is that of a golden horse, O you of divine form, salutations to you! ||57||
Salutations again and again to you who have the form of the sun’s horse; salutations again and again to you who have the form of Kalki’s horse;
salutations again and again to you, Uccaiḥśravas, in the form of the divine horse.
Salutations to you whose nature is the horse of the senses; salutations to you, the horse of the mind;
and salutations to you, the Great Horse, whose form is identical to the holy fig tree (aśvattha). ||59||
Salutations to you who assume the form of the white horse, and salutations to you, the destroyer of sin.
You are Hari in the form of a steed; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Grant me heaven, liberation, and great sovereignty; grant me eternal prosperity. Grant me all riches, and thereafter, grant me liberation.
"By this gift of yours, may Mādhava, the Soul of the Universe, be satisfied.
Having uttered this, one should perform a single circumambulation around [the deity]. (62)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should then present the horse as a gift;
having paid obeisance to the preceptor, he should indeed dedicate that horse to him.
One should also give other various objects as is appropriate for a gift;
one should present wealth to the officiating priests and food, money, and so forth to the mendicant.
Having given [this], through the destruction of his sins, the sacrificer becomes divine;
he goes to the world of the Sun, the world of Truth (Satyaloka), and Vaikuṇṭha. ||65||
One should listen to the Saṃhitā and arrange for the serving of food and other provisions;
one should also offer food to virtuous Brahmins and virtuous women.
Becoming filled with devotion, one should give grass to the cattle, horses, and the helpless, the young, and the weak; and one should feed those who desire food.
O Lakṣmī, he who gives a gift of a golden horse according to his wealth in this manner, being honored by the lords of the gods, goes to the liberated state of Hari. (68)
Mounted upon a golden celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme world of the Sun;
or even one who merely hears this story shall likewise go to the noble abode of the Sun.
He who causes it to be recited or even causes it to be heard likewise goes to the presence of the Sun;
and he who offers praise also goes to heaven, the refuge of happiness.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the great meritorious gift consisting of a horse-chariot.
Having reached a meritorious day, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed.
One should cause an altar and a sacrificial pit to be constructed and procure the materials for worship,
as well as the guardians of the quarters, the deities, and the incarnations of the Supreme Brahman.
One should invoke both the Lord and the Mistress within the auspicious pavilion;
furthermore, eighteen kinds of grain, vessels, and wealth [should be provided].
One should place garments, ornaments, and silver on all sides within the pavilion;
likewise, one should install Gaṇeśa and the other deities, as well as Śrīpati, myself, Janārdana.
One should likewise invoke and worship Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇā, Brahmapriyā, and Haripriyā, and one should bring a golden chariot.
Furthermore, it was yoked with seven horses, possessed four wheels,
and was superior [to others] by virtue of its sapphire water-jar, its protective fender, and its banner.
I am Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Kamalā, resplendent with the charioteer Sūryamukhya at the pole of the chariot. 77.
One should place [the deity] in the middle of the chariot together with the principal queen (paṭṭarājñī),
and one should also place my attendants (pārṣada), adorned with parasols and chowries.
He should likewise station upon the chariot, by my side, virtuous men and women who bear canes and weapons, and who are devoted to the service of worship. (79)
One should place the hosts of gods, sages, and ancestors upon the best of chariots,
as well as Mahālakṣmī, Kaṃbharā, and the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
One should also establish all the auspicious goddesses who are contented;
one should establish Lalitā there, endowed with all powers. 8.1.
One should place jewels, diamonds, necklaces, and golden ornaments upon the chariot;
and on top of a lion skin, one should place a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds, or even more than that. (82)
Having prepared the supporting cloths, one should place upon them the chariot,
along with sixteen or four vessels containing jewels, sprouts, and unbroken grains of rice.
One should place there jars filled with cloth, water, and fruit;
one should worship the deities with devotion, having provided them with silken garments. 84.
O Lakṣmī, one should worship me upon the chariot and perform the consecration (adhivāsana) in my name;
likewise, one should bring other articles specifically for the purpose of giving as gifts.
An umbrella, as well as chowries, silken garments, sandals, wooden shoes, cows, a bed, and a vessel—these too [are to be offered]. (86)
A couch and other beautiful objects, as well as a splendid golden lion, should be fashioned together with the chariot. ||87||
He saw a chariot accompanied by either two or four horses,
with two protectors of the wheels and likewise two attendants at the sides, each equipped with a horse and weapons.

One should worship a chariot made of a thousand pieces of gold, or another according to one's wealth; or at least a chariot weighing more than three palas, and perform three circumambulations around it.
The sacrificer himself, being pure, having taken handfuls of flowers in his joined palms, wearing white garlands and garments, and having performed my oblation with clarified butter— ‖ 3.128.90 ‖
Then, having circumambulated the chariot with other fruits, flowers, and so forth,
one should pray to the chariot and to me, the Lord who is the abode of glory, as non-different from one another.
Homage to you who have attained the supreme abode; homage to you, Nārāyaṇa!
Homage to the yogin whose form is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! ||92||
Salutations to you who have transcended even the cosmic egg, who are the soul of all worlds;
salutations to you, the sovereign of all abodes, the chariot of the Lord of All.
Mahākāla and Mahāmṛtyu are the solstices, and the seasons are indeed the spokes;
all these are called the wheel of rebirth—may you deign to protect me from them. (94)
Grant me the eternal heaven; grant me a righteous destination;
grant me the supreme abode, which is free from time and illusion.
O best of chariots, effect the liberation of my ancestors and my family; becoming a divine celestial vehicle (vimāna), lead them to the imperishable state.
The Muktas reside upon your banner; the Imperishable Abode (Dhāmākṣara) is on the cloth-strip; the Īśvaras are in the body of the staff, and all the Śaktis are in the fender.
Within the interior are the heavenly worlds; in the center is Nārāyaṇa Hari;
all the deities are around him, and all the gods are situated on the outside. 98.
Below, the seven netherworlds (talas) reside, as do Yama and the Bull between the two wheels;
in front are Meru, Puṇya, and likewise Bhakti and the Gurus dwell there. (99)
"I shall indeed give testimony for them; protect me from the ocean of existence.
Having spoken thus, a chariot and other riches should be given to the preceptor.
All other gifts should be given to the destitute as is appropriate;
one should feed all virtuous persons, Brahmins, boys, and girls. 101.
Then he should dismiss everyone and cause a formal dismissal to be performed;
he should cause the Saṃhitā to be recited, relate stories of gifts, and likewise give other instructions.
For both the instructor and the one who gives consent obtain an equal fruit;
indeed, having ascended a divine chariot, he goes to my imperishable abode.
Having enjoyed all the various celestial realms for a long time along with his family,
even that great lord, who established the chariot, goes to the supreme abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedures for the Gift of the Golden Wish-Fulfilling Cow, the Gift of the Golden Horse, and the Gift of the Golden Chariot among the Great Gifts," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 128 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall now describe the gift of the Golden Elephant-Chariot, by the offering of which a person attains the divine abode of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
Having reached an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
within that pavilion, one should arrange the altar, the sacrificial pit, and the materials for the oblation.
Having invited the Brahmins there along with seats and water-jars,
he should also invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as perform the recitation for the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana).
The patron of the sacrifice should cause all auspicious hymns to be sung;
he should perform the invocation of the deities and worship them according to the prescribed rule.
One should have constructed a golden elephant-chariot, shaped like a flower, adorned with jewels and other ornaments, featuring ten wheels and variously decorated gables.

It was well-adorned with a banner, a protective fender, and all necessary equipment; it was exceedingly beautiful, enriched with parasols, chowries, and jewels, and graced by staff-bearers and others.
One should place sesame seeds upon tiger skins and leopard skins, which are resplendent with the beauty of light emanating from objects such as the moon and mirrors.
There, one should station the chariot and indeed the articles to be offered;
upon the chariot, one should place Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, me, the Lord of Ramā.
[He saw] Avatārā, Īśanī, Māṇikyā, Duḥkhahā,
Śrī, Rādhikā, Prabhā, Pāśavatī, Lakṣmī, Jayā, and Ramā.
Lalitā, Kamalā, Padmā, Padminī, Tulasī, Satī,
Sāvitrī, Kambharā, Līlā, Gāyatrī, Mañjulā, and Bhū.
He [worships] Mahālakṣmī, Mahāviṣṇu, Sarasvatī, Mādhavī, Bhārgavī, Suguṇā, Haṃsī, and likewise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
One should install me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, accompanied by Brahmapriyā and Haripriyā, and attended by [my retinue]. 12.
He should indeed station my liberated attendants there upon the chariot,
as well as all divine weapons and whatever divine grains there may be.
Various vessels, sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, and *darbha* grass;
water-pots filled with jewels and adorned with the five types of sprouts. || 14 ||
A lamp, sandals, an umbrella, a mirror, as well as wooden shoes, a bed, a couch, a water-pot, and various kinds of garments. || 15 ||
One should also place there various fruits fit for consumption as food,
as well as wealth in the form of gold and silver, for the purpose of giving.
One should fashion a banner with Garuḍa, a chariot-pole with Vināyaka,
and a canopy beautifully adorned with rows of garlands, its interior well-decorated.
It was joined with sixteen jars, accompanied by sixteen cows,
and [drawn] by sixteen golden elephants adorned with strings of pearls.
With golden trappings upon their backs, with beautiful wheels of golden teeth, with golden stirrups on their backs, and adorned with ornaments for the feet and other decorations; || 19 ||
Having prepared an auspicious chariot adorned with the beautiful sound of tinkling bells,
one should worship me, Śrī Hari, residing therein, as well as the deities and others.
Having performed the circumambulation three times, one should indeed offer salutations and so forth;
one should offer praise while holding a handful of flowers before [the deity]. (2.1)
Salutations to you who are the embodiment of Brahman, who are the refuge of Nārāyaṇa, the dwelling place of the Lord of All, and who consist of ten million liberated souls. ||22||
Salutations to you, whose form is the imperishable Brahman, who are the refuge of ten million powers,
the abode of Brahman, and the very essence of heaven and liberation.
Through your gift, may the merit of sacrifices, sacred fords, vows, moral conducts, and all forms of giving arise here for me. (24)
You are indeed composed of all the gods, and you are also composed of all sacrifices;
you are the abode of the gods graced by all prosperity—protect me! 25.
Purify me from the multitude of my sins, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra, and grant me through this gift a heavenly and then an imperishable state. (26)
Victory to you, who are indeed graced by Him at whose feet the lords of the gods, the incarnations, and the liberated souls bow down! 27.
Taking refuge in Hari, you are the one who leads across the wilderness of worldly existence;
you alone exist as the bestower of prosperity for those devoted to the yoga of liberation.
You are the savior of the ancestors and indeed the prosperer of the lineages;
you are the bestower of happiness—O Kṛṣṇaratha, salutations be unto you! 29.
Having thus made this request and performed a fourth circumambulation, one should bow down;
and one should perform the fire-oblation in the fire one hundred and eight times for Hari.
Then one should practice giving to a glorious and virtuous guru;
thereafter, one should also give other appropriate gifts to the worthy person.
One should give various gifts to Brahmins, mendicants, children, and the virtuous, as well as garments to young girls.
Various kinds of sweet foods, even those that are the essence of milk,
as well as vessels, meals, grains, and silver coins.
One should give away everything according to one's wealth—the house, the hall, and the garden;
a chariot constructed from a thousand palas is considered to bestow imperial sovereignty.
One made of a hundred thousand pieces of gold bestows the station of Indra and grants a son;
even one given weighing more than ten palas bestows prosperity. (35)
When placed upon me, Nārāyaṇa, it bestows the imperishable abode;
when placed upon a great holy person, it bestows the state of lordship.
But when placed upon my devotee who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it grants my own state;
having thus given [the gift] and enjoyed heaven, the giver finally goes to my state. (37)
By hearing, reciting, remembering, causing others to hear,
and likewise by rejoicing [in this], one obtains the fruit of the gift of a chariot.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another unsurpassed great gift:
the gift of the five-ploughed field, which destroys sin and bestows all merit. (39)
Then, on an auspicious day, the patron should have a pavilion constructed,
as well as sacrificial pits, altars, seats, and materials for the fire-offerings and gifts.
Substances such as diamonds and gems for the purpose of worship, sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and all other ritual requisites. ||41||
There, in the pavilion, one should place five water-pots made of gold or other precious metals, containing jewels, along with leaves and fruits.
One should place various kinds of grain there in the pavilion, and according to one's ability, one should set out food for eating and desired delicacies. (43)
One should set aside garments, ornaments, and materials for the purpose of giving;
and having had five auspicious ploughs made of choice wood, one should place them there. (44)
[He saw] oxen yoked to the poles, bound with ropes, adorned with white and black foreheads, beautiful as they were being pulled by men with their fists, and accompanied by other men. ||45||
And [one should fashion] golden or silver [images] endowed with staffs, rays, and so forth,
beginning from five palas and extending up to a thousand palas or more.
Having thus had ploughs made, he likewise had ten bulls fashioned as draft-animals,
yoked to them and adorned with every kind of ornament.

They had silver toe-rings and forehead-marks, were clad in red silk garments, possessed beautiful necks adorned with strings of pearls, and were decorated with tinkling ornaments such as *ghurghura* bells. ||48||
One should consecrate well-adorned golden-horned [oxen] within the pavilion;
one should also arrange suitable carts according to one's capacity. (49)
One should cause a town, a hamlet, a village, or a field rich with crops, or a delightful house, or even a garden, to be fashioned within a golden vessel. (3.129.50)
Thereafter, one should maintain the presence [of the deity] there in the pavilion;
then, one should have learned Brahmins recite benedictions and the proclamation of a meritorious day (puṇyāha).
One should invoke me, Hari, as well as Kṛṣṇa, the ploughman;
and one should also invoke Rādhā, the daughter of Kṛṣṇa, who is Mahālakṣmī and the female ploughman.
Likewise, one should summon the incarnations, the liberated ones, the sovereign goddesses, the gods,
and the world-protectors such as Dharaṇī, Āditya, and Rudra.
One should perform oblations in the fire one hundred and eight times with sacrificial fuel, sesame seeds, desired fruits, leaves, and milk-rice, while remembering me.
The preceptor should offer a caru oblation of milk-rice to Dharaṇī, Āditya, and the Rudras;
likewise, he should offer palāśa fuel-sticks and clarified butter to them.
Black sesame seeds, sugar, rice, and fruits—since the earth is Mahālakṣmī herself, Lakṣmī is truly pleased by white sugar. ||56||
The goddess Dharaṇyā’s daughter is Sitā, the rending of the earth;
she is indeed Dārikā and Putrikā, for she arose having burst through the womb.
For her satisfaction during that oblation, milk-rice (pāyasa) should indeed be offered;
after the fire-sacrifice, one should invite a Brahmin couple and worship them. ||58||
One should honor the virtuous man and the virtuous woman with divine garments, ornaments, and the like, as well as golden necklaces and rings, by providing them with appropriate gifts.
In the pavilion, one should place eighteen kinds of grain, a milch cow,
and a bed furnished with all its accessories and adorned with sugarcane stalks and other items.
Having circumambulated the ploughs while holding a handful of flowers,
one should pray to the Supreme Self, who dwells in the plough as the one who rends [all bonds].
On the white and black [plow], on the white pole, Śiva is stationed;
on the plowshare is Halin, the upholder of Dharma; on the yoke is Viṣṇu, and on the rope is his beloved Nārāyaṇī.
Among bulls you are the god of dharma, and devotion resides in the sacrificial staff;
Śrī Hari dwells everywhere—salutations to you, O Supreme Lord! 63.
All the gods reside within you, who are rich in thunder; salutations to you!
I meditate upon the white goddess, the knower of the essence of the roots of all beings.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the plowman; salutations to the glorious wielder of the plow.
Salutations again and again to you, the Brahman who is the essence of the plow and the all-pervading one.
In this matter of giving, you have been entrusted here, assuming the form of Pañcālāṅgala;
[the fruits of which are] heaven, truth, great sovereignty, and even the sovereignty over the earth.
"Grant me that fruit, and likewise at the end, supreme liberation.
Having spoken thus and bowed down, he placed five ploughshares upon his mouth. (67)
One should offer [these] adorned with equipment and yoked to bulls,
and indeed one should give other gifts as well to the community of monks.
And he should likewise present it to the Brahmins and the officiating priests as is appropriate—
a field of five hundred *vighāṭikās*, fit for cultivation by five ploughs.
Or he may give land of inferior quality along with its garden;
or he may give gold-bearing land, or indeed he should give a house for the sake of peace.
Then, one should give food, water, and so forth in charity according to one's wealth;
thereafter, one should have the twice-born yogis partake of meals there.
To virtuous women, virtuous men, children, the elderly, those blinded by the side-glances of women, and other such helpless people,
one should likewise give gifts according to one's capacity, which destroy all sins.
It shall bestow heaven, it shall bestow sovereignty, and it shall grant the station of Parameṣṭhin;
for as many grains of harvest as there are upon the earth, for so many ages shall one dwell in heaven.
He rejoices together with his family and thereafter goes to the abode of Hari;
there is no doubt that the liberation of his ancestors is surely achieved. ||74||
By the gift of five ploughs, merit indeed arises that lasts for five kalpas;
by that, one truly becomes the lord of heaven (Indra) repeatedly in the celestial realm. ||75||
One who bestows cows, land, sesame seeds, and bulls shall attain Vaikuṇṭha;
by reading or hearing this, one obtains a reward equal to that.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you the great gift of the island of Dhara, which destroys sins, bestows merit, dispels inauspiciousness, and grants happiness. (77)
Having reached an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
one should also have a sacrificial pit and an altar made, and set out jars filled with water.
[He offered] objects suitable for giving and those suitable for the fire-oblation—eight [vessels] fashioned from gold, adorned with jewels, sprouts, and cloths. (79)
One should place all kinds of grains suitable for worship,
as well as a golden representation of the earth consisting of Jambudvīpa, adorned with its boundary mountains.
In its center, it is joined with Mount Meru, delightful and endowed with nine regions;
it is surrounded on all sides by oceans and provided with rivers, streams, and lakes.
It should be provided with all kinds of jewel mines and placed at the side of the deity Varāha,
[weighing] one thousand palas of gold, or half of that, or a fraction thereof.
Having caused it to be made with five palas of weight, one should indeed install it;
there, in the center, one should place me, Śrī Hari, the Lord of Ramā.
Likewise, Muktānikā should place my liberated incarnations, as well as all the beloveds of Brahmā and the beloved women of Hari. (84)
The lords and non-lords, gods and goddesses, as well as the sages; Mahālakṣmī, Śrīgopālakṛṣṇa, and Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Furthermore, having caused the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake to be made, as well as my auspicious temple and the hermitage of Lomaśa, he should likewise establish them there.
One should place there in the pavilion ornaments, garments for clothing, various kinds of wealth, and items suitable for the distribution of food.
One should place a lion skin there, or else a deer skin;
upon that, one should place sesame seeds, grains, juices, and auspicious sugars.
One should also place fruits, silk cloth, and a canopy;
and one should invoke the world-protectors, the guardians of the directions, and the lords of the gods.
Wearing white garments and being pure, he should perform the formal acceptance;
having circumambulated the earth and holding a handful of flowers, he should proceed. (3.129.90)
One whose inner self is permeated by contemplation should worship and also offer prayers:
"Salutations to you, O Soul of all worlds, O Lord Hari, the Soul of the earth! (9.1)
You are the earth, you are the sustainer, you are the nurse; protect us, O Vasundharā!
Salutations to you here, O Vasumatī; grant me always the treasures (vasu). 92.
Salutations again and again to you who reside upon the head of Ananta Śeṣa;
you are Lakṣmī, you are Mahālakṣmī, and you are the contented Narāyaṇī.
You are Gāyatrī, you are Śivā, and you are Māṇikyā in my presence;
you are the destroyer of the suffering of the worlds and the bearer of their embryos—protect me! 94.

You are moonlight, you are radiance, intelligence, wisdom, and the virtuous supporter of the universe; you are fortitude, stability, patience, the earth, the broad one, the nectar-bearing, and the giver of birth. (95)
Protect heaven and grant me a great kingdom; bestow upon me the eternal state, and having been offered to you, make all my ancestors attain liberation. 96.
Having thus bowed, one should offer that golden earth to a worthy preceptor;
or else, one should give half to the Brahmins, as well as other jewels.
Then he should feed the monks, virtuous and holy men who have assembled;
he should give gifts of grain, garments, and fruits. (98)
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations (homa) which bestow happiness;
by that alone, sin is destroyed and merit is obtained through the act of giving. 99.
The man who bestows the gift of earth attains the perfection of Viṣṇu,
accompanied by the liberation of his ancestors, traveling in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
By reciting and hearing this, one goes to Śrīpura and the eternal city of Nārāyaṇa; with the body liberated, one is reborn there.
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of Vairāja, he goes to my imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this great gift consisting of earth been described to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Gift of the Golden Elephant-Chariot, the Great Gift of the Five-Plowshare, and the Great Gift of the Golden Earth," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this supreme great gift (mahādāna) which follows;
it is the Viśvasudarśanacakra-mahādāna, the most magnificent of all.
One should have a radiant wheel made: the best with a thousand palas, the middling with half of that, or the lowest with half of that again.
One should have an excellent wheel made with sixteen spokes and eight rims, adorned with silver bands, and measuring more than twenty *phalas* in height.
Upon His navel, one should fashion me, the auspicious Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, four-armed, adorned with a crown, and beautified by four weapons. || 4 ||
On the initial rim, one should install the auspicious golden goddesses dear to Brahmā and Īśvara— namely Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, Prajñā, Padmāvatī, and Satī.
Māṇikyā, Lalitā, and Haimī Jayā are my beloveds;
likewise, on the second rim, one should worship Jalaśāyin in the east.
To the glorious Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa, who is joined with Kambharāśrī;
and to the Guru Narāyaṇa, who is endowed with a devoted wife and whose own vow is toward his wife. || 7 ||
Lomaśa together with the Kuṅkumavāpī lake, the auspicious Sadguru,
Aja accompanied by Sāvitrī, and likewise Śiva joined with Śivā.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana;
Rāma bearing the axe, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki.
On the third rim, one should have the seven Mātṛkās, as well as the eight Vasus,
and Gaṇeśa together with his family, all accompanied by their vehicles.
In the fourth [layer], he places the twelve Ādityas and also the four Vedas;
in the fifth, the five elements and also the eleven Rudras.
In the sixth [enclosure], one should have the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) and the elephants of the directions fashioned;
and in the seventh, indeed all the weapons, such as the svastika and others.
One should assign the eight Siddhis and the eight Aiśvaryas in the eighth [square].
Having thus caused the Sudarśana-cakra to be fashioned within the pavilion, [one should proceed].
Once it has been prepared with pillars of plantain trees and other ornaments, he should bring the great [image] near the altar;
the Cakra should be placed upon a black antelope skin over sesame seeds.
One should arrange all the requisites, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the eighteen kinds of grain and flavors such as salt and the like.
Also eight full water-pots, jewels, gems, and garments,
as well as garlands, sugarcane, fruits, flowers, and whatever other articles for giving there may be.
One should protect excellent foods and drinks, as well as sugar, wealth,
a cow, a maiden, and Tulasī, and likewise protect against fire.
Then, having become purified by the ritual bath and wearing white garments, the patron, situated within the pavilion, should cause auspicious musical instruments to be played.
Having sat upon his seat together with the officiating priests,
he respectfully performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) and other rites, and then invoked the deities.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should then perform one hundred and eight oblations;
having also performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should offer a handful of flowers.
Having performed circumambulation of the fire-altar (*homacakra*), one should also offer this prayer:
"Homage to the one whose form is the six wheels; homage to the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. (21)
Salutations to You, whose nature is the universal wheel, the Sudarśana;
salutations to You who abide upon the finger of the hand of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 22.
Salutations to you, the compassionate one who is the flame that consumes heaps of sins;
by the gift of the golden discus, grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (23)
Obeisance to You, the embodiment of supreme bliss, whose self is Nārāyaṇa;
to the divine one composed of splendor, who possesses the power to crush the asuras. 24.
Salutations again and again to You who abide in the heart and have transcended all qualities.
The discus resides within Nārāyaṇa, and Hari resides within the center of the discus.
Between the two [lotuses] is Mahālakṣmī; salutations again and again to that Goddess!
You exist as a weapon for the protection of your devotees; protect me. ||26||
Having recited this, one should give the Sudarśana discus to the guru;
likewise, other items suitable for donation should be offered to the twice-born.
At that time, one should indeed bestow gifts upon the distressed, the blind, the wretched, as well as upon women, boys, and girls. (28)
One should feed all kinds of edible foods and likewise perform the *ārātrika* rite; one should also perform the ritual dismissal (*parihāra*) and bid farewell to the Brahmins and others. (29)
Thus, the giver of the wheel is liberated from the bondage of existence in the supreme heaven of Viṣṇu’s world, in the Satya realm upon the ground of Vairāja.
Having enjoyed infinite pleasures and having become one with the essence of Nārāyaṇa, he reached the realm of Vaikuṇṭha as the eternal four-armed Lord. ||3 1 ||
After dwelling there for a long time, he goes to Goloka, the most excellent abode;
from there he goes to Brahmapura, my supreme and imperishable realm.
A devotee, having caused a golden Sudarśana discus, which is eternal and presided over by Hari,
to be made, should worship it at home with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
Even he who crosses the wheel of worldly existence does so by worshipping the discus of Hari;
for him in whose house the Sudarśana resides, the wheels of his sins are indeed destroyed.
The mountains of merit truly perish and are never born again;
indeed, the Sudarśana [cakra] constantly provides protection for the householder. (35)
It certainly increases longevity and bestows abundant prosperity, as well as universal sovereignty or even the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). //36//
Now, O Śivarājñīśrī, I shall tell you that most excellent and secret majesty of my *cakra*, which is superior to all else. (37)
In whose body, house, hand, garment, courtyard, or possessions the Sudarśana discus resides, there sin does not remain. ||38||
The messengers of Yama do not approach, and the rākṣasas flee;
even the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others run far away. (39)
All diseases, such as fevers and the like, never remain;
moreover, through the Sudarśana [mantra], latent impressions (vāsanā) truly reach a state of being uprooted. ||3.130.40||
Afflictions caused by kings, gods, and others are surely destroyed by the Sudarśana;
as are the afflictions of snakes and scorpions, and whatever other poisons there may be. (41)
The supernatural powers of those who dwell there, though well-guarded, are swiftly destroyed in every way by the splendor of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the Sudarśana. ||42||
Furthermore, child-seizing spirits and the like do not afflict that house;
nor does untimely death occur there because of the Sudarśana. (43)
There shall never be a house without offspring where my Sudarśana is present;
where my Sudarśana is present, portents do not occur at all.
May there be no misfortunes where my Sudarśana is present;
may victory always be mine in every way through my Sudarśana.
Furthermore, fears of thieves and tigers do not arise at all, nor do fears of water or fire, nor even fear of earthquakes. (46)
No children are born in that place where my Sudarśana is present, nor is there any fear of miscarriage, nor fear of a woman's widowhood, and so forth. (47)
In Sudarśana, no fear of calamities ever arises;
afflictions do not arise at all, nor does any fear of living beings occur. ||48||
Where my Sudarśana is present, there shall be no fear of weapons, no fear of being struck down, and no affliction from the planets.
Through the majesty of Sudarśana, beauty, charm, prosperity, excellent flavors, and much more arise in abundance, beyond all expectation.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, likewise to the wheel and the most excellent garland-wheel:
a golden garland or a wreath of Tulasī is the supreme wheel. (51)
This is declared to be the Wheel of Brahman (brahmacakra), for it is the supreme Sudarśana;
possessing one hundred and eight spokes, it is the most excellent and great wheel of the virtuous.
Indeed, a garland that has come into the hands of a virtuous person cuts away all sins;
it cuts through all the difficult paths of illusion, root and branch.
It delivers one from the burden of birth and death upon the head;
he by whom the garland is worn around the neck has his head honored. (54)
If a garland is held in the hand, Lakṣmī always dwells in his lotus-like face;
if it is worn on the arm or the forearm, she becomes manifest as Ramā.
The forearm of that person shall always be a beloved abode for Lakṣmī;
and that house in which the Mālācakra resides shall be protected. (56)
I sport with Nārāyaṇa suddenly, with my whole being.
By means of the rosary-recitation, [one subdues] the Daityas who dwell within the wicked senses. ||57||
The dissolution of all impurities certainly occurs;
thus is the supreme Great Wheel of Brahman, the Sudarśana Garland. (58)
O Lakṣmī, one who is a protector at all times should especially give a gift;
namely, a garland made of gold, silver, crystal, or pearls. (59)
One should offer a Tulasī plant as a gift; for it indeed bestows heaven and liberation.
One should give it to a virtuous great guru, or to a high-souled practitioner of silent recitation (jāpaka).
Having worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings, he placed a heart-pleasing garland upon Śrī Hari; the crystal necklace rested upon the Lord's chest.
In her hand she holds a rosary of tulasi beads, by which she has attained honor from Lakṣmī;
she is that very Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, the garlanded one who destroys all impurity. (2)
Bestowing garlands of heaven and granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation, she is brilliantly radiant,
adorned with one hundred and eight jewels upon a thread of heaven.
Adorned with a beautiful crystal or silver [crown], the virtuous Śrīvāsinī is bound with the Brahma-knot and other ornaments. 64.
That garland, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, should be offered according to the prescribed rite after it has been placed upon a pitcher atop a Sarvatobhadra mandala.
Gomukhī, adorned with cloth, should be given together with sugar and other offerings;
it should be presented along with a seat and provided with a covering cloth.
It should be provided with divine curtains, fragrant with fruits, perfectly endowed with divine jewels, and adorned with threads of pearls. ||67||
Indeed, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) accompanied by wealth and grain should be given;
having placed that garland upon a deer-skin, in a jar, and in a cooking pot.
Having placed [the offerings] in the hand of my image of Śrī Hari, one should worship it;
one should bathe my garland with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other such items. 619.

Having worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings, he should again place them in my hand; then, having performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) and offered incense and lamps, he should bow down to me.
Even after offering the sacrificial food (naivedya) to me, one should then feed it to the garland;
for the garland is my consciousness-goddess (cid-devī), and Lalitā is my beloved woman.
The great divine Sadāśakti, the bestower of all merit, should be given together with a svastika and with wealth, grain, and other such things. //72//
Having bowed to the Guru and prostrated again and again, one should offer [the garland] to him;
there, one should pray to the Guru: "I am performing this offering of the garland. (73)
By this merit, may the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa be gracious to me;
likewise, may I always be protected by Rādhā and Lakṣmī with their garlands.
O true Guru, may my sins be destroyed by this offering of the garland;
may Mādhava, ever pleased by the garland, grant me happiness. (75)
Thus one should offer the garland-circle, which removes fear during the giving;
and a fourth part of the garland is indeed twenty-seven [beads].
There may be gems, or auspicious or protective silver;
there is an option or doubt [regarding these], therefore it protects by means of number. (77)
This very protector of hers shall deliver even him;
the offering of the garland is a great gift that destroys all sins. (78)
O beloved, with a rosary there should be constant recitation for me, Nārāyaṇa;
by that, wicked sins are surely destroyed moment by moment. (79)
For one who recites with everything entrusted to me, there is no sin;
this pair of wheels is declared: for one who gives [them], there is no sin.
Two great wheels have been proclaimed: Sudarśana and Mālikā.
Mālikā is the destroyer of worldly existence, while Sudarśana is the slayer of the Daityas.
Furthermore, the third wheel is indeed a finger ornament;
a golden ring-wheel should especially be given as a gift.
Indeed, the giver of a signet ring becomes a sovereign on earth;
the giver of all types of finger-rings even becomes a king in heaven. 8.3.
By giving rings, finger-rings, and so forth, one becomes a creator of the universe;
having fashioned [these] from gold, silver, and other materials, one should worship the twice-born preceptor. (87)
[He saw] a virtuous woman, a great chaste lady, and a devoted wife; a true guru, a teacher learned in the Vedas, and a holy man who was the son of Nārāyaṇa. 85.
Or, having paid homage to one who belongs to the Acyuta lineage, he should then offer it;
having worshipped the rings and finger-rings with excellent saffron, [he should present them]. (86)
One should offer this ornament with the right hand upon the thumb;
there always resides Kamalā-Ramā, the one who takes away gold.
Having worshipped it, one should pray to that ring-finger ornament:
"O Lord, always protect me indeed from the waves produced by the ocean of worldly existence. (88)
O Blessed One, O beloved of the Blessed One, liberation always occurs through gold in my hand; grant it to me, O Illustrious One, while I am afflicted by disease. (89)
O Goddess with waves, having destroyed all my heaps of sin,
O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, immerse me in the wave of the bliss of Brahman.
Having thus worshipped and made this prayer, one should give a beautiful auspicious ring—having three, five, or seven ridges—as a gift. (9.1)
If one is capable, one should give to a twice-born person as a gift one, ten, or twenty beautiful vessels made of gold alone.
And with great devotion, one should give a fourth golden bracelet or bangle to a virtuous person who is a devotee of Viṣṇu upon his hand. (93)
It was equal to a discus, encrusted with jewels, adorned with gems and diamonds,
set with pearls and rubies, and inlaid with the Kaustubha gem.
And one should offer a lion-throne, which destroys all poverty and bestows all prosperity, as well as fortune, and likewise a wife. (95)
It bestows the kingdom of heaven and likewise the realm of truth (satyaloka);
it bestows the world of Brahmā and likewise enjoyment and liberation. ||96||
In this manner, O Lakṣmī, one should offer ornaments for the feet and the ankles, as well as a kāmbikā, a kadalī, a śṛṅkhalā, and a vaṅgaḍī. (97)
It was fashioned from gold and silver, adorned with pearls and gems, bestowing all splendor upon its face, and resonating with the sound of a network of tiny bells. ||98||
In this manner, O Lakṣmī, one should likewise give a golden vessel;
one should bestow a beautiful, well-rounded golden vessel adorned with gems. 99.
All these wheels have been described to you by me, O beloved;
they should be given according to one's capacity, for they truly bring merit through the act of giving.
They bestow heaven, grant great prosperity, and even bestow liberation;
they destroy poverty, disease, and discord, and provide happiness. || 10.1 ||
They cause the expansion of one's lineage from a divine race,
and they increase the good fortune of having divine women as wives and sons.
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, and rejoicing in these,
all such gifts indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of the Great Viśvasudarśana Discus, the Gift of the Mālikā Great Discus, the Gift of the Protector [Discus], and the Gifts of the Great Discuses such as the Ring, Finger-ring, Armlet, Bracelet, Chain, Biṅgiḍī, Bangle, and Natthikā," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, to this most excellent great gift (mahādāna) called Mahākalpalatā, which consists of a golden creeper.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, one should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed;
one should also have an altar and a sacrificial pit made, and install them for the purpose of the oblation.
He should have the Brahmins perform the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana) for the materials to be given away;
then, taking up the items intended for donation, he should place them there in the pavilion.
The officiating priests [prepared] all the ritual requisites, ornaments, garments, and so forth,
as well as the seats for the gods, for Nārāyaṇa, and for me, Śrī.
One should likewise perform the invocation for the goddesses and worship them;
there, in the pavilion, one should [place] ten golden creepers known as Kalpavallīs.

One should place ten golden trees, produced from gold weighing ten units more [than the standard], adorned with fruits and flowers, provided with jewels, silken garments, and the like, and thus decorated and beautified.
One should likewise fashion the wives of the eight guardians of the directions (dikpālas), joined with Vidyādharīs and adorned with Suparṇas, upon each creeper.
On a mountain of sugar, one should cause all the creepers to climb up:
the Aindrī creeper situated upon an elephant, and the Āgneyī creeper situated upon a ram.
In the south is Mahiṣī seated upon a buffalo; in the southwest is Gardabhī seated upon a donkey;
in the west is Makarī seated upon a crocodile; and in the northwest is Hariṇī seated upon a deer.
One should likewise place Kauberī, seated upon a golden vehicle, and Īśānī, seated upon a bull, as well as the sixteen grains there in that pavilion.
Lakṣmī, Śivā, Sāvitrī, Māṇikyā, Duḥkhahātmā, Kambharāśrī, Mahālakṣmī, and the sister of Hari who is ever contented. (11)
One should likewise place essences, fragrances, sweet juices, and jars of clarified butter;
having fashioned these with gold weighing up to a thousand [units], one should indeed install them within the pavilion.
One should also place eight cows and eight jars filled with water containing jewels,
adorned with cloths, rice, leaves, and other such items.
One should worship them according to the prescribed rite, and likewise worship the creepers;
having worshipped with the sounds of the Vedas, one should perform three circumambulations.
One should pray to those creepers accompanied by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who destroy the sins of others and protect those who serve them. 15.
Homage be to the Kalpas that grant fruits; salutations again and again!
Homage be to those that bestow all prosperity; salutations again and again to all supernatural powers! || 16 ||
Salutations indeed to those who are the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī and whose nature is the Self of all;
[to those who are] Svarga, Amṛta, Śrīpura, Vairāja, and Gavāyana.
May they always grant us Vaikuṇṭha, the imperishable abode;
and may you, who are the very form of charity, protect us forever once you have been bestowed.
Having prayed thus and having performed circumambulation once more, one should offer the arghya water to the Guru and the holy ones, while offering portions of it to others as well.
One should indeed give jewels, diamonds, silver, cows, and whatever garments there may be to the mendicants and those who are destitute and without protectors. (3.131.20)
One should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rules, feed virtuous Brahmins,
and likewise feed boys and girls, while also bestowing wealth as an offering.
Then, O beloved, one should offer a gift in return, dismiss [the recipient], and prostrate;
thus one should perform the gift of the Kalpalatā, the fruit of which is great.
Empire arises for him, and he becomes a deliverer of his ancestors;
the earth, filled with crops and other riches, always attends upon him. (23)
Indeed, the supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) arise for the giver of the creeper;
moreover, those wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatās) become celestial nymphs (apsarases) for him in heaven.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this great gift which fulfills all intentions has been described to you; it is auspicious and bestows great sovereignty throughout all the worlds. (25)
Likewise, one should perform the gift of Kalpapriyā; hear now its procedure:
an auspicious image should be fashioned from a thousand bhāras of gold. (26)
Adorned with garments and ornaments, graced by every mark of beauty, she was a beautiful young woman, surrounded by her sons, daughters, and others. ||27||
It is provided with cows, buffaloes, elephants, and horses; adorned with beds and other furnishings;
endowed with wealth, grain, and the like; and possessed of flavorful foods and fruits. ||28||
Having placed that Great Ramā, who is the form of his wife, there within the pavilion,
he should invoke her at the front of the altar and worship her with all necessary materials.
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering and present excellent food offerings and water;
whatever kind of wife one desires, provided she is endowed with the necessary qualities.
She should be fashioned in such a way that she is adorned with erotic ornaments,
accompanied by male and female servants and friends, and graced with the auspicious prosperity of a household.
Having worshipped her, she should perform an oblation into the fire one hundred and more times;
then, having circumambulated the fire, she should place it in her own hand.
Furthermore, one should thereafter pray to the preceptor, or to a virtuous Brahmin, or to Hari, or to Kumāra, or even to a holy person (sati).
This wife, endowed with all the requisites for domestic life and adorned, has been given by me as a gift to this twice-born man. (34)
O Nārāyaṇī, O Mahālakṣmī, you alone are the Supreme Goddess;
O Rame, grant me always the fruit of charity and a virtuous wife.
In heaven, in Satyaloka, in Vairāja, and in Vaikuṇṭha, may my wife be united with me and go along with me; likewise, grant me this fruit.
Having spoken thus, one should place the beloved in the hand of the brahmin preceptor;
that golden image of the beloved shall bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (37)
O Lakṣmī, for thousands of future births, may our marital union remain unbroken;
may it bestow all prosperity and grant eternal bliss. (38)
Bestowing all enjoyments and increasing the lineage of sons and grandsons—this great gift of the Kalpa-tree wife has been described by me to you. (39)
Just as women are desired in heaven or on earth according to their number,
so too should an equal number of dolls be offered as one's own wives.
Having placed them all within the pavilion near the fire,
he should first cause them all to be married according to the marriage rite by the twice-born.
Adorned with garlands of choice flowers, holding them in their hands,
they were radiant with all ornaments and endowed with every kind of decoration.
Then, the wise man should offer all those [gifts] made by his own wife for the sake of charity;
for women thus given according to the prescribed rule [bring benefit] both in this world and the next.
This supreme great gift certainly exists, there is no doubt;
it is indeed the gift of a golden woman, consisting of a substitute for one's own wife. (44)
A woman should certainly not be given as a gift; rather, a golden image should be given.
For the Creator himself has declared that the gift of a woman is indeed a great gift.
In this manner, O Lakṣmī, one should also offer the Lord of Gold for the sake of giving, adorned with all ornaments and beautifully graced by every prosperity. (46)
This great gift of gold is indeed bestower of splendor and conjugal fortune;
I shall describe to you the procedure for it, by the performance of which [it is achieved] never at all. 47.
She shall never experience widowhood; rather, she attains great fortune through her husband.
Having fashioned a golden image, she should worship it there in a pavilion.
There, one should invoke Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Consort of Śrī;
then, one should establish him in the pavilion according to the marriage rite.
Thinking him to be her own golden husband, the woman,
holding the bridegroom’s garland, took his hand and thereafter became his wife.
Then, having performed circumambulation, she should offer herself to her husband as a gift;
thereafter, she should also offer all other various objects.
Whatever kind of husband she has desired, even in birth after birth, such a man, endowed with every excellence, must be given to the Brahmin woman. (52)
This gift is proclaimed as a great gift, a gift unto the husband;
it bestows all auspicious fortune and is the auspicious means for the perpetual fulfillment of the householder's life.
The gift of a son and the gift of a brother, arising from a golden statuette, bestows both heaven and liberation, as well as eternal bliss. (54)
In this very manner, one should perform the rite and invoke me, the Supreme Lord;
that which is offered according to the prescribed rule bears fruit even in the form of a son.
That which is given in the form of a brother indeed bears fruit;
through the gift of an image of Hari, Mādhava, who is Hari himself, becomes united with one. (56)
By the bestowing of a beloved gift, even Kṛṣṇa becomes beloved;
therefore, these gifts should be given according to the prescribed rule. (57)
Through the gift of female and male slaves, female and male slaves are obtained;
nothing whatsoever is acquired that has not been given, therefore one must indeed give on this earth. (58)
Whether given here or in the next world, a gift remains present;
one who gives happiness shall possess happiness, and one who gives suffering shall become possessed of suffering. (59)
A gift of merit should be bestowed upon a householder who has not yet drunk [the water of death], as well as upon the sick, the poor, and those who have knowledge of the world beyond. (3.131.60)
Merit arising from vows and other such acts should be bestowed upon a living being who is facing death;
likewise, other merits consisting of ascetic penances should be given. (6.1)

Virtuous acts consisting of sacrifices, as well as those arising from great festivals, the merits of reciting the scriptures (pārāyaṇa), and whatever merits come from the chanting of mantras (japa); ||62||
All merits arising from giving, those born of performing sacrifices, those resulting from the worship of the gods, and those produced by service to the guru—[all these are surpassed by this]. (63)
In charity, one should give according to the prescribed rules those things produced through service to one's husband,
as well as the virtues such as devotion to the husband (pātivratya), which bestow happiness when given in charity.
Virtues such as devotion to one's wife, the duties of the virtuous which bring happiness, and the duty of benefiting others should be bestowed through the proper ritual of giving. 65.

The merit of knowledge, the merit of digging wells, the merit of *iṣṭāpūrta* and other such acts, the merit arising from assistance such as providing medicinal herbs, and the merit of giving—which bestows happiness—[are all included]. (66)

The merit arising from seeking refuge, that born of truth, as well as the auspiciousness produced by compassion, and the great merit arising from non-violence—these should especially be bestowed through giving. (67)
The merit arising from giving one's throat, likewise the merit arising from giving one's waist,
and the merit arising from giving one's heart— these should be given specifically when making a gift.

The great merit arising from the protection of those who have come for refuge—which originates from providing a support to the supportless—is the gift of life; this should be given especially among all gifts. (69)
The gift of all things is a great gift; the gift of Brahman is the highest of all.
The gift of knowledge is the gift of Hari, and the gift of liberation is even greater than that.
The granting of fearlessness is indeed the most excellent among all gifts; it should be bestowed with every disposition, for there exists nothing superior to it. (71)
The gift of the moon and sun indeed bestows brilliance upon one's eyes;
the gift of higher knowledge (vijñāna) indeed bestows radiance upon the heart.
The gift of liberation bestows eternal bliss upon oneself;
this very gift of fearlessness should be given by one who desires liberation. (73)
The gift of one's body should be performed for the sake of obtaining an auspicious body and so forth;
the gift of one's home should be performed for the sake of easily obtaining a dwelling and so forth. ||74||
The gift of ghee should be performed for the sake of easily attaining nourishment of the body;
the gift of seeds should be performed for the sake of the increase of dharma and progeny. (75)
The gift of water should be performed for the satisfaction of one's ancestors;
likewise, the gift of a preceptor should be made by fashioning a golden image of the guru. (76)
Having caused it to be fashioned according to the rules and having worshipped it along with the *śṛṅgāra* vessel,
one should invoke the Guru and pray to him for the sake of crossing over one's own self.
One should bestow her upon a righteous, virtuous, and devoted worshiper—one who is indeed capable of performing her worship constantly. (78)
To him the image of the Guru should be given, for the fruit of worship is thereby obtained;
if it is not worshipped, the giver would incur the consequence of transgression. (79)
The images of the gods may also be made of gold or silver, or produced from gems and jewels, or fashioned from wood, paintings, and the like. ||3.131.80||
Indeed, those [images] should be bestowed according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the ritual installation (pratiṣṭhā), adorned with all ornaments and endowed with every type of attire. ||81||
All [the images] should be provided with horns, gentle in appearance, and beautiful in form; they should be given together with vessels, perfumes, offerings, and articles for worship. ||82||

Together with the hosts of Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and likewise Ravi, who were worthy of festive ornaments such as strings of pearls and necklaces, and possessed of weapons fit for celebration; (83)
Beautiful and auspicious images should be offered to Vāstu, to the world-protectors (lokapālas), to the lords of the hosts, and likewise to the virtuous attendants. 84.
Adorned with all ornaments and radiant with every grace, they were endowed with appropriate attire and equipped with suitable weapons. ||85||
Provided with suitable vehicles and accompanied by appropriate servants, and endowed with their own strength, they should be given as gifts to bestow happiness. (86)
Mahānārāyaṇī, Brāhmī, Mahālakṣmī, Ramāmṛtā, Kamalā, Śrī, Prabhā, Deyā, Kānakī, and likewise Māṇikī. ||87||
The golden Kambharā-Lakṣmī, the graceful Śrī of auspicious countenance, the elephant-faced Mahālakṣmī, adorned with splendors, should be given. 88.
Gaṅgā, Durgā, Pāśavatī, Satī, Kanyā, Kumārikā, Santuṣā, Jānakī, Devyā, Ramā, Jayā, and Padminī. ||89||
Sāvitrī, Vijayā, and Duḥkhahā, the Mother of the Vedas, should be given;
likewise, Saṃjñā, Svāhā, and the adorned Caṇḍī, joined with Vahni, should be given.
Kātyāyanī and Mahākālī should be given, adorned with their respective attire; Gaurī and Tulasī should also be given, Vṛndā being adorned for the wedding.
Likewise, the Surāṇīs, the Īśānīs, the Mothers, the Yoginīs, and the Muktānīs should be given as gifts to Janārdana. (92)
For the sake of worship, these well-consecrated images should be given with great enthusiasm to a virtuous, devoted twice-born man. 93.
Adorned with costumes, ornaments, offerings, vessels, garments, and the like, temples suitable for their residence should also be provided. 94.
And there were gardens of great prosperity, bearing fruits, garlands, and honey; as well as groves filled with crops and fields indeed rich with sugarcane. 95.
Various offerings consisting of vegetable leaves and the like should be given;
groves, wells, tanks, and lakes should also be bestowed.
All things to be enjoyed, including perfumes, flavors, and foods; grains, treasuries of wealth, and male and female servants—all these should be given away. (97)
Whatever is given is what is obtained; that which is not given is never obtained anywhere.
Therefore, one should give even by fashioning images of wives and female slaves. (98)
Having given thus, one may also obtain supreme happiness in the householder’s life;
having become happy in this world, one further attains universal sovereignty. (99)
In heaven, in Satyaloka, in Vairāja, in Vaikuṇṭha, in Śrīpura, or in Akṣara,
he is born in Goloka as a lordly abode possessing the splendor of Nārāyaṇa.
Endowed with all elegance, possessing the enjoyment of all pleasures, he becomes eternal, overflowing with all bliss and supreme bliss. 101.
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, and rejoicing in this, as well as through giving and causing others to practice it, one shall become a repository of equal merit. || 102 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Great Gifts of the Mahākalpalatā and Suvarṇavallī, the Gift of Kalpapriyā, the Gift of Svarṇakānta, the Gift of Merit, the Gifts of Fearlessness and so forth, the Great Gifts to the Guru, Devas, and Devīs, and the Great Gifts of Temples, Sacred Fields, Gardens, Ornaments, and the like," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 131 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this gift of the seven oceans;
it is a great gift that destroys all sins and bestows the abode of heaven.
Having reached an auspicious day and month, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
one should also have a lovely altar made and procure the ritual materials.
One should have those learned in the Vedas recite benedictory words and auspicious days;
and one should invoke the guardians of the world (lokapālakas) upon their seats within the pavilion.
One should indeed cause seven beautiful ponds to be constructed within the pavilion for the Supreme Lord Hari, for me, and for Śrī Rāmā, the daughter of the ocean.
And there were beautiful golden vessels, weighing from more than seven palas up to a thousand palas, resembling large cooking pots.
First, one should fill the golden vessel with salt;
likewise, the second with milk, and the third indeed with clarified butter.
The fourth [offering] is with jaggery alone, the fifth likewise with curd;
the sixth is also with sugar, and the seventh with sweet water.
These seven oceans should indeed be especially worshipped;
one should place a beautiful golden image of Brahmā in the first ocean.
In the second [day] Keśava and me; in the third likewise Hara;
in the fourth also Bhāskara; and in the fifth the Moon.
In the sixth [house], one should place Lakṣmī, my wife; in the seventh, Pārvatī Satī; and one should establish male and female servants, as well as gems, diamonds, and pearls.
