Those who honor [this] shall dwell in heaven for as long as thirty thousand kalpas;
or one may listen to it, or read it, or even offer one's devotion to it.
He too, having become a lord of the gods, shall dwell in heaven without a doubt;
he attains worldly enjoyment and liberation, along with the wealth of eternal bliss.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Desired Fruits by the Daughters of the Pitṛs and Others through the Recitation of the Two Hundred Names of Lakṣmī, and the Ritual for the Lakṣmī-Saubhāgya-Śayana Vow," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-Santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this Ghaṭalakṣmī vow of yours;
for one who observes the Ghaṭalakṣmī vow, it shall last for seven days in succession.
This world of mortals (bhūrloka) is called heaven because of its abundance of wealth, happiness, and delight;
and even the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) is heaven for the accomplished yogis.
All those realms beginning with Svarga exist within the celestial sphere (div), for they all end in truth;
indeed, these seven divine worlds bestow the attainment of heaven.
However, by virtue of your vow, all [these] attain sovereignty in turn;
it arises solely from the Ghaṭalakṣmī-vow—of this there is no doubt. (4)
In this world, through this vow, auspicious form, supreme longevity, good fortune, abundant prosperity, and vast wealth shall arise for you here.
Listen here to the divine story of the high-souled Agastya.
Formerly, Vahni was commanded by Mahendra regarding the enemies of the gods.
Then, for the sake of their destruction, the fire burnt ten million Dānavas; and of those who were consumed by the flames, thousands of Dānavas remained.
Fleeing in terror, those wicked ones entered the ocean—
namely Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, and Parāvasu.
Virocana and they made their dwelling in the ocean;
and considering them to be powerless, they were neglected by Agni.
Then, after some time, having regained their strength once more, the Daityas again oppressed the gods, as well as humans and all moving beings.
Having severely oppressed brahmins and virtuous men,
they enter the water again for five thousand and seven hundred years, O heroes.
"O Lakṣmī, by the power of this water-fortress they afflict the three worlds";
thereupon Mahendra also instructed Vahni (Fire).
"Let this ocean dry up before long for the sake of destroying the Daityas, since this abode of Varuṇa is the refuge of our enemies. (13)
"Therefore, you must quickly bring about its destruction by drying it up.
Then Agni spoke to Śukra regarding the drying up of the ocean. (14)
O Lord of the Gods, it was indeed unrighteousness that caused the drying up of the ocean;
for within a single yojana of it, there were truly hundreds of millions of living beings. (15)
"For if those living beings were to dwell [there], there would be a great destruction; my sin would become limitless. Therefore, what shall I do? (1.6)
Having heard this, Mahendra then spoke these words in anger:
"The immortals in heaven do not incur the entanglement of merit and demerit."
"O Lord, you are the consumer [of oblations] and free from the stain of sin;
nevertheless, you do not carry out my command—become a human! (18)
Then he said to Pavana and Indra: "Dry up the ocean.
Pavana also replied accordingly: "I shall not perform a sinful deed."
Then Indra cursed him, saying, "O Anila, you too shall become a human.
Thus did those two, named Vasiṣṭha and Agastya, both fall under the power of the curse.
The sage Agastya was born as fire, and Vasiṣṭha as wind;
both were indeed born together from the jar through the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa.
When Urvaśī— the daughter of Śrī Naranārāyaṇa, the most excellent of apsarases—
was invited by Mitra and was traveling through the sky out of desire, ||22||
Later, she was seen by Varuṇa and held captive for the sake of desire;
yet, remaining on the path of truth, she did not welcome Varuṇa. ||23||
"I was previously chosen by Mitra; therefore, I am his wife according to dharma, and not yours now, O Lord Varuṇa. (24)
Varuṇa said to her, "Entrusting your heart to me, you may depart.
She went to Mitra, and Mitra heard what she had said.
Having heard of the deposition of her heart, he then abandoned her in anger;
she, having resorted to the profession of a courtesan, departed, for she had been forsaken by both. (26)
Mitra and Varuṇa both cast into the middle of the jar that fierce seed born of their resolve, which had arisen from the sight of Urvaśī.
At that very time, however, the illustrious Vasiṣṭha was cursed by Nimi to become bodiless; thus being disembodied, he remained within a jar.
Agastya also, due to Indra’s curse, remained there within that jar;
from that jar, the boy Agni-Agastya was born.
Vasiṣṭha was born as Vāyu; there a boy was produced who was a portion of Varuṇa, namely Agastya, while the portion of Mitra was Vasiṣṭha.
As soon as they were born, those two, possessing the memory of their former births and full of discernment,
both performed the Ghaṭalakṣmī vow for the sake of liberation from the curse.
And those two had a pavilion constructed with pillars of plantain trees, adorned with necklaces, arched gateways, garlands, and with cloths, flowers, fruits, and other offerings. (32)
It was provided with earthen jars and the like, as well as sacrificial pits and altars;
it was equipped with the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and adorned with wooden seats and other furnishings.
Adorned with offerings for worship and beautified by a golden pitcher, one should prepare an excellent earthen jar filled with water, which is the supreme source [of the ritual]. (34)
The two of them brought [the bride] into the pavilion and honored her;
they both also summoned their mother, Śrī Mahālakṣmī.
They placed there a golden image in a jar,
and then they bathed it with the five nectars and water.
They adorned and embellished the Goddess;
indeed, they dressed that Mother in red garments and other finery. (37)
They worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains, saffron, and collyrium; having honored him with all manner of articles, they likewise performed the ārātrika ceremony.
With joy, they fed him sweet foods and milk-rice;
with reverence, they also offered him water and betel-leaf. (39)
A golden pitcher, adorned with garlands and cloth,
endowed with the five jewels, and accompanied by a vessel of ghee, [should be placed] at its side.
And those two placed there the supreme, eternal Brahman, the Person the size of a thumb, accompanied by sesame seeds, leaves, and fruits. (41)
And they established me here as Anādiśrīhari,
along with grains, garments, ornaments, and vessels made of jewels in every respect.
Having performed the ritual placement, they both worshipped the cow, who was accompanied by her calf, adorned with all ornaments, and whose horns and hooves were made of gold. (43)
They worshipped her, who was enriched with vessels for milking provided with bronze lids and adorned with ornaments of bells,
and they offered a handful of flowers.
Then the gracious mother, Śrīghaṭalakṣmī, the great chaste lady,
appeared visibly before them and urged them both to request a boon.
Those two chose the most excellent boon: "O Mother, by your grace, may there be liberation from this human birth; please act accordingly. (46)
Lakṣmī then said to Agastya: "The Daityas dwell in the ocean;
after you have drunk the sea, their liberation from humanity will come to pass. (47)
"This Vasiṣṭha shall possess a divine body together with you.
Then the sage spoke again for the sake of granting boons, and Lakṣmī replied.
Vasiṣṭha undertook the auspicious Ghaṭalakṣmī vow on the morning of the day of Agastya’s rising, using white sesame seeds and other offerings. 49.
Having bathed in the waters of sacred fords and wearing white garments, the householder who worships you, Lakṣmī, with either an earthen jar or a golden jar— [3.137.50]
Whoever worships Śrī Hari, Vasiṣṭha, and Agastya for either seven nights or seventeen years, [attains the supreme goal].
One should worship him here and indeed offer him the *argha* in due order:
in Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, and Janaloka.
He shall indeed dwell for a long time in the world of heat (Tapoloka) or the world of truth (Satyaloka);
having exercised lordship over enjoyments for kalpa after kalpa, he shall thereafter go to the Imperishable (Akṣara).
One who offers the water of honor (*arghya*) seven times shall attain the seven prosperous worlds.
"Salutations to Lakṣmī, to Mahālakṣmī, to the consort of Viṣṇu; salutations again and again! (54)
Accept this *arghya*, O Sovereign of All; grant us happiness in every way!
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī; salutations to Hari! ||55||
"Accept this water offering, O Blessed One; grant us happiness in every way!
[The two who] resemble kāśa flowers and are born from fire and wind. (56)
"O sons of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from a pitcher, salutations be unto you both!
Thus one should offer the respectful water (arghya), worship, and a handful of flowers.
O Lakṣmī, may his worlds be eternal for all time;
and for him who performs this throughout his life, his residence shall be in the Imperishable.
When Vaśiṣṭha thus requested Kumbhalakṣmī,
their mother, she said to them, "So be it," and then the mother quickly vanished.
The two sages, having offered their formal renunciation, performed difficult austerities;
then, in the course of time, they beheld the fierce affliction of the Daityas.
Agastya drank the ocean, and then the Daityas met their destruction;
the enemies of the gods were slain and perished by the hosts of deities led by Indra.
Then the gods, led by Brahmā, being well-pleased,
came to that place where those two sages were performing penance, having been urged by them for the sake of obtaining boons.
And Agastya chose a boon, and whatever he desired came to pass for as long as twenty-five crores of thousands of Brahmās.
"We two shall become inhabitants of celestial palaces, both destined for heaven;
Vasiṣṭha shall be among the Seven Sages, and Agastya shall dwell in the southern region. (64)
"Whoever performs worship to us on the day of our rising shall indeed become the sovereign of the seven worlds in due course. (65)
The gods said, "So be it," and they departed as they had come;
Vasiṣṭha and Agastya also then went to Mount Malaya.
Then, after some time, the powerful Paraśurāma requested Agastya,
together with the hosts of sages, for the purpose of drinking up the ocean.
Then Agastya drank [the ocean] again for the sake of the land of Gokarṇatīrtha;
having thus accomplished this great task, those two sages went to heaven.
Thus has this Ghaṭalakṣmī-vrata been described to you, O Lakṣmī;
for seven days it consists of subsisting on fruit and performing worship to you. (69)
Upon the rising of Agastya, the rite bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
thus, O Lakṣmī, your worship should be performed on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, or Kārttika, during the bright fortnight,
[one should perform the rite] together with a pavilion and a garden, and accompanied by the concluding ceremony (udyāpana).
Men and women who perform this shall go to the supreme destination, using the five products of the cow, milk, flowers, and scented water. (72)
One should bathe you with honey, worship you with fruits and flowers, adorn you, clothe you, embellish you, and perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana). ||73||
Then one should feed [the guests] and offer a handful of flowers to the beautiful image; one should ask for forgiveness, bow down, make a request, and dedicate [the merit] to the Guru. (74)
Salutations to Mahālakṣmī for your feet; salutations to Śrī for your ankles;
salutations to Śokahatrī for your shanks; salutations to Ramā for your knees. ||75||
Salutation to the auspicious one for the thighs; salutation to the chest-region; salutation to the hips;
salutation to Padmā for the abdomen; salutation to Kāmaśrī for the breast. ||76||

Salutations to your two hands for the sake of the fortune of good luck; salutations to your arms, belly, and face for the sake of Śrī; salutations to your nose for Kamalā; salutations to your eyes for Padminī.
Salutations to Puṣṭi for the forehead and the locks of hair; salutations to Hiraṇyā for the head; salutations again and again to Hariṇī, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, and Lalitā. ||78||
Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇī, O Vāsudevī, O embodiment of all prosperity;
O Mother, O Sovereign Goddess, grant me that which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
O Padmaja, through this vow which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things,
may everything desired by me come to pass by your grace, O Adhijā!
The patron of the sacrifice should cause the sounds of auspicious songs to be made;
there, well-dressed women and young maidens should also sing songs. 81.
They should worship with red garments, red garlands, and ointments;
with flowers, unbroken grains, water, prostrations, and excellent food offerings. ||82||
Having thus worshipped that auspicious image with vermilion, saffron, oil, the essence [of sandalwood], musk, and collyrium, one should present it to the venerable Guru.
One should also worship the guru with lotuses, sandalwood, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual dismissal and feed the boys and girls.
This supreme Lakṣmī-vrata is the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
for him who performs it, manifold auspiciousness shall indeed dwell in his home. (85)
This vow destroys all sins and increases good fortune and health;
it bestows all delights, pleasures, desired joys, and happiness. (86)
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe another vow, pertaining to Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
one should worship you there, endowed with the initiation of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (87)
Likewise, on the full moon day and on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in all months, one should fashion an auspicious-faced Lakṣmī out of gold.

One should properly worship you, Pāṭalā, who are clad in red garments, smeared with red unguents, anointed with red sandalwood paste, and possess a red complexion, while seated upon a red-colored throne. ||89||
One should bathe you with waters of red saffron and adorn you with red flowers,
red garments, red garlands, red fruits, and so forth.
One should worship with red flowers the Red One within me, Nārāyaṇa;
one should also feed her, worship her, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and likewise bow down to her.
And let the worshipper, established in the vows of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, pray to you:
"O Mahālakṣmī, you are clad in red garments, just as Nārāyaṇa is established in red. (92)
Grant me health, renunciation, great peace, and union with Hari; for I am detached from all others and devoted to the Lord, the Consort of Śrī. ||93||
"O Hari, I shall perform here for you the Sāṃkhyayoga-Mahālakṣmī vow;
by this, may my good fortune become like yours. (94)
May there be the destruction of all obstacles; may all joys be mine.
May all flavors and all supreme blessings and auspiciousness be mine. (95)
Having thus entreated, one should likewise bestow golden Lakṣmī upon the preceptor;
one should also present jeweled ornaments, garments, vessels of grain, and so forth.
One who performs this vow attains service to Hari;
by taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, both worldly enjoyment and liberation come into one's hand.
This vow of the Sāṃkhya and Yoga systems must be performed while fasting;
it removes all sins, bestows a divine body, and is dear to Hari. 98.
She shall become a virtuous wife beloved by Hari, a performer of vows who has cast off her body;
she shall become full of wonder, having attained the abode of the divine syllables. 99.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ghaṭalakṣmī Vow performed by Agastya, the All-Auspicious Lakṣmī Vow, and the Sāṃkhya-Yoga Lakṣmī Vow," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Lakṣmī, listen now to the Rasakalyāṇalalitā vow.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should construct a pavilion with a Sarvatobhadra mandala.
One should fill [the jars] with many kinds of grain and place auspicious jars;
in the central jar, an image made of gold, adorned with ornaments, should be placed.
The Goddess Lalitā, who bestows aesthetic flavor and possesses the beautiful splendor of auspicious rasa,
[is worshipped] on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha.
One should bathe [the image] with honey, sugarcane juice, and ghee;
then one should bathe it with curd, milk, and waters from sacred fords (tīrtha). || 4 ||
One should give ornaments, garments, sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and saffron; one should also bestow articles of adornment as well as flowers and other such offerings.
One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, and likewise the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
one should pray, give a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā), and present a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). || 6 ||
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should honor the virtuous Brahmins;
one should worship a Brahmin couple and bestow gifts such as wealth and other offerings.
One should feed [the recipient] with food, drink, and so forth, along with sweet flavors;
one should bestow a golden lotus, a pair of garments, and a water-pot.
One should give a water-pot filled with sugar or filled with juice;
one should know "juice" (rasa) to mean ghee, milk, curd, honey, and sugar.
One should also feed them sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas), as well as wheat cakes (saṃyāva), fried cakes (pūrikās), ghārikās, apūpas, flour cakes (piṣṭāpūpas), and maṇḍakas. ||3.138.10||
One should likewise feed her milk, vegetables, milk-rice, and curd-rice, while addressing her as:
"O Kamalā, Mādhavī, Lakṣmī, Mother, Ramā, O Daughter of the Ocean! (11)
O auspicious Jayā, Kambharā, Śrī Mahālakṣmī, grant us happiness!
O Padminī, Padmajā, Kṛṣṇā, Nārāyaṇī, Narāyaṇī! ||12||
Oprimordial Śrī Lalitā, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, O Brāhmī, salutations be unto you!
O Vāsudevī, Great Goddess, O Hiraṇyā, whose form is wealth! ||13||
O you who possess all flavors, all happiness, and bestow all that is auspicious, by means of your vow, grant me prosperity and ultimate joy. (14)
Having thus worshipped the golden Lakṣmī,
who bestows the essence [of enjoyment] and is charming with the auspiciousness of the essence, one should present her as a gift to the venerable Guru.
Accompanied by the five jewels and other offerings, fashioned the size of a thumb, four-armed, and endowed with a discus, conch, rosary, and implements of worship. || 16 ||
Likewise, one should give a pair of cows, adorned with ornaments and clothed in garments, along with a calf, yielding milk, and auspicious, to a high-souled Brahmin.
Whoever performs this vow for the sake of the glory of Rasakalyāṇinī according to this rite is liberated from sins at that very moment.
By giving gold, a lotus, and Lakṣmī every month, O King, a ruler is honored in heaven for nine thousand arbudas of years.
Whether she be a woman, a maiden, a widow, or one who is chaste, she enjoys in heaven the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Having obtained the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, one shall attain good fortune and health;
even the giver of counsel rejoices in heaven in the abode of the gods.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another vow belonging to you alone, to be observed on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the very first day of the Cāturmāsya period. (22)
Having risen early in the morning and bathed, the observer of the vow should meditate upon the Lord Hari;
thereafter, he should worship the golden image of Ārdra-Ānanda-lakṣmī.

[He should worship] the Śrī of Nārāyaṇa, who is the size of a thumb, clothed in fine garments, and adorned with ornaments and finery, using darbha grass, fragrant water, and excellent sandalwood paste.

One should bathe [the deity] with white flowers, saffron, unbroken grains (akṣata), and offerings; one should also feed [the deity] with food offerings, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and ask for forgiveness.
Then, with hearts full of devotion, one should pray to Śrī, who is accompanied by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of one's own desires and the giver of what is desired.
Salutation to Mahālakṣmī for the feet; salutation be to you, O Mahāviṣṇu. Salutation to the destroyer of grief for the shanks; salutation be to you, the bestower of happiness. ||27||
Salutation to Kamalā for the thighs; salutation to Ānanda, O Hare, for the waist;
salutation to Īśvarī for the hips; salutation to you, the bestower of prosperity. ||28||
Salutation to Mādhavī at the navel; salutation to you who are the color of gold. Salutation to Poṣaṇakāriṇī at the breasts; salutation to you, Viśvaṃbharā. ||29||
Salutations to Sarasvatī at the throat; salutations to you, Nīlakaṇṭha.
Salutations to Kamaladhāriṇī in the hands; salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to the two arms, to the Protectress, and to the bearer of the Sudarśana discus;
I bow to the one with a moon-like face, to Cāndrī, to Hari, and to the one with the face of fire.
Salutations to the eyes that rain down compassion, and salutations to the abode of mercy;
salutations to the eyebrows that bestow security, and salutations to those who bring about well-being. ||32||
Salutations to you, who are the form of wealth upon the forehead and golden-hued;
salutations to you, who possess all jewels and the *kaustubha* gem upon your crown. ||33||
I bow to Ārdrāśraya and Ānandamādhava, who possess all bodies and all dwellings, who are endowed with all sovereign powers, and who grant all desires. (34)
The house was filled with abundance, including utensils, wealth, grain, and flavorful foods, as well as ornaments, garments, and other such things. ||35||
Make it resplendent with women, male and female servants, attendants, and offspring;
beautified by divine implements and endowed with cows, horses, and elephants. (36)

Abounding in gardens, groves, and fields, increased by fame and honor, rich in vehicles, celestial chariots, and mounts, and possessing excellent progeny in the form of disciples and grand-disciples. (37)
Abounding in joy, delight, and happiness, it was filled with enthusiasm and festivities, accompanied by instrumental music, song, great sacrificial sessions, acts of charity, and drinking. ||38||
Make my house a place constantly engaged in righteous rituals and sacrifices, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, free from obstacles, and devoted to the five great sacrifices.
It was beautiful on all sides with daughters-in-law, adorned by virtuous men and women, and constantly overflowing with the great devotion of the Supreme Lord. (3.138.40)
"Grant me my dwelling in the syllable *va*, which is rich with divine essence at the beginning.
Having thus petitioned and offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should dismiss [the deity]. ||41||
One should offer Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, along with moist objects of joy, to the venerable Guru;
likewise, one should bestow jewels, diamonds, and grain upon the twice-born.
One should feed children, the elderly, and others, and bestow auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
such as conch shells, discs, bracelets, svastikas, goads, and chowries.
One should give sweet foods and garments even to a virtuous person;
one should bestow vessels of ghee and vessels accompanied by gold.
Likewise, one should give vessels of sugar and roasted flour for four months,
as well as full vessels of sesame seeds and vessels of flavorful liquids.
Scented water, flower-water, sandalwood, saffron-water, uncurdled curds, milk, and also water from a cow's horn. ||46||
During the Cāturmāsya, one should always offer Tulasī and lotuses during worship;
in the act of giving, one should offer everything and speak thus before Śrī.
May Lakṣmī be ever pleased with me; may Mādhavī destroy my sins;
may Lalitā be gracious for my good fortune and my happiness. 48.
Having spoken thus, one should bestow everything on the tenth day of the month of Kārttika;
and again at dawn on the eleventh day, having offered a golden lotus.
Having performed the worship, one should complete the vow and bestow it upon a twice-born man, giving him a bed covered with cotton, saying: "May Lakṣmī be pleased with me. (3.138.50)
This is indeed the great Ārdrānana-Rāmā-Nārāyaṇa vow;
by means of it, one attains prosperity and eternal bliss both in this world and the next. (51)
Having enjoyed long-lasting celestial realms, one shall attain the supreme state;
for the listener, the speaker, and the rememberer as well, joy shall be certain.
Having experienced hundreds of great joys within his own home,
he further attains the station of Lakṣmī and the divine abode of Śrīpura.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another vow for you, the most excellent Śāradeya-vrata;
on the day of Bṛhaspati, your worship must be performed. (54)
Having made the pavilion auspicious, provided with arches and other ornaments, and enriched with golden jars, grains, seats, and so forth. (55)
In the center of that, one should have a beautiful elephant-throne made of gold fashioned;
upon that seat, one should install the virtuous goddess known as Śāradā-Ramā.
She has two arms, possesses graceful beauty, and is adorned with all ornaments;
she holds a lute and a lotus in her hands and is exquisitely beautified by her crown and other finery. ||57||
Then, one should place Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī at the sides—
[the goddesses] endowed with musical instruments, possessing divine forms, and holding Vedic manuscripts.

In this manner, one should worship the three goddesses there with perfumes and saffron, with unbroken grains (akṣata), white flowers and the like, and with substances such as incense and lamps. ||59||
One should likewise feed milk, milk-rice (pāyasa), cooked rice, and sweet foods;
one should also give him to drink cool water, rich with fragrance and sweetness.
One should offer betel-leaf and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
one should pray, "May Śāradā-Lakṣmī be pleased; may Vāṇī be gracious to me. (61)
By your grace, may I become a supreme ocean of knowledge;
may Sarasvatī dwell eternally upon the tip of my tongue. (62)
Act in such a way that I may attain eternal bliss in this world;
for the Vedas, the scriptures, weapons, and whatever there is of song, dance, and so forth—[all these are for that end].
O Vāṇī, may my accomplishments not be diminished by you; may they be thus:
Vāṇī, Medhā, Dharā, Puṣṭi, Gaurī, Tuṣṭi, Prabhā, and Mati. (64)
"O Nārāyaṇī, protect me with these eight forms.
Having thus prayed, one should give gifts as well as an offering of flowers.
One should feed children, the elderly, virtuous men, virtuous women, and other ladies;
and one should give wealth, garments, a water-pot, and a book.
One should perform the gift of musical instruments and the offering of ornaments for adornment;
one should provide entertainment and bestow prosperity upon the preceptor.
The observer of the vow should eat both morning and evening while observing a vow of silence;
this vow is to be performed every Thursday for thirteen months.
During the twilight hours, the observer of the vow should likewise maintain silence;
he should not eat in between until the vow has been completed. (69)
One should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) accompanied by a great festival;
one should give a pair of garments to a woman and provide a Brahmin with food.
The observer of the vow should perform the gift of a cow and the gift of a house according to his wealth;
having performed these according to this rule, he should partake of a grand meal consisting of milk-rice and other delicacies. (71)
Through the grace of Śāradā, one is born learned, wealthy, sweet-voiced, and observant of vows; he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||72||
Whether a man, a woman, or a maiden performs the Śāradā-vrata,
she becomes a Brāhmī and shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for thirty thousand kalpas.
He who, having undertaken the vow, performs the gift of knowledge through the bestowal of wealth, and the learned man who imparts knowledge, as well as he who observes the Śāradā-vow; ||74||
He shall dwell even in the city of the Vidyādharas for thirty thousand kalpas;
at the end, he goes to the city of Lakṣmī, and from there he shall proceed to the imperishable Brahman.
Now, O Lakṣmī, hear of another auspicious vow, the Kalyāṇī-kamalā-vrata, which bestows the fruit of all sacrifices and destroys every sin. (76)
It pacifies all evils without exception, is worshipped by all the gods, is the most sacred among the sacred, and the most auspicious among the auspicious. (77)
The auspicious Māgha-śukla-ekādaśikā-vrata is the deity of deities and the most ancient among the Purāṇas; it bestows well-being. (78)
Having performed an anointing with ghee on the tenth day, and having bathed in the morning with sesame seeds and water, one should worship Hari-Kṛṣṇa with all kinds of offerings.
Salutation to Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutation at the feet.
Salutation to the Soul of All; and salutation to Vaikuṇṭha on the face.
Repeated salutations again and again to the one who bears the Śrīvatsa on his chest,
and who holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the gesture of granting boons.
Salutation to Bāhu in all the arms, and to Dāmodara in the belly; salutation to Sukhada in the penis, and to Saubhāgyada in the thighs. ||82||
Salutations to the supporter of all beings at the knees; salutations to the bestower of liberation at the shanks;
salutations again and again to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of sins, at the feet. ||83||
Salutations to Kamalā, the doer of auspiciousness; salutations again and again.
Salutations to Śrī Lalitālakṣmī; salutations again and again to Jayālakṣmī. ||84||
Salutations to the glorious Lakṣmī Māṇikī; salutations to the Śrī of Nārāyaṇī;
salutations to the Lakṣmī who bestows auspicious happiness; salutations to the Śrī of Śivarājñī. ||85||
Salutations to the illustrious Pārvatī-Lakṣmī, the glory of the beloved’s splendor;
salutations to the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī, the glory of Mahālakṣmī. ||86||
Salutations to the glorious Santuṣṭi-Lakṣmī; salutations again and again to the Śrī of Kṛṣṇa.
Salutations to the glorious Rādhikā-Lakṣmī; salutations again and again to Ramā-Lakṣmī. (87)
Having thus bowed to Govinda and having bowed again and again to Śrī,
one should worship both of those bestowers of auspiciousness with all ritual offerings.
With perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and various kinds of edibles;
with water, betel, circumambulations, aratris, and likewise with the offering of flowers. (89)
May my Gopāla, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, be pleased with me;
may my auspicious Mahālakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī be pleased with me.
Having uttered this, the Supreme Goddess should be placed upon the bed;
she should also be worshipped at midday and fed at the beginning of the night.
One should worship with festivities and feed [the devotees] milk-rice and other such foods;
having slept [on the Ekādaśī], one should rise on the morning of the eleventh day and perform a ritual bath.
One should worship the auspicious Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite, together with Viṣṇu, in a beautiful, auspicious pavilion within a lovely *sarvatobhadra* mandala.

And having performed worship at the gift of a cow, one should perform the gift of a bed, the offering of a water-pot, the offering of prosperity, and the offering of jewels, ornaments, garments, vessels, and wealth. ||94||
The observer of the vow should offer grains, food, enjoyments, and so forth in the morning;
he should feed Śrī Mahālakṣmī with milk, auspicious fruits, and other such items. (95)
One should also worship at midday and offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods;
one should likewise worship in the evening and perform a vigil at night.
On the twelfth day, having performed worship according to the prescribed rite even at dawn,
one should bestow gifts upon the preceptor, the virtuous man, the virtuous woman, and the twice-born.
One should feed the virtuous Brahmins excellent and desirable foods;
likewise, one should feed the boys, girls, women, and holy men.
One should give many gifts and then observe the ritual exemptions;
one should recount this narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. (99)
From reciting this, hearing it, remembering it, and rejoicing in it,
there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and also many auspicious blessings.
In a previous birth, having performed the Kalyāṇinī vow as an Ābhīrī girl, she became the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, born as Urvaśī. || 101 ||
In ancient times, a daughter of Puloman, born of a Vaiśya family,
performed this vow and was reborn as Mahendrāṇī, the sovereign lady of heaven.
In the past, having performed this very vow, that twice-born son of a god then became the lord Sūrya, the master of heaven endowed with a thousand rays.
Therefore, the Kalyāṇikā-lakṣmī-vrata, which bestows one's own highest desired object and grants all auspiciousness, should be performed during three days in the month of Māgha. 104.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rasakalyāṇa-Lalitā Vow, the Ārdrānanda-Ramā-Nārāyaṇa Vow, the Śāradeya Vow, and the Kalyāṇī-Kamalā Vow," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 138 ||
The illustrious Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: O Lord Hari, out of compassion for me, please tell me here of that vow which serves specifically to dispel the sorrows that have come upon us.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
In the meritorious month of Āśvayuja, during the bright fortnight, there is the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśikā-vrata);
for the very purpose of destroying grief, there is the Viśoka-dvādaśī-vrata.
On the tenth day, having eaten light food, one should sleep upon the bare ground;
remaining celibate, one should rise early in the morning and remember me.
Having bathed and observed the vow on the eleventh day, one should worship me;
one may remain without food, subsist on fruit, or eat but a single meal.
Having had a golden image of Aśokalalitā fashioned, adorned with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and having worshipped it and fed [the recipient] upon an elephant-throne (gajāsana), || 5 ||
One should cause [the deity] to sleep and perform a vigil in a pavilion constructed of plantain trees;
then, having risen early on the twelfth day and bathed, one should worship once again.
One should perform a bath with all medicinal herbs and also with water consisting of the five products of the cow;
wearing yellow garments, one should worship Lakṣmī and the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu) with blue lotuses.
Salutation to Viśokā for the feet; salutation to Varadā for the shanks;
salutation to Śrī for the knees; and salutation to Abdhijayoṣit for the thighs.
Salutations again and again to Guptā and Viśokakārī at the waist; salutations to Māyā at the belly, and salutations to Poṣayitrī and Bhā at the two sides.
Salutations to Sarvadhartrī at the navel; salutations to Ardhāśrī at the heart;
salutations to Vāṇī at the throat; salutations to Kāntāśrī at the region of the chest.
Salutation to Rakṣayitrī on the two arms, and to Lalitā on the two hands;
salutation to Cāndrī on the face, and also to Kamalā on the two eyes. || 11 ||
Salutations to Surabhidevī in the nose, to Mohinīśrī on the forehead,
to Vyāpikā in the two ears, and salutations to Mahāśrī upon the head.
In a mandala, on a sacrificial mound, or in the presence of an image of Lakṣmī, one should worship me, Hari,
the Lord of Śrī, who am free from sorrow, in the form of gold.
Salutations to Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutations to Your feet. Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved; salutations again and again to Your shanks. (14)
Salutations to Śrī Vāsudeva; salutations again and again to your two knees.
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa; O Blessed One, salutations to your two thighs.
Salutations to you who are the form of bliss; salutations again and again to your penis.
Salutations to Nara-Nārāyaṇa at your hips; salutations again and again to you. (16)
Salutations to your belly, the sustainer of the universe; O Blessed One, salutations!
Salutations again and again to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at your two sides. || 17 ||
Salutations to you at the navel as Padmanābha; at the heart as the Yogi of the Swan;
at the throat as Nīlakaṇṭha; and salutations to Brahmā upon your chest. ||18||
Salutations to the bearer of the discus on his arms, to the holder of the conch in his hands,
to the one of beautiful form in his face, and to the lotus-eyed one in his eyes.

Salutations to you in the nose as the essence of all fragrances, on the forehead as the embodiment of the Guru, in the two ears as the creator of sacred revelation, and upon the head as the possessor of the crest-lock.
Having thus worshipped Govinda with fruits, garlands, and ointments, one should place a winnowing basket before Him and install me, Lakṣmī, therein. (21)
Homage to the two who bestow liberation and joy, and all forms of prosperity;
homage always to the two who effect the removal of sorrow.
O you who are free from sorrow, grant me freedom from sorrow for the destruction of suffering, and grant me boons.
Free from sorrow, they lead to my prosperity; free from sorrow, they lead to all success. ||23||
"You two lords are the destroyers of all my sorrows.
One should worship the winnowing basket, having enveloped it with white cloths and adorned it with fruits. (24)
Likewise, having worshipped with various kinds of garments and a golden lotus, one should feed [the recipient] auspicious milk-preparations and the like.
One should also worship with lotuses at the three times of day and offer food; furthermore, the observer of the vow should drink cool, pure water infused with *darbha* grass at night.
Then one should observe a vigil accompanied by song, dance, and instrumental music;
in the morning, one should worship Lakṣmī, who is free from sorrow, as well as the Lord of Śrī.
Then, one should also worship a married couple according to the prescribed rite for Brahmins;
one should bestow upon them garments, ornaments, food, vessels, cosmetics, and cloths.
One should bestow gifts of wealth and the presentation of jewels and cows according to one's capacity, and one should feed boys and girls. (29)
He should feed virtuous men and women and distribute food everywhere; he should grant exemptions and likewise bestow sacrificial fees.
By this procedure, one should perform the Viśokā-lalitā-vrata;
by means of the Viśokā-dvādaśī, his sorrows indeed perish. (31)
One should perform the gift of a cow, the gift of a bed with its pillows, and the offering of wealth; and one should praise Lalitā, Śrī, and Lakṣmī with heartfelt devotion. (32)
Just as fortune and prosperity do not abandon me and depart, so may I always possess beauty, health, and freedom from sorrow. (33)
May I have supreme devotion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved;
and may Kṛṣṇa, the Child-Kṛṣṇa, together with Lakṣmī, reside in my home. (34)
May he dwell there forever; likewise, I shall perform the gift of the fortune of the winnowing basket (śūrpalakṣmī), as well as a beautiful golden lotus, a karavīra flower, and saffron.
The ketakī, the sinduvāra, the mallikā, and likewise the kesara;
collyrium and red lac, sandalwood, and the kadambaka flower. (36)
I offer ointment, scented oil, and sandalwood;
I offer all kinds of decorative flowers for the sake of happiness. ||37||
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, or even performing this Viśokalalitā-vrata, there shall surely be both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 38.
Now, O Rame, I shall describe to you the vow known as Kṛṣṇalālana; through this excellent vow of tending to Kṛṣṇa, all prosperities indeed come to pass. (39)
This vow consists of three days during the bright fortnights of the months of Kārttika, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha.
On the tenth day, one who observes the vow of moral conduct should eat very light food at night;
having performed the evening worship, the observer of the vow should undertake the religious restriction.
Having risen in the morning, one should reflect: "I shall observe the vow of fasting on the eleventh day," and recite "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa. (42)
Having bathed on the morning of the eleventh day, one should worship the Lord—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Me, the Supreme Person—in the pavilion. 43.
With white flowers, unbroken grains of rice, water, saffron, sandalwood, and other offerings:
"Homage to Vibhūti" for the feet; "Homage to Aśoka" for the knees. (44)
"Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa" for the thighs; "Obeisance to Viśvamūrti" for the waist; "Obeisance to Kandarpa" for the penis; and "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" for the testicles. (45)
"To Dāmodara" [he worships] the belly; "to Vāsudeva," the two breasts;
"to Mādhava," the chest of Viṣṇu; and "salutation to the longing one," the throat. (46)
[One should offer] the face to Śrīdhara, the hair to Keśava,
the back to Śārṅgadhara, and the two ears to Śrutivedin.
"To Hari, who holds the conch, discus, sword, mace, and lotus in his hands—to that Soul of All, obeisance to His head"; thus is the worship. 48.
Having fashioned a golden fish joined with a lotus according to one's means, one should place it in a water-pot; having worshipped it for the sake of the gift, one should indeed bestow it.
Having worshipped a vessel of molasses mixed with sesame seeds and wrapped in a white cloth,
one should offer it along with various fruits as a gift.
One should perform the *ārārtrika* (luminous worship) for Vibhūti and Śrī-Kṛṣṇa,
offering various kinds of food oblations (*naivedya*) in the morning, at midday, and at the beginning of the night.
Having given gifts, he should also cause [the deity] to sleep with festivities of song and instrumental music;
the observer of the vow should keep a vigil and, having bathed in the morning, perform worship. 52.
On the twelfth day, one should also offer prayers and give a lotus to a brahmin;
likewise, one should give a water-pot containing jewels and a cow to the preceptor.
Just as you, O Kṛṣṇa, are never separated from all your divine manifestations, so likewise deliver me from the ocean of saṃsāra with its entirety of suffering. (54)
One should give a bed, one should give wealth, a village, a field, a house, and so forth;
having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should offer ornaments and garments.
One who observes the vow, even if poor, should worship with flowers and offer food for the meal; whoever performs this excellent vow of tending to Kṛṣṇa according to this rule, [attains the fruit].
One should perform the bestowal of prosperity; his supernatural powers (ṛddhi) shall arise at every step. His sins are destroyed, and he shall deliver a hundred ancestors.
Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, one shall not experience the fruit of sorrow;
moreover, there shall be no disease for him, nor poverty, nor bondage. (58)
For as long as one hundred and eight thousand yugas may last, so long shall that king dwell in heaven and be born again [as a ruler]. (59)
Having performed the vow, one goes indeed to the abode of Hari; of this there is no doubt.
And one enjoys all desires together with Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Hari.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in the Rathantara Kalpa, there was indeed a sinful hunter named Paruṣa; he was a consumer of meat, foul-smelling, and exceedingly wicked.
His wife, too, was exceedingly wicked and devoted to infidelity; both of them were intent on harming living beings. Once, in a forest, from a lake—
Taking many lotuses, they went to the city of Vaidiśa for the purpose of selling them, yet no sale occurred.
Despondent at that, both of them, hungry and exhausted, fell asleep on the path near the palace and heard [a sound] softly. (64)

In the pavilion, on the night of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, that excellent woman heard the auspicious sounds of the worship of Śrī Hari performed by the courtesans.
Then the courtesan Anaṅgavatī sang beautiful songs;
having performed worship that night, she gave away many gifts.
To a virtuous preceptor who is a learned Brahmin, one should offer a bed and other such items,
as well as a mountain of salt and even a golden image of Viṣṇu.
Having adorned Hṛṣīkeśa with abundant wealth and various kinds of grain, he fashioned a golden tree with garments for its foliage.
Upon seeing her, the two of them then reached this firm conclusion:
"Let us indeed offer these lotuses here as an act of worship. (69)
Thus, out of devotion, both the courtesan and the man gave a hundred pieces of wealth;
however, although they began to give it, the two of them did not accept it.
The food given for their meal, however, they did not accept,
as they were indeed aware of the greatness of fasting by virtue of their current circumstances.
Having kept watch throughout the night, the morning arrived;
at dawn, the courtesan was given a bed together with a mountain of salt.
With devotion, he gave twelve houses to his preceptor and to the Brahmins,
along with cows accompanied by their calves and provided with clothing and ornaments.
Food should be shared equally with friends, allies, the destitute, the blind, and the wretched;
this is seen as the proper honoring of a hunter as well as of a woman. (74)
In the Śrīharidvādaśikā, there is prasāda consisting of sugar;
thereafter, the water from the nectar of the feet was also taken. (75)
Yayāti and his wife went to their own home, and the courtesan also went to her own home;
those three, being full of devotion, eventually met their death in the course of time.
By offering lotuses there and by the virtuous act of offering [the image of] Keśava,
that hunter, having destroyed all his sins, became a possessor of merit.
In ancient times, there was a king named Puṣkaravāhana in the region of Puṣkarakhaṇḍaka;
after the king's name, that great region became known as Puṣkara.
By Hari, who was pleased by his devotion, and by Lakṣmī, who was satisfied by his vow, this was bestowed upon the king because of his excellent vow of tending to Kṛṣṇa and his resulting prosperity.
The lotus was beautiful, golden, a granter of desires, moving at will, and supreme;
it was [honored] by all the inhabitants of the city along with Kamala.
By means of that which is called a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the king traversed the heavens and the continents;
the seventh continent of this Puṣkara is named Puṣkara. (81)
He became renowned by the names Puṣpavāhana and also Puṣkarāsana; likewise, the queen was honored by thousands of women.
She was named Lāvaṇyavatī and was equal to Kamalā;
indeed, ten thousand sons were born to her by Puṣkara.
And she who was a courtesan was also born as the queen-consort and daughter-in-law of the king;
at the end of their lives, both the monarch and Lavaṇyā were indeed his beloveds. (84)
O Lakṣmī, that wife of Yayāti who became a courtesan abandoned her female body and attained my imperishable abode, the supreme state. (85)
The wife of Kāmadeva was indeed Prīti, who, together with her co-wife Rati, was born as the queen of the gods, the progenitor of joy throughout the worlds. (86)
This vow is proclaimed as the Kṛṣṇalālana-vibhūtidvādaśī-vrata, or alternatively, it is known as the Puṣkarapuṣpa-vrata. ||87||
In any manner whatsoever, on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), one should worship Hari with lotuses; furthermore, gifts and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; rather, one should offer according to one's means with devotion.
Either a golden lotus or a lotus born of water should be given. 89.
If a land-lotus is offered, the Lord of Kamalā becomes pleased;
he bestows universal sovereignty, as well as heaven and the supreme celestial realm.
Truth bestows either the solar, lunar, or Brahma-abode, or even the Vairāja, Vaiṣṇava, or Śrīpura-abode. ||91||
He bestows even Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, the unmanifest, as well as the immortal,
the imperishable supreme abode, and the abode of Brahman.
"I am the Lord of Abundance; indeed, through the vows of the Vibhūti-dvādaśī, O Lakṣmī, I bestow infinite qualities upon the worshiper. (93)
O Lakṣmī, those who have become universal monarchs (cakravartin) on the surface of the earth were born in previous kalpas through the observance of the Vibhūti-dvādaśī vow. ||94||
The lotus, the abode of Kamalā, is made of gold;
by the gift of this lotus, may I be united with Kamalā. (95)
I also dwell within the donor who possesses long life through a portion of myself;
indeed, I bestow the mark of the discus upon the hand of a universal monarch.
O Lotus-born One, the two middle fingers are the conchs and the remaining eight [fingers] are the discs; thus, these very discs belong to Nārāyaṇa himself. (97)
A lotus in the hand and a lotus on the foot belong to a Cakravartin;
likewise, I indeed grant the banner-mark in the hand to the giver of the banner.
To the one who offers a trident, I give a trident;
and to the one who offers a bow with an arrow, I give a bow with an arrow. (99)
I place a most beautiful fish into the hand of the giver of fish,
and I bestow a svastika upon the giver of a svastika.
To the giver of golden banners and the like, I grant everything in every way:
indeed, the earth together with the oceans, and even the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
He in whose right hand there are these six— the banner, the trident, the bow, the arrow, the fish, and the svastika— he is I myself, Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, having placed you in my heart in the form of a virtuous woman,
and holding you upon my left thigh with your pale-white luster, I dwell upon the earth.
O Lakṣmī, you are invisible to people; you shine forth through my service.
At that time, when you were in the form of a virtuous woman, you appeared quite different from who you are now.
You are the embodiment of prosperity, bestowing prosperity through your vows;
on my left hand is a long line of a staff, which awakens me to dharma. 105.
On both my feet there are upward-pointing lines extending across both;
they awaken the inner self within the two abodes of creation, and they too are of that same nature.
By my grace, this may even become a mark of my devotee;
by reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of divine manifestations (vibhūti).

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Viśokalalitā-dvādaśī Vow and the Vibhūtilalitā-kṛṣṇalālana Vow, along with the Example of the Universal Monarch named Puṣkaravāhana and the Characteristics of a Universal Monarch," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, you have described to me the purifying vows; please now announce other new ones that remain."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Kamalā, there are many vows that grant liberation and also bestow various kinds of worldly enjoyment; listen as I describe them to you.
Those actions performed with a desire for fruits indeed yield enjoyment; however, those performed for the sake of my grace truly grant liberation.
Eating only at night for one year is declared to be the *nakta* vow;
the practitioner of that vow should begin it either from the month of Kārttika or from Āṣāḍha.
Beginning from the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], when the year is complete,
one should give a golden Sudarśana discus along with a cow as an offering to the venerable Guru.
One should also feed virtuous people and perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow;
by giving gifts of clothing, one rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should observe the vow of eating once a day, consisting of a meal at midday;
having offered everything to the Deity, one should eat, and never otherwise. (7)
This shall be the vow for a year, and at the end of the year, there should be a great festival;
one should perform the rite of formal completion (udyāpana) and bestow a golden bull.
One should also distribute food to the virtuous and bestow cows;
furthermore, one should observe the vow of eating only every other day for the duration of a year.
One should eat at intervals of one day, and at the conclusion of the vow, hold a great festival;
one should give a golden lotus as a gift and perform the formal rite of completion (udyāpana).
One should give a vessel filled with sugar and feed the virtuous; the observer of the vow attains great merit and, at the end, indeed reaches the station of Viṣṇu.
During the four-month period, one should avoid anointing the body with excellent oils;
this avoidance of anointing is declared to be a supreme vow and a great austerity.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should offer gifts such as oil and also provide various foods;
this is pleasing to me, and by it, one goes to the abode of Hari.
The avoidance of flavors is also proclaimed as the "vow of flavors" (rasavrata).
[These consist of: honey, coconut water, curd, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice. (14)
Or at the end of the year, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana);
one should also give gifts of liquids and the like, and offer fine garments. || 15 ||
One should always perform the vow of desirelessness, which destroys sorrow;
during the Cāturmāsya period, one should always be devoted to celibacy.
When the vow is completed, one should offer a golden Aśoka tree;
one should also offer sugarcane and likewise offer garments.
Having enjoyed these pleasures, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
indeed, the observer of the vow should avoid clipping his nails during the Cāturmāsya period.
One should also avoid shaving the hair during the Cāturmāsya period; having observed this vow known as "not cutting," one should perform a great festival.
At the conclusion, one should perform the rite of completion (udyāpana) and feed virtuous people milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should give gifts of gold, nails, and hair to the twice-born.
O Lakṣmī, one should daily offer an image of my gentle form;
this is proclaimed as the "Gentle Vow" (saumyavrata), lasting for the duration of a month.
In Vaikuṇṭha he shall be liberated with a serene countenance, and here on earth he shall indeed become the moon;
at the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he should give many gifts of jewels.
In the month of Kārtika, having worshipped a golden image adorned with household utensils, one should give it to the Guru; this is called the Saubhāgyavrata.
Then one should offer an image of Viṣṇu and an image of Śrī to the venerable Guru; on other occasions, one should perform various acts of giving while saying, "May Śrī Hari be pleased."
One should observe the Sārasvata vow, maintaining silence during the twilight hours;
having performed this vow for a year, one should offer a pot of clarified butter and a jar of sesame seeds.
One should give a pair of garments, an alms-bowl, and a bell to a twice-born man;
one should give the gift of a cow to the preceptor, as well as the gift of books. (26)
And this Sārasvata vow bestows knowledge, beauty, and other such qualities.
Then, on the fifth lunar day, one should perform the auspicious Sampad-vow dedicated to Mādhavī.
One should worship Lakṣmī constantly, and at the end of the year,
one should give a golden lotus to the preceptor, as well as a milch cow together with her calf.
He, endowed with prosperity, attains the station of Viṣṇu birth after birth;
he should always indeed sweep the entire temple of the Lord, the Consort of Śrī. (29)
At the end of the year, he should present a milch cow as well as a water-pot;
by that, he shall become a king for ten thousand births and thereafter go to the city of Viṣṇu.
This is called the Āyurvrata, which effects the cleansing of sins.
Now, one should perform the Kīrtivrata and always observe eating only once a day.
At the end of the year, one should give ten cows and a golden tree;
there shall be the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, and it will result in prosperity and fame. ||32||
Now, the vow of the Sāman is proclaimed; one should constantly recite the hymn before Hari at the three times of day, and the gift of sesame seeds should be given daily.
One should offer flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) for the purpose of worshipping Hari;
and when the year has been fully completed, one should present a great golden lotus.
One who gives a sesame-cow (tiladhenu) measuring eight finger-breadths attains the supreme state. Then, on the ninth lunar day, one should observe the Vīra-vrata while eating only once a day.
A maiden should feed [the preceptor] for a year; at the end of the year, she should likewise give to the venerable guru a golden bodice, garments, and a golden lion.
One should bestow ornaments, garments, and other gifts upon the maidens according to their merit;
by doing so, one will be handsome for a hundred million births and, at the end, go to the abode of Hari.
Likewise, for one year he should observe the milk-vow on the full moon day;
at the end of the year, he should give five milch cows along with their calves.
He who gives saffron-colored garments along with water-pots goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and shall deliver a hundred of his ancestors.
One should perform the ancestral Śrāddha rite; this is considered the vow dedicated to the ancestors.
Furthermore, during the four months beginning with Caitra, one should offer cool water.
One should cause all the people to drink [the water], and at the conclusion of the vow, one should present a water-jar;
one should also give food, garments, a vessel of sesame seeds, and gold.
This is the Jalānanda vow; by it, one becomes a king at the end of the kalpa.
Then, one should perform the Dhṛtivow, [meditating] daily upon me, Śrī Hari. 42.
Then, one should perform a beautiful ablution with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
at the end of the year, one should also perform the gift of a conch, and [the devotee] goes to the abode of Hari.
At the end of the rainy season, the person who has performed the vow shall not harm any living beings;
he should indeed perform this gift of a cow and the gift of a golden deer.
By this vow of non-violence, one becomes a sovereign at the end of the eon;
then, one should perform the ritual bath in the month of Māgha with cold water.
One should worship the Sun daily and give gifts to the twice-born, such as grain, clothing, ornaments, and so forth; that is called the Sūryavrata.
During the Cāturmāsya, one should worship Mahāviṣṇu and Mahālakṣmī; the observer of the vow should also, according to his capacity, bestow gifts of cows and provide food. (47)
He indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; this auspicious vow is the Viṣṇuvrata.
Now follows the vow named Śīla, which bestows the fruit of good character and health. 48.
Whether a woman or a man, one should observe the vow of celibacy for a full year;
furthermore, one should donate a cow filled with ghee and offer garlands of flowers.
One should feed excellent virtuous men ghee and superior milk-rice (pāyasa);
at the end of the year, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and bestow grain and wealth.
He attains the imperishable state of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
furthermore, he shall not consume oil for a year and should offer a lamp.
One should give gold, a lamp, and a golden discus to a twice-born;
by giving a pair of garments, he indeed goes to the abode of Brahmā.
This is declared to be the Dīpa-vrata (the lamp vow), which bestows radiance as well as beauty.
Now, beginning from the month of Kārttika, one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) only at night.
At the end of the year, one should also give a cow; this is indeed the vow known as Pāyasa, which brings about auspiciousness for the earth, bestows sovereignty, and grants liberation. (54)
Then, one should always avoid perfumes, ointments, and the like for a year;
this is declared to be the vow called "Fragranceless," at the end of which there is the gift of fragrance. (55)
Then one should perform the Kānti-vrata; one should give the gift of a cow every day, and from then on for a year, one must not eat salt at all.
And one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), which bestows the fruits of splendor and fame;
having become a king for a full kalpa, one shall dwell eternally in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, on an auspicious day, one should perform the Brahmavrata by giving a small, beautiful golden vessel filled with sesame seeds to a twice-born man.
The observer of the vow should likewise eat sesame seeds for three days;
furthermore, the observer of the vow should perform the gift of garlands, garments, and ornaments.
He goes to the world of Brahmā and shall attain the state of Nirvāṇa;
the Brahmāṇḍa is proclaimed to extend from three palas upwards according to one's capacity.
Then one should perform the Dhenu-vrata; for three days one should observe the milk-vow (payovrata), and should give a golden bull and a cow that has calved for the first time (ubhayatomukhī).
One should also bestow rice and a golden bull weighing half a pala;
by giving these and through the excellent vow of the cow, one goes to the abode of Brahmā and to Goloka.

Then one should perform the Kalpa-vrata; having fashioned a wish-fulfilling tree out of materials weighing more than a pala, one should give it to a virtuous person along with rice grains containing double-shelled seeds.
By means of a kalpa-gift, at the end of the kalpa, one goes from heaven to my state;
furthermore, one who observes a month-long fast should bestow an auspicious buffalo-cow.
One should give this milch buffalo to the venerable Guru; this is called the buffalo-vow (māhiṣa-vrata). One should also give a beautiful golden image of the earth weighing more than twenty palas.
This is declared to be the Dharā-vrata; by eating only one meal a day, one dwells in the abode of the Lord of Śrī for seven hundred kalpas.
Then that person, who observes the vow of the earth, goes to the imperishable abode;
my devotee indeed proceeds to me and, becoming an attendant, serves me.
In the months of Māgha and Caitra, one devoted to the Guḍavrata should give jaggery;
eating jaggery and drinking jaggery, he should worship with sesame seeds and jaggery.
One should offer me and Lakṣmī, along with molasses, an image made of molasses and molasses itself at the gift of molasses.
This is declared to be the Guḍavrata, which bestows liberation and grants salvation. (69)
Then, one who has observed the fast for a fortnight should present a pair of tawny cows;
he should also perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), which brings about supreme bliss.
At the end of the eon, he shall become a king of kings; that indeed is the Kapila-vow.
Furthermore, eating but once a day for a year, he should always provide food and water. (71)
One shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu at the end; this is considered the Prāpti-vrata.
One should eat only at night on the eighth lunar days and, at the end of the year, give a cow as a gift.
Thereupon he goes to heaven, and at the end, he attains the state of Brahmā; this very vow is called the "vow of the good destination," for it bestows a happy rebirth. (73)
He who gives fuel to a Brahmin for a year, as well as one who gives a cow,
and he who performs this Vaiśvānara vow, goes to Brahman.
On the eleventh day, the observer of the vow gives on the twelfth day a beautiful golden image of the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
At the conclusion of the year, the observer of the vow who gives a golden discus dedicated to Viṣṇu—
having performed this Kṛṣṇa-vow— shall become a partaker of sovereignty at the end of the kalpa.
Having given me away at the end of the year, he shall indeed attain my abode;
moreover, one who subsists on milk-rice should give a pair of cows to a Brahmin at the end of the year.
One attains the world of Lakṣmī; this is called the Śrī-vrata.
He who, on the seventh lunar day, should give away a beautiful, milch cow, [attains that same world]. (78)
One indeed goes to the world of the Sun; that is called the Bhānu-vrata.
On the fourth lunar day, one should eat only at night and, at the end of the year, donate a golden elephant.
The vow known as Vaināyaka bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
during Cāturmāsya, the observer of the vow should offer fruits made of gold and silver.
This fruit-vow, which bestows the world of Viṣṇu, is indeed of great power;
he who fasts on the seventh lunar day should, at the conclusion of the year, offer a golden lotus.
One should also give cows along with a golden vessel; this is proclaimed as the Saura-vrata.
This gift to the Sun bestows the world of the Sun; one should likewise offer it. 82.
Having completed twelve twelfth-day observances (dvādaśīs) by means of fasting,
the practitioner of the vow should give cows, garments, gold, and ornaments to his venerable guru.
O Rame, one attains the supreme state by this vow of Viṣṇu; having performed the ritual release of a bull on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should observe the practice of eating only at night.
One attains the state of Śiva; this is considered the vow for a year.
One should give gold in the measure of a cow's footprint as a gift; this is the vow of the footprint (padavrata).
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a virtuous person;
this is declared to be the "Ghee Vow," which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.
One who sleeps in the open air during the rains should, at the conclusion, give a milch cow;
this vow, known as Ākāśa, bestows the station of Indra.
Thereafter, on the third [lunar day], he shall eat food not cooked by fire;
and at the end of the month, he should indeed perform the gift of a milch cow.
This is declared to be the Śreyas-vrata, which bestows Goloka and grants happiness;
one should fashion an auspicious chariot drawn by horses out of gold weighing more than two palas on the full moon day of Āśvayuja.
One who observes the vow of the chariot while giving gifts shall dwell swiftly in heaven for a hundred kalpas;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings, and thereafter proceed to the supreme state.
He who performs fasts for six months, skipping every other day, and at the end of the year becomes a giver of cows; this is called the Vāruṇa vow.
Having attained the kingdom of Varuṇa, he then goes to the supreme state.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow and bestow a golden moon upon a worthy person.

This Candra-vrata is supreme, bestowing the fruit of the world of the Moon; during the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should constantly perform the penance of the five fires and become a donor of gold and a cow.
This is declared to be the vow of austerity; from it, one attains sovereignty, and thereafter one attains Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Imperishable (Akṣara). ||94||
One should offer a canopy made of cloth or similar materials in the temple;
by the excellent fruit of the canopy-vow, the giver of the canopy goes to heaven. (95)
In the month of Māgha, one should remain wearing wet clothes; on the seventh day, one should become a giver of cows.
Such a practitioner of the Ārdra-vow becomes a king [on earth] and goes to heaven, attaining liberation.
He who, observing the Dhāma-vrata, gives a most excellent mansion as a gift during the month of Phālguna,
indeed goes to the abode of the Supreme Lord.
Having honored a virtuous man and a virtuous woman, one should feed them excellent sweets;
then one may eat the *prasāda* oneself—this indeed is the vow known as *Prasāda*. (98)
It removes all sins, bestows merit, and likewise grants liberation;
it is purifying, the most excellent of all, and the supreme sanctifier of the assembly.
Having practiced eating a single meal a day and, at the end of the year, having gifted a tawny cow,
and being a constant worshiper of Vaiśvānara, he goes to Vibhāvasu.
This Vaiśvānara-vrata bestows divinity and grants happiness; one who eats only once on the tenth day and, at the conclusion of the vow, gives ten cows [attains these fruits]. 101.
One should give a golden leaf; one shall become the sovereign of the Brahmāṇḍa.
O Lakṣmī, this is indeed declared as the Viśvavrata, an ocean of merit.
One should always perform *kīrtana*; this indeed is the vow called *kīrtana*. One should always perform the narration of the sacred story; this indeed is the vow called *kathā*.
One should always perform worship; this indeed is the vow known as Bhajana.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the sixty-one vows have been described to you.
For the sake of benefiting the worlds, since the world possesses three limbs through the recitation, hearing, remembering, and even the performance of this [text]. (105)
Through rejoicing in [the merit], through giving, and even by providing assistance, one certainly obtains the merit of the vow; one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (106)
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "A Brief Description of the Sixty-one Miscellaneous Vows," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Lord of the Imperishable, O Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my Lord;
O Sovereign of Goloka, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Narāyaṇa! (1)
O Infinite One, O Lord of the Indeterminate, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of Immortality, O Consort of Śrī, O Dweller in the City of Śrī! Whatever vows there may be, [those indeed... 2.
For how can there be liberation for one who is not at all able to perform [it]—such as a woman, a child, an elderly person, the sick, or even beasts and birds? (3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Rame, by the remembrance of My name, his liberation shall come;
[O] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Satpati!
O Śrīkṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O glorious Nārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa! O Govinda, O Mādhava, O Viṣṇu, O Master, O Sovereign of Men, O Acyuta!
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Blue-throated One, O Bringer of Happiness to Mahālakṣmī!
O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Ocean of Compassion, O Glorious Son of Gopāla! 6.
O son of Kambharāśrī, you who are the lord of Aśvapaṭṭasara,
whose dwelling has been established at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, abide in my heart.
O Rāma, O illustrious lotus-eyed one, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O All-pervading One!
O Sovereign of the beloved of Hari, protect me and release me from this bondage. || 8 ||
Thus, the chanting of these names of mine indeed bestows liberation;
furthermore, so too does [the chanting] of my abode, the sacred field known as Akṣara.
One should hear and recite the greatness of Aśvapaṭṭasara, the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and of this sacred ford.
One should indeed listen to the narrations of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā,
which consists of one hundred thousand verses and twenty-five thousand more.
One should hear the collection consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses,
which fulfills the desires for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the embodiment of the Saṃhitās; I abide on earth in the form of this second scripture.
In all the worlds of living beings as well as in the worlds of the Lord,
and even in the Imperishable (akṣara), I abide as the essence of the collection [of sounds], having sound as my form.
Whether it be a chapter, a section, a continuous passage, or even a single verse, whoever shall recite this, being the self of all beings, shall become a liberated soul. || 15 ||
He who hears this with a steady mind will become one whose self is Brahman;
those who bow down to my reciter shall become purified.
Those who perform worship of him and go to the sacred ford at Lomaśa’s hermitage shall dwell there perpetually and attain the supreme heaven.
Their enjoyment as well as their liberation has come into my hands through my grace;
they shall proceed to the Supreme Imperishable by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot.
Those who offer praise shall go to the city of Śrī;
women who perform pilgrimage there shall go to Lalitāpura. (19)
Indeed, they shall rejoice with Nārāyaṇī Śrī in the Imperishable Realm;
likewise, they shall abide in the abode together with Śivarājyā Lakṣmī.
Having obtained me, who am dark and beloved, they shall rejoice eternally.
O Lakṣmī, I am the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), and you are a sacred ford equal to me.
And our dwelling place and sacred site are like the Imperishable (Akṣara),
located in Saurāṣṭra and the Ānarta region, all around the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
To the south of Bhadrāvatī and to the west of Śatruñjayā,
on the eastern side of Mount Raivata, in the northern region of the Vyāghrī forest.
O Lakṣmī, this very circular field of one hundred krośas in extent bestows liberation, destroys sin, and grants all the goals of human existence. 24.
Those who have bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake indeed go to heaven and liberation;
for I am Hari, the Maṇḍala consisting of the Kuṅkumavāpī field. 25.
I protect it in every way, even from millions of liberated lords of the gods;
I protect my beloved Badrī at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
By remembering her, a human being indeed becomes capable of burning away sins;
this occurs through the sight of that Badarī, or even by the chanting of her name. (27)
By touching its clay, a man is liberated from sin;
even from thousands of yojanas away, a man is freed by the mere remembrance of Badarī.
Whether a woman or a child, one attains the supreme goal;
by the touch of the leaves and flowers of the Badarī tree, one finds auspicious blessings. (29)
Having plunged into it and drunk from it, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
Meditating upon Badarī with the mind, one obtains abundant desires.
Having gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā, which is adorned with the splendor of Badarī,
one should dwell there for a month as a celibate student and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Wherever he is born, he obtains his desired objects;
[so do] the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
Having seen Badrī and drunk its water, they departed for my imperishable abode—
the refuge of the distressed, the poor, and those of resolute determination.
There is nothing else equal to Kuṅkumavāpikā-Badrī that bestows liberation;
whether one is afflicted by disease, wretched, or old, [one attains it] through the service of Badrī.
Or, if one should relinquish one's life by fate in the vicinity of Badarī, one shall travel in celestial chariots possessing the luster of glowing gold and resembling the sun. ||35||
He goes indeed to the abodes of Kṛṣṇa and rejoices there for eternal years;
he obtains all his desired objects, including all enjoyments and the like. ||36||
In the eternal state, he rejoices in celestial palaces made of all kinds of jewels, adorned with various banners and filled with beautiful women.
In that world where the trees bear the fruit of all desires and the earth is made of gold,
there one is glorified amidst lands of every flavor.
Even by merely remembering Badarī as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā,
one casts off the vital breath and goes indeed to the world of Brahmā, which is higher than the highest.
He who, supported by righteousness and truth, bestows a cow upon the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā through deed, mind, or speech— 3.141.40.
One should bestow gold, jewels, pearls, wealth, grain, and likewise clothing,
for one’s own purposes, for ancestral rites, and also for the worship of the gods.
For one who remains in the imperishable state, an infinite-fold merit is attained;
it is as if one were to give away a single milch cow from among hundreds of thousands of cows.
A cow given right here saves one's sons, servants, and dependents;
likewise, he who bestows a daughter in marriage at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā [is saved]. ||43||
By the rite of marriage performed in his abode, there is infinite merit;
and this jewel from Saurāṣṭra is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, eternally embodied. (44)
O Lotus-born one, even at the time of universal dissolution there is no destruction of this [liṅga] due to my residence within it,
just as there was none for the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices at Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara.
By bathing there, one indeed attains the eternal fruit of liberation from rebirth;
ten thousand tīrthas and sixty crores likewise reside with me, O Rāma.
All of these reside here within my own abode;
therefore, one who gives a golden woman here becomes a dweller in heaven.
He shall obtain a hundred maidens resembling Urvaśī, and he shall become the husband of many thousands of women in their midst. (48)
Where Aśvapaṭṭasara is, that is indeed my field of perfection;
having plundered there, the sinful soul becomes a purifier of the assembly. 49.
The site of Kuṅkumavāpikā is the most purifying of purifiers, the most auspicious of auspicious things, and the bestower of liberation among all givers of liberation.
And on the northern side of Sarasa, from Pātāla, flows the inexhaustible river Śvetadvīpa-Mahāgaṅgā, impelled by Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. 51.
Flowing within the waters, the white river Viṣṇupadī, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, descends here from heaven and remains invisible.
And the Brahmahrada lake is always present at my feet;
from its waters flows the river of nectar from the celestial realm. (53)
Indeed, all the immortals dwell there on the ground of the Horse-Lake;
and a person who performs pilgrimage here obtains the fruit of fasting unto death.
He who bathes for one month in the waters of Aśvapaṭṭasara is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state. ||55||
But he who, out of ignorance, undertakes a pilgrimage to sacred fords and the like in this world, is honored in the heavenly realm, with all his desires fulfilled. ||56||
Once, the divine Lomaśa went to the land of Prayāga;
however, Prayāga was not there, for the sage Bharadvāja was present instead. ||57||
Lomaśa, the king of holy places, asked Bharadvāja:
"O sage, where has he gone today? I have had no sight of him. (58)
Then Bharadvāja said: "Whatever great sins or heinous crimes have been committed by men, they are all cast off upon bathing at Kumbhayoga. (59)
He went to the Aśvasarovara at Prayāga to wash them,
where there is the sacred site known as Kuṅkumavāpī, wherein Lakṣmī herself resides.
Even though the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dwells there, Prayāga has gone there; see, he will arrive quickly.
Lomaśa, having seen the enclosure there, stayed for a moment;
meanwhile, Prayāga arrived, having completely shaken off all his sins.
Having honored him, Lomaśa went to the Badarikāvana;
however, there was no divine Badarī tree there, which is the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Then the slender sage himself was not looked upon by Lomaśa;
he was asked, "Where is the pilgrimage to Badarī, and when will it take place? (64)
The slender body replied, "She has gone and is now at Aśvasarovara in Saurāṣṭra, [worshipping] Śrīpati Puruṣottama in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (65)
In order to serve her beloved lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Life,
that beautiful beloved of Brahmā exists in the form of a maiden among the wives of Brahmā.
Having become the bride and a maidservant of Hari, she shines there together with Lakṣmī;
at times, she appears there as an ascetic on the bank of the Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Muktakoṭikā exists in the form of a jujube tree, extending her celestial palace directly above the oblong pond. 68.
And on the northern ground, those branches which extend over the long pond always remain in the form of umbrellas, impelled by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (69)
O sage, she who is the large-eyed consort of Hari shines there;
she herself is Badarī, and she is resplendent there.
Even here, for the sake of the Blessed One, it exists in another form;
