at the time of Hari’s dwelling, it becomes a provider of shade. (71)
"Knowing this, the venerable sage Lomaśa understood that she would arrive here quickly at the time of midday from the hermitage of the great seer Tantu. (72)
That virtuous maiden Badarī remained there until midday;
then, arriving swiftly by way of the sky, she became Badarikā.
Having worshipped her and likewise having worshipped the illustrious Narayana situated beneath her, Lomasa proceeded to the great Bālakṛṣṇa lake.
Having bathed in Lake Mānasa, he traveled through the air to Saurāṣṭra;
having made his resolve, he then dwelt eternally in my abode.
Knowing the greatness of the earth at the site of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
I indeed [established] that Badarī as Mahālakṣmī together with Nārāyaṇa.
Commanded to remain forever, she dwells upon the bank of the pond;
though her form may be visible at one time, it shall also become invisible at another.
Furthermore, she will become visible again in the assembly of devotees;
likewise, other beloveds of Brahmā shall also assume the form of Badarī.
Becoming thousands of long ponds, subsisting upon that water, they will be visible there; the earth does not become empty.
Likewise, goddesses dear to Hari dwell here as creepers;
one named Anārakalikā assumes the form of a pomegranate tree.
My wife, Uttejinī, exists in the form of a tamarind tree;
and there are two Hingu trees, one called Snehilī and the other Subhagā. (81)
Jāmbuvatī is my wife; there Jāmbikā resides. There also dwell Rāviṇī, Gāyikā, and Rāvaṇikā. ||82||
In this way, I have other dear friends, and they likewise have others; furthermore, a maiden named Dugdhikā-vallī resides there. (83)
Indeed, there are many rows of trees in the form of gardens within the flower-beds; the pearl-like women of divine and beautiful form always serve me there. (84)
In some places they appear as trees and creepers; in some places they are lovely women of beautiful form; in some places they are visible, and in others they become invisible. (85)
In some places they are on my bed, in some places indeed on my elephant-throne; in some places they sport with me in a celestial vehicle.
In some places on the side of the Rāsa-dance ground, in some places even in my pavilion,
and in some places merged within my heart, they become devourers of bliss.
Having attained a state of uniformity in certain respects, they rejoice with intoxicated souls;
yet they become distinct during eating, playing, drinking, and service.
O Lakṣmī, just as you abide in my heart, at my side, and in my presence, so too do those auspicious lotuses like you abide for me. (89)
Wherever their dwelling is, O Lakṣmī, that ground is my imperishable abode;
it is the best of all holy places, the most excellent among the foremost of sacred sites.
In every kalpa, in the land of Surāṣṭra, the holy site of Kuṃkumavāpikā-tīrtha exists by my will alone; it was created by me at the beginning of the cosmic egg.
Surāṣṭra and your kingdom shall be independent on this island-like land;
the dark soil is equal to Kṛṣṇa, for she who belongs to Kṛṣṇa is my very own form.
The land is like a gateway to liberation and purifying in every age, where there exists the river named Subhadrā-Bhadrikā, which was created by me. (93)
By the mere remembrance, touch, or even drinking of a drop of its water, the destruction of sin certainly occurs; likewise, one shall go to heaven and attain the imperishable state. ||94||
Even for a man who is half of me, when he is separated from me for a moment, his sovereign powers dissolve and his feminine splendors are cast down. ||95||
Then, by the Dasyus, Bhadrā Subhadrā, that most excellent river,
who was like a great sacred ford (tīrtha) and the wife of a king, remained within the water.
Bestowing constant auspiciousness upon those who bathe there, she exists as the river Kāryarūpā, the very embodiment of Śrī Puruṣottama, manifesting every form of welfare. (97)
My sister, possessing a divine form and ever contented, dwells at Badarī;
in my own abode, Muktānikā manifests in five forms. (98)
The oceans, lakes equal to the ocean, and likewise rivers—all these holy ones exist within my Kuṅkuma pond, possessing the nature of Brahman. (99)
Indeed, all the Vedas and sacrifices are present here in personified form within this Imperishable One;
so too are the great seers, the ancestors, the perfected beings, and the stainless holy ones.
The truthful, the virtuous, the wielders of the discus, and the attendants who bear the discus worship me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, who am without beginning.
This is a great field of accomplishment, a realm of light, and the supreme beyond the supreme;
this is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is truth, and this is bliss.
This is merit, this is righteous, this is purifying, and this is the supreme teaching of Kṛṣṇa;
by hearing even this, one rejoices greatly in the highest heaven, as if having reached every sacred ford.
One attains the recollection of past births and even the memory of all things;
one understands that which pertains to the three periods of time and also acquires omniscience.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Even Sinners Attain Liberation through Remembering, Beholding, and Other Means Related to the Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, protector of all, omnipresent one!
How does a human being on earth conquer death born of the three periods of time? (1)
By what means can powerful death, which has turned back from no one, be warded off?
Or in what form does death pursue human beings? (2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, O Rame, and also O Lakṣmī born from the ocean; listen, O Akṣaramāṇikī!
Garuḍa, indeed my devotee, sat within my house, chanting my mantra with a rosary and meditating upon my divine form. || 4 ||
Then, being questioned by his father Kaśyapa, the son said:
"O son, how can death be averted for one who is a great devotee and a yogi? (5)
In what form does death indeed arrive and carry one away?
How is it that its touchlessness is experienced here by the embodied being?
Having heard this, the bird spoke to his father: "I shall say this:
through devotion, death turns away from one who takes refuge in the Supreme Self. (7)
A mendicant carrying a staff and bearing weapons, or one who is naked and so forth—the messenger of Death—approaches assuming that very form; by his bite, one does not live.
If three fangs are found embedded in a bite on a funeral pyre, an anthill, a mountain, and so forth, or in a well, a hole, or at the base of a tree, the bitten person does not live.
On the sixth lunar day, in Cancer and Aries, and during the asterisms of Mūla, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and others,
[affliction occurs] in the armpits, hips, throat, joints, temples, ears, abdomen, and so forth.
One bitten on the face, the arm, the neck, or the back is not a victim of Śrīpati;
the remaining [locations] are said to belong to Arka, Phaṇipati, Candra, and Takṣaka, and Bhauma respectively. (11)
Karkoṭaka is Mercury, Padma is Jupiter, Mahāpadma is Venus, Śaṅkha is Saturn, Rāhu is Rāhu, and Kulika is Ketu; these are the planets. (12)
One bitten by a snake of that particular species in those respective planetary positions does not survive:
the big toe corresponds to the first lunar day (*pratipad*), and the two backs of the feet correspond to the second day (*dvitīyā*).
The third day should be for the two ankles, the fourth for the two knees;
the fifth is considered the lunar day for the penis and the vulva, and the sixth for the navel.
The heart is said to be the seventh [stage], and the breasts the eighth day;
the throat is said to be the ninth, and the nostrils the tenth.
The two eyes are to be known as the eleventh [tithi], the two ears are considered the twelfth;
the two eyebrows are the form of the thirteenth, and the conch-shell is considered the fourteenth.
One should bite the head on that fifteenth lunar day at that specific location;
then, bitten by the mouth of Time, the embodied being does not live.
This is considered to be on the right side for a man and on the left side for a woman;
one bitten at such a moment never lives. (18)

However, one should perform the recitation of "Oṃ Garuḍa Svāhā" for one hundred thousand times; while reciting it, one should touch [the body] at the big toe, the sole, the back of the foot, and the ankle. (19)
In the shanks, the knees, the thighs, the penis, the vulva, the hips, the buttocks, the region of the navel, the loins, and the belly and heart. || 3.142.20 ||
In the regions of the sides of the breasts, in the arms, on the palms of the hands, in the fingers, at the elbows, in the throat, at the neck, and at the nape of the neck; ||21||
One should strike on the mouth, the cheeks, the nose, and the temples;
on the ears, the back of the ears, the forehead, the eyes, and the eyebrows. ||22||
One should repeatedly place [the mantra] on the skull, the head, and the crest;
by the consecration with this mantra, that embodied being indeed becomes Garuḍa. (23)
Even in a dream, venomous serpents do not step upon his shadow;
even snakes in the form of Death flee from him out of fear.
Through the application of this mantra, all poison perishes and dissolves:
Oṃ, Lord of Śeṣa, Master of the Nāginīs, You who ride upon the back of Garuḍa! (25)
"O Śrī Hari, bestower of the fruit of Āstīka’s words, remove the poison, remove the poison!"—
by chanting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one becomes perfected;
even Mahākāla will keep his distance out of fear when [the mantra] is employed.
Then, from the recitation of my name, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, [that occurred]. ||27||
Even Mahākāla, though far removed, approaches out of fear of me;
even a body unfit for life lives here, there is no doubt.
One should perform the worship of Śrīdhara, who is accompanied by my retinue.
Having meditated upon oneself as the one named Śrīdhara, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Puruṣottama, the Supreme Self;
salutations to the Imperishable One, and repeated salutations to Māṇikyā.
Salutations again and again to Padmāvatī, Jayā, and Lalitā; salutations again and again to Sukhadā, Prajñā, and Lakṣmī as well. ||31||
Salutations again and again to Rādhikā, to Kriyā, and to Jñānā; salutations again and again to Icchā, to Kamalā, and to Mahālakṣmī. ||3 2||
Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutations again and again to Viṣṇu, who is Śrīdhara;
likewise, [I offer] the consecration, as well as the garment and the sacred thread. 33.
One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food, and circumambulation; one should recite my mantra and meditate upon me as residing within the heart. (34)
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to ten million suns, he has a serene face and is gentle, adorned with a shimmering crown and earrings. (35)
One should meditate upon my auspicious and supreme form—the wearer of the crown, of noble limbs, adorned with a forest garland, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman. (36)
Salutation to Śrīnivāsa, to Kṛṣṇa; salutation to the Lord of Śrī;
salutation again and again to Śrīdhara, who bears the Śārṅga bow, the bestower of prosperity. ||37||
Salutations again and again to you, the illustrious Vallabha, the peaceful and the glorious;
salutations to the dweller of Śrīparvata and to the bestower of welfare. ||38||
Salutations to you, the source of all blessings and the resting place of prosperity;
salutations to the embodiment of auspiciousness, and repeated salutations to the bestower of glory. (39)
"Salutations again and again to the one who lies with Śrī and who is the refuge;
then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should indeed bid farewell to the Lord of Śrī. (3.142.40)
Thus, the one who performs this worship certainly becomes free from poison;
he shakes off his sins and attains my supreme state. (41)
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara, to Śrī Viṣṇu, the Victorious One. This mantra removes all diseases and removes all afflictions. (42)
It removes all sins and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it destroys all poisons and annihilates malevolent spells. ||43||
He who fulfills all desires and bestows my own abode, having himself become identical with my own nature, shall live by chanting [the mantra]; of this there is no doubt. (44)
One should administer an oath by the name of that serpent which dwells in a particular month, in a particular season, and which shares its course with the sun. (45)
By that means, the snake venom is quickly pacified; of this there is no doubt.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the month-snakes, the sun-snakes, and so forth. 46.
The sevenfold array of Hari, whose essence is the sun, dwells together;
yet that single sun is described as manifold through various ritual formulations.
Dhātṛ, Sūrya, the Apsaras Puñjikasthalī, the Rākṣasa Heti, the Nāga Vāsuki, the Yakṣa Rathakṛt, and the lordly sage Pulastya. ||48||
The Gandharva Tumburu also attends upon them in Caitra;
so too do Sūrya, Aryaman, the Apsaras Puñjikasthalī, and the Rākṣasa Heti.
The Naga Kacchanīra, the Yakṣa Ojas, the sage Pulaha,
and the Gandharva Nārada— these preside over Vaiśākha.
Mitra, Sūrya, the Apsaras Menakā, the human Rākṣasa, the Nāga Takṣaka, the Yakṣa Rathasvana, and likewise the sage Atri. ||51||
The Gandharva Hāhā also follows them in the Jyeṣṭhā [nakṣatra];
Varuṇa, Sūrya, the Apsaras Rambhā, and the Rākṣasa Citrasvana [follow] in Citrā. ||52||
The nāga Śukra, the yakṣa Sahajanya, the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭhaka, and the gandharva Hūhū—these dwell in Āṣāḍha. (53)
Indra, Sūrya, the Apsaras Pramlocā, Vārya the Rākṣasa, the Nāga Elāpatra, the Yakṣa Śrotra, and likewise the Ṛṣi Aṅgiras. ||54||
The Gandharva Viśvāvasu and the Apsaras Anumlocā preside over Śrāvaṇa;
Vivasvat Sūrya is the deity, and Vyāghra is the Rākṣasa. ||55||
Śaṅkhapāla the Nāga, Āsāraṇa the Yakṣa, and Bhṛgu the Ṛṣi, as well as Ugrasena the Gandharva—these are the deities in the month of Bhādrapada. (56)
Pūṣan, Sūrya, the Apsaras Ghṛtācī, Vāta, the Rākṣasa, the Nāga Dhanañjaya, the Yakṣa Suruci, and the Ṛṣi Gautama. ||57||
And Suṣeṇa is the Gandharva; these belong to the month of Māgha.
Parjanya and Arka are the Apsarases Senajitī and Varcā, while the Rākṣasa is [Senajit].
The nāga Airāvata, the yakṣa Ṛtu, the seer Bhāradvāja,
and the gandharva Viśva— these indeed follow after Phālguna.
Aṃśu, Sūrya, the Apsaras Urvaśī, Vidyut, the Rākṣasa Chatru, the Nāga Mahāśaṅkha, Tārkṣya, the Yakṣa Kaśyapa, and the Ṛṣi. ||3.142.60||
And the Gandharva is Ṛtusunā; in Mārgaśīrṣa they are Bhaga, Sūrya, Pūrvacitti the Apsaras, and Sphūrja the Rākṣasa.
The Naga Karkoṭaka, the Yakṣa Ūrṇa, the Rishi Āyu,
and the Gandharva Ariṣṭanemi— these attend upon him in the month of Pauṣa.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Sūrya, the Apsaras Tilottamā, Brahmā, Apetarākṣas, the Nāga Kambala, Śatajit, the Yakṣa, and the sage Jamadagni. ||63||
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is a Gandharva, and those two reside among the Aśvins;
Viṣṇu is Sūrya, Raṃbhā is an Apsaras, and Makhāpeta is a Rākṣasa.
Nāga, Aśvatara, Yakṣa, Satyajit, the seer Viśvāmitra,
and the Gandharva Sūryavarcas— these preside over the month of Kārttika.
For these twelve and seven groups, who are conceited regarding their respective stations, are like suns—distinct manifestations of splendor—and they bring about the ripening [of karmic fruits]. (66)
The Apsarases and Gandharvas indeed perform dance and song;
the Yakṣas, along with the Vidyādharas and Grāmaṇīs, also yoke the chariot.
Those serpents, having become ropes, indeed proceed to bind the chariot;
the Rākṣasas, following behind, surely urge the chariot forward.
The sages, such as the Vālakhilyas and others, praise the Lord, the charioteer, with Vedic mantras; they indeed lead him toward the setting [of the sun].
According to the prowess of these very gods, according to their austerity,
according to their application, according to their dharma, according to their reality, and according to their strength.
In the same way, that sun blazes forth, and having been kindled by their splendor,
it dispels all the inauspiciousness of living beings by means of its own radiance.
By these auspicious acts of men, evil indeed is carried away;
by my command, it dispels the evil of those who practice virtuous conduct. (72)
Scorching with heat, chanting prayers, and gladdening all creatures, they indeed protected all beings and acted out of compassion. (73)
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, the Sūryas who have been remembered protect from the time of day, and the Apsarases protect from the delusions of intoxication. (74)
At night, the Rākṣasas protect [the practitioner] from hosts of demons and from evil times;
and when they are worshipped, the Nāgas then protect him from snake venom and other such dangers. (75)
Yakṣas always protect [the sites] from the openings where yakṣas dwell and so forth;
and sages, being honored, protect them through asceticism and mantras. //76//
The Gandharvas, when worshipped, protect the worlds and bestow prosperity;
thus all are composed of time, joined with their respective times.
When worshipped and saluted, they protect those who are devoted.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare the excellent mantra that conquers death. (78)
By the recitation of this [mantra], which has been accumulated, death shall be brought about for those who possess birth;
I am Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Supreme Lord, and my body exists.
Mahākāla is my power (śakti), and his daughter is indeed Death (mṛtyu).
She is the daughter of my sovereignty; that Death was created by me.
"I am the Lord Kālajit, I am Mādhava, the Conqueror of Death;
one should constantly chant my name, bowing while reciting 'Mṛtyuñjaya'. (8.1)
One should recite "Oṃ namo mṛtyuñjayāya svāhā" day and night;
by that, death itself turns away from him—of this there is no doubt. (82)
Evil dreams perish, as do ill-omened birds;
malevolent planets turn back, and even misfortune dissolves away. (83)
Great fear dissolves, the mind-senses indeed go to their dissolution, and all calamities—whether divine or elemental—are utterly destroyed. (84)
Internal diseases and mental afflictions perish, along with all secondary conditions;
sudden misfortunes dissolve and flow away. (85)
Wherever I am, there is not even the slightest suffering, much less any great sorrow; O Lakṣmī, if I am constantly remembered and worshipped, I dwell there.
And there, in the heart, there is indeed eternal bliss with me;
for among devotees, wherever there is Śrī, there is joy.
Both you and I abide as the imperishable Brahman, liberated within His heart;
for there, indeed, time, death, and even sins are purifiers.
Only those who possess good fortune experience happiness and prosperity;
for one devoid of devotion in this world, there arises suffering caused by the planets and other such influences. (89)

Furthermore, O Rame, those who are unrefined and harbor malice cause suffering and poverty, arising from [the influence of] nāgas and other such beings. They become tormentors for those who lack refuge.
Indeed, afflictions flee swiftly from those who have taken refuge in me;
even the messengers of Yama and the omens of death turn back in flight.
One who has devotion as their armor should unite the self with the Self;
having become the innermost Self, one should abide in a state of identity. ||92||
For me, who has attained identity with that [Reality], there exists not even a scent of time—whether through action, mind, speech, body, or the stream of the senses. (93)
The scent of illusion does not exist in him, so how could there be the scent of death?
He rejoices at my side; he is a portion of me, having attained the state of being "mine. (94)
Just as Ramā Lakṣmī rejoices in the world of Śrī, and just as Ananta rejoices, so too does Garuḍa rejoice. (95)
Sanatkumāra rejoices eternally like Śaṅkara;
and as Viṣṇu rejoices, so Nārāyaṇa exults.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa also rejoice;
likewise, the devotee, freed from the noose of time, exults.
O Lotus-born one, that woman who mutters my name becomes like Māṇikyā;
for the splendor of Māṇikyā is eternally of the nature of my own abiding presence.
Wherever I am, there indeed all sovereign powers belong to me;
there, in that which consists of time, māyā, and so forth, neither karma nor suffering exists. (99)
"O Lakṣmī, for one who thus chants, 'Oṃ, salutations again and again to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,' sin shall never touch them. (3.142.100)
Thus has the power of my mantra been described; though difficult to overcome, it is constrained by force.
Yet the power of my name exists as superior to all other powers. (101)
O beloved, the power of my form is always superior to all other powers;
indeed, my own strength is also greater than all other strengths.
Having taken that up, one shall conquer Time, illusion, evil, and karma;
as well as the poison of saṃsāra and the enemies that are the objects of the senses.
Having conquered all poison and drunk the nectar consisting of intoxication,
a mortal attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and becomes immortal in the Imperishable.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this, one who has taken refuge in me rejoices, having abandoned the fear of time and illusion. (105)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature and Power of Time-Death (Kālamṛtyu) and the Exposition of the Recitation of Specific Mantras and the Method of Worshiping the Supreme Lord and Others for the Purpose of Conquering It," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, you have previously described various types of dharma for the Kṛta age, and others even different from those for the Tretā age.
What are the characteristics of the Dvāpara age, in which people, acting with faith, indeed attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa?
What kind of people are they who perform recitation of mantras, [chanting of] names, and devotion—even those devoid of truth—who shall attain liberation or go to heaven? (3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; the duties of the Satya Yuga grant liberation, while the duties of the Tretā Yuga, by their very nature, bestow great sovereignty.
O Lakṣmī, in the Dvāpara age, the bulls [of dharma] bestow the divine worlds of Bhauma, Vairāja, and Vaiṣṇava; whereas in the Kali age, they are debased and touched by impurity.
For the sake of destroying that [evil], I repeatedly assume the form of Kṛṣṇa during the Dvāpara age;
indeed, through my yoga and by association with the virtuous, the sinful cross over [to liberation].
Listen to the characteristics of the Dvāpara age, which have declined from what they were before;
in this age, it is indeed those whose primary quality is devotion who cross over, and no others.
All the perfections (siddhis) that existed in the Tretā age perish in the Dvāpara age;
greed, lack of fortitude, and trade accompanied by deceit [prevail].
Furthermore, the non-determination of reality and the destruction of phonemes are also [effects];
however, the perversion of all actions pertaining to their respective agents is [the result]. (9)
In the Dvāpara age, travel, slaughter, supreme punishment, pride, arrogance, force, injury, and intolerance increase as qualities of rajas and tamas. (3.143.10)
O best of bulls, even the stages of life (āśramas), which have dharma as their purpose, are becoming confused;
there is disagreement regarding the revealed scriptures (śruti) and the treatises (śāstra), and people find satisfaction in excessive logic.
Because of that, a duality arises and certainty is not attained;
through the application of an undetermined meaning, even the true nature of phenomena (dharmatattva) is brought into ridicule. //12//
A dharma established through disagreement becomes confused and perishes;
therefore, the Veda is divided into four parts by Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa.
Furthermore, the Vedas are divided by the sons of the sages due to errors of vision;
new Saṃhitās are also produced by the great seers. (14)
In the Dvāpara ages, they proceed with their own philosophical systems that have divergent meanings;
likewise, the ritual duties of the Adhvaryu priest then arise through various schools.
Through conceptual constructions, as well as through secondary, primary, and eminent forms of exhaustion, that which possesses diverse qualities proceeds in various places. (16)
In this way, faith, confidence, retention, contemplation, and veneration perish through the passage of time; even truth itself perishes. (17)
In this state, submissiveness and stability vanish; deceit and hypocrisy perish, while guile, untruth, and the tendency to deceive increase. (18)
Thus, in the Dvāpara age, false views arise from perversion;
death occurs, and various obstacles arise again and again. (19)
In the Dvāpara age, calamities, diseases, anxieties arising unexpectedly, and attachments to sense objects occur in greater abundance.
In that Dvāpara age, trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs likewise exert themselves according to their strength, and living beings act in accordance with their own nature.
Having observed this, the medicinal herbs entered the earth;
thereafter, in the Dvāpara age, they indeed sprout forth when the ground is tilled by the plow.
But in the middle Dvāpara age, the multitudes of medicinal herbs do not grow there without seed; at that time, agriculture by means of seeds occurs everywhere.
The seed, the root, the branch, the bulb, the stalk, the tube,
the fruit, the leaf, the cluster, the knot, or its sprout— (24)
Then, in the Dvāpara age, those medicinal herbs are born from the earth, having been sown with matted locks, bark, and stalks. Thus they arise from that lineage.
At that time, the livelihood of all people becomes dependent upon them;
thereafter, in the Dvāpara age, the various occupations related to medicinal herbs arise.
Otherwise, their very livelihood would cease at the end of the Tretā Yuga;
they therefore resort to the means of subsistence consisting of trade, agriculture, and commerce.
Then, even water arises from the hands due to the digging of the earth;
at that time, wells and oblong ponds also come into existence all around. (28)
Then those endowed with self-mastery become powerful lords;
yet they also become weak, destitute of people, and deprived of their own sovereignty. (29)
The powerful ones plunder the means of livelihood such as trees and creepers;
they seize women, fields, daughters, sons, wealth, and cows. (3.143.30)
For the sake of establishing the bounds of social order, Brahmā places the mighty Kṣatriya upon the head of the subjects to protect them from injury. 3.1.
At that time, he establishes the castes and stages of life in a state free from fear;
yet then, drought, death, and disease break out on all sides.
Just as the creation of dharma exists, so too does the creation of adharma;
indeed, in the Dvāpara age, they proceed with equal measure among human beings.
The dharmas of the Tretā age exist here and there until the end of the half-Dvāpara;
they too perish once the half-Dvāpara has passed.
Truth mingled with falsehood, non-stealing mixed with theft, non-violence combined with violence, and conduct joined with immorality. (35)
Possession is joined with greed; policy is touched by injustice; purity is touched by impurity; and contentment is accompanied by craving. (36)
Praise of austerity is not distinct [from it]; self-study is for the desire of wealth;
meditation on the Lord is for the purpose of destroying suffering; and devotion is for one's own sake. (37)
Wife, children, and so forth seek half their own interest and half the interest of others;
likewise, servants seek half their own interest and half the interest of others. (38)
Even kings have half their purpose for themselves and half for others;
likewise, even sages are devoted to asceticism for half their own purpose and half for others. (39)
In the Dvāpara age, relationships arise that are half-natural;
religious rites and sacrifices serve as means for accomplishing only one's own self-interest. (3.143.40)
Half [of the food] is brought by rain and half by well-water;
indeed, in the later part of the Dvāpara age, a fixed lifespan no longer exists.
Since sons and others die while their fathers are still living, they are half-true;
likewise, trees bear fruit only when half-grown, as do creepers and women. 42.
In the period of the second half of the Dvāpara age, men become possessed of only partial resolve; people have only half-hearted trust and conduct their affairs with one another [accordingly].
When an auspicious undertaking is being commenced, it certainly bears fruit for that purpose;
likewise, the currents of rivers and the waters of the monsoon yield their results halfway through, as do the seasons with their fruits.
In the Tretā age, when the lifespan of people is half [that of the previous age], they exist here and there;
indeed, in the Satya Yuga, creation occurs in every place through mere volition.
In the Tretā age, the method of creation proceeds from sight;
at the end of the Tretā, creation is by touch; and in the Dvāpara age, it is also from sexual union.
When half of the Dvāpara age has passed, creation from the couple becomes fruitless in some places;
indeed, all mines likewise become devoid of seeds.
Men of futile vigor, whose latent impressions function only partially,
develop attachment toward objects only half-heartedly and proceed from a state of half-love.
Furthermore, in the two ages [the Tretā and Dvāpara], the subjects are half-decrepit and possess only half-strength;
likewise, they are half-dwarfish in stature at the beginning of each age.
Mantras indeed bear fruit only in half their measure, and gurus possess only partial awakening; likewise, charity, vows, compassion, and righteousness truly attain only a state of half-existence.

The disciples abide by only half of their instructions, considering themselves to possess only half of their own strength; and the young wives, having adopted only half of wifely devotion, remain as such. (51)
In this Dvāpara age, the entire family unit achieves only half its purpose;
the stages of life (āśramas) possess only half their virtue, and the social classes (varṇas) have only half their own renown.
The gods grant half of the fruit [of their worship], and their masters are half-protected by the gods;
in battles, there is half-victory, and the soldiers are those who conquer through truth.
The primary [virtues] and those that are half-subordinate manifest as half of the kingdom;
fortune indeed bears fruit as half, and the determination of truth sustains half. (54)
In the Dvāpara age, O Lakṣmī, beings are born with half-essence, yet they possess roots rich in full essence; even oaths are only half-truthful.
The words of merchants are likewise only half-stable, and trust even in great men is established only halfway. (56)
For the Siddhas from Satyaloka are capable of going everywhere;
likewise, the Pitṛs also go only half the way. ||57||
Likewise, the gods also arrive on earth in half that number;
and those residing in the netherworlds (pātāla) and other realms likewise remain in half that number.
In the Dvāpara age, all [beings] are entirely powerless; in the Tretā age, people possess only half their strength.
Medicinal herbs have half their potency, and physicians are merely half-examiners.

Astrologers who understand only half [the science], physicians who practice only half [of medicine], and mechanical devices that accomplish only half [their purpose]—these indeed yield only half-results. (3.143.60)
Broken in the middle, they hang down in the intervals;
though possessed of firmness due to old age, their power of vision is diminished. (61)
Their grasping and their movements have mostly ceased, and their joys have perished;
their hearing and touching have faded away, as have their tasting and smelling.
In the Dvāpara age, beings arise with diminished strength and half the vitality;
they are the abodes of truth, the dwellings of the gods, the schools of the teachers, and the righteous.
When half of the Dvāpara age has passed on earth, approximately half of the sacrificial halls, festivals, temples, and virtuous men perish.
Those jewels that are the essence of truth and those which are the sacred fords—
half of them perish when half of the Dvāpara age has passed upon the earth.

The destruction of half of one's purity, the destruction of half of what is touchable and untouchable, the destruction of half of what is worthy of salutation and unworthy of salutation, and the destruction of half of the worship due to those worthy of worship. ||66||

When half of the Dvāpara age has passed on earth, there is the destruction of half the objects of enjoyment and their enjoyers, the destruction of half the drinks and those who drink them, and the destruction of half the objects of meditation and those who meditate upon them.
There is the destruction of half the human goals and the annihilation of half that which is imagined;
the fruit is the existence of half [of reality], and the initial manifestations have half as their domain. (68)
Intelligence brings half the deliberation, and effort yields half the fruit; friends possess half the influence, and servitude proceeds for half [the duration]. (69)
In the Dvāpara age, when half has passed, cattle will possess only half-trust, birds will be half-servile, and there will be only half-understanding of languages. (3.143.70)
Forms characterized by partial attraction and powers of partial attraction,
as well as the objects of affection and so forth, will exist when half of the Dvāpara age has passed on earth.
Restrained by royal punishments, the subjects abide according to the law;
even that action which is half-performed in public is considered a completed act.
In the Dvāpara age, people do not even count half [of their wealth] in secret;
indeed, in the Dvāpara age, fear of fate overtakes half of the subjects.
In that age, fear of sin is not even reckoned as half;
likewise, fear of treachery and fear of falsehood are not reckoned as even half. ||74||
In this manner, O Lotus-born One, fear of evil deeds is no longer reckoned, nor is sin considered; indeed, only half [of dharma] remains in the Dvāpara age.
But in the subsequent age, that truth survives as only one-third;
and even those three parts of truth and the rest perish entirely in the final two ages.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, embodied beings indeed possess a lifespan of one quarter;
at its beginning it was five hundred years, and in its middle Dvāpara it was half of that.
O Rame, when one-third of that [period] has passed, and in the fourth part thereof,
the lifespan of all embodied beings has indeed reached its reduction by half.
In the Kṛta age, human beings indeed stand eight tālas tall;
in the Tretā, they are six tālas high; and in the Dvāpara, they are four tālas tall.
In the latter half of the Dvāpara age, they will be half that size; then half again, becoming ten cubits tall.
The trees will be four times as high, and the elephants will be half the size of the trees.
In the Dvāpara age, elephants are only half their [Kṛta-age] size, and horses are even less; oxen and other such animals are likewise diminished.
In the Tretā age, they exist with their strength reduced by one-third.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, undertakings are weak and possess only a quarter of their former power;
however, those who possess spiritual accomplishment become tall and long-lived.
Furthermore, they are shorter, with very small bodies, and consequently of even smaller circumference;
their food is ten māṇas, then five māṇas, and then half a māṇa.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, it shall be one māna or half of that;
indeed, during the Satya Yuga, there is travel by day in the sky.
In the fourteen worlds, on the earth, and even in other continents,
during the Tretā age, one's residence indeed depends entirely upon celestial chariots (vimānas).
And at that time, men travel a hundred yojanas in a single day;
in the Dvāpara age it is half of that, and in the latter half of the Dvāpara, half of that again.
At the end of the Dvāpara age it is half of that, and after that, half again;
thus, for those of short stature, the sequence of the feet is contracted.
Without breath control (prāṇāyāma), they possess no power to travel through the sky; they are supported by the earth, dwell on the earth, move upon the earth, and subsist on the earth. (88)
Thus, O Rama, at the end of the Dvapara age, people there will be afflicted by hunger, thirst, and excessive heat; indeed, O Rama, at the end of the Dvapara, people will be full of such suffering.
Abounding in falsehood, endowed with deceit, filled with selfishness and egoism,
and possessed of many impurities, they are born at the end of the Dvāpara age.
O Lakṣmī, at the end of the Dvāpara age, men are born entirely with mean minds, devoid of fortitude, and likewise lacking in profundity. 91.
Women are devoid of prosperity and violate half of the moral boundaries;
likewise, they are arrogant with the pride of "mine-ness," egoism, and the sense of ownership over their own half [of the body].
They indeed become slaves to the afflictions and likewise deprived of even a portion of the Dharma;
consequently, fortunes abandon them and splendors depart from their homes.
Accomplishments depart and supernatural powers vanish;
what remain are merely semblances of accomplishments, for they are indeed false accomplishments.
In the Dvāpara age, cultured people abandon half of their culture;
at the end of Dvāpara, that culture is indeed destroyed by impurities.
And that Time which existed in the past, whose very nature is half-affliction, now proceeds;
the messengers of Time bring about the downfall of men within their dwellings. (96)
The fires, having gone to the left half, proceed clockwise;
at the end of the Dvāpara age, half of the substance offered for worship dissolves.

Everything pertaining to oneself is twofold: the supreme is that which is for the sake of others; indeed, a mind mixed with the state of being other-oriented is merely the "Dvāpara" age of the self. (98)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, human beings indeed resort to various kinds of dharma;
their offspring likewise perform half that which is sinful and half that which is meritorious.
Even while seeking wealth and desire, subjects may undergo decline;
in such a case, one should constantly recite my mantra known as the Gāyatrī.
Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ! We know Śrīghanaśyāma; we meditate upon Nīlakaṇṭha; may Hari inspire us. 10.1.
Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ! We know Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; we meditate upon Anādikṛṣṇa; may that Kṛṣṇa inspire us. 102.
Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ; may we know the glorious Nārāyaṇa, may we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. 103.
One should recite: *oṃ śrībrahmapriyāvallabhāya svāhā namaḥ*.
Likewise, one should recite: *oṃ śrīharipriyāvallabhāya namaḥ*. 104.
One who performs six hundred thousand recitations indeed crosses over the ocean of existence;
therefore, in the Dvāpara age, one should recite this mantra for the sake of liberation.
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī, Lord of Rādhā, Supreme Brahman, Lord of the Gopīs, Lord of Jayā! ||106||
O Lord of Lalitāśrī, O Lord of Prajñā, O Lord of Padmāvatī;
O Lord of Sukhadāśrī, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Śrīmāṇikī! ||107||
O Lord, sovereign of swans, garuḍas, elephants, and horses;
O Lord of the virtuous, Lord of chaste and faithful wives, Lord of all, All-pervading One! 108.
O Blessed One, O Lotus-eyed One, deliver us from the ocean of existence,
from this terrible age of Dvāpara which is indeed characterized by the final period.
Thus he should entreat the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, the Eternal;
he should worship me, wear me [as a sacred thread], and offer me within his heart.
In this way, O Rame, at the end of the Dvāpara age, human beings shall attain liberation through reading and even through hearing my Saṃhitā.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties, Rituals, and Natures of the Dvāpara Age, as well as the Demonstration of Devotion through Mantras and Other Means for the Liberation of Men of That Kind," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-Santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Hari, are the duties of the ages eternal, or are they subject to change? Do the virtues born of one age prevail in another age, or not?
Śrī Puruṣottama said: "The eternal duties of the ages (yuga-dharmas) are indeed inherent to each age;
however, those suited to other ages are overturned by powerful men."
Indeed, the defiled qualities of the Kali age are overturned by those who uphold the Truth (Ṛtambhara),
and likewise, the attributes of the physical body are overturned by yogis who are most powerful.
The laws of time are overturned by virtuous women such as Sādhvikā and others;
likewise, the laws of defects are overturned by perfected beings and holy men.
The laws of the land are overturned by capable and eminent teachers;
the laws of the subjects are overturned by ruling kings. (5)
The duties of ascetics are subverted by those who produce wonders;
the duties of maidens are subverted by assemblies honored by the world. (6)
In this world, festivals and other such events are averted by people who possess perfected speech;
likewise, the duties of the castes are set aside by those who know the conduct and the Vedas of the highest caste.
The physical bases are transformed by people who have renounced the body and attained the state of being bodiless;
however, the mental faculties are transformed by people intent on the practice of attraction.
Where truth exists in a person, there indeed reside the qualities of the Satya-yuga;
where passion (rajas) is joined with goodness (sattva), there proceed the qualities of the Tretā-yuga.
In the Dvāpara age, darkness joined with passion (rajas) begins to prevail slightly;
in the Kali age, indeed, the qualities of darkness (tamas) prevail, wherein darkness itself comes forth.
In the Sāttvika age, indeed, the qualities of Sattva prevail; in the Tāmasa age, those associated with Kali are joined.
In the Tretā age, Sattva and Rajas are combined; in the Dvāpara age, Rajas and Tamas are combined.
O Lakṣmī, in the Kṛta Yuga, Dharma indeed exists in its four quarters;
by that [Dharma], the Blessed One, who bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, is attained.
For Dharma is indeed the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; worship is Kṛṣṇa, as is the libation.
Likewise, the fire-oblation, the twilight prayers, meditation, and concentration—all is Hari. (1.3)
The four feet of Dharma are truth, charity, austerity, and compassion;
I, Hari, am the protector of Dharma, and truth and the others are my feet.
In the Tretā Yuga, Dharma stands on three feet, consisting of truth, charity, and compassion;
in that Tretā age, I too delight in all things such as sacrifices and rituals.
In the Dvāpara age, I am two-footed, consisting of charity and compassion;
in the Kali age, I am one-footed through charity alone, and I delight in being the very essence of charity.
In the Kṛta age I am indeed white; in Tretā I possess a red color;
in Dvāpara I am tawny, and in Kali I become black.
The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas exist within the person;
impelled by the Puruṣa, they also revolve within the selves.
But when sattva, mind, intellect, and the senses are abundant,
then one should know it to be the Kṛta Yuga, in which there is delight in knowledge and austerity.

When embodied beings possess the capacity for rites performed for specific desires and for fame, then the Tretā age is considered to exist externally within the heart as a manifestation of passion (rajas). (3.144.20)
When greed, discontent, pride, hypocrisy, and envy prevail,
as well as a delight in actions performed for desire— that is the Dvāpara age, characterized by rajas and tamas.
When falsehood, sleep, violence, affliction, lethargy, grief, delusion, fear, and dejection are always present, then that state is considered Tamas. ||22||
O Lakṣmī, when the Dvāpara age has passed, people will be harsh in speech,
their natures dominated by desire, and the regions will be filled with various kinds of bandits.
At that time, the religious systems will be filled with heresy, and kings will be devourers of their subjects;
the people will be satisfied only by the touch of genitals and bellies, while rulers will be motivated solely by wealth.
Students are without vows and impure; householders are devoid of wealth;
ascetics dwell in villages; and renunciants are greedy for riches. (25)
In the Kali age, however, the virtuous will have great greed and great thirst;
then servants will abandon their master, and ascetics will abandon their vows.
In the Kali age (Tiṣya), Śūdras will indeed accept gifts, Vaiśyas will be devoted solely to asceticism,
people will be filled with anxiety, and the progeny will be like Piśācas.

All those men who consume food unjustly, who are devoid of worshiping the gods and guests, who are devoted only to women, and who are deprived of offerings to the ancestors and water libations; ||28||
In the Kali age, women indeed become prolific, talkative, and ill-fated;
intent on scratching their heads, they disregard commands in every way. (29)
Likewise, those intent on their own self-interest, their senses agitated by sin, practice deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics. (3.144.30)
In the Kali age, there will be the disease of negligence, constant fears of hunger,
terrible fears of drought, and the upheaval of countries.
The greedy speak untruths through their wicked conduct and ill-performed sacrifices;
yet, there are kinship ties among all human beings across all castes. (32)
In every place, beds, seats, and foods were strewn about in utter disorder; here and there were the killings of embryos, the slaying of heroes, and the murder of the virtuous.
Even when their lifespan is very short, family members die out of order;
they possess little luster or strength, are mostly untruthful, and are unrighteous. (34)
Thieves will abide by the conduct of kings, and kings will act according to their own whims; women faithful to a single husband will not remain, while practitioners of malevolent magic will increase.
Wearing saffron robes and bearing the outward marks of divinity, these people live without hardship for the sake of their livelihood;
having offered away the food of others, they accomplish their own selfish ends. (36)
Candālas shall be the rulers of the kingdom, and Brahmins shall indeed be their servants;
those Brahmins, whose learning, fortune, strength, and eyesight are exhausted, will serve the Candālas. (37)
O Rame, in the Kali age, the Vedas, Shastras, Agamas, and Dharmas take the form of obstacles;
they are indeed utterly destroyed here due to the confusion of dharma.
In that Kali age, there will be neither sacrifices nor marriages;
the cause of mental satisfaction for a couple will be the practice of their own desired conduct. (39)
In the Kali age, all people indeed declare the conduct of the Mlecchas to be the best;
then the god sends down rain of various kinds, and the crops ripen in diverse ways.
All were engaged in the trade of greed, seeking to sell through deceit; there was no one who did not utter cruel words, nor anyone who was upright or free from envy. 41.
In this evil age, there is neither benefactor nor one who returns a favor;
the earth is devoid of kings and is not covered with grain or wealth.
In the Kali age, people will in every way become revilers and fallen; indeed, sectarian circles (maṇḍalas) will arise in both countries and cities. 43.
In the Kali age, even the performance of royal duties destroys righteousness;
the earth possesses little water, yields little fruit, and is devoid of wealth.
They were both protectors and non-protectors, plunderers and lawless ones;
they were stealers of others' wealth and of others' wives, sons, and women. (45)
In the Kali age, people who are fond of violence and harbor evil desires lose their sense of right and wrong; such friends are sweet in speech but wicked at heart.
In the Kali age, there will be thieves, those who steal from thieves, and even those who steal from the thief;
indeed, in the Kali age, insects, mice, and snakes shall even attack them.
In the Kali age, there will indeed be many paths and traditions; these are those who enjoy the fruits of hidden unrighteousness while outwardly displaying virtuous conduct. 48.
Deities, virtuous ascetics, yogis, holy women, and those who enjoy wealth and food—when these humans are satiated by hunger, they indeed promote the prosperity of the evil path. (49)
In the Kṛta age, Dharma lasts for a hundred years; in the Tretā, it lasts for a year;
in the Dvāpara, it lasts for a month; and in the Kali age, it lasts for only a single day.
Moreover, in the Kali age, people abandon that daily religious duty;
they are agitated, wandering about, and afflicted by fear of one another.
Protecting their own lives, they are pitiless, deeply distressed, devoid of moral boundaries, lawless, lacking affection, and shameless. (52)
In the Kali age, people will be devoid of effort, meat-eaters,
dwelling on the shores of the ocean, and entirely subsisting on fish.
At that time, human beings were homeless, clothed in bark garments, and slept upon the ground;
men, beasts, divine beings, birds, and aquatic creatures [all lived in this manner]. 54.
In the Kali age, people for the most part live in a state of social confusion and enjoy its mixed fruits;
there, I, as Nārāyaṇa, impel those who have taken refuge in me.
My attendants, possessing divine bodies yet appearing in the forms of sages and ascetics,
dwell indeed beyond the reach of ordinary perception for the purpose of establishing righteousness.
On the mountains, those of auspicious conduct who subsist on wild roots and fruits give birth to pairs, and from them arise beings composed of dharma.
Endowed with all sovereign powers and possessed of devotion to the Vedas,
many wicked races are slain by my incarnations.
Those dwelling on the shores of the ocean are destroyed by excessive winds, excessive rains, and other such calamities;
thereafter, the sages, my sons, and my attendants [perish] from the forests.
The descendants of Kārtavīrya continue to exist on earth, perpetuating their lineage;
thus is the lineage of what has been done established, and likewise the destruction of the Kali age.
Those sages who are his attendants are born endowed with the fitness for what has been performed;
they possess divine bodies capable of enjoyment and are firm in their vows.
All were practitioners of yoga through dispassion, likewise devoted to the awakening of the Self;
they were contented, established in austerity, most righteous, and characterized by devotion.
Then the Seven Sages, having come from heaven, dwell upon these [mountains];
and there, among them, the Seven Sages truly discourse upon Dharma.
Those Siddhas who remain in the Kali age move about unperceived;
they indeed come into manifestation and become Ācāryas.
The gurus, worthy of protecting the world, dwell among their subjects and even bestow the kingdom upon those born of a noble Brahmin lineage.
O Lakṣmī, when the Kṛtayuga has been thus established, it proceeds once more;
you, who had reached a state of decline during the Kali age, flourish again in the Satya age.
O Lakṣmī, you obtain purity through association with virtuous and chaste women;
yet you are of the nature of an Asurī, a Yātudhānī, a Paiśācī, and a Yakṣa-Rākṣasī.
"O Tiṣyā, you are indeed the embodiment of truth; you are born as divine Lakṣmī.
At that time, in the Satya-yuga, couples will for the most part be devoted to the duties of the household. (68)
And those ascetics who are equal to [true] ascetics are devoted to celibacy;
they are free from desire and utterly devoid of longing, dwelling in the bliss of the Self. ||69||
Furthermore, through the mere application of volition and the mere sight of women,
mental beings— sons, grandsons, and so forth— are likewise produced.
When [the ritual] has been performed upon arrival, they become the very forms of male and female ascetics;
likewise the gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
For by the power of the Kṛta Yuga, they are born devoted to the vows of dharma;
they are born with proportions equal in circumference and height, just as before. (72)
In strength, in yoga, as well as in sovereignty, in prosperities, and in meditative absorptions;
in traveling through the sky and traveling through water, they are born again just as before.
Just as in former times, when the elements were in a state of expansion within the intellect,
so too do they arise when brought into being by the impulse of my volition.
Even the beasts and birds became wish-fulfilling cows;
the trees became wish-granting trees, and the creepers became wish-granting creepers. (75)
Men possess divine bodies and women become celestial damsels;
thus they are born, just as they were in the previous Kṛta age.
But, O Lakṣmī, from the muhūrta called Brāhma until a little before morning, [is the first period];
then from the morning time comes Saṅgava, and after that, Madhyāhnaka. ||77||
Then the period of half of the latter half is evening; after that, the strength is diminished.
In this way, all the ages (yugas) are established, each succeeding one being smaller than the preceding.
Even those with slightly diminished strength, being afflicted by slight decline, are possessed of a progressively decreasing [strength]; therefore, they are not equal in every respect. (79)
Indeed, from the truth existing at the beginning of creation, the subsequent Satya Yugas become progressively weaker; they are certainly not equal to the primordial truth.
Wherever my yogic power is complete, there [the ages] are like the Kṛta; but when manifested with a strength less than mine, the age is made deficient in power. (81)
Know it to be even so: the world is powerless without me;
for wherever I am, there is goodness everywhere—even in the life of a householder.
O Lakṣmī, wherever I am not, there is no goodness even if one is virtuous; in whichever age, O Lakṣmī, I may have been won over by someone, [for that person alone is truly good]. (83)
By him the Kṛtayuga has been won; by him everything dear has been won.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now speak of the virtuous, and then indeed of the holy ones.
For they have indeed become united with Brahman within; therefore, the virtuous call him the "Good" (Santam), the glorious Supreme Self, who extends himself among all creatures. (85)
Being peaceful, those virtuous ones accomplish their own task, which is liberation; likewise, they also accomplish the task of liberation for others.
O Lakṣmī, one is called a *sādhaka* (aspirant) because of the accomplishment of divine deeds;
O Lakṣmī, he alone is a *brahmacārī* (celibate seeker) because of moving within Brahman. (87)

Beneficial to his guru, acting for his own welfare, always devoted to truth and what is beneficial, such a virtuous person is indeed a true celibate; he is a benefactor and the most excellent among the good. ||88||
On account of his causes and his spiritual practices, the householder is called virtuous;
in the Satya Yuga, those householders were indeed virtuous, equal to the truly virtuous.
Those virtuous ascetics in the forest were indeed Vaikhānasas;
and those striving ascetics were virtuous through the practice of yoga.
Dharma is declared to be the high path and the bestower of virtues;
it is the Bull created by the sage Nārāyaṇa and by Brahmā. (91)

The performance of marriage, the agnihotra sacrifice, worship, and so forth, according to the divisions of caste and stage of life, as practiced by the virtuous—that is called the conduct of the cultured (ācāra). ||92||
My remaining attendants, sons, disciples,
and great sages are likewise instructed here for the sake of dharma, so that they may continue the lineage of the world.

It is practiced again and again by the cultured (śiṣṭas) of former and even more ancient times; and because it has been considered the doctrine by those of former and earlier eras, that conduct of the cultured is eternal. //94//
Charity, truthfulness, austerity, devotion, learning, sacrifice, worship, and self-restraint—these eight are the practices that are indeed esteemed as the conduct of the virtuous. (95)
Celibacy, austerity, silence, and even fasting, as well as service to one's parents and likewise taking refuge in a guru. ||96||
This group of six constitutes the dharma of the virtuous; therefore, householders are virtuous.
Having encountered the current of illusion, they do not go along with it, but rather cross over it. 97.

This Tāraka is indeed virtuous; for even though he is a householder, he is a good man, increased by his adherence to the conduct of the refined, and is truly a bull [of dharma] esteemed by the righteous. ||98||
The renunciation of actions unto Me is true *sannyāsa*, which is the duty of the virtuous;
it consists of hymns to Brahman, hymns to the ritual procedure, and hymns to My Lord Hari’s qualities. (99)
The fourfold set consisting of knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, and virtue is set in motion by the learned, the virtuous, and the righteous according to the ancient tradition. (3.144.1) 100.
Those who possess innate [powers] are indeed the virtuous ones and the sages (ṛṣis);
because they "see" (ṛṣanti) the supreme Brahman, they are considered to be ṛṣis.
Indeed, the root *dṛś*, meaning "to go," possesses its true etymological significance among the virtuous;
for those who are the sons of lords may be either born of the mind (*mānasa*) or born of the body (*aurasa*). (1.02)
The sons of the sages and the ṛṣikās were those sages whose wealth was their austerity;
likewise, there were the sons of Brahmā—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
The sons of the sages are those very sages who are the causes of the continuity of the world;
thus, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous are indeed manifold in their truth and righteousness. 104.
Moreover, even virtuous householders engage in truth;
by taking refuge in them, liberation and worldly enjoyment certainly arise. (105)
From reciting, hearing, remembering, and associating with the virtuous, the fruit consisting of worldly enjoyment and liberation arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
In all the ages alike, O Rame, there is but one great quality:
through the chanting of my name, Kṛṣṇa, liberation shall indeed surely come to pass.

In the Kṛta age, Hari is attained through sacrifice; in the Tretā age, He is won by chanting; in the Dvāpara age, Hari is to be reached through service; but in the Kali age, He is attained through glorification.
In that [Kali age], though it is a storehouse of faults, there is the virtue of proclaiming the name of Hari;
Dvāpara, though possessing half as much sin, is virtuous compared to my own birth.
In the Kṛta and other ages, I was not born excessively; all [beings] were born virtuous.
But in the Kali age, I am born again and again, in comparison with the other yugas. (3.144.110)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Analysis and Transformation of the Duties of the Yugas," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 144 ||
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me how your glorification (kīrtana) should be performed,
so that by such an attitude of humility you may be pleased."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
One should perform my kīrtana with a beautiful voice, sweet in its essence, accompanied by musical instruments, rhythmic movement, and vocal concert.
O Rame, may she praise me with dance accompanied by the *tālītāla* rhythm, with small bells and other instruments, and with songs full of many melodies and passions.
I shall explain the science of music (gāndharva) to you according to its true nature; listen attentively.
There are seven notes, three scales (grāmas), and twenty-one melodic modulations (mūrchanās).
And those forty-nine tānas constitute this circle of notes (svaramaṇḍala):
Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and likewise Pañcama. (5)
Dhaivata and Niṣāda—these are proclaimed as the seven notes (svaras).
Sauvīra, Madhyama, and Hariṇa are indeed those three scales (grāmas).
I shall now describe here the divine *mūrchanās* that produce states of ecstasy;
*Hayamedhā* and *Hreṣiṇī* are proclaimed as the first.
The second is proclaimed as Agniṣṭomā, who is of the nature of Agni;
the third is Vājapeyā, who is proclaimed as Śyenī.
The fourth is proclaimed as Rājasūyārāṇikā;
the fifth is proclaimed as Yavarātā Vaṃśinī. || 9 ||
That which is born of gold and is golden is proclaimed as the sixth *mūrcchanā*;
that which is called *gosavanā* and *rāmbhaṇī* is considered the seventh *mūrcchanā*.
The eighth *mūrcchanā* is considered to be Jhañjhāvātīvarṣiṇī;
the ninth *mūrcchanā* is considered to be Brahmadānāgarjinī.
The tenth *mūrcchanā* is considered to be *lālinī*, belonging to Prajāpati;
while *dāgayākṣī* is the eleventh *mūrcchanā*, belonging to Kṣut. (12)
Pānakrāntā, the barking one, is indeed the twelfth mūrcchanā;
Mṛgākrāntā, the crying one, is the thirteenth mūrcchanā. ||13||
Viṣṇukrāntā is Dhāriṇī, for she is indeed the fourteenth mūrcchanā; Santakokilikā is Unmādinī, and she is the fifteenth.
She is Sūryakrāntā, Kālarohiṇikā, and indeed the Ṣoḍaśī;
she is Sarvatobhadrikā, Modamādinī, and the Sāptadaśikī.
Pūrvabhadrā, Bālakaṇṭhī, and indeed the eighteenth mūrchanā;
Ālambuṣī and Hāṃsinī are the nineteenth mūrchanā. ||16||
Sāgarā, Vijayā, Kokilikī, Viśā, Manoharā, Nāradī, and Mānavī—these are the twenty-one mūrcchanās. (17)
O beloved, there are indeed other secondary *mūrcchanās* as well:
the *Mānavyas*, the *Pākṣiṇyas*, and the *Pākṣavyas*, occurring in great numbers.
Sarasvatī and Bhāratī know all those autumnal [melodies], as well as the Brāhmīs, Gāṇyas, Paryas, Apsarases, and Māyūrakīvidhas. ||19||
Yakṣīs, Kinnarīs, Hāṃsyas, Nāginīs, and Vāḍavas; Paitryas, Daivyas, Kṣautyas, Tāḍinyas, and the various Bhauṃkinīs. (3.145.20)
Mainākya, Paikya, Śaukya, and likewise Āyikā—having understood these according to their respective [definitions], the singer (gāyikā) should perform the song (gīti). ||1||
Having understood the short, long, and protracted [vowels], one should employ the musical note (svara) in singing;
then, one should continuously and repeatedly apply the melodic patterns (tāna) during the flow [of the song]. 22.
Those which are called *tānā* and *starā*, occurring in rapid succession within a flow, are distinguished by their momentary differences as they follow the expansion of the *sphoṭa*. (23)
The first is Brahmatāna, while Garbhatāna is the second;
then follow Vyajya, Sañcaraṇa, Aṇu, Yoga, and likewise Ārohaṇa. ||24||
Tanu, Puṣṭa, Viśāla, Vikāsa, Stanapa, as well as Kumāra, Vāmana, Dvistara, and likewise Vikṛta. ||25||
The firm, the milked, the bundle, the revolving, and the surging;
the deep, the level, the upward, the horizontal, and likewise the timid. ||26||
Kalita, agrita, eṣita, and tapta constitute the group of thirty;
likewise, śṛṅgī, toraṇī, staṃbhī, muṣṇaka, and līna as well.
Udbhava, Aṅkuraka, Granthika, Śākhika, Bahumūla, Hasta, Vartula, and likewise Ucchraya; ||28||
Śṛṅga, Guru, Avaroha, Vega, Sthiti, and Ghaṭodara—these tānas have been declared to you; now listen likewise to the secondary (gauṇa) tānas. ||29||
Skanda, Kāku, Puṣkala, Ropa, Santāraka, as well as Taraṇi, Saṃgama, Ati-vigama, Kṣepaṇa, and Mṛdha. || 3.145.30 ||
Sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), mixing (miśraṇa), as well as dripping (galika), cutting (kartana), scraping (ullekha), and speed (raya)—these sixteen are proclaimed. ||31||
The high-lying, the placement of the hare, the bearer of the hundred-thousand, and the twentieth;
likewise, those with liquor, those with vehicles, those traveling downward, and those moving upward. (32)
The womb-vehicle, the transformation, the reversal, the transition, the bridge-construction, and the support-construction—this is proclaimed as the thirtieth [chapter]. ||33||
The mountain, the sleeping, the swooning, the trembling, the leaping, the uttering of "itkṛta," the unmade, the withdrawn, the living, and the bodiless. (34)
The *uttāraka*, *tālavāsa*, *dvicatvāriṃśaka*, *piṇḍaka*, *kīrṇaka*, *yukta*, *bhaṅgī*, and that which is named *lahara* are considered [types of meters]. (35)
Conjunction (*samavāya*) and sequence (*anuvāya*)—these are the qualities consisting of musical notes (*tāna*).
Furthermore, there are others such as high (*tāra*), very high (*tārātāra*), and likewise higher and higher (*tāratama*), and so forth. (36)

O Lakṣmī, those who lack a continuous lineage, who are prone to speaking ill, weeping, and excessive joy, and whose natures are divided— having recognized them as such, one should then avoid praising them.
One should employ various postures and efforts, as well as diverse sequences of breath, along with gestures and emotional expressions accompanied by bodily movements. (38)

O Rame, I shall proclaim those [mantras] which are endowed with the movements of the limbs, joined with the functions of the secondary limbs, and impelled by the manifestation of internal knowledge and so forth. 39.
These names differ in every Kalpa and in every Caturyuga;
I know them all through their designations according to their true nature.
Formerly, the yogi Śrī Nārada approached me for the sake of the song;
I heard everything from him, yet it was indeed deficient in its parts. (41)
Then, O Lakṣmī, he was repeatedly instructed by me for the sake of training; he became your disciple and was taught by you for a long time. (42)
O Lakṣmī, in your presence and within the assembly of the beloved of Brahmā, he sang before me with all his limbs and minor members perfectly complete. (43)
Indeed, he became the remover of the pride of tens of billions of women;
for the sage Śrī Nārada was gazed upon by me with a gracious countenance.
And then my form as a singer was taken into my own service by me;
you know all of this, for you are indeed Nārāyaṇī. 45.
Then Śāradā, the goddess of speech, having heard that song of Nārada, stood motionless for a moment; what then can be said of other women? (46)
The tongue that perceives taste shook her head in many ways, and all the Sarasvatīs became momentarily bewildered. 47.
There, indeed, was much praise for your glory;
I then presented a worthy reward to Nārada.
Likewise, the wish-fulfilling gem, the necklace, and my Sudarśana discus;
the divine Śakti bestowed by me, which distinguishes my sovereignty. 49.
Then the illustrious Nārada was born as an incarnation in the form of a partial manifestation;
indeed, Nārāyaṇa himself was born as Nārada out of compassion. (3.145.50)
In the assembly, Nārada also praised your compassion;
he extolled you in every way as the one by whom that knowledge was taught.
From that time on, O Lotus-born one, my wives and even the Apsarases repeatedly practiced the style of singing in your presence.
Thereupon, O beloved, knowledge began to circulate in many ways throughout the world;
Śaṅkara, having become a Vaiṣṇava, learned a portion [of it] from you.
Then he performed a dance beautified by song as an offering of *kīrtana*.
Being pleased, I gave him the ornament of yoga. (54)
"Remember, Lakṣmī, everything that formerly belonged to you.
Thus addressed, she remembered and beheld everything within herself. (55)
In the divine abode of Śrīpura, he [constructed] a vast music hall extending for a thousand yojanas,
containing a thousand separate chambers.
And there she saw herself assuming a thousand forms,
acting as a teacher seated upon a teaching-throne, performing instrumental music and song.

There, the gopīs, the female attendants, and those who are liberated, as well as the beloveds of Brahmā, the consorts of the Īśas, the wives of the Īśvaras, and the maidens, undergo their training. (58)
As they engage in conversation, the hosts of Apsaras,
the goddesses, the Siddhas, the Yoginīs, and the hosts of Śāradās are instructed.
There were also Gāyatrīs and Sāvitrīs, daughters of Brahmā and celestial maidens;
Gandharvīs and Yakṣīs, Kinnarīs, and hosts of celestial nymphs.
The sons of Kaśyapa were instructed in the purpose of bestowing wealth,
and many Gandharvas born of the previous creation were instructed there as well.
There were also daughters of the Daityas, Dānavīs, and daughters of the Asuras; there were Mānavīs and daughters of the Ṛṣis, as well as maidens who lived until the end of the kalpa.
She saw all the Naga maidens in the music hall, desiring instruction, training even in their own particular art of singing.
Having thus suddenly beheld the divine schools herself,
she was struck with great wonder there and was honored by all the deities.
She considered herself to be the most worthy of honor among them all, standing in the place of respect, acting as she pleased, and deserving of great pride; yet she also recognized her own greatness.
There, seeing me, her husband Kṛṣṇa, singing even a little song—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, her own Lord—[she was filled with joy]. (66)
Rising up, Lakṣmī fell at his feet and spoke:
"O Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa, you who are endowed with grace toward your own consort, salutations to you! (67)
O Hari, ocean of compassion, O Beloved, great honor has been shown to me;
by your grace, O Janārdana, I behold all of this.
In Śrīpura, I am indeed a female singer, performing songs and melodies;
whatever women, men, gandharvas, or celestial nymphs there are in the world— [I surpass them all]. (69)
Indeed, those who are Śāradās and Sarasvatīs are my disciples;
they all study under me by the millions in the concert hall.
The notes, scales, and modulations arise from my own nature and dissolve back into Brahman alone, just as I abide within the heart. (71)
All of this resides within me, and I have a desire to sing;
if there is permission, I shall sing with all the primary and secondary limbs of vocal performance.
"O Supreme Lord, I wish to perform [this] with all my friends. Thus addressed, I, the Lord of Śrī, spoke of the auspicious non-performance [of the rite] regarding Kamalā. (73)
I prepared a very spacious pavilion and arranged seats; having gathered musical instruments, I set them up within the auspicious pavilion.
And all of you auspicious ones, Lakṣmī and the others, who are beloved of Brahmā, arrived at that pavilion and took their respective seats as was appropriate. (75)
O Lakṣmī, they performed a musical concert, and I then became pleased;
I granted them boons again and again upon the surface of the earth.
"If you perform a beautiful song, you shall become my wives;
by this truth, O Kamalā, [you shall dwell] in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (77)
All those women who are dear to Brahmā as well as those dear to Hari reside in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; they are beloved by me. 78.
While this news was thus unfolding for Divyadarśana,
everything then vanished from sight, and only the horse and the charioteer remained visible.
She [saw] the Kuṅkumavāpikā field, her own golden temple,
herself situated as she was within that temple, her friends, and her beloved as well.
Beholding him, Lakṣmī rejoiced, overcome by great wonder;
filled with joy, she rose up toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Embracing the assembly, she performed a concert filled with joy;
then Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa Hari ceased [their performance]. 82.
She desired to drink water, and Lakṣmī then gave her water;
Māṇikyāśrī prepared delicious food, including soup and rice. ||83||
The illustrious Hari Kṛṣṇa ate; Nārāyaṇī gave him water;
Padmāvatī gave him betel-leaf; and Prajñā gave him a garment. (84)
The Lord Kṛṣṇa ceased [speaking] on the couch made of gold;
Lakṣmī and Padmāvatī likewise performed the massaging of his feet.
Prajñā and Māṇikī performed the massaging of His body, while the other beloveds of Brahmā likewise attended to their husband Hari in their respective homes. ||86||
In that very manner they served him, and Hari indeed attained rest;
thereafter, they all accepted the food of his grace.
At midday, they drank water and attained supreme joy;
having obtained a small portion of their husband's grace, they performed their household duties. ||88||
Thus, O Śivarājñīśrī, I have related to you here the entire former account concerning the practice of singing, instrumental music, and so forth. (89)
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reciting this, one shall obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation, and become filled with all bliss. (3.145.90)
O Lakṣmī, those beloved of Hari who, having remembered me and you, shall perform kīrtana, as well as the beloved of Brahmā, will undoubtedly cross over [the ocean of worldly existence]. (91)
Having indeed separated the body from knowledge, which is illusory,
and having separated the senses and made them divine anew— 92.
Having performed the divine internal meditation and having burnt away latent impressions, [one should listen to] my divine life-story accompanied by the chanting of the *praṇava*. 93.
Whosoever— whether a god, a Daitya, a Yakṣa, a Rākṣasa, or even an Asura— that person shall perform [this] by means of the self in the form of Brahman.
Whether a serpent, a beast, a bird, a kinnara, or even a guhyaka,
having offered oneself into me, who am the bliss of consciousness, and having established yoga therein— ||95||
Furthermore, those others who shall celebrate my name, O Lakṣmī, they all, through devotion to me alone, shall attain the supreme state. (96)
O Lakṣmī, even a brief recitation performed through the remembrance of my form becomes divine; it bestows liberation and destroys all sins. (97)
Having become one with me in every respect, one should indeed perform the glorification;
that shall certainly become fruitful, bestowing complete bliss. 98.
The chanting of my name bestows intense fruit upon those possessed of intense fervor;
O Lakṣmī, I myself dance when the female singers dance. 99.
I sing together with the Gandharvas, yet those who bear shields do not see me;
I increase the joy of my devotees and I acquire [merit] for them.
Having increased their affection, I lead them at last to the imperishable state;
they come to me of their own accord and, yielding their desires, do not abandon me.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Scales, Modes, and Melodies in the Saṅgītikā within the Chanting of the Dvāpara Age, and Lakṣmī’s Vision of the Divine Saṅgīta Hall," in the third section, the Dvāpara-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, you who are devoted to me;
as I, a singer, chant my own names, a divine state arises within me here.
O Lakṣmī, wherever there is my singing, my worship, and my glorification,
no great calamities ever arise there at any time.
Indeed, great portents arise for those who are devoid of devotion to me;
their pacification must be performed, otherwise these men shall perish. (3)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"When great portents have arisen, what pacification exists for them?
For the sake of the welfare of all embodied beings, tell me of such a pacification."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the great portents born of the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth;
I shall describe their pacification according to the truth, regarding those [omens] that arise therein.
O Lotus-born One, the Saumya-śānti is for celestial portents, while the Abhayā-śānti is for those occurring in the intermediate space; and the Vaiṣṇavī-śānti is desired for terrestrial calamities.

One who desires victory over an enemy, one who seeks prosperity, one who has been subjected to malevolent magic by others, and one who wishes for the destruction of enemies—[for these, this is prescribed]. (7)
For the sake of destroying great fear, one should perform the rite for peace (*śānti*) that grants fearlessness;
one should also have the most excellent peace performed by virtuous men and Brahmins.
One who is overcome by consumption (rājayakṣman), emaciated by chest wounds, or afflicted by excessive disease,
yet desiring to perform sacrifices or seeking dharma, should cause a gentle propitiatory rite (śānti) to be performed.
In the event of an earthquake, the destruction of food, famine, excessive rainfall, the arising of fear from locusts and the like, or danger born of heedless thieves; ||10||
In that situation, whether the slaughter of animals or even the slaughter of men has occurred, a devotee of Viṣṇu should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite of pacification (śānti).
During the terrible death of embodied beings, one should perform fierce pacification rites;
one should also carry out sacrifices, fire oblations, and the worship of Rudra and other deities.
When there is a destruction of the Vedas, a destruction of the scriptures, among people who are atheistic,
and when the unworthy are being worshipped, one should perform the Brāhmī Śānti rite.
One should cause the supreme worship of Parameṣṭhin and other rites to be performed by those learned in the Vedas,
both for the upcoming consecration and in the event of fear from a hostile army.

One should perform the Raudrī-śānti rite in the event of internal strife within one's own kingdom or upon the destruction of enemies; likewise when the wind blows for more than three days, or during a most terrible storm.
When food is utterly contemptible, when there is a disorder born of wind, or when fear arises,
or when a wind-born disease has occurred, one should perform the pacification rite for Vāyu.
When the fear of drought has arisen, as well as the fear of excessive rain;
when deformed rain occurs, and when bodies of water become corrupted. || 17 ||
When there is danger arising from water, one should perform the Vāruṇī propitiatory rite;
likewise when fear of curses arises, or even fear of a curse uttered through mantras. (18)
When the fear of a false curse has arisen, one should perform the propitiatory rite of Bhārgavī;
likewise when there is a deformity at birth, a disease of the fetus, or miscarriage. (19)
O Rame, one should perform the Prājāpatya pacification when the fruit-bearing trees wither;
likewise, O Rame, when there is a deformity of household utensils or dwellings.
One should perform the propitiatory rite for Tvaṣṭṛ regarding carts and vehicles, as well as in the event of deformities or even fear concerning boys and girls. (21)
In the event of destruction or lack of livelihood, one should perform the Kaumārī rite of pacification;
in the face of danger from forest fires or danger from fire, one should perform the Āgneyī rite of pacification.
When a violation of commands occurs, when there is destruction among servants and the like, or when a disorder consisting of disease arises in horses and other animals; ||23||

One should perform the Gāndharva-śānti rite in cases of disorders such as singing or other vocal defects, when there is pain or obstruction in the throat and similar areas, in diseases of the throat, and in the presence of wounds or sores.
Even when there is an agitation among elephants, one should practice the *Āṅgirasī* peace rite;
likewise, when fear of *piśācas* and the like arises, or when *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and others are seen frolicking. (25)
When suffering is caused by ḍākinīs and others, one should perform propitiation for Nairṛtī;
likewise when the fear of untimely death has arisen or when a bad dream is observed. (26)
