When one has encountered such suffering in hell or similar states, in an evil rebirth, in the abode of Yama, or under the power of Yama and others, one should perform rites for peace regarding Yama. (27)
In the event of the loss of wealth, the loss of property, the destruction of ornaments, gems, and the like,
or indeed the ruin of one's prosperity, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) dedicated to Kubera.
And likewise, when there is an abnormality in the fruits of trees, crops, tubers, fruit-bearing plants, creepers, grains, and roots; (29)
Upon the destruction of his wealth and the loss of his prosperous undertakings,
he should have a terrestrial pacification performed by those learned in the Vedas who are experts in the rites of propitiation.
And during the first watch of the day or at night when there is an affliction,
[one should act] under the asterisms of Hasta, Svāti, Citrā, Āditya, and likewise Aśvinī.
When Aryaman has arisen, or likewise during other portents and when extraordinary omens have occurred, one should perform the Vāyavya rite of pacification.
During the second watch of the day, or at night during a time of distress,
[one should act] under the asterisms of Puṣya, Āgrahāyaṇī, Viśākhā, the Pitṛs (Maghā), and Bharaṇī.

Likewise, during portents or when misfortune strikes, one should perform the fire-related pacification ritual (āgneyī śānti) during the third watch of the day and at night when there is an affliction.
In Rohiṇī, Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), Brāhma (Jyeṣṭhā), Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), Vaiśvadaivata (Uttarāṣāḍhā),
Jyeṣṭhā, and Maitrya (Anurādhā), one should always avoid [the practice] during all types of calamities.
And one should cause the Aindrī-śānti to be performed by Brahmins who are experts in the mantras, during the fourth part of the day or at night, when there is a great calamity. (36)
One should perform the Varuṇa-śānti rite under the asterisms of Āśleṣā, Revatī, Ārdrā, the fierce Ahirbudhnya, Mūla, and the one presided over by Varuṇa.
Indeed, when a calamity arises during the periods of the Mitra-maṇḍala,
or when various wonderful portents occur, one should perform the two types of pacification rites.
Peace indeed becomes armor; it protects one from calamities and the like.
For Peace is considered the wife of Dharma and the daughter of Dakṣa. (39)
She is endowed with righteousness and joined by me; she has been united with my power, is the very embodiment of my energy, and has been invested with my own strength.
Nourished by the powers of those respective deities, she today removes other afflictions;
through rites named "Pacification" (śānti), all calamities flee. ||41||
The deities certainly become displeased due to the misconduct of people;
and from the displeasure of the deities, indeed, calamities arise. (42)
It is known as being of three kinds—celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial—and the pacification of these brings peace therein.
A celestial affliction is proclaimed to be an abnormality caused by the planets and constellations. (43)
The fall of meteors, the burning of the quarters, halos, as well as cities of the Gandharvas, and likewise unnatural rain; ||44||
A rain of blood, the heat of poison, atmospheric calamities, and those affecting both moving and stationary beings arise from Mars; there is also an earthquake born of the earth. 45.
The abnormality of reservoirs of water is also an affliction caused by Mars;
however, when it occurs under the influence of Mars, its fruit should be known as small and it ripens after a long time.
The cloudless [sky] yields middling results, providing fruit during the middle period;
however, if when a portent has arisen there should be auspicious rain, [the result is favorable]. ||47||
Within seven days, a portent should be known to become fruitless;
however, the cessation of portents does not occur except through destruction. (48)
Within three years, a great and wondrous cause for fear shall arise,
affecting either the king’s person, the world at large, the city gate, or the royal priest.
It comes to fruition in one's sons, as well as in the treasury and the vehicles;
for from the very nature of the seasons, extraordinary portents arise. (50)
Pacified by rites of propitiation (śāntika), they bring about auspiciousness;
however, depending on the specific divisions of time and month, they may be auspicious even in the absence of such propitiation.
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, portents, and the sound of thunderclaps;
halos, dust, smoke, and the sun’s setting or rising with a reddened hue. ||52||
The sap oozing from trees, the abundance of fruit-bearing trees, and the increase of cattle, birds, and honey—these are auspicious signs during the months of Phālguna and Caitra. 53.
Turbid with the falling of meteors and comets, the orbs of the sun and moon turned tawny;
they became black, white, yellow, grey, and dark red. (54)
Blood that is reddish like twilight flowers, resembling a turbulent ocean, and the drying up of the waters of rivers—these are auspicious omens in the summer season. (55)
A halo around Indra’s weapon, the appearance of lightning and meteors, trembling, upheaval, and deformity, and the terrible laughing of the earth. (56)
In the rainy season, boats for crossing that shake upon rivers, wells, and lakes, as well as horned animals and boars, are indeed auspicious. (57)
Cold winds and frost, the crying of beasts and birds, the sight of Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas, and the speech of non-human beings; ||58||

In the winter season, smoke and darkness pervading the quarters of the sky, along with the clouds, forests, and mountains, as well as the high rising and setting of the sun, bring about auspicious results. (59)
There was the wondrous sight of celestial women, forms, gandharvas, and divine chariots,
as well as the vision of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, and the speech of non-human beings.
In autumn, the sounds of singing and musical instruments in the forests and on mountain ridges,
the growth of crops, and the emergence of flavors are auspicious omens.
The sky appeared hideous and wondrous to behold due to falling snow and violent winds; it was dark as black collyrium, yet streaked with a tawny hue from the falling of stars and meteors.
The birth of variegated offspring among women, cows, goats, horses, deer, and birds, as well as the transformation of leaves, sprouts, and creepers, are auspicious signs during the cold season. (63)
The images of the deities dance, tremble, and blaze;
they likewise vomit fire, smoke, oil, blood, and fat.
These women delight, weep, perspire, and laugh;
they stand up, sit down, run about, and pant. (65)
They scatter [the offerings], or they consume the treasury, weapons, and banners;
they indeed turn face downwards and wander from place to place.
For such transformations as these are seen to arise suddenly within the lingas, shrines, and sanctuaries; therefore, one should not take pleasure in dwelling there.
Or if there is misfortune for the queen, that country perishes;
and having seen portents during divine processions, one should predict danger to the country. (68)
One should not find pleasure in dwelling there in the palaces of the Grandfather (Brahmā);
for animals, suffering arises from Rudra, and for kings, it arises from the World-Guardians (Lokapālas).
The origin of the generals, such as Skanda, Viśākha, and others;
and the origin of the world-protectors, such as Viṣṇu, Vāsava (Indra), and Viśvakarman.
The suffering arising from Vināyakas affects leaders and teachers, as well as those sent by gods, those sent by kings, goddesses, and the wives of kings. (71)
The suffering arising from Vāsudeva and the suffering arising from the planets cannot be otherwise [alleviated];
regarding sufferings caused by deities, the domestic priest is one who knows the sacred tradition (śruti).
One should bathe the image of the deity, clothe it, and adorn it;
one should worship it with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, food, madhuparka, and other offerings.
One should attend upon [the deity] according to the rules and perform oblations for seven nights;
thereafter, one should always feed virtuous Brahmins at the sacred fire.

On the arrival of the eighth day, one should honor virtuous men and women with delicious food and desired drinks, along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and perform the gift of cows, land, and jewels.
One should give gifts of gold and complete the pacification of the planets;
having caused the recitation of peace-mantras to be performed, one should bring the evil to rest.
When this is done, those obstacles will undoubtedly be pacified.
Furthermore, if a fire should blaze up without fuel in the kingdom of anyone, [this rite must be performed]. (77)
If fire does not burn even when fuel is present, that kingdom will be oppressed by kings;
or if meat, or anything else that is moist, should burst into flames within water. (78)
Where the rampart, the archway, the gate, the royal palace, or the temple of the gods shine with such brilliance, there danger shall befall the king. (79)
Or they may be consumed by lightning; even then there is fear for the king, or fear for the master, wherever fire occurs on dry ground. (80)
Where there are darknesses without a lack of light, dust without rising from the earth, and smoke not born of fire, one should know that there is great danger. (81)
If lightning strikes when the sky is cloudless and devoid of stars, there will be fear;
likewise, if there are stars in the sky during the day, fear arises in the same way. (82)

When there is an anomaly regarding the planets and constellations, when stars appear irregularly, or when there are portents concerning cities, vehicles, mounts, quadrupeds, wild animals, and birds; ||83||
When weapons are blazing and likewise emitting smoke,
and when they emerge from their scabbards, a tumultuous battle shall ensue.
Without fire, sparks are seen here and there;
and by their very nature, bows are also seen to be drawn to their full extent. (85)
If there should be a malfunction of the weapons, one should predict war in that case;
the family priest, having fasted for three nights, should perform oblations there.
Through oblations of fuel-sticks from milky trees, mustard seeds, and clarified butter,
accompanied by the recitation of mantras to Agni, their pacification is brought about.
One should feed the virtuous, the faithful, Brāhmaṇas, children, girls, and women; one should worship the gods and cause a great festival to be celebrated. ||88||
One should give gold, wealth, jewels, cows, land, and clothing;
then there shall be peace from the calamities of fire and weapons. (89)
In those pure [substances] where they are seen moving step by step—whether weeping, or laughing, or exuding many fluids—[they are known as living beings]. (90)
And the trees, free from disease and even without wind, shed their branches;
likewise, those three years old display fruit and roots at the [wrong] time.
In this way, they indeed manifest their own fruit and flower in the interim;
they exude milk, oil, blood, honey, and water.
Those who were healthy suddenly wither away, or once withered, they grow again;
those who have fallen rise up here, and likewise those who have risen fall down. (93)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you of the different results therein:
from weeping, disease comes; from laughing, the ruin of the country. (94)
If a branch falls, there will indeed be a battle that destroys the warriors;
if a young creeper is in full bloom, it will cause the death of children. (95)
It causes dissension within one's own kingdom, as well as the loss of fruits and flowers in the interim; there shall be a decline in cow's milk, and a famine shall descend upon the oils.
In the case of wine, there is a loss of mounts; in the case of blood, a battle shall occur.
If it flows as honey, disease will arise; if it flows as water, it does not rain. (97)
Trees that are healthy yet withered indeed indicate a famine;
however, if new sprouts emerge from those that are dry, it destroys both vitality and food.
For those who have fallen, rising up will bring fear that causes division;
however, if they move from one place to another, there will then be the ruin of the country. ||99||
Even when the trees are blazing and even when they weep at the loss of their wealth, all this misfortune befalls the king regarding those trees he has worshipped. (100)
If a flower or fruit is deformed, the tree foretells the death of the king;
when such signs have appeared among the trees, one must quickly cover those trees.
One should adorn and worship all [the trees] with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings;
one should place a great umbrella over the tree for the pacification of evil. 102.
One should indeed worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Śivā among the trees;
one should offer animals and food, and cause the propitiation of Rudra to be performed.
Having offered oblations into the trees with the mantra "To the Rudras," one should then mutter the Rudra-hymn;
having worshipped [the deity] with offerings rich in milk-rice, clarified butter, and honey, one should perform the gift of land.
One should perform song and dance, and then there shall be peace for Rudra;
thus, O Lakṣmī, it dispels all fear of the subjects and the king. (105)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for Pacifying Celestial, Atmospheric, and Terrestrial Portents," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Excessive rain, drought, and the fear of famine and other such calamities are considered [omens].
Furthermore, rain that occurs out of season, during the day, or incessantly should be understood as bringing about fear. (1)

Furthermore, unnatural phenomena occurring even when there are no clouds should be understood as portending the death of a king; likewise, a reversal of the normal order of cold and heat indicates fear for kings arising from enemies.
Where blood rains down, there shall be fear of weapons;
with a rain of embers and dust, there is the destruction of the city.
There will be great fear for people arising from marrow, bones, fat, and flesh;
likewise, there will be great fear of enemies regarding grains, flowers, fruits, and food.
A rain of dust from fruits is considered to cause fear of disease;
and when there is a rain of grain out of season, danger shall befall the crops.
When the sun is free from dust and the sky is cloudless, if no shadow is seen—
or if a shadow is indeed seen facing the opposite direction— then there shall be danger to the country.
If there is a shower of hail at an improper time, there will be fear of famine;
likewise, if it is white [lightning] in a cloudless sky at night toward the south or the north.
Likewise, if there is a rainbow, the falling of meteors, a city of the Gandharvas,
a flaming horizon, a halo around the sun or moon, or even the darkening of the quarters, there will certainly be fear of a foreign army as well as calamities within one's own country.
For the sake of pacifying that [calamity], one should perform the Sūrya-sacrifice and the Candra-sacrifice;
likewise, one should perform the Parjanya-sacrifice and the Marut-sacrifice. || 9 ||
One should give wealth, goods, gold, and cows as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) there;
having attained peace, those portents will indeed no longer yield their [ominous] fruits.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to other portents as well that announce suffering, which approach or draw near to the city. (11)
Rivers, lakes, and springs either become tasteless, or they turn discolored, turbid, heated, frothy, and infested with living creatures. (12)
If those born of noble lineage carry oil, milk, liquor, or blood [in their dreams],
there will be fear of an enemy army within six months.
O Lakṣmī, these reservoirs of water either roar or blaze as if with fires; likewise, they emit flames, smoke, and dust.
Or if water appears within them, or if the reservoirs contain excellent aquatic creatures, or if the sounds of music are heard, there will be danger from the people. || 15 ||
For its pacification, O King, one should perform oblations with honey, oil, and clarified butter;
one should recite the mantras dedicated to Varuṇa, or have them recited by Brahmins well-versed in the Vedas.
The fire-oblation should be performed in water, and likewise the consecration with clarified butter and other substances;
one should offer honey, ghee, and milk-rice as food for the virtuous yogis.
Likewise, one should give cows along with white garments to the venerable Guru;
one should indeed offer water-pots and present gems and pearls. (18)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another matter regarding the corruption among women:
women who give birth out of season, as well as those whose offspring are born prematurely. (1.9)
Furthermore, there were women who gave birth to deformed offspring, or to twins and triplets; indeed, they were non-human, lacked mouths, and were beset by calamities.
Those with missing limbs and those with extra limbs are born and dwell there;
so too do beasts, birds, living creatures, and reptiles. (21)
In whatever country, village, or family such persons reside, there will be the destruction of that country, village, or family. (22)
The king should banish men and women who have such deficient limbs from his kingdom;
furthermore, he should pacify the female classes being oppressed within his realm with sacrificial oblations.
One should indeed perform the sacrifice of women, consisting of oblations, feeding, and so forth;
as well as the bestowing of garments and ornaments upon women and young girls.
Likewise, there is the worship of the Mothers, the gods, and the goddesses;
and likewise, the worship of the Yoginīs, the virtuous women, and the chaste ladies. ||25||
One should perform the worship of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī;
and the thorough worship of Māṇikyā, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī.
One should perform the worship of Lalitā, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Rati, and Bhakti, as well as the worship of the Kuladevī; likewise, one should cause these to be performed.
And one should also perform the satiation of the Brahmins according to one's desire;
then, O Lakṣmī, peace shall prevail and no misfortune shall arise. (28)
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this indication of impending calamity:
vehicles that do not move when they ought to, and even those that are properly yoked fail to move. (29)
Even when urged from behind, they do not move; there is great danger in that state.
When driven, they do not pull; nor do they pull when not struck. (3.147.30)
The immovable things indeed moved, and the movable things did not move;
and in the sky there arose the sounds of musical instruments and the resonant strains of song and music.
If he causes injury with wood, ladles, axes, or similar tools; or if cows strike him with their tails, or women beat other women. (32)
If there is a transformation of kitchen utensils and the like, a terrible danger from weapons will arise;
for the sake of pacifying that, one should perform worship of Vāyu and the honoring of Brahmins.
One should offer parched grain, ambrosia, and other sweet foods to Vāyu;
one should mutter the great Pavamāna mantras and the Maruta mantras.
One should feed them with *paramānna* (milk-rice) and perform oblations with milk-porridge and other offerings;
one should give abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), by which, O Rame, peace shall be attained.
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñīśrī, to another indication regarding animals:
when wild forest birds enter a village. (36)
Village-dwellers go to the forest, aquatic creatures go to dry land, and land-dwellers go to the water; they cry out fearlessly in this terrible [time]. (37)
At the royal gate or the city gate, jackals, owls, and dogs—creatures that roam by night appearing by day, or those that roam by day appearing by night—are present. (38)
Village-dwelling animals indeed abandon the village; emptiness is truly the fruit therein.
They cry out fiercely during the twilights and form circles.
Wherever they may cry out discordantly, even there emptiness is the result;
if crows and owls cry out above the head during the day. (3.147.40)
For him, a time of calamity may arrive, or fire may break out unexpectedly;
there may even be death, ill repute, or the loss of his position. (41)
A time of calamity shall befall him when it is brought about by his subjects and householders; where the cock crows at nightfall and the cuckoo sings in the winter. (42)
If a female dove cries facing [the sun] at sunrise, it portends danger;
if a carnivorous pigeon enters the house or settles upon the head, it is likewise ominous.
If flies produce honey, the death of the householder will occur;
[this applies when it happens] at the gates of the ramparts, in houses, at archways, in marketplaces, or on streets.
If a carnivorous beast should fall upon the banner, the parasol, the weapons, or other such items;
or if anthills should arise [there], or if honey should flow; (45)
That region goes to ruin and the king likewise dies;
so too do mice, locusts, parrots, and small grass-eating insects.
There, innumerable dogs and monkeys are seen, causing pain, and where the fear of hunger and Māra may descend; they are full of wood, firebrands, bones, and horns. (47)
In that city where even venomous dogs roam about on all sides, or where crows with beaks full of grain fall upon the threshing floors in the town; (48)
There, one should understand that there will be the suffering of famine which causes the wasting away of the body, and there will also be fear of armies in battle for the people. (49)
If a crow is seen during the day while intent on sexual union, either the king there will die or that country will perish. (3.147.50)
If crows fly about at night, there will certainly be the ruin of the house;
likewise, if an owl is seen at the king’s gate or in one's home. (51)

The death of a householder as well as the loss of wealth should be known [to occur] when there are portents involving wild animals and birds; in such cases, one should perform a fire-oblation accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
May the gods protect the pigeons, the village, the house, and the family members;
let five or six twice-born men recite the Rudra-mantras and Indra-mantras. (53)

Indeed, cows should be given at the end of the protection rite; one should perform a sacrifice for the pacification of the planets, and one should also perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu or a sacrifice to Rudra. (54)

One should also cause the material propitiatory rite (bhautikī śānti) to be performed by the best of the twice-born; listen, O Lakṣmī, to another matter regarding the material rites, such as the indications for the thread ceremony (sūcanā) and so forth.
The causeless collapse of palaces, archways, watchtowers, gates, ramparts, and houses, even when they are firm, portends the death of the king.
Where the quarters of the sky are overwhelmed by dust or smoke, and the sun, moon, and stars appear discolored, they portend an increase in fear. (57)
Where Rākṣasas are seen, where Brāhmaṇas act contrary to the Dharma, where the seasons indeed bear no fruit, and where the unworthy is honored by people; ||58||
The constellations are indeed separated and portend great danger;
so too do the rising of comets, eclipses, or any flaw in the moon or the sun. (59)
Wherever there is an anomaly in the planets or the stars, in that place there will be great fear;
women will engage in quarrels, and children will kill other children. (3.147.60)
Where there occurs an interruption of appropriate ritual acts,
the sacrificial fire, though being offered oblations, does not blaze even during rites for peace.
Ants and carnivorous creatures likewise move toward the north;
full jars leak, or the sacrificial oblation is spilled.
Where auspicious words are not heard from any side, where sneezing afflicts one, and where dolls laugh; (63)
The various kinds of food spoil, and the milk flows out from the vessels;
though the gods and Brahmins are present, no divine power is perceived.
The subjects are devoid of devotion toward the gods, the virtuous, and the brahmins; musical instruments are played with dull sounds and out-of-tune melodies. (65)

Where people hate their teachers and friends and are devoted to honoring their enemies; where people show contempt for those who are worthy of worship, those who deserve respect, and the most excellent persons. (66)
In those rites for peace and auspiciousness where atheism arises, either the king dies there or that country perishes. (67)
Now hear the signs that truly appear wherever a king is ill-fated:
the king hates his own subjects, and he comes into conflict with the people. (68)
He seizes the property of his subjects by force, seeks to destroy the people, displays ingratitude, and becomes enraged when entreated. (69)
He reviles the virtuous and does not honor their praise;
out of greed, he forcibly imposes unbearable taxes upon the people. (3.147.70)
Thus, when such a misfortune has occurred, one should perform the sacrifice for Śakra;
one should likewise gratify the Lord of the Gods together with his consort and the other deities.
Food for the twice-born, as well as offerings (bali) for the gods;
worship for the virtuous and the provision of ornaments and such for virtuous women. ||72||
He gave food to the young girls and auspicious gifts to the boys; he also made offerings of cows, land, gold, and the like, as well as the presentation of garments and other gifts. ||73||
An excellent oblation must be performed; by that, peace will surely be attained.
In whatever country or village cooked food is treated as if it were meat, [there this rite is required]. (74)
If curd appears blood-red in color, the village or its district shall perish;
indeed, the abode of the village headman shall fall down without any apparent cause.
Or the house may be broken, and then there shall be the destruction of the king;
if there is a rain of red stones, there will be the howling of dogs on all sides.
There will be the destruction of regions and villages; therefore, one should perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu. An earthquake accompanied by thunder is a precursor of famine. (77)
If it moves from the south to the north, there is great danger to universal sovereignty;
if it moves from the east to the west, the death of the king will certainly occur. (78)
If [the wind] moves from the east to the west, a battle arises among kings;
if it moves from the north to the south, then there will be an abundance of food.
In the first watch there will be illness; in the second, it causes the loss of wealth;
in the third, it brings grain and riches; in the fourth, it bestows middling results. (3.147.80)
If the earth quakes at twilight, it indicates the loss of all one's possessions;
if a crow caws upon setting out on a journey while perched on a thorn or a tree, it brings suffering.
If a crow comes facing one during a journey while perched upon a vehicle, or if it does so in the sky, then death will occur; one should certainly not undertake a journey at such a time.
O Rame, one must not go in that direction when the wings [of the wind] are cast toward the right side;
once gone, one does not return, for death will surely occur.
If a crow flies from the left to the right, there will be death and imprisonment;
if it cries out toward the north, there will be a great famine.
There will be the outbreak of the great pestilence disease among the people, a massive slaughter, and the destruction resulting from the face-to-face combat of two Tārakas. (85)
If it rises with its crest, there will be the breaking of the royal umbrella and the destruction of children and others;
if it rises with its tail, the destruction of cattle will surely occur.
During the Khagrāsa eclipse, there will be war or famine on earth;
during the Prayāṇa eclipse, living beings will possess medicinal herbs, black grain, and cotton.
Dry grass, dried cow dung, and dry wood;
ashes, oil, and molasses—a man devoid of fortune who carries oil with him. (88)
A naked woman with disheveled hair, a sick man, one clad in rags, one who is distracted, one wearing a tattered patched garment, an outcaste, and a vessel for refuse. (89)
A dead bird, an iron object, a widow, as well as mud; leather, a leather-worker, buttermilk, a corpse, and a pregnant woman. (3.147.90)
The prison-dweller, the black bull, the serpent, and also the frog;
the chameleon, the forest lizard, the hare, the muskrat, and the boar. (91)
Grass, bone, a red flower, a cat, a predatory beast, an ironworker, one ground by a machine, a shaven-headed mendicant, or even a wicked person—[these are all considered equal]. 92.
A matted-haired ascetic, a lame man, a buffalo, a deformed person, a donkey, as well as weeping, an ascetic, an enemy, and a person who has been bound. ||93||
A dog fight, a large web of spiders, and ants;
the migration of ants, as well as a stone and salt. (94)
If one should see a sneeze, a field of *gokṣura*, a barren woman, a washerman, or something unpleasant on the road, one should certainly not proceed there at all. 95.
Death, great suffering, failure of one's purpose, and humiliation—these pertain to the left limbs of a man, whereas they pertain to the right limbs of a woman. 96.
If these should throb, one should indeed know it to be a great calamity and destruction;
upon going there, there may be the falling of a staff or the falling of a weapon. (97)
Or if there is the falling of a crown and so forth, it indicates falling itself;
or if one's own falling occurs from the top of a palace, from a staircase, or the like. (98)
Defeat will occur swiftly, as will death and suffering; when such things have arisen, one should immediately perform rites of pacification. 99.

One should perform the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the sacrifice to Rudra, the worship of the gods, the propitiation of the planets, as well as recitation, charity, vows, and so forth; thus peace will certainly prevail.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Peace-Rites and Other Measures for Various Portents," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the portents arising from the heart,
as well as those arising from the body, and the twitchings of the limbs.
If there is a throbbing in the body at the head, there will be the acquisition of land;
if it occurs on the forehead, there will be an increase in status, and if on the eyebrows or the nose, there will be union with beloved ones.

If there is a twitching of the eyes, there is the acquisition of servants; if it occurs at the corners of the eyes, there is the arrival of wealth; but if it occurs at the upper part or the middle, the loss of wealth itself arises.
O Lakṣmī, when the root of the eye throbs, victory will come quickly;
if it throbs below, there is enjoyment for a woman, and at the edge of the ear, the hearing of pleasant news.

The attainment of joy and bliss occurs at the nose; that which arises from the lower lip brings the acquisition of enjoyments; throbbing in the throat results in the gain of enjoyments, as does throbbing in the shoulders.
Trembling in the arms indicates affection for friends; trembling in the hands, the acquisition of wealth.
Trembling in the back portends lack of victory; trembling in the chest, victory shall occur.
If the abdomen throbs, there is the attainment of joy; if the breast, the birth of a daughter. If the navel throbs, there is loss of position; if the intestines, there is the arrival of wealth. (7)

If there is a joint at the knee-joint with others, or an encounter with powerful foes, and if there is a throbbing in the calves, there will be destruction in one's portion; of this there is no doubt. (8)
O Lakṣmī, if there is throbbing in the feet, one shall attain a position in a celestial mansion;
if there is throbbing on the soles of the feet, it results in travel abroad and brings about gain.
For a woman, throbbing on the left side always brings gain; for a man, throbbing on the right brings it.
If these signs are reversed, they grant no gain; of this there is no doubt.
When undesirable visions arise, one should perform fire-offerings (havana), libations (tarpaṇa),
as well as giving gifts of gold and providing food and other such offerings.
For the attainment of happiness, one should perform there either a Vaiṣṇava or a Raudra propitiation.
Now, hear about the sleep-afflictions that arise from the heart in distorted forms. 1–2.
Having observed undesirable omens that yield evil results, one should perform rites for pacification;
however, the emergence of grass, trees, or sprouts from any part of the body other than the navel does not occur.
Pounding [the head] with the dregs of bell-metal, shaving the head, likewise nakedness, wearing soiled garments, anointing the body, and wallowing in mud; || 14 ||
Sinking into mud, a high fall, mounting a swing, the smelting of wrought iron, and likewise the killing of horses. (15)
There is the climbing upon a circle of trees with red flowers,
as well as the act of mounting boars, bears, donkeys, and camels.
The eating of cooked meat, oil, and kṛsara;
as well as dancing, laughing, marriage, and even singing. (17)
Saluting musical instruments that lack strings, as well as plunging into a stream and bathing with cow-dung water; || 18 ||
Even bathing in mud or in dust and water, entering the mother’s womb, and even ascending the funeral pyre—[these are all endured]. (19)
The falling of Indra’s banner, the falling of the moon and the sun, and the appearance of portents celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial; 3.148.20.
Likewise, provoking the anger of gods, the twice-born, kings, and gurus;
embracing young maidens; and sexual intercourse with men. (21)
There is also the wasting away of one's own limbs, purging, vomiting, and so forth;
the journey toward the southern direction, and being overcome by disease as well. (22)
The loss of merit, the loss of fruit, the sweeping of one's house in a dream, the collapse of the house, or playing together with *piśācas* and monkeys. (23)
Likewise, there is dalliance with bears, carnivorous beasts, and wicked men, as well as with wicked women;
furthermore, there is defeat by others and the arising of suffering from others. (24)
Wearing saffron-colored garments, union with a woman clad in saffron, drinking oil, being immersed in oil, and anointing oneself with red flowers. ||25||
The spoiling of foods, the sight of wood, the straying of carts from the path, and the eating of much fried barley-meal; ||26||
Indeed, the sight of prostitutes, the drinking of their breast milk, the bursting of *śataghnī* weapons, and likewise eating the leftovers [of others]—[these are the results]. (27)
Seeing houses of painters and seeing an executioner;
falling into the currents of ponds and the burning of crops. (28)
There is quarreling with water, the sinking of a boat, and seeing the blind;
sitting upon the hips of a dark woman, and shoes placed upon the head. (29)
The arrangement of contradictory syllables, seeing one's own reflection while traveling abroad, the invisibility of a painted image, and the head of the corpse of Gaṇeśa.
The sight of a camel, an obstacle to eating food, as well as shaving, falling into the ocean, and likewise the flow of blood from the *liṅga*. (3.1)
Wearing tattered garments, the anger of a Brahmin preceptor, looking at a barking dog, seizing a hooded serpent, and death. (32)
Furthermore, there is falling upon stones from the moon-chamber and elsewhere, as well as the sight of a cat on the ground, and a black male bird serving as a target. (33)
The sharpening of weapons by the wicked, the bursting asunder of false arms, the consumption of buttermilk and rice-porridge, and even the disappearance of material goods. (34)
Furthermore, seeing enemies while voiding excrement, falling at the feet [of others] during defecation, and likewise seeing six-legged insects while voiding excrement; ||35||
The Greeks and others committed the cutting off of his ears and nose; they saw him naked, smeared with oil, and joined with blood-stained women. (36)
The turning over and the throwing down of the crown and so forth;
the throwing down of the topknot, the throwing down of the ear-ornament, and also that of the teeth. (37)
The falling of the *liṅga*, as well as the blazing of the consort (*patnī*), the sight of a noose around the neck, and likewise death upon being struck. (38)
The killing of a cow or a woman and so forth in a dream, the sight of great portents and the like, the vision of one's ancestors, and fleeing to a foreign land; ||39||
He was insulted by everyone, forced to mount a corpse,
and even held captive by his enemies from the surface of the earth for the sake of wealth.
If one becomes an ant, a vehicle, or a scorpion of that sort, or if there is an elopement with one's wife, these are indicators of the destruction of all one's possessions. (41)
The state of widowhood for daughters, the destruction of temples, the discharge of blood, diseases of the blood, and the manifestation of consumption (tuberculosis). ||42||
The birth of a stillborn child, as well as the death of a pregnant woman;
the falling of a celestial chariot, and likewise the breaking of a cart. ||43||
He was seized by a tiger, killed by a lion in the forest,
harassed by crocodiles, and likewise fell into a deep abyss.
Likewise, being confined in a pit, being imprisoned in one's own house, and even the binding of the feet by many people—[these are the sufferings]. (45)
Even the enjoyment of a Caṇḍāla woman is called the "enjoyment of a Caṇḍāla";
likewise, for living beings, the sight of a terrifying forest in a dream is a vision of fear.
Furthermore, there was the sight of predatory beasts, entering into the midst of fire,
traveling to heaven by means of a vehicle, and likewise going to the cremation ground.
Furthermore, there is the vision of Yama, the sight of the Man of Time (Kālapuruṣa), the vision of a hungry ghost (preta) in a dream, and the sight of the one who bears the noose (Pāśadhara). 48.
Beholding a royal messenger, seeing even Garuḍa,
eating *tulasī*, smearing the ground with cow dung,
being carried away by a whirlwind, and being dragged by a machine. ||49||
Furthermore, there shall be the tearing out of flesh in the assembly, as well as the trampling with feet.
Vomiting mixed with blood, seeing insects during vomiting, being bitten by a black snake, and seeing worms in one's food [are signs of death]. (5.1)
There was the shaking of mountains as well as the shaking of palaces;
there were girls giving birth prematurely, and women suffering from deformed births. (52)
The falling out of facial hair among men and the growth of facial hair among women;
men assuming the dress of women and women assuming the dress of men. (5.3)
If, in a dream, one sees women possessing breasts or men lacking them, this portends the loss of one's country and great danger. (54)
If a king sees himself killed in a dream, the destruction of his kingdom will certainly occur;
likewise, the movement of trees and the movement of creepers [portend the same]. (55)
The departure of maidens to foreign lands is also observed;
there will undoubtedly be a loss of fortune and famine. ||56||
There shall also be the overflowing of rivers and the surging of the ocean on all sides;
by that water, there will be the dissolution of that continent and even of the earth.
Or there may be the dissolution of the earth; no deliberation need be made on this point.
Likewise, there is the movement of temples and the movement of mountains. (58)
And the Śilāsainya monastery shall become fruitful through its teaching;
however, if unknown sounds arise in a difficult place, they bring fear.
In that case, there shall be fear of the destruction of strongholds and fear of the loss of the kingdom;
if there should be an unprovoked roar in the courtyards at night. (3.148.60)
If monkeys or bears laugh in the corners of houses, there arises the spread of disease, a great pestilence, and the destruction of the people. (61)
At the end of the month, the house will surely become empty; of this there is no doubt.
If, in a dream, one sees a shaven-headed man wearing red garments and holding a staff, [the same result follows].
Death occurs there, as does the destruction of even one's prosperity,
if in a dream one sees forest deities who are withered, aged maidens who are emaciated, or women with withered bodies who are pregnant. (63)
With broken feet, they were lame, maimed, and possessed of horns and humps.
The worlds are struck by drought and people die there, of this there is no doubt;
where cattle are slaughtered by barbarians, that is seen even in a dream. (65)
In that place, disturbances caused by barbarians arise; of this there is no doubt—where carnivorous beasts are seen in herds above the city.
The city will meet its destruction; protection can only come through sacrifices to Rudra, for the radiant, radiant maidens weep as they depart from that place.
In that case, there would be the destruction of knowledge, the ruin of one's endeavors, the loss of artistic skill, and poverty and wretchedness would descend. (68)
Where circles of widows are seen on all sides, there are circles of headless trunks; indeed, destruction follows from battle in such a place. (69)
Where animals stray from their proper season among the flocks,
there shall be a violation of dharma in that land and an increase in the conduct of barbarians.
Other such things as well, including the appearance of leprosy and other diseases, as well as bad dreams—these may occur; it is better to speak of them immediately. (71)
Furthermore, there is the rite of inducing sleep, a bath with medicinal paste, and likewise with sesame seeds;
as well as oblations into the fire, the honoring of Brahmins, and the worship of the gods. (72)
The hymn of praise to Śrī Harikṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, the worship of [the serpent], the hearing of the liberation of the king of serpents, and the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa. ||73||
One should perform the sacrifice to Rudra and the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, hold festivals, chant the praises of Hari, and have the story concerning Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa recited in one's own home. (74)
The thorough recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is a great undertaking;
when great danger has arrived, it should be performed as the dispeller of fear. (75)
A dream seen in the first watch of the night yields its fruit within a year;
in the second watch, within six months; and in the third, within three months. (76)

Within four months, the fruit of what was performed during the ten-day period will be realized; furthermore, at that time, the auspicious or inauspicious results of the two dreams will manifest during the night. (77)

What was seen previously appears later, and what was seen before is perceived as having vanished; such is the prevention [of delusion] regarding the vision of these non-existent things in a dream. (78)
One should perform the sacrifice to the planets, the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the sacrifice to Rudra, the Satī-sacrifice,
the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice of feeding, and the merit of giving gifts.
A king devoted to righteousness and desiring the welfare of his subjects should perform planetary sacrifices accompanied by a hundred thousand oblations.
One should examine the ground at the confluence of rivers, in the presence of deities, near a pond, or at a sacred bathing place (daivatīrtha). ||81||
One should dig a pit measuring one cubit and perform one thousand and eight oblations therein; by that, peace is produced.
In the case of a *lakṣahoma*, it should be double that amount, and in a *koṭihoma*, fourfold. Eight officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be appointed, subsisting on roots, milk, and fruits.
One should place jewels suitable for donation within the pavilion;
[one should recite] the Gāyatrī ten thousand times and the Mānastoka mantra six times that number.

One should offer oblations thirty times with the mantras beginning with the *graha* [mantras], four times with those having Viṣṇu as their deity, five times with the *kuṣmāṇḍa* mantras, and sixteen times with flowers and other such offerings.
Ten thousand oblations of *bādara* fruits should be offered into the fire with the *Śrī* mantra; fourteen thousand oblations should likewise be offered. (86)
The remaining five thousand oblations should be offered with mantras dedicated to Indra as the deity;
having performed one hundred thousand such offerings, one should then carry out the Puṣya-bath.
One should bathe the patron with sixteen auspicious jars accompanied by gold; then peace will certainly prevail.
One should give elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, land, garments, and wealth; and here, one should provide a hundred oxen and cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the officiating priests.
When the month is fully completed, the Lakṣahoma is proclaimed;
now hear, O Lakṣmī, the procedure for the Koṭihoma on the bank of a river.
There, sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) are appointed, and the initiation (dīkṣā) is considered to last for one year;
having commenced the fire-oblations (homa) either in Caitra or Kārttika, [the rite continues] for a year.
The patron, subsisting on milk or eating fruits, should cause [the rite] to be performed;
likewise, barley and other grains, rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds [should be used]. (92)
Fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood are recommended, and likewise the "Stream of Wealth" (*vasordhārā*) offering should follow;
in the first month, one should indeed give a meal of milk to the officiating priests.
In the second [month], one should give kṛsarā, which accomplishes dharma, kāma, and artha;
in the third month, saṃyāva; and in the fourth, auspicious modakas.
On the fifth day, one should give curd-rice; on the sixth, a meal of barley-meal;
on the seventh, cakes; and on the eighth, ghee-filled cakes.
In the ninth [month] one should provide sweet rice; in the tenth, barley cakes;
in the eleventh, bean cakes; and in the twelfth, food of six flavors.
Clad in unwashed garments and remaining pure, he should offer oblations for half a day;
this brings satisfaction to Indra and the other gods, fulfilling all desires.
One should cause all the gods to perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
there, one should cause it to be performed according to the rule with a full oblation at every hundred [verses].
For a thousand [recitations], double the amount should be given, up to a hundred thousand;
the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) should be offered to the deities, and one should honor the twice-born.
One should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the prescribed rite;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should give a sacrificial fee consisting of a balance scale equipped with two pans.
Having bound himself, he should weigh himself, and likewise weigh his wife,
using gold, silver, sugar, and diamonds.
One should give a gift; it shall yield the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and destroy obstacles.
May Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the Lord and Master of all sacrifices, be pleased. 102.
Having spoken thus, one should bow to the Brahmins and feed a hundred thousand men;
all calamities perish for him, and merits accrue to him.
One should not grieve over birth and death, nor over deliberations concerning what has been done and what remains undone;
rather, one should perform the supreme sacrifice to the planets and other deities according to one's ability.
O Lakṣmī, by performing this, one obtains the fruit of all ritual procedures for sacred fords and the performance of all sacrifices; this is attained through hearing it and even through reciting it.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Sacrifices to the Planets and Other Rites for the Purpose of Pacifying the Harm Caused by Bad Dreams and the Like," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī, Queen of Śiva; when an auspicious thing is seen in a dream, good fortune arises for the dreamer, and one should not return to sleep. (1)
Mounting a mountain, a palace, an elephant, a horse, or a bull is auspicious; mounting trees with white flowers is also considered auspicious. (2)

The arising from trees and grass at the navel, likewise the state of having many arms, and similarly the state of having many heads, as well as the arising from fruit-bearing trees—[these are the marks]. (3)
Wearing white garlands and garments, wiping all one's limbs clean, touching the moon, the sun, and the stars, and touching the banner of Indra and other such signs. || 4 ||
The act of raising Indra’s banner, witnessing the slaughter of enemies, swallowing the earth and the oceans, and victory in debate, gambling, and battle. (5)
The eating of raw meat, fish, and milk-rice;
even the sight of blood, or bathing in blood. (6)
The drinking of wine, blood, and liquor, as well as milk;
being wrapped in entrails upon the ground; and the vision of a cloudless sky. (7)
Milking a cow by the mouth, as well as milking a female buffalo, a female elephant,
lionesses, mares, and tigresses, is auspicious.
The grace of gods and the virtuous, the grace of gurus and worthy yogis, as well as the grace of brahmins and of chaste wives devoted to dharma—[all these are attained]. 9.
And there is also consecration with water, either that which rests upon the horns of cows,
or lunar water, or the water of the Gaṅgā, or the water of the sky.
This consecration, which bestows sovereignty and brings about awakening, is auspicious;
it is both the consecration for kingship in a dream and the supreme consecration of the celestial abode.
There was also the cutting off of heads, which signaled the destruction of obstacles;
the acquisition of the emblems of sovereignty, and the sounding of stringed instruments. ||1-2||
Likewise, crossing waters, leaping over difficult terrain, and the birth of female elephants, mares, and cows within the house [are auspicious]. (1.3)
Then there is the mounting of horses, as well as the mounting of elephants,
the mounting of bulls, and the auspicious mounting of celestial chariots.
Likewise, there is the gain of excellent women and the embrace of beautiful wives; the worship with gold is considered supreme, yet it is like smearing one's body with excrement. (15)
For living beings, the sight of their parents, teachers, and the virtuous,
as well as the gentle and supreme sight of chaste wives and beloveds, is most excellent.
Beholding deities and pure yogis, as well as seeing clear waters and auspicious festivals, is favorable;
likewise, seeing trees endowed with fruits and flowers is excellent. (17)
The sight of creepers is excellent, and that of gardens bestows auspiciousness. || 18 ||
Beholding gardens with crops, fields, and likewise rivers full of water, clouds, and lakes is auspicious. (19)
The sight of swans is auspicious, as is the sight of cuckoos;
the sight of cātaka birds, peacocks, and garuḍas is likewise auspicious. The sight of pea-fowl, of birds with variegated plumage, and of white birds is auspicious.
The sight of deer, monkeys, and gayals. || 21 ||
The sight of rhinoceroses as well as gaṇḍakas is auspicious;
the bite or the sight of red serpents is excellent. (25)
The sight of coins, silver, and gold;
and the sight of ornaments, necklaces, and divine garments. || 23 ||
There is the sight of auspicious things such as sandalwood, saffron, unbroken rice, and *darbha* grass, as well as the sight of objects of adornment and other auspicious items. (24)
Beholding a courtesan, beholding a female dancer, as well as beholding queens, beholding goddesses, and the sight of a Brahmin woman. || 25 ||
Beholding a maiden, beholding a virtuous person, and beholding a deity;
indeed, the sight of temples, shrines, and palaces is auspicious. (26)
The sight of devotees, the sight of divine temples, the sight of festivals such as the ārātrika ceremony, and the hearing of sacred recitations (kīrtana). || 27 ||
Hearing the discourse, seeing the pavilion and other such things, seeing venerable persons in a dream, and having one's feet massaged by venerable persons; (28)
Massaging one's own body or massaging the feet by a guru or even by one's father bestows victory in all undertakings. (29)
There was also the sight of Gaṇeśa, the sight of Hari’s attendants,
the sight of the bridal procession, and the sight of sacrifices, rituals, and the like.
There was the witnessing of the installation festival, and honor bestowed by the subjects;
there was repeated celebration with women offering unbroken rice grains and other items, along with blessings. || 31 ||
Wearing golden garments and the like, wearing divine garlands and the like, writing, worshiping, and likewise displaying the pleasures of one's beloved. || 32 ||
Furthermore, the raining down of flowers seen in an auspicious dream—such visions in a dream indeed accomplish all goals. (33)
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare to you the omens pertaining to a journey, so that the expedition of both the subjects and the king may indeed be fruitful. (34)
For virtuous men and for all women as well, it shall be fruitful; likewise, it shall be free from suffering, bestowing desired fruits and granting prosperity. (35)
White flowers are most excellent, as are full water-jars and strong men;
likewise, young maidens adorned with ornaments, lotuses, and birds [are auspicious]. (36)
A pregnant saphari fish, meat, and fish; a pair, a bride;
cattle, horses, and elephants; and the Buddha alone is a bull among animals. (37)
The unborn Brahmā alone is the preeminent king; the thirty gods are his friends, as are women, brāhmaṇas, and virtuous Vaiṣṇavas who wear the topknot and the sectarian mark. (38)
Fire is illuminated when possessed of flames; likewise, a king is a true guru when he is learned, righteous, observant of vows, excellent, free from hypocrisy, and skilled in giving gifts. ||39||
A courtesan who is virtuous and chaste, durva grass, fresh cow dung,
gold, silver, copper, rubies, gems, and diamonds.
Pearls, crystals, ornaments, new clothing, a new vehicle, a new woman, and even a new mount—these are [the objects of desire]. (41)
Fresh grain, barley, white mustard seeds, and medicinal herbs;
a human carriage, a blessed seat, and objects made of gold and silver. (42)
The divine chariot, instrumental music, song, the circle of dance, and festivals;
the sword, the parasol, the banner, the whetstone, and the kettle-drums and other instruments. (43)
Weapons, as well as clay, loads of grain, fruit-bearing trees, all royal insignia, and whatever are the insignia of a teacher; ||44||
Ghee, curd, milk, and various fruits;
a decorated man worthy of honor, a svastika, and a vardhamānaka [vase]. 45.
There was also the sight of betel, the *nandyāvarta* design, and the *kaustubha* gem;
beautiful necklaces and vessels, and the hearing of the sounding of musical instruments. (46)
The musical notes gāndhāra, ṣaḍja, and ṛṣabha, as well as sweet songs, and favorable breezes blowing from behind, are always pleasant and bring happiness. (47)
Carnivorous beasts, melodious sounds, the thundering of clouds, lightning, the bow of Indra, and even the trumpeting of elephants—these too [are signs]. (48)
Clarity of mind, hearing auspicious teachings, saluting those worthy of worship, receiving the words of the guru’s blessings, contentment of mind, and that which is pleasing to the mind. (49)
On one side are all auspicious symbols; on the other side is the satisfaction of the mind, as well as the sight of auspicious substances such as saffron and unbroken grains of rice.
A cow with its calf, a horse-rider, a deer, and even a black [antelope]; a female elephant, a parrot, a myna bird, a cuckoo, and the croaking of frogs. (51)
Candraka disregarded the words of his parents as well as the instructions of his preceptor;
he [took] flowers, garlands, and the like, as well as leaves, petals, and food.
The worshiper, the reciter, the servant, even the excellent devotee, as well as the one with yogurt, the lamp, and the fine incense—[all these offer] various kinds of sweet foods. (53)
The sounds of the Vedas, hymns of praise, the play and frolics of children, the playful laughter of maidens, and the glances of young wives. ||54||
Likewise, the clapping of hands, hearing the cry of "Victory!", receiving honor from the assembly and the community, and being summoned by one facing toward oneself; (55)
The sight of wheat sprouts and young grass, the full vessel, prostration, a cry of joy, and by chance the arrival of drops of rain [are auspicious omens]. (56)
Furthermore, the falling of flowers and flower-clusters from a tree upon one's own head at the time of departure is an auspicious omen indicating gain. (57)
There was also a rain of parched grain and the display of offering vessels;
the horses leaped upward, a portending auspicious omen of victory. (58)
Hearing auspicious news, the arrival of gods or teachers, the offering of oblations, the sight of banners, and likewise hearing the music of the gods; ||59||
Hearing the fame of Gālava today, beholding fresh sprouts, seeing the various mudrās, and gazing upon women rich in beauty; (3.149.60)
The sight of her beloved by the wife, the calling of her beloved, dear speech, even the word of command, and the hearing of the name Nārāyaṇa—[these are the means]. (61)
The nourishment and food for all living beings in their infancy consists of suckling at the breast; thus, the infant, the calf, the animal, and the bird are all alike.
Indeed, the philosophical system [of Kaṇāda] along with its mother [the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra] is seen consuming [its own logic], like one eating grains and the like;
it is likewise the act of pleasure for villages, planets, cattle, birds, and living beings. (63)
Gifts were being distributed, and there was festive decoration at the city gate;
there was also festive decoration along the rampart, and colorful patterns on the ground in front of the houses.
A moon-chamber (candraśālā) provided with a banner is seen; that indeed is auspicious.
So too are sacred trees (caityadruma) provided with banners, and grounds containing sacred mounds (caitya) or images (bhautika). ||65||
The archways were indeed auspicious with fresh leaves,
and the walls along the royal roads were smeared with sandalwood paste.
For that is indeed a sanctuary of auspiciousness, where one sprinkles fragrant water;
there too is the beholding of the sandals and the manifestation of the Guru’s form. (67)
There was the sight of the ocean and the sight of the swelling of rivers;
the beholding of divine youths and the beholding of divine maidens. ||68||
Beholding new machines, as well as the arrival of the guru's mantra, listening to narratives, and likewise remembering one's ancestors; ||69||
There is also the recollection of his descent and the witnessing of great festivals and the like;
all fruits that have ripened, even those ripening upon the branches. (3.149.70)
Stems and branches of trees, rich with pods and ears of grain, and beautified by fresh sprouts, bestow prosperity upon sight. (71)
The flowing of ink from an ink-pot, the falling of ink, the oozing of saffron, and likewise the throbbing of the hips; ||72||
Even the offering of betel leaves, the offering of vessels for substances and so forth, everything sweet, and even the morsels of food in the mouth during the pilgrimage [are all offered]. (73)
Auspiciousness arises, bestowing both gain and victory;
likewise, there is the skin of a lion, the skin of a deer, the skin of a tiger, an elephant, and so forth. (74)
A golden plate, a fillet, the roaring of a lion, and the trumpeting of elephants—these indeed are auspicious signs. (75)

Others have performed the placing of substances in the hand, such as the offering of jewels and so forth, as well as the giving of saffron and unbroken rice (akṣata), and even the striking of the palms together (tālikā). ||76||
The gift of the hand is excellent, and likewise the gift of the mind is supreme; among such worthy and auspicious things, this is indeed the most auspicious. (77)
Victory, gain, increase, honor, stability, fame, strength, prosperity, exaltation, fortune, happiness, success, and offspring. (78)
Thus, these and other [faults] arise, especially in the householder's life.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe their opposites, which bring about fear. (79)
If the wind blows harshly against one's face, carrying grit and being dry, it brings suffering;
if an enemy, a base person, or a wicked individual is seen, it portends fear.
However, a shower like a downpour from a pestle, occurring in the reverse order, is not auspicious;
planets in the direct order are praised, Jupiter especially so. ||81||
The moon is most auspicious when facing forward; likewise, a maiden is most auspicious when facing forward during a journey, as are banners, garments, staffs, umbrellas, and feet. (82)
The falling of sandals, ornaments, and the like is considered to bring suffering; likewise, the falling of weapons and other implements leads to calamity. (83)
Upon emerging, [the head] is struck at the doorway; there is also the striking with the tips of the feet, as well as sneezing and being asked contemptuous questions. (84)
If the horse's back is raised or if it goes elsewhere, that is indeed inauspicious and brings suffering;
likewise, the stumbling of the mounts or their becoming entangled with a stake [is ill-omened]. (85)
On the banner of the flesh-eater is a wicked seat that indeed bestows suffering;
"Where are you going? Stay! Do not go!"—such is the sound from behind. (86)
"What would it matter to you if you went there?"—thus was he insulted;
his voice, filled with external sounds of terror, was broken, fearsome, and shattered. (87)
Unpleasant sounds of curses that cause suffering and inauspiciousness [are avoided];
the sound "Come! is praised when uttered from the front, but not from behind. (88)
And also red vessels, a dead body, a skull, husks, ashes, potsherds, bones, broken vessels, and tattered garments. (89)
Executioners who commit evil deeds, a widower, a pregnant woman, a Cāṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, as well as those who carry water and those who hold nooses. (3.149.90)
Likewise, oil-cakes and the like from which the essence has been extracted, fruits that have been broken, hair-ties, and leather; 91.
One who is like iron mud, a eunuch, and one who is insane;
likewise, one who is filthy, has disheveled hair, is afflicted by disease, and wears garments of red ochre. (92)
Anointed with oil, soiled, shaven-headed, naked, as well as a house, fuel, cotton, dry grass, dry wood, and dried cow dung. (93)
Black grain, medicinal herbs that have been parched or spoiled, the sight of a miser, and the sight of damp or soiled objects; ||94||
Next, there is the dragging away by the hand, as well as the forgetting of objects;
then the theft of implements and the disappearance of the principal object. (95)
Insult, shedding tears, stumbling, rolling on the ground, sleeping, fever, obstruction, the breaking of the wheel and other [limbs], as well as the leaking of weapons; ||96||
The sight of one's own anus, as well as the sight of young grass and such things—all these and others like them cause suffering at the time of departure. (97)
At the time of commencing the journey, the arrival of a great personage, as well as the arrival of a chief official, acts as an obstacle and bestows the suffering of impediments. (98)
Having understood these and other such matters, one should go and never return;
after performing the worship of me, Hari, one may depart for another time. (99)
Peaceful rites (śāntikarma) should be performed: fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa), worship (prapūjana), feeding of virtuous Brahmins, gifts, and a great festival.
There is also the worship of the gods, as well as the libation for the ancestors, the sacrifice to the sages, and the complete satisfaction of elemental beings. 101.
Such tasks as these, as well as the chanting of Hari’s names,
narrative sacrifices (kathā-yajña), and whatever rites for pacification (śānti-karman) there may be, should be performed.
O Lakṣmī, when this is performed, misfortunes indeed go to destruction;
through recitation and even through hearing, misfortunes truly vanish.
Moreover, through rites for peace and so forth, there shall always be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Auspicious Omens, Dreams, and the Like, as well as Worship, Peace-Rites, Sacrifices, and Other Such Measures for the Purpose of Averting Adverse Events," in the section concerning the Departure for the Pilgrimage during the Dvāpara Age within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Whether dwelling in a forest, living in the wilderness, or staying on a mountain and the like; being outside a village or in a desolate place—how can such a person be liberated from calamity? (1)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī, Queen of Śiva! Whether one is dwelling in a forest, situated on a mountain, or staying in a desolate place, even if afflicted by hardship, one is liberated through the remembrance of me.
By remembering, worshipping, or even bowing down to my devotees,
one shall be liberated from all kinds of bondage, even in a solitary place.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"There are many devotees of yours; out of compassion, tell me who among them is powerful, bestows swift nourishment, provides assistance, and removes my distress."
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Even without service, worship, propitiation, or devotion, Hanumān, upon being remembered even for a moment, is the destroyer of all suffering.
Service to others is dharma; Hanumān possesses the quality of being a refuge.
The capacity to dispel suffering without guile shines forth in Hanumān.
By mere incense he arrives; by mere praise he is seen;
and by mere remembrance, having come, he fulfills the desires of those who take refuge in him. (7)
Hanumān removes the affliction of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and wicked women such as ḍākinīs, as well as the planetary spirits of childhood and the sky.
Indeed, lifelong celibacy shines forth in Hanumān;
my own form is the form of Brahman, and celibacy is always considered to be that very form.
Having obtained the power of Brahmā and being endowed with the strength of devotion,
Hanumān performs his task as your helper in your austerities.
Even while remaining invisible, the Lord, assuming the form of the wind, swiftly arrives;
having destroyed ghosts, spirits, and other such beings, he liberates the afflicted from their disease.
Wherever the illustrious Hanumān resides, established according to the rite of installation,
or wherever there is his image, there no affliction arises.
Whether in a forest, or even in a wilderness, on a mountain, in a city, or in a town;
whether in a village, a hamlet, a small settlement, or even while dwelling in a cowherd station.
On a sandbank, on a height, in the lap [of a mountain], on a boundary, in a field, on dry land, in a house, on a path, in a square, on a tree, in a pit, and in a temple. (14)
Wherever Hanumān’s banner is, or his image,
whether in that forest, on the ground, or even upon a rampart or in a camp— there [he shall be].
The classes of spirits and the like do not approach; nor do fevers, obstacles, planetary influences, and so forth;
nor do ḍākinīs, śākinīs, bhūtas, bhairavas, and piśācas. (16)
Sorcery, heroes, diseases, afflictions, night-stalkers and the like, as well as miseries, headless corpses, spirits of the dead, and Brahmarākṣasas; ||17||
Enemies, yakṣas, kuṣmāṇḍas, mechanical devices, mantras, and tantrikas;
malevolent spells and all forms of sorcery flee in every direction. (18)
The yoginīs, the mothers, the daityas, the gaṇas,
and the dānavas fled upon seeing the exceedingly powerful Lord Hanumān.
The Kākinī and Kāminī spirits, the Brahma-grahas and the Caura-grahas,
as well as the Mārī-grahas, are destroyed upon hearing this hymn of Hanumān.
Tigers, serpents, kings, women, and likewise enemies—all these evils are bound by the remembrance of the glorious Hanumān. (21)
By its power, there occurs an increase in lifespan, health, sovereignty, and so forth;
likewise, headaches, abdominal tumors, snake-nooses, and the like [are removed]. (22)
Ignorance, as well as portents of death and whatever misfortunes there may be, are undoubtedly destroyed by the recitation of Hanumān’s hymn; of this there is no doubt. (23)
The Yātudhānas, the Pramathas, the Asuras of terrible aspect, the Ketavas who oppose all that is auspicious, and the reptiles and other such beings; ||24||
Terrible sins, hardships, fanged predators, calamities, and quarrels are destroyed by the hymn of Hanumān. (25)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the worship and other rites of Hanumān.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, at dawn, the observer of the vow [should proceed]. 26.
Having bathed, worshipped the gods, and paid homage to the ancestors with offerings,
one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, adorned with pillars of plantain trees.
It was auspiciously adorned with necklaces, diamonds and other gems, pearls, leaf-patterned arches, colored creepers, banners, and water-pots.
One should cause it to have four doors, twelve pillars, and a canopy of fine cloths;
moreover, one should have the mace symbol placed upon the banner in the pavilion as well.
One should cause a pit to be made in the center measuring two cubits in size,
and a triple-line boundary (trisetu) as appropriate, using vermilion and saffron mixed with water.
One should offer a vessel of fragrant oil, vermilion, a meal of black gram,
fried cakes, sweetmeat balls, chickpeas, and grains of rice.
Sesame seeds, the essence of milk, milk-rice, and milk as well;
kidney beans, ghee, sweetened food, fruits, and flat cakes. ||32||
One should also cause purikās made with milk and jaggery to be placed there;
one should set down jaggery-rice cooked in milk within that pavilion.
Coconuts, dates, and dates from the *khārikā* tree, as well as jackfruit, all kinds of nourishing foods, and whatever fruits are nourishing; ||34||
Then, according to his capacity, the observer of the vow should supervise the pavilion, having first caused the twice-born to recite the words for an auspicious day and blessings. (35)

One should cause the expiation to be performed and also cause the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) to be made, for the sake of destroying all that is inauspicious and likewise for the attainment of all that is desired. ||36||
I perform this installation rite for Hanumān for the sake of peace;
by the grace of Hanumān, may it reach completion free from all obstacles. (37)
One should worship Gaṇeśa and likewise install Rudra;
there, one should place the jar of Hanumān as the principal deity. (38)
Añjanī and her mother, as well as Maruta as his father;
Śaṅkara, the father of the elements, and Skanda who is a celibate student. ||39||
One should likewise establish the virtuous ones such as Sanatkumāra, the Mātṛkās, the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the Nidhis, and the Brahmavrata.

One should establish the Brahmacharya, as well as the deity of the site (Vāstudeva) together with his divine retinue; likewise, one should install the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas), the protectors of the worlds (Lokapālas), and the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
The Garuḍa-vyūha and the Śeṣasarpa-vyūha born of the venerable Vāsudeva;
the venerable Lalitā, Mahālakṣmī, Rāmāditya, and Nareśvara. ||42||
One should likewise station and worship monkeys of that same species,
as well as the mace that destroys all sins, which stands upon his feet and possesses a serpent-like form.
One should place the Brahma-garland and likewise the Vardhinī jar;
having invoked the sacred waters (tīrthas) therein, one should then deposit gems.
One should sprinkle all the five nectars (pañcāmṛtas), whatever vessels are used for the fire-oblation (homa), and all the materials for worship with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).

Having thus invoked the deities, one should worship them with sandalwood paste and other offerings, as well as the sixteen types of excellent materials and so forth; thereafter, one should cause the fire to be established.
One should offer oblations into the fire-pit with ghee, along with desirable foods and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of arka flowers and likewise with fuel-wood such as that of the arka tree.
Having performed the worship of the planets, one should offer oblations to all the deities:
clarified butter, rice, fruit, leaves, flowers, sugar, and so forth.
On the altar, one should place the principal deity Hanumān, fashioned from gold, silver, copper, gems, or stone. (49)
Having brought it there, one should establish it and again cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
one should bathe it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and massage it with fragrant oils.
One should cause him to be consecrated, purify him, and bestow garments upon him;
one should adorn the Son of the Wind and then cause him to mount the chariot.
One should cause him to be paraded through the city with musical instruments, festivals, and songs on all sides;
one should worship him, prostrate before him, and bring him to one's own home along with all the subjects. (52)
Having worshipped it at the site of the altar, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water;
one should let it rest for one night and then raise it up in the morning.
One should perform the entire worship of the deity as well as the fire-oblation (havana),
and cause the mantras of Hanumān, combined with Vedic mantras, to be recited.
Listen, Lakṣmī; I shall tell you the great mantra of Hanumān: Oṃ, obeisance to Hanumān, the destroyer of suffering; grant happiness, phaṭ svāhā! ||55||
If one recites the twenty-syllable mantra ten thousand times daily for one month, it shall destroy all suffering. (56)

Om. Of this great mantra of Śrī Hanumān, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), and Śrī Himācala Hanumān is the deity (devatā). For the sake of attaining all that is desired, for the destruction of all that is undesired, and for the propitiation of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa...
I shall perform the recitation of the mantra of the Śrī Himācala Hanuman Stotra. ||57||

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, who possesses great strength, who possesses supreme heroic vigor, who has the great Hanuman as his mark, whose body is like adamant, who is a celibate youth, and who binds the hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kuṣmāṇḍas, vināyakas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, śākinīs, kākinīs, yoginīs, vetālinīs, kṛtyās, grahas, and bands; who binds diseases and the like—come, come! Approach, approach! Cause to enter, cause to enter! Cause to penetrate, cause to penetrate! Quiver, quiver! O you who bind all faces, bring my enemy under my control! Klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ.
Crush, crush! Kill, kill! Grind, grind! Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ phaṭ svāhā. ||58||

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Hanumān born of Brahmā, Rudra, and the Maruts, for the warding off of all suffering; cut, cut all kinds of fevers! Expel, expel all misfortunes! Oṃ hrāṃ śrīṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Śrī Himācala Mahāhanumān, who destroys suffering and is worshipped by Lakṣmī. Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hruṃ hraiṃ hroṃ hraḥ āṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ jauṃ sauṃ, come, come, come! Oṃ haṃ oṃ haṃ oṃ haṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Powerful One!

O wielder of the mace, take away, take away all poison! Tear asunder, tear asunder the forest of the sky! Cut, cut! Kill, kill! Dry up, dry up! Delude, delude! Inflame, inflame! Strike, strike! Tear asunder, tear asunder all illusion! Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great-Tailed One! Agitate, agitate all powers! Perform, perform the liberation from all bonds! Uproot, uproot all pains! Slacken, slacken all fetters!

Cut, cut away evil ignorance! Reveal, reveal your own vidyās! Destroy, destroy all misfortunes! Accomplish, accomplish that which is unaccomplishable! Dwell here in this image, dwell here! Display, display your miraculous power! O mountain-hero Hanumān, burn, burn my enemies to ashes! Kill, kill! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! ||59||
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and then perform the fire oblation;
thereafter, one should worship Śrī Hanumān and carry out the concluding rites.
On the morning of the third day, having worshipped the gods and likewise performed the fire-oblation,
one should raise up the monkey and worship him.
Having placed it upon the palanquin, one should bring it to the front of the temple;
having performed a circumambulation, [one should place it] facing either east or north.

Having placed [the vessel] before the temple, one should worship, offer the bali-oblation, perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), and likewise perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa). ||63||
One should apply collyrium to the eyes and offer garments, ornaments, and so forth;
one should also perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), resonating with the seed-syllables.

Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅa āṃ, to the self consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; Oṃ, salutation to the heart. Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ aṃ iṃ, to the self consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; Īṃ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ uṃ, to the self consisting of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose; Ūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.

Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ eṃ! To the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; aiṃ! To the armor, huṃ! Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ oṃ! To the self of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating; auṃ! To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ! Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ taṃ aṃ! To the self of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness; aḥ! To the weapon, phaṭ! ||65||
Then, having touched the deity: *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the deity are here.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*, the life-force (*jīva*) of the deity is established here.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*, all the sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of the deity are here.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ! May the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths of the deity abide here; svāhā! ||66||
Placing his thumb upon the heart of the image, he should recite:
"May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths move within her;
may no one whatsoever cause harm to the divinity of this image. (67)
Having restrained [the breath] with the *praṇava* and meditated upon him as if he were still alive,
one should then whisper the Hanuman-mantra into her ear and bow down.
One should install [the deity] upon a lion-throne in the temple and pray thus:
"O God, by your installation, may all inauspicious things reach their ultimate dissolution. (69)
O monkey, make all the Kuru warriors happy in every respect;
one should offer incense, lamps, food offerings, betel leaf, and water.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite and then offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
Having lit cotton wicks, one should recite this *nīrājana* prayer: ||71||
Here is the lustration rite:
Victory, O powerful monkey! Victory, O powerful monkey!
