You are Hanumān, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by gods, men, and sages. 72.
O son of the Wind-god of mature majesty, who brings victory to the three worlds; O crusher of the pride of the enemies of the gods, who removes the peril of fear! Victory to you! ||73||

Obeisance to the Conqueror! Through the recitation [of his name], the afflictions caused by spirits, piśācas, and fierce grahas are destroyed; they perish upon hearing the roar of Hanumān and from the trembling of the earth. (74)
With the assistance of Raghuvīra, having crossed the exceedingly vast ocean and accomplished the purification of Sītā, he set Lanka ablaze. (Jaya0 75)
O giver of delight at the feet of Rāma, protector of those who have sought refuge; O Hanumān, fully blissful, bestower of the fruit of desires! Victory! 76.
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and likewise perform the rite of release;
one should feed Brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, and devotees, and bestow sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should constantly worship the God; he shall destroy all that is inauspicious.
One should gaze upon the banner and other symbols, and recite the mantra without interruption. (78)

Having meditated upon vermilion, oil, and a garland of arka flowers, one should always offer them; thus, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and even Lakṣmī herself shall come to dwell among men. 79.

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Hanuman Mantra, its Recitation, and the Consecration of Hanuman’s Vitality," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, you are Hari himself who has become an incarnation;
I know this in every way, that you have been born for the sake of uplifting the worlds.
How can there be deliverance for those who have not attained your yoga—those unfortunate ones who are sinners burdened by the five great sins? (2)
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me here: how can You deliver those who are associated with the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, and sexual intercourse with a chaste wife? (3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the means for their deliverance;
it is certain that my grace toward even the most sinful is like a blazing fire. 4.
Indeed, out of compassion for the world, I have established sacred fords (tīrthas) that are both animate and inanimate, and truly wondrous.
By the mere touch or even the sight of it, sins indeed blaze up;
the Aśvapaṭṭasara tīrtha is the destroyer of all sins.
Nārmada Śuklatīrtha, as well as Bhagukṣetra, and the great Oṃkāra Tīrtha, which destroys all sins. || 7 ||
Somanātha, Dvārikā, Gomatī, Svarṇalekhikā, and the Nārāyaṇahrada tīrtha, which destroys all sins. || 8 ||
The Bhadrāvatī, the Sābhramatī, the Godāvarī, the Sarasvatī,
the Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī, as well as the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
Gokarṇa, the sacred field of Mādhura, as well as Kapālamocana,
Haridvāra, Viśālā, Kaurava, and likewise Puṣkara.
Sambhala, the Brahmaputra, the Gaṇḍakī, the Kāñcanī river, the Gāgarā, the Sindhu, and likewise the Pampā lake. || 11 ||
Setubandha, Jagannātha, the supreme Kāpila Tīrtha, and the lake named Mānasa, which destroys all sins. (12)
And Kedāra, where bodies fall; the great river Cerāvatī; Menakāṅgī; Śikṣāṅgī; and Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara. || 13 ||
The Kṛṣṇā river, the Kaubera lake, the river Mannāmikā, the Cāṅga and Śikṣāṅgikā rivers, the Śālavīnā, and the Triaṅgi lake. || 14 ||
Also the Nārāyaṇa lake, the lake named Śrīstana, the lake called Dvikalā, and the river Līnāyānākṣiṇī. || 15 ||
The river Obī is known as Coralakā, and the Nīparā flows from Yūra;
the Mahādīrghā is called Nārāyaṇī, the destroyer of all sins. || 16 ||
The Volgā, the Śāvanarī, and I, the river Ambarikā;
the Dvīnadī and the Rānanā, as well as the Pralayāya lake.
The Nāyajharā is the best of rivers, as is the Caṇḍasarovara;
likewise the Kaṅgū river, the Āmajhānā, and the Parīmā river.
The Supāravaryaka lake, the Mekāñjī, and the great river;
also the Vinipāda lake and the lake named Sulava. (19)
O Lotus-born One, such holy places as these have been created by me upon the surface of the earth for the destruction of great sins and other evils.
Indeed, out of compassion for the sake of deliverance in all regions and districts,
people who bathe there attain purity and supreme liberation from me.
Wherever my incarnations occur and wherever the sites of those incarnations are located,
there the people who perform acts of merit are liberated from all sins.
Wherever my image is installed, wherever sacrifices are performed,
and wherever the ritual bath and the purificatory ablution (avabhṛtha) take place— there people are liberated from their sins.
Where the gods move about, and the virtuous who purify the assembly, and where the truthful dwell—there one is liberated from sins. (24)
Where there are people practicing celibacy, where ascetics reside, and where there are virtuous ones whose conduct is Brahman— there one is liberated from sins.
Where the grace of Brahmā resides and where the feeding of Brahmins takes place, and where the Vaiśvadevas eat, there one is liberated from sins. || 26 ||
The sacred ford of the father is a supreme sacred ford, and the sacred ford of the mother is superior to that;
the sacred ford of the guru is more excellent than that, and there one is liberated from sins.
A devoted wife is the supreme sacred site, and a husband devoted to his wife is a sacred site;
likewise, a disciple who serves his guru is a sacred site—one is liberated from sins by these. (28)
Videha is where the virtuous dwell and embodied beings are established in Brahman; by the mere mention of it or by entering its temples, one is liberated from all sins. (29)
Wherever austerity, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, and Vedic study exist, and wherever cows are worshipped, people are liberated from all sins. (3.151.30)
One should sacrifice one's life for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or for the sake of a righteous cause;
one should also sacrifice one's life for the sake of the gods, for the sake of the ancestors, and for the sake of one's mother.
One should sacrifice one's life for the sake of one's master, for the sake of one's husband, and for the sake of truth;
one should also sacrifice one's life for the sake of dharma, for the sake of sacrifice, and for the sake of liberation.
Then all sins are surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
One may even practice fasting or cast oneself down from the Bhṛgu cliff. ||33||
Or one may enter a blazing fire, or enter the water at a sacred bathing place;
then all sins are destroyed, there is no doubt. ||34||
Having given food to a learned man even until the end of his life, one's sins are destroyed and the sin of killing a Brahmin is removed. ||35||
Having bathed at the final purificatory rite (avabhṛtha) of sacrifices, one is released from sins;
one should give one's entire possessions to a virtuous and learned person who is an embodiment of Hari.
His sins are destroyed by giving gifts and by serving the virtuous;
by merely bathing at Triveṇī, all his evils are destroyed in every way. (37)
He bathes regularly at the three sessions of the day, bows to all the deities, and subsists on a single meal; thus, his sins perish in every respect. (38)
By bathing in the water from Hari’s feet, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the duration of a year, a drinker of intoxicants is liberated. (39)
A thief of gold is liberated from his sin when struck with a pestle by kings;
one who has had sexual intercourse with a woman forbidden to him should perform five or six *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
If he associates with those who have fallen [from their status], he should indeed perform those same vows;
or else, remaining diligent, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year.
Or one may give the gift of all one's possessions, which purifies all sins;
likewise, traveling to sacred fields such as Gayā and the like is destructive of sin. 42.
Having reached the day of the new moon, whoever worships me as Hari after feeding virtuous brāhmaṇas is liberated from all sins. (43)
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [one should offer oblations] to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to the destroyer of all beings.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka, one should offer eight handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds to each. (45)
One should worship the God of Dharma and is thereby liberated from all sins;
[one should observe] celibacy, sleeping on the ground, fasting, and honoring the virtuous. (46)
One should perform [this rite] and remember Kṛṣṇa; one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the Sun on the seventh day.
One should also feed virtuous people and is thereby liberated from all sins, having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped me, Hari. (48)
On the twelfth lunar day, one should feed the virtuous and is thereby liberated from all sins;
one should constantly perform recitation, visit sacred fords, and worship the gods and the virtuous. (49)
One who performs this constantly with faith is indeed liberated from all sins;
and he who gives gifts at the beginning and at the end of an eclipse [is likewise freed].
By [giving] diamonds, gems, grains, and other materials, as well as lands, houses, and food, one is liberated from all sins. (51)
Even one who is joined with great sins, if he dies at sacred pilgrimage sites while being purified by his observances,
shall abandon his life according to the rule and be liberated from all transgressions.
Whether her husband be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or defiled by a great sin,
a virtuous and auspicious woman devoted to her husband shall deliver him.
But for that woman who is devoted to her husband and eager to serve him, no sin exists either in this world or in the next. (54)
The virtuous man who is devoted to the Supreme Brahman, the virtuous woman who is devoted to Lakṣmī, and the disciple who serves his guru as Brahman—these are liberated from all sins. (55)
One who has bathed at Phalgutīrtha and other such sites shall obtain the fruit of all merit;
moreover, he who bathes according to my command shall be delivered from great sins.
One should give one's entire possession to a virtuous person; one should give it to Śrī Hari, and one should give it to Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī; thus one is liberated from all sins.
One should give riches in the form of treasures to the god Viṣṇu;
one should also give for the sake of sacrifice, and thus one is liberated from all sins.
One who is content with whatever is obtained by chance should never go outside the house of a Brahmin; such a person is not touched by sins.
He who, having himself endured sufferings, brings happiness to others,
becomes a vessel for all blessings and is never touched by sins.
He who eats the remains of food, who partakes of what is graciously offered by his guru, and who is content with whatever is obtained as alms— for him no sin exists.
Likewise, one who follows a virtuous conduct and lives by not begging,
being content with whatever is obtained spontaneously, is never touched by sins.

A person who is always immersed in the narrations of Kṛṣṇa and bestows the knowledge of Brahman, being liberated through the awakening found in the company of the virtuous, is freed from all sins. 63.
He who is Brahman himself, a knower of Brahman, a devotee of Brahman, served by those most devoted to Brahman, and possessed of self-discrimination—he is never touched by sins. (64)
Just as one who grasps according to need, just as one who mocks through renunciation, and just as one who delights in meditation, is never touched by sins. 65.

Free from thirst for the pleasant and the unpleasant, with hunger extinguished by gain and loss, and devoid of activity regarding what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped—he is not touched by sins. (66)
Whether one is wretched, or destitute, or wealthy, or even a king—one should serve the virtuous according to one's ability; thus, one is liberated from sins.
One should indeed bestow the nine treasures at the sacrifice and is thereby liberated from sins;
one should also assign the Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, and Kacchapa.
One should likewise offer Mukunda, Nanda, Nīla, and Śaṅkha;
and by offering Mahāśaṅkha, one is liberated from all bonds.
A treasure is not to be recognized by its number, but by the act of giving;
even a poor man, having given to the Divine, is considered a lord of treasures like Padmanidhi.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe the giver who is the lord of treasures: one who possesses great conch-shells yet does not give is called a miser. (71)
Even one who possesses very little wealth should diligently give his own money for the sake of the gods, for the sake of a sacrifice, for the sake of truth, and to a virtuous ascetic.
To a virtuous person devoted to Viṣṇu and established in Brahman for the sake of merit, that substance known as Padma belongs; for he is indeed the lord of the Padma treasure.
Whether it be very little or much, whether it be his entire property or his own personal wealth, he who offers it while setting aside only what is necessary for the maintenance of his journey; ||74||
Wealth obtained from gods and others is considered his Great Padma Treasure;
that wealth is declared to be *sāttvika*, for he who gives it is indeed *sāttvika*. (75)
"In the next world, Lakṣmī indeed makes his wealth immeasurable;
for the sake of my devotees, being pleased, you surely grant him everything. (76)
Therefore, for those devoted to the gods and free from greed, these two treasures—divine by name, filled with compassion, and shaped like lotuses—are indeed inexhaustible. (77)
Listen, O Makara, I shall speak: wealth acquired through hardships is enjoyed by one who is solely intent on his own interest; indeed, he gives nothing away in charity. (78)
Desirous of profit, he should give for the sake of interest at the end of the year for the sake of increase, having abandoned the old friendship and established ever-new friendships. (79)
In this way, the destruction of a substance indeed occurs through successive stages;
even in the case of weapons such as swords and arrows, they perish upon being gathered together.
That wealth which is not given away and is intended solely for one's own sake is like a treasure buried in the earth;
at the time of death, that entire possession is lost and will be taken by others. (81)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the tortoise who, having acquired wealth through great effort, neither enjoyed it nor gave it away, and out of greed did not even trust anyone. (82)
For indeed, that which is useless is cast into the treasury in the depths of the earth;
yet when accumulated by a single person, it is seized even by others at the time of death. (83)
For that [fish] is indeed carried off by kings or by bands of thieves;
the *mākara* is said to be *rājasa*, while the *kācchapa* is always *tāmasa*. (84)
The *mākara* is half-sinful and the *kacchapa* is full of sin;
listen, Lakṣmī, and one should diligently acquire the *mukunda* treasure. (85)
But even after depositing it in a treasury or in the earth, he repeatedly takes it out again and again to bestow it upon courtesans, dancers, and singers. (86)
Just as wealth spent on vessels, calamities, or afflictions always results in loss, so too does wealth belonging to one devoted to sin result in the loss of that which is named Mukunda. 87.
Even a doer of evil must indeed be awakened; he is the treasure-hoard that holds the sheath of Mukunda.
Listen, O Padmaja, for I shall also tell you of Nanda and the treasure-hoard.
For he who delights in passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) shall indeed be the support of the Kula;
all the members of the family enjoy the substance out of a spirit of love. (89)
Praises are also born [for them], they have many wives, and there is the enjoyment of wealth for their own sake as well as for the benefit of others. (3.151.90)
He shows laxity toward former friends and forms attachments with others;
such is his own wealth, for it is indeed of the nature of a treasure in a grove. (91)
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the treasure Nīla and likewise the Uttara;
by means of his own wealth, Nīla indeed always becomes one of sattvic nature. (92)
One who collects clothing, grain, and so forth, constructs tanks and similar works;
this is a treasure lasting for three generations, and one should cause mango groves and the like to be established. (93)
He indeed performs religious duties and gives a garden to Viṣṇu;
I shall describe Śaṅkhanidhi, O Lakṣmī, listen, for he brings about calamity. (94)
O Rame, Śaṅkha himself consumes the wealth of one person until it is exhausted;
neither his family nor his lineage enjoys that wealth. 95.
With his attendants eating poor food and wearing no fine garments, and desiring only to nourish his own interests, he would give to another man in vain. (96)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the great conch, the treasure; it is not for the sake of enjoyment alone.
For wealth exists only among others, not even slightly in one's own house. (97)
Thus, having understood that the treasures are for the sake of awakening, one should employ them;
by doing so for the sake of sacred sites, deities, and the virtuous, one is liberated from all sins. (98)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Destroying All Great Sins and Other Evils, and the Explanation of the Names and Purposes for the Employment of Wealth by the Nine Treasures," in the Third Section on the Lineage of Dvāpara within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to those sons who effect the removal of sin, who are endowed with the strength of dharma, and by taking refuge in whom there is liberation. || 1 ||
From Dharmadeva, Śraddhā indeed gave birth to a son named Kāma;
that Kāma, when applied for my sake, is intended for liberation. || 2 ||
From Dharmadeva, Śrī indeed gave birth to an auspicious son named Darpa; though Darpa was employed for my sake, he is destined for liberation. (3)
From Dharmadeva, Dhṛti gave birth to a son named Niyama;
he was appointed for my sake and is intended for liberation. (4)
From Dharmadeva, Tuṣṭi gave birth to a son named Saṃtoṣa;
he has been appointed for my sake and is intended for my liberation. || 5 ||
Likewise, Puṣṭi bore a son named Lobha to Dharmadeva;
"Lobha, when employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (6)
Likewise, Medhā bore a son named Śruta to Dharmadeva;
and this [son], being employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (7)
Likewise, Kriyā gave birth to Daṇḍa as the son of Dharmadeva;
Daṇḍa, when employed for my sake, is ordained for liberation.
Policy followed by punishment, and discipline followed by policy—
these three, when applied by me, truly lead to liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Buddhi gave birth to a son named Bodha;
this Bodha, when employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (3.152.10)
Likewise, from Dharmadeva, Lajjā gave birth to a son named Sunaya;
one who is joined with Sunaya is prepared for liberation through Kṛṣṇa. || 11 ||
Likewise, from Dharmadeva, Vapu gave birth to Vyavasāya;
and Vyavasāya, being employed for my sake, shall become the bestower of liberation. ||12||
Likewise, Śānti bore a son named Kṣema to Dharmadeva;
Kṣema, when employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (13)
From Dharmadeva, Siddhi likewise gave birth to a son named Sukha;
and Sukha, being united with Kṛṣṇā, is destined for liberation.
Likewise, Dharmadeva gave birth to Kīrti and a son named Yaśas;
that fame, when united with Kṛṣṇa, is ordained for liberation.
And if all these grandsons of Dharma are indeed engaged for my sake,
they shall all lead to liberation and become destroyers of sin.
Kāmaputra is Mahānanda; Harṣaputra is Atimānaka;
Niyamavirāma is Santuṣṭi; and Tarpaṇa is the son of Santoṣa. || 17 ||
The son of Greed is Accumulation; the son of Sacred Learning is Determination; the son of Punishment is known as Suffering; and the son of Policy is Increase. || 18 ||
Vinaya was the son of Abhyudaya, Śāntanu was the son of Bodha, Tejas was the son of Sunaya, and Āyaka was the son of Vyavasāya. (1.9)
The son is the protection of security; the son is known as the joy of happiness;
the son is the festival of fame; and indeed, O my son, grandsons are the fruit of dharma.
When applied, O beloved, they all bestow liberation and destroy sins;
through yoga, these divine [mantras] should be joined by the virtuous, for they truly cause one to cross over [saṃsāra]. 21.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to those who indeed bestow sin and cause the destruction of merit;
they are the sons of Adharma, who promote wicked deeds and conduct. (22)
Himsā was the wife of Adharma; from her was born a son named Anṛta.
Anṛta is said to be untruth, which causes suffering and brings about evil. (23)
His sister was Nirṛti, and his two sons were Naraka and Bhaya;
likewise, two daughters are considered to be Māyā and Vedanā.
Likewise, Māyāsuta was born, as well as Mṛtyu, the snatcher away of all beings;
and from Vedanā, the son named Duḥkha was also born. (25)
From Death were born Disease, Old Age, Sorrow, and Thirst, as well as Anger;
and Nirṛti gave birth to her son Vināśa, who is difficult to endure.
Brahmā, however, spoke these beneficial words to the son of Nirṛti, who was difficult to endure, hungry, emaciated, having the voice of a crow, and with a downcast face: ||27||
"Do not devour this world, my son; I shall provide for your livelihood.
May your dwelling always be in the abode of the unrighteous. (28)
Food that has been kept overnight, that contains insects, or has been looked upon by dogs;
food placed in a broken vessel, or that has been touched by the breath of the mouth—[these are forbidden]. (29)

Food that is left-over, even if it has been steamed, or that which has been licked, or that which is unconsecrated, or that which has been defiled by a woman in her courses—if you eat such food, it shall belong to you as your own. (3.152.30)
O Yakṣa, whatever has been offered or given without faith, by those who have not bathed, or with contempt; whatever is abandoned or wicked—all that has been entrusted to you by me. (3.1)
Your dwelling shall be among those who break the ranks, the deceitful, those who alter the cooking of food, the fraudulent, the quarrelsome, and the wicked. (32)
While the aged bull is left unfed and unattended, and while the young ones are deprived of nourishment, your dwelling shall always be in such a house. (33)
You shall overcome those mortals who observe fasts in vain, those addicted to the vices of gambling and women, and those deceitful ones who follow the "cat-like" way of life.
But for those who inflict suffering, for the wicked, for those who betray trust, and for those who oppose those seeking refuge—there shall always be your dwelling in their homes. (35)
O merciless one, you must indeed always remain in this house, which is difficult to endure;
you must never stay in a righteous home or in a temple of the gods. (36)
He who is pure within and likewise without regarding the consecrated food and other matters according to the rule, who is free from greed and has conquered desire—abandon his house as well. (37)
Abandon even that house where there is no loving-kindness toward children, the elderly, women, and men, as well as toward one's own kinsmen. (38)
O Yakṣa, avoid that house where women take delight and have no desire to go outside, and which is always filled with modesty. (39)
Avoid that house where there are beds and foods suited to one's age, yet where there is no service to the virtuous. (3.152.40)
Avoid that house where compassionate ones, ever established in virtuous deeds, reside, provided it is equipped with common utensils. (41)
Avoid that house where those seated on their seats rise up suddenly in the presence of their teacher or even in the presence of the elders. 42.
That house whose door is not pierced by young trees, shrubs, and the like, and which possesses the beauty of a garden—that dwelling is auspicious; avoid the others. (43)
Avoid that house where no sound of men piercing the vital points arises, nor where such speech is not heard within. (44)
Avoid that house where there is no worship of the deities, ancestors, mortals, and guests, and where one eats only what remains from their grace. (45)
You should avoid men and women who speak the truth, who are forgiving by nature, non-violent, free from regret, and devoid of envy. (46)
Abandon that woman who is devoted to serving her husband, who avoids the company of unchaste women, and who is nourished by the food remaining from the family and her husband. 47.
Always abandon that auspicious brahmin who possesses Vedic knowledge, is of a sattvic nature, worships the gods, is devoted to sacrifices such as the *adhvara*, and is contented and tranquil. 48.
Abandon that unbearable, powerful Kṣatriya who is a protector, a donor, one who follows the path of Dharma, devoted solely to justice, and full of devotion. (49)
But abandon the Vaiśya who is established in his livelihood, devoted to truth and righteousness, non-violent, intent on charity, devoted [to you], and a servant of the cows. (3.152.50)
Abandon the Śūdra who is devoted to service, faithful, peaceful, and sincere;
where the husband and wife are mutually supportive in their amorous dalliance. (51)
Abandon that house in every way where the son is devoted to dharma and liberation, yet performs worship for his teacher, the gods, and likewise for his father. (52)
And there, his wife performs unbearable tasks; do not dwell there, where one must apply ointments morning and evening and attend to the worship of the gods. (53)
You are unable even to look upon the home of the virtuous, which is purified by their feet, where beds are not seen by the sun, and where fire and water are ever-present. (54)
Lamps that illuminate like the sun, possessing the supernatural power of the gateway of giving, worthy recipients of the grace of the virtuous, they are houses of fortune and vessels of merit. (55)
Where Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī are worshipped, and where there are indeed virtuous men and women, how could there be any fear of misfortune? (56)
That house where there is a bull, sandalwood, a lute, a mirror, honey, clarified butter, sweet food, ghee, and copper vessels— that is not your refuge.
Where there are thorny trees, where there are intoxicating creepers, and where the wife is devoid of marriage—that is an anthill; dwell there! (58)
In that house where there are five men, three women, and likewise three lineages, yet which is dark and devoid of fire—that house shall be your dwelling. (59)
One goat, two female donkeys, three oxen, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants—dry up this house, O unbearable one! (3.152.60)
Likewise, the hoe, the sickle, and the basket; the cooking pot and other vessels; all such implements, as well as the pestle and the mortar. (61)
The bed of women, as well as other things, are scattered here and there;
your dwelling is a house that is unclean and filthy. (62)
The pestle and mortar shall be the seat for women, and the threshold shall be the place for their counsel;
dwell in that house, O intolerable one! (63)
Just as grains, both ripe and unripe, are trampled where they lie in a house, so too are students there; roam about as you please, O Unbearable One! (64)
Where fire is placed upon the lid of a cooking pot or within the hollow of a ladle in a house, that indeed becomes the abode of all calamities without exception.
In whose house there is human bone, death shall abide day and night;
therein your dwelling will be unbearable, as well as that of other rākṣasas.
Where there are Padma and Mahāpadma, where there is a young woman eating sweetmeats, and where there are bellowing bulls—abandon that house by all means. (67)
Where weaponless deities and those with weapons are fashioned by men for worship without any battle, abandon that temple. (68)
Do not dwell in that house where the citizens and countryfolk no longer perform their long-established great festivals as they did before. (69)

Go to those whose auspicious marks have been destroyed by bathing with water from a winnowing-basket fan, by the drops of water from their clothes, or even by the water on the tips of their nails. 3.152.70.

The house should be endowed with local customs and the traditions of one's kin, accompanied by festivities; it should be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, and graced with auspicious rites for the deity. (71)

O unbearable one, do not touch that house, which is endowed with purity and right conduct, which is the grain for the world, worthy of worship, and a constant refuge; do not even look upon those who dwell therein.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, at the beginning, Brahmā gave a dwelling to Duḥsaha for the sake of his residence;
indeed, Duḥsaha became the companion of Adharma.
Duḥsaha had a wife known by the name Malinī;
she was the daughter of Kali, skilled in quarreling, and one who relied upon the nature of affliction. (74)
She had eight sons and eight daughters who were terrifying;
[the sons were] Dantākṛṣṭi, Ukti, and Parivarta as the third. ||75||
Aṅgadhṛk, Śakuni, Gaṇḍaprāntarati, Garbhahā, and Sasyahā—listen also to these names of the Kanyās. (76)

The first is the Impeller (niyojikā), the second is the Obstructer (virodhinī), the third is the Seizer (svayaṃhārakarī), the fourth is the Deluder (bhrāmaṇī), and the fifth is the Stealer of the Season (ṛtuhāriṇī). ||77||
The eighth is the destroyer of memory, the destroyer of seed, and likewise the one who causes enmity;
these are the givers of fear. Now hear from me their respective functions.
The "Tooth-drawer" (Dantākṛṣṭi) resides in the teeth of infants who have been born;
it causes the onset of fever. Its pacification is achieved by scattering white mustard seeds upon the bed and by wearing a linen garment. (79)
Thus speaks the one named Tathokti; let there be an end to this unbearable state. For the sake of its pacification, Janārdana must be glorified with auspicious hymns.
The *parivarta* indeed effects the turning of the fetuses;
one should perform protection with *rakṣoghna* mantras and white mustard seeds. (81)
Indeed, one who wears [the grass] on his limbs causes the limbs to throb inauspiciously;
however, by touching her lap with *kuśa* grass, that throbbing then ceases.
Furthermore, when a bird such as a crow perches [on a tree], that omen is always inauspicious; in this case, one should abandon the undertaking and turn back. (83)
And at the end of the Gaṇḍakāla period, Gaṇḍaprānta also dwells there;
he utterly destroys all undertakings, but his obstruction is averted by the praise of the deity. (84)

One who possesses a *gaṇḍa* [yoga] indeed attains dissolution through baths with cow urine and mustard seeds, through the worship of the corresponding planets, and by performing festivals for the Dharma and other such rites. //85//
The destroyer of embryos and the destroyer of the fetus perishes constantly through purification;
he is destroyed by means of divine garlands, protective rites, and mantras. (86)
A crop-stealer destroys the abundance of grain in a portion of the field;
therefore, one should provide protection by wearing a pair of worn-out sandals.

Likewise, by walking with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), by the entry of a Caṇḍāla, by the offering of the bali-oblation outside, and by dwelling at the feet of the virtuous; ||88||
But she who incites men toward theft, sexual misconduct, intoxicants, and the like, should bring about their pacification through association with the virtuous. ||89||
Through the performance of initiations and other rites, through religious duties, vows, and the frequenting of sacred fords,
she indeed creates discord between husband and wife.
Relatives, friends, parents, and sons should always perform its pacification toward one another by following the conduct prescribed in the scriptures. 91.
A girl who steals for herself even takes grain from the threshing floor;
likewise, she takes milk from the cows, and even takes the clarified butter from that milk.
One steals prosperity by taking highly valuable goods from a kitchen; likewise, one steals food that is half-cooked or that remains in a storehouse for food. (93)
When food has been served, she eats together with those who are eating;
likewise, she carries off the food that remains as the leavings of men. (94)
She even steals the perfected power from the workshops and halls of industry; she is likewise a stealer of milk, taking the milk from the udders of cows and women. (95)
Clarified butter from curd, oil from sesame seeds, liquor from a distillery, dye from safflower and the like, and even thread from cotton—[these are forbidden]. (96)
For the sake of pacifying that [evil influence], one should perform an auspicious pairing of two peacocks;
furthermore, one should place an artificial woman there, both in the house and on the ground.
Likewise, one should recite the protective mantra of Lakṣmī:
"O Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Lalitā, Kambharā, Sati!
Strike down the wicked Hārikā; let Hārikā meet her destruction! (98)
Having prayed thus, one should cause it to be placed in the house, on a spot of ash, or in a cow-pen;
by means of the smoke from the sacrificial fire, the deity, incense, ash, and so forth, [the evil] is destroyed. 99.
For one who dwells in a single place, another [woman] indeed produces agitation;
moreover, that woman who causes him to wander brings him suffering.
Then, one should perform protection for him with scattered white mustard seeds, on his seat, his bed, and on the ground wherever that man resides. 101.
Furthermore, she who takes flowers from other women is a debtor;
she should instead perform worship at sacred fords, temples, shrines, and on the peaks of mountains.

For the pacification of that [fever], a physician skilled in treatment should administer excellent medicines appropriate for the season and perform ablutions in rivers, confluences, or excavated pools.
She robs women of their memory, for she is indeed the destroyer of men's memory;
this is due to her frequenting secluded places as well as her devotion to Lord Hari.
And through unctuous food and drink, there may be its alleviation; furthermore, another [wind], known as *bījāhāpariṇī*, also carries away semen and the *rajas*. 105.

The pacification of that [anger] is said to occur through eating food purified by the grace of Hari, and by pilgrimage to sacred fords, when the one who holds the fruit of desires in his hand [is present]. (106)
One who is hateful should offer sesame seeds smeared with honey, milk, and ghee as an oblation for the sake of pacification; one should perform the sacrifice to Mitravindā.
O Lotus-born One, I shall now describe the other offspring of these princes and princesses, beginning with their naming ceremonies and so forth.
From the extraction of the teeth, two daughters—Vijalpā and Kalahā—are born;
both cause affliction, and pacification should be performed through the rite of fire-offerings (homa).
In the rite of offering (balikarman), one should scatter sprouts of dūrvā grass smeared with honey, ghee, and milk,
and likewise offer them into the fire while invoking Mitra.
From Tathokti was born a son named Kālajihva, who oppresses the wicked;
and from Rama were born two sons, Parivarta and Suta, who were deformed and hideous.
Since those two [the crow and the owl] take refuge in the tops of trees, moats, walls, and the ocean,
and cause the destruction of the fetus, a pregnant woman should not ascend them.
O Lakṣmī, his son, known by the name Piśuna, held the trees, the moat, the rampart, and the great ocean upon his limbs. 11.3.
The strength of men who have conquered their minds through the practice of yoga resides in the bones and marrow;
furthermore, there are five types of birds: the hawk, the crow, and the pigeon.
The vulture and the owl—these are considered to be the hawk that bestows death; the crow brings about the end of time, while the owl brings about the state of a rākṣasa.
A pigeon that is greedy brings disease and leads one upon the path of Yama;
furthermore, if hawks and other birds perch upon its head, [the same result follows].
A man should avoid a house whose roof is occupied by a pigeon;
for the hawk, the pigeon, the vulture, the crow, and the owl take delight in such a dwelling.
Once he has entered, he should report the end [of the matter] to those dwelling in that house;
for even in a dream, the sight of pigeons and the like is not auspicious.
The sons of Gaṇḍaprāntarati, who dwell in Rājasvalya and reside at Śrāddhaparva— during those times, one should not approach a woman.
The son is the destroyer of the womb, and the daughter is the one who wets;
one enters the womb and devours it, while the other, having consumed it, causes delusion.
From that, children are born—frogs, tortoises, and reptiles—or it indeed becomes feces; thus she becomes pregnant. (121)
One should avoid cremation grounds, burial sites, and crossroads at night;
one should avoid the shade of trees and must not cast off one's upper garment.
The son of Śasyahaṃsa, Kṣudraka, destroys the prosperity of Ṛddhikā;
indeed, the field of the sower does not bear fruit when sown on an inauspicious day.
The daughter of a procuress, one who is intoxicated, insane, or negligent, and a young girl—these enter for the destruction of all embodied beings. 1.24.

Through the *virodhinī* [yoga], they cause others to engage in unrighteous acts and the like, such as union with the wives of others; it has three sons: *nodaka*, *grāhaka*, and likewise [the third]. (1.25)
In a household devoid of proper conduct, there is indeed one who covers over the darkness and another who practices slander; the former is the giver, while the latter is the receiver.
O Rame, the third [son] generates anger through darkness and causes extreme suffering;
these three sons, born of me by theft, are to be taken away by me myself.
The one who takes everything away, the one who takes half, and likewise the one who takes away vigor—they always dwell in the house of misconduct and the house of afflictions. 128.
The son of Bhrāmaṇī, named Kākajaṅgha, who was devoid of righteousness, took delight in pleasure, sang, ate, and indulged in laughter. (129)

The maiden who has three sisters, she who lacks breasts, she who lacks secondary sexual characteristics, and she who kills her offspring—for her, the world does not perform the proper marriage rite. (3.152.1) 30.
Or else, having passed the proper time, one steals her two breasts;
likewise, by not giving the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and by failing to honor one's mother. (131)
Another steals the ornaments of a married maiden;
the third, however, dwells in the midst of fire, in smokeless places, and in the lying-in chamber.
Having entered a place devoid of lamps, weapons, clubs, living beings, and mustard seeds, she carries off the newborn child; thus, that [child] perishes. (133)
She is named Jātahāriṇī, a most terrible eater of flesh;
therefore, one must take great care to protect [the child] diligently in the lying-in chamber.
Smṛtihā was his son by name, as were Pracaṇḍa and Attukāman; Līka and Caṇḍaputra were also his sons, and they were all born from the womb of a Caṇḍāla woman. ||1 35||
Worldly people indeed cause the lineage of unrighteousness to dwell and carry it away;
those who destroy the seed strive for the destruction of the seed in one devoid of purity.
The two sons of Vidveṣiṇī were manifesters of harm toward men;
however, even though one was a sinner, he made his own virtues known in the world. (1.37)
But the second [type of person] draws away from the world the virtues of friendliness;
thus all these are difficult to endure, by which the subjects suffer hardship. (1.38)
Their pacification must be performed with various offerings and honors,
through sacrifices dedicated to Rudra, Viṣṇu, the gods, the spirits, and Caṇḍī.
Through the worship of Hari with devotion, through vows and acts of propitiation, through special services to the virtuous, and through wonderful and worthy offerings; || 3.152.140 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told that which destroys the sins of the wicked, as well as rites for pacification and other purposes, and portents occurring in connection with them. (141)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Lineage of Dharma, Description of the Lineage of Adharma, the Residences of Duḥsaha, and the Description of the Oppressions of the Descendants of Duḥsaha," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Which direction is considered best for a journey, and which is considered inferior? When is it deemed appropriate?
When is the departure most auspicious, and at what time is which action considered excellent? (1)
When might it become inauspicious regarding the conjunctions of constellations, days, and lunar days?
Tell me all that for the sake of the welfare of the world. (2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Kṛttikā has Agni as its presiding deity; Rohiṇī has Brahmā as its deity;
Mṛgaśirā has Soma as its deity; and Ārdrā has Rudra as its deity.
Punarvasu has the Sun as its deity; Puṣya has Jupiter as its deity;
Aśleṣā has the Serpents as its deity; and Maghā has the Ancestors as its deity. || 4 ||
Pūrvāphālgunī should be known as having Padmajā as its presiding deity; Uttarāphālgunī should be known as having Aryaman as its presiding deity. || 5 ||
Hasta has Savitṛ as its deity, while Citrā has Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity;
Svātī has Vāyu as its presiding deity, and Viśākhā has Indra and Agni as its deities.
Anurādhā has Mitra as its deity; Jyeṣṭhā, however, has Śakra as its deity;
Mūlā has Nirṛti as its presiding deity; and Pūrvāṣāḍhā has the Waters (Āpa) as its deity.
Uttarāṣāḍhā is proclaimed to have the Viśvedevas as its deity;
Abhijit has Brahmā as its deity, and Śravaṇā has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Dhaniṣṭhā has Vasudeva as its deity; Śatabhiṣā has Varuṇa as its deity;
Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā have Aja (the Unborn) as their deity; and Revatī has Ahirbudhnya as its deity.
Puṣya has the gods as its deity, Revatī has the Aśvins as its deity, and likewise Aśvinī;
Bharaṇī has Yama as its deity—these are declared to be the deities of the lunar mansions (ṛkṣa).
Brahmāṇī is established in the east on the first and ninth lunar days;
and Māheśvarī is in the north on the second and tenth lunar days.
On the fifth and the thirteenth [tithis], Vārāhī is situated in the south;
on the sixth and the fourteenth, Indrāṇī is situated in the west.
On the seventh day and on the full moon, Cāmuṇḍā resides in the northwest;
on the eighth day and on the new moon, Lakṣmī is considered to reside in the northeast.
On the eleventh and thirteenth days, Vaiṣṇavī is indeed in the southeast;
on the twelfth and fourth days, Kaumārī is in the southwest.
One should never engage in going or other such activities in the presence of the Yoginīs.
[The asterisms are] Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, and Punarvasu. (15)
Puṣyā, Hastā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā bestow excellence upon setting out;
so too do the five asterisms beginning with Hasti (Ārdrā) and the three Uttaras. (16)
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Punarvasu are excellent for putting on new garments; they also increase one's good fortune.
Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūlā, Viśākhā, and the three Pūrvas are downward-facing; indeed, activities pertaining to the lower regions should be performed under them. (18)

The digging of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like; the excavation of the earth, caves, and pits; the digging of a temple’s foundations; the digging for hidden treasure; and grass [are all forms of injury]. (19)
One may perform calculations, the commencement of astrology, and entering underground caves;
these very things will succeed, and all subterranean undertakings will be accomplished in every way.
Revatī, Aśvinī, Citrā, Svātī, Hastā, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Jyeṣṭhā—these are considered to be side-facing (pārśvamukha). ||21||
One may perform the taming of elephants, camels, horses, and bulls, as well as buffaloes and cows; one may carry out the sowing of seeds and the navigation of boats and other such vessels. (22)
The movement and arrival of wheeled vehicles, machines, and chariots [should be undertaken] under Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttarās. (23)
Śatabhiṣaj and Śravaṇa—these nine are considered to have upward-facing mouths;
under these, one should cause the consecration for kingship and the binding of the turban to be performed. (24)
One should cause all of these to be made with their faces turned upward and raised;
however, the fourth, sixth, eighth, and likewise the ninth are inauspicious.

The new moon day, the full moon day, the twelfth, and the fourteenth; likewise, the first day of the bright fortnight is auspicious, as is the second day of the dark fortnight when it falls on a Wednesday.
The third lunar day is auspicious when joined with Mars; the fourth with Saturday; the fifth with Jupiter; and the sixth is auspicious on Tuesday and Friday. (27)
The seventh [tithi] falls on Wednesday or Monday; the eighth falls on Tuesday or Sunday;
the ninth falls on Monday; and the tenth falls on Thursday. (28)
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is pervaded by Jupiter; the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) falls on Wednesday;
the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) is occupied by Venus and Mars; and the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) is excellent when it falls on Saturday. (29)
On the day of Jupiter, both the full moon and the new moon are to be understood as most auspicious;
the sun burns away the twelfth lunar day, while the moon burns away the eleventh.
Mars burns the tenth house, while Mercury burns the ninth;
Jupiter burns the eighth, and Venus burns the seventh. (3.1)
Saturn burns the sixth lunar day, and indeed there is no movement [of the traveler] on that day; nor is there movement on the first, ninth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days. (32)
One should avoid setting out on a journey on Wednesday from afar; likewise, the sixth lunar day in Aries and Cancer, and the eighth lunar day in Virgo and Gemini. (33)
The fourth lunar day in Taurus and Aquarius, the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra, the tenth in Scorpio and Leo, and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces. (34)
These [asterisms] are burnt; human beings, including embodied souls and others, must not travel during them.
When the Sun is in the three Viśākhās and the Moon is in the three Pūrvāṣāḍhās, [these are the times]. (349)
O Rama, the triad of Dhaniṣṭhā is for Mars; the triad of Revatī is for Mercury;
the triad beginning with Rohiṇī is for Jupiter; and the triad of Puṣya is for Venus.
One should also avoid the three Uttarā-phalgunīs when Saturn is present;
this is an accidental conjunction (autpātika-yoga) that causes death, disease, and other calamities. ||37||
At the root is the Sun; in Śravaṇa is the Moon; in the latter Proṣṭhapadā is Mars;
in Kṛttikā is Mercury; and in Punarvasu, O Lakṣmī, is Jupiter. (38)
Pūrvaphalgunī with Venus and Svātī with Saturn—these are indeed Amṛta-yogas, which accomplish all undertakings. (39)
Five *ghaṭikās* are proclaimed for Viṣkambha, seven for Śūla,
six for Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, and nine for Vyāghāta and Vajra.
On every day of Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti, these death-yogas (mṛtyuyoga) must be avoided, for they cause the destruction of one's undertakings. ||41||
The Sun is auspicious in Hastā; Jupiter in Puṣya; Mercury in Anurādhā is auspicious;
Rohiṇī is excellent for Saturn; and Śatabhiṣaj is excellent for the Moon. (42)
Revatī is most excellent for Venus, while Aśvinī is auspicious for Mars;
these are the Siddhi-yogas that destroy all defects.
Bharaṇī is for Bhārgava (Venus), Citrā for Soma (the Moon), and Uttarāṣāḍhā for Bhauma (Mars);
while Dhaniṣṭhā is for Budha (Mercury). ||44||
When Śatabhiṣā falls on a Thursday, Rohiṇī on a Friday,
and Revatī on a Saturday, these are indeed considered to be Viṣa-yogas.
Puṣya, Punarvasu, Revatī, Citrā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Hastā, Aśvinī, and likewise Mṛgaśīrṣa. ||46||
Śatabhiṣā is also suitable for the rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarma);
likewise, Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Ārdrā, and Bharaṇī. ||47||
Aśleṣā and Kṛttikā—these [nakṣatras] bring death during a journey.
Six periods (daśās) are to be understood for Āditya; fifteen are recorded for Soma.
Eight [verses] are to be understood for Maṅgala; seventeen are recorded for Budha;
ten are to be understood for Śanaiścara; and nineteen for Guru. (49)
The period of Rāhu lasts for twelve years, while that of Bhārgava lasts for twenty-one;
the period of the Sun brings misery and causes agitation as well as the destruction of kings. (3.153.50)
The period of the Moon bestows prosperity and likewise grants the pleasure of desired food;
the period of Mars brings about suffering and leads to the destruction of sovereignty and other blessings. 51.
The period of Mercury bestows celestial women, grants sovereignty, and brings about an increase in the treasury;
the period of Saturn causes the destruction of the kingdom and brings suffering to one's kinsmen. (52)
The period of Jupiter bestows sovereignty and grants happiness, dharma, and other blessings;
the period of Rāhu causes the loss of kingdom, brings disease, and results in suffering. ||53||
The period of Venus bestows elephants, horses, and the attainment of kingdom and women;
Aries is the domain of Mars, while Taurus is proclaimed as that of Venus. (54)
Mercury is the field of Gemini, and Soma (the Moon) is that of Cancer;
Leo shall be the field of the Sun, and Virgo the field of Mercury. (55)
The sign of Libra is the domain of Bhārgava (Venus), and Scorpio is that of Maṅgala (Mars);
Sagittarius is the domain of Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), while Capricorn and Aquarius belong to Śani (Saturn). 56.
And Pisces belongs to Jupiter; it is desired for fields and brings profit in buying.
Where there are two full moons, there should be two Pūrvāṣāḍhās. (57)
That should be known as the intercalary Āṣāḍha; Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā constitute the month of Alaṃkṛti.
Deer, snakes, monkeys, cats, dogs, pigs, birds, mongooses, and mice are auspicious when encountered on the right during a journey. (59)
A Brahmin maiden, a corpse, an elephant, a conch shell, a kettledrum, the earth, a flute, a woman, and a full water-pot are auspicious sights on a journey. (3.153.60)
Jackals, camels, donkeys, and the like are auspicious on the left side during a journey;
so too are cotton, medicinal herbs, oils, cooked food, charcoal, and serpents. (61)
One with disheveled hair, wearing a red garland, naked, or possessing inauspicious marks;
hiccup occurring in the east yields fruit, while in the southeast it bestows distress and grief.
In the south she is the giver of loss and the giver of grief and torment;
in the southwest she is the giver of sweet food; and in the west she is considered the giver of wealth.
In the north it is a quarrel, but in the northeast it brings death.
Having drawn the Sun in human form, one should [draw] his asterism. (64)
One should establish the first three [syllables] on the head, the next three on the face,
and place one each upon the two shoulders, the pair of arms, and the two hands.
One should place five [syllables] in the heart, one in the navel, and also one in the secret place;
one each in the two knees, and the remaining ones one should apply to the feet.
A man whose [ascendant] is situated in the feet (caraṇa) becomes short-lived due to the star;
if it is in the knees, there is travel to a foreign land; and if it is in the private parts, he will have another's wife.

One who possesses it at the navel is content with little; one who possesses it at the heart is a great lord; one who possesses it in the hand becomes a thief; and if it has fallen from its place onto the arm, he becomes a beggar.
If [the planet] is situated in the shoulder, one becomes a lord of wealth; if in the mouth, one obtains sweet food;
and if on the head, one is enriched with silk garments—such is the fruit according to the respective asterism.
The Moon in the seventh house is excellent for growth; in the bright fortnight, it is best when situated in the second.
It also bestows gain when located in the fifth or the ninth, even during the period of conception.
There are twelve states of the moon; listen, O Lotus-born One!
The periods (daśā) indeed occur in groups of three constellations, beginning from Āśvinī.
In two and a half [years], the first [period] brings about departure from enlightenment;
the second brings about loss, and the third is considered to bring about death. (72)
The fourth is the bestower of victory; the fifth period, however, bestows laughter.
The sixth bestows the delight of play, and the seventh bestows happiness and joy. (73)
The eighth period brings sorrow, while the ninth period bestows enjoyments;
the tenth period causes fever, and the eleventh period produces trembling. (74)
The twelfth [tithi] bestows stability, and its fruit is considered equal to ten [times that of the first].
[If Venus] is situated in the birth sign, it produces contentment; in the second house, it is a destroyer of happiness. (75)
In the third year there is honor from the state; in the fourth, it brings about strife;
in the fifth, it bestows a wife; and in the sixth, it shall be a giver of wealth and grain.
In the seventh [house], there is pleasure and worship; in the eighth, it causes doubt regarding life;
in the ninth, it bestows the accumulation of wealth; and in the tenth, it grants success.
In the eleventh lunar mansion the moon bestows victory, and in the twelfth it brings death.
One should undertake an eastern journey starting from Kṛttikā and travel through seven constellations.
One should travel to the south when Maghā and the following asterisms are rising; to the west when Anurādhā and the following are rising;
and a journey to the north during the seven asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā is always considered most excellent. (79)
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are for assuming a disguise; Mṛgaśiras, Aśvinī, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hastā are indeed auspicious.
In the giving away of a daughter in marriage, on journeys, and in rites such as consecrations, Venus and the Moon situated in the birth sign are always considered to bestow auspicious results. (8–1)
The Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are indeed givers of auspiciousness in the second house;
in the third house, Mars, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon are considered to be givers of auspiciousness. (82)
Mercury is excellent in the fourth house; Venus and Jupiter are the fifth houses;
likewise, the Moon and Ketu are proclaimed to be excellent in the fifth house. (83)
Saturn, the Sun, and Mars are always considered excellent in the sixth house;
Jupiter and the Moon in the seventh, and Mercury and Venus likewise in the eighth. (84)
In the ninth house, Jupiter is most excellent; in the tenth, the Sun, Saturn, and the Moon;
in the eleventh, all the planets; and in the twelfth, Mercury and Venus. (85)
The crocodile is best with the lion, the ram is most excellent with the virgin;
the fish is [best] with Libra, and the crab with Aquarius. (86)
The Bull is favorable with Sagittarius, while Scorpio is favorable with Gemini;
in this way, everything indeed becomes conducive to affection and bestows auspicious results. (87)
Starting from its very rising, the sun remains established in a zodiacal sign;
it proceeds through six signs during the day and through six signs during the night.
In Pisces and Aries, there are likewise five ghaṭikās;
in Taurus and Aquarius, four; and in Gemini and Scorpio, three. (89)
Five ghaṭikās are proclaimed for Aries and Cancer, six for Leo and Scorpio, and seven for Libra and Virgo. (3.153.90)
If Aries is the ascendant, she will be barren; if Taurus, she becomes a passionate woman;
if Gemini, she is fortunate; and if Cancer, she becomes a courtesan. (9.1)
In Leo, she will have few sons; in Virgo, she will be endowed with beauty. In Libra, there will be beauty and prosperity; in Scorpio, she will be harsh. (9.2)
In Sagittarius she will possess good fortune; in Capricorn she will be one who goes to the low; in Aquarius she will have few sons; and in Pisces she will be endowed with detachment.
Libra, Cancer, Aries, and Capricorn are considered movable signs;
Leo, Taurus, Aquarius, and Scorpio are considered fixed signs. (94)
Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Gemini are the dual-natured signs;
travel should be undertaken with these after a long time, whereas one should enter [a city] under a fixed sign. (95)
One should have the installation of a deity and marriage rites performed on days of dual nature; Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Śreṣṭhā are excellent, while Riktā should always be avoided as a lunar day.
The three lunar days [known as] Nandā are the first, the sixth, and the eleventh;
the three lunar days [known as] Bhadrā are the second, the seventh, and the twelfth. ||97||
The three lunar days are the eighth (Aṣṭamī), the third (Tṛtīyā), and the thirteenth (Trayodaśī);
and the other three are the fourth (Caturthī), the ninth (Navamī), and the fourteenth (Caturdaśī), which are the "empty" (riktā) days. ||98||
The fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days are considered auspicious when full.
Mercury is mobile, Jupiter is swift, Venus is gentle, and the Sun is fixed. (99)
Saturn is cruel, Mars is fierce, and even the Moon is likewise;
one should travel with the *cara* and *kṣipra* [nakṣatras], and enter [the city] with the *mṛdu* and *dhruva* [nakṣatras].
One must fight with fierce and terrible [enemies], and victory shall be attained; of this there is no doubt.
The consecration of a king and fire-rituals are recommended on a Monday. (101)

Traveling, setting out on a journey, acquiring a house, a palace, and so forth, as well as the office of a general, valorous combat, and the practice of weapons—these are auspicious under Mars. (10.2)
Accomplishing tasks, mantras, and journeys are auspicious under Mercury;
recitation, worship of deities, and clothing or ornaments are auspicious under Jupiter. (103)
Giving a daughter in marriage, mounting an elephant, and sexual union with a woman are auspicious under Venus;
establishing a deity and entering a new house are auspicious under Saturn, as is tethering an elephant.
Having thus observed all this, one should proceed with the undertaking of action; O Rame, both enjoyment and liberation shall arise from reading and hearing this.
The lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, the lunar days, the astrological conjunctions, as well as the planetary periods, the omens, the hiccup, and likewise the locations. || 106 ||
The ascendants, the hours, and everything else—perceive them all as my own form;
indeed, for an embodied being, whatever merit they possess, that very thing manifests before them.
O Lakṣmī, there I was remembered, worshipped, fed,
served, saluted, propitiated, and attended upon.
I bring about all good fortune and I transform the distressed into the well-situated;
and by knowing me everywhere, no destruction of one's undertakings occurs.
Everything is fruitful for the devotee, but fruitless for the atheist;
for one who possesses self-control the fruit is supreme, while for one lacking self-control it is inferior.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Success or Failure of Actions and Their Results Based on Specific Nakshatras, Yoginis, Tithis, Yogas, Dashas, Omens, Hiccups, Locations, Ascendants, and Ghatikas," in the Third Section (Dvapara-santana) of the glorious *Lakshmi-Narayaniya Samhita*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious story of Sarojinī.
Formerly, she was the daughter of a potter who desired [the sage] Kardama.
For the purpose of fashioning all vessels such as jars and the like,
he brings suitable clay by means of vehicles such as donkeys.
Because she was not desired by her mother, father, brother, or anywhere even by her sister— despite being fit for marriage— she therefore did not wish to choose a husband at all.
That virtuous woman lived in her father’s house, devoted to celibacy,
dedicated to serving her elders, and intent upon the dharma of good conduct.
Attached to their own resolve and content with even the smallest things, these spirits dwell in the house of the poor; therefore, their desire does not increase. || 5 ||
Indeed, that virtuous woman lived contented with her own nature;
then, in the course of time, her mother named Ghoṇāvatī fell ill with fever.
Having reached heaven, she departed; the lotus pond grieved:
"There is no happiness equal to a mother; there is no support like that of one's own birth-giver. (7)
For daughters, the mother always shines like heaven within the home;
even for poor children, the mother is considered their supreme wealth.
Without giving to his own daughter, the mother does not eat or drink;
without remembering her own children born of her, she does not let the day pass.
Even when she has forgotten or is asleep, the mother calls her children; she nourishes them like gods and serves her own.
Even for birds, nectar indeed resides within the mother’s lap;
even their eggs are always nurtured by the warmth of the mother’s belly.
Even for a mere moment of separation, a mother finds no happiness;
yet that mother goes to heaven today, even though her father is old.
Since he too will go to heaven while his livelihood remains dependent on his son,
I must therefore always remain here; for if I were to dwell in the house of my brother’s wife without affection, it would indeed be a hellish experience for me.
"What indeed must be done by me today, and likewise what must be done hereafter? (14)
Thus, in this manner, she remained perpetually sorrowful and devoid of passion;
then, at the twelfth ancestral rite (śrāddha), the lords of the earth arrived.
And although relatives possess relations, they are merely connected by kinship;
yet there, a desire was formed for the sake of the lotus-pond alone.
Her father informed him of this, and he too gave his consent;
by the formal betrothal, that maiden was given to the potter.
Then, at an auspicious moment, the girl was married with great blessings by her father, named Cakradhvas, to one called Nāladharāya.
That maiden also became serene and abandoned her grief entirely;
she went indeed to the home of her husband and, established in happiness, enjoyed worldly pleasures.
However, the bodily marks of a maiden indeed indicate the loss of her husband:
namely, a beard, long lips, and likewise a flat nose. (3.154.20)
When a squinting-eyed woman comes to her husband's house with her big toe and ring finger not touching the ground, then at that very moment— 21.
Her husband contracted a fever, and having become emaciated, he indeed died;
she became a widow due to the defect of her bodily marks. ||22||
Then, having reached her father's house and being protected by her brothers,
she— childless and without support— grieved for herself again and again.
After another year, she was again requested by another potter;
she was married by her father once more and went back to her husband's house. (24)
She indeed enjoys even greater happiness than before in the house of a happy person;
however, due to the influence of bodily marks, the power of planetary afflictions, and likewise again— ||5||
Her second husband, named Ratnaka, also died;
being childless, she grieved repeatedly for that virtuous husband.
Lamenting his own misfortune, he returned once more to his father's house;
meanwhile, his father, having reached the end of his time, fell under the power of death.
From that time forward, Sarojinī remained dependent upon her brother;
after one year had passed, she was sought in marriage by a potter as his third wife.
Entrusted by her brother, Sarojinī went to the house of her husband and lived there happily for a year, experiencing even greater comfort than before.
Then her third husband, named Lāladāsa, also died;
she grieved exceedingly in her mind, indeed reviling her own fortune.
Then, having arrived at her brother’s house, she lived there constantly in misery;
and again, after another year, she was requested by another potter.
Given by her elder brother according to the prescribed rites, she indeed went to the house of her husband;
she enjoyed happiness for only one year, and then even her fourth husband died.
Having returned once more to her brother’s house, childless and deeply distressed,
she passed her days in misery while remaining dependent on others.
Then once, his brother’s wife, desiring refuse, gave instructions for cooking earthen vessels, for the sake of obtaining fuel from the refuse. (34)
Within this boundary, you must gather fuel, firewood,
leaves, twigs, branches, logs, and stalks for the purpose of the sacrificial hearth.
At that very moment, Sarojinī became afflicted with fever due to the cold;
she forbade herself from proceeding further and fell asleep upon the surface of the ground.
Then the brother’s wife, becoming enraged, uttered insults;
but having heard them, she did not reply, for she was afflicted by the suffering of fever.
When Sarojinī did not come even though she had been summoned, her brother’s wife went to the hut, took Sarojinī by the hand, and [led her away]. (38)
He also forcibly dragged her away and commanded that fuel be brought;
afflicted by fever, Sarojinī cried out, "I will not go! (39)
She struck her brother’s wife, and she in turn struck her;
thus a quarrelsome battle between the two ensued, with each seizing the other by the hair.
Even upon merely hearing the news, the neighbors gathered at his house;
the family members arrived, as did the villagers and friends. (41)
By means of various conciliatory words, they all pacified their distress; yet thereafter, a constant enmity arose between the two, intensified by the wrath of their eyes. (42)
Furthermore, a constant battle of glances arises between their eyes;
there is a war of words with the Gālikās, and even quarrels break out. (43)
As the days passed in this manner, her brother succumbed to the power of time;
she had no protector at all, for her brother’s wife was now left with excellent sons.
He then forcibly expelled her from his own house;
she too, having assumed the status of a mature woman, abandoned the village and lay down on the riverbank. (45)
Right there he saw a dream that was the cause of his suffering, [the vision of] his own mother from a previous birth, acting as his slayer while seated upon him. (46)
In her own home, for the sake of selling it, she indeed slaughters a goat kid;
having killed many kids, she maintains her belly.
Seeing herself in such a state as a female executioner, she died;
thereafter, she went to the city of Yama and experienced sufferings there.
Then, having become a Piśācinī for a thousand years, I was born in the house of a potter and became Sarojinī. (49)
Thus, having seen this as if in a dream on the riverbank,
she rose up from there and understood it to be the fruit of her own karma.
"For indeed, everything previously done is later obtained by all embodied beings;
since goats were formerly killed by me, my boons are therefore perishing. (51)
"All my husbands have died because of my own actions; therefore, having become a female mendicant, I must certainly depart. (52)
Having thus reflected upon the affliction of karma, the affliction of the planets, and that born of one's own nature,
and considering such suffering to be the fruit of past actions, he went to the forest to the hermitage of a virtuous woman.
There shines the divine female renunciant, the illustrious Satīśvarī, a Vaiṣṇavī and celibate practitioner accompanied by thousands of disciples. (54)
Her form consists of divine splendor and destroys sins at the mere sight;
she is solely devoted to the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (55)
She is auspicious, endowed with the wonders of hearing from afar, seeing distant things, and so forth;
she removes the suffering of others, is devoted to the practice of yoga, and has conquered her senses. (56)
At that hermitage, no men ever entered;
there were only certain young maidens devoted to the fire-oblation and wearing the sacred thread.
Some were devoted to meditation, others were intent on garlands and the recitation of mantras; some virtuous women were dedicated to asceticism, their beauty enhanced by their matted locks.
Some were naked, some relied on tree bark, and others on skins;
some wore garments made of leaves, bamboo, or mats, while others relied on woolen blankets and the like. ||59||
All were devoted solely to Brahman, truthful, virtuous, and observant of vows dedicated to Kṛṣṇa;
they had established their affection directly upon Kṛṣṇa and were intent upon the path to liberation.
Even the gods Vāyu, Sūrya, and Śaśin, as well as the fires, do not touch them;
they move about with their daughters, and attendants serve them in their dwellings. ||61||
In that place, enmity between the deer and the king of beasts is indeed natural,
yet there, desire, anger, and the like truly abandon their inherent nature.
In this auspicious hermitage of virtuous women, where youthfulness does not exist at all, even that which is present remains pure and attains a state free from the qualities of material nature.
Indeed, the menstruation of virtuous women has been dissolved through their ascetic power;
they shine with divine bodies like goddesses in the ether of consciousness.
There are pits of water, fire, and steam where cold and heat coexist;
there, the supernatural powers (siddhis) exist through mere speech, resolve, and thought.
Some goddesses dwell in mountain caves, some have entered into huts,
some have made their abodes in the sky, and others even sport in the atmosphere.
Some were knowers of the Veda, some were performers of ritual action, some were devoted to the Sāman chants, and some were awakeners to the Ṛg-verses. ||67||
Some are constantly devoted to wisdom and likewise assume many forms;
others abide in meditative absorption, and thus these virtuous women shine forth.
Having gone there, she was Virūpākṣī— ugly-faced, with long lips,
hairy shanks, a flat nose, and flat feet.
With a large nose, red hair, a small mouth, and slender breasts, Sarojinī, the daughter of a potter, remained without any support. (3.154.70)
At the very gate of the cow-pen of the hermitage where the deer indeed roam, she, endowed with great majesty, rolled upon the ground covered in dust. (71)
That purifying dust was indeed rubbed upon her body;
yet, seeing that devotee who was purifying but whose limbs were inauspicious, [he was struck with wonder]. (72)
O Lakṣmī, the young women approached the sorrowful girl;
having bowed to all the young women, he went together with them to another hermitage.
Where that virtuous lady, the illustrious Satīśvarī, the Guru, was resplendent;
having offered her salutations, she wept and fell at the feet of the Guru.
Seeing her miserable and distressed, the virtuous mistress felt compassion and said to her,
"Do not fear," and likewise gave her bark garments.
Having been questioned regarding her circumstances and having understood [the truth], she took refuge in dispassion;
protected among virtuous women, she manifested the purity of her body. (76)
The virtuous lady Satīśvarī gave her a monthly vow,
consisting of the practice of heating oneself with five fires and subsisting on a diet of fruits and roots.
I shall constantly perform the recitation of my mantra one thousand times;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (78)
Thus she constantly recited this with one-pointed mind;
and at the end of the month, having performed thirty thousand recitations, the illustrious Satīśvarī [was attained].
And being pleased, she called her and said, "Drink this water born of my grace.
Sarojinī drank the water, which was the nectar of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (3.154.80)
Then she indeed manifested with a divine form, equal to the sun, like Lakṣmī, like Durgā, like Sāvitrī, and like Śacī. ||81||
She became endowed with the wonder of divine power and great sovereignty,
together with the wealth of divine vision, divine hearing, and a divine mind.
She shone in the midst of virtuous women like a supreme pearl;
her entire body became like a divine lotus-plant. (83)
A most auspicious and supreme body, adorned with the marks of all the best six lines on its limbs, capable of traveling through the sky, and obtained through divine grace, was born. 84.
Out of compassion, Kuṃbhakartrī indeed became a protector of Brahman;
then she constantly served the noble Gaurī, the true sovereign. ||85||
By means of divine ascetic power and yoga, through the command of his merit-accumulations,
and also by many acts of service, he gratified Gaurī.
Then Satīśvarī asked her: "Tell me your heart's desire; O upholder of Brahman, what do you wish? I shall grant your heart's desire. (87)
Then Sarojinī said: "May the Supreme Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be my husband. (88)
Standing at the soles of Lakṣmī’s feet, I shall serve the Supreme Lord;
wherever Lakṣmī is, there I shall dwell together with her as her companion.
Without my beloved Lord of Lakṣmī, nothing else pleases my heart;
indeed, I desire only that liberation which consists of service as a maidservant. (3.154.90)
"Therefore, act in such a way that through this attainment I may become one who has fulfilled her purpose.
"So be it," the virtuous Mistress then said to Sarojinī. (91)
He gave her two great mantras for the purpose of recitation:
Oṃ, may we know Mahālakṣmī; may we meditate upon the Consort of Viṣṇu;
may that Lakṣmī inspire us. (92)
Oṃ. Let us know Nārāyaṇa; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May that Viṣṇu inspire us. ||93||
Having received both mantras, she constantly recited them and worshipped them;
devoted to meditation and service, she perpetually honored Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. (94)

At the end of the year, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa became clearly visible before her and spoke to Sarojinī: 95. At the end of the year, those two, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, having become manifest before her eyes in a state of great serenity, spoke to Sarojinī.
"Tell me, what is it that dwells in your mind? That is indeed a dilemma.
Having heard this, she bowed with devotion and chose him as her boon.
"Standing at the soles of Lakṣmī’s feet, I shall always serve Hari.
"So be it," they both said, and they accepted the lotus. (97)
Śrī and Rameśvara created two forms for the lotus-born goddess:
one was a divine, fragrant lotus, rich with stalks and flowers; the other was a single [form]. (98)
The second maiden-form was described as Padminī;
there, Hari indeed took that Padminī by his own hand.
Then Sarojinī and Vallikā became a divine wife equal to Lakṣmī, possessing the very form of Lakṣmī’s sister, within the midst of the water.
There, Lakṣmī, enriched by the petals of lotuses, always resided;
and the lotus-pond was ever enriched by the service of Lakṣmī’s feet. 101.
From that time forward, Lakṣmī has always shone within the lotus;
purified by the dust of Lakṣmī’s feet, she serves Śrī Narāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, in former times Sarojinī always became the sustainer of the world through devotion;
then, by devotion to her guru, she became the maker of the jar and the upholder of Brahman.
Through devotion to the Lord Guru Satīśvarī, the planets and other influences became neutralized;
likewise, all bodily marks that were indicative of misfortune were likewise removed.
Having attained that cessation, they then became divine in form;
thus, through constant devotion and daily service to the virtuous, [this state is achieved].
Through the grace of virtuous women who know Brahman, one attains divinity;
by the mere sight of holy yogis, sins are destroyed.
Through service, divine qualities that grant supreme liberation are obtained;
likewise, obstacles such as time and karma, which cause suffering, are overcome. (107)
All those [obstacles] indeed go to dissolution through the fruit of service to the Guru;
both malevolent planets and auspicious ones, as well as inauspicious times and auspicious ones, [are overcome]. 108.
The unfortunate becomes fortunate, and even the earthly body shines divinely;
the short-lived attains long life, and poverty turns into wealth. (109)
Indeed, even sins attain the nature of merit through service;
by reading, hearing, or even remembering this, one obtains that same fruit.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how the daughter of a potter, Sarojinī, due to the sins of her previous birth, after the death of her four husbands, departed for the hermitage of the holy Satīśvarī out of renunciation; and there, through devotion to Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and service to her guru, upon the destruction of the defects of the planets and physical ailments, attained the original form of Kamalinīvallikā who takes refuge in Śrī Lakṣmī, as well as the attainment of the form of Ramā known as Padminī," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Lord, regarding those fourteen Manus who have been mentioned by you as being honored by the world— O Kṛṣṇa, tell me here of their origin.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"The Manus, who are indeed portions of My own self, appear fourteen by fourteen in every Kalpa;
they are the lords of all kingdoms and also the promoters of Dharma."
Even the fourteen lords of the worlds who promote righteousness were all created by me alone; they remain engaged in their respective duties.
Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa,
Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, and Vaivasvata is the seventh.
Sāvarṇi, Dakṣasāvarṇi, Brahmasāvarṇi, Dharmasāvarṇi, and Rudrasāvarṇi is recorded as the twelfth. || 5 ||
Devasāvarṇi and Indrasāvarṇi are the fourteenth;
the lifespan of each Manu is indeed seventy-one [yugas] plus a fraction.
The duration of the fourteen Manus is more than one thousand [years];
and the duration of Brahmā is also more than one thousand [years], plus one day.
There are one thousand and more nights for the Creator;
at the end of two thousand and more [years], there is the dawn that brings about creation and dissolution.
It shall consist of the ten worlds, from the netherworld (pātāla) up to heaven;
in the east, on the bank of the celestial river, is the Vaiṣṇava [sanctuary] with many assembly halls.
The righteous-souled great Ṛṣi Dharmatapas performed a sacrifice;
O Nārāyaṇa, I am pleased with him because of his name, Dharmatapas.
He granted him an excellent boon according to his desire: even while engaged in worldly activity, he chose the auspicious state of renunciation.
The fruit of my asceticism and the fruit of my sacrifice—the station of a Manvantara—were first granted by me to him; thus he became Svāyambhuva.
The mind-born son of Brahmā, who was devoted to the protection of his subjects,
took the virtuous woman Śatarūpā as his wife.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were their two sons.
Now, there was a brahmin named Vāraṇa on the bank of the river Varaṇā.
This thought occurred to him: "I shall see the earth [in its entirety].
Just then, a virtuous guest traveling through the sky arrived at his house.
The twice-born man gave food to him, whose name was Khākhapada;
