then, as he set his mind on the journey, the virtuous man spoke to him.
"Having smeared your feet with mantras and medicinal herbs, wander about like a ball.
Having said this, he applied that very medicinal paste to both of his feet.
Indeed, in half a day, the twice-born one traveled a thousand yojanas through the sky and descended upon the snowy mountain and the watery earth.
The foot-ointment produced from the supreme medicinal herb was washed away;
unable to travel by way of the sky, he remained upon the surface of the earth.
The excellent Apsaras named Varūthinī beheld him;
she was infatuated and thought within her heart of performing service for him.
Going before him with extreme devotion, righteousness, religious observances, virtuous conduct, and true propriety, she indeed served him.
The twice-born one, being pleased, granted her a boon:
"O Prajāvatī, may you be possessed of sons and grandsons, and honored by the three worlds. (22)
Having thus bestowed this blessing, the twice-born one likewise remembered me;
then, bowing down, he spoke to the Gārhapatya fire in a low voice.
O Fire, become the protector in the form of Brahmā and in the form of Kṛṣṇa,
so that today, while the sun is still present, I may behold my own home.
Just as virtuous and holy men who have arrived were served by me, and just as Vedic ritual was not abandoned by me at its proper time; ||25||
And just as my mind never turns toward the wealth of others or the wives of others, by which the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is eternally worshipped. (26)
"By that truth, O Fire, lead me indeed to my own home.
As he was speaking thus, the Gārhapatya fire itself [appeared].
Then a bird in the form of a ram, possessed of wings, came before him;
the twice-born man, having mounted its back, quickly reached his own home.
Varūthinī also, having bowed to that brahmin and accompanied by his blessings,
reached the divine Gandharva named Devakeli.
Therefore, she conceived a fetus endowed with the splendor of the Brahmins' blessings;
that boy was born radiant, like a blazing fire.
Because he shone with his own radiance, he became known by the name Svarociḥ;
and Svarociḥ indeed departed into the sky in a celestial chariot.
The river Manoramā,
which formerly belonged to the Gandharva Kanyakendīvāra, became a Vaiṣṇavī goddess through her ascetic penance.
In the region of Saptasārasvata, the virtuous and beautiful Sarasvatī,
who was united with the Sarayū, desired Svarociṣ.
She requested him with righteousness and humility for the sake of a husband;
having made him her husband, she went to his house along with him across the river.
Wandering together with her through groves and parks by means of his celestial chariot,
he once beheld a beautiful doe in a forest.
He touched with his right hand that celestial woman, who was endowed with divine qualities, fearless, standing motionless, and who had come close to him.
That doe, having vanished, was indeed born as a divine goddess;
then, overcome with wonder, he addressed her, saying, "Who are you? (37)
And she said to him: "I am the deity of this forest;
having been entreated by the gods, I have come here, stationed before you. (38)
"O Mahāmati, you must indeed cause a son to be born to me by this woman.
Having been addressed thus, Svarocis immediately took her as his own beloved. (39)
And upon her, he then begot a radiant son;
at the very moment of his birth, the celestial drums resounded.
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsarases danced;
the father gave the child his own name, Svārociṣa.
O Lakṣmī, Svārociṣa shall be the second Manu;
his presiding deity shall be the Vidyā named Padminī. (42)
He learned from her entirely those foundations and treasures by which the treasures, such as lotuses and others, are clearly known upon the earth. (43)
Through the grace of the deities, by serving the virtuous, and through treasures bestowed upon one, wealth increases even in the human state. (44)
Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Kacchapa, Mukunda, Nandaka, Nīla, and Śaṅkha—these are the [sons] of Manu. (45)
In their very homes, they were eternally the fulfillers of all desires:
wealth, jewels, weapons, elixirs, musical instruments, and minerals. (46)
Grains, enjoyments, ornaments, and divine things were always present for Manu.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen also to the beautiful third mantra. ||47||
The son of Uttānapāda was known by the name Uttama;
he was the celebrated son of Suruci, who shone with the prowess of the sun.
That knower of dharma married a woman of the Bābhravya lineage named Bahulā;
devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, he lived together with her.
To behold Śeṣanārāyaṇa, he worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa;
he also worshipped Śeṣa, and indeed he worshipped the daughter of Śeṣa as well.
He gave ornaments to that auspicious woman, and she was indeed delighted;
the auspicious Kalyāṇī, who had no other sons, then bestowed a blessed blessing upon him.
A son of great heroism shall be born to you from this wife;
he will be a wise lord of a Manvantara, possessing an unimpeded and excellent wheel. 22.
Then, when the time had come, an excellent son was born to the king;
celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
The assembled sages gave him the name Auttama;
as he was the son of Uttama, he became renowned by the name Sadauttama.
The sages and gods shall establish him in the state of Manu;
now, O Lakṣmī, I shall speak of the fourth Manu—listen to him.
There was a king on earth renowned as Svarāṣṭra, a man of great prowess;
for a long time he indeed performed penance on the sandy bank of the Vitastā. (96)
His wife, the virtuous queen, a yoginī capable of assuming any form,
became a doe and dwelt constantly in the forest in the vicinity of the king.
Devoted to the holy life, the king heard from Vyomaśāradā:
"O King, by the power of her asceticism, this woman Utpalā has [become] yours."
"For a divine son shall indeed be born, named Tāmasa Manu;
therefore, bestow your seed upon her for the sake of benefiting the world. (59)
Having heard this, the king granted union to the menstruating Utpalā; indeed, by mere touch, Utpalāvatī conceived a child.
Then that Utpalāvatī, having the body of a doe, gave birth to a son;
thereafter, all the sages gathered together in that forest at that time.
Beholding that mother, who was indeed a dark-brown doe of a tamasic nature, he thought: "Let this fourth Manu be Tamasa by name."
Thus, this very son, having quickly propitiated the Sun,
obtained all the divine weapons in their entirety, including the means for their withdrawal.
O Lakṣmī, he will shine forth having become the Manu named Tāmasa;
now listen as I tell you about the fifth Manu.
There was a highly fortunate seer named Ṛtavāk;
at the end of his life, Revatī was born to him, unfortunate and increasing his afflictions.
By that [act], even the king of sages obtained a long-lasting disease. Ṛtavāk said to Revatī: "Through your yoga, my son... (66)
"O Revatī, you who have been born as a giver of disease due to your immoral conduct, fall down quickly! When he had thus uttered this curse, the constellation Revatī fell.
In Saurāṣṭra, on Mount Kumuda, indeed in my region of Vastrāpatha,
that mountain Kumuda became known as Raivataka because of its falling down.
On Mount Raivata, that maiden Revatī was born from a lake;
and the king of sages named Pramuca [found] the maiden near his hermitage. (69)
Indeed, he took up and nourished the newborn girl as his own daughter.
Then, after some time, there was a king there named Durgama.
He arrived and called out to his beloved Revatī;
then Pramuca gave that daughter of his to Durgama.
There, by the power of his asceticism, he made the constellation Revatī join with the Moon in the sky as before; then he spoke to his son-in-law: (72)
"O protector of the earth, let that which pertains to your marriage be told; what shall I give you?
The king said: 'Through your grace, O joy, I choose a mantra as my son.'"
The sage said, "So be it; thus shall Manu become your son.
Taking her with him, the king went to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having bathed, worshipped me, and bowed to the sage Lomaśa,
Durgama went to the city of Durganagara on the bank of the Gaṅgāvatī.
From him, a son named Raivata Manu was born of Revatī;
in another kalpa, he will also become the son of Sūrya, known as Revanta.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this Raivata shall be the fifth Manu;
I have described him to you, and now hear as I speak of the sixth Manu.
O beloved, because he was born from the eye of Parameṣṭhin in a previous birth,
he is called Cākṣuṣa even in this present birth.
Remembering his past lives, he was born there, resting upon the lap of his mother, the wife named Giribhadra, who belonged to a kṣatriya lord of the earth. (79)
The woman who carried him was born from the bed of Giribhadra,
in the house of a queen named Vikrānta and his Haiminī wife.
Having placed that newborn there and taking the infant, she departed; having placed the prince in the house of the learned Brahmin, she took that child [of the sage]. (8.1)
The Rākṣasī even snatched away the child of the Brahmin and devoured him;
thus it was that he, though raised upon the queen’s couch in the royal palace, [met such a fate].
He became renowned by the name Ānanda, and likewise Arthamānasa;
he performed most intense penance, and Brahmā, having arrived in his presence, [spoke]. (83)
Brahmā addressed him as "Cākṣuṣa," turning him away from his asceticism;
he established him as the sixth Manu, and thus he shall become the sixth Manu.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I recite to you the seven-syllable mantra:
"The wife of Sūrya, the daughter of Viśvakarman, renowned as Saṃjñā. (85)
Ravi begot an auspicious son, Vaivasvata, upon her;
for this Vaivasvata, O Lakṣmī, will become the seventh Manu.
Because he was born from one who possessed the same phonetic quality (*savarṇa*) as his predecessor, he became renowned as Sāvarṇi.
Now, O beloved Nārāyaṇī, listen as I speak of the eighth Manu. (87)
In the previous Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Suratha;
defeated in battle by his enemies, he went to the forest in sorrow. (88)
Then a distressed Vaiśya named Samādhi arrived there;
seeing him so sorrowful, the king asked, "Why indeed do you grieve? (89)
The Vaiśya said to the king: "I lived happily in your kingdom, but now I have been cast out by my wife and children, who were driven by unrighteous greed for wealth."
Deprived of wealth, wife, and sons, having taken my property, he has come here in misery, cast out by his own kinsmen and relatives. (91)
Thus, I do not know the state of my sons' welfare or lack thereof, nor that of my wives, my kinsmen, my daughters, or my household members. (92)
Is there peace in their homes, or is there now no peace? How are they? Are my sons well-behaved, or are they ill-behaved? (92)
The king said: "Why does your mind continue to cling with affection to those wives, sons, and others by whom you have been cast out? (94)
The Vaiśya said: "It is so; nevertheless, the mind is a source of suffering.
What can I do? For even my illusory power (māyā) runs toward those [objects] in the mind. (95)
By those who, greedy for wealth, abandoned affection for their father and rejected my husband and kinsmen—even though they were full of love, my heart remains with them. (96)
I know them to be perverse, yet even knowing this, I do not abandon them;
for the mind is inclined toward love even for kinsmen who are devoid of virtue. (97)
On their account, sighs and dejection arise within me;
what can I do that is not harsh toward those who are ill-disposed? (98)
Some living beings are blind by day, while others are blind at night;
some beings have equal vision both by day and at night.
Even those possessed of knowledge are born blind with delusion, suffering from one misery after another;
even selfless beasts and birds are likewise of such a nature.
They suffer for the sake of wives and sons; men are just like deer.
Indeed, through illusion, they wander in the pit of "mine-ness" within the whirlpool of delusion. 101.
This very [knowledge] is considered the bestower of boons for the liberation of the devotees of Viṣṇu;
it is that supreme, eternal Vidyā which serves as the cause of liberation. 102.
For she is the cause of bondage to saṃsāra and the deluder of those who lack devotion;
indeed, that eternal Mother of the World shall become the very soul of the world.
Furthermore, that which consists of yogic sleep (yoganidrā) proceeds within the domain of Viṣṇu;
through austerity, Māyā is mastered and she becomes the bestower of liberation.
Thus, O King, those two Vaiśyas, acting together for the sake of knowledge,
performed severe penance while remembering Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī.
And Lakṣmī, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, granted them her vision;
she bestowed a boon upon the king, saying, "After you die, you shall obtain birth."
From Sūrya you shall become the Manu named Sāvarṇika;
this Vaiśya shall be wise and endowed with prosperity and happiness.
Having thus granted them the boon they desired, Lakṣmī,
being praised by them with devotion, immediately vanished from sight.
Having thus obtained a boon from Lakṣmī, Suratha, the best of Kṣatriyas and son of the Sun, shall become the eighth Manu, Sāvarṇi.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Births and Other Details of the Eight Manus," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O beloved Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the ninth mantra.
In Surāṣṭra, there was a king named Dhanavarman who possessed a very small kingdom. (1)
Constantly feeling anxiety upon seeing other great kingdoms, I thought:
"I am not a sovereign lord adorned with royal ornaments; I am but a petty king in a small town."
Without fame and universal sovereignty, there is truly no peace in my heart;
therefore, I shall indeed exert effort incessantly for the sake of imperial dominion.
Having reflected thus, he departed from his own village together with his wife, sons, and kinsmen, proceeding to the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭā for the sake of pilgrimage and ascetic practice.
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he bowed at his feet before him;
once a seat was offered, he sat down and was questioned regarding his welfare.
He replied to Lomaśa with kindness: "May it be well with you;
[may it be well with] your village, sons, daughters, wife, cattle, fields, and farmers."
"O Guru, by your grace, may all here indeed be well;
yet my heart remains unsatisfied with this petty village-kingdom."
"He desires a great kingdom; tell me the vow for its attainment.
Having heard this, Śrī Lomaśa first spoke to him of the vow for the purification of the body.
Having bestowed the mantra of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, which bestows great merit, he said:
"Worship the Lord here beneath a tree in this mango grove."

O King, you who have heard the scriptures, who are well-versed in recitation, possessed of great devotion and long-standing fortitude, accompanied by your wife and sons, perform the highest austerity.
Homeless, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, free from passion, sleeping on the ground, possessing the character of Brahman, they lived without any possessions. || 1.1 ||
Constantly bathing at the three sessions of the day and performing the triple worship every day, [they recite]:
"Om, svāhā to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord. (12)
Let all these, devoted to this mantra, perform penance here for one year;
thereafter, let them remain here for another year as reciters of the Lakṣmī-Gāyatrī.
"Oṃ, may we know Mahālakṣmī and meditate upon the consort of Viṣṇu;
may that Lakṣmī inspire us"—with these words, let them dwell for a year. 14.
"Śrī Hari will surely grant your desired success immediately.
Having been told this, they bowed to the Guru and worshipped him with pure devotion. (15)
Having bathed at Aśvapaṭṭasara and Vāra, they went to the mango grove;
there, in the forest, those practicing austerities spent a month, a year, and likewise another half-month.
O Lakṣmī, being pleased at that time, I went toward them along with you; I came before their very eyes, and Dhanavarman too was filled with joy.
The entire family, along with everyone else, bowed down to me with great agitation;
the king was quickly urged by me for the purpose of granting his desired boon.
Having honored him with a hospitable welcome, he requested an excellent boon:
a supreme sovereignty that surpassed all other human kings.
"I grant you the sovereignty renowned among men, saying 'So be it.
O Dhanavarman, together with your family, you shall become a great Manu."
For he who is the future ninth Manu, Sāvarṇa, the son of Dakṣa, shall indeed be named Dakṣasāvarṇi, [the seventy-first]. (21)
"Reside for that length of time in the heavenly world with your own independent realm.
As soon as this was said, right there appeared a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the sun.
Resounding with the cries of gods and apsarases, that beautiful [city] came into existence upon the earth;
meanwhile, out of compassion for me, the king passed away along with his family.
Devadeha, the independent lord of the Tārakas, went to heaven;
for when the time arrives, he will indeed become the Manu Dakṣasāvarṇi.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the ninth Manu has been described to you;
now I shall tell you the tenth Manu, who is of the same color as Brahmā.
He first set his mind upon a certain dull-witted Brahmin named Brahmasāvarṇi,
who was living on the shore of Bālakṛṣṇa Lake.
"I shall perform extensive austerities; for what happiness is there here in the state of a brahmin?
In a kingdom, however, there exists supreme happiness, filled with all enjoyments. (27)
Having reflected thus, the dull-witted Brahmin named Balīśvara himself remained constantly living in the water of the lake for ten years.
While meditating, he beheld me, the Lord of Śrī, his beloved master;
and I, remaining in samādhi, saw him with my nāḍī being devoured by a fish.
My devotee’s entire skeletal frame was covered with moss;
indeed, I went into his presence along with you in order to uplift him.
And having entered within, I raised up that lord of the Bālīs;
he possesses neither skin, nor a collection of vessels, nor sense organs. (31)
How does he see and hear, and how indeed does he touch and speak?
How does he stand and move, and from where does the movement of the vital breaths arise? (3)
There is no blood, nor marrow, nor belly, nor cavities;
such indeed is my body, the devotee, which abides within me at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Having entered his body as its cage, the constituent elements were fashioned by me; they were brought to growth, and thus the sinews, marrow, and so forth came into being. (34)
All the channels there were also renewed by me;
blood was filled therein, and subsequently, hair grew forth.
His body, covered with skin and endowed with the senses, vital breaths, and mind, having reached the heart during that perfect state of meditative absorption, emerged from it. (36)
As soon as he rose from the water, he saw me standing before him—
the glorious Supreme Self— bestowing that boon upon him.
He too, beholding me as Hari, requested the fruit of his ascetic penance;
he worshipped me repeatedly with mere water and indeed with his heart.
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of Siddhis, Lord of the World, Lord of Māyā, Lord of lords, Lord of kings, O Master! ||39||
"Grant me sovereignty here, and also the status of a Brahmin forever.
"So be it," I said, granting this boon to that high-souled one.
He fell at our feet and offered auspicious lotuses at our feet;
he drank the nectar of our feet. ||41||
The food offered by us two, consisting indeed of milk, was consumed by him after he had quickly drunk water, like one who is bodiless (videha). ||42||
Having cast off his body, that king of devotees, possessing a divine form, went to the celestial realm in a chariot together with me and you. 43.
Offered by me to the gods, he dwells even in the world of the gods;
then, after some time, he attained the state of being the son of Brahmā.
By the power of my worship and through his own austerity, he shall himself become the Manu known as Brahmasāvarṇi, attaining the supreme status of a Manu.
O Lakṣmī, he shall indeed obtain Brahminhood endowed with sovereignty;
now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I declare the eleventh mantra. 46.
In former times, there was a farmer named Dharmasāvarṇi, belonging to the Vaiśya caste, who was devoted to righteousness and supported a family consisting of a host of deities. ||47||
Born in the region of Surāṣṭra, he was known by the name Ānandavarṇīti;
he practiced devotion to the Blessed One and exerted himself in the vow of celibacy.
He always remains a perpetual celibate (ūrdhvaretas), dwelling even in the tiger-infested forest on the bank of the Soḍhu river, seeking shelter beneath the Śiṃśapā tree. 49.
With great dispassion, he performed the japa of Śrī Hari;
there, for ten years, he consumed only sugar-cane stalks as his food. (3.156.50)
Then, indeed, he propitiates me, the Imperishable, through fierce austerities;
he finds no sleep and even abandons the deluding illusion.
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O Hari Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe! O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama! ||52||
Thus he constantly cried out and chanted the name of the glorious Narayana;
twenty years passed happily for him as he was chanting. (53)
Then that farmer Devānīka became intent on meditation on the full moon day of Śarad, which was exceedingly radiant with the splendor of the moon.
There, in that forest on level ground near a śiṃśapā tree,
he saw me, divine and with a face like the full moon, arrived there.
Rising up suddenly, the Vaiśya fell at my feet;
he worshipped me with auspicious flowers and such, as well as sugar, tubers, and roots. (56)
That [teaching] was set in motion by me for the sake of the boon; he too requested it:
brahminhood, divinity, great sovereignty, and prosperity. (57)
Having been told by me, "So be it," he was dissuaded from the fatigue of his asceticism and went to the great sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭa, the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
I and the invisible being both returned to our own abodes;
the host of gods then took refuge with me while dwelling in the family of the sages.
In due time, having cast off his body, that highly meritorious man went to the auspicious abode of Truth— the world of Brahmā itself— within the house of Dharma.
The brahmin Dharmasaṃgṛhī was the mind-born son of Dharma;
in his lineage were my ancestors in the sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā.
Those worthy of your worship reside indeed in the vast region of Saurāṣṭra, as well as in Jālāyana, Sauvīra, Sārakaṭa, and Gairika. (62)
My ancestors indeed dwell in Gokṣura and Kṣārapāṭa;
that son of Dharma, Devānīka himself, [resides there] with masses of merit.
Indeed, by my will, having attained the status of a Brahmin and the name Dharmasāvarṇi,
you shall become the eleventh Manu, O lord of kings.
For that duration of time, he shines in the Hall of Dharma in Satyaloka.
Now, O Lakṣmī, my dear, I shall speak of the twelfth Manu; listen. (65)
On an uncultivated plot of land on the bank of the Nārāyaṇī,
there lived a compassionate Śūdra named Ghṛṇeṣika, who was devoid of righteous deeds.
Devoted to supporting his family, he was especially engaged in the occupation of fishing;
once, a rain fell and the waters overflowed their banks.
Then, like the great river Nārāyaṇī spreading out as the ocean, these [waters] indeed swept away houses and villages and carried them off in this flood.
Then the Śūdra, accompanied by his wife and son and provided with a house,
was indeed carried away upon a boat in the midst of the water.
A small house made of wood, even with its foundation, floats upon the water; at that time, he offered himself for the sake of Rudra’s protection. (3.156.70)
If, having regained my life, I should obtain my own home,
then together with my kin I shall always perform the auspicious worship of Rudra.
I shall avoid fish and I shall not commit any act of violence;
I shall subsist on wild roots, fruits, and the like, through devotion to Rudra.
"I shall perform only my religious duties; may the husband of a virtuous wife protect me.
Having thus made this vow, he remained with his family at home by the water.
He performed worship of Rudra, who was in his own form, saying:
"O Hara, remove my distress; O Lord of Satī, remove my suffering and protect my life! (74)
O Mahādeva, O Mahākāla, you who possess the nature of Brahmā and Viṣṇu!
Victory to you, O Śambhu; victory to you, O Rudra; victory to you, O Lord of Śrī Pārvatī! 75.
"O Antaka, protect me! I am yours; grant me life!
Thus did he worship, absorbed in that [deity] along with his family. (76)
By the will of Rudra, his boat, which was floating upon the water, reached the shore;
and when the floods subsided, he too emerged from the house onto the ground.
Having descended, he went a long distance to where the city of Śrīvana was located;
there, he sustained his life with alms, such as vegetables and other food.
Then, accompanied by his family, he went to a forest region on the outskirts and propitiated Rudra, setting aside his own wicked qualities. (79)
In this manner, a period of five years passed for him while he subsisted solely on fruits and roots; at that time, Rudra arrived.
Accompanied by Satī, exceedingly gentle, and like a great ascetic, he spoke:
"O compassionate one, how do you dwell in the forest? What is your desire? (81)
"I am Rudra; speak what you desire, for I am pleased with you; I shall grant it.
Then Ghṛṇeṣika chose the status of a son and also sovereignty.
"So be it," Hara said, and having received the worship, he vanished.
And at the end of the year, Ghṛṇeṣika, along with his family, was seized by fever.
Having cast off his body, he went to the divine realm, having become an attendant of the gods,
to where Rudra Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, shines resplendent.
There he became the son of Rudra and always resided in the house of Rudra;
he will become the Manu Rudrasāvarṇi, possessing the enjoyment of imperial sovereignty. (85)
Thus has this twelfth Manu been described to you;
O Lotus-born One, hear now of the thirteenth Manu, Devasāvarṇi.
In former times, there was a Brāhmaṇa on the bank of the Dīnā river in Ketumāla;
he was a Vaiṣṇava, devoted to sacrificial portions and other rites, and a worshiper of the gods. ||87||
With the sixteen and other ritual offerings, he indeed worships Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Satī, Hara,
and Gaṇeśa, and he certainly gratifies the ancestors.
He constantly gratifies the gods in sacrifice with clarified butter and other offerings;
and I, being pleased with him, became present within the scope of that sacrifice.
He obstructed her for the sake of a boon and requested that most excellent boon:
"For the sake of your imperial sovereignty, and also for the sake of worshipping you as a deity. (3.156.90)
"O Adhvaryava, grant me also the station of Brahmā.
"So be it," I said, and I granted that boon to that great-souled one.
Having granted a boon to him named Sudharman, I indeed vanished;
he too, casting off his body, [was born] in the house of the patriarch Ruci.
O Lakṣmī, this very son born of Mālinī, indeed named Deva,
shall become Raucya, known by the name Devasāvarṇi.
And then the deities, having assembled together, will perform the installation of this thirteenth deity, Manu. (94)
Ruci, indeed the son of Brahmā, lived the life of a religious student.
Then his ancestors said to him, "O dear son, enter the state of a householder."
"Indeed, through a son, there shall be the deliverance of the ancestors as well as their satisfaction.
Thereupon, he performed the *śrāddha* rite and established the life of a householder.
And upon Mālinī he begot a son, Raucya Manu;
this very one shall be the thirteenth Manu, possessed of great strength.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Births and Life-Deeds of the Manus from the Ninth to the Thirteenth," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"The wise Prajāpati Ruci, even though he was unwilling, accepted the life of a householder with that beautiful woman; tell me that in detail. (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, how you attained the state of a householder; how you protected the duties of the virtuous while also acquiring the duties of domestic life. || 2 ||
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, sleeping little and eating little, Ruci lived, O Lakṣmī, entirely devoid of all attachments.
Seeing him without a fire, without a dwelling, eating but once a day, without a fixed hermitage, and free from all attachments, his ancestors spoke to Ruci.
"My dear child, why do you not take a wife—
one who is meritorious, purifying, bestowing happiness, righteous, and the means for attaining heaven and other realms?"
It bestows liberation from debt, grants the attainment of family fame and honor, is auspicious,
destroys bondage, and causes the exhaustion of all latent impressions.
Together with his wife, by serving all the gods, the ancestors, the virtuous,
the sages, and guests, he shall attain heaven.
Thus, without a wife, you incur the debt to the gods, the debt to the ancestors, and likewise the debt to the sages, and you fall into bondage day after day. (8)
O son, without the birth of a son, without the satiation of the gods,
and without the gratification of the sages, you shall certainly not attain the supreme goal.
The affliction that exists in taking a wife is greater than that which exists without a wife;
it persists both in this world and in the next. Therefore, my son, become a householder. (3.157.10)
For one who is without a wife, without sacrifices, and devoid of lineage, there will surely be hell after death; therefore, my son, become a householder.
Having heard this, Ruci replied to his ancestors with auspicious and righteous words:
"O ancestors, I believe you; let there be obeisance to you as I speak. (12)
Celibacy is the very form of Brahman, equal to Brahman, and the bestower of liberation;
desiring liberation through it, I have no interest at all in heaven.
Thus, for me who has attained such awakening, the taking of a wife is considered a descent into the lower realms, afflicted by the suffering of evil, afflictions, and disease. (14)
The restraint of the self, the senses, and other principles is considered the giver of liberation;
that [restraint] would not exist for one who has taken a wife and is filled with the passion of desire. (15)
The mud of karma, arising from the union of the doer and the deed, increases as a latent impression (*vāsanā*); born through many lifetimes, this mire of action continues to flourish. (16)
This self, though smeared with impurities, must indeed be washed by the discerning through immersion in the sacred ford of Brahman and by the waters of contemplation, devotion, and the like. (17)
O ancestors, I wash away the long-adhering mire consisting of latent impressions; being devoted to celibacy, I make myself fit for you. 18.
Indeed, I am able to effect your deliverance;
by the power of celibacy alone, I cast off my bonds and my faults.
Thus addressed, the ancestors said: "O son, that is indeed fitting;
celibacy is truly the path to liberation, of this there is no doubt. (3.157.20)
In the past, obstacles were encountered on the path—sins, inauspiciousness, and evil calamities, as well as egoism, possessiveness, illusion, and countless other karmic actions. (21)
All actions performed in the past,
whether meritorious or non-meritorious, which were intended for experience, must be washed away entirely right here.
While eating those [foods], washing them, and making them new and free of defects,
one should offer everything to Kṛṣṇa, abandoning all bondage for the sake of liberation.
For one who maintains their livelihood here [in this manner], no bondage arises;
there is the exhaustion of past karma and the fruit of liberation without obstacle. (24)
Thus, O son, the washing away of actions is appropriate through this sequence; for this lack of discernment, which produces the mire of sin, is certainly not to be counted [as a valid means]. 25.
Therefore, having taken a wife, enjoy [the world], renounce it, and liberate yourself;
having performed the supreme service [to others], go to the eternal and imperishable state. 26.
Having heard these words of her father, Ruci said to the ancestors:
"The path of action is indeed ignorance; do not involve me in that. (27)
Ignorance and action are both equally hellish;
freedom from action is declared to be perfection; I shall achieve this freedom from action. ||28||
Having heard this, his ancestors gave him this true reply:
"One must perform such actions by which knowledge is acquired. (29)

Through knowledge, that which is called ignorance or false knowledge shall go to dissolution; yet, O son, by the non-performance of prescribed duties, ignorance and false knowledge flourish. (3.157.30)

Furthermore, the non-performance of what is prescribed and the performance of what is prohibited lead to bondage; if there were restraint even in the non-performance of what is prescribed, that too would be a destroyer of dharma.
That would not lead to liberation; rather, in the end, it causes a downward rebirth.
It is not a washing away of sins, but rather their very accumulation.
One is completely consumed by the sins arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties;
therefore, one should perform auspicious acts that have been prescribed for the purpose of preventing the occurrence of such transgressions.
"Since the householder's life is ordained to follow the life of celibacy, my son, if that action [of renouncing it] were hell, it would be like an antidote to poison. (34)
Destroy the poison of transgression by means of the engagement with the householder's life;
having fully performed the duties of the householder, O forest-dweller, destroy that poison.
Therefore, O son, always destroy the poison of worldly existence through renunciation;
abandon the body, senses, and so forth by attaining the realization of the Self as Brahman. (36)
Then, through the contemplation of the Supreme Self, abandon the notion of your own individual self;
having thus ascended this sequence, achieve the supreme ascent. (37)
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors became invisible and went to their own abode;
Ruci, reflecting in his mind, set his heart upon obtaining a wife.
Remembering Brahmā as his father, he performed much penance once again.
Brahmā, having arrived, said to Ruci: "You shall become a Prajāpati. (39)
Having created progeny, obtained sons, and performed Vedic rites,
he entered the four stages of life and established them among his subjects.
Having enjoyed the ever-new fruits of karma resulting from the yoga of giving, and having thereafter brought satisfaction to your ancestors, you shall attain supreme perfection. ||41||
When satisfied, those ancestors will grant you a wife and sons as desired;
when fully gratified by the performance of their commands, O Grandfathers, what would you not give?
O Lakṣmī, having heard these words of the Creator, Ruci herself was pleased;
she praised the Creator and worshipped him with water and flowers.
Then Brahmā vanished there on the riverbank;
thereafter Ruci, having gratified the ancestors, praised them with prostrations and the weight of devotion. 44.
I bow to the eternal Grandfather, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa;
to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. 45.
I pay homage to the imperishable abode of Śrī-Brahman and to the liberated Maheśvaras;
I pay homage to all powers and sovereignties, and to the qualities and the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas). 46.
[She saw] the weapons, all the bhūtas, the vibhūtis, as well as the Īśvaras, the Muktānikās, the avatāras, and the Mothers, Śrī, Ramā, and the others. ||47||
I pay homage to those known as the Vyūhas, and I pay homage to the Virājas;
I pay homage to the virtuous knowers of Brahman who dwell in Satyaloka. ||48||

I pay homage to those ancestral spirits honored in the śrāddha, and to those who are the presiding deities in the śrāddha; I bow to those who are gratified by the gods themselves during the śrāddha. 49.
I bow to those who are gratified in heaven by the great seers (maharṣis),
and likewise, I bow to those who are gratified by the perfected ones (siddhas).
I bow to those who are worshipped even by the Guhyakas for the sake of supernatural powers;
and I pay homage to those ancestors who are worshipped by humans on earth. (51)
And I pay homage here to those ancestors who bestow their own desired worlds—those who, being gratified by the performance of śrāddha rites, are worshipped with faith by the brahmins. ||2||
I bow to those who bestow the station of Prajāpati and are satisfied by their wives;
I bow to those highly honored ones who grant the fruit of lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika).
I bow to the ancestors who are gratified by the Kṣatriyas and honored at sacrifices;
I bow to the ancestors who are worshipped by the Vaiśyas and who subsist on the *kavya* offerings.
I bow to those whose food is honored by Śūdras, to those honored with food during auspicious times,
to the ancestors honored by Asuras, and to those who subsist on the food of Rākṣasas.
I bow here to those inhabitants of Pātāla who are gratified during the Śrāddha rites— those whose food is the Svadhā offering and who are honored by the depths of the netherworld.
I bow to the ancestors who are worshipped by all, including the Nāgas and others, with every kind of enjoyment— those dwelling in heaven, those in the intermediate space, and those situated on earth.
I always bow to the Pitṛs who reside in celestial chariots, who possess embodied forms, who are honored by practitioners of yoga, and who are auspicious bestowers of liberation from suffering. (58)
I always pay homage here to those ancestors who have taken form, who consume the *svadhā* offering, who bestow all desired fruits, and who grant even liberation while residing in heaven. (59)
May they be satisfied— those who grant desires to those who have wishes, who bestow the state of divinity and sons,
who grant the stations of Indra and Sūrya, and who bestow cattle, heaven, a home, and power.
May all those dwelling in celestial chariots, clothed in rays, and bestowing nectar—whether in the moon or the sun—be satisfied with water, food, perfumes, flavors, and other offerings. (61)

Those who consume the food offered into the fire, those others who are the eaters of oblations (haviḥ-bhujaḥ), those who dwell within the bodies of Brahmins, and those who dwell within the bodies of virtuous people; ||62||
May those who partake of the funeral offerings attain satisfaction through the water and other gifts offered by me;
may they, gratified by the black sesame seeds and vegetable leaves, experience joy.

May all those ancestors, who consume what is left by others, who are worthy of worship by the immortals, and who bestow heaven, attain satisfaction through these offerings of flowers, perfumes, and food. 64.

May those ancestors who have been worshipped daily, those worshipped monthly, and those worshipped on the Aṣṭakā days, as well as those worshipped at the end of the year and during festivals— may they, my ancestors, be satisfied.

White ones, honored by Brahmins, have the color of the sun; those honored by Kṣatriyas are golden-colored; those worthy of worship by Vaiśyas are golden-hued; and blue ones are worshipped by Śūdras. ||66||
May they attain satisfaction through flowers, perfumes, juices, incense, water, food, fruits, leaves, and the oblation of clarified butter poured into the fire; to them I bow.
I also bow to those who, preceded by the gods, consume the offerings to the ancestors (kavya), whose garlands are prosperity— namely, the bhūtas, pretas, asuras, rākṣasas, and the fierce pitṛs.
May the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa ancestors likewise attain satisfaction, being gratified by me with faith. (69)
May the Agniṣvātta protect the eastern quarter, and likewise the Barhiṣads the southern;
may the Ājyapas protect the western, and the Somapas mine in the north.
May Yama always protect me from Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas, from evil spells and incantations, and from the bodies of Asuras and Pretas. (71)
May the thirty-one classes of ancestors, being satisfied, grant me what is beneficial:
the Viśvas, the Viśvabhujas, the Dharmas, the Dhanyas, and likewise the Śubhānanas. (72)

They are to be propitiated, they bestow prosperity, and they are the makers of prosperity; they are the nine prosperities, auspicious, health-giving, the performers of welfare, and the causes of capability. (73)
And those with more auspicious bases—thus are the six groups of fathers (pitṛgaṇas):
the excellent ones, the most worthy ones, the givers of boons, the givers of nourishment, and likewise the givers of contentment.
The sustainers and protectors of the universe, those seven groups of ancestors, are great, high-souled, honored, and possessed of mighty strength. ||75||
These five groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas) are thus: Mahimavantas, as well as Sukhadās, Dhanadas, Dharmadās, and Bhūtidās. ||76||
"May all four Gaṇas indeed be satisfied when worshipped by me.
As Ruci was thus offering praise, a mass of splendors appeared before him.
Then Ruci, rising up before him,
praised those who were formless, unworshipped, composed of light, and present there.
I pay homage to those ancestors who are accessible through meditation and possess divine forms; I also bow down to Indra and the other lords, as well as Dakṣa, Mārīca, and the leaders of the sages.
I bow to Manu, the Moon among sages, the Sun, and Īśvara; to the ancestors, those who dwell in the waters, the lords of the planets and constellations, and those honored by Vāyu and Agni.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to those who dwell in the sky and those who reside on earth and in heaven;
I also pay homage to the divine sages and progenitors, the givers of imperishable rewards.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to Kaśyapa, the lord of creatures; to Soma and Varuṇa; and to the lords of yoga, the perfected ones, and the virtuous.
Salutations to the Self-Existent Supreme Lord from the hosts of the seven worlds; salutations again and again to Soma and to those who uphold Soma. ||83||
I bow to the yogis who have the form of fire and who stand at the sacrificial altar;
I indeed pay homage to the ancestors, who abide in splendor and whose forms are the moon, the sun, and fire.
I bow to the perfected ones who possess the nature of Brahmā, who are devoted to celibacy, who reside in Satyaloka, and who abide as lords beyond the veil of ignorance. ||85||
I bow to the Vairāja, Vaiṣṇava, and Bhauma forms, to the Śrīs dwelling in Śrīpura, to those abiding in the unmanifest nectar, and to those residing in Goloka. (86)
I bow to Vaikuṇṭha, the imperishable abode, and its incarnations;
and I bow to all the female incarnations and the liberated women.
I bow to all the liberated attendants and to the divine powers, and to the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī. 88.
I bow to all the beloveds of Brahmā, as well as the beloveds of Hari, along with their weapons, qualities, and manifestations; may they be gracious toward me. (89)
Thus praised, those auspicious ancestors emerged from his splendor;
provided with the offered food, flowers, and other gifts, they stood before him.
The prostrated ones spoke to him again: "O son, remain accompanied by your wife;
from her a son shall be born to you, the great Manu named Raucya."
Others shall also become your sons, and they too will be rulers of the earth;
and you, having become Prajāpati and having created the fourfold progeny, [shall rule].
"O devotee, your office has ended; you shall attain perfection leading to liberation.
And we shall cause those who recite this hymn to attain prosperity."
By the recitation of this hymn, satisfaction lasts for twelve years;
even if a śrāddha rite is performed imperfectly, it becomes endowed with merit through the chanting of this hymn.
When this was said, O Lakṣmī, the Apsaras Pramlocā, beautiful to behold, suddenly rose up from the middle of the river together with the girl. 95.
For she was indeed the beloved of Puṣkara, the son of Varuṇa; he said to Ruci, "O Ruci, take my daughter as your wife. (96)
"May Manu be born from her; she has been given by me.
When Ruci said, "So be it," he gave him his daughter Mālinī. (97)
Ruci took her hand, and from her a son was born;
he was the god Raucya Manu, who will indeed be the thirteenth.
The great devotee, a true worshipper, shall be liberated at the end of his term of office.
This [account] concerning the father, including the narrative and the rites of worship, is pure and sinless. (99)
By reciting it, one is released from suffering and likewise endowed with prosperity;
one obtains wealth and enjoyment here, and may even attain liberation at the end.
One shall obtain the fruit of worshiping the ancestors, as well as a lineage, heaven, and even abundant prosperity; one may also attain supreme liberation.
One shall obtain increase in righteousness, as well as health, wealth, grain, and so forth;
one attains all desires earned through the propitiation of the ancestors. (102)
He enjoys all forms of bliss, joy, and every happiness;
through devotion to his father, his state as a householder becomes free from worldly defects. ||103||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Vision of the Ancestors by the Prajāpati Ruci, His Praise, the Instruction for the Purpose of Domestic Life, and the Description of Domestic Life," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; I shall speak of the fourteenth Manu, named Indrasāvarṇi, the auspicious son of Bhūti in the future.
There was a disciple of Aṅgiras named Bhūti, who was exceedingly prone to anger;
he was fierce, a giver of curses, and harsh-spoken out of rage even over a trivial matter.
Knowing him to be of such a nature, out of fear, no one at all approaches the vicinity of his hermitage; even the gods are terrified.
For this very reason, Mātariśvan (the wind) did not blow excessively harshly;
the sun did not commit excessive evil, nor did Parjanya (the rain-god) create excessive mud.
The moon was not too cold, nor did the fire burn excessively;
even the trees, the creepers, and the grasses were afraid of it.
Even outside the proper seasons, flowers and the like, as well as an abundance of fruits, constantly appear;
moreover, the seasons themselves proceed according to their own order within that hermitage.
The waters of the rivers flowing near his hermitage,
as well as those contained within my own water-pot, indeed remain there out of fear of him, O Rame.
For such was that Bhūti; being childless, he performed austerities for a long time out of a desire for a son, enduring the afflictions of cold, wind, and fire.
Restricting his food, he became emaciated even though he did not obtain what he desired;
nevertheless, he desisted from his asceticism and came to recognize me as the Supreme Lord.
Once, his elder brother named Suvarcas summoned him to his own sacrifice;
therefore, he [Śukra] desired to send one of his disciples who was about to depart.
He said, "I am going to the sacrifice of my elder brother, which is called the Śāntidharma;
you must perform the vigil for the fire in my hermitage."
"Ensure that the sacrificial fire does not go out; thus maintain the hermitage. Having thus instructed his disciple, he went indeed to his brother's sacrifice.
Then Śānti went to the forest for the sake of sacrificial fuel, flowers, fruits, and other necessities;
having returned, she performed the service of the hermitage, such as sweeping and other chores. (13)
Indeed, as soon as he went to the fire-sanctuary for the purpose of offering oblations, the fire was extinguished;
seeing this, he became lost in thought.
Terrified by the fear of spirits and exceedingly distressed, he lamented:
"What shall I do? What indeed must I undertake in this situation? (15)
If my preceptor sees this sacrificial fire-altar with its fires extinguished,
he will then swiftly employ me in a difficult calamity.
"If I were to establish another fire here in the place of the sacred fire, the Guru, seeing me directly, would reduce me to ashes. (17)
Thus, having been born as the cause of my teacher’s anger and his curse,
and seeing that the fire has now been extinguished, my teacher will surely curse me.
Or else, the enraged fire will surely burn me then;
let that which was destined to happen come to pass, for what is not to be will not come to be.
In that situation, a means must be employed for the pacification of the offense;
indeed, the request for forgiveness should be made by the one who committed the offense. (3.158.20)
"This is the duty that must be performed by me here; this is my foremost obligation.
Having reflected thus, that wise one then sang a hymn of praise to Agni.
Having gone for refuge to the Purifier (Fire), he offered praise with a single-minded heart:
"Oṃ, salutations to the one whose essence is infinite power and fierce power, the Lord Hari! (22)
Oṃ, salutation to the one who is the embodiment of the means for accomplishing the sacrifice for all worlds;
who presides over one, two, and five [sacrifices], and who possesses a sixfold nature in the Rājasūya.
Salutations to you who possess the visible form of a god, whose conduct is divine;
salutations to the powerful one who is the form of semen for all those possessing bodies. 24.
You are the mouth of all the gods, of the lords, and even of Hari;
you are the digestion of all beings, as well as of foods that possess flavor.
Consuming the oblation that has been offered, you indeed bring about the state of being a cloud;
having assumed the form of rain, you cause the multitude of medicinal herbs to flourish.
Living beings dwell happily upon its fruits and other products;
with its sacrificial fuel-sticks, people—and even the gods—perform their sacrifices. (27)
O Vibhāvasu, the Daityas and Rākṣasas as well, those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and even those born from the earth, all have you as their support.
O Fire, all are nourished by you; all increase through you;
all are protected by you; likewise, protect me. (29)
Among the gods you are indeed luminosity, and among the Siddhas you are splendor;
you abide as poison among the Nāgas, and as the portion of wind among the birds.
Among human beings you are anger, and among the hosts of beasts and birds you are arrogance; in trees you are hardness, and in the earth as well, you are firmness.
In water you alone are fluidity; indeed, you are speed among the winds.
You are pervasive like the sky, abiding within all beings. (32)
You alone are threefold, eightfold, and even thousandfold;
indeed, you are the enjoyer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings through the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and the like.
Even among the weapons you alone shine brilliantly amidst the streams [of flame];
O Jātavedas, homage be to you, and let there be salutation to you, O tawny-eyed one! 34.
O Consumer of Oblations, homage be to you; homage be to you, O Carrier of the Sacrificial Offering!
O Purifier, homage be to you from this day forth; homage be to you, O Purifier of the Universe! (35)
Salutations be to you, the maker of ripening; salutations again and again to you, the nourisher.
You are light, you are the great Āditya; O Vibhāvasu, let there be salutation to you! 36.
You are the fire Hiraṇyaretas, O seven-tongued one; salutations be unto you!
Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, and likewise Lohitā—[these are your tongues]. (37)
Dhūmrā, Sphulliṅginī, Viśvā, and Saptajihvā are your auspicious [tongues];
Kālaniṣṭhākarī is the first, and Pralayakārī is the second. (38)
The third is to be understood as *laghimā* (levity); the fourth is the power of acting according to one's will (*kāmakāriṇī*).
The fifth bestows freedom from disease (*rogadā*), and the sixth brings about the state of being a *sarvapudgala* (the universal person). ||39||
The seventh is the flame that bestows happiness; protect us from great fear because of them. O tawny-eyed one, red-necked one, black-colored one, O consumer of oblations! 3.158.40.
Save me from this fear, O Fire, O Consumer of Oblations!
You are known as the submarine fire and the Vāḍava fire; you are the digestive fire within the stomach.
O Vaiśvānara, drinker of Soma, consumer of oblations, protect me from fear!
Touched by your flames, this substance becomes pure. (42)
By means of your ashes, may all be pure; make me pure as well.
O son, protect me here from the fear that has arisen, just as a father protects his son.
O Fire, come forth openly for the sake of this devotee;
protect me so that the preceptor Bhūti does not consume me with his curse. (44)
Thus praised, the Fire-god appeared before Śānti in a magnificent form;
pleased, he approached and said to Śānti, "Have no fear of me, your preceptor."
"I am pleased with your devotion and even with this hymn; choose a boon.
Śānti said, "I am free from fear by the mere sight of you."
May the preceptor Bhūti come and behold you seated upon your throne;
may he also become the distinguished son of the preceptor who is childless.
Thus addressed, Analadeva, filled with serenity, replied:
"The boon you have requested is for the sake of your preceptor, not for your own sake. (48)
Being even more pleased than that, I grant it: "So be it!
Your son, named Bhautya, shall be the lord of a Manvantara. (49)
The fourteenth, beginning with Mahendra, shall be established; he will be wise and, moreover, a preceptor who loves peace—of this there is no doubt.
I indeed exist within the sacrificial pit, endowed with flames amidst the fuel-sticks;
by this hymn of praise, my worshiper shall be freed from sin and become a sharer in the merit of the sacrifice. (51)
"And he shall be free from calamities; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Agni dwelt there in the sacrificial pit, laughing.
Then Bhūti arrived and became filled with affection;
he asked his disciple the reason for both that affection and his tranquility.
Śānti related the entire account exactly as it had occurred for the sake of his welfare;
then, becoming pleased, that guru indeed bestowed the Vedas upon his disciple.
There was born there a son of Bhūti named Manu Bhautya;
Śuci was the Indra, and likewise the gods accepted Bhautya as their Manu.
And there, they worshipped in every way the Manvantara named Indrasāvarṇi and the deities with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and excellent sandalwood paste.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this one named Indrasāvarṇi shall become the fourteenth Manu; he has now been described to you.
O Śivarājñī-lakṣmī, having heard these words, one obtains an excellent progeny, all desires, wealth, knowledge, intellect, and a beautiful wife. 58.
One obtains health, strength, a grandson, a son, supreme magnanimity, auspiciousness, intelligence, victory, and great preeminence among kinsmen. (59)
He attains the destruction of his enemies and the favor of the gods;
moreover, he is liberated from all sins merely by hearing [this]. (3.158.60)
One obtains sacred learning, the Dharma, honor, and one's own desired prosperity;
one acquires cattle, the earth, sovereignty, and preeminence. ||61||
From that, one attains longevity, prosperity, and detachment;
likewise, one attains spiritual advancement, heaven, and glory.
But those Manus are portions of myself; they have been established by me, and I rejoice in them.
The worship of him is indeed my own worship; his story is considered to be my own story.
There, I cast forth that fiery energy which bestows the status of a universal monarch;
indeed, by means of their propitiation, those Manūs became my devotees.
There will be others as well in other kalpas, and those who have already existed—
they too are considered to be my portions, the Manus.
All the lunar days beginning with Manv-ādi are essentially composed of vows;
they bestow great merit, are purifying for those who give gifts, grant heaven, and bestow the status of a king.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the origin of the Manus;
tell me what you wish to hear, for I shall indeed speak of that.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of the Fourteenth Manu," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"I am satisfied by the nectar of your words, which grant eternal joy. If it pleases you, we shall indeed travel in a celestial chariot to sport together."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Let all those who are dear to Brahmā, as well as others who are dear to Hari, be ready; we shall go to the Himavat mountain."
Thus addressed, they all quickly prepared themselves along with Śrī;
having adorned themselves, they ascended the celestial chariot.
Filled with great enthusiasm, the women went with their beloved Hari in a celestial chariot that moved through the air to behold various lands.
Having beheld Mount Catuṣṭilā and gazed upon the Anarta country, and having seen Camatkārapura and the Śrīgiri of Nārāyaṇa; || 5 ||
Having beheld Suvarṇadvīpa and having crossed the ocean, and having seen the Nārāyaṇa lake and crossed the Sindhukī marshland; || 6 ||
Having bathed in the river and purified myself, and having beheld the mountain like a stone,
I shall gaze upon Indukuśa and behold Kārukāra.
Having beheld Śrīnagara and Kaśyapāra, they went to the Himālaya;
and having beheld the Saptasindhu mountains, they proceeded to the Nandāsatī.
Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇā, Brahmā, Priyā, and the others, being honored by her and having received the worship offered by her,
embraced her with their lotus-hearts.
Having purified Queen Nandā, they gazed upon the forests;
and they also beheld the beautifully adorned and well-suspended Gaṅgā.
It was crowded with Gandharvas and others, constantly frequented by gods and other celestial beings, sprinkled on all sides by the rut of divine elephants, and surrounded by lordly elephants.
It was a refuge for ascetics, frequented by gods and brahmins,
covered with rows of white swans, and adorned with *kāśa* grass as if with chowries.
It was meritorious, very cool, heart-pleasing, increasing the joy of the mind,
subject to waning and waxing, delightful, and frequented by hosts of the twice-born.
Its waters were as sweet as nectar; it was graced by ascetics, serving as a ladder for ascending to heaven and destroying all impurities.
It possessed very cool and swift-flowing water, was frequented by hosts of great sages, and caused longing in all the world while captivating the heart. || 15 ||
It bestows merit upon all the worlds and grants the path to heaven;
it resounds with the cries of geese and cranes and is adorned with aquatic flowers.
Her navel was deep with its whirlpools, her broad hips were like islands,
she was rich with eyes like blue lotuses, and her face was like a fully blossomed lotus.
Clad in a garment of snow-white foam, possessing the ruddy sheldrake as her lower lip, displaying rows of cranes as her teeth, and having eyebrows formed by schools of darting fish; (18)
Her beautiful breasts were like water-jars situated within the cavity of the water’s edge; she resounded with the tinkling of swans as her anklets and wore a series of bracelets made of lotus stalks.
It was fragrant with the pollen from the trees and creepers on its banks,
and it was difficult to behold because the solar disc was reflected in its multitude of waves.
[The river] whose two banks were agitated by the blows produced by the tusks of Indra’s elephant,
[was further disturbed] by the temple-juice from Śakra’s elephant and by the sandalwood paste from the breasts of celestial women.
[He saw] a pond of fragrant water, intensely frequented by bees out of greed,
[visited] by ascetics rich in austerity, by gods, by celestial nymphs, and by the wives of men.
She bestows happiness and peace, removes sin, and makes her voice heard;
she is resorted to by hosts of liberated sages, gods, ancestors, and humans.
He beheld it frequented by yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, hosts of siddhas and cāraṇas, as well as deities and divine trees.
Having descended into that river, the beloveds of Brahmā and the beloveds of Hari bathed;
there was the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, possessing ten million forms.
He bathed in the water together with them, filling their minds and instilling in them fragrance as well as the liquid essence of erotic passion.
Having been reunited with her former companions, Gaṅgā felt her purpose fulfilled;
moreover, through union with Śrī Hari, she attained eternal satisfaction.
Then, having put on their garments and assumed the finest ornaments,
they ascended the celestial chariot and beheld the Himalaya.
It was surrounded by many towering, pale-white peaks,
and it was also inhabited by ascetics with white matted hair.
Whiter than a silken cloth by its thousands of waterfalls and rivers,
whiter than heaven by its thousands of peaks of the Himalayas.
With dark-blue Devadāru forests serving as his lower garment,
he has a white cloud for a turban and a blue cloud for an upper robe.
In some places he has the moon and sun as his crown; in some places he is endowed with the bodily elements;
his central body is smeared with snow, while his sides are anointed with sandalwood paste.
In some places it was marked by the feet of apsarases stained with red lac;
in some places it was touched by the sun, and in others it was shrouded in the darkness of shade.
In some places, it flowed with purifying water through mouths like caves;
in other places, it was graced by groups of Vidyādharas sporting there.
In some places it was sung by hosts of kinnaras and even by kimpuruṣas;
it was a refuge for ascetics and was frequented by siddhas and divine men. (35)
With regions where the winds had ceased and adorned with dark-green meadows,
and in some places covered with flowers, it stood like a great garden.
In some places it was frequented by deer, where great trees were shattered by elephants;
it resounded with the roars of lions and tigers and was filled with deep caves.
It possessed great peaks like snow-capped umbrellas and was adorned with hundreds of waterfalls and cascades,
its various regions resembling forests of bamboo thickets.
It resembled an aged ṛṣi and was like the thousand-headed Vṛtra;
its path was blocked by snow, and it stood there imitating the color of silver. ||39||
Beholding the mountain, they all indeed attained supreme joy;
they gazed upon the diverse forests, which were exceedingly delightful.
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, along with *karṇikāra* and *śāmalī*;
with *nyagrodha*, great *aśvattha*, *śirīṣa*, and *śiṃśapā* trees. ||41||
And they were filled with great nimba trees, nirguṇḍī plants, haridru trees, kāleyaka trees, devadāru trees, nimba trees, and padmaka trees. ||42||
With *kapittha*, sandalwood, *bilva*, and red sandalwood trees;
with *vātāmra*, *iṣṭaka*, *akṣoṭaka*, and *arjuna* trees. ||43||
With *abjaka*, *hastikarṇa*, *sumanasa*, and *panasa* flowers, as well as with *prācīnāmālaka*, *kovidāra*, and *dhanaka* flowers. ||44||
With *samarāṭa*, *kharjūraka*, *nārikela*, and *khārika* trees; with *priyālu*, *iṅguda*, *tantumāla*, and likewise *dhava* trees. (45)
With *kāśmīrī* leaves, *āmātaka* fruits, mangoes, and *sarjaka* trees; with nutmegs, betel nuts, long peppers, *plakṣa* trees, and *khadira* wood. ||46||
With *kaṭphala* fruits, with *lavaṅga* and other spices, with cardamom, with flowers and silken cloths, and with *kiṃśuka*, *khadira*, *mandāraka*, and *kovidāraka* trees; ||47||
With *yavāsa*, *śamī*, *vetasa*, and *ambuvetasa* trees;
with *raktātiraṅga*, *nāraṅga*, *karavīra*, and *ciñcu* trees. ||48||
With *hiṅgu*, *jambīraka*, *licikā*, *priyaṅgu*, *jāmbu*, *rāvaṇa*, *kaṭaguṇḍa*, and *khalīlaka*. (49)
They were adorned with red Aśoka trees, Aśoka trees, Kallas, and Śrīpādapas, as well as Āmalakas, Udumbaras, and Campakas.
With white campakas, royal campakas, mucukundas, and kunda flowers;
with parūṣakas, kadambas, pārijātas, and galāṭakas. ||51||
With *kirāta* trees, as well as *ketaka*, *saubhāñjana*, and *nikoṭaka*; with *vallaka* trees, *badarī* trees, and likewise *akṣoṭaka*.
With *kañjarī* trees, *sarjaka*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamālaka* trees; with mangoes, *āraḍūsa*, *barbara*, and *rāmaphālaka* trees. ||53||
With *sītā* fruits, *yāma* fruits, and nectar-like *rāyaṇa* and other fruits,
as well as with *tumburu* trees, *thūraka* plants, and *hastadhūraka* shrubs.
With *ceriṭa*, *arjuna*, and *tilaka* trees with red filaments;
with *madhuka*, *tulasī*, *vṛndā*, and *tigmagandhaka* plants. ||55||
And with *bakula*, *karmada*, *punnāga*, and *ketaka* trees; with *yūthikā*, *jātīphala*, *locas*, sesame, and *kuśeśaya* lotuses. (56)
With *pāribhadraka*, *haridrā*, *kadamba*, *kuṭaja* and other trees;
with *mustaka*, saffron, *kaṃbhā*, *nīpa*, and likewise with groves of *pālī* trees. ||57||
With red flowers, with *sūryamukha* and *sāraghava* trees, with fruit-bearing trees, with pomegranates, *bandhūka*, *kuñjala*, *mallikā*, and other such blossoms; || 58 ||
With *kurabaka* flowers, *bījapūra* fruits, camphor, and *aguru* trees; with *guggulu*, sugarcane, *hintāla* palms, and *cakramardana* plants. (59)
With *pīlu* trees, *dhātakī* trees, *cirabilva*, and *lodhra*;
with *kṣīrikā*, *aśmaka*, *navaraṅga*, and *trikhaṭvaka* trees.
With *bhallātaka*, *indrayava*, *guñjā*, *karamardaka*, *aviṣṭaka*,
along with *drākṣā* and *putrajīvaka*.
With *kaṅkola* and *lavaṅga*, with creeping vines of betel,
with black pepper and jasmine, as well as with *muktaka* and *trapusa* flowers.
With *kuṣmāṇḍaka* gourds, *cirbhaṭa* cucumbers, *paṭola* vines, *kāravella* bitter melons, *karkoṭaka* eggplants, *vārtāka* tomatoes, radishes, and *svādukaṇṭaka* plants. ||63||
They were adorned with *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kalhāra*,
and mustard plants, as well as with *somavallī*, *saṃdhinīvallī*, *sañjīvanī* grasses, *kākālī*, *kāsamardī*, and *śakandala*.
With forests of pulse-bearing plants, grain fields, bamboos, and rattan canes;
with thickets of reeds, cotton plants, golden trees, and *bhūtṛṇa* grass.
With ginger, ajamoda, kuberaka, priyālaka, white water lilies, blue lotuses, land-lotuses, and kaseruka; ||66||
The beloveds of Hari beheld the forests adorned with lotus stalks, wheat, black mustard, and wild rice.
Likewise, they saw there birds of various forms:
peacocks, woodpeckers, sparrows, and cuckoos.
He saw kadamba ducks, swans, koyaṣṭis, khañjarīṭakas,
ospreys, kālakūṭas, khaṭvāṅgas, and likewise hunters.
Likewise, [he saw] *gokṣveḍakas*, jars, *dhārtarāṣṭras*, parrots, cranes,
*dhātukas*, ruddy geese, *kaṭukas*, *ṭiṭṭibhas*, and *bhaṭas*.
And pigeons, lotus-birds, sārikās, and likewise hallaras;
also quails, prabhadrakas, and even garuḍas and cocks. ||71||
Cocks, black sparrows, partridges, swans, woodpeckers, sparrows, francolins, and ḍiṇḍamas; ||72||
They beheld bhūliṅgas, sīrapādas, and bhṛṅgarājas; they saw dātyūhas, sparrows, kāraṇḍavas, caṣas, and cātakas.
They beheld parrots, peacocks, cranes, and swans;
they beheld flocks of birds born of many different species. ||74||
They beheld various kinds of beasts of prey and wild animals as well—tigers, maned lions, leopards, śarabhas, and wolves. (75)
Bears, hyenas, monkeys, golangulas, pragenḍakas, vanaras, hares, cats, wolves, and bhallukas; ||76||
Elephants, buffaloes, gayals, yaks, bulls, wild asses, sṛmaras, rams, and even antelopes; ||77||
Also the kukura, nīlaka, karāla, śambara, rāmaśarabha, toraṇa, kālapuccha, and varāhaka [dogs]. (78)
The women beheld horses, donkeys, reṇḍīyara animals, and citraka deer, as well as lakes and rivers with white waters. 79.
And the beloveds of Hari gazed upon the mountain’s caves and its water-channels, which were warm and cool in their respective parts.
Then, in front of me, I beheld the auspicious hermitage of the seer Atri,
endowed with natural splendor and free from the evils of violence and the like.
There was no falling of snow for five yojanas in every direction;
Kṛṣṇa, honored by Atri, and the Kṛṣṇās went before him.
In its vicinity is a beautiful, great, white peak, where indeed the clouds gather together and let fall snow. (83)
Now, in front of it stands another supreme peak, exceedingly lofty;
there, the clouds constantly and repeatedly pour down snow-water. (84)
Between the two peaks there is a summit that is exceedingly lofty;
upon its slope, on the western side, there are auspicious groves of trees. (85)
Pervaded by darkness and dense with the abundance of fruits, flowers, and the like, the sun does not shine there, nor does the moon gleam. (86)
Nevertheless, there is indeed light there by day;
there are jujube trees (badarī), and great seers dwell there. (87)
Then a celestial chariot, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
descended from the sky into Viśālā, illuminating all directions.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as the great sages devoted to dharma, quickly approached the celestial chariot, overcome with wonder. (89)
Having beheld the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Śrī and the beloved Master, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman and the Highest Lord; 3.159.90.
They all suddenly worshipped with water, sandalwood, and excellent fruits;
Nara and Nārāyaṇa were also worshipped by the Supreme Soul. 91.
Both brothers were honored by all the Nārāyaṇī goddesses;
the great ṛṣis were also honored, saluted, and asked for forgiveness.
Then, having given gifts and served those best of holy men with heart-felt dispositions, he bowed to Vṛṣa and Hari with devotion. (93)
Then, having ascended the celestial chariot, they proceeded ahead;
Himācala himself became the lord of kings and went along with Sainaka.
Full of eagerness, he went toward Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot for the purpose of worship;
having bowed and performed the rites of worship, he then requested permission to return to his own abode. 95.
Desiring to meet Hari, he too went to his abode;
indeed, all around the mountains were ramparts made of white and golden stone.
In the center is a vast valley, adorned with lakes and the like, provided with gardens and such; there stands a palace accompanied by a city. ||97||
The beautiful and most enchanting Himalaya exists;
indeed, the celestial chariot descended there upon the ground of the rampart. 98.
In the home of Himālaya, indeed, Menā and Himālaya offered a welcome and performed worship for Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 99.
They both performed what was appropriate for Hari, Haripriyā, and the others;
Parvata obtained supreme bliss from the sight of Nārāyaṇa.
They caused the Supreme Lord, together with his beloved, to dwell in a magnificent palace, and they quickly prepared nectars and excellent foods for him. || 101 ||
He quickly fed him and then performed the waving of lights (ārātrika);
thereafter, Śrī Hari, served joyfully by his beloveds, took his rest.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with Brahmapriyā and others, beheld the earth from his celestial chariot and proceeded to the home of Himālaya," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Then Himādri indeed arrived for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Soul,
having placed gold in various ways into vessels over golden fires.
And in silver vessels, there were unsurpassed corals, as well as gems known as māṇikya and likewise ruby (padmarāga) jewels. || 2 ||
Having filled basins with diamonds, emeralds, highly radiant sapphires,
and gems known as vaidūrya, he arrived there.
And others set in gold, as well as diamonds and other gems,
emeralds in the number of shells, and brilliantly radiant sapphires.
Karkoṭakas, sūryakāntas, candrakāntas, syamantakas,
sphatikas, gomedakas, and likewise dhūlīmarakatas.
He brought royal jewels, Brahma-jewels, and pearls,
and worshipped Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
She gave garlands of jewels and necklaces of gems;
she gave strings of diamonds and likewise strings of pearls.
Himālaya worshipped Hari with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and the like, as well as with lamps and other offerings;
Menā worshipped Satī in the same manner.
Thus, after the worship, the Mountain led [him] to the auspicious abode of Menā,
which measured more than a krośa and was resplendent with a lake.
The steps all around that lake truly shine beautifully,
surrounded on every side by trees made of gold and silver.
With various mani-jewels and flowers blazing with the luster of excellent ornaments, and with leaves of emerald and blue lapis lazuli as their petals; || 11 ||
In that lake, lotuses with petals of ruby and clusters of diamond filaments, fragrant and radiant, truly shine forth.
The emerald leaves with blue lapis lazuli centers shine upon the body of Vallikā, truly causing great wonder.
The ground of the lake was divine and naturally soft, strewn with various jewels and serving as a refuge for aquatic creatures. (14)
It was the refuge of cowries, oyster shells,
and conchs, as well as of sea-monsters, fish, and fierce creatures along with tortoises.
It is adorned with countless emeralds and the tips of vajras,
and it is beautified by rubies, sapphires, and great blue gems.
With crores of puṣparāgas, karkoṭakas, and anantakas; with rājāvartas, pieces of tuttha, and crores of rucirākṣas. || 17 ||
Likewise, with millions of sun-stones, moon-stones, and other dark-colored gems ending with the last of the letters, as well as with jyotīrasa, crystal, syamantaka, and white stones. || 18 ||
It was also filled with *gomedaka* and *pittaka* gems, as well as *dhūlīmarakata*, *prarāja* jewels, and *vaidūrya* stones possessing fragrant scents. (19)
Likewise, the pleasant ground all around the lake was strewn with pearls, Brahma-gems, and other pearls. (3.160.20)
The water of the lake was pleasantly warm, which destroyed the coldness caused by bathing;
its water was abundant, delicious, light, cool, and fragrant. (21)
It does not injure the throat nor does it overfill the belly;
it produces supreme satisfaction and great happiness within the body. (22)
In the midst of the water there arose a magnificent palace with walls of gold,
composed entirely of every kind of gem, its floor radiant with the luster of moonstones.
With beautiful steps made of vaidūrya, with pillars of pure coral, with great columns of indranīla, and with pedestals fashioned from emerald; ||24||
In such a palace, which was radiant with networks of diamond rays, beautiful, and captivating to the sight, Acyuta was worshipped by Menakā for the sake of adoration. (25)
Mādhava remains eternally protected, subservient to the desires of his devotees;
he sleeps upon the coils of the serpent’s body and is adorned with every ornament.
Likewise, one foot of the illustrious Lord,
the Supreme Self, is bent at the knee, while His second foot is placed upon the king of serpents.
His foot rests upon the lap of Lakṣmī as he reclines on the coils of Śeṣa;
his arm, adorned with armlets, is placed upon the hood of the lord of serpents.
With one hand holding his head by the hair resting on the back of his fingers, and the other hand hanging down with its palm bent and its wrist resting upon his knee. ||29||
With his third hand slightly bent at the region of the navel, and his fourth hand holding a cluster of flowers placed near the nose; || 3.160.30 ||
His feet were massaged by Lakṣmī with hands resembling lotus petals;
he wore a crown adorned with a garland of *santāna* flowers, and was decorated with necklaces and armlets.
Adorned with ornaments such as armlets and finger-rings,
he shone with the beautiful jewels set upon the hoods of the lord of serpents.
His conduct regarding unknown objects is established by the Himālaya; he is constantly honored by Menā and worshipped with the flowers of the *santāna* tree. (33)
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and he was incensed with divine incense;
[he was offered] delicious fruits, heart-pleasing [foods], nectar-like substances, milk-rice, and so forth. ||34||
Having been fed by Queen Menakā, Utpalaśīrṣaka fell asleep;
and as he lay on his most beautiful side, he was beheld by all of them.
Beheld by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Hari,
though possessing a physical form, arose in his divine splendor into His presence.
Having bowed down and embraced him in his heart, he paid homage to Puruṣottama, the beginningless Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World. (37)
The Guru of incarnations, the Guru of emanations, and the Guru who is himself a partial incarnation—the Guru of all Nārāyaṇas has come to my house. (38)
Having said, "I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose," he worshipped the cause.
Having performed the worship, the serpent became invisible there within the image.
Beyond that, the Supreme Lord went to the abode of Himādri,
which was composed of all kinds of jewels, endowed with divine splendor, and full of prosperity.
It was provided with all utensils, furnished with every kind of food, endowed with all beverages, divine, and adorned with soft seats. ||41||
It was pervaded by every kind of fragrance, adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatā),
granting all desires, and accompanied by ten million male and female servants.
Adorned with a throne of gold, diamonds, and jewels, Menakā indeed seated Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon it. 43.
He worshipped with supreme affection and performed the *ārātrika* ceremony;
there, Hari took the nectar-food and the offerings.
Having caused his abode to be purified, he went forth into the sky before the sight of Adri by his command;
swiftly traveling by celestial chariot, he reached the auspicious peak of Kedāra.
The Great God Kedāreśa appeared before the Lord of Śrī and worshipped the Supreme Soul, who was accompanied by Brahmā, his beloved consort, and others. 46.
Having received worship with many jewels and the like, as well as fruits, flowers, and so forth, Hari went before him to Mount Kailāsa.
And Śaṅkara, accompanied by all his gaṇas and joined by Satī, beheld Mādhava, who was served by the enemy of Tripura and attended by the wish-fulfilling tree.
Kubera also approached and worshipped the Supreme Lord;
together with the Guhyakas, he worshipped Hari, the Lord of Śrī. 49.
Then Hari, having received worship with all kinds of jewels, fruits, and flowers,
beheld Mount Saugandhika as well as Mount Suvela.
They beheld Mount Candraprabha, as well as the divine lake of pure water,
the Caitraratha grove, and likewise the Sarvauṣadhi mountain.
Having beheld the divine forest called Viśoka on Mount Kakudmin, and having then seen Mount Vaidyuta and the Vaibhrāja forest; ||52||
Then, having beheld Mount Aruṇa and Lake Śailoda, and having beheld Mount Gaura and the lake with golden sands; ||53||
Beholding the shining silver mountain Himavat, the circle of the earth, and the ocean of clouds above, they proceeded forward.
Having seen the rows of mountains and the lake Śrīmatasara,
the wives of Kṛṣṇa, seated in their celestial chariots, gazed upon them with great joy.
Together with Kṛṣṇa, they descended all around that bank;
they sported with their Lord and engaged in water-sports. (56)
They embrace Mādhava, they bathe him, they bathe themselves;
they gladden him, they rejoice, they bathe, and they rejoice as well. (57)
