Held within the heart by the illustrious Hari, they delight their beloved;
delighted and consisting of their beloved, these women please their dear one. 58.
The women of that place delight their husband with various gestures;
indeed, O beloved, they take up lotuses and apply them [to him]. (59)
Some struck their beloveds with water splashed from their hands;
and being struck by their beloveds, they then became filled with joy.
At that time, beautiful women were seen, their breasts heaving with panting and dancing,
as the knots of their tresses were loosened by the forceful blows of their lovers' hands.
Some women, under the pretext of bathing, embraced their lovers; thus, having delighted their lovers again and again, the women [proceeded]. (62)
Emerging and standing upon the bank, they adorned their limbs;
they made their bodies beautiful and decorated them with ornaments.
Having prepared themselves, they remained situated in their celestial chariots out of longing for their husbands;
then, by means of those chariots, they all went to the white mountain.
Then they went to Hanumat-parvata, which was rich in the beauty of its forests;
there, Śrīpati, the Supreme Person, was worshipped by Hanumān.
Even while established in austerity, Hanumān was honored by Lakṣmī;
in former times, that monkey was a protector who acted as an assistant on the mountain.
Then, by way of the celestial chariots, they went to the golden Gaṅgā;
having drunk its waters there, they proceeded to the city of Śiveśvara.
Having reached the most excellent and purifying Vārāṇasī, which is graced by the Varaṇā river,
and having beheld the beautiful Gaṅgā and Śiva, the Lord of the Universe,
they spent the entire night happily in the abode of Viśveśvara.
Śaṅkara, however, showed great honor to Kṛṣṇa in many ways, providing him with food, clothing, drinks, massages, and other such services. (69)
Propitiated with comfortable beds, enjoyments, and other luxuries, Mādhava, the Supreme Lord, spent the night in a palace resembling Vaikuṇṭha.
Having received worship and partaken of food and other offerings, he took his leave;
then, beholding Mount Vindhya from afar, he quickly departed by means of a celestial chariot.
Having beheld the seven-layered mountain, Bhṛgukaccha— the city of Śrī— and then Gopanātha, he [saw] his own Lomaśabhūmi.
They all went to the city and attained the highest rest;
then, in the evening, those women stood before their lord, the Master.
Having first provided food and other necessities, they questioned the Supreme Lord:
"O Keśava, to whom do all these jewels, diamonds, and so forth belong? (74)
When and from what were all these material things indeed produced and offered to the Himalaya? For they are certainly not divine. //75//
"O Lord, since even a mere fraction of the Kaustubha and other jewels does not exist within these [trees], we wish to hear the story of those precious gems. (76)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Acceptance of Worship Offered by Himādri, the Visiting of Kedāra, Kailāsa, Mānasa, Rohanūmata, Mount Kāśī, Vindhya, Saptapuṭa, Bhṛgukaccha, Gopanātha, and Others, the Arrival at Lomaśa’s Pond, and the Desire to Know the Origin of the Brahma-wives’ Material Diamonds and Other Jewels," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O beloveds of Brahmā, to that which you have asked concerning the origin of the jewel;
I shall here relate this ancient narrative born of the devotion of Bala and Prabalā.
In Vaikuṇṭha, all those attendants who dwell there are dear to me;
among them, Bala and Prabala were stationed as two [foremost].
Those two divine attendants and gatekeepers were sent by me to the abode of the illustrious Lalitā-lakṣmī, known as Śrīpura.
Requested by Śrī Lalitā Mahālakṣmī, those two [messengers] went toward me; commanded by me, they both departed for the city of Śrī named Śrīpura.
Having been honored by Lalitā, those two were appointed as gatekeepers;
they were armed, unwearied, and utterly devoted to their master.
Wearing crowns and auspicious attire, adorned with jewels, gems, and other ornaments, they have faces encircled by halos of splendor; they are gentle, with eyes like lotuses.
Then, every day, Lalitā’s countless female friends and maidservants arrive at the abode of Śrī in the morning, bringing with them water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other requisites.
Having bathed in the divine Śrīnirjhara spring and having gathered fresh, fragrant flowers from Kṛṣṇa’s garden, they depart.
Some [brought] kadamba flowers, some bakula flowers;
some brought aśoka flowers, and some auspicious kunda buds.
Some [brought] only *śrīkusuma* flowers and *pārijāta* blossoms;
some, *śṛṅgāra* flowers; and others indeed, lotuses.
Some, however, took only campaka flowers, some lotuses from the dry land,
and others brought clusters of yūthikā blossoms.
Some carry thousand-petaled lotuses as well as kadamba flowers;
thus, assuming thousands of forms, they proceed.
Some went taking pastes of sandalwood and saffron,
while others took all the articles suitable for adornment.
Others, having gathered collyrium and other such items, as well as fragrant oils and some essences of scent, go forth for the purpose of worship.
Others depart taking tulasī leaves;
others take fruits, and still others take food and golden rings.
Taking away other gifts— jewels, necklaces, umbrellas, chowries, incense, lamps, and offerings— they depart toward Śrī.
Innumerable people were indeed passing through, and a great crush occurred at the city gate;
there was also a tumultuous clamor from the female companions and the Pūjikās.
At the city gate of Lalitāśrī, there arose the sound of hearing what was not being spoken,
produced by the flow of young women emerging under the influence of that divine possession.
A great crush occurred there at the city gate, causing a state of paralysis;
it was the seat of the powerful and likewise the seat of the strong,
being trampled by young women falling down on both sides.
And some indeed caused them to ascend onto the altar-platform.
Having lost their way in the crush and trembling with fear of the throng,
those women— while their powerful younger brother stood nearby— placed their hands together in añjali.
She gently requests her circle of friends for permission to depart;
moreover, bowing with conciliatory words, she speaks so as not to cause any disturbance.
But Bala, endowed with strength, spoke even as he requested:
"Let them go slowly, let them go slowly; let them not cause a crush here. (23)
"Since even our seats have been powdered and crushed, I take delight even while women are thus speaking of peace. (24)
As they crushed one another and fell upon the city gate, the collapse of both Bala’s army and his attendants occurred.
Then, the footprints of her friends appeared upon him;
his crown was destroyed and his attire became smeared with dust and mud.
His weapons and other implements likewise fell from his hands;
when this falling occurred, Bala indeed became filled with rage.
From Jayā, Prajñā, Pāśavatī, Māṇikyā, and her other companions—from the elbows, from the hands, from the sides, and likewise from the chest—[the goddesses emerged]. || 28 ||
Rising up with great speed, he struck the door-bolt and shouted insults at his fallen companions. (29)
Then, seizing him by the hand, lifting him up, and raising him high, he cast him far away.
Seeing that Balarāma was enraged and that they were falling helplessly during this untimely crush, his friends were overwhelmed by the force of the impact.
He was censuring [the donor], yet giving [himself away], standing there as a repeller of obstacles. ||3 1 ||
As he was striking with his two elbows like one intoxicated with rage, Jaya and the others cried out to him, "Fall! Fall! 32.
"You are not fit to remain here, filled with wrath at the women's gate;
one who is powerful, ever-fitting, gentle, and repeatedly enduring of all things is fit for this place. (33)
He possesses a handsome form and sweet speech that is pleasant to hear; he is humble and patient, and in him no harshness is found.
Though powerful, he bears himself like a woman and acts as a devoted servant.
Even when oppressed, he does not utter a reproach nor indeed a cry of distress;
on the contrary, he offers praise and bows down in salutation.
"This one is always powerful and worthy to remain here, but this other one is not. || 35-36 ||
Indeed, let it fall soon upon the creation of the Creator in this universe;
enjoy the fruit of your elbows and the fruit of your own ill-behavior. (37)
Thus addressed, he suddenly became pale, on the verge of falling down, filled with rage, and overcome by pride against the strength of Nārāyaṇa. (38)
Considering himself superior, he replied with indignation:
"Jayā, Aprajñā, Pāśavatī, Māṇikyā, and the other women. (39)
"Those who have indeed told me 'fall upon me'—let them fall, even the wise ones, anywhere within the cosmic egg, upon the earth, bearing the fruit born of separation. (3.161.40)
"The sorrow born of separation from Hari, and likewise that born of separation from my own abode"—
when these words, consisting of curses, had thus been uttered between them, [41]
Having heard that, the goddess named Śrī Lalitā went there quickly;
having learned the entire account, the beautiful woman grieved for a moment. (42)
Then Bala, Jaya, and the others also prayed most intensely for the cessation of the curse, so that even upon falling [from heaven], they might attain liberation. ||43||
Lalitāśrī said: "Indeed, it was born by my will;
there is no grief regarding the crushing or the falling."
I too must go to that place where you, my female friends, are—where the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), resides. ||45||
He will come to that place himself, there is no doubt, for the sake of the task of uplifting the world and to fulfill the heart's desire of his friend. (46)
"You shall be known as Prajñā and Jayā, and you shall also be Pāśavatī; you shall be Māṇikī, and you shall become the wives of Kṛṣṇa along with me. (47)
There shall indeed be no suffering from falling or separation upon the earth;
through constant union with Kṛṣṇa, you shall be possessed of happiness. 48.
Furthermore, this attendant Bala, who was mentioned by Hari, was appointed to my city gate and received a curse out of anger. (49)
By the will of Kṛṣṇa he is indeed small, and likewise by my will;
yet this Bala is truly filled with wrath within the cosmic egg of Brahmā.
But because he was born with an asuric disposition accompanied by anger, [the gods] thought, "He will seize [us]; once dead, he shall attain liberation. (5.1)
The relics arising from his body, which are of the nature of transformation, exist on earth;
and in heaven as well, there are excellent jewels and material gems. (52)
"They shall become worthy of worship everywhere on all sides"—it was for the sake of accomplishing this very great task that I, too, [acted]. (53)
Even Nārāyaṇa desired the downfall of the Goddess,
and he desired the downfall of Bala for the sake of the jewel.
Whatever I have desired shall come to pass exactly so;
this divine attendant Bala is the supreme devotee of Nārāyaṇa.
The most excellent of great devotees, he is purifying and the sanctifier of the world;
even the jewels arising from his purifying body are themselves purifying.
And being upheld, these purifiers shall cleanse the worlds of sin,
and they shall also protect them from sufferings and calamities.
And ornaments made of jewels produced from his body shall indeed come into being;
furthermore, Maṇimūrti Hari shall dwell upon the surface of the earth.
In this way, O friends, the liberation of Bala from the gods and indeed from Nārāyaṇa will soon take place; thereafter, he will quickly return to the earth.
I shall also appear on the surface of the earth in a graceful form as the princess, the servant of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (3.161.60)
In the south, I shall become Lalitālakṣmī in Kāñcī;
for the sake of performing many acts of deliverance, everything shall be suitable.
Having spoken thus at the city gate in the abode of Śrīpura, Lalitālakṣmī, after addressing them, went to her own seat, and Jayā and the others quickly prostrated themselves.
Having obtained birth as he desired here on the surface of the earth within the cosmic egg,
Bala also manifested in this world with the nature of an asura.
From Kaśyapa and Diti, indeed, there was a son named Bala;
he was a great Asura, a Daitya, the elder brother of Sukeśī and others.
Having performed penance for a hundred years on the summit of Mount Meru while meditating upon Viṣṇu, he was born endowed with the memory of his former lives and filled with great joy.
Placing his head upon the earth and likewise his feet in the air,
he appeared as if entered into a state of meditative absorption (samādhi), enveloped by a network of creepers.
A bird’s nest was formed upon the back of a creeper at his feet;
bound by the creeper, it remained motionless for a hundred years.
His flesh became withered as he remembered Nārāyaṇa in his heart;
then I went before him for the sake of releasing him from that curse.
I personally cleared away all those creepers;
and by my two hands, he was created and attained some degree of knowledge. (69)
He perceived my two hands by their mere touch as being tender;
and when he was quickly bathed by me, he indeed raised his face upward.
He prostrated like a staff and wept, shedding tears;
with his limbs overwhelmed by love, he entreated for liberation from the womb.
Viṣṇu said: "O devotee, you have always been my devotee and likewise my purifier; by granting me your vision, you have become even more purified than that. (92)
Listen quickly, for you shall be released from this womb of a female demon;
abandon your asceticism, go to the world of Indra, and display your strength! ||73||
When the crores of gods will not be able to defeat that devotee Daitya,
they shall then perform service to him.
Being pleased, you will grant them an excellent boon;
indeed, you shall be requested by them to assume the form of sacrificial fuel at the sacrifice.
All of them together shall indeed carry out that killing of yours, and the diamonds shall arise from your own body. (76)
Various kinds of gems and various kinds of jewels shall also be yours;
then your liberation will swiftly come to pass, without a doubt. (77)
Having spoken thus and given me his discus, he indeed became invisible;
abandoning his asceticism, he went to heaven and requested a battle with Indra and the other gods.
In battle, Mahendra gave him combat and was defeated by him;
even the Sun and the Moon were conquered, and the guardians of the quarters were likewise vanquished.
Even the world-protectors have been conquered by Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana;
Indra and the others were utterly defeated by it, and it cannot be overcome by them.
Having become subject to another's will, the gods performed service for Bala;
by that service, Bala was exceedingly pleased and offered them a boon.
He dispatched the gods; and those gods, having reflected upon that matter and remembering the words of Viṣṇu, requested their own respective gains.
If there is no boon to be granted, if your word is true, and if you are pleased with my service and am devoted to Narayana; ||83||
Then grant one supreme boon, most desired by all the gods:
let you yourself become the sacrificial fuel there, for Nārāyaṇa is the sacrifice itself in person. (84)
"Having come together with us—the gods, daityas, nāgas, sarpas, and dānavas—you shall indeed attain liberation through this oblation. (85)
Thus addressed, the Daitya Bālaka became exceedingly pleased and said to Viṣṇu: "This fuel is my supreme good fortune. (8.6)
In this world, death for the sake of the gods and total self-surrender are the most excellent;
for saṃsāra is indeed characterized by death, yet death for the sake of the deity is sublime. (87)

If it can be obtained for the sake of cattle, for the sake of the teacher, for the sake of Mādhava, for the sake of dharma, or for the sake of righteous deeds—then what gain could be greater than that? (88)
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what supreme fortune has come to me today, that I have been appointed by the gods to stand before the mouth of Lord Viṣṇu! (89)
"Today my self-surrender shall become most auspicious.
Having reflected thus, he then granted the boon, saying, "So be it."
And the gods, having obtained that boon, eagerly caused a sacrificial ground to be prepared on the western slope of Mount Meru.
There, the gods, Daityas, Dānavas, and birds were summoned,
as well as the great sages, the ancestors, human beings, trees, and creepers.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, as well as those born from elemental spirits (bhūta), kuṣmāṇḍas, kinnaras, nāgas, gandharvas, and serpents (bhogins). ||93||
The serpents, the foremost of the Asuras, the Apsarases, as well as the rivers, the oceans, the forests, and the lofty mountains [all came there]. (94)
The clouds, the lightning, the thunderbolts, and the multitudes of medicinal herbs— all these principles, having been invoked, arrived there at that great sacrifice.
At that moment, Bala assumed the form of sacrificial fuel (samidh) there, in the sacrificial rite initiated by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others.
While he was being sprinkled with the waters of the *vardhinī* vessel during the sacrifice, he sat down;
at that moment, having taken the form of a sacrificial fuel-stick (*samit*), he became as large as a great mountain.
A great mass arose from trees, creepers, and plants;
it was rich with rice, flowers, and fruits, and its essence became desirable ghee. ||98||
It was not known that he had then taken the form of a living being in the form of an oblation;
indeed, all the oblations were seen there on the mountain at that time. 99.
Perceiving the mountain-like mass of the oblation to have been turned away,
the gods then performed the purificatory sprinkling and carried out the fire sacrifice.
At that time, his oblations in the fire numbered in the hundreds of thousands;
they consisted of seeds, grains, clarified butter, fruits, and flavorful juices, and were fragrant. (101)
The auspicious limbs of that pure being,
cast into the fire like sacrificial fuel, became seeds of jewels.
Then, seeing those seeds in the vessel, which were as radiant as the sun and moon,
the gods and others, knowing their value, took them up.
Then, [he saw] the gods, the yakṣas, the siddhas, the wind-eaters (gandharvas),
humans, and great ṛṣis performing sacrifices on all sides.
At that time, there arose a very great grasping for the seed-jewels;
gods and other beings leaped up from the pit and seized them from the path of the sky.
Taking hold of one another, they went far away in their celestial chariots to their own homes; and because of their mutual pulling, there was then a great crush.
In the sky, there was a great scramble for the sake of the jewel-seeds;
and as they scrambled, those seeds which fell from the path of the air—
And those who fell by the force of their celestial chariots— whether they had fallen by their own hands or otherwise—
landed upon mountains, in oceans, in rivers, and even in forests.
Then, by virtue of their respective qualities, seeds and jewels came to exist within trees, in the paths of the clouds, upon the earth, and even in the lakes.
At that time, various things endowed with the quality of being worthy of being placed [upon others] came into existence.
Thus has the origin of the various kinds of jewels been proclaimed to you. (3.161.110)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of the Attendant named Bala from his Abode of Śrīpura due to Mutual Curses by Jaya and Others, and the Production of Jewels from the Physical Elements of the Body of the Daitya Bala in the Form of Fuel at a Sacrifice," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Śrī, Ramā, and others, as well as my beloveds beginning with Jayā;
all those jewels indeed possess great qualities."
Even those things that destroy spirits, demons, poison, serpents, and diseases may be endowed with excellent qualities, and likewise, they may also be devoid of such qualities. || 2 ||
Diamonds, pearls, rubies, emeralds, sovereign gems, sapphires, lapis lazuli, and topazes—these are the various species [of jewels]. (3)
Karketana stones, sapulaka, rudhira, and likewise sphaṭika; coral, pearls, and glass—these indeed are the gems.
Having examined the shape, color, quality, defect, and its result, the value of these is determined; it is not otherwise.
Those [auspicious moments] which are employed on the day of the family star (kulagna) or on a defiled day inevitably become full of defects and deprive one of prosperity.
Therefore, one should examine jewels before accepting or even wearing them; at an auspicious time, by accepting only those that are auspicious, one shall thereby obtain supreme prosperity.
The diamond-gem (vajramaṇi) shall possess great power over all things;
wherever the seeds of the *balā* plant, bones, and sacrificial fuel-sticks are cast, [there it prevails].
Various types of diamonds, known by the name "vajra," have arisen;
namely those from Haima, Mātaṅga, Saurāṣṭra, Pauṇḍra, Kaliṅga, and Kosala. (9)
The Veṇātaṭas, the Sauvīras, the regions endowed with Vajrodbhava, those from Ātāmra, those from the Himavat mountains, those from Mātaṅga, and the Kapīśins.
Those born in Saurāṣṭra are copper-colored; those originating from Puṇḍra are considered dark-complexioned;
those arising from Kaliṅga are gold-colored; and those from Kosala have a yellow luster.

Those from the banks of the Veṇā possess the luster of the moon; those from Sauvīra have the hue of clouds; those from Samyak are equal on all sides, excellent in quality, beautiful in color, and light. 1.1 The inhabitants of the banks of the Veṇā are as radiant as the moon; those of Sauvīra have the splendor of clouds; those of Samyak are uniform in their qualities across all their parts, possessing excellent color and being light. 1.1
That diamond which is free from lines, spots, crow-feet,
stains, and fractures, even if it is only the size of an atom, is indeed the supreme diamond.
If that [sword] has a sharp and keen edge, and if the deity resides within it, then when held, it grants gain, is unfailing, and bestows all happiness. (14)
Just as its color is, so is the celestial abode; just as it is luminous, so too is its priceless nature and its designation as a deity conceived. || 15 ||
Indeed, deities dwell within the vajras, distinguished according to their colors: Hari resides in the green directions, while Varuṇa himself dwells in the white ones.
When they are yellow, Śakra himself resides there; when they are tawny, Agni dwells there;
when they are dark-blue, the Pitṛs are present; and likewise, when they are copper-colored, the Maruts are there.
A Brahmin should wear a beneficial gem that has the luster of a white water-lily, crystal, or conch shell;
a Kṣatriya should wear a gem resembling the color of a hare or a brown eye.
A Vaiśya should wear a ruby that resembles the leaf of a plantain tree, which bestows prosperity;
a Śūdra should wear a gem resembling the luster of a polished sword.
Or red as a hibiscus flower or coral, or resembling the juice of turmeric;
kings should wear these two diamond colors, which bestow benefit. (3.162.20)
The king indeed should wear a diamond that consists of all colors;
even if it is rounded at the bottom and top, such a gem may be possessed of many hues. ||1||
It is suitable for a king and not for other castes, for it brings suffering to them;
it is a source of prosperity for the virtuous, but a bringer of calamity to others. (22)
If its horn is seen to be crushed or shattered, it should never be worn by those seeking their own welfare, even if it possesses all other qualities. (23)
A diamond with shattered and cracked points, containing specks of impurity within, destroys prosperity; it should never be kept in the home.
If one part of it has a reddish luster, or if it possesses a blood-red color, this will surely cause death; such a gem must never be worn anywhere.
The edges, sides, and facets of a diamond are six, eight, and twelve respectively; its qualities, produced from its source, consist of its lofty, even, and extremely sharp points. (26)
It is pure according to the six parameters, stainless, clearly possessing a sharp edge, light, endowed with the correct color, free from defects, and likewise well-proportioned in its sides. (27)
One should wear the Vajra, which enriches the firmament with the brilliance of Indra’s rainbow, which is difficult to obtain, and which increases longevity, women, and wealth;
it is the protector of prosperity, cattle, and grain, and the promoter of all forms of success. (28)
It removes the fear of predatory beasts, fire, poison, tigers, thieves, and water. ||29||
This jewel, which wards off the malevolent spells of the Atharvans from afar, consists of twenty measures of rice; it is a diamond of the highest quality and value.
A diamond that is deficient in its qualities, luster, oiliness, and weight is considered inferior; it is indeed [inferior] in terms of price, profit, happiness, and so forth. //31//
If it is half [the size], its quality is said to be half; if it is a quarter, its quality shall be a quarter;
and if it is half of a quarter, its value shall likewise be a quarter. ||32||
Indeed, even a thirtyth part, a hundredth part, an eightieth part, or even a thousandth part of a diamond may be subtle, yet it remains potent in its quality. ||33||
The weight of diamonds may be equal to eight mustard seeds;
yet that diamond which is endowed with all excellent qualities floats upon the waters. (34)
Even among the entire category of jewels, its wearing is possible;
yet, even in the slightest measure, its weight is inferred from the act of wearing it. (35)
Therefore, one must certainly uphold even a single atom;
for even a small diamond, if it possesses a flaw, may be worth only a tenth of its value. (36)
A diamond with many manifest defects may have a value of only one-hundredth part [of a flawless one];
for a diamond with many defects, the price is very small even when used as an ornament. (37)
Even when donned and worn, such a thing is faulty and brings about swift ruin; indeed, it is quite enough to wear even a flawed diamond as an ornament.
A woman should never wear a diamond, even one possessed of excellent qualities;
she who desires the birth of a son must never wear it at any time.
A vajra that is long, flat, short, or devoid of qualities should not be worn; likewise, one made of iron, topaz, or gomedaka [is to be avoided]. (3.162.40)
By means of beryl, crystal, and various kinds of glass, skillful artisans produce replicas that resemble diamonds. (41)
The examination of those [gems] should be performed by means of alkaline solutions and touchstones;
for whatever gems exist on earth, as well as other metallic ores. ||42||
One may scratch all things with a vajra, yet it cannot be scratched by them;
it possesses the weightiness of all jewels, as well as excellence and a hundredfold radiance. (43)
The cause is the vajra, the reason is lightness, and the radiance is a hundredfold;
the vajra-lineage indeed carves the unborn state all around. ||44||
Diamond is engraved by diamond; diamond is not engraved by anything else.
Diamonds, pearls, gems, and whatever other kinds [of jewels] there may be— ||45||
For those [flames] that are obstructed, there is no upward movement;
for some, it may be seen somehow or other because they have been diverted horizontally. //46//
When being drawn across obliquely, it is obstructed at its sides;
its tip is shattered like a vajra, it is discolored, and it possesses lines and dots. (47)
If he possesses the rainbow, he bestows sons and other kin, as well as wealth and grain;
indeed, such a king bears the thunderbolt of Indra with the brilliance of lightning. 48.
By means of valor, one obtains sovereignty over that very earth;
thus has the Vajra-ratna been described to you, O beloveds of Brahmā, and after this [follows] what is beyond it.
I shall describe the gem consisting of pearls; listen attentively.
They are individually distinct as being clear, translucent, intensely lustrous, or stained with impurities.
Pearls and gems indeed originate from elephants, clouds, whales, conchs, fish, serpents, oysters, and bamboo; they are born from both earth and water.
That which originates from oyster shells is considered the best among all types of pearls;
that which originates from oyster shells is to be pierced, for the remaining types are indeed unpierceable. || 52 ||
Even if it lacks the feathers of a vulture, that auspicious [conch] produced from bamboo, elephants, fish, chariots, shells, or boars is highly praised.
The pearl originating from a conch or produced from an elephant is the lowest grade;
it is the color of the middle of an elephant's forehead, or yellow, or likewise lusterless.
The conch of Śaṅkha is of the smallest size, measuring one *vṛhatkoṇapala*;
the best conchs are those considered to be of pure lineage, like elephants.
In those [signs], the pearls produced are round but lack luster;
whereas those produced in Pisces (Mīna), though small, are perfectly round.
Extremely minute and the color of the back of a pāṭhīna fish, they are indeed born within the midst of the ocean from the mouths of fish.
The pearl known as *bhūtalottha* (earth-born) possesses the luster of a boar's tusk and has a brilliance equal to the tip of a sprout; some consider such a pearl to be auspicious. (58)
That color produced from stone and that produced from bamboo have an appearance identical to it;
yet even those bamboos are enjoyed everywhere by worthy people, whereas yours are not at all.
The jewels born of serpents, both round and brilliant,
become as if washed by the luster of the edges of swords.
Wearing ornaments of gold and pearls, he shall be meritorious and endowed with splendor;
he will surely possess royal fortune and be rich in majestic power.
Desiring to ascertain the value of the jewel, he should indeed place it upon the roof of his house at an auspicious moment, having first provided great protection for it.
Then indeed great-sounding drums resound in the sky, flashes of lightning occur, and clouds also appear. (63)
In whatever treasury or house such a pearl exists, there are no serpents, obstacles, demons, or mental afflictions. (64)
O gods, where there are no calamities or diseases—that pearl which comes from a serpent—and furthermore, that pearl which arises from a cloud; 65.
They indeed carry it away along the path of the sky, possessing a radiance like the rays of the sun;
at night it shines just as during the day, where it abides by its own splendor.
Even the entire earth made of gold would not be a sufficient price for such a jewel, since it bestows both gold and jewels.
He before whom this jewel shall appear will enjoy the entire circle of the earth;
furthermore, the fortune and splendor of both his subjects and his king shall increase. (68)
Indeed, even at distances of thousands of yojanas, such calamities do not occur;
for these pearl-like teeth of Bala’s were thus liberated. (69)
Whatever sacrificial fuel was prepared there at that sacrifice, from those [plants] seeds were produced at various times, indeed possessing diverse colors and forms.
Indeed, those pure pearls which fell into the waters of the oceans—
charming with the luster of moonbeams— are truly born from oyster shells.
They were on the island of Siṃhala, in Saurāṣṭra, Tāmraparṇaka,
Pāraśava, Pāraloka, Kaubera, and the land of the Pāṇḍyas.
Indeed, those produced from oyster shells arise from both Hāṭaka and Hemaka;
that which originates from an oyster shell possesses a color that is not inferior and is endowed with excellent qualities and luster. ||73||
And it arises endowed with shape and measure during the stages of growth and so forth, whether in Vardhana, Pārasīka, Pātāla, or Siṃhala. (74)
Indeed, the value of a single pearl born from a mother-of-pearl shell that has been polished on a whetstone amounts to two thousand silver coins.
A gem that is half a *māṣa* less [in weight] has a value ten parts less;
one that is three *māṣakas* heavier has a value of two thousand. ||76||
The price for two and a half *māṣakas* is one thousand and five hundred;
the price for two *māṣakas* of superior quality is one thousand;
and the price for one and a half *māṣakas* of superior quality is indeed five hundred.
Two hundred and fifty [units] of that jewel which weighs six guñjās of guggulu. || 78 ||
That agallochum which weighs four *guñjās* is considered to have a value of two hundred;
likewise, that agallochum which weighs two *guñjās* is considered to have a value of one hundred.
The value of a single *guñjā* is indeed fifty *mudrikās*;
sixteen *guñjās* constitute a *dharaṇa*, which is known as a *dārvika*.
A balance-beam weighing thirty *gruñjas* is called a *ratna*;
however, those that are inferior *ratnas* are worth thirty [units] each. || 8.1 ||
Those worth twenty [units] or likewise those worth ten;
then, for its examination, one should place the juice of a citron in a vessel.
Having been cast into [the crucible] and heated, the gem is rubbed with radish roots;
if it leaves a streak, it is indeed artificial or of inferior quality.
Having placed it inside a clay-coated vessel, one should cook it in fire;
then in milk, then in curd, then in ghee, and again in water.
Then, by rubbing it with cloths, it becomes endowed with quality and luster;
such a pearl is indeed excellent, true, and free from blemish. (85)
An ornament set with gold that resembles white glass should be worn;
however, if there is doubt as to whether it is artificial, it must be examined again.
One should soak it for a night in hot saline oil or water.
That [substance] should be rubbed with rice grains while placed between two dry cloths. ||87||
If it does not undergo discoloration, it should be known as genuine. It is white, of the proper proportions, glossy, heavy, transparent, and perfectly pure. || 88 ||
A pearl that is brilliant, well-rounded, and possessed of excellent qualities does not bring even a single fault or misfortune upon its owner. (89)
Thus have I described to you the pearl gems, which are dear to Hari;
now I shall speak of the rubies—listen to them according to their origin.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin, Value, and Superiority of the Vajramaṇi and Muktamaṇi Gems," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having obtained the seed of Bala’s blood as fuel, the god Sūrya went by way of the sky; the lord of Laṅkā obstructed him.
And indeed, seeds fell into the ocean and into the Gaṅgā of Rāvaṇa;
from them were produced radiant jewels.
Those lotuses born in water are indeed radiant with beautiful color;
likewise, those arising from Saugandhika and Kuruvinda are endowed with excellent qualities.
Some were made of crystal and radiant, while others were of many colors,
appearing like the bandhūka flower, the guñjā berry, the indragopa insect, or the juice of the japā flower.
Resembling the pomegranate, the kiṃśuka flower, vermilion, and the blue lotus, they possess the color of lotus, saffron, and lac-dye, and are endowed with radiance. || 5 ||
Those [crystals] which, being made of crystal, shine intensely with their own luster when clearly struck by the rays of the sun,
they color their sides with redness.
Some have a luster mixed with saffron and indigo, others possess the radiance of fierce red lotuses; some have the appearance of lotus flowers, while others have the brilliance of vermilion.
Others possess the luster of the eyes of cakoras, cuckoos, and cranes; and yet others possess the brilliance of the finest red lotus flowers. (8)
These rubies born of crystal are generally similar in their brilliance, hardness, and weight; they are endowed with blue and red lusters.
These gems from the Saugandhika mine are generally uniform;
the gems produced from Kuruvinda are inferior to these in color.
Those who are without radiance, inwardly dense, and lacking great power—
such as these are found in the Andhra country and likewise in the Tumburu region.
Those that possess similar qualities are born; indeed, they are considered to be of little value.
An abundance of color, heaviness, oiliness, evenness, and translucence—these are the marks of excellence. (12)
The brilliance and great size of jewels are indicators of their excellence; however, those that resemble gravel and are possessed of flaws, impurities, and the like, are not so. (13)
Lacking luster, rough, and discolored, they are not excellent;
likewise, by wearing a flawed gem, one incurs grief and anxiety.
One incurs death, suffering, and loss of wealth; there is no doubt about this.
Furthermore, five [gems] that are of a different species become like rubies (padmarāga). || 15 ||
Also those born in Kalasapura, as well as those born in the region of Tumburu,
those born in Muktapāṇīya, those originating from Siṃhala, and the Śrīpūrṇakas.
Those gems originating from the Kalasa river possess a combination of white and yellow;
those from Tumburu are copper-colored, while those born in the Siṃhala country are black.
Pearls are by nature devoid of the word "namas," are endowed with the syllable "śrī," are full, and lack brilliance;
when joined with husks, they become copper-colored and even oily.
Those who, when rubbed, lose their luster are of low birth;
he whose head is pressed by the finger and bears a dark streak along its side [is likewise so];
and he who possesses the qualities of another person standing nearby.
Even if it is equal [in appearance], that pearl-gem would indeed be of inferior value.

When a doubt regarding its artificiality has arisen, one should rub it on a whetstone; then, by means of what arises from its own kind, it shall scratch the other, and the other shall scratch it in return.
Just as it is impossible to scratch a ruby or a sapphire with anything other than a diamond or a kuruvinda gem, so too,
wherever there is a scratch, that jewel is indeed not called supreme.
Or, even if it were artificial, provided that it is marked with lines. ||23||
A gem that is artificial or flawed should never be worn at all,
even alongside a genuine gem or one equal to the Kaustubha.
Just as even a single outcaste defiles many twice-born men,
so too does a corrupt person destroy even virtues.
One who wears the ruby of truth, even while dwelling among enemies,
shall not be overcome by calamities nor overcome by obstacles.
It is not overcome by calamities, misfortunes, or defects;
it is endowed with the brilliance of its own color and is excellent, whereas that which lacks these is indeed inferior. (27)
The most excellent jewel should always be worn, never an inferior one;
for that which is worn by one who possesses nothing of value renders it worthless. (28)
Now, O beloved of Brahmā, I shall describe to you the emeralds found here;
Vāsuki took them from the sky while gathering the seeds of the *balapitta* fuel-wood.
When Garuḍa pursued him there, he checked his progress,
and seeds fell upon the ground of the Māṇikya mountain.
Thus, upon the Turuṣka trees, in the nalikā groves and creepers,
and on the shore of the White Ocean, emeralds then came into being.
Even though the seeds fell from the opening of Garuḍa’s beak, from them were born [trees] possessing throats like parrots and blossoms as red as śirīṣa flowers. ||32||
Resembling the backs of fireflies, with the luster of moss and water-grass,
and like white water-lilies and young shoots, they possess a brilliance like the coils of a serpent.
Likewise, those gems known as *patraraṅga* are born from bile;
by means of those produced from the seeds of the serpent’s coils, all poison is pacified.
That which cannot be cured by any collection of medicinal herbs or mantras—the poison produced from the fangs of a great serpent—is pacified by these [remedies]. ||35||
That gem which is extremely green in color, soft, radiant, and possessing a luster like the midst of gold powder is considered the most excellent. ||36||
Possessing all structural qualities and likewise endowed with a uniform form, it illuminates the hermitage upon being touched by the rays of the sun. (37)
And that which becomes endowed with internal luster through the application of lightning-like radiance, and is green like a grassy meadow—that indeed is the most excellent. (38)
Where there are many colors, yet with a clear core in the center, it is cloudy, glossy, and pure, with the luster of a peacock feather on all sides. ||3.9||
That which is deficient compared to the former should be understood as slightly inferior; for it is considered variegated, harsh, soiled, hard, and gravelly. (3.163.40)
Emerald mixed with lead from stone is not of the highest quality;
likewise, it is of that same inferior sort when fashioned from fragments of emerald or when joined together.
Those who desire their own welfare should not maintain that [hostility], nor should it ever be conquered;
for by its very power, even the rays of the *bhallātaka* tree fall into imbalance through the winds.
Those artificial emeralds must never be worn;
likewise, pearls equal to diamonds and emeralds equal [to them] are also [prohibited]. (43)
For those whose radiance indeed moves upward, straight, or crookedly,
it perishes instantly when observed from the side.
These emeralds of mixed origins should be understood as bringing auspiciousness when used for bathing, sipping water, recitation, and the performance of protective mantra-rites. (45)
And even when the means for giving cows, gold, and so forth have been performed, as well as in rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests, and in the worship of gurus; (46)
While [beings] were being afflicted by various collections of defects arising from poison, [the Buddha appeared], free from defects, endowed with virtues, and joined like refined gold. (47)
Emerald should always be worn during battle and in the pursuit of victory;
emerald is proclaimed to have a value exceeding that of ruby.
When there is an excess of defects, even in a sapphire, a loss of value occurs;
thus have sapphires been described, and now I shall speak to you of blue gems (nīlamaṇi).
The seed of the *samid* tree from the pair of eyes that fell upon the land of Bala in the coastal region of Siṃhala became that earth in many places on all sides.
They have become like sapphire; these blue ones are of many varieties—resembling the hue of a blue lotus, a bee, or a bow (the rainbow), and even equal to the throat of Śiva.
Resembling mountain peaks, with the luster of ocean waters, and possessing crests like peacocks;
they are blue-black in hue, equal in brilliance to the neck of a peacock, and endowed with great qualities.
Clay, stones, and rock fissures, as well as gravel mixed with cracks, and those with the appearance of a layer of mica, are also considered defective in color. (53)
One who wears an indranīla obtains all the qualities of a padmarāga;
whatever examination applies to a padmarāga, that same [examination] applies to an indranīla as well.
To whatever extent a ruby thrown into the fire would pass through it, a sapphire thrown there would pass even further through the flame. (59)

Just as the auspicious examination of a gem is for the sake of its true nature, so too, that very examination must be understood; yet it is not for the sake of the qualities themselves, since those qualities are subject to destruction. //56//

The jewel must be placed in fire, for it may indeed prove to be defective; such a jewel would bring misfortune to the owner, as well as to the one who made it and the one who caused it to be made. (57)
Mirror-glass, blue lotus, karavīra, beryl, crystal, and so forth—even these gems indeed become equal to sapphire. 58.
When there is an excess of hardness and weight, their excellence arises.
[The sapphire] is the color of indranīla, copper-colored, and has the luster of oleander or blue lotus. (55)
That sapphire in whose center the blue radiance of Indra’s bow shines forth is called an *indranīla*; it is highly precious and very difficult to obtain. (3.163.60)
That [gem] in which the quality of blue predominates so much that it renders all other qualities into blueness, even when situated among a hundred other virtues, is called Mahānīla.
Whatever price is assigned to a ruby of the measure of a single *māṣa*,
that same price is also assigned to a sapphire on account of its superior qualities.
Now I shall describe the Lakṣmīs, the origin and other details of Vaidūrya;
for they indeed arise from the seed-syllables of the *samidh* [fuel-sticks] consisting of the sound of the demon Bala.
Indeed, on the distant mountain where Kāmarūpa and Kāmākṣī reside, there are [beings] of many colors, endowed with splendor, delight, and beauty.
Those beautiful vaidūrya gems, shining like clouds in the rainy season,
though full of brilliance, have indeed become like sparks of fire.
Those with the luster of a peacock’s neck, resembling bamboo shoots, and those like the feathers of a bow are also excellent, bestowing supreme fortune. (66)
The girikācas, śiśupālas, kācas, and likewise sphaṭikas,
as well as the varieties of vaidūrya known as dhūmras, are all equal.

Śiśupāla is known as "glass" (kāca) because of his lack of writing [or merit], and he is "light glass" (girikāca) because of his insignificance; and he is "crystal" (sphaṭika) because of his brilliance. ||68||
The price of two *pala*s of *guru* is considered equal to that of an *indranīla*.
Indeed, differences in name, appearance, and quality give rise to differences in price. (69)
Oiliness, lightness, and softness are always the signs of genuineness;
when worn on the wrist, they bestow gain, and their value is sixfold.
This value would be abundant in mines and in the land;
sixteen māṣas constitute a suvarṇa, and a seventh part of that is known as a saṃjñaka. (71)
A *śāṇa* is four *māṣas* in measure; a *māṣaka* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*. A *dharaṇa* is proclaimed to be the tenth part of a *pala*.
When the weight reaches a higher degree, the price increases due to its heaviness;
now, for the sake of your understanding, I shall describe the Puṣparāga gems of Lakṣmī. //73//
The seeds of the bark-fuel of the demon Bala fell upon the Himalayan mountains;
from them were born the highly virtuous puṣparāga gems.
The varieties of gemstones known as *padmarāga* are yellowish-white;
those that are yellowish-red are called *kauruṇḍaka*.
Those that are transparent, red, and yellow are designated as *kāṣāyaka*;
those that are slightly blue, white, and glossy are designated as *somānaka*. (76)
Those which are extremely red are considered indeed to be *padmarāga* rubies; those which are very blue are *puṣparāga* topazes, designated as *indranīla* sapphires. (77)
Pure Vaidūryasadṛśa bestows the fruit in the form of a son upon women who always wear it; of this there is no doubt. (78)
Now I shall describe the *lakṣmīs* here; from the *karketana* gems, the seed of the nail-fuel of Vāyubala arrived. (79)
Then he scattered karketana gems into the lotus groves; they became like honey, soma, and blood, resembling copper-yellow fire.
Those that are blue, white, or rough remove defects such as disease;
those that are glossy, pure, uniform in color, yellow, variegated, and heavy [are auspicious]. (8.1)
Those karketana gems that are free from the defects of lines and scratches are purifying;
one should wrap them in a gold leaf and heat them with fire.
If that karketana gem becomes radiant, it destroys disease, dispels afflictions, bestows long life, and grants a lineage of happiness. ||83||
When worn as an ornament, this bestows wealth and grain, and it also grants honor, kinsmen, and radiant splendor. (84)
Some are blue, deformed, withered, and likewise turbid; lacking the brilliance of luster, their complexion becomes like that of a donkey. ||85||
Those who possess no virtues indeed cause suffering and must never be supported; they are like those who, having encountered the rays of the sun, are consumed by its fiery halo.
Those which are born as the most precious *karketana* gems are indeed such;
now, O you who are dear to Brahmā, I shall describe to you the *bhīṣma-ratnas*.
The seed of the power of the demon Bala, ignited by fuel, fell upon the Himalayas; from that, in the region to the north,
there arose formidable [plants] shining like conch shells and lotuses, and resembling Syonāka flowers.
Indeed, those [jewels] born with the power of sustaining the throat are bestowers of prosperity.
Upon seeing one who wears the Bhīṣma-jewel, wolves, leopards, śarabhas, tigers, panthers, and elephants flee far away. (3.163.90)
If the Bhīṣma-jewel ring, endowed with all virtues, is worn, it indeed bestows great satisfaction during the rite of libations to the ancestors. || 91 ||
The poisons of snakes, birds, mice, and scorpions likewise become auspicious;
by wearing this, fear of water, fire, thieves, and enemies is surely destroyed. || 92 ||
One should avoid from afar that which resembles a cloud, has moss-like streaks, is rough, yellowish, lusterless, discolored, or soiled, because such a stone brings about loss.
The price should be determined according to the quality, taking into account the excellence of the place, time, and other factors.
Now, O beloveds of Brahmā, I shall indeed speak of the *pulaka* gems for you. 94.
The serpents scattered the seeds of the claws of the demon Bala upon the mountains, upwards, and even into the northern rivers.
From that region, indeed, the maṇis and pulakas were produced;
[they are found] in Dāśārṇa, Vāgade, Melakaka, and also in Kālagaka.
Some were the color of guñjā seeds, collyrium, or honey; others were as white as lotus stalks.
There were also excellent ones with the luster of gandharvas, fire, or plantain trees. (17)

Those with variegated patterns resembling a conch, a lotus, a water-pot, or the sun, which are free of lines and possess fine hair-like filaments (pulaka), are auspicious and bestow prosperity; indeed, they are thus proclaimed.
If those bearing the fierce forms of crows, donkeys, asses, jackals, and wolves, with faces like vultures and mouths full of flesh, are held [in the hand], they bestow death. (19)
The price for a pala-bhāra of these is five hundred mudrikās;
now I shall describe to you the gem known as rudhira, which brings prosperity.
The Fire-god took the seed of the *samidh* tree called Rūpa belonging to the demon Bala;
he cast it into the Revā river and certainly also into the low-lying ground.
Resembling indragopa insects and like the beaks of parrots,
those who were nourished with the color of blood indeed became blood-red.
Those that are white like the moon in the middle, of pure color, and shaped like a balance scale, as well as those resembling sapphire, indeed bestow servants and sovereignty. (103)
When polished, those known as *suravajra* bestow gain and grant prosperity;
now I shall describe the auspicious *lakṣmī* gems known as *sphaṭika*.
In the lands of Kāverī, Vindhya, Yavana, Cīna, and Nepāla, the seed of the plant known as Medā belongs to Balāsura; it is indeed Lāṅgalī.
He even cast that oil into the path of the sky, and it indeed became crystal—
white as a lotus stalk or a conch shell, yet possessed of a slight variation in hue.
Indeed, they became destroyers of sin, possessing the value of worthy qualities;
then Śeṣa forcibly took those who were in the form of sacrificial fuel and seeds.
He first cast them upon Kerala and other regions; from that they became corals, possessing the color of a rabbit's blood and resembling the hue of guñjā and japā flowers.
Sunīlā and Devakaromā are born; they are indeed distinct from those [others].
A coral (vidruma) that is clear, soft, glossy, and beautiful in its form is beneficial;
it brings wealth and grain in this world and destroys the pain and fear of poison.
Thus, gems are born from their respective seed-lineages;
those produced from mines and even those gems originating from fire are likewise born.
O you who are dear to Brahmā, I have described all these gems to you.
For my devotee Bala, these [qualities] arise without cause;
through their retention and recitation, they also bring about the remembrance of me.
Then Bala went by means of a celestial chariot to my very abode.
And Jayā and the others, my female attendants, are present here.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Origin and Qualities of Padmarāga, Marakata, Indranīla, Vaidūrya, Puṣparāga, Karketana, Bhīṣma, Pulaka, Rudhira, Sphaṭika, and Vidruma Gems," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "O Beloved, regarding those fourteen Manus who have been proclaimed by the Blessed One— tell me of those among them which were your incarnations, along with their respective deeds."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, I shall describe the incarnations that destroy the Daityas and protect dharma, along with their causes. || 2 ||
At that time, Svāyambhuva Manu was the Indra known as Viśvabhuk;
likewise, the Daitya Bāṣkali performed severe penance.
The Daitya brought under his control Agnidhra and the other sons of Manu,
as well as Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
He brought even Vasiṣṭha and the other seven ṛṣis under his control;
he also brought the Jayas, the Amitās, the Śukas, and the Yāma gods into subjection.
Even Viṣṇu, having been urged by Nārada for the sake of slaying the Daitya,
hurled his great discus, Sudarśana, at the forefront of the battle.
Then he severed the head of the Daitya and liberated the gods;
O Rame, this was my first incarnation in the form of Viṣṇu.
Then, in the second Manvantara, that of Svārociṣa,
the Daitya Purukṛtsara indeed [conquered] Vipaścit as Indra and the gods.
In that manner, he afflicted Ūrja, Stamba, and Niścala;
he also afflicted Ṛṣabha, Cāruvīra, and Dambholi.
He oppressed the Seven Sages, the Tuṣitas, and the Pārāvatas;
he also tormented the sons of Manu, Ekala, Vinata, Vidyut, and Ravi.
And he tormented Nabhāsa with his great bow reaching to his ears;
and sometimes he dwelt within the water or in the form of a cloud.
Indeed, even though I was entreated by Mahendra, I assumed the form of a white elephant with wings, shining like a mountain, in order to obstruct his present course.
In the forest, he suddenly seized a four-tusked, two-trunked Daitya who was fighting with weapons in battle, overpowering him by force. || 13 ||
"By killing [enemies] with my tusks, my two trunks, and by trampling them with my feet, I, that very Gajanārāyaṇa, shall then become manifest upon the earth. (14)
Renowned and honored by the worlds, bestowing both liberation and worldly enjoyment— this second incarnation of mine, O Rame, is called Gaja.
And in the third Manu, Auttama, there was the Dānava Pralamba, who possessed great strength;
he [conquered] Mahendra and likewise the one named Svaśānti.
He will cause distress to Rathaujas, Urdhvabāhu, the sinless Śaraṇa, Maṇi,
Śaṅku, Sutatapas, and the Seven Sages.
Having caused those gods— the Vaśavṛttas, Svadhāmans, Śivas, Satyas, and Pratardanas— to fight, he will bring them under his own control.
The sons of Manu were Paraśu, Vinīta, Māja, Śuci, Suketu, Suvala, Devāvṛdha, and Sumitraka. || 19 ||
Having acquired them through great exertion, he will conquer all of them in battle;
then, having gone into the midst of the great waters, the Dānava will take up his residence there.
Then, requested by Manu, I shall become the Lord in the form of a fish within the waters;
indeed, I shall cause Lambaka to die.
And this is my third incarnation, assuming the form of a fish,
occurring on earth during the time of the fourth Manu, named Tāmasa.
The asura Bhīmaratha, strengthened by the Bhaimaratha asuras,
set out for victory over the one named Śibi, Indra, and likewise the sons of Manu.
Jānujaṅgha, Nirbhaya, Navakhyāti, Naya, Vivikṣipa, Priyabhṛtya, Haviṣkandhi, and Kṛta—[these were the sons]. || 24 ||
He brought under his control Kṛtabandhu, Prastalākṣa, Daśa,
the Ṛṣis, Jyotirdhāmaka, Dhṛṣṭa, Kāvya, and Hemaka.
At that time, he indeed brought Agni, Ceta, and Caitraka under his control;
likewise, he brought the gods, the *surāgas*, the *svadhīs*, the *harīs*, and the *haritakas* under his sway.
Then, having been entreated by the gods, I, Rāma, acted;
I [struck] that great asura Bhīmaratha who was situated at the bottom of the ocean.
"Assuming a great body in the form of a tortoise, I shall destroy [the enemies] in the midst of the waters;
this is my fourth incarnation, bearing the form of a tortoise. (28)
In the time of the fifth Manu, Raivata, on this earth,
he whose enemies were pacified bound one named Vibhu while Indra was ruling.
The two Daityas, accompanied by hosts of Daityas, [attacked] the sons of Manu as well as Mahāprāṇa, Sādhaka, Pratyaṅga, and Naramitraka.
He conquered Śuci, Paraghna, Vanabandhu, and likewise Dṛḍhavrata;
he also defeated Ketuśṛṅga and oppressed the Seven Sages.
Devaśrī, Vedabāhu, Ūrdhvabāhu, Svadhāmaka, Hiraṇyaromaka, Parjanya, and Satyanāmaka. ||32||
In this manner, he oppressed the gods who were free from passion and desirous of the horse-sacrifice, as well as the Vaikuṇṭhas and the immortals, in many ways on all sides.
And having been entreated by the sages dwelling in that forest,
I assumed the form of a swan and slew Śāntaśatru.
And this is my fifth incarnation, assuming the form of a swan;
thereafter, during the time of the sixth Manu, Cākṣuṣa.
The great Daitya Mahākāla became the bringer of sorrow to the gods;
having conquered Indra, who was known as Manojava, he also defeated the sons of Manu.
Uru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tāpasa, Satyabāhuka, Kṛti, Agniṣṇu, Atirātra, Sudyumna, and Nara. ||37||
Having thus conquered these gods, the noble ones, the Bhāvyas, and the Pralekhakas, as well as having conquered the Pṛthukas, the Prasutas, and even the Ṛṣis; || 38 ||
Haviṣmant, Sutanu, Svadhāman, Vairāja, Abhimāna, Sahiṣṇu, and Madhuśrī—these are indeed the seven [sons]. (39)
"Having conquered the sovereignty of the three worlds, Mahākāla will indeed rule;
then, entreated by the people, I shall assume the form of Hayagrīva. (3.164.40)
"O Lotus-born One, having become the Daitya Mahākāla, I shall destroy him;
this is my sixth incarnation, possessing the form of Hayagrīva. (41)
And in the seventh Manvantara, O Lakṣmī, during that of Vaivasvata,
the great and wicked Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa conquered all the gods.
Likewise, [he worshipped] the Maruts, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Gaṇas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, and the divine Aṅgirases. ||43||
In that manner, the king of the Daityas conquered Indra, who was named Tejasvin,
and he oppressed the sages, including Bharadvāja and Gautama.
He brought under his control Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and Atri, as well as the sons of Manu.
And [he begot] Ikṣvāku, Laviṣyant, Nediṣṭha by name, Nabhas, Pāṃśu, Viṣṭi, Sarjāti, Karūṣaka, and Pṛṣadhra. || 46 ||
He made Sudyumna and all others his own followers, devotees of Viṣṇu;
at that time, I myself, Hari, was entreated by the Earth with devotion.
"Assuming the form of a boar, I shall slay Hiraṇyākṣa;
this is the seventh incarnation, the Boar, the protector of the earth and other realms. (48)
And in the eighth Manvantara, named Sāvarṇya, King Bali—
the Daitya son of Virocana— became a great devotee of Indra.
And under his control, all the hosts of gods— those possessing the luster of nectar, those performing great austerities, and the principal ones— remained as if by force.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Vyāsa, Gālava, Dīptimān,
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Paraśurāma— even those sages were under his control.
The sons of Sāvarṇi were Arvavīra, Vijaya, Satyavāk,
Kṛti, Nirdeha, Sagati, Variṣṭha, and Gariṣṭhaka.
When all the subjects of Bali had become submissive to his word and were suffering,
I was then entreated by the gods and sages and assumed the form of a dwarf.
Having become a beggar Brahmin, I shall seize the throne of Śakra;
I shall send Bali to liberation and dispatch him to heaven, giving him over to Jiṣṇu.
O Lotus-born One, this is my eighth incarnation as Trivikrama; in the ninth period, during the Manvantara of Dakṣasāvarṇi, I shall appear as Kālakākṣaka.
He brought under his control Indra, whose name was wonderful,
as well as that Indra who was a portion of Kārttikeya, and these sons of Manu.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Dīptiketu, Padmahasta, Nirākṛti,
Pṛthuśravas, Ṛcika, Bṛhaddyumna, and Bṛhadguṇa.
In this manner, he brought under his control the Seven Sages, as well as Medhātithi, Vasu,
Jyotiṣmat, Sabala, Dyuti, Kavya, and Havyaka.
Likewise, at that time, being entreated by the gods, I become Padmanābha for the sake of the Pārās, the Sudharmas, and the Marīcigarbhasuras.
"I shall slay Kālakākṣa and I shall make the gods happy;
for this, O Lotus-born One, is my ninth incarnation as Padmanābha."
In the tenth Manvantara, under Brahmasāvarṇi, the great Asura Baliśatru brought Indra, named Śānti, and the seven Ṛṣis under his control.
Āpomūrti, Haviṣmat, Satya, Sukṛtin,
as well as Nābhāga, Apratima, and Vasiṣṭha— these were the ṛṣis.
The sons of Manu were Sukṣetra, Bhūmisena, Jayadratha, Anamitra, Vṛṣabha, Śatānīka, and Suparvaka. ||63||
The great asura brought under his control those of excellent valor and supreme energy;
he even brought the gods, who were sitting at ease with their vital breaths restrained, under his subjection.
Requested by the gods at that time, I myself, assuming the form of Hari, shall indeed slay that enemy of Bali with my mace; I shall take my pleasure in this.
O Lotus-born one, this tenth incarnation of mine is in the form of Hari;
in the eleventh, Manu will be Dharmasāvarṇi, and Indra will be Vṛṣa.
The great Daitya, the Ten-necked one, brought the deities under his control,
as well as the birds that travel at will and those who take delight in their own creative transformations.
And he [appointed] Ekaikarucika, as well as the gods and the sons of Manu:
Sarvatraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, and Guru Pūru.
He brought under his control Kṣetravarṇa, Dṛḍheṣu, Ārdra, and likewise Putraka; he also subdued the Seven Sages, Agnitejas, and Haviṣyaka.
I am Viśva, Viṣṇu, and Vistara; I am the one possessing oblations and the form of Varuṇa.
Entreated by the sages, I appear in the form of Śrī as the creator of delusion.
"Having become a charming woman, I shall slay this great asura who seeks to carry me away; my eleventh incarnation, assuming the form of a beautiful woman, shall take delight [in this task]. (71)
In the twelfth [manvantara], during the Rudrasāvarṇi period, the preeminent asura named Tāraka indeed brought Indraka, whose domain is Truth (Ṛtadhāman), under his own control.
The sons of Manu were Devavanta, Upadeva, Vidūratha,
Devaśreṣṭha, Mitravanta, Mitradeva, and Savīryaka.
Likewise, there are the Mitrabindus, the Mitravāhas, and the Pravāhas;
as well as the Svadharmans among the gods, and the Rohitakas and Haritakas.
He is the enemy of the gods (Indra), the son of Tapa, the seven sages, and he is also called Ityapi;
he is the ascetic, the son of Tapa, the embodiment of austerity, and one who delights in penance.
Then the gods indeed made a request to me for Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and Vidyuti, for the sake of bringing about the end of Tāraka.
Tāraka also became possessed of great strength due to the boon granted by Śaṅkara;
for man is indeed the principle of consciousness (cetanatattva), while woman is illusion (māyā), which is insentient (jaḍa).
"Having obtained these two boons, death shall indeed not come to me; being free from disease, I conquered all beings and ruled over the kingdom born of the three worlds. (78)
Therefore, for his destruction, I have attained the state of a neuter;
in that form, O Kamalā, I shall indeed destroy Tāraka.
This new incarnation is a neuter lion;
from that, a creation consisting of neuter beings arose, superior even to me.
O Lakṣmī, this twelfth incarnation of mine has been proclaimed; at that time, men, having meditated upon and worshipped me as the Neuter Hari, [attained their goal]. 8 1.
They shall attain supreme liberation, free from the marks of male and female,
during the thirteenth Manvantara, that of Devasāvarṇi, under Raucya as the lord of heaven.
Even the Daitya named Ṭiṭṭibha brought Indra under his control;
[he likewise subdued] Citrasena, the son of Manu, and Dhṛti, who was devoted to austerity and dharma. (83)
He brought under his control Vicitra, Gharma, Kṣetravṛtti, Dṛḍha, Sunetraka, as well as the Ṛṣis and Sunaya, the seer of reality. ||84||

He is steadfast, imperishable, of the form of night, free from longing, and without creative manifestation; then [he beheld] the gods, whose body-hairs are the heavens and whose own dharma is their nature.
The ṭiṭṭibha brought even his own kinsmen and the gods under his control;
then the gods and others sought to destroy that ṭiṭṭibha who dwelt upon Mount Meru.
Seeking me out, I assumed a long peacock form;
in that peacock form, I shall cause the ṭiṭṭibha to be killed. (87)
O Lakṣmī, this thirteenth incarnation of mine has been proclaimed;
I shall be the great king Māyūra, and I will receive worship in that age. (88)
In the Bhautya Manvantara, fourteen Indras will belong to the Sāvarṇi cycle; among them, the great Asura Śuci, having become Indra, shall exercise sovereign rule over the three worlds.
The sons of Manu were Gabhīra, Dhṛṣṭamūru, Tarasvin,
Abhimāna, Gabhīra, Grāha, Jiṣṇu, and Pravīraka.
He brought under his control Saṃkrandana, who was difficult to subdue,
as well as the Seven Sages, Agnibāhu, Agnidhra, Śuci, and Māgadha.
He himself brought Śukra, Ajita, and Mukta under his control, as well as the Cākṣuṣas, the Karmaṭhas, and the pure, radiant gods. ||92||
Likewise, he himself brought the hosts of gods under his control by means of his speech;
and at evening time, when Hari and I were requested by Brahmā, [he did so]. 93.
For the sake of the dissolution and destruction of the demon Indra,
I shall indeed cause Śakraka to be slain by the Sudarśana discus.
O Lakṣmī, this Sudarśana Hari is my final incarnation;
it is said that there will be many others as well at the end of the kalpa.
By the force of necessity, my incarnations indeed become innumerable;
for in whose hand or on the sole of whose foot there appears a fish or a bow-bannered [fish]. (96)
Whether it be an arrow, a trident, a svastika, a discus, a lotus, or even a water-pot—
I am that very Nārāyaṇa himself, manifest yet bearing a concealed form.

I am the one who abides in the true Dharma, whose actions are virtuous, and who is all-knowing; though possessing sovereignty, I am without the need for worldly power, and though divine, I conduct myself as if non-divine.
Through association, meeting, union, sight, or even touch;
through living together, remembering, or serving—He is certainly the bestower of liberation. 99.
Fortunate embodied beings, having known me and propitiated me through service, attain my extraordinary bliss on the path to liberation. (3.164.10)
Thinking me to be a mere human being, those sinful Asuras—full of great envy and transgressors—depart from afar. (10.1)
Even those established on the path to liberation will go to many hells, despite their signs of omniscience and their divine qualities and so forth. (10.2)
Having known Me, those men and women, as well as animals, birds, and those of Śūdra birth, who take refuge in Me, shall attain My imperishable state. (10.3)
Even those who are devoted to unrighteousness become purifiers through union with me; for desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, and envy—[are likewise purified].
Through my yoga, both evil qualities and merit and demerit are devoid of attributes;
for those who are united with me by whatever disposition they may have, [those qualities cease to exist].
For those who have become eternally disciplined are never again separated from me;
indeed, my yoga bestows liberation upon gods, humans, and rākṣasas alike.
By my mere resolve, the heaps of eggs belonging to Śūdras, birds, animals, and the wives of Daityas and Dānavas are delivered [from suffering].
By my slight good fortune, evildoers are purified;
that very rite which belongs to one named Pāpa becomes purifying when performed for me. 108.
"I am independent; my traditions indeed teach me what is virtuous.
Let this be virtuous, and thus I maintain it, for that is indeed virtue. || 109 ||
"Even that which is not a bull may become a bull for me through my resolve, or a bull may cease to be a bull. Having reflected thus, they serve me, the Supreme Lord, in embodied form. (3.164.110)
Their liberation rests in his hand for all rites, both here and in the hereafter;
by reading or hearing this chapter, there shall be deliverance.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purpose and Other Details of the Fourteen Incarnations of Hari during the Fourteen Manvantaras," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"What kind of auspicious and virtuous deed should a living person perform here, by which he may be happy everywhere and in the next world? (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: My worship should be performed, for it bestows supreme happiness in the hereafter;
likewise, the worship of the ancestors should be performed, and by that, the worship of the gods becomes auspicious.
One should perform the most excellent gift (dāna) as well as the auspicious "living funeral rite" (jīvacchrāddha);
by performing these here with one's own hand, their fruit is obtained in the hereafter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Lord, tell me how and of what nature the *jīvacchrāddha* (the funeral rite for the living) is to be performed;
explain its procedure, and tell me everything that is to be offered therein.
Śrī Puṣkottama said:
In a temple, in the residence of the virtuous, in a monastery, in the presence of the Lord,
in a school, on a sacrificial ground, on a mountain, and on the bank of a river— (5).
One should perform the *jīva-śrāddha*, which bestows happiness, in a forest, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in a place containing a shrine (*caitya*), on a holy spot, or even in one's own new home.
But when one contemplates the Dharma, it should be performed with reverence;
through faith, it is offered by one's own hand, by the heart, and through meditative realization.
That *śrāddha* should be understood in every respect as being proclaimed fivefold:
the *pārabrāhmika*, the *paitrya*, the *daiva*, the *aiśvara*, and the *bhautika*.
Whether in childhood, youth, or old age, or even when death is imminent,
this must be performed in its fivefold form by virtuous people at any time whatsoever.

When the *jīvacchrāddha* has been performed, the living person is liberated while still alive—whether he be performing actions or not, whether he be ignorant or even possessed of knowledge. (3.165.10)

Whether he be learned in the Vedas or not learned in the Vedas, whether he belongs to one of the four castes or is a human being of any other status, whether he is established in a stage of life (āśrama) or is a renunciant (tyāgī), he should indeed perform the śrāddha in five ways.
Having remembered Hari, the Supreme Brahman, in great temples,
a living person on this earth should offer daily food offerings (naivedya) to Hari.
One should offer ever-new great offerings (mahānaivedya) to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, consisting of fifty-six types of enjoyments; that leads to the fruit of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). 13.
Every morning, one should likewise offer to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa mung-bean sweets, milk, sugar, and so forth.
One should give betel leaves and betel nut for the sake of satisfaction;
the fruit of that act shall be inexhaustible happiness for oneself, the giver, in the next world.
At midday as well, one should offer auspicious sweet foods;
one should present cooked dishes seasoned with ghee, clarified butter, and sugar.
One should offer vegetables, split pulses, soup, various cooked rice dishes, cakes, fried pancakes, milk-based preparations, and other dairy products. (17)
Delightful fermented rice-gruel preparations mixed with various spices, as well as foods to be chewed, swallowed, licked, and sucked, along with fruits. (18)
One should offer bulbs, flowers, petals, leaves, and knots as food to Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods, who is indeed accompanied by all forms of prosperity.
One should always thus offer royal enjoyments in vessels made of gold and other materials; that which is offered directly in such bowls and dishes is indeed the Śrāddha itself.
While living, a livelihood was granted by me to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of a means of subsistence;
that indeed bears fruit in the imperishable abode of Goloka and also in Śrīpura.
Everything given to the Supreme Lord becomes inexhaustible;
even when it has been returned by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, it is obtained even in the state of liberation.
Whether in Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the unmanifest, or even in the immortal realm,
whatever is given here to the Lord is obtained there multiplied by infinite qualities.
In this manner, waters that are sweet, cool, and pleasant,
as well as those desired in all seasons, should be offered to Śrī Hari.
Those things given in the form of livelihoods are obtained for one's satisfaction;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, mouth-fresheners should be given for the sake of purity. 25.
He also offered betel leaves, cloves, cardamom, camphor, and betel rolls, as well as areca nut powder, khadira wood powder, and other desired fruits.
Furthermore, at the time of rising, water, fruit, and leaves, as well as whatever foods are warm or cold, should be offered for the purpose of a meal. (Verse 7)
All those cooked in ghee, and those cooked in oil;
all those cooked by fire, and those cooked by the sun. ||28||
Edible offerings that are seasonally ripe and possess fragrant flavors should always be presented to Śrī Hari during the third watch of the day. (29)
In the evening, for the sake of food and drink, one should offer purīs, polikās,
milk, vegetables, sour gruel (āranāla), and water to Śrī Hari.
One should indeed always provide for him, and one should assign a garden for his livelihood; one should also bestow fields and likewise grant palatial residences and dwellings.
One should give villages, houses, and land that provide a means of livelihood to the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||3||
One should even secure a livelihood through wealth for the sake of maintaining a continuous flow of worship;
that which one performs with such faith is called *jīvacchrāddha*. (33)
Year after year, one should offer food accompanied by water once;
or otherwise, one should give a monetary offering (nāṇaka) as a sacrificial oblation on a platter (sthālanaivedya).
One may give it every month, or likewise offer it at every festival; one may also bestow it every fortnight, or even at every sacred occasion.
Thus, this excellent livelihood has been granted to Śrī Hari;
it shall be for the sake of inexhaustible fruit and shall provide eternal satisfaction.
O Lakṣmī, this Śrāddha pertaining to the Supreme Brahman has been described by me to you;
now listen as I also describe the Śrāddha pertaining to Īśvara. ||37||
In whatever part of the temple there are my incarnate images—the manifestations such as Vāsudeva and others, and the perfected ones such as Kapila and others—[there I am present]. (38)
One should offer the sacrificial food (nivedya) to Śrī and Lakṣmī, to the male attendants (pārṣadas) and those auspicious female attendants, and to the lords such as Vairāja and others. (39)
One should offer here sweet food, drinkable water, fruit, bulbs, leaves and the like, betel-leaf and such, milk, and even living honey. (3.165.40)
All that is declared to belong to Īśvara; it is given for the sake of a return fruit.
O Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you that which is ancestral, offered to the ancestors. (41)

Whether in water, at the root of *darbha* grass, at the foot of a tree, or upon the ground; or in the hand of a Brahmin, or in the mouth of a Brahmin—one who is living should give for the sake of satisfaction. (42)
One should offer balls of raw dough and cooked savory foods during the meal; one should offer vegetables, leaves, fruits, roots, and milk for the sake of satisfaction. (43)
And one should also reverently offer the *daiva* śrāddha to the gods—to the Ādityas, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Vasus as well. (44)
Likewise, one should offer auspicious gifts to other deities as desired;
for that is declared to be the *daiva-śrāddha*. Listen as I describe its procedure. ||45||
Having examined the ground according to the rules by means of its scent, leaves, sap, and so forth,
one should indeed prepare an auspicious sand altar on that site which is free from thorns and obstacles.
In the center, having smeared a most beautiful pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit at most according to the prescribed rite, and having applied [sacrificial substances] and established the fire; ||47||
Having added fuel according to the scriptures and having enclosed the area on all sides,
he should strew grass around it according to the scriptures as handed down through the traditional lineage.

Having completed the entire rite beginning with the invocation of the fire (agnimukha) and having fully worshipped the fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), he should offer oblations separately with fuel-sticks and the like, as well as with the sacrificial porridge (caru). 49.
One should also offer oblations with clarified butter, having extracted it for oneself among the gods and others;
then, for the sake of their satisfaction, one should offer all the elements that constitute reality.
Oṃ bhūḥ, salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
Oṃ bhūḥ, and to the beginningless Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, svāhā! ||51||
Oṃ, salutation to the incarnations of Bhuvaḥ and likewise to the Īśvaras;
Oṃ, svāhā to the incarnations of Bhuvaḥ and likewise to the Īśvaras. ||52||
Oṃ Svaḥ! Salutations to the creations of living beings, to the ancestors, the deities, and so forth.
Oṃ Svaḥ Svāhā! To the creations of living beings, to the ancestors, the deities, and so forth. ||53||
Oṃ bhūḥ, obeisance to Vedhas; Oṃ bhūḥ, svāhā to Vedhas.
Oṃ bhuvaḥ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, svāhā to Viṣṇu. ||54||
Oṃ svaḥ, obeisance to Śaṃkara; Oṃ svaḥ, svāhā to Śaṃkara.
Oṃ mahaḥ, obeisance to Sureśa; Oṃ mahaḥ, svāhā to Sureśa. ||55||
Oṃ janaḥ pitṛbhyo namaḥ; Oṃ janaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ svāhā.
Oṃ tapaḥ prakṛtaye namaḥ; Oṃ tapaḥ prakṛtaye svāhā. ||26||
Oṃ, truth; obeisance to Hari. Oṃ, truth; svāhā to Hari.
Oṃ, protect my sense of smell, Kṛṣṇa, the upholder of the earth; to the god Kṛṣṇa, the fragrance in the nose; obeisance to Bhūḥ. ||57||
Oṃ, protect my Kṛṣṇadharā; [protect] the fragrance in the nose for Kṛṣṇa, Bhūḥ Svāhā!
Oṃ, protect my Kṛṣṇadharā; [protect] the fragrance in the nose for the wife of Kṛṣṇa, Bhūr Namaḥ Svāhā! ||58||
Oṃ, protect my earth for me, O Kṛṣṇa; protect the sense of smell in my nose for the sake of the Consort of Kṛṣṇa: Bhūḥ Svāhā!
Oṃ, O Hari, protect my water for me; protect the sense of taste on my tongue for the sake of Hari: Bhuvaḥ Namaḥ. (59)
