Oṃ hare, protect my water; for the sake of Hari, [I offer] the taste on the tongue; to Bhuvaḥ, Svāhā!
Oṃ hare, protect my water; for the sake of the wife of Hari, [I offer] the taste on the tongue; to Bhuvaḥ, Namaḥ!
Oṃ hare, protect my water; protect the taste on my tongue for the Consort of Hari; to Bhuvaḥ, svāhā!
Oṃ pareśa, protect my fire; protect the form in my eyes for the Supreme Lord; to Svara, namaḥ! ||61||
Oṃ, O Supreme Lord Agni, protect my eyes and form; O Supreme Lord, [protect] my voice; Svāhā!
Oṃ, O Supreme Lord Agni, protect my eyes and form; obeisance to the voice of the Consort of the Supreme Lord; Oṃ. ||62||
Oṃ, protect my fire for me, O Supreme Lord; protect my form for me, O Consort of the Supreme Lord; svāhā to the sun!
Oṃ, protect my wind for me, O Brahman; protect my touch for me, O Skin; salutations to the Great God, the Divine Brahman. ||63||
Oṃ, protect my Vāyu, the Brahman; [protect] touch in the skin for the sake of the Great God, the Brahman; svāhā!
Oṃ, protect my Vāyu, the Brahman.
To the skin, the touch, and the wife of Brahmā, Mahārī, obeisance. || 64 ||
Oṃ, protect my Vāyu, the Brahman; protect my touch within the skin for the sake of the Greatness of the Consort of Brahman, Svāhā!
Oṃ, protect my hollow space, the supreme ether.
In the ear, the sound; from the supreme ether, salutation to the person. || 65 ||
Oṃ, O Supreme Ether, protect my cavity;
O Supreme Ether, [protect] sound in the ear for the person—svāhā!
Oṃ, O Supreme Ether, protect my cavity.
In the ear, one should offer sound to the consort of Paravyoman; people [should thus perform] salutation. || 66 ||
Oṃ! Protect my supreme etherial cavity;
protect sound in my ears for the sake of the Consort of the Supreme Ether; Oṃ Jana, Svāhā!
Oṃ! Protect the dust of the Lord of Liberation from me.
Obeisance to austerity for the sake of liberation from thirst for material objects.
Oṃ! Protect my two eyes of liberation;
obeisance to austerity for the sake of liberation from thirst for material objects, svāhā!
Oṃ, protect my dust from Mukteśa;
[I offer] obeisance to austerity for Mukteśa’s wife, Tṛṣṇā, regarding material wealth.
Oṃ, protect my dust from Mukteśa.
To the substance, to thirst, to the wife of liberation, to austerity, Svāhā!
Oṃ, Bālakṛṣṇa, protect my truth; [protect] faith in dharma for Bālakṛṣṇa; obeisance to Truth. 69.
Oṃ Bālakṛṣṇa, protect my truth;
[protect] faith in dharma for Bālakṛṣṇa; truth, svāhā!
Oṃ Bālakṛṣṇa, protect my truth.
Salutations to Śraddhā, the wife of Bālakṛṣṇa, who is Truth; obeisance to her. ||3.165.70||
Oṃ Bālakṛṣṇa, protect my truth;
protect my faith in dharma. To the wife of Bālakṛṣṇa, truth, svāhā! Oṃ Lord of Life, protect my life!
Salutation to the lord of life, who is the movement and the very breath of existence in the hereafter. ||71||
Oṃ, O Lord of Life, protect my life;
for the sake of the Lord of Life in the next world, may my life be well-sustained—svāhā!
Oṃ, O Lord of Life, protect my life.
To the beloved wife of the Lord of Life in the next world, obeisance, svāhā! ||72||
Oṃ, O Lord of Life, protect my life;
may there be life for the wife of the lord of life in the hereafter, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Brahman, to the illustrious Puruṣottama, svāhā! ||73||
Oṃ, obeisance to the father, svāhā to the father; obeisance to the grandfather, svāhā to the grandfather. Oṃ, obeisance to the great-grandfather, svāhā to the great-grandfather. ||74||
Oṃ, homage to the beings, to the beings svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the subtle ones, to the measures (mātrās) svāhā! ||75||
Oṃ, homage to the sense-faculties; to the sense-faculties, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the vital breaths; to the vital breaths, svāhā! ||76||
Om, obeisance to the internal organs; svāhā to the internal organs!
Om, obeisance to the Self; svāhā to the Self! ||77||
Oṃ Kṛṣṇa! Cut through the earth; cut through the sense of smell; cut through my sin! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Svaḥ svāhā! ||78||
Having thus offered separately for each, one should indeed offer with pure ghee alone either a thousand times, half of that, or one hundred and eight times. ||79||
One should offer oblations of clarified butter alone one hundred and eight times separately to Mahālakṣmī,
and likewise with the Prāṇa-mantras and others, using clarified butter alone.
Oṃ, seated in the vital breath, I offer the nectar.
O Hari, enter me for the sake of burning away [impurities]; svāhā to the vital breath!
Svāhā to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the glorious Hari, the lord of the vital breath! ||81||
Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā, bhuvaḥ svāhā, svaḥ svāhā, bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā.
One should offer oblations in this sequence, as well as whatever is prescribed for the śrāddha ceremony according to the rules.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for the satisfaction of the Supreme Self,
and thereafter one should also present it for the satisfaction of the consort of the Supreme Self.
Having thus completed [the offerings] to the gods and the ancestors, one should indeed assign [the food] by one's own name;
one should also present it to the spirits (bhūtas) and others, and likewise offer it to those who are indebted.
Then, having become free from debt, he should feed many lords of yogis;
he should feed virtuous men, holy women, and children—both boys and girls. 85.
One should also feed one's kinsmen and provide excellent food for the gurus;
furthermore, one should give garments, ornaments, and blankets to those who are worthy recipients among the Vaiṣṇavas.
Vehicles, beds, carriages, vessels of bell-metal, copper, and so forth;
gold, silver, a cow, sesame seeds, fields, and all forms of wealth.
One should also give groups of male and female servants as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and one should offer delicious funeral cakes (piṇḍa) separately in eight varieties.
For three days, one should offer caru and a meal of milk to Śrī Viṣṇu.
Whether [the deceased] has died or not, one should perform this; while living, one performs it, and having died, one obtains the fruit.
Having acted in this way, there is no longer purity or impurity for one who has died here;
since he is liberated while living, there is indeed no birth-impurity (sūtaka) for him.
For those who cremate the body, the period of impurity (sūtaka) lasts only as long as the bath; there is nothing more than that.
In their lineage, whether it be a daughter or a son, whoever increases the family line [is purified accordingly]. 91.
He too shall certainly be liberated and become one who effects the deliverance of his ancestors;
by the performance of a Śrāddha for the living, the ancestors are released even from hell.
By this rite, he is released from the debt to his mother and father; when the time arrives, he is freed from dwelling in a pit, from cremation, and from being carried by water. 93.
Whatever may be entirely free from fault for the sake of his liberation, that very work performed by himself causes his debt to dissolve. //94//
One should give material food to cows and cattle, as well as to birds such as parrots;
one should also offer it to insects, moths, other living beings, and fish and the like.
One should give water to trees and other such beings, as well as grains to embodied beings;
one should offer food to mendicants and present them with clothing and alms-bowls.
Whoever should bestow [it] in every way with his own hand according to his ability—for such a deceased person, there is no waiting for twelve days at all. //97//
He travels swiftly by means of a celestial chariot, seated upon a bull, to the world of merit;
or else, the *ātivāhika* deities who move upward lead him there.
O Lakṣmī, in this manner the Śrāddha that bestows life should be performed;
it shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation when one offers what has been earned by one's own hands. (99)
Cooking with one's own hand, eating with one's own hand, acquiring wealth with one's own hand, and giving with one's own hand. (3.165.100)
Whoever performs this [rite] conquers both in this world and in the next;
moreover, by merely hearing it, one becomes endowed with such merit.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Jīvacchrāddha," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "In this world, two things prevail: nectar and poison.
Sudhā is nectar and gara is poison; indeed, these two alone are savory. (1)

O Hari, if that [state] were to belong to the Wheel, or if it did not belong to it, what kind of thing would it be—such that, having known it, these people of the world might become dispassionate or take it up? (2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, a great poison arose;
the yogi Śrī Śaṅkara drank it, and the great sages praised him.
O Blessed One, O Hara, you have neutralized the most terrible poison called Kālakūṭa;
O Treasure of Compassion, everything has been well protected and established by you.
You are capable, you are the Great Lord, you are the protector, O remover of poison;
you are ever victorious, O excellent yogin, for you are Brahmā, free from all attachment.
Having heard this, Śambhu laughed and said to the other sages:
"The poison called Kālakūṭa is not poison; rather, it is the world that is the fierce poison."
He who can withdraw that poison is indeed capable; what need has he for this?
A yogi should, with every effort, withdraw the illusory poison.
Those who remove the poison of illusion are indeed Śaṅkaras; for they bring about welfare—whether as gurus, gods, or virtuous beings who are exceedingly pure.
For those great-souled yogis are indeed bestowers of peace and liberation;
for those virtuous ones are capable of removing the poison of saṃsāra.
The virtuous ones such as Sanaka and others, as well as the yogis such as Śuka and others, and the truthful celibate women who bring about the destruction of latent desires; 3.166.10.
This saṃsāra is of two kinds: indeed, the embodied and the unembodied.
The embodied consists of the forms of husband and wife, while the unembodied consists of latent impressions (vāsanā).
False knowledge is the cause of latent impressions (vāsanā), and by the power of these impressions,
householders who possess passion experience the enjoyment of sense objects.
Hatred toward passion is its friend; it even provides assistance in what is undesirable.
These two defects, [attraction and aversion], are the motivators and the desistors [of action]. 1.3.
That activity, which consists of both engagement and withdrawal, is endowed with qualities and performs action;
for that which possesses action, its arising is the connection with the first moment.
Increase, nourishment, and firmness, as well as decrease, decay, dissolution, and so forth—arising again according to one's karma, it culminates in dissolution. (15)
Thus, even while wandering here in the wheel of saṃsāra, one possessed of discernment and free from passion,
hatred, and the like, becomes liberated from bondage.
O Lotus-born One, there are many poisons; listen as I speak of them:
the sweet poison of family pride arises from birth. (17)
Mother, father, friend, and kinsman are a great poison of conceit;
"my house," "my garden," "my field," and "my chest. (18)
"Mine is wealth, mine is gold, mine is clothing, and mine is the most excellent food;
my word is always to be honored, for that which is spoken by me is indeed the truth. (19)
This supreme and invincible speech is indeed mine and must be honored;
victory is mine, my resolve is mine, and it is to be honored by no one else.
And that which has been determined by me must be accepted in every way by people;
for this intoxication is said to be a great poison, by which one is utterly tormented. (21)
Power is said to be the supreme poison, for it causes affliction and brings about conflict; likewise, knowledge of the arts is a poison, and even the poison of prosperity brings about destruction.
But sense objects, O Lakṣmī, are like poison, causing one to fall into great hells;
for the possession by sense objects is indeed like poison, whose onset is incurable.
O Lakṣmī, craving is the supreme poison; passion is a most potent poison;
hatred is a fire-like poison; and anxiety is a lethal poison that brings about destruction. (24)
Desire is the deadliest poison among all poisons, more virulent than any venom;
it arises from hell, is the giver of hells, and bestows the state of dwelling in hell. (25)
Delusion is likewise a poison that brings about what is undesirable and bestows great suffering;
one who is deluded does not know his duty, and being consumed by delusion, he perishes.
Existence is supreme poison, and sovereignty is indeed a deadly poison;
greed for the tongue, the genitals, and the belly is the poison that brings about the end of time.
Atheism, and the disparagement of one's teacher and parents, are a heavy poison;
by which [poison] one is suddenly slain and falls into ruin in the downward path. || 28 ||
A curse is poison for those who are suffering; lack of affection toward the virtuous is poison;
and unrighteousness is poison that burns one’s heavenly merit and destroys prosperity. (29)
Censure, theft, and violence—these three are roots;
they cut away the doer and bring about his destruction before long. (3.166.30)
Miserliness is the intolerance and envy that burns the eye; through these, the heart and mind are likewise scorched, and the man is consumed by each of his own respective abodes.
Thus, enveloped by poisons and shrouded by ignorance, this hell-being exists in every way; this poison is indeed most difficult to endure.
Born from sprouts, born from sweat, as well as born from eggs and born from a womb—they wander indeed due to the absence of renunciation, driven by ignorance, latent impressions, and karma. (33)
The body, consisting of six sheaths and containing the vital fluids, is indeed sustained;
the first birth is considered to be from the father, consisting of the bestowing of the seed. (34)
Birth from the womb is considered the second [stage], while the form of a child is the third;
the third begins with the sacred thread ceremony (*brahmasūtra*), and marriage is the fourth. (35)
The fifth [state] arises from total renunciation; the sixth, however, occurs after death;
the seventh is the attainment of liberation, after which no further birth exists. (36)
The bondage of action is that of the seed, the animal, and the human;
furthermore, there is the unshakable, the ancestral, and the seventh, which is indeed the state beyond rebirth.
In this way, these births are indeed permeated by poison;
moreover, the mere implantation of the seed is called "birth from the seed" (baijika). || 38 ||
That which is obtained at birth from a womb like that of a beast is the "beastly" birth of a child;
[it consists of] the Manu, the Mantra, the Gāyatrī, and even the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 39 ||
One enters human beings as bulls and takes on human birth; marriage and the bondage of ritual action are a state of existence equal to a prison. (3.166.40)
Having abandoned everything—including that birth which consists of the bonds of karma and takes the form of the married state—he who becomes dispassionate attains renunciation (saṃnyāsa). ||41||
The birth of one who has gone for refuge to Hari is declared to be infallible;
even at the time of casting off the body, during the state of being a ghost, it effects the union with the subtle body. 42.
The embodied soul, joined with merit and demerit, wanders; that is birth.
It is called "the state of the deceased" (pretyaka) when it exists anywhere for the sake of rebirth. //43//
Having performed disinterested devotion for the sake of liberation, having discharged one's debts, having severed bonds, and having dissolved and destroyed all poisons; ||44||
He who departs for the abode of Hari—that indeed is a birth from which there is no rebirth;
he possesses unsurpassed joy and is truly a partaker of the great nectar.
Having reached his seventh birth, death no longer exists for him;
thus, O Lakṣmī, these six poisons indeed become vast.
Cruel, burning, and indeed cooking on all sides are the many sufferings within the womb, and likewise upon the path of birth.
Whether on the ground or upon a bed, in childhood or in youth, in enjoyment or in yoga, in worldly affairs or in old age and dependence; ||48||
For the discerning person, there are only sufferings in the face of incapacity, poverty, disease, death, the state of a ghost, and likewise in the southern region or a poisoned pit. (49)
Among animals, humans, yakṣas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and gods;
among the hosts of ancestors, the enjoyers of pleasures, gandharvas, and the throngs of apsarases.

In the realm of Indra, in the realm of Brahmā, in the natural state, in the world of Virāj, in the abode of Prajāpati, in the realm of Puruṣa, and in the maw of Time—therein lies suffering, a most great poison. (51)
The earthly, the watery, the fiery, and the windy; the ethereal, the mental, the intellectual, and likewise the egoic. ||52||
Ordinary poison and suffering exist at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end;
present sufferings will become lethal poisons.
In place, time, and action, various sufferings [arise];
like a tree whose roots have been severed, one falls helplessly to the earth. (54)
Due to the exhaustion of their merit-tree, even the gods fall to the earth;
likewise, suffering born of evil is forcibly experienced as mere suffering. (55)

It occurs for hell-beings even in hell, for kings who have not attained their heart's desire, and likewise for ascetics and those of the [four] castes due to the non-performance of what has been prescribed. (56)
Suffering exists for those submerged in the fear of saṃsāra, even for those free from passion, as well as for insects, birds, wild animals, domestic beasts, elephants, and horses. (57)
Poison is suffering, and for one who does not abandon that which is like poison, it is indeed suffering;
for all those who dwell in celestial palaces and hold office for the duration of a kalpa, there is only suffering. (58)
And for Manu and others who pride themselves on their positions, the land was a source of poison;
so too it was for the gods and the Daityas, due to their mutual desire for victory. (59)
The poison and suffering of both Rākṣasas and kings exist throughout the three worlds;
hermitages exist for the sake of labor, but true rest comes through knowledge.
Knowledge given to an unworthy recipient results in suffering; therefore, one should strive to obtain the status of a worthy recipient.
Through constant association with the virtuous, the state of being a worthy recipient of truth arises.
O Rāma, by her grace, the Brahman should be held by the virtuous;
likewise, the Supreme Brahman should be held in the eyes, and Hari should be held in the ears. (62)
Kṛṣṇa is to be meditated upon in the skin during yoga; Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon in the seat of taste.
Parameśa is to be meditated upon in the sense of smell; the Lord himself is to be meditated upon in the feet.
The pervasive Īśvara is to be meditated upon in the anus and the genitals as the inner self.
The Lord of Māyā should be held in the mind; Narāyaṇa should be held in the heart;
Mādhava should be held in the intellect; and Ṛṣīkeśa should be held in reflection. (64)
The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is to be meditated upon in the earth; the One who reclines on the waters (Jaleśaya) is to be meditated upon in water;
the Lord of Light (Dhāmeśa) is to be meditated upon in fire; and the Lord of the Cosmic Man (Virāṭpati) is to be meditated upon in the wind. ||65||
Mahāviṣṇu is to be held within the ether, but I am to be held within one's own self;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, I am to be seen, and likewise Hari is to be heard.
I alone am that which is to be smelled, tasted, and touched;
I am that which is to be thought, understood, and acted upon—I am Hari.
"I am indeed that which is to be willed; I am to be spoken; likewise, I am the Lord;
I am that which is to be grasped, that which is to be traversed, and that which is to be created. (68)
I am indeed to be gladdened; I abide in each and every reality (tattva).
In the vital breath, in departure, in movement, in drinking, and in stability, I abide. (69)
Let the self-possessed one worship me as the all-pervading Self moving within,
residing in food, in water, in the vital breath, and situated in the mind.
One should worship me, Hari, the Supreme Person, as abiding in consciousness,
as abiding in the senses, as abiding in the subtle elements, as abiding in time, and as established in the individual soul.
One should worship me, who abide in all things, as the nectar and the imperishable Lord within, the innermost Supreme Self, for the sake of cutting through the poison of saṃsāra.
Having abandoned the poison of the impurity of ignorance, [behold] me, who am the object of knowledge—the gracious Hari, the Lord of lords, the innate master dwelling within. ||73||
Having known this directly, one shall indeed attain the vast state of immortality;
therefore, one should constantly practice that knowledge which is my own domain as the primary focus. (74)
Endowed with this single knowledge, joined with the affection of devotion, and having abandoned the poison of attachment, he attains Me; of this there is no doubt. (75)
In this world or even in the next, there remains nothing for him to do;
for he is liberated while living, since even his latent tendencies have dissolved away. (76)
Devoted to knowledge and devotion, he is a knower of Brahman in the ultimate sense;
thus, he is liberated from saṃsāra and freed from the poison of suffering.
Abiding in the refuge of the Guru, one goes to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self;
the yogi’s all sins and poisons are digested.
Even while playing, one would not be tainted by various kinds of poisons;
O Rame, the meditation on Śrī Hari remains forever free from poison.

One who is of a Brahmanical character should practice meditation through association with the Guru; he should attain a state of total absorption in me, and finally, even a state of complete merging into me.
For my devotee indeed finds even poison to be nectar;
thus, all poisons appear as nectars to him. ||81||
The elements are subtle measures; the objects of the senses arise from the objects; there are both qualities and non-qualities, as well as actions and those which are heavy. 82.
All those [poisons] are imagined as nectars within me, the Supreme;
thus indeed is the devotee a consumer of poison, capable [of it], and no other ever. ||83||
Indeed, he would be capable of supporting the earth, water, and fire;
likewise, he would be able to support the wind, space, the eightfold functions, and the lords. (84)
He shall be able to sustain both Prakṛti and Puruṣa,
and he shall be capable of sustaining Time as well, for he is of my own nature.
He shall also possess the nature of the syllable (akṣara) and is indeed capable of sustaining the liberated;
for as I am, so is he—the destroyer of the very beginning of worldly existence.
One who possesses the state of the Lord, whose self is the Self, becomes capable of acting;
having attained the supreme state of the Lord, one becomes the master of all actions. ||87||
One should recognize poison through experience and contemplate its remedy;
or, having consumed non-poison or even a potent poison, one should destroy that poison [with mantras]. 88.
The virtuous are said to be non-venomous, whereas I, Hari, am of fierce venom; yet through association with the virtuous, even one who is venomous becomes free from poison by drinking from me. (89)
"Out of affection for me, who am free from poison, and through devotion, you have propitiated me;
by my grace, liberation shall come swiftly—this is my solemn promise, O Rame."
Whether situated in the womb, being born, or whether he be a child, a youth,
or even an old man, the embodied soul is liberated by the grace of the Supreme Self.
Whether born from an egg, born from a sprout, or even born from sweat, a man or a woman who possesses my grace is liberated. ||92||
Even embodied beings, who are portions of My very self and distinguished by their union with Me, having become perfected through My nature, attain the supreme goal. 93.
Those devotees who have been beheld by me, who are my own portions and have taken refuge at my feet, cross the poisonous ocean of saṃsāra as objects of my compassion. 94.
Just as oil rises upward when mixed with water, so too the embodied soul, through union with Kṛṣṇa, rises upward and is surely delivered. 95.
Just as fire, when kindled, naturally rises upward, so too the embodied soul, when nourished by my supreme devotion, rises upward. 96.
Just as a yogi indeed proceeds to the door of Brahman through great sovereign powers, even so does he proceed to the Supreme Brahman through my sovereign powers. 97.
Just as Gopī, having attained the unborn [Viṣṇu], became Gāyatrī, so too a cowherd, having attained Hari, shall reach Goloka. ||98||
Just as Lakṣmī, having attained Hari, obtained a dwelling in his heart, so too the devotee, having attained Hari, shall obtain a dwelling in the Imperishable. 99.
Just as an illusion, having reached Hari, dissolves into Hari,
so too the devotee, having reached Hari, completely dissolves into Hari.
Just as a wife clinging to her beloved does not perceive any separation from him, so too the devotee, absorbed in Hari, does not perceive his own individuality.
Just as sugar attains the state of being the very essence of milk,
so too does one who performs dark deeds attain the state of milk within devotion toward Kṛṣṇa.
Just as a liquid mind indeed merges into a vessel of oil,
so too my affectionate devotee, being full of love, merges into me as non-different.
Just as Ānanda and Pramoda are not separate from their own bliss within themselves, so too is the devotee of divine form not separate from the Supreme Self. 104.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this power of neutralizing poison has been declared by me to you;
by reciting or hearing this, one dispels all poison.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Poisons of Saṃsāra and the Means for Their Removal," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Keśava, for a devotee or a female devotee who has fallen into calamity, how may there be the destruction of that calamity, and how may there be the destruction of sin? (1)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: For an embodied being who is without vows, incapable, and devoid of knowledge, this hymn known as Vyāpahaṇa is intended for the destruction of calamities, sins, and the like. (2)
Having become single-minded, one should praise the Supreme Lord,
as well as his incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, and the ancestral deities.
One should praise the sages, gurus, devotees of the Lord, holy men, and practitioners;
then, having become one who seeks no other refuge, one should pray, and thus become possessed of happiness. || 4 ||
O Rame, I shall recite to you this divine hymn that bestows all accomplishments;
it swiftly grants all desired objects to the listener, the speaker, and the reader.
Salutations to the primordial Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self;
to the Great Blessed One, the Lord of the imperishable liberated souls, the Transcendent Self.
Salutations to the sovereign lord of the three worlds, to the inner controller of all,
to the Supreme Brahman, to Puruṣottama, and to the one who descends in incarnations.
The all-knowing one, the abode of all, the dwelling place of Śrī, who is established in everything;
may he, who resides in the supreme syllable and is the Lord of the liberated, dispel my sin. (8)
May the Lord Narayana, the supreme Brahman, the divine self, the Supreme Ruler, the Blessed One, indeed dispel all calamity and sin. 9.
May Hari— the Lord of all, beginningless and endless, the possessor of all knowledge,
the bestower of everything, and the giver of happiness— ward off sin and calamity.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, worshipped by the universe—may the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dispel all evil. 1.1.1.

Beloved by Brahmā, yet indifferent to what is dear or not dear, the lovely one, the peaceful, the master overflowing with affection—may He, who captivates the beloved of Hari, protect us and dispel all calamities. 12.
Served by the circle of liberated ones, attended by groups of emancipated beings, most desirable, supremely lovely—may He remove our sins and calamities. (13)
May the supreme one— the incarnate, the perfect, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest, the Lord of the high and the low— remove my sins and calamities.
May Śrīpati, Śrīdhara, Śrīhṛt, Śrīmān, Śrīda, Śriyānvita, Śrīpāda, Śrīhari, and Kṛṣṇa dispel the calamities of sin. 15.

May the Lord of Lakṣmī, the bearer of Lakṣmī, the one who has taken Lakṣmī to his heart, the one endowed with the granting of Lakṣmī, who is exceedingly gratified by the service of Lakṣmī, remove the calamities arising from sin. 16.
May the Lord of Rādhā, who bears Rādhā, who dwells in the heart of Rādhā, and who is united with Rādhikā;
may He, whose soul is Rādhā and who is Kṛṣṇa to Rādhikā, dispel my sins and calamities. (17)
May the Lord of Māṇikī, whose vehicle is Māṇikī, the Master of Māṇikī, who wears a fresh necklace of rubies, remove the calamities of sin. (18)
May the Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the cowherd girls, worshipped by the cowherds and cowherdesses, the protector of cows and the dark-hued Kṛṣṇa, remove my sins and calamities. 1.9.
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa— the best of men, the king, the protector, the supreme among humans,
the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha— dispel all calamities arising from sin.
May Vasuda, Vāsudeva—the bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
the eater of nectar and the giver of nectar—dispel those who cause one to fall into sin.
May He who is the giver of the earth, who stands upon the earth, who is the abundance of the earth, who increases the fortune of those on earth,
the Lord of the existence of the earth and the unmanifested, and who removes sin and calamity— may He protect us.
May Hari, the protector of the Vedas, the upholder of the earth, the bearer of the deep thunder, and the possessor of wisdom, [grant us refuge].
May the Swan, the observer of the divine, who milks the cows of heaven and is free from sin, drive away all evil. ||23||

May the compassionate ascetic, the virtuous mendicant, the fierce sacrifice, the forest-dweller, the child, the eminent physician, and the one who removes the calamities of sin, dispel [all evils]. (24)

May the wise Kṛṣṇakānta Śāstrī, the sovereign emperor who is the cause of incarnation, whose nature is possession, a partial manifestation, a digit of power, and prosperity, remove all evil and misfortune. 25.

May the Supreme Lord—who is full, who is the supreme manifestation, the sovereign, the inner controller, the creator of his own form as the image, the pervasive presence in the temple, the one well-established in yoga, and the remover of the calamities of sin—dispel [all obstacles]. 26.
May the Supreme Lord, who dwells in all abodes, who possesses manifold forms, and who is the teacher of both the insentient and the sentient, remove my sins and calamities. (27)
May Nārāyaṇī, Śrīpureśī, Mādhavī, Puruṣottamī, Kārṇī, and Śrī Lalitā Lakṣmī dispel my sins and calamities. 28.
May Bhārgavī, Lakṣmī the destroyer of sorrow, Śivarājñī, Vaiṣṇavī, Padminikā, and Padmajā remove my sins and calamities. (29)
May Kaṃbharāśrī, Mahālakṣmī, Vāsudevī, the Supreme Sovereign, the Imperishable Śrī, the Blessed Goddess, remove my sins and calamities. (3.167.30)
May Pauruṣī, Prākṛtī, Devī, Māyeśī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Pārabrāhmī, and Mother Ramā dispel all sins and calamities. (3.1)
May Padmā, Vairājī, Gaṅgā, Revā, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, Gomatī, and Gopī—abounding in abundance—dispel my sins and misfortunes. (35)
May she who is Sādāśaivī, Māheśī, Brāhmī, Brahmapriyā, Satī, Sādhvī, Svāminī, and Cāndrī, remove the calamities of sin. (33)
May Tulasī—golden, made of gold, deer-like, and possessing a golden form;
Vaikuṇṭhā, Vṛndā—dispel all sins and calamities. (34)

May the perfected one, who is the mother, whose form is accomplishment, the wonder that is the daughter of the Moon, the nectar of immortality, and the one possessing nooses—may she dispel sins and calamities. (35)
May the solar radiance, the retinue of Īśvara, and the goddess Rati—[who are] affection, devotion, and the form of the vow—dispel sins and calamities. (36)
May the gentle, ancient, divine, contented, and satisfied Abjikā—Kamalāmbā Śāradā—dispel my sins and calamities. (37)
May Aindrī, who consists of pure bliss, whose power is consciousness and whose form is knowledge, the yoginī established in the heart, remove my sins and calamities. (38)
May my mother Mohinī, Nandinī, Padmekṣaṇā, Urvaśī, Pativratā, and Svarṇavarṇā dispel my sins and calamities. (39)
May the auspicious and purifying Vidyā, the bestower of wealth and the sustainer of riches, the daughter of the ocean who removes distress, being peaceful, dispel sins and calamities. (3.167.40)

May Śrī—the knower of all states of being, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the granter of fearlessness to her devotees, who occupies half the body of [Śiva], the giver of life—dispel sins and calamities. 41.
Endowed with good fortune, rich in splendor, adorned with all ornaments, and her limbs radiant with every grace, may she dispel sins and calamities. 42.
May Gaurī—the prosperity of crops, the prosperity of jewels, the prosperity of wealth, the mistress of the household, and the bearer of grain and food—dispel sin and calamity. 43.
May Rohiṇī, the nourisher, the maiden in the bloom of youth, the delighter of the gods, and the most beautiful woman, remove my sins and calamities. 44.
Consisting of goodness, bestowing goodness, upholding goodness, and united with goodness—may she, who is the essence of being, consciousness, and bliss, dispel sins and calamities. (45)
The liberated attendants, the devotees, the other devotees, the Sādhyas, the Īśvaras, the female Īśvarīs, and the Great Liberated Ones—may they dispel my sins and calamities. (46)
The conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the Kaustubha gem, the crown, the forest garland, and the flower garland of Hari dispel all sins and calamities. (47)
The staff, the umbrella, the chowrie, the armlet, as well as the bracelet, the chain, the girdle, and the black antelope skin—these dispel sin and calamities. (48)
All the qualities, sovereignties, wonders, perfections, and powers of Śrī Hari dispel sins and calamities. (49)
Śālagrāma, as well as the sage Śālaṅkāyana, the Gaṇḍakī river,
the Triveṇī, and the Śāla tree— these dispel sins and calamities.
Badarī, the sages dwelling in Badarī, Nara, Hari, the Gaṅgā, Himavat, and gold—these dispel sins and calamities. (51)

Viṣṇu reclining on Śeṣa, the Ocean of Milk, the milk-born goddess Lakṣmī, the white king of serpents, and those who have renounced food and worldly attachments—these dispel sins and calamities. ||52||
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and Prabhākara, along with the Gaṇas, the Rudras, and the Rudrāṇīs, dispel all sin and calamities. (53)
The Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, the Moon, the luminous stars, the planets, and even the comets—may they all dispel sin and misfortune. (54)
The swan, Garuḍa, the bull, the lion, the deer, the elephant, Śeṣa, the peacock, and the sun—may these dispel sin and misfortune. 55.
Kārttikeya, Mahākāla, the great vajra, and the trident—the Kāladaṇḍa weapon—may these dispel your sins and calamities. 56.
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, the lords of lords, the guardians of the quarters, and the guardians of the worlds dispel sin and calamities. ||57||
Space, touch, fire, taste, and likewise earth—these subtle elements (tanmātras), as well as the vital breaths, shall dispel sin and calamities. (58)
May the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Kinnaras, as well as the Guhyakas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃpuruṣas, dispel sin and calamities. (59)
The mothers of the gods, as well as the mothers of the hosts,
and all the mothers of living beings, may they dispel sin and calamities.
Likewise, the Apsarases, the goddesses, the lunar mansions, and the lunar days;
the fortnights, the months, and the years—may they dispel my sin and misfortune.
Fever, diseases, the seasons, debts, as well as Rākṣasas, Daityas, and wicked Dānavas—may they dispel sin and calamities. (62)
The oceans, rivers, wells, ponds, oblong lakes,
tanks, and pools— Varuṇa dispels their sins and calamities.
The cows that rain down all desires, the creepers that fulfill all wishes,
and likewise the wish-fulfilling trees— may they dispel my sins and calamities.
Sacrifices, sacrificial rites, injunctions, and even the Vedas; the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the meters—these all dispel sin and misfortune. (659)
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he has a thousand arms, is all-knowing, and dispels sin and calamities. (66)
May Pāvaka, the purifier, Vahni, Saptārcis, Saptajihvika, Svarṇaretas, Brahmamukha, and Pāpāpaha dispel all calamities. (67)
Generosity, self-restraint, compassion, the divine, the gods, the goddesses, the virtuous, the holy men, and the meritorious—these dispel sin and misfortune. (68)
The elderly, those worthy of worship, the devotees of the Lord, the single-minded followers of Hari, astrologers, and divine beings—may they dispel our sins and calamities. (69)
The observance of vows, meritorious deeds, the practice of well-performed actions, service, faith, and meditative cultivation dispel sin and calamities.
Yoga, all forms of knowledge, truth, detachment, and mastery—these, as well as the worship of Hari and his command, dispel sin and calamity. (71)
May the household deities, the village deities, the field deities, those dwelling at the boundaries, the gate deities, and the external deities dispel sins and calamities. (72)
The deities of the dwelling, the deities of the ancestral rites, the deities of the sacrifice, the great festivals, the sacred fords, and the abodes of the gods—these dispel sin and calamity. (73)
Temples, shrines, monasteries, and places of sacred discourse—all these sites of liberation dispel sins and calamities. (74)
Mothers, fathers, elders, kinsmen, virtuous wives, devotees, boys, and girls—may they all dispel our sins and calamities. (75)
All expiations, sacred *darbha* grasses, the weapons of the gods, and the offerings to the gods and ancestors dispel sin and misfortune. (76)
The divine chariots, the paths to the gods, the celestial ways, and the deities,
as well as the escorting gods, shall dispel all sins and calamities.
Lightnings, dense clouds, earthquakes, and likewise calamities—
those gods who receive offerings dispel sins and misfortunes.
The treasures, the quarters of the world, the Manus, and likewise the Kalās,
as well as the fourteen worlds, dispel sin and calamities.
The Vyāhṛtis, the Prāṇāyāmas, the Yāmyas born of the lineage of Dharma, and Dharmadeva along with his wives—may they dispel all sins and calamities. (3.167.80)

The deities of the sacrificial pit and the pavilion, those dwelling upon the branches of the banner, and the deities of the fuel-sticks, vessels, and other implements—may they all dispel sins and calamities. (8.1)
O Lakṣmī, the feet of the true guru, the nectar-water from his feet, and the remnants of food consumed by the guru dispel sin and calamities. (82)
The water from the feet of Satī, the water from the feet of Sādhu, and the meritorious water from the feet of Viṣṇu dispel sins and calamities. (83)
The company of the virtuous, service, taking refuge [in them], their commands and words, as well as their favor and blessings—these dispel sin and misfortune. (84)

The sacred ford of the mother, the sacred ford of the father, the most excellent sacred ford of the guru, the sacred ford of the husband, and the sacred ford of the virtuous wife—these dispel sins and calamities. (85)
Gotīrtha, Avabhṛthatīrtha, Paṅktitīrtha, Dakṣiṇa,
Sannyāsatīrtha, and Mantra— these dispel sins and calamities.
The sacred thread, the necklace made of Tulasī beads, the offering [of one's possessions], and that which is called the surrender of oneself—these dispel sins and calamities. (87)
May their state of being yogis, their excellence, their steadfastness, as well as their Vedic learning, their essence of Brahman, and their devotion, always purify me. (88)
May the purifying Kuṅkumavāpī, the purifying Śrī Narāyaṇa, and the purifying Śrī always purify me, who have come for refuge. 89.
May Dharma, Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Bhakti purify me here through their service; may they purify me, this devotee, as I am now offered unto them. (3.167.90)
Praising her thus and bowing upon the ground, O Lakṣmī, one who maintains a pure livelihood—his calamities perish and his sins indeed turn back. (91)
Whoever recites or even hears this divine hymn of dispelling, and offers leaves, flowers, and so forth, becomes pure at that very moment. (92)
One desiring a daughter shall obtain a daughter; one desiring victory shall obtain victory;
one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth; and one desiring sons shall obtain sons. ||93||
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking enjoyment shall attain enjoyment;
one seeking prosperity shall obtain prosperity; and one seeking a kingdom shall attain a kingdom. ||94||
One desiring heaven shall attain heaven; one desiring liberation shall obtain liberation;
and one longing for the destruction of suffering shall achieve the destruction of suffering. ||95||
One seeking a husband shall obtain a handsome husband; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
and one seeking happiness shall likewise obtain happiness as well as good fortune.
One who desires fame shall likewise obtain preeminence;
by praising [him], one shall attain whatever desires one may seek. (97)
For whomsoever this merit is recited while being read, diseases arising from wind, bile, and other humors shall not afflict them. (98)
For him there shall be no death, nor contact with the venom of fangs;
he shall not suffer untimely misery, for he has dispelled [all such things] by your praise.
One who recites this hymn of removal shall obtain all the merits of every sacred ford, the merits of sacrifices,
and the merits of gifts and vows.

The killer of a cow, the ungrateful person, the slayer of a hero, the slayer of a Brahmin, as well as the slayer of a child, the one who betrays those who have sought refuge, and also the betrayer of a friend’s trust. || 101 ||
A killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a woman, or likewise a slaughterer of animals—
by reciting this praise, he becomes pure, having cast off all sins.
Having offered devotion, one who possesses all merit then goes to that which bestows liberation;
this hymn, known as Vyapohana, provides a refuge for the refugeless.
Having praised Lakṣmī with this [hymn], one should bow to me and then offer prayers;
having meditated and become one with Brahman, one is liberated from these bonds. 104.
Having uttered this with devotion, there remains nothing that ought to be praised;
therefore, in times of impending calamity, one should recite the *Vyapohana*. 105.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, wherein the hymn of *vyapohana* for the purpose of destroying all calamities, sins, bonds, and the like has been declared.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this meritorious account which destroys all sins, bestows all merit, and concerns the gift of a daughter at a sacrifice. || 1 ||
Having performed a sacrifice, having fed and satisfied the virtuous twice-born,
and having given gifts to mendicants, young girls, and children, they were most skilled in bestowing sacrificial fees.
He who bestows his daughter in marriage shall indeed obtain the merit of ten million sacrifices;
he should offer oblations of milk-rice and fruits into the fire within the sacrificial pit in the pavilion.
One should satisfy the ancestral deities with sweet foods, grains such as *kaṇa*, auspicious sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and continuous streams of ghee for nourishment.
Then, one should invoke Kumāraka there in the pavilion—
he who is learned, handsome, renowned, and born of a noble lineage.
He was endowed with youth and brought joy to the hearts of maidens;
he was fortunate, and his character, dharma, virtues, and other qualities were already well known from before.
Having seated him in the presence of the assembly near the fire,
[he should act] with the Brahmins as witnesses and with the fire as witness in the pavilion.
Then, in the presence of the gods who partake of the sacrifice, the father of the girl should worship them with water, flowers, and other offerings, and proclaim her name, lineage, and so forth. (8)
Having observed his fitness for the purpose of the gift, one should have him recite the *svastivācana*;
one should cause him to perform the purification of the body and give him a sacred thread (*yajñopavītaka*).
In the sacrifice, one should cause the Vaiṣṇava and Pārameśvara mantras to be imparted;
there, one should protect the Tulasī plant and then apply the sectarian mark (tilaka).
One should have a crescent moon fashioned with unbroken grains, saffron, and sandalwood; the bridegroom, resplendent and wearing auspicious attire, should bear garlands of flowers.
One should offer ornaments to him and then worship his feet;
one should cause the madhuparka to be given and cause him to consume that which is most pleasing.
One should also cause the sacrificial oblation of milk-rice and other offerings to be offered;
or else, one should have delightful musical instruments played and likewise have songs sung.
One should have Vedic Brahmins recite Vedic mantras and songs,
[invoking] all the gods, Hari, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and Narāyaṇī.
Having paid homage to the fire and the Brahmins, the father approached his daughter,
who was adorned with many ornaments and graced with excellent finery.
Adorned with divine garments and the like, gratified with honors and gifts,
and propitiated for the sake of marriage, she was brought into the pavilion.
In the presence of all people, he should establish himself as a preeminent Vāmaka;
he should bow to the fire, the twice-born, the virtuous, the sages, the elders, and the assembly.
One should also bow to the Kumāra and honor him with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata);
one should apply saffron and akṣata to the forehead of the Kumāra.
"May Nārāyaṇa be pleased with me; may Gaṇeśa be pleased;
may all the deities be pleased; may my desired object be accomplished."
Then, having spoken, the maiden should sit upon the seat offered by the Brahmin;
holding the water in her own hand, she should perform the supreme *saṃkalpa*.
"I am a maiden, a virgin, in the presence of Nārāyaṇa; I have come to the sacrifice in the assembly of the gods for the purpose of being offered. (21)
"To whomsoever my father shall give me in marriage, I will become his lawful wife in the presence of the fire; may there be no obstacle for me here. (22)
Having spoken thus, that maiden should release that water upon the ground;
then her father, or her brother, or her mother, or a kinsman [should perform the remaining rites].
Then, according to the manner previously described, the preceptor should take water in his own hand and likewise give that water into the hand of the boy.
He should also cause the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) to be made and have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) recited;
he should then proclaim his authority as the giver of the girl in the presence of water as witness.
Then one should recite the boy’s eligibility for receiving gifts:
"I, [Name], belonging to the [Gotra] lineage, am here in this pavilion at the sacrifice. (26)
"I shall accept the gift of the maiden for the sake of dharma, with fire as my witness";
having thus made this resolve, the youth should pour water upon the ground. (27)
"I shall protect this maiden, my wife, for as long as I live;
I shall practice our shared duties in the presence of Nārāyaṇa. (28)
After the utterance of "iti" and so forth, the father should recite the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):
"I give this gift of a daughter to this bridegroom, the young man. (29)
"O gods, fire, and other witnesses, this daughter of mine is given to him of such-and-such lineage and name; may she be born as his wife. (3.168.30)
Having spoken thus, he should place the bridegroom’s marriage garland around the neck of the bride through the agency of the girl herself, and cause her hand to bow in salutation.
O beautiful one, she should cause the left hand of the bridegroom to be placed upon her right hand;
adorned with the fruit of desire, she should offer herself in full splendor.
She should form this resolve in her heart: "I am the wife of you, the bridegroom. And the bridegroom should say: "And I am the husband of you, the bride. (33)
The twice-born and others stationed within the pavilion should honor them with flowers;
the groom shall place the garland he himself holds around the neck of the maiden. (34)
Then both, having risen with their garments tied together,
circumambulated the fire four times and returned to their own seats.

Having stood and performed prostrations and other rites, they should then sit down and perform the oblation with ghee and other substances; thereafter, the father should bestow wealth and other gifts.
Others gave gold, garments, a mansion, a carriage, and an excellent vehicle; others gave various auspicious wedding gifts. (37)
Thus, the giving away of one's own daughter in a sacrifice constitutes a Daiva marriage;
with the gods as witnesses, it is indeed the most excellent, the highest of the high. (38)
By the gift of a chest and so forth, the fruit of giving heaven is obtained;
likewise here, by the gift of a trough or a water-jar. (39)
By the gift of a water-pot, one obtains the fruit arising from the gift of the cosmic egg;
likewise, by the gift of cows, land, grain, gold, and so forth, during that sacrifice.
The fruit arising from the gift of the earth and Mount Meru shall belong to the couple.
[The cow] should have horns of gold, hooves of silver, and be provided with a divine garment. (41)
A milch cow with her calf, accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee, should be given; this yields the fruit born of the gift of the world of cows. 42.
As long as the calf's face, complete with its feet, is visible within the womb, for that long the cow is to be known as the Earth; the donor shall attain universal sovereignty.
Massaging those who are weary, nursing the sick, worshiping the gods, honoring the ancestors, venerating the elderly, serving the virtuous, and attending upon one's husband. (44)
The worship of Śatī, as well as the sweeping and cleaning of the temple, and the cleaning of vessels and the like used for food scraps by virtuous yogis—[these are their duties]. (45)
And the pleasing of Brahmins—all that is like the gift of a cow;
it destroys sin, bestows merit, grants heaven, and likewise grants liberation. ||46||
By giving one's own desired object to a virtuous person, one may attain liberation;
by giving one's own desired object to a twice-born brahmin, one may attain heaven. ||47||
By the gift of a married couple, one attains heaven and liberation;
by giving land, lamps, food, clothing, and clarified butter, one shall go to prosperity.
By giving a house, grain, an umbrella, a garland, a tree, a vehicle, clarified butter,
water, a bed, and ointment, one attains heaven.
The giver of the Veda attains the world of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the gods to reach;
as do those who give the meanings of the Vedas, the sacrificial scriptures, and whatever treatises on Dharma there may be.
Likewise, by giving the *saṃhitās*, one shall attain the world of Brahmā;
he who is capable but does not accept [the gift] shall attain the worlds of the donors. (51)
One should accept even from those of evil deeds what comes unasked:
kusha grass, vegetables, milk, clarified butter, curd, and purifying water.
Clothing, oil, sandalwood, saffron, garments, and so forth—
when obtained unasked, these may be accepted by the will of Nārāyaṇa.
That which is obtained by the will of Nārāyaṇī should be accepted by the wise and virtuous;
it should be accepted with detachment and dispassion, and likewise given away to others.
Whatever is given by a husband and wife at a sacrifice, even if it be very small, certainly becomes inexhaustible and yields infinite fruit; there is no doubt in this matter. ||95||
A daughter given away in a sacrifice is born in the form of Lakṣmī;
the groom who receives her is likewise considered to be of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa. ||56||
At that time, in the sacred field of Ācyuta-adhvarabhavana, a gift given indeed becomes imperishable when witnessed by the gods and others. (57)
In this manner, the gift should be bestowed; that indeed is the divine (daiva) form of marriage.
All sins are destroyed, and there shall be the arising of all merit. ||58||
Such a supreme gift does not exist at all in the world of mortals;
listen, O Lakṣmī, to another [gift] which likewise destroys committed sins. (59)
The offering of performed actions to Kṛṣṇa is the destroyer of sin;
such an offering is declared to be beyond the qualities (nirguṇa) and does not lead to worldly enjoyment.
Or he may speak of the faults of a brahmin, a guru, a deity, or a king;
having bowed down, he should ask for forgiveness and touch his right ear.
Furthermore, one should likewise speak words for the sake of maintaining the state of faultlessness;
even when this has been done, no punishment for faults shall apply to him.
He who, for the sake of the gods, gives away even his entire possession along with his very life,
his karmas— even those born of fierce deeds— perish.
Now I shall further proclaim to you the auspicious undertaking of renunciation, which destroys time, illusion, evil karma, fear of Yama, and so forth. (94)
Having performed a sacrifice, one should indeed take up the supreme Vaiṣṇava renunciation;
having attained self-knowledge, one casts off all sins.
Having undertaken the renunciation of karma, one dispels even sins;
by resorting to the holy ford of the virtuous, one shall likewise cleanse all evils.
Now I shall declare another [rite], which is a secondary rite for Vināyaka;
it wards off the sufferings of the wicked and the extremely wicked, and bestows happiness. (67)
In his dreams he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men;
furthermore, his undertakings become fruitless, and he sinks down without apparent cause. (68)
When such hardship has arisen, a king does not obtain his kingdom, nor does a maiden obtain a husband, and a pregnant woman does not obtain a son. (69)
One should perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules at an auspicious moment in the morning;
following the application of an ointment of white mustard seeds, fragrant substances, and clarified butter, one should wash the head.
One should smear [the image] with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances and cause a benediction to be recited;
then, having brought water from a lake in four jars.
Having placed clay, yellow pigment (rocanā), perfumes, and guggulu,
one should bathe the embodied being— who has experienced the dream— on the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) with those waters.
In ancient times, the ṛṣis bathed Indra and liberated him from evil;
even so, we consecrate you, and may the purifying verses (pāvamānyas) cleanse you. ||73||
The Blessed One Varuṇa, King Bhaga, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati;
Indra, Vāyu, and the Seven Sages—all these granted him fortune (bhaga). ||74||
Whatever misfortune resides in your hair, at the parting of your hair, or upon your head; whatever is on your forehead, your ears, or your eyes—may that always go to destruction for you. (75)
Having bathed, one should apply mustard oil to the ears and the head;
then, taking kusha grass with clarified butter, one should offer oblations with pieces of shala wood.
One should likewise offer the Kuṣmāṇḍa and the Rājaputras accompanied by the Svāhā-call,
having spread kuśa grass everywhere upon the ground at a crossroads.
Uncooked rice, variegated and fragrant flowers, wine, food, milk-rice, ghee, curd, and rice with jaggery. (78)
Having placed [the offerings] on the ground and bowed to Śiva, one should feed the virtuous Ambikā;
and with dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, one should pray for the well-being of the virtuous lady.
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me fortune, O bestower of good fortune! Grant me sons, prosperity, all desires, and freedom from obstacles. (3.168.80)
One should satisfy the learned Brahmins and the virtuous with gifts, food, and sandalwood;
one should worship the preceptor and the planets, and offer one's prosperity to Nārāyaṇa. 8.1.
Or rather, O Lakṣmī, having made Duḥkha (Suffering) into an embodied form, one should worship him—one who is emaciated, lame, black-complexioned, with withered hands, and possessed by grief. 82.
With sunken eyes like those of a blind man, hungry, with visible veins, white-haired, ugly, filled with anxiety, and covered in filth; (83)
"O son of Adharma, you who are honored, go far away;
having received this offering of kṛsarā-rice and oil-cake, be happy. (84)
Having thus worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should then dismiss [the deity] at the bank of a river or at the abode of Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by a black cloth.
Having been dismissed and honored, that god of suffering indeed departs;
thus, O Lakṣmī, the god of sin should be worshipped by those who desire happiness. (86)

He was black in color, with stout feet and long hands; his eyes were filled with darkness, his face was black, and he was overcome by fear; he was a performer of cruel deeds and a violent oppressor. ||87||

Having worshipped with black flowers and collyrium, one should offer the bali-oblation consisting of black gram and the like, as well as milk-rice and so forth; then, one should cast it away in the forest.
When this is done, the personification of sin indeed departs far away;
thus, O Lakṣmī, one should worship the God with ease and attain happiness. 89.
With a serene countenance, gentle, well-nourished, white-complexioned, and beautifully adorned;
wearing golden garments, his entire body was rendered radiant, and he was in the full bloom of youth.
Adorned with all ornaments, one should offer the bali-oblation consisting of milk-rice, sweet foods, fruits, and the like, along with auspicious flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
Having worshipped [the deity] endowed with Dharma, endowed with devotion, and joined with virtuous vows and observances, in an auspicious and meritorious temple or likewise in a palace.
Having offered prayers and prostrated with devotion, one should cast [the image] into the water, [saying]:
"O Soul of all, O Lord who bestows great bliss upon all the worlds! (93)
By your dwelling here, great bliss is constantly produced for me; O Avimukta, remain forever and always make your abode here.
By your very glance, O Lord of the World, men become lords in heaven;
by your grace, O God, human beings on earth are made happy. (95)
"By that, may I indeed be happy; O God, be gracious and grant me a boon. Having thus entreated the God, and having worshipped and prostrated before Him, [he remained] in happiness. ||96||
The worshipper should cast [the offerings] into the midst of the water and shall become happy;
whether it be a man or a woman, or neither of these two, [it shall be so] according to the stated method. //97//
Having worshipped [her], one shall obtain fortune, prosperity, and supreme wealth; as well as a son, cattle, land, a wife, and even the expansion of one's lineage. (98)
He constantly attains freedom from suffering and partakes in great festivals; he shall also be immensely prosperous in this world and in the next. (99)
Having fully accomplished great enjoyments, he proceeds to the world of liberation;
neither does his ruin occur, nor does it arise for him unexpectedly.
Suffering and even poverty do not arise unexpectedly;
prosperity, happiness, and all things increase, along with the highest enjoyments. (101)
From reciting, hearing, or worshipping this, there shall be fruit:
one shall become happy and wealthy, and shall become a donor again and again. (102)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatly Fruitful Nature of Giving Away a Daughter at a Sacrifice, Offering [the Merit] to Kṛṣṇa, Taking Up Sannyāsa, Attending upon Vināyaka, and Worshipping Men of Sin, Suffering, and Happiness," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Why is it that even though they are eternal, even though they possess knowledge, and even though they know the state of death, embodied beings still go there? Tell me the cause.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Everything crooked is the domain of death; indeed, those who are crooked go toward death. They practice a devious way of life, for desire and the like are truly killers.
These very enemies, who always dwell within one's own body, are the slayers;
for those devoid of them—namely, for yogis and the virtuous—there is truly no death, O Rame.
Death is indeed declared to be hell, and it is produced by birth and so forth;
birth is obtained through the power of karma, and karma is acquired through latent impressions (vāsanā). || 4 ||
If that [sin] is consumed by peace, self-restraint, and service to the virtuous,
one should wash away the self with devotion to Hari and attain purity.
Then, death in its painful form, known as mortality, does not arise;
having attained a divine state, he goes to the eternal Brahman.
He shall indeed become long-lived and possess eternal sovereignty;
by my power, his bodily elements, which are otherwise subject to death, become divine.
Both negligence and delusion perish in every way for him;
indeed, those two, appearing in the form of death, never enter him at any time.
For my devotee who is free from illusion and established in yoga,
even divine illusion arises as something devoid of bondage and the like.
Then that eternally liberated self proceeds into Brahman alone;
even so, O Lakṣmī, you likewise become thus, just as you were born from the ocean.
You abide by my yoga, free from divine illusion;
you are eternal, perfectly established in equilibrium, and devoid of increase or decrease.
Just as I am, so indeed are you; likewise, Lakṣmī also becomes devoted to me. My will is such that it is produced in exactly that same way by her.
In the past, a battle took place between the Self and the ego;
by means of the ego, this body was made into its own kingdom. (13)
By him, all the fragrance born of his own kingdom was taken away;
only a foul odor remained—a poison that brings death and misery.

The conscious self, having observed its own misdeed—which consists in the destruction of knowledge—and having observed its own engagement in what is not the Self, took up the weapon of discernment. (15)
He abandoned that evil ego, which bestows death;
yet even as it was being struck by that exceedingly swift weapon, the ego persisted.
Having abandoned the healthy portion of water, he entered the earth;
and all the delicious flavor produced by his own kingdom was likewise taken away by him.
The poison that remained, its potency already experienced, was death-dealing and painful;
moreover, he himself cast a weapon at him for the sake of his destruction. (18)
Being struck down, Ahaṅkāra entered the region of light;
there he assumed a beautiful form belonging to his own kingdom.
Then the conscious self (cidātman) again cast at him a sharp weapon called discernment (viveka), which left him both deformed and powerless. (3.169.20)
Although being struck, the ego entered the realm of air;
there it assumed touch, which is known as "good," belonging to its own kingdom.
Seeing him still standing there as before, Kusparśa, for his destruction, once again discharged a weapon at him. ||22||
The ego-sense, spreading through the subtle ether, grasped the sound residing therein;
and having perceived that sound again in the same manner, it remained as a residual trace.
As soon as the conscious self (cidātmā) seized a weapon and began to slay him, egoism (ahaṃkāra), though previously without support, entered into that conscious self. 24.
The conscious self, having become the Guru, also instructed the ego-sense;
that ego-sense then held fast to the thought: "I am of the very nature of Brahman. (25)
Then, through the conceit of being the very nature of Brahman, he attained the state of Brahman;
though he was merely illusory, by the word of his guru and through meditative worship, he attained the state of Brahman.
The conscious self (cidātman) struck him with discernment, yet it did not cause any injury;
therefore, remaining established in the Self, he was born free from death. ||27||
Having abandoned one's own individual nature and attained the state of the conscious self, one reaches the condition of being invulnerable and takes recourse in the divine sense of "I. ||28||
Having resorted to divine intellect, he attained the Supreme Self;
established in the self through divine intellect, he was born forever invincible. ||29||
Having attained the state of liberation through supreme devotion to the Supreme Lord, no obstruction whatsoever arises for those liberated ones who possess divine principles. ||3.169.30||
In this way, O Lakṣmī, destruction indeed follows from death through the act of surrender;
[it occurs] through the surrender of the self, of all the senses, and of all actions. (31)
Indeed, the offering of the mental modifications together with the self into Brahman is devoid of qualities;
for in Me, who am beyond qualities, there is no death that brings suffering to the worlds.
O Lakṣmī, diseases are of two kinds: physical and likewise mental;
their arising is mutual among those that depend upon one another. (33)
For wind, bile, and phlegm arise from the body when they are in a state of imbalance;
indeed, their equilibrium is declared to be the healthy state and that is what is called health. (34)
Just as a medicinal herb is suppressed by its opposite, so cold is suppressed by heat, and heat is suppressed by cold. (35)
Likewise, when there is a mental affliction, the mild is crushed by the sharp;
sorrow is overcome by joy, and joy is overcome by sorrow. (36)
If there is equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, that is the health of the self;
their imbalance is indeed disease, and for that, massage is prescribed. (37)

One who possesses suffering strives for happiness, while one who is happy even remembers suffering; both these states arise from the qualities [of the mind] and belong to the mind, not to the Self. (38)
Nevertheless, having acquired momentum, that embodied being flows along with its current and forms attachments, imagining them as his own mental states. (39)
If one obtains from the mouth of a true guru that ancient wisdom which is of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, then the mind desires its own dissolution. (3.169.40)
One strives for its destruction with the weapon of wisdom;
indeed, the self itself becomes the warrior, having mounted the chariot of Brahman. (41)
Then, O Lakṣmī, the self shall conquer the state of the Supreme Brahman;
one should utterly renounce all external requisites, the Vaiśya, and material wealth.
Being free from attachment and without possessiveness, one will then attain perfection;
for as long as the thought "this is mine" arises, death remains present. (43)
When the notion "this is mine" no longer exists, death has passed away for him;
for him, the eternal truth "I am Brahman" shines forth clearly.
O Lakṣmī, for such a person of discernment, there is indeed an infinite sovereignty over the universe consisting of both the moving and the stationary. 45.
Nevertheless, he has no sense of "mine-ness"; what can death do to him?
Having placed the state beyond death at his feet, he has gone to the eternal Brahman.
O Lakṣmī, even while one dwells in the forest living on wild produce,
death clings to one's very hair if one has not abandoned the sense of "mine-ness."
Having perceived with the inner self the illusion of "mine-ness" regarding both external and internal things, one remains as the nature of the inner Brahman; this is liberation from the great fear.
All activities in the world are born of desire;
if, after reflecting, one becomes free from desire and withdraws the mind, [then liberation is attained]. ||49||
By the very withdrawal of the causal [state], further nourished by the power of repeated practice,
he crosses the flow of illusion and attains the eternal Brahman.
One should hang upon the essential path—charity, vows, austerity, and sacrifice;
for even that which is essential becomes essence-less if one pursues it without having made desireless.
Whatever one may pursue after having performed the offering to Hari, which is of great essence,
all that shall serve for his crossing over or indeed act as his helper.
Suppression is indeed the seed of liberation, while exertion is the seed of worldly existence.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the ancient verse concerning how this occurred for the individual soul.
Once, while he himself was happy, the Self questioned Abhimāna, who stood by his side and was repeatedly a powerful obstacle to his happiness. (54)
How and by what means is your destruction to come, if you are one whose vow is true?
Tell me, so that upon your destruction I may attain happiness. (55)
Then that personification of egoism, displaying the strength of his beard, spoke angrily to the embodied being: "Listen, I shall tell you the truth. (56)
No one arisen from this world can indeed bring about my destruction here,
except for Nārāyaṇa or a person who is a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata).
I cannot be slain by any being possessed of attachment; for whatever power or weapon is used to slay me, that very power and weapon are themselves destroyed.
Indeed, he will not be able to kill me as long as that which nourishes the seed remains, so that I may manifest once again.
If he strives to kill me by means of sacrifices and other rites rich in sacrificial fees, my nourishment shall arise from his desire for dharma; thus do I manifest myself.
Even if he strives to kill me through silent recitation or through silence, my nourishment here consists in his sense of "I-ness" (sāhaṃbhāva); by that, I manifest myself.
If one strives to kill me by means of the Vedantas or the paths of knowledge, I manifest myself through that very effort, thinking, "He has been killed by me," thereby nourishing the ego.
If one strives to kill me through renunciation and dispassion, my delusion manifests elsewhere; nourished by that [effort], I appear.
Even those who have renounced the world may live as negligent, with minds turned outward, malicious, and eager for quarrels, their intentions corrupted by the gods. (64)
Even if he strives to slay me through fortitude and the vow of celibacy,
I shall arise once more through the nourishment of the seed known as the pride of victory.
If he strives to strike me down through the attainments of ascetic power and sovereignty, or by means of the miraculous feats and yogic perfections such as Madhumatī and the rest; ||66||
I am born again through the extreme nourishment of those things whose nature is seed;
and even if one strives to kill me by means of practices for the sake of liberation, [it is impossible].
I dance and I laugh at that ignorant one who is satisfied with his own means;
I, the eternal one, am invincible to those who desire such things.

If even a slight sense of "mine-ness" or attachment toward what is contrary [to liberation] or toward what is desired by oneself should arise, then having obtained existence therein, I become a creator of the bonds of saṃsāra. (69)
The state of "mineness" is a condition of the mind; it perishes when the mind is destroyed.
Just as the defects of the earth vanish when glass is absent, there is no doubt about this. (3.169.70)
Nevertheless, even for glass, the state of being broken does not perish;
likewise, the sense of "mine" within the self does not ultimately perish. (71)
Upon reaching the dissolution, the earth dissolves into water;
in this sequence, the dissolution of the principles (tattvas) occurs within the principle of Mahat. ||72||
When the mind dissolves, when Māyā dissolves, when the state of being a living soul is obstructed, and when the nature of the Self shines forth, may there be death for me—death as non-rebirth. (73)
The sudden manifestation of the Self occurs through the power of the Supreme Lord’s grace;
for it is held that by offering everything to Him, my own [limited] existence comes to an end. (74)
O Lakṣmī, having been addressed thus in the past by his profound self-conceit, this very person should indeed strive toward me, the Supreme Lord, the Immutable.
Through the state of total surrender and other such means, that sense of "I" perishes; and the sense of "mine" also dissolves, having fallen into the Supreme Self. (76)
Just as salt, once fallen into the ocean, is always dissolved and never sprouts again anywhere, so too does Kṛṣṇa prevent the sprouting of this [seed].
Having understood this, the virtuous person strives for the supreme surrender of the self in its entirety—even of the body, senses, mind, vital breath, ego, and the great principle (mahat). //78//
Indeed, by offering even the existence of sattva, rajas, and tamas—which possess the qualities of being, consciousness, and bliss—one performs the offering of everything. (79)
Indeed, for devotees through the offering of everything to Me, all things become My own nature by virtue of their union with Me; they do not lead to bondage. (3.169.80)
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell the story of my devotee;
there, on the shore of this lake, was a devotee named Sādhubhāvāyana. (81)
Having contracted all his mental functions (vṛttis), he became established in meditative absorption (samādhi);
at that moment, the personification of ego (ahaṃkāra-puruṣa) appeared near him.
Terror-inspiring, of fierce form, black in color, and exceedingly robust, he laughed and spoke to that abode of goodness within his heart: 835.
"Who are you, and why indeed do you expel me from my house?
I am established in a vow, yet possessed of egoism and situated within the realm of merit. (84)
In giving, there is the egoism of "I am," established in the dharma of heaven;
and in sacrifice, there is the egoism of "I am," established in the activity of the agent. ||85||
The sphere of sacrificial fees is established in the state of being a sacrificer,
while the ego-sense is situated in the sphere of purity at the sacred ford.
Even in service, the egoism remains fixed in the thought "I am doing it";
and in recitation, the egoism is established in the function of destroying sin.
Even in the practice of celibacy, there is the egoism of one who stands thinking "I am a practitioner of vows";
even in knowledge, there is the egoism of one who is established in the thought "I am a scholar. (88)
Even in dispassion, there remains the ego-sense, established in the thought "I am indeed faultless";
and even in renunciation, there is the ego-sense: "I am indeed the destroyer of saṃsāra. (89)
Even in meditation there is the sense of "I," thinking, "I am the meditator, I am the practitioner of yoga";
even in samādhi there is egoism, thinking, "I am the Lord, possessed of illusory power. (3.169.90)
Thus, while some maintain that my departure occurs in one fortnight, others hold that my life continues in the other;
therefore, I am never truly dead. (9.1)
With a single spirit of offering, I go; and when offered, I take refuge in merit, action, its fruit, devotion, the self, livelihood, and the mind. (92)
If my intellect and I are both offered unto the Supreme Lord,
then we all shall go to that auspicious refuge which is the locus of offering.
"Leaving aside the one to whom [the mind] is offered, we shall proceed by means of the act of giving;
therefore, O virtuous one, offer up your intellect—this illusion adorned with the three qualities. (94)

Likewise, ignorance and knowledge, the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) which rests upon the Bull (Śiva), all states beginning with dharma, and the mind as well, which possesses dharma—[all these he created]. 95.
All the sense organs, the deities, the internal functions, all external instruments, the subtle elements, and their respective objects—[all these constitute the ego]. ||96||
The objects, the five elements, the elemental products, and the sense-organs,
as well as their fruits, the qualities, and whatever actions there may be— ||97||
Relinquish all strivings, as well as all latent tendencies, mental cultivations, relationships, and likewise all conditioned formations. (98)
Offer yourself with devotion to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
then I, together with my own family, shall go [to him], and not otherwise. 99.
Having heard this, he suddenly recognized me as his friend, rose from his meditative absorption,
and offered himself unto me, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Bhagavān Bhavāyana rendered the entire ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) excellent;
having become entirely absorbed in me, he offered it as a self-surrendered gift. || 101 ||
Thus, having abandoned yoga, meditative absorption, and the like, she offered all her ritual actions, consisting of service, unto the illustrious Pauruṣottamī Nārāyaṇa.
Then his pride dissolved into the Supreme Self;
he too became eternally liberated, having become one with me, the indweller of the imperishable.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this complete surrender is the means for destroying suffering;
it is the means for liberation, as it consists entirely of offering oneself to Me.
From reciting and hearing this, freedom from possessiveness arises;
likewise, from practicing it, primordial liberation also arises. (105)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of Death, the Means for Their Destruction, and the Dissolution of Pride through the Method of Offering to Kṛṣṇa by Way of the Example of the Sages," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O beloved Kṛṣṇa, out of compassion for living beings, please describe here those universally accepted duties leading to liberation which bring about the destruction of delusion.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, together with all your companions;
I shall declare the beneficial duties that bestow both spiritual perfections and liberation.
O Lakṣmī, you know that my supreme abode, the imperishable, the highest ether, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the place of liberation.
In the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Goloka is eternally served by me,
who am myself served by the multitude of gopīs beginning with Rādhā.
The first is the supreme abode, the second is the imperishable state, and the third abode is Goloka; that is my place of liberation.
In the fourth realm, indeed Vaikuṇṭha, I, Nārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Lord, dwell, served by Lakṣmī and others, as well as by my attendants and the rest.
In the fifth, O beloved, I, as Vāsudeva, together with Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others,
