always dwell in the unmanifest abode, the place of liberation.
In the sixth world, called Amṛta, I dwell by the name Bhūman;
I am the dispenser of justice for the lords, the Great King of Kings.
In the seventh abode, Śrīpura, I dwell as the Lord of Lalitā;
worshipped by Mahālakṣmī, I assume the form of Mahāviṣṇu.
This very Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī, united with Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, who is my fortunate mother, exists upon the earth even today. (3.170.10)
In the eighth realm, which is primordial, composed of Māyā, and pertaining to the Puruṣa,
I dwell as the Lord, being the very essence of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
For that is the place of liberation for the form of the Great Being;
it is the ninth [level], belonging to Sadāśiva, known as the eternal Kailāsa.
The tenth abode is Vaiṣṇava, served by Śrī Viṣṇu;
and the eleventh abode is Vairāja, which contains millions of Īśvaras.
The twelfth is indeed the Mātsya, and likewise the thirteenth is the Kaurma;
the fourteenth is the Vārāha, and the fifteenth is the Kāpila. ||14||
Then I shall take away the sixteenth [incarnation], that of Vāsudeva;
and then the eighteenth, that of Pārtha, followed by that of Dāttātreya.
The twentieth is the abode based on the Haṃsa; the twenty-first is the Nārasiṃhaka;
the twenty-second is the Ārṣabha; and the twenty-third is the Vāmana.
The twenty-fourth is based on Paraśurāma; after that, the Yājña;
then also the Rāmadhāma, and the twenty-seventh is like that of Kumāra.
The twenty-eighth is Hayaśīrṣa, and after that, Nārada;
the thirtieth is Rājarājāḍhya, while the thirty-first belongs to Vyāsa.
The thirty-second is Buddhist; the thirty-third is associated with Māhinī;
the thirty-fourth is not neuter; and likewise, there are innumerable [forms] within the syllables.
Indeed, these many forms of mine and likewise my incarnations exist within the regions and boundaries of the Imperishable; thus I sport there.
Furthermore, from that [source], my abodes are infinite;
they have been created in such a manner for the fulfillment of the aspirations of my devotees. (21)
O Dear One, all places of liberation are attained by human beings according to their devotion and their station, through the power of their worship;
likewise, there are many other such places here in this world.
The realm of Vaikuṇṭha within the covering of water, as well as the Satyaloka abode of Brahmā.
And also Badaryāśrama itself, belonging to me, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
that place is auspicious, bestowing liberation, and granting worldly emancipation. (24)
I alone remain there in the abode named Śvetadvīpa, which is free from food and frequented by liberated souls; there I abide as Śeṣa, served by Lakṣmī and others.
The lunar station as well as the solar station shine for me there,
and likewise my divine golden form is situated within the fire.
Also the region of Kubera, that of Yama, that of the Maruts, and that of Indra;
likewise the region of Īśāna, Kailāsa, that of Śiva, and the region of Varuṇa in the waters.
Indeed, my abodes are innumerable, equal in bliss to liberation;
likewise, there are places that grant happiness even in the netherworlds (pātālas).
O Lotus-born One, all those things existing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) that are peaceful indeed become fit for liberation in this very life.
For even the abodes of the lords, though they grant long-lasting happiness, are indeed equal to liberation,
since they are peaceful at the time of universal dissolution.
Indeed, all those [beings] who are subject to destruction become worthy of eternal liberation through my desire. (31)
O Lakṣmī, without the syllables and words, the Great Abode shines; and without others, the worlds and divine stations shine and dissolve within it.
When I, possessed of yoga, become the very nature of the Supreme Brahman,
united with Rādhā and united with Ramā, then the abodes are created by me.
O Lotus-born One, all things indeed manifest from Brahman within the abode of the Imperishable; for all things have Brahman as their essence and culminate in Brahman.
And in some cases, even the abode of the syllable (akṣaradhāman) dissolves entirely within me—the Lord who abides in the supreme abode, the beginningless Supreme Brahman. (35)
My supreme abode exists eternally, from which the imperishable and other [entities] repeatedly manifest,
and by which even millions of liberated souls shine forth.
And those who have taken refuge in me, or those who have taken refuge in my incarnations,
or those who have taken refuge in my lords, or those who have taken refuge in my form— ||37||
Those who have taken refuge in my portions, or those who have resorted to my majesty;
those who have taken refuge in my saints, or those who have fully resorted to my power. ||38||
Devoted to meditation on me and intent upon my service, they are attached to serving my virtuous male devotees as well as my virtuous female devotees. (39)
Those who have taken refuge in my poetic art, or those who have resorted to my divine possession;
those who have taken refuge in my lineage, and those who have resorted to my wives.
Those who have dedicated their very selves and all their possessions for my sake—all of them abide on my path; they have taken refuge in my way. (41)
Those who have set out upon my path and those who are traveling along my path—all of them, filled with affection for me, have come into my presence. ||42||
They indeed attain liberation; led by me, they are brought to my abode. Having ascended the path of gradual progression, they reach the supreme state. ||43||
Human beings, seers, gods, ancestors, as well as sages; the virtuous, the perfected ones, noble men, truthful women, and chaste wives—[all these are present]. (44)
Those Vaiṣṇavas who have surrendered themselves to Me, as well as those who have taken refuge in My yogis—they all indeed [attain the goal] in due order. (45)
By the power of worshipping my own portion, they will gradually come to me;
and through them, the dharma of liberation, which is progressive in nature, shall flourish here.
For those knowers who directly take refuge in me through the Vedic compendium,
there shall be attainment of my city-abode even without following the sequential path.
Thus indeed many have gone to my state by taking refuge in me;
those who worship my true nature shall gradually attain my state. 48.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I compassionately established the path to liberation in this world; having followed it, those who have taken refuge in me shall cross over the forest of worldly existence. 49.
Once, the illustrious Mānasā Muni was seated on the ground beneath a banyan tree on the bank of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, chanting the praises of Hari.
He beheld a yogi who had reached the further shore of knowledge and realization, who was skilled in the meaning of all principles, and who could distinguish between pleasure and pain. ||51||
He remembers his past births, is skilled in discerning merit and demerit, knows himself,
and indeed understands the destinies resulting from the actions that govern embodied beings.
He was moving about like one who is liberated, perfected, tranquil, and a master of his senses;
he was blazing with Brahmanic splendor and possessed knowledge of the art of invisibility.
Thus, as he proceeded slowly followed by invisible devotees of the Lord,
the illustrious Mānasa rose up and prostrated before the yogin.
He gratified him, who is named Consciousness and Bliss, with greetings and other courtesies;
for he was indeed pleased by his disposition, faith, devotion, and service.
The illustrious Cidānanda spoke appropriately to the sage Śrīmānasa:
"Listen, O holy one; impelled by Kṛṣṇa, I shall speak here out of compassion. (56)
The entire world belongs to Kṛṣṇa alone;
everything is fashioned for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, and everything is employed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, for the purpose of liberation and the attainment of divinity. (57)
That which is directed toward another, setting aside Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of attaining worldly goals, may grant the attainment of worldly ends, but not eternal liberation. (68)
Through various actions and solely through the application of merit,
mortals indeed attain auspicious states of existence, such as residence in the world of the gods.
Therein is no ultimate happiness, nor therein is there eternal stability;
rather, from that great position, one falls again and again, having attained it only with difficulty. (3.170.60)
Such foul destinies as these, many and terrible, ending in downfall and accumulated through evil deeds, have been reached by me and by you in the past. (61)
It is filled with desire, anger, great delusion, thirst, passion, and the like;
for there indeed is death again and again, and there is constant brooding over it. (62)
Various kinds of food have been eaten, and countless breasts have been drunk from;
various mothers have been seen, and fathers likewise of diverse sorts. (63)
The various pleasures of men as well as of women, and likewise their various sufferings and many lamentations—(all these arise from the mind). //64//
In various places, they repeatedly beat their chests; they even struck their heads and committed suicide in many ways. (65)
Separations from loved ones, numerous dwellings together with those who are disliked, and the destructions of accumulated wealth for those who have fallen into suffering. (66)
There are insults and great hardships from kings and from one's own kin, as well as physical and mental agonies that are exceedingly terrible. (67)
Insults of a terrible nature, killings and cruel imprisonments, the extreme hardships of dependence, and likewise the agonies of disease; ||68||
There are also the torments born of Yama, falls into hell, many births and diseases, and dreadful old age and ailments. (69)
All the calamities that cause terror, arising from the pairs of opposites, have been experienced by me and by you again and again in this world. (3.170.70)
Indeed, through your beginningless union with Kṛṣṇa, the mental net has been abandoned,
and the bodily [net] too has always been abandoned in Śrī Hari, the Supreme Self.
And you shall dwell happily here at this supreme, purifying site of Hari’s feet, in the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, which bestows liberation like a divine pearl. (72)
Having reflected upon everything, I attained supreme detachment and took refuge at the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having abandoned worldly ways, though afflicted by suffering, he maintained virtuous conduct;
having experienced every form of pain, he followed this path. (74)
Then, by the grace of the Supreme Self, I also attained perfection;
thereafter, I [saw] the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī.
Having seen, bowed to, and worshipped [it], I shall go to the supreme state;
having performed my pilgrimage, I shall not return here again. (76)
And upon seeing you again, divine perfection was born within me here; until the final dissolution and until the creation of beings, my own destinies have become auspicious. (77)
I find no higher [attainment] than this; thus, this is the supreme perfection.
I have entrusted all that is auspicious to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. (78)
Not even a trace of auspicious merit remains for me to enjoy from that;
henceforth, I shall go to the supreme abode of Śrī Hari. (79)
The state of the supreme Brahman is the most excellent; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
Indeed, I shall not return again here to this world of creation, which is full of suffering.
"O knower of the Self, seeing you here as my supreme divine devotee of Lord Hari, I am pleased with you; tell me, what may I do for you? (8.1)
This auspicious time has arrived to offer one's mind to the Lord;
through the service of a self-surrendering devotee, everything is attained.
Through faith, great liberation is attained; there is no doubt in this.
Just as you have become faithful here, so should you demonstrate service. (83)
I am greatly pleased with your devotion and your worship of Hari; ask whatever you desire, and I shall explain it all to you. (84)
I hold your devotion in high regard and I honor you greatly;
since I have achieved my purpose through you, tell me quickly, what shall I give? (85)
Having been addressed thus, the illustrious Mānasaka, having honored that divine personage, Cidānanda, with excellent gifts, questioned him at length with great intelligence. (86)
How does the body come to destruction? How does the body come into being? How does the embodied soul, while wandering through saṃsāra, become completely liberated from saṃsāra? ||87||
How does illusion dissolve, and how does one enter into illusion?
Having abandoned one body, how does one attain another? (88)
How does the self experience its own acquired merit and demerit?
And having exhausted both merit and demerit, how does it attain Brahman? ||89||
Where does the karma of this disembodied living being reside? Upon what support is one meditated for the sake of destroying the fruits of karmas? (3.170.90)
How and by what power is divinity established here?
How is there eternal liberation, and how is there the state of being permeated by the Imperishable? ||91||
"Explain how even that very similarity could come to be; examine those [points]," thus did the mental [son] Lakṣmī ask Citānanda. (92)
But Cidānanda, out of compassion, remembered me, the Supreme Lord, and after reflecting upon all the questions according to their proper order, he spoke the answer. 93.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Abodes within the Duties for Liberation and the Mutual Questions between the Illustrious Mānasa and Sacidānanda Yogins," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Thus impelled, the powerful yogi, full of consciousness and bliss,
spoke all the answers to the questions in due order, O Rame, from his heart.
Listen as I describe them to you in due order, O Kamala,
those life-prolonging actions that a living being performs until the end of his existence.
The continuity of such a lifespan is established here itself as supreme;
likewise are merit, service to assemblies, service to the virtuous, and auspicious blessings. (3)
Generosity, restraint of the senses, celibacy, auspicious austerity,
the practice of yoga, and devotion— all these indeed promote longevity.
Service to the sacred fire, the use of medicinal herbs, non-violence, the consumption of ghee, and eating the remains of sacrificial offerings—
these indeed increase one's lifespan.

The holy ford of a chaste wife, the holy ford of a mother, the holy ford of dharma, and the worship of the gods—indeed, freedom from passion and non-indulgence in sensual pleasures; these truly bestow long life.
Offering to the sages (ṛṣyarpaṇa), likewise offering to the gods (devārpaṇa), offering to Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇārpaṇa),
offering to the eternally liberated (nityamuktārpaṇa), and offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa) are indeed bestowers of long life.
Friendship with those who dwell in heaven bestows heavenly life;
thus, the fortunate man who performs such action attains both longevity and renown.
One whose self is overwhelmed by the exhaustion of life-span resorts to perverted practices;
when destruction is imminent, his intellect turns away from the truth.
Relying upon his strength and power, as well as pride and self-conceit, the man lacking self-mastery excessively indulges in enjoyment, even that which is contrary to his own welfare. (3.171.10)
He indulges in extremely harsh practices and consumes excessive amounts according to his capacity;
he eats spoiled food, meat, and drinks that are mutually incompatible in their qualities.
He eats heavy foods in immoderate quantities, even when his previous meal is undigested, and repeatedly;
he indulges excessively in excessive physical exercise and sexual intercourse;
and out of constant greed for wealth, he subjects himself to the burden of carrying heavy loads.
He indeed becomes exceedingly impetuous with the desire for victory. || 13 ||
Bound by the fetters of karma, a person overeats food mixed with corrupted tastes and suppresses the urges of urine, feces, and other bodily excretions. (14)
He indulges in proper sleep and does not indulge in sleeping during the day;
yet, being overcome by his sense of taste, he consumes even undigested juices.
Becoming filled with disease and affliction, he experiences the decay of the body;
though exceedingly tormented, lacking energy, and utterly defeated by great hardships.
Abandoning fortitude, he would suddenly face death, even if he encounters adverse circumstances such as imprisonment and the like. || 17 ||
By such contrary conditions, the body quickly perishes;
its heat is obstructed, it becomes agitated, and the vital winds (vāyu) become excessively forceful. || 18 ||
Suddenly severing the bonds, it casts the vital breaths out from the internal cavity;
it pierces the vital points (marmas) that maintain the health of the living being. || 19 ||
Then, upon the immediate destruction of knowledge, the individual soul falls from its station;
here, enveloped by the subtle body, it abandons the perishable gross body. (3.171.20)
Indeed, conscious of birth and death, he goes elsewhere;
others see him departing and abandoning his gross body. (21)
Nevertheless, they do not attain detachment, nor do they worship me;
they die in that very same state, abandoning everything right here.
They experience pain at the time of death through the striking of their vital organs and so forth; likewise, they undergo intense suffering during the transition into the womb.
Living beings experience sensations produced by birth, produced by the body, and joined with repeated death; there is no end to them. (24)
When he indeed abandons the body and is seen without breath, he is devoid of warmth, breathless, stripped of splendor, and his consciousness destroyed. (25)
And when he is abandoned by me and by Brahmā, he is then said to be a "dead self";
for by whichever channels the bearer of the body perceives the objects of the senses, [by those same channels he departs]. (26)
By the cessation of their vital breaths, there would be the dissolution of the channels;
when the vital points (*marmans*) where the channels reside are pierced, [the body] is beloved no more. (27)
As he departs, he becomes unpleasant; he perceives nothing at all, yet, endowed with life and accompanied by the subtle body, he breathes out three times. (28)
As it departs, it quickly causes even the gross and slightly insentient body to tremble;
having fallen away from the body, it is indeed enveloped by its own karmas. (29)
Accompanied by immeasurable sins and merits, possessing a subtle body,
he proceeds to another state of existence, which is fashioned in three ways according to his past actions.
Having attained a human state where merit and demerit are equal, one proceeds to that destiny;
even in this very world, one surely experiences various high and low enjoyments according to one's own actions.
Indeed, through impure actions, people go to the lower realms;
they go to that place where they are cooked in hell as the fruit of their deeds. (32)
Those who possess merit indeed proceed to the higher realms consisting of stars, even to the lunar orb and the solar orb as well. (33)
Having enjoyed such delightful things as these, upon the exhaustion of their merit, they fall again;
they go to the earth, undergoing rebirth and death once more. (34)
Furthermore, impelled by their karma, they go again to heaven or to hell;
and even in heaven there is no satisfaction upon seeing a more radiant splendor. (35)
The gods—whether in their low, high, or middling states—both covet and seize;
having reflected thus, the wise man should regard the subtle body as belonging to the Lord Hari. (36)
Having made this offering, one who has become divine indeed departs for the imperishable state;
likewise, [one offers] the eye, the function of the eye, the eyeball, and the deity. (37)
The object, as well as form itself; knowledge, awakening, and the knower; reflection, determination, and conceit; and the entirety of experience—[all these are the self]. (38)
Likewise, O Keśava, having offered himself, the formative impressions (saṃskāras), and even his memory, and having performed the offering of all that has been offered as a self-surrender; ||39||
Having either fashioned or cast off a subtle and divine body,
and having abandoned union with material nature (prakṛti), he established himself in the yoga of Brahman.
Having completely burnt away all latent impressions through my meditation, I rejoice;
the Supreme Brahman, Hari, the Puruṣottama, indeed enters into me. 41.
Thus, having abandoned the three bodies, one attains the eternal Brahman;
[one abandons] all objects such as fragrances and the like, as well as all outward flows in every way.
Likewise, having placed within me the internal currents, as well as the fruit and enjoyment,
and having abandoned the triad, he goes to me, the Supreme Lord.
O Lotus-born one, upon the exhaustion of karma, the destruction of the gross body occurs;
upon the exhaustion of merit and demerit, the destruction of the subtle body arises.

Through the flow of the bliss of Brahman and the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), this subtle body (liṅgadeha), which consists of latent impressions, dissolves by means of my [true] being. 45.
There is also the dissolution of the body, which has ignorance as its cause;
hear now how the attainment of the Self by the body truly occurs. (46)
O Lakṣmī, the union with a body occurs through various causes for that God who is of the nature of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss and who is likewise bodiless. 47.
This self is pure and divine; it resides either in the Imperishable (akṣara), or in a region of the Imperishable, or at its boundary, or in the presence of the objects of Māyā. 48.
By its very nature, it assumes the qualities of proximity like a crystal;
those very qualities, being foreign, lead it to be designated as something else by others. (49)
Having attained those illusory phenomena which consist of the rules governing manifestation, I have been revealed and have become active, endowed with those very regulations. (3.171.50)
In this way, the self thinks through the functions of the principle of illusion (māyātattva) and so forth;
whether it be a conclusion, self-conceit, reflection, or cogitation—[all these constitute the nature of the mind]. (51)

He indeed knows that which consists of the radiance of Māyā, as well as that which consists of his own radiance; he knows both his own cognition alone and that which is mixed with the radiance of Māyā.
This mixture and delusion is indeed designated as ignorance (avidyā);
by means of it, the self engages in actions consisting of merit and demerit. //53//
Indeed, auspicious and inauspicious actions arise for this [agent] through illusion;
and a taint from those auspicious and inauspicious [actions] arises for him upon their experience. (54)
Through its attachment to knowledge, it is also smeared by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced thereby;
and that attachment which exists in the impression consisting of dharma resides in that which has a transparent nature. (55)
When these arise in the *ādhāra* within the living being (*jīva*), the *jīva* wanders through transmigratory existence;
even though it is joined with the subtle body (*sūkṣma*), it strives for the sake of attaining its own desired enjoyments and so forth. (56)
Endowed with those subtle elements, this [self] obtains the gross material body;
having attained gross inertia, it becomes exceedingly inert through being cooked by the gross elements. (57)
Possessing gross states and enjoying sense-objects, he becomes greedy for karma;
having repeatedly obtained various fields of action, again and again, [he wanders]. (58)
He enjoys enjoyments consisting of pleasure, which are granted by the impressions of his past fortune;
and from that, he subsequently obtains a long-lasting fruit to be experienced for a long time through them.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even though he is unattached, he obtains inexhaustible fruit to be enjoyed throughout many births, due to the very nature of attraction. (3.171.60)
Having drawn forth other qualities, he establishes his own sovereignty,
just as one who is not a king, yet being powerful, seizes a kingdom and becomes a ruler.
In this way, this embodied being is born, possessing the yoga of attraction;
though devoid of illusion, he becomes possessed of illusion, and once born, he does not cease.
One who enters into an ever-deepening state of attachment is not liberated;
just as a leather-worker does not abandon even a foul-smelling hide-drum.
Enveloped by the accumulation of karma, he does not abandon this wretched body;
he undergoes auspicious, inauspicious, or mixed karma. (64)
Just as a fruit-bearing tree, when it comes into flower, yields abundant fruit,
so too shall there be great merit for him who acts with a virtuous mind.
Likewise, one goes toward evil through evil committed by the mind; then, joined with the mind, this [being] proceeds as one who is greatly indolent.
Just as a servant gives to his master, so does he eat;
and when he desires enjoyments once more, his life-span comes to an end.
Impelled by desire, this being is led into the dwelling of the womb;
through its mind and its merits and demerits, it lies within the womb, powerless. (68)
The semen, mixed with blood, becomes the *kalala*, the precursor of the body; it enters the womb, conforming to its past merits and demerits. (69)
One enters the *kalala* stage according to the influence of past karma; another enters the *budbuda* stage according to his own karma. (3.171.70)
By virtue of their own karma, one enters the flesh, another the muscle,
one enters the internal cavity, and another a well-formed doll of limbs.
One enters into a statue limb by limb, while another even enters into an embryo;
this occurs either quickly or after a long time, according to the influence of past karma.
When the effigy has been fully nourished with flowers and water, and has been sustained by heat and other means over time,
the living soul indeed enters it through its own karma.
Due to its subtlety and its unmanifest state, the individual soul (jīva), possessing a subtle body, enters [the womb] indeed; there it becomes attached by means of karma determined within.
Therein dwells the Great Brahman, the protector even of the seed;
I too reside there together with that Supreme Brahman, the seed of seeds. 75.
He is the doer, the instigator, the nourisher, the creator, the protector, and the observer;
He is the witness, the unattached one, and the bestower of the fruits of action. ||76||
And for all embodied beings, I am the eternal seed of seeds; I abide as the impeller of the evolving principles that fill [the universe].
"Living beings live by means of the vital breath, the sense organs, and other life-sustaining factors;
that very life-force, having entered all the limbs of the embryo at that time," (78)
Established in the support of the vital breaths (prāṇas), he immediately bestows [consciousness] through wisdom;
by means of that, he causes the limbs and so forth to move, and thus he is called "the living one" (sajīva). ||79||
Just as a small amount of liquid gold transforms an entire copper statue into one made of gold, so too does it transform the body into one consisting of the living soul (jīva).
This conscious being performs this entry into the living soul, just as fire, having entered a lump of iron, makes it its own form. (81)
Likewise, having entered the insentient, this [consciousness] should determine it through its own consciousness, just as a lamp, though itself shining, illuminates the house. //82//
And just as one situated in a single place illuminates both itself and another, so too the Person (puruṣa), though residing within the heart, illuminates the three bodies. ||83||
There, in the womb, he experiences until the ninth month that which was previously performed and is suitable for gestation;
likewise, in the tenth month, [he experiences] the effects of his actions from a previous birth.
Knowledge also arises, and then he moves outside;
the karma of the womb reaches its exhaustion, and the karma of childhood arrives. (85)
For the sake of enjoyment, that fool, being under its control, experiences what he himself has done; then, becoming a youth, he is by nature desirous of sense objects. (86)
When one engages excessively with sense objects, evil arises;
when one turns away from sense objects, merit arises for him. ||87||
Generosity, religious observance, celibacy, service, the meditation on Brahman, self-restraint, tranquility, compassion, sacred pilgrimage, vows, discipline, and self-control [are the means]. ||88||
Avoiding deceitful conduct, refraining from the property of others, serving one's mother and father, and honoring the deities and guests. ||89||
Worship of the guru, non-violence, purity, restraint of the senses, the practice of auspicious deeds, and conducting oneself according to the conduct of the virtuous; 3.171.90.
If one should perform these [rites], Dharma becomes nourished;
and Dharma, when well-protected, protects both this lineage and the celestial realm. (91)
One should serve the virtuous and maintain a firm standing among the good;
one should observe every conduct in which there is uninterrupted peace. (92)
He who protects this Dharma shall not fall into an evil rebirth; he constantly attains success in both his religious duty and his worldly aims. (93)
Indeed, rules of conduct and observances have been declared solely for the sake of worldly prosperity;
thus is the world restrained by teachers who are knowers of the scriptures. (94)
And the embodied yogi who abides in this discipline shall become such here that poison does not touch him at all, just as it does not affect one who knows the science of poisons. ||95||
Saṃsāra does not touch one who abides in self-restraint;
nor does illusion, nor the fruits of action, touch one who is established in yoga. //96//
The yogi, having become liberated while living (jīvanmukta), is released from the body;
established in yoga throughout all worlds, the liberated embodied soul is preeminent. ||97||
He is indeed the teacher who bestows liberation in this world, for he is free from attachment;
whatever auspicious merit has been acquired by an embodied being through the path of Dharma, [it is his]. (98)
Either through excellent auspicious enjoyments, or after a long period of time, his crossing over from saṃsāra will come about by means of the practice of the virtuous. ||99||

Either after the exhaustion of the fruit of evil deeds, or through birth among animals, birds, and the like, the destruction of sin occurs suddenly for the virtuous through their association with the wise. (3.171.10)

Through the use of vehicles, carriages, shade, and the like, as well as through the application of leaves, flowers, and so forth, and by virtue of attending upon the virtuous, merit is produced for him. (101)
From that, through a virtuous birth, one attains either heaven or the higher realm;
from there, one reaches the world of the Lord, and from there, one proceeds to liberation. ||102||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, having performed and experienced [the results of] one's actions, one is liberated from karma.
Long ago, at the time of creation, a person was indeed born by my very command. 103.
Having fashioned a body for himself, he created the three worlds—
the stationary and the moving— by means of primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of the three guṇas.
Having then created her whose nature is my own Māyā, he gave her to the Puruṣa;
she is Prakṛti, by whom this entire world of bodies is pervaded.
The Puruṣa, variegated by Māyā, then created Pradhāna; and through union with the Puruṣa, various principles indeed arose from Pradhāna.
From that, the Virāṭ was born; from him, Brahmā; from him, the gods; and from them, these creatures beginning with human beings, whose forms consist of the nature of light.
All this is composed of illusion; that which is perishable is the supreme imperishable.
Beyond that is the immortal abode, my supreme abode situated above it.
Commanded by me, the lords created a creation consisting of ten million worlds;
even after observing that, Brahmā created the fourfold [beings].
Having established the measure of time for them, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) ordained both creation and dissolution for the sake of happiness.
Happiness is indeed mingled with suffering, and the body is impure;
all physical forms are headed for destruction, and cyclic existence bestows terrible misery. (1.11)
Abounding in the bonds of birth and death, it is difficult to cross for those who are greatly deluded; yet it is easily conquered by the unattached, even by the virtuous who possess doubt. (11.2)
Finding weariness with worldly things and seeking the supreme state, they indeed attain it;
having abandoned this very body, they truly depart.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this has been told to you: here, the liberation from the body, how the body is acquired, and how that attainment of liberation occurs.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of the Destruction of the Body, the Causes of the Acquisition of the Body, and the Causes of Liberation from the Body," within the section on the Dharma of Liberation in the third period (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the abode of Māyā is produced;
for by means of knowledge (vidyā), a living being crosses over it and thereby conquers ignorance (avidyā). || 1 ||
The knowledge of Brahman is indeed considered the supreme knowledge and the knowledge of the Self;
for by the meditation upon the Supreme Self, that ignorance is utterly destroyed. || 2 ||
Ascertainment accompanied by affection, as well as reflection of that same nature, and likewise meditation upon Śrī Hari accompanied by knowledge of His majesty. (3)
The repeated awareness of one's own true nature, conjoined with the realization of perfection and consisting of knowledge, is said to be that which leads to the attainment of the Supreme Brahman.
O Rame, that indeed is true knowledge by which the Supreme Brahman is attained;
for it dispels ignorance and bestows the Supreme Brahman itself. || 5 ||
Just as the purification of gold indeed occurs through four means—by means of a touchstone, by cutting, by heating, and by hammering—so too is the purification of the mind. || 6 ||
In the same way, the removal of the illusion regarding the self occurs through the fourfold means:
association with the virtuous, knowledge, dispassion, and supreme devotion.
Through association with the virtuous, there is indeed the cessation of the flow of the qualities;
through higher knowledge, there is the gradual reversal of the formative predispositions.
Through dispassion comes the destruction of latent impressions and the turning toward Hari;
through affectionate devotion comes attachment to Hari, and from that, non-attachment to Māyā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, may there be the departure of Māyā through the grace of the true Guru;
by the favor of Kṛṣṇa, the destruction of Māyā shall swiftly occur.
By the dwelling of Hari within one's own self, there is the cessation of Māyā, just as all wild beasts flee upon the presence of a lion. || 11 ||
Just as the departure of base beings occurs through dwelling with a king,
so too does the departure of the senses residing in the body occur through dwelling with death.
Just as mice depart from a house because of the presence of a snake, so do festivals depart from the heart because of the presence of fear. ||13||
Just as the disappearance of all anxieties occurs during a great festival,
so too does the disappearance of Māyā occur through the residence of Hari.
Wherever I dwell, there Māyā does not abide;
I reside within my devotee, and there Māyā is not found.
He who is absorbed in the One Path, the Dark One (Kṛṣṇa), contemplating Brahman,
remains silent, free from all modifications, and does not maintain anything other than Me.

One should abandon each preceding stage for the sake of the next; thus one may cross over the bondage of existence, being free from malice, patient, tranquil in mind, and having conquered the senses. (17)
Free from dejection and hatred, fearless in the acquisition of Brahman, with mind conquered and disposition subdued, my devotee is liberated; I am pleased. (18)
Endowed with pure contemplation toward all living beings as if they were oneself, and free from egoism, pride, and the like, he is indeed liberated in every respect. (19)
He who remains the same in life and death, in stability and adversity, in pain and pleasure, in fainting, in gain and loss, and toward the pleasant and the hateful— he indeed is liberated.
He does not covet anything, nor does he despise anyone;
free from the pairs of opposites and devoid of passion and the like, he is liberated in every respect. ||21||
Ajātaśatru— though without kinsmen, without offspring, and even without a wife,
having renounced dharma, artha, and kāma, and being free from desire— is liberated.
Devoid of both merit and demerit, he exhausts only that which has already begun (prārabdha).
One who has brought about the destruction of the principles that initiate the body is one whose mind is tranquil. ||23||
He who is devoted to Śrī Hari through non-dual love and service, having attained the realization of the Self, becomes my very self and is liberated. (24)
One whose abode is hope and who possesses divine vision should behold the world as impermanent—resembling an ashvattha tree, fraught with birth, death, and old age. (25)
Endowed with dispassion, tranquility, and other such qualities, and being free from defects,
he indeed abandons his bondage to the self and attains liberation without delay.
Upon seeing me—who am devoid of a body born of illusion and who delights in divine fragrance, taste, touch, sound, and form—one is swiftly liberated. (27)
Having seen me—the Lord who is neither gross nor subtle, who is causeless and supreme, devoid of qualities yet the enjoyer of qualities—one is instantly liberated. ||28||
Having abandoned all desires and even internal states of existence through his intellect, the devotee who is imbued with my being gradually attains nirvāṇa. ||29||
Freed from external and internal purifications, devoid of dualities, truly without possessions and free from attachment—he is indeed liberated. (3.172.30)
The ascetic, rich in my devotion and freed from all other impressions, having attained the eternal Brahman—everlasting, imperishable, and upward-tending—[ascended]. (3.1)
Being tranquil, he approaches me, the Supreme Brahman, higher than the highest;
perceiving the Self within the self, he indeed attains my supreme state.
Having withdrawn all the senses, one should hold their functions within the mind;
having fixed the mind within the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāvanā), one should then hold that within the intellect (buddhi).
Having constantly restrained the intellect and likewise its corresponding memory, and having fixed the latent impressions upon those very impressions, one should offer the impressions into the Self.
One should offer oneself into the dark, beginningless, and glorious Puruṣottama;
thus, having attained union with Me, one becomes fit for eternal liberation.
Such a supreme saint is one whose conduct is exclusively focused on the One;
existing while perceiving Me in his own form, he enjoys my bliss. (36)
With an unceasing light accompanied by the inner eye,
he beholds within himself the Self— me, his Lord, the Supreme Person.
Thus, fixed [in meditation], he perceives his own self as me there, just as a person indeed perceives himself in a dream, thinking, "This is I. (38)
In this way, he clearly perceives himself as his own true nature, just as one who has bathed perceives the clinging film of water upon the body. (39)

If some skillful person were to extract [the mind] and demonstrate it separately from that [body], they might likewise extract the body and demonstrate it as distinct from the subtle [mind]. (3.172.40)
One should draw forth the subtle from its cause and demonstrate it as distinct;
and one should also demonstrate the cause by separating it from Māyā. ||41||
Just as someone might demonstrate illusion by separating it from the living soul, so too does the yogi demonstrate the living soul by separating it from Hari. ||42||
Just as a yogi, having separated himself from the body, may manifest his true self, so too should one manifest me, the Supreme Self, by separating me from the individual soul. ||43||

Nevertheless, that self which is not of the nature of the intellect cannot be distinct from the Infinite (Bhūman), for I am all-pervading; [otherwise] it would obstruct His sovereignty over all things. (44)
I completely restrain that [individual soul] by manifesting my power within it;
having entered me, it becomes liberated from me and enjoys my sovereign powers.
Indeed, his illusion has ceased; he has gone to me, the supreme imperishable.
Just as illusion does not exist there, so too it does not exist here.
Wherever he may dwell, my devotee is indeed free from deceit;
devoid of [worldly] qualities yet possessed of divine attributes, he is a vessel for the state of liberation. ||47||
For when the embodied one perceives himself as disciplined by me, there is no lord over him here; he is the master even of the three worlds.
He becomes one-fold, two-fold, three-fold, ten-fold, and thousand-fold;
he assumes various other beautiful bodies according to his will. (49)
For him there is no disease, no old age, no death, nor even sorrow;
he, the self-controlled one, exercises lordship even over the gods.
Indeed, having abandoned the notion of a physical body, one attains the supreme Brahman;
for one who has reached the state of Brahman, no fear of destruction arises. ||51||
When beings are being afflicted or destroyed, he indeed has no fear, nor does he have any affliction from the terrible sufferings and sorrows arising from attachment and the like. (52)
The one whose self is disciplined, who is free from longing, and who is filled with peace, is not shaken;
death does not pierce him, nor does time swallow him up.
Nothing else more blissful than this is seen in the world:
having properly yoked one's own self, it becomes established in me, Kṛṣṇa. (54)
With the suffering of thirst having ceased, he sleeps happily within himself;
casting off this human body, he attains a form according to his desire.
Therefore, once liberated, one should cultivate detachment; no further injunction is required.
One who perceives the Self does not desire even the greatest sovereign enjoyments.
Established in the Self, the great liberated one, who is liberated while living and free from the body, may dwell even in a city; yet his mind does not abandon the external world.
Though staying within the city, he dwells in his own abode;
even while in that abode, the liberated one casts out the mind toward the external world.
Even in whatever hut one may dwell, the mind does not leave its side;
even though it dwells within this very body, one's own mind remains outside. (59)
Even regarding an object consisting of the body, it does not release it for even a moment;
it does not release it from the sense organs, the physical seats, or the subtle elements.
The mind does not leave the cakras, beginning with the mūlādhāra, for even a moment;
nor does it leave the mind for even a moment upon any other subtle reality.
Since he is free from all latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding the three kinds of bodies everywhere, he perceives me, Hari, as the single Self both within and without. ||62||
Since everything here is complete within him, he is similar to that;
indeed, he perceives me as the most perfectly complete, and nothing else.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and possessing ears everywhere— having become such as this, he beholds me.
Even while maintaining his own body, he indeed beheld the absolute Brahman;
having attained the Self, he was then filled with supreme joy.
Having made the celestial chariot his support, he then attains liberation through me;
this is not easily understood by one whose inner self is confused.
For those who perform ritual actions, there is the world of the gods; for the wise, the eternal void;
for the perfected ones, the abode of truth; and for the devotees, the eternal Brahman.
For that supreme goal, O Lakṣmī, is the eternal Brahman, wherein there is immortality, well-being, happiness, and perpetual joy. (68)
Relying upon this means of accomplishment, even sinful women who have reached their final state all attain the supreme goal; how much more so, then, those who are deeply learned? (69)
Those who are devoted to their own duty, faithful to the virtuous, seekers of the welfare of others, knowers of Brahman, steadfast, and eternally dedicated to the Supreme Spirit; ||| 3.172.70 ||
There exists no other happiness whatsoever beyond my world;
having understood this and abandoned delusion, one shall attain the supreme goal. ||71||
This dissolution of māyā, which is liberation, has been shown to you;
through union with me alone, who am the goal, it is joined to the supreme state. (72)
O Lakṣmī, his thirst for you does not remain directed toward any other object once he has abandoned me;
for that very reason, this devotee shines in my supreme state.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Dharma of Liberation, the Means for the Dissolution of Māyā, and the Attainment of the Abode of the Supreme Brahman," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 172 ||
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; I shall here relate the conversation between the two yogic spouses of old, which is worthy of being heard and bestows the supreme goal.
In former times, there was a yoginī named Śrutiphalā who had a yogi as her husband,
named Sadvidyāyana, who had reached the further shore of both knowledge and realized wisdom.
Having ascended to a state of doubt, she questioned him solely for the sake of instructing the world:
"O Lord, I am always established in the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the three bodies."
I am devoted to the service of my husband, yet I am a servant of Hari; I am intent on the duties of the body, yet I abide in the nature of desire.
Devoted to the service of the gods, I abide with pure intention;
awakened by my husband, I abide intent upon the knowledge of liberation and free from attachment. (5)

Moreover, O beloved, the mental [state] that follows the path of the body's objects proceeds here and there according to the nourishment of the constituent elements, just like a river flowing downward.
This mind of mine, by its very nature flowing downward, drags me away;
O Lord, when shall I then become one whose stream flows upward? (7)
"When shall I attain liberation? When indeed shall I find eternal happiness? To what world shall I go, having taken refuge in you, my beloved? (8)
You remain here having abandoned all ritual action, though you are capable and still possessed of desire;
your wife, however, has no other resort and is always dependent upon her husband.
Thus, through my union with my husband, I indeed protect both spiritual discipline and desire like a bull; yet, even so, this bondage of karma remains mine.
No one who has fallen into the pursuit of enjoyments attains liberation;
yet, O Lord, you know all that—how then can there be liberation through action? (11)
We have heard that wives attain the worlds won by their husbands;
but if the husband here is devoid of such worlds, what is the fate of the wife there?
"Having obtained a husband such as you, what destiny shall I indeed attain?"—
thus questioned, the best of sages named Sadvidyāyana [replied].
With a tranquil soul, yet smiling within his heart, he said to his wife Śrutiphālā:
"I have no desire, nor do I have any worldly bond; I do not consider the nature of the body to be mine. (14)
This self is not the wife, nor is this self recorded as the husband;
the body of the man is the husband, while the body of the woman is the wife. (15)
Thus is worldly convention established; this very state is known as "existence" (bhava), and it is also called the "bondage of saṃsāra," especially in the form of the marital union.
Even more than that, the state of having offspring is conceived as a cause for bondage;
for desire, attachment, latent impressions, and so forth, are attributes of the body and not of the Self.
Behold me, possessing a divine body, in the form of Nārāyaṇa;
I am Brahmā as my lord, Viṣṇu as my lord, and the god Maheśvara as my lord.
Considering her husband to be the Supreme Brahman, she who serves him is liberated;
the cowherd women, out of desire, are liberated again and again at the beginning of every kalpa. (19)
By the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī belongs to Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, O beautiful lady, considering me to be the form of Brahmā, serve me.
Then you will certainly attain the world of the virtuous Yoginīs;
or else, having resorted to the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), worship me, the Supreme Lord.
"Then you will indeed attain the nirvāṇa of Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
Having said this, that yogi [emitted] from his own body Kāma, who was of beautiful form.
Having separated [the essence], Kāma indeed consumed it with fire and became like ashes;
he then gave the well-formed, though quality-less, lump of Kāma to his wife.
By that touch, he became divine and liberated, as if his very form were released;
through his longing for the vehicle of true knowledge, Kāma assumed a divine nature.
Having witnessed that supreme marvel, she whose speech bore fruit said to her husband:
"O Lord! You have conquered indignation, you have conquered desire, and you have conquered the senses! (25)
"O you who have conquered all possessions, I now recognize that you are divine;
my suspicion born of desire has ceased upon seeing your divine form. (26)
I behold you, the Lord, in a dark form consisting of four arms;
I perceive all your divine activities as well, without a doubt. (27)
My fickleness has vanished and my feminine intellect has departed today;
having attained divine delight, I shall by force become divine for you. (28)
"Tell me, however, that knowledge which is appropriate for me and brings happiness.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself; and Kāma too, possessing a divine form, [did the same].
Desiring the boat of true knowledge, she suddenly entered his body;
having seen it there, she who was the fruit of the Vedas then became free from doubt.
Just as in Kṛṣṇa, so too in his devotee; all those divine qualities residing within the body truly come to be—both the base qualities become virtuous qualities.
Desire, affection, happiness, service, nurturing, pleasure, and auspiciousness—when directed toward Śrī Hari by a devotee, these become divine among the virtuous. (32)
Those very attachments that were formed toward wives, sons, kinsmen, children, and householders, when directed toward the virtuous, become the opened door to liberation. (33)
"I have obtained the Lord of Yoga; I am blessed and have attained divinity.
I have no bodily activity, nor am I a passionate woman, for I am divine. (34)
I am indeed not a woman, but the Self, eternally blissful and liberated;
the body is possessed of bodily objects, while the Self is adorned by its own inherent purpose. ||375||
The path of the two is divided; what natural feeling could there be?
Thus, that beautiful woman, though of the very nature of Brahman, [was transformed] in a mere moment. (36)
Then the Brahmin’s wife, a knower of Brahman, perfected and free from attachments,
having attained such knowledge, spoke thus to her husband, Vidyāyana.
O fortunate one, all activity is attached to the body and not to the self;
here, action consists of that which is perceivable and visible through the organs of action and the organs of knowledge.
The identification of the self with the body, thinking "this is action" and "this is not action," constitutes bondage;
therein one also falls into delusion because of the predominance of the notion of action. (39)
Every person devoid of knowledge is deluded by the bondage of the body;
as long as there is identification with the body, liberation from action (naiṣkarmya) will not arise for him.
Through the body, the senses, the mind, and so forth, one experiences auspicious and inauspicious [results], which cause birth, enjoyment, old age, and disease, and which bestow bondage. (41)
Indeed, the true nature of the principles does not abide in inaction;
they remain joined with action, for action prevails among all beings.
Indeed, actions born of creation lead to various bodily distinctions;
such as the Agnihotra and other rites for a Brahmin, as well as the study of the Vedas. (3)
For a Kṣatriya, the teaching is governance; for a Vaiśya, it is trade as well as agriculture;
for a Śūdra, it is service; and for one whose nature is Brahman, it is the study of the Veda, fire-offerings, and so forth. (44)
In the case of one with a wife, there is hospitality and the acquisition and nurturing of wealth;
in the forest, the forest-dweller’s livelihood; and for the virtuous, the wandering for alms and so forth. (49)
Even through the practice of the discipline of Brahman, freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) does not truly exist;
for this innate nature, embodied as the body, is inherently fickle. 46.
The bodily humors are fickle, and the mind is likewise restless;
the intellect is a cluster of senses, and the consciousness is as flickering as its objects. (47)
The formative predispositions (saṃskāra) are as flickering as a flame in a vessel, and the stream of consciousness is also unstable;
likewise, knowledge, desire, volition, and states such as aversion depend upon their respective objects. (48)
They live for sense objects, and restlessness is established in their nature; indeed, this entire monkey-like being is born of the principles (tattvas) and has action as its inherent nature. 49.
How could that which is devoid of activity remain for the sake of attaining peace?
Therefore, for the purpose of transforming it, one should resort to unwavering steadiness. (3.173.50)
Through entry that is utterly motionless, one attains immovability;
such is that Supreme Brahman, which is completely full everywhere. (51)
One should always take refuge in that which is motionless and gentle for the sake of the Gentle One, through action, mind, speech, heart, self, and all [faculties]. (52)
Thus, just as a lamp placed in a windless spot within a granary, though flickering, indeed becomes extinguished by itself due to the oil; ||53||
It moves indeed, yet it may remain for a moment free from agitation;
or it may enter into dissolution there in that space and attain a state of inactivity.
And thus, this conscious self, though enveloped by the flickering [senses], remains itself.
Having attained cessation within the ether of consciousness (cidambare), one becomes free from activity;
one becomes as steady as a gem, possessing the luster of a gem-lamp, just as a gem-lamp is steady when endowed with its natural radiance. ||55-56||
Wind may or may not become oil, yet even that exists through the power of thought;
likewise, this Acyuta always abides as the bestower of splendor.
For objects of the senses residing within the body, O gentle one, are indeed like the wind.
Whether the jewel is enjoyed or not enjoyed, it remains indifferent;
||58|| so too, O wife, whether the attributes of the body are experienced or not, the Self is like that jewel for you and for me—indifferent and devoid of karma. ||59||
Having attained the Supreme Brahman, why do you fear the worlds?
O liberated Supreme Goddess, abandon the doubt, "Where shall I go? (3.173.60)
I am eternally Brahman, and I shall go to the supreme state;
through knowledge, worship, devotion, and other means, you too shall go with me.
For those household duties are indeed dharmas; they are not non-dharmas, nor do they lead to hell. When joined with me, the seasonal duties and mental duties have attained a divine state. (62)
Through the yoga of knowledge and through the yoga of Brahman, the Supreme Self, I am divine;
by my yoga, O wife, you too have attained divinity.
Who will proclaim this supreme, secret, and innate state—concealed, bestowing liberation, and free from bondage? (64)
The enjoyer does not attain the supreme, most excellent state of one who does not enjoy; how then, O beloved, could he speak of the higher states that have been described by me to you?
Rākṣasas and all obstacles exist for all embodied beings;
having abandoned them on the path of Brahman and the path to heaven, one shall become happy.
"O beloved, having taken refuge in the Supreme Self residing within myself, I have brought all the Rākṣasas, who can assume any form at will, under my control in every way. (67)
In the middle of the eyebrows, one obtains the meditation upon the Guru, the venerable Supreme Self, wherein resides that Supreme Brahman, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (68)
O most virtuous one, you always see that [Self] as your wife; worship Him!
These channels—Idā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā—are the paths. 69.
Just as even the deities beginning with Brahmā, having united with their beloveds,
worship that Kṛṣṇa who is beyond the imperishable, so too do the great ṛṣis.
Worship him, O fair-browed one, whom the wise, the virtuous, the peaceful, and those who have conquered their worldly goals worship; always abandon concern for the body.
It cannot be smelled by the nose, nor can it be tasted by the tongue;
it cannot be touched by the sense of touch, nor indeed can it be seen by the eye. (72)
And after hearing that, indeed, serve the Supreme Brahman with your self together with your mind and with an intellect firmly grasped in Brahman. (73)
That Supreme Brahman, which is without smell, taste, touch, form, and devoid of sound, is attained through His grace by serving Him. (74)
From which the Tantra proceeds and wherein it is established, and depending upon which the vital breaths, beginning with prāṇa, come into operation. ||75||
Worship that witness of all, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the most excellent Master, the Consort of Śrī, the infallible One, O beautiful lady. (76)
"I am not your husband, nor are you my wife; you are the husband, Śrī Puruṣottama.
Worship that Puruṣottama, the divine Self of us both. (77)
One should place the prāṇa in the heart, the apāna in the anus, the samāna situated at the navel,
the udāna in the region of the throat, and the vyāna throughout the entire body.
Having conquered yourself among them, contemplate the Supreme Lord;
Vaiśvānara, the sevenfold fire, resides within the vital breaths that move through the body. (79)
The smeller, indeed, through the sense of smell, experiences the odor to be smelled in the earth;
the drinker, through the tongue, experiences the taste to be drunk in water. || 3.173.80 ||
The seer perceives the visible form with the eye, and experiences it within the element of fire;
the toucher perceives the tangible touch with the skin, and experiences it within the element of wind.
The hearer, by means of the ear, experiences the sound to be heard within space;
the thinker, by means of the mind, perceives his own object of thought.
The cognizer, by means of the intellect, indeed causes the object to be known;
likewise, the self, through the supreme self, experiences everything that is to be experienced. //83//
But that which is enjoyed by means of the supreme self is divine, not worldly;
the worldly leads to bondage, while the divine, when offered, leads to liberation. (84)
In this very manner, movement is performed by the two feet;
likewise, grasping is done by the two hands, and conversation and speech by the voice. (85)

The evacuation of excrement through the anus, the experience of pleasure through the generative organ, and so forth—he is indeed the goer, the giver, the speaker, the emitter, and the one who causes delight. (86)
For Vaiśvānara, the inner self, is indeed the Supreme Self; He performs that [action].
I am not the doer, nor are you the doer; therefore, there is no bondage from karma.
One should indeed surrender the conceit of being a knower into the Supreme Self, and one should also surrender the notion of being an enjoyer into the Supreme Self. ||88||
In this state of being, I am never a man, nor are you ever a woman;
for he who is I is indeed you, and we two both abide in the Supreme.
There is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from the Supreme Self for us two;
you are the Self and I am likewise the Self, both abiding within the Supreme Self.
In that [Self] wherein we both abide, everything is held and surrendered;
this being so, how could there remain for me even action? (91)
When everything is completely surrendered to the Lord of Gods, whose nature is actionless, then whatever world belongs to Him is also eternally ours both. (92)
The supreme state is indeed the sky of consciousness, the eternal abode of the imperishable;
it belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone, and it belongs to us as well. ||93||
Where Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, resides, there I shall go, and you too shall go; of this there is no doubt. (94)
Worship that Supreme Self, the Lord and Master who is your husband;
abandon wretchedness, doubt, and fear, which lead to a low rebirth. 95.
Accept knowledge, dispassion, righteousness, and flawless devotion;
indeed, establish her as the fearless bestower of the supreme abode itself. 96.
Thus addressed, his own wife— who understood the fruit of the Vedas exceedingly well and delighted in the awakening to Brahman— attained supreme joy.
She bowed at the feet of her husband and became like Lakṣmī herself; thereafter, all her actions were entirely characterized by divine dedication to me. 98.
He always conducts himself according to the scriptures, worships me, the Supreme Lord, attains supreme bliss, and partakes of the essence of Brahman. ||99||
Although she was constantly occupied with her household duties, she remained ever-covetous of the home;
though united with her husband, she was always devoted to Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Reply—beginning with the attainment of the world of the Supreme Brahman through the method of total renunciation and actionlessness—to the question posed by the wife Śrutiphala regarding her departure to the world of the Kvalas and other matters, addressed to the sage Sadvidyāyana," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, as to how even the absolute Self, though rich in past actions, enters a body; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is.
In the ether of the self, it exists together with its own subtle karma;
from volition, joy arises, and by that, one engages in desire. (2)
Then, the vital breath (prāṇa) proceeds from the union of semen and blood;
once the semen is held by the prāṇa, the downward breath (apāna) proceeds there.
The semen is impelled by the *apāna* [vital air], and the *rajas* is also drawn upward;
by that *samāna* [vital air], the two being mixed, the lower seed-nature (*bījatā*) is produced. (4)
Udāna leads the embryo into the abdomen for its integration;
it certainly joins the integration at its place, the navel, for the sake of the umbilical cord.

And Vyāna is involved in the mixing [of elements] there; it pervades for the sake of digestion, and indeed, that which has been digested takes the form of offspring, nourished by the woman's nāla (umbilical cord).
Having attained birth, it indeed goes outside; that is considered to consist of the six sheaths. From the mother, the body hairs, blood, and flesh exist therein.
From the father [the seed] come the sinews, bones, and marrow; these possess strength within this material body composed of the elements. It is in such a body as this that "māyā" is defined.
The body is said to belong to the illusory self (māyātman), whereas that which is bodiless is free from illusion;
yet the self always resorts to me through the senses and other faculties for its own nourishment.
I am indeed the body, whose nature is to be nourished and which is of the form of illusion;
by the very existence of my body, the individual soul exists and experiences.
Therefore, the body is always illusion (māyā), the source of all objects of experience;
the self, through its own karma, undergoes bondage to the body by means of the vital breaths.
The Caturhotṛ sacrifice is the summit; the Hotṛ priest attains this bond.
The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the fourfold [set] from which one is liberated.
These four priests each consist of seven [elements]:
the nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, the ear, and also the mind. (1.3)
Intellect and the organs of sense—these seven are the causes of the qualities (guṇas):
namely, smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. (14)
That which is to be thought and that which is to be understood—these are actions and the causes of action; likewise, the smeller, the eater, the seer, the toucher, and the hearer as well. (15)
The thinker, the perceiver, and the doer—these seven are the causal agents.
Such beings consume and offer up their own internal states as oblations.
He who is unattached to these seven is indeed liberated in a sevenfold manner;
being devoid of causes and the like, I am untainted by karma.
I have no agency whatsoever; therefore, I am eternally liberated.
Devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," I abide in the state of liberation.
Otherwise, however, bound by the illusion of the four hotṛ-priests, I am ignorant; not eating the true foods, I am destroyed by the sense of "mine-ness."
Eating food for the sake of the body, nourishing it while possessed by the sense of "mine," this person,
consuming what is not the Self, is destroyed by Māyā.
Illusion, craving, and the forms of thirst increase one's attachment to sense objects; by drinking that which should not be drunk, this person is brought to ruin through illusion. ||21||
"O Lord, that which is not offered is unfit to be drunk, and that which is not presented is unfit to be eaten.
Or rather, this water—whether it be for drinking or for the senses—is indeed fit for the body. (22)
This food, though delicious, is indeed unfit for consumption; it is merely physical and elemental. One who cooks for his own sake is neither bound nor liberated. (23)
That which is subtle—whether it be food or drink, auspicious or inauspicious—is perceived by the mind, as well as by speech, sight, hearing, and touch. (24)
That which is grasped by the tongue, that which is grasped by the nose, and that which is reached by the hands, the feet, the genitals, and the anus; ||25||
Whatever is grasped or enjoyed by the intellect, the mind, and the ego, along with the external sense-spheres— whether individually or collectively, whenever it may be— [is that which is perceived].
Whether in a dream, while awake, at the end, in the middle, or at the beginning—
whatever is eaten or drunk, all that is for one's own sake and is indeed composed of illusion.
While being cooked, the embodied soul is indeed struck with nooses, whips, and other instruments;
all that is abandoned for the sake of one's own self when one has left behind the Supreme Self.
Indeed, even that which is fit to be eaten or drunk becomes devoid of quality;
likewise, for one who knows the yoga of the qualityless, the fire of knowledge proceeds. ||29||
It is the reducer of all to ashes and the destroyer of the bonds of illusion;
it is the sacrifice of Yoga for Hari, with the renunciation of everything as its sacrificial fee.
For one who has performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of serving the virtuous and who has plunged into the river of liberation,
this cycle of worldly existence born of food and drink no longer exists.
Although active and existing in the present, that Puruṣa is indeed inactive;
through union with the Supreme Puruṣa, he bestows ten million liberations here.
Even while living with his beloved, his desire is not illusory; and even while living with her husband, her passion is not illusory for him. (33)
For one's own sake, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, and indeed for the sake of the Supreme Brahman;
the transition to another body is for one's own purpose, resulting in the experience of auspicious and inauspicious [karmas]. (34)

O Lakṣmī, the goal of Kṛṣṇa is, in every way, the granting of the abode of the Supreme Brahman; whereas the goal of the individual soul—consisting of its own self-interest, full of thirst, possessed of latent impressions, and stained by passion—is [otherwise]. (35)
Karma previously acquired persists, but it is destroyed by taking refuge in Me;
indeed, by the complete surrender of everything to Me, the fruit of action perishes.
Through taking refuge in the virtuous and in my own form, divinity shall arise;
for as there is union with me, so indeed is there divinity.
Just as a wife attains auspicious worldly divinity through union with her husband, so too does the sky attain a divinity endowed with brilliant radiance through its conjunction with the sun. (38)
Just as copper attains divinity and loveliness through its union with gold, so too is the divinity of people brought about by knowledge through its union with virtue. 39.
By means of dress, [the state] of kings is established; by divine ornaments, that of the gods;
and by gold, that of the classes of ancestors through their merit.
The divine nature of the perfected ones was brought about by their sovereignty; that of the ascetics by their austerities; and that of the disciples and the groups of servants by their service. (41)
The Gandharvas attain divinity through songs; the virtuous through dedication to Acyuta; and chaste women indeed through truthfulness and their vows.

The divine state of all celibates everywhere is attained through the vow of Brahman; for the lords, it is through the attainment of my station; and for the liberated, it is through union with me. ||43||
Divinity always resides within my limbs as the very essence of all fortunes;
O Lakṣmī, that divinity of mine is eternal and inherent to my own nature.
Having obtained one such as I, my devotee, endowed with divine nature,
attains eternal divinity and rejoices in my abode.

And through my yoga, his divine powers—such as illusion (māyā), the senses, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the elements, and the subtle constituents (mātrā)—are mine; therefore, I am indeed Nārāyaṇa. 46.
By my yoga alone, infinite living beings have attained the state of Śiva;
by my yoga and through devotion, countless men have become Nārāyaṇas.
Those who have been born and those who are being born are indeed residents of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as residents of Goloka and inhabitants of the Supreme Abode. ||48||
Those who dwell in the Imperishable (Akṣara), as well as those who dwell in other abodes, those who reside in the world of Īśa, and those who dwell in the world of Māyā; ||49||
Innumerable crores of beings are born as Viṣṇus and as forms of Viṣṇu;
likewise, countless Vairāja Brahmās are also born.
Furthermore, primary puruṣas are born in infinite numbers;
and even those who are liberated are born in infinite numbers, having gone to the abode.
Even while singing they rejoice, and being filled with joy, they dance for Hari;
what then need be said, O Lakṣmī, regarding even a mere atom of contact with Māyā? 52.
Even Māyā, the great sovereign goddess, rejoices there upon attaining me;
she is the imperishable, supreme Vidyā, and even Māyā undergoes transformation.
If a supreme devotee knows this divine procedure in this way, his yoga is always divine; what cause for lamentation could there be in that? (54)
Thus, through my power consisting of yoga,
she becomes divine and preeminent among all, being solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
The one Teacher dwelling in the heart is I, the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
united with me, my devotee carries out [his duties] and performs [his actions]. (56)
The one Guru residing in the heart is I myself, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
the devotee, instructed by me, carries out and performs [the divine will]. (57)
The Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, is my sole kinsman dwelling within my heart; instructed by Him, this [body] carries out and performs its tasks. (58)
There is one Lord dwelling in the heart, Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa;
embraced by Him, the devotee enjoys bliss. (59)
I alone am the inner controller, the Supreme Self residing in the heart;
impelled by me, this [individual soul] proceeds and acts.
I alone am the hearer, the eater, the knower, and the thinker;
likewise, I alone am the smeller, the toucher, the seer, and the taster.
I alone am the one who causes joy, the grasper, the goer, and the relinquisher;
by me alone has this been experienced—[the other] eats, knows, and rejoices.
I am the Guru, the Supreme Brahman; my abode is this [universe] in every way.
By performing the rite of offering everything to the Guru, one is not smeared by action. ||63||
Thus, for one who lives here, there shall be liberation while living;
at the end of the body, there shall be eternal liberation in my very abode.
I bestow upon him my own unbroken, imperishable abode, which is the refuge of bliss;
and he shall eternally possess a state of being perfumed by the imperishable, enriched with every happiness.
"Released by my meditation, he attains similarity with me;
through my grace, he obtains all my sovereign powers. (66)
O Lakṣmī, this Brahma-mahāvidyā has been revealed to you here;
by attaining it alone, a man or a woman becomes one whose very form is Brahman.
For this purpose, I previously established within this sphere my own knowledge—the single-syllable Brahman "Om"—known by the name of the letter *da*. (68)
Having obtained that [knowledge] which bestows the highest good, all those who enjoy the status of asuras, gods,
and sages fled with zeal, each according to their own nature.
All the serpents, celestial rishis, and dānavas, having each resolved upon various interpretations of the syllable *da*, remained established according to their respective natures.
Through the letter *da*, the disposition of snakes toward biting arose;
indeed, the disposition of asuras toward deceit was born of their own nature. (71)
At that time, the cultivation of generosity arose among the gods by their very nature;
meanwhile, among the great seers, the cultivation of self-restraint arose by their very nature. (72)
Thereafter, the disposition of compassion arose among the virtuous; from that, the disposition toward charity arose among human beings. (73)
Upon seeing the women, a feeling arose within him with the sound of the letter 'da';
they were all naturally performing the supreme erotic sentiment born of their own nature. (74)
The kings' disposition was directed toward milking the earth and the kingdom,
while the disposition of the Rākṣasas and Daityas arose toward inflicting punishment.
The disposition of the elders toward dexterity was innate;
however, for those engaged in ritual action, it resided in their destiny, while for the industrious, it resided in their fortune.
The state of wretchedness among the miserable arose from the letter *da* as their innate nature;
likewise, the divine state of the lords arose from it as their innate nature. (77)
For the Piśācas, however, a disposition toward foul odors arose as their innate nature; for gamblers, however, a disposition toward wickedness arose as their innate nature. (78)
In the teaching of the teachers, there arose the state of being born of intrinsic nature;
in the conquest of the quarters through the strength of the arms of the givers, there arose the mental cultivation.
Among householders, that conception arose regarding pregnancy for the sake of a good son;
among animals, that conception arose regarding food in relation to their teeth. (3.174.80)

From that [event], the inclination toward performing śrāddha rites for the ancestors on the Darśa festival and other occasions arose; likewise, among the subjects living in their respective regions, a sense of devotion was awakened. (8.1)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, at that time there were indeed various conceptions of Brahman;
for they all arose from their own nature and became the performers of action. 82.
Yet for some, that [knowledge] did not lead to divine liberation;
therefore, Brahman was taught by me once more, saying "He is indeed. (83)

At that time, it occurred to those seeking liberation that service to the virtuous arises from one's own nature through the syllable *sa*, and that for householders, the state of being virtuous bestows liberation. (84)
From that, there arose renunciation (sannyāsa), as well as all duties such as ritual actions;
truth, the vow, the dharma of truth, the world of truth (satyaloka), and the nature of the eternal Self (sadātmatā). ||85||
Furthermore, [He possesses] eternality, as well as existence, consciousness, and bliss;
He is the self of all, possesses a formal embodied form, and is endowed with attributes. (86)
Fortune, a well-disposed mind, chastity, equanimity, as well as impartial vision and the capacity to grasp the essential meaning. ||87||
The possession of supernatural powers, the vow of celibacy free from emission, worship of the Lord of the Gods, and service to Śrī Hari, the all-seeing one. ||88||
Thus, I have performed japa as well as the golden worship of the Sun,
followed the eternal conduct of the Ṛṣis, and attained both sāyujya and sārṣṭi.

Sālokya (residing in the same world), sārūpya (having the same form), sahabhāva (being in the same presence) in every way, and svāmisevakabhāva (the state of master and servant)— such are the dharmas born of the letter 'sa'.
Human beings, gods, sages, and even the ancestors, as well as the ascetics and the souls of devotees, indeed embraced the path to liberation. ||9 1 ||
They performed hearing, service, total surrender, and formal offering;
thus, having obtained the Guru who is the Supreme Brahman and the giver of liberation, one attains it from him. ||92||
Having realized their own self as having attained the state of Brahman, they worshipped; and having experienced the Supreme Lord as residing within themselves, they worshipped him.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, the world of living beings, according to its own nature, experiences both the real and the unreal, even after having received [instruction] from a teacher. (94)
Wandering through the world with virtue, one becomes a practitioner of virtue;
he who is ever devoted to the conquest of the senses is truly a celibate student (brahmacārī). 95.
Wandering through the world with evil, one indeed becomes an evildoer;
likewise, one who delights in the pleasures of the senses acts according to desire out of passion.
But one who practices Dharma is devoted to sacrifices and rituals according to the Dharma;
one who practices merit is devoted to austerity and the observance of vows. ||97||
But one who has abandoned ritual observances and actions, remaining solely established in Brahman, moves through the world in the form of Brahman and becomes truly fixed in Brahman. ||98||
Celibacy is the form of Brahman; one whose conduct is Brahman is always happy.
For such a person, Brahman itself is the fuel, Brahman is the fire, and Brahman is the source.
Having fully attained all that is Brahman, he reaches the Supreme Brahman;
