the self is Brahman, the teacher is Brahman, for he is established entirely within Brahman.
Concentrated in that supreme Brahman, possessing the virtue of Brahman, and devoted to that celibacy which is the supreme Brahman—he attains me. || 101 ||
Whether it be a man, a woman, a eunuch, or any human being whatsoever— whoever may be a knower of their caste, a rememberer of past births, and possessed of discernment— (10.2)
Having attained the Supreme Brahman, he indeed rejoices with me;
whether here or there, all his actions indeed grant liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Body is Acquired, the Experience of the Fruits of Auspicious and Inauspicious Karma, the Attainment of Brahman, the Foundation of Karma, the Offering of Fruits, the Acquisition of Divine Form, Eternal Liberation, Abiding in the Imperishable, and the Realization of Sārūpya," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā* within the Dharma of Liberation.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Thus, the Lord himself, known as Sadvidyāyana, spoke these many bulls of liberation to his wife Śrutiphalā, who was born from a lotus. || 1 ||
And he spoke thus concerning the ocean of saṃsāra, which is devoid of a bottom,
where the fish of the senses find their livelihood, and which is tossed about by the waves.
It has a path constructed by the boat of the elements, is connected to the hope for sense-objects,
abounds with fish that are the subtle elements as its food, and has winds such as grief and joy.
[The ocean] has desire, anger, and the like as its crocodiles; delusion, confusion, and the like as its whirling currents;
attachment, aversion, and the like as its whirlpools; and latent impressions as the coolness of its waters.
Having crossed over the shoreless ocean known as karma— consisting of merit, demerit, and the like—
through the yoga of Hari, I have entered the supreme realm.
Divine, endowed with divine qualities, resplendent with divine cattle,
eternal, golden-hued, truly fearless, and worthy of the Vedas.
Where there are rivers consisting of bliss, where the trees are filled with joy,
where the wish-fulfilling creepers are delight, and where they are the abodes of the essence of affection.
Where indeed festivals are held by the Lord, who is endowed with every excellent quality,
and who possesses eternal youth, beauty, tenderness, and love.
Therefore, there is no other giver of happiness than this; indeed, there is no other happiness than this.
Having attained it, there is no sorrow, nor suffering, nor likewise fear.
Indeed, there is no seed of impermanence there, nor is there a three-branched tree;
there are not even seven secondary branches, nor sixteen terminal branches.
Here there are no matted-haired sages practicing the yoga of mental invocation,
nor are there enclosures of bamboo pillars, nor any ground elevated by the height of [sacred] lineages.
There were no sharp-edged thorns nor any *kaṅkara* stones there;
indeed, there was neither heat arising from the sun's rays nor coolness produced by moonlight.
There is neither smoke from fire, nor even shadow produced by a canopy;
there are no clouds, no urine, and the five fires are not present there.
There are no passions arising from attachment, nor is there a mass of erotic sentiment;
there is no field of bondage there, nor are there fetters that obstruct.
Indeed, there are no rubies or other such gems there;
rather, there are flowers of five colors and fruits possessing the three tastes.
There are no trees or shrubs there, yet those very things exist there;
there dwell swans with the hue of rubies and sweet voices.
Satiated by necklaces of pearls, they utter the words "I am he, I am he";
there their splendors are unobstructed and devoid of boundaries.
There, the cows have many horns and fulfill all desires; they are Nārāyaṇī cows, great and truthful, who remove all suffering.
The Kṛṣṇadevas become guests, dwelling in the sky;
they are initiated and are also constantly beheld by their Lord.
There, eternal festivals for her companions indeed take place constantly; yet, during unions with their beloved husbands, their amorous dalliances are devoid of satisfaction.
"I have taken refuge in the supreme ground, which is unshakable, changeless, and imperishable"— thus did he, whose path was true knowledge, proclaim that which is the fruit of the Vedas.
"Ha! Ha! I am blossomed with joy," he sang again and again, remembering the auspicious place;
recollecting that ground which is the fruit of the Vedas, he spoke once more.
He danced to the rhythm, speaking and even teaching;
and at that time, he attained a state of spiritual moisture in the presence of Śrutiphala.
Having regained his composure, he spoke again: "Blessed are you, O Supreme Goddess!
I am she and you are he; I am he and you are she—for this Self is indeed the Supreme Lord. (24)
For those peaceful ones who have attained that, there is no fear anywhere—neither above, nor below, nor across; nor is an end to the ground found. (25)
Indeed, there are divine forest groves belonging to Hari there,
where a beautiful woman with three faces does not grow even when turned upside down.
Indeed, mountains and hills dwell there;
they bathe at the confluence of the Pārameśvara in the river that carries Brahmā.
Satiated by bathing, with diminished desires, firm in their vows, and radiant like gods,
they enter the Self within themselves and worship the Supreme Self.
Those who know the forest of the Self dwell and rejoice here;
such is this supreme forest of the state that those most devoted to Brahman have realized.
Through my yoga I have attained [the goal], and you, O fruit of the sacred revelation, have attained it as well;
I have reached the supreme Brahman, the abode of knowledge, and I am now free from fear.
Overwhelmed by the bliss of Brahman, I do not perceive harsh odors, nor do I experience harsh tastes, nor do I see harsh forms. ||3.1||
I do not touch rough to the touch, nor do I hear a harsh sound;
I do not form rough thoughts, being completely immersed in the bliss of Brahman. (32)
I desire nothing, nor is there any object of aversion for me; I dwell within the net of Brahman, overflowing with the bliss of Brahman. (33)
Bathed in the bliss of Brahman, I offer the entire earthly or watery universe as an oblation into the Supreme Lord during the Brahma-yajña. 34.
Whether it be the fiery, the airy, or the ethereal, or the qualities and so forth; whether it be subtlety, or even internality, or action, or consciousness—(35)
Whether it be intrinsic nature or the artificial, whether insentient or sentient, or even consciousness itself—I offer it all, overflowing with the bliss of Brahman. (36)
Having indeed offered up the perishable nature, I offer myself into the imperishable state within the Unfallen One; thus liberated and overflowing with the bliss of Brahman, I am free. (37)
For one who is impartial toward all beings, free from deceit, self-conquered,
and completely liberated on all sides, there is truly no fear for me.
For association only with the virtuous, meeting only with those who are liberated, a state of identity with the devotees, and non-difference from Śrī Hari; 39.
Having thus obtained these supreme gains, I rejoice in every way;
immersed in true knowledge, I experience the sweet fruit of the fruit of sacred learning. (3.175.40)
In this manner, O Lakṣmī, within the very vehicle of true knowledge, he completely brought his wife—who was of the nature of Brahman—to the fruit of the Vedas through instruction. 41.
Now once, a most devoted king named Alarka, the son of Madālasā, having indeed conquered the entire earth, [ruled]. (42)
Standing at the foot of a tree, he set his mind upon peace;
for the sake of peace, he reflected that the entire earth had indeed been conquered. (43)
Even with sharpened arrows and weapons, there is still no peace;
for the mind is indeed fickle and wicked—only by conquering it does one attain supreme peace.
Thinking "I shall attain [it]," he cuts my mind with sharp arrows;
here, I cut his senses and instruments with my shafts. (45)
Having reflected thus, he fixed extremely subtle arrows upon his bow;
then, his mind having become embodied, it stood present before him. (46)
O Lotus-born One, they declared that Alarka was beyond the range of arrows:
"These arrows will not kill me, O Alarka, for I am without a covering. (47)
"Those [arrows] will return fruitlessly and pierce you; you shall die.
Discharge other arrows by which I might be destroyed."
Having heard this, Alarka replied: "O Mind, you, joined with the sense of smell, perceive many odors; it is through its assistance that you live. (49)
"Then I shall destroy your sense of smell with sharp arrows, and that will be your death.
Having heard this regarding his sense of smell, the Alarka replied fearlessly: |||50||
"O King, these arrows will not kill me while I am out of their range;
turning back, they will pierce your vital organs, and you shall die. (51)
"Release other arrows with which you shall destroy me.
Having heard this, Alarka then said: "Indeed, this tongue is my helper. (52)
She is always a provider of pleasant service to the mind by bestowing flavor;
likewise, this skin is always a provider of pleasure by bestowing touch. (53)
Likewise, this faculty of hearing provides assistance in the acquisition of sound;
similarly, this faculty of sight also acts as an aid in the acquisition of form. (94)
In the same way, all these other signs and so forth,
as well as the sense organs, indeed exist as aids to the mind.
This intellect, acting as a thief, seizes what has been given to the mind;
and egoism, having joined with them here, eats it all with pride. (56)
"Having heard this, the intellect, together with all [the senses], said to Alarka: 'I shall strike each of these in every way with subtle arrows.'"
"O Ālarka, these arrows shall not touch you, nor shall they ever touch us;
for these [arrows] are gross, while we are subtle—there is no contact, and no talk of death. (58)
Fruitless and turned back, they will kill you in their rage;
yet even as he released his arrows at that time, they too were turned back and rendered fruitless.
They struck Alarka, and Alarka fell into a swoon;
he then remembered me, Śrī Hari, in the form of Dattātreya.
Having manifested myself, I indeed granted him life;
the arrows were extracted from his body, and he truly rose up. (61)
I discharged arrows at him— arrows consisting of one-pointed concentration and strength—
which were unattached to the subject, the object, and so forth, and were established solely in their own essential nature.

He [the opponent] also [encountered] those sharp, subtle, and internal arrows of mine, joined with the Brahma-weapon and released from my mantra-endowed yoga-arrows, which were drenched by the discharged missiles.
Having reached them, he quickly released [his power] toward all the senses and other faculties;
some struck them down swiftly, while others indeed fled.
Furthermore, having bound them with nooses by means of the rays of his concentration,
he cast them into the lake of Brahmā, and they there attained dissolution.
Then, having become divine beings, they attended upon Alarka who was liberated;
thereafter, possessing a divine form, he attained the highest perfection.
Together with his mother and his brothers, he indeed attained liberation;
while giving this very instruction, listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which bestows discernment. (67)
"Alas! Everything external conquered by arrows is indeed impermanent; everything pertaining to the body has been practiced until this day, yet there is no internal [transformation]. (68)
By the grace of the true guru, today all the senses and other faculties, which were previously full of defects, have indeed been conquered individually and rendered virtuous. (69)
Having cast them into the Brahma-lake, they were indeed made divine;
thus, having become one of divine form myself, I worship Keśava.
Without the offering of everything else, there is indeed no happiness anywhere;
by surrendering one's own self to Kṛṣṇa, the supreme and eternal happiness is attained. (71)
Even in a battle created by illusion, victory shall be eternal;
[this occurs] through the practice of yoga toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, King Alarka attained eternal peace.
Even though her fruit had been heard [of], she indeed attained peace through service to her husband. ||73||
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the three enemies who exist everywhere in their triple nature—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which bestow bondage when impelled by Māyā. (74)
These three are your enemies in the world; they recur thrice, thus making nine.
Exhilaration, affection, and bliss—these three are your children of the nature of *sattva*. (75)
Craving, anger, and the possession of hatred—these three arise from rajas;
fatigue, drowsiness, and delusion—these three arise from tamas. (76)
These nine enemies indeed obstruct consciousness within the body;
they constantly cause it to remain solely within their own respective natures. (77)
When the person, desiring to conquer them, seeks the assembly of liberation, he then strives to abandon the city and entrusts them to me. (78)
He is liberated only to the extent that these [passions] have been conquered;
for greed is a great defect if it has not been utterly subdued. (79)
O Lakṣmī, for others, victory may result in fruitlessness due to craving;
yet, impelled by that [dispassion], a person never finds such craving anywhere at all.
Afflicted by thirst, one runs toward low ground in this world and may even fall;
indeed, one does not perceive what should not be done, for one pursues lower and lower states. 81.
From that arises anxiety and fear, and from that comes the state of passion (rājasī gati);
then, moreover, the state of darkness (tāmasī) arises, and one engages in action.
When birth and karma are exhausted, there is death; then rebirth, and again death.
But when greed is conquered, there is freedom from craving, which is indeed eternal great bliss.
That sovereignty of one's own self bestows the bliss of Brahman;
it is a great kingdom, a divine reign whose essence is the beloved Supreme Brahman. ||84||
Kṛṣṇa, the King and Supreme Lord, considers that kingdom to be my own kingdom, just as a king himself considers his own self to be his own domain. 85.
If the individual soul (jīva) were indeed to become the king by abandoning the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the true king, then that [soul] would be rootless and merely a deceiver. 86.
What is the use here of this kingdom inherited from one's father and grandfather by the living soul—whether it be the earth, the royal body, ritual action, or even righteousness? (87)
That which is enjoyment is the kingdom, and that which is existence is indeed the king;
yet there is no kingdom in the body, nor is there a kingdom even in the mind. (88)
Sovereignty does not reside in the group of senses, nor does sovereignty reside in the sense objects;
the living being alone is subject to everything, for you do not consider the [objects] to be subject to the living being. (89)
Whence indeed can there be sovereignty or even kingship for the individual soul (jīva)?
For those [objects] are never entirely dependent upon the jīva at any time.
Then, having failed to obtain the kingdom and having abandoned the false realm of sense-objects, one should become happy by taking refuge in the King who is the Supreme Self. ||91||
For those states born of the body, produced by karma, composed of the elements, and likewise transitory, are always present; in that regard, there is no sovereignty belonging to the self.
Thinking "this is mine," one clings to it falsely;
when it perishes without having been asked [for], then one realizes the truth. 9.3
"I have no kingdom, I have nothing, I have no body—how much less anything else!
Thinking thus, a person possessed of knowledge should gather the divine kingdom. (94)

One should not consume fragrance for one's own sake when it has come under one's control; that is the earth. One should not take flavor for one's own sake when it has come under one's control; those are the waters. (95)
Fire, having come under its control, does not take up its own form;
wind, having come under its control, does not take up its own touch. (96)
I shall not employ speech for my own sake, for that [speech] has come under the control of space;
I shall not engage in mental reflection for my own sake, for that mind has come under the control of the self. 97.
I have no effort for my own sake, for my self has come under my control;
rather, it is for the sake of the gods, for the sake of guests, for the sake of living beings, and for the sake of the ancestors. (98)
All my undertakings are dedicated for the sake of liberation; indeed, everything for me is an offering to Brahman, and even my dharma is for my own release. 99.
Thinking thus, O Lakṣmī, a person is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence;
having spoken thus to his own wife, he who was named Sadvidyāyana— [3.175.100]
Again he said: "I always abide in the fruit of the Vedas;
I am a Brahmin, I am liberated, and I am also one who follows the dharma of a householder. (101)
I am devoted to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
I am not as you perceive me to be, filled with desire.
The entire kingdom of Śrī Kamaleśa, both on me and on you on this earth, belongs to him;
you too shall come to know this with such an understanding, and not otherwise.
"O beloved, Nārāyaṇa is my wealth; by that I am wealthy.
There is but one path, the Supreme Brahman, by which those who know It proceed. (1.04)
Whether in households, forest retreats, the dwellings of teachers, among mendicants, or in other such abodes, sovereignty belongs to the Supreme Lord Śrī. 105.
Having stayed there and obtained leave, one should proceed further to the divine place, the celestial abode; in its midst, there is no fear from any other location.
Since your beloved wife is devoted to the fruit of sacred learning, most excellent in Brahman, and a speaker of Brahman,
you have no fear of the next world through the application of true knowledge and right conduct.
Devoted to the contemplation of my nature, you shall attain my very self;
I am the Self, the Supreme Self, and I have attained it—of this there is no doubt. (108)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge for Crossing the Ocean of Saṃsāra and Other Matters," in the section on the Dharma of Liberation within the third period (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having heard this again, Śrutiphalā questioned her lord once more:
"I am fulfilled; nevertheless, this quest for knowledge is profound. (1)
This cannot be understood or practiced by one of small mind;
tell me here the dharma of liberation, both extensive and concise.
O Lakṣmī, having heard these words of his beloved, the sage Sadvidyāyana, who acts for the welfare of all women, spoke clearly indeed. (3)
The lower fire-drill is the form of the wife’s intellect, and the husband is the supreme upper fire-drill;
when these two rub against each other through austerity and sacred learning, the fire of knowledge is born therefrom.
The intellect is the woman and the self is the man; thus they are called husband and wife. And the Supreme Self, the supreme teacher, dwells within them both.
Through all actions, Janārdana, who is the Self of the self, should always be propitiated—
whether by those two [the male and female deities] residing in the bodies of women, or by those residing in men.
This knowledge, the knowledge of Brahman, has been declared by me in brief; you are that very [knowledge], eternally liberated and increased through awakening. (7)
I am liberated and always nourished by the intellect; the intellect is both my beloved wife and my own self, and through these two, Brahman is attained.
The intellect has the Vedas as its fruit, and consciousness is the vehicle for true knowledge;
the Self of these two is the Supreme Brahman, Lakṣmī, and I, the Puruṣottama.
By taking refuge in me, consciousness becomes liberated and divine; and the Self, having true knowledge as its vehicle, becomes the Greatly Liberated (Mahāmukta). || 3.176.10 ||
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate the auspicious story of a teacher and his disciple—
the instruction of the teacher named Muktistotāyana to his son.
O Dear One, the disciple Siddhiviśāyana questioned his own guru:
"What is said to be the supreme good? Who is the Supreme (Para) and who is the Non-Supreme (Apara)?"
Whence am I and whence are you? What is the supreme truth and the highest bliss?
From what are beings born, and by what do living creatures live? (13)
What is truth and what is austerity? What qualities have been proclaimed by the virtuous? Which paths lead to auspiciousness, and what is considered eternal happiness? (14)
O learned one, tell all of this by which liberation is produced, so that people who fear cyclic existence may become desirous of emancipation. (15)
The gurus are indeed saviors who grant liberation, for they are compassionate, the protectors of those who have come for refuge, and purifiers. (16)
Having heard that from Siddhiviśāyana, Muktisrotāyana taught it to his disciple, whose inner treasury was filled with the desire for liberation.
Listen, O Lord of the Siddhas; I shall tell you everything exactly as it is.
Indeed, the worship of the Supreme Lord is considered by me to be the highest good. (18)
He alone is the Supreme Lord, the cause of all causes; He is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (19)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, the teacher of Māyā, the syllable Om, and so forth, is the Lord who is the cause of all incarnations.
The renunciants are of a virtuous nature and are likewise the very forms of Hari;
the saints are His incarnations, while the lords are His other manifestations (vyūhas). ||2 1 ||
Furthermore, they are indeed the lower Brahman, the letters, and the liberated ones;
and all those who desire liberation are even lower than that.
All others besides oneself are hungry and full of craving;
the supreme reality is declared to be the Self (ātman), while that which is not the Self is always the inferior.

Indeed, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), characterized by the three *māyās*, was born from the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*); likewise, the sense of "you" (*tvaṃbhāva*) was born from that, through the perception of duality regarding what is not the Self. (24)
The designation "I" and "you" is illusory and does not belong to the Self.
The Great Principle (mahat-tattva), as it was being born, emitted the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra). || 25 ||
The state of duality arising from egoism exists in every way as a form of delusion.
Upon its abandonment—the relinquishing of the notions of "I" and "mine"—there is the bliss of one's own true Self.
When the Self enjoys that which is offered by the Supreme Self, that is the supreme bliss.
For indeed, through union with Śrī Hari, that very state is unassailable throughout the three periods of time.
That which is born from union with the Blessed Lord is declared to be eternal truth and bliss;
it is never subject to destruction, nor can it be taken away, nor is it exhausted, nor does it decay.
Such is that state, consisting of a mass of great bliss;
having attained it, everything else indeed becomes mindless and tasteless here.
The giver of that is the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari himself, the Supreme Controller,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Infallible One.
From Him indeed the incarnations arise, and even the lords themselves proceed from Him.
From that indeed arises Īśvarī, and from her Māyā is born. || 31 ||
The sages, as well as the gods, humans, and the immobile beings,
and indeed all embodied creatures who dig into the earth—
all these are born from Śrī Hari; they live only because he has entered into them.
Arranged by Māyā through the reality of the Āpūraka,
and pervaded within by Parāpman, they live for long or short durations;
their "living" consists of a collection of actions— merit and sin— earned by themselves.
As long as those unseen forces arising from karma persist, so long do those embodied beings live; and upon their destruction, they always die.
Truth is indeed the supreme Brahman, and liberation is eternally considered to be truth.
The Self is Truth, consisting of consciousness and bliss; Śrī is the truth that never departs.
Dharma is the eternal truth of the virtuous, which is said to bestow liberation.
Indeed, austerity is the highest goodness, and renunciation is the supreme austerity.
When capability exists, endurance is called the supreme austerity;
knowledge is declared to be wisdom, and that austerity shall always be the giver of liberation.
He who knows the dwelling within Brahman as well as the departure from Prakṛti— || 38 ||
Thus, he who attains the distinction between consciousness and the unconscious reaches the supreme goal.
He who desires nothing and identifies with nothing, even while remaining in this world, is fit for becoming one with Brahman. (3.176.40)
Having made an offering unto Me, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Consciousness and Bliss, one should remain [in that state]; one is liberated, there is no doubt about this.
Long ago, Brahmā was questioned by the Brahman-sages regarding the supreme goal of liberation.
How should one perform action rightly, and how may one be liberated from evil?
"Which paths are auspicious for us, and what are the southern and northern routes?
Having heard this, Brahmā said to them: "One should always perform service to one's guru. (43)
The gurus are the bestowers of liberation; the virtuous and noble people are auspicious;
they all are the washers away of sins and the granters of a treasure-trove of merit. ||44||
Those who, being unasked, offer what is beneficial are pure and noble teachers;
the instructions bestowed by them should be accepted, for they are considered true virtues. (45)

Those qualities by which a conscious being attains nourishment in the states of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—as well as in bliss—are indeed of divine form; others are considered base qualities (*durguṇa*). ||46||
Impelled by the qualities (guṇas), the self performs actions that bring happiness, or auspicious deeds that grant the next world or the supreme abode. 47.
Action that bestows one's own abode is considered good, the very best kind of good;
action that bestows the world beyond is considered better than good. ||48||
In this world, action endowed with righteousness is called a virtuous deed;
Brahman is truth, austerity is truth, and service to the guru is truth. (49)
Truth is good; one is liberated from sin by one's own duty. Service to sacred fords, service to the virtuous, and service to one’s parents are indeed purifying.
Knowledge of the Self, knowledge of Hari, and devotion—which destroys all sins—as well as service to one's mother, service to cows, and service to virtuous women, are indeed purifying. (51)
Devotion to the gods, devotion to the guru, and meditative absorption destroy sins;
celibacy and renunciation are the destroyers of all sins. (52)
The householder’s stage of life bestows heaven when dedicated to me, but it bestows liberation as well;
the forest-dweller’s stage is for those free from passion and brings about the destruction of the activity of māyā.
Having thus understood that Dharma has faith as its characteristic, they practice it:
through generosity, service, sacrificial fees, truth, merit, and goodness. (54)
Benefiting others becomes for you sacred pilgrimage sites and divine vehicles;
knowledge, detachment, sovereignty, meditation, concentration, and self-surrender likewise become so. 55.
The recitation of mantras, extreme contentment, and the vehicles of accomplishment belong to them;
likewise, worship, supreme devotion, love, and service. (56)
Surrender is falling for refuge; they are the vehicles to liberation.
All those paths are auspicious, but Hari is forever the most auspicious of all. 57.
Having gone there, the steadfast one enjoys that eternal, divine bliss;
having become identical with Nārāyaṇa, he enjoys every supernatural power.
Those paths have been described to you, and likewise other [paths] have been proclaimed;
now I shall speak of the southern ones, those who bestow the womb, and the excellent wheel-bearers.
Having taken the merit of his human state, he indeed becomes a god for a long time;
then, taking the remainder, he returns to the human state by the southern path.
Taking his evil karma, he goes to the kingdom of Yama for the sake of cessation;
taking the remainder, he is born among animals or, thereafter, somewhere among humans.
Thus, indeed, on the southern path consisting of eighty-four lakhs [of verses],
that very southern path revolves like a wheel.
There, within the right channel of the body, the principles (tattvas) reside;
indeed, the unmanifest root-illusion (mūla-māyā), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), is established there.
The preceding part is in a state of equilibrium, while the subsequent part is in a state of disequilibrium;
it is the eternal reality, both non-productive and stable, yet characterized by the power of procreation.
From the uneven qualities (guṇas), however, the Great Principle (mahattattva) is born;
in the body, that takes the form of the intellect (buddhi), which is indeed the feminine form of the conscious self (cidātman).
From that, the one named ego (ahaṃkāra) arises as a son, existing in a state intermediate between the two.
Consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), it is born and functions within all bodies.
From that, the subtle elements and the sense organs are produced;
from that, the mind is also born, and from that, space and the vital breath as well.
From that, fire arises; from that, water; and from that, earth is produced.
All of these exist here within the body in the southern region. (68)
With its nine gates opened, or likewise with two gates closed;
or with one gate in excess, or with one gate deficient, and so forth. (69)
It consists of six sheaths, five types of harshness, and nineteen subtle elements;
it possesses consciousness, the eight qualities, manifold qualities, and the essential nature.
And it is always stained and impure, possessing qualities unlike those of the noble ones; furthermore, at the end, these three streams of dharmas likewise [cease]. (7.1)
They consist of white, black, and that which is neither white nor black;
they are conditioned, and through those very conditions, they indeed constantly arise anew.
Sattva indeed becomes a lamp; rajas provides motion;
tamas brings about cessation; thus, it is indeed characterized by activity.
When the quality of sattva prevails, there is affection, joy, and celebration;
happiness, clarity, and rising prosperity, as well as magnanimity and fearlessness. (74)
Faith, forbearance, fortitude, truthfulness, contentment, as well as straightforwardness, compassion, equanimity, non-violence, purity, dexterity, and skill in good action. ||75||
Vow, service, attendance, freedom from desire, modesty, endurance, trust, assistance, renunciation, contentment, and joy. (76)
Virtuous conduct that is stainless, peaceful action that brings auspicious vision, equanimity, and celibacy free from the sense of "I" and "mine. (77)
Generosity, sacrifice, and study—these qualities belong to the mode of goodness (sattva).
Through these qualities, those of steady disposition arise, characterized by virtuous conduct. (78)
Free from sorrow and abundant in dharma, they go to heaven as gods;
having attained sovereignty, mastery, and lightness, they enjoy these in the celestial realm. (79)
These gods known as the Ūrdhvasrotasas are indeed considered by you to be the most excellent; whatever they desire, all that they enjoy and distribute. (3.176.80)
Now, I shall describe the characteristics of the royal assembly in brief: it is characterized by activity, legal procedure, enthusiasm, momentum, and exertion. (8.1)
Suffering, form, exertion, pain, heat, upwardness, sovereignty, union, causal discourse, pleasure, strength, and pride. ||8.2||
Valor, wrath, quarreling, calumny, protection, battle, envy, desire, bondage, slaughter, sale, and cutting off; || 83 ||
Intolerance of the faults of others, anxiety, envy, falsehood, censure, praise, flattery, conceptualization, and the provocation of asceticism; (84)
Service, attendance, servitude, and acceptance;
negligence, censure, policy, array, and salutation. ||85||

Blessings, rites for prosperity, the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*, sacred knowledge, auspiciousness, affection, and the longing that "this is mine"—[all these are forms of attachment]. (8.6)
Pride, illusion, loathing, vigilance, and likewise theft;
hypocrisy, arrogance, passion, devotion, joy, and desire. (87)
Gambling, dancing, singing, and activities such as these are indeed characterized by passion (rājasa).
For dharma, artha, and worldly prosperity are truly the fruits of the passionate nature. || 88 ||
Endowed with those qualities and joined with the sovereignty of dharma and other virtues,
those men indeed go to this very world of Manu and rejoice there.
They long for the next world; they satisfy the ancestors, they offer oblations, they give gifts, they receive them, and they are born again and again.
Now, I shall describe those qualities arising from *tamas* which belong to the *tāmasas*. (3.176.90)
Delusion, fear, greed, sleep, rigidity, corruption,
lack of renunciation, ignorance, wavering, confusion of memory, atheism, dualistic tendencies, blindness, dullness, and depression. (91–92)
False pride, enmity, corruption, and deluded states of mind; evil, dependence on others, laziness, and ignorance resembling smoke. (93)
Destruction, cessation, breaking, and dissolution—these are the qualities of tamas;
for all activities are indeed governed by those characterized by tamas. (94)
Slanderous speech, anger, excessive renunciation, arrogance, intolerance, and envy—these indeed belong to the quality of darkness (tamas). || 95 ||
Futile undertakings, futile giving, and futile eating—
as well as lack of faith and fragmentation— these indeed belong to the quality of darkness (tamas).
Humans who have transgressed the boundaries of conduct, as well as Daityas and Rākṣasas,
have fallen into the downward hell and are destined for the animal hell.
Dānavas, asuras, pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, and others—cruel, harmful beings who subsist on flesh—also come into existence. (98)
They are born among stationary objects and moving beings, even among domestic animals;
they are born among draft animals, donkeys, camels, and carnivorous creatures;
likewise, they become biting insects, worms, beetles, and birds.
And there are also egg-born creatures, both those with many feet and those with four feet.
Those who are insane, deaf, mute, and those whose conduct is shrouded by sinful diseases—these are the arvāk-srotas; they are immersed in darkness and are characterized by tamas.
Thus indeed do these embodied beings become possessed of virtuous conduct in this world through association with the good, in whatever manner it may be. || 10.2 ||
Through association with the meritorious,
even those such as Caṇḍālas— who are full of sin, being murderers or destroyers— ascend to higher abodes;
and by means of the practice of dharma, they too are born again into a beautiful state.
Having entered a womb, they indeed ascend upwards again by turns at some point.
Brahmin-sages, gods, virtuous ones, and sages—these happy men go to heaven through that dharma which is permeated by the Lord through the quality of goodness (sattva). || 105 ||
Whether through devotion, surrender, service, or even by grace,
those who have come for refuge surely attain the state of liberation, though perhaps after a long time.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, everything regarding the connection with the body and so forth has been told.
By means of the very entrance to the abode of perfection, through the stream of liberation,
he attained stainless discernment and reached supreme peace;
the disciple also obtained the most divine vision belonging to the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Concise Dharmas of Liberation, the Dharmas of the Body, and those Pertaining to Māyā," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Lakṣmī, one who knows that the creation arises from Māyā is not deluded;
he is the one whose hands and feet are everywhere, and whose eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides. (19)
He who possesses ears everywhere—knowing Him indeed, one is truly liberated.
He is the one of great power, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), residing in the heart of all.
He is the Lord of all, the bestower of all light, the Infallible (Acyuta), the most excellent among men.
The gracious Śrī Hari and I say: having known Me, one is completely liberated.
"Knowing me as Viṣṇu at the first creation, as myself as Svayaṃbhū, and also as Śaṅkara,
those who aspire to Brahman are liberated.
[This is for] the sages whose souls are purified and who are satisfied with the knowledge of the supreme self."
My eternal world belongs to those who have achieved perfection through Vedic study and sacrifice.
My eternal world belongs to those wise people who are devoted to Brahman and whose minds are untainted by the performance of ritual acts, ending in constant remembrance of me.
He whose senses are under control, whose objects of sense are free from passion,
whose mind is pure, and whose intellect is unerring;
he who possesses knowledge and devotion, and in whom service is ever established.
He goes to that auspicious Brahman and is not born again thereafter. || 8 ||
One should first conquer the village that is to be burned; then Brahman shines forth.
Realizing that "all this has been created by me," one should thereafter renounce it.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the two feet, the anus, the generative organ, the two hands, and likewise speech as the tenth. (3.177.10)
The mind is the eleventh, the intellect (citta) is the [twelfth], and the ego (ahaṃ) is the fourteenth;
space is the first element, and the ear is said to be its internal organ (adhyātma). || 11 ||

In that context, sound is the *adhibhūta* (the objective element), and the quarters of space (*diśaḥ*) are the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity). Wind is the second *bhūta* (element), and the skin is the *adhyātma* (the internal organ) therein.
The tangible is the *adhibhūta*, and lightning is the *adhidaivata* therein;
fire is the third element (*bhūta*), and the eye is said to be the *adhyātma*. (13)
In that [element], form is the adhibhūta and the sun is the adhidaivata;
water is the fourth bhūta, and the tongue is said to be the adhyātma.
Taste is the elemental object there, and the moon is the presiding deity;
earth is the fifth element, and the sense of smell is said to be the internal subject.
Smell is the elemental (adhibhūta) therein, and wind is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) therein;
the feet are the internal (adhyātma), and that which is to be traversed is the elemental (adhibhūtaka).
In this context, with respect to the deities, it is the eternal Viṣṇu himself;
with respect to the self, the anus is said to be that which leads to a downward course and carries away what has been drunk.
Emission is indeed the objective element (adhibhūta), and Mitra is the presiding deity there (adhidaivata).
Procreation for all worlds is called the organ of generation (upastha) with respect to the self (adhyātma).
The semen and the menstrual flow are the Adhibhūta, while Prajāpati is the Adhidevata;
here, the two hands are the Adhyātma, and action is indeed the Adhibhūta.
Śakra is the presiding deity there, acting as the agent of grasping for awakening;
and that which is the eastern speech, Vaiśvadevī, is here said to be the Sādhya-self.
Speech is to be declared as the *adhibhūta*, and fire (*vahni*) is the *adhidaivata* therein;
likewise, the mind (*manas*) is the *adhyātma*, while volition (*saṃkalpa*) is the *adhibhūta*. (21)
The moon is the presiding deity, for that is considered the kingdom of the mind;
likewise, the ego is the internal self, the creator of all worldly existence. || 22 ||
Egoism is the *adhibhūta*, and Rudra is the *adhidaivata* therein;
the mind is the *adhyātma*, and Vāsudeva is the *adhidaivata*.
Cognition is the element pertaining to the external world, while thought indeed brings about dissolution;
the intellect, moreover, is the supreme progenitor of all things pertaining to the self.

The object of perception (adhibhūta) should be understood as Brahmā, and the presiding deity therein (adhidaivata) is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), the deity of deities and the fourth [in the hierarchy]. || 25 ||
Thus, I am the abode of all and the presiding deity of all gods;
having known this triad and abandoned it, one should satisfy the fourth with the three.

The conscious person who is free from attachment to qualities and the like, who practices celibacy, and who offers everything to Me—by pleasing Me, such a person is liberated as a partaker of the fruit therein. (27)
This vow, consisting of Brahman, is the one state of supreme bliss;
established therein, this conscious being is indeed liberated in every respect. (98)
Having restrained desires within oneself, with craving extinguished and dedicated to me, and seeing the Self in all beings, one is fit for becoming Brahman. 29.
For by the cessation of all the senses, the internal fire is kindled;
the conscious self shines forth, and the serene self increases. (3.177.30)
He is self-luminous, the supreme light, transcending all splendors;
he has passed beyond the wheel of illusion, the wheel of time, and the wheel of karma. ||31||
Having transcended the entire world and abandoned the Person who is so difficult to relinquish, one attains the supreme station of Brahman, the ether, the space of consciousness. 32.
Then, liberated from all illusion, he abides among the liberated ones;
having performed his ablutions in the lake of Brahman, he is resplendent with a divine birth.
Shining like the Omniscient One, appearing both as one and as many,
he rejoices in the imperishable abode and delights in the eternal Lord.
Having been liberated, the assemblies of Brahmins, the lords, the gods, the great seers,
the ancestors, human beings, and all living creatures always praise him for the sake of liberation.
I am the supreme Brahman, the Lord; there is none higher than me.
Hari is the king of kings of all, the highest among the disciplined.
(26) 36 He by whom the virtuous are protected, and the liberated devotees are protected.
They rejoice in this world and enjoy happiness after passing away. ||37||
The renunciant who is a devotee of knowledge attains the supreme goal;
free from dualities, full of devotion, and full of affection for me, he goes to me alone. (38)
Liberated from all conditioned phenomena and free from all dualities, liberated from all evils, he attains the supreme goal. ||9||
There are four stages of life, all of which subsist upon the householder's state;
indeed, for one established therein, it is superior to reach the end of the householder's life.
For one who maintains a wife, however, the five great sacrifices lead to liberation; eating what remains after serving the deities and guests, he who eats the remnants (vighasa) is not defiled.
One should wear the Vaiṣṇava rosary, [observe] initiation, [follow] the practice of begging, [maintain] the right mindset, and [avoid] women;
having studied me, even while performing one's own duties, one is liberated. (42)
Whether a householder or one who has retired from worldly life, whoever desires liberation for himself should practice actionlessness after granting fearlessness to all beings.
The sage who brings happiness to all beings, who is friendly, who has restrained all his senses, and who has dedicated his own activities to Hari, attains the supreme goal. 44.
He who does not rejoice at gain, nor become dejected by lack of gain, and who feels a sense of revulsion in his mind toward gain that comes through being honored; ||45||
One should act continuously without obstructing living beings;
for the sake of shelter, one should resort to an unobstructed mountain cave. (46)
One who knows liberation should, through purified intellects, make Kṛṣṇa his own;
thus he becomes worthy of Śrī Hari’s trust and shall acquire liberation. 47.
Even while remaining established in the duties of a householder, one should practice the conduct of the wise;
being undeluded, one should perform my supreme devotion through the appearance of a deluded man. 48.
He who is perfected in his vows is liberated from all bonds;
by fixing his mind on me as the Beloved, he shall be liberated—of this there is no doubt. (49)
He who desires nothing and despises nothing is fit for becoming Brahman even in this very world. (3.177.50)
Having abandoned all action consisting of the qualities (guṇas) within the glorious Supreme Self, one who is attached to me with affection is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
For whoever should remember Hari at the time of death for even a single breath,
he, having approached me then, is fit for immortality.
If, however, one restrains the self within the Self for even a mere moment and worships me,
being beheld by me, he indeed becomes fit for immortality.
In this world, some people desire only the Dharma; some desire knowledge and discernment; and some desire only dispassion.
Some speak of place or time; some even speak of destiny.
Some say it is bathing at the three periods of the day, while others say it is not bathing at all.
Others, however, say that food alone is the cause, while others likewise say fasting;
some are devoted solely to ritual action, and others are devoted to tranquility.
Some praise liberation; some, various kinds of enjoyments; some, wealth such as gold and silver; while others, however, praise the state of possessionlessness.
Others again are devoted to worship, while some are intent on sacrifice; some indeed follow the path of violence, while others observe the vow of non-violence as their merit.
Some resort to sacred fords, others to service, and still others to doing favors; some practice sincerity, while others perform meditation or austerity.
Some say that self-study, worship, and giving are [the means]; others speak of truth;
others again of renunciation, and still others of falling from a cliff, as did Bhṛgu.

Some [praise] renunciation and others detachment; likewise, others [praise] the householder's life, while others praise dwelling free from the pairs of opposites, and still others praise total self-surrender.
O Lakṣmī, all those auspicious distinctions of dharma bestow prosperity;
if they are connected with me, they all without exception bestow liberation.
Deprived of my yoga, they are cast into the mire of saṃsāra;
whatever merit, demerit, or a mixture of both is acquired by them through their actions, [that is what they receive]. (63)
Whether in this life or another, that which has not been experienced does not perish;
for the connection with a body exists for the sake of experience, and by that, transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is indeed certain.
Among all these, however, consciousness is the supreme good in every respect;
and devotion to Kṛṣṇa bestows liberation, being eternal and the source of happiness. (65)
But those who perform other actions joined with worldly desires rejoice here in this world, being born again and again.
Those who perform their duties for Hari while renouncing the fruit are the ones who perceive the truth;
yet He enjoys everything [offered] like a lotus leaf [remains unstained by water]. (67)
For even a wise man, though fully endowed with all enjoyments, is not defiled;
just as a drop of water, though resting upon a leaf, is not adhered to.
Thus, this conscious self, when offered unto Me, is not bound;
the devotee who is united with the offering of all things is not tainted, even though he remains immersed in the world.
Even with a thousand [teachings], one of dull intellect does not attain awakening;
whereas even with a fourth part, the wise man prospers in happiness.
For the wise man who knows the means attains ultimate happiness;
one should travel by chariot only as far as the path for chariots allows.
When the track of the chariot has vanished ahead, the charioteer must proceed on foot;
and when the movement of the feet has ceased, he must proceed with the gait of a swan.

One who moves like Garuḍa, one who moves like an elephant, one who moves through the sky, and even one who moves everywhere—the disciple of the Guru, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, must proceed in this manner. //73//
As long as there is water, one should proceed ahead by boat or by arms;
having reached the far shore, one should then leave the boat and proceed by means of a vehicle.
Having transcended the entire surface of the earth, he should proceed ahead by means of a celestial chariot;
but when beyond the range of the celestial chariot, he should move together with Viṣṇu.
Even beyond the reach of Viṣṇu, he should proceed ahead together with the liberated;
having cast off that which consists of *māyā*, the liberated one goes to the supreme goal.
Austerity is the most excellent medicine, and knowledge is likewise the supreme dosage;
the essence of devotion provides nourishment, and one who is strengthened by these attains my state. (77)
Whatever is difficult to attain, difficult to behold, difficult to overcome, or difficult to follow—all that can be accomplished through austerity, by my service, and by my grace. (78)
Through pure meditative yoga and likewise through devotion rich with love, the great-souled ones attain my supreme realm. (79)
Having made my meditation firm, people with clear minds and who perceive the Self attain me, who am full of eternal bliss. (3.177.80)
Action is indeed declared to be death; freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) is considered immortality.
That which is thus immortal, eternal, constant, and imperishable is bliss. (81)
Having tasted Me, who am under control and abide within oneself, one knows Me and shall not die;
having attained the consumption of the nectar of immortality, one becomes immortal, a sovereign among the liberated.
Having transcended all conditioned phenomena and having restrained the self within the Self, one who has realized the Supreme Brahman shall go to that state both here and beyond. ||83||
Indeed, when a being attains clarity of mind, there arises a delight in serving the virtuous;
having attained such clarity through the virtuous, one obtains Hari, the Lord of the virtuous. (84)
Such is the destiny of those liberated through the perfection of consciousness;
this is the eternal destination of those who are dispassionate and devoted.
"For householders who possess devotion, she alone is the eternal goal"—thus spoke the king of sages named Sadvidyāyana, O Lakṣmī. (86)
He related many discourses whose fruit is hearing for the sake of liberation;
Śrutiphala, however, asked: "How is it that you remain established in bondage? (87)
Then Vidyāyana said: "For this is indeed the dharma intended for the age, even for insects, moths, beasts, and birds. (88)
O beloved, this is the duty of even reptiles: the supporting of their wives;
women are to be protected and nourished, and once they have been taken in marriage, they must not be abandoned. (89)
O beloved, one who abandons his wife falls from radiant glory and from dharma;
for service, the lineage of the family, and the pursuits of dharma, pleasure, and wealth depend upon her. (3.177.90)
"O beloved, everything belonging to a householder is always dependent upon his wife;
therefore, I am bound to you, for you are my wedded wife. (91)
He who does not know the duty toward a wife, nor his own duty arising from the state of being husband and wife, incurs great infamy and goes indeed to the hells. ||92||
In this very way, the husband is considered the supreme dharma for women;
through the favor of the husband, women always obtain the fruits of pleasure and progeny. (93)
For he is called a *pati* (lord) because of his protection, and a *bhartṛ* (supporter) because of his sustenance;
by granting sons, he is a granter of boons—thus Dharma is considered the supreme husband. 94.
Thinking thus, I consider this a well-done deed; therefore, I shall remain bound to you. You must always be protected by me with every effort. (955)
The constant desire of the virtuous is the protection of their own offspring;
for by procreating a son, a father always becomes one who has fulfilled his duty. (96)
"Having become a mother of sons, you must now liberate me from my debt.
Thus addressed, she who was devoted to knowledge was further enlightened regarding the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
Having been led toward divinity, she conceived a noble son; there, her mind-born son was indeed quickly born.
Named Nirvāṇa, he was indeed consecrated by her suddenly; and having been initiated by his father as well, he grew up as a bestower of awakening. 99.
Then, O Lakṣmī, the husband, who was endowed with ten thousand fruits of the Vedas, married the auspicious and delusion-free maiden, the virtuous daughter of Vaikhānasa.
The king of sages, Sadvidyāyana, having attained supreme meditative absorption,
went to the divine abode of Brahmā, my own supreme and blissful realm.
By reading, hearing, reflecting upon, and even retaining this [text], one who possesses the vital breath becomes liberated; of this there is no doubt. (102)
Indeed, he who has reverence for the dharma of liberation would be capable of making thousands of people and women those who have sought refuge in him his own.
Even while constantly enjoying worldly pleasures, one should possess knowledge and detachment;
placing one's feet upon the head of Māyā, one goes to my imperishable state.
Having obtained the desired gains, one should indeed proceed toward supreme liberation;
even a woman, enriched by the dharma of liberation, shall become a divine Nārāyaṇī.
By Your grace, may she become liberated while living in this world, even while possessing all enjoyments; and at the end of the body, may she go to the supreme abode. 106.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Adhyātma, Adhibhūta, Adhidaiva, Adhidevatā, and so forth," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Choose, O Lakṣmī; I shall tell you the beautiful story of a devotee, a householder who is ever self-surrendered, which grants liberation.
There was a mendicant devotee of mine, a lord among sages named Bhikṣāyana;
he had a beautiful wife whose name was Ayācitāñjali.
The mendicant always bathes three times a day in the lake;
his wife, meanwhile, takes water from the Aśvapaṭṭa [tank] and brings it to the temple.
"Established in the three daily ablutions, she indeed performs worship to me constantly;
thus, in the home of that couple, there is always my presence. (4)
While I worship my own image, my livelihood is sustained by the food, water, and clothing given by the devotees. (5)
Having worshipped those two and me in the morning, [one should perform] the service of the temple:
sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, offering incense, and lighting lamps.
Furthermore, there is the gathering of flowers and other offerings, the heating [of the vessel], the cleansing of the bowl,
the waving of lights (ārātrika), as well as the offering of the cooked food (sthālīpāka-nivedana) and the presentation of water.
They should also offer betel-leaf and perform the ritual dismissal;
thus, they should always respectfully practice the offering of oneself.
Every day, I indeed perform the practice of alms-gathering for these two;
whether it be some devotee who has arrived, or even another person seeking a pilgrimage.
Both of them, my devotees who are satisfied with whatever they obtain by chance, offer food and other necessities to me alone, even when they are themselves well-provided for. (3.178.10)
Practice the very duties of the householder with devotion;
for these two, desire, anger, greed, and delusion do not exist for their own sake.
Having accepted me as Hari and always considering me to be situated within,
they perform all their activities, both those pertaining to the body and others.
Food, drinking water, anointing with oil, decoration, as well as dress, festival, delight, and likewise sexual pleasure; || 13 ||
Remembering me alone through divine vision, they perform everything;
without the surrender of the self, they never act according to their own will anywhere.
Indeed, every resolve of those two was centered on Me,
as they took alms, placing Hari within every morsel of food.
And for those who remember me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
whether on a bed, on a swing, during physical exertion, or even at other times, [those two shall grant their grace].
They proceed only by remembering me and never depart from me;
for my pleasure, they have bound water-jars and other vessels to carry water in the heat.
They always provide me with cold water, drinks, and so forth;
likewise, they give warm water when it is cold, as well as warm food and other such things. (18)
For my sake, those two indeed perform acts of penury such as wearing tattered garments,
and they offer gifts like umbrellas during the rainy season, as well as keeping a vigil on the Ekādaśī day.

Likewise, during religious observances, the bringing of fruits and flowers for my sake, as well as singing, dancing, the sound of musical instruments, rhythmic clapping, and acts of pleasing adornment; || 3.178.20 ||
They constantly speak for my sake and they speak of me;
thus conducting themselves, the two of them listen to my discourse.
In this world, desire is indeed considered a hell rooted in latent impressions; for those possessed by desire, there is no liberation at all. Therefore, one should renounce desire. ||22||
With palms joined in supplication, his wife, having heard this, questioned that sage:
"O Brahmin, you say that my husband is a mendicant who will be my savior. (23)
I ask you to dispel the doubt that has arisen through this discourse:
desire is said to lead to hell; for those possessed by desire, there is no liberation at all. (24)
"We two are established in the dharma of householders, yet desire exists therein. How, then, could liberation be attained? Therefore, the mind-born [desire] must be abandoned. (25)
Having heard that, Bhikṣāyana spoke to his own dear wife:
"O wife, it is true that all worlds are indeed illusory, even those [described as] hells. (26)
O wife, apart from offering to Hari, all things are devoid of merit when offered to Him;
therefore, desire, anger, and greed must be abandoned—even greed itself must be renounced. (27)
Indeed, he should attain the state of being devoid of qualities within Nārāyaṇa, the supreme reality;
for this bondage, which yields hellish rebirth, exists solely for the sake of the bliss of one's own self. (28)
When the wife is offered to the Supreme Self through association with the Supreme Lord, and through that association with Hari, O wife, Māyā perishes therein. (29)
Indeed, all actions free from deceit become devoid of worldly qualities, just as all vegetables, sweet foods, water, and fruits [become so when consumed by one free from desire]. || 3.178.30 ||
Whether illusory or material, that which is offered to Kṛṣṇa is indeed beyond the three modes of nature;
likewise, the eyes, hands, chest, feet, hips, and mind [are offered]. (3.1)
O beloved, every action performed by us two in the constant worship and service of Śrī Hari becomes free from all qualities (nirguṇa) when offered to Him. 32.
For those things such as the body, the senses, and their inherent nature are indeed devoid of qualities;
therefore, for us there is no hell, but rather the eternal Dharma. ||33||
By that practice of service and other such duties, merit arises through association with Hari:
"I am a beggar and you are a female beggar; indeed, our alms are always Hari. (34)
For us two, Kṛṣṇa is the mendicant, devoid of qualities, the Supreme Lord; through union with Him, our activity is likewise characterized by Kṛṣṇa and is indeed devoid of qualities. (35)
Therefore, O wife, in every undertaking remember Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord; think not of me nor of you, but of Kṛṣṇa alone, both in union and in separation. (36)
Thus, there is no bondage for you here in this world or in this body;
nor is there any bondage for me, O beloved, who acts solely for the sake of others. (37)
Even though she was being instructed in this manner, O Lakṣmī, that virtuous female mendicant did not place even the slightest bit of trust in him. 38.
He reflected once more: "This desire is defiled by nature; it is indeed sin, which brings about hell and bestows suffering. (39)
Thus she constantly thought and always worshipped me;
one day, I appeared before them directly, within the range of their vision.
To destroy her doubt, I touched her with my own hand;
she swooned at my form, which was adorned with every ornament.
The innocent woman quickly sent me word while she was in her husband's presence:
"Without sexual union, I can by no means endure even his mere touch. (42)
All forms of bliss were indeed bestowed upon her, and she became supremely happy;
from that very moment, her state of being free from desire became divine.
Volition is born of desire; that [desire] was forever destroyed from within her.
Free from desire, she became liberated in form and empowered by the vow of Brahman. ||44||
Even the mendicant, touched by her, became entirely free from desire;
from that time forward, those two, radiant as the sun, were established in the vows of Brahmanical conduct.
They became distinguished, worshipful to the gods, and worshipful to the world;
thus, through my constant service, I rendered them free from desire.
By means of my yoga, even women and men become truly free from desire;
thus, they all proceed to the supreme state. (47)
Having met their death at the proper time and being established in celestial chariots,
they became liberated in form and went to my imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, in this world, for a man and a woman who thus offer themselves to me, I destroy all defects and bestow divine virtues. (49)
For the compassionate Supreme Soul, who is capable of accomplishing everything, this scripture has appeared in the world for the sake of His devotee; indeed, I shall deliver the devotees.
O Lakṣmī, whatever various kinds of alms are given by me to my husband, all of that becomes devoid of merit due to my connection with him. (5.1)
Listen, O Kamalā; I shall tell you various things:
whatever is most dear to oneself, all that is considered to be of the nature of alms.

Whatever is desired in the states of dreaming, waking, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), or liberation—that which has not been offered [to the deity] must certainly not be accepted; having given it to me, one should partake of it.
May he who takes refuge in me grant me every kind of food, sweet upon the tongue;
may he give me whatever delicious drink is desired. (54)
Whatever garments are beautiful, as well as attire, ornaments, and the like, along with gold, silver, diamonds, and other gems—let one offer these to me. (55)
One should offer to me unguents and the like, perfumes and the like, and collyrium and the like;
one should present to me crowns and the like, beds and the like, and ritual balls and the like.

He should offer me canopies and the like, seats and the like, as well as vehicles and the like; he should offer me temples and the like, mounts and the like, and celestial palaces and the like. ||57||
One should offer me incense, lamps, flowers, sandalwood, and so forth; one should also offer me elephants, horses, cattle, and the like, as well as male and female servants. ||58||
May he present to me all delightful forms and sounds worthy of being heard; may he also provide me with all kinds of tangible objects and everything that is to be grasped. ||59||
One should offer those who are to be sent forth to me as partakers of happiness and objects of joy; one should present all kinds of sweet foods and offer sprays of *tulasī*.
One should give me, the mendicant, the essence of oil, camphor, and so forth;
one should always offer me a son, a daughter, a husband, a wife, and all one's possessions.
He should entrust all my weapons and all my machines to me;
he should entrust to me the performance of sacrificial rites, such as yajñas and yāgas, as well as the oblations and other rituals.
He should offer me the crops, as well as the ears of grain and the individual grains;
he should also offer me medicinal herbs rich in sweet juices, honey, and so forth.
One should also offer me the sixty-eight arts and the nine treasures;
a person should bestow everything upon me, both the manifest and the unmanifest.
May he grant me all income and production, as well as the increase of wealth and material goods—whether pertaining to the heart, the body, or the senses. (65)
By offering me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or even water, one may well attain learning,
wisdom, discernment, skillfulness, and the possession of virtuous qualities.
One should offer all that is righteous and beneficial to others to me;
for those intentions which are fruitless and those which yield results only at the end [are not to be offered]. (67)
He should offer me all his works and all his efforts,
as well as all his sovereignties and all his powers.
May he bestow upon me all his states, all his wonders, and all his endowments of the quality of beauty. (69)
I am for the sake of others, and as a monk, I bestow an infinite number [of gifts]; having taken what is requested through begging, I indeed give it away eternally. (3.178.70)
I bestow upon you sovereignty, heaven, the divine worlds, enjoyments, new riches, pleasures, festivals, delights, and joys. (71)
I give wealth, grain, garments, and excellent dwellings; I give herds of cattle, male and female servants, sons, and daughters.
Furthermore, there is the station of Dhiṣṇya, as well as that of Mahendra, Vaiṣṇava, and Brāhma;
also the sovereignty of the guardians of the quarters, or the lordly state, or the supreme station of Vairāja.
I shall grant you the sovereignty of the world-protectors, the status of a great seer, the position of a preceptor, or even the eternal station of Sūrya or the kingdom of Candra.
I grant Vaikuṇṭha, or the Immortal, or the Unmanifest, or Goloka, the Imperishable, or Śrīpura, or Brahmaloka, or the Supreme Abode.
I beg from you; everything always pleases me.
I enjoy this which I receive through giving, and having enjoyed it, I give it away infinitely. (76)
I thoroughly consume my merit and sin, as well as my good and evil deeds; having received what was undesired given by people, I bestow back upon them what is desired. (77)
Having obtained non-gain, I bestow upon myself the nature of gain as its fruit;
and having obtained even a small amount, I bestow it in many ways according to my desire. ||78||
I bestow abundant Lakṣmī and exceedingly vast riches;
I grant manifold powers and bestow victory at all times.
Whatever may be mine in its entirety,
all that I give to him who offers everything to me and remains as one with me.
"O Lakṣmī, I am thus capable of giving everything in its infinite extent;
if there are indeed beggars who beg for my sake, they shall surely receive it. (8.1)
And from them they enjoy [their rewards], for which I grant infinite fruit;
these many kings, brahmins, and sages—so it is said. (82)
At the conclusion of my ascetic penance, they indeed begged me alone for a son;
thus I became the son of beggars, repeatedly and in vain solicited by them.
I am Gaṇeśa of Śaṅkara; Hari Kṛṣṇa of Vṛṣa;
and Vāmana of Aditi, as well as Kapila of Kardama.
I am Gopāla to Vasudeva, and Ṛṣabha to Nābhi;
and I am Anādi-Śrīkṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to Kaṃbharā. (85)
From Atri was born Jamadagni, and from him likewise came Paraśurāma;
Rāma was also the son of Śataratha, as well as that of Brahmā.
Births such as these are indeed of the nature of mendicancy;
everything exists within mendicancy, and even "I" exist within mendicancy. (87)
"O Bhṛgu, these mendicants are my vessels of great affection, my very forms;
you, O supreme mistress, were given by Bhṛgu as alms.
Even Padmā was obtained through alms, and likewise Nārāyaṇa. (88)
Likewise, Duḥkhahāśrī was obtained, as well as Lakṣmī and Māṇikī. ||89||
Through alms, wisdom, Padmāvatī, Kamalā, and Ramā are obtained;
by reading or hearing this, one becomes possessed of enjoyment and liberation. (3.178.90)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Sage Bhikṣāyana through Acts such as Offering Everything to Śrī Hari, Even While in the Householder State, and the Greatness of Alms," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! In the city named Bhāvuka, there was indeed a Vaiśya who was helpless;
having lost his father in childhood, he was nourished by his mother. || 1 ||
The mother, named Nityāśrayā, always protects her son Veśin alone,
as he is the very root for the increase of the lineage.
That widow always goes to the temple of Kṛṣṇa in the presence of the brāhmaṇas to hear the sacred narrative, by which her suffering is utterly destroyed. 9.
Through the knowledge of this narrative, auspicious fortitude arises instantly;
torments perish, sufferings vanish, and there occurs an absolute dissolution of anxiety.
That beautiful woman listened to the Saṃhitā named Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
for two years, she listened to all the narratives.
Having heard those various stories, she became one whose form was that of Brahmā;
virtuous, chaste, and endowed with dharma, she remained there as a bodiless being (videhinī).
Then she understood the meaning of her own name, "Nityāśrayā," for she thought:
"In the eternal Lord Hari, my Master, my refuge truly exists."
Hari is the husband, the lord, the master; I am his wife.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is eternally to be served from time immemorial.
The cowherd boy is the manifest, imperishable son of Kambharā;
he is the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, the master of millions, billions, and hundreds of thousands of Lakṣmīs.
He alone is the beloved Lord and Master Nārāyaṇa, the fulfiller of all desires for his own devotees, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having thus attained such knowledge and being firmly established in her vow of austerity,
she performed the service of the form of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Indeed, by her a beautiful image was caused to be made for me upon a copper plate;
and the vow of its worship, consisting of self-surrender, was constantly observed.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to how she performed her service.
Having risen in the morning, she [prostrated] upon the ground, saying: "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! (13)
She recites the one hundred and eight names beginning with "iti" using a rosary;
then, remaining on her bed, she performs meditation upon my form.
The feet, shanks, knees, thighs, hips and so forth, the waist, the navel, the belly, the chest, the back, and both sides; || 15 ||
Meditating upon the throat, the mouth, the two cheeks, the temples, the forehead, the two eyes, the ears, and the crest-lock, she then performs her ablution.
Anāthamātā is devoted to me, O Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa;
she indeed performs the chanting of my name and offers a water-pot during her bath.
He himself indeed offers Tulasī leaves and flowers to the Sun and to the ancestors who dwell in heaven, even from the very stalks. ||18||
Having gathered sandalwood and ground it, she indeed returns home silently;
having placed my image upon the seat, perform the invocation, the offering of the seat, and so forth.
He offers me water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping;
likewise, he offers water, sandalwood paste, water, and flowers.

Even without the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one may worship using substances designated by the name "five nectars," such as cloth, a sacred thread, and myrobalan fruit for the purpose of adornment. 21.
That virtuous woman offers me rice for all my adornments, as well as the finest saffron, and incense made from sandalwood powder.
In the early morning itself, she offers a lamp with oil, an oblation of chickpeas and the like, fruit, a vessel of sesame seeds, or molasses.
He offers water just as it is obtained, and likewise presents it;
he indeed performs the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) preceded by the ringing of bells. ||24||
Every morning, he always performs circumambulation, prostration, praise, and the auspicious dismissal, preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers. (25)
Then indeed she performs her household duties, the fondling of the child, the protection of the child, the giving of breast milk, and the feeding of the child. (26)
Content with what she receives as a servant, she indeed provides for his nourishment;
satisfied with food, clothing, and other necessities, she serves her husband Kṛṣṇa. (27)

Then, assuming the form of a maidservant for the sake of performing the duties of service, she went to the house of a merchant with the desire to prepare vessels, ointments, and other such items. (28)
Having completed his service for the master, he obtained food, fruit, and other provisions from the merchant’s wife at midday; taking these, he returned to his own home. (29)
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa comes to me because of my worship and other services;
that excellent family constantly hears the chanting of His names. (3.179.30)
All that became devoted to me; even the old merchant, though possessed of beauty, met his death in due time, while my constant refuge remained in his house.
Chanting "Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," I was drawn by her and went indeed into the presence of the merchant. (32)
I appeared directly before him and likewise before that woman;
having bestowed upon me divine touch, he indeed led me to that imperishable abode.
From my divine celestial chariot, I beheld that entire household;
indeed, I took delight with that helpless woman, for they had all become devoted to me.
For at midday, having likewise performed her daily household duties for the merchant, she would return to her own home after feeding her own son. (35)
Having caused [her] to drink milk, she eats while remaining fixed in the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa;
in the evening, she also performs the lustration rite and my worship.
Having given me food and having prepared it for herself as well, she then goes to sleep, placing the child at her side and me beside her too. (37)
Thus, the eternal Vaiṣṇavī power indeed constantly resorts to me;
even as a child, having witnessed his mother's devotion, he became the most excellent of devotees.
Just as his mother was, so too was her son—a highly devoted soul who, even in childhood, was self-realized through playful acts such as honoring the Lord with flowers and other offerings. (39)
Having established an artificial image made of clay upon a seat of sand,
he worshipped my image with mud, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
Holding blades of grass and leaves lying on the ground, he offers them with devotion, thinking them to be flowers; likewise, he regards water as his mother. (41)
He respectfully offers food from a vessel broken by clay, and he also gives other things such as ripe nimba fruits. ||42||
She performs circumambulations like a staff and likewise offers a garland;
she indeed entreats Hari for forgiveness, compassion, and favor. (43)
He renounces all that, even together with his friends;
indeed, he delights at the forefront of his home while worshipping me, Nārāyaṇa.
When time had passed in this way, that youth became a supreme devotee, and his mother too began to worship me; I was then pleased with them both.
Then Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin, arrived there;
he requested alms from me, who was then constantly engaged in providing refuge.
He gave me one flat cake and provided buttermilk for my meal;
sitting there in the courtyard of the house, I ate a little. ||47||
I likewise gave half a *roṭaka* to that boy, and I provided him with a small amount of buttermilk and milk. (48)
The young son, filled with wonder, said repeatedly to his mother:
"O Mother, this buttermilk has become milk through the grace of the Brahmin. (49)
"This sweet-filled cake, though smeared with ghee, has become even more delightful; therefore, this most excellent Brāhmaṇa is truly marvelous. (3.179.50)
Having heard this supreme marvel, the mother, bewildered, gazed upon the Lord;
as she fixed her gaze upon his gaze, he then became four-armed. (51)
Divine, with divine limbs and adorned with all divine ornaments upon every part of my body, I became Puruṣottama, marked by divine signs and accompanied by Lakṣmī. ||52||
Then, upon merely beholding me, the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Śrī, she fell at my feet and cried out, "Save me! (53)
And my son, named Keśī, recognizing me as the Supreme Lord,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the protector of the helpless, fell at my feet.
The boy praised me, and his mother, overwhelmed with emotion, also offered praise:
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of mercy! O Mādhava, protector of the helpless! (55)
O Śrī Hari, O Lord, deliver me from this worldly cycle of existence;
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my Master! (56)
By you, in the form of a brahmin, the mother and son have been delivered;
"you are the protector of the protectorless"—truly, these words of yours are so. (57)
O Supreme Lord, indeed many discourses of yours have been heard by me;
having attained supreme dispassion, you have been served by me, O Janārdana. (58)
Having attained knowledge and recognized you as my lord, I worship you forever.
O Lord, this child is yours; please look after your son.
O Śrī Puruṣottama, lead me to Your abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
O Lord, Beloved, Friend, Kinsman, and Protector, O Śrī Hari, protect me! 3.179.60.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, she offered a handful of flowers to me;
she also grasped my feet and wept, overwhelmed with love. 61.
O Rame, my feet were then bathed by her tears;
and her son, offering himself to me, likewise shed tears of love.
"Grant me liberation, O ocean of compassion, Supreme Lord, Consort of Śrī!"—
thus he spoke, placing his hands upon his chest and fixing his gaze upon his heart.
Just as a son embraces his father, so did he embrace me;
tears were shed by me toward my most devoted son.
As soon as he was bathed by them, he came to possess divine vision;
and I, O Rāmā, beheld his mother with a compassionate gaze.
She too, divine and possessing divine vision, then quickly turned away:
"Out of compassion for me, these two knowers of the three times have resorted to perfection; my persistence was in vain. (66)
But those two became like Lakṣmī and Muktā, sporting divinely there with divine requisites brought together according to their will.
They both worshipped me, yet they did not release me;
"O Kṛṣṇa, dwell here," they said to me again and again. (68)
Or rather, they both then said, "Lead us both together";
then, having greatly contracted his form, he again assumed the appearance of a brahmin.
