Those two, possessing divine forms, served me with their hands as fans;
I, indeed, considered their liberation.
Taking them both together, I placed them upon the celestial chariot Sūryābha—
the son Keśin and his mother Nityāśrayā, who was indeed without a protector.
He swiftly led me to my own abode, the imperishable supreme state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am the protector of the helpless and their deliverer. (72)
I am the beloved of my devoted ones, the bestower of liberation, moved by great compassion;
through reading and hearing this, auspicious enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass. (73)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Bestowing of His Vision and Liberation upon Anāthā, Nityāśrayā, and Their Son Keśin, after Witnessing Their Devotion to the Bhāgavata," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another beautiful story concerning my devotee.
In the city named Māyā, there lived a devotee of mine known as Vyāghra.
From childhood she possessed a divine nature, was affectionate toward the virtuous, pure, and devoted to the Vaiṣṇavas; likewise, the ascetics and the female renunciants would come to her.
He indeed goes quickly to visit the virtuous for the purpose of seeing them, performing such services as massaging their feet and fetching water. (3)
In his hermitage, he always performs the purification of vessels and other such tasks, as well as the sweeping;
he partakes of the sacred remains (prasāda) and constantly serves the virtuous.
Thus, the devotee, filled with devotion, received a great blessing:
"Live long! Remain for a long time! Be happy and prosperous! (5)
Then, although he was engaged in the service of the virtuous, once,
due to his childish nature and greed, he [caught sight of] a golden chain that had fallen.
He seized the ornament of Vāsudeva by way of theft;
meanwhile, the virtuous men went to another village, while the tiger took the chain.
Having obtained it during the cleaning and other rites, he indeed kept it hidden;
having brought it to his own home, he placed the golden chain in a casket.
No one indeed knew that he was thus protecting him;
even his mother did not know of the chain within the chest.
Even his father, the wandering minstrel named Kūṭadeva,
did not know such a chain— a golden chain within a wooden box.
She recognizes it herself when held, and she sees it even in the dark;
furthermore, she places it back there, hidden within the chest.
Then the virtuous one named Śyāma, a worshipper of Viṣṇumūrti,
went to another village for the sake of worship, taking with him his chain as far as he desired.
Not seeing her at the time of worship, he reflected that she must have fallen;
he then repeatedly sent messengers through his devotees to inquire in Māyāpura.
His devotees questioned the tiger as to whether he had seen [the sage] or not;
out of both greed and fear, he gave them this reply.
Thus, due to the sin of theft committed by the non-existent tiger,
the two hands of the gold thief were indeed filled with finger-rings.
Gala-kushtha (ringworm) appeared on both his thumbs in every way, and his body became afflicted with white leprosy; this was the fruit born of theft and sin.
He devoted himself to me, the Blessed One, and even applied medicinal treatments;
yet his leprosy did not subside at all, and he became exceedingly miserable. (17)
And although he was a partaker of the sin of stealing gold, he became a recipient of the fruit of serving the virtuous;
there, indeed, he heard the narrative associated with Lakṣmī.
He had heard that the fruit of stealing gold would be leprosy,
and he had also heard that its atonement was the gift of gold.
If one who has stolen gold performs the Brahmakṛcchra vow as well as the Brahmakūrca vow for seven days, he is liberated.
Then, while this [matter] was indeed undisclosed, he practiced the Brahmakūrca vow in secret, causing internal pain; yet, having made it public outwardly, he performed the Brahmakūrca penance.
On the first day, he drank water boiled with *khadira* leaves;
on the second day, however, he drank water boiled with *kiṃśuka* flowers.
On the third day, however, he drank water boiled with bilva leaves;
on the fourth day, he drank water boiled with lotus seeds.
In the fifth month, however, he drank water boiled with udumbara fruits;
in the sixth month, he drank water boiled with darbha leaves, and after that, [the same].
Worshipping me repeatedly, he observed the fast on the seventh lunar day;
he also performed a rite of propitiation before my image, which destroys all sins.
"O Hari, while I was performing the cleansing there, gold was obtained by me;
that sin has indeed manifested in the form of leprosy upon me—forgive that! (26)
Furthermore, I shall bestow a golden garland upon that virtuous man;
I have also performed expiation through the Brahmakūrca vow.
"May this disease of mine be destroyed; have mercy for the sake of my devotion.
Save me, protect me, O Lord of the World, O Śrī Hari, O Puruṣottama! (28)
"You are the one who effects the rescue from sin; protect me, your devotee.
Thus he entreated him most fervently, shedding profuse tears.
He reflected that death would come when his leprosy was not cured.

While he was thus reflecting, I fell asleep; and in a dream, I appeared in his presence, manifesting my form bearing the conch, discus, and mace. Laughing, I said to him: "O devotee, why do you grieve? Speak!"
He said to me, "O ocean of compassion, out of greed for gold, this chain belonging to the virtuous Viṣṇu was obtained by me, and it has now fallen upon the ground. (32)
"She remains protected in my home, and I enjoy the fruit of *kuṣṭhaka*;
having heard this story, I have performed the expiation for the theft of gold. (33)
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, destroy my sin through the Brahmakūrca vow"—
thus did he pray, and then I [appeared] in his presence.
Suddenly interrupting the dream, I brought him to the waking state;
he too, having quickly arisen there, beheld me as the Supreme Lord.
Overwhelmed and choked with love, he prostrated himself like a staff; filled with affection, he danced and likewise begged for forgiveness. (36)
Then, in order to remove that fault, I said to him:
"Give me the golden chain; indeed, your sin will be gone."
Then the tiger, having stood up, gave me the chain;
I then placed that chain around my own neck. (38)
The virtuous ones went to that place where they had been;
and having gone to Mūrtikaṇṭha, the virtuous one saw her there.
Beholding that golden garland again and again,
he rejoiced and recounted to everyone the supreme wonder of Hari.
For the sake of His devotees, the Blessed Lord indeed provides both acquisition and preservation;
He thinks only of His devotee in both prosperity and adversity. (41)
To whomever one may be devoted, for that person's sake the Blessed One himself bestows his own blessed state along with all his personal sovereignty.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, Vyāghra, the king of devotees, was instantly freed from leprosy and became cleansed of all sin. ||43||
He was born fortunate and handsome, just as before;
therefore, I myself, Nārāyaṇa, protect my dependent.
Whether it be a sinner, or one filled with impurity, overwhelmed by the defects of illusion, burdened by hundreds of millions of latent impressions, and devoid of righteous deeds and the like; ||45||
Moreover, [consider] me who has come to you for refuge, who has renounced his life for my sake, whose every activity is for my sake, and whose meditation and worship are for my sake. (46)
I shall protect people in every way through the surrender of all things unto me;
listen now to another divine story that destroys the torment of sin. 47.

In the village of Dhanagrāma, there lived an excellent Brahmin named Uttama, who served as the priest for the village; he lived with his family and was primarily devoted to the ritualistic portion of the Vedas. (48)
He is indeed the facilitator of the ritual section for people of all castes;
he is the preceptor even of the king, and he also performs the king's business.
The food of kings is indeed said to be heavy, as is the food of thieves;
likewise, the food of people who do not give and of those who have fallen from their status is heavy.
O Lakṣmī, what is eaten does not digest; even what is drunk does not digest;
and clothing, vessels, and the like, once accepted as a gift, do not digest either. (51)
The acceptance of gifts such as beds, cows, and gold never decays;
he is indeed the most excellent "earth-god" (brāhmaṇa), known as the village priest.
Out of greed, he caused all the castes to seize wealth and other possessions;
he ate, drank, consumed food, took pleasure, and rejoiced in his home. (53)
And his prosperity in the house became most excellent, surpassing that of kings;
there were necklaces of gems, golden garlands, and couches and seats of gold.
There were various mansions, as well as numerous male and female servants, and also cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, along with elephants, horses, chariots, and the like. (55)
Everything of his became prosperous; he had sons and daughters who bestowed happiness, and his wife was endowed with devotion, possessed of righteousness, and faithful to her husband.
Then, due to his burden of giving, the accumulation of wealth by the wicked,
and the food, drink, and other provisions provided to those sinners, he suffered from dropsy and fell into great fear.
The belly is afflicted by that, and indeed a large protuberance hangs down;
what is eaten does not digest, nor does what is drunk ever mature.
Even then, not even for a single moment did he experience happiness through his supernatural powers;
nevertheless, he went to the hermitages of physicians for the sake of curing his illness. (59)
Despite the administration of many medicinal remedies, the dropsy was not cured at all; on the contrary, it increased day by day. (3.180.60)
Then, on one occasion, that Brahmin went to the sage Devāyana;
having prostrated deeply before the holy man, he informed him of his own ailment.
The saintly man gave him a garland of the names of Hari and a sprout of Tulasī, saying:
"O Hare Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, make me free from suffering! (62)
Thus he instructed the Brahmin to perform the recitation a thousand times;
and so, every single day, he too joyfully performed that recitation daily.
He always worships me solely for the sake of destroying his disease;
the afflicted one worships me constantly, but the one seeking worldly prosperity does not worship me at all.
Afflicted by worldly power, he served me for his own sake;
yet he served me as one who performs devotion before me at the end of a year [of practice]. 65.
Out of compassion, he granted his own vision for the sake of curing the disease;
having formed a circle of holy men, he went toward his house.
He too, for the sake of curing the disease, joyfully gave food and other provisions, as well as various gifts such as gold, silver, and garments to the virtuous. (67)
He also prayed most earnestly for the sake of curing his disease;
having become a virtuous guru, I placed my hand upon his belly. (68)
Then, so that a miracle might indeed occur, the great disease of ascites departed from his belly in embodied form. (69)
Deformed and filled with fear, he fled and ran about;
yet in a moment, his ailment vanished, the Brahmin became healthy, and he was restored to well-being.
Then the water became dry and the digestive fire (jāṭhara) became auspicious;
we all, being virtuous, quickly attained invisibility. ||71||
Having recognized me as Nārāyaṇa, he then worshipped me repeatedly;
thus, O Lakṣmī, that devotee was rendered free from all affliction by me at that time.
He too, at the end, went to my supreme imperishable abode;
from reciting and hearing this, there is health, worldly enjoyment, and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cure of Leprosy for the Leprous Thief Named Vyāghra, a Devotee of the Cāraṇas; the Cure of Dropsy for the Devotee, the Village Priest Named Uttama; the Vision of the Lord, Liberation, and Other Matters," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of Virāla. A devotee named Virāla was a resident of Māñjuṣṭha village. (1)
He was indeed a wealthy Vaiśya living with his family, engaged in the trade and sale of foodstuffs, garments, and vessels. (2)

The subject (dharmin) is one who possesses wealth exceeding a hundred thousand [gold pieces] and is devoted to the service of the virtuous, by whom a beautiful and most splendid hall of Dharma was caused to be built. (3)
Where virtuous guests arrive and find rest—travelers, ascetics, holy women, and those weary from their journeys. (4)
Wherein he caused to be constructed that most excellent and auspicious food-sacrifice (annasatra),
wherein there was sweet food endowed with flavor, as well as milk and boiled rice.
The monks always receive fried cakes, soups, vegetables, and other foods;
they eat them constantly by the hundreds, and he bestows words of blessing upon them.
Even Virālavaiśya constantly gave gifts with his own hand—
alms to children, to the helpless, and even to women.
She causes the chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu to be performed,
and she herself performs my worship in this manner, as well as causing it to be performed, every single day.
He had five sons, seven daughters, and two wives;
all of them worship me, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having gathered together in the evening before me, they perform kīrtana;
they tell delightful stories and listen to one another.
Thus, for Virāja, who was endowed with merit and great prosperity,
a severe case of consumption (rājayakṣmā) arose before he had even reached old age.
Constantly increasing, the disease has caused him to become emaciated;
many medicines have been administered, and likewise, various mantras have been performed.
Many meritorious deeds were performed and great efforts were made for his sake, yet the disease did not perish; the merchant became consumed by anxiety.
The family is consumed by anxiety: "The father, who is worthy of honor, is about to die;
what should be done? Where should one go? Indeed, for the sake of protecting the father—" (14)
As they were reflecting thus, the auspicious Kuṅkumavāpikā appeared—a holy site that removes disease, where the Lord of Śrī himself resides in person. (15)
When this thought had arisen in their minds, they then departed together with Janaka for the sacred site of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Proclaiming my name and likewise remembering me, the Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the remover of disease.
Then, having arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, they sat down beneath a banyan tree; remembering me, they drank the water.
Having reached the inexhaustible water-vessel, all those radiant ones bathed;
then they gave gifts of gold, silver, and garments.
They gave alms-bowls, foods, sweets, and blankets, saying, "May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be pleased with us. (3.181.20)
Then, perceiving his devotion, Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin,
went to the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake into his presence.
Then, that man named Virāla, considering his death to have occurred at a sacred ford, remembered me within his heart; may Nārāyaṇa protect him.
Then, having gone into his presence, I indeed questioned Virālaka:
"O wealthy man, from where, for what reason, and how have you come here? (23)
"O Tīrthakṛt, how did this disease come to be, and for how long has it persisted?
Remembering his death with great distress, Virālaka wept aloud. (24)
He grieved there in many ways and questioned me, the Brahmin: "Salutations to you, O sage; you are aged, so if you know the deity [responsible for this], please tell me. (25)
Tell me, O Brahmin, how disease arose for one who has performed so much merit;
indeed, no sin was committed by me in this birth. (26)
Indeed, many various kinds of meritorious gifts were bestowed.
From my childhood, I have been one who serves the virtuous, and I am a worshiper of Śrī Hari. ||27||
My family is indeed always endowed with devotion toward the Supreme Lord;
together with my family, I perform religious observances joined with devotion. (28)
"Nevertheless, show me how this wasting disease came upon me. Having heard this, he who was in the form of a brahmin spoke all of Virāla's story. (29)
He indeed related the account of his previous birth to the lotus-born one:
"Listen, O merchant; you are highly meritorious in every respect in this present life."
Indeed, whatever action was performed in the past cannot be escaped by anyone;
in a previous birth, you were a Brahmin named Gaṅgeśvara.
On the holy bank of the Sābhramatī, at the temple of Viṣṇu, you became a priest;
nearby there were fields of grain and gardens.
The seats of the Vaiśya were indeed beautiful, yet the Vaiśya met his death;
his wife, having become a maidservant in the palace, then performed service there. (33)
There in that temple, that virtuous woman gave cows and bulls;
likewise, she also gave fields and gardens to the temple.
Unable to practice agriculture, she became a servant in the temple and dwelt in the refuge of the gods, having no other support and relying solely upon you.
She indeed performs the service of the bulls with grass and other fodder, as well as milking and so forth;
likewise, she carries water and performs sweeping and other such tasks.
She serves Gaṅgeśvara, remaining ever obedient to his command;
whatever grains, vegetables, fruits, and other things grow upon the earth [are hers].
Having brought those [grains], you first give them to the Brahmin;
you must always cook them well and offer the most delicious food as a naivedya to Viṣṇu.
Having granted her favor, you then took the food;
the servant, having prepared it, offers the flowers, garlands, and other items to Viṣṇu.
Thus she constantly serves you as well as Viṣṇu the Lord—
free from guile, endowed with devotion, offering everything, and possessed of virtue.
Now, being greedy for the sense of taste, you prepare excellent sweet food and offer it secretly within the temple to Viṣṇu. (41)
Having eaten and attained satisfaction, you then give even that coarse food—namely wheat cakes—to your female servant. (42)
Thus you have always acted with partiality toward the giver;
that which ought to be given first to the donor was not done by you at that time.
The breaking of the line of seating that was committed there became your sin in the past.
Once, during a period of excessive rain, there was a great flood on the Sābhramatī. ||44||
Pervading the field, the grove, and even the temple, that [water] indeed surged with great velocity and increased rapidly, overflowing its banks. 45.
The cows, the bulls, and the servants all climbed onto the ground at the site where the temple was to be raised, being afflicted by great fear. (46)
That servant-woman, the farmer's wife, being terrified when you arrived with water, clung to you;
longing to preserve her life, she embraced you for the sake of survival. (47)
You, as well as that Karṣukī, Ratnamālā,
the cows, and the bulls— all for the sake of their livelihood— remembered me in my embodied form.
Then I reflected upon this for the sake of protecting the devotees and yogis:
"O merchant, even when the time of death has arrived for embodied beings," (49)
The mind is turbid, powerful, difficult to restrain, and accompanied by latent impressions;
it quickly undergoes a transformation upon contact with the body of a woman. (3.181.50)
Then, at that moment and in that place, your mind underwent a transformation;
you were overcome by desire during the embrace in the flood of water. (51)
Having realized this, I abandoned you and even rejected your servants;
though I had come for the sake of protection, I did not provide you with protection there. (52)
O twice-born one, seeing the destruction of Dharma, I did not provide protection;
you were carried away by the force of the current along with the greedy woman.
Cows and bulls were also swept away in that flood;
all of them died, though they were endowed with merit yet possessed a slight degree of sin. ||54||
O Brahmin Gaṅgeśvara, you were then a defiler of the assembly;
now indeed you are wealthy and possessed of the merit of service to Hari. (55)
The field, the gift, the female cultivator, and the servants are indeed yours;
this Brāhmaṇa woman who was your wife before your death is your second wife. (56)
Immediately after, having died from grief, she shines here as this merchant's wife;
those five sons who were bulls are indeed those who have died in the waters of the Pūru. (57)
"O merchant, these seven daughters, the two cows, and [my other possessions] have perished in the waters;
yet, by the fruit of my worship, this wealth and prosperity now exist. (58)
"O merchant, this disease of yours has arisen today because you eat desired food for your own sake while sitting apart from the row; yet this deceitlessness of yours brings joy. (59)
A female farmer enjoys the merit of giving fields, gardens, and the like;
a Brahmin woman, however, enjoys the merit of dharma through her devotion to her husband.
The gods, wealth, cattle, and human beings all enjoy happiness;
you, however, as the worshiper, are endowed with wealth, grain, jewels, women, and progeny.
I have incurred the fruit of consumption as the result of the sin of breaking the row;
yet, through the power of devotion, both you and I [are restored] for the sake of the family.
I, Mādhava, have come for the sake of liberation for one who has reached the sacred ford;
tell me, Virālaka, whether it be liberation or freedom from disease. (33)
"What do you desire? Hari, assuming the form of a Brahmin, shall say here:
"I will by all means bring about the destruction of the sin of eating what is forbidden. (64)
"O merchant, become free from affliction, or indeed attain liberation right here.
Upon hearing this, he was suddenly thrilled and, having prostrated before Puruṣottama, [he departed]. (65)
He asked me, "Does my life still remain in this world, or not? I replied to him, "Not even a moment of life remains for you beyond this point."
"But you are my devotee and have come to my abode as a seeker of the sacred ford;
therefore, out of compassion for your desire to destroy disease, I grant it to you."
Whether you desire long life, liberation, or indeed both,
I remove birth, death, old age, and disease for those who seek my refuge.
Thus addressed, that eminent merchant then gave a seat, as well as water for honoring (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and fruits to me in the form of a Brahmin.
Musk, saffron, camphor, as well as saffron filaments,
sandalwood, fragrant heartwoods, and likewise excellent jeweled necklaces.
Garlands of flowers, woolen blankets, crowns, bracelets, earrings, rings, and also chains made of gold. (71)
He offered fragrant essences, a parasol, fly-whisks, golden sandals,
various other gifts, as well as sons, daughters, and both his wives.
Then the merchant offered all his wealth to me, O Lakṣmī;
he honored me according to the prescribed rite and declared, "I am yours. (73)
"Save me! Protect me! O ocean of compassion, do as you wish; I am indeed yours.
Thus did Virālaka speak to me, O Acyuta, at that time.
He said to him, "O merchant, may you become free from disease immediately;
stay upon the earth for only one year, and thereafter there shall be liberation. (75)
"You shall indeed go; there is no doubt. Having performed the ritual ablution at the sacred ford, return home.
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (76)
Chant this mantra constantly, worship your beloved Kṛṣṇa, remember me always, O merchant, and perform the pilgrimage to the five sacred fords (pañcatīrthī). 77.
Constantly practice the service of the virtuous, the holy men, and the noble women; likewise, perform the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and the sacrifice to all beings.
Perform for me acts of charity, fire-offerings, and the presentation of food offerings;
for in this essence-less cycle of existence, the constant service of Hari is the only true essence. (79)
Service to the virtuous is the supreme essence; indeed, association with the virtuous is the medicine.
Service to me truly bestows liberation upon the virtuous, for it destroys latent desires.
By the power of serving the virtuous, latent impressions (vāsanā) indeed dissolve here;
honoring the good is the means for destroying the sins of infinite births. (81)
Worthy worship is the destroyer of misfortunes that have already begun for the poor; worthy worship is also the destroyer of obstacles and the multitude of diseases. (82)
The virtuous are like wish-fulfilling gems; they grant what is well-conceived.
The virtuous are like wish-granting trees; they bestow the highest desired object.
The virtuous are indeed wish-fulfilling trees that grant even the fruit of immortality; the holy ones are cows of plenty that milk forth eternal happiness.
Those holy ones bestow both spiritual accomplishments and worldly prosperity;
indeed, through their blessings, they transform even meager fortune into great fortune.
Those virtuous ones, by means of my yoga, cause me to attain divine nature and reach the imperishable state;
they ward off the messengers of Yama, and they are my heart. 86.
For they indeed burn away evils, increase merits, bestow good fortune, and remove calamities. (87)
O merchant, always perform service toward them that bestows grace;
and also, O gentle one, always carry out the five sacrifices with sincere devotion. (88)
O Gaṅgaka, perform service to cows and service to the Dharma, which bestow heaven; always engage in the study of discourses on self-knowledge. (89)
O devoted one, always perform my worship alone;
at the end, having granted you my vision, I shall lead you to my imperishable abode.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, sexual misconduct, theft, and even the killing of an embryo—such are the great sins for which there is atonement in the realm of Yama. ||9.1||
By him who has served the virtuous, such clarity has been attained;
by him who, through total self-surrender to the holy ones, has received their word of blessing. (92)
The burning away of those various sins occurs swiftly;
for the virtuous person, there is no atonement whatsoever equal to service [to the Guru], nor any other. 93.
O Lakṣmī, for a virtuous person who is indeed immersed in service, there is no world of Yama;
even insects, birds, and the like, as well as outcasts and murderers [attain it]. (94)
Even courtesans and thieves were uplifted by their service to the virtuous;
so too were beasts, birds, trees, creepers, and shrubs. (95)
Through the practice of the virtuous, they attained the supreme good in the Lotus [World];
the great path of devotion to Kṛṣṇa proceeds only among the virtuous. (96)
From that, it subsequently proceeds among the virtuous throughout all worlds;
by this, people cross over saṃsāra and reach its further shore. ||97||
Those who are devoted to the service of the virtuous surely go to my world, having enjoyed infinite heavens as well as the stations of the lords. 98.
And they rejoice in Vaikuṇṭha, in Goloka, and in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman).
Thus was that Virālaka, the king of devotees, instructed by me. 99.
By my command, the wealthy man departed for his own home filled with joy;
there he served me in every way, and at the end of a year, he met his death.
Having performed supreme service to the virtuous, he went to my imperishable abode;
in this way, O Lakṣmī, both the listener and the speaker who possess devotion shall go to that abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of the Vaiśya named Virāla in a Previous Birth, His Attainment of Śrī Hari in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Destruction of His Consumption, and His Liberation," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇīśrī, listen to this story and another as well.
Formerly, there was a king named Pṛthvīdhara in Karṇapura.
Ruling over a fragmented kingdom, he protected his subjects according to dharma;
in his courtyard every morning, there were always more than a hundred mendicants.
Indeed, helpless young boys and girls,
as well as helpless widows, find satisfaction through the gain of food, eating at this perpetual gift of rice.
Having gone to the temple of Viṣṇu, King Pṛthvīdhara himself performed the worship of the image of Nārāyaṇa with tulasī leaves.
Constantly uttering "Salutation to Viṣṇu," he performs [this] ten thousand times a day,
meditating upon and remembering me, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person.

Having offered incense, a lamp, food offerings, water, and betel leaf, as well as performing the waving of lights (nīrājana), hymns of praise, and circumambulation, one should prostrate like a staff. || 6 ||
He gives a gift of one hundred silver coins, as well as a hundred garments, and he always gives a single cow; thereafter, he remains constant in his giving.
Having offered a handful of flowers to Śrī Hari, he goes to his own home;
thus he worships me constantly, subsisting on food offered to me.
He lived always as a devotee, avoiding violence and sexual misconduct;
for one whose merit was performed in a previous birth, such devotion arises.
And his mind remains fixed on the Dharma even amidst the splendor of sovereignty;
thus, O Lakṣmī, Pṛthvīdhara, having performed his auspicious daily rites, always remains so.
He goes to the court of justice and there indeed delivers a verdict;
then, every evening, he always listens to my discourse.
From the assembly of the virtuous gathered for the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, the saintly, perfected, and wise ones dispel many doubts. (12)
The king partakes of the water from the feet of the virtuous, and at the conclusion of the discourse, he performs a recitation accompanied by musical instruments. (13)
Thousands of people—women and men alike—are chanting his praises:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare! (14)
"Hare Viṣṇu! Hare Jiṣṇu! O Anādi-Kṛṣṇa! Hare!
Hare!"—in this manner they performed your worship, beginning with the accompaniment of musical instruments.
Then the virtuous ones indeed retired to their monasteries; thereafter, the king, having performed the evening worship of the gods and obtained excellent food, [did likewise].
While repeatedly reciting "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," he becomes absorbed in meditation as he turns my rosary. (17)
Thinking "he is indeed sleeping," the king also practiced virtuous conduct;
his queen, named Madhuvindā, was a devoted Vaiṣṇavī.
Just as a virtuous woman endowed with devotion to her husband, O Brahmins, worships Me—the Supreme Self—regarding this world as terrible; ||19||
Bondage is that which is rich in suffering and defects, permeated by latent impressions (vāsanā), and subject to decay;
whereas liberation is the eternal Supreme Self, and she [the Goddess] is indeed the Self itself.
She regards me as the giver of liberation, serves virtuous people, and, possessing a tranquil character like that of a king’s daughter, she worships me, Janārdana. (21)
As is the king, so is the prosperity; thus the subjects become endowed with virtue.
His sons and others also worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī. 22.
All my subjects, belonging to all the social orders, likewise devoted themselves to me;
they gave gifts, performed recitations, and offered their service. ||23||
And for the virtuous, even while performing acts such as cleaning the dwelling and so forth, they offer [these services] to the holy ones;
thus indeed it is for Vaiṣṇavas who conduct themselves continuously in this manner. 24.
The Blessed One remains gracious, and the rain-cloud pours down its rain;
all prosperities rejoice as if they were sentient beings endowed with fortune. (25)
The cows rained down all desires, the trees bore fruit,
the crops yielded grain, and the earth itself bestowed its essence.
For that devotee of mine, O Śrī, there were likewise no enemies.
There were no calamities, and that king became rich in happiness.
In due time, his first son was born blind from birth;
nevertheless, he performed the birth celebrations for that son according to the prescribed rites at the proper time.
He remained known as one born blind, for he did not open his eyes at all;
meanwhile, the king indeed performed the ritual service of Viṣṇu during a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
For the purpose of opening the eyes, one should perform the worship of the sun and the moon,
and offer an unbroken lamp of ghee in the temple of the deity.
A year passed for him in blindness;
then the king, suddenly abandoning all hope, set his mind upon asceticism alone.
Leaving the royal palace, he took a seat in the shade beneath a grove of trees in a garden and sat down to perform his ascetic penance.
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa," he turned his rosary;
the king, subsisting on fruit, ate but one meal a day in solitude.
Holding a śālagrāma stone before him, he worships me and remembers me as well, even though he is clad only in bark garments and seated upon a deer-skin. (34)
Deprived of all enjoyments and longing for his son and eyes,
he frequents me day and night there in that hermitage, dwelling among the trees.
The king endures the rain, the cold, and the heat, and he serves me;
with devotion, he performs worship of my Śālagrāma stone, O King. (36)
Performing the three daily ablutions and bowing to the sun, she who wore five locks of hair and honored the ancestors passed a year in this manner. ||37||
Thus, at the end of the year, the king meditated upon me repeatedly during the night and praised me;
O Kṛṣṇa, your name is indeed "Hari," for it removes all suffering. (38)
O Mādhava, why do you not remove the suffering of me, your devotee?
You are entirely capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise in every way. (39)
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever merit there is, that is indeed Your favor and grace;
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever sin there is, that is indeed Your opposition and indifference. (3.182.40)
If you display such indifference toward a devotee, then what is the fate of that devotee who has been abandoned by his protector? (41)
O Mādhava, protect your son as well by granting him sight;
having shaken off his sin, restore his vision to him. (42)
Having spoken thus, and having quickly heard my prayer, he prostrated himself like a staff;
then, observing the asceticism of his son, I arrived here for the sake of his eyes. (43)
Matted-haired, carrying a staff, virtuous, smeared with ashes, and clad in a deer-skin,
he appeared within that circle of trees, holding a water-pot in his hand.
Uttering "Hare Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu" in the presence of the virtuous, he departed, saying, "Victory to the yogin, the lord of the earth, who is in the guise of an ascetic! (45)
Having uttered these words, he gave him the auspicious water from his water-pot;
the king, for his part, was struck with the utmost wonder.
This sudden arrival in the guise of a holy man—whence has this guest come?
Could he be that divine and infallible one who fulfills my heart’s desire? (47)
"A guest must indeed be honored, especially one who is virtuous.
Having reflected thus, the king rose and fell at his feet. (48)
He offered a seat and likewise presented the arghya and madhuparka;
he also performed worship with flowers, perfumes, fruits, and other offerings. ||49||
Having offered his salutations, he then inquired regarding the reason for their arrival:
"I am blessed; I have fulfilled my purpose by the sight of these holy people. (3.182.50)
The supreme water in the form of a sacred ford has been obtained from his water-pot;
its mere sight is purifying and makes all the senses holy. (51)
Today, by the power of my good fortune, I shall obtain the touch that destroys sin at the feet of the Holy One, as well as his service and his grace. (52)
"Out of compassion, through divine favor, and by the accumulation of merit," having said this, he stood before him in silence with palms joined in reverence. ||53||
"I am Sādhusvarūpa; may you be endowed with the highest good. Is all well with you, O King? Or tell me, what is the reason for your asceticism? (54)
The king said: "Indeed, by the grace of the virtuous, I am well;
I possess sons, I possess wealth, and I am devoted to the virtuous. (55)
"Nevertheless, my son remains unvirtuous and does not see me at all;
O holy one, he is as if born blind—tell me, what could be the cause? (56)
"O Lord, for the sake of attaining his vision, I perform penance in the month of Mādhava;
it consists of worship, and I have no other desire. (57)
If one’s son is sightless, his kingdom shall indeed be blind;
even if he himself is not sightless, blindness in the home and blindness in the lineage bring great suffering. ||58||
How can this blindness go far away? You know; show me!
Thus, through the meeting with you, a holy man, I shall indeed have fulfilled my purpose. (59)
The speech of the virtuous is divine, always true in meaning and bestowing success;
the heart of the virtuous is indeed gentle and removes all suffering. (3.182.60)
Beholding the virtuous is meritorious, and serving them likewise bestows liberation;
the favor bestowed by a holy man fulfills all desires. (61)
Having spoken thus, he ceased; and then, O Lakṣmī, I said:
"Listen, O King, in a previous birth your son was an ascetic."
Just as I was dressed in the garb of an ascetic, so too did that brahmin Durvoḍhaka become an ascetic; he was poor and desired a kingdom. (63)
He performed austerities on the bank of the Revā at the Śuklaka tīrtha, where many men seeking the merit of sacred fords come and go. ||64||
Men and women bathe at that sacred ford and depart from its side;
Durvoḍhaka, observing them, remains established in that place of austerity.
O Lakṣmī, the sense organ is powerful and the mind is likewise powerful;
when an object comes before it, whether approaching or departing, it becomes restless.
The restraint of those [senses] must always be practiced by the ascetic;
for if the senses and the mind are not restrained, austerity is fruitless. (67)
At what moment will the turbulent mind not lead one astray?
There is never any certainty or trust in that mind. (68)
Once, you yourself, as king, set out for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites together with your family,
accompanied by a limited number of attendants and enriched with all necessary provisions.
On the day of the full moon, he went to Śuklatīrtha on the Revā river to bathe,
at that spot where this virtuous ascetic, the Brahmin, was performing his austerities.
Then you made your dwelling in a mango grove a short distance away;
having recognized him as an ascetic, a holy man with matted hair, you stood before him. (71)
Accompanied by his wife, he performed prostrations and likewise offered worship; the queen, filled with devotion, presented fruits and other offerings. (72)
Having washed the feet of the virtuous one, your beloved drank the water—she who was radiant with beauty, youth, loveliness, nourishment, and grace. ||73||
Upon seeing her, delusion arose in this ascetic brahmin, and he secretly cast his two eyes full of desire upon her. (74)
Then that brahmin [bestowed it] upon the queen who was his disciple,
as well as upon the holy female attendant at the holy ford, and likewise upon the king’s mother.
Driven by desire and intent upon sovereignty, he performed austerities with longing;
yet, with his senses and mind unsubdued, he then committed the sin of a wicked glance.
Indeed, those who are infatuated with another's wife and employ their wicked eyes are truly born blind and blind from birth, for they possess passion. (77)
Thus, at that time, the sin of delusion indeed arose for this brahmin ascetic, who was infatuated by the beauty of her form. (78)
Therefore, in order to prevent the arising of delusion, beautiful women always do not even show their faces, solely for the sake of protecting the Dharma. (79)

Excellent noble women always maintain the garment of modesty as a covering over their faces when appearing in public, for the sake of protecting their devotion to their husbands and other virtues. (3.182.80)
Because [wrong] view causes delusion, they do not even grant an audience;
veiled by their shawls, they remain where the sun cannot be seen. (8.1)
Then, O King, that ascetic passed away in the course of time;
this son of yours was born from her womb, begotten by him while he was still infatuated.
This kingdom is the fruit of his asceticism, obtained by that great-souled one;
and he has indeed obtained the fruit of his evil gaze, known as this [present] birth.
O devoted one, gratified by your austerities, worship, and other offerings, I, the Blessed One who resides at Śālagrāma, have come here. (84)
Thus, I am Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, the granter of your desires;
speak, O King, and I shall give you here whatever is pleasing to your mind. (85)
"I have come here for the sake of food; whatever you desire, I shall give to you.
Thus addressed, the royal sage named Pṛthvīdhara then spoke.
He requested the sight of his son, devotion at my feet, and finally,
the imperishable abode as well as a lineage consisting solely of devotees.
Having heard this, I gave it to him, saying, "So be it; it shall happen thus.
Then, having offered water from my water-pot, I vanished from that spot.
With a serene mind, the king, having completed his ascetic penance,
departed for his own dwelling situated in the village, clad in bark garments.
Honored by the subjects and recognized as a worthy recipient of boons,
his desires fulfilled, he was further gladdened by shouts of victory.
He then went to his own palace while excellent musical instruments were played on all sides; indeed, the queen attained a state of great joy.
The king went toward his son and quickly gave the water offered by me;
by the touch of that water, the eye was restored to the son's eye, and he regained his sight.
Then his right hand became left, and through the touch of the water, it regained its sight;
a great festival arose, and the fruit of his asceticism was fully realized. (93)
Then a young son was born, who indeed remembered his past lives at all times;
consequently, he constantly recollected the fruit of his own evil vision.
He too was born as a great devotee of the Lord, endowed with righteousness;
by name he was King Citradhvaja, powerful and devoted to the virtuous.
O Lakṣmī, he always honors me; he governs the kingdom entrusted to him by his father according to policy and indeed delights his subjects. 9.6.
When his father passed away, I then caused him to reach his own abode, the imperishable realm of Viṣṇu, by means of a celestial chariot.
Thus, by Viṣṇu, the fulfillment of the desire of his own devotee— who had indeed been strengthened by ascetic penance— was accomplished through the granting of the sight of a son.
O Lakṣmī, being pleased and becoming subject to devotion on this earth, I utterly destroy the external and internal blindness of my devotees. (99)
I bestow the divine treasure-trove of knowledge, which illuminates the Self,
by means of which they cross over the darkness of Māyā and proceed to the supreme state.
From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, and from worshipping me,
there shall be enjoyment and liberation, as well as prosperity, happiness, and final release.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Life of King Pṛthvīdhara, His Birth as a Son Blind from Birth, and How the Blessed Lord Granted Him Sight," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, on the bank of the river Śatrūñjayā there was a devotee named Sāgara, a Śūdra who was a protector of the forest. || 1 ||
Accompanied by his sons and retinue, and equipped with weapons, he—appointed to the kingdom of Pālikā—guards the forest at Pālikātāna. || 2 ||
Once, that king, born in Pālikātāna, went into the forest regions for the purpose of hunting, accompanied by a limited number of servants.
Having entered that forest, the king took that servant Sāgara with him there as a guide for the path among the deer and other wild animals.
This Śūdra, too, is a devotee of Hari;
he indeed commits no violence, for as one who practices non-violence, he truly fears the sin of harming the king.
He led him toward a remote region devoid of wild animals;
here, deer come, go, and even dwell.
Having spoken thus, he led the lord of the earth, the king named Vanapāla,
to a place where there was water, a delightful forest, and beautiful regions.
Wandering from forest to forest even within the vast wilderness, he led him to that region where there were human habitations here and there until evening.
Pointing out, "The deer is here; the deer is there," he led the king on a circuit while chanting the name of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Praying within, he said, "O Blessed One, please forgive me for this offense committed here together with the king, arising from our pursuit of game."
"O Lord, I do not wish to kill the forest-born deer myself at any time, nor do I wish to cause such violence to be committed by others at any time."
Therefore, this king shall be led by me out through the gate, so that deer may not be found there and no violence may befall me. (12)
"There would be no sin of violence; therefore, protect me in that way, O Mādhava!
Perhaps some wild animal might not encounter the king here on this path. (13)
"O Inner Controller, O Lord, ordain all things accordingly for my benefit.
Thus did that righteous and pure Śūdra devotee pray to me. (14)
Drawing that king along, he goes before him here and there, describing it in many ways; O King, in this case, it must indeed be a sword.
Here there may be a variegated deer, as well as a horned animal and a sṛmara;
here there is also a gavaya, a hare, or perhaps a geṇḍuka here.
Whether it be a hyena, a black deer, or a boar that appears here,
he goes on and on, eager and binding his hopes upon each one.
He offers water and fruits to the king and even serves him;
nevertheless, that king finds no satisfaction except for deer.
Thus, evening fell within the forest;
and the king, though still intent on capturing the deer, then became hopeless.
When the sun had set, they all took rest within the forest;
hungry and despondent, they stayed indeed beneath a banyan tree on the shore of a lake.
Then, by the turn of fortune, another forest-dweller who had been wandering through his own forest returned at that time toward his home. (21)
Having heard the voices of men there beneath the banyan tree,
he emerged by a side path and returned once more to the shelter of the banyan.
There he saw the king accompanied by a limited number of attendants; he bowed to them with devotion, stood before them, and questioned that monarch.
"O King, how is it that there is rest for the group of servants here tonight? If there is work to be done, I shall remain at your command to serve. (24)
"I am a servant, knowledgeable of forest paths, familiar with wild creatures, and accustomed to dwelling in the woods;
I understand everything in the forest and shall carry out the king's command. (25)
Having heard the account and that his daily activities had been fruitless, the king then spoke of his entire futile wandering in search of game.
Then, having heard this, another forest-dweller named Dakṣagarva said to the king:
"O King, this forest is not like that; it is never inhabited by such deer. (27)
"By whom was this path shown, which yields nothing but affliction? There are no deer in this forest, yet wood-gatherers wander here. (28)
Furthermore, there is another forest for deer on the southern bank of the river;
there, success in hunting is always achieved. (29)
"O King, you have surely been deluded by someone; you are proceeding here in vain. This exertion of yours in this forest will indeed result only in hardship. (3.183.30)
Thus addressed, the king then realized his own deception; for he understood that the futile wandering had been brought about by the Śūdra Sāgara.
Alas! Men are indeed betrayers of trust; having dragged a king onto a wrong path, they lead him toward his death.
Trust should never be placed in strangers, whether in the forest, at home, or on the battlefield; by placing trust in them, kings may encounter great hardship.
We, seeking deer, have been deceived here by Sāgara;
we have been led far astray in a forest devoid of deer and rendered fruitless. (34)
This man, who indeed exists as one whose conduct is hypocritical, is a fit recipient for punishment;
he must be abandoned through the infliction of punishment, and instruction must be given by me in this matter.
Having reflected thus, the king then spoke to the forest-dweller named Dakṣagarva: "Stay, or go to your own home."
"Come here with me tomorrow morning for the sake of hunting in the forest;
indeed, I shall grant you an excellent reward as you desire. (37)
"O Dakṣagarva, having offered salutations and demonstrated the necessity [of your presence], go or stay only if deer are easily obtainable; otherwise, do not. (38)
He went to his own home at night and did not return to that place in the morning;
the king, having become enraged, [went] to the ocean at dawn.
He asked, "Tell me, how did you bring me here to this forest, where there is no hunting at all, and where wandering in the wilderness has become futile? (3.183.40)
"You have indeed caused this suffering; therefore, you must be punished in every way.
You shall receive your monthly wages from my treasury. (41)
"Since I have been deceived here by you, who are truly a servant,
therefore I shall inflict punishment upon you, a deceitful seeker."
Having spoken thus, the king quickly addressed his other servants with these words:
"Bind the forearms and feet of this wicked man here with stones."
"Grind this wicked man to powder and throw him beneath the banyan tree!"—thus addressed, those other servants and soldiers became filled with rage. (44)
Seizing those terrible rocks, the fierce ones crushed them; having broken both his ankles at the foot of that banyan tree, they shattered his feet as well.
Having cast [the child] down from that place, all those wicked men, filled with pride, departed for another forest to hunt, along with the king. (46)
Then Sāgara, realizing that [the Lord] had arrived there by the power of destiny, wept bitterly in many ways, remembering me, Puruṣottama. 47.
O Blessed One, why do you not provide protection for your devotees here?
And O Kṛṣṇa, why do you not likewise bring about the destruction of the wicked? (48)
Having understood that there is great sin in violence, I, out of compassion for the deer, have indeed opened the way for the king. (49)
O ocean of mercy, I am your devotee; how can I, being compassionate, lead a cruel king—who would slay deer—to kill these young fawns? (3.183.50)
Today I have obtained the fruit of non-violence, which is indeed of a violent nature;
alas, O Kṛṣṇa, even you must endure what was done by one who has taken refuge in you. (51)
But this is a supreme wonder: that you do not protect your devotees, O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Hare Viṣṇu, O Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (52)
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Victorious One, grant protection!
If You do not come quickly here to this dense forest at the banyan tree, [all will be lost]. (53)
"Furthermore, on that day, my death will surely come here;
due to the hardship of walking, no one at all will give me water. (54)
They will depart for the realm of the vital breaths (Prāṇa), and my destination will be wretched;
even my family members will not know of my death here.
O Hare-Nātha, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Hari! O Hari, son of Śrī Kambharā, Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Ramā! ||56||
Come quickly, O Lord of Kamalā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Master!
O Lord of Padmāvatī, O Lord of Prajñā, O Lord of Śrīmāṇikī! ||57||
O Lord of the liberated, Lord of Brahmā, Lord of creation, Lord of the universe!
O Lord of devotees, Lord of the wretched, O Hari, Lord of the beloved of Brahmā! 58.
Come quickly, O Blessed One, you who possess a body for the sake of protecting your devotees;
O Lord of Saurāṣṭra, O glorious Master of the cowherd boys! 59.
"How indeed, O Blessed One, shall I endure this painful agony born from the crushing of my ankle joints? Here, my very life-breaths are indeed fainting away."
Having spoken thus, she bowed to me and immediately fell into a state of fainting;
O Lakṣmī, as long as Sāgara remains my devotee, so long shall I remain with him swiftly.
Taking the leaves of the sandhinī plant and its excellent juice, he quickly went to his side, assuming the form of a forest-dweller.
Having drawn them out with his fingers, he applied them there to the two broken places;
meanwhile, the two bandages were also quickly fastened around the forearms.
And the bones, as before, were restored to their natural state, free from disease, endowed with strength, and rich in blood;
they were touched by me again and again. (64)
Indeed, the prevention of his fainting was accomplished by me for the sake of my devotee; he was raised up, that suffering was removed, and everything was made whole once again. (65)
He was fed, and then made to drink excellent, pleasing water;
he was treated with affection by a loving gaze and brought to his own home. (66)
He worshipped me, who had assumed the form of a forest-dweller, with great devotion;
having provided a beautiful seat in his house, he performed service for me.
O Lakṣmī, his wife Hīrukā and his sons and daughters also served me in many ways at midday with meals and other refreshments.
I have eaten, I have drunk water, and likewise I have accepted service consisting of massaging the feet, rubbing the limbs, and so forth. (69)
Then this devoted Sāgara questioned me regarding himself: "O Lord Hari, O ocean of mercy, how can this suffering be mine?"
"By what sin has this state of having my legs broken come upon me?
Indeed, I have not harmed living beings, nor have I consumed meat, liquor, or similar things. (71)
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, even when touched [by others], one never acts falsely;
nor is theft or adultery ever committed at any time. ||72||
"But this deception of the king was performed by me, O Lord, for the sake of protecting living beings; no sin has been committed by me herein. (73)
"How was my foot struck? How did this suffering come upon you, O people?
Tell me truly, O Lord, or tell me what such karma must have been. (74)
"In this present life, I have neither committed nor even remember [such an act].
If it were done by me while I was unaware, then tell me that which dispels my doubt. (75)
Then, O Kamalā, I informed him of his past deeds;
for in this birth, he had indeed committed no such cruel act. (76)
Then I said: "Listen, O Sāgara, to what was done in the past:
you were indeed an elephant-keeper, the protector of the king's elephant. (77)
"You are indeed Dharodara by name, a Śūdra with a family here, who served as the elephant-keeper for this king, your father Dharmapāla. (78)
Once, while you were serving as a servant in charge of elephant care, when the elephant’s rut manifested, you [restrained] that young elephant. (79)
She made many efforts to bring the madman under her control,
indeed by placing *gokṣura* and other substances, as well as those made of iron, beneath his soles.
Likewise, with iron bolts, iron chains, and the like;
with fierce bhalla-javelins, bamboos, and long iron-tipped fruits.
Having split the feet of the elephant and rendered it powerless, you completely obstructed it as it became motionless and came to that place. ||82||
The fool struck excessively at his feet;
at that moment, even the bone of one of the elephant's legs was shattered. (83)
Furthermore, when that elephant desired to rise up again, you mercilessly struck it on its forefeet with iron clubs. (84)
The bone of the second foot went to powder on its side;
thus, by the power of his cruelty, the bones of both feet were shattered. (85)
"You were then cursed by the elephant: 'You shall become my protector and my slayer;
indeed, by my very trunk, your foot shall be broken. (86)
In the course of time, you have indeed met your end as Sāgara;
the elephant has also met its end, and this is that very prince. (87)
This very elephant, formerly known as Vanapāla, now has his feet broken;
he is the king today, and you are the forest-guardian today. (88)
"Your feet were broken by him as the fruit of those [deeds] previously committed.
Do not grieve; you are my devotee, and you have indeed been protected by me today. (89)
Action performed in the past does not abandon any embodied being;
O devotee, you have received the fruit of the action you yourself committed.
However, out of devotion and through non-violence, I have protected you;
yet even a slight offense on the part of the king has become the cause for this. (91)
"You should not grieve over the breaking of your foot in the forest;
take refuge in me, the Supreme Self, and behold my divine form. (92)
"I am Nārāyaṇa himself, come here in my four-armed form; go this very day to the king when he has returned home in the evening. (93)
"Tell me the entire account that provides protection and bestows happiness;
having heard it, that king will surely honor me. (94)
"By means of your yoga, I shall indeed bring about the liberation of the king.
Do not fear, O lord of devotees; I shall remain with you. (95)
Having spoken thus to the lotus-born Brahmā, the Blessed One vanished from that place;
the devotee, remembering Hari, went to the king's palace during the night.
He related the entire auspicious account to the king;
having heard it, the king was struck with wonder and repeatedly begged for forgiveness. (97)
Having come for refuge, he praised me, the protector of devotees, repeatedly recognizing his own previous birth as an elephant. (98)
Having attained supreme wonder and realizing that the body is transitory, the king became a devotee and took refuge in me along with his family. (99)
Then my father and my kinsmen also constantly attended upon me,
having ruled the kingdom and performed service to the virtuous, offering devotion at every opportunity.
They attained me, the Supreme Lord, the abode of Śrī, the imperishable and true state;
O Lakṣmī, from reading and hearing this, there is both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord made the feet of the Śūdra named Sāgara, whose feet were broken, free from pain, along with the account of his previous birth," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this purifying story of my devotee Vṛkṇadeva, which occurred in the past and destroys all sins.
In the city of Dhruvālaya, there was a servant named Vṛkṇadeva, who by birth was a Śūdra but was exceedingly righteous; he was a messenger.
Of the atheistic king named Bhāvaśūra,
Vṛkṇadeva was my devotee, while Bhāvaśūra himself was an atheist.
A constant dispute arose between the two friends;
Vṛkṇadeva always said, "O King, worship the Lord Hari."
Bhāvaśūra replied: "Revere both fortune and karma," thus repeatedly addressing the king when the great festival of Vṛkṇadeva’s vow had arrived.
He says, "Perform acts of charity, worship,
and religious duties," yet the king considers all such charity and worship to be mere falsehood.
There is no heaven, nor merit, nor likewise anything such as dharma;
everything arises from its own inherent nature, for as is the field, so is the growth.
Just as a son begotten by a queen through any seed whatsoever becomes a king, so too does the established order follow the lineage.
One born from a royal lineage in a poor family becomes wretched;
for one's innate nature, one's own past actions, and destiny prevail everywhere. (9)
A kingdom never presents itself to one who lacks the fortune for it;
nor does poverty ever present itself to one who possesses the fortune for sovereignty.
Just as the rays of the sun, having entered into water, become cool, and cold water, through contact with a great fire, becomes hot; || 11 ||
Indeed, everything born of the earth attains the state of earthliness within the earth;
likewise, by the power of the mine and through its inherent nature, the great becomes light.
Indeed, it arises exactly as ordained; in that regard, devotion holds no weight.
Rather, it is destiny that possesses weight, or else it is karma that possesses weight.
Indeed, action born of nature proceeds like inherent disposition;
a biped moves by means of two [feet], while a quadruped moves by means of four. || 14 ||
The hundred-footed [centipede] moves by means of its hundred [feet], and likewise is its formation;
the elephant eats with two faces, and the tree [stands] with a thousand roots.
Just as Kārttikeya [is surrounded] by six faces and Brahmā by four mouths, so too is the ocean the portion for the submarine fire (vāḍavāgni). 16.
Action performed at the proper place and time arises as destiny;
through that, one may obtain a kingdom, happiness, heaven, and the ancestral lineage. || 17 ||
"Understand from me, Vṛkṇadeva, that devotion has no causal efficacy in this matter.
In this way, the king constantly rebuked Vṛkṇadeva.
Then, after a long period of time had passed in this manner, the king once asked Vṛkṇadeva: "Tell me, how were you cut down?"
If devotion is indeed the cause of one's own desired happiness, then why, by the power of devotion, do you not abandon this state of being cut asunder? || 3.184.20 ||
Then Vṛkṇadeva spoke to King Bhāvaśūra:
"This state of being maimed has arisen from past action; indeed, it can be wiped away through devotion. (21)
O King, Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu is indeed the fulfiller of the desires of his devotees;
if a devotee desires sovereignty, the Lord Hari surely grants it.
If a devotee desires health, Narayana certainly grants it;
whatever desires he may long for, Hari surely fulfills them all.
For one who has desires, the Supreme Lord is the fulfiller of those desires;
for one who is free from desire, the Supreme Lord is the bestower of great bliss. ||24||
Everything indeed proceeds from truth; Mādhava is pleased by devotion.
When Hari is fully gratified, he grants everything—of this there is no doubt. ||25||
Then Bhāvaśūra said: "You speak everything falsely;
being cut off does not pass away, nor does health remain established in the lap. (26)
I have no confidence in devotion as I do in ritual action;
nevertheless, O Lord, I shall indeed make some wager here. (27)
"I am the king, uncut; you are the servant, cut, as you proceed.
This is determined by action; it does not change. (28)
If the power of devotion were the cause for our exchange,
then let there be a swapping here between us two, such that the state of being uncut and cut is reversed.
Then, considering the power of devotion, I shall perform the worship of Hari;
otherwise, I will by no means consider your words to be true.
Having heard these words of the king, even though he was being cut to pieces,
he then remembered me, his lord, with supreme devotion in the presence of the monarch.
In the presence of all the people, the king spoke as follows:
"O Soul of All, let it be so! Thus he spoke again and again.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, having come under the influence of Vṛkṇadeva solely through devotion and affection, I remained hidden right there in that state of being cut down.
Having pulled out the severed arm of Vṛkṇadeva, I cast it into the two hands of the king;
at that moment, the king’s forearms likewise became severed.
The two elbows became hunched and the veins were drawn tight; the two hands acted like dry wood, rapidly stretched out and extended.
While everyone there was looking on,
the two hands of King Vṛkṇadeva suddenly became severed and turned away from him.
They became free from constriction in their channels, capable of performing their respective functions;
richly endowed with redness and possessed of nourishment, they were able to carry out whatever tasks were desired. ||37||
Seeing such a great marvel, the people smiled;
the king, however, considered it the fruit of his own excessive speech arising from atheism.
He considered devotion to be truly the transformer of karmas;
he regarded the power of devotion as supreme and abandoned atheism. (39)
"In this way, indeed, Vṛkṇatāroga was born of his [former] birth; I took delight in him.
Then, for the sake of honoring his devotion, he was exchanged between those two. (3.184.40)
Then the king became devoted [to the practice], having abandoned the pride of his actions as well as the pride of his innate nature, by the power of his severed state.
Then the queen named Śīladharman lamented;
indeed, her sons, daughters, servants, and subjects also grieved exceedingly.
Vṛkṇadeva, seeing the king cut down, lamented;
he prayed to the Supreme Self for the removal of the king's disease.
Then the king also received the mantra from Vṛkṇadeva:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (44)
Then he recited his rosary one hundred and eight times;
at that very moment, I, the protector of devotees, appeared before him in an instant.
The Lord, bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the Vaijayantī garland, together with Śrī Lakṣmī, quickly appeared in the sky within the splendor of Brahmā. 46.
King Vṛkṇadeva beheld me as divine;
all his subjects then likewise gazed upon me, their Lord.
They uttered cries of victory, bowed down, and praised the Imperishable One;
they considered themselves blessed and fortunate to have obtained the sight of the Supreme Self. 48.
Indeed, through the power of eating but one meal a day, many have attained the vision [of me];
however, I have caused my divine form to disappear and revealed this auspicious body.
Having performed this, he went into the presence of the king; as soon as the king was touched by him, his atheism suddenly vanished, and the king became devoted to righteousness.
As was the devotee, so was the king; both became righteous.
The king, his subjects, and all others attained supreme joy. ||51||
They celebrated with joy and festivity upon obtaining the sight of me;
and they all worshipped me, Nārāyaṇa, with great reverence. (52)
Then the servant Vṛkṇadeva questioned me, his lord:
"Tell me now, how did my state of being cut off come about, and how was it removed? (53)
Then, O Kamalā, I related to my devotees the entire account born of my previous birth—that very sin which brings about the state of being cut asunder. (54)
Formerly, you were a monkey-monk and a protector of monkeys; having made the monkeys play and having caused the people to dwell in their abodes. (55)
He maintained his livelihood by obtaining food, clothing, and other necessities from the villagers;
he had two leopards, five mongooses, and seven monkeys.
At that time, two snakes and eight scorpions came under your control;
through their various playful antics, you maintained your household livelihood. (57)
All those householders were instructors of various living beings, and they too had made those creatures play in the sky for a meal. 58.
Then, they acquired means of subsistence and maintained their livelihood;
while they were living in this manner, established at the edge of the village.
While everyone was asleep at night, a wolf came from the forest;
having perceived its scent, the monkey first fled quickly.
It leaped away out of fear of him, but it fell upon your chest;
then the monkey's two hands fell upon your forehead and eyes.
Then, with his claws, he tore the hide from your forehead;
though you were suddenly asleep, you perceived a supreme fear, like a beast.
Seeing that monkey of his own, you struck him with an iron rod;
at that moment, both his forefeet and those of the leopard were broken.
He let out a cry of fear, and other animals also shrieked;
having seen you, the forest-dweller who causes terror, they were struck with fear.
A cruel wolf, a predator of monkeys, has indeed drawn near not far away;
having raised a great cry, you [struck] that wolf with a sharp spear.
Having rushed forward, you then tore open his heart;
he fell down and died, yet you remained fearless.
At that time, living beings such as bears and others became fearless,
even though the monkey remained constantly confined within his own bonds.
Without reflection, you suddenly broke his two legs out of anger;
thus the monkey who had taken refuge with you met with great suffering there. (68)
He was one who had sought refuge and relied [on him], as well as one who provided his livelihood;
he was protected like a son, yet struck with an iron staff.
The hands of that man who had uttered harsh insults were broken;
and with pieces of cloth, medicinal herbs, and other means, service was rendered to his feet.
At the end of the month, those two forefeet became free from pain;
however, they remained forever bent, mangled in appearance, and crooked. ||71||
The fruit of that [action] has been obtained by you in this very birth as this state of being maimed;
it was only now that this suffering of yours arose.
Furthermore, you [should recite] the verses concerning the play of the monkey and the bear, which originated in a former age, [namely those] of Jāmbavān and Hanumān. (73)
You sang of the form of battle, joined with the rescue from the mountain of Droṇa;
indeed, you sang of the form of my own connection, endowed with the sentiment of devotion. ||74||
By the merit of that recitation, even though you were cut down, you have become endowed with great prosperity;
even while remaining under the protection of this king, you are wealthy.
"You abide here possessed of devotion and you cause firm devotion to arise;
indeed, the power of your devotion has been born, by which I am truly under your control. (76)
I have come for your protection, and your state of being cut down has been prevented.
Listen, for this king Vṛka here was born dead.
Thus, this king remains together with you, holding nihilistic views;
he acts with hostility toward religious duties and the like, according to his former nature. (78)
It was solely because of the wolf that the monkey’s leg was broken;
the fruit of that action shall belong half to the wolf alone. (79)
This king has attained the state of being cut down; your sin has passed onto the monarch.
Listen also to how this Vṛka indeed attained the status of a king.
In his third previous birth, he was a wrathful Brahmin named Prāṇadhara; people called him "Life-taker" (Prāṇahara). ||81||
Causing agitation and bringing affliction during religious rites, rituals, festivals, weddings, recitations, or acts of giving, he forcibly takes an excessive amount. (82)
Insatiable through excessive speech, by force, and even through strife,
he would indeed seize wealth, food, and all kinds of goods by sheer violence.
Just as the austerity of even an ascetic becomes fruitless through anger, so too does the austerity of one who is full of craving and prone to wrath become in vain. (84)
Nevertheless, due to his slight worship of the gods and other rites, as well as his meager asceticism, and likewise because of his mass of sins, he went to the abode of Yama upon death. (85)
Then Citragupta reported his good and evil deeds; [the king said:
"Tell me first what you wish to eat, and I shall satisfy your desire. (86)
Having heard these words of King Yama, he became filled with intense anger and said:
"O Yama, I must first experience the fruit of my own sin. (87)
Then, joined by Yama to experience the sufferings of the realm of Yama,
he endured the torments of hell and, through the remainder of his karma, attained the state of a wolf.
In that matter, his death occurred at your hand;
indeed, because of the merits he performed in the past, his reign was very short. (89)
The inherent natures born from previous lives are never abandoned by anyone;
due to the defects of his former nature, he takes pleasure in quarreling. (3.184.90)
Nevertheless, O Devavr̥kṇa, you instruct him every day with auspicious words for the sake of devotion; by this means, his merit increases. (91)
Fruit from a tree and the like ripens slowly; likewise, ghee is produced slowly from milk.
The fruit of a son is obtained slowly from a wife, and purification through sacraments occurs slowly.
Gradually knowledge, gradually wisdom, gradually the acquisition of wealth and so forth, and gradually through repeated associations—delight arises for those who persist in practice. (93)
Thus, in the course of time, merit also proceeds for this king;
meanwhile, his evil has diminished to a mere fragment and now persists only slightly. (94)
Nevertheless, by means of the yoga of devotion, and likewise by my own yoga, all that sin shall go to its destruction. (95)
And at dawn tomorrow, this king's state of being cut asunder will pass away;
his cruelty and atheism as well—everything will be destroyed. (96)
"My devotee shall become single-mindedly devoted just as you are;
and in the end, both of us shall indeed dwell in my abode. (97)
These sons of yours, beginning with the monkeys, whose cruel dispositions have been severed, have now been born as humans;
they too shall attain liberation.
Having thus granted the boon, I indeed vanished;
and on the very morning of the day after tomorrow, the king's [limb] will become severed.
"He performed service for me," [he said]; "O Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
In time, King Bhāvaśūra went to my divine abode. (3.184.100)
Even Vṛkṇadeva and the others attained liberation in due time;
thus, O Lakṣmī, I constantly provide protection for one who is truly devoted.
Through the yoga of devotion, the welfare of living beings is certainly attained;
through the yoga of devotion, devotion arises, and likewise my union [with them] occurs. || 102 ||
Association with the virtuous is a treasure for men that destroys even great sin;
though practiced only slightly, it bears fruit and bestows liberation upon both the listener and the speaker.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Vṛkṇatā through the Devotion of the Bhakta named Vṛkṇadeva, the Liberation of King Bhāvaśūra by means of Bhakti-yoga, and his Previous Birth Story," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen to the beautiful story of the devotee named Mañjulakeśa, a resident of the village of Halavāda.
In the city of Halavāna, there dwells a Brahmin named Lakṣmī who possesses beautiful hair;
he is exceedingly devoted to me and has exerted great effort in the practice of dharma.
Constantly bathing at the three sessions of the day, performing the worship and salutation during the three junctions of time, he would worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Satī, and the Sun at dawn.
While performing the recitation of hymns, he constantly prays to Hari: "O Hare, Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu! May devotion to You be mine forever. (4)
Your majesty is supreme, yet Your servitude is absolute;
likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, toward Your devotees, I have no thought of fault in You.
May I always have the company of those virtuous ones who are your exclusive devotees;
and may there always be the vision of your forms as well as those of the virtuous.
May my mind be firm in the Dharma; may I possess resolute determination.
May there never be for me even the slightest contact with liquor, meat, and the like.
May there be no eating of forbidden foods for me, such as onions and garlic;
likewise, may my restless mind never turn toward theft at any time. (8)
May I never have the inclination to revile your devotees, nor may I even entertain the thought of censuring the gods. (9)
May I never have association anywhere with the Asuras or the nihilists;
may there be no attachment to sense objects, and may my love always be for You alone.
O Kṛṣṇa, let my self-offering always abide in you;
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, let my devotion as a faithful wife always abide in you. (1.1)
Thus, accompanied by his family, he constantly seeks my favor;
for he would never drink unstrained water, nor even one that has not been offered.
He does not eat food, fruits, and so forth, unless they have been offered; nor does he use clothing, garments, ornaments, and the like, unless they have been offered.
One should not employ a vehicle or even a mount without having first offered it;
likewise, whatever ornaments or articles are to be used for enjoyment must indeed be offered.
That great devotee of the Lord indeed employs [all things] for his own spiritual purpose;
he performs the worship of me, Nārāyaṇa, constantly.
Then, for the sake of alms, he goes into the city; having obtained food by begging, he returns home, cooks it, and offers it to me. (1.6)
Together with his family, he partakes of food accompanied by tulasī leaves,
and he also recites the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
And he causes those who have come to the hermitage to hear [the teachings], O Lakṣmī;
this god on earth is accompanied by his wife and joined by his sons and others. (18)
Then, that great devotee firmly maintained his religious duty;
yet at times, his kinsmen would even invite him to a feast for his own kin.

But that man was a brahmin; however, he did not eat at the meal of his kinsmen, nor did he eat rice and other foods cooked with unstrained water or without being consecrated by ritual preparation. (3.185.20)
Knowing this, he does not eat even that which is defiled by onions and the like,
nor does he ever eat food mixed with garlic and such.
For this reason, his kinsmen grieve for him;
yet he, with his beautiful hair, indeed endures everything.
Then once, Mañjula went to the house of his relative; the relatives, however, said to him, "For your sake, [we have prepared] this pure [food]. (23)
"Having cooked the food, we shall indeed give it to you; eat this which provides satisfaction.
Having thus gained his confidence, [they served him] even a small portion of the prepared meal. (24)
Having recognized [the wine], they became filled with rage and gave it to him at the fine meal;
Mañjulakeśa, however, having recognized it by its fragrance in the food contained within the vessel. (246)
He abandoned that meal which was mixed with a small amount of liquor and accompanied by sugar and saffron; indeed, he abandoned even the water in that house.
Then Mañjula, enraged by that betrayal of trust, cursed him, saying:
"He who, having gained my confidence through a meal, gave me wine! (27)
"Let him be distracted, intoxicated, and utterly deranged.
When this was suddenly spoken in the presence of the people at that time, [28]
Mañjulaputra’s father-in-law fell into a state of wild madness;
his mind became bewildered and he quickly abandoned all sense of propriety. (29)
Her speech became wicked and her conduct likewise wicked; she was made naked.
Her father-in-law, known by the name Pāśupateśa, was punished with a curse.
Dejected and deprived of his luster, he caused various kinds of affliction;
standing in the presence of people, he urinated while naked. ||3 1||
He cries out, dances, claps his hands, leaps, and even runs; he shouts, laughs, and sings incoherently. ||32||
Having obtained alms-bowls and robes, he even tears them apart and rends them;
he utters unspeakable words and performs bestial actions. (33)
