Thus, indeed, by the fault of the curse, he suddenly fell into a state of mental derangement and committed many unforeseen outrages.
His family became greatly distressed by that affliction;
they then entreated the brahmin for the cessation of the curse. (35)
He said: "Let even those with beautiful hair abandon the eating of forbidden food;
let them instead perform purification through great penance and vows. (36)
Therefore, after purification, let them perform this auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice known as Brahmakūrca, and let them also give gifts of cows.
And let them take up the Vaiṣṇava mantras of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa there for the purpose of performing acts of devotion; from that, well-being will arise. ||38||
Thus addressed by the Lord of Pāśupata, the householders abandoned the eating of forbidden food and performed the Brahmakūrca penance. (39)
They performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and gave gifts of excellent cows;
Omana-ādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
At that time, they received this mantra as well as other mantras;
they became Vaiṣṇavas and chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa. (41)
Even though all this was done, his mental agitation did not cease; then Mañjulakeśa, being exceedingly devoted, remained without food. (42)
Remaining on his seat for seven days, he performed the recitation of Bālakṛṣṇa’s names,
and having gathered together his kinsmen, he made fervent prayers to them.
Then, for the sake of protecting my devotees and indeed to fulfill their desires,
I assumed an invisible form and listened to the kīrtana and other devotional acts.
When the seven days have passed, on the morning of the eighth day, during the worship, the waving of lamps, and the concluding rite,
I am present in person within the Śālagrāma stone.
I revealed to them my divine form, attended by Śrī, standing in the midst of a circle of splendor, and resplendent with rows of golden necklaces. (46)
He is clad in divine raiment, richly adorned with ornaments, and beautified by an excellent crown;
he holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and is auspicious, bestowing blessings.
Seeing me with such a serene face, so lovely, having arrived for the sake of protection, they fell into a state of delusion. (48)
The mental fluctuations of all of them were fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, while all their senses were absorbed in me, the radiant one. 49.
Just as they had attained samādhi, so too did they become absorbed;
they obtained the supreme bliss of my form, the highest which is difficult to attain.
Through my very bliss, they became happy, joined with the bliss of Brahman; devoid of any memory of anything other than me, they were cognizant of their own true nature alone. (51)
Just as they had become liberated, established in their true abode with steady consciousness,
so too, having granted them momentary bliss, [the Lord] then effected the dissolution of his splendor.
I quickly assumed the form of a virtuous sage, wearing saffron robes and holding a rosary in my hand, while chanting "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
Proclaiming the name of the Blessed One, calling out, and leading them outside— all of them, hearing my voice, arose from their state of meditative absorption.
They beheld before them me, Hari, in a virtuous form;
filled with love, they bowed down, overwhelmed and with their minds fixed on the divine. ||55||
Chanting "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," they approached me;
they all prostrated like staffs and fell at my feet. (96)
Having seen that face which was perceived in meditative concentration, those seeking the state of a holy man beheld its brilliance;
and having seen that radiance, they beheld that very serenity.
Seeing that youthful state as well, they concluded: "The Lord has arrived in a virtuous form for the sake of protection and indeed to fulfill the desires of his devotees. (58)
They offered him the guest-water (arghya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), an excellent seat, and water;
they gave him fruit and suitable food, and they gave him their very hearts. ||59||
They offered up all their possessions and fell repeatedly at his feet;
they massaged his feet with their arms and embraced me closely.
Having washed their feet with water, they then drank milk, saying,
"We are blessed, for through the power of devotion we have approached the Blessed One."
Blessed is this Mañjulakeśa, the father of the devotee of the Lord of the Daughter;
blessed is our son-in-law, whose father is devoted to Hari. (62)
Blessed is that virtuous and chaste daughter named Kṛṣṇalīlā,
whose father-in-law attained the grace of the Blessed Lord.
Oh, by means of devotion, the liberation of hundreds of householders and hundreds of kinsmen certainly occurs.
Wherever a devoted follower of the Lord resides, even in a village, the villagers attain liberation through the power of that devotion; of this there is no doubt.
In whatever village there may be a devotee, the sins of the embodied beings do not remain there at all; O Kamalā, they perish through the chanting of the devotee's praises.
Wherever a devotee walks— on the road, in a garden, or near a house—
there all obstacles perish, and there is auspiciousness at every step.
Wherever his food and dwelling are within the boundary of a village,
the messengers of Yama, overcome by fear, do not enter that place at all.
Wherever the devotee dwells— whether on earth, in water, or in the sky—
that place is in every way a sacred ford (tīrtha), auspiciously delivering embodied beings from sin.
Wherever there is a devotee, there the gods arrive, duly honored;
even the liberated Nārāyaṇas and Lakṣmīs arrive and dwell there.
The spiritual accomplishments, yogic powers, and various forms of sovereignty—these riches, which are like wish-fulfilling trees, abide within the company of those devotees. (71)
The Vasus and the Pārṣadas also dwell in the house of the devotee;
the devotee is in every way a moving, conscious holy place (tīrtha). ||72||
Victory is there, prosperity is there, aesthetic delights are there, and great supernatural powers are there; where the devotee shines, there is dharma and supreme liberation. //73//
Indeed, by the grace of that devotee, even those who commit offenses against a devotee become highly meritorious, for devotees are compassionate. (74)
Indeed, our own sinful fortune has been turned into merit;
today, through this connection with a devotee, the meeting with a devotee has become blessed. (75)
Liberation is indeed granted even to those who harbor hatred by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, liberation is brought about for us haters by Mañjukeśa.
Today the sacrifice is fruitful, the gifts are fruitful, the Brahmakūrca vow is fruitful, and life itself is fruitful. (77)
Our riches are fruitful, and our eyes as well, in whose home Hari himself shines forth in the form of a holy man. (78)
O Blessed One, forgive our sins arising from the drinking of intoxicants and the like;
O Blessed One, Supreme Person, forgive this offense of your devotees. (79)
O Lord of Ramā, let this curse given by Mañjulakeśa at Pāśupateśaka—
which has resulted in old age and madness— be revoked.
O holy Hari-Kṛṣṇa, quickly bestow Your grace upon us, so that he may regain his health and his mental confusion may dissolve. (81)
Thus they entreated me, and Mañjukeśa also then repeatedly entreated me for the sake of destroying the mental instability caused by the Lord of Paśupati. ||82||
Having heard [his prayer], and having granted the water from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) to fulfill the devotee's desire,
he quickly caused both the Lord of Pāśupata and the Brahmin to drink it.
I then quickly dispelled his mental agitation within the lotus;
thereupon, that radiant and pure one suddenly became composed once more. (84)
Then he massaged my feet and prostrated like a staff;
with a voice choked with emotion, he said, "Forgive me. (85)
"O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of compassion, grant me liberation," he said to me;
I granted him courage, and he worshipped me with supreme devotion. (86)
He indeed gave him everything suitable for a worthy recipient, including that which is pleasing to the heart and conducive to contemplation;
thus, through the practice of devotion, he removed his state of mental distraction.
Then he bestowed devotion upon him and gave him this mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (88)
They received this mantra and recited it with the utmost devotion;
and the villagers, having heard of the saint’s miraculous power, arrived there.
O Lakṣmī, thousands of people, including Brāhmaṇas and others, having thus beheld me and witnessed that auspicious wonder directly, took refuge in me.
O Lakṣmī, all those Vaiṣṇavas, having been consecrated by me with mantras and endowed with my blessings, worshipped me. ||91||
Then, having granted an excellent boon to Mañjukeśa, I said:
"Everything shall come to pass exactly as you wish, according to your word."
This lord of the Pāśupatas, indeed together with his family, shall attain supreme liberation through my grace at the time of death. (93)
But those devotees in this village who shall worship the Supreme Lord will attain the ultimate perfections, being perfectly established in spiritual realization. 94.
Here, the followers of Yama shall not go; obstacles shall depart to a great distance.
And through your majesty, O devotee, devotion shall abide here among the worlds. (95)
Having spoken thus, I withdrew my virtuous form and became invisible;
those devotees, having attained devotion and having worshipped me, [attained liberation] thereafter. ||96||
And at that time, O Lakṣmī, those attendants, having become my own attendants, went with their retinues to my imperishable abode by means of celestial chariots, possessing beautiful forms. 97.
Mañjukeśa, too, being devoted to me, went to my imperishable abode;
through that yoga, other men as well have attained the supreme state. (98)
Likewise, they went to the refuge of Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms;
O Kamalā, in this way, I am always the destroyer of the devotee's suffering. 99.
From reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this, there shall surely be both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the majesty of Śrī Hari. (3.185.10)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Lord Granted Liberation from the Curse and Ultimate Salvation to the Brahmin Pāśupateśa, Who Had Attained Insanity Due to the Curse of the Devotee-Brahmin named Mañjulakeśa," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen to this purifying story of the devotee.
Of the one named Bāṇāṅgaṇa, who resided in the village of Vairāḍhya.
Bāṇāṅgaṇa was indeed a Śūdra, a wicked Śūdra who was the lord of those bearing banners;
he indeed produced liquor from the juices of trees in many ways.
He constantly performs the duties inherited through his family lineage,
and by engaging in buying and selling, he also maintains his household.
Then, on one occasion, having joined a large caravan, he went to the Raivata pilgrimage site to perform his ablutions,
to conduct trade, and to perform the circumambulation.
Thousands of people go to Revatācala in Kārtika,
as well as to the Vāmana-tīrtha and the Nārāyaṇahrada in Saurāṣṭra.
Also at Revatīkuṇḍaka, Bhaveśvara, Mṛgīsthala,
Dāmodara, Nārasiṃha, Svayaṃbhū, and Parameṣṭhin.
At Rādhā’s abode, at the river Svarṇarekhā, at the holy site of Śrī Hanumān,
at the Gaṅgā, at Ambā, and at Dattapāda— in forest after forest— (he performed his worship).
In Sītāvana, Rāmavana, and likewise Pūrvajāmbūvana;
in Boriyā, Droṇikā, and Sthalyā, as well as in Kāṣṭhahārivana. || 8 ||
Furthermore, at Devasarovara, in the mango grove, and again at Bhaveśvara,
they perform circumambulation, encompassing the Kumudācala mountain.
Bāṇāṅgaṇa also, accompanied by carts for the sale of liquors,
goes forth together with tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of men.

Those who are tamasic—whether devotees of Rudra, or Śākta, or those who have taken refuge in Bhairava—who drink liquor in many ways and treat it as a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) during the month of Kārttika; || 11 ||
Then virtuous women and men, householders and ascetics alike— even Vaiṣṇavas— go on pilgrimage and perform circumambulations.
The sages, the virtuous, truthful stories of various kinds,
as well as those concerning Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and the truthful Śaṅkara.
Of Sarasvatī and Vedhas, of Gāyatrī and Raivata, of Revatī and Vāmana, and of the virtuous women and the virtuous men as well. (14)
And twice-born ones and scholars perform [this] here and there;
likewise, scholars, the learned, the elderly, and yogis as well.
The Yoginīs and the Mothers also sang hymns of praise,
and Bāṇa’s army, with divine vision and devotion, offered him a drink.
To those beggars who approach him on foot near his residence,
he gives drinks with a meritorious vision and through service.
Then, at night as well as in the morning, he hears various divine hymns of praise and songs of devotion that grant liberation. (18)
O Lakṣmī, there he heard a speech concerning Viṣṇu, proclaimed by Viṣṇu itself—
speech that was righteous in nature, filled with devotion, and conducive to welfare.
A holy place (tīrtha) should always be established by those who desire to cross over the cycle of worldly existence;
for on this earth, a holy place is indeed twofold, as both [the external and internal] are obtained there.
There are two types of sacred sites (tīrtha) existing on earth: the immobile and the mobile.
The immobile consists of water-sites and the like, as well as mountains and temples. (21)
Sacred images, groves, forests, trees, shrines, and sacred grounds—these are the birthplaces of the gods and the lands of origin for the virtuous. ||22||
The dwellings of Brahmins, places of dust, and cow-pens—all these indeed become stationary sacred fords (tīrthas). 23.
Having gone to them, men who serve these stationary deities cross over [the ocean of saṃsāra] with pure disposition through bathing, drinking, immersion, and beholding. (24)
Indeed, sins first blaze forth from stationary objects;
thereafter arises the dawning of merit, and from that, devotion emerges. (25)
Through devotion, there is satisfaction of the deity; through that satisfaction, the vision of the gods and others occurs directly.
Indeed, the divine state arises, and from that, divinity itself comes to be.
Through divine contemplation, the devotee attains detachment on all sides;
he gains supreme affection and finds the highest devotion. ||27||
Through supreme devotion, liberation occurs gradually even over a long period of time;
however, for one possessed of intense spiritual fervor, liberation indeed comes swiftly, even from a stationary state.
In some cases, liberation might occur for a particular individual, but it is not so for all;
therefore, fixed holy places (sthāvara-tīrtha) do not indeed bestow swift liberation.

O Lakṣmī, when there is dullness of faith, even regarding the slow, medium, and other velocities [of spiritual progress], a slowness arises even in respect to liberation, due to the attainment of purification after a long time.
Therefore, among all stationary holy places (tīrthas), mobile ones are indeed superior;
for here, the mother is a mobile tīrtha, and the father is also a mobile tīrtha.
The husband is a moving sacred ford (tīrtha), and the chaste wife is a moving sacred ford;
the sage is a moving sacred ford, and the virtuous woman is a moving sacred ford. ||32||
The holy ford of the virtuous is mobile, and the holy ford of the yogis is mobile;
the holy ford of the community is mobile, and the holy ford of pilgrimage is mobile. ||33||
The devotee is a moving sacred ford, and the ascetic is the most excellent moving sacred ford;
indeed, the devotee who has offered himself to the Lord is the supreme moving sacred ford.
The deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are portions of Hari;
indeed, Satī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are the moving tīrthas.
The Yoginīs, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, sacred fords, and moving beings; wish-fulfilling cows and men who are observant of vows. (36)
Devoted to the celibate life, free from the faults of meat and liquor, and rich in dharma, these people are indeed mobile shrines who are devoted to me. 37.
These [places] purify through being seen, as well as through touch and service, in which neither liquor nor meat—forms of evil—is found. (38)
Having undertaken the vow of non-violence, they worship the Supreme Lord; having firmly established themselves in the vow of truth, they perform chanting and recount His stories. (39)
Having undertaken the vow of non-stealing, they give away their possessions;
having observed celibacy, they serve the most excellent of gurus.
Having established themselves in compassion and their vows, they also provide service to the helpless, as well as service to teachers and the service of gurus in accordance with dharma. ||41||
Virtuous people perform meritorious deeds consisting of total self-surrender;
having abandoned the sense of bodily identity, they cultivate the contemplation of Brahman. ||42||
They serve [the teacher] as their own self, and likewise as their lord;
they serve them with the thought of liberation, and likewise with the thought of being liberated. ||43||
O Lakṣmī, thus frequented, this supreme moving tīrtha quickly shakes off all sins and swiftly bestows liberation as well. (44)
They have been seen, touched, bowed to, and likewise honored and fed; they have been given drink, carried, massaged, and anointed. (45)
The virtuous were propitiated, honored, and adorned;
they were delighted, gladdened, made to laugh, and likewise celebrated.
They have been offered, taken up from the beginning, carried along, and laid down;
they have been adorned, saluted, served, and held within the heart. (47)
They were made related, brought into contact, and embraced upon his own chest;
they were consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana), adorned with garlands, and rendered fragrant by means of liquid perfumes and other substances. ||48||

For the virtuous quickly purify those who have been bathed with them, as well as those who have been anointed with oil; likewise those who have been perfumed, those who have been forgiven, those who have been remembered, and even those who have been sipped water for purification.
They were perfumed, illuminated, and anointed with saffron; they were smeared with sandalwood paste, circumambulated, and likewise prostrated themselves like a staff.
For the virtuous indeed purify quickly even those held within their own hearts;
the company of the virtuous is the supreme sacred ford, being Nārāyaṇa himself in person. (51)
The Agnitīrtha is indeed purifying, and the Sūryatīrtha is likewise;
the Sādhutīrtha is the purifier of purifiers and the sanctifier of the assembly.
The grace of a saint is rich in merit and the destroyer of all sins;
the touch of a saint is a great initiation that annihilates all evil.
Even the mere sight of the virtuous destroys the sins of the senses;
the instruction of the virtuous is a sacred ford that destroys the impurities of the self. (54)
The supreme resolve of Hari exists as the very resolve of the virtuous;
and I, O Lakṣmī, dwell in every way within the hearts of the virtuous. (55)
Indeed, all holy places of pilgrimage dwell at the feet of the virtuous;
and all merits dwell upon the shanks of the virtuous. (56)
Indeed, all merit-bestowing sacrifices reside in the knees of the virtuous;
likewise, all the gods and goddesses reside in the thighs of the saintly. (57)
In the well-guarded [region] reside moral conduct, vows, and austerities;
in the excellent waist reside the supernatural powers and all perfections. (58)
In the belly of the virtuous man dwell all the sages; within his stomach reside the fires;
and in the navel of the virtuous man, the sovereign powers of yoga abide in every way. (59)
The most virtuous ancestors dwell upon the chest of the righteous man,
and all forms of charity always reside at his sides.
All the oceans dwell within the belly of the virtuous; indeed, all the celestial mansions dwell upon the hips of the saintly.
Even Mount Meru, the refuge of all, dwells upon the back of the virtuous;
indeed, all powers dwell upon the shoulders of the virtuous.
In the throat of the virtuous man dwells even the supreme abode of Brahman;
indeed, in the arms of the good reside the guardians of the quarters, such as Mahendra and the others.
O virtuous one, the *vyūhas* always reside in the two elbows of the saint;
and O Lakṣmī, all the glories (*śrīs*) reside in the hands of the saint. (64)
In the palms of the hands of the saint, both enjoyment and liberation reside;
in the collection of the saint’s fingers dwell the planets, such as the moon and the sun. (65)
In all the channels of the holy one, all rivers dwell;
in all the hairs of the holy one, all wish-fulfilling trees dwell.
On the back of the neck of the virtuous one, Mahārudra shines;
on his impurity dwells Mahāmāyā, and in his vigor resides Hiraṇmaya.
O Lakṣmī, a person shines when freed from the snares of Māyā;
O Lakṣmī, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) shines through the actions of the virtuous.
In the chin of the virtuous man, Kamalā, the bestower of prosperity, shines resplendent;
in the lips of the virtuous man, divine powers always dwell. (69)
I am indeed present in the mouth of the virtuous as the impeller of all their actions; for on the tongues of the good, all the Vedas abide as my own words.
In the nose resides the abode of the virtuous known as Bhūmā, and from its radiance comes Vairāja;
in the two cheeks reside both Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka for the virtuous. (71)
In the two cheeks resides the Great Being Sadāśiva,
and upon the brow shines Saṃkarṣaṇa as Mahākāla.
In the two eyes reside the knowledge of Brahman and direct realization;
on the forehead is the splendor of Brahman, and all abodes are present there.
The imperishable Brahman resides in the head, and the Supreme Person in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
indeed, all those liberated ones dwell within the hair of the virtuous.
All powers reside in the will; for the virtuous, they are lords within the mind.
Worship resides in the intellect; for the virtuous, they are dear to Brahman within the heart.
The Blessed One dwells in the virtuous; through association with the virtuous, one attains Nirvana. Indeed, when the virtuous are pleased, all the heavens are present.
For the virtuous, dissolution occurs at sleep, while creation occurs upon awakening;
their meditative absorptions (samādhis) occur in deep sleep, and for the wise, the state of Brahman is found in meditation.
The *Upaniṣad* is in solitude, the *Sudarśana* in the *Mālikā*, the *Brahma-weapon* in discernment (*vijñāna*), and the *Nārāyaṇa-weapon* in the self (*ātman*). ||78||
In all the bones of the virtuous, pools of nectar always shine;
in the body of the holy man, there are divine states, and on his palms, they are like wish-fulfilling creepers.
Between the breasts is the lineage of Dharma; both paths are the two breasts;
and upon the seat of the virtuous are the pedestals of all the deities.
Indeed, all goddesses always reside within the ritual action of the virtuous;
and in the worship of the virtuous there, the satisfaction of Hari truly exists. (81)
Thus did that lord of the banner hear this delightful story,
and he came to understand the sin of selling liquor from the words of the scriptures.
He grieved in his heart: "The selling of liquor must be abandoned by me forever, and I must undertake another effort that is free from blemish. (83)
Just as wine belongs to a potter, so too is the breaking of earthenware vessels his work; therefore, the sin of drinking wine must be abandoned.
Having reflected thus upon the virtuous servant who was devoted to bhakti, the liquor-drinker bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake and offered this prayer. (85)
"O holy man, I am a potter by trade, a drinker of liquor, and a maker of wine;
yet today, having heard this story and bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake, I [have become pure]. (86)
"Having come for refuge to Bhava, perform what is pure and shake off your sin.
Having heard this, the servant of the Holy One (Santadāsa) indeed offered the Vaiṣṇava water.
He granted his grace and bestowed the Brahmakūrca vow;
he gave the Vaiṣṇava mantra and presented a garland of Tulasī.
To Bāṇa, who came with his family to the arena seeking refuge:
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! ||89||
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, obeisance unto You!"—
giving this mantra for chanting, He made him a true Vaiṣṇava.
The preceptor Hari gave him his blessing: "You shall meet [your goal].
Having received this supreme blessing, Bāṇa went to his own abode. 91.
He departed and abandoned his occupation with liquor;
indeed, he took up the occupation of making earthen vessels. (92)
He sent me, the Supreme Self; he constantly offers praise to that devotee who is affectionate toward him, together with his family and all his loved ones. 93.
Indeed, supreme devotion, accompanied by purity, is seen to be eternal;
it worships Me, eats what is offered to Me, protects Me, and unites with Me. 94.
Together with his family, he observed the Cāturmāsya vow, subsisting on fruits and other such items;
and in the month of Kārtika, he performed the worship and the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to the rules of the vow.
Then, on the night of the eleventh day, he performed a vigil;
consequently, at the very dawn of the twelfth day, I became pleased with him and revealed my own form to him.
Endowed with splendor, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, and accompanied by Lakṣmī, he beheld me, prostrated like a staff, and worshipped me with supreme devotion. (97)
Together with his family, he repeatedly fell at my feet for refuge and then entreated me: "Lift me up from the ocean of existence! (98)
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence!
Then he gave me water for my feet to drink. 99.
Then that virtuous soul, together with his family, drank [the water];
he was swiftly freed from bondage, his mind fixed upon liberation.
At that time, O Lakṣmī, I quickly cast off my body and caused him to ascend this most excellent celestial chariot.
I sent him, together with his attendants, to my imperishable abode;
then, when the exhaustion of his lifespan had arrived, his family as well [followed].
Abiding in my true word, he gradually attains my imperishable abode;
thus, for that very devotee, his impurity is removed through the yoga of the virtuous.
Having kindled it all, he gave his imperishable abode to him;
Bāṇa’s retinue attained liberation, and his family followed after them in succession.
Having become that purifying and imperishable Vaiṣṇava state, he went to liberation;
by reciting, hearing, or remembering this, liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of how Liberation was Granted by the Lord to the Liquor-Seller named Bāṇāṅgaṇa through his Meeting with a Saintly Person, as well as the Manifestations of the Saint’s Form," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this auspicious story of another as well.
In a city named Dhavala, there lived a leather-worker who subsisted on the dead.
He always dwells on the outskirts of a village where hoofed animals die;
he is one who carries away the carcasses of livestock from the midst of the village.
A purifier of hides, he remained untouchable and stayed far away;
indeed, he and his entire family were always sinful eaters of dead meat.
Having established a residence in a certain place and having carried out the sale of hides,
he obtained with that wealth wheat and other grains, as well as vegetables, fruits, and the like.
Having purchased it and brought it to his own home, he cooks it and eats it;
and at times, [he eats] with forest cats, jackals, and likewise rabbits.
In some places, that flesh-eater provides food for his family with boars, hyenas, and the like, and in others with tortoises and fish.
Thus, by birth, by his occupation, and by his food, that most sinful leather-worker,
known as Mṛtādana, was always to be avoided from afar and lived in isolation.
Then once, when the rainy season had set in, a flood of water arrived from all sides with great force day and night.
There, at that time, some living beings were carried away by the forest-dwellers—
both the dead and the living, as well as even domestic animals.
Even those who roam in the pasture of grassy fields were unable, due to the force of the previous wind, to reach their homes during the rain. ||3.187.10||
A single cow, carried away by the force of the current, was still alive near the height of a cobbler's dwelling. || 11 ||
Being pulled along by the waters, she was then seen as she emerged;
out of compassion, the cobbler desired to lift the cow up. (12)
Well-fed himself, powerful, firm, and capable of crossing,
the eater of the dead tied a rope measuring one hundred cubits around his waist and plunged into the water.
Having placed a second rope around the necks of the householders,
he then threw another strong rope, knotted at the end, around his own neck.
Wherever the cow fell, she was suddenly carried away by the force of the water;
having crossed it with speed, she stood before him on the lower ground.
The cow is carried away by the full [water], and the leather-worker is also carried away;
those who stand on the bank holding the rope run after that very bank. (1.6)
By the dexterity of the leather-worker Tarata,
the end of a knotted rope was indeed placed around the neck of the cow.
Having quickly formed a knot, he placed it upon his two horns;
having made a loop in the rope, he tied its hanging end around his waist.
Then the householders said, "Let them pull it by force," and the rope was pulled by the householders while they held it with their own hands.
The leather-worker was dragged to the bank by the force of the current,
and the cow, bound by a rope around her waist, was also pulled along.
Drawn toward the shore and reunited with her kinsmen,
she arrived at the bank alive together with the shoemaker.
Then the cow, satisfied by the preservation of her life, uttered this blessing to them:
"By my protection, all your sins have been destroyed. (22)
Whatever fruit there is in the gift of a cow, whatever great fruit there is in the livelihood of cows,
and whatever fruit there is in the service of cows— may all that be yours.
Whatever fruit is said to result from the gift of a cow giving birth while being milked, may that fruit be yours through my preservation of your life. (24)
May that fruit which comes from a golden cow, the fruit born of a tawny cow, and the fruit of a Gomedha sacrifice—may all that come to you through my protection. (25)

Whatever fruit results from protecting the earth, whatever fruit results from protecting the subjects, and whatever fruit results from protecting a maiden—may that fruit be yours through my protection. (26)

May the fruit that comes from protecting a chaste woman, the fruit that comes from protecting children, and the fruit that comes from protecting a Brahmin—all that may accrue to you through my protection. (27)

May that fruit which arises from the protection of the virtuous, that fruit which arises from the protection of the gods, and that fruit which arises from the protection of those who have come for refuge—may all that be mine through your protection. (28)

May whatever fruit results from protecting the frightened, whatever fruit results from protecting living beings, and whatever fruit results from the gift of liberation—may all that accrue to you through my protection. (29)
May the fruit that comes from protecting the Dharma, the fruit that comes from protecting the fetus,
and the fruit that comes from serving one's mother— may all that be yours through my protection.

May the fruit that comes from worshipping the gods, the fruit that comes from protection at the time of death, and the fruit that comes from the holy sites of the Gaṅgā—may all that be yours through my protection. (3.1)
May the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such crimes, those arising from the injury of animals, and the sins of consuming meat, all dissolve through my protection. (32)
For one who gives up their life for the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, for the sake of the virtuous, or for the sake of the gods, there is the destruction of all sins.
For my sake you have given up your lives; for my sake you have lived your lives. You are the protectors of me; may you live, served by prosperity. (34)
May you enjoy worldly prosperity, liberation, and great opulence equal to that of heaven;
may your lineage always remain devoted and full of devotion toward the cow and the Lord of Cows. 35.
May your affection for Gopāla, the beloved of the gopīs, Govinda, and the cowherd boy, as well as your residence in Goloka, be with you. (36)
Thus, trembling, agitated by fear, afflicted by cold, and likewise hungry, the cow then gave them auspicious blessings. (37)
Then, gradually taking refuge with that pregnant, white cow,
the leather-worker led her to his own home and protected her there.
She gave her the finest morsels of fodder and served her with grass and water;
yet no one comes for her, nor is there anyone to take her away. (39)
Thereupon, that cow made her dwelling in the house of a leather-worker; having eaten grass, she would return and stand by his side in the evening. (3.187.40)
Just as a leather-worker serves his own [hide] according to his strength, so too does even a poor man, striving for the sake of a cow, repeatedly offer grass and water. 41.
He brings [the food] from a field, or from a forest, or from a distant place;
for one who thus habitually consumes the food of a dead man, [this is the consequence]. 42.
The fruit of serving cows and likewise the fruit of receiving a cow's blessing were obtained by him once in the morning; however, he was then impelled by the eater of the dead (the jackal). (43)
"Today I shall plaster the house with white clay and cow dung.
Having reflected thus, he took Sītā and a digging tool along with his wife. (44)
Taking two bamboo vessels for the purpose of fetching earth, he went to the riverbank where auspicious white clay could be found. (45)
And with a spade, Sītā dug up the earth in a pit;
it was dug to the depth of a span on the bank, reaching down to the level of the ground below.
Then, by the power of destiny, a beautiful sacrificial oblation (caru) made of copper and filled with gold and silver emerged from the midst of the earth. 47.

"Indeed, by eating this dead matter, [the poison] will quickly [take effect]; therefore, having extracted the gold rings from them, place them in a bamboo vessel, well-concealed with earth, inside the house. (48)
Five bowls were brought, but no one knew of them; they were all cast into a hollow within the house and well concealed. (49)
Considering the service of cows to be the fruit [of his merit], he, together with his wife, served the cow;
and the copper vessel that was indeed in the pit remained exactly as it had been.
Having buried it empty and concealed it with earth, he indeed went home;
then, using the coin as required, he enjoyed all kinds of pleasures in every way.
He enjoys food, drinks, garments, and sweets;
he consumes his earned wealth in such a way that others do not even know of it. (52)
She attends to guests who arrive by that path, and she also attends to guests staying in the cow-pen or in the area of tree-shade. ||53||
He also offers fruits, sugar, and even honey-mixture (madhuparka); he gives clothing, water as required, and chickpeas and other such items. (54)
He gives to the virtuous food that has been cooked in ghee, cooked in oil, or even cooked by fire, as well as food ripened by the sun or ripened by the seasons.
The virtuous yogi gives what is appropriate and does not serve what is inappropriate;
he serves his family and the virtuous, and he listens to devotional songs. ||56||
He who listens to my delightful, well-spoken, supreme, and purifying discourse—hears that non-violence is the highest dharma, and one who eats only the remnants of a sacrifice is liberated. (57)
The eating of meat is a great sin that leads to the city of Yama;
one who eats fish is a consumer of all kinds of flesh and is never liberated at any time. (58)
One who has fallen due to eating what is forbidden to eat never attains liberation anywhere;
the messengers of Yama torment and cook him in the abode of Yama. (59)
They constantly cook that meat-eater in a great fire;
they cut him to pieces, kill him, and cast him into hell.
Intoxicants, meat, theft, and sexual misconduct—these are defilements that are terrifying and most dreadful; they must never be committed by human beings. (61)
This human birth is indeed obtained on earth for the sake of liberation;
liberation is to be achieved by men, and thus faults and sins must be abandoned.
Even if one has consumed liquor, meat, and so forth throughout many lifetimes— as a human, a bird, or even as an animal— there is no end to that sin.
In this human state, indeed, meritorious deeds that grant heaven must be performed;
furthermore, devotion to Hari must be practiced so that liberation may be attained in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]. 64.
Thus the leather-worker indeed heard that purifying discourse;
then, through association with the virtuous, a desire for liberation suddenly arose within him.
He undertook the observances, including non-violence and the renunciation of meat and other such things, as well as eating only vegetarian food and the constant service of Śrī Hari. (66)
Service to the virtuous, service to cows, avoidance of sin, giving gifts to worthy recipients as is appropriate, and likewise the chanting of the glories of the Lord; ||67||
He always undertook such observances as the festivals of the gods and the Cāturmāsya vows— rules that grant liberation.
Then Sādhu, whose name was Dharmaśālāyana, while wandering through the forest,
arrived naked at the vicinity of a cobbler’s house.
The leather-worker saw him, a yogi whose mind was absorbed in yoga,
auspiciously reciting prayers with a rosary while remembering the Supreme Self.
[He saw] the sage who was sky-clad, tranquil, changeless, and firm in resolve; who maintained his vows and conduct, was free from passion, handsome, and wore matted hair. (71)
The shoemaker, having gone to him, joyfully offered his salutation:
"Welcome to you, O illustrious one; O virtuous man, may victory be yours forever. (72)
"Come and dwell here with me; I am a leather-worker by birth.
If you so desire, O virtuous and sinless one, purify my home. (73)
Having heard this, Śālāyana said, "May there be auspiciousness for you, O speaker of truth; may the Blessed One also be with you, who are a devotee of the virtuous. (74)
Even one who is divine in nature becomes subject to his will; what then need be said of a virtuous person?
For even those born from the womb of a *caṇḍāla* become purifiers when they are devotees of the Blessed One. 75.
For all subjects are indeed bound by leather;
they are born from leather, with leather as their womb and leather as their source. (76)
They cause them to bathe with hides and decorate them with hides;
indeed, they perform massages and other such treatments upon the hide itself using oil and other substances. (77)
They even offer ornaments and garments to their leather-clad bodies;
since the entire world is made of skin, who is not a tanner? (78)
Brahmā is a leather-worker, and his sons are leather-workers;
you are a devotee who is a leather-worker, born into the lineage of a leather-worker. (79)
In the matter of being a leather-worker for living beings, there is no distinction whatsoever;
those who are deluded regarding the nature of the "skin" are considered true leather-workers. (3.187.80)
For they are considered to be free from delusion regarding the realm of the skin (the physical body) and to have the form of Brahman;
these holy ones dwell in the abode of Brahman, possess the form of Brahman, and are dear to the Great One (Brahman). ||81||
As long as this self exists within the body, it is a leather-worker;
when it becomes bodiless through devotion, that liberation is a creator of Brahman. ||82||
I am indeed the Self, possessing a virtuous form and the form of Brahman;
through devotion to Hari consisting of love, I become the very embodiment of Brahman. (83)
O devotee, through the practice of yoga you have indeed become the very form of Brahman;
for those who are devoted to the virtuous are themselves virtuous in form and performers of virtuous deeds.
He whose entire wealth is said to be the virtuous goal and the Self of Brahman—he alone is free from sin, a meritorious soul, and a purifier of the assembly. 85.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous man then went to his home;
the cobbler, a king among devotees, offered him a gracious welcome.
He offered a beautiful seat and performed the washing of [his] feet;
indeed, together with his entire family, he drank the nectar of those feet. (87)
She massaged his feet and likewise rubbed his body;
she offered him sweet madhuparka, as well as sugar and parched grain flour.
He gave various excellent ripe fruits, and he also provided water and a bed for the sake of rest. (89)
The sons, daughters, and the couple all massaged the body;
having fed him, they did so indeed to relieve his fatigue from the journey.
He attained supreme sleep, and they all performed massage for him,
as well as the rubbing of his body and the fanning of air with fans.
In this manner, they performed service for Dharmaśālāyana;
then, having fallen asleep, Dharmaśālāyana woke up. (92)
Having drunk water, he sat upon his seat engaged in the recitation of the Mālā-mantra; and the Mṛtādanīs and others stood before him with a spirit of devotion. (93)
The holy man said: "Devotion to the Supreme Self must always be practiced;
furthermore, service to cows and service to the virtuous must be performed here for the sake of liberation. (94)
Receive this divine mantra from me together with your family;
thereafter you shall attain the celestial heaven and then liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed, that cobbler, together with his family, then received the mantra of the saintly Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (96)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Then, following the path described by the saintly ones, he worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa. (97)
Then he indeed went on a pilgrimage together with a virtuous man to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
There, at that sacrifice, he bestowed gold in many ways as a gift;
likewise, he caused a temple to be built upon the shore of the lake.
He constructed his own auspicious hermitage for the purpose of worship,
and there he dwelt together with his virtuous son and his lineage.
Then once, while I was pleased within the lotus, he arrived there; I granted him a vision of My own four-armed form, possessed of great splendor.
He honored his family, including me, the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
having washed my feet, he drank the water from them. 102.
An exceedingly radiant celestial chariot arrived swiftly from the abode of Brahmā;
there, at my command, the deceased man ascended it.
Together with that cow, I brought him to my own abode there;
all the rest of my family and the gods then went to heaven.
Having enjoyed the merit resulting from the conduct of the cow, they shall go to my supreme abode;
likewise, [they shall enjoy] the great merit of serving the virtuous and the fruit of devotion to me.
O Lakṣmī, they shall enjoy that which is delightful and filled with eternal bliss;
thus, by the service of cows, the sin of eating meat has been destroyed.
Through the arising of merit, his meeting with the virtuous, the acquisition of wealth, residence at sacred fords, and supreme liberation— all these came to pass for him.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and even reflecting upon this, there shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and the eternal state is attained. (108)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Sins such as Meat-Eating and the Attainment of Merit, the Meeting with a Holy Man, and the Attainment of Heaven and Liberation for the Leather-worker named Mṛtādana, through his Saving the Life of a Cow," in the Third Section on the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious account of the thief’s liberation. There was indeed a thief named Śaṅkudhara in the city of Mālava. || 1 ||
Making his dwelling in the abode of thieves, he nourishes the circle of thieves; intent on the journey of theft, he remains at night bearing weapons and other such gear. (2)
He may even assume a different appearance and perform different actions;
having understood the distinction regarding entry, one must act with every possible effort in every way.
Having made an appointment at night, he indeed commits the theft of wealth;
sometimes from a horse, sometimes from a camel, and sometimes from a long-eared donkey.
Having indeed cast down his burden of wealth, he runs far away;
even so, having gone to another country and having stolen riches, [he flees]. || 5 ||
Having brought [the wealth] to his own home and divided it with the thieves, he guards his own portion;
he celebrates a festival, eats, consumes, and rejoices.
"Theft must be carried out by all means, and no other task exists for him; he is intent on the effort of stealing, his thoughts are on stealing, and he is devoted to the meditation of stealing. (7)
He remains there, a thief who fills his own belly while supporting his family,
whenever there might be a festival or some great occasion for the gods.
Wherever a non-Buddhist teacher gathers a following of more than a thousand people—
whether at a shrine, a temple, on a mountain, at the edge of a village, or on a riverbank— (9)
And there in the temple, this circle of thieves goes about;
they search everywhere, for where indeed are the riches? ||3.188.10||
When, where, or how does the house of a wealthy man ever become deserted?
Where is the path for entry, or where and how is the exit? (1.1)
How is attainment achieved? How is one's own protection secured? And how is concealment maintained?
Thus, devoted to his own meditation, he travels with his caravan while carrying the stake. (12)
Having committed theft in various other towns, he would carry off wealth;
once, during the latter part of the night, such a man had a dream.
It became an infinite source for the acquisition of gold and jewels;
he perceived that it had formerly been a royal capital in the forest.
In that forest, in a remote and desolate place, he saw in a dream an excellent treasure-chest, inlaid with gold and jewels, which had been protected by kings in former times. (15)
Just as no one else knew of his hidden treasure, so too,
having risen in the morning and eaten, he departed under the pretext of going for recreation.
Just as he saw in a dream an ancient forest, a path, a cluster of trees, stones, and the earth covered with spreading grasses. (17)
There, having gained confidence, that thief saw everything exactly as it was, including Prācīnavasati indicated by ancient marks.

Furthermore, those latent predispositions (*saṃskāra*) sown in a previous birth that have endured for a long time will sprout within this lotus-like life, in another birth; of this there is no doubt. (19)
In former times, many thousands of years ago, this thief was the treasurer of King Suhotra.
Then, at that place, the city of Suhotra was built by his father, Janaka, who was named Kāñcana; thus it became a golden city.
For that treasury of the king of the Lunar dynasty was indeed intended for protection;
then, after some time, the treasures were removed to another location.
And although they were all led away and deposited [there] by means of a ruse, they were entirely [seized] by the treasurer named Apajāpaka. ||23||
Furthermore, the treasury was so carefully concealed that others did not perceive even the slightest distinction between the gold and the jewels. (24)
Right there, for the sake of his own inherent purpose, he remained under a guise;
then, after some time had passed and a long period had indeed elapsed.
Apajāpa was indeed unable to lead away Guptakoṣaka;
in this very manner, he died there in the new city of Mālavī.
On account of the sin of theft, he was indeed sent by the agents of Yama to the city of Yama;
there he was beaten with iron rods and made to suffer in the cauldron.
Bound repeatedly with nooses, mallets, and staffs, he was treated like a criminal;
only after exhausting the fruits of his evil deeds was he released there in that desolate forest.
He took the form of a hungry ghost and did not allow anyone else to go to that place;
he constantly delighted in the forest and beheld only the treasury. (29)
He consumed all forest produce and dwelt even among the trees of the treasury;
in this manner, eight hundred years of his life indeed passed away.
At that time, in that secluded place upon the eastern ground,
a brahmin named Sumantuka arrived to perform austerities.
Having recognized in the forest a delightful and auspicious site suitable for penance—free from obstacles, abounding in trees, creepers, and pillars, and possessing excellent waterways. ||32||
Not far away, taking refuge in the shade of a banyan tree,
the ascetic performed penance while worshipping Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person.
Then, when a year had passed, this deceased man, considering that ascetic to be a virtuous soul and the one who would effect his own deliverance, [approached him].
Assuming the form of a Kirāta, he went before him under the shade of a banyan tree,
bowing and praising the asceticism of that high-souled one.
Sumantu alone knew him to be in the form of a ghost through his ascetic power;
nevertheless, he offered a welcome to him as he arrived at the banyan-tree hut.
To that forest-dweller, who was dark-complexioned, emaciated, and indeed suffering, the king of sages asked: "O embodied one, O forest-dweller, is all well with you here? (37)
The king inquired after the welfare of the ascetic on account of his majesty;
the sage, for his part, asked about his dwelling, his village, his religious duties, and his activities. (38)
Having become sincere, he related the account from the beginning:
"Formerly, I was a treasurer here, full of deceit and sin. (39)
Having died and gone to the city of Yāmyapura, having experienced sufferings and torments, and having obtained some small remaining fruit of his deception; ||3.188.40||
"I am born here in this forest as a ghost; release me out of compassion!
Thus did Upavān speak to him, yet he did not show him the treasure at that time.
That compassionate sage, muttering the Gāyatrī mantra, gave water to him for the sake of the deceased's liberation; and his state as a ghost vanished.
However, due to his nature as a thief and through deceit,
this man became a thief named Śaṅkudhara in the city of Mālava.
Accompanied by his previous conditioning, he was indeed an expert in theft; thus, O Lakṣmī, for this man who was devoted to stealing, by the power of that strong conditioning— (44)
In a dream, he experienced the memory of his former birth as Koṣa;
thereupon, he went to that very Koṣa in a secluded forest.
He scrutinized everything marked with the signs described in his dream;
then that man, who was full of greed, became pleased.
Right there he saw the banyan tree, the former site of the ascetic; though the ascetic was no longer present, the auspicious banyan tree remained. (47)
But Sumantuka, having attained a divine body through his asceticism, remains hidden within a banyan tree as an ascetic of celestial form. (48)
Then Śaṅkudhara did not see that ascetic at all;
he saw only the banyan tree, for he did not bow to the banyan tree as he had done before. (49)
Having considered his treasury to be satisfied with the gold produced, he went there;
and being well-pleased, he returned to his own home that very evening.
Then, being alone, he reflected repeatedly within his own heart:
"How indeed can I bring wealth from there to this place? (51)
And so that others may not know, it must indeed be taken away;
having made your dwelling there in the forest, you shall gradually return here. ||52||
"But I must always bring [him] alone by means of a stratagem.
Having reflected thus, he went forth alone under the pretext of theft. (23)
Having spoken thus to his household members, he took up weapons and went to that forest;
and there, even in the darkness, he began to dig slowly and stealthily.
Having dug until dawn, he went for a moment beneath a banyan tree to rest;
returning there again, he dug slowly and steadily once more. (55)
Fearless indeed in the middle of the forest, alone and without apprehension,
he remained there until a sound came from that banyan tree like that of a human being.
Having heard this, he looked all around in alarm; yet, seeing no human being at all, he became increasingly apprehensive. ||57||
He dug slowly until a stone slab laden with rocks arrived there;
having lifted that single stone onto the surface of the rock, [he placed it]. (58)
He thoroughly inspected eight copper vessels containing gold,
silver, ornaments, coins, gems, and diamonds.
Having observed all those various objects designated as substances that he had seen in his dream, in every respect and in their entirety, he attained the highest peace.
Then, having covered these vessels each in its proper place, he should place a heap of grass, leaves, and so forth upon them.
He quickly threw branches of thorny trees upon him;
then, having returned to the banyan tree, he indeed took a moment's rest.
Reflecting on how the theft of the goods was to be carried out at night,
he lay down for just a moment, contemplating the entire plan he had devised.
At the end of a ghaṭikā, he rose and stood before him;
the king of yogis, Sumantuka, appeared in person, laughing repeatedly.
Having become motionless for a moment and reflecting upon that great seer and ascetic,
he quickly recognized him as one seen before and bowed down to him.
With a serene face, the preta, remembering his former births, quickly spoke to that Lord of Sages, the deliverer: "O Guru, in the past I was a preta. (66)
"In this matter, I have been rescued by you; I am a human being, a thief named Śaṅkudhara, devoted solely to the act of stealing. (67)
Maintaining myself through theft, I wander about as a sinner;
O best of Brahmins, O ocean of compassion, my former preceptor, grant me deliverance! (68)
"Act in such a way that there may be for me both prosperity and liberation.
Having heard this from the one formerly devoted to him who now stood for refuge, the sage—
Filled with compassion and reflecting upon her deliverance, Sumantu said:
"I shall bring about your supreme welfare; of this there is no doubt. (3.188.70)
I shall speak; O disciple, perform it with respect accordingly.
Listen to this brief instruction; I tell you that which is suitable for you. (71)
In former times, you were of the lunar dynasty and a great lord of treasures;
thereafter, having gone to the city of Yama, you experienced various torments.
"Born as a Preta, you have indeed become a human being through my compassion;
nevertheless, your state of being a thief has not been destroyed here—I tell you this."
"Whatever wealth you have dug up or excavated, and whatever else may be there—with that, perform a sacrifice here, conducted with the assistance of Sumantu. (74)
"And I myself, Sumantu, dwell right here beneath this banyan tree;
all people in the world know me as an ascetic who has attained perfection through yoga. (75)
"Sumantu shall also perform the sacrifice; speak thus as well:
'Cause trust to be established among all the subjects. (76)
Then, sages, seers, and deities, as well as Brahmins, virtuous men, and noble women, will come here to this sacrifice. (77)
"I shall spend my wealth; I shall perform the supreme sacrifice.
When this is done, your merit will be great and your highest welfare will be attained. (78)
Accept this purifying mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which sanctifies those who sit in the same row:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (79)
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Hari Viṣṇu, O Bāla Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī! O Supreme Lord, O Ocean of Mercy, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Ramā! || 3.188.80 ||
In this manner, perform the chanting always, day and night;
all your sins will utterly perish. (8.1)
O dear one, by my blessing, the merit of this sacrifice shall belong to you alone;
likewise, may there be purity of self for you, as well as devotion to me, Śrī Hari. (82)
My words shall bear fruit; of this there is no doubt.
You shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as shall your family members. (83)
Having spoken thus and having understood his mind, the sage then gave him a mantra;
the king of sages, Sumantu, sent him from that hermitage.
Having heard the excellent news from the dwellings of the brahmins, the hermitages of the sages, and from virtuous women and holy men, the learned ones quickly arrived there for the sacrifice. ||85||
O Lakṣmī, at that time, the king of sages, Sumantu, by mere resolve,
created mountains, rivers, and heaps of all kinds of objects.
Then Brahmā and the other deities appeared there in person;
the great sages, the ancestors, the virtuous, and the noble women also arrived. ||87||
Then the sage performed the Viṣṇu-sacrifice for seven days;
at the desire of Sumantu, Viṣṇu became manifest there in person.
Then the fires themselves directly accepted the sacrificial food;
at the final oblation, Sumantuka remembered me, the Supreme Lord. 89.
Then, for the sake of performing auspicious rites for my devotees, I went there;
well-honored by Sumantu and others, I partook of the sacrificial offerings.
Then Sumantuka caused the gifts of the materials excavated there to be given away by the hand of Śaṅkudhara, amounting to ten million gold pieces.
He caused crores of silver coins, crores of gems, and crores of diamonds to be given away with great wonders. (92)
No one at all understood from where the wealth had come;
indeed, they all considered it to be entirely a miracle of Sumantu. (93)
A great cry of victory arose through gifts, sacrificial fees, and other offerings;
the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and other sages were all satisfied. (94)
All embodied beings were also satisfied there at that great sacrifice;
and at the concluding bath, Sumantu caused his disciple to perform the ritual immersion.
There he requested me to grant an audience to his devotee;
indeed, I [granted it] even to Śaṅkudhara along with his family.
He showed himself, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and indeed purified them all in accordance with the words of Sumantu. 97.

Having shaken off all the sins of the devotee and bestowed upon him a treasure of merit, he takes hold of him for the journey to heaven and establishes him in the eternal realm in the celestial sphere.
Tāraka, however, bestowed a great heaven upon Śaṅkudhārin;
and Śaṅkudhārin departed with his family while the virtuous looked on.
Having become possessed of a divine body, he quickly went to the abode of Dhruva;
indeed, having enjoyed the fruit of the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice in the abode of Dhruva.
Then he, together with his family, will indeed go to Vaikuṇṭha;
thus, O Lakṣmī, by the power of Sumantu, he became a king among devotees.
Even the thief, having become free from theft and having performed an auspicious sacrifice through my compassion for the virtuous man and by the grace of the Supreme God, [attained his goal]. (102)
Being honored by all the worlds, he became renowned and attained the eternal state.
Thus, through the influence of a saintly person, even sinners and the wicked [attain liberation].
Those who are free from sin are born and indeed go to the supreme state;
by reading and hearing this, one may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Sins, the Performance of Sacrifice, and Liberation through the Yoga of Sumantu and Karṣi for the Thief named Śaṅkudhara," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; the grace of Hari toward the virtuous arises only through constant attendance [upon them], and certainly not by any other means.
The direct realization of Hari occurs either through his grace, or through service, or even through perpetual meditation; of this there is no doubt. (2)
Steadfastness in the form of Hari is difficult for embodied beings;
nevertheless, it is certainly achieved through the yoga of practice—of this there is no doubt.
O Lakṣmī, my form is a wish-fulfilling gem that grants whatever is thought of;
it bestows heaven, prosperity, great bliss, and liberation whenever they are desired.
The vision of the Self is the vision of Īśa, the vision of Brahman;
it is the divine vision of the liberated ones, and from that comes my vision as well.
Whatever is intended is obtained entirely from the form of meditation;
and through such contemplation, the illusion of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" surely perishes.
Even the illusory memories of one who practices meditation perish;
even Māyā herself, appearing in the form of the three qualities as house, son, and wife, perishes.
Likewise, for the meditator, that which is called illusion (māyā), consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā), surely perishes;
craving is indeed destroyed, and the attainment of peace arises. || 8 ||
When the devotee, through the power of meditation on Hari alone, becomes absorbed in Him and remains truly without rising again,
then the falling of the body occurs.
The separation from the modifications of the material elements occurs, and likewise, the destruction of the subtle body comes about through the power of meditation. (3.189.10)
Within the self alone, the stream of consciousness—the state of meditative absorption—increases;
this very divine consciousness increases as a substantial form. || 1 1 ||
Having indeed become that very form of meditation, one is properly joined to the image; and through that yoga, for the living soul, which is conscious and of that nature— || 12 ||
Indeed, at the time of departure, that conscious being himself attains a form equal to the form of Hari.
This one, whose true nature is the form of Brahman, shines forth with a divine appearance;
the embodied self, the very soul of Brahman, manifests resembling Hari.
O Lakṣmī, by the will of Śrī Hari, the most excellent among the liberated shines forth;
great affection is the cause of supreme bliss, both for me and for Hari.
Thus, those who are always affectionate, noble-souled, great-souled, and virtuous— being themselves purifiers— they indeed purify and cleanse sinful people.
Since their work consists solely of compassion,
which bestows liberation and uplifts the sinful, they carry out that task by my command.
Therefore, even sinners who have taken refuge in the virtuous attain liberation; indeed, embodied beings surely achieve supreme liberation through association with the good.
Even courtesans, violent men, thieves, those who commit adultery, murderers,
the fallen, the wicked, and even the hateful cross over [the ocean of existence] through association with the virtuous.
Whatever pride is repeatedly fostered in the world by people through association with the wicked, that very pride is surely crossed over if association with the virtuous is established. (3.189.20)
The virtues of the good should always be accepted, and their faults should always be avoided by the virtuous.
One who perceives virtues indeed crosses over, while one who perceives faults sinks down.
One should honor the virtuous and disregard one's own kin;
for the righteous indeed deliver him who honors the virtuous. (22)
But those who indeed show contempt for the virtuous fall;
having their merit burnt away, they go to a low birth.
Those who, upon seeing some incidental condition arising from the physical nature of a virtuous person, perceive faults in that saint, become his revilers. (24)
Those who are always rich in faults indeed possess a vision focused on defects;
they constantly imagine evils in virtuous people.
They always proclaim these as defects that cause the destruction of one's reputation:
desire, anger, greed, pride, delusion, attachment, arrogance, envy, lack of foresight, and likewise, a voidness of respect for others. (26)
Lack of nobility, lack of invitation, indifference, thirstiness, pride, and the viewing of non-restraint constitute wrong view. ||27||
Possessiveness, greed, and external latent impressions; outward-directed activity, the quality of passion (rājasatva), the quality of darkness (tāmasatva), and lack of awakening. ||28||
Subservience to the tongue, gluttony for the genitals and belly, unrighteousness, association with kings, possessiveness, and arrogance; ||29||
Ignorance, lack of fitness, sleep, worthlessness, falsehood mixed with truth, deceit, dishonesty, hypocrisy, and excessive gluttony; || 3.189.30 ||
Folly, theft, and great indolence—these are the very vices that those who are full of malice and prone to reviling falsely attribute [to him]. (3.1)
The wicked conceive evil thoughts and become possessed by sin; they regard their own actions as right, and likewise toward the virtuous.
Just as one's own latent tendencies are, so too should one project them onto the virtuous;
just as one's own wickedness is, so too should one project it onto the virtuous. ||33||
Furthermore, toward those who have taken refuge in them, these people instill wicked qualities;
they cause them to perceive faults, non-existence, and contempt. (34)
All the wicked actions of the virtuous incite non-cultivation and expel their virtues; they speak with constant faults. (35)
They say that conduct is entirely wicked, and likewise their behavior is corrupt, sinful, and impure, like that of the Daityas or the Dānavas. (36)
For the demonic ones indeed project a demonic nature onto the virtuous; they attribute their own various evil qualities to the good, even while perceiving them as virtues.
They display hatred through their eyes; they harbor hatred even in their gait. They show hatred in their bowing and their glances, and they even speak hatred with their speech. (38)
For they demonstrate to others that what ought to be done by the virtuous is actually not to be done or is a wicked deed; thus they provoke groundless strife.
"This was done by this virtuous person; that is indeed appropriate.
For this person is not truly virtuous, nor does virtue exist here at all. (3.189.40)
Who would touch his feet? Who would salute such a one? Who would bow to him? Who would serve him? Many such as he have been seen. (41)
Those like you, devoid of discernment, consider such people to be virtuous;
we, however, do not even look upon their faces at any time.
Thus they constantly engage in censure, seizing upon faults; through wicked talk, they cause others who possess faults to seize them as well. (43)
Likewise, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to this demonic conduct of the asuras, who indeed have no affection for the virtuous. (44)
Those in whom the defects of desire, anger, theft, untruthfulness, deceit, backbiting, and sexual misconduct prevail, possess a rajasic state. ||45||
Those people are indeed possessed of faults, yet they are powerless to abandon those faults;
on the contrary, with their minds attached to sense objects, they remain submerged in fault.
Therefore, when the virtuous undertake the refutation of those faults in order to cause them to abandon them, then those of wicked mind— ||47||
Those who seek to expose faults engage in the censure of the virtuous, saying, "This man is ignorant of what should and should not be said; this virtuous one truly does not know how to speak. (48)
Possessing knowledge of only a single part, yet lacking vast knowledge, he considers himself a scholar and conducts himself devoid of true insight. ||49||
"He does not follow me anywhere, nor does he accept what I say; being intoxicated by the excellence of his own words, he is intent on refuting us. (3.189.50)
He knows nothing of the hermitage, nor does he know our bulls;
he simply destroys the enjoyments and other riches appropriate for the life of a householder. (51)
"Therefore, this virtuous man lacks discernment; he is indeed a fool.
In this way, they revile the virtuous one who offers beneficial instruction.
For such people as these, there is never any affection even for the virtuous.
Without affection, trust does not arise in the words of the virtuous. ||53||
Due to lack of conviction, there is indeed no faith that increases the knowledge of greatness;
for through lack of faith there is no practice, and from a lack of practice, there is no meditation at all.
There is no service, no cultivation [of the path], nor indeed any realization of identity; consequently, there is no attraction at all—so how, then, could there be any greatness? (55)
He has no joy in hearing his stories, nor even in hearing news of him; he lacks enthusiasm for receiving his commands—how then could there be deep affection? (56)
Listen, Lakṣmī, for just as you possess the notion of being my mistress, so too do I possess the state of being your servant; in that regard, no distinction exists. (57)
Whether beaten, assaulted, reviled, saluted, or insulted, you were never at odds with them, but remained their servant. (58)
With your entire being, you always delight in my non-existence; you serve me as a devoted maidservant, naturally embracing my virtues. (59)
In that regard, there is never any sense of inferiority toward me, your master;
likewise, among those in the assembly of the virtuous, there is indeed never any sense of inferiority.
Even for those who possess no state of equanimity, but rather an exalted contemplation,
there is greatness, divinity, and freedom from qualities among the virtuous.

In all virtuous actions, one should cultivate the thought that they bestow excellence; in activity toward both the auspicious and the inauspicious, one should cultivate the thought that they bestow merit.
For those in whom these qualities indeed exist, their mastery over the virtuous is always present;
cultivated, it yields divine fruits and becomes the bestower of divine liberation.
It shall effect the severance of the bonds of illusion, time, primordial matter, karma, and so forth;
[it acts] just as affection exists toward one's own wife, toward a son, and toward family members. 64.
Just as one feels affection for one's parents, for one's daughter, and for one's male and female servants, so indeed should one act toward the virtuous.
Even a worldly feeling of affection attains a divine state when directed toward the virtuous;
through the attainment of the virtuous person's favor, every undertaking is successfully accomplished.

Just as a wife perceives no faults in her own beloved husband, nor does she perceive wicked deeds or evil dispositions, but rather perceives only his excellent qualities; so too [should one view the Lord]. (67)
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, for those whose vision toward the virtuous is pure,
even their faults appear in every way as virtues alone.
Having attained union with those virtuous ones and their auspicious clarity,
and having received their blessings as well as the attainment of their service, ||69||
Having obtained affection, and likewise having obtained love offered by themselves,
and having attained supreme delight in the Self, they cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
They will indeed possess affection, even greater than that for their wives and sons;
purified by such virtuous love, he alone crosses over Māyā.
Whether a man, a woman, or a eunuch, one is liberated through affection for the virtuous.
This I speak as truth, indeed as truth: I become the very form of the virtuous. (72)
The greatness of My nature is known from the virtuous alone and never from any other source;
the virtuous are My heart, and My dwelling is always with the virtuous. (73)

Satisfaction arises for me alone in pleasing the virtuous; I delight in them, for the holy ones are purifiers, their very forms sanctifying from the tips of their nails to the crown of their heads. (74)
Listen, Lakṣmī; those who are wicked toward others truly cause distress to the virtuous during meals, drinking water, sitting, and acts of hospitality. (75)
In the matter of hospitality and service, they cause virtuous people to toil;
they even compel the righteous, their elders, and great men to perform the duties of servants. (76)
Those devoid of wisdom, acting in such a manner, quickly accumulate a heap of sin;
some, regarding virtuous men as equal to their own wives, [invite them] to a fine meal. (77)
Some prepare and cook food for their own consumption, while others provide vessels and cool water for the purpose of drinking. (78)
For those who beg from both—the virtuous man as well as the servant—seek two things:
some ignorant ones ask for a ball and such, while others ask for their own seat for sleeping. (79)
Some ignorant people cause the virtuous to be treated and made to endure just as they would a slave; likewise, they treat warm water and fresh, hot food in the same manner. (3.189.80)
Indeed, some ignorant people cause their own welfare to be proclaimed by the virtuous in assemblies, just as masters have it done by their servants for their own benefit. 8.1.
They cause praise to be made for the virtuous just as they do through a messenger, and likewise through a bard or a herald. (82)
Some, intoxicated with pride and arrogant in their own minds, have the virtuous carry their own chests— burdensome with their contents— by the hands or even upon the heads of those very people.
Some wicked ones indeed forcibly humble virtuous and humble people;
those wicked ones repeatedly cause their own praise to be performed.
Indeed, such sinful people, heaped with mountains of evil,
devoid of wealth and food in this world, wander about and come to their end.
Under the pretext of instructing virtuous people, they accomplish their own selfish ends;
devoted to their own interests, though skilled in such matters, they go at last to the abode of Yama.
Even those who are proud and maintain their own existence among the virtuous,
being driven by the workings of egoism, go to the abode of Yama.
Those who cause sudden harm in the abode of the virtuous, and who falsely attribute blame and stains to the holy ones; 88.
But those who are merciless and who bring ill-repute upon the virtuous, being haters of the company of the good, surely go to the abode of Yama. (89)
Listen, Lakṣmī, for they likewise revile holy men for wearing [such] dress;
those who never give even a worn-out piece of cloth anywhere. (3.189.90)
They indeed revile a fine, high-quality garment given by others—even one that is pure, beautifully colored, and radiant—reviling it by calling it "royal. (91)
Likewise, they indeed censure the alms-bowl, the vehicle, and the mount of the virtuous;
similarly, they censure the hall, the mansion, and even the hut of the holy man. ||92||
They despise even brilliance, they despise the gift that is offered,
they despise the presentation of wealth, and they despise the rubbing of sandalwood paste.
They revile the use of medicinal herbs and the like, as well as the protection [of property] as it has been performed;
they revile wealth such as cows and buffaloes that has been acquired by virtuous means.
Filled with envy, they revile acts such as helping others, which are practiced by the virtuous; they also revile the wandering for alms and ascetic penance.
Upon merely seeing the abode of the virtuous, the virtuous women blaze with splendor;
likewise, upon beholding the divine assembly, the Asura people blaze forth.
At the end of their bodies' lives, these people enter into a cycle of sinful existence;
they are indeed tormented repeatedly in the worlds of Yama and in miserable wombs.
Therefore, one should always worship my virtuous representative wearing my garb; perceiving him as myself, one should serve him and please him with auspicious offerings. (98)
One should please [the Lord] through devoted service and likewise by offering all one's possessions;
having cultivated devotion to Hari, one should also please virtuous people.
One should constantly serve the guru, always serve one's parents,
serve one's husband with devotion, and please the virtuous man with devotion.
One should worship the Lord with various sentiments and glorify Hari with faith;
one should always offer everything to the Deity and sustain one's family. 101.
Having offered all food as an oblation to Kṛṣṇa, one should eat; not otherwise.
For those who conduct themselves in this manner, both enjoyment and liberation rest in the palm of their hand.
From reading, hearing, remembering, and even retaining this, one shall obtain the fruit of serving the virtuous, and upon the end of worldly enjoyment, there shall be liberation. ||103||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fulfillment of All Desires through the Attainment of the Lord Cintāmaṇi by Meeting with a Holy Man," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this wondrous tale.
There were one hundred devotees from the great land of Saurāṣṭra who had come together in a group. || 1 ||
The sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā, Somanātha, Raivata, the Svarṇavatī, the Kṛṣṇabhūmi, and the beautiful Gopanārtha. || 2 ||
To establish such sacred fords (tīrthas), they came to Saurāṣṭra;
having crossed the Mahī and the Vāpī on the way by boat, they proceeded further from there.
Having crossed the Sābhramatī river, they arrived at Gopanātha;
from there, having established the great Siṃhavana as a secret Prayāga, [they proceeded].
Having entered, as they were proceeding swiftly toward Somanātha,
they then reached the Siṃhāraṇya forest where armed robbers were stationed.
Among them, the lord of the plunderers was named Sāmāntavikrama;
he was accompanied by cavalrymen and endowed with warriors equipped with weapons and other gear.
Standing nearby, neither too far away nor too close,
his followers raised shouts and cries that were terrifying.
For the sake of plundering, they quickly set up a cordon around the Saṅgha on all sides;
in the midst of it, through terrifying threats, they stationed a hundred men to guard the Saṅgha.
The ornaments of the women and whatever articles of adornment belonged to the men, those fierce ones brought together in one place and had them fashioned [into weapons].
They took all the fine garments belonging to those in the community;
then the merchants, who were foremost in the community, bound them with ropes.
Those plunderers indeed bound Padmacandra, Śaṅkhacandra, and Śṛṅkhalacandra, as well as Vanacandra and Vālicandra. ||11||
They struck others with sticks and so forth to instill fear;
all those merchants, being terrified and tormented, became silent.
Severely beaten, they gave all their possessions to these plunderers;
however, among them was one named Vanacandraka, a Vaiṣṇava and a devotee of mine.
His wife, Sukhādevī, was devoted to me, O Rāma;
from their childhood, both were my devotees and worshipped me incessantly.
