By virtue of their union with me, whose name is Sāyana-ayana, those two Vaiṣṇavas dwell endowed with devotion, taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa. || 15 ||
In that time of distress, those two devotees then remembered me;
the other cowherd boys as well wept and remembered the Lord.
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, protect the pilgrims from the robbers; O Kṛṣṇa, you are Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the helpless in the forest. 17.
You are the savior, the liberator from suffering, and the protector; you are the father, the mother, and the guru. May Hari-Kṛṣṇa and Bāla-Kṛṣṇa protect me. 18.
"Since we who have committed sins are being plundered here in the midst of the forest, nevertheless, O Mādhava, grant protection to your own devotees. (19)
We shall offer devotion unto you and we shall indeed give you our gifts;
O Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, protect our all! 3.190.20.
"We shall bestow wealth and other offerings at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, provided that you grant us protection from wicked robbers. (21)
"All our ornaments, whatever excellent garments we possess, silver coins, and gold coins—we shall give these at Aśvasarovara. (22)
"Having undertaken the vow for the month of Kārtika, we shall perform it with fruits and other offerings, and we shall also daily recite the Mālā-mantra one hundred times. (23)
"Having stayed for one month each in the monasteries of the virtuous during the month of Māgha, we shall perform service in accordance with the commands of the virtuous. (24)
Thus Vanacandra and the others, afflicted and plundered by robbers, performed various acts of penance for the sake of liberation from the robbers. (25)
Sukhādevī, the wife of Vanacandra, as well as those women who had joined the Saṅgha, likewise entreated me.
O Hari! O forest-dweller! O performer of pastimes in Vṛndāvana!
O Kṛṣṇa, hidden within the midst of the assembly of gopīs, protect Your maidservants! 27.
You are the powerful one for the weak; you are the Blessed One for those who are devoted.
You are the creator of joy for your female servants; O Kṛṣṇa, protect these servant-girls.
In the forest you are the companion of the cowherd girls; in the secluded place you are the friend of Rādhā;
on the bed, O Kṛṣṇa, who brings joy to Kamalā, protect your maidservants. 29.

At the time of dissolution, You are served by the liberated; at the time of creation, You are the Lord of the devoted; in the Rāsa dance, You are enamored of all—O Kṛṣṇa, protect Your handmaidens! 3.190.30.
O Lord of those distressed in calamity, protector of those who have sought refuge, remover of the suffering of enemies—O Kṛṣṇa, protect your maidservants! 3.11.
In the womb, You are the nourisher of the embryo; in childhood, You reside within the stainless heart;
in youth, You are the object of love—O Kṛṣṇa, protect Your maidservants!
In old age, You are the best of the learned; in battle, You are the man who grants victory.
O Kṛṣṇa, you are the support for those who have no support; protect your maidservants. || 33 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, may he who was formerly the Asura Rohiṇāṇḍa, yet is the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, protect us—he who was slain by you. 34.
In the past, you were the primordial Śrī Meru-Nārāyaṇa;
when Meru was falling into the abyss, protection was provided by you.
In the past, when the cosmic egg was being consumed by the fire of the sun,
protection and peace were provided by you, the primordial Viṣṇu in the form of Nārāyaṇa.
O Śrī Hari, whose nature is the primordial Lord Nārāyaṇa, in the past you brought about the destruction of the demon Dhūmra and provided protection for Candra. ||37||
By you, O Nārāyaṇa of beginningless sacrifice, sacrifices were set in motion;
for in ancient times, you became the Brahman-Nārāyaṇa who is the teacher of Rudra from the beginning.
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you were Nārāyaṇa, the Sun, for the purpose of regulating the dwellings of the gods; O Kṛṣṇa, protect us, your maidservants! 39.
Possessing the forms of Nāga, Śāstā, Ananta, Garuḍa, and Nārāyaṇa,
you, the beginningless Ārṣa-Nārāyaṇa, became Dhruva for the sake of stability.
O Supreme Lord, for the very purpose of overcoming the Daityas beginning with Śurānanda,
you became the primordial, wise Nārāyaṇa.
You became the beginningless hero Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the righteous; you are the beginningless Bhadranārāyaṇa for the sake of liberating those who have been burnt.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you were Harinārāyaṇa, the husband of the daughter of Tuṅgabhadrāsana; protect us, your maidservants! 43.
In the past, you were the protector of the treasury of the Rākṣasa named Kośa for the sake of its destruction;
you are the beginningless Śrībīja Nārāyaṇa, the guardian of the seed. ||44||
In former times, you were the primordial being for the sake of the liberation of the sons of Dharmavrata;
O Kṛṣṇa, may the beginningless Śrīvara Nārāyaṇa protect us. 45.
By the curse of the great virtuous Sudarśanī, the world became composed of women;
for the sake of its protection, you attained the state of the beginningless Nārāyaṇa as both woman and man.
O Śrī Jala-Nārāyaṇa, you who are without beginning, having slain the Makara demon, protect the worlds; O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, protect your maidservants. (47)
In the past, you were the primordial Śrī-Śīlanārāyaṇa;
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of protecting the righteous dharma, protect these female servants. 48.
In ancient times, you were the primordial Nārāyaṇa who increases the fortune of Śrī;
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of destroying tigers, fire, and other dangers, protect your maidservants. 49.
In ancient times, you were the beginningless four-faced Nārāyaṇa;
you are the bestower of desired boons upon the Brahmins Rādhanikā and Puṇyarāta.
In ancient times, he was Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa;
for the sake of sanctifying the holy places, he became the beginningless Tīrtha-Nārāyaṇa.
For the sake of devotion, you became the beginningless Śrījīvanārāyaṇa;
in the sacrifice, you became the illustrious Ardhaśrīśvaranārāyaṇa. ||52||
You became Pitṛnārāyaṇa, the deliverer of the ancestors, in the first half of the Ādya [Kalpa];
you became Plakṣanārāyaṇa for the sake of instructing in liberation through devotion.
O Lord of Gods, O Kṛṣṇa, in the human sacrifice (naramedha), you became Nārāyaṇa, the foremost among men, and protected the devotees; now, protect your female servants.
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you were Ādinārāyaṇa, who commanded King Sūryavarcas; O Kṛṣṇa, protect these female servants.
O Lord Rājanārāyaṇa, you who are without beginning, you existed even in the past;
O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of the demon Māyūrakā, protect your maidservants! 56.
In ancient times, you were the unborn Nārāyaṇa, the eternally glorious celibate student;
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of protecting those who observe lifelong vows, protect these servant girls.
For the sake of destroying the demon Hālaka and also for the sake of restoring Śiva to life, you, the primordial Śrī Śivanārāyaṇa, appeared in the past. (58)
O Kṛṣṇa, you were formerly the beginningless Śrī-Svarṇanārāyaṇa; for the sake of reviving Kubera, please protect these maidservants. (59)
In ancient times, you, the beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa, created the fire of the mountain Aruṇācala, which was red with flames and consumed the forest of the wicked among the people.
May he who was formerly Anādisāvananārāyaṇa, together with Lakṣmī worshipped by Nirvāṇikā, protect you. 61.
In former times, through devotion to King Aṃśumat, you became Nārāyaṇa;
may that Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Śrī Sādhu, protect us. 62.
May that primordial Śrī Bhaktanārāyaṇa, who indeed brought back to life the sage Śāla when he had been cursed, protect us. 63.
In the past, for the sake of liberating the lord of the earth who wore armor, you yourself became the primordial Lord Śrī Medhanārāyaṇa; may he protect us. 64.
In the past, for the sake of destroying the great asura Analāda, you became the beginningless Śrī-Vahni-Nārāyaṇa; may he protect us. (65)
For the sake of destroying the disease of the womb, you became Rasanārāyaṇa;
as such, O Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, protect your female servants.
O primordial Śrī Cakranārāyaṇa, you existed even before creation;
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, who brought about the destruction of the Daityas, protect your female servants.
Anādi-satya-nārāyaṇa is for the purpose of establishing the Dharma; Anādi-śrī-hiraṇya-nārāyaṇa is for the sake of the stability of the mountain.
For the sake of his devotees, you were formerly the beginningless Śrī Nairañjaninārāyaṇa, and you were also the beginningless Śrī Puṇyanārāyaṇa;
may that Kṛṣṇa, who brings an end to the curse of Puṇyavatī, protect us.
You became the primordial, illustrious, great Brahman Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, protect these maidservants so that the desires of the Apsarases may be fulfilled;
for you were, in ancient times, the beginningless Śrī Gurunārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the purpose of bestowing the knowledge of Brahman, protect the maidservants;
you are the one who grants the auspicious initiation at the sacrifice of King Bṛhaddharma.
May that beginningless and glorious Ācārya Nārāyaṇa protect us—he who was formerly the beginningless, illustrious Mahāvidyun-Nārāyaṇa, the Unborn. (73)
O Kṛṣṇa, you who are the slayer of the Daitya Vidyutstava, protect your female servants;
you were formerly the beginningless, glorious Madhu-nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of the demon Madhubhakṣa, protect these maidservants;
you were indeed the beginningless Lord Nārāyaṇa in the past.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of destroying the Daityas during the Tiṣya age, protect these female servants;
for you were formerly the beginningless, glorious, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, protect the maidservants during this golden festival of the Creator;
for you were formerly the primordial Śrī Mokṣanārāyaṇa.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who are without beginning, O beloved Keśava, O Lord of Brahma-priyā and the others, protect us from these robbers! 78.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of those dear to you, show mercy! Grant us protection quickly from these plunderers; we have come to you for refuge. (79)
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, those women also performed meditation upon Hari;
I myself, as Hari, arrived there and remained invisible for a moment.
While listening to my words of praise concerning my past deeds,
the plunderers gather their coins and other wealth together in one place.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn by the Great Saurya Confederacy when Harassed by Robbers," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; both the girls and the boys, being greatly distressed, offered praise to me for the sake of their own protection—what I heard at that time, I shall relate.
He who, having liberated from hardship his own daughter Divyādevī— the daughter of Divodāsa— who was bereft of fortune, established her in the imperishable state.
May that Lord Bālakṛṣṇa protect us, his female attendants; for in the past, through the yoga of your holy one, the Bhilla woman and the Bhilla attained liberation. (3)
In former times, O Kṛṣṇa, King Subāhu, together with his wife, attained the path of liberation through your majesty by taking refuge in a holy man.
O Kṛṣṇa, you protected the maiden Aśokasundarī, the daughter of Satī and Śaṅkara, in the past; now protect us, your servants.
In former times, you took the form of a woman for the sake of destroying Vihuṇḍa;
as the husband of Kāmodā, may he protect us, his female servants.
"You are the bestower of liberation upon Śuka; protect our own daughters.
There is one named Khaśa, a servant of Viṣṇu, and his beautiful wife is Rāmaṇī."
And her daughter Līlāvatī was brought forth before you, O Lord;
for in the past, O Kṛṣṇa, O All-pervading One, you have [purified] the sins of courtesans.
O Lord, having performed meritorious deeds, you then created the people of merit;
in former times, you also made courtesans and yoginīs.
O Kṛṣṇa, you became the bestower of liberation to Sumara’s wife, the dog-eater named Rakṣā; may He protect us, His female devotees. 10.
The Lord formerly made Kauśika the Garuḍa and the singer,
as well as a Vaiśya named Mālava and others who were skilled in singing.
May he who led us to the world of Brahmā protect us, O female attendants;
may he who granted liberation to the Brahmin Harimiśra protect us. 1-2.
In ancient times, you presented a mace to the great queen Cidambarā, the wife of Jiṣṇu,
and provided her protection from the Rākṣasa Bhadraka.
May she, whose subjects are living beings and who has her own attendants as servants, protect us;
she who possesses sovereignty in battle, is beloved by Brahmā, and is the daughter of Gadā.
May he by whom even Nārāyaṇa was made black protect us;
may he by whom the lords of battle were likewise liberated protect us. (15)
May that Mādhava, by whom liberation was granted to Bindumatī and to the wife of Yayāti, provide protection from the plunderers who are like lions.
May that Kṛṣṇa of lovely qualities, by whom Nārāyaṇa— who bore the crescent moon upon his axe— was delivered, protect his own female devotees.
May that Kṛṣṇa, who led the cowherd’s wife Sucandrakā and her husband, the cowherd, to the imperishable abode, protect us. 18.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect us, by whom Hari— the first among men— was led toward the imperishable path of Brahman.
May that Kṛṣṇa—Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa—who in former times liberated the vultures as the Supreme Self, protect us. 20.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect me, who granted liberation to Jīvacandra;
he who effected the release of the sons of Śatānanda and Vinodinī. ||21||
May that very Śrī Hari by whom Kṛṣṇa was created protect us;
may He who grants liberation even from the women of Kāśī protect us. 22.
May that Kṛṣṇa—who is the primordial Kṛṣṇa, yet appears as the infant Kṛṣṇa—protect us, by whose power the sparrow was protected through the act of mating with the bull. 23.
May that Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, by whom the liberation of Citraketu and Queen Mālatī was formerly accomplished, protect us. 24.
May that Kṛṣṇa, by whom the virtuous have been made excellent, protect us;
may he who made the fire-bodied Kṛśānu emaciated protect us. ||25||
May that very Lord Kṛṣṇa, by whom the sound of the flute was made to resound again and again for man and woman alike, protect his own female attendants here. 16.
May the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, who protected Vipula and Devaśarman, grant liberation and protect us from this suffering. 27.
May that very Lord, by whom the sages were formerly settled at the sacred ford named Gokarṇa, protect us from robbers.
May that Kṛṣṇa, who ordained the welfare of Kuvalāśva, Uttaṅka, Satyavrata, and Gālava, protect us. 29.
By whose majesty the powerful Kṛṣṇa became a saintly Brahmin who resounds with spiritual power; may he protect us from robbers. 30.
The son of Keśariṇī, Ālambāyana, indeed attained liberation;
by his majesty, may that Kṛṣṇa protect us from robbers. (3.1)
May Bālakṛṣṇa, our beloved and dear one, who led hundreds of thousands of virtuous men from Gokarṇa to the imperishable abode, protect us, O dear ones! 32.
May that Kṛṣṇa, by whom the Śabara, the Rākṣasa, the vulture, and even the dog-eater were liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, protect you, his servants. 33.
May that Kṛṣṇa of ours protect us from robbers—He who, seeing the fame of Śāpa to be supreme, cut off her head; O His own female servants! 34.
May he by whom Bhāruṇḍa the Puṣkasa was delivered protect us;
may that Kṛṣṇa by whom Vṛṣādarbhi was made free protect us. (35)
May that Kṛṣṇa protect you, his servants—he by whom the thief Naraśāya was liberated, and by whom the wealthy were set free. 36.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, who possesses divine beauty, who is the protector of Kundadhārā and who protected the Jāṅgalas at the sacrifice, protect our daughters. 37.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved, who has liberated even Śambhalavāra along with its people, protect his own female attendants here. ||38||
In the divine lineage of the host of gods, Bālakṛṣṇa was born;
may that very Lord protect his own female devotees here. (39)
Salutation to the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
salutation to the one born as Śrī Kambharā, Lakṣmī, and Gopāla. ||40||
May that glorious Hari, by whom the eminent brahmin Dīrghaśīla was liberated from the noose of Yama, protect his own female servants. 41.
May this very Lord and Protector, by whom the Brahmin woman Brahmāsati was liberated by the Supreme Self, protect us, his own female servants. 42.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect you, his servants—he by whom the great queen Kālindharā and the king named Vaivarta were liberated. 43.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect you, his devotees—he by whom even Vṛṣagamana, the son of Romapāda, was liberated through Viṣṇu. 44.
May that Bālakṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa protect us—he by whom Viṣṇu formerly liberated the thief Nagnabhaṅga. ||45||
O maidservants, may that wielder of the discus, by whom the demon Bhaṇḍāsura was slain through the gateway of Lalitā—
that Kṛṣṇa-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa— protect us here.
May that Lord Kṛṣṇa, by whom millions of maidens from the Lalitā-mānasa lake were accepted in the past, protect you, his female servants. 47.
May He who grants liberation protect us—He by whom Pīvarī and the others were established in their vows with all their desires fulfilled. (48)
May this Kṛṣṇa protect us, his female servants, from robbers—he by whom Vasiṣṭha and Agastya were liberated from their curse, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow! 49.
May that beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa protect us, by whom the cruel hunter was liberated along with his wife. (50)
May she who brings liberation even to Puṣkaravāhana protect us—she who creates the lotus-lake, the virtuous sovereign endowed with compassion. 5.1.
May that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by whose grace Padminī became equal to Kamalā, protect us from robbers. 5.2
He who provided protection to the brahmin Dharmatapas, and he who granted the status of Manu to Suratha—He is indeed the Lord of Śrī. ||5.3||
By that Supreme Self, Dhanavarman was sent to heaven,
and likewise, O twice-born one, Bali was established in his kingdom among men.
By whom Ānandavarṇin was likewise established among men, and by whom the Śūdra Ghṛṇeṣika was established in the kingdom of Mānava. ||55||
May Kṛṣṇa, by whom Bhūti was rescued and who saved his servants, protect us—he by whom the demon Bālaka was uprooted and turned into jewels. (56)
May that Viṣṇu, by whom Bāṣkali was destroyed, protect us;
by Gajanārāyaṇa as well, Purukutsara was slain.
By that wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Pralamba was destroyed when he took the form of a fish;
and Bhīmaratha was indeed slain by him in the form of a tortoise.
For by him indeed, Śāntaśatru was slain in the form of a swan,
and Mahākāla was destroyed by him as Hayagrīva.
May that Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, protect his own female attendants;
may Vāmana and Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of Kālakākṣa, protect them as well.
May Hari, the slayer of Bali and the enemy of the gods, dispel our suffering;
and may the Lord who took the form of a woman, the destroyer of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, protect us.
May Hari, the slayer of Tāraka, protect us— even he who assumed the form of a eunuch—
by whom, in the past, the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird was destroyed while it was in the form of a peacock.
May he by whom Śuci was slain protect us—that wielder of the discus—and likewise [the sons] of Sādhubhāvāyana-Ṛṣi and of Śrīmānasa. 63.
May Kṛṣṇa, who brings about liberation even for Cidānanda, protect us—he who indeed liberated Sadvidyāyanī, his wife, who is the fruit of the Vedas. 64.
May he who brought about the liberation of Alarka’s mother protect us;
he who is the gateway to the stream of liberation and likewise the path to the attainment of perfections.

May that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose wife offers her hands in supplication without being asked and whose husband is a sage who wanders for alms, protect us—he by taking refuge in whom even he has been liberated. 66.
May that Great King Bālakṛṣṇa, by whom the mother Nityāśrayā and her son Keśin were liberated, protect us here. 67.
He by whom his mother Cāraṇī and his son Vyāghra were delivered;
he by whom his father, the virtuous Kūṭadeva, and Śyāma were delivered. (68)
May Kṛṣṇa protect me, by whom the supreme Bhūdeva and the Ṛṣi Devāyana were likewise liberated from distress. 69.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, whose life is dear to him, protect Virālaka the Vaiśya along with his family, whom he rescued from bandits. 70.
May he who rescued King Pṛthvīdhara and Queen Madhuvindā, as well as the wretched Durvoḍhaka, protect us. (71)
May he who protected Sāgara, Śūdraka, the king named Venapāla, and Hīrukā, the wife of a Śūdra, grant us protection. (72)
May this Kṛṣṇa, by whom Vṛkṇadeva, Bhāvaśūra, Śīladharma, and Asatī were likewise liberated, protect you, his female devotees. (73)
May he who protected Mañjulakeśa, Bhūdeva, Pāśupateśa, the eminent Brahmin, as well as Bāṇāṅgaṇa and the Śūdra, protect us. 74.
May he who [is] Mṛtādana, Santadāsa, Dharmaśālāyana, and Śaṅkudhara, and by whom they were uplifted, protect his female attendants. (75)
And this lord of robbers, named Sāmantavikrama, is plundering our entire wealth; O Kṛṣṇa, alas Kṛṣṇa, protect us! (76)
We are yours here, we are yours here; protect us, your servants!
O Inner Self, O Pervasive Self, O Infinite One, protect us here! 77.
And the children likewise offered hymns of praise to Kṛṣṇa;
hearing this, O Rame, I suddenly assumed a hundred forms there.
Horsemen, camel-riders, armed warriors, and soldiers from the mountains have indeed arrived from afar with the speed of fifty [miles] for the sake of protection. (79)
They raised a loud outcry, saying, "Let the thieves be ready!
We shall surely kill them here; let the sons of our mothers be born! (80)
Thus making the sounds "sphoṭa" and "dhūṣkṛtī," they caused the camels,
horses, and other animals to turn back in all ten directions in an instant.
And the king’s attendants, surrounding those groups of thieves in a circle, went before them to overpower, punish, and beat them. (82)
Then, overcome with rage and having abandoned all hope for their lives, they fled from the Middle Country, uttering sounds of abuse and shouting "sphoṭa! (crash!).
Then, O Lakṣmī, my attendants quickly let out shouts of "dhūṣkṛti";
a mutual battle ensued, consisting of those shouting "dhūṣkṛti" and the golikās. (84)
All those exceedingly arrogant ones were pierced by me with my ball-machines;
all fifty of them died there, having been struck through by the balls.
I led all of them, who had died, to heaven by means of my hands;
having thus liberated those merchant devotees, I then comforted them with gentle words.
All those men, women, girls, and children, having sought refuge, fell at my feet as I stood in the form of an army. ||87||
Then, from my own accumulated wealth, I gave them all their possessions—ornaments, garments, and so forth—each according to what was his. (88)
They all became happy; I touched their beaten limbs, and they became free from pain as well as free from fear.
Then, O Lakṣmī, I suddenly caused the armies consisting of horses, camels, and soldiers to vanish,
and I alone became the four-armed Nārāyaṇa.
I caused Vanacandra and Sukhādevī to have an audience with me;
at that time, I also granted my own audience to all the others.
Overcome by supreme wonder, they all fell at my feet; those devotees, equal to the most devoted, had sought refuge in me. (92)
Then, in the circle of the forest, I gave them my mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (93)
O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, Ādi-Kṛṣṇa, Narāyaṇa;
O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, grant me protection! 94.
Then, O Kamalā, he bestowed the great Vaiṣṇava initiation upon him,
after which he traversed all the forest regions beyond.
Having asked everyone if they were well and shown them the way to the sacred ford, O Lakṣmī, I vanished there; they too [proceeded] slowly toward Prabhāsa.
From there they went to Raivata, and from there they arrived at Aśvapaṭṭa; meanwhile, the various acts of merit consisting of pilgrimages and gifts were performed. (97)
At that time, they all performed my worship in the form of offering their very selves; likewise, they rendered service to the virtuous. (98)
All being restored to health, they performed devotion to me at every sacred site;
then they went to Camatkārapurī, the city of gold. 99.
Then they reached their own country and always offered devotion unto me;
having been delivered and protected, at the end of their bodies they attained my abode. (3.191.1) 00.
O Lakṣmī, those who are devoted to me have been brought by me to [the highest state];
even those who are thieves and plunderers, if they know my true nature, [attain that same goal]. (101)
"Indeed, I have brought them from heaven to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha at the end;
thus, being devoted to compassion, I protect them and lead them there."
I release those who have taken refuge in me from the noose of existence and I uplift them;
by reading or hearing this, there shall likewise be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, assuming the forms of royal soldiers and others, slew the plunderers and protected His devotees following the praise of women and children for the sake of their protection from robbers," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this purifying story of a devotee.
In ancient times, there was a brāhmaṇa named Dhaniṣṭhakoṣa who possessed abundant wealth and other riches.
He was a performer of sacrifices and offerings, a worshiper of the five deities (Pañcāyatana),
devoted to piety, exceedingly generous, and likewise possessed of the wealth of a thousand cows.
The lord of fields, gardens, and forests was endowed with industry and exertion;
indeed, there were always millions of gold and silver coins in his treasury.
Though highly honored by the Lord of Yuddhapura in many ways,
King Mālavasiṃha also constantly offered auspicious betel-leaf.
He bestows upon him exalted dignity within the assembly hall of the great palace;
he receives his very consent regarding the affairs of the kingdom, which are exceedingly difficult to bear.
Just as one honors the foremost and most eminent person, so too should one honor a Brahmin at all festivals, in pleasure gardens, and at water-stations.
In all assemblies, he considered the twice-born to be worthy of every honor;
and the affection of the subjects became firmly rooted in him. || 7 ||
He indeed bestows wealth among his subjects for the sake of providing assistance, even without a written document; for truthfulness is the very price of one's word.
He provided assistance with clothing, food, and other necessities to the distressed, the poor, the protectorless women, the virtuous, and the mendicants.
He restored many gifts of houses, numerous temples,
religious rest-houses, and the highly dilapidated monasteries of holy men.
He caused water-stations and food-distributions to be established like a king;
the king, for his part, remained everywhere providing him with assistance.
The treasure of Dhaniṣṭhaka constantly attends me, the Supreme Lord;
having bathed and worshipped me, O King, he then meets with me thereafter. (12)
Having worshipped the five deities and others, he always eats and never otherwise;
his family is devoted to me, and they always worship me, O Rame.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, intoxication with sovereignty, intoxication with wealth,
and likewise intoxication with youth, lead a person astray.
The violent onset of the senses, the presence of sense objects, and even the fickleness of the mind cast the devotee into impurity. (15)
Whether constantly engaged in dance, or constantly in a musical assembly, or constantly in the state of erotic passion, the quality of *rajas* increases. (1.6)
Constant engagement with sense objects and constant attachment to material things forcibly carry away the mind, which by nature flows downward like a river. (17)
In the same way, this devoted one’s conduct was such that he frequented royal assemblies and attended upon courtesans and the like during dances at night and other times. (18)
Due to living together with female slaves and other such factors, their minds became corrupted; though they were beautiful, they were lustful and deluded by the desire for wealth.
With gestures of allure, various services, and shared dwellings, the courtesans cast my devotee, who was a treasury of wealth, into delusion. (3.192.20)
They gradually caused him to become immersed in most delightful sense-objects;
like those who can be won over by wealth, having obtained wealth, they remained before him as objects of enjoyment. (21)
Although he was my devotee, having abandoned devotion and fallen into the company of kings,
he thereafter generally made his constant residence in the royal garden.
He indeed looks after his own family only occasionally after a long time,
since he spends much of his residence in the garden together with the king.
The king also constantly associated with that childhood friend, sharing in drinking, eating, games, and the pleasures of dance and song. (24)
Thus, for a devotee who is joined with sense objects through external activities, my worship, recitation, and meditation are all accomplished gradually, step by step. (25)
Having suffered injury and reached dissolution, my devotion became impaired;
he remembers me only occasionally, and especially so when it concerns women. (26)
Accompanied by courtesans, he lived devoted to sexual indulgence;
meanwhile, his sons, daughters, and his virtuous, law-abiding wife remained there.
By name Snehalatādevī, my most devoted wife, grieved for the condition of her husband; yet she worships me, Śrī Hari, as the supreme devotee. 28.
She indeed prays for the protection of her husband’s dharma through worship, for the abandonment of unrighteousness, and for fame, renown, and birth in a noble lineage. (29)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Puruṣottama Mādhava!
Quell that restlessness which exists in the mind of Your devotee.
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Kānta Keśava, please liberate me from the addiction to sexual intercourse with my husband.
O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that the king may also become devoted to you, and likewise that even the courtesans may become devoted to you, the Supreme Soul. (32)
O Kṛṣṇa, show mercy so that the subjects may also become devoted;
from this day forward, I shall observe a vow of eating but one meal per day until the end of the year.
And with a concentrated mind, I shall serve you, O virtuous lady of the Saṅgha;
I shall perform your worship every day for the duration of one ghaṭikā. (34)
During the period of birth-impurity, I shall perform worship for you with the sixteen services;
I shall also provide a golden swing and a golden image of you.
I shall cause her to be fashioned, endowed with splendor, joined with Rādhā and Ramā, accompanied by Padmāvatī, and graced by the beautiful Māṇikī. (36)
Endowed with fortune, likewise delightful, richly adorned, and in the full bloom of youth—
such an excellent and auspicious bedstead shall I indeed have fashioned.
Your implements, moreover, are made of gold and silver:
the two fans, the fly-whisks, the parasol, the sandals, and the ornaments. (38)
"For your satisfaction, I shall have you massaged daily with the finest fragrant substances and the essence of oils, using golden and jeweled implements. (39)
I shall perform anointing with liquids, worship with Tulasī leaves, and offer oblations of ghee and desired foods for the sake of His supreme satisfaction.
"O beloved Keśava, I shall cause annual festivals to be held for you;
deliver my husband, a merchant, from his addiction to courtesans. (41)
She has come to you for refuge and fallen at your feet;
burn away the sins of my husband and do what is pleasing to me. (42)
Having spoken thus on the day of the festival of lights for Hari,
Snehalatikā performed my worship and observed the vow for an entire year.
That virtuous woman observed all the prescribed rules;
indeed, she brought the vow named Patisaṃskāraka to its full completion.
On that very day, he performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) of his vow like a mountain of food (annakūṭa),
and also celebrated a festival for Kṛṣṇa on the first lunar day (pratipad) to complete the vow.
He caused a pavilion to be constructed, adorned with plantain pillars, beautiful and provided with archways and the like, and equipped with sacrificial pits and altars. ||46||
It was provided with lion-thrones, graced by Brahmins and deities,
and equipped with the full array of offerings for gods and ancestors, as well as the materials for the act of giving.

It resounded with the sounds of sacrificial fires being kindled, Vedic rituals, and the chanting of the Vedas and mantras; it was filled with the noise of the recitations performed by virtuous men and women who were devotees of Viṣṇu.
It resounds with musical instruments, proclamations, songs, and the like, augmented by the sound of giving,
and is presided over by inhabitants of the worlds such as Satyasvara.
Possessing a divine nature through visits to sacred fords, it was resplendent with the attendants of Kṛṣṇa,
graced by the playful movements of the beloved of Brahmā, and adorned with banners and flags.

It is adorned with the excellent maṇḍala named Sarvatobhadra, which is preeminent in meaning, and is provided with vessels such as the sthālī, kalaśa, and pātra, as well as gifts of beds and other articles. (51)
Where Mādhava is worshipped with the requisites for worship, and where oblations of various kinds are offered into the fire; ||52||
Where the Vedic chants and mantras are recited by the Brahmins, and where gifts consisting of gold and silver are bestowed; ||93||
The Brahmins partook of the desired foods and delicacies, and with hearts full of contentment, they bestowed blessings that grant all forms of prosperity. (54)
Then, as the *pūrṇāhuti* was being offered with streams of clarified butter,
the aged Nārāyaṇa-Nara arrived there at the pavilion.
O Lakṣmī, he who was I in the form of a brahmin, possessed of exceeding splendor, is indeed that very same person.
Both the gods and the sages offered me a welcome and performed the rites of hospitality.
They gave me an excellent seat, and Agni honored me as well;
there I sat down, O twice-born one, having been fully honored by all.
"Whose sacrifice is this? I asked the wise twice-born one;
that twice-born man, Soma-āyana, replied to me with a gesture of his finger. (58)
For this creeper of affection, there exists today a sacrifice arising from the completion of her vow;
may that which is desired for the sake of attaining her goals be fulfilled here.
"I shall do as you wish," I said immediately there at that sacrifice;
listen, Lakṣmī, for a great marvel then occurred in that garden.
The palace in which the great merchant, the king, and the servants resided became shaken, as if trembling during an earthquake. ||61||
At that time, I took no pleasure in anything other than the palace together with its gardens;
yet, by my very will, that terrifying trembling arose then. (62)
The palace collapsed because of him, crushing many courtesans;
the king and the merchant were in the middle story at the time of the palace's fall. (63)
They fell there with broken limbs, yet they survived in fear;
having fallen together, they regained consciousness and were reunited. (64)
As they were calling out to one another, he asked, "O wealthy man, what is your condition, O King?
The wealthy man replied, "My foot is broken at the knee. (65)
The king said: "My hand is broken at the joint of the wrist;
there is no other suffering here, and the lives of both of us remain. (66)
"Death has certainly not occurred; this has been brought about by the Supreme Lord.
By both of us, having abandoned the path of Śrī Hari, the way of courtesans was followed. (67)
This evil was grasped by her, and its fruit is this destruction;
nevertheless, it may be due to former merit or through the merit of her relatives. (68)
"Let us live here within the heart, in the space granted by Kṛṣṇa;
from this day forward, we shall indeed abandon all association with courtesans. (69)
"We two shall worship the Supreme Lord and observe our vows,
if indeed we may escape from this difficult place where no space can be discerned."
"We two shall surely emerge alive from this broken middle;
let us worship Nārāyaṇa here, and he will grant us protection. (71)
Having thus reached their decision, the two of them chanted "Hare Kṛṣṇa.
O Lakṣmī, they were protected by the merit of the sacrifice of the creeper of their mutual affection. (72)
Then, immediately after the final oblation of the sacrifice in Yuddhapura,
the collapse of the royal palace was heard from the mouths of the people.
The nihilists, however, claim that the fruit arising from transgression occurs in the sacrifice; yet that is not the reality there, for no transgression occurred in the ritual. (74)
Indeed, that was brought about by my will and by the sin of the merchant; even courtesans become stained with impurity through the falling away of my devotees.
They have indeed died by their own sin, but my devotee has been protected by me;
even the king has been protected by me for the sake of devotion through the power of his devotion.
Then the believers said: "The wicked have died because of their own sins;
yet, due to the merit of the sacrifice, the merchant and the king did not die. (77)
And the men, having gone quickly to the entire Kāṭamāla tree,
slowly moved it far away and cleared away the stones and earth.
The merchant and the king, who were living together in the lower part of the wood,
slowly extracted the two [beings] while providing medicinal treatment for their broken limbs.
All those courtesans were found to be composed of corpses, with their hair disheveled;
they were indeed dead when discovered, and they entered the city of Yama.
Upon touching the elder, the merchant and the king quickly regained their natural composure in hand and foot;
and having heard the news of the sacrifice, they were indeed exceedingly delighted. (81)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, assuming an aged form, touched them both with His two hands; Mūḍhamāra then vanished.
All their suffering vanished, and the two met within the pavilion; they beheld the meritorious rite and heard of the woman’s vow. (83)
Then, having understood that the vow was for the sake of purifying her husband, for the sake of purifying the king, and also for the sake of purifying the subjects, the woman [undertook it]. (84)
The subjects, the king, and all the wealthy men praised the devoted wife:
"Blessed is this woman, a devotee of Hari, seeking liberation, and purifying. (85)
For the sake of the welfare of her subjects and others, she observed her vows for a long time; and by her, her own possessions were offered for the sake of divine rites. (86)
By her merit, this king and the merchant have been well protected;
we all shall worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. (87)
The king also spoke clearly there in the pavilion, just as the merchant and the subjects likewise spoke in the pavilion. (88)
We shall abandon all calamities and sinful deeds;
we shall worship Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the eternal Bālakṛṣṇa. ||89||
"We shall perform expiation for the sinful deeds we have committed;
we shall become devotees of Viṣṇu and, in the end, go to the abode of Hari."
Thus, hundreds of thousands of spectators arrived there—both men and women—who had come either for the sake of the sacrifice or for no particular reason at all. (91)
All the people born in the kingdom, their minds transformed by the power of the aged Brahmin, were indeed terrified at the sight of the Vaiṣṇava initiation.
The elder brāhmaṇas accepted them, abandoned their vices, wore tulasī garlands around their necks, and took up my name, "Bālakṛṣṇa. (93)
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā"—having received this mantra, they indeed became the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas. (94)
They all undertook a vow during the bright fortnight of Kārtika:
"You yourself shall eat but one meal a day, and you must perform my worship every single day. (95)
There was a constant distribution of food for a period of one ghaṭikā;
then, I granted my auspicious vision there in the pavilion.
Four-armed and of divine form, accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Ramā, and joined by Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, and Śrī—He is most enchanting. (97)
Adorned with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, the Kaustubha gem, and a necklace, his face was enriched by a halo of divine splendor, and he was decorated with armlets. (98)
It was frequented by divine liberated attendants and great sages,
and it was highly honored by the sacrificial fires, the deities, and the gods.
Seeing that I, the Supreme Lord, had arrived for the sake of fulfilling the desires of Snehalatā,
they worshipped me and drank the water from my feet.
The lords of the earth accepted the remnants of the sacrifice and partook of them;
then they all brought the sacrifice to completion and performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
The king, the merchant, and likewise the subjects bathed in the Luṇī river;
at that time, O Rame, whatever sins they possessed were utterly consumed.
This great ablution, the *avabhṛtha*, effects the destruction of all sins.
For those who have committed great sins and offenses become pure by bathing there.
The king and the merchant immediately remembered the courtesans for the sake of their liberation,
due to the power of wine and the merit of the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
And all those women who had been released by the king and the merchant from the abode of Yama quickly arrived there on the bank of the Luṇyā river, escorted by messengers.
They reached the water and swam about, and having been sprinkled with water by me,
they were instantly freed from sin and endowed with divine bodies.
Then, by means of celestial chariots, they all went to heaven for a long time;
thereafter, they shall proceed to the eternal abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme self.
Thus those subjects were liberated and made into Vaiṣṇavas;
the king and the merchant were freed from their vices and endowed with devotion by the woman.
Then, having received worship, I quickly vanished from that place;
at the end of my lifespan, [I encountered] the Brahmin Somāyana, who was like a creeper of affection.
May Dhaniṣṭhaka, Koṣa, Vaṇija, King Mālava-siṃha,
and all my Vaiṣṇava subjects attain my imperishable state at the proper time.
O Lakṣmī, having purified even one who is devoted to another's wife— provided he is endowed with devotion and free from deceit— I lead him to liberation.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this,
even one of sinful conduct shall become pure and go to my abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari granted liberation to the merchant Dhaniṣṭhaka, who was addicted to courtesans, through the performance of the vow of devotion made by his own wife," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the liberation of the slayer of a Brahmin.
There was once a king named Rājīva in a village called Vāṭāsīna. || 1 ||
His queen was the virtuous Kundanadevikā by name;
she was devoted to her husband, possessed of sons, dedicated to dharma, and ascetic.
Devoted to me and to Śrī Hari, and intent upon vows and meditation, she does not look upon the sun and is untouchable by other men; with her, I sport in some place.
Devoted to her husband's service, intent on the worship of the gods, bathing, and other rites,
she observed the Cāturmāsya vow and celebrated the festivals of Hari.
Devoted to the virtue of giving and characterized by altruism,
she had consecrated all her auspicious possessions for the sake of honoring and serving the virtuous.
She is the one who serves the poor, the helpless, and cows; she is a worshiper of the Sun;
she bestows honor upon maidens, and she is intent upon my propitiation.
She always provides food and clothing to guests, visitors, and others;
she performs pilgrimages to sacred sites and is ever devoted to the worship of her husband’s feet.
Thus, she was endowed with refined conduct, constantly reciting her rosary,
devoted to beholding the gods, and always engaged in listening to sacred discourses.
She indeed knows the welfare and well-being of her own subjects;
she is devoted to the dharma of non-violence and dedicated to the vow of truth.
By her merit, the kingdom indeed shines and rejoices greatly;
and her subjects are free from fear, free from disease, and possessed of abundant prosperity.
O Lakṣmī, just as gold does not become fragrant when it is not treated with perfume,
so too the husband falls to a low state even when his wife is of noble character.
Her husband is a cruel king who does not acknowledge the gods;
full of arrogance, he considers dharma, ritual action, and the like to be utterly useless. (12)
He does not value the Brahmins nor the virtuous, nor indeed the righteous; lacking discrimination, he shows contempt even for those worthy of worship. 1.3.
He performs neither bathing nor giving, neither worship nor even virtuous vows;
he visits no sacred ford, offers no honor, and does not perform even righteous deeds.
The property of the gods, the wealth of Brahmins, the wealth of the virtuous, and the lawful coinage belonging to others—whatever such is obtained even by force. || 15 ||
The greedy-natured man indeed seizes everything and never releases anything to anyone, whether by theft,
by force, by taxes, by hair-pulling, by war, or by oppression.
Whatever is obtained through deceit or fraud, he indeed considers all that to be just;
he perceives injustice as justice itself, for such is the nature of a king’s duty.
Whatever wealth belongs to the subjects—fields, land, houses and the like, as well as businesses and revenue shares—the subjects themselves are indeed my wealth. (18)
Sons and daughters, cows and bulls, horses, elephants, vehicles, mounts, and livestock—he knows all these as well as everything belonging to the king. (19)
The kingdom belongs neither to the king nor to anyone else, whether it be insentient or sentient;
for the king is the lord of the earth, and the subjects indeed belong to the monarch.
"Since the king enjoys the earth, he indeed enjoys all other earthly beings as well as all its transformations"; thus does the lord of the earth reflect. (21)
Moreover, he had harbored a particular hatred toward brahmins from birth, thinking:
"Brahmins surely consume sweets and sacrificial fees in vain. (22)
Thinking, "These Brahmins are merely wandering for alms and are manifest thieves," he sees the Brahmins and drives them far away. (23)
He indeed punishes in many ways and even seizes what has been begged;
listen, O Brahmins, for once there were twenty Tīrthaṅkaras endowed with Lakṣmī. (24)
Those many wandering devotees arrived at Vāṭāsīna;
on the way, they were honored by the queen for the sake of obtaining rest.
Through food, clothing, drink, and the like, as well as by gifts and vehicles,
the king then realized that they indeed possessed wealth even before him.
And after that, under the pretext of [visiting] a sacred ford, the king gave them a vast amount [of wealth].
Having heard this, the king, out of greed, summoned the brahmins into his presence.
He then plundered all that wealth belonging to the Brahmins,
and out of anger, he confined them all in prison on that very day.
Then the Brahmins, becoming enraged, uttered a formidable curse:
"Your kingdom shall be destroyed, and you shall be deprived of your family and all else. (29)
Become a forest-dweller and a hypocrite, for you are indeed a base mendicant;
having enjoyed the fruit [of your actions] for twenty years, you shall assume a bestial body.
"O atheist, O merciless one, having encountered all these miseries, you shall suffer them;
for the curse was pronounced by the brahmins during the day, while you, O Lord of Vaṭodara, were at night. (3.1)
Accompanied by his army, he came and seized Samastaka in battle;
having appointed Deśapāla to his own kingdom, he placed [the others] in fetters.
Having liberated the brahmins and provided a means of livelihood for the queen,
he then protected the king's family there.
Although he searched everywhere for the sake of recovering the lotus,
he nevertheless departed quickly from his own city by a secret path.
Due to the fault of the brahmins' curse, King Rājīva went to the forest region of the Narmadā for twenty years.
In the forest, I experienced the suffering of a beast, characterized by wretchedness;
then the queen, along with her sons and daughters, began to serve me. (36)
Known by the name Kundanadevī, she was devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
yet even Rājīva, though dwelling in the forest, was indeed distressed by his own sins. (37)
He committed much evil, such as plundering and slaughtering animals;
yet while he was thus dwelling in the forest, a certain Brahmin [encountered] the Narmadā river.
While going to bathe in that forest, Rājīva also met him nearby; he too questioned that brahmin: "Tell me now. (39)
"Where are you going? What is before you? Give me everything that is here!
The Brahmin replied, "Before me there is but a small amount of travel provisions and wealth. (3.193.40)
"O forest-dweller, I will not give you anything except what is necessary for the mere sustenance of my journey.
As they were thus disputing there, a battle broke out between them. (41)
A Brahmin was struck by Rājīva and crushed in the chest with stones;
that Brahmin was reborn there as a preta on the bank of the Narmadā. ||42||
He coiled around the king, the slayer of living beings and the murderer of a Brahmin;
the king, rendered ill-fated by the curse, was then further afflicted by the Rākṣasa.
She wandered through the forest lands like one who was distraught, intoxicated, or dull-witted;
nevertheless, Kunda-nadevī remained devoted to the conduct of Brahman.
Once, while he was asleep in the forest, he saw him— distressed,
tormented by hunger and thirst, and possessed by a rākṣasa in a state of madness.
Having fallen into the conduct of beasts and adopted the manner of Rākṣasas, he was even devouring a dead animal or a bird. ||46||
He was remembering and uttering the words "Kundanā" and "Kundanā," and he was dark-complexioned,
hairy, and likewise wore coarse matted locks.
He appeared as if someone else, though he was known [to be otherwise], with all his true nature laid bare—
whether a Śabara, a Pāraśava, an executioner, or a dog-cooker.
Likewise, when observed, it is indeed terrifying even to behold—like a body that is extremely foul-smelling, filthy, and decrepit. (49)
Seeing that forest-dweller, a personification of sin, repeatedly uttering "Kundanā, Kundanā," she— [3.193.50]
For a moment she reflected, "Who might this be in a dream?
Then, overcome with fear, she said: "Who are you in the middle of the forest? (51)
And he said, "I am named Rājīva, the lord of Kundanāpa;
I am afflicted by the sin of a curse, and especially by a Rākṣasa."
"Kundanā must rescue me; only then will I attain a good rebirth.
As long as Kundanā hears these words of the king while she is asleep— 53.
Then the sleep of the queen departed;
at dawn she awoke, having risen filled with grief, distressed by the suffering of her husband.
Beholding the visible [reality] as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of her hand, that virtuous woman, filled with haste, bathed and worshipped me, Śrīpati, the remover of suffering. 55.
With her face overcome by grief and her mind scorched by excessive sorrow,
Satī, having uttered my name, praised me with eyes clouded by tears.
O Lord, you are one whose desires are fulfilled; indeed, nothing remains for you to attain.
Nevertheless, tell me, how have you come here into this cycle of existence? (57)
If it is for the sake of fulfilling the desires of your devotees, then fulfill my own wish;
if you consider me to be your devotee, disciple, or servant. (58)
Rājīva, who was held by a *rākṣasa*, was to be liberated from the suffering of the forest;
for if there is the destruction of karma through the experiencing of its fruit, it must happen in every case. (59)
O Compassionate One, your compassion is in vain, your arrival is in vain,
and your devotion is in vain, since you have not fulfilled the purpose of one who seeks every goal.
I am indeed a woman seeking wealth, yet I am likewise your servant;
therefore, grant me deliverance through the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, if compassion does not arise in you for one who has committed evil, then I shall give my own merit to him; by that means, you must deliver him.
O Kṛṣṇa, if you have no compassion for me when I am being consumed by the rod of Brahmā’s curse, then you ought to show mercy to me and protect my husband. 63.
If a full punishment is ordained for one who slays a Brahmin, then I consider it right that you now apply that very punishment to me. (64)
I am indeed his half-woman, seeking half of his merit and demerit;
may half of the merit born from my devotion accrue to him. (65)
May half of his sin also abide here with me;
thus, O Nārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu, by means of justice and according to rule. (66)
He may even deserve to drink it in exchange for a suitable ransom;
therefore, he becomes the slayer of the Asuras himself and the bestower of liberation.
O Blessed Keśava, bring happiness even to Rājīva;
for the sake of my peace, who am your devotee, grant my prayer. (68)
"Just as the effort for the *pārijāta* tree is undertaken by you for the sake of Bhāmā, so am I Bhāmā; I shall be your servant, and I request my own *pārijāta*. (69)
"O Kṛṣṇa, in age after age, Bhāmā has been made content by you;
through the gift of the Pārijāta tree, make me content as Bhāmā was."
I shall please you here with devotion; you, in turn, please me with a gift.
A woman and a man please one another through service and the giving of wealth.
O Protector, you ought to act in such a way as to grant favor in all circumstances;
for though she has a protector, O Lord, you regard her situation as one of being without a protector.
Thus spoke Rājīva in Araṇyaka: "Kundanā, Kundanā. (72)
He indeed demands his ransom; therefore, deliver him and show mercy!
As long as you do not deliver him, I shall remain in a fast unto death.
Having spoken thus, Queen Kundaṇā, seated alone, without water, without food, and free from all worldly desire, undertook a fast unto death along with Lakṣmī. (74)
Having conquered sleep and subdued her appetite, and having resolved upon death, she closed her eyes and became absorbed in meditation within her heart. 75.
She made me turn upon the rosary so that I would not desist from recitation;
through the functions of concentration and meditation, she bound me within her heart. (76)
Though firmly held by his great speed, she did not waver for even a moment;
desiring the release of the lotus, she became intent upon me alone.
Having understood her mind, I, remaining within, quickly emerged from the outside in a beautiful form for the sake of her liberation.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Ramā,
richly adorned with all ornaments, and likewise served by his attendants.
With a serene countenance and tranquil, he was intent upon bestowing boons;
his form was pervaded by a halo of splendor, and he was adorned with divine ornaments.
Seeing me standing before her in such a state, she was quickly awakened from within the interior of the jasmine flower and emerged from her meditative absorption. ||81||
Beholding me as the Supreme Self, the virtuous woman rose up quickly and immediately fell at my feet and embraced me closely to her chest.
By the mere touch of me, divine vision was born within her;
she beheld in the forest her own husband, whom she had seen in a dream. (83)
She quickly pointed out her own husband with outstretched hands;
she then entreated him to liberate her suffering husband who was possessed by the Rākṣasa. (84)
Right there, for the sake of my husband's liberation alone, I suddenly took the form of Garuḍa and, having mounted him, carried her along with the one named Kunda.
Wherever that rājīva bird dwelt in the forest, I would come there, descend from the sky, and enjoy myself together with her. (86)
Then, with the water from his own water-pot, he sprinkled the lotus as it was revolving; thereupon, the Rākṣasa who had been leaping about ceased.
Having quickly drunk the water, he indeed became possessed of a divine body;
and after praising me, he went to heaven by means of a celestial chariot through my power. ||88||
Then Rājīva, having become composed in mind and possessing excellent radiance, recognized me as his own wife as well as the Supreme Lord. (89)
Kundanādevikā bowed at my feet and prostrated like a staff; she then reported the entire matter to him.
Then, having been sprinkled again with water by me, he became purified;
he performed the destruction of his sins as I caused him to drink water from my own hands. (91)
Having placed him upon Garuḍa, I brought him to the city of Vāṭāsana;
the queen caused the mantra to be given, and the king abandoned his pride.
He received my mantra, as well as a necklace and a garland of tulasī;
he became a Vaiṣṇava, a devotee of the Lord, possessing a disposition of faith. ||93||
The sons, daughters, and all the subjects likewise attained a state of serenity; then, having provided for their security and well-being, [he departed]. (94)
Having spoken these words to me for the purpose of my departure from this imperishable world, she quickly vanished before the king of Vaṭodara. (95)
Having become a brahmin, I went there indeed for the sake of alms;
then that king, named Bhāskaravikrama, was requested by me.
"Speak, O Brahmin; I shall grant you whatever is within the scope of your desire.
Thereupon, he said to me, "I request the protection of the lotus. (97)
To restore the kingdom to Vāṭāsīna, King Rājeśvara, being so magnanimous, quickly replied, "So be it. (98)
Having spoken thus, he dispatched a messenger with a similar letter to the chief official;
and I, a brahmin, likewise caused the kingdom to be bestowed upon Rājīva.
Having again granted my vision to the queen and the king, I then vanished; thereafter, after some time, I took my delight.
I brought Rājīva, Kunda, Nādevī, as well as their sons, daughters,
and that entire Vaiṣṇava family to the imperishable abode.
In this way, through my devotion and the propitiation of my wife in the past,
even the sinful Rājīva, though a slayer of a Brahmin, was protected from the forest.
The Rākṣasa was liberated from the Rākṣasas, and even the Rākṣasa himself was set free;
indeed, the entire family of King Rājīva was delivered from sin.
Indeed, through the power of Kundanā’s ascetic observances and fasting,
and by her devotion in worshipping me, her own kingdom was recovered once again.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, through devotion to me, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained here;
likewise, by reading and hearing this, one shall obtain enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Lord and Liberation from Suffering through the Supreme Devotion of Queen Kunda-nadevī—Who Was a Brahmin-Slayer, Overpowered by Rākṣasas, and Deprived of Her Kingdom—King Vāṭāsīnāra," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Nārāyaṇīśrī, listen to the life-story of the Lord of the lotus-like devotees, the destroyer of women's distress, named Devaviśrāma.
There was a king named Cakradhara, the lord of the city of Virāma;
he had a minister named Devaviśrama who was exceedingly righteous.
He was one who brought about the prosperity of the kingdom, desiring the welfare of his subjects;
he was ever intent on the effort of protecting the realm and a constant worshiper of the gods and other deities.
He was devoted to the path of Dharma and dedicated to the true Dharma;
he was intent on serving virtuous men, women, and chaste wives, and was an exemplary servant.
Whosoever are destitute of wealth, they beg for a divine rest;
he too grants their desire and indeed satisfies the mendicants.
Even those seeking wealth were highly satisfied and uttered great blessings, saying, "May you have heaven, a kingdom, and a great empire! (6)
The righteous king also constantly served the Supreme Lord;
there were no thieves, nor rogues, nor deceitful men, nor impostors.
Those who delight in deceit do not even desire the kingdom of their own king;
for as is the king, so is the minister, always inflicting punishment upon thieves and the like.
Those who are intent on malevolent magic, those who live by means of mantras, tantras, and the like, and those who are slayers or murderers—these are never pleasing to him at all. (9)
Then once, the female servants of Bahucarā’s mother—
women who were yoginīs and knowers of mantras— went out for alms in Rame.
Wherever kings who are lords of charity are heard of, and likewise wherever there are people who give alms, it is in those very places, O Rame, that these beggars indeed solicit wealth.
Gold, silver, garments, vehicles, and even mounts;
diamonds, rubies of various colors, and diverse kinds of gems.
They beg for ornaments and they obtain what is begged; likewise, they present that same Great Goddess who wanders through many [forms]. (13)
"The mother, who has performed many deeds, will give a hundred thousandfold to the giver.
Recalling these supreme words, those women accept the gift. (14)
Then, wherever the merchants, kings, or people give to them, at those city gates and house doors, those women [stand]. (15)
Having made their seats firm, they proclaim themselves in groups;
indeed, having undertaken the vow of fasting, they perform that penance which is but strife.
Victory, victory to you, O Mother who wanders far! Victory, victory to you, O Mother who wanders far!
You are the giver of wealth to the generous; victory, victory to you, O Mother who wanders far! (17)
Thus playing cymbals, they sing aloud in the courtyard of the house;
for five or seven days they remain there and do not depart.
Then, having suffered defeat, the masters of the houses even give [the goods], and they take back gold, silver, wealth, and so forth in many ways. (1.9)
But if they do not surrender the wealth or property as desired,
one should resort to fasting by force and strive even through quarrels.
Having seized them, they indeed depart; women do not act otherwise than by force.
All such yoginīs, numbering ten, are of this nature. (21)
They indeed resorted to force for the sake of wealth; then the minister gave them money—a hundred gold coins—but even having received it, they were devoid of satisfaction.
Just as a thousand gold pieces are [valued], so too is everything else—gems, diamonds, ornaments, and so forth—as well as wealth separate from the king. (23)
Ten thousand gold coins and garlands of gems and pearls—though they were thus pressed with persistence, they did not go out. ||24||
Then, when seven days had passed while the distribution of a thousand gold coins was being given, those [women] were not yet satisfied.
Then they performed impure rites and incantations for the destruction of the minister,
and they also performed defiled spells for the destruction of the king.
Then the minister, having fallen down, became agitated and deeply unconscious; however, regaining consciousness within a moment, he rose up again. ||27||
The king, too, having reached such a state, fell into a swoon; then, having risen again, he performed all those rites of malevolent magic.
Neither the minister nor the king, being unable to endure it, had the head of the one most worthy of honor cut off by their own soldiers. (29)
Then other weak and cruel women fled out of fear of death,
taking the wealth that had been given and abandoning the corpse of the deceased woman.
They set out running and proceeded toward the interior of the city;
everywhere among the people in the world, it was said that the king had committed the murder of a woman.
Furthermore, the infamy arose that even his minister had committed the murder of a woman;
[he was accused of being] one who sets fires, one who administers poison, one who raises a weapon, or one who performs malevolent incantations.
These women are assassins, givers of curses, and likewise givers of enmity;
there is no fault whatsoever in their destruction, for she who takes away life deserves to be killed.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, there is no fault whatsoever in such non-destruction;
nevertheless, worldly rumors arise concerning the killing of women. (34)
All those who cause infamy have their course marked out by the world; they bring reproach upon the subjects and even upon the king himself. (35)
Indeed, without even knowing the cause—such as malevolent magic or the like—they falsely proclaim their infamy, saying, "The king is a killer of women" or "He is a murderer of his ministers. (36)
Then the Wheel-turning King spoke auspicious words to the minister named Devaviśrama for the removal of his blemish.
O Great-Minded One, how can there be cleansing for one who speaks of what ought to be done?
Just as contentment among the subjects serves as the cleansing of slander. (38)
Although there is no sin in killing a woman who practices malevolent magic, one should nevertheless perform a vow for the sake of pacifying the ill repute she incurs. (39)
"O minister, having reflected upon what is beneficial, tell me what is auspicious;
let that which is appropriate be done so that it may become a righteous deed. (3.194.40)
The minister said: "O King, summon a splendid assembly and there declare your intention to the elderly subjects. (41)
Having heard this, the king acted accordingly; and there, men and thousands of women—both elders of the subjects and common folk—came to the assembly hall.
Then the minister pointed out a domestic priest who was exceedingly righteous, highly learned, well-versed in the treatises, and a master of the Vedas. (43)
Knowing the dharma, the place, and the time, and being urged by the words of the ministers and commanded by the king, he proclaimed the dharmas in the assembly hall.
May the venerable assembly, as well as the elderly women and men, listen;
I shall declare the characteristics of dharma in accordance with the scriptures. (45)

Dharma, characterized by impelling, accomplishes one's purpose and bestows liberation; whereas that which is contrary to it, being non-beneficial and having an adverse purpose, brings about a downward state of existence and is not dharma. ||46||
That which the noble ones indeed praise while protecting it is called *dharma*, for it is a bull;
but that which people censure is proclaimed to be *adharma*.
That by which there is the upholding, nourishing, and likewise the protection of the worlds, and by which happiness, security, and well-being may arise—that is called Dharma. (48)
That conduct which is established according to place, time, and a worthy recipient brings happiness and is Dharma; that which brings suffering is Adharma. (49)
Through righteousness, fame arises, as well as constant happiness and peace;
likewise, there is prosperity, advancement, heaven, and eternal liberation.
That alone is the dharma by which a king makes his subjects happy:
worship of the gods, as well as charity, religious observance, compassion, and the giving of sacrificial fees.
Constantly helping others is the duty of all embodied beings;
likewise, bathing, recitation of mantras, salutation to the gods, and dedication to the divine [are their duties].
Honoring the elderly is dharma, as is honoring the king;
right conduct is indeed the primary dharma, for unrighteousness is its opposite.
Dharma is indeed the conduct of the virtuous, but not so that of the wicked;
it consists of non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, the vow of celibacy, austerity, and self-restraint. (54)
Dharma alone is declared supreme, yet service to the elderly is difficult to find;
service to the virtuous and association with the good are proclaimed as the highest dharma. (65)
Benefiting living beings according to one's ability is considered the bull [of dharma];
making others pleased is dharma, for being pleased is indeed difficult to attain. (56)
Lack of faith, as well as agitation, failure to provide assistance, lack of service, violence, falsehood, forcible seizure, and association with the wicked. (97)
That indeed becomes unrighteousness and must always be abandoned by people;
for a gift given with faith is considered to be righteousness itself. (98)
That which is taken by force is indeed the unrighteousness of a plunderer;
it would be a malevolent rite (abhicāra) if, through mantras, it were to destroy lives. ||99||
For kings, unrighteousness itself is a cause for the destruction of life;
even the killing of a leader through malevolent magic is unrighteous.

Violence committed at the wrong place, at the wrong time, or against an unworthy recipient, as well as violence arising from a corrupt intention or the act of an assassin, is indeed proclaimed to be unrighteousness (adharma). ||61||
When such unrighteousness manifests in a man, a woman, a boy, or even a girl,
it assumes the very form of an assassin.
Even an unrighteous person who possesses weapons and the like must certainly be restrained; likewise, an assailant must be slain by all means for the sake of protecting one's life. (63)
When an assassin is not killed by the one whom he intended to kill, that very person is indeed swiftly slain [by the consequences]; therefore, an assassin must be put to death. 64.
This very nature of the Dharma has indeed been declared by me in your presence;
herein is the worship of women who are devoted and have wandered far [in spiritual practice]. 65.
Although a thousand gold coins were paid according to the proper measure, the women, firm in their resolve, still sought to take him by force and by violence. (66)
They performed malevolent magic against the king and his minister, causing a great pestilence;
therefore, they were murderous sorceresses like Pūtanas.
These are said to be indeed rākṣasīs, harmful and characterized by tamas;
they are knowers of mantras who employ them for the purpose of malevolent magic against enemies.
"They must certainly be killed; there is no fault in this, for such is the established law.
"All of them indeed deserve death, but only one among them—" ||69||
Compassion was shown, not cruelty; that alone is dharma and nothing else.
For in that act of slaying the wicked, there is indeed dharma.
Since the destruction of life is indeed the very nature of living beings, there is no fault in killing a woman; it is just like the slaying of Pūtanā. (71)
There is indeed no fault in killing one who must be slain; understand that to be the Dharma.
One should have no compassion for a lioness, a female elephant, a female snake, or a female scorpion. (72)
Compassion is not approved for a Rākṣasī who kills living beings;
therefore, people should never show compassion toward one who is murderous. (73)

When an action is undertaken that results in the loss of life, compassion must not be exercised at all; when an action is undertaken that does not result in the loss of life, indifference toward it is appropriate. ||74||
Such indeed is the nature of those who lead the people;
therefore, let you speak here regarding the destruction of this sorceress.
"Whether it be evil or merit, or neither, or both—having heard this, those honored in the assembly spoke most exceedingly in accordance with dharma. (76)
There is no fault in killing an assassin, nor is there any fault in the killing of one who is intent on performing malevolent magic. (77)
However, for the sake of purifying such speech as "a woman has been struck," a sacrifice to Viṣṇu must be performed, which brings peace to all slander.
"Such is our view: let the king perform this meritorious deed.
O Lakṣmī, the words of the subjects were thus honored by the monarch. (79)
And the minister accepted it in the assembly for the sake of complete purification;
then, having taken an auspicious moment, he performed the sacrifice.
The pavilion, the excellent sacrificial pit, the installations of the deities, as well as the worship, the gifts, the meals, and the clarified butter. ||81||
Various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), oblations (havyas), fuel-sticks (samidhas), articles for the worship of Viṣṇu, offerings to the ancestors (kavyas), and garments [were presented]. ||82||
The king, his ministers, and the subjects gave appropriate gifts of food and wealth;
they performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), for at that time I was indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having become an outcaste, I went there and begged for food;
the minister gave me food from afar, and at that time I was delighted.
Then I, who purify the row [of diners], ate the food; I took a mouthful of water and likewise performed the washing of my hands. (85)
Indeed, as soon as the water was drunk,
smoke of a blackish-grey hue emerged from the king's body and became the minister’s horse.
Indeed, from the body of the minister, the sinful woman Kṛṣṇā emerged;
that female yoginī died and truly became a woman in the form of a murder. 87.
Drawn by the dog-cooker himself, she vanished from that dog-cooker;
she was instantly consumed by fire from the head of that dog-cooker.
Having assumed the form of lightning, she quickly became a traveler through the sky;
possessing a divine form, she praised me, Śrīpati, the Lord of Ramā. 89.
"O Blessed One, you have arrived here at this sacrifice for the sake of my liberation from this unchaste woman,
and for the fulfillment of both the sacrifice and the king's purpose."
Even the killing committed by the hand of a devotee leads to liberation;
even my sinful killing, through union with you, bestows heaven.
It surely grants liberation; merit is now born within me:
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Śrīpati, Supreme Lord! || 92 ||
"Deliver me, your servant, who has wandered much through the power [of my past deeds]";
having spoken thus, she quickly attained the heavenly state by the glance of the Blessed One. (9.3)
In the course of time, through devotion to Hari, that virtuous woman went to Vaikuṇṭha;
thereafter, the king, his family, and even the minister [attained] the Supreme Lord.
Having recognized me and Hari as well, the people offered worship;
then, at that very moment, I assumed four arms and took my place upon an auspicious seat at the sacrifice.
Having been seated, he sat down and then granted me his favor;
he gave the form of gold from the sacrificial vessel (caru) to all of them, and they too accepted it.
Indeed, they have all become purified by coming to me;
thus, the stain of their slaughter has been destroyed by me for both of them. (97)
The liberation of the yoginī Kāṇḍikānāmikā was indeed accomplished by means of boons for the sake of heaven and for the liberation of the king and his minister. (98)
Having joined them with blessings and established them within their families,
I then, after some time, caused them both to dwell in heaven.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have made those two followers of the king partakers of liberation;
in this manner, I have performed everything after the sacrifice out of compassion.
Even as he manifested his disappearance during the sacrifice, they beheld him; with their minds fixed on him, the men and women remembered him, and they too went to that imperishable abode.
In this way, O beloved, I have destroyed the sin of killing a woman;
both the reciter and the listener of this shall obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Sin of the Murder of the Yoginī Woman by the Minister named Devaviśrāma was Averted by Śrī Hari through a Sacrifice at the Command of King Cakradhara," in the Third Section on the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this story that destroys all sins,
which took place in Saurāṣṭra at Māyūrapurī on the bank of the river Matsyā.
In that great garden lived its keeper, Mālī, who was a householder named Harṣula;
he was a devotee of Hari and devoted to righteous deeds.
He became intent upon bathing, worship, charity, and other such acts according to his capacity.
Hṛṣula’s wife was named Vidrumavallakī.
She too became devoted [to her husband], yet she was childless and filled with grief;
[he then acted] through the application of medicinal herbs as well as auspicious mantras and other such means.
She did not shine with the beauty of pregnancy despite her many hopes,
when she became despondent at the approach of old age.
Then, abandoning her hope, her husband took another auspicious woman as his wife,
who shared half his dwelling, according to the dictates of fate.
She became pregnant and was named Citrapallavā;
Harṣula, for his part, was filled with joy through his thoughts concerning his future son.
Desiring a son, he performs acts of charity, religious duty, vows, and meritorious deeds;
he also honors the virtuous and offers them hospitality with fruits and food.
He performs worship in every way even for those who have arrived as guests;
filled with faith and desiring a son, he accepts their blessings.
With a devoted heart, he daily brings fruits and other offerings from his own garden to the temple and serves the shrine and its surroundings. (3.195.10)
Vidrumavallakī was likewise possessed of variegated foliage;
she was devoted to her husband and filled with fear of sin. (1.1)
Indeed, because she was childless and especially due to her old age, Vidrumavallakī constantly felt a sense of perpetual humiliation. || 12 ||
A painted village that is pregnant deserves measurement on all sides;
for great suffering has indeed befallen Vidrumā due to her co-wifehood.
Even there, perceiving the intense suffering of her rival wife who possessed a son, she constantly worried that an abortion might occur.
Indeed, she prepares fresh foods that are pungent, sharp, and hot, and gives them to the pregnant woman, ensuring they are seasoned with her own taste. (15)
Nevertheless, the miscarriage did not occur; consequently, she again gave her a medicine for miscarriage to be taken with her food.
The miscarriage did not indeed occur; the months were completed for the birth.
The birth of a son took place, and Mālin, being joyful, attained great delight. (17)
Citrapallī became radiant, and the coral lute was dried;
even Harṣula gave gifts to the twice-born according to his ability.
And he gave gifts of cows, food, and also garments made of fruits and flowers with roots of gold and silver, to a worthy and virtuous man.
Overwhelmed with love, he performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for his son;
from that time on, he built a small hut for his guest in the garden.
There, being joyful, he would honor those who had come or arrived,
whether they were guests or virtuous holy men, with food, fruits, and other offerings.
Having obtained a son in his old age, he indeed cultivates the company of the virtuous;
he constantly delights in the chanting of Hari's names and likewise sings them as well. (22)
He indeed worships my image with fruits, flowers, and other offerings with true devotion;
thus a year has passed for my son, entirely auspicious in every way. (23)
Vidrumavallakī, enraged and afflicted by grief due to intense burning,
