and filled with jealousy toward her son, thought of administering poison.
Having dug up the root of the poison and extracted even a small amount of its juice,
that sinful woman gave it with milk for the child’s drink, leading to his destruction.
Then the illustrious Lord said: "Since I am the protector of my devotees, I assumed the form of a holy man and manifested my divine majesty before her at that time."
I went there to Harṣula’s house, like a guest, to that garden; Harṣula then honored me with offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as fruits, water, and other refreshments.
She honored me with sweet foods, auspicious meals, seats, and other offerings;
and Citrapallī, being pleased, attended upon me with great joy.
But one Vidrumavallikā knows about the drinking of milk; she will give him the juice from the root of a poison-tree, and by that the boy will die. (29)
With a serene mind, she became devoted to the service of the virtuous;
that sinful woman waited for when death might come to her child.
A child who has fallen asleep after drinking milk is comforted by its mother;
therefore, O virtuous one, she dwelt for a long time in his service. (31)
The child became lifeless due to the onset of poison;
indeed, no one else knew of Hari except for Akrūra.
When they had all indeed become intent upon serving the virtuous,
Nandā— that coral creeper— also went for the purpose of purification.
Thereupon, having seized a dead lizard,
she brought it to the side of her son’s cradle and threw it upon the ground.
Then others, not knowing [the truth], were thus insulted by her as she cast them off slowly;
then, seizing a staff, she shouted excessively with force.
"Run here, run here! This son of yours has been bitten by a lizard, my lord!
And this lizard is being beaten here by me with blows from a staff! (36)
"Sister, come quickly! My son has been bitten by this creature here!
Thus she spoke, and even as she said so, she struck the dead lizard with her staff.
One should make a great outcry so that others hear it;
having heard that supreme clamor, they will indeed falsely accuse him of treachery. (38)
Accompanied by the virtuous man, they all ran toward the son's abode,
driven by the power of their life-breaths, as if they had heard or seen that their son was dead.
And they all wept, but their mother, like a female osprey,
was even more filled with grief than she would have been had she been separated from her own son.
The virtuous woman became immersed in grief due to the loss of her son;
her father also fell into sorrow and wept aloud with an unrestrained voice. ||41||
There in the garden, many farmers and others, afflicted with grief upon hearing of their son's bite, arrived from all sides. ||42||
Suddenly beholding death, they were submerged in an ocean of grief;
and I recognized Vidrumavallakī, who was engaged in a deception.
She too became afraid there, thinking, "This man is a virtuous and powerful one;
what if he should discover the poison given by Vidrumavallī? (44)
"Then my husband will surely bring about the destruction of my life.
Having fallen into such fear, she grasped the feet of the virtuous man. (45)
Furthermore, he gradually produces the perception of being massaged, yet even through that perception and by means of the sensations of the touch of fingers, he thinks, "This is my own fault. (46)
She informed him for the sake of protection, saying, "Do not make it public.
She was then told by me: "I am indeed a virtuous person who acts for your benefit. (47)
"In this matter, I shall act solely for the benefit of all, free from any sin;
let the servants of the virtuous not grieve over the death of their son. (48)
"I am indeed capable of dispelling grief in every way; by means of the *sañjīvanī* lore, I can restore a dead child to life. (49)
"I am indeed able to do this; therefore, let those who are dear to the virtuous not weep.
I shall restore even the iguana to life; let them find happiness here."
Having spoken thus, I suddenly took water in my hand, consecrated it with my own name, and placed it into the mouth of the dead child. ||51||
By the mere touch of the water, he indeed became endowed with breath;
the boy was suddenly restored to life and became free from poison.
The lizard also, through contact with the water, was restored to life as soon as it was thrown;
then, having paid homage to me, she ascended a celestial chariot that had arrived from heaven. (53)
Having ascended, the goddess Godhā went to the auspicious heaven.
Beholding this great marvel, Harbulā and the others recognized me as their supreme refuge;
they offered devotion and received the mantra.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
(95) They all worshipped me with their whole being and then begged for my forgiveness;
they all celebrated a supreme festival in the presence of the saintly. (96)
For a day and night, I, a virtuous man named Sañjīvanāyana,
dwelt in his beautiful house, attended to in a magnificent garden.
Full of joy, he served me for the sake of increasing his son’s lifespan;
I bestowed upon him the words, "May he live for a hundred thousand years. (58)
His son, named Sañjīvana, also obtained a lifespan of one hundred thousand years from me; for my grace toward a devotee is indeed infinite. (59)
And Citravallī, being well-pleased and greatly rejoicing at the longevity of her son, served me again and again with massages of my body.
When midnight had passed, the wicked coral creeper came to me in secret and said: "Lift me up; have mercy! (6.1)
Indeed, a great sin—the killing of a child—has been committed by me, a woman, out of jealousy and the feelings of a co-wife; forgive me, do not cast me out. (62)
"And destroy my hidden sin, O Lord of the World!
Having spoken thus, she performed a massage of his feet and a rubbing of his body.
Out of compassion, for the sake of destroying the sins of my devotee, I have indeed looked upon her with a divine form and a divine vision. (64)
As soon as she was touched on the body with his two arms,
the personified sin of child-murder emerged trembling from her body.
By me, through the gift of water, she was quickly consumed and brought to dissolution;
the coral creeper swiftly became free from fear.
Lakṣmī, Citrikā, and likewise Vidrumā were my devotees;
their son Harṣula and Godhā were also delivered from sin.
They were protected, guarded, nourished, and fully satisfied; then, having risen in the morning and received respectful offerings and food, [they departed]. (68)
As soon as he desired to depart, the devoted Harṣula asked, "O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, what may be done for you? (69)
And there he gave instruction to him and also to the two women:
"One should seek the company of the virtuous, and likewise, Hari should be served. (3.195.70)
Even when place and time are adverse, Janārdana protects;
I am the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (71)
I provide protection for my devotees whenever dharma is indeed violated;
even if a devotee is possessed of faults, I do not take those faults into account.
For me, who has attained the company of the virtuous and who recognizes their greatness, I do not take account of any fault, even if I am entirely a servant. (73)
From association with the virtuous, merit indeed arises that destroys sin; therefore, one should always cultivate association with the virtuous followers of Śrī Hari. (74)
In this same way, my incarnations should always be remembered by people;
their divine sports and the regions of their birth should be remembered for the removal of sin. (75)
Whether at the time of death or during a crisis of place and time,
the remembrance of the True Being (Sat) and the others destroys sin and bestows liberation.
One who cannot endure the excellence of others should certainly not practice envy;
through envy, all harm and sin arise, as does censure and death. (77)
Consequently, even a journey to the regions of Yama brings only suffering;
therefore, both male devotees and female devotees should diligently abandon envy. (78)
One should always maintain a cheerful disposition toward others, for it bestows happiness even upon oneself; I truly become pleased with one who performs service for others. (79)
Rivalry with co-wives should be made pleasant, and likewise, that which must be done should be made pleasant;
one should act in a way that is dear to the husband, for by that alone am I truly pleased.
Therefore, that evil quality must be abandoned by the devoted man and the devoted woman;
and my form, served by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, should be meditated upon. 81.
Even if she is not seen while being meditated upon, she should nevertheless be constantly meditated upon within the heart with faith; I bestow my grace upon her.
I become subject to him alone and grant whatever he desires;
that indeed should be understood as discernment, which perceives the virtues of devotees. (83)
Observing one's own faults and also the practice of perceiving the virtues [of others]—that which was spoken by the virtuous Hari should be accepted as beneficial. (84)
Thus instructed, the devotee shall attain great stability;
his sensory faculties will become intent upon the service of Śrī Hari and the virtuous. (85)
Whosoever should abide [in this way], for him there will quickly arise serene devotion to Hari;
through the grace of Śrī Hari, all his essential truths [will be revealed]. (86)
Purifying things are produced, and millions of evils and the like perish;
my devotion attains nourishment, and from that, one obtains what is desired.

Therefore, one should apply the senses toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, toward me, and toward saintly persons; association with the virtuous should always be cultivated for the sake of attaining purity and liberation. 88.
One should never engage in harmful or malicious association with anyone;
nor should one ever practice criticism upon observing the physical actions of the virtuous. (89)
By that, divine vision shall arise, and love for Kṛṣṇa increases;
affection for the virtuous grows, and one attains merit and liberation. ||3.195.90||
When the yoga of Hari is directly realized, one should not contemplate any incompleteness;
for firm devotion must be maintained toward Me while I appear in human form within the field of perception.
Indeed, by means of seeing me and so forth, the self should be realized as one whose desires are fulfilled; association with me should be cultivated in every way for the increase of devotion. (92)
I fulfill the heart's desires of such a devotee;
I forcibly bestow my own supernatural sovereignty even upon one who does not desire it.

Therefore, having obtained Kṛṣṇa—the beloved, the lord, and the master—directly before one's eyes, and having served him, the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) should then be accomplished through Hari. 94.
As long as there is no destruction of passion and hatred, nor the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), so long will there be no state of exclusive devotion toward me, the Supreme Self. 95.
Whatever desire for pleasure arises from the impulse of the senses, that must always be destroyed by offering it indeed unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (96)
Indeed, having established this connection with the great ones, one's latent impressions (vāsanā) must surely be destroyed—
that by which the desire for objects other than Kṛṣṇa arises.
That devotee is indeed of the nature of Brahman; him I truly encompass.
He is my exclusive devotee, the one who effects the liberation of countless embodied beings. (98)
And as the inner controller, I am the fulfiller of all desires;
I am the giver of the fruits of all actions and of all prosperities. 99.
Because whatever arises from the body and so forth is produced by karma,
therefore, having indeed brought that [karma] forth from the body, it is accumulated.
I grant him what he has obtained from that very source at the appropriate time;
I also bestow upon him the most excellent fruit of my service, even in abundance.
Therefore, service to me should always be performed by people endowed with faith;
I fulfill their desired object, even if it is contrary to their past karma (prārabdha). || 10 ||
Even in times of adversity, one must serve the virtuous, just as I have;
for they are like the wish-fulfilling vine, auspicious and the fulfiller of all desires. 103.
My service toward wife, son, wealth, and the like is excessive;
likewise, my service toward husband, wife, and parents is indeed excessive. (104)
Through service to me, every happiness in this body comes to the embodied soul;
and at the end of the body, he attains even my own supreme, imperishable abode.
Whatever kind of disposition toward me arises in anyone throughout their life,
I grant them that very same state at the end.
To him who has rendered service to me directly, and to her by whom service was performed directly,
I grant that supreme state which takes refuge in me.
In every way, I provide protection for them against the restraints (yamas) and so forth;
for such a person, there is no fear of untimely death, nor indeed any fear of the effects of time and karma.
"For he is a devotee of mine, Kṛṣṇa, the Controller of the universe;
being pleased, I lead him to my abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara)."
At the end of the body, my devotee indeed goes to my abode in every way;
whether through remembrance, or even through fainting, or through agony, he attains it. (3.195.110)
Indeed, by attaining Hari, the virtuous must know that it is surely their own welfare;
for that welfare becomes supreme both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, devotion should be practiced toward me alone and toward the virtuous as well; for, having abandoned affection for anyone other than me, true devotion is difficult to attain.
Having abandoned the characteristics of a devotee and even one's own personal pleasure,
one should constantly do what is pleasing to the Master, according to His own taste.
The practice [of devotion] must be maintained, for it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Let my devotees worship me in this way; I shall grant them everything they desire.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, in the form of a holy man, restored to life the son of the devotee named Harṣula—who had been lost due to his first wife giving birth to a son by a second wife—and thereby destroyed the sin of child-murder," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Thus, O Nārāyaṇī, that auspicious [teaching] which bestows liberation was then instructed by me to those two women and to Harṣula.
Moreover, even though this coral creeper is devoid of grown offspring and the like, she asked me, "O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, how is it that I am possessed of sons? (2)
O beloved, I shall become likewise; indeed, show mercy toward me. By her prayer, such good fortune has come to that devoted woman.
And through my service there, I obtained a new, auspicious son-granting [boon];
when I spoke thus, she became truly pleased.
Furthermore, I have given them an instruction that is exceedingly purifying, for one who possesses devotion toward me, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (5)
One should constantly abide by his direct instructions; whatever task Kṛṣṇa’s devotees might say, that too should be performed with haste.
One who desires such [a state] should await the word of Hari;
likewise, one should indeed hold my form within the mind continuously.
Constantly possessing ever-fresh faith, one should uphold [this teaching] and not abandon it;
devoted to meditation upon me, one should consider all desires as already fulfilled.
Meditating for a long time upon my form, one then attains the supreme goal;
or, by practicing service to the virtuous, one likewise reaches that highest state.
One should grasp only the virtues of the virtuous, abandoning their faults; one should likewise seek out virtues in the Supreme Lord and in the saintly person, regardless of their outward appearance.
One should always practice good conduct, which is the cause of the favor of the virtuous;
[one should do so] in behavior, speech, action, in association with the virtuous, and in service.
One should not entertain doubt at all, for bad association leads to doubt; rather, with full confidence, one should perform what is desired by the virtuous and likewise by Hari.
That alone shall indeed bestow liberation; one shall attain victory without a doubt.
I am the deliverer of the lowly, and I uplift those who have taken refuge in me.
A virtuous person should serve Hari with enthusiasm;
for indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is unattainable for servants who are full of zeal.
The attainment of various kinds of objects shall come about through attaining Me; those who take refuge in Me become eternally blissful through My happiness. 15.
He who completely renounces all objects of sense between me and them,
and who always worships me alone— he is liberated and he is dear to me.
The activities of one's own senses should be offered to the Supreme Self;
then all divine actions become dedicated to Me. 17.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa himself, his satisfaction proceeds;
likewise, through union with Hari himself, his own state becomes that of Brahman.
For one who possesses that, there remains no further duty to be performed for the sake of liberation;
for all the organs of knowledge take their own food from Him alone.
Hari is the direct object of that perception, as are the eternal qualities of Hari;
likewise, Hari is the object of the senses, which are the instruments of action.
Whoever possesses this, for him there shall indeed be eternal bliss;
upon the attainment of divine qualities and the like, everything becomes permeated with Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, in this very matter, one should always act and be so:
the form of Hari belongs to the virtuous, and likewise the essence of Hari belongs to the virtuous.
The fragrance of the virtuous and of Hari, as well as the sound of the virtuous and of Hari, and the touch of the virtuous and of Hari, always brings about purification and liberation. (23)
Beholding Hari, touching him, serving his body, and even massaging his feet—these acts are always purifying and cleansing for the virtuous. (24)
The residence of the virtuous in the abode of Hari, as well as the observance of His command, is undoubtedly purifying and always bestows liberation through their conduct. (25)
One should offer only that which is fit to be enjoyed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and never otherwise;
one should offer it to Kṛṣṇa, who is the true person whose very self is the form of Kṛṣṇa. (26)
That which is offered attains divinity, and its enjoyer shall go to liberation;
through union with Hari, that reality becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and its enjoyer likewise becomes devoid of qualities.
For it immediately purifies the internal organ, making it devoid of qualities;
indeed, bondage does not arise for that which is devoid of qualities through the experience of enjoyment.
Having understood this, even the five [senses] and likewise other objects should always be served as divine, purifying, and gracious in nature. (29)
Those who are not dedicated should certainly not be served; indeed, they should be avoided from afar.
For those who conduct themselves in this manner, distraction never arises.
There shall be no bondage, and meritorious liberation will be held in the palm of one's hand;
all desires are purified, and cherished goals are always accomplished. (31)
My abode always dwells within him, bestowing happiness;
having discerned this, the virtuous should cultivate association with such people as well as with Hari. (32)
One should always cultivate the company of the virtuous, for it bestows the supreme good;
there is no such object or substance that, through union with me, would not attain a divine state or grant liberation. (33)
Through my yoga, everything—whether superior or even inferior—is pure. ||34||
Knowing this, everything—including my entire physical body—must be offered to Me;
for indeed, I become the refuge even for one who has thus attained Me.
For one who is established in the Self that is Brahman, who is endowed with the qualities of a guru, who is free from attachment everywhere, and who indeed possesses affection for me; ||36||
Indeed,
even in that abode, my entire sovereignty belongs to me, who am the knower of my own majesty and the treasure-trove of my own grace.
Through that, sovereignty obtainable by my grace is acquired;
from constant association with the virtuous, one should attain the perfected Dharma.
The Dharma of the Siddhas indeed bestows liberation; one should acquire that by resorting to the virtuous.
I, Hari, am the Dharma to be realized (sādhya), and I am attained through the state of perfection (siddha). ||39||
Even for one who has the direct attainment of Hari, direct union with Him, constant service, and perpetual vision of Him, there still remains worldly, illusory pleasure. (3.196.40)
If his soul still desires and remains unsatisfied, he goes to hell; indeed, that ignorant person who does not abandon thirst must be understood as such. 41.
Having attained the realization of what is real and what is unreal, one should then abandon the pleasure of illusion;
yet, having abandoned the bliss of the Self, one delights in the pleasure of illusion. (42)
For that person who enjoys the happiness of Hari while remaining within the Self, no eternal duties whatsoever remain to be accomplished. (43)
That very wise one, whose self is liberated and whose self is devoted, is superior to all;
indeed, by the power of worship, he becomes Nārāyaṇa himself. ||44||

A woman may become Nārāyaṇī, just as Rādhā and Lakṣmī are known as Ramā; this occurs for one who has attained the company of the virtuous, through the realization of one's own self as the Supreme Self. (45)
Indeed, a direct divine vision arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
For one who possesses the company of the virtuous, there is the manifestation of the Self.
Even in the vision of the Supreme Self, independence may arise through grace for one who exerts effort in the endeavor to see the Self and abides in the company of the virtuous. ||47||
If, relying upon my majesty and establishing inner vision,
one beholds one's own true nature, one perceives it as radiant and effulgent like the sun.
In the stainless self-luminous [consciousness], he indeed beholds me, the Supreme Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, and shall become possessed of eternal bliss. 49.
Whether it be a woman or even a man who is my exclusive devotee, having surrendered all their possessions for my sake, they go to me in the supreme state.
While all ritual actions are being performed, Hari himself should be contemplated and held in mind, just as he has been seen and just as he has been heard.
Hari, who is to be enjoyed, served, and loved, am I;
by him, devotees indeed go to the supreme, imperishable abode of Brahman.
With a tranquil mind, one should behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa for a long time through inward vision;
then, because my very form is identical with Him, all forms of bliss are to be attained.
This living soul, within the bodies of embodied beings in this shoreless ocean of saṃsāra,
[wanders] through eighty-four lakhs of bodies that are like mines of karmic conjunctions.
Indeed, as a woman or a man, he has been born many times again and again;
likewise, men have been enjoyed by him, and women have been enjoyed by him repeatedly.
All the milks were drunk yellow; the inner chambers were inspected;
and likewise, death and birth were seen again and again. (56)
Even though the notions of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" have been established in various ways toward the body and bodily objects, he has attained his abiding place within that very body. (57)
Indeed, all those former bodies have been forgotten;
likewise, when this other birth is attained, they are forgotten in the same way.
Therefore, in this very body, attachment must indeed be abandoned as is appropriate;
egoism and possessiveness must be relinquished through knowledge, just as was done previously.
Having abandoned attachment to sense objects through discernment and becoming attached to me, Hari, that embodied being who so engages shall be liberated by taking refuge in me. (3.196.60)
For the sake of liberation, for the sake of discernment, for the sake of greatness, and for my own sake as well,
the holy ones— pure, purifying, and possessing the form of the Fish— should always be served.
Then, through service, having attained exclusivity and divinity, and having reached the supreme imperishable abode by virtue of union with the attributes of the Imperishable; ||62||
"Just as millions of liberated ones serve me, so too does this person;
therefore, he should serve me with the thought, 'I must stand in the ranks of those liberated ones. (63)
Other happinesses are incomplete, trivial, and likewise momentary;
having reflected on this, one should practice exclusive devotion toward me, which knows the secret. (64)
In this world, one should render one's own mind free from greed regarding illusory objects, so that no attachment arises toward their beautiful forms and such. (65)
By the power of that [meditation], even while traveling toward the abode of Hari along the path, the supernatural perfections (siddhis) approach him; yet he should certainly feel no greed for them.
He who has taken refuge in me certainly goes to the further shore beyond primordial nature;
having become single-minded, he enjoys my own exalted bliss.
For one whose remembrance of my form occurs during all their activities, there shall indeed be stability in every respect toward the Lord, O Sovereign Lady. (68)
Whatever happiness anyone may desire, that very happiness should be received from my presence;
indeed, I grant all of it to him, and not from any other source.
My kingdom is a kingdom of devotees; no division exists therein.
Therefore, one should always be a queen and never a courtesan.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I instructed you;
and thereafter, with hearts moistened by affection, they worshipped me with supreme devotion.
Eagerly they served me fruits of the finest quality;
yet they remained intent on propitiating me, who possessed such a virtuous appearance. (72)
Eager to serve him, they made a firm resolve to dwell with him;
then, out of their persistence, he who was of virtuous form spoke to them at that time.
And he consented to stay there for many days and nights;
during the day, they respectfully bathed him with silent tears.
They offered worship with many garlands of flowers, ornaments fashioned from flowers,
flower-cloths, and floral decorations.
A crown of yellow flowers, as well as bracelets and armlets—these ornaments made of yellow flowers were fashioned by them and worn by me. (76)
At that time, I indeed wore all kinds of garments, sevenfold in form, fragrant and variegated.
A swing was made for the branch of a kadamba tree using ropes;
it was fastened and adorned with beautiful sprouts, flowers, arches, and other ornaments. (78)
Having seated me upon the swing, those three, their hearts filled with deep emotion, began to rock my beloved lord, the protector of their lives. (79)
They caused them to drink the juice of sugarcane as well as that of oranges,
coconut water, and fragrant sweet water.
At night, filled with eagerness, they performed kīrtana accompanied by various musical instruments;
thousands of people arrived there, longing for a vision of him.
Consequently, they became purifiers through their sight, touch, and so forth;
and by receiving his grace, they returned to their own abodes.
And Harṣula’s two wives also served me at night with total self-surrender, with faultless intent, and through divine ministrations. (83)
Then, her most excellent wife was named Vidrumavallakī; after all had fallen asleep and past midnight, she went of her own accord into solitude.
Having come there secretly and alone, she who desired a son served me, the Supreme Lord, by massaging my body. (85)
Slowly placing her face near my ear while remaining silent, she entreated me:
"O Blessed One, O Keśava, grant me a son."
"O Hari, I am entirely pleased with the service of this devotee.
"So be it," I said, and touched her, saying, "May you be blessed with a son. (87)
Her fortune having been fully opened up, she became clear-minded in many ways;
then, with even greater devotion, she served me as she desired. (88)
I was asleep, and she had then departed to serve her husband;
she became one who had attained her heart's desire, pregnant and beautiful. (89)
Then, when the time had arrived, Harṣula gave birth to an auspicious boy; indeed, he obtained great joy from that one son who was so brilliantly radiant.
Having thus obtained a son named Vidrumavallakī, thereafter she became a worthy recipient of honor, always beautiful and endowed with every auspicious fortune. 91.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that devotee was then delivered by me through her service;
and being pleased, I also delivered her from the sin of killing a child. (92)
I have revived the child and likewise accepted his service;
in this very manner, I always provide protection for my devotees.
However many individual souls (jīvas) there are who remain joined with bodies, they all exist as possessed of defects; yet, by means of devotion, they cross over [to liberation]. //94//
"Out of devotion, I shall quickly deliver these men, even those who are sinful.
Then, having been honored and saluted by them, I desired to depart. (95)
Suddenly, in the guise of a holy man, I vanished in an instant;
Harṣula and the others daily remembered me in meditation according to how they had seen me.
They practiced devotion with their whole being and served the virtuous;
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, they went to the highest heaven.
Having reached my imperishable abode, which is higher than heaven, they have gone from heaven to that supreme state;
thus, through desireless service, they attain the stainless Brahman. 98.
Through service a son is obtained; through service happiness is obtained;
and through service one also obtains fearlessness as well as freedom from sin. ||99||
Through service one obtains millions of enjoyments; through service, eternal happiness;
and through service, I, Śrī Hari, the bestower of all perfect desires, am attained. (3.196.100)
Through devotion I deliver the devotees; through service I accept them;
through identity I cause them joy; and beyond that, I bestow everything.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and likewise practicing this,
there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation, and eternal prosperity shall come to pass.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s Instruction in the Garden of the Devotee named Harṣula and the Attainment of a Son by Harṣula’s Senior Wife," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the slayer of his father.
In Saurāṣṭra, there was an old, devoted farmer who had a family. (1)
In the village of Paṭolaka, near the city of Koṭināra,
there was a man named Śāṇadhara, who had five sons and grandsons.
The father of seven daughters, who possessed gardens, fields, and wealth in cattle,
worshipped both Śrī Hari and me daily during his agricultural labors.
Whatever may be produced, he should indeed offer it all to me;
thereafter, he eats together with his family, including the new rice and other such foods.
All kinds of leafy vegetables, grains both cooked and uncooked, as well as bulbs, roots, and whatever else is suitable—greens, sprouts, and excellent fruits. (9)
Whatever she obtains with effort— ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as milk, curd, honey, and other flavorful substances— she should offer it all to me in every way.
He enjoys vehicles, mounts, and likewise various utensils,
having constantly offered them to me, as well as water and food in every respect.
"He indeed accepts [it]," said my devotee, who is devoted solely to faith and devotion, regarding the Mūlakṛṣṇapura Tīrtha as well as Prācīsārasvata. (8)
The great holy site of Somanātha, the holy sites beginning with Gopanātha, the holy site of the river Svarṇarekhā, and likewise Kuṅkumavāpikā; || 9 ||
Indeed, one who proceeds while advancing, endowed with devotion and faith—
whatever was previously performed by such a devotee as their past karma [is exhausted].
That was attained in another birth and has become manifest in this life;
formerly he was Gopāla, always intent upon the protection of cows.
Then, seizing those cats from the bull,
he tore off all their wings, leaving the cats wingless.
Having been made thus, those wingless gadflies indeed cast themselves upon the ground;
having all fallen to the earth, they were likewise afflicted by hunger and thirst.
They die in extreme agony after repeatedly uttering curses:
"May you likewise become miserable, for you have made us handless! (14)
Because of the curse [pronounced] daily upon the dying gadflies,
even in this very birth, the hands of that Śāṇadhara [were likewise affected].
And on both his feet, upon all the thumbs and toes, a great disease arose consisting of oozing leprosy, producing a foul stench and discharge. (16)
Although very many medicines were prepared by physicians,
the discharge from his throat was certainly not cured, nor was there even the slightest destruction of the disease.
The gods were also honored in many ways, and likewise, acts such as giving and merit were performed repeatedly and in manifold ways. (18)
Nevertheless, his club grew, while his claws gradually perished;
the tips of his fingers vanished, and his middle sections were falling away.
Then, from the very roots, all his fingers and thumbs fell away;
thus, in accordance with his past karma, he experienced supreme suffering.
Having constructed a fodder shed in the garden field by means of my sons and others,
I always take delight there, where my father is protected upon a comfortable couch.
Rubbing his hips again and again, he moves toward the side regions;
there he voids excrement and discharges urine all around.
He even utters sounds of spitting, and no one approaches his side;
the ground all around his house has become exceedingly foul-smelling. (23)
To such an old man, who is covered in foul-smelling filth and infested with flies and crows, the sons always provide food.
They spray water from afar and give gifts from afar when they have not cultivated their minds;
such is the gradual result for flies that have been deprived of their wings. (29)
The aged soul, bearing its curse, continues to eat; it does not depart from the body.
Even here in this body, hell has arrived for its experience, which is truly dreadful.
It is not cleansed by anyone at all; rather, it increases through medical treatment.
Even his hands, feet, and hoods have been devoured by decaying leprosy.
And the swift mace, having reached the edge of his forearm, [struck];
O King, Lakṣmī [beheld] the birds, animals, and reptiles in the world.
They kill animals and insects through an untimely death, which indeed brings great sin;
[or they kill] a mouse, a mongoose, a monitor lizard, a sparrow, or a frog. (29)
In this world, those ignorant ones obtain only cruel fruit that brings about total destruction;
likewise, they cause the death of the offspring of living beings.
Indeed, a curse falls upon those who have committed no offense in vain;
for even the cursing of vehicles—horses, bulls, elephants, and camels—is likewise in vain. (31)
Even when engaged in their own tasks, they repeatedly inflict beatings;
by their curse, the master’s entire wealth and happiness perish.
Women are beaten by ignorant men and even by children, saying "you are dogs";
by their curse, those strikers are themselves consumed. (33)
Also those who are diseased and miserable, even those deprived of water and food;
those who are poor and destitute of wealth, and those bereft of household prosperity. (34)
Action once performed remains present in every way, even after a long time;
thus has this formidable action of his come to fruition. (35)
Even in the midst of extreme suffering, sons and others do not die if their minds are broken;
the family, its desires shattered, became one whose hopes were destroyed. (36)
Then, their faith shattered, the sons held a consultation:
"Our father, though afflicted by the disease-wind of the garden, does not die. (37)

And if, due to the dwelling of a sick person, the land becomes covered with diseased crops in the form of grain, or if one afflicted with oozing bile and leprosy should die, it would be auspicious. (38)
Due to the abundance of his past sins, death does not indeed come to him;
nor does disease arrive, for it becomes pacified and even increases [in strength]. (39)
"What should be done? Where should we go? Indeed, no remedy appears.
Nevertheless, it is an ignoble act for sons to commit violence against their father. (3.197.40)
"He must certainly be killed here, or cast away elsewhere into a pit;
or he should be carried off into the water while still alive—such indeed is the slaughter of a father! (41)
"Protection is appropriate here; what need is there for this unbearable vow?"—such was the deliberation that arose among the five sons. (42)
Thereupon, the youngest brother, being spontaneously filled with righteousness and affection and knowing the fruit of serving his father, spoke thus in the midst of his brothers.
Nārāyaṇa himself is the father, and likewise Brahmā is another father;
the father is declared to be the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), for he must indeed be served by those born of his lineage. 44.
The fruit of sons' service to their father is heaven and liberation;
therefore, he should be served even if he is diseased or of ill conduct. (45)
Then, having heard the words of his younger brother, the second one also spoke:
"What you have said is fitting and brings auspiciousness; however, this applies when one is in good health and well-situated. (46)
Moreover, a suffering greater than death itself is observed here;
therefore, service is a miserable slavery that increases all kinds of diseases.
Indeed, whoever should be intent on serving this [disease], he too would become ill; for this disease is contagious, being born of transmission and similar contagions from others. ||48||
Therefore, even though service may be appropriate for him, it would destroy all his health and result in evil consequences; hence, I do not approve of such service.
Then the third said: "In our service, we shall constantly employ another person—whether a male servant or a female servant—providing them with a good salary. || 3.197.50 ||
The fourth said: "That is indeed appropriate; nevertheless, not even a single man or woman would serve [him] even for wages. (51)
"Therefore, that which must be done here—let it be considered what that might be.
Then Jīvana, the eldest son of his father, spoke.
Immersion in the waters of a sacred ford, or in a river or even the ocean, as well as various forms of leaping from a precipice, are indeed shown in the scriptures. (53)
Falling from a mountain, burning in fire, plunging into water, lying in a pit in the earth, or fasting at sacred pilgrimage sites; ||54||
For those with incurable diseases, for those devoid of passion, for renunciants,
and likewise for those desiring heaven, such falls upon the female organ grant the attainment of their desired goals.
In the end, one must indeed perform the act of throwing oneself from a cliff for one's ancestors,
if a servant neither appears nor serves for wages.
Having reflected thus, he appointed these five to serve the younger brother; however, out of contempt, he became dejected in mind. (57)
He became devoid of faith and then appointed a servant;
many such servants arose, [staying] for one day or even two days.
Some servants serve for five days, while others do so for only half a day; those who, being filled with compassion, do not perform service at all, indeed depart [from this world]. (59)
"Since we have not obtained servants in this way, these five sons of yours are highly esteemed;
let it be arranged that his falling from a mountain be carried out to his liking. (3.197.60)
When questioned, his father, upon hearing it, said "No," being overcome by excessive passion;
likewise, when asked about the blazing of the fire, he said "No" to them.
Though questioned regarding the neck-noose, he nevertheless said "no" to them;
for one possessed of the sense of "I" in relation to the body does not accept death.
When asked about being cast into a pit in the earth, he likewise said "no" to them;
neither death nor being carried away by the current of a river was pleasing to him.
Indeed, life is dear even to this father whose body is afflicted with disease;
for even when the physical frame has become extremely wretched, the individual soul (jīvātman) still clings to existence in this world.
The state of being the eternal substratum and the quality of affection, as well as identity with it like that of a sacrificial animal, prevail even for a human, a god, or a man of knowledge. (65)
What indeed is so surprising in this world for the ignorant?
Even a father [feels such attachment] toward his own body when it is diseased, aged, and leaking fluids. (66)
Having attained such an identity with them, he truly could not bring himself to abandon them;
like one who is distressed, he said to his sons, "I cannot bear to die."
Just as you give me food and water from afar, so let it be given to me either in the garden or in the forest nearby. (68)
"O sons, self-destruction is certainly not desired by me;
great fear is seen arising even when one forcibly exerts oneself toward the abandonment of life. (69)
I shall remember the Supreme Self; let them cast me far away from here.
Only after fully experiencing the fruit of my karma do I desire to die in every way.
Thus addressed, those sons, full of deceit, spoke in private:
"So be it, father; we shall indeed cast you into the forest."
"We shall provide food and other offerings there, but certainly not in the garden;
rather, first a holy site (tīrtha) must be established, for that brings auspiciousness. (72)
There shall be total merit and the washing away of all sins at the Mūladvārāvatī tīrtha, which is situated on the shore of the ocean.
Having bathed him there, father, we shall lead him to the vicinity of the garden;
we will keep him in the forest out of fear of the transmission of disease. (74)
Having spoken thus, all those sons, who were indeed disguised as pilgrims,
placed their father upon a cart and went to the vicinity of the ocean.
Having gone to the shore at the water's edge, they bathed him;
they said, "O father, remember the venerable Lord Nārāyaṇa."
If a substance or the like has been placed on the ground, or in a pit, or elsewhere—if it is to be seen or spoken of—then show it and announce it. (77)
You may perform the leap from a cliff or cast yourself into the waters of the ocean—
acts that grant access to heaven— but fix your mind upon Kṛṣṇa.
Thus addressed, the father said: "Such was my past karma (prārabdha);
O sons, you are not at fault in this matter, for such was my death. (79)
Since such is the fruit here of many past sins,
even though there are five sons, a wife, and daughters.
"Let my death in the ocean be as it is—wretched and helpless—but let there be much gold and silver coinage. (81)
"Let them know that which was previously deposited by me beneath the hearth;
for that, accumulated over many years, amounts to more than a hundred thousand. (82)
"Let others not know at all; let them know my five-fold wealth.
Having said this, he meditated upon Śrī Hari, his sole kinsman and protector. (83)
O Kṛṣṇa, he quickly remembered me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord, with all his mental faculties unified in a single-pointed concentration within his heart. 84.

Having caused the manifestation of the body to disappear and having withdrawn the functions of the senses, one should fully concentrate the internal manifestation upon the individual self (jīvātman). ||85||
In His own form, He is Saccidānanda, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Ramā, and the husband of Māṇikī. ||86||
When the end of her life was at hand, she praised with devotion her lord, the master of Padmāvatī, the husband of Brahmapriyā, and the protector of the virtuous.
The sons, however, lifted him up and threw him into the waters of the ocean;
they remained on the shore watching him, and bathed under his pretext. ||87||
At that time, his sons thought that their father’s body was submerged in water while he was still alive, or else that he had died and been devoured by some creature. ||88||
There, those sons wept with an artifice arising from their devotion;
for the removal of their sins, they remembered the Supreme Lord Hari and me.
"Forgive me, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa; the killing of one's father is terrifying—it is the destroyer of merit, the destroyer of heaven, the destroyer of liberation, and the bringer of ruin."
We have indeed committed that [offense] against you in the ocean; forgive us, O Supreme Lord.
We shall perform the sacrifice to Viṣṇu with abundant ancestral wealth. (91)
"Provide for the deliverance of my father, whether to heaven or to liberation"—thus did she seek refuge at my side when her father passed away. (92)
Then his seven daughters and his wife undertook a fast within the house;
those women, being weak, powerless, and unable to speak against the inevitable end, [remained there]. (93)
Having learned of the killing of their father, they performed a fast unto death;
yet those women honored me in their home with sixteen excellent offerings.
They offered praises for the sake of protecting their father and maintained the integrity of their vows;
indeed, they performed my worship with a hundred thousand tulasī leaves.
Then, O Lakṣmī, that Lord who bestows auspiciousness upon his devotees suddenly spoke:
"I have appeared instantly in the ocean, in the vicinity of my father's body. (96)
Having fallen into a swoon in the midst of the water, that sick man was touched by me;
then his disease was quickly destroyed, and he regained his hands and feet along with his fingers.
The aged Śāṇadhara became robust and possessed a divine body;
then, lifted up by me, he was brought from the midst of the waters to the shore. (98)
In the presence of his sons, he was restored with all his limbs complete and freed from disease;
and both he and his sons beheld me bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Then they all quickly vanished from sight out of respect;
however, those who had remained in the house for the purpose of fasting reappeared there.
I spoke to those women, and Śāṇadhara was restored to life by me;
free from illness, he is coming quickly with his sons to the city. (101)
"Having visited the sacred ford of Somanātha, they shall indeed come here.
Having been told this, they worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their beloved Lord. (102)
They waited for the enclosure and for the arrival of their father’s guide;
then I vanished, and at the end of the day, my father returned home.
He arrived together with his son, bringing about a festival of joy;
indeed, the entire family became exceedingly delighted, as did all other people.
Those who knew my greatness were filled with wonder;
they declared that devotion was the cause of their health and the preservation of their lives.
Then a great sacrifice named Vaiṣṇava was performed by my sons;
there, the gods, sages, ancestors, and I myself were gratified with the food offered therein.
Through sacrificial fees, the poor were satisfied; through food, those who bear bodies;
and through devotion, both I and Śrī Hari truly became pleased at the sacrifice.
Thus, by me, the compassionate and high-souled one, protection was afforded to my father and to those devoted to me, even though they were killers of their own fathers. 108.
Then, at the end, they shall attain liberation in my supreme, imperishable abode;
by reading or hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.
Health arises and good fortune also increases;
there shall be the destruction of obstacles and even the destruction of enemies. (3.197.1–10)
My devotee shall obtain security and well-being;
indeed, he shall attain heaven, prosperity, as well as his own desired livelihood.
Being entirely pleased by your devotion, I grant whatever is desired:
sovereignty, long life, wealth, grain, sons, and daughters. (112)
"O Daughter of the Ocean, I give everything to the female devotee and likewise to the male devotee;
thus, being subject to devotion, I abide and I provide protection. (1.13)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord destroyed the disease, provided protection, and eradicated the sins of the farmer named Śāṇadhara—who had contracted the disease of falling leprosy due to the karma of his previous birth and was thrown into the ocean by his sons out of fear"—in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, the excellent brāhmaṇa Nimbadeva—
In Saurāṣṭra, however, he became a devotee in a small village named Sadālaya. || 1 ||
He constantly worships me with devotion, possessing knowledge of dharma, wisdom, and dispassion;
he is ever intent on helping others and is devoted to charity. || 2 ||
He who knows the Self considers non-violence to be the supreme dharma, service to the virtuous to be superior to that, and service to Hari to be far higher still. (3)
He performs service to the cows and the appropriate service to Brahmins;
he also respectfully performs service to his subjects and service to guests. || 4 ||
Truthful women and men, virtuous ones, as well as guests and travelers who come to his own door— he, being of pure disposition, serves them all.
He performed a feast of food for the sake of the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the needy; he performed a sacrifice of animals, providing assistance to the lame and the aged.
Such is Nimbadeva that he worships me day and night;
having gone to my temple, he meditates upon Puruṣottama.
He always performs for me the cleansing, the offering of lamps, the offering of incense, the excellent presentation [of flowers], the offering of water, and the offering of food.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Hari, O All-pervading One! 9.
Thus praising me, he goes toward his temple and returns to his own home, causing people to hear [my name] and leading the subjects to take refuge in me. (3.198.10)
Now, in that village there was a bull named Grāmapālita;
he was massive in body, exceedingly strong, well-nourished, white, and marked with footprints.
And Mahākakughnī and Mahāśṛṅgī, adorned with beautiful forms,
[reside] on the outskirts of the village, during the day, on a spot shaded by the Pippala tree.
He sits down in some village, and he wanders even along the royal highway;
at night he roams through the fields and even through the vegetable gardens.
Returning again at dawn, he stands upon the village grounds;
such is this bull whenever he gazes abroad. (14)
One sees Nimbadeva in the middle of the village, on the road, in the field, at the crossroads, at the outskirts, in the garden, or wherever else one may behold him.
Meanwhile, a being of terrible form rushed swiftly on four legs to kill Nimbadeva, to crush him, and to destroy him.
Just as one, remembering a former enmity, runs after a deer out of anger for the sake of avenging that past hostility, so too is this [the case] for him from his previous birth. (17)
Thus, when many such occasions arose, Nimbadeva would quickly protect his own [son] through skillful means, whether entering a marketplace or a house. (18)
Having ascended the sacrificial altar and climbed upon a tree with a high seat, he constantly protects his own [body]; he travels along the road as if afraid.
Leaving that street where the bull was standing,
he indeed went by another road from his house for the sake of his business outside.
On the royal highway, at a crossroads, in a field, in a garden, at a city gate, at the threshold, on the ground, or wherever else— indeed, it does not come within the range of his vision.
Thus Nimbadeva always proceeded with a fearful mind,
and Vṛṣabha also constantly groomed Nimbadeva.
"When shall I meet him? I shall kill him while remaining thus fully prepared.
As much time passed in this manner, once, he went to the temple of the god.
Then, at the onset of night, by good fortune and through the conjunction of fate, Nimbadeva, though devoid of a staff, went into his presence for the purpose of seeing him.
Having encountered that unarmed man on the street,
that powerful bull, filled with rage, rushed toward him with great speed.
Then, while making a roar like a bull in order to kill Nimbadeva,
a cart arrived from behind, and then a second one followed.
On the narrow path, there was no space on either side;
the bull ran forward, finding nowhere to run.
And thus, upon that path which was like a noose on both sides and bestowing death, Nimbadeva immediately remembered me, Hari, at that time. (28)
There he saw a very firm stone lying fallen;
lifting it quickly with his hand by force, he held it in his grasp.
With all his might, he suddenly struck the bull on the head with his hand; he struck it so as to kill it in every way.
Then the bull split open the forehead of his head;
from that blow, he quickly fell into a swoon and experienced two rounds of dizziness.
He fell there upon the ground and died in an instant;
thus, there is no fault in killing an assailant, and so it came to pass.
One should never place trust in those with fangs, those with horns, nor likewise in those who bear weapons, in the mindless, in thieves, or in those driven by hunger and thirst. (33)
One should never place trust in kings, courtesans, enemies, elephants, clawed beasts, or those who are characterized by darkness (tamas).
And likewise for fires, waters, planets, and those who seek their own interests.
One should never place trust in young women or in wicked people. 35.
One must never place trust in machines that have become worn out, nor in vehicles used for amusement, nor in those that are predatory or prone to causing laughter. (36)
One should never place trust in the young, the sick, those possessed by anger, the renegades, beggars, or fools. (37)
One must never place trust in those whose intellects are unrefined, who are indolent, who destroy the Dharma, who are nihilists, or who seek only pleasure. (38)
One must never place trust in those who are unacquainted, the deceitful, the greedy, those who lack women, or those who are lustful. (39)
One must never place trust in clouds, in heat, in dust, in winds, nor in darkness or those things characterized by darkness. (3.198.40)
One must never place trust in those who are deluded, intoxicated with pride, naturally prone to excessive bowing, or who grant entrance into their inner circle. (41)
One must never place trust even in travelers, in caravans that meet for a moment, in those who possess bodies such as kings and the like, or even in women who are independent. 42.
One must never place trust in wicked co-wives who are characterized by negligence and who do not remain within the bounds of propriety. 42.
One must never place trust in people devoid of faith, nor in actors, dancers, and yogis, nor in those situated in gambling dens or on the battlefield. 44.
One must never place trust in barbers who are devoid of affection in their hearts, who assist those of a different caste, and who are addicted to drinking liquor. 45.
One should never place trust in those who watch for flaws by nature, who are envious, negligent, or unaccustomed to new things. 46.
One must never place trust in those who speak with many pleasing words, who act in opposition to the path of political ethics (nīti), and who do not follow the sacred scriptures.
One must never place trust in those who reject mental cultivation (*amanaskā*), who destroy their own reputation and fame, and whose minds are habituated to disputation. (48)
One must never place trust in those who live by the profession of plucking [roots], those who act with falsehood and injustice, or those who obstruct the truth. (49)
One should never place trust in mountain caves, forests, wildernesses, or lakes, even for those whose sensory faculties and mental functions have been stilled. (3.198.50)
One must never place trust in those who are unsteady, tall, dwarfish, or hunchbacked; nor in those who are one-eyed or lame. (51)
One must never place trust in those whose channels are constricted, nor in those who have abandoned their families,
nor in those who have forsaken their country and subjects.
One must never place trust in courtesans, in women who are mere ornaments, in women who have sought refuge, or in women related to kings. 53.
One should never place trust in regions of excessive rain, in meadows, on the ground, nor in mountains or mud. (94)
One must never place trust in physicians whose conduct is unknown, in cremation grounds that are formidable, or in medicinal herbs whose properties are unknown. (95)
One must never place trust in food provided by an enemy, in perfumes provided by an enemy, or in persons sent by an enemy. (56)
One must never place trust in parrots that have been nourished by an enemy, birds that have been protected by an enemy, or those whose wings are connected to an enemy. //57//
One should never place trust in women who are excessively prone to anger, in husbands who are excessively prone to anger, or in people who have overindulged in food. 568.
One should never place trust in those whose dwellings are excessively dilapidated, nor in those whose bodies are excessively aged,
nor in medicines that have become too old.
One must never place trust in those who are addicted to mantras and tantras, those who are experts in elixirs (rasāyana), or in asuras and rākṣasas.

"Regarding this person there is pride, and regarding that person there is pride"—thus, one must never place trust in those who crave honor, who are double-tongued, and who are utterly devoid of integrity. 61"
One must never place trust in women who are separated from their husbands, widows, deceitful women, those devoid of passion, or those who have attained supernatural powers.

One must never place trust in those who are disoriented regarding the directions, those possessed by spirits or ghosts, those afflicted with wind-related diseases, or those who have fallen under the power of a foreign army.
One must never place trust in those who move by crawling, those who strike with their hands, those that dwell in the water, those that travel crookedly, or in people who are hungry. (64)
One must never place trust in spies, those living in the forest, those who have entered a foreign kingdom, nor those who have taken refuge while harboring ill will. 65.
In every way, one must never place any trust whatsoever in those dark-natured deities who have been installed for the purpose of performing acts characterized by transgression.
One must never place trust in the words of fools who are overwhelmed by times of calamity, nor in those people who act solely to achieve their own self-interest. 67.
One should never place trust in those who have made their homes within the borders of many householders, many servants, many kings, and even many yogis. 68.
One must never place trust in those who roam at night, in those who seize by force, in those who are suffering, or in those whose conduct is unknown. 69.
One should never place trust in those who are agitated, those devoid of passion, those bound by vows, those of forceful temperament, or those devoted to external activities. 3.198.70.

One must never place trust in those who dwell by grassy riverbanks, in those whose boats have been wrecked, in those who are high-minded, or in those who are angry one moment and pleased the next. (71)
One must never place trust in those Daityas who are attached to their bodies, senses, and so forth, nor in the wives of others, nor in a gathering of many people. (72)
During a festival, one must never place trust in those who are jealous, nor in paramours and their mistresses, nor likewise in illegitimate sons. (73)
One should never place trust in stepmothers, the blind, merchants, and fallacious logicians, nor in those who are devoid of devotion to me. //74//
One should never place trust in those who are diseased, wounded, flushed with excitement, trembling, or prone to excessive dreaming. (75)
One must never place trust in those who are ignorant, unlearned, unpracticed, beginners, or those who have not mastered their craft. (76)
One should never place trust in those who possess partial practice, whose roots are not uprooted, whose stature is boundless, and who take their support from the sky. //77//
For in every such case, O Lakṣmī, one who places trust [in you] inevitably encounters suffering, loss, misfortune, or even death; there is no doubt about this. (78)
Nimbadeva, having thought thus, then killed the bull;
that sin of cow-slaughter clung to him, and Nimbadeva fell into a state of unconsciousness.
He quickly turned black and afflicted with leprosy;
somehow or other, he suddenly returned to his own home.
Having summoned the brahmins, he confessed that killing;
the twice-born ones also told him that the expiation for the sake of a Viṣṇu-sacrifice was one year.
He also performed the practice of eating but once a day, which is equivalent to the gift of a thousand cows;
he performed all of this and gave the sacrificial fee at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Nevertheless, his dark complexion did not lose its liveliness;
yet he fell into despondency and remembered me, Hari.
Knowing him to be supremely devoted, Nārāyaṇa and I appeared before him;
manifesting in a divine form, he touched him with his own arm.
Instantly, Śveta became a devotee, possessed of a pure mind and established in well-being;
I gave him the mantra, and he received it with supreme devotion. (85)
Bālakṛṣṇa Hari, the Lord who directly bestows liberation upon me, then spoke this mantra at all times. Thus he spoke. 86.
When the time had come, my devotee Nimbadevaka attained liberation;
thus, indeed, the destruction of the sin of slaughter was brought about by me at his sacrifice.
Indeed, by my power, no evil remains for my devotees.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in a previous birth, he was a servant of Nimbadeva. (88)
Even after receiving his full wages, that lazy man, being both negligent and wrathful, does not perform his work completely. (89)
That servant died of fever and indeed became a bull;
possessing the memory of his former birth, he constantly gazed upon his master.
Having repeatedly observed that he constantly incites others to action and even insults his own kin, he manifests a state of enmity toward him. (91)
Rushing indeed to kill his own master out of fury and rage—such a bull surely meets his death by the hand of his master. (92)
Having incurred a debt, he was born again as his son—handsome, wise, and a performer of many tasks. (93)
But Nimbadeva, having given everything to his son in his old age, constantly worships me, the Lord; together with his family, he rejoices.
Even my son, Gokulavardhana by name, serves me;
indeed, through devotion to me, even that son has attained liberation in this very body.
O Lakṣmī, in this way, the faults committed are surely destroyed by my majesty, as well as by devotion to me, meditation, chanting, and taking refuge. 96.
Through the practice of serving the virtuous, all sins are destroyed in every way;
this is true even by serving devoted women who are themselves chaste. 97.
Through this blessing, all evils are destroyed in every way;
all obstacles perish, and likewise, it is the destroyer of all calamities. (98)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Sin of Cow-Slaughter was Averted for the Devotee Named Nimbadeva by the Blessed Lord," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; out of compassion I shall tell you that which must always be practiced by all people: the devoted service of the true scriptures. (1)
And the study of this *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* should be practiced by women, by men, and indeed by all embodied beings. (2)
The various modes of my devotion, as well as the means for attaining liberation, the causes of heaven, and the processes by which the worlds are sustained; || 3 ||
All these many things have been spoken here by me out of compassion;
indeed, I have declared that my devotees are exclusively devoted and auspicious.

Those who possess the notion that the body is the self, as well as those who possess the notion that Brahman is the self; those who are said to be intent on their own interest, and likewise those who are intent on the interest of others and possess divine qualities. (5)
But those who are divine, established in the Self which is distinct from the three bodies,
worship me directly in that Self which is supreme light.
They behold my eternal form, whose nature is supreme light;
within that very form, they behold me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Though they remain here in this world, these beings possess divine vision; they are exceedingly radiant, as if sporting visibly with their own selves.
You reside in the city of Brahmā, just like those dear to Brahmā;
indeed, the state of Brahman, which bestows supreme bliss, must be realized by you devotees through spiritual practice.
For those men or women who harbor human thoughts toward me, their lord, they shall have fear of obstacles, thinking, "May I be separated from him. (3.199.10)
"Due to my absence, there might never be any failure to reach my abode;
therefore, my devotees in this world certainly do not perform [rites] for me [in such a manner]. (11)
Some practice human meditation, while others practice divine meditation;
however, just as my divine meditation is directed toward me, so too is it directed toward my own self.
Divine contemplation should be practiced, but not the contemplation of the body as the self;
for embodied beings, the contemplation of the body as the self becomes a source of obstacles.
Upon seeing the very form of Pārvatī, Brahmā was overcome by delusion and faltered;
from that, the great sages known as the Bālakhilyas were born.
Upon seeing me, the enchanting Māyā, Śaṅkara likewise became infatuated;
and Nārada, out of a sense of embodied existence, desired to marry her.
In this way, many others also have gone, having been freed from delusion;
yet for those who possess a body, a great obstacle consisting of delusion arises. (1.6)
For those endowed with divine nature who dwell in self-abidance,
the state of Brahman indeed arises, just as it did for Śuka and Sanaka and the others.
All my divine sports should be understood as arising from passion;
through affection for me, that Yoginī indeed becomes the bestower of liberation. 18.
May there be for me intense affection and deep attachment toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and may that supreme love remain ever firm within my own self. 1.9.
By this affection, the illusory affection of devotees is dissolved;
it does not allow the state of illusory affection to persist within them. || 3.199.20 ||
One should always practice meditation upon me with constant affection;
for a steady state of meditative absorption is the cause of the Great Samādhi. (21)
When one's conduct becomes firm, there shall be single-minded devotion toward me, Keśava—
the Lord who is a mass of eternal bliss and the bestower of great happiness.
One should constantly establish steadiness in me during all activities;
when such practice has arisen, the self is restrained within me. (23)
With his senses and internal organ fully absorbed, he is born in Me;
thus, through the cessation of the mind, when all [modifications] are restrained, he becomes one with Me. ||24||
Excessive love exists there; it is the cause, and nothing else, O Rame.
Through affection, the mind of devotees becomes thus firmly established in Me. 25.
May they suddenly find residence within my own self, and may I too dwell within them with love; indeed, may this become a direct reminder of my own form. (26)
Even the knowledge of the Greatness [of the Lord] increases constantly through love;
love joined with the knowledge of the Greatness attains the state of being established in the Self that is Brahman. ||27||
He would not perceive illusion; he would perceive me, the eternal Brahman, the imperishable one of divine form, filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss. 28.
Therein, indeed, in one's own essential nature— the imperishable, eternal Brahman, which is the pervasive, all-encompassing radiance of consciousness that is always of a single flavor— (29)
One should behold me, the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as the divine and beloved; one beholds no other form. (3.199.30)
This is the divine state of Brahmā, as well as the state of supreme knowledge;
it is also the state of divine gnosis, known as the dissolution of cognition. (3.1)
When the supreme deity Kṛṣṇa is directly perceived,
that embodied being who constantly undertakes the practice of this [meditation] attains the supreme and most excellent state, O Lakṣmī, just like yours.
To the extent that the greatness of direct perception is indeed known by me, [I shall explain it]. || 33 ||
By his grace, there shall arise within his heart a corresponding light;
and he beholds that light, which consists of consciousness, as it increases.
To whatever extent he perceives his own greatness increasing, to that same extent he perceives the Praṇava, and likewise my own form. ||35||
Through my grace, one finds that which is increasing in the form of Brahman;
gradually, one beholds the complete light everywhere. ||36||
He indeed hears the sweet sounds of the notes of my names,
while he is immersed in the sound of Brahman and absorbed in his own eternal Self.
That state of being free from illusion and liberated, which consists precisely in becoming Brahman, is the experience of my own majesty to the extent that it is most intensely realized. (38)
To that extent, there is the vision of me, the Supreme Self, who am the state of Brahman—for me, who have reached the highest pinnacle and who know my own majesty. (39)
Sovereignty consisting of the power to control Time, Māyā, and so forth, has arisen;
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and He is equal to Me.
I am the sustainer of all incarnations, the controller of time and illusion; I transcend the qualities (guṇas), am changeless, and am the Lord of the lords of all lords. ||41||
For the sake of the welfare of embodied beings here, I appear according to my own will like a mortal;
and for the sake of my devotees, I perform all activities just like a mortal.
In this regard, those of deluded intellect and limited knowledge, possessing only the eye of flesh, rely upon their own personal experience and thereby imagine various faults. (43)
O Lakṣmī, I am always faultless and ever like a wish-fulfilling gem; for all those faults that enter into the conceptualizers reside in their own conceptions.
Those who perceive me as desirous indeed become desirous themselves;
those who conceive of me as angry likewise become angry. (45)
Those who are themselves dissolute consider me to be dissolute; those who are themselves deceitful recognize me as a deceiver. (46)
The Asuras of meager intellect indeed know me as non-divine;
however, those who truly know me as divine and human know me as divine.
They indeed become divine and even non-divine deities;
those who know me, the Lord, as being without fault, perceive me even in human form.
Even those who are possessed of faults become faultless through my power, for he has all the external senses and the internal ones under his control. (49)

He whose very resolve is under control and who possesses the certain realization of Kṛṣṇa before his eyes—he alone is considered always complete, blessed, and one who has achieved the goal of life. (3.199.50)
As is the liberated one, so is he; as it is in the syllable, so is it here.
As is the divine, so shall he become here, endowed with all sovereign powers.

O Lakṣmī, he would consider his own fortune to be merged with the fortune of Śrī Hari and not separate from it; indeed, he would consider himself blessed. In this world, which is scorched by the forest fire of lust and other passions, he would think: "I am blessed, since for me... [verse 52]
The primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa met him in person. ||53||
But when the virtuous have gathered around him, they grant liberation and destroy defects;
by their grace, I shall conquer the internal enemies such as desire and the rest.
And by the power of my good fortune and through the grace of Śrī Hari, I shall perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa in the form of Brahmā, which bestows liberation. (55)
Such devotees of mine are considered by me to be fortunate;
they have indeed attained all perfect qualities and employ the wish-fulfilling gem. (56)
Indeed, there is no incompleteness in them, for they are made perfect by being my refuge;
since I, the Lord of Rādhikā, have appeared before their very eyes in person.
For they possess abundant merit arising from previous births, and because of this,
there has arisen for them a great yoga through association with the virtuous, which bestows liberation.

If, however, there should be a sense of incompleteness in the devotee who has taken refuge, that [incompleteness] is removed by means of the knowledge of the greatness [of the Lord], which is rich in self-abidance. 59.
If the state of self-abidance is weak, it causes suffering even during meditative absorption;
yet when the inner sounds are heard, they seem as if they are splitting the cosmic egg.
But at that time, one who lacks firm abidance in the Self fears even within meditative absorption;
indeed, through the reality of the Self, one becomes fearless and attains identity with Brahman.
The yogi in meditative absorption perceives therein the splendor that consumes the cosmic egg;
then, being devoid of abiding in the Self, he fears it as something without refuge.
Or else, Hari himself, purified by love, becomes his companion on that path;
for one who knows the Self and has Hari as his companion does not experience fear.
For the knower of the Self, all latent impressions of sense objects shatter;
yet, through one-pointedness, his mind finds cessation in Kṛṣṇa.
Having surrendered the flow of all the senses into me, Kṛṣṇa, my devotees should remain steadfast; no obstacle shall arise for them.
When the mind of the devotee has become single in its power and single in its activity,
and is firmly established in Me alone, then it cannot be drawn away.
For that [state] is indeed free from latent impressions (nirvāsana) even through delightful objects;
it is restrained within my form and devoid of thinking of anything other than Me.
In this way, the minds of the virtuous become truly fixed upon me;
abandoning all else, those whose sole purpose is Kṛṣṇa perform my worship.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am to be attained through compassion and I am the granter of all desires;
for the virtuous, the great devotees of the Lord, worship me in nine ways.
For those who are devoted to Brahman, who know the Self, and who understand my majesty, their devotion becomes firmly established and their service to me ever increases. (3.199.70)
In that way, he becomes established in identity with me;
nevertheless, he should not be exalted by the virtuous, for in such exaltation there is the destruction of the seed.
For the grace of Hari and that of such [deities] indeed turns out fruitless;
therefore, everything, including prosperity and the like, should be established in Me alone. (72)
Intellect, mind, ego, consciousness, and the functions of the senses, as well as the body and the qualities of the body, should all be established within Me, the Lord. (73)
One's state of being a connoisseur of aesthetic rasa should be constantly surrendered to Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, my sovereign Hari, the husband of Śrī Lakṣmī and Rādhikā. (74)
The aesthetic flavor of singing should also be offered to the Lord;
chanting, gestures, and emotional states should be offered to Me, the Supreme. (75)
If the state of being [the aesthetic] flavor (rasa) were to exist elsewhere without its dedication to me, it would be something else entirely.
In that case, there would be attachment, and by that, there would be a falling away from the path of the highest goods. ||76||
For one who is single-mindedly devoted, a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, such flavor could never arise in any objects or worlds other than Me. ||77||
He whose taste is found in my words which partake of my playful qualities,
and not elsewhere— he alone is my beloved, a connoisseur of the aesthetic flavor of poetry.
When a devotee experiences delight upon the touch of my limbs by a yogi, he is considered truly delighted;
he is not a connoisseur of the pleasure of touch anywhere else. //79//
My own vision is the vision of my devotees;
he whose gaze is imbued with that essence and has no other desire to see is a connoisseur of my form. (3.199.8)

He who finds true delight in nothing else, but whose supreme taste for flavor lies in the delicious food, betel, and other offerings presented by me— he is my [beloved]. He who finds true delight in smelling the fragrances and other things offered by me— [he is my beloved].
My connoisseur of that fragrance is not elsewhere than in the scent and so forth [of my body]. (82)
The grasping of divine objects is in my hands, and the circumambulation of my temples is performed by my feet. (83)
He whose speech consists of the essence of my stories and the like, who possesses the primordial bliss through union with me, and whose constant flavor is found in my state—[to him I bow]. (84)
All these and others are indeed full of flavor for my sake:
the mind, the intellect, as well as the consciousness, the ego, and even the vital breath. (85)
Indeed, all the qualities of my assembly belong to that devotee who possesses joy toward my form, as well as toward embodied beings and even sense objects. 86.
For among the divine devotees, there is in every way an excellence of aesthetic flavor (rasa), as well as an absolute devotion directed toward me alone. ||87||
Whether waking, sleeping, or even in a state of unconsciousness, for one who is established in the fourth state (turya), all aesthetic delight is considered to reside in Me alone. ||88||
The true state of being a connoisseur (rasikatā) is considered to belong to that divine devotee; [it resides] always in the heart of such a devotee who is a connoisseur. 89.
I, Anādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, am speaking; behold my divine form, which is immediately perceived as supernatural within the heart of one who gazes upon me.
The splendor of Brahman shines forth in that light, and I am the Lord within it;
therefore, my form should be held fast by devotees through singing and chanting. 91.
And my mind, imbued with faith, is centered upon my form;
it cannot be drawn away by any other object whatsoever. (92)
For the Blessed One is capable of removing all illusory obstacles in their entirety; indeed, he is the Lord of all lords.
By him the terrestrial globes were supported, and likewise the stars in the sky;
by him indeed the rising and setting of the sun and the moon were established. ||94||
