By him were created the clouds, the water-bearers that bestow moisture;
by him were created the seasons, which yield trees, creepers, and fruits. (95)
By his command, even the oceans do not overstep their own shores;
by a mere drop of his creative essence, the forms of his progeny are brought forth in all their manifestations. 96.
I am that glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who possesses a human form, by whose will the soul—which is indeed beyond the reach of the senses—is sustained. (97)
I am indeed the Lord both outside and within the heart, and even in the divine abode; here, as the Master, I am united with my devotees for their supreme liberation. 98.
Knowing me to be such, as one whose sphere is the knowledge of my majesty, my devotee should offer me devotion free from fear. 99.
For such a wise person, the state of Brahman exists here;
indeed, the illusory powers do not enter his heart.
Indeed, for one who is equanimous toward pleasure and pain, a divine state arises even when being honored or beaten, or when riding an elephant or a donkey.
Whether toward an enemy or a friend, gold or iron, beauty or ugliness, and whether in dishonor or honor, he indeed abides in equanimity. (102)
Indeed, my residence is always within the heart of such a person;
even the gods and lords perform his worship. 10.3.
He becomes the deliverer of those wandering in saṃsāra from the ocean of existence;
he also becomes the support of the worlds and possesses sovereign power. 104.
Endowed with countless auspicious qualities, he even bestows liberation;
my own form always dwells within his form, O Rāma.
All my senses dwell within his senses; my entire inner organ rejoices within his inner organ.
Therefore, by virtue of its identity with me, it remains capable—just like me—of illuminating the eyes and other organs of all living beings. (107)
Nevertheless, by abiding in goodness, one endures even the insults inflicted by lowly beings; for the dharma of forbearance is indeed the mark of a virtuous person.
That very Great Self is indeed patience, the supreme capacity;
[it arises] from the company of such a holy man as myself and from the offering [of oneself]. 109.
All desires are fulfilled, and one shall attain both heaven and liberation;
by reading or hearing this, O Rame, one obtains worldly enjoyment and final emancipation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of How Śrī Hari Explained the Perfection in Brahman, Sovereignty, and Other Qualities of His Exclusive Devotees," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of Bhāṇḍabhakta;
in the city of Bhāṇḍīya, there was indeed a Śūdra named Bhāṇḍa who was a king among devotees.

In former times, there was one named Kālīndara, skilled in singing and instrumental music; Kālīndara was exceedingly proficient and possessed a passion for musical instruments from his very childhood.
He understands the art of instrumental music in accordance with vocal melodies; moreover, many musical instruments come from afar to his hall. (3)
The inhabitants there practice the playing of musical instruments,
as well as dances accompanied by the rhythmic clapping of hands, which are essentially composed of such hand-clapping.
Many female dancers also arrived and practiced in that same manner, consisting of movements involving the throat, palms, thighs, and hand-claps.
Then, courtesans and maidens perform [rites] for him in that hall;
year after year, they celebrate a great festival there.
In that assembly, they give demonstrations of their training;
thus, the singers and dancers there are exceedingly skilled. (7)
Debateurs, jesters, and people of many forms—both men and women—receive excellent rewards according to their learning. (8)
Consisting of gold, silver, jewels, or ornaments,
or in the form of costumes and musical instruments, it was presented by the assembly.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, a very great festival arose every year;
because of that, he became famous as Bhāṇḍa Kālīndara.
Virtuous kings, truthful merchants, and high-ranking officials come to the festival to bestow rewards. (11)
King Bhāṇḍīra also performed honors for them, as well as hospitality for the kings and others, according to their merit and according to his wealth.
Being worthy, he also offers a welcome as is appropriate;
in such an assembly as this, this Kālīndara is a supreme king of devotion.
He installs my beautiful golden image upon a throne situated in the assembly hall, which is enriched with the splendor of every ornament.
[He saw] the beautiful one named Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Rādhā,
in a radiant pavilion resembling the assembly hall of heaven.
Before beginning the singing and other performances, one should first worship me;
then, having worshipped the kings, the virtuous men, and the foremost of chaste women.
Then, having bowed with devotion to the elders, the Brahmins, and the foremost of the merchants,
he first performed for me a beautiful song rich in supplication.
Victorious is Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the cause of all, the Lord of Śrī, and the sovereign of all prosperity;
victorious is Nārāyaṇa, the ultimate goal of the Vedas.
This beloved of Rādhikā is the Lord of lords. || 18 ||
Victorious is the Lord of Kamalā, the Consort of the Maiden of Brahmā, the Beloved of the multitude of liberated souls, the Sovereign!
Victorious is the Lord of the Abode and the Lord of Avatāras!
Kaṃbharā’s son is Bālakṛṣṇa. || 1.9 ||
Victorious is the Lord who is born as Gopāla, the leader of the Māṇikīs, the sovereign of the imperishable, the supreme master,
the inner self within all worlds, and the Primal Lord.
Victorious is Kṛṣṇa Hari, the Lord of Pārvatī! ||3.200.20||
Victory to the Lord of the Gopīs! Victory to the Lord of ascetics! Victory to the King of kings of all lords!
Victory indeed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava!
May the Lord of lords, the Master of masters, be victorious! || 21 ||
May Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa— the protector of devotees and the bestower of the desires of his own people— deliver me;
likewise, [may he deliver] those of the merchant class and dancing women.
May the Lord of Lords deliver the singer. ||22||
May Acyuta, the Lord who is especially the friend of the distressed, fulfill the longing of his devotees;
he whom Kālindī’s son praises as being beyond both Time and Māyā.
To him for the sake of enjoyment, liberation, and peace. ||23||
Thus, having repeatedly heard the song of me, Kālīndara, as I was accompanied by the dancing girls and the people, I became truly pleased. (24)
O Lakṣmī, accompanied by Rādhā and others, I showed them my own form and bestowed my grace upon them;
for Nārāyaṇa is subservient to his devotees. (25)
There, in that assembly hall within the gathering, I manifested an exceedingly brilliant mass of splendor, born from my own form.
There, my form gradually appeared, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and endowed with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, the Kaustubha gem, and other ornaments. (27)
Richly adorned with divine ornaments and attire, with a gracious and auspicious countenance, He was accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī, as well as by His divine attendants. ||28||
For a moment there, all the women and men were bewildered;
for a moment, they indeed became stunned and blind by the masses of splendor.
That splendor suddenly dissolved, and I became a performer of the dance of men;
seen by them in that beautiful form, I vanished in an instant.
Out of a slight devotion for my devotees, I have thus displayed this form;
indeed, the entire assembly repeatedly desired to behold that form. || 3.1 ||
Thereafter, all those Vaiṣṇavas constantly took refuge with Kālīndara, the great devotee; through their faith in me, they all became [true] Vaiṣṇavas.
All of them constantly worship me; they perform hymns of praise in the morning, recount my stories, and offer worship to me with various articles.
They all partake of the food offering, which is the very form of my grace;
likewise, having gathered together, they all perform the evening congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana).
O Lakṣmī born from the storehouse, that hall of food is indeed always [open] through my divine grace by means of the practice of eating but one meal a day. 35.
There, my constant glorification arises, which brings me great joy;
there, virtuous men and virtuous women always come and go. (36)
Likewise, other devotees of mine perform my worship daily—beautifully at dawn, at midday, and in the evening. (37)
Through constant devotion, they indeed became purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
Once, the virtuous Kamalāyana went to the city of Bhāṇḍīra.
My devotee Kālīndara, a great devotee and a swift servant of the holy men, set out on a pilgrimage at the onset of night. (39)
She gave Lakṣmī to the virtuous guest, offered him a welcome,
presented the honey-mixture (madhuparka), provided him with lodging, and served him with devotion.
After evening, an assembly of spectators gathered there;
in that place, Kālīndara asked Sata about his own ultimate liberation. (41)
"O virtuous one, tell me how that ultimate and perfect auspiciousness may come to be. The virtuous Kamalāyana began to speak thus in the assembly.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is most dear to all, has out of compassion appeared here in the human lineage for the welfare of embodied beings. 43.
Having himself assumed a human form, he dwells indeed upon the earth;
and the virtuous and compassionate ones who depend upon him also move about there. 44.
The benefactors of the worlds teach His qualities;
having heard those qualities, human beings practice devotion. ||45||
Through devotion, well-being surely arises and one attains the state of the Imperishable;
this is for those people who grasp the qualities of the virtuous, supreme Self. (46)
They perform service to the holy ones as well as to the illustrious Supreme Soul;
they worship that Lord and the holy ones, and thus they cross the ocean of worldly existence. ||47||
But those who grasp at faults fall into the ocean of existence;
their latent impressions increase through the sin of grasping at faults. (48)
But those who, with divine vision, praise and accept the qualities of the virtuous Hari which grant liberation, they go to the supreme goal. (49)
Purity arises in the hearts of those who serve the virtuous;
a virtuous person is equal to a hundred Brahmins, and Lord Hari is equal to a hundred virtuous persons.
In whatever measure he associates with the virtuous day and night, in that same measure his divine nature toward Hari and the saint increases. (51)
In that very way, purity and association with the virtuous increase;
great merit increases, which bestows the supreme well-being of others. (52)
The sins of the senses perish through association with the virtuous;
therefore, those adorned by goodness—the virtuous—should be served with every offering. 53.
Service to a saintly person is service to Hari; by that, one attains the supreme state.
Wherever a saintly person dwells, that house is always a bestower of liberation.
That temple where Kṛṣṇa dwells bestows liberation;
that land where the holy Hari resides bestows liberation. (59)
That bed is purifying upon which a virtuous man, possessed of peace, sleeps;
on whatever day one may have the sight or service of such a saintly devotee of Hari. (56)
That day is declared auspicious, a liberation that destroys all sins;
it is a beneficial assembly and gathering where there is the meeting of a holy man. (57)
Furthermore, association with devotees destroys sin and likewise bestows liberation;
so too does the company of virtuous Vaiṣṇavas and service rendered to saintly women. (58)
Association with the virtuous is indeed the treasury of men that bestows liberation;
gifts, merit, food, and so forth should always be given to the saintly. (59)
Everything should be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for that brings about liberation;
through such services as these, the wise man should accomplish liberation.
One should avoid improper place, improper time, and the company of the unworthy;
one should cultivate the company of the virtuous and perform righteous deeds, for by that, liberation shall be attained in this very life.
Association with the wicked is destructive to devotion; one should abandon it.
Furthermore, one should avoid association with the corrupt, for it is an obstacle to liberation.
Through the connection with past conditioning, purity arises in the heart;
through the dawning of past merit as well, purity arises in the heart. (63)
Through the grace of Śrī Hari, purity arises in the heart; and through the grace of the saints as well, purity arises in the heart. (64)
Through the human effort known as service to the virtuous and likewise to Śrī Hari,
supreme purity arises by means of the act of surrendering all that one possesses.
He whose inner organ is stainless becomes attached to the company of the virtuous;
having performed service to the saintly and service to Hari, he attains their grace and favor.
Having obtained the favor of Hari, having obtained the favor of the virtuous, and thereafter having received a boon from Hari, the high-souled among the righteous; ||67||

Having attained Śrī Hari, the Lord who assumes the human dance, through right understanding, and having met with holy men who bestow liberation, he formed an association with the virtuous devotees of Hari. (68)
Having obtained supreme knowledge from them, he attains divinity through devotion to them;
by divine grace, the devotee goes to the highest state by means of a celestial vehicle.
The cessation of volitions, latent impressions, and illusions, as well as the attainment of liberation, occurs through association with the virtuous who have taken refuge in Hari. (3.200.70)
The mind of those joined in affection for Hari-Kṛṣṇa becomes absorbed in Him;
likewise, it becomes so for those of exclusive devotion through service free from hypocrisy. (71)
One who is devoted to service and devotion is superior, not one who is intent upon renunciation;
the servant seeks countless liberations, while the renunciant effects his own liberation.
Because the devotion of one who worships as a servant is greater toward Kṛṣṇa, he who possesses the power of superior devotion is the best and is capable of liberating countless beings. (73)
One who has desisted [from service] is weak and inferior, while by serving His devotee one becomes strong; such a servant is considered firmly established in the command of Kṛṣṇa. (74)
In that case, even if some fault such as verbal harshness should occur, this divine ordeal itself must not be rejected; rather, that very fault is actually a merit. //75//
A person who perceives faults is indeed a Dānava or an Asura;
he who grasps at faults in Kṛṣṇa merely mimics the dance of men. (76)
Hari, the bestower of auspiciousness, fulfills the desires of his devotees here;
he satisfies the longings of women and grants the cherished wishes of men as well. (77)
Then the Daityas, by means of their own experience, conceived [the idea] that his divine deeds—which merely by being heard remove sin—were born of karma. ||78||
Because of those faults—lust, anger, and greed—they go to a downward state;
yet this does not apply to Hari, the virtuous one who brings about the welfare of the world.
Even a scent of fault may arise regarding the divine Supreme Self;
however, one who perceives faults is demonic, therefore one should not imagine any fault.
But toward Hari, whether they be great devotees or even very small ones, one should never, in any way, impute even the slightest fault. ||8.1||
Kṛṣṇa is divine; Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes are divine—may they grant auspiciousness! The virtuous are divine; the pastimes of the virtuous are likewise divine and bestow liberation. (82)
And there exists the divine command of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
he who is divine in this regard is indeed considered great. (83)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, Śrī Puruṣottama,
has appeared here in person, assuming the dramatic role of Nara as the promulgator of the command.
Having thus resolved, the devotees abide following His word;
through their service, liberation surely occurs, just as by His command.
The devotees are marked by the Command; they seek liberation and go toward liberation.
But those who are non-devotees are worldly beings, seekers of sense objects. (86)
The objects of the world belong to those devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
however, for the non-devotees, objects are merely intent upon the savoring of sensual desires.
Village songs, desirable forms, touch and smell born of the body, and the eating of forbidden food—these are the objects of enjoyment for those who crave sense-objects. (88)
The movement is black, the form is black, and the touch is exceedingly fragrant;
even the very scent of Kṛṣṇa [is present] in the water, food, fruit, and ornaments. (89)
A leaf of tulasī blessed by Kṛṣṇa, as well as a garment, musical instruments, singing, splendor, and the like, along with amorous gestures, laughter, and songs; || 3.200.90 ||
The playful dalliances and amorous gestures performed by the Blessed One for his devotees are present;
yet the vulgar remain in external things, while the true devotees abide in Keśava.
Just as village folk are not at all able to abandon their village enjoyments,
so too devotees are not at all able to abandon the enjoyments of Kṛṣṇa.
Even those devotees established in meditative absorption engage in the narration of Śrī Hari’s deeds;
they are drawn toward the singing of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities alone, and not toward others. 93.
When one is established in sattva, meditation on Hari arises, which brings peace and happiness;
however, when in a state of rajas or tamas, meditation on Kṛṣṇa is difficult to sustain.
The manifestation of the object of meditation does not occur at all in a heart that is rajasic or tamasic;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa, who assumes the human drama, must be seen externally as one worthy of being beheld. 95.
At that time, the virtuous and beautiful ones were indeed outside;
they were to be served by those of passionate nature through external states and the abundance of worldly pleasures.
Or rather, when there is profound reflection upon the nature of the Self,
then the state of being characterized by darkness (tāmasa) as well as that characterized by passion (rājasa) dissolves through knowledge.
The mind, naturally restless like a monkey, is restrained;
however, if it is not restrained, one must constantly chant the name of Hari externally. 98.
One should perform the playing of the satālī and the supreme chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories;
by that, the qualities of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa) are destroyed. 99.
One should serve the virtuous and receive instruction from the mouths of the virtuous;
one should indeed achieve peace that bestows immortality through their glorification.
O Kṛṣṇa, a very firm refuge is the promoter of serenity; by means of such a refuge, the forceful currents of the qualities are stilled for the practitioner of devotion. (101)
One should take refuge in the Supreme Self through faith; or else, one should take refuge in the Supreme Self for the sake of one's own interest or out of affection. 102.
Or rather, the refuge of the Supreme Self should be established through knowledge;
the three previous ones are indeed weak, while the one born of knowledge is powerful. (103)
People who trust in the words of the virtuous take refuge in Hari; however, those motivated by self-interest do so for the sake of attaining sovereignty, power, health, wealth, and the like.
People who are affectionate due to their physical beauty, kinship, or friendship, once having become tender, surely take refuge [in one another]; they do not endure separation.
Having realized the majesty of the Supreme Self through the power of association with the virtuous, those foremost among the wise take refuge in Hari; they are the ones who find eternal shelter.
The wise, however, know Hari as the Lord of all lords,
the substratum of all qualities and the absence of qualities, and likewise the master of divine māyā.
The Lord, the all-pervading one, who is the locus of both defects and their absence, the locus of both right and wrong,
the subtle, the great, the long, and likewise the locus of both desire and desirelessness.
It is endowed with sovereignty and lack of sovereignty, possessed of fear and fearlessness,
containing both the existent and the non-existent as its entire treasury, and filled with all manner of wonders.
It is the substratum of both action and inaction, and likewise the substratum of all things as appropriate;
there is no possibility whatsoever for anything to exist apart from Hari.
For Hari is indeed the great refuge of both the unprosperous and the prosperous;
everything is possible in Kṛṣṇa, who lies within the body of all.
In that case, when [the self] is associated [with the body], action is possible everywhere, just as it is with the body;
even in the case of dissociation, everything is indeed possible when one is freed from illusion (māyā). || 112 ||
That which is equal to illusion (māyā) is like illusion, and that which is non-illusory is equal to itself;
therefore, it is appropriate, and no obstacle arises in its support. || 113 ||
Thus, when Kṛṣṇa is fully relied upon through knowledge as the Supreme Lord,
he becomes the treasury of all arts and the bestower of all supreme blessings.
All ritual practices performed with the proper support indeed become successful;
there is no doubt about this. Having accomplished that [support], one should bring about liberation.
O Kālīndara, always knowing this, take refuge again and again; worship Nārāyaṇa Hari, the supreme abode, just as one seeks the ultimate source of a crop.
Having spoken thus, the saint departed toward another appropriate direction;
and Kālī, Indirā, and the others, abiding by his word, took refuge in me, O Lakṣmī.
Then I led them to my supreme syllable, the highest state;
at the end of their bodies, those partakers of devotion reached my firm refuge.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and practicing this, there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation by my grace; O Rame, may I always abide [in you]. 11.9.

Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation through Supreme Devotion of Kālīndarabhāṇḍa, a Resident of Bhāṇḍīra Village, Accompanied by Dancers and Others, and the Instruction of the Great Sage Kamalāyana," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the devotee, the dancer named Rāyaṇadeva, which bestows devotion.
In the great village of Ākhoṭaka, there lived a devotee named Rāyaṇadevaka together with his family; he indeed resided there and always worshipped me. || 2 ||
The merit performed in a previous birth follows one everywhere.
In a former life, he was a peacock living near the gate of a village. (3)
He dwells constantly around the trees at the edge of the settlement,
for the virtuous who arrive there, as well as the pilgrims and those seeking sacred sites.
Those who dwell upon the earth, having reached a garden or a village,
stay or remain for two days in a grove of trees.
There they perform service, cook, and eat;
they drink in every way the water that has been offered to Hari.
They also cast away their leftover vessels, leaves, water,
and food into the groves of trees for the sake of the birds dwelling there.
Animals, birds, insects, and other creatures eat the remnants of food, drink the water, and pass away [therein]. (8)
By the grace of Hari, the peacock eats and drinks both food and water; likewise, by the grace of the virtuous man, one properly drinks and eats even that which is pleasing.
Thus, for him who had attained such serene faith, his great and powerful merit reached its peak while his evil was brought to destruction; then, in due course of time, he passed away.
By virtue of his merit, the bird entered the womb of Kastūrikā, the wife of the Śūdra named Hārītaka, and took birth as a human being.
After his stay in the womb, in the eighth month,
the great sage Bodhāyana, who was deeply devoted and virtuous in dharma, arrived there.
Then the Brahmin went to the house of Hārītaka for the sake of alms; and Hārītaka, having recognized him as a learned astrologer and a god-like Brahmin, made a request.
"Accept this alms-food consisting of milk-rice, clarified butter, and sugar;
remain steady here for this day and dispel my doubt. (14)
Having spoken thus, she gave alms consisting of sweet food, ghee, milk,
flour, fruits, honey, a seat, and excellent water.
Having cooked it and offered it to the Supreme Self, Bodhāyana then ate the prasāda and gave all that remained away. || 16 ||
Having even consumed his own family for the sake of the family of Hārītaka,

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the delightful story of the great-souled Gāyaka on the day of his vow, which has brought me great satisfaction. (1)
In the city named Ālā, there was a devotee of Vratardī, a Vaiśya who was highly skilled in all musical instruments such as the vīṇā and the mṛdaṅga. || 2 ||
In front of him lived many male and female disciples who, being inclined toward singing, resided there for the purpose of practicing the arts of music and the like. (3)
From various regions and distant lands, they arrive on the day of the vow;
having heard that he is the master of the science of song and having received instruction, they depart.
Now there was a king named Puṇḍravarmā, the ruler of the city of Nimbataka; he was righteous and entirely devoted to the worship of the Blessed One. || 5 ||
Having heard that the best of singers was in Saurāṣṭra on the day of his vow,
the king summoned him to his own capital for the sake of singing.
The messenger went and informed that singer of the king's words:
"O best of singers, the king says to you, 'Come to the royal festival.'"
Vrataratna replied thus: "O King, I shall not become a singer at your festival;
I am a devotee of the Blessed One who has offered himself in self-surrender."
Without Hari, my tongue shall never sing of another;

"So how can I sing of the illusory qualities of kings here?

The singer of vows, the singer of Kṛṣṇa, and no other singer;

Come, O Kṛṣṇa, come, O Kṛṣṇa; come, come, O Beloved!

Therefore, my devotees should be served—those who are truthful, whose latent desires have been uprooted, who are intent on divine rites and meditation, and who have taken refuge in the Savior. ||92||
Free from obstacles and devoid of all impediments, they have taken refuge in my divine Bhāgavata dharma and in my service. ||9 3||
By providing refuge for the virtuous, by engendering clarity of faith, and by acting in accordance with the command [of the Guru], the imperishable abode shall come into one's hand. (94)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, [I have wandered] on the earth, in heaven, in Satyaloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, in Goloka, in the imperishable Śvetadvīpa, in Śrīpura, and in the immortal realm. ||95||
Those who dwell in Avyākṛta or Badarī, relying upon me—Muktā, Muktānikā, and all those who have offered their very selves to Kṛṣṇa—are liberated. ||96||
Those who enjoy eternal bliss, as well as those who observe vows and sing praises, have all attained liberation from me, serving eternal bliss. ||97||
Whosoever in this world, being masters of any art, offer that art unto me, they all, by my grace, go to the imperishable abode; of this there is no doubt. (98)
Whatever dharma, virtue, art, or ritual action they may have before them, let that indeed be their own means for propitiating Śrī Hari. (99)
Therefore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is to be propitiated by men and by groups of women; and the virtuous are also to be propitiated. (3.202.100)
Then the state becomes divine—the body, the mind, and likewise that which is internal;
the qualities, the actions, the conduct, and the service are all entirely divine. (101)
Having become Hari and having attained Hari, that person who offers himself rejoices;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, by reading or hearing this, one rejoices in me.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vaiṣṇava Status and Liberation of King Puṇḍravarman along with his progeny through the Yoga of the Devotee-Gāyaka named Vratadin," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of the weaver. In a city named Dhurilā, there was a weaver known by the name Tūlavāyī.
He lived there with his family, always honored by the king and the subjects;
he was skilled in weaving fine threads and the like, as well as in the manufacture of thread.
With his claws, he fashions with a fraction of his power threads that are subtler than the subtlest;
indeed, those threads are like the fibers of a spider's web, produced by a loom of thread.
From his subtle portion, beings are born who are exceedingly delicate and subtle;
by his threads, the garment of the sky is woven and sustained within that sky.
It is not seen at all within the rays; thus it becomes subtle.
A golden ring and a garment can both be stretched out [within it]. (5)
Likewise, a lower garment, an upper robe, and a turban are produced;
indeed, garments suitable for a queen's attire arise from those very threads.
This weaver indeed joins together the shuttle,
the loom, the joining-pin, and the needle— all these subtle tools— for the act of weaving.
The most subtle, the subtler, and the subtle, resembling the subtle;
the gross-subtle, the medium-gross, the gross, and likewise the grosser. (8)
Indeed, very thick threads with bodies of dullness come into being;
various beautiful phālikās and kukkaṭīs also come into being.
And in the hall, cotton-spinners produce bobbins for the threads using their fingernails and mechanical spindles.
From spinning wheels and whirling frames, beautiful threads are produced;
indeed, many men and many women serve as laborers. ||1||
They produce threads of cotton and others as well,
along with threads of equal fibers and bracelets according to their purpose.
They were neither deficient nor excessive, free from knots, breaks, or joins; devoid of defects such as coarseness or thinness, and auspicious.
It is well known that the people, as well as kings and merchants, generally wear garments made from these very fibers. (14)
The great seal (mahāmudrā) of cotton-weaving seals [the practitioner], increasing human prosperity;
its excellence always shines forth in threads and in the cloths produced from them. 15.
Such was this cotton-carder, an achiever of great deeds;
nevertheless, he maintained devotion toward me in all his undertakings. (16)
The name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is present in machines, in iron implements used for spiritual practice, and everywhere—even in plowshares and sickles. (17)
The name of Kṛṣṇa was engraved upon their clothing, on the walls, and in the hall;
so too were all the male servants and the female servants marked.
Indeed, they chant the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
Tūlavāyī himself constantly worships me, Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed and worshipped me, he afterwards ascends the vehicle;
[he partakes of] my grace, the food offering, the rice, water, fruits, and so forth.
He always eats together with his family as if offering himself to Me; having offered Me garments, vessels, seats, and so forth, he employs them for My sake. (21)
Such a devotee of mine, being composed, worships me;
yet this weaver, due to his lack of concentration at the loom, quickly [produced]—22.
In the Cakravega hell, my hand fell and was crushed; from my shoulder, the hand became detached, and my King of Devotees fainted. (23)
He too quickly remembered me and requested protection for his heart;
and all the servants of karma, having recognized the chanting of my name, [did the same].
Having gathered there at his side, I became a physician, a skilled king of healers, and arrived as one who bestows medicine. ||25||
Taking with me the *sandhinī*, *raktarodhā*, *poṣiṇī*, *sthitisthāpikā*,
and *oṣadhī* herbs, I quickly arrived.
Having offered water with my hand to his mouth, I restored him from his fainting fit;
then I joined the base of the neck of the pregnant cow to his headless trunk.
And with the *raktarodhanikā* [bandage], I ensured the stabilization of the blood; with the *poṣiṇī*, I bound the arms, hands, and fingers as was appropriate. (28)

Having performed nourishment and established stability through the *sthitisthāpinī* [mudrā], which makes [the task] easy to accomplish, I likewise bestowed fortitude and remained seated upon my throne. ||29||
Then, beholding me in my divine form, their minds were captivated;
they attained supreme confidence and indeed regarded me as Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They praised him, bowed to him, worshipped him,
and made requests for forgiveness, for deliverance, and for liberation from the snare of Māyā.
O Kṛṣṇa, they requested the company of the virtuous, devotion, and knowledge;
I said to them, "So be it," and [bestowed] my supreme knowledge.
O Lakṣmī, I granted divine vision of myself to all of them;
saying "So be it," I bestowed upon them enjoyment, liberation, and prosperity.
Then, after a period of time, he brought about their disappearance from that place;
and at the end of their bodies, he led them gradually to my imperishable state.
When Tūlavāyī had become old and was bound for liberation, I again granted my own vision to Tūlavāyī. (35)
Tūlavāyī questioned me for the welfare of the worlds:
"What is your nature within the Abode, and what are the millions of liberated ones like? (36)
What is your home and dwelling like? What are even the lords like? And what are the sovereign goddesses who descend like? Is this indeed the truth? (37)
What are those holy ones like, and what are your liberations like?
What are your supernatural powers like, and what am I like, who have taken refuge in you? (38)
"O Mādhava, tell me, how shall I dwell in your abode?
O Lakṣmī, I have thoroughly pacified my desire to be fanned like cotton. (39)
Listen, O devotee; I shall become manifest here before your divine vision.
In every way, I shall indeed be present within that abode, possessing a divine form.
Mādhava, an ocean of boundless virtue, beauty, charm, and brilliance, is the embodied form of all liberated souls who are to be beheld. 41.
I am always two-armed, yet by my own will I assume other forms,
possessing many shapes with thousands of arms and more.
I become all tastes, all fragrances, and all forms;
I become all touches, all sounds, and all bliss. ||43||
I am a youth, the lord of countless liberated souls who are dear to Brahmā; I am the husband of countless liberated souls who are dear to Hari, possessing a robust body. (44)
I am worthy of service and the fulfiller of all desires within my imperishable state;
in that very imperishable abode dwell millions of liberated souls. (45)
All of them have me as their supreme goal; they are divine, possessing forms equal to my own, enriched with all divine qualities, embodied, and oceans of bliss. ||46||
Such are my liberated young colts—extremely beautiful, radiant, most charming, and indeed captivating. 47.
My syllable is the supreme ether, the supreme abode, and the supreme home;
it is fashioned of gold and resplendent with a row of thousands of crores of pillars.
It consists of a thousand times ten million jars, filled with all supernatural powers and accomplishments;
enriched by a thousand times ten million chambers, it extends over a vast area.
Indeed, all desires and all ritual forms exist there in their perfect manifestations;
there are couches composed of every luxury and lion-thrones of every kind.
The highly precious elephant-posture exists in my abode;
such is that supreme realm where I dwell with the Śaktis.
Accompanied by those who are liberated and possessing a divine form, millions of incarnations of Kṛṣṇa manifest from me alone. (52)
Innumerable Nārāyaṇas, Rāmas, and millions of men, as well as sages of countless abodes, come into being and descend [into the world]. (53)
Vāsudeva and others, as well as millions of Hiraṇyagarbhas, Vairājas, Īśvaras, Bhūmans, and even Brahmās [are all subject to this]. (54)
The Rudras and the foremost Viṣṇus become millions of lords;
having obtained great sovereignties from me, they likewise become millions of incarnations.
And those who become lords, partaking of the excellence of pure beings—for them, indeed, all powers have been made manifest by me. (56)
They indeed become sovereign ladies, the powers that constitute the essence of saṃsāra; and because they are mines of bliss, they are therefore truly real.
They were virtuous women, embodiments of Brahman, devoted to celibacy,
the very personification of moral conduct and vows, and practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Those very Lakṣmīs who descend [to earth], those Kamalās, those Śris, those Ramās, those Rādhikās, and those Sampads—they all become [manifest]. 59.
In my sovereign abode, there are indeed mandalas of such a kind;
from such worlds, the attendants come here.
Those devotees who are solely intent on renunciation are my divine forms;
they truly become holy men (sādhus) who bring about every auspiciousness.

Those liberated ones who abide in the service of the virtuous possess divine forms; they attain the states of living in the same world (sālokya), sharing the same power (sārṣṭi), having the same form (sārūpya), and being in union (sayogika).
Such indeed are the liberations that bestow divine bliss;
likewise, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are all-seeing and all-hearing. //63//
They possess the nature of all attainments, they are characterized by the fulfillment of true desires,
they are the yielders of all wishes, and they are always filled with perfect bliss.
My female attendants will become embodied and complete in every way;
having been liberated, you, O Tūlavāyin, shall dwell there with them.
"Every day, a divine youth, possessing divine sovereignty and identical in form to my own image, filled with perfect bliss, shall reside here. (66)
While you dwell there, there will arise for you a supreme state free from conceptual construction, such that no other object of vision shall remain for you. (67)
For you who have become Brahman, nothing other than Me exists as an object of perception there;
indeed, all this is the Supreme Brahman, and no other vision exists.
Even those [objects] are not within the range of one who has attained identity with Me;
therefore, the Imperishable (akṣara) is the range, but You are not within Your own range.
You shall attain such a supreme state of Brahman there;
you will always remain immersed in my embodied form.
In Your vision, there are indeed no liberated ones, nor the Imperishable, much less the Lords;
whence could there be Māyā or individual souls? Everything is of the nature of Brahman in You. //71//
O weaver of cotton, such shall be your state there;
through my grace, your liberation will likewise come to pass.
That state is considered to be non-conceptual, bodiless, and characterized by identity with Me;
those who are liberated while remaining here are My liberated ones, the jīvanmuktas. ||73||
But those whose meditative concentrations are accompanied by conceptualization perceive the individual souls as illusion, as well as the principles, the lords, and all abodes in every respect. (74)
Even while observing them, they are not bound by illusions, time, or karma; nor are they slain, nor do they cling to them at all. //75//
They proceed here without being stained by the body, senses, and so forth;
indeed, these are my devotees who have offered themselves to me.
Those who possess knowledge of the Dharma and are rich in detachment always offer devotion to me;
these virtuous ones here, possessing devotion with conceptualization, are liberated by me. (77)
And likewise, even householders and ascetics who know the scriptures, as well as female renunciants and virtuous women who are free from passion, become [liberated]. //78//
Those who abide in the state with conceptual thought constantly practice those ninefold forms of devotion toward me with love, offering their entire being. (79)
May there be for me the hearing of Your stories and the proclamation of Your divine pastimes;
may there be the remembrance of my form and the massaging of my feet and other limbs.
The crushing of the feet and even the bodies of the virtuous is my worship with sandalwood and other unguents; saluting me with words is my adoration. (81)
Having offered me my entire servitude and a seat near me, servitude consists of obeying all commands and conducting oneself with constant attendance. (82)
Friendship, a state of affection, and constant unity in action; as well as the offering of oneself and the offering of everything that belongs to oneself. ||83||
Dwelling together in every way, as well as service like that of a wife—such is the devotion of a yogin who still possesses conceptual thought. (84)
In every way, by being absorbed in me, she indeed becomes a bestower of happiness;
through such devotion, affection, and service toward me. (85)
That which consists in bringing about [the deity's] presence through knowledge and a sense of exaltation is considered *upāsanā*, and it illuminates all that is divine. (86)
Indeed, that which is called "upāsanā" (devotional service) is the repeated and manifold application of the streams of all types of knowledge toward Me, Hari. 87.
My reflection, my resolve, and my memory are all of Śrī Hari;
I am the divine youth Kṛṣṇa, served by millions of liberated souls and others. (88)
Within the syllable *akṣara*, my lineages exist—the Muktas and the auspicious Muktānikās.
I am Hari, endowed with all ornaments and captivating to all.
Possessing an infinite abundance of sovereign power and being the locus of infinite qualities of disappearance—such as this is my knowledge and realization; that indeed is worship.
That embodied being who fully accomplishes devotion, affection, service, worship, and steadfastness in speech is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). ||9.1||
Thus, he becomes one possessed of conceptual meditative absorption (savikalpasamādhi) in this world;
then, having attained the state of Brahman, he becomes attached to me, Mādhava.
By means of the body, mind, speech, action, and the functions of the senses; by the self, by mental cultivation, and by latent impressions such as feeling and the like. ||93||
Through meditation, through retention, through dedication, and through restraint;
through identification, through melting, and through unification—just like one who is bodiless (videha). //94//
That devotee becomes bodiless (videhī), possessing the state of non-conceptual absorption;
having attained such supreme, divine joy, he rejoices in me.
Thus I have told you everything; O weaver of cotton, act quickly!
Go swiftly to my supreme abode, which is filled with all bliss. 96.
Thus addressed by me, O Lakṣmī, that cotton-carder bowed to the Lord;
casting off his body, he indeed became divine, possessing a liberated form. 97.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he went to my imperishable abode;
in this same way, other devotees of mine as well, who perform the work of winnowing cotton, [attain that state]. 98.
In due course, I have led them all to my imperishable state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, should one become a devotee, full of devotion, and a worshiper of me. 99.
Having granted him my vision, I lead him to my supreme abode;
I surely bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and I provide protection in every way.
Through reciting, hearing, remembering, and likewise protecting this, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and attain my supreme bliss. (101)

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, having protected Tūlavāyī by name—a weaver of thread—through his devotion, as well as his workers, granted him a vision and bestowed liberation," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the beautiful story of my devotee named Jāṅgaladeva, who was indeed a wood-gatherer. || 1 ||
A Śūdra named Jāṅgaladeva, a wood-gatherer who was exceedingly devoted, lived with his family in the village of Niśāra as a faithful householder. || 2 ||
Rising daily at dawn during the hour known as Brāhma-muhūrta,
he bathed in the well, meditated upon Hari, and offered me a *roṭaka*.
Then, having offered water along with *āranāla* while bowing down to me,
he burned incense made of fragrant wood, *gundrā*, and other substances before me.
Having offered me wild fruits, flowers, leaves, and cotton seeds, this devotee took leave of his wife and children. || 5 ||
Taking his rope and his axe, he goes to the forest every morning;
and having diligently cut various kinds of dry wood, || 6 ||
Having bound his load at midday in a place shaded by trees, he eats the roasted grain he has brought along, mindful of me with his mind fixed on me.
Having indeed found rest after that, when his exhaustion has subsided, he surely returns to his own home,
carrying the burden of firewood upon his head.
Whenever he cuts dry wood or a dry branch from the tree,
at each such instance he remembers Hari, bows to the tree, and then cuts it.
"If a leaf, a flower, or a fruit is obtained, he gives it to me," he says, "O tree, go to union with Nārāyaṇa. (3.204.10)
"Hari-Kṛṣṇa! Hari-Viṣṇu! Bāla-Kṛṣṇa! Supreme Lord!
O Inner Controller, grant auspiciousness to this tree," he says. (11)
For such is my devotee, who reflects upon the excellence of trees;
even in the midst of the forest, he worships me, the Lord of Śrī, the best of persons.
And many other wood-gatherers, having come to him through their own spiritual practice,
became his devotees and Vaiṣṇavas, intent upon the chanting of the Name.
In the forest, beneath a Pippala tree, upon an altar,
my stone image was joined together by wood-gatherers.
Established there for the purpose of being seen on that auspicious moment of the day, they gather at midday and worship me, glorifying my name. ||15||
They worship me and Hari with fruits, water, leaves, and the like;
thereafter, they all eat wild tubers and go to rest.
On an auspicious day, they celebrate a new and ever-fresh great festival,
adorned with leaf-pavilions, archways, and flower garlands.
They dance and chant with devotion, using mṛdaṅgas and other instruments;
such is the dancing and chanting for me of those devoted to kīrtana.
O Lakṣmī, when [the devotee] is born as my beloved, then—at the time of worship, during dancing, and during chanting—I become invisible in form while listening to him. 19.
Then, having assumed the form of a virtuous mendicant, I went at that time to the circle of wood-gatherers at the Pippala tree on the sacrificial platform.
That man of virtuous form was honored by them with words of welcome, likewise worshipped, fed with fruits, tubers, and other foods, and had his feet massaged. ||21||
Then, while being massaged on my body, I was saluted by the people; and as I stood there, they questioned me, saying, "How indeed is the Blessed Lord? (22)
If Janārdana were formless and perceivable here only by the eyes, how could there be liberation for wood-gatherers and forest-dwellers? (23)
Then, out of compassion, I bestowed supreme knowledge upon Kamala there, and I indeed revealed the Vaiṣṇava light within her own heart.
When gathering wood, one must indeed remember Nārāyaṇa;
and when carrying away wood, one should always remember Śrī Hari. (25)
Even when tying up the load, the Supreme Lord should be remembered;
even at the time of sale, one should say, "May people sell Hari. (26)
May people sell Rāma-fuel, Keśava-fuel, and Kṛṣṇa-branches; may they sell Kṛṣṇa-fuel and black wood. (27)
Thus, at every step, this Nārāyaṇa should be proclaimed:
"The beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the bestower of liberation. (28)
The glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, should always be remembered;
He alone is the bestower of liberation, the inner self, and a treasure-house of compassion. (29)
He is the Lord who bestows heaven, who grants happiness, and who provides all forms of prosperity;
He is the giver of eternal bliss and the one who enables crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Let them constantly recite this purifying mantra of the Supreme Lord. 3.1.
Let the wood-gatherers offer everything to me, the Lord;
through devotion, all that they do shall become merit-bestowing and lead to the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya). ||32||
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa exists as the cause of all causes; Hari is the bestower of light upon all who illuminate. 33.
By whose light all this shines and vibrates, and who, as the Supreme Lord, abides in the imperishable abode at the beginning of creation. (34)
The Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, the Lord of Muktā, and the Lord of the beloved of Brahmā;
by His own will, He brought forth both Prakṛti and Puruṣa into manifestation. (35)
From those two, creation was produced in the past, entered by Nārāyaṇa;
from those two came Pradhāna and Puruṣa, and from those two came the Golden Person (Hiraṇyapuruṣa).
From him were born Virāṭ, from him Brahmā, from him the great seers and the gods;
and from him were born human beings, as well as cattle, birds, and trees. ||37||
Thus all this has been born and created by the glorious Supreme Self;
the elements, the senses, the objects, the deities, and so forth, have been permeated by the Supreme Self. (38)
Hari dwells within them according to their capacity, and He is present therein;
Hari is the impeller toward action, and Mādhava is the illuminator.
Hari Kṛṣṇa is the eternal companion of the individual soul in the world beyond;
even in this world, Hari himself is the friend and witness of all people.
Having observed the karma performed by living beings, the Lord, who bestows fruits, grants to those beings the rewards consisting of bodies, houses, and other forms of prosperity. (41)
He bestows heaven or even hell according to one's karma;
know thus that Kṛṣṇa is always the witness. 42.
The Blessed One, possessing form, has thus attained the state of being the inner controller of all;
he is all-pervasive, yet he also exists within the range of vision. ||43||
The Lord Hari himself exists in the form of the virtuous;
by worshipping the virtuous, one performs the eternal worship of Kṛṣṇa. (44)
The Supreme Hari, the ocean of mercy, appears indeed in a virtuous form;
Kṛṣṇa, the purifier of devotees, dwells among the righteous through his grace. 45.
Devotees intent on serving the virtuous cross the ocean of worldly existence;
for embodied beings, the virtuous are always the supreme Brahman and the means to liberation. 46.
Those for whom all this shines forth in their vision as the form of Brahman, possessing minds free from conceptual construction, are saviors even of the sinful. (47)
But those who perceive the soul, the Lord, and Māyā as one with Brahman—those seers of Brahman are happy;
through their happiness in Kṛṣṇa, they bring joy to the people who have taken refuge in them. 48.
Free from desire, anger, and other such passions, with their minds fixed on Śrī Hari,
these beings, though bodiless, wander about like ordinary people.
They cause others to practice devotion to Hari and instruct people;
they deliver all people—men, women, and eunuchs alike.
They cultivate delightful discourse, they protect the most excellent virtues, and they liberate others from bondage; such are the virtuous ones who possess the form of Kṛṣṇa.
The virtuous are indeed the liberators from the ocean of worldly existence for living beings of many species who are experiencing the fruits of their respective karmas.
And where the virtuous dwell, there Nārāyaṇa himself dwells, having assumed a human form, though remaining unmanifest. (53)
Although endowed with all forms of splendor, he desires the dramatic dance of a man; for in certain instances, out of compassion, he assumes the noble deeds of one who transcends humanity.
The virtuous know that Blessed One as Mānava, and no others; however, others come to know Mādhava through their association with the virtuous. ||55||
Those who take refuge in, feel affection for, and delight in the Supreme Self are indeed liberated from the cycle of worldly existence; in the end, they go to the abode of Brahman.
In Him, Kṛṣṇa, they take delight; there they play, full of joy;
right there they bring bliss to others and enjoy an abundance of happiness. ||57||
Whether knowing or even unknowing, whoever feels affection for Kṛṣṇa in his human form,
having indeed transcended the qualities (guṇas), goes at the end to the imperishable state.
Because Kṛṣṇa possesses a divine form, those who take refuge in him become divine through that connection;
though they may possess non-divine forms, they go to Brahman. ||59||
Because Hari, the Lord of Māyā, is himself free from Māyā,
even ordinary persons who have taken refuge in Him cross over Māyā indeed by the power of Hari.
Even those women of Vraja who were always affectionate toward Hari through the nature of desire have indeed attained liberation, their bodies now devoid of material qualities.
All those beloved of Brahmā were affectionately devoted to Bālakṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; they attained a state of qualitylessness (nirguṇatva) within the qualityless Kṛṣṇa.
Out of desire, affection, virtue, or self-interest, they had become attached to the Supreme Self;
then, their bonds exhausted, they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the gunas.
Mādhava Kṛṣṇa is devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa) and his form is existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
Those who attained union with him became free from qualities and reached divine perfection.
Thus, through affection for Hari, whose nature is truth, liberation becomes certain;
likewise, through affection for a saintly person, there is liberation, for saints are the very forms of Kṛṣṇa.
Through association with the virtuous, they surely proceed to the supreme, imperishable abode of Hari; for the single-minded devotees of Hari desire only the service of Hari.
They do not desire heaven, nor liberation, nor the world of the Supreme Self;
they do not long for sovereign powers, nor do they desire identity with the Divine.
They do not desire proximity, nor unity at any time;
those who possess such desires would be full of longing, indeed the very lowest of the low.
That [offering] is indeed called *truṭi* when it consists of devotion through the offering of one's entire self;
in the case of the offering of oneself (*ātmanivedita*), there is the offering of even one's very volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Since they do not form any further intentions for their own self-interest once it has been accomplished, they are indeed free from desire; thus, they are the most excellent of all in every respect. (3.204.70)
By the command of Hari they desire service, but not by their own will;
the fruit of service is declared to be supreme, for everything is completed therein. (71)
Through service to Kṛṣṇa, the fruit of serenity is fully attained;
there is no other fruit superior to this that resides in the hearts of those free from desire. (72)
The highest state is obtained through service; what then is the use of states such as *sālokya*?
For they never desire oneness, since that destroys the state of servitude.
How can there be service, how can there be clarity, or how can there be happiness when there is a sense of oneness?
Therefore, indeed, those who possess desireless devotion become dear to Hari.
Kṛṣṇa thoroughly protects those devotees who are free from desire for worldly rewards;
he accepts with love their service performed out of love. ||75||
Even to devotees who do not desire them, the gracious Lord Hari,
the Sovereign in the Imperishable, bestows his own great sovereign powers.
Thus, those devotees who are contented become as dark-complexioned as Kṛṣṇa; by His grace, the Lord of Māyā always sports together with them all. (77)
They are dear to Him as He is dear to Himself; contented, wise, and happy, they are indeed desireless and supreme devotees who are beloved by Him. (78)
In eating, lying down, bathing, walking, and sexual union;
in action, playing, mocking, speech, diversion, laughing, and maintaining composure—79.
Janārdana protects those who dwell with him free from desire;
without doubt, such constant devotees are dear to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
O Lakṣmī, having been thus instructed by me, who was disguised as a holy man,
all those wood-gatherers became practitioners of the yoga of knowledge.
Then, having recognized me as the supreme holy one whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, they took refuge in me,
rejoiced, and thereafter made their request.
If, through the grace of the virtuous Guru, there is a vision of the Supreme Self, then we are fit to be your disciples; in that case, grant us that which bestows liberation.
Then I said this to them: "Perform meditation indeed within your hearts;
you shall behold right here Śrīnātha, the Supreme Lord, Mādhava, Hari. (84)
Having been addressed thus, they fixed their gaze upon Keśava within their hearts;
meanwhile, they beheld me, Kṛṣṇa, dressed in the guise of a holy man.
From the form of the saintly one, they beheld the Supreme Lord in a divine form with four arms—the beloved of Śrī, the beloved of Rādhikā, the Supreme Sovereign. (86)
All those wood-gatherers beheld that imperishable, most brilliantly radiant abode of Śrī Hari, resplendent with countless millions of liberated souls.
There, a beautiful lion-throne and a most excellent elephant-throne were present;
upon them sat I, Hari, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor.
They gazed upon the Lord of the lords of lords, the Master who is the husband of Rādhā, the consort of the beloved of Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among persons. 89.
Beholding him in the form of a holy man, who was being served by infinite, liberated beings enjoying absolute bliss, he suddenly perceived this within his heart.
Then they all saw the ascetic standing outside;
filled with affection, they suddenly gazed upon that holy man.
Having risen and recognized me as the Supreme Self who had arrived in the forest, they honored me,
embraced me, and then drank the water from my feet.
And having received the grace granted by me, they ate with great joy;
all of them attained a divine state and prostrated themselves like staffs.
Rising again and again, considering themselves blessed and filled with joy,
they danced to the rhythmic clapping of their hands and likewise performed songs of praise.
They made my soles very red with their tongues;
they all rolled in the dust near my feet. (95)
Then they attained peace and paid homage to me, the eternal one;
they requested service just as it was seen in my abode.
Having uttered "So be it," I immediately vanished from sight.
Then those [sages], free from conceptual construction, became truly knowers of my worship.
In the course of time, they became divine devotees and, casting off their bodies,
went to my supreme abode where the Sādhyas indeed dwell.
In this way, I rescued thousands of wood-gatherers who were devoted to me, such as Lakṣmī, Jāṅgala, Deva, and others, all of whom were intent on their devotion. 99.
O Lakṣmī, those who were there with desires have been led toward heaven; those who were free from desire have likewise been led to Vaikuṇṭha and the imperishable realm.
Some, O Lakṣmī, were led to the exceedingly brilliant realm of Goloka,
and others were led to Śrīpura, the abode of Lalitā.
Some were led to the sacred abode of Śrī Badarī, others to Śvetadvīpa; some were brought to the unmanifest realm (Avyākṛta), and others to the immortal state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these wood-gatherers have been rescued by me;
through reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained. 103.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how the wood-carriers, headed by Jāṅgala-deva, beheld Śrī Hari in the form of a saint through their devotion and attained liberation at the end," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the supremely purifying story of my devotee named Vātsalyadhīra, who performed his duty as a merchant. 1.
In the village of Nāgaśālāyana, there was a Vaiśya who was devoted to me,
possessing wealth such as a family, riches, gardens, cows, fields, and other assets.
He was highly esteemed by the worlds and by the king;
he was a worshiper of the brāhmaṇas and was exceedingly devoted to meditation upon Hari and me.
He was constantly devoted to worship and recitation, intent upon devotion and chanting;
he served holy places, saintly persons, and virtuous women, and he served both cows and the gods.
Honoring the elderly and devoted to the duty of giving food,
that wealthy man offered excellent wealth year after year for the sake of sacrifice.
He indeed gives in this manner; he also gives for the purpose of planting trees, and he likewise gives for the excavation of ponds, wells, and tanks.
He bestows gifts even for the restoration of ruined temples and the like, and he also gives for the sake of assisting the helpless, children, and the wretched. (7)
The virtuous merchant, possessing excellent righteousness, indeed provides fodder and morsels of food for the bulls, horses, parrots, and birds such as pigeons.
He established almshouses for food and other necessities, auspicious rest-houses,
delightful water-stations, and sacrificial altars at crossroads and other public places.
Within his domain, he established water-stations, food-distribution centers, and shelters providing refuge,
and he instituted an excellent, continuous stream of worship for the gods.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, his wealth is constantly given away even in charity;
yet that coin of steadfast affection increases eternally and remains inexhaustible.
Such a devotee of mine performs a supreme great festival during the vow, like a king, with excellent offerings of great value.

He indeed causes a grand festival to be celebrated with instrumental music, singing, songs, and the like, as well as with hymns of praise, devotional worship, dances, celebrations, and other such festivities.
With the food and water offered, as well as with desirable foods, fruits, and milk-rice (pāyasa),
he indeed gratifies all those who have gathered for the great festival.
What was given in the past, and what is obtained here from that, and even what is given from that—everything shall become imperishable when it is given to Nārāyaṇa. || 15 ||
Thinking thus, one should indeed give; what is given shall become inexhaustible.
It shall increase and never diminish; therefore, one should especially practice giving.
There shall be great merit as the fruit of giving, the highest heaven,
and also the grace of Hari, whereby satisfaction arises within one's own self.
In every way, the gift of flavors, food, and wealth, as well as houses, fields, gardens, cows, and milk, bestows happiness. (18)
The gift of substances and implements should likewise be given inexhaustibly;
it must be bestowed in every way by those endowed with prosperity, and thus prosperity shall accrue to them.

One certainly does not obtain what is not given—such as a woman, wealth, a house, and so forth; rather, everything is obtained only when it has been given, including the happiness born of the senses and the body. (3.205.20)
O Lakṣmī, steadfast in his affection for children, he wrote the names of Kṛṣṇa at every sacrificial session and in every place— on door-panels and at water-stations.
In huts, on walls, in vessels, and even upon garments and objects, she chants the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the Beloved of Śrī. (22)
To such a devotee who was constantly worshipping me,
I went to his house, having become an ascetic with matted hair.
And I was invited by him to a meal on a grass seat;
I, in turn, requested the devotee to wash my feet. (24)
Having filled a golden pitcher with water mixed with fragrant scents,
he affectionately washed his feet and drank the water born of that grace.
Then, moreover, the King of Devotees was quickly offered by me once again fragrant oils for the purpose of massaging his body. (26)
With a serene mind, he likewise massaged my limbs;
then, having been addressed by me, he proceeded to bathe me with warm water.
Then, full of zeal, he himself arrived there quickly with warm water;
though he had been rejected by me, he entreated me for the sake of his wife.
Then, at her husband's command, that devoted wife named Mañjulikā quickly and confidently approached me to bathe me. (29)
With a serene mind, that virtuous woman offered me a golden seat;
though I was clad in nothing but a loincloth, I sat down upon that auspicious seat.
That virtuous, chaste, and devoted woman, full of love, repeatedly massaged my entire body with her two hands and bathed me. 3.1.
I indeed showed her that transformation consisting of the waking state;
nevertheless, she bathed me with respect, free from all doubt.
Repeatedly touching her all over her limbs,
the devoted Mañjulī remained with a serene mind and did not undergo any change of emotion.
Steadfast, firm, and endowed with righteousness, she praised him with palms joined in reverence:
"Be gracious, O liberated soul, for I am performing service unto you. (34)
"May I perform service for you without any doubt, so that it may be according to your husband's command;
for Nārāyaṇa is truly a virtuous man, the divine-formed Hari himself. (35)
Indeed, service to him is obtained by a woman only through good fortune; if you have my husband’s permission, I am yours, for I am devoted to my husband. (36)
Having been addressed thus, O Lakṣmī, I likewise summoned her husband and said:
"Let your wife be given to me; she troubles my mind. (37)
Then my husband, having honored my feet, granted it, saying, "So be it. And she too, through her devotion to me, became manifest by my command, O Rame.
Then, without even touching her, I quickly became divine with four arms—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (39)
She too, considering herself blessed, fell at her feet;
and her husband, though steadfast through affection, was overwhelmed with love.
Recognizing me as Hari in the form of a holy man, he fell at my feet;
he summoned his devotees and performed service at that very moment.
With garments, ornaments, sandalwood, saffron, and other such things, he offered me everything—food, water, and fruit. (42)
She also prepared a couch, a golden seat, and exquisite ornaments worthy of the highest honor;
she performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and then gave me a bed. ||43||
Then I, the Lord whose nature is that of a saint, was honored by all; and the devotees made their requests, while I, firm in my affection for them, responded accordingly.
O Supreme Lord, the enjoyment has been obtained; let the divine state be granted.
Let knowledge endowed with greatness, which is higher than the highest, be granted by you. 45.
O Lakṣmī, I have bestowed supreme knowledge upon him and upon them;
affection should be cultivated toward me, the Blessed Supreme Lord. 46.
One should offer everything unreservedly to me, Mādhava, and one should practice complete detachment from all things pertaining to worldly existence. 47.
Dispassion must be protected in every way for the sake of severing bondage;
likewise, attachment to Me, Kṛṣṇa—namely, love, affection, and extreme tenderness. (48)
Women and men must by all means offer themselves to me; they should strive constantly, for it is by that means that I am attained. 49.
Through this affection, may my remembrance of Hari be unbroken within my heart;
by that means, may the manifestation of His form always abide with me, bestowing happiness.
But other thoughts, once they have arisen, certainly lead to further impulsion;
however, when dissolved along with *māyā*, they truly become seedless.
The perfect intentions of those possessed of full love, who are always practitioners of the yoga of devotion, fall within my range of perception; they never become objects for others. 52.
But if, due to an association with an improper place, time, or company, a delusive thought should arise regarding what is contrary [to reality], then distress will occur in the heart. (53)
Just as pain would arise from the thrusting of a sharp needle into the eye,
so too would a sharp-pointed shaft, having entered the heart, surely cause agony.
Just as such a thought, once arisen, causes distress to one who has taken refuge [in it], so too should such supreme love be directed toward me, Keśava. (55)
My affection has been increased by my knowledge of his greatness;
furthermore, it may even be natural due to the acceptance of the garland of choice. (56)
The necklace, the garland, the excellent garland, and the mantra are considered my boons;
affection for their acquisition arises like that of a maiden for her beloved. (57)
Affection may arise even for one who is unseen, for he is the support of all and the protector; indeed, every disposition of the devotee becomes one of total self-surrender to him. (58)
Even when grasping the hand, affection increases greatly;
when offering one's entire self, affection increases boundlessly. (59)
Affection arises from association with the Guru; the Guru is considered to be a virtuous person.
By attaining the company of the righteous, one shall obtain my own majesty.
Even regarding the body, its objects, and material possessions, one who possesses discrimination should abandon attachment and increase their affection for me, Hari Kṛṣṇa. (61)
One should never consider the inert body or anything pertaining to the body as one's own;
"I am the conscious, divine Self, who has taken refuge in the Blessed One. (62)
I am of the nature of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss; I am liberated, established in Brahman.
Māyā does not exist for me in this world; there is nothing apart from Hari.
Thus, one who possesses discernment becomes entirely devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
free from the notions of "I" and "mine," he is devoid of all attachment and the like. (64)
I have no mother and no father; I have no wife and no wealth.
I have no son and no daughter; I have neither house nor garden. (65)
In previous existences, many fathers and others were born;
yet, due to ignorance, I have forgotten them here, and so it is with these as well. (66)
For the Self, there is no mother; how then could there be a father, or a home?
And where, indeed, could egoism, possessiveness, attachment, and aversion possibly exist? (67)
Thus, for those who possess discernment, all notions of "mine-ness" and the like perish;
yet, toward Me alone, Śrī Hari, the sense of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" arises.
Truth indeed bestows liberation; by means of it, devotees cross over, while those who sink down—devoid of discernment—are bound in saṃsāra and do not cross over. (69)
Just as in a theater, mature youths assume appropriate costumes for the sake of the stage in order to perform a drama. (3.205.70)
Skilled in various garments, they wear fine attire;
they prepare them with great beauty and adorn them splendidly. (71)
They fashion youths and women of beautiful form; there, if one who wears a disguise encounters people who provide such disguises, [he may be captured]. (72)
If, out of delusion, he should regard his parents as the ones who gave him birth, then he would indeed remain ignorant, utterly devoid of all discernment and the like. ||73||
Likewise, even the body is merely a disguise; one should not, however, conceive of parents as being within the body and so forth, while abiding here in the form of the Self that is Brahman.
In this very way, just as many [seeds] have gone into various species,
so too do those two [the parents] produce the body of this [child].
Having thus created such detachment toward wife, children, wealth, and prosperity, one should indeed abandon affection for them and cultivate affection for me, the Supreme Lord. (76)
Then, the sense of "I" regarding the body shall perish, and consequently, the sense of "mine" regarding bodily things will vanish;
the power of abiding in the Self will increase eternally, bestowing the imperishable state.
Through discernment, the pride of belonging to a caste or stage of life shall dissolve;
indeed, a firm inclination toward liberation alone will arise within one's own self. (78)
Taking him by the arm, she should indeed take refuge in her beloved Kṛṣṇa;
for him, enjoyment and liberation will be as if held in the palm of his hand—of this there is no doubt. (79)
Even a householder should be considered a true saint if he worships Kṛṣṇa, being established in such knowledge and possessing detachment. || 3.205.80 ||
Since Hari is indeed not far away and he is easily attainable for the virtuous, therefore all bonds perish; that very virtuous one alone is to be served. 8.1
O Lakṣmī, he exists as the Brahman-Self, devoid of the state of being the body and so forth; because everything has been offered up as his own Self, nothing whatsoever remains.
Furthermore, even for those who possess renunciation and have abandoned their homes and such, if pride should arise at any time, it dissolves through this yoga. (83)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that merchant-chief was instructed by me;
together with his wife, sons, and others, he became equal to a great saint. (84)
Together with his family, he dedicated all his activities in every way to Kṛṣṇa;
in particular, he attained self-realization and came to know my own greatness. (85)
Then, having attained detachment, that king of devotees, together with his wife,
desired the Vaiṣṇava initiation, which is virtuous and esteemed by the holy.
At my command, he bestowed wealth and riches upon his sons;
himself steadfast in affection, he remained joined with Mañjulikā and Satī.
He received initiation and the mantra, and became a virtuous ascetic;
thereafter, his wife became a virtuous practitioner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
At that time, I made this virtuous man named Vātsalyāyana;
endowed with detachment, he undertook an effort for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites. ||89||
But I immediately vanished; having bowed to my subjects and taken leave of my sons, I went to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
He reached the supreme imperishable field, Kuṅkumavāpikā,
where he beheld me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as previously envisioned.
She established a sacred bathing place there and dwelt in the hermitage of the illustrious Lomaśa;
the great virtuous Mañjulikā lived among those dear to Brahmā.
Both of them, virtuous in form and knowers of the Self, attend upon me;
O Lakṣmī, behold these two as they abide here, and look at the chaste Mañjulikā.
This is that very same servant of yours, pure and filled with devotion;
she who was once in my house, a virtuous woman free from doubt. (94)
Having remained here for the sake of offering herself by her husband's command, that divine Brahmayoginī, possessing a celestial form, now exists here today. (95)
And Vātsalyāyana is a virtuous man, possessing the form of Brahman;
he is established in the Self, perfectly wise, and devoted to affection. (96)
He does not take account of illusion, time, or even karma;
for by my power, he abides in the elevation of all the principles (tattvas). 97.
This [consciousness] indeed moves through the sky with this very body in every way;
it moves without restraint across the ocean, the mountain, the forest, and the cloud. (98)
Whether in fire, moon, or sun, on the Lokāloka mountain or in the sky, or on Mount Meru, the one who has reached the further shore of yoga goes there and returns again to his own abode. 99.
"By my grace, that best of saints now constantly meditates upon my form;
he is now capable of sustaining, creating, and destroying."
O Lakṣmī, through my worship and through service performed without hesitation,
he has attained divine status by means of my yoga, remaining forever like one who is liberated.
Thus, those who practice devotion become possessed of divine forms;
by reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, being pleased by the devotion of the merchant Vātsalyadhīra and his wife Mañjulikā-devī, granted them His vision, and how they both became perfected saints," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the forest-guardian,
a Śūdra named Tilakaraṅga who dwelt in the wilderness.
In Mahākālavana, O Lakṣmī, there was a forest guardian named Tilakaranga, who was exceedingly devoted, a worshiper of Śiva, and full of deep contemplation. || 2 ||
Having made his dwelling in a grove of trees on the bank of the Sureśikā river,
he wanders about daily with his weapons, guarding the forest.
Subsisting on wild roots and fruits, or at times eating food obtained by chance,
he lives with his family, feeding on grains ripened by the seasons.
Even while dwelling in the forest, he constantly refrained from harming living beings,
was devoted to the dharma of compassion, and worshipped Śaṅkara at the appropriate time.
Having bathed in the morning and filled a water-pot, he goes to the temple of Śrī Śaṅkara and performs the ritual ablution with bilva leaves and sandalwood paste.
She also offers golden flowers upon the pericarp;
even at midday, she who carries water, having offered them and worshipped Śaṅkara, [performs her rites].
Then, having received the food offering (naivedya), he eats it in the evening as well;
[he offers] incense, a lamp, excellent food offerings, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa). || 8 ||
Having performed propitiation and salutation, he performs recitation;
thereafter, he sleeps right there upon the altar in the presence of Śaṅkara.
Having risen early in the morning and swept [the area], and having performed the recitation of the Gālava hymn followed by the remembrance of Śambhu, he then proceeds to bathe.
His wife, Śikhādevī, likewise performs the worship of Śaṅkara daily according to her ability, and she even bathes the Liṅga herself.
On that day, a woman devoted to yoga resided there in the temple;
meanwhile, some men and women who were traveling on the road passed by the enclosure.
If they come and rest there, that goddess Śikhādevī gives them water, fruit, and dry land, honoring them as is appropriate.
Even as he spoke of Śaṅkara’s qualities, virtues, and wonders,
Śaṅkara indeed became pleased upon beholding the devotion of his devotee.
Once, having become a Vaiṣṇava and desiring to go on a pilgrimage, he arrived there,
having applied the Vaiṣṇava tilaka and carrying a fine basket upon his shoulder.
With a śālagrāma stone held against his belly, he cried out "Nārāyaṇa" repeatedly;
seeing him, Śikhādevī then gave him a dwelling upon the altar.
Having placed the casket there, she went to the Sukeśikā river to bathe;
and having bathed, and having bathed the Śālagrāma stone, and having worshipped it, [she returned].
He arrived and sat down for a moment, steady, upon the seat on the altar;
meanwhile, Tilakaranga also came from within the forest.
Having brought roots and tubers, she placed them upon the altar;
