And now, moreover, you are indeed engaged in eating meat;
since you are a slayer of men, you will certainly become a slayer of monkeys as well. (17)
O monkeys and human-like beings, that sin born of killing a man—namely, the very act of killing a child and certainly the killing of a woman as well—[is incurred]. (18)
O Cāṇḍāla, you are born again among humans who are difficult to find;
yet for the sake of your belly and for the sake of your family, you perform acts of violence. (19)
Furthermore, there are those torments of Yama and the downward path once more;
for the sake of those by whom you were previously cast down, you strive again.
"What kind of preeminent fool are you? What profit do you have from those who fall?
Behold, O fool, the true essence of a human being lies indeed in righteous action. (21)
Likewise, behold your own liberation, the auspicious destroyer of sins;
[behold] Dāmodara-Nārāyaṇa at the holy ford on the river Svarṇāvatī. ||22||
Behold! Perform merit and quickly abandon violence; be happy.
Become a purifier in this world, a devotee, and worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||23||
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake, perform the destruction of all sins;
likewise, having bathed in the Revatī pool and in the Vāmana pool.
Having bathed in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, at the holy site of Śrīsomatīrtha, and in the Sarasvatī river, may you be happy. (25)
Bathe in the city of Mūladvāravatī and from there go to heaven;
having established an auspicious sacred site for the sake of concealment, go to Gavāyana.
O fool, worship Govinda, the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
having shown compassion, having maintained righteousness, and likewise having practiced devotion to Hari.
By these [means], one goes to the world of Brahmā, which is eternal, ancient, and everlasting;
for the Supreme Lord resides at the sacred ford of Kuṅkumavāpikā. ||28||

He indeed possesses both divine and human bodies; he is the creator of Brahmā and the Lord of his beloved; he alone is the Blessed One, the creator of the world, who remains stationed within its protector.
The glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī and the Supreme Sovereign,
dwells like an ordinary human being, served by men and women.
Even at the end of the body, by the mere remembrance of him, even a great sinner is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme imperishable abode.
Go to him and worship that cowherd boy, the son of Kambharā;
take refuge in that self-possessed Supreme Lord who dwells within the heart. ||2||
Therefore, one must directly realize the knowledge of the majesty of that Lord of Rādhā and Ramā; from this, eternal liberation arises. 33.
From intense affection for the Blessed One, clarity of mind arises;
through that, liberation—which bestows the abode of the Blessed One—is placed within one's grasp. (34)
"O Cāṇḍāla, listen; I shall tell you: affection must indeed be shown in every way, just as toward a newly wedded wife's husband, so too toward one's first-born son. (35)
Just as [the mind of] a child toward its mother, or that of a greedy person toward wealth, or that of a hungry person toward food, or that of one terrified by fear toward a protector; ||36||
Just as [the thirst] of aquatic creatures is for water, and just as that of a moth is for fire, so should affection always be directed toward the Supreme Lord, the bestower of happiness. (37)
The Lord of Lords is to be touched by the skin, contemplated with the eyes, heard with the two ears, and tasted through kissing and other such acts. (38)
O Hari, his very fragrance is to be taken up and his form is always to be perceived;
the Blessed One is to be embraced and Mādhava is to be glorified. (39)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is to be gladdened, and likewise, the offering of everything to Hari must be performed;
furthermore, the daily practice of reciting the qualities of Hari should be carried out.
Affection for Kṛṣṇa arises through the knowledge of His majesty, qualities, and so forth;
or rather, such affection arises spontaneously only in a true devotee.
Just as one feels toward a wife, children, or wealth, so too when one attains natural affection for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, one is fit for becoming Brahman. 42.
Those of divine intellect possess innate affection;
their divine actions are for the sake of Hari, and their love for Him flourishes ever more. (43)
If pride exists as an obstacle to the nourishment of affection, it must be destroyed by all means, for it creates hindrances on the path to the highest good. (44)
All things of an evil nature must indeed be destroyed with effort;
those who seek liberation must destroy them with the thought that they are extreme enemies. (45)
If those of evil nature who dwell within the body act like friends,
yet are actually obstacles to liberation, they should be destroyed through association with the virtuous.
One should always cultivate the company of the virtuous; the company of the virtuous is a great medicine.
I am the Self, powerful, having Kṛṣṇa as my helper, and possessing excellent righteousness. 47.
Whatever he desires, he surely accomplishes; being capable even of liberation, one who has taken refuge in Hari shall uproot the impulses of passion and darkness.
Superimposition upon the body, evil association, and the accumulation of past actions—all these causes of illusion and delusion must be destroyed through the company of the virtuous. 49.
Through discernment, the superimposition of the self upon the body must be abandoned by means of the words of the virtuous;
and through association with the virtuous, evil company must be abandoned by means of gathering with the good. (3.211.50)
All the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) created in previous births that lead to evil deeds must be destroyed here by the great ones through their constant devotion to the virtuous. (51)
For a man of extreme wickedness, the fruit of his sin is torment;
then calamities arrive for the sake of his destruction.
Suddenly, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) runs hither and thither in every direction.
Nevertheless, calamities continue to increase and do not depart to a distance. ||53||
Then, becoming dejected in mind, he approaches people who are even more miserable;
and having heard of a virtuous or elderly person, he reports his misfortunes to them. (54)
Having received the words of the virtuous, one performs the worship of vows, as well as association with the good, devotion, service, and the remembrance of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (55)
Thus, by the power of the seed-syllable, his impurities are indeed dissolved;
consequently, his heart becomes stainless and pure.
There, Kṛṣṇa shines through the speech of the virtuous, worthy of devotion;
He gradually becomes manifest, and people become meritorious. ||57||
In this way, even impure conditioned phenomena attain purity;
likewise, an outcaste attains the status of a Brahmin, and a wicked person likewise attains the state of a good man. (58)
Through the favor of the virtuous, even a pauper quickly attains the status of a king;
likewise, through the favor of the virtuous, even a fool attains scholarship. (59)
Through the grace of the virtuous, even a sinner attains merit and heaven;
through the grace of the virtuous, even a wicked man becomes a purifier of the assembly.
In order to attain extreme clarity [of mind], one must always behave without guile in the presence of the virtuous, following their conduct accordingly. (61)
In whatever matter they have interest, that should be accomplished without hesitation; in whatever matter they have no interest, that should always be abandoned immediately. (62)
Abandoning pride, worldly shame, and arrogance regarding one's own virtues, one should indeed perform service to the virtuous and hold their words in the heart. (63)
Whatever obstacles arise in serving the virtuous, all those negative qualities must be abandoned; only that which bestows clarity should be adopted. (64)
Those qualities by which people indeed become serene are considered true virtues;
and that alone is called dharma by which serenity arises. //65//
That which causes displeasure to the virtuous is indeed a fault;
it must certainly be abandoned by a devotee, for one should instead cultivate delight in the virtuous.
For the virtuous are indeed pleased with one who is compliant and devoted as a servant;
by embracing the virtues of the good, the faults residing in the heart perish. (67)
The virtuous and great ones should be served, for they bestow divine nature; through the grasping of their qualities, devotion toward the Supreme Self increases. (68)
By grasping the quality of selflessness in the virtuous, one shall attain selflessness;
by grasping the quality of freedom from anger in the virtuous, one shall attain freedom from anger. (69)
By perceiving the quality of selflessness in the virtuous, one shall attain selflessness;
by perceiving the quality of freedom from delusion in the virtuous, one shall attain freedom from delusion. ||3.211.70||
Just as one who possesses a divine form becomes endowed with divine beauty upon grasping the qualities of the virtuous,
so too does one become [divine] upon grasping the quality of lordliness (bhagavattva) of the virtuous.
Indeed, by such devotion one becomes supreme, possessing great sovereignty and other virtues;
he has no relish for anything else, and his interest is always fixed on Kṛṣṇa and the virtuous.
Devotion exists toward Kṛṣṇa, the true person, while its absence exists toward others; for those such as you, service to Hari increases among the virtuous.
Supreme servitude, which is ever-increasing, stainless, and rooted in love, sometimes indeed transforms into lordship through the grace of the Lord. (74)
Just as lordship arises out of compassion toward a disciple or a servant, so too may the state of servitude in a slave transform into the state of being a master. //75//
There is no partiality toward the virtuous in the presence of Hari;
whether a woman, a Śūdra, or even a Cāṇḍāla, one attains the supreme goal through devotion. (76)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even by that monkey, the forest-dweller Kapikṣaya was awakened;
he attained that wonder and attained awakening. (77)
He indeed considered himself one who had accomplished his purpose and a partaker of merit,
since from that monkey he had obtained auspicious knowledge that bestows liberation.
Then he questioned the monkey: "Who are you here, who bestows knowledge and liberation, and who destroys the faults such as violence? (79)
"You dispel the fault of illusion and destroy all ignorance;
yet you wander in the forest—tell me truly, who are you here? (3.211.80)
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and I have been born anew through your words;
I shall become especially so once I have known you, the Purifier.
Having heard this, the monkey said: "We and these forest-dwellers who are red-colored monkeys—all of us are the deities of heaven. (82)
We all become possessed of divine bodies and dwellers in heaven;
we enjoy the merit of heaven, and when that merit is exhausted, it passes away. (83)
Nothing new is earned there, since heaven is a land of enjoyment;
this earth is the land of action, and merit performed here meets with its fruit.
For the sake of merit, on Mount Raivata, monkeys in human form, having gathered fruits, leaves, and other offerings, performed worship by dedicating them to the deity. (85)
Having partaken of this auspicious, purifying, and liberating favor, as well as the water from the Svarṇarekhā and the Nārāyaṇa lake. (86)
Having drunk from the lake of Dāmodara, we increase our great merit;
having bathed in this sacred ford, we, desiring liberation, seek our future release.
We are not monkeys, but gods in the form of monkeys, so that we may never again take birth in the human world at the end of our stay in heaven. (88)
"Let us establish a holy place here so that liberation may be attained by us;
you too, O consumer of fruits, should likewise establish a holy place. (89)
Accompanied by your family, you shall attain the supreme goal after going to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake to visit the yogi Lomaśa.
"Receive the mantra of Hari; therein you shall attain purity.
Having been addressed thus, that Cāṇḍāla bowed down to the host of deities.
Having quickly drunk the water of the Nārāyaṇa-kuṇḍa, which was as clear as a crane's throat,
he went to the abode of Lomaśa, prostrated before him, and spoke.
Afterwards, having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he received the mantra from Lomaśa out of his compassion, after [Lomaśa] had related the entire account.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! This devotee, together with his family, became devoted to me, Hari. (94)
He undertook the pilgrimage to Aśvapaṭṭasara and became purified;
by my grace and through his devotion to Lomaśa, his sin was destroyed.
Then, when the appointed time had arrived, he abandoned his body;
at that moment, all his wives and children likewise abandoned their bodies.
Chanting "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmīkānta, Ramāpati," they attained divine bodies and became yogis liberated from worldly existence. 97.
And a celestial chariot attended by my attendants arrived there;
having ascended it, they all went to my beloved, the imperishable abode. (98)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by my very grace, eternal welfare has been brought about for this devotee, a Cāṇḍāla, through his association with the monkey. (99)
In this way, others as well, purified by devotion to me and by devotion to the virtuous, serve me and those virtuous ones; they too attain the supreme goal. (3.211.10)
By reading, hearing, or remembering this, those with desires attain prosperity, while those free from desire attain my supreme state. 101.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Outcaste Named Kapikṣaya, Together with His Family, through Devotion to Hari by Means of Instruction from a Monkey-Formed Deity," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the iron-smith Nālīka, my purifying devotee. 1.
My devotee Nālīkara lived in the city named Vakranadā;
he was indeed an iron-smith residing there together with his family.
Long chains of clods, as well as small pegs,
ribbons, earrings, strips, and leaf-shaped clod-ornaments.
He also makes many clay vessels and iron implements, as well as carts and the ritual instruments for the planets.
During the movement of the bellows, in inhalation and exhalation, he meditated on the venerable Narayana;
likewise during the raising of the iron-beater, its lowering, and the hammering of the iron.
In tasks such as the forging of iron, one should remember me, Nārāyaṇa;
regarding the bellows as the goddess Ramā and the fire as Nārāyaṇa.
Regarding the garland as a moving staff, he always worships me, Hari;
and perceiving Māyā as a forge for iron—that is, a forge for the mass of his sins—he [worships me].
Considering clods of earth to be mere illusions, he strikes them for the sake of liberation;
and he regards the sounds arising from the striking of iron as the sacred syllable *praṇava*.
Thus Nālīkara, devoted through the vision of Brahman and possessing self-realization,
conducts himself endowed with devotion and worships my very form as well.
Having bathed in the morning and bowed to the image in the home, he offers incense;
having lit a lamp, he also presents a garland of flowers and sandalwood paste to Me.
Having offered me the essence of fragrance, the food offering of milk and sugar, and having presented fried cakes, as well as water and betel-leaf; || 11 ||
Having offered [the food] to me and asked for my forgiveness, he then eats and even drinks;
in this very same manner, he does so even in the iron workshop for Mādhava.
Having remembered [the deity], having gone [to the shrine], having paid homage, and having offered incense and a lamp, as well as a garland of flowers, sugar, and other excellent fruit; 13.
Having delivered [the goods] at the proper time, he then performs his duty;
with a pure mind and devotion, he carries out my iron works. (14)
Once, this devotee of such a kind had a profound thought:
"Worship should always be performed at night together with many others. (15)
The Saṅgha should perform the distribution [of alms], for it is the means of liberation for many;
thus, with a virtuous mind, [one should consider] the people and kinsmen of one's own village.
He spoke in order to establish a circle of devotion, and even then,
they established that supreme circle of devotees with great joy.
At the beginning of night, men and women would gather for two ghaṭikās and daily begin the auspicious chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa. ||18||
All the people residing in the city, having heard of and witnessed that auspicious deed,
offered mangoes there and joined him in the circle of devotees.
Thousands of people, filled with enthusiasm,
offer their devotion through all the festivals of Śrī Hari, as well as with instrumental music, dance, and other such performances.

O Lakṣmī, those who are diligent for their own spiritual welfare perform worship with erotic sentiments and other offerings, as well as vigils and other rites, at the appropriate times and with great zeal. (21)
Beholding their devotion,
I then became pleased with that devotee, the blacksmith, who promotes devotion unto me.
Once, for the sake of increasing their devotion, a most brilliant and radiant splendor issued forth from the forehead of my image and was shown to them in its brilliance.
And because I quickly performed the ritual slaughter (śāmita), they, out of devotion and reverence for me, showed me exceptional devotion filled with deep feeling. (24)
And they became knowers of me, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, as I remained in embodied form;
they indeed constructed a temple for Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
There, they performed a continuous stream of worship and other rites according to their means.
"O Daughter of the Ocean, I dwell within this image together with you. (26)
I remove the sufferings and calamities of all every day;
those who offer me honor perform acts that destroy disease and misery. (27)
I destroy all afflictions— those arising from the internal, the divine, and the elemental— and they indeed become established in well-being.
And they worship me with intense emotions, proclaiming my wonders and other such feats.
Then, on one occasion, she became a female ascetic, assuming the garb of a *tāpasī*.
And I, having become an ascetic yogi, arrived at the onset of night at a spot near the temple, observing the circle of devotees.
Just as some wretched, destitute beggar has appeared, so too are you of a miserable mind—a female mendicant devoid of vows. (3.1)
Just as a common woman is soiled and devoid of the merit of bathing in the Dharma, even so am I defiled, yet I captivate the minds of those who behold me. (32)
But having made a single small child, filled with excrement, urine, and the like—a Garuda in the form of a boy—I stood before her in my belly. (33)
Thus, seeing that trio and observing them approaching the front of the temple like beggars in distress, they became filled with compassion.
Having summoned them, they seated them comfortably upon the altar and offered them food produced from the grace of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with devotion, they gave us milk for our offspring;
and having partaken of food and drink, O Lakṣmī, we remained in a state of happiness.
On the balconies they sat and chanted His names; at the crossroads they began the *rāsa* dance with rhythmic clapping and beautiful dancing. (37)
Indeed, countless men and women, full of devotion, offered their worship;
and as they performed the kīrtana, they took rest for a moment. (38)
Then, having risen, I performed kīrtana with you there in that courtyard, dancing to the accompaniment of hand-claps and anklets. ||39||
Having seen both me and you at that time, they attained supreme wonder;
and being pleased, they repeatedly questioned me, who am peaceful, for the sake of their welfare.
"O holy one, show us compassion and speak something that bestows welfare here.
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, I then gave them my own knowledge.
He indeed declared that the cause of love for the Blessed One is His majesty;
furthermore, confidence in that love is also a cause when one possesses knowledge of His majesty. (42)
One should take refuge in Hari, the controller of Māyā, Puruṣa, and Kāla, as well as of nature, qualities, and actions, and of the principles that are both insentient and sentient. ||43||
One should take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the independent creator of all, the cause of all incarnations, and the bestower of all powers. 44.
A person who possesses knowledge of His majesty should take refuge in the Supreme Self with love;
by serving that Lord with affection, one shall attain the supreme abode. 45.
One who possesses discernment should by all means effect the destruction of latent impressions;
for whatever liking or desire I have for worldly objects— (46)
Having indeed discerned how much [of that] it is, one must remove it from there;
for how much pure desire or longing remains toward Hari? (47)
Having discerned whether [the qualities] in Māyā and in Hari are equal, inferior, or even superior, one should always strive diligently to increase them in Hari. 48.
Whatever may be laughable in illusion is entirely baseless; however, in that which pertains to *māyā*, there is perishability, the quality of bestowing suffering, and the power to cause bondage. (49)
Having understood that [the world] arises as a collection of objects, one should abandon it;
one should renounce attachment to illusory things, which binds even those who are liberated. (3.212.50)

Indeed, through association with the virtuous, through connection with Kṛṣṇa, and through the chanting and singing of Kṛṣṇa’s glories, the destruction of the latent impressions of aversion arises very swiftly. (51)
Delight in Kṛṣṇa indeed arises directly from yoga, especially through its specific practice;
thus, by the yoga of repeated practice, love for Kṛṣṇa increases. (52)

For one who has tasted the nectar of the Lord, there occurs a swift destruction of attachment toward worldly enjoyments—whether they be pleasant or otherwise—as they are illusory and equal to impurity. (53)
The divine nature consisting of Nārāyaṇa shines forth as composed of Brahman for this devotee who is fixed in the Blessed Lord;
such is the supreme, virtuous state of being Brahman.
That supreme state is the great Bhāgavata, full of joy, free from the conceit of *māyā*, and adorned with the nature of the Blessed One. (55)

For the sake of destroying latent impressions (vāsanā), as well as for the sake of attaining love for Hari, one should cultivate steadfastness in the Self and also the highest form of dispassion (vairāgya). ||56||
One should achieve the knowledge of the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇa, self-surrender, steadfast devotion to the Blessed One, and cultivate association with the virtuous. (57)
One should accomplish service to those virtuous ones who are established in the self free from latent impressions;
having attained the favor of the virtuous, one shall conquer illusion and go to the Supreme. ||58||
One may attain supreme steadfastness through knowledge derived from taking refuge in the Supreme Self;
by the assistance of the company of the virtuous, one's steadfastness toward Hari becomes firm.
Through devotion fixed upon the Self, there arises likewise firmness of fortitude;
and for the steadfast one who has attained the state of liberation, no obstacles ever arise. (3.212.60)
Furthermore, even the supernatural powers (siddhis), which take the form of obstacles to devotion, do not approach [the devotee];
for indeed, the powers come only for the purpose of testing one whose devotion has reached maturity.
By the command of Śrī Hari, they repeatedly entice him who has taken refuge [in Him];
nevertheless, he should not look at them, for having conquered them, he goes to the supreme abode.
For such a devotee, Kṛṣṇa himself comes under his control—he who is free from the latent impressions of māyā and has dedicated everything to Kṛṣṇa. (63)
Hari is always pleased with one who has surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
yet, Śrī Hari is sometimes even more pleased by the heart of a devotee who possesses excessive love for Kṛṣṇa.
One whose armor is bound by the cord of love becomes unable to proceed;
for him alone the Blessed One is the protector, the master, the beloved, and the bestower of liberation. 65.
And he who removes the suffering of illusion dwells entirely within his heart;
for such a devotee, indeed, divine qualities arise. 66.
Truthfulness, purity, and all other such qualities arise from taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa;
they are born even in one possessed of devotion through Kṛṣṇa’s divine knowledge. (67)
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa Mādhava is the controller of time, karma, and inherent nature, as well as of illusion, the individual soul, and even the lords.
The Lord of Śrī, the Master, is the creator, the nourisher, and the destroyer of all creations;
that very Gopāla-bāla resides within the hearts of all. (69)
The Lord, the sovereign of Rādhā and Ramā, remains untainted;
knowing this, he established a firm relationship with Hari Kṛṣṇa. (3.212.70)
Even the divine qualities belonging to that Śrī Hari manifest in every way for the devotee as all forms of sovereignty.
Just as one obtains the quality of light through association with the lamp of the eye, so too do the qualities of Hari enter into the devotee through union with Him. (72)
By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he becomes independent and equal to Kṛṣṇa;
having attained perfection in all actions, he becomes eternally perfected. ||73||
Just as Indra came to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, having been driven away by hosts of apsarases and deprived of Urvaśī’s company, in order to cause an interruption to their ascetic penance.
Thus, by means of *siddhi*, those possessing *siddhi* are cast out by one who has attained *susiddhi*;
and by a devotee of Hari, even the primordial *māyā* is cast out through His power. (75)
The gods indeed become endowed with the qualities of the Blessed One;
those of demonic nature are never born possessing the qualities of the Blessed One. (76)
But when sinners enter the shoreless ocean of compassion of the great holy ones, certain virtues indeed enter them through devotion to the Lord. (77)
For the virtuous, when pleased by service, destroy one's evil qualities;
they destroy one's demonic nature and bring about a divine disposition. (78)
But he who, out of pride, despises poor people who are devoted to him—even a celestial being shall fall into a demonic state by the mass of that person's sin. (79)
He would be cursed and consumed by the power of Brahman; virtues do not enter such a person.
Therefore, one must never, under any circumstances, treat the wretched with contempt.
One should behave like a wretched person before those who are wretched; by this, Kṛṣṇa is well-pleased.
The Blessed One never shows mercy toward those possessed of pride. 8.1
Virtuous qualities never arise at all in those who are malevolent;
by harming one who is gentle, devoted, and humble, one's merit is utterly destroyed.
This is certain, there is no doubt in this matter: for those who are weak should not be despised, even if they are outwardly impure, provided their hearts possess pure intentions. (83)
For those virtuous ones are devotees of the Blessed One, worthy of honor, and bestowers of liberation;
within their hearts, the Blessed One, the inner guide, shines resplendent. (84)
Indeed, the Lord of the distressed, the protector of the helpless, exists together with them;
for Mādhava becomes enraged by the insult of his devotees. (85)
One who treats him with contempt will swiftly meet destruction by his own hand;
yet, being subservient to the devotion of the destitute, he quickly causes others to bring about [the destruction] of that person. 86.
"Alas, we are wretched, soiled, and swarmed by flies;
filled with fear and dejected in mind, we have come here for the sake of food. (87)
"You have not shown contempt, but have honored us with respect;
therefore, we are here with hearts full of joy and endowed with happiness.
You are devotees of the Blessed One, truthful, and servants free from pride. (88)
And let them request a boon, if it pleases your mind. (89)
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, when I had bowed to my own image and desired to go far away, at that moment the boy passed stool. (3.212.90)
Nālīkara led the water and gave it to his wife;
that woman, named Kundaṇikā, received the offering from your hand. (9.1)
With sincere devotion, you have performed the cleansing of my impurities;
for this reason, even greater clarity has indeed arisen within me. (92)
He granted his own divine and wonderful vision to his devotees—[the vision of] the beautiful dark-complexioned Lord of Śrī, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. 93.
O Lakṣmī, I likewise displayed my beautiful form to you,
and I manifested my true nature as the child Garuḍa.
Then the devotees, having achieved their purpose, felt it within their hearts;
they danced after beholding him and, full of zeal, offered worship. || 95 ||
At that time, they chose a boon for the sake of liberation and nothing else;
having granted the boon, saying "So be it," [the Lord] vanished in an instant. (96)
I entered the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa together with you,
and at that moment, Garuḍa suddenly entered the form of the bird.
Having thus granted them my own vision, I bestowed upon them supreme happiness;
then, as time passed, [I fashioned] a lotus from ironwork.
In his chest there arose a disease of breath, with the movement of breath occurring in every way;
indeed, he was afflicted by the disease known as *dama*, O King of Devotees. (99)
Being unable to perform his task, he prayed to me while I was present in my physical form;
I immediately manifested myself and had him drink milk from my hand.
Having touched his heart with my hand, the disease was destroyed;
then, quickly becoming invisible, I always dwell and take delight within his form.
When his lifespan was exhausted, I brought Nālīkara and Strī,
as well as Kundaṇikā, by means of a celestial chariot to the supreme, imperishable abode.
In this way, I lead other devotees as well to my own imperishable abode;
and those who worship me with devotion likewise take on my qualities.
They perform service to the virtuous in every way with a spirit of love;
having attained the favor of the virtuous, they shall go to my abode. 104.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and even practicing [this], there is indeed enjoyment and liberation; it is the supreme goal according to one's desire.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Nālīka the Blacksmith’s Vision of Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Garuḍa through Devotion, His Liberation, and Other Matters," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Śrī, consort of Nārāyaṇa, listen to the auspicious story of the leather-worker named Maṅgala, which is filled with devotion to me. || 1 ||
In the city of Droṇikā, there was a devoted and very serviceable cobbler named Maṅgaladeva,
who lived as a householder engaged in the work of leather.
Of buffalo-cows, cattle, antelopes, as well as lions, tigers, elephants, and other species of animal-bodied beings. || 3 ||
He purifies the hides of dead animals through various processing methods,
and indeed sells those processed hides for high prices.
Having prepared seats made of skins that serve as purifiers,
he also gives them to the virtuous, including those of deer and even of lions, the kings of beasts.
Having gone daily to the assembly of the virtuous at the monastery of the holy ones every day,
he performs the sweeping of the crossroads and other areas, as well as the city gates and so forth.
Having taken the dust from the feet of the virtuous upon his head, heart, face,
and body, he bathes in that dust and even rolls about in the very soil.
Oh, what fortune! O leather-worker, I bathe in the dust of the merit of the virtuous;
having attained the favor of the virtuous, I shall go to the supreme state. (8)
Speaking thus, he drinks even the water from the feet of the Great One,
and he eats the food left over by the virtuous, served upon a bed of leaves.
This body, which was impure as a leather-worker, has become pure through the grace of the virtuous;
all my sins have been destroyed, and my state as a leather-worker has vanished.
Oh, how wonderful are the saintly! Oh, how wonderful is Kṛṣṇa! Oh, how wonderful is my birth here!
Though born from a low caste, I am indeed most fortunate through this service.
Knowing His majesty in this way, O Kṛṣṇa, one remembers Kṛṣṇa;
one even writes the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa upon pieces of leather. 12.
He gives gifts to the virtuous, seeking his own welfare as well, having fashioned various other implements made of leather. (13)
Having written down the name Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he sold it;
and he wrote "Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa" upon the courtyard of his house and upon the archway.
O Rame, everything belonging to that devotee consists of Kṛṣṇa;
even his marketplace was established by him as the "Marketplace of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
And it was decorated all around on the walls, doors, archways, and floors with [images of] Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, O Hari, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Ramā! (16)
O Beloved Lord, O Consort of Kamalā, O Śrīkaṃbharāja, O Gopāla-bālaka, O glorious Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme Sovereign! 17.
O Blessed One, destroying evil and bringing merit, you abide within;
thus [you are worshipped] everywhere by these names and likewise by means of images and so forth. (18)
"The entire marketplace has been decorated, and likewise my house has been decorated;
such is this devotee of mine who, having bathed, performs worship unto me. (19)
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as food offerings and fruit,
he also presents betel leaf, water, and other items, and performs the ritual dismissal.
Having eaten the food born of his grace, he indeed exerts himself;
for all his servants and laborers perform my worship as well. (21)
Having undertaken their work, they perform it incessantly with joy;
and at night, having gathered together, they engage in conversation and even practice kīrtana.
They sing my verses and rejoice with festivals; if it is a day of religious observance, they remain awake until dawn. (23)
In the morning, having gathered together, they perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of their vow;
they feed and honor many devoted leather-workers.
They also honor with material gifts those others who have arrived—whether they be virtuous persons worthy of such treatment or others—who are in their own city. (25)
And to those who come to them, they even give footwear;
thus indeed do they perform service in many ways, possessing the consciousness of devotion.
May the virtuous be well-disposed toward them and grant their blessings, saying:
"May these devotees be happy, and may their devotion bear excellent fruit without obstacles. (27)
May the servants of virtuous women and holy men be long-lived, purifying, free from all calamities, and endowed with merit. (28)
Thus, by the grace of the virtuous, they receive such blessings;
then once, on the full moon day of Āśvina, when the moon was [at its zenith], (29)
When the full moon had arrived and the great festival was underway,
those leather-workers indeed fashioned an image of Hari for the Kaumudī celebration.
Having seated her upon a beautiful seat in the moonlight,
he worshipped her with sandalwood paste, lovely garments, and splendid ornaments.
They performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites; they offered oblations to Viṣṇu consisting of parched grain soaked in milk and mixed with sugar. || 32 ||
Having placed that uncovered offering in the great hall,
they eagerly performed the rāsa dance before the Blessed One.
With the rhythmic clapping of their hands, feet, and other limbs, they glorified Acyuta; and immersed in love, they wandered about in a circular formation. (34)
They circumambulate me, Hari; they sing with great eagerness for leaping;
they converse with rhythmic claps and leap about in various ways.
Having sat down, they rise; out of confusion, they roll about and then stand up and walk away;
they clap their hands and offer them, facing forward and facing backward. (36)
In this way, my servants enjoy great joy and bliss,
O Lakṣmī, when the ground in the middle of the night shines like the milk of the moon.
Then I, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, being greedy for the elixir of devotional love,
became single-mindedly intent on the rāsa dance, and I both see and hear.
Just as they do not see me even when I am in embodied form, so it is with you;
and I have become gracious, bound by love, their dear Lord.
Listen to what happened there: a serpent, greedy for the song, approached from his dwelling nearby and settled still in a corner of the house. (3.213.40)
Having heard the song filled with the essence of the rāsa dance, having heard the rhythmic chanting of the tāla,
and having smelled the auspicious puffed rice placed in the vessels along with milk and sugar— 41.
Seeing them situated in a desolate place, he approached them slowly and slowly;
having tasted the milk with his tongue, he drank the sweet liquid again and again. ||42||
Purified by grace, he quickly departed with some fear;
then, having found rest at the end of the dance, he went forth to obtain further grace.
And all those devoted people, row by row,
served the poison-smeared pṛthuka grains to the thousand embodied beings in that assembly.
Having eaten the *pṛthuka* grains, all those people— knowing their great power,
including everyone from children to the elderly— [became] possessed by the poison of black serpents.
Having all eaten and drunk water, they slept for a moment in the courtyard;
then many of them fell into a toxic stupor, on the verge of death.
They became scorched by the poison and were deprived of the luster of their bodies;
then others, touched by the diminished venom, suffered intensely. 47.

There was the provocation of poison in others and in his own people, and a dizziness in their heads; moreover, there appeared tawny, blue, and green wave-like lusters within the rays of their eyes. (48)
They indeed performed an examination and quickly understood that the poison was present; they all openly declared, "The pṛthuka grains are infused with venom. (49)
Then, having been consumed, a fainting spell that brings death indeed approached;
everyone quickly drank ghee for the sake of neutralizing the poison.
The emetic they took, though containing poison, became a remedy that neutralized poison;
nevertheless, many of those devotees were as if dead from the poison.
Other people there entreated me to bring them back to life;
many women, sons, husbands, and kinsmen wept there. (52)
They remembered me, the Supreme Lord, the giver of life who dwells within; they remembered their state of distress, their weeping, their worship, and their vows.
Beholding her devotion, I became pleased and quickly manifested myself in the form of a holy man, with a medicinal box for curing abdominal ailments placed upon my hip.
Having heard the account of what had occurred, I remained in the presence of those who caused my grief;
then, quickly reporting the news and having placed water in a jar, [I departed].
There, having cast medicinal juice and offering water for rinsing the mouth,
I suddenly poured it into the mouths of those who were unconscious and in a state resembling death.
Then, by the touch of the water on their palms, they regained consciousness;
they became as if immortal, having recovered their life-breaths and the movement of their awareness. (57)
They all suddenly arose like those waking from sleep;
established in their own state, they there recognized their own calamity as if in a dream. (58)
Poison was turned into nectar by the sage through the power of medicinal herbs and water;
then, they all gathered together and gave food to the sage. (59)
Those people, who had been restored to life, provided him with delightful drinks and seats for his rest during the latter part of the night, and they massaged his feet.
Those people, immersed in service, questioned that very virtuous man:
"O Blessed One, how does an obstacle arise for those who have attained steadfastness? (61)
Then the virtuous one said to him: "Indeed, an obstacle arises by the will of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of testing;
it is certainly not considered a true obstacle."
From that, there arises firmness in the grace of Kṛṣṇa and firmness in devotion;
and He, appearing in person, effects the destruction of all obstacles. (63)
In times of distress, however, there shall be remembrance of Śrī Hari by His devotees;
and when a miracle is displayed, their firmness in devotion shall become great.
Aha! This Blessed One exists as the preventer of all suffering;
his service should be performed, for it is auspicious, bestowing liberation and happiness. (656)
Thus do these volitions always arise when observing sovereignty;
but when observing the lack of sovereignty, they mimic the dance of men.
"Fatigue would surely arise toward Kṛṣṇa, for he is not [merely] this [human] Lord;
my service performed here for a long time has indeed become fruitless. (67)
Just as I am weak, powerless, and dependent on others, so too is he weak, incapable, and dependent on others. (68)
Just as desire, anger, greed, delusion, and fear exist in me,
so indeed do desire, greed, anger, delusion, and fear exist in Kṛṣṇa.
"Therefore, this Blessed One is certainly not [divine], but rather a human being.
Thus, possessing an ordinary mind, he regarded Kṛṣṇa as an ordinary mortal.
One whose divine disposition has perished imagines faults as if they were his own; therefore, one should always contemplate Hari with a mind empowered by a divine disposition. (71)
One should consider one's own fullness [in this way]: "There is nothing for me to attain except Hari;
there is no other supreme goal to be accomplished by me, for everything remains as a means to attain Hari. (72)
Indeed, Hari himself is present here; that supreme abode is there. The realm of Brahmā is also there, and the liberated souls dwell there as well.
Since Hari is present here, everything—the earth and so forth—is supreme;
the assembly is divine, the devotees are divine, and the men and women are divine. (74)
O Blessed One, in their union my joy exists as being composed of the Lord;
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, since Hari dwells here.
"The Blessed One exists here in the form of a virtuous being, in embodied form.
Such are the thoughts that arise in the heart of a devotee who knows the Self. (76)
The gods and lords are liberated and made happy by his abundance;
that very Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), shines here.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond the supreme, the imperishable, all-pervading abode of Brahman—He has come here. ||78||
The great king has met [with us] here; the end of my good fortune is not yet seen.
Indeed, through the power of that Kṛṣṇa, our life shall be restored once more. (79)
In the divine, eternal, and supreme abode, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines forth,
worshipped by countless great liberated souls who are equal to Himself.
Indeed, within each single hair of those who have been liberated by the divine grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there resides a splendor resembling ten million times ten million suns.
The entire radiant splendor of such countless liberated ones dissolves into a single hair-pore; such is that Imperishable.
There exists indeed a divine abode of Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
and there are also such abodes as well as the splendors of those very abodes.
All things attain dissolution within the single hair-pore of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
such is the sovereign power (bhūti) of the Supreme Self. 84.
Such is the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the capable and most great Hari;
moved by compassion for embodied beings, he is endowed with all powers for their ultimate welfare. (85)
Assuming a divine human form, he is born among men like an ordinary man; concealing his great sovereign powers, he exists in human shape. (86)
Through devotion to him, all sufferings come to rest;
there is no bondage for him from time, karma, or māyā. (87)
Through service to that glorious Hari, protection is always attained, just as protection has indeed been provided for you here by me while I exist. (88)
In the same way, Kṛṣṇa effects His own protection through the agency of the virtuous; He does so for the conscious beings who are His devotees, as well as for all the principles of Māyā. (89)
Indeed, his entire body becomes pervaded and subject to him;
everything indeed comes under the control of this great-souled one.
In all those principles, even among the liberated lords of syllables, and even among those such as the individual souls under the influence of māyā, Kṛṣṇa exists as the all-pervading one.
Kṛṣṇa is the impeller of all, independent, and the controller; he is endowed with all sovereignty, the supreme remainder of all, the source of all auspiciousness, and the Lord. ||92||
Having manifested on earth in the likeness of a man, he performs the dance of humanity;
therefore, O men and women who possess divine nature, serve that Hari.
They all indeed attain the entire sovereignty of Śrī Hari;
possessing the nature of Brahman and being of the essence of Brahman, they serve Hari with love. (94)
Even in the world of Brahmā, those of such form serve the Supreme Lord;
therefore, here on earth, Hari—manifesting in a virtuous form—is the supreme protector who should be served. ||95||
"Nārāyaṇa himself, the fulfiller of the desires of his devotees, resides within the virtuous;
thus, O Lakṣmī, Maṅgala, Deva, and the others were described by me at that time. (96)
Some perceived Kṛṣṇa within me, while others perceived me as Kṛṣṇa; thus, with intense devotion, they served that form of the Holy One again and again.
Satī, the wife of Maṅgaladeva, known by the name Vibhāvarī, served me with great devotion through such acts as massaging my feet. 98.
Then, having been entreated by them again and again for the sake of liberation, I said,
"So be it," and revealed my own divine body.
He was endowed with a lute and wore a crown; his form was dark and beautiful, more handsome than the beauty of ten million Cupids, a radiant youth.
He is the Lord of Śrī, saluted by Rādhā and others, served by the beloveds of Brahmā, and attended by millions of liberated great female devotees.
And having shown me in such a form, you then vanished from their sight in an instant; they, however, were once again overcome with great wonder.
They danced and offered hymns of praise upon the direct vision of Kṛṣṇa;
thus they constantly worshipped him with perpetual and supreme devotion.
When the time had arrived, I brought them by means of a celestial chariot to that supreme and transcendent abode of divine syllables, and I established them there among the liberated ones.
I protected my devotee Maṅgaladeva and his wife Vibhāvarī in their service at my feet, which are established in the imperishable state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I then provided protection for the leather-workers;
moved by compassion, I gave them a mantra in the form of a virtuous man.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! They chanted this, they worshipped me, they remembered me, and they went to my supreme abode. (1.07)
From reciting, hearing, remembering, and even serving this,
as well as from worshipping it, one obtains divine prosperity, heaven, and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord, having personally appeared through the devotion of the cobbler devotee named Maṅgaladeva, warded off poison," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious account of the chariot-maker who dwells in Sutāra village, which is rich with devotion to me. || 1 ||
On the bank of the Raṅgamayī river, there lived in the city of Sutāra a very pure chariot-maker who was my devotee and possessed a family.
All wooden vehicles, carts, and chariots; all wheel-less carriages, wooden seats, and couches. || 3 ||
He manufactures mats, couches, and beds, as well as deceptive objects such as beautiful wooden vessels and wooden puppets. (4)
The best of craftsmen indeed constructs boats, elephants, horses, cows, and bulls,
as well as various other implements, by means of his own skill.
He also made chests and small trunks with beautiful four-sided tops;
in all those works, he even inscribed the name of Hari.
Having first written his own name as "Haridāsa," he then indeed writes "Hari" upon all objects.
And in his house, within a wooden shed, he fashioned a wooden image of the Supreme Soul, Lord Śrī Hari,
inside the lattice-work of the dwelling.
He indeed established that beautiful image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my own, and worships it every morning.
Together with Śrī, [he was honored] with flowers, leaves, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and saffron;
with ornaments, garments, liquid offerings, incense, lamps, food offerings, and water.
Having thus worshipped daily, one then consumes the *prasāda*;
furthermore, after distributing it to others, one proceeds with one's duties.
During his exertion, Haridāsa, the king of true devotees, remembered me, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, as well as Harikṛṣṇa and Bālakṛṣṇa. 1-2.
Then, on one occasion, a reflection regarding the domain of the gods and others occurred to him:
"Setting aside all other endeavors, let me apply myself solely to the task of making images. (13)

For those whose meditative absorption becomes divine in nature for the purpose of emanation, there is likewise remembrance of the gods during activities such as [painting] forms, colors, and so forth. (14)
There should be constant chanting and the offering of worship in embodied form;
having reflected thus, Haridāsa became eager for the sake of Hari. (15)
With devotion, he undertook an endeavor centered on the form of Hari;
he fashioned a most beautiful image of Puruṣottama. (16)
The form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa adorned with a ruby, as well as the pair of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa and both Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. || 17 ||
Vāsudeva together with Śrī, Viṣṇu accompanied by Kamalā,
as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Śeṣa.
He fashioned Śrīpati, resplendent with divine beauty, seated upon Garuḍa, seated upon an elephant, seated upon Māṇikī, seated in a celestial chariot, and seated in a chariot.
The Lord, who destroys suffering and is accompanied by Śrī and the cows,
as well as Matsya, Kūrma, Vārāha, Kapila, and Hari.
Vāsudeva, Rājarāja, Pṛthu, Datta, Nṛsiṃhaka, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Paraśudhara, Yajña, and Vāmana. ||21||
Rāma, Kumāra, Vyāsa, Hayagrīva, and Nārada;
Bālakṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, and the Lord of Nārāyaṇī. ||2||
Hara and Satī, Brahmā and Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Prajñā, Pārāvatī, Durgā, Gaṅgā, and likewise Kālikā. ||23||
He fashioned auspicious images of Sūrya, Vahni, Candramas, Gaṇeśa, Kālabhairava, Nanda, Sunanda, and the Liṅga. ||24||
He fashions auspicious images from pieces of wood from various trees, including those with spreading branches, banyans, and śiṃśapā trees. ||25||
He indeed fashions them in various ways— small, medium, and large—
adorned with colorful ornaments, refined, and marked with distinct features.
While chanting the name of Hari and constantly fashioning images, he does not perceive them at all when their forms shine within his heart. (27)
Sitting in secret and remembering me, he assumes my form;
with his mind one-pointedly focused within his own heart, he is born as my very self.
The dissolution of all the functions of the senses indeed occurs within me;
in whatever manner that may be, he strives like a yogin and meditates with steadfastness. (29)
Whether half a day or a full day passed for him as if in deep meditation,
even so, immersed in love, he did not emerge from that state of absorption.
Since the form of Mādhava exists as a wish-fulfilling gem, the desires held within it become fulfilled from its presence. (3.1)
Thus, for Haridāsa, who was possessed of such certainty,
no form whatsoever arose that could take the nature of an object to be accomplished.
For that long, he remains steadfast in meditative absorption, absorbed in my form, desiring to behold a new form worthy of being fashioned, one that is most beautiful. (33)
Then, when the form of my embodied compassion arises—
having seen and repeatedly held that form which is the likeness of what must be done— (34)
Having practiced this, the devotee then goes outside, and not otherwise;
for such is the true nature of the form of the deity to be accomplished as it was seen.
From wood, by means of artistic skills, he fashions a beautiful, gentle image with a smiling face, equipped with all suitable and excellent weapons. (36)
He thus enhances the beautiful wooden form made of wood, richly adorned with appropriate ornaments, exactly as it was envisioned in his heart.
Having made such an arrangement, he sells it beautifully colored;
thus [is the case] for all the gods and for the ascetic-yogins like Hanumān. (38)
Having purchased virtuous women and deities, he sells them;
he meditates upon all the deities, and especially upon his beloved. (39)
She meditates upon Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person;
therefore, from my likeness, I shall fulfill even that which she desires.
He became renowned in the world as Haridāsa, the very body of Hari;
indeed, even kings had their chosen deities consecrated by him.
Haridāsa, too, having performed [the rites], gives away only the most auspicious [gifts].
Haridāsa has made a vow that there shall be none other than Nārāyaṇa.
Except for an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa, no human image should ever be made by me; for an illusory image would indeed be contrary to devotion. (43)
An image of a human female must never be fashioned for those who harbor base thoughts;
likewise, an image of a human female must never be fashioned for those who lack devotion. (44)
For his devotees, however, auspicious rites should be performed together with their chosen deity;
in this way, he indeed constantly protected the state of self-surrender.
Then, O Lakṣmī, being pleased, he approached for the sake of testing him;
having become a sovereign emperor, he traveled along the road under the pretext of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Possessing elephants, horses, and chariots, accompanied by an army of more than a thousand soldiers, and attended by thousands of queens, female servants, and male servants. ||47||
Adorned with necklaces of jewels, diamonds, pearls, and the like, and graced by a parasol,
he sat upon the back of a great white elephant accompanied by a golden female elephant.
Seated there, attended by fly-whisks and honored with shouts of "Victory!", he was surrounded on all sides by warriors bearing missiles and weapons. ||49||
O Lakṣmī, you are my wife, the sovereign empress, most excellent and beautiful; likewise, you are honored and served by the preceptor, the ministers, the chiefs, and others.
Adorned by a multitude of young female attendants who were as beautiful as thousands [of stars],
she was protected by servant-maids dispatched by me and honored by my servants.
Likewise, seated upon a celestial chariot rich with great gold and jewels,
she approached me together with me, having been previously sent forth by me.
"O Emperor, being such as I am, I went forth previously to a grove of trees on the bank of the river Raṅgamayī under the pretext of a pilgrimage. (53)
Having taken refuge at the excellent bank of the sacred ford known as Mahāśālagrāma-tīrtha for the sake of stability, I descended from my elephant. (54)
Accompanied by my army, I dwelt there with my mind intent on bathing, worship, and other rites;
then the subjects residing in the city named Sutārā arrived.
The gurus, the brahmins, and the mendicants were filled with curiosity; they were also possessed by a desire for sacrificial fees and an eagerness to behold [the spectacle]. (56)
Everyone came to the city to see the king;
yet even so, that king of devotees did not come, knowing him to be illusory.
Then, having performed the ritual for the sacred ford according to the traditional rules, and having given many gifts thereafter, I heard of the auspicious images. (58)
He also saw images installed on the banks of the sacred ford;
he questioned the men who had arrived there concerning the preeminent artisan.
They replied, "The king of artisans resides in this city;
though summoned by me through messengers, even Haridāsa did not come."
He said that he would never go into the presence of anyone other than a true devotee of the Lord, nor to Nārāyaṇa Hari himself, unless he were accompanied by a devotee of Hari. (61)
Then I spoke my name as Kṛṣṇadāsa:
"I am Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsavarya, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa. (62)
"Come, O best of artisans, for the sake of the image at my command.
Having been addressed thus by the messengers who had gone there, he too, upon hearing it, arrived.
Taking up garlands of flowers, they placed them upon the king's chest;
for, knowing him to be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, they bowed down with great devotion.
The king also showed him great honor, as was fitting for one who is highly discerning.
The artisan was questioned by me, the king, regarding the fashioning of the image of Lakṣmī.
When asked even about the price for the purpose of purchasing the images,
he gave me an image of Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Rādhā.
Having obtained Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa with a thousand silver coins,
I gave him a ring and furthermore a hundred pieces of gold.
Having given him a reward, I said to him:
"Fashion one image for me and one image for my queen. (68)
"I shall give you as much gold, gems, and diamonds as you desire.
He replied, "O King, I am a devotee, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (69)
I always fashion images of the manifestations of Nārāyaṇa, as well as of Nārāyaṇa himself, and of the gods and the deities.
I do not perform even a human-like act, nor do I perform a magical one;
for one whose mind is occupied with such contrivances, one would not contemplate Nārāyaṇa. (71)
"O King, I did not at any time think of the illusion or the illusory puppet, nor even of the making of that puppet who was your queen. (72)
"Recollection would indeed belong to a human being, and there would be a loss of my devotion;
therefore, I shall certainly not fashion a doll for you—forgive me. (73)
Although you are a devoted worshiper, you are indeed of a rajasic nature;
and this great illusion of the King exists to delude you.
I shall not remember him, Nārāyaṇa, without Lakṣmī;
for if you are with the Queen [Lakṣmī], then he is indeed with Mādhava. (75)
"If both of you remain like devotees and continue in service, and it pleases you, then I shall create an image together with the Lord of Śrī. (76)
I do not act out of mere selfishness, nor do I desire a reward;
salutations to you, and may you forgive me, for the king is to be honored by his subjects. (77)
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, Haridāsa, the king of devotees, went home;
for I, the King, followed behind him after having thus thoroughly tested my devotee.
Having reached his house on foot, the people were filled with wonder;
that king of devotees, out of discernment, gave me a wooden seat.
He gave and showed the food and water offered to Śrī Hari;
he sat down for meditation upon my entire image. (3.214.80)
Disregarding my fear and maintaining auspicious fortitude toward Hari, I then became absorbed in meditation, immersed within his heart; thus, I came to dwell in his heart.
The king was in the form of Rāma, and the queen was in the form of Lakṣmī, each according to their respective roles;
having recognized Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and me, he quickly rose up. (82)
He welcomed me by prostrating like a staff and circumambulated me;
he suddenly began to chant praises and danced, overwhelmed with joy. (83)
Then, however, those other people who were there as spectators at that time, having seen that great marvel and likewise having heard what was uttered by the devotee, [were amazed]. (84)
For Nārāyaṇa himself came to my house having become a sovereign emperor, and the Great Queen Lakṣmī arrived; thus, I am truly fortunate. (85)
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for the inhabitants of the village of Sutāra!
Oh, what supreme auspicious fortune for my wife, the illustrious Mānavī! 86.
Today the fortune of my family, of my servants, and of the wives of my servants is most excellent, since Hari, the Beloved, dwells in our home. (87)
That Śrī, the beloved of Hari, who has come to his house in the form of a queen—may she bring about the welfare of Śrīmān Avyaya and the liberation of Haridāsa. 88.
Oh, what a fruit for the maker of the image that Lord Hari is present in his very home! Oh, what a gain for one who has offered himself that the Lord Himself is present in his home! (89)
My art has become well-mastered; my life has become a true life.
I have directly attained Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, united with Śrī.
Upon hearing this, the people also honored the King, the Lord of Fortune;
they prostrated themselves like a staff, and Bhakta fell at his feet.
O Lakṣmī, meanwhile my own supreme four-armed form, divine and enchanting, was revealed by me together with you, Lakṣmī. 92.
In that very moment, the entire army on the riverbank vanished;
a great wonder then occurred there.
Then, the Blessed One appeared to me in person at my home; having granted me his vision, he accepted my worship, bestowed a boon, and imparted the means for liberation. ||94||
Having offered my devotion, I then stood for a moment with you and spoke to that devotee who knows the Self. (95)
To whoever worships me in this manner, for their sake I am in every way like a wish-fulfilling creeper; I fulfill their heart's desires.
Those artisans who, devoted to meditation upon me, shall fashion my image with pure intentions, free from greed and self-interest; (97)
"I shall grant them liberation, just as you have done here, O King of Devotees.
Having spoken thus, he revealed his true form within the house to Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī. (98)

And when I have been established for the purpose of worship, even though I have vanished from that established image, the devotee nevertheless constantly meditates upon me and likewise remembers me. (99)
When the time had not yet arrived, he arrived at that house by means of his celestial chariot;
he beheld the illustrious wife of that man and likewise his servant, Haridāsa.
Having caused those two to ascend to the divine state and having brought them to my imperishable abode,
I likewise brought others to my imperishable realm in due course of time.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this chariot-maker, my devotee, has indeed been delivered by me. By reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained. 102.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord Granted Liberation to the Chariot-maker named Haridāsa and His Family through Devotion," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of the stone-gatherer;
formerly, in the city of Sudāma, there was one named Dāmaśila.
This man, along with his family, resided there, engaged in the business of mining and selling stone;
indeed, hundreds of people served as his laborers, carrying out the enterprise.
Desiring to build a temple for the King of the Gods, they extract massive, long stones from the earth and send them to foreign lands. || 3 ||
The peaks are variegated, and the palaces are of diverse kinds;
they are made of white stone, divine, and adorned with the excellence of artistic craftsmanship.
The finest artisans produce those [images] fashioned from that stone through their skills;
for indeed, the excavation of stones takes place during the day upon the surface of the earth at the mines.
It is performed constantly by those who are experts in that matter and are urged by Dāman;
indeed, Dāman Śilāda is the overseer, the measurer, and likewise the appraiser.
He conducts inspections at the proper time regarding the mines and the ground,
and the laborers strive in the extraction and the hoisting.
With his cart and wagon, he possessed an abundance of many goods;
there, Dāmaśila indeed came for the purpose of trade to those who sought to purchase.
He purchases at the proper price auspicious stones that are suitable for images,
highly valuable, and likewise fit for temples.
Suitable for houses, suitable for walls, and others suitable for mats—
she gives these, possessing various values and qualities, to the one who seeks them.
The servants place those [women] upon a wagon belonging to Dāmaśilāda,
as well as upon bulls, camels, excellent elephants, and likewise upon *geṇḍakas*.
The excellent charioteers draw [the chariot] with buffaloes and mechanical horses;
for the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa himself provides protection everywhere.
It performs [actions] in ascending and descending, in extending, in rising up and withdrawing, in turning over and tearing asunder. ||13||
Some there weigh a hundred bhāras, some are even heavier than that;
those weighing half of that and half again are constantly being excavated. (14)
In some places, indeed, a cart meets its destruction due to the extreme weight of the rocks;
for on the rocky surface, the cart is crushed to powder and becomes mere refuse.
"In times of sudden calamity and the like, Lord Hari indeed protects [his devotee].
Having reflected thus upon his servants of karma, Śilāda’s son considered Uttama to be the best.
"Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, O Beloved, O Consort of Śrī, Hare!"—such is the worship, the congregational chanting, and the loud proclamation of Hari. (17)
He constantly instructed him in protection by which one attains liberation;
he himself performs worship and even causes his servants to do so as well. (18)
Upon the rocks he inscribed the names of Kṛṣṇa, which are endowed with merit:
the Kṛṣṇa-rock, the Rāma-rock, and likewise the Nārāyaṇa-rock. (19)
Lakṣmī-śilā, Rama-upalā, Rādhā-upalā, Hara-upalā, Deva-upalā, Mandira-aśmā, Mūrti-upalā, and Satī-śilā. (3.215.20)
The Viṣṇu-stone, the Brahmā-stone, the Parameśvara-stone, the Devī-stone, the Sūrya-stone, the Tīrtha-stone, and the Guru-stone. (21)
Mokṣaśilā, Ātmaśilā, and likewise Muktīśilā;
similarly Avatāraśilā and Golokaprastara;
Vaikuṇṭhaśilā, Cakrāśman, and likewise Śālagrāmaśilā.
The Bhagavat-prastara and also the Janārdana-śilā. || 23 ||
By him, for the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa, the sections on stones were composed under the names Yogaśilā, Jñānaśilā, and Dhyānaśilā. (24)
O men, by means of the yoga of the stone, I shall proclaim Nārāyaṇa;
they shall utter his auspicious name, which is supreme and the destroyer of sins. (25)
With this intention, Dāmaśilāda indeed inscribed upon the stones the names of Hari, which are truly bestowers of liberation.
Even human beings, under the pretext of stones, take up the names of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
indeed, the classes of his servants and the names of the merchant-princes are truly purifying.
Thus, by means of his devotion, true devotion consisting of kīrtana was brought about;
even ordinary men and women were purified by the sacred names. 28.
For him, a most great merit, consisting of a serene mind, has arisen;
indeed, it increases continuously as a form of grace toward me.
O Rame, hearing of the devotion of that devotee, virtuous, pious, and righteous mendicants and travelers come to his house. (3.215.30)
Having gathered together, they perform worship and the chanting of my glories, having indeed installed an image of me made of *śilājatu* in their home. (31)
They always worship him with devotion, great festivals, and excellent offerings;
they perform singing, dancing, and vocal music in the *rāsa* dance before him. ||32||
Having offered me incense, lamps, and the like, as well as food offerings and water,
they receive my grace and then depart.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the assembly of the virtuous truly attained nourishment in the palace of Dāmaśilāda; at that time, I was especially pleased.
Remaining constantly in the state of non-existence regarding the image, I accept the service performed and provide protection in every way. (35)
Now once, while the master was at home, all the servants were at the quarry, a distance of one krośa away, intent on extracting stones. (36)
Long and massive boulders were cast out by them and placed upon a cart,
but that cart was quickly broken.
Among the servants and laborers who were walking by the side of the cart,
two or three indeed fell upon the cart onto a surface of stone.
Alas, alas! Then, indeed, grief arose among the people there;
they even began to pray for water to drink. (39)
They gave water, and then they fell into a swoon, on the verge of death;
then others remembered me, Lord Nārāyaṇa, their protector.
With great effort, they suddenly raised the cart and the stone together with other men in order to relieve the burden that had overwhelmed them. (41)
Two or three of those servants were expelled;
deprived of their means and their light, they stood facing death in great misery. (42)
They continued in that state until Dāmaśilāda, having been informed by the servants, went quickly to his home with devotion. ||3||
Just as he approached the mine after indeed remembering me, Nārāyaṇa,
I arrived at the mine from the forest, disguised as a holy man.
Seeing those who were mendicants seeking food begging for water, I was filled with supreme wonder at their conduct. ||45||
I remained motionless for a moment, while they entreated Acyuta:
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, Friend of the Wretched! Revive these miserable men! (46)
Just as there is no killing of a human being for one who protects his devotee, you are the provider of protection to the destitute; you are the fulfiller of the desires of your devotees. 47.
You are the destroyer of all suffering; protect your own people.
No medicine would be effective here against one who is as shattered as a heap of pulverized bones.
In this body, when the blood has been exhausted, there is no life without you;
for these [beings] have no life without wonder or without spiritual attainment (siddhi). 49.
"These deer are as good as dead; no one other than you, O Yogi, is capable of reviving them, restoring them to health, and healing their fractures. (3.215.50)
Hearing those who were speaking thus, the virtuous one took water in his hand and gave it to them for sipping from the mouth.
Having established a protection and placed the ashes from his belly into both hands,
he diligently rubbed them all over the bodies of the broken ones.
Then they attained well-being; they were joined together and made free from pain, and they became filled with blood just as they had been before. ||53||
Just as those who have risen from sleep bow down to a virtuous yogi, so too,
having regained their life-breath, they found rest for a moment before the presence of the Holy One.
The virtuous man accepted alms and then ate water and food;
they all likewise properly partook of my gracious gift.
Then, pacified by [her] peace, they sat down while serving her lotus feet and asked me for the supreme means that destroys sin.
I have indeed related to them exactly as it is the supreme wisdom of Nārāyaṇa, which is likewise his form in manifestation.
Service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, and likewise the visiting of sacred pilgrimage sites—these indeed become destroyers of sin through the grace of the Lord. (58)
Through association with the virtuous alone, knowledge of Śrī Hari arises, as well as through the study of authentic scriptures and by listening to His narrations. (59)
Through the power of past impressions, consciousness arises for Hari;
through the practice of yoga, there is the sudden destruction of all impurities.
Through the path of the yogi and the path of Brahman, the form of Kṛṣṇa shines forth;
such is the beautiful synthesis that exists within the body. 61.
In the Vairāja [state], it exists as both subtle and gross, without distinction;
however, in the human body, these are the channels (nāḍīs), while in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), they are the rivers.
The cavities within the body are the oceans in the cosmic egg;
the soles of the feet are the netherworld (pātāla), the head is the realm of truth (satya), and the waist is indeed the earth.
The channels of the senses within the body have as their causes the channels of the senses of the Virāj; therefore, these two become one in essence. (64)
Those devoted to the practice of yoga reach the tip of the tongue through meditative absorption;
then, the yogins behold the end of the Vairāja-tongue.
In this way, through meditative absorption, they reach the limit of all the sense faculties;
then the yogins behold the end of the supreme sense faculties.
The Suṣumṇā exists in the center of this body, ascending from the navel toward the head;
the Iḍā is on the left, while the Piṅgalā is always situated on the right.
Having reached the head at the end of the Suṣumṇā, one beholds the Vairāja;
that [Suṣumṇā], being long from the Brahma-randhra, leads to the Vairāja yoga.
Indeed, in the form of rays of light, she [issued] from the Vairāja Puruṣa as far as the aperture of the Mahāpuruṣa; thus she is designated as "Tejaḥkiraṇā" (the Ray of Light).
Because she has attained identity with the Imperishable (akṣara), she indeed resides within Hari;
having reached identity with the subject (pramātṛ), she exists as the nature of rays.
Therefore, by way of the Suṣumṇā path, the yogi goes to the supreme state. ||3.215.70||
The ray emerging from Hari is the end-point of all incarnations;
for it exists pervasively among both lords and individual souls.
That is Brahman, that is consciousness, and that is indeed pure being and light. (71)
By his light all this shines, endowed with the radiance of knowledge;
and through an excess of affection, the splendor of one such as he increases.
Whether one is awake, asleep, or in deep sleep, wheneversoever there is a state of absorption in Hari for anyone through affection, he shall go to that very place.
Through the volition of Hari, and also through the power of Hari, as well as through the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will of Hari. ||74||
Living beings and their lords proceed forth, acting with knowledge and engaged in activity;
all living beings are under the sway of karma and are indeed not independent.
Indeed, through His knowledge, action, and will, the Lord is in every way the bestower of the fruits of actions for those who possess knowledge, action, and will. (76)
Those powers of Hari impel knowledge and the other faculties of men according to their respective past actions; by that means, the process of creation proceeds.
Indeed, through the practice of meditation upon Hari, the living beings of creation become divine;
possessing divine vision, they then behold the Sudarśana of Brahman.
That Brahman, devoid of the qualities of Māyā and the like, is the qualityless (nirguṇa) Taijasa Brahman;
endowed with its own divine attributes, it is the eternal Brahman with qualities (saguṇa).
The great-souled ones, who have obtained the true fruit of association with the virtuous, attain the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, the eternal Parabrahman. (3.215.80)
These yogis indeed go to Him, the Lord of the virtuous, who possesses a divine form in human shape—the Supreme Self of divine form. (81)
Many become divine, equal to Him, possessing the form of Brahman;
just as the beloved of Brahman is divine, so too are the liberated ones indeed innumerable.
Just as Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Satī, and Sarasvatī are divine, so too do men and women become divine when they have merged with the Supreme Self. 83.
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa, who is Nārāyaṇa, is indeed to be worshipped as the protector;
he is the giver of liberation and the giver of heaven, and the one who possesses the attainment of the path of Suṣumṇā. ||84||
In the home, Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana, must be constantly remembered;
Hari dwells in the form of the virtuous, and he, the refuge of the virtuous, is to be served. (85)
Having spoken thus and having rendered them fearless, I then gave this mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (86)
Then, O Lakṣmī, regarding me as their guru, they led me—who possessed the form of a saint and was a source of wonder to people—back to my own abode. 87.
They fed them exceedingly and caused them to drink desirable drinks;
they respectfully served them milk-rice mixed with sugar. ||88||
They indeed worshipped him and then begged for his forgiveness;
they drank the nectar-water from his feet, and I too drank it at that time.
Endowed with blessings and made objects of His compassion through grace, may enjoyment and liberation indeed arise for you always according to your desire. (3.215.90)
Then, O Lakṣmī, I was desirous of going to you, longing for a vision of Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of obtaining a direct encounter with Kṛṣṇa. (91)
When they made their request, I directed them there, saying,
"So be it," and they beheld me as Hari, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Having attained supreme wonder like those who have realized yoga directly, they then quickly manifested as divine beings of celestial form. (93)
They danced and sang, and being filled with extreme joy, they rejoiced;
they worshipped me, the Supreme Brahman, the protector, the savior of their very lives. 94.
Then, while they were looking on, I vanished from that image;
from that time forward,
those thousands of devotees became worshippers of the image, offering themselves entirely to me.
Then, when the time had arrived, Dāmaśilādaka offered food.
I brought his many devoted servants as well as his wife, named Kalā,
by means of a celestial chariot to my supreme, eternal, and imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, protection has been afforded by me, devotion has been inspired, knowledge has been granted, and auspicious power as well as liberation have been bestowed. (98)
In this way, at the end, I grant liberation to my devotees;
I also bestow divine nature upon them, for I am to be attained through devotion alone. 99.

From the recitation, hearing, remembering, or even praising this, there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation, as well as the desired, auspicious goal; I am the beloved Śrī Guru, the Master, the Lord, and the refuge for all. (3.215.100)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord protected the servants of the devotee named Dāmaśilāda, who was a stone-gatherer, and brought about the final liberation of Dāmaśilāda and the others," in the third section (the Dvāpara cycle) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to the beautiful story of my devotee named Sañjayadeva, who was an expert in the arts and crafts.
He was a devotee of me, Nārāyaṇa, residing in the city of Kutarka;
together with his family, he constantly worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī.
He knows the artisan in many ways, as well as those things produced from wood, stone, and minerals.
Trees, creepers, clusters of blossoms, and so forth; as well as gods, sages, humans, and the like.
