He understands, according to their respective natures, all kinds of beings— beasts, birds, serpents, insects, and so forth— as well as the principles (tattvas) and other such things, through his creative power (kalā).
In every kind of artistic craft, Sañjayadeva indeed paints me as Hari, yet in between [the figures], he depicts me in a subtle form, possessing a most minute physical appearance.
Just so that others might not know, [I placed] the essential [element] in such a way;
within the craft [was] an inner craft, and within that, the auspicious me.
For by remembering me, he makes that [work] "with seed" (sabīja),
since it becomes divine when offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, like the excellent yoga of Kṛṣṇa himself.
Thus the devotee always performs dedication to Kṛṣṇa;
every craft made of me is permeated by my essence and is graced by successful effort.
The devotee perceives within his own heart that devotion as being composed of His very essence,
wherein Nārāyaṇa and I myself are fashioned and come into being.
In all arts and crafts, he regards me as Nārāyaṇa Hari; he meditates upon me, acts for my sake, bows to me, and even worships me. (3.216.10)
Rising daily at dawn, he meditates upon me and performs my worship:
the bathing of my image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), likewise the bathing with sacred waters (tīrtha), and the offering of the respectful water (arghya).
They always offer me ornaments, cosmetics, and garments;
likewise, incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, and water.
Having bowed down and performed prostrations like a staff, he offers me fragrant oil, the essence of it, along with a costly seat and couch, while offering praise.
One should constantly seek that which is beneficial, both of this world and the next:
the company of the virtuous, service to Kṛṣṇa, and the chanting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s glories. (14)
At the onset of night, Sañjaya constantly performs [his ritual] at home together with his own wife Keśavatī and his son Suradeva. || 15 ||
He performs dance and song, listens to the wonderful stories of Kṛṣṇa, offers auspicious food offerings, and distributes the sacred remnants (prasāda). || 16 ||
Having eaten what is pleasing, he always thereafter applies himself to exertion;
thus indeed does Sañjayadeva remain steadfast in devotion to me. 17.
Under his command, other artisans and laborers remain;
they too, through the application of their respective crafts, worship the Supreme Lord.
Then once, the king named Khaḍgavarman, the lord of Vihāra, summoned him for the construction of his own new palace. (19)
In every corner and at every spot throughout the seven stories of the palace,
there were statues installed for the sake of representing all well-known species of beings.
The king issued a command, demonstrating generosity even in the expenditure of wealth,
as he gave to the craftsmen and artisans, satisfying them.
This devotee, filled with great joy, accepted the king’s command;
having duly honored the auspicious-eyed goddess of the earth according to the prescribed rite, he departed.
Having dug there for auspiciousness, the king himself laid the foundation with his own hand;
thus the seven-storied palace was completed, resembling the celestial abode of Indra.
In various places, they also installed great images that were beautiful,
diverse, gentle, and captivating.
Of Nārāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa, of Rādhā and Śrī, of Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī, and of Māṇikī and the wives of Brahmā. ||25||
Also the auspicious forms of the incarnations of Śrī Hari,
the lords, as well as the images of the goddesses and the great sages, gods, and yogis.
Of goddesses and deities, of humans and birds, of wild animals and domesticated creatures—of all embodied beings. ||27||
Likewise, there were images of purifying, auspicious, and famous beings, as well as beautiful sights of rivers and things born from the earth. (28)
He caused even those things visible to sight to vanish from view: the mountains, the planets, the lightning, the sky-dwellers, the clouds, and the oceans.
Having constructed such a great mansion at various locations,
he established me, the subtle and infallible Nārāyaṇa, within it.
With a serene mind and full of devotion, he offered the site for the dwelling;
the king, having summoned the brahmins, caused the ritual worship of the site (vāstupūjā) to be performed. ||3 1||
The king indeed caused oblations, feasts, and acts of worship to be performed;
he gave gifts, sacrificial fees, and rewards. ||32||
To the artisan, he gave an elephant adorned with golden ornaments,
as well as five villages, and likewise male and female servants.
The king bestowed appropriate wealth and other gifts upon the artisans;
then, having mounted the lordly elephant adorned with ornaments, he returned to his own palace.
Just as Sañjayadeva was proceeding, at that very moment,
an elephant on the path suddenly became frantic and overcome with excessive rut.
Invincible and exceedingly powerful, wandering about with a distracted and frenzied mind,
he became impossible to discipline, possessed by great delusion and transgressing his vows.
He is one who restrains the elephant-keepers, he is unapproachable, and likewise he is terrifying;
he is the performer of great nourishment and is endowed with a great, rushing speed.
Unrestrained and wandering on a wrong path, he ran about;
the men, terrified, fled indeed for the sake of protecting their own lives. (38)
No one remained where the elephant went;
Ambālikā, along with her attendants, was exposed and fell to the ground. (39)
Sanjaya the elephant-driver also fell down,
and the elephant, seizing my devotee Sanjayadeva with its trunk, struck him down.
The devotee suddenly threw it far away, and it fell into a pit;
indeed, in the middle of that bottomless pit, he fainted from the agony of the fall. (41)
There, the elephant remembered me, Hari, the protector of devotees, within his heart;
meanwhile, O men, the pit dug itself as far as the elephant had gone.
People gathered around him for the purpose of beholding and protecting him;
but prior to that, O Lakṣmī, I had already gone to the side of my devotee. ||43||
Touching him with both hands, I dispelled his fainting fit and his pain;
I granted him the vision of my own self as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having grasped him by the hand, do not lead him out from the pit;
he shall become healthy, devoted, free from disease, and devoid of all affliction and suffering.
And while traveling on the road, deluding men, the Blessed One said: "He has indeed come here for my protection. (46)
"By performing those [acts], I am free from disease and remain here without affliction;
thus, let everyone worship Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. (47)
Having said this, he pointed with his finger at me standing before him—
Kṛṣṇa, who had assumed the form of a brahmin, his beautiful body pervaded by splendor.
They bowed down to Hari and to me, who possessed divine human forms;
they prayed for their well-being, and I also gave them instruction.

All that is auspicious arises through devotion to Kṛṣṇa and through service to the virtuous; therefore, everything that ought to be done should be performed for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (3.216.50)
The favor of the virtuous is to be obtained, and likewise their virtues are to be attained;
the virtuous, who are always superior even to the gods, are auspicious and worthy of honor by those seeking liberation. 51.
They are to be worshipped like Viṣṇu and served like Viṣṇu;
the command of the virtuous is to be obeyed and held in the mind. (52)
One should behave without guile before the virtuous like a servant;
and seeing virtuous ones who are equal to Kṛṣṇa, one should bow down before them. ||53||
The virtuous, who are the very forms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, should be contemplated within one's own heart;
they are great, capable, divine, and auspicious in every respect. (54)
The purifiers, who are the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, are supreme, free from transformation, and have gone beyond Māyā; I too am within that Māyā.
"Indeed, the destruction of my delusion will come about through service to the virtuous;
all the sins of me, a commoner, shall go to their complete exhaustion. (56)
Thus, one who perceives the virtues of the virtuous shall become an ocean of merit in this world;
whereas those wicked people in the world who revile holy yogis— ||57||
They speak mutual slander and describe the faults of the virtuous, saying, "How these so-called holy men are indeed devoid of discernment! (58)
They do not know how to remain in the world, nor how to eat, drink, or speak;
they do not even know how to wear clothing or give it away. //59//
They do not know how to offer a welcome to one who has arrived as a guest, yet those who give counsel strive to proclaim their own greatness. (3.216.60)
"Desire, greed, attachment, and anger exist in him just as they do in me; 'this man is not virtuous,' 'he is a liar,' 'he is indeed virtuous'—thus do people perceive his faults. (61)
Such beings, with skin for their eyes, dwellers in the abodes of hell, and enjoyers of suffering, are born here as the servants of Yama after death. (62)
Sometimes such virtuous ones who are oriented toward liberation are not born at all;
they should be known as demonic beings in this world, for they cause harm to the righteous.
"You are indeed experts in the arts and crafts, especially this Sañjaya;
he shall maintain my form in every respect within all the arts."
In all those places, my devotion toward this object [of worship] arose;
through such application of devotion, Janārdana appeared in the form of a brahmin.
I have arrived as your protector, pleased by my service;
having served the virtuous Hari, may you go to liberation, the supreme state.
The image of Kṛṣṇa is to be worshipped like Kṛṣṇa himself, honored like Kṛṣṇa himself, and served like Kṛṣṇa himself;
likewise, the saintly are to be fully worshipped, honored, and served like Kṛṣṇa himself.
Kṛṣṇa is great and holy, endowed with all sovereign powers and other attributes;
he is the protector of all, omnipresent, and possessed of infinite power. ||68||
They enter the bodies of others and protect them from calamity and misfortune;
indeed, Kṛṣṇa, having entered their form, remains there for the sake of protection.
Having entered the image directly by His own will, He shines forth;
yet for me, He remains directly present just as before, and my boundary [of devotion] is always and in every way the same.

Indeed, out of respect, she must be protected by the virtuous at the forefront of their forms and at the forefront of their existence, having entered directly and in every way into the hearts of the virtuous. (71)
Therefore, I indeed abide here eternally; for the virtuous are to be served, and the boundaries of conduct must be maintained, which are equal to my own embodied form.
But those atheists who, regarding the image of the Existent as mere stone, consider virtuous men to be merely material beings, revile them. (73)
My words and the words of the virtuous are indeed granters of liberation;
yet those who treat them as false and meaningless are merely deluded by illusion.
The revilers and sinners will surely go to the suffering of hell;
in them, no knowledge of the self, the other self, and so forth, ever arises. (75)
No certainty arises for me regarding the form of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, no well-being whatsoever ever comes to such as him. (76)
Indeed, their wickedness does not reside in their physical forms alone;
rather, it exists likewise toward those who are virtuous and similarly toward their own chosen deities. (77)
Due to their lack of control over their own destiny and other such factors, atheism arises among many evildoers;
they do not acknowledge the incarnations of the Lord at all. (78)
Those wicked ones do not even consider Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Śrīpura, the imperishable abode, or the realm of Brahmā as manifestations of his glory.
Likewise, wickedness arises from association with the wicked;
indeed, wickedness also arises through the connection with prior sins and the like. (3.216.80)
Through association with the words and discourses of nihilists, as well as with the defects such as lust, anger, and pride, wickedness arises. (81)
The heart of the wicked does not retain the devotion of the virtuous toward Hari; therefore, one should never associate with a wicked person who is like a donkey or worse. 82.
Human beings seeking liberation in this world must certainly not engage in worldly affairs; rather, they should listen to the divine and excellent stories of Hari, which bestow divine awakening. 83.
The divine pastimes recounted by the virtuous should always be heard by servants, and association with the virtuous and with Nārāyaṇa should also be cultivated. (84)

My divinity is to be realized by the virtuous; my abiding in the form of the two awakenings (bodhi) is to be understood. My majesty is to be known, and one such as I is to be realized by the virtuous. (85)
I shall provide protection in every way for such a devotee,
just as protection was afforded here to Sañjaya when he fell into the pit by me.
"Abiding in the image, I shall provide supreme protection so that they may worship me;
through non-violence, I am Kṛṣṇa dwelling within all living beings. (87)
In every way, I must be conducted here by my devotees who are full of compassion;
non-injury is a powerful dharma, and bringing joy is the supreme dharma. (88)
One should please [the teacher] through the disposition of offering all one's possessions, and never harm him—whether by body, speech, mind, action, or even service. (89)
He shall please me and the virtuous, and from that he shall obtain heaven and liberation;
for anger, egoism, pride, and other such faults, which are injurious, must indeed be abandoned.
One should always abide in tranquility; Janārdana is to be worshipped, as are the holy sages who possess the sublime nectar of the Lord's feet. (91)
Having spoken thus, and having given to my devotees the mantra centered on me—*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*—[he departed]. ||92||
Having accepted the worship offered by the devotees, I quickly vanished;
meanwhile, the elephant was seized with great effort by the king's men.
Then, having pacified him with hospitable attentions, they gave him to Sañjaya.
Now, O Acyuta, when my lifespan is complete, I shall have abundant food for my devotee.
O Lakṣmī, for the purpose of bestowing liberation, I went in person to his house;
taking that devotee, as well as others, upon the elephant-vehicle.
Having displayed his divine power, he quickly brought me along with my army to the supreme,
divine, imperishable abode, as well as other master craftsmen.
O Lakṣmī, having thus protected the men and the devoted women by leading them to the supreme abode, I was seized by the hand and cast into a pit.
Artisans fashion my image and worship me;
through their devotion, possessing divine nature, they go to my supreme abode.
In whatever manner such [stones] may be, I dwell within those very Śālagrāma stones; likewise, I dwell among virtuous, chaste, and holy women, as well as among yogis. 99.
I am present everywhere within all consecrated images,
and I dwell especially within those who fulfill the minds of my devotees.
Wherever my dwelling may be—whether on wood, a wall, or a stone slab—everything indeed becomes divine through association with me, who am divine. (101)
Through my yoga, women, men, trees, and so forth become divine by my yoga; they always become givers of liberation. || 102 ||
Faults become virtues, and indeed the inert become conscious;
by my yoga, whatever things there may be, they all become divine.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord Protected and Liberated the Artisan Sañjayadeva from an Elephant through His Devotion," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this auspicious and purifying story of my devotee named Saṃbharadeva, concerning Citrakṛt. 1.
In the great village of Nimbakāla in Saurāṣṭra, there lived a devotee named Saṃbhara-deva together with his family; he was highly skilled in the art of painting.
He became the independent creator of all forms, assuming whatever appearance was required—whether that of a human, a beast, or even a bird. (3)
Just as the form, color, nature, visibility, and activity of insects, trees, creepers, and the elements such as earth and water arise [from their own causes]. || 4 ||
Just as her radiance, just as her smile, and just as her various gestures and postures were,
she then suddenly displayed them all within the paintings by means of the brush.
And also upon cloths, on walls, in dramatic performances, and in images;
in palaces, in temples, and in every way within the chambers of mansions.
And upon pieces of bark, wood, and clay figurines, that painter brings forth all the various qualities and states of nature.
Endowed with such arts, he worships me incessantly and indeed creates my subtle form within all manner of paintings.
Having made himself exceedingly subtle, he indeed knows his own task as accomplished;
yet that painting in which Hari is not present is a painting of fruitless action.
Wherever there is a painting of Hari’s form, that painting is fruitful in its purpose;
likewise, his very actions were always permeated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
His livelihood was always devoted to painting and centered on Kṛṣṇa;
even in his dreams, while engaged in the act of painting, the Lord Śrīpati appeared before him.
Rising early in the morning, she would call out my name: "O Nārāyaṇa!
Rādhākṛṣṇa! Harikṛṣṇa! Śrīmatkṛṣṇanarāyaṇa!
Having thus remembered and called out, she would then bathe and worship the Lord.
And with all the services that have been obtained, he offers incense and lamps.
Having offered the food offering, prostrated like a staff, performed the water-salutation, the waving of lights, and circumambulation;
and having requested forgiveness, one should partake of the excellent prasāda.
He enters the picture gallery and engages in painting pictures; many other artists also become present there. (15)
Those very same servants, through their association with devotion,
worship me alone— the Supreme Self, Śrīnātha, the son of Kambharā.
The protector of cowherd children, the beloved lord of Brahman, the husband of Māṇikī, the lord of incarnations, the lord of the liberated, and the destroyer of suffering. || 17 ||
Having gathered together at night, they all glorify the Lord of Ramā;
they dance before the image and likewise sing songs.
Then Saṃbhara-deva, impelled by the circle of devotees,
offers a description of the Form for the sake of attaining meditation upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Let my painters listen; Hari shines within my heart.
I shall describe Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, exactly as He has been seen. (3.217.20)
The Lord of the Imperishable, the husband of the beloved of Brahmā, possessing a divine human form,
pervaded by a halo of splendor, and having the brilliance of ten million times ten million suns.
He was illuminated by all his excellent limbs from which nectar flowed,
and he possessed golden hair reaching fifty-six and a quarter finger-breadths in height.
The Lord has golden hair and a golden form, consisting entirely of gold;
his face bears a serene smile, and his belly hangs down like a ball.
With eyes reaching as far as his ears, beautiful with the glow of ten million rays of light, his gaze filled with love, he possesses divine, direct vision. ||24||
He has a broad and elevated forehead, marked with a *tilaka* above the center;
on the right side of his forehead, there is a *tilaka* situated at the hairline above the eyebrows.
In the upper corner on the right side and in the upper corner on the left side,
his forehead shines brilliantly, adorned with a tilaka as dark and beautiful as a sesame seed.
On the upper part of his left side, there was a fine mole at the hairline where the parting was made;
on his beautiful cheek, near the corner of his left eye, he bore another mole. (27)
On the right cheek, it is endowed with four minute sesame seeds;
and above each of the two ears, it is endowed with a single minute sesame seed.
His divine eyes were as beautiful as sesame flowers and captivating to the mind;

he was adorned with two ears graced by long earlobes. He was beautified by teeth like jasmine buds, rich with a fine, white luster, and shone with a pair of lips possessing the glow of ripe, red bimba fruits.

He had a full face and a beautiful chin, with fine, reddish-brown hair; on his forehead was a saffron tilaka, with a crescent mark of saffron in its center. His forehead was adorned with long lines extending to both temples, shining with a central line resembling a half-moon.
A fine black mole shines upon the left side of the throat above the collarbone; a black mole in the hollow of the neck indicates one who is fortunate. (33)
The tongue resembles a red lotus and is presided over by Sarasvatī;
there is also a *tila* (mark) one finger-breadth deep below the pit of the throat.
On the right shoulder there is a small sesame seed, and below that another sesame seed;
and below that on the arm, there is indeed a third sesame seed as well. (35)
And below that, a fourth auspicious *tilaka* is also present;
furthermore, a fifth *tilaka* is located on the upper part of the forearm near the elbow,
and the sixth *tilaka* is on the upper portion of the forearm above the elbow.
At the joint of the elbow, there is a subtle *tila* of five;
above the elbow on the back part, a *tila* is situated.
In the forearm (*karanālī*), the *tila* is subtle, and in the wrist (*karabhra*), there is a *tila*. (37)
On the back of the hand there is a beautiful cluster of six sweets (laḍḍukas),
while on the palm there are a fish, a bow, a banner, a trident, and likewise arrows.
There are auspicious wheel-marks on her palms, which are red and possess the luster of the moon;
her fingers are tender and endowed with reddened, elevated nails. (39)
Her beautiful lines of body hair shine with a golden hue;
there is a conch-mark at the tip of her middle finger, and discus-marks on all four fingers.
On his index finger there is a barley-grain mark, and his hand is as radiant as the moon;
on his left shoulder, at the base of the collarbone, a dark mole shines beautifully. ||41||
Below that, near the arm, there are three very subtle sesame seeds;
and on the back of the shoulder, there is an extremely minute sesame seed of red color. ||42||
On the left side of the belly, near the flank of Nala, a single mole shines beautifully;
moreover, the navel is deep and depressed, and the belly is radiant. (43)
Three folds shine at the navel, and the belly is beautifully proportioned;
on the right side of the belly, three sesame-marks shine forth. (44)
There is one sesame mark on the right shoulder blade and two sesame marks on the right side of the abdomen; the breast-marks are dark in color, hairy, and endowed with beauty. (45)
His chest is broad and elevated, marked with the Śrīvatsa sign;
below the chest, there is a small mole situated above the belly.
Indeed, a beautiful mole exists on the left arm at the side of the belly;
moreover, a most splendid tilaka mark is also present upon the left arm. (47)
Likewise, there are two fine sesame seeds at the joint of the left elbow;
a single sesame seed resides on the forearm, and the nails of the fingers of the hand are auspicious.
There is a conch-shell line on the middle finger, while there are discus-marks on all four [fingers].
The palms of her hands and her nails were red, resembling land-lotuses;
she was radiant, possessing a form that emitted a captivating luster, enchanting to the mind,
capable of shattering the fortitude of women, and as beautiful as ten million gods of love.
Her divine form shines forth, full of the bloom of youth;
she is endowed with a sacred thread, and her neck is adorned with a radiant necklace. (51)
In one hand she holds a rosary, while in another she holds a pen;
her form shines forth, endowed with weapons such as the discus and accompanied by the sacred narrative.
On the hip of Bālakṛṣṇa, the form of Lakṣmī shines;
indeed, on the linga in the middle, two sesame seeds shine above and below.
Two very beautiful sesame marks reside on the right hip, and two sesame marks shine upon the lower part of the right thigh. (54)
Both knees are beautiful and likewise shine, being perfectly rounded;
moreover, there is a mole on the lower part of the right leg, beneath the knee. (55)
Likewise, a black sesame mark shines beautifully in the middle of the inner flank;
a sesame mark on the joint of the left thigh is most excellent and beautiful. (56)
Beside that, on the part of the thigh, there is indeed a great mark of a wound;
furthermore, on the hip of the dwarf, there is a very minute mole. (57)
Upon her left thigh sits Śrī, resembling the full moon;
she is invisible, radiant, divine, and the fulfiller of all desires. (58)
The shanks of the Supreme Self resemble the trunks of elephants and are well-developed; the hands of the Lord of Śrī-Ramā extend down to His knees. (99)
Indeed, a single sesame seed exists on the lower part of the left forearm;
it is auspicious near the wrist and at the edge of the foot’s hood.
A second auspicious mark, a subtle tilaka, is situated upon the line;
and on each foot, three ankle-bones indeed exist externally.
The soles of the feet resemble *kammānika* flowers and are as delicate as the *śirīṣa*.
And upon the red-hued [surface], there is a thick book adorned with a line of hair.
Indeed, the hairs above the joints of his fingers and thumbs are golden;
likewise, all his nails shine like the moon and are elevated.
On the palms of the feet of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, there are divine marks;
and on his form, the subtle marks described by Samudra are also present.
The *phullaliṅga* of the Supreme Self measures nine finger-breadths;
and on both feet, two auspicious upward-pointing lines (*ūrdhvarekhā*) exist, O knower of Brahman. (65)
The voice of Hari is always sweet and flows like nectar;
in Bālakṛṣṇa reside supreme generosity, beauty,
compassion, loveliness, and the possession of auspicious qualities.
The inexhaustible prowess of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa prevails;
all sovereign lordships and likewise all powers are truly present [in him]. (67)
All the splendors of adornment and all wonders come to pass;
all marvels exist as the riches of the sovereign of kings. (68)
For all glories indeed possess the quality of attraction for him;
here, truly, are all states of sweetness and all oceans of bliss.
All festivals and all joys exist within the Supreme Self;
He is the fulfillment of all desires and the inner controller of all. (3.217.70)
Like Hari, he possesses the state of being more beautiful than all that is beautiful, the state of being the giver of all, omniscience, and the constant capacity to assume all forms. (71)
Standing by his side were Śrī Rādhikā, Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, Ramā, Nārāyaṇī, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Kamalā, and others. ||72||
The beloveds of Brahmā, the liberated ones, the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as maidens and cowherd girls who are the beloveds of Hari, all serve this [Lord]. (73)
The liberated attendants, as well as the mounts and weapons, serve his lordships, along with the manifestations that are equal to him.
For the sake of the liberation of all living beings, he exists within human existence;
he alone is of divine form, whether he be a human or even non-human. (75)
The Blessed One himself exists here in person, even in human form,
accompanied by his own splendor as well as by liberated attendants and others.
The sphere of activity of the Supreme Lord proceeds with his entire retinue; there is no distinction whatsoever between his human and divine states. (77)
Wherever Kṛṣṇa is, there exist his abodes, the liberated souls, and the Śaktis;
all are divine, embodied, possessed of form, and resemble Kṛṣṇa. ||78||
Those men and women become divine in form and liberated;
indeed, all of you are divine yogis of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Let them worship here Tamana-Adikrishna Narayana, the beloved of Sri-Kanta,
the son of Gopala and Kambhari, who holds a flute in His hand.
Let them constantly chant the name of the Lord of Śrī, let them meditate upon the Consort of Kamalā, and let them serve the Beloved of Māṇikī; thus may they attain supreme bliss. 81.
Thus, that devotee of mine, standing in the midst of the circle of devotees,
constantly instructs the devotees with words that bestow auspiciousness.
The devotees regard Sambharadeva as their own teacher, the painter; they indeed honor him, offer devotion, and serve him. ||83||
Then, on one occasion, being pleased on the full-moon day of Āṣāḍha,
I observed the worship of the Guru and the worship of the deity performed by them in that house.
Quickly assume the auspicious form of the god Saṃbhara;
the god Saṃbhara is in the house, while I am in the courtyard. (85)
Beholding those two deities, Saṃbhara and Deva, all the people who were their worshippers, as well as the painters, were filled with a confusion mixed with wonder. (86)
And having gone there repeatedly, they saw in the courtyard and the house how two forms of the teacher existed separately and truly. (87)
Then they conducted an investigation at home and at the crossroads;
they performed the *ārārtrika* rite for both of them at the same time. (88)
The radiance within the body of the householder became obscured, while the light of the lamps situated at the crossroads was unobscured. (89)
They beheld Hari within the center of their bodies and recognized him as the one who wanders;
yet, because he was in the form of a teacher within the house, they thereafter called him Śrīguruvai.
From the house, Sambhara quickly went outside the sacrificial altar toward Hari;
while everyone looked on, Hari suddenly became concealed within Sambhara.
Considering this to be a most great marvel, they, filled with longing, offered praise:
"O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Hare Viṣṇu! O Lord Nārāyaṇa! O Master! (62)
"Please show us your grace so that we may behold you directly once more.
They danced before their guru and performed hymns of praise.
They performed various acts of worship toward the Guru and the image;
then, at the hour of midday, on the auspicious occasion of offering the food oblation (naivedya).
Then I myself appeared there again in the form of a Guru, O Rame;
and then you beheld me, the Guru Hari, in a divine form.
Then [he saw] the Lord of Śrī, endowed with four arms and marked by the discus and other signs, radiant, wearing a crown, and bearing the emblems described by his preceptor. (96)
Adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, crests, and rings, and distinguished by garments and ornaments enriched with chains and precious gems. 97.
They brought food and fed me, and likewise performed the nightly lamp-offering;
they indeed gave me water, betel-leaf, and excellent fragrances. ||98||
Men and women alike massaged my feet on all sides;
they offered words of blessing to me, and I bestowed upon them the gift of liberation.
"Quickly perform worship; the painter shall vanish from the image. They all, with joyful minds, took refuge in me in the form of their guru.
[He meditated upon] Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī.
Then, when another period of time had arrived and his lifespan was coming to an end, (101)
Possessing a divine form, he came with an elephant to bring [her];
he showed his own elephant to the wife of Saṃbhara-deva.
Then he revealed to me his own divine form;
thereafter, he granted me a vision of himself to Saṃbhara-deva.
Having thus fashioned that devotee Saṃbhara with a divine body,
as well as his wife named Citrasaritā with a divine form.
Having arranged for a golden palanquin and placed her upon an elephant,
he led her to the supreme imperishable abode, as well as others whose devotion had reached its fruition.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I raised up this painter as my follower;
by reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord granted a vision and liberation through the devotion of the painter named Saṃbhara-deva," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen to the story of the devotee Mauktikeśin, who dwelt on the banks of the Jharaṇā river and who removed the charcoal [of his sins]. || 1 ||
Mauktikeśī is my devotee, the king of the brothers of the Pārtha clan;
he is indeed the eternal illuminator of the mines and pits of his lineage.
There, thousands of people working as charcoal-makers were digging up the *kula* trees— dark-colored *pārtha* species— in the mine day and night.
Having worshipped me in the morning, he then proceeds toward the mine;
there, for a moment, he causes my worship to be performed by his servants.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrīśa, Hare Hare! (5)
Having thus prepared and caused [the vessel] to be made,
he quickly enters the mine-cavern along with his workmen.
They bury fragments of black stone and charcoal in a cave,
and they worship me, the Blessed Lord Śrīpati, at the moment of their exhaustion.
Having eaten at midday, those engaged in ritual action rest;
then Mauktikeśī awakens the people as if with divine light.
Without the worship of Kṛṣṇa, this vast and deep abyss of worldly existence—
which is bottomless and composed of latent desires— cannot be crossed by anyone at all.
There are countless tens of millions of crossings over birth, death, old age, and disease; likewise, there are crossings over karma, where the waters are driven by various activities. (3.218.10)
Without devotion to Hari alone, a person does not attain the end;
one who is unattached and associates with the virtuous attains the ultimate goal through dispassion.
These two exist in the heart, opposed and having different domains:
one leads [the soul] into illusion (māyā), while the second leads it to the Supreme Self (paramātman). 12.
One says, "I shall enjoy illusory sense-objects," while the second says, "I shall certainly not enjoy illusory sense-objects. || 13 ||
In that state, there is only one mind, illusory and perceiving illusory objects;
the second, the self named the living soul (jīva), constantly effects negation.
Having discerned thus, one should know the Supreme Lord by means of the self;
one should abandon all other objects here that obstruct liberation. 15.
Vāsanā, joined with the mind, is the impeller even toward sense objects; arising from the words of worldly experience, it even says, "Enjoy! (16).
Aroused by the discourse of the virtuous and dwelling within the self through meditation,
she indeed issues the prohibition, "Do not enjoy," regarding illusory things.
Worldly talk should be cast out, and the nectar of the discourse of the virtuous should be retained;
[for they are] father, mother, friend, kinsman, sister, brother, and maternal uncle. (18)
"Son, wife, queen, cow, horse, clothing, house, and wealth—'this is mine' and 'this is yours'—such are worldly attachments. (19)
Driven by the causes of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," they are cast into the abyss; they wander through the ritualistic sections of the Vedas and are born again and again. (3.218.20)
Having indeed taken to heart the words of the virtuous who bestow what is auspicious:
"He is neither father, nor friend, nor kinsman; he is not brother, maternal uncle, nor sister. (21)
Son, wife, queen, cow, horse, clothing, house, and wealth—none of this is mine, nor is it yours; rather, it belongs to the Supreme Self.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my father, mother, friend, kinsman, and husband; I, however, am the eternal servant of Śrī Hari, endowed with consciousness. ||23||
The father and mother are indeed the givers of liberation; I am their servant, possessed of great devotion.
For me there is no bondage, no Māyā, no ego-sense, and nothing that is "mine."
Through association with the virtuous, I am eternally pure, a devotee of Hari, and liberated;
for latent impressions (vāsanā) are indeed bondage, while liberation is the dissolution of those impressions. ||25||
In this saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering, happiness indeed exists in the dark state;
the worldly sounds of the virtuous contend as awakeners. || 26 ||
For those who possess great strength in that knowledge called discernment, which is constantly engaged in battle within the heart, victory shall indeed belong to them alone. (27)
Where Nārāyaṇa resides, and where the virtuous who grant liberation dwell, there alone victory abides; the power of illusion is indeed fruitless there. (28)
Kṛṣṇa dwells in the hearts of the virtuous, and victory always belongs to the virtuous;
for the saintly, whose very nature is instruction, reside within their hearts. (29)
Likewise, for those in whose hearts Kṛṣṇa always resides through the medium of this narrative,
strength and victory arise that grant the attainment of liberation.
Through association with virtuous outsiders, the virtuous within flourish; through association with non-virtuous outsiders, the non-virtuous within flourish. (31)
The strength of those who are nourished increases, while for those who are not nourished there is decline;
therefore, the virtuous should be supported, but never the wicked.
In whatever measure the virtuous may become pleased, in that same measure their livelihood is secured;
the satisfaction of the virtuous is nourishment, and through that, there is the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa. ||33||
When this is born, victory indeed arises for the individual soul;
one attains the kingdom of liberation and the great bliss of service to Kṛṣṇa. (34)
For the devotee who strives for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and likewise for the sake of serving the saintly,
the Lord, the self-sovereign ruler, is the witness as he fights.
Indeed, the Lord certainly becomes pleased when he sees death in battle;
for one who dies in battle, there is victory, and the Lord is pleased with him. (36)
He knows that this man has met his death out of devotion to his master;
he has certainly never turned his back [in battle], and therefore he deserves victory.
The master indeed grants him a reward even greater than victory;
therefore, one should fight with powerful men, facing them head-on and chest-to-chest for the sake of victory.
One must die facing the enemy with chest forward in battle for the sake of pleasing one's master;
one must die with devotion and according to dharma, keeping the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) present before one’s heart.
One who possesses the Discus within his body must die by serving the virtuous;
through devotion to Hari in human form, he shall go to the depths of the mountain cave.
Bad association must be abandoned in every way, while good association should certainly be cultivated;
the stories of the virtuous should be heard, and Kṛṣṇa should always be held within the heart. (41)
One should go for refuge to Hari solely for the sake of immediate supreme bliss;
certainly not for the sake of bodily comfort, nor even for the acquisition of wealth, sons, or kin.
One should not go for refuge to Hari out of greed for kingship or other such things;
one should go for refuge to Hari endowed with a state of desirelessness.
Since attachment to sensual existence arises as an obstacle to liberation, and since one must seek refuge in the destruction of desire, that [attachment] should therefore be abandoned. 44.
That which provides refuge from desire should be grasped, and that which is preceded by the absence of desire should be grasped;
for liberation arises with certainty through that which is thus grasped. (45)
When their desires are fulfilled, those who seek the attainment of their wishes worship Hari with true devotion;
but when their desires are not fulfilled, they abandon even that devotion entirely.
Even the wise abandon their understanding; what then can be said of the state of being a Blessed One?
On the contrary, they even practice atheism and engage in censure. //47//
Those who are motivated by their own self-interest fall indeed into the hells;
therefore, one should serve the Lord Hari with a state of desirelessness. 48.
Out of compassion, he indeed fulfills the desires of those who possess longing;
he bestows upon his devotees who have sought refuge the fruit born of taking refuge in devotion. 49.
The Lord, taking into account the devotee's dependence upon Him, surely bestows infinite merit;
yet, being under the devotee's influence, He makes even great suffering appear small for that devotee.
Indeed, the boundary of actions was bound by that very wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
Hari, remaining within, always bestows fruit according to one's *prārabdha* (commenced karma).
The Supreme Lord, who is independent, the creator of all, and the controller, bestows [results] with impartiality, yet especially out of compassion. ||52||
And if those who have committed exceedingly evil deeds should become His true masters,
Śrī Hari, out of compassion, [renders] even their very many karmas [ineffective].
Those things which are to be enjoyed over a long period of time, though they may be harmful and even cause suffering,
he indeed makes them enjoyable for only a short time and of little value.
One completely wards off the pain of a thorn with a splinter;
likewise, the giver of food and clothing wards off the suffering of extreme poverty. (55)
Only the devotees of Hari recognize this grace of his, and no others;
whereas the non-devotees impute faults to Hari, even where there are none.
Having cast aspersions on [the Buddha's] lack of lordship, they even abandon his refuge; they revile those equal to themselves and speak unspeakable nonsense. (57)
Having recognized him as my Lord, I have indeed spent all my wealth in every way;
and by one who has offered his very self, the virtuous have been honored.
Nevertheless, he has not removed even the slightest bit of my suffering; nor have I recognized his benefit to me—what will he do for me hereafter? (59)
Therefore, I have abandoned this [body] which possessed the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
having thus abandoned it, one proceeds from there into the hell of Māyā.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, for one's own ultimate welfare, devotion to Kṛṣṇa must indeed be practiced with disinterestedness; it is never for the sake of attaining worldly desires.
Mādhava does not accept the service of a devotee who possesses desire;
for the presence of desire in a servant is a defect characterized by longing. (62)
Thirst, desire, and longing are indeed the very embodiments of transgression; therefore, one who is devoted to Bhakti should never harbor longing for Hari under any circumstances. (63)
If one's longing remains unfulfilled, it constitutes an offense against the Supreme Self;
indeed, such an offense is a great transgression against Nārāyaṇa.
He cannot endure malice, suffering, censure, the description of faults, the disparagement of virtues, or false ascriptions. (65)
Hari does not forgive even the slightest offense committed against Him or His devotee; therefore, such an offense must never be committed under any circumstances.
The refutation of the formless nature of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the denial of His possessing qualities (saguṇatva), and likewise the disparagement of the virtuous; ||67||
A great offense indeed, which brings about rebirth in the great hells, must never be committed—whether knowingly or unknowingly—even when engaged in battle. (68)
In the supreme divine world, in his own imperishable state, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, exists with a divine form. (69)
Served by countless divine Brahmas and liberated souls, that Lord Māṇikīpati dwells here in human form out of his compassion.
Just as a human being composed of the elements is seen here [in this world] by her, so too is he divine;
yet he does not exist as one composed of the elements, but is divine according to the syllable.
That which is our eye is composed of the elements (bhautika), and it exists as something graspable like itself;
yet Hari, out of compassion alone, reveals [the truth] to us here.
Just as he is devoted, so should he be received, for he is under the sway of compassion;
he alone, with his assembly of devotees, is to be understood as the divine form. (73)
Therefore, there is nothing beyond that which is to be attained or even known;
yet, if one's own devotee truly desires to behold the abodes of all perfections, [then he may do so]. (74)
Then the compassionate Lord reveals it in every way;
that divine and imperishable abode exists together with it.
He possesses splendors together with Hari, as well as sovereign powers;
he is joined by his own abode, the Imperishable, and his retinue.
Kṛṣṇa exists upon the surface of the earth and is perceived by the eyes of men;
yet his imperishable abode is like that of a human, and his qualities are identical to those of worldly activity.
Just as liberated beings are equal to humans and their activities are like those of ordinary folk,
there is not even the slightest difference between those who abide in the celestial abodes and those who dwell on earth.
Those with the eyes of divine samādhi perceive the most excellent divine realms;
wherever Kṛṣṇa is, there is His abode, and there the liberated Śaktis reside.
All of them accept the food, water, clothing, wealth, prosperity, houses, and other offerings presented by devoted human beings, just like ordinary men.
Nevertheless, being free from desire, they accept those divine objects for the sake of the welfare of their devotees; by association with them, [the devotees] attain birth [in that state]. ||81||
Givers obtain that divine form in the imperishable state;
such is the case for Kṛṣṇa himself, as well as for his virtuous devotees at all times. (82)
For such greatness is indeed to be experienced, bestowing divine liberation;
for one endowed with the greatness of Kṛṣṇa, calamities truly do not occur. 8.3.
A devotee of Kṛṣṇa, even if he be a pauper, must never be treated with contempt;
for by insulting a pauper, there occurs the destruction of Kṛṣṇa who resides within him. (84)
All the activities of Kṛṣṇa, whether they be mundane or divine, should be understood as divine even for his devotees by one who knows devotion. (85)
Hari delights with devoted human beings for the pleasure of the minds of his devotees;
he also delights in desire and likewise delights in laughter.
He delights in the company of women with gestures that are in keeping with their nature;
nevertheless, his state of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) is a source of wonder even to ten million women.
Śrī Hari, assuming ten million forms and destroying desire and pride, takes human form for the sake of His own devotees and performs actions like an ordinary man. (88)
He may indeed manifest desire, anger, fear, greed, delusion, sorrow, and envy at times; yet all of that brings about auspiciousness for men.
Whatever has been heard, spoken, seen, meditated upon, or even rejoiced in—
all the deeds of Śrī Hari indeed grant liberation to human beings.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, appearing in human form, indeed fills the minds of men;
through the sense of shared humanity, the duty of service toward Hari arises in men. (91)
From him, when served and propitiated, one may find the supreme good—even a pauper, even one in a state of servitude, even a female slave, and even one devoid of merit. (92)
For one who has taken firm refuge [in him], there shall always be joy;
"The supreme good has been attained by me, and my companions shall be liberated. (93)
I have achieved my purpose; you too have achieved your purpose who abide by my words.
You are my true selves, and I am always the one who perceives the Self.
There exists nothing other than Hari as a reality to be perceived; all that appears to me is illusory.
Thus, my dwelling is here upon this earth, yet also in the supreme, imperishable realm.
There is no doubt in this matter; knowing this, one should worship Him.
The Blessed One will provide protection both in this world and in the next. 96.
Having thus instructed them and received their promise, they went to the mine for the sake of the work;
meanwhile, Hari, for the purpose of testing them, caused a flow of water against the wall of the mine.
Having fashioned a pit in the form of a great river, he brought [the water] together;
indeed, by the breaking of the walls through the excavation, it was like the flow of a mighty river.
A torrent suddenly arose there in that abyss;
all of them were satisfied by knowledge and freed from the fear of death. ||99||
Remember me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and rejoice;
for the water there in the cavern became like a lake.
Broken, submerged, and devoted, they worship me, the Lord of Ramā;
yet those who are established in the Self and possess knowledge have a firm refuge in their hearts. (10.1)
Joyful ones regarded me as their inner self, as if in meditative absorption;
my devotee Mauktikeśī remembered me while digging the earth. 102.
Submerged in the waters within the depths of the earth, I, with supreme devotion, worshiped Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī;
and then [I saw] those servants who were free from suffering and devoted to Him. (103)
There, in the midst of the water within the pit, I, the destroyer of the waters, appeared;
with my Sudarśana discus, I dried up the all-pervading water.
In a mere instant, indeed in a moment, I even blocked the current;
my devotees became truly at ease upon seeing the Sudarśana discus.
Upon seeing me, they were indeed immersed for a moment in eternal bliss;
then they worshipped me and prayed for the imperishable state.
I said to them, "Let it be so for the sake of liberation alone," and having instructed them on the firmness of devotion, I then quickly vanished from that place.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Thus did Mauktikeśī, the lord of the mine, bestow this mantra upon them. (108)
By the mere recitation [of the mantra], they all became possessed of divine knowledge.
Then, after some time, other men likewise [attained it] from Mauktikeśin.
By means of this celestial chariot, I have brought you to my abode, the imperishable, supreme state.
Thus have the deceptive ones of the Kula lineage been tested, as if they were pits dug in the ground.
O Lakṣmī, they have been protected and even liberated by him who is drawn by compassion;
through the recitation and hearing of this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighteen chapter, titled "The Description of the Testing and Liberation through Devotion of the Devotee named Mauktikeśin, the Lord of the Stone-Carbon Mine," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of that hunter,
a devotee residing in the village of Piñjala who served saintly persons.
There was a hunter named Cakradhara, devoted to violence;
though of the Śūdra caste, he was a thief for the sake of supporting his family.
Even one who is a great thief of domestic animals belonging to their owners, as well as a killer of wild animals such as hares and the like, [is reborn as a small insect]. || 3 ||
Driven by cruelty, he would commit acts of violence for the sake of satisfying his own life-force;
then, on one occasion, drawn by the lure of hope, he went into the forest.
In a thicket of trees, pillars, and bamboo, he saw the great seer Pautimāṣya in the form of a deer,
as well as his wife in the form of a doe.
By name they were Sāma and Kṛṣi; they were like a doe, possessing the form of a female deer, subsisting on leaves, flowers, and grass, and eating fresh sprouts and fruits.
Seeing that they were handsome and beautiful deer, the hunter took up his arrow;
meanwhile, the sage, perceiving him, vanished along with the doe.
Cakradhara, too, having become suspicious that the two had gone into the thicket of trees,
set out immediately to search for them, proceeding step by step.
Then, by the voice from the sky, the great sage said to that hunter:
"O sinner, do not set your mind here in vain upon one who is himself full of sin."
"I am not a deer; I am the great seer Pautimāṣya, who subsists on forest fare.
Together with my wife, I always wander here in the forest, dwelling in happiness. (2.219.10)
O great sinner, go elsewhere; you have fallen even from liberation. Having attained a human body, why do you not desire liberation?
Having heard this, the hunter said: "Constantly desiring sense-objects, I am a meat-eater here for the sake of obtaining nourishment for my lust."
Then Pautimāṣya said: "Lust is what leads you to hell, for in it there is unrighteousness—namely, the harming and the devouring of living beings. (1.3)
"Do not think that your dwelling will always be in hell;
do not, by casting human existence into desire, carry yourself to hell. (14)
Listen, hunter, if it pleases you, I shall tell you a story for your own benefit; for association with the virtuous is indeed a means of deliverance. (15)
This desire is a defect born of the body, arising from food, drink, and so forth;
it takes the form of semen as its gross portion, produced from the bodily constituents.
Throughout the body, there are particles of semen that provide nourishment;
these indeed constitute the gross, material form of Kāmadeva. (17)
Then, the mind also, which always resides within the *manovaha* [channel], moves from moment to moment throughout all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) within the body. (18)
Forming an intention through vigor, one draws [the seed] into the wombs;
it is produced when concentrated at the root of the *sivanī* channel. || 19 ||
And that [intellect], having attained non-difference with the mind,
becomes pervaded within the mind, conjoined with the subtle-form mind.
Through causes, the force of latent impressions, and action, [semen] flows from the penis;
therefore, desire is threefold and it always exists in three bodies. ||21||
The cause is subtle, consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) and having the nature of the mind;
the gross form consists of semen (vīrya), which is illusory (māyika) and does not belong to the Self. //22//
The Self exists as the very nature of Brahman, the controller of all the senses, and is distinct from hair, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and sinews. ||23||
Vigor possesses the nature of the six sheaths; the seventh is that which brings about enjoyment.
It dwells at the impure gate and departs through the impure gate. (24)
The bondage of the impure body bestows the city of Yama, the realm of sin;
from desire arise violence, anger, and delusion, as well as impure mental impressions and thoughts. (25)
Birth, action, death, suffering, and likewise agitation—all these arise from that evil desire; therefore, abandon it and conduct yourself according to dharma.
The seasonal gift must be bestowed; this is the eternal dharma.
One should not seek excessive enjoyment, for it creates an obstacle to the path of liberation. (27)
The virtuous sages and noble women are devoted to renunciation;
immersed in the bliss of the Self, they cast away desire far from themselves. (28)
Through the practice of yoga, they protect the bodily constituents in every way;
by constantly restraining the mind, they uproot latent tendencies.
Those lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins) are born with upward-directed semen;
they are devoid of the flow of perspiration and free from nocturnal emissions. ||2.219.30||
Immersed in the bliss of the Self that is Brahman, those stainless ascetics are born;
indeed, they are as capable as the Lord (Īśa) and as sovereign in their prosperity as Viṣṇu.
Those who are devoted to celibacy become creators of emanation like Brahmā, possessing the power of the Supreme Lord; for them, even fire and wind rise up as they approach. (32)
Those who know the Greatness (Mahiman) go forth in embodied form to offer a welcome;
at the end of their enjoyment, the supreme Brahman is to be attained by one who follows the dharma of Manu.
There is no end to craving for enjoyments; rather, craving increases through enjoyment.
Therefore, having renounced enjoyments, worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa. (34)
O wielder of the discus, go for refuge indeed to Hari, the wielder of the discus; having utterly shattered the wheel of illusion, become established in the wheel of Brahman. 35.
Thus addressed by the sage, O Lakṣmī, Cakradhara, who was of auspicious intent, indeed had his mind transformed by those instructions. (36)
He indeed desired a vision of his teacher, Pautimāṣya;
and for the sake of that vision, the teacher assumed a human form.
He granted him his own vision, caused him to drink water,
gave him the water from his feet, and utterly destroyed all his sins.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having given him this Vaiṣṇava mantra, he caused him to perform worship with the leaves of Vṛndāvana. ||39||
The hunter also thereafter worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
having returned home purified by the sacred ford, he caused his wife to be purified as well.
Having forever abandoned violence and theft, he who worships me, the Supreme Lord, and always worships Kṛṣṇa at the Tulasī tree, worships me. (41)
Even while undertaking a journey, he carries out the service of the virtuous with wild fruits obtained through their grace;
from that time forward, he has performed the service of the good constantly with forest-grown fruits.
He indeed assumed the form of a holy man and thereafter became one wearing matted locks;
his wife likewise wore matted locks, smeared herself with ashes, and was a worshiper of Tulasī. (43)
She became perfected in her vows and distinguished by her practice of eating only the remains of offerings;
thus, with a pure mind, out of devotion and according to the sage's wish, I [acted]. (44)
When the time for his liberation had arrived, I, Hari, appeared before him in a divine form; and he, along with the woman, beheld me.
Covered in dust and overwhelmed with emotion, they bowed at his feet and fell prostrate, having hurriedly offered him a welcome for the sake of their liberation. (46)
While the two elephants were immersed in love, they quickly offered me forest fruit;
then, casting off their bodies, they ascended with divine forms. 47.
O Rame, having been sent by me, those two went to Vaikuṇṭha;
thus was liberation attained by the hunter through the association with a true guru. 48.
In the same way, however, for those who are devoted to the virtuous, their latent impressions (vāsanās) perish and their mind becomes eternally pure. (49)
By your grace, as well as that of the virtuous, my faults such as lust and anger, and whatever other sins exist, shall perish; and I shall become possessed of a divine form.
O Lakṣmī, they go to the supreme Brahman, which bestows eternal bliss; by reading or hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained. 51.

Thus ends the two hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Hunter Cakradhara’s Sins, such as Violence, Were Destroyed through Association with the Sage Pautimāṣya, and His Subsequent Liberation through Devotion," in the Third Section on the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen to the story of that devotee, a slanderer indeed, who resided in the city of Saṃbhala and had offered himself to Me.
There was a devoted attendant named Vāṭadhara, a servant of King Sutārasiṃha, the lord of the earth. || 2 ||
He was skilled in the art of statecraft, clever in pleasing the king, diligent in legal proceedings, and experienced in the exchange of goods and other such matters.
He was an object of favor for the king and queen, a refuge for Māna, devoted to the Rāṇa family, and one who rose above the caste of his own residence.
He perceives with a sharp intellect and acts accordingly with his mind;
he investigates with knowledge and deliberates with wisdom.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the faculty that determines objects; thought (*mati*) has the senses as its domain;
knowledge (*jñāna*) is the clarity of discernment; while wisdom (*prajñā*) is fresh intuition. || 6 ||
In this way, consciousness dwells within the enclosure (vāṭadhara) like one skilled in his craft;
it certainly seeks out the enclosure for a task that is otherwise impossible to accomplish.
Therefore, he brings a task to completion and is praised by kings and others—
just as an elder, a minister, a judge, and a teacher are.
Although this Vāṭadhra is thus possessed of excellent conduct,
nevertheless, being subject to his own nature, he occasionally practices backbiting.
From the queen to the king, O King; from the king to the queen; from the king to the minister;
from the minister to the subjects; and sometimes from the queen to the king. (3.220.10)
He speaks in such a way that it may remain unmanifest so that others do not understand it, but the listener alone understands it. 1.1.11.
Then once, on the occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), the queen gave abundant gifts to the Brahmins, the poor, and the virtuous, including food and other provisions.
The Queen of Dvīpī gave away as a gift the wealth that was in her own hands—such as concealed jewels and gems—which the king did not know of at all. (1.3)
The keeper of the enclosure, having been appointed to give the island-born elephant, understood the situation;
thereafter, the queen gave auspicious food and gifts to the virtuous.
The virtuous who take refuge in Hari partake of the desired foods;
among them, there was one ascetic named Ghaṭyayana who remained detached.
He dwells in one place for only a moment, not longer;
indeed, while he is eating there, [the food] arises in rows.
When one ghaṭikā had passed for him, he arose, abandoned his meal, went to another tree, and stood there for another ghaṭikā. || 17 ||
Having drunk water from there, he indeed went to another place;
thus, staying for but a ghaṭikā, he repeatedly goes to yet another spot. (18)
The gatekeeper, seeing him restless and having abandoned his food, searched for him throughout the evening and quickly found him where he was. (19)
Having gone there, bowed, offered the fruit, and performed a salutation,
he asked the reason for her agitation while bowing repeatedly.
Ghaṭīyantra then said to him: "O Lakṣmī, the cause of your fickleness is that you do not remain in one place for more than a single ghaṭikā; yet, that very quality is your true virtue. (21)
Bondage shall not exist anywhere, and passion shall never arise; possessiveness shall not occur at all, and dispassion shall be constant. (22)
Non-possessiveness itself is his vow; by it, however, [the body] is protected.
Long-term residence leads to bondage; therefore, one should not practice long-term residence. (23)
Whether in water, on land, or among trees, staying for a long time is fraught with danger;
for holy men, a stable posture should last no longer than the time it takes to milk a cow or a single ghaṭī.
The seat of the hour-glass (ghaṭī) is within Māyā, while the eternal seat belongs to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; having understood this through discernment, my practice is the restraint of mental agitation. (25)
From association, affection is born; from affection, the sense of "mine" arises.
Through that [sense], attachment occurs, and through that, latent impressions (vāsanā) are produced there repeatedly. (26)
Co-dwelling is indeed bondage; separation is the supreme liberation.
Latent impressions must be abandoned in every way; association must be renounced by the high-souled one. (27)
One who possesses discrimination should attain a state free from latent impressions through dispassion, by being devoted to the Blessed One and established in the Self. (28)
And by perceiving the defects of suffering, there shall be freedom from latent impressions:
"I am the self, a devotee of Hari; I do not belong to Māyā nor to karmas. (29)
I am of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss, distinct from the perishable body;
I am firmly established in the refuge of Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable Lord.
I have no passion for illusion (māyā), nor any taste for the objects of the senses;
I dwell in and rejoice in the internal Śrī Vāsudeva.
Thus, for one who is constantly discerning and possesses firm dispassion, the sprout of attachment does not arise even when in contact with the most excellent objects. (3.2)
Even while dwelling in delightful divine enjoyments, he remains disengaged in mind; being unattached and indifferent, he is considered one who is free from latent desires.
They should grasp the virtues of the virtuous and recognize their divine nature;
they too shall become enriched with divine qualities and always victorious over illusion.

But those who seize upon the faults and defects of the virtuous, being indeed enveloped by desire and the like, they truly come into existence as those whose nature is dominated by desire and the rest.
Afflicted by desires and other such passions, they wander about in extreme misery;
they obtain neither liberation, nor a good heaven, nor even worldly prosperity.
For those who revile, the sinful, and the wicked—whether men or women—who perceive divinity only in the company of the virtuous, surely fall into the hells. (37)
They go to the supreme state of Brahman, their divine nature greatly increased;
for their senses indeed become blunted by Māyā. (38)
Whether he be a king or a householder, even one who is prosperous and possessed of enjoyments, having attained such knowledge as this, he conducts himself beyond the realm of sense objects;
through the conjunction of his previously commenced merit, he remains even while situated in the midst of sense objects.
Nevertheless, he remains like a holy man, free from attachment like a yogi;
for even while eating, he is truly a non-eater, just as a lotus leaf remains untouched by water,
or as one with acid-ridden teeth performs the act of chewing chickpeas.
Thus, he becomes entirely incapable of grasping sense objects;
consequently, the illusory latent impression (vāsanā) of one who is thus blunted dissolves away.
He who knows even slightly the flavor of illusion has no latent impression [of it];
therefore, one should cast off the flavor of illusion from the heart. 43.
In the directly perceived form of the Blessed One, one should recognize all-encompassing perfection;
by that alone, all undertakings are accomplished for the yogi of devotion. 44.
Having engaged in the company of the virtuous, one must understand this very point:
for one who knows thus, Hari certainly fulfills every desire. ||45||
The latent impressions of one who offers their mind [to Kṛṣṇa] perish right here;
for him by whom the mind has been offered to Kṛṣṇa, there is not even a moment without Kṛṣṇa. (46)
In separation, it acts like an eon; or there may be a great burning in the heart.
When Kṛṣṇa has arrived, peace shall arise, and the desire to behold him increases day by day.
Upon hearing of Kṛṣṇa’s majesty, great joy shall arise;
and toward activities related to Kṛṣṇa, a supreme inclination shall emerge. (48)
One should always be intent upon carrying out the instructions of Kṛṣṇa;
such a person, even though far away, dwells in the presence of Mādhava. (49)
But one who transgresses commands, devoid of love, and unfaithful—such a self-interested and wicked master should be understood as being far away even when standing right beside him. (3.220.50)
Therefore, just as the Lord Mādhava dwells within one's own heart,
so indeed should His residence be established by oneself in the imperishable state.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Recite this mantra daily and worship the Imperishable Lord. (52)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Ramā;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Lord of the Universe! ||53||
Thus, cause the wise king and his subjects to hear this constant devotion to Śrī Hari; through that, their highest good shall come to pass. (54)
Thus did that virtuous Dhaṭyayana, a servant of Hari adorned with excellent qualities, give this instruction on prosperity to Vāṭadhara.
Vāṭadhra also went home and performed worship as he had been instructed;
and he constantly engaged in devotion, chanting "Hare Kṛṣṇa."
Ghaṭyayana, however, departed for another village while remembering Hari;
Vāṭadhra, moreover, became a great devotee who brought about liberation. (57)
He indeed bestowed upon the king, the queen, and the subjects the mantra that grants liberation;
he caused them all to perform the worship of Hari with the name "Kṛṣṇa" in every way.
Indeed, in this world, virtuous qualities truly arise in one who is endowed with devotion.
Nevertheless, the innate nature of a base character does not cease. ||59||
Even if one were as great a devotee as Garuḍa himself, his inherent nature as a serpent-eater does not perish; it remains a quality of his very birth. (3.220.60)
Even monkeys devoted to Rāma do not abandon their animal nature;
for even a lion, though devoted to Pārvatī, does not give up his violence.
Even though he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, that Kṣatriya does not abandon battle;
even though he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, that Kirāta does not abandon his forest-dwelling way of life.
The cow and the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa do not abandon their grazing;
this sky-clad mendicant, a devotee of Viṣṇu, likewise does not abandon his mendicancy. (63)
To report to an enemy or another person one's own hidden qualities—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—as if they were concealed, is indeed considered malice (*piśunatā*). 64.
Whatever fruit arises—whether it be affliction, war, or even strife; or despondency, agitation, anger, or even destruction—[all these result from such actions]. (65)
Therefore, one should never engage in backbiting toward anyone;
rather, one should look for virtues and not point out faults. 66.
One who perceives virtues proceeds happily and is even born as a meritorious person;
one who perceives faults becomes miserable and is even born as a sinful person. (67)
Slander indeed brings about harm, whereas instruction bestows virtue;
one must never engage in slander, but should occasionally offer instruction.
If there were such fitness, then even instruction would not be otherwise;
[this applies] toward father, mother, brother, sister, mother-in-law, and wife. (69)
One should never speak maliciously even to a master, a kinsman, a disciple, a daughter, a son, a daughter-in-law, an elder, or a child. (3.220.70)
One must never speak slander against the king at any time, whether to the king, the queen, the minister, the prince, or to the subjects. (71)
Due to the fault of his low birth, he once committed slander,
reporting to the king that the queen had made a gift.
She gave secret treasures such as diamonds and gems to the twice-born, and she also provided food for the virtuous and bestowed ornaments upon them. ||73||
Then the king, having learned that Guptadhana had given [the wealth] as a gift, summoned the queen and asked: "Tell me, where was the wealth and so forth given? (74)
Whatever was given without my command, or whatever was done that was not desired by me—that was indeed done for me.
All your wealth was kept hidden and always preserved for your own sake;
it certainly could not have been for the purpose of giving, and thus what was given was not properly done.
A woman must not do anything at all without having obtained her husband's permission. ||76||
O Queen, let that beloved wife who is not truly dear go to her father; she who secretly squanders wealth will eventually bring about total ruin. (77)
"Such a beloved wife as this should not have been protected by me in the house;
go, O Goddess, to your own father and dwell there for a long time in happiness. (78)
Having been addressed thus, that beautiful woman was overcome with great sorrow and wept;
then the king [bestowed gifts] for the sake of Khavāsa, who was in the form of a door-keeper. (79)
For he inflicted punishment that stripped them of all their possessions and placed them in fetters;
the doer, the one who causes it to be done, and the one who approves of it are equal in this matter.
Thus the king imposed punishment; he seized the house-gardens and even confiscated the wealth and property of the devoted Vāṭadhārin.
Vāṭadhra, though bound in fetters, worshipped Hari most piteously;
and the queen, stripped of her honor, remained in her own palace deprived of food.
For Vaiṣṇavī, established in her vow, quickly became desirous of death;
she thought, "In the practice of charity there is no suffering; how has this suffering come upon me? (83)
"May Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the remover of suffering, take away my pain"—thinking thus, she remained standing before my image, having undertaken a fast. (84)

Even one who is in shackles, or likewise one who is confined by a fence, or one who stands in a fast unto death—there shall indeed be no punishment for such a person regarding the act of giving, provided he considers it as being directed toward Hari. ||85||
Having reported the arisen suffering, he meditated upon the Lord within his own heart; yet that event spread even among the subjects, despite being kept secret. (86)
Grief suddenly entered among the subjects, the classes of brahmins, the virtuous, and the women, for the king had not acted as was appropriate. (87)
Thus, news proclaiming the gift spread everywhere:
"Indeed, charity is the duty of kings; a virtuous deed has been performed by the queen. (88)
"For the king who enjoys his kingdom, there is no deficiency whatsoever in his wealth";
thus indeed did the livelihood among the subjects become exceedingly prosperous. (89)
For the sake of destroying the queen's sorrow and for the peace of Vāṭadhāra,
the subjects also remembered Hari and gave blessings that bestow happiness.
When that seven-day fast had passed, at night in the prison cell, Mādhava—
namely I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— appeared.
Thus, as the protector of my devotees, I went to the queen’s palace,
adorned with a crown, necklace, and the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Having granted her my own vision, I gave the drink of milk to the queen;
thereafter, I likewise gave the drink of milk to Vāṭadhra.
Having offered words of consolation,
he, appearing in the form of a brahmin, possessing great splendor and being the best among those who know the treatises on dharma, approached the royal palace.

He offered me the royal throne, and when questioned by me regarding his health, he told me that he was free from disease and that his family lived without hardship, provided he observed the proper conduct.
The king related the account and the cause of his distress;
he then instructed the king that a woman has independent authority over her own property.
Even in that regard, she who performs meritorious deeds is fit for the form of giving; indeed, the husband of a virtuous woman who is devoted to him truly crosses over [to liberation]. 97.
The gift of a cow, the gift of jewels, and indeed the gift of ornaments shall deliver her;
for the gift of a husband, even one who is a king of great sin, is the supreme gift that delivers her. (98)
Therefore, O King, honor a virtuous woman as is fitting, and likewise honor the Vāṭadhra here, who performs his duties with integrity. (99)
Having said this, I myself manifested my own form, pervaded by light, to the king;
he rejoiced and fell at my feet.
He begged for forgiveness and liberation in the abode of Nārāyaṇa,
and I became invisible, having accepted the worship he had performed.
The king honored the queen and his own attendants with respectful offerings;
likewise, he caused a festival to be celebrated and made auspicious proclamations regarding gifts.
He pacified the quarrel with affectionate words and gifts,
and likewise showed honor to Vāṭadhra by returning his daughter to him.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that queen was protected by me at that time;
though she was desirous of death and had fainted from hunger, she was given milk to drink.
Even Vāṭadhara, my devotee, was protected from royal punishment;
then, when the time had arrived, he informed the king of his devotion. (105)
Then, by means of my own celestial chariot, I brought the queen and Vāṭadhara to the imperishable,
supreme abode, which is free from all malice.
From reading, hearing, or remembering this, there is the destruction of sin;
one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as heaven and one's own desired supreme delight.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection and Liberation by the Blessed Lord of Vāṭadhara Piśunakhavāsa and King Sutāra Siṃha, as well as the Queen of Dvīpa," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the housebuilder.
In the city of Takṣaśilā, there was one named Śivajaya. (1)
He was devoted, skilled in architecture, an expert builder of temples and houses, knowledgeable in the layout of cities, and a constructor of divine abodes and other structures. || 2 ||
The preeminent artisan, through his own intellect alone, brings about the creation of artistic wonders;
he is the builder of the royal palace, having manifested a new kind of craftsmanship.
Capable of assuming nine forms and moving within the range of the nine stories and so forth, he constructs palaces resembling celestial abodes out of countless jewels.
Once, a sage named Vṛṣaparvan approached him;
he was a great devotee of the Lord, a worshiper, virtuous in conduct, and well-restrained.
Rising up suddenly, Śivajaya offered a welcome;
full of devotion, he presented the sage with water for his feet and the honey-mixture.
He seated him upon a beautiful, pure seat, offered water,
and performed the massaging of the sage's feet and the rubbing of his limbs.
The sage, with a joyful mind, inquired after his welfare;
he too, upon arriving there, said to him, "I am well."
That house where the feet of a virtuous man are honored with faith is indeed divine; any other is merely a cremation ground.
Today all my merit has perished and my demerit has increased;
yet I am blessed, for that divine personage truly shines today within my home.
Having spoken thus and observing a vow of silence, he said to Vṛṣaparvan:
"Teach me, who have come to you for refuge, that which is the supreme welfare."
Then, O Lakṣmī, Vṛṣaparvan, having remembered Anādinarāyaṇa, instructed him in many ways for the sake of Śiva’s victory and for liberation.
O Śivajaya, listen: affection for Kṛṣṇa bestows liberation, whereas lack of affection for Māyā arises from the perception of her as inferior and so forth.
Affection for Kṛṣṇa arises from the cognition of His supreme excellence;
that excellence is such that He is Himself the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord. (14)
Savitṛ, the sovereign of all abodes, the lord of the virtuous, the lord of all who are liberated, the lord of all sovereignty, and the lord of Ramā. || 15 ||
Among all the Blessed Ones, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa is the most blessed;
he is the inner self above all and the bestower of the fruits of all actions. ||16||
The Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is that within whom nothing whatsoever exists independently;
for without His will, even the powerful wind cannot move a single dry leaf. 17.
He indeed does not act for the sake of movement; he is the impeller himself.
That very Blessed One is here on earth in the form of a holy man (sādhu). 18.
Possessing a form according to his will, he dwells filling the minds of his devotees;
divine, with divine conduct, and in every way of divine form.
