For every action arising from his body becomes a giver of liberation, for he in whose heart such greatness of Hari exists. (3.221.20)
Twenty-one people indeed rescue that devotee: ten from his lineage, ten from his family, and he himself as the twenty-first.
If they were to accept in every way the virtue of that devotee, [they would say]:
"Oh! Indeed, a purifier who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa has been born in our family. (22)
"By that [act], our great fortune will result in our deliverance;
through the merit of the devotion he has performed, we, his family members, shall also attain it. (23)
Those who possess such virtues cross over [the ocean of existence]; of this there is no doubt.
Others as well, possessing virtues, become partakers of merit. (24)
They indeed cross over saṃsāra and go to the imperishable abode—those who proclaim the qualities [of the Lord] and those who truly grasp those qualities. ||25||
Those who accept words of praise go to the abode of Kṛṣṇa;
[so do those engaged in] discourse about the devotee, singing of the devotee's virtues, and offering salutations to the devotee. ||26||
Praising devotion, the grace of devotion, and these [deities] who grant liberation—these belong to the devotee;
likewise, those who harbor hatred toward the devotee, as well as their relatives and others, [belong to the enemy]. ||27||
Whosoever they may be, those who go to hell are impelled by Yama:
the wrathful, the envious, the proud, the deceitful, and the lustful. (28)
Those who are hateful and those who are slanderous certainly go to hell;
but those who, having completely abandoned such faults, worship Janārdana, [attain liberation].
Devoted to love for Kṛṣṇa, filled with love for the Lord, and intent on the service of the Lord, they go to the abode of Hari.
Indeed, they become endowed with excellent qualities equal to the qualities of the Blessed One;
a devotee possessing the qualities of the Blessed One brings about liberation for those who have taken refuge in him. ||31||
Protecting his own dharma, likewise achieving freedom from passion, established in the Self and established in Hari, the affectionate one attains the supreme state. ||32||
Whether in an auspicious place or time, or at the beginning of the waking state and so forth in a favorable setting,
or even in an inauspicious or contrary situation, the devotee, casting off the body— (33)
Favored by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he indeed proceeds to the supreme abode—whether he be a non-devotee, a hater of Hari, a hater of the virtuous, or a slanderer. (34)
He who is indeed empty of dharma and so forth, even regarding auspicious places and the like, goes always to the terrible abode of Yama after casting off the body. ||35||
Whatever state of mind has been practiced will arise as one's destination at the end;
whether death is auspicious or inauspicious is not the cause for a good or bad rebirth. (36)
The devotee attains the upward path, whereas one who is other than that faces a miserable state.
The all-seeing Guru Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of mercy, leads his own devotee to the imperishable abode; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Or rather, by the power of the worship of his own Nārāyaṇa, the devotee [attains this]. ||38||
Worshipping Kṛṣṇa, he himself becomes independent and goes to the imperishable abode;
like the Lord Himself, he is capable of the dissolution and creation of universes. (39)
What is the measure of this body’s maintenance or its abandonment?
Indeed, such a devotee as this is truly rare upon this earth.
One should become such a devotee in whom there is no deficiency;
one should become such a wise person in whom there is indeed no attachment elsewhere. (41)
One who observes such vows shall attain devotion to Lord Hari;
one who possesses such qualities shall attain the state of the Imperishable Brahman. ||42||
One should cultivate such a divine state, looking upward beyond the world of illusion;
one’s residence shall be at the pinnacle of liberation, raining down eternal bliss.
That alone is auspicious, O Śivajaya; anything else is inauspicious.
Listen to all wholesome deeds; having heard them, practice them.
He for whom the time for the sake of Hari is both morning and evening,
and in whom the worship of Kṛṣṇa is his very principle— he is indeed skilled.
That place where the image of Hari is present—in one's home, in a shop, in a temple, on the ground, in a field, in a garden, or during religious observance—is considered auspicious. (46)

But that action which is for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of the goal, for the sake of the gods, for the sake of the self, and also for the sake of liberation—that action is considered skillful. (47)
Indeed, that association which is with the virtuous brings about the knowledge of Dharma and happiness; it destroys latent impressions, produces love for Kṛṣṇa, and is truly auspicious. (48)
That mantra which destroys delusion, bestows knowledge, and illuminates the heart;
which is divine, joined with the name of Kṛṣṇa, and is indeed skillful, is the destroyer of sins. 49.
That initiation which bestows the state of Brahman, which is purifying and destructive of sins, which produces knowledge and grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa, is indeed auspicious. (3.221.50)
That meditation which bestows peace, destroys the agitation caused by the suffering of illusion and so forth, grants eternal bliss, and confers a divine state—that indeed is wholesome. (51)
He who bestows divinity, likewise destroys faults,
is a savior, a purifier, a benefactor in liberation— he is indeed skillful.
She who causes one to drink the nectar-milk of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who nourishes devotion, who reveals liberation, and who is indeed auspicious—she is the Mother. 53.
He who is a father, a teacher in the exertion of protecting righteous deeds and the like, and a guardian of the great path to the world of Brahmā—he is indeed skilled. (54)
That brother who maintains or even causes to be performed an action that grants liberation, being skillful, bestows upon him a divine splendor that grants liberation. //55//
That sister who gives food to her brother, which has been offered to Brahman, is indeed skillful;
she bestows the blessing that grants liberation through Brahman.
That wife who bestows yoga upon Śrī Hari, who is His servant, who binds Kṛṣṇa, and who bestows prosperity—she is considered auspicious. (57)
That son who, through devotion to Kṛṣṇa and religious observances, delivers his own father and wins his father's favor, is considered truly skilled. (588)
That husband who, being truly devoted, bestows the bliss of Brahman and causes [his wife] to drink the essence of Brahman which grants liberation— he is indeed skillful.
But those householders who cause others to abandon the deceptive, bitter, and sorrow-inducing [world] and bestow upon them liberation— they are always skillful.
Likewise, those such as subjects and kings who are assistants toward liberation, yet turn away from it because they do not attain liberation themselves—all of them are considered skillful. (61)
Those qualities which bestow happiness, provide service to the virtuous, grant devotion to Hari, bestow joy upon others, and bring about liberation—these are considered auspicious. (62)

Those riches which are for the sake of the Lord, for the sake of the virtuous, which bestow the yoga of merit, and which are for the sake of helping others and attaining liberation, are considered auspicious. (63)
Those prosperities which are for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of the gods, and given through the duty of charity;
those which are for the sake of devotion and for the sake of the guru—those are divine and always auspicious. (64)
Cows, buffaloes, bulls, horses, elephants, vehicles, and female slaves—when they are for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and for the sake of the virtuous, they grant liberation; indeed, they are auspicious. (65)
Whatever body, mind, speech, senses, or powers one possesses, if they are for the sake of Hari, they are indeed auspicious and grant liberation. 66.
Whatever beds are very soft, as well as golden vessels, diamonds, gems, silver, jewels, and wealth—all that is for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and is indeed auspicious. (67)
When their joys, enjoyments, festivals, and pleasant associations are for the sake of Hari, for the sake of the virtuous, and grant liberation—verily, they are auspicious. (68)
Those practices, arts, sciences, and supreme knowledge of the knower;
those manifestations for the sake of Hari, for the sake of the virtuous, and those which are skillful—may they be auspicious to you. (69)

Those two, skilled in means, are considered divine: they manage income and expenditure for the sake of Hari, accomplish the goals of their mission, follow the path to liberation, and bring about the destruction of the bonds of illusion. (3.221.70)
Charity, vows, observances, right conduct, worldly consensus, the stages of life, and the prescribed paths—all these are for the sake of Hari; may you be virtuous. (71)
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, when always offered to Hari, take for him the form of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha); they are ever auspicious and bestow liberation.
May your teachings, your humility, your poverty, and your dwelling in the forest lead to your residence in a great palace; may all your efforts for the sake of the deer be auspicious for you. (73)

Those whose activities for the sake of Kṛṣṇa persist during waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and whose activities for the sake of liberation persist in the fourth state and in the liberation of Brahman—they alone are truly skillful. (74)
For one who possesses exceedingly affectionate and virtuous people, as well as Lord Hari, and whose undertakings are directed toward liberation, all is well for him in every respect. (75)
He who always possesses devotion in his home, in his heart, toward his family, toward Hari, toward the virtuous, and toward the path of liberation—for him there is well-being in every respect. (76)
In whose house there is worship of Hari, as well as hospitality toward the virtuous, and welfare for the gods and chaste women, all is well with him in every respect. (77)
In whose house there is the constant prasāda of Hari and food, for him the state of eating vighasa is supreme; he is virtuous in every respect. (78)
For one who has surrendered all possessions for the sake of Hari and has offered his very self, the yoga of desireless devotion is in every way auspicious. (95)
He who possesses no view of illusion indeed possesses the auspicious divine vision at all times; for him, the constant appreciation of virtues is entirely wholesome in every respect.
Faith in the words of Hari, which are words of truth, and the preservation of that faith, as well as every effort for the sake of liberation—this is his welfare in every respect. (8.1)
For one who possesses faith, choice, surrender, humility, steadiness, servitude, and devotion to Hari, there is well-being in every respect. (82)
I shall now describe those unwholesome qualities here which are indeed destructive:
atheism, unrighteousness, being devoid of devotion, and the abandonment of vows. (83)
Censuring, doing harm, and violence are indeed unwholesome acts; so too are eating what is unfit to eat, drinking intoxicants, and passing a day in vain. (84)
Association with the wicked, association with evil, delusion, arrogance, pride, and the infliction of suffering upon others—these are indeed always unwholesome. (85)
Lust for another's wife, longing for another's wealth,
backbiting, and deceit— these are indeed always unwholesome.
Lack of devotion to the Dharma, being devoid of the means for self-realization, ignorance, illusory delusion, and indeed constant unwholesome actions—[these are the causes]. (87)
Craving, envy, fear, and greed, as well as the avoidance of respectful conduct and the pursuit of actions that lead to further rebirth—these are indeed always unwholesome. (88)
Having understood this, always perform virtuous deeds indeed;
abandon the unwholesome, O Śivajaya, and you shall attain liberation.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā!
Recite the mantra and chant the name: "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare. (3.221.90)
"Having crossed over Māyā, you shall go to the world of Brahmā, the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, Vṛṣaparvan accepted the worship and departed for the forest. (91)
Lakṣmī sent me, Śivajaya, to Acyuta Puruṣottama;
he indeed performed everything auspiciously and abandoned all inauspicious things. ||92||
He became a great devotee, intent upon meditation, dedication, and worship; other excellent artisans also honored Mādhava in his house. (93)
They engaged in the company of the virtuous and performed the most excellent vows and festivals;
then once, on the morning of the twelfth lunar day, following their vow, they— ||94||
They performed worship for me during the night, followed by a vigil;
they also carried out the concluding rite (udyāpana), as well as hymns of praise and dancing. ||95||
There I appeared, possessing divine splendor and four arms;
seeing me, Hari, the beloved of Śrī, they all rejoiced on every side. (96)
Then they worshipped me with objects imbued with love arising from their hearts;
they requested liberation, and having said "So be it," I vanished.
Then, after some time, Śivajaya, accompanied by his devotees, cast off his body and went to the imperishable abode, escorted by my attendants. 98.
O Lakṣmī, in this way my devotees go to my imperishable abode through worship, adoration, self-surrender, and communion. 99.
Through association with the virtuous, even those who are not divine proceed to the supreme, divine state;
and those of good renown as well as reciters likewise attain the highest welfare.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation of Śivajaya, the Builder of the Temple, through the Yoga of the Sage Vṛṣaparvan," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of the spider-weaver;
a weaver lived there, sporting on the bank of the river named Kamalā.
And in that monastery, he became a maker of fish-traps and nets;
he set snares on the feet of birds and on the horns and feet of beasts.
Just as there may be nets corresponding to the bodies of fish and other creatures, he creates them from threads and ropes and sells them everywhere. (3)
And by means of the wealth produced from that, his sustenance is indeed maintained;
he, known by the name Saṅgarayādaska, resides in the city of the Creator. || 4 ||
Having purchased their snares at this marketplace,
those possessing nooses bind aquatic creatures, tree-dwellers, and forest-born beings.
Once, having placed baskets upon his shoulder,
that fisherman went to the city to sell them, crying out, "Buy the baskets!"
Carrying a small bundle in his belly, he spoke loudly for the sake of alms;
then the time arrived for him, and at midday, hunger arose.
Having purchased food from the market, he indeed came outside the city;
having gone to the bank of the Kamalā, he ate and drank water.
At that moment, a virtuous mendicant named Śuklāyana, who had approached with the desire to beg, was seen holding a garland in his hand and around his neck.
Chanting "Hare Kṛṣṇa" by name, remembering Kṛṣṇa within his heart, upholding the dharma of non-violence, and reflecting upon discrimination; || 3.222.10 ||
Carrying only what was necessary for his journey and free from the pairs of opposites, he indeed approached him.
Om, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! || 11 ||
Having announced himself previously, he later sat down near him;
though soiled in his clothing and physical appearance, he was radiant within his heart.
Drawing his mind toward him, he gazed with a gentle look;
then, as if desiring and longing for silence, he maintained his vow of silence and became steady.
Seeing the detached yogi, who was steadfast and deeply trustworthy, the spider, though not impelled by fate, spoke as if impelled by it: (14)
"Salutations to you, O holy man! From where do you come, how [did you arrive], and what do you desire? The holy man replied: "Salutations to the Inner Controller; may it be well with you. (15)
"I desire some food accompanied by a drink of water.
The fisherman, with a gracious heart, gave him parched rice.
And roasted chickpeas, even slightly seasoned with salt—may you always have such auspicious, healthy, and pleasant food. (17)
"May you have a peaceful sleep through my offering of rice grains," having said this, he remembered Śrī Hari and offered [the gift] to the Inner Self. (18)
He ate rice and other foods, and having drunk, he then attained satisfaction;
at that time, he indeed inquired about the occupation of the fisherman.
The fisherman spoke truthfully regarding his occupation with nets;
having heard this, the saint meditated on Kṛṣṇa for a moment and then gave him instruction.
Listen, O Saṅgarayādaska; I shall tell you what is beneficial for you in every respect.
There are eighty-four lakhs of birth-channels for embodied beings here in this world. (11)
In that regard, the human body indeed is the supreme means ordained for liberation;
for it is through the accumulation of merit over many births that one attains the human state. (22)
The embodied soul obtains a body; from that, through merit, one indeed attains heaven;
through devotion, liberation; through one's own duty, prosperity; and through discernment, happiness. ||23||
A human being should always accomplish virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
one should avoid a life that is like that of cattle and characterized by violence. 24.
Through violence, one obtains the realm of Yama and the abode of hell;
likewise, through violence, evil, malice, and misfortune are likewise produced. (25)
Confusion arises, as well as poverty and the destruction of people; for those who commit violence, there is a downward course and the state of going to hell. (26)
The sin of violence arises for those who set snares and for those who are robbers;
likewise, the sin of violence arises for even those who construct nets for living beings. ||27||
The killer, the eater, the one who rejoices, the accomplice, the giver of weapons, the giver of nooses, and the giver of nets shall all share equally in the karmic fruit. (28)
For one who makes nets, the sin of violence inevitably arises;
the embodied beings caught in the net seem to hiss at you as they breathe out through the mesh. (29)
"May those who curse one who wears a net and is bound by a net suffer misery;
therefore, I, being virtuous, shall instruct you here for your own happiness. (3.222.30)
The merit resulting from saving a life has that as its fruit—supreme happiness;
the demerit resulting from harming a living being has that as its fruit—intense suffering. (3.1)
Abandoning the work of the net and the activity of the net, collect rags;
with rags suitable for clothing, sin does not arise anywhere. (32)
Having attained the means for self-realization, perform what is beneficial for yourself:
bathing, meditation, worship of Hari, service to others, and self-surrender. (33)
Having served the virtuous and attained merit, go to heaven after worshiping the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
Having performed vows, festivals, and acts of charity, go to the supreme heaven;
do not, however, weave a net that causes harm and brings about sin. (35)
Make human life meaningful by attaining liberation and other goals;
always listen to the discourses of the scriptures and worship Nārāyaṇa. (36)
Having known Nārāyaṇa alone, proceed to the supreme state;
remember Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Consort of Kamalā. ||37||
He alone is the Lord of Syllables (Akṣareśa), the Lord of Māṇikī, the Lord of Rādhā, and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
He is indeed the Blessed One here on this earthly plane of Manu as well. 38.
The Lord of the Divine Abode is born directly in human form;
all his deeds, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [are as follows]. (39)
Indeed, those very things are to be contemplated;
they are truly bestowers of liberation, granters of great peace, and givers of auspiciousness.
Desire, anger, fear, sorrow, joy, victory, defeat, hunger, thirst, action, and sleep—all that is his auspiciousness. (41)
Whatever action of his may be censurable, blameworthy, base, or cruel, it should all be understood as bestowing auspiciousness; no fault exists in Hari. (49)

Because Hari is devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa) and because He is divine among the virtuous—those who have attained a connection with Hari—He possesses both qualitylessness and divinity. ||43||
Having understood that [the virtuous] indeed abide [in this way], one should certainly serve the holy ones;
having attained affection for the virtuous and having established affection for Hari, [one attains the goal]. (44)
Only by abandoning attachment to anything else can one attain steadfastness toward the Supreme Lord;
through such constant practice, the latent impression (saṃskāra) becomes powerful. ||45||
By that, an excess of affection for Kṛṣṇa arises repeatedly;
likewise, it exists for the devotee even during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. 46.
The vision of the divine form of Śrī Hari arises;
likewise, through great affection, the sight of Hari occurs for virtuous women. 47.
The Gopīs beheld Hari with excessive longing;
the Daityas, his enemies, beheld Hari with excessive hatred. (48)
The vision of Viṣṇu by the gods occurs repeatedly through the excellence of their own nature; the vision of Brahman by yogins occurs through the yoga of extreme identification. 49.
For the wise, the vision of Brahman occurs in every way through supreme knowledge;
likewise, the vision of Kṛṣṇa occurs through service performed with devotion.
Through the practice of constant devotion, grace from Hari arises;
by His compassion, the vision of Śrī Hari is likewise granted at all times. (51)
And through the benedictions of the virtuous, when purity is attained in every respect, there is the vision of Hari everywhere—in the hearts of devotees and externally as well. (52)
Indeed, for one who possesses partiality toward the devotees of Kṛṣṇa just as toward their own family members, that association with the virtuous is indeed eternal. (53)
For such a devotee, millions of faults perish;
latent impressions are destroyed, and the virtues of the virtuous arise. (54)
Without affection for Hari, association with the virtuous is one whose root has perished;
yet he who is devoid of pride, seeks liberation, and possesses divine vision [remains steadfast]. (415)
Knowing the greatness of Hari for the sake of the saintly wives of devotees, let association with the virtuous always remain firmly rooted as that which is to be understood by him. 16.
Unable to endure the separation from such devotees, the Lord—
though residing in the imperishable realm (Akṣara) and beyond the senses— descends here out of compassion for their ultimate welfare.
Assuming a human form by his own will, he wanders upon the earth;
one should constantly conduct oneself in accordance with his example. (58)
Unwavering devotion is the means for propitiating Hari;
for one who possesses the grace of Hari, there is the favor of the virtuous. (59)
For the sake of attaining clarity, one should not seek physical comfort;
association with the virtuous should be nourished by both body and mind. (3.222.60)
This is the manifest Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World, the Incarnate Supreme Brahman, the glorious son of Gopāla. (61)
These virtuous devotees of Hari are inhabitants of the imperishable ether;
all of them here are liberated, including even the women who are equal to Lakṣmī.
Through yoga, this earth has become the imperishable abode of Bālakṛṣṇa;
we all have become divinely liberated through our association with Nārāyaṇa.
Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is the abode, and likewise the liberated souls and the Muktānikās;
this is our great fortune that we have met with the divine ones.
Dwelling together with these is everything divine for me;
for Hari is to be served, and indeed, the virtuous are to be served.
Their commands must be obeyed; from that, one attains divinity.
Indeed, the virtues of the virtuous arise from the observance of the commands of the virtuous.
One should constantly serve the virtuous as if they were gods and likewise as if they were Kṛṣṇa;
meditation on Kṛṣṇa is the supreme duty, and devotion should be practiced in manifold ways.
Likewise, one should abandon evil, which is of a wicked nature, by serving the virtuous;
the power toward what is beneficial should be increased, and internal enemies must be conquered. (68)
Whether manifest or hidden, Kṛṣṇa is to be understood as being near oneself;
he is the witness of all that is manifest, omnipresent, and the bearer of manifold forms. (39)
The inner self, the supreme self, the lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Māṇikī—He directly perceives everything; the Supreme Lord exists everywhere.
Whether in the stationary or the moving, the gross or the subtle, or otherwise, there is nothing that exists without the desire for it; yet the powerful wind moves even a leaf without such a desire.
The giver of the fruits of all actions, he remains supporting everything;
indeed, the power of support exists in him alone, both upon the earth and likewise in the water.
He possesses the power of satisfaction and likewise the power of supporting the sky;
that Supreme Lord is the giver of the light of the moon, the sun, and fire.
Such indeed is this capable man here;
Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā, grants his own vision to him.
In this way, the Lord Hari should be contemplated incessantly in the mind;
for He alone indeed removes the sufferings of those who have taken refuge in Him. (75)
He is capable of providing protection; he exists possessing a divine nature, yet at times, through human states, he even endures suffering.
At times he experiences fear, desires, forgives, and indeed cries out.
In this world, all actions performed for Hari are indeed auspicious, even if they appear sinful. ||77||
That Lord has saintly devotees who are as dear to Him as His own self;
oh, how this Blessed One remains subject even here to the will of His devotees!
"By his majesty, his devotees become doers of good, and the holy ones grant us liberation"—thus one should cultivate such greatness. (79)
One whose intellect regarding Hari is always extraordinary, like that of the virtuous, should constantly cultivate that [intellect] and never the evil intellect born of worldly attachment. (3.222.80)
One should perceive the defect inherent in intrinsic nature and not cultivate worldly familiarity;
by that means, the defect of improper mental impressions departs from the heart. (81)
One should increase that true devotion performed by the body, senses, and mind, which consists of the offering of one's all and bestows the state of supreme liberation. 82.
Service to the virtuous is considered the primary means for attaining liberation;
indeed, the righteous should be constantly served even in times of adversity. (83)
One should listen to the virtuous discourse concerning the news of Hari for the removal of sins;
and for the sake of liberation, one should offer everything—body, home, wealth, and so forth. (84)
One should know the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Māṇikī, as the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, and the Lord of Rādhikā. ||85||
Indeed, the Vyūhas such as Vāsudeva and others, the Mūrtis such as Keśava and others, and the Avatāras such as Matsya and others belong to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa. (86)

Having attained such greatness, a person who takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, just as Satī took refuge in her husband or as a wife [takes refuge] in her husband. ||87||
Thus, having abandoned the practice of weaving nets, you, Saṅgarayādaska, should instead engage in the weaving of cloth, mats, and the like. (88)
Worship Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman; attain liberation and the highest state.
Possessing true devotion, go to the divine, eternal, and imperishable abode. 89.
Thus the virtuous Śuklāyana, having sat down on the riverbank,
gave him his blessing and made him a devotee of Viṣṇu who serves with devotion.
For the battle, suddenly withdrawing its own net, went as it were into the house and split apart the long tube of passion. 9.11.
Having done so, he kept me in his house and abandoned his state of being a monk; together with his family, he served me and caused many devotees to be established [in the faith]. (92)
O Lakṣmī, since even my devotion and worship grant liberation, from that time forth she protected the dharma of non-injury in every way. (93)
And he [Kṛṣṇa], out of affection for his servant and other such feelings, made me an object of his perception in embodied form;
then, when the time had arrived, Mādhava came with his chariot.
I went to that house to lead my imperishable abode,
as well as her husband Saṃgara and his wife Rūpāvatī, onto the chariot.
Having seated him and restored his divine body, he went to the imperishable abode;
other multitudes of my devotees as well, led by me, have gone to the Supreme.
O Rame, I have set ablaze the entire mass of all sins; out of compassion, I have established purity for my devotees and those who are devoted to the virtuous.
Even those who are sinful, associated with the wicked, ignorant, and attached to sense-objects, become pure and enjoyers of Brahman through association with the virtuous. (98)
Whether they be women, animals, or even the dull-witted and impure, by resorting to the service of the virtuous, they become purifiers of the assembly. (99)
Neither Brahmins, nor gods, nor cows, nor vows, nor observances, nor restraints, nor sacred fords are as excellent as virtuous people; indeed, they are the most excellent of all.
Indeed, her entire divine and purifying form, from her nails to her hair, is truly like Nārāyaṇa himself, and Nārāyaṇī is like Lakṣmī herself. ||10.1||
The grace of the virtuous is divine; likewise, the touch of the virtuous is supreme.
Indeed, service to the virtuous bestows happiness, destroys suffering, and grants the vision of Hari.
From reading, hearing, remembering, and even reflecting upon this, there shall be the destruction of sin, the attainment of merit, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation. (103)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of How the Holy Śuklāyana Caused Jālaka, the Devotee of Saṅgara-Yādava, to Abandon His Work and Attain the Lord," in the Third Section on the Lineage of Dvāpara within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of Ajapālaka,
which took place at Nandipattana near the river Candraprabhā.
There was indeed a Bharavāṭa named Udyamaśrī, whose wealth consisted of goats;
he possessed five hundred goats as well as one hundred cows. (2)
Five hundred rams, a hundred donkeys, ten dogs, and twenty female buffaloes. || 3 ||
He possesses ten groups of servants for various tasks,
and he has six wives and seventy sons and daughters.
On the bank of a river, in a forest, on a grassy meadow rich with fodder,
or on ground abounding in thick, beautiful medicinal herbs and lush vegetation.
She dwells in Suvṛttikā, not far from Nandipura,
where the dwellings of other herdsmen and cattle-keepers are located.
Indeed, she who is of the nature of sound exists as the one who partakes of forest food and the like;
there dwells the great glory of exertion, along with fame and likewise long life. (7)
In whose dwelling many forest-dwellers frequently arrive, accompanied by their livestock, wealth, and families, to serve as guests; || 8 ||
He also welcomes them all with milk and other offerings;
for holy men, ascetics, perfected ones, and yogis are arriving there.
Virtuous women also come frequently to his service-chamber;
he honors them all and pleases them with meals.
Through gifts, honors, and great respect, as well as by massaging their feet and other services,
women, sons, daughters-in-law, and even servants were constantly attended to at all times.
They serve virtuous men and virtuous women with great devotion,
regarding the holy ones as Lord Hari himself, with a disposition of offering their very selves.
Hari dwells visibly among the virtuous, and Ramā herself dwells among virtuous women;
even the gods dwell among guests, for they are indeed worthy of worship.
While he was thus performing service and worshipping me,
his lord, twenty virtuous women who were practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga arrived at his house.
There were indeed elderly Vaiṣṇava female ascetics devoted to piety; with their milk and other offerings, as well as gifts of forest-grown food, [he honored them]. (15)
He offered them honor and a welcome, and provided lodging in a temporary hut;
there those women, devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, stayed.
Divine and endowed with divine qualities, they bathed in the river and worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa, their Lord of Life, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having offered food to the Supreme Soul, they ate;
and having taken rest, they performed the evening congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana). ||18||
The reciters performed the nightly lamp-offering and recounted the life stories;
meanwhile, thousands of cowherd women, boys, and girls gathered to listen to the narrative.
Having learned of that supreme circle of virtuous women,
those mothers, whose dispositions were ever immersed in the form of Hari, arrived from all sides.
They worship and sing praises of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their beloved Lord;
among them, one named Satīśvarī attained the status of a preceptor. ||21||
The virtuous women of the cowherds, as well as all the cowherds, listened with faith and a spirit of devotion to the excellent narrative of Hari.
The virtuous lady Satī spoke this beautiful narrative from the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, which bestows excellent liberation and utterly consumes all sins. (23)
By him whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa, the world is indeed conquered;
for that mind alone is truly conquered which is held fast in the Supreme Self.
The senses proceed toward their objects along with the mind; however, that mind which has not been conquered follows after the object to which it has gone. (25)
Having turned back the movement of the mind toward the movements of the senses, one should fix that mind upon Hari; then the senses will be conquered.
Upon the destruction of passion, dispassion arises; by that, the mind becomes conquered.
Through love for Hari, the mind does not go elsewhere; thus, the mind becomes conquered. (27)
Through abiding in Brahman, passion, desire, and the like are indeed destroyed;
the notion of enjoyment perishes, and by that, the mind becomes conquered. (28)
The mind of one who is immersed in the divine bliss of Śrī Hari, the Lord of Śrī, and who is endowed with the knowledge of His majesty, shall be conquered. (29)
For one whose state of consciousness persists through the destruction of the state of the body, his mind becomes inert and devoid of effort, and thus it is conquered. (3.223.30)
Perpetual contentment consists in turning away from the illusory objects of desire;
his mind is considered always satisfied and steady, and his intellect ever-conquered. (3.1)

Through the destruction of the identification with the body, through the power of abiding in the Self, and through the abandonment of the latent impressions of attachment, the mind shall be forever conquered. ||32||
The mind is said to be in the form of a woman, and the individual soul (jīvātman) assumes the form of a man;
when the mind abandons its enjoyment, the mind becomes naturally conquered.
"I am the self, the conscious woman; the Supreme Self is my man.
He is my husband, my enjoyer, and the giver of happiness; there is no other supreme agent of my enjoyment. (34)
He is the manifest Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, the beloved of Śrī;
he is the protector, the sustainer, the creator, the dear one, the lord of life, and the master. 35.
He is the Master, the Radiant One, and the Desireless One, overflowing with all-bliss;
this Supreme Person is my beloved, the bestower of my bliss. (36)
The ruler of the lords, the source of all incarnations and those who descend from them,
this very Lord of Goloka has attained the state of being the Master of the cowherd girls.
He is the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, the Master of the female attendants, and the Lord of the liberated women; He is Kṛṣṇa, resplendent in the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma).
In Śrīpura, Avyākṛta, and Amṛta, he is the Lord of Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Kamalā; the Lord of Lalitā and Māṇikī; and the Lord of Prabhā and Padmāvatī. ||39||
He is the Lord of Brahmapriyā and he is the Lord of Haripriyā;
he is the Lord of Viśālā and Badarī, and the Supreme Lord of Śvetadvīpa.
He is the Lord of Lakṣmī, who dwells upon the shore of the Ocean of Milk; he is the husband of Sītā and the husband of Satī;
Kṛṣṇa is indeed the husband of every virtuous woman and the husband of Kumbhakārī. 41.

The Lord of all those who are liberated, the Lord of the perfected ones, the Lord of all female companions, the Lord of all female servants, the Lord of even my mere life-breath—He is the Supreme Person. 42.
Knowing this, one should worship Hari, the beloved who is the refuge of all happiness;
when one's mind becomes fixed on Kṛṣṇa, that indeed is considered victory. (43)
And this Blessed One dwells within my heart, within my own self;
possessing the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, he shines among virtuous men and women.
The illustrious Gopālabāla shines in Akṣarakṣetra;
he is the manifest treasury of all happiness, Vāsudeva himself. 45.
Indeed, it is the source of great happiness for humans, gods, ancestors, perfected yogis,
lords, and millions of incarnations.
Whatever joys indeed belong to the liberated ones and to those who abide in the realm of Brahman—
all those belong to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā.
If such a Lord exists even at the tip of a single hair, He is our Master Kṛṣṇa, the treasury of all happiness, who has now been met by us. 48.
Before that abode of bliss, indeed, stand all the other abodes of bliss belonging to all the world-protectors, to the hosts, and to the lords of those abodes. (49)
Of the planets, the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, and also the Aśvins;
of the Sādhyas, the Vadhūs, and the Rudras who dwell in heaven.
The abodes of the suns, of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as those of other celestial beings, are indeed like hells compared to the realm of this Supreme Self. (51)
Having abandoned this beloved Lord of Śrī, who is designated as hell itself, how could I, the Supreme Goddess, resort to others whom you perceive as happiness? (52)
Having thus understood this greatness, a virtuous woman endowed with divine disposition should abandon delusion, which leads to hells; her mind is forever victorious. (53)
Then, the illusory latent impressions (vāsanās) constantly come to dissolution;
such is the illusory desire for the body and the desire for enjoyment. (54)
She who is eternally burnt is never born again, for she has been uprooted;
such is the majesty of Hari that she does not recognize here on earth. 55.
For such a person, even toward an ordinary man there would be a disposition of desire;
likewise, affection for a son, a friend, a wife, a husband, and so forth, is also a bondage. (56)
The mind of that woman, who dwells in the pursuit of her own self-interest, turns toward it;
she, being dragged down by affection for her family, would abandon the Supreme Self.
Or, due to the affliction of disease and the like, or from the failure to obtain sense objects, she may abandon [her practice];
however, her mind should always remain fixed on Keśava for the sake of attaining those objects. 58.
But when sense objects are not obtained, that [state] becomes vulgar;
consequently, one falls away from devotion to Hari and does not find the path to liberation.
Therefore, one should cultivate toward Hari a love that is natural, devoid of self-interest;
it should not arise from beauty, nor from desire, nor from greed, nor even from gain. (3.223.60)
Affection should not be cultivated for one's own sake, but rather it should be natural, arising from the knowledge of the majesty and the wondrous power of his divine qualities. (61)
One should always cultivate affection for him whose destruction never occurs;
for in Hari reside divine qualities such as truthfulness, purity, and happiness.
Furthermore, his affection is boundless, as are his sweetness, excellent character, friendship, compassion, love, pity, tranquility, forbearance, and delight. (63)
Joy, the performance of benefit, endurance, divine nature, fortitude, magnanimity, eternal bliss, and the protection of those who seek refuge. (64)
These virtues come even to devotees through service;
indeed, virtues manifest even by listening to the accounts of the virtuous.
Affection for devotees endowed with such qualities arises in Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, one should perform service to Hari through body, mind, and speech. (66)
One's physical form should be conducted according to the pleasure of Hari;
austerity and other practices should be performed in accordance with the pleasure of Hari.
One should always perform service with faith toward Hari, the virtuous, yogis, and saintly women; thus, firm affection for Kṛṣṇa shall arise.
Bitter speech should not be spoken; rather, one should speak that which is true and beneficial. One should neither engage in disputes with great men, nor seek victory over them.
One should speak words that are free from pride, gentle, authoritative, and full of humility;
one should utter excellent speech and honor the commandful words of Hari.
The word of Hari should always be accepted with reverence, even if it is harsh;
the word of Hari must indeed be accepted, even if it is unworthy of action or seemingly impossible.
In this way, let there be love for Hari; likewise, let there be love for the virtuous, upon seeing, hearing of, meditating on, worshipping, and serving Hari. (72)
One-pointed concentration upon the embodied form of Śrī Hari in His presence brings about the attainment of one's desired goals;
likewise, there is a vision that is ever-new and transcendent. ||73||
One should maintain this steadily for a long time and indeed look at nothing else;
such a vision is truly the cause of love for Hari.
Whether externally or internally, such a vision is the cause of affection;
for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, love arises only toward one whose gaze is steady. (75)
Furthermore, the virtuous find no pleasure in a man or a woman who gazes elsewhere, nor in a beast, nor in a painting, nor in a door with flickering eyes. (76)
With a mind that has many streams, a flickering gaze is cast;
by that gaze, one does not find delight in that [object], as it goes elsewhere. (77)
Just as a lustful man might look upon a woman of desire with a single-minded focus, so should one behold the Lord, one's husband, with a state of being entirely absorbed in love. 78.

Not even the slightest thing that has occurred in the interval should be brought into connection [with the present], just as the bride’s first sight of her husband at the very first moment is entirely new. (79)
That vision indeed brings about firmness of form and steadfastness, bestows a radiant luster, and is eternally fresh; it is the very cause of affection.
Indeed, one must practice such single-minded concentration while listening to the narrative; for by hearing of his life-story, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, becomes manifest. (81)
Among all the sense organs—whether the eye, the ear, or even the mind—these must indeed be restrained, for they are especially fickle. ||82||
The faculty of desire is even more restless than those [other senses], because it is so fickle;
therefore, having restrained the mind, desire itself must be restrained along with the mind. (83)
Otherwise, during meditation on or worship of Śrī Hari, vulgar forms and sense objects that cause affliction would manifest as creators of obstacles. (84)
If the mind, which is the powerful indicator, indeed proceeds toward vulgar objects of the senses such as sight and hearing, then one must apply careful discernment. (85)
There is no gain whatsoever in departing from Hari to dwell in another realm, because all sense objects are givers of suffering and causes of bondage through illusion. (86)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Śrīvallabha is the embodiment of bliss;
one should remain there for the attainment of eternal bliss. (87)
The stage of perfection is a divine stage, a treasure-trove of joy and delight;
everything indeed arises from Kṛṣṇa, therefore obtain great happiness. 88.
In other cases, there might even be some slight happiness for one who exerts effort;
however, that [happiness] is mostly full of suffering and likewise brings about rebirth in hell. (89)
Therefore, listen to the story, behold Kṛṣṇa, and contemplate him in every way;
go indeed to that bliss which comes from Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved, and not from any other.
Thus, through affection for Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain the desired perfection:
opulence, prosperity, beauty, and the Lord Śrī Rādhāmāṇikī. 91.
Through devotion to Him, one attains everything equal to Viṣṇu and Nārāyaṇa;
whether in this body or upon death, everything is attained in His abode in every way.
Therefore, one should always abide in Hari with the eye, the mind, the speech, the ear, the heart, as well as with desire and even with the very self. 93.
In this way, for one who possesses love for Kṛṣṇa through constant devotion, or for a woman who possesses love for him, there indeed arises the state of being a worthy recipient of Kṛṣṇa’s love. 94.
Consequently, his divine abiding would be like that of Kṛṣṇa, or it would be like that of Lakṣmī;
there would be no deficiency in Hari, nor any inferiority in her, Śrī.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the great virtuous Satīśvarī instructed the cowherdesses and the cowherds, who were affectionate toward the Blessed One, for the sake of liberation. 96.
The cowherd women, the cowherds, and others such as Bharavaṭa and Udyamaśrī took up the highest form of devotion. 97.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā"—this mantra and the supreme name Satīśvarī they received. (98)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Beloved, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of Ramā!
O Bestower of Liberation, O Dear One, O Granter of all Desires, O Supreme Person! 99.
Thus they took up these names and performed their recitation with reverence; the virtuous women, having performed their worship and eaten their morning meal, went to another village.
The male attendants and female attendants likewise went forth repeatedly;
they performed worship and adoration of Bālakṛṣṇa at all times. || 10 1 ||
Indeed, through their devotion, the Blessed One suddenly manifested together with Rādhā and Ramā, as well as with Māṇikī and Śrī.
Having seen him in his four-armed form during the great festival at home,
in the temple on the day of the vow, specifically on the morning of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Then thousands of people attained supreme wonder,
having received his very sight as well as his grace and the auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having granted the boon for the sake of liberation, the Lord vanished;
O Lakṣmī, I, being that very person, then, when the time had arrived, produced the glory of effort.
I led the cowherd boys, the excellent devotees, and the gopīs, who were overflowing with love,
to my own abode, the eternal and supreme Goloka.
Thus, through his association with the virtuous women, the compassionate Lord delivered even the cowherds and their wives from the world of illusion by means of his affection and devotion.
Thus, those women and men who shall worship me with total devotion,
all will go to my supreme abode, which is served by their beloveds.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, or even practicing this, enjoyment, liberation, and great bliss shall be attained; it is offered by me. 109.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotion and Liberation of the Cowherds, beginning with Udyamaśrī and others, through their Service to the Chaste Satīśvarī," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; on the land of Maru, there was an oxherd named Dīrgharaṃbha in the village known as Citrordhva.
On the other side were his camels, numbering more than a hundred, which fed upon the *śamī* tree;
he was a dweller in high lands, a camel-herder, and a seller of wool. (2)
One who sells camels, as well as one who trades in grain, and one who transports grain from one region to another region; || 3 ||
Generally living in the forest as a protector of camels,
he dwelt there at night together with ten camel-herders.
Then, in the exceedingly dense Śamī forest, camels such as Dīrgharaṃbha and others moved about on all sides, having placed a fire around it.
Seated upon woolen blankets, they chant the praises of Rāma;
likewise, gathered together, they engage in conversations and songs concerning the gods.
Having offered the milk of camels into their hearts to the Lord, they drink it;
and having prepared *roṭakas* with *śamī*, *śimbī*, and sour gruel, they eat them.
If any travelers happen to come along the forest path,
they respectfully offer them milk, flat cakes, and other such provisions.
Thinking, "One must perform service for others by giving food and blankets," they offer even the finest blankets.
Or, virtuous people who have come for a pilgrimage meet on that path; they offer them food and water, and perform the rites of welcome and so forth. (3.224.10)
Constantly desiring meritorious and virtuous deeds with the very thought of Rāma,
they serve the assembly of the righteous according to their wish with a spirit of devotion.
Then once, while they were traveling toward Tripuṣkara to perform the Arbuda pilgrimage,
they encountered a circle of virtuous monks and nuns on the road.
And with the sounds of musical instruments, they proclaimed: "Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Janārdana!
Narasiṃha, Hara, Viṣṇu! Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta! (1.3)
Having seen them, Dīrgharaṃbha went to them, prostrated himself,
and gave them milk, cakes, and water at midday.
In the evening, those virtuous men, though full of longing, found rest there;
that night, all the camel-herders attended upon the holy people.
They likewise heard the chanting of his names and stories of Rāma;
indeed, they heard the excellent work called the Rāmāyaṇa, the supreme Vaiṣṇava text.
Bowing low, he asked how his own welfare might be attained;
then Rāmāyaṇa replied with the means for achieving that welfare.
Service to the virtuous, the auspicious chanting of Rāma’s name,
and the ninefold devotion to Viṣṇu are indeed the means for attaining well-being.
There is the constant salutation of Rāma, worship with many articles,
and daily worship within the heart through mental offerings.
And the meditation on Rāma is a means for attaining what is auspicious; thus, with his body bristling with joy from love and his speech faltering with emotion, he meditated. (3.224.20)
A devotee engaged in the worship of Hari should be intent on contemplating His essential nature alone, whether performing external worship or internal adoration. (21)
This one, esteemed by all devotees, is indeed distinguished among all in devotion;
however, one who lacks single-minded concentration and is devoid of affection is not praised.
He who possesses abundant faith in worship and service, and especially who possesses faith and reverence for the narration and the chanting [of the Lord's names]. ||23||

His majesty is supreme, his friendship toward devotees is excellent, and for him, even a long duration of time passes like a single moment when engaged in the worship of Rāma and similar practices. (24)
The ninefold service of Hari, which for him is renewed every day—may this never, at any time or place, become secondary or stale for him. (25)
He whose faith and devotion are constant, ever-new, and ever-bright, is liberated here; and she too is liberated—whether he be a man or a woman on this earth.
Even devotees situated at a distance are like this when they stand in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
if they are not like this while standing by his side, they are considered as far away as those who are distant. ||27||
Therefore, one should strive without interruption for the attainment of the arising of joy through hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and divine vision. 28.
The story of Hari should be heard from the mouth of a virtuous person who has attained identity with Kṛṣṇa; it sustains the intended meaning accompanied by the remembrance of Śrī Hari. (29)
Furthermore, one must repeatedly contemplate and investigate the meaning of what has been heard, together with a loving visualization of the Form; this destroys latent tendencies. (3.224.30)
Then, one should perform pure meditation (nididhyāsana), which is a recollection born of mental impressions (saṃskāra); through this, Mādhava becomes pleased with him out of faith and love. 31.
By that, there should be a spontaneous and constant manifestation of Hari within;
once there is such manifestation, there shall always be the direct perception of the divine form of Hari.
In this way, love for Hari should be cultivated; through that love, love from Hari will arise.
From the mutual love of both, identity is then born.
Celibacy, steadfastness in the Self, detachment, hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, and taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa—these are declared to be the causes for direct realization. (34)
Reflection and meditative absorption bestow the fulfillment of the devotees' desires;
hearing alone does not directly grant the fruit of realization.
Latent impressions do not perish without nididhyāsana;
the knots of the heart are destroyed by constant meditation on the indivisible Kṛṣṇa. (36)
Indeed, for one who possesses profound contemplation and is a direct seer [of reality], fullness of desire and bliss exist; but not for anyone else. //37//

Whether it be the external form of Kṛṣṇa seen by the observer, or likewise the thought within the heart, or the constant remembrance of His form by the rememberer— in each case, Keśava swiftly manifests Himself.
For one who does not proceed in this way and who does not apply effort in this way, the Lord—the divine self who is the soul of the universe—does not manifest at all within the heart. (39)
Therefore, the means for the direct realization of Kṛṣṇa within the heart are said to be hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and love. 3.224.40
Through love that is ever-sustaining, Hari shines forth like a beloved;
therefore, one should likewise reflect upon the heard and seen Hari. (41)
One should practice remembrance accompanied by love and endowed with faith; upon that, Hari’s affection arises, which leads to union with His abode. 42.

As long as the identity of the individual soul with the body persists, one must recognize that there will be great obstacles to love for Kṛṣṇa, which produce further worldly existence and rebirth. (43)
Therefore, the realization that this Self is distinct from the body and so forth must be attained by the discerning person from both a true teacher and the scriptures. (44)
And the delusion regarding the identity between the insentient and the sentient must be destroyed;
[one must realize] the true natures of both the insentient and the sentient in every respect. (45)
Furthermore, those phenomena by which the distinction between these two is to be understood must be awakened;
for through that, the delusion of identity will perish along with its very root. (46)
Inert, composed of suffering, diseased, perishable, and deformed;
subject to decay, pervaded by saliva, urine, and impurities, and possessed of birth, death, and old age. ||47||
Bound by fractures, existing in many states, illusory, composed of the elements, and consisting of a mass, this body always exists as a form that is subject to decay and manifold in nature. (48)
The sense organs, which are indeed qualities of the subtle body, produce suffering, defects, agitation, and anxiety; such are they. (49)
I am not such as this; I am of the nature of consciousness, possessed of bliss, free from disease, eternal, changeless, and devoid of decay. (3.224.50)
I am of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss; I transcend birth, death, and old age.
I am indivisible, stable, and one; I am divine and free from illusion. (51)
I am non-material, devoid of the elements, luminous, free from laughter, uniform, stainless, unattached, the seer, and immortal. //52//
My divine powers are the impellers of the faculties of the senses;
being such, I am indeed the conscious one, possessing the nature of liberation.
Thus, one should properly contemplate the discrimination between the self and the non-self;
having learned this from the mouths of the wise or from the scriptures, one should cultivate it. (54)
When knowledge is matured, there is no confusion between the attributes of the body and the attributes of the Self;
therefore, one should be established in the Self, which is also called being established in the Blessed Lord. 55.
In this state, the human being becomes truly of the nature of Brahman and of the nature of liberation;
neither latent impressions (vāsanā) remain for him, nor delusion, nor even torments.
He who has not firmly established this discrimination between the Self and the non-Self is afflicted by the attributes of the body, such as suffering and the like, being driven by delusion. (57)
As long as there is laxity in practice, so long shall one remain under the sway of the notion that the body is the self;
like a beast, let him continue in the animal-like state characterized by "I" and "mine. (58)
[It is] of the nature of identity with the body, senses, and so forth; it deludes through desire and volition;
it is filled with attachment to the fluids of male and female, with suffering, thirst, and sin. (59)
Thinking "I shall eat sweets," that [desire] brings suffering even when one delights in oneself;
by such a disposition, he surely goes to illusory hells.
One should strive so that there may be no rebirth in the hells; one should achieve steadfastness in the Self through service to Hari and to the virtuous. 61.
With love and an awareness of his majesty, one should abandon attachment to the body;
with faith one should serve the holy ones, and with devotion, Janārdana.
One should remain constantly under the command of Hari and the saintly person;
one should protect the duties prescribed by the scriptures and acquire knowledge of His majesty. ||63||
In this way, there would be freedom from latent impressions; however, due to affection for Kṛṣṇa, that [freedom] is quickly attained.
Devotion toward Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the knowledge of His majesty, increases. (64)
For one devoid of knowledge of the Lord’s majesty, the qualities born of devotion perish;
for one endowed with knowledge of His majesty, those very qualities become the bringers of auspiciousness. (65)
All these abide in the heart just as they do for the virtuous;
yet, upon the arrival of the [true] qualities, all latent impressions (vāsanās) quickly perish.
If death occurs for a devotee who worships while a residue of latent impressions still remains, his birth will be radiant among the gods and other celestial beings.
Therefore, it shall indeed bring about prosperity and enjoyment in the home of devotees;
and having attained the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), liberation will then become certain.
For a devotee who possesses the latent impressions [of devotion], there is no going to the realm of Yama;
the fruit of devotion is considered to be either the world of the gods or the world of the Lord. (69)
Having become a devotee, even a great universal monarch (mahācakravartin) shall go to the Imperishable; Kṛṣṇa, whose compassion is boundless, is the supreme goal for the devotee.
Having rendered him free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), he protects his own devotee;
for even the illusory manifestations of the abode of Kṛṣṇa [are withdrawn] from his presence.
To those who know the Self, even the hells appear as such;
having experienced them and then abandoned them, they proceed from there to the imperishable state.
Chanting the name of Rāma, touching and beholding Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa,
having become divine, stainless, and of the nature of Brahman, he attains the supreme state.
He goes to the abode of yogis, the supreme state of the liberated;
situated in the midst of the circle of the virtuous, he enjoys great bliss in the Imperishable.
Whether they be devotees or non-devotees, those who behold Hari directly, or touch him, or serve him, indeed become divine beings. (75)
If those who are not devotees, yet possess a focused mind and serve with hearts full of joy,
then they abandon their latent impressions and proceed to the supreme state.
Even those devotees who serve the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, with a mindless [unfocused] mind, will eventually reach His state in another birth. ||77||
For those whose devotion is characterized by intense spiritual urgency, the Lord is most proximate; for those whose devotion is characterized by mild spiritual urgency, Janārdana is most remote. (78)
The chanting of Hari’s name without a focused mind, as well as seeing, touching, serving, and so forth, will never yield the complete fruit anywhere. (79)
But that meditation which is devoid of the mind would be lacking in spiritual radiance;
therein, the form of Nārāyaṇa would never manifest at all.
Therefore, devotees [should practice] in both ways—whether through external or internal worship.
They should cultivate the Great Lord through practices such as loving devotion and one-pointed concentration. ||81||
By the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, at the end of their bodies, they immediately went to the abode of the Beloved of Śrī, Goloka; liberated, they possessed divine forms. ||82||
Others, however, having attained merit and having reached and completed their rebirth through devotion and other such means,
shall go to that state upon the exhaustion of that merit.
But for those [devotees], service consists of offering everything like the gopīs;
their touch, sight, and glorification are established as the threefold form [of the Lord]. (84)
They proceed swiftly to the divine liberation whose essence is Kṛṣṇa;
yet everything performed without mindfulness is fruitless and does not bestow liberation. (85)
"O camel-herders, you must indeed perform that task in such a manner—with love, with affection, with a devoted mind, and with the whole of your hearts. (86)
Service, glorification, and even the touch of Śrī Hari by the virtuous—through these, liberation will swiftly come to those devotees who are rich with intense affection. (87)
For forest-dwellers, chanting [the Lord's names], service, and devotion are the means to liberation;
for Brahmins, the six duties and ninefold devotion lead to liberation. (88)
For the virtuous, meditation is the desired bath, and likewise, service is the worship;
detachment, steadfastness in the Self, and steadfastness in Kṛṣṇa lead to liberation. (89)
For women, serving Hari with a sense of endearment toward a lover, filled with affection, offering everything, following His will, and maintaining the state of a servant leads to liberation.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Recite this supreme mantra and chant the name of Bāla Kṛṣṇa as well. 9.1.
Having meditated upon mental worship of the Supreme Self, let them perform it;
let them remember His deeds, and thereby let them attain liberation as well. 92.
Having spoken thus, all the virtuous ones, including those who recite the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts, took their leave of me;
and having been honored and fed, they departed from there. (93)
Dīrgharambha and all the others followed the virtuous method of instruction and took refuge in the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī. 94.
Hare Kṛṣṇa! Hare Rāma! Hare Viṣṇu! Hare Prabhu!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Lord of Sītā, Lord of Rādhā, All-pervading One! 95.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, those camel-herders, having gathered together, constantly performed worship for me, their Lord, in the forest and at home with love and devotion. (96)
Then, after some time had passed, he who possessed a divine form and four arms came to lead Dīrgha, Rambhā, and the others to liberation.
Rāma, the lord of Vaikuṇṭha, resplendent together with Sītā,
brought him and the others by means of a divine celestial chariot.
Those camels which had been given as gifts to the virtuous were also taken away by him,
who approached assuming a divine form.
Carrying beautiful birds of golden hue, adorned with all ornaments and making a jingling sound from their tiny bells, I approached.
Having transformed each and every one of those devotee camel-herders into divine beings and having mounted them upon camels,
he brought them to my celestial abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, all these camel-herders were made divine by me, the compassionate one, through my devotion in the course of narrating the story of Rāma. (102)
From reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this, there shall arise enjoyment, liberation, as well as desired prosperity and wealth. (103)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Dīrgharava and the Other Camel-herders through Their Association with the Holy Man named Rāmāyana," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of the devotee named Ratnaprabha, the son of Kharapāla, which bestows the state of liberation.
On the bank of the Lūṇī river, in the city of Lūṇī, there was an excellent Kṣatriya named Ratnaprabha, who was the protector of a thousand donkeys. ||2||
With his long ears, he indeed carries away grains and other goods from one place to another,
from one country to another, and from one village to another, again and again.
And for the merchants, kings, and others, he performs their business by means of donkeys, bringing and carrying goods for a wage earned through labor.
In this manner, he brought many grains, vessels, and likewise sacrificial fuel from the forest, from fields and threshing floors, from the city, and from other cities.
He causes [the goods] to reach another village or the center of the village by means of donkeys;
indeed, having taken the wage for the labor, he conducts the journey home.
Then once, having loaded two thousand measures of wheat onto the backs of donkeys,
he departed from the village of Lūṇī.
Accompanied by forty fierce-tempered servants, he proceeded fearlessly toward the capital city of Yuddhapurī on a day of scorching sunlight.
As he was traveling on the road, he became exhausted by the heat;
and perceiving that the donkeys were likewise exhausted, he too succumbed to fatigue.
Indeed, he dwells there for two ghaṭīs by the side of a water-channel in a grove of trees;
that circle of virtuous men there is truly abundant with forest produce.
Likewise, Ratnaprabha and the others, having given water to the donkeys and having partaken of food such as *roṭaka* cakes, went before the holy men.
Having bowed down and uttered "Victory to Śrī Rāma," the holy men stood before him,
offered a welcome, and then bestowed their blessings.

Having repeatedly understood the fatigue born of activity in going and coming, they have declared that for the sake of one's welfare, the auspicious refuge in Nārāyaṇa is through meditation (dhyāna). 13.
The best of virtuous men, Narasiṃhasvāmī, who was served by holy men,
instructed everyone for a mere hour regarding Acyuta.
Alas! All that has been done in this world is as if undone if service to Kṛṣṇa is not performed;
indeed, all such acts are then fruitless for the embodied soul, just like being in the womb. 15.
Just as a donkey laden with a burden of sandalwood perceives only the weight and does not perceive its fragrance, so too is he devoid of bliss. ||16||
Likewise, one who is devoted to worldly toil in this world, devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, is called a bearer of burdens, but not a knower of the essence of the Self. (17)
Since there is no difference perceived between a donkey and a human in terms of being carriers of labor, that human is indeed like a donkey in that regard. (18)
Just as donkeys, who are mere animals, fall under the control of the potter, so too do other potters fall under the control of their own actions, which are themselves like animals. 19.
Those men who are devoid of devotion, devoid of righteousness, bereft of human purpose, and lacking in the merit of charity, are like donkeys. (3.225.20)
Those men who are devoid of visiting sacred fords, who are bereft of ritual bathing and worship, and who lack service to the virtuous, are like donkeys. (21)
Deprived of their own welfare and attached to tastes and such, men in this world who are intent on gratifying their genitals and bellies are like donkeys. (22)
Bearing the burden of their families yet devoid of the path to the highest good, men who swallow mouthfuls of the fodder of sense-objects are like donkeys. (23)
Those men who tread paths devoid of moral boundaries, who are bereft of service to their parents, and who lack the realization that all beings are the Self, are like donkeys. (24)
Exerting effort only for the sake of food, devoid of austerity and vows, smeared with ashes yet naked, these men are like donkeys. (25)
Those men who are devoid of even a trace of devotion to the five deities, who are atheists, and who lack respect for their guru, are like donkeys. ||26||
Even householders who are devoid of faith, who avoid sacrifices and offerings, who are intent on sexual indulgence and greedy, are like donkeys. (27)
Having four legs, a tail like a fool's, and coils that wind around their dwelling places, yet devoid of the memory of the gods, householders are like donkeys. (28)
Hearing vulgar speech, their ears hang down; crying out in distress, they run after the objects of the senses like household donkeys. (29)
Unpeaceful, wandering among the winds of sense objects like illusory travelers, householders waste their lives in vain, like donkeys. (3.225.30)
For even those who have bathed at holy pilgrimage sites and are drenched in the waters of the scriptures,
yet remain ignorant of its greatness and devoid of wisdom, wallow in the ashes of their sins.
When there are seven sons, the donkey carries the burden;
when there are many husbands, the wives carry the burden. (32)
The burden of a camel does not diminish even when seven young ones are present; likewise, the burden of a father does not diminish even when many sons are present as householders. (33)
Even for a camel that is decrepit, there is running for a hundred *krośas*;
even for a human being who is old, there is running for a hundred *krośas*. (34)
The donkey roams in the village; the man roams in the house.
But neither roams anywhere in Hari—what difference is there between a donkey and a man? 35.
A man with a long neck is always like a camel; when there is food to eat, the man with a long neck is like a camel.
When devoid of devotion to the meal, what difference is there between a man and a camel? (36)
One is constantly beaten with clubs, while another is [beaten] with words; since both are indifferent to the removal of suffering, what difference is there between a human and a donkey? (37)

*Khara* is that which possesses the senses and their objects; it gives those (*tāni rāti*), thus it is *khara*. *Nara* is known as that which gives the meaning of Nārāyaṇa (*nārāyaṇārtha*) to man (*nare na*). || 38 ||
If a man, having abandoned Nārāyaṇa, should fall into hell, what difference is there between a donkey and a man, other than that which arises from their physical bodies, such as hooves or nails? (39)
Since the movement of both the donkey and the man is unrestrained,
and there is no limit to their actions, what indeed is the difference between the donkey and the man?
If a man bathes [at sacred sites] but never chants the name of Hari, he is indeed a donkey; he who does not utter the name of Hari is truly a donkey. (43)
Therefore, having risen early in the morning and bathed, one should chant the name of Nārāyaṇa;
one should worship the Supreme Self and feed the Lord, the Consort of Śrī. 42.
Then one should partake of that merit and drink the water of its grace;
one should serve virtuous men and always worship Śrī Hari. ||43||
One should indeed practice the chanting of the Name;
one should contemplate the form of Kṛṣṇa during dreams, while awake, and even in deep sleep. (44)
When the senses possess outward activity, that state is proclaimed as waking;
at that time, the forms of Hari and the saintly devotees are to be perceived externally. (45)
Indeed, the virtuous should be served with all external efforts;
they should be served with discernment by one who is awake, dominated by the quality of goodness (sattva). 46.
Even through delusion, those in the waking state dominated by *rajas* should be served;
those in the waking state dominated by *tamas* should be served when one is afflicted by grief, fatigue, and the like. (47)

The functions of the sense organs, however, having resorted to the heart and the throat, have reached the physical seats [of the senses]; this indeed is the state of dreaming, while [the state] when they are asleep is deep sleep. 48.
Then, in that dream, one should serve the virtuous with discernment;
at that time, when the dream is dominated by the quality of goodness (sattva), one should serve Lord Hari. 49.
They should be attended upon with a deluded intellect during a dream dominated by *rajas*;
they should be served with grief, fatigue, and the like during a dream dominated by *tamas*. (3.225.50)
When the mental modifications (vṛttis) dwell slightly within the heart, that is the state of "half-sleep" (ardhasuṣupti).
Indeed, for a moment, one should practice service to the equanimity (sāmya) during the sleep of the sattva (sattvasuptika). ||51||
For a moment, service characterized by agitation should be performed during the sleep of the rājasa state;
for a moment, service characterized by the offering of absorption should be performed during the sleep of the tāmasa state. (52)
By implication, there is also absorption in Kṛṣṇa, as well as wandering among His devotees;
at that time, Hari appears even slightly in the presence of true devotees, but not elsewhere among those who are illusory.
Then, the dissolution of all things within the supreme Self is the state of deep sleep;
and the oneness of the Self with Śrī Hari is the fourth state (turya), which is deep sleep.
The enjoyment of that, delight in that, and the surrendering of one's consciousness therein; likewise, the surrendering of bliss and even the surrendering of one's very life. ||55||
The offering of one's life-breath, as well as the offering of all mental formations,
and the offering of all enjoyments— that is always the state of perfect deep sleep within Hari.

It should be practiced by the devotees of the Blessed One where there is the great bliss of Brahman, the destruction of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," and the dissolution of agency and possessiveness. (57)
When one offers oneself to Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva,
then Hari— the Supreme Brahman, the inner witness, the observer of karma—
becomes the seer residing within the self; for that is indeed the supreme state of the Fourth (turya).
Even there, the Blessed One is to be served, as in the fourth state (turyaka) within samādhi.
For the virtuous are likewise to be served when merged in the form [of the deity], just as in the fourth state;
by means of the vision of the abode, the power of the abode, the senses of the abode, and its splendor. (3.225.60)
The Blessed One is to be served by one's own self through the rites of the *dhāman*;
the Supreme Brahman is to be served as the Brahman-self in the supreme state.
Then, by means of his own self, Nārāyaṇa, who is the fourth state (turya), should be served by Śrī with her divine, single-flavored, and spiritual body. 62.
This state of liberation here is mingled with the abode of liberation; it is to be rejoiced in within Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (63)
All states of existence must be offered to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
childhood, youth, and old age must be surrendered to the Supreme Self.
Femininity or masculinity must indeed be bestowed upon the Supreme Self;
likewise, maidenhood, boyhood, the state of husband and wife, and womanhood [must be bestowed].
Asceticism and even death must be surrendered to Mādhava;
likewise, reflection, the drop (bindu), the resonance (nāda), the sound (dhvani), and the words.
For the supreme (parā), the intermediate (aparā), the visionary (paśyantī), the middle (madhyā),
and the articulate (vaikharī)— all these, born of Brahman and being the very forms of Brahman, are to be offered unto Hari.
The supreme speech is that which consists entirely of the description of Brahman, as well as the discourse of the virtuous concerning Kṛṣṇa, consisting of recitation and song. || 68 ||
A description of the playful deeds and character of Hari, and a description of devotion.
There is a description of the incarnations and a praise of those who are virtuous. (69)
Even the description of devotees is called the Supreme Speech;
that which bestows liberation and consists of divine sounds is all proclaimed as the Supreme. (3.225.70)
That [devotion] which is to be offered to Hari is indeed pleasing to Hari and brings happiness;
whereas other [forms of devotion] concern worldly objects and engage one in mundane affairs. (71)
That speech which is true to reality, of the nature of truth, yielding the fruit of *ṛta*, and bestowing merit—such speech, ever perceiving [the Truth], should always be offered to Hari. (72)
She is always considered the [goddess] of the lords, the gods, and the sages;
she bestows the light of existence and happiness, and should be offered to the Supreme Lord. (73)
Furthermore, that which is intent upon another purpose, consisting of censure or praise, aimed at accomplishing one's own worldly ends, and arising from a portion of delusion or error; (74)
That speech which is moderate, yielding both merit and demerit as its fruit, should be offered in every way to Hari Kṛṣṇa by one endowed with devotion. (75)
Alternatively, vitandā is speech that is either devoid of other meaning, or causes agitation through a flawed meaning; it is base, vulgar, and fruitless in both respects. (76)
That *vaikharī* speech, which is devoid of fruit for both the listener and the speaker, devoted solely to disintegration, and accompanied by mere affliction, is always the lowest. (77)
That [speech] too should be offered to Kṛṣṇa, provided it arises according to the proper place and time;
furthermore, there is another kind which has a single determined meaning, and yet another which possesses many meanings. (78)
Whether its meaning is obscure or clear, speech of all four kinds should always be offered to Kṛṣṇa; for it is divine and bestows liberation. (79)
The words, sentences, and means of valid cognition, which are established by logic, should be offered unto the Supreme Self; they should be offered unto the Supreme Self. ||3.225.80||
The principles of the elements and their derivatives are to be offered into the Supreme Self;
the triad of the object of meditation, the act of meditation, and the meditator are to be offered into that Supreme Self. 81.
