The categories of the object of enjoyment, the enjoyment, and the enjoyer should be offered into the Supreme Self;
devotion, which is the act of worshiping, should be offered into the glorious Supreme Lord.
O Indra, the powers belonging to Indra should be offered to Mādhava; whether they be human qualities or those of a donkey, they should be cast into the Lord Hari. (83)
Having then become divine, she would assume the form of a claw among people;
for that Nārāyaṇa, the divine space is indeed the imperishable ether.
"In that regard, one should cultivate delight in the act itself, not a delight in scratching.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, were Ratnaprabhā and the others instructed at that time.
By the virtuous Narasiṃhasvāmin, the yogi Hari:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (86)
Having been given the mantra, they were purified and became my Vaiṣṇava devotees;
then, they regarded their guru as the god Nṛsiṃhasvāmin himself.
They worshipped them exceedingly and fed them with great respect;
and they, who bring about auspiciousness, accepted blessings from them.
Having bowed to the virtuous, the donkey-herders went to another village;
indeed, in their own home, they worshipped Hari according to the aforementioned method, crying out, "Hare! Hare! (89).
Through their devotion, through such worship, through knowledge, and through service to their guru,
I quickly became pleased with the keepers of the donkeys.
Once, having made Garuḍa into a donkey and standing upon that donkey, I was traveling along the road when I encountered them ahead. (91)
Bearded and dressed in the garb of a Kṣatriya, looking as splendid as one ready for a journey, he said to them: "Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory to you, O Rāma Janārdana! (92)
"Victory to Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu! Victory to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!"—thus was Śrī Puruṣottama reminded by these names. (93)
Having quickly dismounted from the donkey, they offered their salutations;
and having heard the name of Hari, they too became joyful and indeed gathered around me. (94)
Just as beloved kinsmen, sons, or even parents would quickly restrain me and seat me upon a woolen rug. 95.
Greatly delighted on the road, they gave them water, fruit, and likewise food;
they also asked about his home, his arrival, and his activities.
Then I showed him my supreme divine abode in the highest ether, as well as the account of my deeds known as Nārāyaṇa and my arrival at the holy ford.
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, they became exceedingly devoted to me, Nārāyaṇa; knowing me to be their supreme devotee, they served me with heart-felt massages of their limbs. 98.
Thinking of me as the supreme saint, they prostrated themselves like a staff;
then, I quickly revealed my four-armed form to them.
Accompanied by Garuḍa, he bestowed that very same gift upon the path of the righteous;
he granted them grace regarding the fruits and other things they had consumed.
Wearing blankets on their shoulders and likewise carrying staffs in their hands,
with leather sandals upon their feet, they danced with eager excitement.
With long cloths upon their heads and wearing washed tunics, they danced with extreme joy and repeatedly rolled upon the ground. 102.
Grant me liberation, grant me Your state, O Hari, whose vehicle is the donkey!
Grant us Your divine abode, O Kṛṣṇa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa! 103.
Having uttered this, they suddenly placed the dust of his feet upon their faces; then, those charming ones, with one-pointed devotion like those in meditative absorption, beheld my vision.
Then, O Lakṣmī, they vanished; and in another moment, having regained their radiance, they praised me and considered themselves to be of blessed fortune. (105)
There on the path, they constructed an altar for Nārāyaṇa;
they constantly performed devotion always on the bank of the Luṇī river.
When the time was ripe, O Rāma, I gradually led even those thousands of them to my own abode, the imperishable state of liberation, by means of Garuḍa.
Thus have the devotees been uplifted by me through the practice of yoga;
from the recitation and hearing of this, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained. (108)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotee Ratnaprabha, the Ass-herder, Attaining the Lord and Liberation through the Holy Yoga of Lord Nṛsiṃha," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; on the bank of the Ājīvanī river in Saurāṣṭra, there was a physician named Gadārdaneśvara.
Having established his residence in Jīradurga and knowing the essential principles of medicinal herbs,
the Brahmin, together with his family, set up his own shop in Jīradurga and there performed medical treatment for the sick using those medicines.
Indeed, his name became renowned as one who knew the art of destroying diseases. Far and wide among the clusters of villages and throughout the people of the land,
the subjects would come to his house for the removal of their ailments.
He too, having remembered Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, gives the medicine;
that indeed becomes fruitful, virtuous, and a remover of disease.
It is combined with sacrificial ashes and the sugar-like grace of the Lord.
Powders made from Tulasī leaves, medicinal woods, and minerals; ashes and other substances; mercury preparations processed by fire that act as emetics in autumn;
and likewise fermented liquors (āsava) that destroy phlegm and cure chronic fevers.
Purgatives, pills, digestive stimulants, and those that destroy wind; seeds of trees that bestow power and nourish the bodily constituents;
powdered products derived from living organisms; and husks that remove disease.
Whether derived from leaves, flowers, or even the powders of bark,
whatever [medicine] one gives to a sick person destroys the disease in every way;
it also swiftly removes the poison arising from the venom of snakes and other creatures.
In the clinic of such a physician, ten men perform grinding, as well as massaging and cooking.
They always diligently prepare medicines—extracting the essence, powdering, and incinerating—as appropriate for each case. (12)
At the start of the rainy season, Gadārdana himself goes to a riverbank within the sacred field,
taking vessels made of glass and other materials to a place teeming with living creatures.
Having caught reptiles, cochineal insects, indragopa beetles, ants,
and creatures that cause red swellings, he places them in a vessel.
Indeed, by the thousands, those who are fierce toward living beings meet their destruction;
for even lizards and the like fall into pits and other such traps when incited by stimulating oils. (15)
Having seized it and placed it in a glass vessel, the king of physicians deprives [the patient] of life;
merciless for the sake of his own gain, he is a destroyer of another's life. (16)
Even though he was a Brahmin, he became devoted to the ways of Rākṣasas and intent on the path of violence;
indeed, through greed for coins and out of craving, he became a perpetrator of harm.
Thus, Gadārdana, the destroyer of beings, from time to time became a slayer who caused the destruction of ten million creatures for the sake of medicinal herbs. || 18 ||
Even the creatures, fainting and tormented, cursed that twice-born man:
"May even all living beings take away the life-breaths of you, the destroyer of our lives! (19)
Having repeatedly encountered suffering like ours within eighty-four hundred thousand wombs, go again and again to death. (3.226.20)
Thus cursed with many curses of intense force,
that physician gradually became possessed by fever at the time of the ripening of his karma.
For the destruction of the fever, he suddenly administered pills and other remedies;
yet the fever did not subside, but on the contrary, it increased even further. ||22||
Indeed, an obstacle that has arisen from one's past karma (prārabdha) is not destroyed even by ten million means;
likewise, great suffering arising from a curse does not dissolve through other means.
[He is the master] of the physician, of Yama the King, of the god, and of the bull; what then need be said of the powerful Lord and of man? (24)
It dissolves only through the grace of Śāpadanta and not otherwise;
the creatures here have perished—whence could one obtain his grace? (25)
For chronic fever has acquired power over the physician; like a ghost, it constantly withers him who is devoted to the destruction of diseases. (26)
Then, in order to dispel that [fever], he constantly drinks decoctions;
yet, because those decoctions have not struck the *apra-ārabdha* (uncommenced) portion [of karma], they produce the opposite effect. ||27||
They cause the destruction of blood and likewise increase heat;
they also create minute pores within the channels and the masses of flesh.
Then all those boiling fluids that cause wounds receded;
yet even in his urine, excrement, and spittle, a portion of blood flowed forth. (29)
Even the physician, despite his excellent treatment, became more ill than the patient;
for in one who is beyond recovery, there is neither wisdom, nor strength, nor medicine, nor remedies.
Even when applied by those skilled in wholesome means, they prevail against great evil;
O Lakṣmī, [this is] for the pacification of the renowned physician who has exerted himself.
Other physicians also arrived from afar for the purpose of treatment;
having performed the root-therapy, they administered medicinal drugs. (32)
Nevertheless, not even a trace of this [merit] destroyed by sin is seen;
and having their hopes shattered, they return to their own homes. (33)
Indeed, the flow of blood from the physician has not subsided;
O Lakṣmī, by the medicines he applied there, it has instead increased even further. (34)
Thus a year passed for him, suffering like a denizen of Yama; then his mother, having risen from the ashes, was herself consumed by the physician.
She too, having undergone a transformation, broke out with boils all over;
her body became filled with pus, foul-smelling, and cracked on every side. (36)
The hellish vessel became filled with pus and excrement;
no one could go near its side, and the physician, tormented by pain, wept. (37)
Afflicted by the bites of insects and creatures that have arisen [within him], he suffers;
with his flesh being devoured by these creatures, he cries out in extreme agony. (38)
O Rame, the king of physicians has encountered such great suffering;
he constantly resorts to me solely for the destruction of his misery. (39)
"I am indeed not capable of destroying the suffering caused by the curse;
for I am situated within the heart of the one who cursed, and thus I am constrained."
I myself am the giver of the curse; how then could I again be the one who releases from the curse?
For without that curse, I have no power to bring about the liberation of a living being.
For such a physician who attends even to me, suffering does not cease at all, nor does death occur. (482)
He takes food that sustains life and is light for his stomach;
therefore, his vital breaths do not depart, as they are bound by the experience of the curse.
The king of physicians also performed many meritorious acts of giving;
yet his vital breaths, possessing a radiance equal to the city of Yama, did not leave their place. (44)
Through the application of medicinal herbs, a slight recovery of health is observed; for a month, health is maintained, and the flesh and marrow increase. (45)
Furthermore, living beings are born there by the thousands;
insects bite them in many ways, just as in the hell-pot of Yama here.
Thus, by the power of the curse, this physician remained in such a state; ten years indeed passed for this patient in this manner. (47)
However many living beings have been killed by him, that much suffering from Yama has already manifested here directly; nevertheless, more remains. (48)
In the meantime, Lakṣmī and her six sons, due to association with sinners and excessive diarrhea, gradually met their death one after another. (49)
The six daughters of Gadārdana became widowed and childless due to the fault of their association with him. || 3.226.50 ||
Yet all these women became widows because of their fathers' transgressions, [arising] from sitting, lying down, clothing, eating, and performing activities together with them. (51)
Through birth and through the inheritance of property, evil is transmitted among people;
it is like the fear felt by those householders toward the creatures they kill. (52)
And likewise, due to his curse, suffering befell his household members;
all this intense and swift-flowing misery arose right here. (53)
Thus, having reached the state of being without offspring, only one wife remained;
she too, overcome with anxiety, summoned her brothers in every way. (54)
He gave all his wealth to them, so that his house became as if empty;
even his wife and brothers were bound by the snare of wealth. (55)
All those who consumed wealth for their own enjoyment quickly became afflicted with disease and died;
indeed, due to their addiction to sinful wealth, they were left without any lineage.
One must not eat the food of a physician, for one would thereby become liable to penance; O Lakṣmī, a physician is indeed a "hundred-killer," and his food is considered to bestow sin. (57)
Behold, these physicians are indeed merciless, always like the messengers of Yama;
they are engaged in cutting, killing, inflicting death, and attending to corpses and the like. (58)
And by practicing with naked corpses, by gazing upon naked corpses, and by constantly seeing corpses that are naked, foul-smelling, and infested with insects; ||59||

In the performance of medical treatments and the application of cauterization, emetics, and so forth, physicians who take the lives of others are impure and equal to the messengers of Yama. (3.226.60)
One must not eat the food of those sinners who take life without direct experience [of its consequences]; for such food brings about one's own destruction.
Indeed, not everyone in this world is equal to Dhanvantari;
for only those who know the truth, who are meritorious, non-violent, and pure [attain such status]. (62)
They are always considered worthy of worship, being like the sons of the Aśvins;
for they are the bringers of welfare to the world and are entirely free from the path of violence.
Just as those who employ medicines according to their requirements are devoted to them,
yet free from injury to living beings, so too are those who practice with wood, minerals, and other materials.
Those physicians of the gods are difficult to find, yet worship of them bestows merit.
Then, O Lakṣmī, after some time had passed, that wife of Gadārdana—
Afflicted by the disease of consumption, she was known by the name Mukundinī;
she was a Vaiṣṇavī devoted to her husband and endowed with faith, pure disposition, and virtuous qualities.
From her childhood, she became a devotee of Hari;
she was one who bathed [in sacred waters], a worshiper, full of devotion, virtuous, and entirely devoted to her husband.

She is one who constantly performs vows, charity, and austerities; she is a constant attendant upon the virtuous; she is devoted to the stories of Kṛṣṇa; and she is adorned by purity and contentment. (68)
Through body, mind, speech, and actions, she was a servant of the virtuous;
she was eternally devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa and endowed with the ninefold devotion. (69)
She is the performer of offerings such as necklaces, food oblations, and incense; she is a worshiper of Viṣṇu, one who offers herself in surrender, a great devotee of the Lord, and beloved by Hari.
Devoted to virtue and truth, virtuous, endowed with a nature united to Dharma, divine and possessed of divine qualities— O Blessed One, she is eternally steadfast.
O Lakṣmī, you are devoted to meditation and intent on surrendering everything to me, Hari;
yet such a devotee as you is deeply distressed by worldly association.
"Indeed, half of my husband's entire being is enjoyed by his own wife;
thus she remains devoted to me, though she is afflicted and overcome with grief. (73)
When her year had passed and she was emaciated, her husband died;
then, a widow dependent on others, she wept like a female osprey.
Having observed her husband’s miserable state, and remembering her daughter, son, and others, as well as remembering her deceased brothers and likewise her own own wretched condition; ||75||
Deprived of fortitude, she cried out with wailing like one afflicted by consumption;
and hearing her lamentation, the gods then stood stunned for a moment.
The seasons and even the principles (tattvas) became momentarily inert;
then, O Lakṣmī, I, the inner self, suddenly perceived my own [true] nature.
Dwelling in the heart of Mukundinī, I became affectionate and sorrowful;
yet my inner self granted me fortitude through right reflection.
Having regained consciousness and summoned her fortitude, she, O Lakṣmī, repeatedly remembered me, Hari: "O Lord! O Lord! Have mercy! (79)
Have compassion for this devoted woman who is in distress and widowed;
be kind to her who remains, having lost all her possessions.
"There is no limit to my sufferings; rescue me from the ocean of existence!
First kill me, and then kill my husband. (81)
May my destiny be that of a virtuous wife, not that of a widow;
therefore, having kindled the fire, I shall indeed burn alive. (82)
Chastity is always appropriate; widowhood is terrifying.
You have compassion; please come and restore him to life, free from disease.
"If this is not so, grant death to both of us simultaneously.
Having spoken thus, my devotee meditated upon me within her heart for a moment. (84)
Meanwhile, my attendants were sent by me to that husband of hers,
[to find him] as he was being led away by the messengers of Yama, suffering and seeking refuge.
Having gone quickly, my attendants, who were seekers of wealth, separated him from me;
he was seized, brought back, and once again made to enter my body. (86)
Suddenly the body rose up, as if bound by some unseen fetter;
those seeking the corpse stood stunned, filled with great wonder. (87)
Some said: "The experience of the results of sins was incomplete;
having returned for further enjoyment of those sins, he was not protected by the messengers of Yama. (88)
But others then said, "By the devotion of his truthful wife, he has indeed risen up through her great devotion; he shall surely become free from disease. (89)
Others said: "This sinful man exists merely as a mental impression (vāsanika);
he does not go to the next world alone, leaving behind his own wife."
But others then said, "For the lines of karma are indeed difficult to overcome";
thus they desisted and ceased their insistence upon him.
Then, O Lakṣmī, by the power of my wife’s devotion,
I appeared before her in person, divine and embodied, along with my attendants.
The four-armed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, possessing a divine body,
said to Mukundinī, "Choose a boon from me."
She too, rising suddenly, fell at my feet;
Gadārdana, for his part, seeing me, slept as if free from disease.
Rising up, they quickly prostrated themselves at my feet upon the ground;
and being commanded by me to grant a boon, those two spoke.
Grant us liberation, O ocean of compassion, Supreme Lord, Consort of Ramā!
For everything has been carried away by Time, and we two have indeed been rendered homeless. (16)
The physician of physicians is Mahākāla, and his physician is the Supreme Lord;
both have been utterly driven away here by your attendants at the call of Yama. (97)
"O Supreme Lord, grant us liberation or assign us whatever you desire.
To these two who were thus entreating him, he replied, "So be it," and [placed them] upon a celestial chariot.
Having caused her to ascend to the supreme heaven, he sent her off with his attendants;
at that time, Satī, the consort of Mukunda, was [elevated] by the power of her devotion to the True Being. 99.
Leaving heaven, she quickly went to the world of the virtuous (Satyaloka) with her husband;
for my attendants [brought] that Mukundinī together with her lord.
Having established the world of virtuous people, they indeed departed for my abode;
thus, when the end of time arrives, those two shall go to the supreme state.
O Lakṣmī, by the power of his devotion, that physician abandoned the southern region (Yama’s realm) and went to the world of the virtuous (Satyaloka),
even though his heap of sins was great.
Nevertheless, by the power of a woman and through my compassion, he has attained dissolution;
for a husband receives half of the merit performed by his wife.
Vows, gifts, and so forth, as well as devotion—everything attains half [of its merit] through [the recipient].
In this way, it applies to relatives, sons, wives, friends, and others as well. 104.
Even when performed under the name of a *preta*, merit accrues to the deceased;
therefore, people perform the *śrāddha*, sacrifice, and gift-giving on his behalf.
O Rame, there is indeed no other means for granting liberation equal to devotion;
by reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall surely come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sufferings of the Physician named Gadārdaneśvara Due to His Sins and the Liberation of His Wife Mukundinī Through Devotion," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to this beautiful story of a devotee named Deśyāvana,
who was a protector of monkeys and mongooses.
The yogi Deśyāvana was the son of Candrāvana;
he dwelt at Gauvādikheta on the bank of the river Gomaṇḍalī.
The son was indeed instructed by his father in the care of monkeys and mongooses,
as well as in making the monkeys dance and in pitting the mongooses against one another in combat.
She becomes a monkey or a king; she is a monkey accompanied by a gurgling sound.
Wearing a fine garment, she remains bashful in the presence of a monkey. (4)
She behaves like a queen and is well-trained in dancing;
yet, when there is a lapse in her dancing, the monkey strikes her out of anger. || 5 ||
Then the monkey, having gone between the pit and the bamboo pole by means of the rope, moved along like an actor— a performer holding a bowl as his parasol.
This female monkey, moving upon the stage, plays the ḍamaru drum;
she displays a monkey to the people with her hand holding a staff.
Seeing him, people, their hearts filled with devotion, offered wealth and food;
then the monkey descended from the new cart.
Having yoked two jackals and placed the female monkey upon them,
he himself, acting as the charioteer, drove it like a king.
The two Nakulas stand by the side of Vānarī like two attendants;
holding beautiful chowries, the people gaze upon them with curiosity. (3.227.10)
As the two monkeys were carrying those two jackals, the monkey struck them with a staff; meanwhile, the two enraged jackals stood facing him at the front of the vehicle. 11.
Having emerged and come forward, and having leaped up and shouted in anger,
they watched as he fought properly with the monkey.
There, while the people were watching, one jackal fought with the monkey;
the second, seizing a female monkey by the ear, carried her away and vanished.
Then, leaving the arena, the female monkey fled toward the forest;
meanwhile, the male monkey also ran after her to bring back the jackal.
The jackal ran after the female monkey to bring her back,
while the mongoose climbed up the two bamboo poles behind him.
For as he watched, the female monkey was carried off by jackals;
thereupon, a battle ensued between the local forest-dwellers and the forest-dwellers from that region. (16)
Furthermore, there was the dyeing of the jackal's fur and his request for forgiveness;
he begged for alms from the people, and his wife in Purikā likewise entreated them. (17)
Thus, constantly in villages, market towns, and cities, he goes again and again and causes the beasts to perform laughter and dance. (18)
With the wealth produced from that—such as new clothes and flour and so forth—he always maintains himself and remains constantly together with his wife. (19)
Filled with compassion, he also tended to the livestock;
by nature devoted to his duty, Deśyāvana went out every morning daily.
He bathes, bows down to the dark one of variegated luster, and gazes upon him;
he carries water and fruit, and food prepared in the city. (2.1)
Having offered [the food] to Viṣṇu and given it to the animals and his own wife, he then eats; not otherwise, while remembering me, Nārāyaṇa. (22)
O Lakṣmī, my devotees everywhere—whether refined or unrefined—whoever they may be, worship me as the Lord in whatever manner they can. (23)
Exhausted by devotion, I strive to fulfill their hearts' desires;
for even Śūdrā Purikā, having bathed, serves me every day.
On my cart, he indeed preserves my beautiful form and auspicious luster;
he knows no other dharma, but knows only the taking of refuge. ||25||
The blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the most excellent in splendor, will effect our deliverance;
therefore, nothing should be consumed, not even water, without first offering it to Him. 26.
Indeed, not a single day should be spent fruitlessly without devotion to Hari;
for Hari dwells as the inner self within the monkey, the mongoose, and even the jackal.
O Lakṣmī, in this manner those two—the monkey and the mongoose—perceive [the distinction] everywhere, whether in a woman or a man, in a tree, or in that which is insentient or sentient. (28)
Therefore, those two—pure, affectionate, and devoted—are approved by me;
having fashioned a sport during the day, they produced and provided for their own sustenance and food. (29)
Fully content with whatever is obtained, they perform chanting at night, accompanied by the sound of hand-drums and other instruments: "O Kṛṣṇa! O Rāma! O Lord of Ramā! (3.227.30)
Thus they indeed constantly perform worship at the onset of night;
on the full moon day, they offer sweet food before me.
Having bestowed it upon the animals, those two then enjoy that which arises from my grace every month; thus they observe this vow continuously.
O Rame, for those who always drink water mixed with *tulasī*, there is no cause for devotion other than that; neither forest, nor land, nor home, nor wealth matters. (33)
Affection is the cause therein; the heart is the cause of devotion;
faith is the cause therein, and merit is the great cause. (34)
Thus, while both were dwelling on the bank of Gomaṇḍalī,
once a community of holy men (sādhus) indeed approached them from the side, seeking to perform a pilgrimage.
Both of them went quickly and bowed at the feet of the holy ones;
they then requested a moment's rest from their lords. (36)
Even the virtuous, having beheld the riverbank and the shade of the trees, found rest for a moment and drank the cool water. (37)
On that full-moon day, by the conjunction of good fortune, sweetmeats were prepared;
indeed, the entire *saṃyāva* was offered to Śrī Hari. (38)
O Lakṣmī, those who gave with devotion to the virtuous and the virtuous who ate while mindful of me—therein the saṃyāva attained increase. (39)
Having known this through my inner self, I increased the saṃyāva;
all twenty virtuous ones were satisfied, and it became that large in extent.
Even as the *saṃyāva* was being carried forward, it did not diminish in the slightest;
indeed, even the virtuous realized that to be the very power of devotion.
In the midst of that [assembly], the leader of the circle, a virtuous man named Sudhāmara, taught these words, considering him a worthy vessel and a devotee.
Listen, O devotee: Hari is always to be served, as are His saintly ones;
Nārāyaṇa dwells among the virtuous, fulfilling their desires and intentions. ||43||
Neither birth, nor wealth, nor sovereignty is the means for attaining Kṛṣṇa’s grace; affectionate devotion and service to the virtuous are the means for attaining Kṛṣṇa’s grace. (44)
O Blessed One, the virtuous are the ultimate goal, and likewise the Blessed Lord himself;
indeed, Naimiṣa forest is the sacred field where the mind becomes blunted [of its worldly desires]. (45)
The senses become dulled, withdrawn, and steady;
turning away from sense objects, they become givers of peace. (46)
In that field which possesses the form of a holy sage and is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, one should bathe in the waters of the company of the virtuous and perform meritorious sacrifices. 47.
There, the supreme accomplishment of the Dharma of Liberation occurs swiftly;
likewise, for those seeking liberation, meditative absorption and its perfection arise quickly. (48)
The monkeys are indeed the sense-faculties, while the two jackals are the ego and the mind;
one should always bring those mongooses—the former karmic actions—under their control. 49.
One should cause those who are under one's influence to abide in righteousness, knowledge, detachment, devotion, service to the virtuous, and in the form of Hari. (3.227.50)
A wise person should always abandon envy, which is defined as the inability to endure the excellence of others;
likewise, pride, which obstructs all [virtues], should be diligently abandoned by the wise. (51)
One should constantly cultivate goodness (sattva), from which a delight in the Dharma arises; that which is called goodness is the Kṛta Yuga, wherein there is meditation upon Hari. ||52||
One should indeed restrain the impulses of rajas that impel one toward actions driven by desire;
the Tretā Yuga should be understood as characterized by rajas, and in this age, service performed with the body is what must be practiced.
One whose self is joined with rajas and tamas is said to be of the nature of the Dvāpara age;
therein, one should abandon greed, the desire for gain, and thirst [for worldly things], and practice service to Hari.
The Kali age should be understood as consisting of darkness (tamas), wherein illusion, falsehood, and the like prevail;
in such a time, one should seek the company of the virtuous and constantly worship them. ||55||
Through the loud chanting of Viṣṇu’s names, the force of the Kali age is turned back;
according to one's prior karma, the ages manifest within the heart.
Therefore, meditation, self-abidance, and the supreme sense of one's own greatness must be practiced with particular care, for they are not in contradiction with the duties of the age. (57)
For one who worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there is indeed no fear born of time or karma;
thinking "I have achieved my purpose," he should serve the most excellent of holy men.
One should practice the ninefold devotion with the realization of offering all one's possessions;
indeed, by taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa and His saintly devotees, the Kali age is destroyed from the heart.
Where there is the dwelling of Kṛṣṇa, there Kali does not exist;
where the virtuous reside, there Māyā does not exist.
The Dharma of the great devotee is essentially the state of being a great Vaiṣṇava; it consists of the offering of everything and, being auspicious, it should always be protected. ||61||
Theft, backbiting, and deceit must never be practiced under any circumstances;
one should seek the company of the virtuous and always place trust in the good. (62)
The bounds of conduct must be observed by the virtuous just as they were by Kṛṣṇa;
service to the virtuous must always be performed just as it was by Kṛṣṇa. ||63||
For those in whom there is violence, intoxication, theft, falsehood, as well as deceit, atheism, and guile—they are not grounds for trust. (64)
But they take no pleasure in the company of the virtuous, nor in the virtuous themselves, nor in Hari; indeed, those sinners, who delight in strife, constantly harbor malice toward them.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should serve the virtuous and never the atheists;
by serving the Lord of All through the company of the virtuous, one should acquire liberation. 66.
But he who, in the company of the virtuous, worships with faith and single-minded devotion,
indeed goes at the end of the body to the supreme, imperishable abode of Hari.
He may go to Goloka or Vaikuṇṭha, to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa;
he may go to Śvetadvīpa or to the city of Śrī, and attain immortality.
For those possessing divine vision, these [realms] are present in every way right before them; for those possessing worldly vision, those abodes remain far away. ||69||
Just as the individual soul exists in the body, and the glorious Puruṣottama exists within that soul,
one should perceive the divine abodes nearby through the vision of being identical with Him.
Wherever Kṛṣṇa is, whether in the heart or outside, there indeed reside all abodes and all the sovereign powers of Kṛṣṇa.
Those devotees who possess such understanding are considered equal to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the merit born from the sight of them is identical to the sight of Kṛṣṇa himself. (72)

Through the meeting with all such [saints] as these, liberation—which is indeed difficult to attain by other means—is obtained; for by the grace of the virtuous, that which is hard to reach becomes easy. (73)
Out of affection for those who have taken refuge in them, the virtuous lead them to the Imperishable;
having indeed caused their latent impressions (vāsanās) to perish, they lead them to the supreme state.
Whether it be a group of women, a group of men, or any embodied being possessed of desire,
the virtuous, having purified them and made them divine, lead them to the Imperishable.
Listen, O Deśyāvana; indeed, remember Hari, the Lord of the dance.
By means of the rope of the flute, remember in every way that divine, imperishable abode. 76.
When the monkey was on the rope, he remembered Viṣṇu; when on the umbrella, he remembered the umbrella-bearer.
In the first bamboo joint he reached Goloka, and in the second, Vikuṇṭha.
"Remember that divine chariot where that female monkey is stationed;
remember there the Brahma-chariot, the illusory form of Viṣṇu as a monkey."
Remember also the jackal as egoism (ahaṃkāra) and the second as the mental faculty (mānasa);
by those two that Māyā is joined; deliver her to Viṣṇu.
But remember there the Guru Nakula, the seer of all;
for the divine Guru, established in the syllables of the rope, will deliver you.
Produce the great sound arising from the hand-drum, "Oṃ Nārāyaṇa Mādhava," so that it may indeed be heard constantly by all living beings. (8.1)
Behold devotion consisting of service, like a dancer who protects the stage;
behold likewise alms-gathering as the journey toward liberation, composed of eternal substance.
Behold those embodied beings who have come for refuge and the gift of alms; through their association with the virtuous, they become purified and focused in mind. (83)
Behold me, the virtuous and immortal Hari, as your inner controller;
behold Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of knowledge and liberation, who seeks your welfare. (84)
Behold your own self as the one to be instructed, the protector of monkeys and others, the master, the controller, and the one who ordains the performance of the play upon the stage. (85)
Behold the stage, the birth, the body, and the entire household;
behold death as the end of the play and the casting off of karmas. (86)
Behold how it delights the minds of the spectators;
by acting thus, behold that your own satisfaction has become eternal. (87)
Thus, by constantly perceiving in this way, you shall attain the supreme state;
having realized the Brāhmī Upaniṣad within your heart, there is no fear.
As long as latent impressions (vāsanā) exist, so long does the play (khela) continue;
through dwelling in the Upaniṣad, the play shall always become [the state of] play.
Supreme peace shall prevail; O descendant of Deśyāvana, act accordingly. Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! ||3.227.90||
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Person! Worship the Supreme Lord eternally; thus, remain composed in mind. (91)
Having spoken thus, the virtuous one, together with his maṇḍala and well-honored by Kamalā, became gracious in mind and departed after bestowing words of blessing. (92)
Then, having looked at the vessel held [before him], this one who speaks of what is to be taught saw the saṃyāva, full of grace, exactly as it was. (93)
He considered it a marvel, a great wonder, and even the grace of Hari;
he and his family likewise enjoyed that very same divine favor. (94)
Indeed, together with his family, he attained divine vision; Hari stood before him, at his sides, and behind him, surrounding him on all sides.
Wherever he looks, there he beholds the Soul of the Universe—in what is above, below, on the ground, in a vessel, in a garment, in a chariot, or even in a monkey. (96)
In the jackal, the mongoose, and the dancer, he beheld the Supreme Self;
the devotee attained a divine state and held that which was imagined within his hand.
O Lakṣmī, my form as Nārāyaṇa became visible everywhere; that was indeed the grace of my virtuous guru, and it was truly auspicious for me. 98.
By means of which his entire supreme vision of Brahman was born;
then, perceiving that his word had become effective, people began to arrive in great throngs. 99.
But having obtained a vision of him, even those who are impure become purified;
they receive my mantra from that devotee and indeed depart from there.
They become fulfilled by the sight of the Great Bhāgavata;
then, when the time had arrived, I appeared before him. 101.
Accompanied by a celestial chariot and surrounded by my attendants,
O Lakṣmī, I likewise caused divine bodies to be fashioned for you as well.
Having caused the monkeys, mongooses, and jackals, as well as Kīśapa and Kīśapā,
to ascend the celestial chariot, he brought them to my presence.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, she granted liberation through the yoga of devotion to all who enjoy my grace, as she stood in the midst of the circle of the liberated.
By reciting, hearing, reflecting upon, and practicing this,
one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as eternal, divine heaven.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Kīśapāla, the Sudhāmarasādhu of Deśyāvana, through an Occasional Narrative," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; I shall tell you another story.
In the city of Pārvatī, there was a devotee named Harṣadharma who was a barber. 1.
He lived there with his family, engaged in the work of serving the king;
the ruler there was named Svarṇadhanvā. || 2 ||
This barber, together with his family, performs service for him.
The barber’s wife was a virtuous woman named Nigamikā. (3)
Devoted to her husband, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, and highly virtuous,
she was intent on vows, charity, and the recitation of prayers, and she found delight in Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly devoted to the service of the virtuous and always possessing a divine disposition,
she had five sons and five beautiful daughters.
All of them are devotees of the Blessed One, Vaiṣṇavas endowed with devotion; they cry out to me, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the gopīs and the Consort of Śrī.
They also constantly devote themselves to me in their homes with offerings and worship;
they always honor me with the sixteen types of service.
Abiding always in their physical forms, I accept their worship with affection;
likewise, even the barber, having always bathed and performed my worship, [attains his goal].
Only after offering me the food-oblation and eating it himself does he go to the king's palace;
for a servant indeed serves the king with his whole being, not a barber.
Likewise, the sons and daughters of the barber, as well as those of the royal household,
serve me appropriately after performing my worship and other rites.
Every day, that barber’s wife, Nigamikā,
would rise first in the morning, bathe, and perform the cleaning of the house and its surroundings.
Having made the water warm and having bathed Keśava, as well as me and the Śālagrāma, with all kinds of offerings; || 1-2 ||
Having prepared fruit, rice, sweetmeats, flatbread, curd, and milk—auspicious, warm, and even somewhat thick—he offers them to me as well. (13)
Then, having performed the ritual waving of lights (nirājana) and offered the formal dismissal (parihāra),
she raises her husband up, bathes him, and likewise offers the water used for washing her husband's feet.
Having drunk the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet, she worships her husband as well; afterwards, she offers him whatever he desires and whatever is pleasing to him. (15)
Then he gives food and water as is appropriate to guests, to virtuous people, and even to the destitute, and he also offers it to the cow.
Having offered water to the Sun and presented the *arghya* to Viṣṇu,
one should thereafter give flour to the swarm of ants.
Having offered everything to the ancestors so that it becomes pure once more, and having then presented water along with food and other offerings to the husband; || 18 ||
Having first offered the food, water, and fruit to her daughters and others, Nigamikā herself eats the remaining remnants of the prasāda. (19)
"With every morsel, I offer it to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa";
remembering this, she eats, and likewise she drinks water.
In the center, a dog, a mongoose, a monkey, a parrot, a sparrow, a cow, a bull, and even a female cat shall come; having given to them, one eats, and not otherwise.
Such was that devoted servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
having completed her household duties, she would set out with great speed early in the morning. (22)
A most virtuous woman from the city proceeded toward the queen’s residence;
she slowly approached Queen Pañcadevī, who was lying asleep upon her bed.
She massages her limbs and rubs her feet;
for the sake of the queen, she also quickly prepares warm water. (24)
He provides tooth-cleaning powder, mouthfuls of water for rinsing, and so forth;
he performs the preliminary acts of purification and bathes him with waters.
There was also the rubbing with fragrant unguents and the cleansing of the body;
likewise, there was the grooming of the hair and the beautifying of the hairstyle and so forth. ||26||
Wearing ornaments such as elegant dress and finery, applying collyrium to the eyes, applying red lac-dye, and coloring the nails, lips, and so forth. ||27||
Having given everything as it was required and having honored her like the Goddess Śrī,
Vāyudā pleases the Great Queen with a fan.
She performs all household duties beautifully, as well as the midday and evening services and so forth. (29)
The barber-woman completes the queen's duties up to the offering of betel;
she daily prepares a bed rich with flowers and perfumes.
The queen sleeps happily while the barber’s wife massages her;
the queen indeed falls asleep, while the barber’s wife enters into a deep slumber. (31)
Having gone home, she constantly performs service for her husband, consisting of massaging his feet, and thereafter the barber’s wife sleeps.
Having performed excellent service for the king, her husband would always return home at the end of the night and then attend to his barber-wife.
Blessed is the faith of servants; even more so that of those who serve as slaves;
and even more so, O Lakṣmī, that of women whose souls are endowed with devotion to their husbands. (34)
This world is bound by karma and is indeed subservient to karma;
yet, one who is under the sway of a desireless state of being acts as a sovereign devotee.
Both the barber and his wife know the bondage of karma;
service to a king is a bond of karma, yet this exertion is for the sake of obtaining wealth. (36)
Indeed, without the acquisition [of resources], the maintenance of the body cannot be accomplished at all;
food, wealth, and clothing are obtained through service to the king. (37)
Nevertheless, those two, being full of devotion, perform service to me out of a desire for eternal bliss, rather than through false service and the like. (38)
The embodied being, under the influence of karma, must act for the sake of the body, senses, and objects;
however, one who desires liberation must act for the sake of the Self through knowledge. (39)
It should be performed for the sake of Śrī Hari with the disposition of total surrender;
thinking thus, those two always practice service unto me. (3.228.40)
In Rājagṛha as well, those two always perform worship of Me;
they also repeatedly sing My praises and the song of the cowherd girls.
As they spoke of the Rāsa-līlā and related its story,
the queen and the king, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, fell asleep.
In this way, one should worship others as well, and even cause them to practice devotion:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. ||43||
O Kṛṣṇa, for those two devoted ones who constantly mutter "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" again and again while chanting and causing others to chant, such was their discipline in the service of the King. 44.
Once, however, when it was evening and the barber had departed from the house, she remained in the house, intent on service to that very king. (45)
Indeed, at the moment of his departure, ten virtuous men and ten virtuous women of great renown arrived. 46.
Through great fortune and great merit, the virtuous come;
indeed, everything should be done with reverence for the sake of welcoming the virtuous. 47.
Abandoning hundreds of tasks, one should practice the service of the virtuous;
for householders, the duty of hospitality toward guests is always considered the highest dharma. (48)
Furthermore, for the sake of the virtuous and the saintly, it is certain that one must abandon everything and remain devoted to service; this is the supreme dharma. 49.
The human body exists for the sake of liberation; the virtuous on earth exist for the sake of liberation. Therefore, people should swiftly offer their entire being to them in yoga. (3.228.50)
Otherwise, what benefit is there in a human body without service, when guests come to one's house and are satisfied with greetings and the like? (5.1)
That house shall always be purifying and worthy of being a dwelling for Lakṣmī, provided that the guests within it do not indeed depart with disappointed hearts. (52)
If they are treated with disrespect or are dissatisfied, that house is considered as if burnt;
it indeed becomes devoid of merit and bereft of fortune and prosperity. ||53||
That house which provides refuge for virtuous renunciants, ascetics,
and yogis is always a divine abode of the gods and the most excellent of sacred pilgrimage sites.
That house where there are no virtuous people and no service to guests is declared to be a cremation ground; indeed, impurity (sūtaka) always exists therein. //55//
In that house where virtuous people reside, the deities dwell;
all obstacles are warded off, and spiritual accomplishments abide there. (56)
Holy places of pilgrimage come there out of a desire for the feet of the virtuous;
there, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent. ||57||
Where Nārāyaṇa is, there are Rādhikā, Kamalā, and Ramā;
there dwell the liberated ones, possessing divine bodies and beloved by Hari. 58.
That family in which the virtuous man has compassion is like Videha;
indeed, it partakes in liberation, is considered divine, and is held to be a destroyer of sins. (59)
That family is most excellent, Vaiṣṇava, and bestows liberation,
in whose house the wise and steadfast holy men eat and drink.
Those men who sleep while chanting the name of the Lord, Nārāyaṇa—
the sons, daughters, and even women— attain a divine state.
All indeed become liberated through the attainment of the company of holy and virtuous people;
for service to the holy is an inexhaustible treasury, whereas any other is subject to exhaustion.
Therefore, after serving the virtuous, feeding them, and likewise putting them to rest,
and having obtained their permission, I shall indeed depart from there.
Having resolved, "I too shall serve the queen," the barber-woman welcomed the virtuous ones and joyfully offered them the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
She gave him seats and offered sacrificial fuel and water;
likewise, having prepared warm fruit and sweet food, she gave it to him with joy. (65)
Then she fed all the virtuous men and women,
and she also provided massage for the bodies of the virtuous women and the holy men.
The virtuous women, devoted to steadfastness, spoke of it;
the virtuous wives recounted it as they passed half the night. Thus, [the night] departed. (67)
Then, while all the virtuous men and women were asleep, the barber’s wife,
being very eager to serve the queen, began to reflect for a moment.
Having bowed and received the command, she went quickly toward the queen;
meanwhile, even though the time had passed, the barber’s wife [remained there].

Thinking that she had not arrived, she became greatly enraged and desired to inflict punishment, saying, "Tomorrow I shall surely seize all her property; another barber has been entrusted to me by her."
"I shall expel her from the village, or I shall place her in shackles"—thus did she become enraged; indeed, the Lord himself knows this.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, during the first watch of the night, I, the Blessed One, quickly assumed the very beautiful form of another barber for the sake of my devotee. (72)
Having reflected thus—that she attends upon virtuous women for the sake of serving me and for the purpose of pacifying the angry queen—she serves the holy ones as my devotee. (73)
"The enraged queen will bring about the destruction of my devotee's livelihood;
may that not happen to my devotee, my servant, and likewise to the virtuous. (74)
"This woman, who is devoted to me and endowed with righteousness, must be protected by me;
for that entire family, full of devotion, must likewise be protected. (75)
Reflecting thus, she who protects her devotees thought, "I shall not remain as I am," and having become a barber woman, she went quickly to the queen's palace during the first watch of the night.
All services were performed by me for the queen while she was in good health;
indeed, in the form of a woman during the night, I attended to her adornment, meals, and so forth.
The purification of vessels, the offering of drinks and fragrant foods, the provision of a beautiful bed, and likewise the presentation of betel leaves and other such items. ||78||
The thorough massaging and rubbing of the queen’s body, the fanning with a fan, and engaging her in conversation; ||79||
At that time, during the night, I performed all the instructions and so forth;
listen, Lakṣmī, to the very instruction which I myself gave.
The discourse of the scriptures should be heard, for the teacher is indeed to be honored in every way;
likewise, charity should be bestowed with faith by the queen, the wife of Dharma. (81)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa should always be served with the intellect; the notions of "I" and "mine" should be abandoned, and pride should never be indulged in under any circumstances. (82)
One must protect the distressed; one should not show anger toward a servant.
One should show compassion toward female slaves, and one must not seize property even when it has been lost.
Whether it be food, wealth, a home, service, or even safety, the Supreme Self is to be worshipped; for upon that queen rests the grace of Hari. (84)
By that [means], liberation in the Imperishable (akṣara) always occurs;
she becomes stainless, a great liberated one, resembling Kṛṣṇa. ||85||
Like Ramā, she is not bound by auspicious or inauspicious karmas;
yet, through excessive devotion, like Lakṣmī, she attains oneness with Hari.
Or else, having become his wife and remaining distinct from him, she serves him with devotion; by the grace of Hari, she always becomes independent in her duties. (87)
Established in Brahman and possessing the character of Brahman, she attains liberation in the Imperishable;
but that queen who is devoted to worldly enjoyment and devoid of service to Kṛṣṇa— ||88||
Having died and gone to heaven, and having enjoyed [its fruits], she is born here again in the mortal world;
thus, through many births, perfected by devotion, she shall be liberated.
And by the grace of the virtuous Guru, one shall go at the end to the imperishable state;
indeed, by the grace of Śrī Hari, all latent desires (vāsanās) here come to an end.
Having cultivated association with the virtuous and having worshipped the Supreme Lord here, one should make this human birth meaningful—that which bestows the eternal kingdom of liberation. 91.
"This Self is of the nature of Brahman; one should indeed perceive Kṛṣṇa within it.
Having thus instructed Queen Lakṣmī and having served her, [he departed]. ||92||
Having put her to sleep as if she were awake, I then departed from that dwelling;
at that moment, the barber's wife arrived there at midnight.
Trembling and filled with fear, she approached the bed to serve that great queen; bowing low, she begged for forgiveness. (94)
A great deal of my time has passed in the course of this glorification;
O Great Queen, please forgive me, for I did not come to serve you. (95)
Having heard this supreme marvel, the queen was overcome with doubt:
"How indeed can she be the very same servant who departed after serving us? (96)
Having arrived, she begged for forgiveness despite having committed no offense; reflecting thus, he said to her, "How is it that you are not my wife? (97)
"You have arrived; tell me, how can you grant forgiveness? Now [tell me] all about my service and so forth during the night. (98)
"Having done this, you are going to your own home; why indeed do you ask for forgiveness?
The barber's wife replied, "I have certainly not come here today to serve you. (99)
"I have arrived at this very moment; why do you speak to me as if I were deluded? O venerable one, do not joke in this way; I was not present here. (3.228.10)
"Perhaps some other woman has performed service for him.
Upon hearing this, the queen was momentarily bewildered, and then she felt at ease.
Having cast off her sleep, that mistress of creatures fell asleep;
meanwhile, that barber-woman was returning to her own home.
At that moment, he saw a woman in his own house who possessed many forms,
appearing then identical to himself in beauty, age, and attire.
For a moment, overcome with wonder, she asked the beautiful, smiling woman: "Who are you? How and from where have you come here to my house, O lady who resembles Kamalā? (104)
O Lakṣmī, at that time, having transformed my own beautiful form,
I revealed Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu.
For your sake, having assumed the form of a barber, I served her;
yet because she was served by you, the queen then became enraged.
"She has resolved that everything must be taken from you through non-service;
therefore, having assumed your form, I have served that mistress of creatures. (107)
"O blessed lady, I am here as your devotee, come for the sake of your welfare;
you, along with your husband, sons, daughters, and others, shall always be mine. (1.08)
Practice this constant meditation of mine as your own sphere of activity;
I shall lead your family, who are devoted to me, to my supreme abode, which is your sphere of attainment.
Having spoken thus, she detained me on the bed for a moment;
then, having bestowed supreme bliss upon me, she vanished in the next instant.
But in the dream, O sons, they saw me as a barber, and all of them—even though they were virtuous—saw me thus; then at dawn, they woke up.
They described and beheld the forms of Hari to one another,
considering it their supreme good fortune that they had seen Brahman.
Then, having bathed again in the morning and eaten, those virtuous ones departed;
and that divine housewife went to another village with the barber’s wife.
Even the barber served me, as did his family;
then, after some time, I led them all away by means of excellent celestial chariots.
O Lakṣmī, Hari, under the influence of my compassion, truly regarded my supreme abode as the imperishable;
and the king, the queen, and the others likewise accepted my conduct.
Having determined that he was divine, they indeed approached him along with their progeny;
and in the course of time, they too went to my supreme, imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by me, the compassionate one,
have these devotees been uplifted under the pretext of serving the holy man named Kalyāṇadhāman.
By reading and hearing this, there shall likewise be enjoyment and liberation;
O Rame, by Your grace, may there be the fulfillment of my every desire.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord, being pleased by the service of the barber’s wife named Nigamikā— who remained devoted to the service of the saintly Kalyāṇadhāma and others— manifested in the form of Nigamikā and performed service to the queen, and protected and liberated the family of the barber," in the third section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this story concerning the birth of a devotee.
There was a cowherdess who was my devotee, residing in the city of Ārdraśṛṅga.
In the tiger forest— a region filled with lions, tigers, and predatory beasts—
dwells the goddess named Rūṭāṇakī, purified by her past impressions (saṃskāras).
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you a great wonder concerning a devotee. In a previous birth, she was a Śūdra fisherwoman on the bank of a river. (3)
But Satī remained on the fisherman’s boat;
she always dwelt upon the ground situated at the confluence of the Śatruñjaya and the ocean.
She, whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa, indeed carries those men who travel to the great pilgrimage site of Gopanātha across every shore by means of her boat.
That virtuous woman indeed leads with her true devotion those holy men who arrive,
even bringing them to the further shore without accepting any material gifts.
But once, a certain saint named Śrī Haricaitanya, a king among yogis, took up some goods and carried them to the opposite shore.
To reach the further shore,
that perfected one, the best of holy men, indeed proceeded upon the water by means of his two sandals, having approached the riverbank.
He travels through the sky by means of his own perfected ascetic power,
yet he also wanders at will upon the earth along the banks of rivers.
Having arrived there by chance and seeing him,
that fisherwoman indeed bowed down and earnestly requested him to come onto her boat.
The best of yogis, however, desiring the welfare of the best of wise women, boarded the boat while worshipping me; and being gratified by her devotion, he gave instruction there.
Worship Kṛṣṇa, worship Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama;
worship the saints and virtuous women—you shall attain the supreme goal.
In this body, your self is in the form of a female fisherman, possessing the nature of consciousness;
for this body always remains under the control of the individual soul (jīvātman).
Just as the boat is under your control, so too is the body under your control;
just as the boat is the visible form, you are the seer and the impeller.
Likewise, the body is of the nature of the seen, while the Self is the seer and the impeller;
the body is pervaded by suffering and the like, whereas the seer is devoid of suffering and the like.
In that regard, there shines forth another, some omniscient being, within that seer.
He who impels one toward virtuous deeds and restrains one from wicked deeds—
the inner self in the form of a witness— is that very Lord Hari;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the noble beloved of Kṛṣṇa.

Worship Him alone, who is honored by the lords of yogis, by holy men, and by virtuous women; serve Him with exclusive devotion consisting of pure love. Always behold that Lord, the beloved Kṛṣṇa, within your heart.
Constantly practice meditation upon the Lord of the Gopīs, who is endowed with His own essential nature. ||19||
Abandoning external objects, behold Mādhava within your heart;
offer all your senses unto that Kṛṣṇa.
Having turned back the functions of the senses, fix them upon that Kṛṣṇa;
acquire the great bliss that is the mass of being, consciousness, and bliss. 21.
Become the eternal enjoyer of Kṛṣṇānanda, equal to Ramā; for by attaining the enjoyment of Kṛṣṇa, all other pleasures become like poison. ||22||
In that way, they shall indeed become so; therefore, enjoy Kṛṣṇa as your lord and master.
[Listen to] the divine and human exploits of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 23.
Always proclaim with devotion all the wonderful deeds of the Lord of Ramā, which indeed bestow both heaven and liberation. (24)
Constantly remember all the amorous gestures, pastimes, and military expeditions, as well as festivals and other events, of the Lord of Śrī.
All those divine exploits of the Lord of Ramā, whether mundane or supramundane, inferior or superior, [are worthy of being heard]. 26.
Hari can make the insentient sentient and the sentient insentient;
always maintain association with such a powerful Hari.
Abandon negligence, great indolence, great delusion, and pride;
having abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," always remain established in the nature of the Self. (28)
To cross the ocean of saṃsāra, remain steadfast in the presence of the virtuous;
becoming devoted to Hari, worship Hari as your husband forever. 29.
Abandoning the state of the body, take refuge in the state of Brahman;
offer all enjoyments, both gross and subtle, to Hari Kṛṣṇa.
Reflect thus: "I am the Self, not the body";
and bear this divine state: "I am indeed the Beloved of Śrī. (31)
Having thus attained solitude, engage with actions free from attachment;
abandon the sin born of identification with the body, and abandon the path to the realm of Yama.
Having worshipped the Lord of Śrī and finally beheld the divine Lord of Ramā,
go with him by means of that celestial vehicle to the realm of the divine syllables.
Abandoning your state as a fisherwoman, attain the excellence of wisdom; through association with me, the virtuous one, become truly devoted to Viṣṇu. 34.
"Either in this birth or in the second, go to the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, was she indeed instructed by the virtuous one upon that boat. (35)
The wise fisherwoman indeed attained supreme awakening;
then the king of ascetics, having reached the opposite shore, disembarked.
Having bestowed unsurpassed knowledge upon the boatman's wife, he departed for the sacred ford;
thereafter, she chanted the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa day and night.
By the power of destiny and through the turn of time, that fish-eating woman died and was born as a human, an Ābhīrī woman possessing many buffaloes. (38)
Once again, she became a highly fortunate woman, a virtuous devotee of the Great Lord (Mahābhāgavata),
a servant of the holy ones, and from her childhood devoted to celibacy.
The desire for marriage was never entertained by her; indeed, that longing was burnt away, so that even while she possessed youth, she remained as if established in old age.
By the power of her past impressions, the yoginī was indeed one who remembered her former births;
by her very nature, she became firmly established in the Self and devoted solely to it. 41.
By name she was Ruṭāṇakīdevī, devoted to divine knowledge;
that virtuous woman was always intent on serving the holy and was a practitioner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. 42.
Offering herself completely, full of renunciation, and endowed with dispassion, she incessantly performs the turning of garlands and the chanting of the names of Hari. (43)
Having constantly prepared the milk of buffaloes, making it wholesome and sweet in the form of *pāyasa*, he indeed feeds [them] with devotion. (44)
Having bathed in the morning, worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa and offered the *arghya* to Him,
and having likewise given the *arghya* to the Sun and to the ancestors, he should perform the act of dedication (*samarpaṇa*).
Having offered the ancestral rites (śrāddha) with milk-rice, prepared foods, fruits, and water,
she then caused the virtuous men and likewise the chaste women to take their meal.
She always eats what is pleasing to the eye and conducts herself as one who purifies the assembly, just like Lakṣmī, just like Gaṅgā, and just like the goddess Sarasvatī. ||47||
Thus, she who has Brahman as her supreme goal shines forth as the goddess Rudrāṇikā in the house of him where virtuous men constantly arrive. ||48||
And virtuous women also come, knowing her to be a devoted servant;
they perform kīrtanas, rāsas, and auspicious great festivals. 49.
Thus, indeed, in the house of her devotee Bhajamānā,
once midnight had passed and all embodied beings were asleep.
A certain Daitya, wearing iron earrings, arrived from the forest;
his body was as tall as a palmyra tree, black in complexion, and excessively hairy.
Young, strong, and well-nourished like another banyan tree,
he seized that sleeping, great virtuous woman with extreme agility.
Having taken [him], he traveled by way of the sky and arrived in a great forest;
there, with agility, he descended into a dense thicket of trees.
Having placed that beautiful Ruṭāṇakī upon the earth, the Daitya slowly awakened her; and as soon as she became conscious, [he spoke].
In the midst of the forest, he saw his own wife,
who had been brought there and brought under his control by a forest-dwelling Daitya named Āyasakuṇḍala.
Moreover, she was a great devotee, courageous, virtuous, and a sovereign lady;
indeed, she was a highly blessed Vaiṣṇavī goddess equal to Durgā. ||56||
Though she was powerful like Kṛṣṇa and virtuous, she felt not the slightest fear;
in her heart, she remembered Kṛṣṇa, her beloved, the Lord of the universe, her husband. 57.
If I am your devotee and have been made your own by you,
then I abide solely in devotion to you, even if I am equal in splendor to Śrī herself.
I am indeed one who has surrendered her very self to you, a follower of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
for my hand has always been taken by you as my lord.
If the virtuous and those to be won over have indeed been served by me;
and if I have surrendered all my possessions for your sake and am dear to you.
Then come to me, O Viṣṇu; you, Kṛṣṇa, quickly go before me. Having arrived in person, grant me protection from this terrible demon.
"If I am not born to you here, or if I have become devoid of devotion, then let the Daitya Bali touch you, if it pleases you. (62)
"O Beloved, do as you wish; O Blessed One, exert yourself according to your own will regarding your own power, or else remain indifferent. (63)
Having spoken thus, she then offered worship into my heart;
the Daitya, for his part, then endeavored to please her with words and many expressions of devotion.
Though he is eager and indeed urges her to engage in various kinds of conversation,
she remains silent, with her mind fixed on me, and does not speak at all.
The Daitya danced before her, repeatedly provoking much laughter;
nevertheless, with her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, she did not direct her thoughts outward at all.
Then, even at home while asleep, everyone became as if inert—the virtuous men and women, the simple folk, and the great dignitaries alike. (67)
Ruṭāṇakya’s father, named Durvāraṇa, was also asleep, and his mother, named Khaṭamiṣṭādevī, was likewise fast asleep. (68)
At that time, all the other villagers were fast asleep;
in that darkness, no one noticed the abduction of Ruṭāṇakī. (69)
Then the queens, who were like beasts with a sense for scent, being wide awake and not even slightly drowsy, perceived the odor of the Daityas.
The queens indeed perceived that Daitya had arrived in such a manner,
having taken the goddess Ruṭāṇakī with him as he traveled through the darkness-filled sky.
They raised a tumultuous clamor and loud cries like those of cattle;
hearing that danger had arrived, they all remained wide awake.
Fearing tigers, they placed fires all around the logs;
indeed, they made loud, long-sustained sounds on every side.
Fearing him to be a lion, they all did not recognize the Daitya at that time;
thus an hour passed away, even though protection was maintained on all sides.
The queens did not remain calm; agitated, they roared like [distressed] cows.
But one queen, enraged, quickly went to the seat of Rūṭāṇaka. (75)
Carrying her seat upon her two horns, she began to wander;
then she was called out by everyone: "Ruṭāṇaki! Ruṭāṇaki! (76)
"Where has she gone, and why does this queen even destroy her seat?
For when summoned, that passionate woman did not give an answer. || 77 ||

She was not seen among the people, nor even in the house among virtuous and chaste women; then, having become a source of suspicion, it was said that the little girl had been carried off by someone. (78)
Then indeed, all of them, overwhelmed with grief, wept and went out in every direction to search for him; yet they did not see him anywhere within the boundary.
Having lost all hope, they returned; they remembered me, the Supreme Lord.
All the virtuous women and men performed the chanting of my names.
Then, accompanied by the Discus and Garuḍa, I went to the forest [to see] Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Ārya-Kṛṣṇa-Mādhava.
As that king of the Daityas was dancing, I cut him down with great agility;
having drawn his splendor into myself, I placed him upon Garuḍa.
Having gladdened her with affection, I quickly led her to her home;
by the mere touch of me, that virtuous woman became most divine.
"O Lakṣmī, possessing divine sovereignty, she is indeed just like you;
thus, by way of the path through the sky, she was brought to the house in the city of Ārdraśṛṅga. (84)
Having thus established my vision for all devotees and having bestowed that divine, refulgent form, I remained for more than a ghaṭikā.
Accepting the service rendered by the virtuous men and women, [he partook of] milk-rice, a meal, worship, the drinking of water, betel-leaf and other such offerings. (86)
When I, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, had finished eating and was ready to depart, my devotees, immersed in love and full of longing, made this request: ||87||
"O Kṛṣṇa, lead us away with you if we are your devoted servants;
for the saintly Rukmiṇī, the virtuous men, and the virtuous women likewise entreated him. (88)
O Lakṣmī, at that time I gave them my auspicious mantra:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā*. (89)
Then he gave the water from his feet, prasāda food, and milk-rice (pāyasa),
having instructed the unripe men there to offer their devotion.
He [saw] the virtuous Pakvā, the holy people, the chaste Ruṭāṇakī,
as well as her mother, her father, and that queen.
Having likewise granted divine bodies to the liberated men and women,
and having placed them upon the back of Garuḍa, he led me to my imperishable abode.
He brought those others who were unripe [in merit] at the proper time to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, protection has been provided by me for women who are indeed full of fear.
That Muktānikā has become the beloved of Brahmā in my imperishable syllable;
today she exists in your realm under the name Rūpeśvarī. (94)
"This young woman is my wife; behold her, wedded to me. Here are ten other virtuous young women who are my wives. (95)
Those women here, Mandārakalikā and the others, are your friends;
they are my beloveds, dear to Brahmā, in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Only those with divine vision understand this story, and no others;
my divine wonder has been recounted by me for your delight. (97)
In this way, I always and in every respect protect my devotees;
I also grant liberation to those who have reached maturity and bestow upon them the imperishable abode. 98.
Those who would constantly devote themselves to me with the disposition of offering all that they possess—for them, I truly become connected to them, and they likewise become connected to me. (99)
I shall always and in every way protect those who have surrendered to me from time,
Yama, karma, the senses and so forth, and from all defects.
From reciting, hearing, reflecting upon, or even speaking of this, there shall surely be enjoyment and liberation; my attainment bestows happiness. (101)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari protected and liberated the fisherman’s wife Rūṭāṇakī and the virtuous Ābhīrī devotees from the demon in her previous birth," within the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to [the account] of that fish-eating fisherman dwelling in Matsyapattana, who nevertheless performed acts of devotion.
It is indeed the uplifter of the story arising from the assembly of the virtuous;
it purifies sinners and likewise destroys the delusion of Māyā.
And there was a fisherman named Dhīraparva in Matsyapattana,
who was always the master of a hundred boats at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā river and the ocean.
He whose boat, manned by servants, constantly catches fish with nets from the time of Brahmamuhūrta until sunrise.
A constant capture of a hundred thousand fish occurs in the net—
fish that are minute, large, or very long, and whose bodies possess various distinct qualities and dimensions.
For them, a sinful nature characterized by violence arises during the festival of Dhīraparvan;
even one whose lifespan is a hundred thousand years [is diminished] by excessive violence during the festival of Dhīraparvan.
Life is constantly diminishing, measured indeed by a hundred days;
within the span of two years, seventy thousand [days] pass away. (7)
Due to the curse of a fish, thirty years of his life were cut short by sins;
after those thirty years had passed, he took up the occupation of a fisherman.
Having accumulated one hundred thousand years, thirty-two [years] have now passed;
and in the final month of the thirty-second year, during the rainy season, there was a downpour of rain.
For seven days, rain fell continuously everywhere in the regions of Kṛṣṇa,
and likewise throughout the lands of the Tuṅgabhadrā.
O Lakṣmī, it was constantly like the edge of a pestle;
at that time, the waters of the rivers did not flow with their usual force. || 11 ||
Abandoning the path of the sārins, many humans there, as well as virtuous forest-dwellers, frequented the paths of the bhūs and the sense objects.
Even beasts and birds were swept away by the floods of water;
many among them died, dragged far away by those currents. ||13||
All those who were without support died; those with support clung to wood, while others, clinging to trees and such, remained alive in the midst of the city.
They arrived at the confluence of the Matsyapaṭṭa and the Kṛṣṇasāgara; indeed, they then beheld embodied beings even in that great water as if they were alive.
Dhīraparvan commanded all his own servants, who were protectors of the mechanical ships,
as well as the captains of the hundred vessels.
Let them not act like fish-catchers as long as there is danger from the river; let them instead capture living men from the midst of the flood.
In every way, the gift of life— indeed, mere life itself—
must be bestowed here upon those who are carried away by the current during this dissolution.
Food should also be given, such as dry grain and roasted chickpeas and the like, as well as blankets, garments, and other items for warding off the cold. (19)
In this manner, indeed, protection was ordained there by Dhīraparvan through the giving of wealth, food, clothing, boats, and other such things, as well as by means of his servant-men.
Men, women, children, and the elderly, having come into contact with wood—whether clinging to bamboo poles, great trees, or suspended from branches—[perished]. (21)

Indeed, there were thousands of men attached to grass-baskets and the like, as well as those dwelling in corpses and such; there were also ascetics, virtuous men, virtuous women, the dispassionate, and even Vaiṣṇavas who carried various objects on their shoulders. (22)
Then the devotees, who were devoted to Nārāyaṇa, were protected while they lived. ||23||
From the great ocean of merit obtained through their blessings,
there also arose the emergence of the great merit of the gift of life.
Merit and demerit cannot be exhausted without experiencing their results;
this yoga occurred because of the exhaustion of his lifespan within seven days. (25)
Indeed, life is diminished by sins and increased by merits;
the former [karma] is experienced first, and that which is later is experienced last. (26)
Indeed, the fruit arising from actions such as violence and killing is repeated death;
by that very act of slaughter, the executioner shall suffer it in the abode of Yama.
The offering consisting of the fish-eater Matsyamāra, a deed impelled by intense agitation, was previously obtained for the sake of enjoyment, yet it was joined with the noose of Time. (28)
Joined by the messengers of Yama, [he experiences] the suffering born from the slaughter of ten million fish and other creatures;
at the end of seven days, when the force of the rain has diminished on that day.
Seated upon a mechanized boat, attended by servants and accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, he went out onto the water to view the shoreline.
At the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and the ocean, where the great current flows with immense force,
he went as far as one krośa into the vast waters of the sea.
Then, on the deck of the ship, there occurred the wondrous tossing of tree branches;
unexpectedly, a great surge of water arrived. (30)
And even when a great flood arises unexpectedly, resulting from the mutual impact of two massive walls of water, [it does not cause harm]. (33)
Having leaped with great speed into the sky from the front part of the great ship,
as soon as he has gone downward in front, [the ship] is then submerged by the great waters at its rear.
Suddenly, she was tossed violently into the air,
and then the prow of the boat was driven down into the depths of the water by the two walls of waves.
Then, indeed, turned upside down by the waters of the great-velocityed rivers at her side,
she sank for a mere moment into the waters of the ocean.
Having reached the surface of the earth, she was indeed without support and without companions;
Dhīra, Parva, and all the others had died, having fainted in the waters. (37)
Those sinners were swiftly led to the realm of Yama by the messengers of Yama;
meanwhile, the corpses were devoured by fish, and the wealth was taken by servants and men. (38)
The boats were taken away by the sailors, but their lives were taken by the attendants of Yama;
and their merits and sins were taken away by those deceased family members.
Just as those provisions for the journey departed along with their owners,
so too were they led at the appointed time by messengers toward the abode of Yama.
Citragupta announced their sins in the presence of Yama;
the King of Dharma, however, punished them all according to their deeds.
And after casting them into Kālasūtra for a long time,
he then cast those who killed fish into the hell known as Galapāśa.
Then he cast them for a long time into a pit of alkaline mud;
thereafter, he threw them into a sacrificial pit containing weapons.
Then he cast them into the Forest of Sword-leaves for a long time;
thereafter, he cast them into a fire-pit filled with great flames.
Then he threw them into this pit there, which was teeming with living creatures;
therein, scorpions, chameleons, and other venomous biters stung them.
Then Yamarāja cast them into Lālāmukha,
and thereafter into the pits of fish and other creatures, and into that which is called the Salt Ocean.
He cast them into a net-boat while they were being tormented by his soldiers;
