there, they became like fish, serving as food for great fish and other creatures. (47)
Torn apart by fish and devoured again and again,
they are revived once more and undergo further sufferings.
Then, by the command of Dharma, at the conclusion of the severe punishment for all their sins, they were all expelled from the sacrificial pit after a long period of time.
They became hungry ghosts (pretas), suffering indeed in a vast, parched forest; after a thousand years, having endured those torments of the pretas, they were released.
Fish born in the salt ocean at the confluence of the Black Sea were caught by fishermen using nets and machines, and then they were eaten. (51)
Thus, as they reach the end of their experience of the evils they have committed,
they then attain a superior merit born from the gift of human life.
All of them became the young sons of Vaiṣṇavas—of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and ship-owners—in the city of Matsya. (53)
Those who, by means of ships, carry out the trade of goods belonging to many countries, perform a most excellent and wealth-bestowing enterprise, and not one involving violence. (54)
Such were your auspicious sons, endowed with devotion;
wherever they were, they remained filled with happiness in my house, which abounded in wealth, grain, and prosperity. ||55||

They were devoted to the Brahmins and devoted to the virtuous; they were intent on the dharma of non-violence, dedicated to the worship of the gods, generous, and eaters of the remains of sacrificial offerings. ||56||
They were devoted to the service of cows, worshippers of virtuous men and women, full of faith in the service of temples and other sacred sites, and endowed with sound judgment. (57)
A temple for Nārāyaṇa was indeed built by them there;
and there, Hari, together with Lakṣmī, was installed according to the prescribed rites by the twice-born.
Then a devoted brahmin, a twice-born named Nirvāṇanāvika,
completely renouncing the life of a householder, entered the stage of renunciation.
Having become a virtuous priest, he always resided there in that temple;
he was a supreme Vaiṣṇava ascetic named Nirvāṇāyana.
He performs service to the gods, service to devotees, and service to the virtuous;
he celebrates divine Vaiṣṇava festivals and causes them to be celebrated as well.
In the evening, men and women gather to tell stories;
people come for the sake of hearing them, for that city has indeed become Vaiṣṇava.
Once, drawn by devotion for him and moved by compassion,
I became a saintly Vaiṣṇava and went there to hear his discourse.
Seeing that I had arrived as a guest, that virtuous and noble man seated me on an auspicious seat and offered me a welcome and other courtesies.
Following the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā,
Hari himself compassionately taught it there to the members of the assembly.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is pleased by the hearing of this narrative;
for that Kṛṣṇa who is heard of in this story manifests here in person. (66)
The fruit of this discourse is indeed affection for Hari through the knowledge of His majesty,
as well as self-abidance, devotion to the Lord, and liberation in His abode.
There is the destruction of illusion and delusion, the constant acquisition of service to Hari, and likewise a divine state forever filled with eternal bliss. 68.
That fruit of the narrative has been declared; thus, this story should be heard with reverence.
For a devotee full of love, not even a single ghaṭikā passes without Kṛṣṇa.
Without the dark-eyed one, he would not be able to remain in any way whatsoever;
he exists as one possessed of knowledge, devotion, and detachment.
A firm and unswerving devotion to Hari arises in him;
even for the goddess Śrī, her love for her beloved remains constant and undying.
She is exclusively and fully devoted to Hari, eternally charming;
she is intent upon accomplishing her own purpose and seeks that goal through Kṛṣṇa alone. (72)
The mind never goes elsewhere; it always dwells within Hari alone. Through devotion, it certainly accomplishes its own purpose as well as the purpose of Kṛṣṇa. (73)
A woman who loves Kṛṣṇa and is devoted to Kṛṣṇa should always be attached to Hari;
having abandoned her own self-interest, she should accomplish every task for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. (74)
She should possess the disposition of offering her all and be ever dedicated to Hari;
in this way, women become truly charming, passionate, and self-surrendered. (75)
Their lord Kṛṣṇa is their deliverer from the great ocean;
for their ultimate welfare, Kṛṣṇa is born as their husband in human form.
Indeed, for the sake of bestowing grace, Hari, the king who grants liberation, is born as a sage-ascetic for the welfare of the virtuous. ||77||
Those women who take refuge in Him— the Lord who is the embodiment of kingship, the embodiment of the virtuous, and the embodiment of the husband— become divine and liberated from ten million bonds.
With divine vision, they know Harikṛṣṇa as the Supreme Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the Lord of Māpata.
Just as embodied beings drink the water of the Ocean of Sweetness,
they are satisfied according to their bodies, according to their capacity, and according to their strength.
All embodied beings, from ants up to the great fish, nevertheless never reach the further shore of the ocean. || 8.1 ||
Just as mosquitoes and others, as well as eagles and others, fly through the sky according to their respective capacities, attaining happiness in flight. (82)
Nevertheless, they do not reach its end; it is called "the boundless sky.
Likewise, no one at all reaches the limit of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra. 8.3
Just as an embodied being standing on the ground perceives the moon as a mere plate, yet when he has reached its proximity, he perceives it as truly vast. ||84||
Just as a person situated upon the moon perceives the moon’s far shore,
so too does the devotee, standing near, find the boundless Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, the power of worship when it is slight is said to be like that of a lamp;
however, when it is greater than that, its power truly arises like a forest fire. ||86||
That [light] is even greater than that, like the fire of the great elements;
that is considered even greater than that, equal to the abode of Brahman. 87.
Filled with the splendor of Brahman, the devotee attains Mādhava—the boundless, supremely divine Kṛṣṇa, who is beloved and enchanting. ||88||
The great liberated one, whose nature is Brahman, serves the Supreme beyond the supreme—the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Lord of Ramā. 89.
By the power of devotion and practice, a woman attains the Lord of Māṇikī—the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of Brahman, the Great Sovereign. (3.230.90)
Just as an increase in oil, light, and so forth occurs, so too does one who has attained liberation experience the great, divine bliss of Kṛṣṇa. (91)

Whether a man or a woman who has offered themselves [to Him], they become the best among the liberated, with their very self being Kṛṣṇa, their form being Kṛṣṇa, and overflowing with the bliss of Kṛṣṇa. 92.
Through the power of devotion and practice, even oneness with Kṛṣṇa arises—eternal and unchanging, like that of Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, and Māṇikī. (93)
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, Kṛṣṇa is eternally to be worshipped. O Hari! O Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa! O Lord of Śrī! O Lord of Akṣara! O All-pervading One! 94.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Let the servants of Nārāyaṇa indeed chant this mantra daily. (95)
"May they be self-surrendering, with all their certainties directed toward Kṛṣṇa.
Having said this at the conclusion of the narrative, I indeed became four-armed at that time.
O Lakṣmī, he is adorned with all the splendors of the conch, discus, mace, lotus, jewel, crown, and earrings, and is hailed with the cry of "Victory! (Jaya). ||97||
Worshipped by their hearts with devotion and with waters of sandalwood, and saluted for the sake of their own liberation, I said to them, "So be it. (98)
Suddenly drawing their minds away into the ether of consciousness (cid-ambare),
when the appointed time arrived, I led them to my own imperishable abode.
I led some to heaven, others to the true realm of Vairāja,
others to Śrīpura, and likewise others to immortality.
He caused those devotees— the ferrymen who protect living beings— to attain Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, the unmanifested state, and the supreme abode.
[He saw] those who protect the virtuous, those who protect women, those who protect children,
those who bestow the gift of life, and his devotees who were born of a second birth.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, sometimes for the sake of the Blessed One, for the sake of virtuous women and the virtuous, or even for the sake of cows, [I protect] those who perform meritorious deeds, despite their great sins.
Even at another time, when merits have arisen for the virtuous yogin,
I lead him to the supreme, imperishable abode, the highest state.
From reciting this, hearing it, remembering it, or even reflecting upon it, there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation, and one’s desired goal shall be attained. (105)
Even by the mere remembrance of Śrī Hari, the sins of the wicked are destroyed;
and through the songs of the glory of the devotees, all their evils are purified in every way.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of how the fishermen Dhīra, Parva, and others, who were fishers in their previous birth during the Dvāpara age, after undergoing torments in the realm of Yama, attained births as boatmen due to their former small merit, and there performed worship and obtained liberation," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*.
Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of this Jalla, known by the name Tārakādarśaka, who caused [you] to be impaled upon a stake.
In the city of Cambāvatī, indeed, on the bank of the Rāvī river,
in the fortress of the great prison that inflicts the punishment of the trident-staff.
He was appointed as the overseer of the stars and the one who impaled [criminals] on pikes—
those great offenders who had been punished with the king's rod.
Killers of women, killers of cows, killers of children, and killers of men; those who destroy images and those who ruin temples—all of these shall be punished by impalement on a stake.
The great king of Cambāpurī, named Supathānaka, whose gaze was like that of a star, caused them to be impaled upon the tips of stakes. || 5 ||
He protected the spear-wielder Tārakādarśaka and Jallādaka; for in the midst of that fortress stood spears that were always suspended in the air.
Winged creatures, desiring to eat flesh, indeed hover about;
merely by remembering her, a trembling of the hair arises even in one possessed of fortitude. (7)
Upon seeing him, even a weak person experiences paralysis of the heart;
and upon hearing of his punishment, even virtuous people remember the Supreme Lord.
Even for sinners who remember the Lord, saying "O Lord of Lords, protect me!",
that place becomes as terrifying as the abode of Yama.
There, in that fortress, he lived day and night in a state of filth; he received a salary from the king and sustained his life with it. (3.231.10)
Even before inflicting punishment upon the wicked with his trident and staff,
he causes them to hear the names "Kṛṣṇa" and "Nārāyaṇa."
Protect me, Mādhava; O Govinda, protect me again from sin!
Here I am, O Kṛṣṇa, surrendered to you in the form of a stake.
"I am experiencing this fruit of my own sin; no one else here bears the blame.
I shall never commit such an evil act again, if only I may be liberated from this transgression. (13)
"Let all men listen: I am ascending by my own karma.
Let them not grieve for my destruction; rather, let them grieve for their own evil deeds. (14)
May relatives, fathers, mothers, kinsmen, sons, and daughters not commit sins, nor may they suffer upon the stake. || 15 ||
And those friends and the people of the world who behold me here—
let them uphold my dharma, and not speak otherwise.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having thus uttered all of this, he [beheld] him, who was adorned with a staff. || 17 ||
Having bound a cloth over his eyes and been slowly raised by the people,
he is placed upon the sharp-edged tip of the stake with his back toward it.
In the middle part, along the spinal column, one should balance [the body] very slowly so that the pain enters the back, making the arm supine.
Then the devoted Jallādaka cried out, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa indeed! and made the sinner hear, "Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa! (3.231.20)
Likewise, when the destruction of evil and liberation arise, or again, how a virtuous birth may come about for one who is flawed—[all this occurs] in such a manner. (21)
At the time of his final breath, uttering the name of Hari, he gives water mixed with *tulasī* to that sinner upon his lips.
There, the king’s attendants played various kinds of musical instruments,
so that no sound of suffering, lamentation, or the like could be heard at all.
Then, once the life-force has departed from the stake,
he removes the corpse from the ground and casts it into a fire-pit, or else [gives it] to a relative.
By the king's command, he gives exactly as it is to the householder;
in this same way, that Tārakādarśa sends even the offender.
Whether it be the realm of Yama or the heaven called Kṛṣṇa, having proclaimed my name, I know that Hari-Kṛṣṇa dwells within me; indeed, I delight in that.
My devotee Tārakādarśa is engaged in the chanting of my names;
having performed this act of penance and then bathed, he offered a garland.
Holding [the image] in his hand, he even recites the name "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" a thousand times;
likewise, he even performs seven days of fasting as an expiation.
He begged forgiveness from Kṛṣṇa for his sin regarding the trident: "Forgive me.
Then, at the auspicious holy site on the banks of the Rāvinī river in the Jambū region... [29]
Having bathed, he indeed gives away as a gift the wages earned on that day;
he constantly serves the virtuous and performs the remembrance of Hari.
Constant meditation on Hari, as well as His worship, devotion, the offering of food, and the offering of betel-leaf and water; ||31||

Having performed the offering of incense, the lamp, prostrations, the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), as well as hymns of praise and the request for forgiveness, one should perform the dismissal with the word "namaḥ. (32)
Then, having eaten the prasāda that was offered, he indeed performs his duties; appointed to the state of a servant, he stands before him with humility. (33)
Whirling a rosary in his hand and chanting "Nārāyaṇa," he looks upon his devotees and offers salutation to the Inner Self.
Considering everything to be the abode of Brahman, he indeed remains immersed [in it];
such is my devotee Jallāda, whose vision is like that of Tāraka.
Having attained firmness in devotion, he would call together men and women in the courtyard of his own house in the evening, and perform kīrtana at the onset of night.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Victorious One, Lord of Rādhā and Ramā;
O Govinda, Mādhava, Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī! ||37||
Thus, having gathered with men, he recites for two ghaṭikās;
at the conclusion of the recitation, he performs my worship as well as the ārātrika ceremony. ||38||
He bestows grace upon all devotees through that which is offered to Me;
at night, he indeed goes to sleep while holding the rosary around his neck. (39)
"O Raṭan, I am indeed Bālakṛṣṇa-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
thus, through his devotion, I have become pleased before him. (3.231.40)
Indeed, I remain invisible; yet I hear the chanting and other such acts, I behold the worship as well, and I always accept it out of affection. 41.
Then, on one occasion, I thought of delivering my devotee;
I resolved that food, water, and clothing must be given to him by me constantly. (42)
This man must be liberated from the procedure of impalement;
he is my devotee and is entirely free from passion regarding the act of impalement. (43)
Nevertheless, for the sake of sustaining life or seeking wages, one commits that act;
yet such violence is indeed a sin, even if it is prompted by a stake.
In this matter, my devotee is distressed and performs expiation;
therefore, he must be released from his liability for the act of impalement.
Having reflected thus, O Lakṣmī, I then became the superintendent of the prison;
assuming the form of the prison superintendent, I went toward the king. (46)
And I reported to the king the behavior of Tārakā’s display of the stars:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you; then do whatever pleases you. (47)
Indeed, this Tārakādarśaka has been appointed by you on a salary to inflict punishment with the trident upon the wicked. (48)
This devotee, endowed with compassion, performs penance;
he regards the impalement upon a stake as a sin for the embodied being who deserves punishment.
He mutters "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" for seven days and does not eat;
gentle-hearted and compassionate, he is at times completely surrendered to compassion. (3.231.50)
It appears to me that he might at some point disregard my command, for he is of a gentle nature and thus not fit for such a task. (51)
In that matter, another person who is always capable and cruel should be appointed;
for in whatever task one has complete confidence, there is indeed no fear from him.
"I am afraid of this; therefore, remove it.
Grant him protection for the forest where there is no harm. (53)
"Because there is no fear for you regarding defeat, nor regarding your own command and policy.
Having spoken thus, he issued the order in that very place and in that very manner. 54.
Having caused it to be written and having made the forest my domain, I vanished; meanwhile, by the king's command, a letter arrived at my abode of happiness through a messenger. (55)
Even by the sight of the stars, that grace of Hari is considered attained;
indeed, my removal from this place of sin exists through the will of Kṛṣṇa. ||56||
"Lord Hari, the protector of his devotees, will do what is appropriate.
Thinking thus, he abandoned the site of the trident-holder and departed quickly.
He quickly took charge of the forest regions with generous stipends;
endowed with great happiness, he dwelt in the forest districts. (58)
Always accompanied by his family on the auspicious bank of the Rāvinī river, he lived on wild fruits, tubers, leaves, pods, and seeds. (59)
With grains, auspicious herbs, foods, juices, and likewise with fresh honeys,
he indeed sustains his life-journey, which results in happiness.
Having recognized my greatness, he serves me even more intensely;
mounting his camel at night, he does so even during the day along with his soldiers.
He constantly surveys the great forest and conducts himself like a king;
meanwhile, the forest-dwellers [provide for him] with milk, curd, iron, and bricks.
The forest-dwellers pay him great honor with sweet foods, sugar, and the like; they also present him with edible offerings consisting of newly harvested grain.
And the lords of the fields and groves [should be entrusted] to the official in charge of guarding the boundaries,
so that someone may indeed be released from hell or from prison.
Just as one undergoes a royal consecration, so did he obtain happiness;
thus indeed Tārakādarśa became happy through the power of compassion.
His devotion indeed increased through meditation, worship, and honoring;
he constantly performed the turning of the rosary a thousand times.
Thinking thus, and especially regarding Nārāyaṇa as the source of security and well-being, how could I not worship Mādhava, who has bestowed happiness through his own self? (67)
My devotee worships me in many ways through acts of devotion;
by him, a beautiful image made of clay has been fashioned in his own hermitage. (68)
Black hair from the yak-tail is well-arranged there;
two eyes are joined by two black spots made of cowrie shells. (69)
Then two clusters of flowers were placed as ear-ornaments upon their ears;
likewise, a garland made of lotus seeds and a garland of *guñjā* berries were offered.

Crystal bracelets were fastened upon his arms, and auspicious rings were placed on his forearms; furthermore, finger-rings were fashioned from *darbha* grass blades, and chains were made of *muñja* reeds.
They subsisted on fruits and wore garments of bark;
they also possessed woolen blankets, deer skins, and flower ornaments.
These very [weapons], appearing at their proper times, were presented to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
he assumed his four-armed form, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Likewise, at his side was the auspicious goddess Lakṣmī, a young woman beautifully adorned, endowed with all ornaments and fashioned from excellent forest materials. (74)
It was beautifully adorned in its various places with saffron, lac-dye, and other substances;
the vessels were made of forest leaves, and the hut was constructed from bamboo and similar materials. (75)
Services appropriate for the forest were performed by that practitioner of devotion;
he protected the cows, which yielded excellent milk, for the sake of the Blessed One. (76)
Well-nourished in the forest by an abundance of grass, fodder, and the like,
they would thus always bathe at dawn and worship Ramā and the Lord.
Having properly adorned [the deity] with flower garlands and the like, with sandalwood and other [unguents], with honey, sweet roots, the heartwood of trees, fruits, and so forth; ||78||
An offering of sweet juices and sweet tubers, as well as water, betel-leaf, a lamp, incense, circumambulation, and hymns of praise. (79)
He always offers salutations for forgiveness of his offenses, prostrations like a staff, handfuls of flowers, and requests for pardon; thus he acts constantly. (3.231.80)
At midday he takes his meal; in the evening, having offered worship, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and food, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth, he always performs kīrtana.
His wife, Kṛtaśalyā, rising every morning and bathing daily, would bring flowers and fashion garlands and other such offerings. (82)
She indeed offered herself to Kṛṣṇa and bowed hundreds of times repeatedly;
then, having made a request for forgiveness and prostrated before her husband, she attended to her household duties.
In this manner, she provides food for the virtuous at midday,
and likewise in the evening, she offers sweet sacrificial oblations.
Having removed the ornaments, attire, and other finery from the Lord Śrī,
and having dressed Him in suitable garments, she indeed puts Him to sleep at night.
In the morning, she puts on a most excellent and new attire, beautifully adorned;
and she offers to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow everything that has been cooked and prepared. ||86||
Out of devotion, he daily ate food, water, and vegetables mixed with Tulasī leaves, together with his family, including his sons, daughters, and others. ||87||
While Tārādarśa was conducting himself in this manner, I, having assumed the form of a guest and become one with matted hair, went to the forest. (88)
In the evening, my family welcomed me with affection, recognizing that I was a virtuous man chanting the name of Śrī Nārāyaṇa. (89)
I was fed and honored; I was given drink and my limbs were massaged; I was laid to rest upon a bed, awakened in the morning, and saluted with reverence.
Having been bathed, honored, fed, and presented with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
he was properly entreated for his favor and for liberation.
When this was uttered and established by those most devoted ones, saying "So be it," I was then transformed into a divine form with four arms.
Endowed with glory and pervaded by divine splendors, full of serenity, and subject to the devotion of his devotees, he bestowed a blessing for the sake of liberation. (93)
Having offered grace and flower garlands to the head of the ten families, he suddenly vanished right there while they were looking at the image. 94.
Having attained a state of great wonder, they obtained divine vision;
from that time forth, they beheld me in my form endowed with Lakṣmī and the Sudarśana discus.
They behold the eternal divine [form] directly, just like parents;
indeed, by my divine grace, they have become those who have accomplished all that was to be done.
Then, when the time had fully arrived, by means of a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot,
O Lakṣmī, I led them to my imperishable abode, which is higher than the highest.
Thus, liberation has indeed been granted by me, the compassionate one, to my devotee; I am especially present in the hearts of those seeking liberation for the sake of their protection. 98.
Men who are sinful, of sinful conduct, and associated with the wicked, may take refuge in me or in the most excellent of holy men out of a desire to destroy their sin. (99)
Having shaken off their sins and bestowed merits upon them in every way,
and having made those embodied beings pure, he then granted them divine bodies.
I shall lead you to heaven, or to the truthful Śrīpura, or to the immortal realm;
or to the unmanifest Vaikuṇṭha, or to Goloka, the imperishable abode.
I shall cause you to attain the supreme state, as resplendent as that of a king of kings;
there, you shall always perform service at my feet.
O Rame, from reading this, hearing it, touching it, or even by its mere presence, enjoyment, liberation, divine attainment, and final emancipation arise.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Prosperity and Liberation through Devotion of Śūlīprada, Tārakādarśa, and his wife Kṛtaśalyā," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of Agnidasa as well. There was a Śūdra named Jvālāprasāda who was a forest guard.
Formerly, at Vṛtraprasthavana on the bank of the river Kālindī,
he dwelt in that forest together with his family.
He was one who ate wild roots and fruits, as well as one who worked with wood;
likewise, he was one who worked with fodder, creepers, grass, stalks, and medicinal herbs. || 3 ||
Even the thought of non-violence, for the sake of sustaining one's life, turns useless pieces of wood into charcoal. (4)
Having gathered heaps of wood, he offers fire there;
from that, embers arise which have extinguished flames and are of great value. || 5 ||
He constantly sells half-burnt *maṭṭhī* and *kulaśa* stones;
by means of those goods, he becomes wealthy and performs meritorious acts of charity.
He knows that when this wood is burned, countless species of living beings are consumed there in the heap; for me, his sin is great. (7)
For the sake of its pacification, a gift consisting of a twentieth part [of one's wealth] should be bestowed;
religious duties should be performed, and one should serve virtuous women and holy men.
Festivals for Śrī Hari should be celebrated, as well as worship and vows;
offerings should be given at the temple, and gifts should be bestowed upon the destitute and the homeless.
One should give to the homeless; one should give to the dweller at a sacred ford;
one should give for the sake of helping others; and likewise, one should give to the performer of sacrifices. ||3.232.10||
Then, indeed, the purification of sin arises, and never otherwise;
having understood this, one should bestow one's own things and personal wealth upon a worthy recipient.
He indeed makes offerings with faith to righteous people;
he gives food to those who come for the sake of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Likewise, he gives gifts of clothing, offers forest-grown medicinal herbs,
and provides fuel-sticks to virtuous men for the purpose of maintaining the sacrificial fire.
He constantly worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhā, the Lord of Ramā,
the Lord of Kamalā, the Lord of Prabhā, the husband of Śrīmāṇikī, and Hari.
He bathes constantly in the Yamunā and offers arghya to the Sun;
he also offers water, ancestral oblations (śrāddha), fruit, and food to the ancestors. ||15||
"He gives what is appropriate to a guest and he also gives to mendicants;
yet now he has fashioned a wooden image of me, Śrī Hari. (16)
She was shining together with the illustrious goddess Māṇikī, possessing her own splendor,
with a gracious countenance, peaceful, and adorned with the erotic sentiment of love.
Every morning, having risen and bathed, he indeed attends upon her, who is complete in all her limbs and adorned with divine ornaments.
Seated upon a beautiful wooden throne, accompanied by her attendants,
she was offered water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), a bath, and anointing with oil and other unguents.
With cow's milk, ghee, curd, rich sugar, and honey,
he performs the bathing and the consecration upon his big toe.
Having performed the cleansing with a cloth, the brushing of the teeth, and likewise the gargling, [he should provide] ornaments and such, as well as divine garments. (21)
She bestows upon me all the articles of adornment—scented sandalwood, saffron, flower garlands, crowns, and other floral ornaments. (25)
Incense, a lamp, and an offering of food consisting of excellent, desirable fruits;
water, milk, milk-rice, curds, and the finest cooked foods. (23)
He gives me betel-leaf and likewise the finest mouth-perfume;
he performs circumambulation, prostrates like a staff, offers the arghya-water, bows down, and recites hymns of praise. (24)
He performs a request for forgiveness for his offense, offers himself as a pledge, and, having withdrawn from worship, presents food that has been offered. (25)
He enjoys only divine grace, as does his wife,
the goddess named Prabhāvatī, as well as their sons, daughters, and others.
They eat that food through his grace, and because of that, they proceed with diligence;
likewise, they perform worship for me at midday and even at night.
The offering of food, the drinking water, the waving of lights (ārātrika), as well as hymns of praise, and the chanting of the glories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu, the Lord of Bālakṛṣṇa and Ramā. || 588 ||
O Lord Rādheśa-Māṇikīsvāmin, O Śrīpati, O Lord of Kamalā!
Having made you their excuse, they lead me before you. (29)
They sing beautiful songs and thereafter they sleep;
in this manner, all of them remain constantly engaged in devotion.
Then once, a great yogi named Narāyaṇāyana,
accompanied by hundreds of virtuous men and women, arrived at his hermitage.
Prabhāvatī and Jvālāprasāda likewise offered a welcome to the virtuous;
they both rendered due honor to the holy women and the best of saints.
Seats, water, sweet foods, fruits, honey, juices, as well as tubers, legumes, and cucumbers; |||33||
Greatly delighted, they gave roasted grains, dried foods, parched flour, chickpeas, as well as vegetables and leafy greens.
At that time, the virtuous men and women were serene, satisfied, and forever happy;
they performed evening ablutions, meals, drinking milk, and worship. (35)
They performed the kīrtana of Śrī Hari with instrumental music, singing, and excellent rhythms;
many people indeed gathered there for the festival at night.
Thousands of men and women, longing for the sight of the virtuous one, as well as the inhabitants of the city of Vṛtraprastha, also arrived. (37)
The forest on the banks of the Yamunā became like heaven because of the people;
at that time, men remained there after having obtained the sight of the holy ones. (38)
And they sat in the assembly hall, eager to hear the discourse;
there, Nārāyaṇāyana indeed taught for their benefit.

Through affection and the yoga of devotion toward Kṛṣṇa and those who are virtuous, through service to chaste women, through the worship of images, and through the adoration of deities; || 3.232.40 ||
Through service, there shall arise purity, divinity, and likewise liberation;
indeed, the direct attainment of the Supreme Lord shall come to pass.
Through devotion, the presence of the Supreme Self arises; through affection, there occurs here the destruction of illusion, and the person becomes possessed of divine vision. (42)
He perceives Govinda directly, both within and without;
freed from the veil of illusion, he becomes like the Lord himself. (43)
From here, one beholds Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the imperishable abode;
therefore, the saintly, virtuous women, and likewise Hari, are to be propitiated through service.
Through the blessings of the virtuous who are full of serene faith, Hari becomes manifest;
for Nārāyaṇa dwells among the virtuous, bestowing upon them the bliss of liberation from the cycle of rebirth. 45.
For the sake of attaining divine bliss, one should serve the virtuous as well as Lord Hari;
with faith and discernment, one should cultivate the highest association with the good. (46)
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and service to the virtuous—these bestow liberation; all these auspicious qualities should be acquired. (47)
One who seeks his goal must never hastily place trust in those who are wicked;
for if that were done, vices such as craving would always continue to increase. (48)
A mortal who possesses a state of nihilism is like saline soil; there, the seed of affectionate devotion does not sprout, but rather undergoes combustion.
For association with the wicked is indeed the cause of one's downfall; a great evil arises from the company of those who are of bad character. (3.232.50)
Association with the virtuous is a treasury of all merits and the destroyer of sins; those who do not recognize the value of such association act contrary to the true purpose of human life. 51.
They indeed form evil associations, and because of that, they fall into an inferior state through quarreling, disputing, sleep, and sinful deeds.
Furthermore, afflicted by their own faults, they die due to the performance of improper deeds;
they undergo rebirth, death, hell, and even a downward course.
They find the city of Yama and are subjected to torments there;
but the discerning ones in this world, having realized that the body is merely inert matter, [do not suffer].
Having understood that the senses, the mind, and the intellect are composed of illusion, as well as the three qualities, primordial nature, and various latent impressions; ||55||
Knowing that they bestow bondage upon the living soul, one should become free from attachment;
for one who is devoted to constant practice, latent impressions and the like are destroyed.
For those who practice renunciation, the formative impressions (saṃskāras) do not arise, being devoid of their root;
for within their hearts dwells the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He does not allow entry for the faults within the interior of the heart of one whose mind is devoted [to worldly things];
for one possessed of the conceit of a body, the Lord does not shine in the heart. (58)
In the heart, which is composed of darkness and devoid of light, Māyā increases;
through that, the notions of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" reach full growth, and by means of them, the latent impressions (vāsanās) [thrive].
Beings are born in many ways, and the thread of craving increases;
again, sins arise through craving for sense objects. (3.232.60)
Therefore, thinking "I am the conscious self, the controller of the body and so forth; I am a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, whose abode is Brahman," one should abandon thirst. (61)
One who desires happiness should always remain vigilant and discerning;
one who seeks their own true welfare must constantly strive for the sake of Hari’s happiness. 62.
The defects shall not indeed afflict him; they perish by the power of Hari.
Latent impressions and other such factors do not overcome a person who is established in the Self.
For one who seeks the service of the virtuous, who is sincere, devoted, and humble,
faults do not prevail, as they are destroyed by the grace of the virtuous.
A wicked nature is indeed destroyed along with its very roots through association with the virtuous;
therefore, the defects of embodied beings who associate with the virtuous shall dissolve away.
From childhood itself, one should cultivate association with the virtuous, devotion to Acyuta, and indeed, affection for the devotees of Hari; one should act so as to bestow Hari [upon others].
By means of that [practice], firm devotion toward Hari indeed arises during youth;
and by the power of that devotion, desire and other passions shall certainly not afflict the embodied soul.
One should always serve the virtuous who are peaceful and free from mental afflictions;
thus, affliction shall go to dissolution and youth shall be preserved.
One should never imagine any malice toward virtuous people;
for when one imagines faults in others, faults arise from that very sin. (69)
Through lack of discrimination, one is indeed afflicted by imagined defects;
therefore, one should behold the divine holy men who have Nārāyaṇa as their very self. If any defect should ever appear in the virtuous themselves, [it is merely an illusion].
This is not a fault, but rather a virtue; it is truly divine, without a doubt.
One should conceive of things in this divine manner so that one may likewise possess divinity.
He who perceives faults becomes faulty; he who perceives virtues becomes virtuous.
Having understood the three bodies to be distinct, one should serve the peaceful and virtuous;
through such service, one attains the eternal, supreme state of the Lord.
One should practice the guileless worship of Hari, which brings auspiciousness to the good.
Through the attainment of Hari's grace, the state of being green (or favorably disposed) arises in the follower.
Firmness in knowledge and firmness in affection toward Hari among the virtuous bestow liberation.
Service arises through affection, and from that affection comes eternal remembrance;
indeed, absorption in Him occurs only when there is such vision throughout the three states of consciousness.
But once direct realization has arisen, nothing further remains to be done.
First there is the vision within the body of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in his human form; thereafter, indeed, there is the vision within the senses.
Then indeed there is perception within the internal organs, and from that, in the individual soul (jīva);
thus the divine Lord resides within the body, the senses, and the self.
He who, having observed the physical nature of Kṛṣṇa, considers his divinity, and he who, having understood his mental nature, likewise considers his divinity; ||71||
Having cultivated his own meditation, he should likewise contemplate his divine nature;
he should conceive that all divine pastimes of Kṛṣṇa are bestowers of liberation.
Thus, through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, both the internal and the external instruments—the body and all else—indeed become entirely divine. (81)
The divine Lord Hari is perceived through the divine [vision] by the practitioner of devotion; He is not perceivable by that which is non-divine, even though one has become a human being. 82.
Therefore, all the devotees of the divine Yogi Kṛṣṇa are divine;
even the social orders are divine, and even desires and the like are divine. 8.3.
Everything that is prepared for the sake of Kṛṣṇa by a devotee indeed becomes divine;
the Lord Kṛṣṇa, out of great compassion, acts for the welfare of all living beings. (84)
From that supreme world beyond the syllable, he is born here on earth for the welfare of people, and he also causes them to engage in his own true company. 85.
And though possessing a human form, he performs worldly activities like a man;
yet let men know that even these are indeed his divine sports (līlā). 86.
"May all these divine spectators indeed be givers of auspiciousness.
Thus did the Blessed One [speak] regarding his own dependents, for whom he had created divine [forms] by his own will. (87)
He grants his own vision and company exclusively to his devotee;
therefore, the senses and other faculties of the devotee indeed attain the state of Kṛṣṇa. 88.
Due to their connection with divine Kṛṣṇa, they are divine and not illusory;
for as Kṛṣṇa is indeed divine, so too are the saintly devotees divine. (89)
Indeed, those who do not perceive faults, even if they are devotees, are divine like holy men;
for both men and women are always divine who do not perceive faults.
Association with the virtuous is truly divine; the virtuous are divine, and so is Hari.
All of them are faultless, bestowers of liberation, and entirely free from the effects of Māyā. ||91||
Whosoever should harbor a perception of fault toward them, his mind was indeed previously cursed by his parents, and thereafter by the virtuous. ||92||
Through transgression against the virtuous, one's intellect becomes corrupted by their curse;
for the virtuous, though appearing weak like ordinary men, are beloved of the Lord. (93)
At the very time of their being crushed, Hari himself, dwelling within the heart, becomes afflicted;
by that, the intellect of the one who has been cursed is thoroughly chastened. 94.
Indeed, the wicked person is burned by grasping at faults and is never pure;
one should constantly strive to destroy that [tendency] by serving the virtuous. (95)
With body, mind, materials, and senses, one should always be devoted to service for the sake of obtaining the grace of the virtuous. (96)
By serving with the spirit of offering all that one possesses,
he indeed attains purity, freedom from curses, divine nature, and the quality of perceiving virtues. Having attained such purification by propitiating Kṛṣṇa, he shall go to the imperishable state.
And having propitiated the virtuous, one shall attain the divine hermitage of Nārāyaṇa. ||98||
Therefore, let virtuous people constantly serve [the wise] for the sake of liberation;
having burned away this [world] with the fire of knowledge, let them offer their own selves as oblations into the fire of Brahman. //99//
Having thus instructed her, O Rame, he gave her the mantra of Hari:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (3.232.100)
He gave them the nectar from his feet for us, O Nārāyaṇa;
and having rested at night, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous ones bathe in the morning.
Having worshipped their own feet and consumed fruits and water,
and having spoken words of blessing to the devotees, the holy men departed for the sacred ford.
Those devotees, imbued with the grace of Jvālā, constantly served me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, with affection. (103)
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, they celebrated a festival when the morning had dawned following the night vigil on the eleventh day.
As they were dancing and chanting praises, I appeared before them on the ground, four-armed, accompanied by Māṇikī and Śrī, and adorned with divine ornaments. 105.
Having received all the honors offered by them, I vanished in an instant;
yet, bound by the cords of love, I continued to dwell eternally within that very form.
When the time arrived, he brought me to his abode, which was radiant with flames,
as well as his wife Prabhāvatī and thousands of devotees.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the devotee been rescued by me from the ocean of worldly existence; by reading or hearing this, one shall obtain deliverance from existence. 108.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, through the meeting with the saintly devotee Nārāyaṇāyana, brought about by the devotion of the devotee named Jvālāprasāda—who was formerly Aṅgārāgni—secured the liberation of himself, his wife, and thousands of other embodied beings," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the liberation even of the poison-giver;
in the delightful region of Kāśamitra, in the city of Śrīnagara which brings great happiness.
On the bank of the Jhillīmāsā river lived a devotee named Lavādana;
he was a householder, an eminent brāhmaṇa, well-versed in the sciences, and highly righteous.
There was a king of Śrīnagara named Śrīmān Aveśvara, of renowned lineage, possessed of great honor, and esteemed by the lord of Śrīpura. (3)
Constantly honored by him and placed at the head in the assembly, he was the foremost in the court of justice and held in the highest esteem by the subjects. (4)
Then another king, Lavādana, conducted himself like a king,
having established all the prosperity of his kingdom under the Department of Education.
Highly skilled in military matters and likewise expert in administrative affairs,
he remained thus wise and was held in the highest esteem even by the queen.
Such was this preeminent one, who was indeed the king’s own guru;
he performed the affairs of state as well as whatever duties pertained to the kingdom.
Perceiving harm to the king, the subjects, the army, or the kingdom, he—
free from doubt and equal in intellect— averts that harm.
He protects the king, the subjects, and the armies when they have fallen into calamity;
as a believer in the gods in this world, he remains a worthy recipient of honor.
He alone is worthy of the eternal Sun, Hara, Viṣṇu, the Moon, the Creator,
Fire, Indra, Suvarṇa, Māyā, and the individual soul (jīva).
Devoted to the ten sense-bases, he also performs the ten types of dharma:
the gift of water, the gift of leather, and the gift of prosperity in many ways. (1)
The offering of medicinal herbs, the offering of ornaments, as well as the offering of clarified butter;
the gift of a bow, the gift of gold, the gift of a maiden, and the offering of sacred stories. || 12 ||
In this way, he performs these very duties as well as other appropriate ones;
he even carries out the offering of houses, fields, dwellings, groves, and gardens.
This great man is capable of bestowing the royal fortune;
being such a devoted servant, he serves the ten gods.
Even one who possesses knowledge and is righteous in nature may, at times, possess a tamasic disposition;
he performs a tamasic deed, such as the great act of violence inherent in punishment.
Whether it be a king, a prince, his own son, or another subject,
he inflicts punishment upon one deserving of punishment in accordance with the treatises on Dharma.
Then, as time passed, the king became mature and youthful;
he gradually became intent upon hunting and sexual union.
For he indeed forcibly commits sexual intercourse with his subjects;
therefore, this lord of men incurs such censure among his people.
Constant fear arose from the cause of the oppression of his subjects. The king had five sons and twenty daughters. (19)
There were also seven queens who were young women;
nevertheless, drawn by the power of desire, he was constantly engaged in sexual intercourse.
He became exceedingly devoted to sin, consuming wine, spirits, and human flesh;
then, indeed, for the sake of restraining him and for the devouring of living beings, [the gods acted].
They repeatedly entreated him to administer the punishment of dharma;
however, Lavaṇa also lamented, thinking that such an act would constitute treason against the king.
"If I do not punish him, it would be an offense against my subjects; what should I do in this matter?
While reflecting thus, the path gradually became clear to him.
"The kingdom must be given to the crown prince; the king has become useless. He will have to be disciplined by his own lack of virtue. (24)
Then, on one occasion, Lava informed the king—who was established in courage—of auspicious words, beneficial for his welfare, that had arisen from a gathering of wise men. (25)
Samsara is indeed devoid of essence; its essence, however, lies in liberation, which comes either through service to the virtuous or by taking refuge in Narayana. (26)
Indeed, for embodied beings, the destruction of sin as well as liberation arises when the Prāṇayāma has been undertaken; likewise, sovereignty, prosperity, and kinsmen [are attained]. (27)
They do not protect the great king, the universal monarch;
rather, it is Dharma alone that protects him when practiced, for Adharma never protects anyone at all.
In the world beyond, it is Dharma alone that, when practiced, protects a person;
but Adharma, like an enemy, afflicts one both in this world and in the world beyond. (29)
Having attained renunciation, the Blessed One is to be worshipped by one who desires his own welfare;
having entrusted the burden to a worthy son, liberation should be achieved by one who seeks happiness. (3.233.30)
There is no limit to sensual desires; they increase along with craving.
They cause one to fall into hell, tormenting and burning one mercilessly. ||3.1||
Having abandoned the desires residing in the heart, one should practice dedication to Nārāyaṇa; for worldly activity, devotion, and desires cannot coexist. 32.
One who possesses the goal of dharma should abandon worldly affairs and desires in order to practice devotion;
therefore, you must bestow the kingdom upon Prince Śānteśvara.
"That will be auspicious for my worthy eldest son.
Having heard this, the king was consumed within as if by a flame of fire. (34)
O Lotus-born One, for one who is possessed by craving, everything—even nectar—is indeed poison;
there is no doubt that even words of benefit and words of renunciation turn into poison.
He, however, spoke with propriety to his own preeminent and supreme teacher:
"O Teacher, that which is suitable for me has been presented by you from Lava. (36)
Nevertheless, after some time has passed, I shall grant it to him accordingly;
meanwhile, my son's fitness for the kingdom will reach full maturity. (37)
"Therefore, after practice, I shall grant you the kingdom; there is no swiftness [in this matter]. Thus addressed, the preceptor remained silent and looked at the king.
The king, too, constantly reflected upon his own interest with guile:
"This man is my preceptor, the teacher of the kingdom, and the chief presiding officer of the assembly. (39)
"One preceptor must indeed be removed from his position, while another is to be established;
then there will be security for me and constant well-being. (3.233.40)
Having reflected thus, at the end of three months he sent him away from his place;
Lavādana also, recognizing it as the will of fate, abandoned his own position.
Having attained cessation, he indeed constantly worshipped those ten gods;
and the king truly increased excessively among his own subjects through sexual union.
Having forcibly carried off beautiful maidens from the subjects,
he indulges his desires among them and, having achieved his purpose, lets them go.
Out of extreme rage, abuse toward the subjects increased:
"This king must indeed be destroyed; he is a banisher of the principal [brahmins]. (44)
Indeed, the same word is heard everywhere among all subjects; therefore, even a king who is addicted to sexual misconduct with his subjects must certainly be destroyed. 41.
"Otherwise, there will surely be a great loss among the subjects.
Having thus resolved, all those foremost of the subjects [prepared] for the eating of the *lava* fruit.
Impelled by destiny for the destruction of King Mimi, they indeed went toward the commander-in-chief accompanied by Lava. 47.
They also told the story of the one named Sūryakānta, who was firm in his vows;
for indeed, the king would have met his destruction had he not resorted to righteousness.
"Even though you are the teacher of the people, you must certainly resort to firm policy;
this king must by all means be deposed from his royal position. (49)
Having heard these words to the core, Sūryakānta said, "So be it.
Then they all went to the crown prince Śānteśvara.

"This king remains on a wrong path, and no one is found fit to correct him with their feet; you, however, must be dismounted from your vehicle and established [on the right path] by the subjects with respect. (51)
"Know this for yourselves: otherwise, there will be a great calamity.
Then the prince likewise spoke thus to the queen: "So be it. (52)
All of them declared this conclusion regarding Śreṣṭhottamā;
and she, the discerning woman, being under the influence of destiny, spoke thus: "So be it. (53)
Then a great assembly was convened by the subjects for the sake of a return;
there were the queen, as well as other queens, and the princes, the best among the subjects. (54)
The commander-in-chief and the chief minister arrived for the purpose of reaching a decision;
they presented their resolution to the new chief. ||55||
But Gartamanī, though the chief, did not approve of the decision;
rising up, he departed and reported the unfavorable matter to the king. (56)
In a sudden fit of rage, the king said to Gartaman: "Let the commander-in-chief cast the prince into prison! (57)
Having heard from Gartamaṇi about the queen, the subjects, the former prime minister, and likewise the adversaries, the king’s soldiers [acted] by the king's command.
Then, hundreds of the king’s soldiers ran about on all sides, having been dispatched to quickly place those who opposed the king in fetters.
Many were held there, indeed bound in fetters;
then Lavaḍana was there with the queen and the prince.
Having approached the commander-in-chief and deliberated with him, he took extremely potent poison and went for refuge to the king. (61)
Then she placed a garland of flowers containing poison around the king's neck;
having smelled its fragrance, the king gradually fell into a swoon.
Then, having died, Gartamaṇi quickly fell from his position;
Lavaṇādana was honored by the subjects in the place of the chief.
All those held in prison were released by this Lava;
Prince Śāntiśvara was consecrated upon the royal throne.
It was proclaimed even among the subjects that the Lord of Men had died;
then those queens and the princes performed the funeral rites for the king.
That Lavādana performed the sacrifice for the sake of the king's purification;
likewise, the brahmins, the helpless, the virtuous, and the maidens [were purified]. (66)
The subjects were fed and satisfied with gifts of gold;
and the young children were gratified with gifts of cows, houses, and maidens.
Through his religious acts, the king was joined with merit at the sacrifice;
yet in the city of Yama, there are torments such as the glowing iron bed (sūrmi) that bestow manifold sufferings. (68)
Having enjoyed heaven, the king subsequently returned by virtue of the merit of his sacrifice;
he became the crown prince, and as king, he indeed governed the kingdom righteously.
He was constantly devoted to the virtuous and solely dedicated to Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, a thousand virtuous men always ate at his home.
He ruled a righteous kingdom, approved by Lava and Anumān.
Now, there was a supreme saint named Kiṃśukāyana, a true guru. (71)
O Blessed One, he established Ātmaniṣṭha, Lavādana, and his guru;
likewise, he established King Śānteśvara and the commander-in-chief Sūryakānta.
Then he taught the foremost of subjects, which bestow welfare and auspiciousness:
that embodied beings in this world are born and pass away through their actions. (73)
Dharma, knowledge, detachment, devotion to Hari and to the virtuous, as well as whatever merit has been earned through service and charity—these indeed accompany one [to the next world]. ||74||
A king who is righteous is like a father, but one who is unrighteous should be punished like an enemy. Through a righteous ruler, the constant welfare of his subjects is ensured. (75)
A king who indeed promotes the service of the virtuous shines among his subjects;
but one who follows the conduct of a cat or a crow is despised by his subjects.
But that king whose heart is stainless, who is devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa, who has conquered his senses, and who protects his subjects, prospers through the blessings of the virtuous. (77)
Someone may be virtuous in childhood but act contrary to that in youth;
yet another, though wicked in childhood, may become righteous in youth. (78)
Through association with the virtuous, an embodied being—from childhood until the end of life—shall always become a true person established on the path to the highest good. (79)
An evil man, through association with the wicked—and by virtue of living together, social interaction, sharing food and drink, and mutual contempt—increases in wickedness itself. (3.233.80)
Virtues and vices are seen in both the child and especially in the youth;
through the power of merit in childhood, one may become righteous even in youth. (8.1)
Through tranquility comes peace of mind, and through self-restraint comes the taming of the external senses;
by means of these two, all defects such as desire, anger, and the rest are to be eliminated. (82)
Both of these are beneficial for renunciants and householders alike; however, for those devoted to the service of the virtuous, their faults are destroyed at their very root. (83)
The individual soul, when skilled in discrimination, may destroy the entire circle of defects;
but Kṛṣṇa, the witness and inner self, shall lead it to the supreme abode. 84.
The Blessed One, whose form is auspicious, manifests on earth for the welfare of living beings; by serving Him, the Lord of Śrī, one is liberated. (85)
Although Śrī Hari, while remaining in His own abode, is indeed capable of bestowing liberation, nevertheless, those who become loving devotees here [in this world]— //86//

Indeed, those women and men who are full of love for Hari find even a moment's separation from Him unbearable; yet, for the sake of attaining that bliss which comes with His union, they endure it. (87)
Out of devotion toward them, and in order to fulfill their desires, He assumes here a form filled with compassion, joy, and other qualities, so as to bestow [these] upon them. (88)
Having granted his yoga, he fulfills all the heart's desires of his devotees;
indeed, he becomes like one of their own kin solely for the sake of increasing their love. 89.
That very compassion of Hari must be understood as manifesting in the birth of one belonging to the class of devotees,
through His countless divine virtues, sovereignty, majesty, and splendor.
Filling the hearts of men and women and remaining under their influence, he did so by being a son, a husband, a friend, and a companion. (91)
He proceeds as father, mother, and virtuous wife;
he exists as disciple, teacher, and king. ||92||
Having brought them happiness as they desired, he established the supreme Dharma, while the destruction of the Asuras occurred as a secondary consequence. ||93||
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā, withdraws by His own will after the satisfaction of His devotees [is complete]. 94.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, who was once a cowherd boy, is to be grasped with devotion;
[one must abandon] lust, anger, deceit, greed, pride, envy, and malice. (95)
Having abandoned all evils and having burned them away, one should worship that Lord of Māṇakī with devotion and by serving the virtuous;
thus, that Lord becomes fully propitious. 96.
The sin of one who sets fire to dwellings, one who administers poison, and one who commits the murder of a woman—indeed, even for the virtuous—is destroyed by service to Kṛṣṇa. 97.
The sin of one who serves Kṛṣṇa—the sin of killing a child, the sin arising from killing a cow, the sin of destroying a king, and likewise the sin of killing a mother—is dissolved. 98.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
By constantly reciting this mantra, purification from sin will occur. ||99||
Having spoken thus, Kiṃśukāyana bestowed the mantra upon Kamalā;
right there, he made all those hundred thousand subjects excellent Vaiṣṇavas.
Indeed, they took refuge in me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
then Lavādano, along with the ten gods, [took refuge] in me, Puruṣottama.
Everyone else—the kings, the subjects, and so forth—worshipped him with particular distinction;
yet those who had surrendered their very selves worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 102.
Then those virtuous ones indeed proceeded to Badrī-Nārāyaṇa;
for He had become pleased by the service rendered during Lavaṇāsura’s old age.
O Lakṣmī, I appeared before him with a divine form,
having shaken off the great sin of the poison-giver by means of that celestial body.
Having thus established my divine and imperishable abode,
he brought all the queens, as well as the commander-in-chief and the new king.
Pleased by her devotion, he led her gradually to all the imperishable stages;
and he led his subjects, who were endowed with devotion, to the purifying state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, all of them have been liberated by me through the agency of the virtuous; they have been rendered free from the bonds of Māyā in the supreme, imperishable state.
The great sin of administering poison has entirely dissolved through devotion;
in this way, O Rāma, all sins are completely dissolved by devotion.
By the power of my worship, they surely attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
by reading and hearing this, there shall always be enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Garada—the chief of the Lavādanas—through his devotion to the Lord and his service to the saint Kiṃśukāyana, as well as the liberation of his queens and subjects," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the wielder of weapons. Formerly, there was a man named Vikhaṇḍalavarman who was a bearer of arms.
In the village of Nāndala, on the auspicious bank of the Mahī river, there was a great Kṣatriya, a mighty ruler of the forest-dwelling Kirātas and the thieves. || 2 ||
He was the punisher of robbers and likewise a wielder of bow and arrow;
he was the protector who ensured safety on the road for those traveling with their wives.
He was the protector of the armies setting out for the sake of marriage, and he was the savior of merchants and those whose minds were troubled on all sides; thus he bore that name.
Upon hearing his name, thieves always flee far away;
thus the Punisher is a source of terror even to those who punish.
But a devotee, having taken recourse to the path of righteousness in his heart,
[should protect that wealth] which has been bestowed by merchants and likewise by kings for the sake of protection.
He subsists on that very amount of wages and not otherwise;
in appearance he is like a messenger of Yama, yet he is always possessed of compassion and righteousness.
In protection he was like a king, and in the path of political ethics like Śukra;
in awakening he was equal to Bṛhaspati, and in devotion he was like Garuḍa.
One who knows the Self conducts himself with a disposition of offering all things;
however, upon encountering an individual intent on unrighteousness, he inflicts punishment.
He always punishes a wicked or deceitful man according to his deserts;
indeed, he slays one who is exceedingly evil by force, using the stroke of a weapon.
Thus, the thought that "the sin of killing and so forth certainly occurs" arises constantly in his heart; yet, during worship, he always asks for forgiveness. (11)
Having bathed in the morning and performed the worship of my image with the sixteen articles, and having offered the waving of lights (nīrājana) and the offering of sweet food as a gift; || 12 ||
Then, having offered water and mouth-freshening betel-leaf,
he placed his weapon before me and begged for forgiveness.
I am neither cruel nor a violent hater; I am not self-seeking nor a libertine.
May my weapon not prove wicked against one who has fallen and is free from fault.
"O Lord, let my weapon not fall upon one who follows the right path, a devotee, or one who is exempt from punishment;
let my weapon not be defiled by fault through ignorance."
May this not lead to my defeat in the punishment of the wicked;
may I not be tainted by sin through the practice of policies that fall outside the bounds of ethics.
Even though this is so, if at any time sin should overcome me through the force of human ignorance, indeed due to the offense of one who is wretched; || 17 ||
"O Kṛṣṇa, I am in every way deserving of punishment; if I am to be forgiven, then let me be forgiven.
Thus has this devotee of mine [spoken], casting his sword, arrows, and other weapons before me. (18)
Having offered [the food] daily and then eaten that which arises from grace, he drinks the nectar of the feet and departs for the sake of protecting those who are to be protected. (19)
In the village, the forest, the threshing floor, the courtyard, or the field, Vikhaṇḍala joyfully protects all things that must be guarded in every way.
At midday, he always eats the food offered to me as a sacred remnant (prasāda);
in the evening, having returned from the boundary, he performs worship at home.
Having offered me flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, excellent water,
the waving of lights (nīrājana), hymns of praise, betel leaf, and fragrant scents,
and having even laid down my weapons before me; ||22||
Furthermore, he constantly prays: "Forgive me indeed for the evil born of ignorance. (23)
I am yours; I am your servant; I am your devotee, absorbed in you.
Having attained identity with you, I become your remnant (śeṣa). 24.
O Lakṣmī, having thus always entrusted me with his weapons and his duties,
he indeed goes to sleep upon his bed while remembering me.
His wife, named Harasatī, serves him;
she is a great devotee of me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the glorious Lord Narāyaṇa. (26)
When he beholds me as Nārāyaṇa within his husband, he perceives nothing else;
while I abide within the form of his husband, he performs all service unto me.
He performs separate service for my image, my lord, including bathing, decoration, ornaments, and the like, as well as the waving of lights and excellent food offerings. (28)
[He offered] a drink, betel-leaf, the gift of a breeze, the swinging of a cradle, and likewise songs arising from his sweet throat, filled with my playful charms. (29)
She also spoke of the avoidance of sleep,
and then the beautiful woman performed her own daily duties.
Thus, those who are exceedingly devoted to me worship me incessantly;
and virtuous men and women also go to that purifying home.
Having eaten and drunk, and having cast off their fatigue, they proceeded to that supreme sacred ford (tīrtha). Then, on one occasion, the holy man Nirmohanāyana arrived.
Having been honored, fed, and massaged in his feet during the night,
he instructed them in the supreme means for attaining liberation.
Forgiveness is a weapon superior to other weapons, auspicious and bestowing all peace;
forgiveness is the splendor of the powerful, and forgiveness is the austerity of ascetics.
He who endures all oppressions is indeed considered Nārāyaṇa;
for forgiveness always exists in the earth and in the mother of all embodied beings. (35)
Forgiveness, consisting of divine qualities, is always found among the virtuous;
it indeed bestows victory in this world and is a companion for heaven and liberation. (36)
Forgiveness is the weapon that destroys all offenses;
for in desire, anger, pride, greed, and arrogance, forgiveness alone bestows peace.
Forgiveness is the weapon of the weak, just as it is the weapon of the discerning;
for the virtuous, forgiveness is indeed a weapon that both disciplines and delivers.
Kṛṣṇa, as the inner self, is always present in the hearts of those who are forgiving; through his grace, he provides protection for such a person especially. (39)
It is called the "Teacher" (śāstṛ) because it protects; for that is considered by people to be a weapon.
Indeed, it is the Teacher because of the fear of illusion and the fear of karma. (3.234.40)
Neither is the weapon that truly governs the body, nor is it the weapon that governs the senses; likewise, that which is called "excessive truth" (atirṛtam) is not such at all. ||41||
The body and the senses are the effects of Māyā and are perishable;
even if they are protected in ten thousand ways, they surely perish at the time of dissolution.
The protection of that which is perishable is indeed fruitless and serves only its own specific purpose;
likewise, a weapon is useless, and such effort is a burden devoid of result. (43)
The forest is indeed subject to destruction, and the boundary likewise;
indeed, everything such as fields, gardens, and so forth, proceeds toward destruction. (44)
Thieves are subject to death, and so too are the crops;
likewise, you, the Teacher, though embodied, are likewise subject to destruction. (45)
One whose nature is subject to death is trained by those who share that nature; that is the wonder of it.
Indeed, it is better to avoid contact with the mud altogether than to wash it off later. (46)
Therefore, weapons for the body do not indeed grant liberation;
rather, those weapons that grant liberation must be concealed in every way. (47)
These divine weapons, O Vikhaṇḍala, must be guarded, maintained, and employed for the sake of liberation; learn them from me now. 48.
Youth is indeed the form of the enemy, and the weapon against it is the acquisition of vows;
desire is the great enemy there, and the weapon against it is celibacy.

Latent impressions are the enemy, the mother is that weapon, and one's own established nature is the shield; discrimination is the knowledge of distinctions, and the repeated worship of Śrī Hari is the recourse.
Renunciation, detachment, and constant outward indifference—these indeed are the weapons that destroy Māyā. (51)
Constant taking of refuge in Śrī Hari, association with the service of the virtuous, the ninefold devotion to Śrī Hari, and worship with supreme feeling; ||52||
Serving the guileless saints by offering them everything one possesses, meditating on Śrī Hari within the heart, and surrendering one's own self through the body. ||53||
Constant contemplation with the mind, perpetual manifestation of the intellect regarding Hari, and the dedication of all activities, such as bliss and the like, to the Lord of All. (54)
The tasting of flavors and so forth occurs only through the grace of Kṛṣṇa and not otherwise;
all things such as sound and touch belong to Kṛṣṇa alone and not to others. (55)
By these weapons, there occurs the destruction of illusion as well as the dissolution of karma;
through desireless action, peace arises for one who is free from craving.

Those whose undertakings are free from desires and conceptual constructions are indeed devoid of the qualities (guṇas); by association with such holy beings, one attains the divine state of being beyond the qualities.
Through the attainment of Hari, one gains divinity; through direct yoga, there is liberation.
In one endowed with knowledge of His majesty, love for Hari arises. (58)
Through affection, may the imperishable vibration of Hari arise within one who is attached;
and from that, the senses as well shall proceed, taking His form.
The internal organs indeed arise as the temples of Kṛṣṇa;
the self becomes the throne of that Nārāyaṇa. (3.234.60)
Therefore, the self—consisting of the state of Brahman—rejoices, rests, eats, exults, delights, and causes others to rejoice through states of identification [with that]. 61.
Engaged in worldly affairs yet maintaining the contemplation of Brahman everywhere, one is liberated from the bondage of karma and becomes Brahman itself; of this there is no doubt.
With a steady mind, the divine one, being Brahman itself and absorbed in Brahman, takes firm refuge in Kṛṣṇa and delights in Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt. (63)
Kṛṣṇa, the deliverer from the lowest state, accepts that which is offered in refuge;
He purifies even the fallen and sports together with those who love Him. 64.
Mādhava surely grants a true state of existence to one who is devoted to him;
such a person attains the ultimate station, the highest good, when everything is offered to Mādhava.
When all effects of primordial nature dissolve into the abode of the Imperishable,
the splendor consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss shines forth for the devotee.
In that light, the Lord Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa shines forth, stationed within as the regulator of both the conscious and the unconscious. 67.
Possessing a divine form, divine garments, and the splendor of divine ornaments,
he was being served by countless liberated souls who had become like the Great Brahman.
[He is] with infinite powers, such as Rādhā, Ramā, Muktānikā, and others, who bestow the bliss of performing worship and massaging His feet. ||69||
He alone provides service at His own feet to the one who serves Him;
He alone, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, dwells upon the earth.
For the ultimate welfare of the worlds, having thus reflected upon the Supreme Brahman, whose form consists of divine qualities and purposes, one should take refuge in Puruṣottama.
Those who have taken refuge and reached the state of perfection see Him directly;
those with subtle vision perceive the subtle Inner Self within.
Those of gross vision perceive that Lord as a gross form within the gross;
yet Māyā, unconfined by bodies, remains merged in equality within the Imperishable.
Then he is subtle, then O Kṛṣṇa, he is perceived here in a subtle form; when the consciousnesses have dissolved, devoid of any other principles. ||74||
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, the subtle [form] is perceived there in its subtle aspect;
for Māyā is a state of instability, as are conscious beings who are subject to karma. 175.
Then, among them, Kṛṣṇa is perceived in a gross form;
for those possessing divine vision, the sight of Kṛṣṇa is endowed with divinity.
Just as the vision of those who do not possess divine sight regarding Kṛṣṇa is merely worldly,
so too are all the powers of Hari, whether subtle or gross.
But all powers and illusions, whether conscious or otherwise, have been deposited by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow within subtle and gross objects, one within the other. (78)
Whether they manifest individually, or as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*), or as being without qualities (*nirguṇa*),
all those perfections indeed belong to the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The most excellent devotee of the Lord, who has offered his entire being, enjoys all lordly powers;
he who is devoted to his husband attains all sovereignities.
In Lord Hari, the Lord of gods and Master of liberation, only His own state remains;
the Lord bestows everything else that is His own upon that devotee. ||81||
The great weapon of affection always brings even one's master under control;
by that very weapon of affection, Hari should be disciplined within the heart.
One should be bound by the snares of affection so that one does not wander far from the heart;
this alone is the imperishable liberation for embodied beings, the very divinity in this world. (83)
That state which is the enjoyer of the bliss of divine enjoyment and lordship must first be attained here on earth through the direct presence of the Guru, Kṛṣṇa. 84.
Then, existing in Brahmapura, that very same [power] shines forth;
she is the enchanting love of Hari, which always bestows great bliss. (85)
One who has attained a state of identity with the Lord, the Master, obtains that same bliss which is eternally found in Hari by ten million Abjakāma gods.
He obtains infinite pleasure for the eyes, infinite pleasure from touch, and incomparable bliss from kissing, when the mistress is his lord. (87)
One obtains the great bliss of embracing within the Supreme Self;
likewise, this initiation is the tasting of the divine essence of all the senses. ||88||
And thus he obtains a festival of divine joy and delight, as well as divine gladness, peace, coolness, and that which is mingled with nectar. (89)
One obtains those very joys which arise from the twenty-four principles when there is the beloved Śrīhari as the master, the lord of fortune, and the sovereign.
Whatever joys exist within the three worlds, one attains them all in the form of the Lord, the glorious Supreme Self. 91.
Having thus given this instruction to Lakṣmī, Nirmohanāyana stayed for the night and, being highly honored, departed for another sacred site.
In the morning, Vikhaṇḍala performed the devotion as prescribed, accompanied by knowledge; his wife also, who was of the nature of Brahman, did the same.
They cultivated such devotion, filled with affection and ever-increasing, and they performed everything appropriate for the worship of the image. (94)
Pleased by their devotion, I appeared before them, manifest as the most beautiful Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with four divine arms. (95)
Laughing, I accepted all the most excellent offerings presented to me; having partaken of the food offering (naivedya), I gave away the consecrated remains (prasādika). ||96||
Having eaten with delight and having drunk the nectar-like water,
they both immediately assumed divine forms equal to my own.
Both of them, free from delusion, prayed for liberation;
I, having placed those two divine beings upon my celestial chariot, [led them] to my own imperishable abode. (98)
Accompanied by his attendants, he fulfills the intentions of those two;
they both abide eternally in the imperishable abode of Kamalā, having attained liberation. (99)
Thus, through this connection with the virtuous, his two own followers were uplifted;
O Lakṣmī, by reading or hearing this, one shall attain liberation.
The devotee who is devoted to me obtains heaven, or the world of truth (satyaloka), or sovereignty, or the state of lordship, or enjoyment, or liberation, or whatever else he desires. 101.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Lord and the Liberation of the Weapon-bearer named Vikhaṇḍala and His Wife Harasatī, Occurring in the Context of the Righteous Nirmohanāyana," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the virtuous story of Jīrṇodbhava, which took place in the city of Ārāma on the extensive bank of the Vīṇā river.
And there was a great, industrious farmer named Jīrṇodbhava,
who possessed a hundred sons, a hundred servants, twenty wives, and was full of strength.
He was the father of a hundred sons, adorned by four hundred grandsons, and graced by two hundred great-grandsons; he dwelt in a magnificent mansion.
Thus, Kṛṣīvala was born into a family of noble lineage; he was exceedingly pure, constantly devoted to the gift of dharma, and dedicated to the service of cows and other such duties.
He possesses five hundred head of cattle, two hundred buffaloes,
one hundred horses, and eight hundred bulls.
He possesses fields, groves, great gardens, lands for crops,
fodder, forests, and elevated tracts of land.
A yojana from here, on the bank of the river Vīṇā, lies his land;
there he practices agriculture, sowing seeds according to the season.
Various kinds of grains are produced everywhere as food;
there are also legumes, tubers, roots, flowers, and leaves.
Fruits, ears of grain, pods, and *veṣavāṭaka* (seasonings); knots, stalk-grains, leafy vegetables, and likewise *bhājikā*—these are the [varieties]. || 9 ||
All kinds of fermented gruel and whatever is bitter or pungent will, in every way, grow for him in fields such as the great marshes. (3.235.10)
Various medicinal herbs also spring forth when sprinkled with water;
men and women likewise exert themselves, devoted to the labor of agriculture.
By sowing seeds, they produce many kinds of edible grains;
from all that has been produced, they take a full twentieth part. (12)
For the sake of Dharma, he indeed gives gifts and performs acts of worship;
in his house, which is ever-restored from decay, there dwell homeless holy men and twice-born brahmins.
