Those who consume what is moist and solid food, who are devoid of worship, the Dharma, and other virtues, who are alienated from the duties of their religious order, and who lack knowledge, are characterized by tamas. ||73||
"How may the destruction of our misdeeds come to pass for us who are bound like trees?
O Brahmin, a great Plakṣa tree will proclaim our deliverance. (74)
Having thus heard this desire for the truth, the Lord of the Plakṣa tree, Druma,
reflected in many ways for the purification of all the trees.
In which the supreme power of Śrī Hari exists equally—unimpeded, eternal, and devoid of even the slightest diminution. (76)
To that tree which is worthy of refuge, the giver of liberation, the destroyer of sins, and likewise the bestower of peace; which brings an end to illusion and whose essence is the form of Nārāyaṇa.
He spoke to them of the Badarī tree, which is eternally frequented by the assembly of the virtuous;
"Listen, all you trees, to that which destroys all sins. (78)
Equal to Kṛṣṇa and the bestower of liberation, she who is the young yoginī resides indeed within the Badarī forest at the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (79)
Bālabadarīdevī, who is Māṇikyā, the supreme mistress;
she is Badrīśvarī, Śīlaguptā, and always a perpetual celibate.
Mahāmuktānikā, who wears a circle of ten million pearls, that auspicious Badrikā brings about the elevation of those born as trees. 81.
Through seeing, touching, hearing the name, prostrating, and through meditation, as well as through taking refuge and the practice of yoga, she exists as the destroyer of evil. (82)
Whatever evils there may be among the species of trees, whether innate or adventitious, that Badarī shall destroy them all. (83)
Where Nārāyaṇa himself, an ascetic for the sake of celibacy, resides;
and for whose sake that Badrikā also became an ascetic woman of Brahmanical conduct. (84)
The divine, supreme power of the Lord, which removes all sins, destroys all impurities, and is endowed with every capacity, exists as the upward-tending force. 85.
In that regard, for the purpose of destroying evil, all the lords of the earth should go as is appropriate every year on a pilgrimage to those various trees. 86.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and likewise to Nara, and having worshipped Badarī with fruits, flowers, juices, and other offerings, one should bow down to her. (87)
One should touch that divine Badarī and dwell in the place within its shade;
one should embrace the Badarī with one's chest and likewise consume its nectar.
One should likewise catch that breeze and circumambulate [the deity] clockwise;
one should offer incense, a lamp, and food offerings, as well as seek forgiveness and offer praise. (89)
O Supreme Goddess, you should act; destroy the web of our sins!
Deliver us from the great suffering of birth as trees; grant us liberation! 4.1.90
Having thus prayed to that Goddess and bowed down, one should go to one's own respective forest;
by constantly remembering Badarī and Nārāyaṇa, one shall attain liberation. ||91||
The goddess Badrikā grants liberation to trees in a single birth;
thus, those trees who have performed the pilgrimage shall go to the supreme goal. 92.
Then, when the trees requested their own departure for the sake of the journey,
Hari spoke to them always in the presence of Hari in Śvetadvīpa.
"O trees, remain firm; nevertheless, for the sake of attaining liberation, you shall become seekers of the journey, departing by means of the subtle body. (94)
As long as even a single subtle toe remains stuck within the depths of the earth, may you all possess life for that long. (95)
Even when your subtle body has departed for Badarī on pilgrimage,
you shall return and take up residence again in your own body, known as the gross one.
"All you trees who have set out on the pilgrimage to Badarī shall attain liberation from this abode; listen, for I am Śvetanārāyaṇa himself speaking. (97)
Having thus obtained the grace of Hari, those trees thereafter became *badarī* and *yājñika* trees, and having worshipped Nārāyaṇī, [they attained their goal].
Having burned away their own sins through the power of Badarī, trees indeed attain liberation; likewise, they attain it in a single birth.
They shall surely go to the divine abode by serving the Badarīśī;
through union with the Lord of Badarī, Plakṣā is said to be the bestower of liberation.
The divine Goddess Badarī, who brings about liberation for all, is born directly from her refuge in Nārāyaṇa; she is Māṇikyā, the young Yoginī. 101.
She asked about divine stories that bring liberation even in the Tiṣya age,
concerning her beloved Nara-Nārāyaṇa at the excellent Badarī hermitage.
Whatever stories concerning Badrī were asked regarding Nara and Nārāyaṇa, they were all answered by their lord, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Those various [mantras] exist in the Tiṣya-khaṇḍa as bestowers of liberation, being centered upon the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī. 104.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation and Majesty of Śrī Naranārāyaṇa at the Badarī of Śrī Māṇikya, and the Introduction of the Narrative," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Badarī, to the narrative of your devotee, how you attained the state of a jujube tree through the power of devotion. (1)
In ancient times, there was a royal sage named Badara in the snowy region;
he was a highly fortunate devotee, a supreme Vaiṣṇava, and one who ascends to the higher realms.
He ruled over half the earth by means of divine powers and instruments;
for him, there were hundreds of thousands of pleasure-palaces and comforts beyond measure.
Indeed, they were made of gold, adorned with gardens of wish-fulfilling trees,
the dwellings of celestial maidens, and opulent in their various heights.
Each one shines like the sun with masses of splendor like the moon;
by their radiance, the night on earth then exists as if it were dissolved.
An illusion of constellations and stars arises when the celestial chariot is small;
then, the moonlight blending together makes the sky appear like milk.
Even within the clouds,
the rays of the celestial chariots of the high-souled Badara spread forth, shining like rainbows.
A divine celestial chariot called Satyābhidha, which moves by truth, belongs to him;
indeed, that king, the sovereign of yogis, travels to the assembly of Brahmā by means of it.
The second is the noble world of non-perception (asaṃjñin), which involves wandering through the world of the ancestors and so forth;
the third is named Tridiva, and the fourth is the station of Indra (aindrapada).
The fifth is named Bhāskara, and the sixth is likewise Kaumudaka;
the seventh is designated Dhruva, and the eighth is named Kailāsa.
The ninth is named Dharmasaṃjña, and beyond that is Merusaṃjña; then Śvetavāha, Kṣīravāha, and others known as Talas.
And those [steeds] indeed were named Lokāloka, possessing the speed of thought,
each endowed with qualities corresponding to its name, and reaching beyond the very limits of the quarters.
Those celestial abodes were indeed filled with every kind of divine enjoyment;
within them all were forms made of jewels and gold.
The auspicious images of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, appearing as divine couples joined with Śrī Māṇikyā Mahālakṣmī. (14)
Established upon elephant-seats and worshipped with the auspicious jujube fruit, they were enriched with the splendor of every ornament and offered every kind of fragrance and essence. || 15 ||
Among them are divine messengers, attendants, gods on earth, stainless holy men, and those traveling in celestial chariots; among these, the best of Bhāgavatas are preeminent.
They were great devotees of truth, virtuous women devoted to moral conduct;
they possessed the joy of the moon, faces with the luster of the moon, and were endowed with a golden radiance. || 17 ||
Among them, O Goddess of Badarī, there exist great devotees of Badara,
and among them, the chanting [of his name] occurs constantly.
By association with whom even the gods and others attain the eternal Brahman;
there has never been such a devotee by whom the entire world was filled. (19)
In every place, the cry of victory for this king resounds, accompanied by the great clamor of those rich in devotion to the chanting of Hari's glories.
In whichever direction Badara’s celestial chariots travel, in that direction the divine sages bow with devotion, and his wives dance. (21)
In their celestial chariots, they worship the splendor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; filled with joy, they perform the lustration ceremony, present offerings, and then depart.
In the great kingdom of Badara, in villages, hamlets, cities, and so forth; in towns, ports, royal capitals, and even in cowherd settlements—in every such place. ||23||

Virtuous ascetics and female ascetics are honored with food, clothing, and other gifts; likewise, Brahmins who are without support are honored with sacrificial fees and by those who provide auspicious refuge.
Just as women who are destitute and others are won over by those who provide for their desires,
so indeed do the sacrifices of Brahman arise in every village through the offering of jujube fruits.
In every region there were food-distributions, and in the land of Badara there was a lotus-pool; everywhere there were water-stations as well as wish-fulfilling creepers.
Even those who obtain but a fragment of my path enjoy the fruit through mendicancy;
they drink the sweet, satisfying juice and worship me. (27)
Indeed, there were circles of Vaiṣṇavas in every small village;
morning, noon, and evening, they glorified and worshipped me. (28)
Having come to the earth as narrators of divine stories, they cause my story to be recited and the Saṃhitā to be read; thus they enlighten others and worship me. (29)
Indeed, the most excellent and supreme festivals arise among the subjects on the days beginning from the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika up to the twelfth.
On all Jayantī days, associations with the virtuous arise;
there is the honoring, observance, worship, and so forth of vows and festivals. (3.1)
For him, the completion of the rite and great respect arise even among his subjects;
moreover, for that king, there occurs the constant giving away of many cows. (32)
How could there be a new Śeṣa, since that king, having placed the serpent Śeṣa upon a celestial chariot, took him away? (33)
He went to Pātāla and said, "Restore what remains of the previous [creation];
this Śeṣa of mine is most powerful and shall support the earth."
Leaving only his tail behind for the sake of examination, he indeed dropped the golden ball below;
then, the golden serpent suddenly and swiftly placed that terrestrial globe upon his head.
The pride of the one who remained with only the root was indeed uprooted;
his arrogance vanished, and he did not bow before that Badara who still possessed gold.
He requested that his own crown be held [by the Lord] upon his head for the sake of honor;
otherwise, there would be the destruction of the fame of one who had been insulted by the mountain-king.
Because she had no place in the world, she begged for Golaka again;
then Badara indeed gave him to her to hold upon his own hood.
Then the wise ascetic Svarṇaśeṣa brought the earth for the sake of Pūrvaśeṣa and his own abode as a remnant of gold.
Thus, Svarṇaśeṣa was a man of great discernment. 39.
The great yogi Patañjali was born as a Vidyādhara;
through all the arts of yoga, he performed the upliftment of the world. (4.2.40)
O Badrī, in every house of such a devotee as Badara,
there were streams of Kṛṣṇa, and in every house there was devotion.
The entire universe has indeed taken refuge in me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, whose original form is served by Śrīmāṇikyā. ||42||
Listen, O Goddess Badrīprabhā; at that time, seeing the earth as more prosperous than heaven, other protectors of world-ages [desired] that kingdom. (43)
Desirous of prosperity, many contended with King Badara; having encountered Badara, they fought and indeed suffered defeat. (44)
Indeed, a devotee may be conquered through devotion alone, but never by any other forms of combat;
for how could he ever be defeated when the Lord himself dwells visibly in his home? ||45||
For many hostile kings were slain by the arrows of the king;
they were all killed in the ocean known as the Himavat-samudra. 46.
Situated to the south of the regions of the Kiṃpuruṣas, in the middle,
it extends for two thousand yojanas and possesses sweet water.
Then this ocean named Mānasa became sweet-watered;
it was an ocean of ever-cool water, endowed with all kinds of jewels.
"Listen, O Goddess Badarīprabhā, she who is currently staying here on Mount Badarī, the king of mountains in the Himalayas, in order to conquer King Badara. (49)
Once, the great asura Hemānala,
accompanied by an army of one hundred million, came through the sky from that other half of the earth.
By way of the sky, together with tens of thousands of celestial chariots,
he suddenly engaged in battle with Badara in the Kiṃpuruṣa region.
Then Badara’s aerial chariots, along with their armies,
possessing divine powers, descended from the sky into the ranks of the asuras.
Thousands of celestial chariots belonging to the Asuras were indeed destroyed;
their armies, having become like sweet waters in the ocean, entered into the sea-monsters.
Hemānala, the best of asuras, fought with Badara;
indeed, their armies fought against one another, determined to end their lives.
With showers of divine weapons, with celestial arrows, and with divine missiles, as well as with flashes of lightning and nooses born of Varuṇa; ||55||
With various vajras and staffs, with vast wheels of time, and with mantras, tantras, great machines, illusions, and conjurations; ||56||
They fought with artificial representations of wind, fire, serpents, gavayas, and Garuḍas; with scorpions, mountains, and trees;
and with various snow-capped mountains and unsurpassed celestial spheres (graha-golas). 57.
Enraged, they struck one another with maces that were capable of splitting boulders. ||58||
For after repeatedly slaughtering the armies of the Asuras,
they enter the ocean of nectar and become established there in well-being.
Furthermore, having regained their strength and health, they return to the battle;
yet, struck down by Badara, they enter the ocean once again.
Then King Badara, the best of devotees, having seen the asuras situated in the ocean, reflected within himself: (61)
"How can I bring about their destruction in the ocean, so that they may never again emerge safely from within it into the battle? (62)
All water would take the form of the ocean, and it would become the nature of the snowy mountains;
those Asuras situated within would be dead and turned into stone.
Having reflected thus, Badara called to mind the goddess Candrā;
and she immediately appeared there to assist in the task of the gods.
He set his mind upon the destruction of the Asuras, the slayers of the gods;
having arrived, he spoke suddenly to the high-souled Badara.
"Speak, O King, of your task, as well as that of the gods;
I shall quickly accomplish it for you, even if it be entirely difficult to achieve."
Badara performed worship, a welcome, salutation, and praise for Śaśin; he offered him an excellent seat and bowed down again and again. (67)
O compassionate one, creator of peace, moon of heaven, great lord!
You, the bestower of grace upon devotees, are victorious, O giver of nectar! 68.
The life of all the worlds resides in your arts, and the sweetness of medicinal herbs proceeds from your application. (69)
Through union with you, growth and nourishment arise, as does the cessation of burning;
the medicinal herbs have you as their support, and embodied beings have those herbs as their support. (4.2.70)
O Moon, lord of the night-lotuses, lord of the night, who brings joy through union with your beloved;
O Śaśin, lord of the stars, you are truly victorious as the dispeller of darkness. (71)
O Moon, you who possess the color of milk, O cool-rayed one, you are ever victorious!
O cool ocean, embodiment of nectar, may you accomplish the purpose of your devotees here. (72)
The Asuras, repeatedly approaching, crush human beings;
they afflict the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and the devotees again and again. (73)
Afflicted by my arrows, they have entered the ocean of snow;
let them indeed be crushed by mountains of ice and boulders.
Act in such a way that they do not come here again from outside;
for you are the herb that destroys both the worlds and the asuras.
"Consider the cold weapon as already [neutralized]; therefore, quickly prepare the medicinal remedy.
Thus was the Lord of Night requested by Śrī Badarīprabhā. (76)
He took from his own neck and gave to Badara— a noble moonstone gem—
to his devotee who was performing the work of the gods.
He said, "O King, place the jewel here in the cold ocean;
the cold ocean will suddenly become a great mountain consisting of cool stone. (78)
Right here there shall be a cool ground, of this there is no doubt;
O King, dwell in a celestial chariot in the sky, and not upon the earth. (79)
Do not succumb to the cold; act accordingly.
Here I go; quickly cast the jewel into the water.
Thus addressed, Badara quickly placed the celestial chariot in the sky,
bowed to the moon, and hurled the jewel into the oceans.
Then all the waters, indeed afflicted by the cold fire,
became solidified there in the cold ocean like cool stones.
The cold ocean attains the state of cold land and becomes a snowy surface;
then, the waters are tossed upward and scattered in all directions by the heat.
Those peaks, composed of white golden stone, suddenly came into being, and the sky became cool. (84)
Showers of hailstones fell suddenly from the sky;
by them, indeed, the mountain peaks began to swell.
Those great touches were born and indeed grew;
thus that mountain was produced, measuring a thousand yojanas in extent.
Endowed with moonstones, he was like the Himavat mountain showering snow;
on the earth, he was like the snowy mountain with its moon-gems, shining with the luster of jujube fruits.
The Asuras, who were engaged in battle upon the water and the stones at its base, were crushed and obstructed; having turned into the very substance of the stones, they died. ||88||
And through that great transformation, all calamities were pacified;
then the worlds, the seers, the sages, and likewise the deities [were restored].
Having heard this, the Rākṣasas, Asuras, Daityas, Dānavas, humans, and birds joyfully came to behold the land of Himālaya.
The ancestors, the world-protectors, the perfected ones, the celestial bards and dancers, the gandharvas, the kinnaras, the heralds, the genealogists, and likewise the panegyrists; ||91||
The Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Sādhyas, the yogins of Śaṅkara, the Gaṇas and the goddesses of the Gaṇas, as well as the Mātṛs and the Vasus. ||92||
Those residing on Mount Meru and those dwelling in the other world, possessing divine bodies, arrived;
they rejoiced in many ways upon beholding the cool, golden moonlight.
They greatly increased the prosperity of King Badara;
all those guardians of the quarters praised him and bestowed honor upon him. (94)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa became exceedingly pleased;
the entire kingdom of Badara, consisting of the Himalayas, came to belong to him. ||55||
At that time, there was no forest nearby him;
however, the gods and others made that mountain, which was equal to Mount Meru, habitable for his residence. (96)
Seeing this, they felt longing and repeatedly requested the king;
the king, however, granted a residence in the Himalayas to ten million deities.
All the classes of gods made their respective dwellings appropriate to their lineages upon the golden peaks; thus did that abode of the gods come to be. (98)
Indeed, another heaven appeared upon the earth as the Himalaya;
likewise, there were wish-fulfilling trees, wish-fulfilling creepers, and even wish-fulfilling grasses.
And forests planted by the gods all around the Himalaya extend for a circle of one hundred yojanas on every side at the base of the earth.
Indeed, groves of all kinds of divine medicinal herbs were planted,
as well as wonderful gardens filled with fruits, leaves, juices, and other delights.
Indeed, having been brought repeatedly from the heavenly realm and likewise from their own respective worlds by others,
auspicious riches were deposited all around.
The seven sages dwelt there, and Śaṅkara also resided there;
likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the goddesses, and hosts of Apsaras took up their abode.
Gandharvas, cāraṇas, kiṃpuruṣas, kinnaras, and gods—
as well as many other deities— indeed dwelt upon the Himalaya.
Thus the great Himagiri was born upon the earth as Candragiri;
and the surface of the earth became mingled with heaven, adorned by divine portions.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the fourth section on the lineage of the Tiṣya age, is the narrative of the great devotee, the royal sage named Badara; the battle with the demon Hemānala; the entry of the demons into the cool ocean at the center of the earth out of fear of Badara; the transformation of that cool ocean into the form of the Great Himālaya mountain consisting of cool stones through the casting of a moon-given moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*) into the cool ocean following Badara’s hymn of praise; and the desire of the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds to dwell upon this divine Himālaya.
The second chapter, titled "Description of the Forest Gardens and Wild Groves planted by the gods and others with celestial herbs, which were provided by Badara," ends here. || 2 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Badrīramā Pārvatī, to what occurred so fiercely—the cause of the gods' flight and how their protection was restored once again. || 1 ||
But while the gods remained steadfast and Himācala was confident,
there Hemānala was tormented upon a surface of golden stone.
That peak suddenly fell from its base into the sky,
and an earthquake also occurred among the other peaks.
A terrifying sound arose, like that of the fire of universal destruction;
there was frequent shaking of the earth, and a rain of stones fell upon the ground.
And from the surface [of the earth], stones radiant with gold fly upward;
likewise, they are impelled and cast forth from below by the fire of gold.
Then, by the power of yoga, the demon Hema rose up again from the stone slab by force; indeed, this was a great marvel.
The gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as all embodied beings such as the deities, were overcome with fear upon seeing that terrible calamity.
They then remembered the glorious Blessed Lord, the Master beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
as well as King Badara, the great devotee of the Lord.
Then Hemānala also appeared in the sky to fight with the mace;
his body was like a mountain, radiant as if made of ice and stone.
Whichever deity he beheld there on the mountain, he crushed;
meanwhile, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the Lord of the celestial chariot appeared.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Badarī,
arrived there by celestial chariot at the place where the asura Hemānala was.
Beholding that divine chariot, he rushed toward Hari to fight;
the Blessed One then quickly girded himself and took up his mace.
Having placed Śrī Ramā in the celestial chariot, he came outside;
the great king Badara also arrived there immediately.
Seeing the great asura Hemānala revived once again, the king was struck with great wonder; wielding his mace, he fought with him.
Struck even by Kṛṣṇa with a small myrobalan fruit using his mace, the Asura became exhausted;
with his waist broken, he fell to the ground.
Bādarāyaṇa lifted him up while he was still alive from that pit and cast him right back into the same snowy pit where he had been.
Then Mādhava established the Himālaya mountain there;
and Badara then [established] the supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Indeed, having failed to rise again, he entreated him in many ways;
the Blessed One said, "O King, listen to the story of Haimānalī."
In a former kalpa, he performed austerities for the sake of propitiating the Wielder of the Discus;
having placed his hand upon Hari’s head, he did so for a thousand years.
Then, indeed, for a thousand years he stood upon one foot;
then, indeed, for a thousand years he remained suspended from the branch of a banyan tree.
With his face turned downwards, he performed penance while gazing at me, Hari, with his hand;
then, for a thousand years, he kindled a fire upon his head.
Hanging from a branch, he performed most rigorous asceticism;
for a thousand years, he remained without food, subsisting only on air.
His body became suspended within the matted roots of the banyan branch.
A corpse of dried flesh and bone came to be within the branches and roots.
There he took the form of a matted-haired ascetic, climbed upon by ants;
covered with earthen anthills, he became completely concealed.
Not leaving my form upon the palm of my hand, he became an anthill;
and at the end of ten thousand years, I became pleased.
Standing in his hand, I drew out the essence of consciousness; and as I gave him the milk of the banyan tree, I bathed that body of his.
Then, by the force of the rain, all the dust was shaken away;
the asura Hemānala, having lost his vigor, stood with his face turned downwards.
Gradually regaining consciousness, as if waking with his eyes opened,
he then gazed all around at what was before him.
I manifested my four-armed form endowed with splendor;
the Asura, having joined his palms in reverence, bowed to me within the mass of his matted locks.
Having attained knowledge of that which is not his own domain, his mind became serene;
yet, as if desiring to know further, he became agitated toward me.
Having been thus awakened by me for the sake of granting a boon, he, being overwhelmed, then chose [this] for the purpose of completing his ascetic penance. || 3.1 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, if you proceed here to grant a boon, if indeed you are true to your vow, and if I am worthy and a fit recipient; 32.
Therefore, having beheld the two feet of Śrī, I have fallen into delusion;
for the two feet of Śrī are tender, radiant, and the refuge of all auspiciousness.
"Make them so that they may be touched and seen by me, and likewise eternal; let the two feet of Śrī become those that touch my body. (34)
Grant me likewise a supreme and most excellent kingdom, replete with majesty;
grant me also such power that no beings may overcome me.
"I shall indeed become dependent on Śrī alone, and never on anyone else anywhere;
if you grant me that boon, then I shall surely abandon my asceticism. (36)
Otherwise, O Mādhava, you are a speaker of falsehood and are not to be trusted;
go back just as you came, for I am indeed performing penance for a long time.
O Badrī, having been thus entreated while everyone was listening, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, spoke these words: "So be it. (38)
"When the ripening of their karma has arrived, all this will become true.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor, vanished from sight. (39)
This Hemānala suddenly abandoned his asceticism and went home;
having gone to Mount Meru, he set forth for battle with a mace.
By the power of his former asceticism, half of the earth was won by him in this kalpa;
at that time, he ruled as a sovereign king like another Viṣṇu.
And he approached even Badara to conquer his kingdom, by means of no one whatsoever—neither a supernatural being nor a physical being. (42)
Yet that asura will surely meet with defeat at some point;
thus has he obtained this boon, he who is like a peak of the snowy mountain.
Though he had previously risen from the depths of the earth by the power of his asceticism,
he has now indeed been cast back into this pit by you with a jujube fruit.
However, as long as Śrī does not fall at his feet upon that body, this Asura shall not be defeated. (45)
This man shall dwell motionless within the womb of the earth by the power of Śrī’s feet;
having obtained her imperishable feet, he will become steadfast in soul.
Therefore, O Badarī-māṇikya, worship my beloved Śrī here for the sake of her residence, and likewise for the sake of the work of the gods. ||47||
Even for one to whom a boon has been granted by me, this is for the sake of truth and victory;
otherwise, all your effort here will be fruitless.
Thus addressed, King Badara praised the Supreme Goddess:
Māṇikyā, Śrī Mahāmuktānikā, and Śrī Bālayoginī. (49)

Salutations to the Goddess who abides in all that moves and is stationary, whose splendor consists of wonder, who is indeed Nārāyaṇī, who is non-different [from Him], and who is the consort of Bālakṛṣṇa’s body. (4.3.50)
Salutations to the illustrious Puruṣottamī, the consort of Hari, the wife of Brahmā;
salutations to you, the wife of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||51||
Salutations to her whose complexion is like a ruby, the sustainer; salutations to Śrī Hari.
Salutations to the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; repeated salutations to the Supreme Brahman.
Repeated salutations to the Mother who perfectly accomplishes all that is required for the meal;
O Goddess of gods, be gracious for the pacification of the golden fire. (53)
"O Mother, this great asura cannot be defeated in battle by Śrīkānta without the nectar;
therefore, you who accomplish the purpose of the gods, must indeed crush him. (54)
Salutations to her who destroys all; salutations to you, the protectress.
Salutations to you, the wife of Mahānārāyaṇa, and to you, Māṇikyā. ||55||
Having thus entreated that Śakti, he performed worship with his heart;
then he offered flowers at her ruby-like feet.
Then, that supreme Lakṣmī, who dwells within the imperishable Brahman,
suddenly appeared before him with a serene countenance and radiant splendor.
She is the perfect counterpart to the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
a young woman pervaded by splendor, she bears the discus, the lotus, and other [emblems]. ||58||
Likewise, she held a goad and an excellent trident in her hands,
gazing again and again at Kṛṣṇa— her beloved, dear one, and very life.
Eager to carry out his command, she was devoted to that task, powerful,
slender yet fully nourished, and endowed with fresh youth.
She was golden-hued with the luster of refined gold, possessing long and beautiful lotus-eyes;
she had a nose like a parrot’s beak, teeth as white as kunda flowers, lips red as the bimba fruit, and a touch as cool as ice.
Richly adorned with garments as radiant as lightning, she shone with the Kaustubha gem;
she was graced by ornaments upon her ears, nose, forehead, arms, wrists, and feet.
Her waist was girt with a girdle; she was adorned with erotic ointments and collyrium; she shone with her braided hair and topknot, and was marked with a crescent of vermilion.
She has beautiful breasts, beautiful hips, and a beautiful waist;
she is endowed with a radiant halo and is adorned with nails that shine like the moon. (64)
Resplendent with the exquisite beauty of lac-dye, adorned with a line of golden hair, and overflowing with the great essence of love—she is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 65.
Her excellent chest was covered by fragrant flower garlands and swarms of bees;
she was enchanting with the beauty of her two thighs, which resembled land-lotuses. ||66||
Always desiring not to leave her beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
that great chaste woman, ever united with Him, held the hand of Śrīkṛṣṇa.
She, who dwells upon the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is the vessel of the Lord's love;
though she is the Supreme Sovereign, she appears like an ascetic woman, with a body as cool as a mountain. 68.
Endowed with all sovereign powers and other perfections, an ocean of the quality of maternal affection, possessed of infinite beauty, and praised by many female companions. (69)
With her eyes fixed upon the face of the Blessed One, overflowing with bliss and supreme joy, she laughed and spoke to the two Supreme Persons regarding the jujube fruit.
"Speak, O King; I shall provide for your welfare immediately here.
I shall also swiftly accomplish the work of the gods and the work of Kṛṣṇa in this matter. (71)
Having heard this, the king requested Śrī for the purpose of crushing the asuras;
by the will of Nārāyaṇa, she too rushed forward on foot to slay them.
At that moment, the chief of the Daityas became like a block of ice in the pit;
then Nārāyaṇa quickly spoke to Lakṣmī, Māṇikī.
O Nārāyaṇī, stand quickly here with your feet upon the asura;
once struck and touched by your feet, this asura shall never again emerge from within.
That evil-minded one will likewise rise up by the power of the boon he received;
therefore, perform the task for Badara and for the welfare of the gods. (75)
Then, with a distressed heart, the illustrious Māṇikyā said to her lord:
"How indeed can I live here all alone, without Kṛṣṇa? (76)
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who are without beginning, you are forever my husband;
and I am your wife, O Kṛṣṇa, devoted solely to my marital fidelity.
"I cannot bear to remain even for a moment alone in this cold wilderness without my husband.
O Kṛṣṇa, do as you wish; instruct me in a vow that is consistent with dharma."
Having heard this, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, reflected and said:
"O Badrī, become a many-rooted tree made of ruby at Māṇikya. (79)
The goad and the trident, as well as the two spikes, are your great weapons;
together with your husband, you shall be the destroyers of all the asuras.
"Always remain as the beautiful Badarī tree, a female ascetic dwelling among the trees;
having touched the golden fire with your feet, crush it within the earth. (8.1)
O Goddess Badrīdevī, may you always be immovable and eternal;
you were praised by King Badara and desired by Vadara. 82.
"Since you have come here, drawn by me with a jujube fruit (badara), you shall forever be known by the name Badarī and shall be fruitful. (83)
This very Badarikāśrama shall become a divine abode;
I, the best of ascetics, shall dwell eternally in the shade of the Badarī tree. (84)
I am born as the son of Dharma, whose essence is Nara and Nārāyaṇa; I wear matted hair, observe virtuous conduct, and live as a celibate student, finding my beautiful dwelling at your feet. (85)
I manifest here as Nara and Nārāyaṇa for the sake of the world's welfare,
as long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth shall remain.
"In the meantime, O Badrī, I shall remain here in the guise of an ascetic, while you shall remain as an ascetic woman;
we two shall dwell here in the cool, white hermitage of Himavat. (87)
Furthermore, even the fire within the earth, constantly crushed beneath the soles of your feet, shall indeed become deeply asleep as your devotee. (88)
"Act in such a way that the supreme welfare of the worlds may likewise be secured.
Having spoken thus, Queen Māṇikī quickly became Badrikā. (89)
Having caused a shower of stones to fall upon the head of the Asura Hemānala,
Māṇikyā remained firm there, having planted her very feet upon him.
The eternally divine goddess Vārkṣī is Badrīramā;
she is the ascetic lady united with the ascetic Nārāyaṇa. ||91||
He dwelt there suddenly with the wielder of the discus, the son of Dharma;
all calamities were pacified, and the fear of the asuras came to an end.
The gods and others remained motionless and worshipped the Mistress of Badarī,
while they also paid homage to Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The gods and others call this place Badrinātha, Badrikā, Badara, as well as King Nṛpa, and indeed Badarikāśrama itself. (94)
O Queen of Badarī, your abode is divine, purifying, and beautiful;
from that time forward, the gods indeed [visited it] again and again for six months.
The ancestors perform the *tīrtha* rite at Badarikāśrama on the peak of the Himavat for two months, while human beings do so for four months. (96)
Having performed the pilgrimage to Badarikāśrama, they afflict Hemānala—the embodiment of sin residing within their hearts—at Himālaya. 97.
O Queen of Badarī, having become purifiers by your very sight, embodied beings likewise become purified and liberated by the sight of me as well. 98.
Just as I dwell in the supreme abode, the world of Brahman, which is according to the syllable, so too do I dwell here together with Badrikā, accompanied by Māṇikya. 99.
"I dwell in every way, O Badrī, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds;
thus you are in every respect the most excellent, honored by all trees. (4.3.100)
"You dwell here on the Himalaya as an ascetic who shares my nature;
you are Nārāyaṇī, Badarī, and Māṇikyā, my river. (101)
I am the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person joined with Nara;
indeed, I am to be worshipped under the names Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Śrī Badarīśvarī, this excellent narrative of the devoted Badara has been proclaimed by me, composed with great devotion.
Badarī also, through constant devotion, manifested in the form of nectar;
she exists as the very fruit of the Badarī tree, just like your own daughter.
The seed is in the form of a man, and I dwell within the womb of the fruit;
by that [seed], O Badarī, other jujube trees are produced here.
"This place is my representative form; my primary abode, however, is on the mountain far from here, whose divine nature cannot be reached by travel. (106)
Behold that, O Māṇikī; for it is not within the range of vision of men, since there is no path for men, but only the path for those who are liberated. || 107 ||
From reciting, hearing, or remembering this, liberation shall occur;
likewise, there shall be the pacification of demonic afflictions and the attainment of the state consisting of Brahman.
May the supreme power that bestows all that is most auspicious arise,
and may all forms of prosperity dwell near those who listen to the stories of Badarī.
There shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and there will be no defeat for Tiṣya;
for I, as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, dwell indeed within the heart of the listener.

Thus, in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, [is described]: the re-emergence of Hemānala; the calamities such as the hurling of the mountain peak; the casting of [Hemānala] into a pit by Badara and Hari; the account of Hemānala’s former penance; the granting of boons and the attainment of the boon of being trampled by the feet of Śrī; the transformation of Śrī Māṇikyā into the form of a jujube tree (*badarī*) for the purpose of crushing him; the crushing by her feet; the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the forms of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; the jujube tree becoming the form of the fruit; and Nara becoming the form of the seed.
The third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Badrikāśrama Tīrtha and the Description of the Original Badrikāśrama as Being Separate and Distant," etc. || 3 ||
The illustrious Badrīśvarī said:
O Viṣṇu, Nara and Nārāyaṇa; O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
O Hari, beloved of Kṛṣṇā; O Kṛṣṇa, who removes the suffering of Śrī, Māṇikī, and Ramā! || 1 ||
O Nārāyaṇa, tell me how that King Badara attained the state of a jujube fruit, and how the man attained the state of a seed.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Badrīramā, to that purifying and auspicious narrative, which grants liberation to devotees and destroys the sins of sinners. (3)
Badara was indeed a great devotee; [he possessed] a kingdom, wealth, houses and the like, riches, women, vehicles and mounts, as well as subjects. || 4 ||
Having dedicated his treasury, his jewels, the earth, and even his own body and belongings—
all for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— he indeed conducted himself like a true saint.
He always employed his male and female servants in the service of holy men;
in his palaces dwelt virtuous people, the devotees of Hari.
O Badarī, kīrtanas were held constantly in his abode;
indeed, he surrendered everything for the sake of practicing devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Once, having attained the state of self-surrender, the king reflected:
"Everything has been offered by me to Hari, the Supreme Self. (8)
Everything is indeed illusory, and so too has the Self been described;
as well as that which is earthly, watery, fiery, and even vital breath.
Everything was offered to the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus:
the house, the vehicle, food and so forth, as well as garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Fragrant substances, perfumed oils, and so forth—all such inanimate objects that are useful for the sake of Kṛṣṇa arise as fit and worthy of service. (1.1)
But this body is exceedingly base, filled with foul odors, impure, deformed, and moist; it is of no use to the Wielder of the Discus.
It is indeed perpetually impure, filled with filth and urine;
it is bathed in marrow and flesh, a despicable corpse, a mere carcass. (13)
In every way, he is of no use to me, my master;
he is proclaimed to be a living corpse, a dead man, ashes, excrement, or earth. (14)
How may this composition for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and for the sake of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa be useful? And how might it not be useless? (19)
How might that which was nurtured by me for a hundred thousand years and served with auspicious deeds be of benefit here for the sake of the virtuous? (16)
Indeed, let this human body become meaningful;
through penance, I shall likewise make it divine, fit for enjoyment by the virtuous and by Hari.
Or, out of devotion, I shall place it in use so that it remains worthy of service;
for the virtuous never offer service to a king.
The king’s body performs service like that of a wretched man;
therefore, this body of the king now functions fruitlessly.
I shall indeed make that [abode] fruitful through asceticism and propitiation;
for that abode which does not belong to a deity is considered a cursed place.
That head which was not employed in bowing to the gods is indeed contemptible;
those two eyes which were not for the purpose of beholding the gods are likewise contemptible. (21)
Those ears which do not hear the words of the gods are also to be condemned;
and that forehead which does not possess the grace of sandalwood paste and other offerings worthy of the gods [is likewise to be despised]. (22)
That forehead should always be understood as unfortunate, like the forehead of a bear, upon which the nose that perceives the fragrance of Lord Hari never exists. (23)
That face, resembling parched sesame seeds and flowers, is full of hollows and lacks beauty,
since it never utters the words of Śrī Hari.
There is neither praise nor joy in that mouth which is like the face of a fool;
it is a tongue that does not know the flavor born of the grace of Nārāyaṇa. 25.
But she should be understood as being like a ladle or like a female frog, devoid of virtue,
if her face— though beautiful and lovely— is not to be enjoyed by Hari;
for it must be understood that even for excellent women, such a face is eternally eclipsed by Rāhu.
And that face of the man is considered to be equal to the face of a monkey. ||27||
That mouth which does not know the taste of the nectar from the face of Hari Nārāyaṇa is indeed like the hole of a mouse, devoid of the essence of betel.
That throat which is not immersed in the song of Hari’s glory, however melodious it may be, should be understood as being like a *kīcaka* reed—merely a hollow sound of empty resonance. (29)
That chest which is not worthy of Hari, nor has it been resorted to by Śrī Hari, and wherein there is no dwelling of Hari—that chest is but a bird’s nest in a tree. (4.4.30)

That chest upon which Kṛṣṇa himself does not lie, even though it is adorned with necklaces like a living man’s, should be understood as the impure chest of a corpse, with its breasts hanging down in vain. (31)
Those two breasts which were touched by the lotus-palms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s beloved hands have indeed become inauspicious lumps, resembling knots on a mango tree.
Those two shoulders which were not embraced by Kṛṣṇa’s hands remain stiff;
that back which was touched while lying on Kṛṣṇa’s bed has indeed become like wood.
That belly which was pressed against the belly of the Beloved of Ramā was not at all fearful;
that navel which was gazed upon by Kṛṣṇa was not like a pit or a hole.
That which has never been touched by Kṛṣṇa—the hips, the loins, and the private parts—should be understood as the abode of Yama, a refuge for all sins. (35)
The hips, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet are like the buttresses of a tree trunk, having never experienced the touch of Kṛṣṇa. (36)
The mind that experiences separation from Kṛṣṇa is indeed considered to be the Raurava hell;
the intellect devoid of Kṛṣṇa is the pit consisting of the Kumbhīpāka hell. (37)
That mind which is devoid of the dark [qualities] is like a jackal;
that ego-sense which is empty of the dark is destructive like a she-wolf. (38)
The three qualities (guṇas) are devoid of Kṛṣṇa, for they consist of the three defects (doṣas);
the three states (avasthās) are likewise devoid of Kṛṣṇa, for they are indeed the three sins (aghāt).
That form which is devoid of blackness is always considered to be *śvitra*;
that taste which is devoid of blackness is indeed the river Vaitaraṇī. (4.4.40)
The scent, devoid of blackness, resembles a vessel of impurity;
the sound, separated from blackness, is indeed like the cry of an owl in every respect. (41)
Indeed, touch devoid of Kṛṣṇa is like the fire of poison;
likewise, delight, affection, happiness, joy, and festivals are all void when deprived of Kṛṣṇa.
All those hell-beings, O Ānanda, are of the nature of hell because of their awakening;
indeed, everything joined with the dark [karma] is so, whether it be very small or great. (43)
That indeed is divine, eternal, the great nectar that bestows liberation, and that which becomes beneficial for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and for the virtuous. ||44||
That which is considered base becomes excellent when honored by the gods;
even marrow, bone, skin, and so forth, become worthy of use when employed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
That divine human body is entirely meaningful, for it bestows liberation;
even trees become meaningful by taking the form of vehicles for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. (46)
Elephant tusks become grass-curl ornaments and seats;
from the hair of yak-tail tufts, auspicious whisks are produced. (47)
Even the musk of the musk-deer is considered suitable for use by Kṛṣṇa;
furthermore, the skins of deer, lions, and other animals serve as seats. 48.
Even mother-of-pearl and other such gems become ornaments, and offerings of roots, tubers, and fruits arise for Hari. (49)
From the Supreme Self, sweet foods arise from grains, and even drinkable substances such as milk and other products derived from cows come into being. 4.4.50
Honey from bees is sweet and edible;
silk cloth produced from insects is useful for the sake of black [clothing]. (51)
Even minerals, which are of the nature of earth, can take the form of weapons;
likewise, a conch shell, which originates from a marine creature, can also take the form of a musical instrument. (52)
Even gems arising from the body and pearls are worn as a garland by Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved; indeed, everything that is useful is accepted by him.
Indeed, even the backs of a swan, Garuḍa, an elephant,
a horse, or Viṣṇu become fit for auspicious seats.
However, this human body is indeed of no use to Kṛṣṇa, nor is it of use to the virtuous;
therefore, it is always useless.
Thus the king reflected in many ways upon his own body:
"Could even collyrium, though black, become the seat for Krishna's eyes? (56)
A man’s body, even if equal to that [of a woman], is indeed useless for this reason;
whereas a woman’s body finds its purpose like that of a maidservant for the sake of Hari. 57.
There is no human body equal to that which does not exist for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, by me, [this body] must be for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, and likewise for the sake of the virtuous man and the virtuous woman.
The purpose of being a seer, a sage, or a forest-dweller must indeed be fulfilled;
the kingdom has been enjoyed and everything that was to be done has been accomplished—nothing remains. (59)
My son Viśāla is young, capable, and skilled in the duties of kingship;
having entrusted the kingdom to him, I shall dedicate this body to Kṛṣṇa.
Having reflected thus, that Badara summoned the subjects; making his heart open and having obtained the consensus of the people, [he spoke]. (61)
With a great festival, he entrusted the righteous burden of the kingdom to his son named Viśāla, and thereafter set his mind upon liberation.
Having reached the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa on the Himalayas,
he reflected upon his own body as being useful for the service of the virtuous.
For the sake of serving Nārāyaṇa,
he remained in meditative absorption (samādhi) as was appropriate, suddenly fixing his self within the Supreme Self.
Having attained an excess of affection for those two lords, Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
he became completely absorbed in them, forgetting his own body.
Filled with the fire of Brahmā and intensely radiant with the fire of knowledge, he was suddenly liquefied by the flame of passion and became bodiless (videha).
While all the best of sages were looking on, it turned into a liquid,
[passing through] the hair, blood, flesh, sinews, bones, and marrow.
And all these [qualities], including vigor, became of the nature of nectar at the foot-base of the glorious Badarī, whose form is Śrī Māṇikī-Śrī. (68)
Then all that liquid, in the form of food, quickly dissolved;
this great wonder occurred as it was offered at the feet of Śrī. (69)
Just as the final state of one's contemplation is, so does the embodied being become;
thus, King Badara quickly attained the state of the essence.
Indeed, in the form of a liquid and edible substance, he dissolved into the roots of the banyan trees;
and in the form of a most delicious essence, he entered the trunk of the banyan tree.
Suddenly pervading the branches, he likewise became the form of flowers;
he also became the form of fruit, and from that, jujube fruits (badara) came into being.
This is a great marvel that has occurred: Badara, having made his own body into liquid essence, has brought it forth in the form of a fruit. (73)
The bael fruits were sweet, ripened in every way, fragrant, beautiful, large, and providing complete satisfaction. ||74||
Then all the jujubes became sanctifying, born from the essence of the splendor of rubies, produced by his grace. (75)
Then the divine Nara-Nārāyaṇa took some [of them];
the Blessed One indeed ate the sweet fruits among the food offerings.
Then other sages, gods, gandharvas, humans, and deities—
whosoever were there on the Himalaya mountain— all indeed ate the excellent fruits.
A single fruit was produced that provided satisfaction for an entire year;
indeed, being filled with honey, it brought complete satisfaction to all the ascetics.
Praise arose throughout the fourteen worlds regarding the excellent nectar-like bilva fruits on the Himavat mountain. (79)
Having heard [this] through tradition, the ancestors, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas indeed obtain the gifts of Nārāyaṇa which grant satisfaction. (4.4.80)
Sages, humans, gods, and other embodied beings came to the mountain for the sake of obtaining the fruits [of their penance], and Nārāyaṇa also bestowed them. (81)
Having obtained fruits that were indeed exceedingly sweet and delicious, they all ate them and attained a year-long satisfaction that bestows happiness. (82)
Whoever eats its fruits attains divinity;
they obtain strength, nourishment, and valor a thousandfold. (83)
Having heard [of them] again and again, they come; and having led [them there], they depart, after beholding Himālaya, Badarī, and the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
The inhabitants of the egg rejoice in various jujube fruits;
a great festival has arisen for all those who eat jujubes. (85)
Having beheld Mount Maināka in the ocean, as well as Badarī with its rubies, and having beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is the very essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; ||86||
Indeed, they regarded the ascetic with matted hair as a new creation;
for the sake of pilgrimage, he had come to the excellent sacred site of Badarikaśrama.
The excellent vehicles, the attendants, the celestial hosts, millions of lords, the goddesses, and the divine beings arrived with the desire for the fruit [of their devotion]. (88)
Just as the jujube fruits are taken away, so too do fresh ones immediately spring up all around the tree. (89)
This Badara, O Great King, was the essence of the sap of the *badara* fruit; through supreme devotion, he became embodied as a fruit, a body fit to be enjoyed by all.
It is imperishable and undecaying, likewise devoid of numerical measure;
it is the divine essence, consisting of the essence of Brahman, the supreme essence of Śrī. ||91||
Indeed, by the grace of Nara-Nārāyaṇa and also by the grace of Lakṣmī, he was always born as one whose very nature consists of fruit and progeny. 92.
He was always like a fruit made of ruby, possessing divine fruit;
and the goddess Badrī, though in the form of a tree, was always fruitful. (93)
Even the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa became possessed of a son in the form of a fruit;
though established in the vow of celibacy, he became the father of Badara.
Māṇikyāśrī was always devoted to virtuous conduct and vows; as a young yoginī, she always possessed sons like the *badara* fruits upon her bamboo staff. (95)
These jujube fruits, indeed identical with Nārāyaṇa, became divine, characterized by the nature of the *lakṣya*, and fit for the consumption of the liberated. 96.
Therefore, the enjoyer of the jujube fruit experiences great bliss through the form of Kṛṣṇa;
he alone, as an enjoyer of the bliss of the Divine Form, dwells in the Badarī forest. 97.
Indeed, all the auspicious jujube fruits on that jujube tree are free from illusion and consist solely of the single reality (caikatattva). //98//
Thus indeed, O Goddess Badarī, the jujube fruit attained its state;
through supreme devotion, having reached a state of liquid essence, it remained within the tree. (99)
For it is held that for the great devotees of the Lord, everything is offered unto Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, everything indeed becomes divine.
Even illusion becomes non-illusion, and even the body becomes bodiless; likewise, qualities attain the state of being quality-less, and the inert becomes divine and conscious. || 10.1 ||
"Everything indeed offered to Kṛṣṇa becomes identical with Kṛṣṇa;
such, O illustrious Goddess Māṇikī, is the narrative concerning your devotees. (102)
O Goddess Śrī Badarī, I have proclaimed this divine [account] which bestows liberation;
by reading or hearing it, one shall obtain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the supreme goal.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of King Badara’s Attainment of Essentiality through Penance and Devotion at the Foot of the Badarī Tree, Resulting in His Transformation into the Essence of Taste and the Form of Badarī Fruits," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Badarī, to the account of Nara as well;
there, in that seedless jujube fruit, Nara indeed attained the state of being a seed.
Having seen and eaten those most excellent fruits, which were indeed as delicious as nectar, the gods, great seers, deities, humans, and other embodied beings [were filled with wonder]. (2)
They fervently entreated Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as well as Māṇikī, with the desire to lead Badrī to that region.
O Viṣṇu, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Lord who bestows all assistance!
This Badarī is the most excellent of wish-fulfilling trees, bearing the noble fruit of nectar.
Endowed with compassion, she dwells here in the imperishable abode;
and here the jujube tree has attained the state of fruit, yielding a juice that brings satisfaction.
Such nectar as this does not exist in heaven, nor among people, nor in asceticism or truth;
it is found neither in the world of men, nor in Pātāla, nor even on Mount Meru or Lokācala.
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, ocean of compassion, grant us in these worlds this [gift] which bestows inexhaustible fruit and grants inexhaustible satisfaction. (7)
Just as we gods, the *ṛṣis*, and the great *ṛṣis* are devoted [to you],
may we indeed become dwellers of forests and wildernesses, subsisting on these fruits.
O Lord, you perform penance for the sake of the welfare of the entire world;
may you likewise bring about the supreme good by granting the attainment of Badarī.
Even sinful beings in this world who partake of the jujube fruit shall become sinless and go to the supreme state.
Indeed, compassion should be shown toward the worlds; for there is no fruit superior to this, which bestows liberation, purifies, grants merit, and yields the fruit of sacrifice. (11)
It increases the ascetic power of those who practice austerity, bestows eternal satisfaction,
is more delicious than the nectar of the gods, and is the supreme source of gratification for the ancestors.
It increases the strength of the virtuous who dwell in forests and wildernesses,
accomplishes the purity of the inner heart, and is dear to Hari.
For the jujube fruit is indeed the fruit of Brahman, as well as the fruit of divine nectar;
it is likewise the fruit of Lakṣmī, the fruit of devotion, and the fruit of Śrīmāṇikī.
O Lord, this imperishable fruit of truth is not obtained elsewhere;
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having given it to us, make us successful in our purpose. 15.
This fruit is called *badara*, and likewise there was a king named *Badara*.
Furthermore, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Māṇikī, Badrī, Pārvatī, and Ramā are all beloved by Hari.
You are Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and all of you are benefactors of the world;
may you bestow your favor through the act of offering this jujube fruit.
Thus requested, Hari, moved by compassion for the sake of fulfilling the minds of you all, my devotees who were begging for jujube fruits, spoke to them. (18)
I wish to give these jujube fruits so that they may remain unbroken;
for these, possessing divine forms, shall indeed become seedless.
By giving these to you, there shall certainly be no long delay in your attainment;
for there exists but one tree of the jujube (badarī) that is likewise immovable.
And he cannot be uprooted for the purpose of crushing the Hema-asuras;
rather, it shall be such that there will be a succession of lineages like that of the jujube trees. (21)
All effects produced by me possess seeds;
without a seed, that lineage does not grow or continue unbroken. (22)
From the root, the trunk, the fruit, the leaf, the stem, the stalk, the eye,
the branch, the fiber, and the knot— may there be an increase of the lineage.
In this context, the increase of the lineage through the seed is considered superior;
for by those born of the lineage, the deliverance of their ancestors is accomplished. (24)
"In the case of decrease, there would be no new acquisition nor even a reduction;
therefore, I shall place seeds here within these jujube fruits. (25)
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Badarī,
with a gracious soul, at that very moment beheld his own partial incarnation, Nara.
Bowing low and humble, with palms joined in reverence, the man spoke:
"O Hari, if you have any desire, I shall fulfill it immediately; tell me what it is."
Formerly, by your will, when Rādhā came into being from Śrī Puruṣottama in the imperishable abode, at that time I attained the state of Kṛṣṇa. ||28||
By your command, I always dwell in Goloka together with Rādhā;
yet, when the goddess Ramā was born from your own form, [I entered her]. (29)
Then, having attained the state of Nārāyaṇa, I became a dweller of Vaikuṇṭha;
indeed, it was at that time that Ramā manifested from your form.
In former times, I existed in the form of Vāsudeva and in the form of the Vyūha,
when Mahālakṣmī was born as Lalitā from your own essence.
At that time, in ancient days, I was indeed Mahāviṣṇu in Śrīpura;
when Lakṣmī was born from your body, I then became Viṣṇu.
And Śrī was born from your form; at that time, by your command, I became the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, and Kamalā was born from your form. (33)
At that time, when you were dwelling in the snowy mountains having made Māṇikī Badarī your place of service, I became Śvetanārāyaṇa in Śvetadvīpa.
Then, in this world, I shall become your brother, Nara, your younger sibling; I am your mind-born son, the son of Dharma. Speak, and I shall do whatever you say.
For those who are the four sons of Dharma are indeed Nārāyaṇas;
among them, the eldest is Hari, who exists in the Imperishable, while you are Śrī Puruṣottama. (36)
Kṛṣṇa resides in the realm of Goloka, and Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha;
you are that very Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is moral character.
O Supreme Lord, you abide here together with Māṇikya;
I am a human being who is a portion of you, so show me the command and I shall carry it out. (38)
Having spoken thus, he bowed down to that Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Badarī.
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "O brother, you are a doer of auspicious deeds. (39)
There exists one who acts for the benefit of the world, possessing my own prowess and form;
you abide as the very embodiment of my heroism, strength, power, and other attributes.
Indeed, these devotees, the gods and others, pray for Badarikā;
they desire jujube fruits for the sake of achieving their constant sustenance. (41)
Today there exists only one Badarī, namely Mūladevikā;
yet indeed, countless jujube fruits have been produced from her. 42.
They indeed become seedless when requested by the gods and others;
all of them are given and consumed by the gods and others. (43)
They will provide satisfaction only once and not more;
however, they would indeed be the perpetuators of the lineage if they were to do so forever. (44)
At that time, there shall be happiness for the world through those who provide inexhaustible lineages;
furthermore, there shall be the increase of the lineage of Badarī and the feeding of ascetics. (45)
On the earth and in the heavens, others shall subsist on fruit;
in all worlds, the lineage of Badarī shall exist for the sake of others.
"Furthermore, I have desired seeds here within these jujube fruits;
therefore, O younger brother, having assumed the form of a seed, enter into these fruits. (47)
With roots whose essence is you, there will be tens of millions of other jujube trees (*badarī*) even in forests, wildernesses, gardens, fields, and jungles. (48)
"By your command, O Badarī, even the most excellent jujube fruits in all the worlds shall become like seeds; therefore, become possessed of seeds. (49)
Thus addressed, that devotee, by the command of Nārāyaṇa,
suddenly assumed the form of a seed and entered into the root of the *badarī* tree.
When all the jujube fruits had ripened, that soul in the form of a seed was born;
this man, born from the womb of the jujube tree, was born as a founder of a noble lineage.
Nārāyaṇa, being pleased upon seeing the man who was the essence of the seed, remained there separately even while in the guise of an ascetic.
The auspicious Badarī became gracious and indeed gave birth to Vaṃśavatī;
then Nārāyaṇa spoke with supreme reverence to the gods and others.
Indeed, this is the majesty of the jujube fruits and of Badarī, which destroys all sins;
for it is from this root that the jujube trees shall arise upon the earth and in heaven.
In Candra, Meru, Satyaloka, Jana, Tapas, and Mānava; in Lokāloka, Raivatādri, Puṣkara, and Dakṣiṇakuru. ||55||
In the regions of Brahmā, in the eastern lands of Amarīśaka,
in the world of Gaurī, and likewise in the open plains and in the lands of Oṣṭra.
In Pātāla and other realms, in the auspicious abodes of sages, on the banks of rivers, in forests, and even in the forests of lions; ||57||
Indeed, throughout all the forests of Dharma there will be Badarī trees;
some shall yield fruit in every season, while others shall be eternal and inexhaustible in heaven and other realms. (58)
Some possess qualities such as their specific location and so forth, yielding fruit according to the season;
some yield fruit during the rainy season, while others produce fruit in the cold.
Some will be trees that bear fruit in the hot season;
others likewise will bear fruit in the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra.
And in various regions there will also be Badarī shrubs that are like daughters,
auspicious and bestowing large fruits that are ripe, desirable, sweet, and nourishing.
Those people who shall perform worship with jujube fruits (badara) in the month of Māgha, for them there shall be the fruit of worshipping Lakṣmī herself; of this there is no doubt. (62)
On a day in spring, on the eleventh lunar day, on the full moon day, or on the new moon day,
one should go to the vicinity of the root of the Badarī tree.
Having gone to the base of the venerable Badarī on the eleventh day of Phālguna, on the full moon day of Phālguna,
or on the new moon day of Phālguna, || 1150 ||
One should indeed first worship the goddess Badarī with an offering of water;
one should offer hidden sugar and present sweet food upon the root.
One should also offer milk, as well as incense, a lamp, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
one should offer saffron, gulāla, sandalwood, and water.
One should offer the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), a thread for the lower garment, collyrium, vermilion for the sake of adornment, and a garland of flowers. ||67||
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering, circumambulation, and acts of salutation;
one should also offer betel-leaf and present a pleasing fruit. (68)
One should offer a banner to Badrīdevī; salutations be unto you, O Nārāyaṇī!
Salutations to you, O Śrīmāṇikī; repeated salutations to you, O Ramā! (69)
Salutations to the illustrious Puruṣottamī; salutations again and again to Padmāvatī.
Salutations to you, O Bālayoginī; salutations again and again to the goddess Kārṣṇī.
Salutations to you, the daughter of Himavat, who bears the trident and the goad;
you are Lakṣmī, you are Satī, you are Śrī, you are Ramā, and you are Rādhikā, O Sovereign. (71)
You are Pārvatī and Mahālakṣmī; salutations to you, O Brāhmī!
Salutations to you, O Badarīśvarī; repeated salutations to you, O Hariṇī! ||72||
Salutations to you, the bestower of fruits upon ascetics and the sustainer of nectar;
salutations to you, O Mother Badrī, who are worshipped by the three worlds. ||73||
Your shadow is considered the destroyer of the beginningless shadow of Māyā; Your root is the root of Brahman, the warder-off of primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti). (74)
Your branches are the branches of the abode that transcend the abode of the syllable (akṣara),
and your leaves are indeed parasols that bestow the sovereignty of Brahman.
Your fruits have been enjoyed, which bestow the fruits of yoga upon yogis, granting the fruits of all yoga and bestowing the Supreme Brahman. ||76||
Your seeds indeed cause the destruction of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the worlds;
the jujube trees of your lineage destroy the sins of sinners. (77)
The consumption of your fruits bestows the fruit of liberation;
the touch of your leaves bestows the abode of Brahman-bliss. (78)
Bowing at your feet brings about the destruction of all asuras;
O Badrī, the sight of your form is the vision of Brahmā himself. (79)
O Badarī, bathing in the waters rich with your fruit is equivalent to plunging into the Brahma-lake;
sleeping beneath you is the consecration of all sacred fords.
Offering water and other gifts at your root grants satisfaction to the ancestors;
even the offering of your fruit alone during a *śrāddha* ceremony bestows ten-thousandfold satisfaction.
O Badrī, the gift of your fully ripened fruits bestows the essence of Brahman;
it grants all flavors, increases all prosperity, and augments every form of wealth.
Where Badarī indeed is in the vessel, there is my imperishable abode;
where the goddess Śrī-Badarī is, there is the sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama. ||83||
A living being whose life has departed within the Badrī forest is fit for liberation;
indeed, the messengers of Yama never enter beneath the Badrī tree. (84)
Indeed, beneath Badarī lie the destroyers of the sins of the wicked;
one who beholds Badarī at the time of death attains heaven and liberation.
One who eats the fruit of the *badarī* tree goes to the supreme goal when dead;
one whose bed is strewn with *badarī* flowers goes to the imperishable state. (86)
For one fallen into calamity, the worship of Badarī brings about the destruction of that calamity;
for one who serves Badarī, no evil dream ever arises anywhere. (87)
Likewise, the afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* perish;
for those who constantly resort to Badarī, the torments of the planets are always destroyed. (88)
On the auspicious day of Māghī, a garland of jujube fruits should indeed be worn around the neck;
and on that auspicious day of Māghī, ripe and sweet jujube fruit should be eaten. (89)
On an auspicious day, the juice within the jujube fruit should be ground inside the body;
furthermore, on the day of the vow, one should perform a bath with water rich in jujube fruits.
Therefore, whatever fruit may result from the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of sacrifices, the fruit of all sacrifices shall come from the worship of Badarī; of this there is no doubt. ||91||
One should offer jujube fruits made from ripe fruit, and for the sake of the rite for the deity, one should also offer wood from the jujube tree. 92.
Likewise, one should offer ripe jujube fruits for the purpose of the oblation;
one should also offer jujube fruits for the purpose of eating fruit.
One should offer these, together with sugar, mixed with ghee, and likewise combined with milk, to the ascetic practitioner of penance. ||94||
Having gone to the foot of the Badarī tree on the full moon day of Māgha, one should partake of food;
all the gods eat that, and the ancestors as well are satisfied. (95)
One should give gifts at the site of Badarī to a virtuous Brahmin;
indeed, what is given to a destitute woman becomes inexhaustible. 96.
In ancient times, a brahmin named Suśīla,
having offered a auspicious jujube fruit (*badara*) into the hands of his father during a *śrāddha* ceremony, indeed attained the station of Indra.
By uttering the names Badara, Badarīnātha, Badrikā, Badarikāśrama, and the seed-syllable of Badrī, a mortal becomes one with Brahman. (98)
Remembering Badarī, Badara, Vadriśvara, and Himāśrama,
one who casts off the body at the time of death shall go upward to the supreme goal.
Having remembered the goddess Śrī Badarī, that woman will go to the imperishable realm;
she shall become the wife of Hari and the sovereign friend of Māṇikyā.
A human being shall attain liberation at the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa;
even beasts, birds, insects, and aquatic creatures as well [shall do so]. 10.1.
Grasses and other plants that take refuge in Badarī shall attain liberation upon death;
this Badarī is the abode where Nara and Nārāyaṇa reside. (102)
Through the practice of that [rite], those who have indeed committed sins will attain enjoyment, liberation, and the prosperity of heaven and other realms; they shall truly become purified.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Badarī Tree’s Possession of Seeded Fruit in Response to the Gods’ and Others’ Desire for Constant Attainment of Badarī Fruits, the Seed-Nature of Nara, and the Greatness of Badarī," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Badrīśvarī said: O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord Nārāyaṇa;
O Viṣṇu, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, ascetic Lord of Badarī! (1)
When and where in ancient times did the Brahmin named Suśīla live, by whom the satisfaction of the ancestors was accomplished with a jujube fruit, thereby granting them heaven? (2)
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Badrīramā, to the narrative of Suśīla;
it took place in the auspicious land called Vihāra, in the vicinity of the hermitage of Pulaha. (3)
On the auspicious bank of the Gaṇḍakī, in the city of Mauktikāhāra,
there lived a preeminent Brāhmaṇa named Suśīla, who indeed possessed a large family.
His father was named Śrīśīla; he was always industrious, learned, yet overcome by greed and devoted to the fear of expenditure. || 5 ||

He is impoverished by expenditures for the sake of his family, yet he accumulates wealth and other possessions; he is devoid of festivals and the like, and is bereft of enthusiasm for religious vows and such.
In matters of honor such as greatness and the like, he was as devoid of expenditure as a miser;
even in his dress, his carriage, and his food, he was as coarse as a forest-dweller.
He manages his livelihood by obtaining alms for activities such as the worship of gods;
he is devoid of hospitality and the like, being solely devoted to dry sacrifices.
He gave his offspring milk to drink and provided them with flour-porridge;
he ate his midday meal without vegetables and the like, and it was devoid of ghee.
He eats kṛśara rice himself and also feeds it to his wife;
he feeds only vegetables to his sons and others, and likewise to those of similar status.
The Brahmin father, though devoid of charity and other virtues, was possessed of fortune and good character and was diligent in his duties;
having gone himself to the riverbank, he bathed and brought back fruits and other offerings.
Having personally gathered the sacrificial fuel, he indeed offers it into the fire;
even there, he offers only a single drop of ghee, and nothing more.
The Brahmin wears only a loincloth and a fringe, and no further clothing;
indeed, he carries himself with only a sacrificial thread over his shoulder.
"Even though he is a householder, this man behaves like an ascetic or a sage under the influence of greed;
for he never eats anything that has been kept overnight in his home."
Having obtained vegetables, or bulbs, roots, or leaves,
he brings them from the forest, the wilderness, or even the jungle and eats them.
In time, this brahmin had ten sons and seven daughters,
all of whom were adorned by the dharma of brahmins.
His eldest son, named Suśīla, being diligent in his duties, attained renown for his knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences throughout all the villages of Pārśva. (17)
Noble, generous in giving, and devoted to the festival of Dharma, he nourished his family with food, clothing, and all enjoyments. || 18 ||
He was a worthy recipient of royal honors and the like, honored and respected by the people; he was proficient in sacrificial rites and other duties, a Vaiṣṇava who was like a king among devotees.
Devoted to the vow of serving the virtuous and dedicated to the service of holy women,
he was intent upon the duty of hospitality, the service of cows, and the service of the village.
He was always a reciter for children and a storyteller;
such was his own son, devoid of the dharma of hair (asceticism).
Seeing that he was profligate, his father sent him far from home;
consequently, having abandoned his own house, he went to another city.
Having been shown great honor by the king, he dwelt there with a tranquil mind, ruling the kingdom known as Dārābhāgya and being esteemed by his subjects and the king alike. (23)
The king, the lord of the unfortunate in matters of wives, known by the name Dāreśvara,
gave a palace for his residence to the learned and virtuous man.
On the occasion of the solar eclipse, he gave land, fields, gardens, great groves, vehicles, and food sufficient for his livelihood as gifts.
Having received due honor, this brahmin became serene through the attainment of auspicious prosperity;
with a tranquil mind, he worshipped Hari, the Lord of Śrī, his own beloved.
Having obtained a livelihood suitable for his own journey, he was indeed satisfied,
having completely abandoned all external adjuncts that fall within the sphere of worldly acquisition.
Every day, he recited the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in the city at the assembly place of the multitude of subjects.
The king, as well as the lord of his wife,
attend daily to various narratives that are indeed devoted to devotion for Bhakta.
Having heard again and again those accounts concerning the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa that have emerged from the mouth of this Vaiṣṇava, he indeed rejoices.
At the conclusion of the discourse, he indeed causes the proclamation of festivals with offerings of food and other delights:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa! Bālakṛṣṇa! Śrīpati! Puruṣottama! (3.1)
"O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Badarīśvara!
Having thus performed the kīrtana and offered the naivedya, [he said: 32.
Then, having shared out the prasāda, the members of the assembly go home;
the brāhmaṇa performs worship to Hari in the evening and worship again in the morning. (33)
Having performed his midday devotions, he indeed takes his meal;
people are eager for the opportunity to meet with him both morning and evening.
Those seeking liberation, with pure minds, constantly approach him for their own spiritual welfare;
to them, the best of brahmins imparts the mantra that bestows liberation. (35)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
In that city, many Vaiṣṇavas indeed became accomplished in this way. (36)
Among both men and women, there were many groups of highly virtuous devotees;
performing acts of devotion, they worshiped the Lord Śrīprabha. (37)
Just as it was in the city, so too in the other villages, there arose communities of devotees who took refuge in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||38||
Then, considering the auspicious brahmin Bhāgavata to be the most excellent of devotees and worthy, the king gave him his daughter Kundanikā. (39)
Virtuous and fortunate, having obtained the chaste Kundanikā as his wife—a divine princess—he rejoiced through the grace of Lord Hari. (4.6.40)
She too, equal to Lakṣmī, virtuous, devoted, and chaste, worshipped her beloved lord, the noble Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (41)
For she was noble, endowed with great supernatural power, a mistress of generosity, and beloved;
she was always dear to Kṛṣṇa and was born devoted to Kṛṣṇa. 42.
The son-in-law shone in the royal palace, his fortune increased;
his fame spread everywhere, and his father heard of it. (43)
Sent by their father, the sons and daughters also came, filled with great enthusiasm, to see their eldest brother and their own sibling.
Queen Gālavī, his mother, also came to see her son;
however, the father remained alone at home, deeply ashamed due to the fault of his renunciation. ||45||
Moreover, being intent on greed for wealth, he was the guardian of the riches in the house;
by the turn of fate, a fever came upon the Brahmin Śrīśīla. (46)
Having met death through the exhaustion of his lifespan in an utterly secluded house, when his death was gradually discovered by his kinsmen, the funeral rites were performed. (47)
O Goddess of Badarī, for the sinner, the miser, and the greedy man, death occurs in solitude even though he has many family members. (48)
Due to the fault of greed, that brahmin was driven away by the mountain of latent impressions;
he attained the state of a ghost there, assuming a spectral body within that house.
For when wealth has entered the house, it dwells there as if having made its abode;
no other gains entrance, and this [wealth] afflicts whoever has already entered.
That being became well-known as one devoted to the behavior of a preta; having given no gifts in his past, he obtained neither food, nor sustenance, nor water. (51)
Afflicted by hunger, he cries out somewhere during the latter half of the night;
