and for those set upon their departure, I am the one who brings about their end.
I am the one who bestows rewards, excellent gifts, and satisfaction; I am the father and the lord who honors those who arrive with welcome respect. 46.
For those who have taken refuge in me, I am the great support as their protector;
for the protectorless, I am the excellent protector; and among the multitude of wives, I am the husband.
Among all forms of good fortune, I am the Moon of Great Good Fortune;
and among vast riches, I am Eternal Prosperity. (48)
Among supernatural powers, I am the supreme power; among gains, I am the giver of self-attainment;
and among services, I am the service of the limbs in the act of total surrender. 49.
I am the attentive service of those who desire to hear, and I am the virtuous conduct of the well-behaved;
I am the goodness of the good, the patience of the patient, and the intoxication of the renouncers.
Among all things, I am the virtue of morality; among those possessed of vigor, I am vigor;
among women, I am beauty; and among men, I am the beard. (51)
I am the lac-dye upon the bride's feet, and I am the slow, hesitant gait;
yet I also possess the natural restlessness born of our recent union. (52)
I become favorable toward embodied beings who do me service;
I am favor, compassion, pity, and benefit toward the virtuous. (53)
Among victors, I am victory; among those who know the Self, I am knowledge;
among poets who are almost omniscient, I am logic; and among poetic compositions, I am the poem. (54)
I become the belovedness of those who are beloved, the warbling of those who know mantras, and the praise of those who offer praise; I am the very spectacle for all who look on. (55)
I am the attachment of those who are attached, and the knot of those who tie knots; I am the innate nature of those established in their nature, and the expansion of those who expand. 96.
O Nikāmadeva, know me to be the conscious one among the conscious;
I am the witness of all, the initiator and the withdrawer. (57)
I am the giver of the fruits of all actions; I am subtle for those who live subtly, and I am gross for the gross; I am always visible to those who possess vision.
I am invisible to embodied beings who are deprived of divine vision;
I am within the range of those whose goal is me, yet I am far from even those who hate me. (59)
I am the life of all beings and the existence of the insentient; I am in the navel-lotus of women and I am the manhood in men.
For I am the nectar of the gods, the accumulation of merit for the ancestors, the state of Brahman for the seers, and the principle of justice for human beings. (61)
Among warriors, I am battle; among the learned, I am vast knowledge; among virtuous women, I am truth and dharma; and among wives, I am devotion to the husband as a deity.
I dwell in the wifely devotion of wives, in the service to fathers of sons,
in the spirit of charity of the wealthy, and in the sacrificial altar of kings.
I am the leader of the Apsarases in their assembly, the chief of the Gandharvas in singing, the foremost among dancers in the art of dance, and the presiding lord in the assembly hall.
I am entirely Vyāsadeva in discourse, fire in the sacrifice, victory in battle, and statesmanship in exertion. (65)
Among the milk of cattle and other animals, I am the bull; among trees, I am the *guñjā* plant; and among the preparations of split pulses and the like, I am the alms begged by mendicants. (66)
I am in the inner sanctum of temples, at the gateways of palaces,
in the courtyards of villages, and in the halls of justice of cities.
I am in the *pippala* trees in the forests, at the thresholds of every house,
in the *tulasī*, in the sacred sites of the Vaiṣṇavas, and even in the forest of the Vaiṣṇavas.
I abide in sacred fords; I am present on earth and in the abodes of my devotees.
I am in all times, yet I am in the time of Brahmā, and I am in the evening rite of circumambulation and lamps.

I am in the lunar mansion of Jayantī and others; I am in the most excellent image for worship; I am in every friend; I am in every person; and I am in every scripture that contains my teachings. (4.25.70)
I am in the Dharma; I am in the holy life; I am in the one who has faith and the giver.
I am in front of the fortunate, but behind those of ill fortune.
I am below the sinful, but above the dwellers of heaven. (71)

Among those who offer themselves to me, I am the inner self within the body, senses, and mind; among the Brahmins, I am their speech; and among forms of illusion, I am that which consists of the quality of goodness (sattva-guṇa). ||72||
I am the fear of those who act unjustly, and I am the instruction for those who are to be disciplined;
I am the final determination of disputes, and I am entirely pervaded by the fruits [of action] in every way.
In this stream of similar beings and in the progressive sequence of the world of speech,
I dwell as non-dual Brahman, the distinguished and imperishable.
Therefore, I am the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the non-dual Brahman characterized by distinction;
whoever knows me as such, in my true form, O God who fulfills all desires, [attains the goal]. (79)
One who knows me does not perish; there is no doubt that such a person goes to liberation by regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa as their beloved, noble, and sovereign Lord Bālakṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nikāmadeva said:
O Lord of All, O Nārāyaṇa, how do you realize yourself as the distinguished non-dual Brahman? Tell me this in brief. (77)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said:
That which is the gross Māyā, consisting of all effects, is the specific attribute;
whereas the subtle Māyā, the state of equilibrium, is the triad of qualities (guṇatraya).
But distinct from those two insentient [elements] is the imperishable Brahman;
it exists as the inner abiding pervader, for both of those are indeed subordinate to the Imperishable.
The gross selves are characterized by being consumers of the fruits of all actions;
the subtle selves are characterized by being devoid of the fruits of action and the like.
Indeed, distinct from those two forms of consciousness is the imperishable Brahman;
it exists as the inner abiding, all-pervading reality, for both of those [consciousnesses] reside within that supreme imperishable.
That imperishable, however, is truly one alone, devoid of a second.
The divine abode called Brahmā belongs to the Supreme Self who is the Supreme Brahman; it is eternally known as Light, consisting of the splendor of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. 82.
That one [reality], however, is here distinguished fourfold by its qualifiers;
that is the abode of Brahman, the non-duality of the two distinct [aspects] with their respective qualifiers. (83)
O twice-born one, I have described to you my abode called Akṣara, which is qualified non-dualism;
it exists in all ways, at all times, within both insentient and sentient beings. (84)
The imperishable Brahman, endowed with all wonders, shines forth;
it shines resplendently there in that abode of the imperishable, which is indeed the distinguished non-duality.
I am indeed that very one—Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama—who is singular and devoid of any equal or superior. (86)
I am non-dual; there are never two supreme lords.
Therefore, I am the venerable Supreme Lord, the Non-dualism of the Distinct (Viśiṣṭādvaita). ||87||
Beyond the supreme Brahman and the imperishable, the soul of all who has reached the imperishable Brahman—the distinguished, non-dual imperishable Brahman—therein I abide alone. (88)
Brahman, which resides in all that is insentient and sentient, is considered superior to me;
and thus, O Brahmin, I am always the pervader of that which is pervasive. (89)
This reality has been told to you for the sake of knowing my true nature:
I am that very one, manifest everywhere—even within the imperishable and within the manifest splendor.
O best of the twice-born, the imperishable Brahman joined with me exists everywhere;
and the threefold creation exists within that imperishable, endowed with it as its qualification. 9.1.
There are imperishable syllables and there are also liberated ones, as well as other abodes;
and that abode is capable and likewise possesses form through my yoga.
He is also engaged in service to Mukteśvara, who resembles me; he attains similarity with me and is certainly the eternal support of all. 93.
This very person is the imperishable Puruṣa; he himself is the Brahma-Puruṣa.
That alone is the pervasive, divine, and ever-luminous stage. 94.
Therein, all objects of enjoyment that have manifested, as well as the instruments of enjoyment and all forms of prosperity, exist in every respect. (95)
Whatever their support, whatever their nourishment, and whatever their degree of prosperity—
even those who are liberated dwell indeed in the abode together with the liberated women.
Through perfect union with my form, there is the full, indivisible, imperishable, immutable, and eternal abode; indeed, dwelling therein is liberation.
"O Nikāmadeva, through my yoga you have gone to that imperishable state;
for where I am, there indeed exists that eternal, imperishable abode."
That land and all its riches exist here in me, the Lord;
for indeed, the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the imperishable abode are present right here. 99.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the Beloved of Śrī, resides in Akṣara; He shines here as the Lord of all, the husband of Your daughter.
Through my yoga, there is no liberation for you to attain;
here, direct association with me bestows liberation upon you in this imperishable state.
"Always you have been liberated from me; behold your own divine abode!
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led him to the imperishable realm (akṣara-pada).
He suddenly revealed Nikāmadevaka, who was liberated,
as well as Muktānikā, the divine and eternal queen of the gods.
Having shown Badrīpriyā, Bālayoginī, the virtuous Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, and Haripatnī, he vanished from sight.
O Badrikā, you are indeed that very same Bālayoginī who was there,
possessing the hue of a ruby and serving as the consort of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
On earth, that Māṇikī became the invincible mare Vāhā;
she was endowed with the power of Brahmā and possessed the nature of both Jayā and Lalitā.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Yoga Consisting of the Nature of the Supreme Brahman and the Discernment of the Supreme Brahman as the Essence of Viśiṣṭādvaita," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; thereafter, Anādinārāyaṇa spoke to that devotee Nikāmadeva concerning the fearless Yoga.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Nikāmadeva, to this supreme Nirbhīka-yoga (the yoga of fearlessness), by knowing which one has no fear of Māyā, Time, and other such karmic forces.
For one who meditates daily upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, there shall arise no fear regarding the enjoyment of the merit gained from rivers, gifts, sacred fords, or austerities. || 3 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, for him by whom all merits have indeed been placed in me,
that supreme, imperishable, and fearless abode is surely attained.
The worship of me through ritual action is always superior to all other actions;
likewise, my remembrance and approval utterly destroy fear in every way.
Even a slight attachment to illusion and sin here belongs to those great souls;
for such great souls, the remembrance of Hari constitutes their atonement.
By merely remembering me for a moment, one shall go to my abode;
how much more so for one who is constantly devoted and free from fear of association with others?
The knower of yoga stands beyond the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
that very yoga is the constant activity of the mind directed toward Me alone.
Whether walking, standing, breathing, speaking, entering, eating, or enjoying, one should remember me, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, in every way.
Even if one is engaged in all worldly activities, if one directs the mind toward me,
there is no defilement from enjoyments for that person who dwells amidst those enjoyments.
Memory is my supreme dharma; it is indeed meditation, austerity, and sacrifice.
It is all purity and the highest peace; everything is established in my remembrance.
That which is difficult to attain, supreme, far-reaching, beyond the range of perception, and imperishable—
even so, by my grace, it shall surely be attained by me, its rememberer.
Whatever deficiency there may be in hundreds of sacrifices, such as errors in ritual procedure and the like,
is rendered faultless and, on the contrary, complete by my remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"In this world, there is no purification for those who have committed evil deeds equal to mindfulness;
that mindfulness of mine both burns away all existences and bestows liberation. (14)
But for one whose practice of meditation has reached perfection, liberation occurs in this very birth;
my memory, like fire, consumes the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the rememberer.
When Hari is established in the self and established in the mind, all sins are indeed dissolved by themselves; thereafter, no fear exists.
Since I am present within the mind of the one who remembers me, quarrel, defilement, fault, passion, agitation, and decay shall not overcome his mental faculty.
The lunar day, the month, the moment, the astrological conjunction, the moon, the ascendant, and the auspicious day—all these are auspicious in every way only when Govinda is remembered therein. (18)
That is a wound, that is the supreme loss, and that is the ultimate calamity, in which moment Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is not meditated upon. (19)
The Kṛta Yuga belongs to him in whose heart Janārdana resides;
the Kali Yuga belongs to him in whose heart Janārdana does not reside.
In whose heart Govinda resides—in the front, the back, in front, above, below, all around, in the middle, or in a circle—he is indeed one who has accomplished his purpose. 21.

For one whose mind is fixed upon the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, whether in regard to the auspicious or the inauspicious, the great fruit is heaven, which is devoid of suffering, defects, and the like. (22)
Even one who does not renounce the life of a householder, if he always remembers me,
cuts through the illusion of human agency, for his actions are indeed offered unto me.
He in whose heart Hari dwells is patient toward offenders, endowed with compassion for the ignorant, and filled with joy toward the righteous. (24)
One should remember me, Nārāyaṇa, during acts of renunciation and enjoyment, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and especially even during evil deeds. (25)
Abiding in his heart, I constantly bestow upon him gain, victory, fame, and wealth, as well as peace and supreme bliss.
I am the bestower of liberation upon countless birds, trees, and animals;
what then need be said of those men who have taken refuge in me and remember my sovereignty? (27)
Why is the shade of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet not resorted to—a shade free from cold and heat, bestowing the state of immortality, and destroying the fear of Māyā? (28)
For him whose mind is fixed on me, his lord, there is no fear of a curse, nor likewise any fear of a king, nor even any fear of Yama.
Meditation, when accompanied by mindfulness, is always pure and supreme;
by it, even one who eats sin is never defiled in this world.

But he whose mind is directed toward Me, Hari, in the same way that it is directed toward sense objects, and who is likewise devoted to the virtuous in the company of the good—he is liberated here and grants liberation to others. 3.1.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, which takes up residence in the heart, rescues those richly endowed with association with those who associate with His associates from the ocean of sin. (32)
That is true knowledge where Śrī Hari is; that is the sacred narrative where Mādhava is;
that is virtuous action where I am present; and that is the true mind which is offered unto me.
That is the tongue which praises Hari; that is the skin which touches the Lord; those are the hands which embrace me; and that is the body which exists for my sake. (34)
The fruit of my head is prostration; here, the fruit of my hands is my worship of You.
The fruit of my mind is contemplation of You; the fruit of my speech is the praise of Your qualities. (31)
A heap of sins equal to Mount Meru is instantly destroyed by the remembrance of me;
and conduct, whether good or bad, when offered unto me, leaves no stain. (36)
Hari is the protector of the helpless; Hari is the strength of the weak;
Hari is the giver to those with desires; Hari is the refuge of all. (37)
O Brahmin, taking refuge here in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the supreme sacred site (tīrtha), which destroys illusion, time, karma, and the like. (38)
Whether he be a Śūdra, a leather-worker, or a Cāṇḍāla, if he is endowed with devotion to me, I consider him as purifying as a Brāhmaṇa; for he has attained union with me. (39)
If the panegyrists of the wealthy praise me in such a manner,
I shall first make them lords of wealth here and then release them from their bondage.
Just as fire, having completely pervaded a forest, burns both the dry and the moist,
so too, established within the heart, do I burn away latent impressions and the like.
Just as the lords of beasts do not resort to a great forest that is ablaze,
so too do pride and the other [afflictions] not resort to me while I am thus radiant.
To whatever extent my devotion and my trust are intense, one obtains the fruit accordingly; herein, my grace is especially distinguished. (43)
Embodied beings sink and perish, submerged in their children, wives, family, and so forth;
but if they indeed sink into me, they immediately cross over by my power.
I do not see liberation for him at any time in the future, by whom the gateway to liberation—the service of the virtuous—is closed. (45)
One should always worship me, the Supreme Self, both within the heart and externally;
one should meditate upon me, the all-pervading, embodied, beautiful Lord, the Beloved of Śrī. 46.
[Know me as] the Guru, the husband, the master, the beloved witness, the infallible one—Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. ||47||
O giver of honor, by meditating upon me in this manner, honoring me, and respecting me,
you will certainly attain, my dear son, my eternal and imperishable state.
Thus enlightened, the brahmin Nikāmadeva was filled with reverence;
having attained great joy, he spoke fearlessly to Sāma.
Dancing, singing, laughing, leaping about his body, and repeatedly making gestures,
he spoke fearlessly while singing the *sāman* through the power of divine possession.
I have taken refuge in Bālakṛṣṇa; what can Time do to me?
He is the Lord of the Imperishable, the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Brahmā, and the Supreme Person.
I have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord Adhokṣaja, who bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus; what can death do to me? (52)
I have taken refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the infallible Acyuta, born as Gopāla; what can Māyā do to me? (53)
I have taken refuge in Ādhava, who descends in all forms, who is served by all powers, and who is the son of Kambharā; what sin can it do to me? (54)
I have reached the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa, and the Aśvasaras lake; what deed will it perform for me? (55)
I have taken refuge in the Blessed One, the Narayana of all abodes, the beloved of Radha; what can thirst do to me? (56)
I have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Savior from Māyā, the Lord of Śrīmādhavī, and the Master of Māṇikī; what can my desire do to me? (57)
I have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord, the inner controller of all, the manifest master of the Bālayoginīs; what can delusion do to me? (58)
I have attained Hari, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of Liberation, the husband of Muktānikā, and the beloved Lord of Brahmā; what will worldly prosperity do for me? (59)
I have taken refuge in the Lord of lords, the husband of the Goddess of lords, the husband of the beloved of Hari, the master of masters; what can darkness do to me?
I have taken refuge in the Lord of Padmāvatī, the master of both the insentient and the sentient, the Lord of Lakṣmī; what can latent impressions do? (61)
I have taken refuge in the Lord of the virtuous—the child who is of one form, many forms, and indeed universal form; what can bondage do to me? (66)
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Salutations to the one who dwells in Akṣara, salutations to the resident of Goloka. 63.
Salutations to the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to the dweller of Śrīpura;
salutations to the beloved of Lalitā; salutations to You, the beloved of all. 64.
Salutation to you, the beloved of the youthful Yoginī, the beloved of Badarī;
salutation to you, Vāsudeva, the lord of all gods. ||65||
Salutations to the dweller in the nectar, salutations to the dweller in the unmanifest;
salutations to the dweller on Kailāsa, salutations to the dweller in Hiraṇyagarbha. ||66||
Homage to the one who is the consecrated abode of the Siddhas; homage to the one who dwells among the gods and others;
homage to the one who is the dwelling place of the ancestors; homage to the one who takes human form. ||67||
Salutation to the Abode of All; salutation to the Dweller within my own self;
salutation to the One residing in the heart of Sureśvarī; salutation to the one whose nature is infinite. ||68||
Salutations always to the one who dwells within the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the inner self;
salutations to you, O Supreme Bliss; salutations to you, who are filled with wisdom. 69.
Salutations to you, O Śrī Puruṣottama, bestower of knowledge and realization;
salutations to you, O Viṣṇu, creator of the universe; salutations to you, the cause of all. 4.26.70.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the cowherds and cowherdesses; salutations, O accomplisher of all aims!
Salutations to you, O bestower of grace; salutations to you, O Lord, giver of liberation. (71)

Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa! Victory to you, Viṣṇu! O Mādhava, giver of fearlessness to me! Victory to you, the peaceful one, the bliss of consciousness! O Keśava, the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss! 72.
Victory, O living one, victory-giver, victory to you, O Janārdana manifest!
Victory to you who have transcended the worship of seeds, the womb, and other such [rituals] prescribed in the scriptures and elsewhere! 73.
You are my guru, you are my father, brother, friend, kinsman, and mother;
you are my liberation, you are supreme bliss, and you are my all-in-all, O Acyuta. (74)
You are the savior and the protector; you are the leader and you are liberation.
The entire world shines forth as a manifestation of your form. ||75||
O Blessed One, you are the Supreme Brahman, difficult to be approached even by the gods and others;
yet you have been reached here by me through the power of the young Yoginī. (76)
Who knows you, O Lord of the self, who are attainable by the liberated, the highest beyond the high, that eternal Person, the ancient Supreme Being? ||77||
The great sages dwelling in heaven, though they have not reached the ultimate form,
worship your incarnate forms which are within their range of perception.
The incarnations worship you, the one who descends as a person;
the innumerable Nārāyaṇas worship you, the supreme refuge.
Those liberated ones who belong to Nārāyaṇa worship you as their supreme Lord;
the virtuous and liberated ones worship you, the true Lord, in all conditions. (4.26.80)
O Blessed One, due to my ignorance regarding the natural disposition of humans and other beings, you ought to forgive everything I have done that was not done for you. (8.1)
O Lord Hari, may my devotion to Your pair of feet remain unshakable in every state, everywhere, at all times, and in every way. (82)
May my affection for you alone be constant and eternal;
O bestower of the fruits of all desires, may my devotion to you be firm. (83)
What mortal is able to compose a hymn of praise for the Infinite One?
Nevertheless, O Lord, forgive these words of mine; homage be unto You! (84)
Through the yoga of the Supreme Person, fearlessness arises;
through your yoga, a person attains the state of the Supreme Person. (85)
The unfortunate becomes fortunate, and the wicked attains goodness;
even the luckless shall become blessed through this praise of yours, O Puruṣottama. (86)
Even those who are to be excluded from society, if they have come to you for refuge, all become possessed of virtuous character and are born as purifiers of the assembly. ||87||
Those who possess unwavering devotion for Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all—even if they perform the work of outcasts—they are the very best among the best of Brahmins. (88)
Even those who practice ritual purity, O Kṛṣṇa, are devoid of true detachment;
they all dwell in cremation grounds, filled with every kind of impurity.
Those who are devoted to your meditation and dedicated to your worship, they enjoy your grace; they are always eaters of the remains of the sacrificial feast.
Having constantly propitiated you, Śrī Hari, the bestower of all happiness, and having attained you, the Supreme Self, nothing remains to be desired. 9.1.
May that Kṛṣṇa, who is meditated upon by the virtuous, desired by the virtuous women, and drunk in by those who have attained yoga, abide within my heart. 92.
I worship with the flowers of my inner dispositions and offer the cupped hands of faith;
having offered myself as the sacrificial fee, I surrender to you, O Supreme Lord. (93)
Just as ghee residing within the bodies of cows does not provide them with strength, yet when it is extracted, combined with ritual action, and given to them, it bestows strength; so it is here. (94)
Likewise, although you reside within the hearts of men, you do not exist for their strength;
yet you alone, having emerged in person, abide as strength itself. 95.
O Kṛṣṇa, even without my propitiation, you have come under the sway of my compassion;
O Nārāyaṇa, O Acyuta, your manifest human form has been seen by me. (96)
And may you always manifest your divine form, if I am a worthy recipient here and if I am a vessel for your compassion. (97)
My status as a Brahmin has also gone; it has been surrendered to you alone.
If my state of liberation exists at all, it is because I am devoted to you in every respect. (98)
Thus entreated by the illustrious Badarīdevī, the Supreme Lord, out of mere grace, revealed his divine form to the Brahmin. 99.
It is established in the Imperishable, filled with countless incarnations,
and served by liberated beings, their consorts, and deities such as Kamalā.
Likewise, out of compassion, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa showed the eager Badarī, which is graced by the illustrious Bālāyoginī, to the seeker.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn and Other Matters Following the Attainment of Divine Knowledge by Nikāmadeva, After the Instruction on Fearless Yoga Given by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess Badarī, to this supreme and divine story of the wife of a yogin who was intent on his goal; it is also a bestower of liberation. || 1 ||
As soon as he beheld the divine Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Nikāmadeva suddenly became motionless in a divine state. || 2 ||
Just then, the virtuous Sureśvarī quickly arrived there for the purpose of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with auspicious lotuses.
Accompanied by a thousand lotuses grown in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
Satī arrived with sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, and flowers for the purpose of worshipping Kṛṣṇa.
She beheld her husband motionless, established in divine samādhi;
without speaking, she quickly [offered herself] to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus.
Having offered lotuses, sandalwood, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
and having offered all kinds of beautiful flowers to the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Just as she sat down before him in order to massage his feet,
the radiance emerged from the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, her beloved.
O Badrī, it pervaded the palace and then the courtyard;
dense and thick, it pervaded the expanse of the sky.
She became like the moon, bestowing sweetness, coolness, and what is desired;
then she became like lightning, and thereafter equal to the fire of heaven.
Then that fiery [form] became composed of the great elements in the sky;
it was suitable for the lords and accessible to the inhabitants of heaven.
From there she is accessible to Brahmā and the other gods; from there, she is to be beheld by the foremost of lords in the abode of Śrīpura, just like the splendor of light.
After that came the splendor of Vāsudeva, then the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, and finally the splendor of the Imperishable; that entire abode of the Imperishable became illuminated by those two.
Muktā, Muktānikā, Brahmapriyā, Haripriyā, Samastā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Lalitā, Jayā, and Ramā. (12)
The powers of Rādhā and Padmāvatī were beheld by those two,
as well as the groves, palaces, and auspicious temples within that abode.
There are various palaces, auspicious abodes of the liberated, and the primary temple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 15.
Thus the female companions and the male companions beheld him situated in the midst of many palaces, enriched with a thousand and one pitchers.
Gardens and monasteries were beheld, filled with divine enjoyments, and endowed with celestial and super-celestial beauty, sweetness, and brilliance. (17)
The male attendants and female attendants were beheld there by the two of them;
the wish-fulfilling trees, the trees of Brahmā, and the creepers of Brahmā were beheld. || 18 ||
In them, fruits and flowers are displayed with abundant splendor and sweet flavors;
they consist of an infinite array of enjoyments, accumulated through countless means.
Infinite male and female servants, infinite sovereign powers and riches, and liberated souls with bodies of eternal perfection were beheld. (4.27.20)
The Supreme Lord, residing in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, was beheld within His abode, served by liberated souls and their female companions.
Even Saurāṣṭra was beheld within the supreme abode of the divine syllable;
likewise the divine Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and the beautiful hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
And there, the divine abodes of the great sages were also beheld, possessing powers numbering in the hundreds of billions, trillions, and quadrillions.
There you are beheld by the beloveds of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
and there you, O Badarī, the beloved of the Lord, abide as Māṇikyā.
Then, in the all-beautiful palace of Kṛṣṇa, they beheld a divine elephant-throne,
endowed with every prosperity.
Then, O Badrī, the Supreme Person, the Ancient Being, the most excellent of men, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—divine, youthful, and exceedingly beautiful—was present there. (26)
The Lord had golden hair and a golden beard, was clad in golden garments, and possessed a brilliant luster; he was the embodiment of all beauty and was endowed with a gentle smile.
He is resplendent with two eyes as cool and vast as infinite moons;
from his lotus-like eyes, which are rich with the essence of love and bestow all bliss, he is born. ||28||
Adorned with a facial orb radiant with gentle smiles and rich fragrance, he reveals the awakening of the love for the exquisite sweetness residing in his reddened lips. ||29||
His teeth possess the splendor of excellent seed-pearls radiating white luster;
within his ruby-like tongue lies the wealth of the unmanifest state of Śrī’s form.
He is adorned with garlands of mandāra flowers and other blossoms hanging from his two well-developed shoulders;
his forearms are graced by the beauty of his arms joined together, and his wrists are enriched with jeweled chains.
In the palm of his right hand, he holds a fish, a trident, a bow, and a banner;
the entire surface of his chest shines with a row of moon-like nails. ||32||
His chest was adorned with lines from the Kaustubha gem spread across a series of jewel ornaments;
he was enriched by the splendor of golden garments and other finery, and graced by a girdle upon his waist.
He was resplendent with foot-ornaments jingling with tinkling bells,
and his feet were endowed with soft, golden sandals adorned with variegated auspicious designs.
His entire body, including the soles of his feet, bears all the marks such as the red lac-dye;
above his head shines the supreme parasol of the Supreme Lord. (35)
Even though the two auspicious chowries, held by Śrī and Lakṣmī, were small in size, there stood the virtuous Bālayoginī with a fan. (36)
To that Kṛṣṇa to whom Sureśvarī offers betel-leaf,
Nikāmadeva shines here as the staff-bearer of Śrīkṛṣṇa.
Thus was Śrī Kṛṣṇa, possessing a divine form, beheld by the two of them;
then, by His grace, they beheld Kṛṣṇa’s gardens and palaces. (38)
Having entered within, everything was indeed beheld by them; and infinite bliss and joy were gathered there by those two. (39)
Temples were constructed and divine splendors were bestowed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
those who were satisfied, those of eternal nature, and even those who were liberated were beheld by Him. 4.27.40.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa was beheld as the very embodiment of Dharma, and likewise the illustrious Kaṃbharā-Lakṣmī was beheld as the personification of Devotion. 41.
The young woman was satisfied, having beheld the power of Kṛṣṇa;
and having thus seen his grace and received it, the two of them then ate.
Satiated by the vision of Nārāyaṇa, they both arrived at Goloka;
the entire imperishable abode suddenly underwent dissolution.
In Goloka, that very Mādhava in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa himself—was beheld by them. ||44||
Holding his flute, accompanied by Rādhikā amidst the circles of gopīs,
he was seen delighting in the rāsa dance and gladdening the throngs of cowherds.
Devoted to the excellent service of cows and subsisting on food such as milk and curd, he beheld Kṛṣṇa, who is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||46||
Then, that Goloka was seen by them to have vanished, and at that very moment, Vaikuṇṭha was observed to have appeared. ||47||
There, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Lakṣmī, was beheld—served by countless attendants, the infinite, primordial Rāmaṇa. (48)
Then that great, indeterminate abode was beheld by those two;
therein, in that abode, dwelt Vāsudeva, served by Vāsudevyā and others.
Adorned with all powers, the Blessed One was indeed beheld by his brothers, Pradyumna and the others, in the abode of Śrīpura.
Served by Lalitāśrī Mahādevī and her infinite powers,
he is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, residing in that abode known as Amṛta.
For the Blessed One is the Infinite; he, the Lord of Kamalā, was beheld by him.
Thereafter, Sadāśiva was seen in the form of Kailāsa.
That very Blessed One, the golden Mahāviṣṇu, whose form is of gold, was beheld by those two within the abode of Hiraṇyagarbha.
And there in Vaikuṇṭha, he beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who assumes the form of Viṣṇu, accompanied by Padmā and Śrī.
Then, in the sun as well, that very Lord Nārāyaṇa was seen, golden-hued;
and in the fire, the Blessed One was seen assuming the form of fire.
That very Blessed One, the foremost among men, was perceived by those two as an ascetic at Badarikāśrama, and then as Śeṣaga in Śvetadvīpa.
That very Blessed One, the beloved of Lakṣmī, was beheld in the milk at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, assuming the forms of all his incarnations.
Then the Supreme Person, who is without beginning, was beheld by those two as being accompanied by Koṭyavatāra and endowed with Koṭikṛṣṇa.
Then that very Self, in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin),
was also beheld by Sureśvarī within her own heart and in the mind of Nikāmadeva.
In every limb of the complete image and within the bones of the young female yogini, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was beheld. (4.27.60)
Having thus displayed his own supreme divine majesty to them, the Lord Acyuta thereafter vanished from their sight.
That man, born suddenly on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara,
stood upon the earth there, having resolved to bathe;
he touched Nikāmadeva and Sureśvarī with both his hands.
At that time, those two became possessed of physical eyes, just like ordinary human beings.
Having fulfilled their desires and having attained the vision of the Self within all beings, the two fell prostrate and, with eyes filled with tears, offered praise to their Lord, the Master. (64)
O Kṛṣṇa, we have been purified by your compassion; we have been purified by the gift of your daughter.
O Kṛṣṇa, we have been protected by your presence and have also been liberated through your grace. (65)
We have achieved our purpose; nothing remains for us to seek.
You, the Supreme Lord, have been found by us here once again after a long time within this ocean of worldly existence.
Existence has gone, existence has passed away; fear indeed has gone to its end.
The realization of Brahman has arrived, and the bliss of Brahman has been fully attained.
Or else, send me right there where you yourself abide, O Great Imperishable;
or else, protect me right here at your feet, O Janārdana.
You are truly Brahmeshvara, the savior from birth and death;
since there is neither birth nor death for you, you are indeed the Savior (Tāraka).
O Blessed One, you are the soul of all; may you grant us our every desire.
Apart from you, the Supreme Self, nothing exists in the world.
Only by knowing you as the universal form and the supreme is one liberated;
by beholding you alone, who abide in all things, meditative absorption (samādhi) remains forever established.
He who gives up his life while meditating upon you indeed goes to the abode of Brahman;
having established you within the lotus of his own self, nothing remains to be attained.
Meditation that reveals Kṛṣṇa is the liberator from all bonds;
oh, how great is our supreme fortune that you have met us here! (73)
For fire is seen from churning; so are you [seen] from the surrender of all things.
May your compassion lead to our liberation, for there is indeed no other cause or path.
Hearing, reflection, meditation, knowledge, pilgrimage, austerity, and vows—these are not the causes of liberation here; rather, your grace alone is the cause in this matter. (75)
When all desires residing in the heart are surrendered unto you, the Lord, then the attainment of the state of immortality shall come to pass here through your grace. (76)
You are the all-knowing and all-seeing, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who acts as the lamp for the self;
having dissolved your own latent impressions (vāsanā), you lead [beings] to the imperishable abode.
Having uttered "Oṃ, obeisance to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," the two of them offered their salutations; at that moment, Śrī Bālayoginī appeared.
The virtuous woman arrived to offer the most excellent, well-sweetened, cool water fit for drinking to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 79.
Having known through her divine vision that her parents would soon be liberated,
she quickly approached Hari, who was not far away, and suddenly made him drink water.
That young yoginī offered the water of her faith to her parents;
meanwhile, they cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! (81).
Out of compassion for their lord and master, they spoke with divine voices, having been transformed in body by drinking the water of his grace. (82)
Possessing divine forms and radiant with splendor, and free from the abandonment of their portions,
they became liberated right there, as if they had reached their own abode.
Meanwhile, a magnificent celestial chariot appeared, adorned with the finest elephants,
graced by strings of pearls and gems, and resounded with shouts of victory and other joyful cries.
Illuminating the sky, the earth, and heaven according to the syllables [of his name],
he descended near the temple onto the grounds of the bridge.
With shouts of "Victory!", they worshipped their lord Harikṛṣṇa, the husband of Śrī and Lord of Ramā, with divine flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sandalwood, and other offerings. 86.
Descending from their celestial chariots, they took the nectar-like dust of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet upon their heads, placed it there, and drank the water.
While all the worlds were watching, those two boys, possessing divine bodies, were likewise held by the hand of Bālakṛṣṇa in a celestial chariot.
There, both Vipra and Sureśvara, along with Nikāmadeva, were seated; they were saluted by the daughter, Hariṇī, and Badarī. (89)
Having bowed down with a ruby and having also prostrated before the dark-complexioned kinsmen,
they both, after bowing to everyone, departed for the imperishable abode by means of a celestial chariot.
O Goddess, beloved of Badarī, it is a supreme wonder that millions of embodied beings have attained such a state, while their parents were united with the Supreme Self.
At that time, your parents were considered to have sent forth the imperishable abode;
those who shall hear this supreme narrative with the highest devotion [shall attain it]. ||2||
Or they will cause the worlds to hear it, and they shall attain the supreme goal;
indeed, service to Kṛṣṇa bestows liberation, and service to the virtuous also bestows liberation. 93.
A mantra wards off poison, and fire even removes cold;
yet these two are always faultless, for the mantra is Kṛṣṇa and the fire is indeed the True Being (Sat).

Liberation comes through association with the virtuous, just as it does from the yoga of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, liberation is attained, just as it is through the company of the saintly. ||95||
Through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, the divine nature of his form is manifested here;
indeed, even the attainment of all goals remains, and no other happiness is left. 96.
Through the practice of the *Bālayoginīgītā*, a woman becomes the wife of the Supreme Self, a maiden becomes his consort, and a man becomes his servant and attendant. (97)
Those with desires shall become abodes of prosperity; those free from desire shall attain liberation.
Those who have not attained perfection shall reach perfection, and even those who are bound shall attain freedom from bondage.
Even by merely hearing it, they are led to the state of Brahman; through honoring it, they attain the nature of Kṛṣṇa; and through profound meditation, they attain the state of the Supreme Lord. 99.
"O Badarī, they shall attain [this] in every way," so said Śrī Puruṣottama;
this is the song of Bālāyoginī, which bestows the excellent yoga of Bālakṛṣṇa.
One should constantly listen for the sake of liberation; one should go unto the Supreme Person; one should enjoy happiness in the state of Kṛṣṇa; and one should sleep upon the bed of Hari. 101.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa granted His vision—whose form is the abode of all abodes—to Nikāmadeva and his wife, and how He brought about the divine liberation of Nikāmadeva and his wife while they were still in their physical bodies," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the Supreme Soul, which brings liberation to the fisherman devotee who has sought refuge. 1.
There is a city named Jvālālaka on the bank of the Bhadrikā;
there dwells one born of the fisherman caste, known by the name Nigaḍabhrāma.
During the day, he made his dwelling near the Bhadrā river,
intent on the work of catching fish and striving to support his family.
Taking his net and going to Bhadrā’s pond,
he would always catch fish and return home in the evening, subsisting on fish.
Having sold the fish in excess, whatever wealth he obtained,
with that he would buy food, vegetables, leaves, and so forth, and support his children.
By that deed, he supported his sons, daughters, and wife;
then once, together with his wife, for the purpose of washing clothes— (6)
Accompanied by his net and his device for ensnaring [beasts], he went to the Bhadrā river;
standing on the bank, he cast his net into the deep waters.
Then his wife, intent on washing her garments,
was indeed washing the clothes there in that lake of pure water with those waters.
While she, intent on meditation upon her garment, was immersing the cloth in the water,
her husband caught his own husband, the fish, in a net.
Having seen [this] and suddenly heard the terrifying roar of the *timi*,
she beheld her husband bound by the net of the fishermen and obstructed by the *timinī*.
Being dragged along with the net containing many fish, she, having fallen into distress and being powerless to protect them, uttered a curse. (11)
Then, assuming a human voice and becoming extremely distressed, she said:
"O fisherman, may you never be released from the whirlpool of worldly existence."
May I repeatedly become a *timiṅgila* fish, swallowed by a *makara* and caught in the net of a fisherman, so that I may suffer here as I do from the loss of my husband. (1.3)
"Likewise, may your wife also always remain sorrowful.
Having spoken thus to the fish-wife, she wept, obstructed by her offspring.
Then, having heard that wonder from the fishermen, they saw within the water a female fish crying out for her husband, who was tormented by the net. (15)
But she, Matsyā, knowing thus within herself, uttered a curse;
then suddenly casting off her garment, she approached the presence of her husband. (16)
Having reflected upon the means for the fish's liberation, he placed the fishing line in his hand;
then, having released it from his master’s grasp, he slowly retrieved the net from the water.
Fearing the curse, she released the fish so that they might be unbound; by means of loosening the net, the fish escaped from the net. (18)
All of them, emerging from the net unhurt, entered the water, speaking cheerfully: "May you live for a hundred thousand years! (19)
She was always a devoted wife, dedicated to the service of her husband;
she was compassionate toward fish and avoided acts of violence and the like. (4.28.20)
"May the fisherwoman be ever joyful here through our protection";
having spoken thus, the fish and the others entered into the midst of the water. (21)
Then, having heard this, the fisherman was struck with great wonder;
though he was overcome by hunger, seeing his wife’s deed, he became filled with compassion.
He consented and released the net without effort on the bank;
he asked his wife, "What is this sudden pulling of the net? (23)
He then informed his wife of that curse uttered by the fish;
and the fisherman, having heard it, was seized with fear for his future births.
Day after day, seeing the endlessness of the sufferings born of the fish-womb,
he [felt compassion] for the female fish who had bestowed the curse and for the woman who had granted liberation.
At that moment, having cast away his net and set it ablaze in the fire, the fisherman offered words of praise, saying, "I have been liberated from sin. (26)
From that time on, he subsisted on fruits, roots, grains, and vegetables;
O Badrī, the company of holy men is a source of merit and bestows a favorable rebirth.
All these sages had become fish in that water at Bhadrā; there, the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [resided].
Having stayed many times upon the elephant, the great sages, driven by a longing for that sacred bathing place, became fish when he went there to bathe. (29)
But that great fish which was seized, as well as the other fish that were there, became the great seer Pipplāyana in the form of a fish. (4.28.30)
The twice-born one was like the Omniscient One, looking upward, and a treasury of all sciences;
his wife was Matsyā, who was named Pāṭhāyanī.
O Badrikā, other fish and such creatures in the water became knowers of the Vedas, O Brahmins; but that fisherman remained a sinner, bearing the punishment of the great seers.
A husband is rescued by a compassionate wife who understands the proper time;
one who creates bondage goes to hell, while one who severs bondage attains honor.
One who bestows the state of life and existence attains all the heavens;
however, one who causes fear surely falls even from heaven, the abode of happiness. (34)
Then the fisherwoman, having bowed, asked the fish in the water:
"Who are you? How have you become fish? And how is your speech so auspicious? (35)
"How can you explain this state of being in the form of a fish? O abodes of compassion, please tell us.
Thus urged, the brahmins replied, dispelling the delusion caused by their fetters: 36.
Here, the Lord Śrī Bhagavān Himself, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
mounted His elephant in order to wander from the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Hari comes to the forest of Rasālā, rests here upon this green sward, and bathes and sports on the bank of the Bhadrā in its excellent waters. (38)
In many ways, she was together with Śrī, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Priyā, and others, as well as with Mādhavī, Lalitā, Muktā, Jayā, and her attendant associates. ||39||
He delights in those waters with them; he enjoys their fruits and protects the water.
Devoted to compassion, he surely bestows his grace upon those who approach him. (4.28.40)
He bestows that grace upon the sages, the attendants, the aquatic creatures, and the beasts and birds; having obtained it, they proceed with great reverence.
Here Mādhava serves various kinds of sweet foods;
here the Lord celebrates festivals and bestows gifts.
For that purpose, O Brahmins, many who are wretched and servants dwell here in vain, desiring gifts and favors. (43)
And we brahmins also dwell here for the sake of the tigers alone—hundred auspicious householders with Pipaṭhāyana at our head. (44)
Behold, beneath these glorious mango trees there are hermitages;
nevertheless, forest-dwelling rākṣasas come here for the sake of water. (45)
Sometimes by night or even by day, wicked men who perform many cruel deeds harass the brahmins and strike them down in certain places. (46)
They carry off our women and seize our property; though we are capable of retaliating, we remain committed to non-violence. (47)
Through the power of obtaining the Lord and without affliction, we dwell here in various places within the waters, having become fish in the midst of the water. (48)
In some places, however, we wander through the mango groves of Surāṣṭra, appearing again and again as human beings, deer, or perfected sages.
Speak indeed, who are you here, and why do you cause harm? How is it that you bear such cruelty and violence even toward a human being?
This auspicious human body, which bestows both liberation and heaven, is difficult to obtain;
how then can you, as an agent of action, go to the hells through violence? (51)
Violence, theft, adultery, deceit, trickery, falsehood, slander, and the attribution of faults—these are the givers of rebirth in hell. (52)
Eating meat, drinking liquor, malice, impurity, causing distress, seizing the property of others, and anger—these are the givers of hells. 53.
Service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, granting supreme fearlessness, non-violence, eating only what is offered as grace, and refraining from criticism [are the marks of a devotee]. (54)
Benefiting others, giving gifts, purity, worship, beholding [the divine], association with the virtuous, and eating food and fruit—these are considered the bestowers of heaven. (55)
These [offerings] provide sustenance merely by their ownership, yet they are the givers of heavenly realms;
however, suffering arises from violence, and that sin leads to hell. (96)
The destruction of another's life for the sake of one's own belly is a pitiless act, even though there are fruits, tubers, and various kinds of food available. (57)
He who is a meat-eater goes to the supreme Raurava hell;
living beings must never be killed, for fruit that is fit to be eaten is what brings about purification.
Cow's milk should be properly consumed, but a cow must never be killed under any circumstances;
likewise, the fruit, flower, and leaf produced by trees and such should be eaten.
Trees should not be destroyed for the sake of fruit and such when they yield them naturally; likewise, the milk of a living mother should be drunk, but she herself must not be killed. (4.28.60)
Honey may be taken from flowers, but they must never be destroyed;
taxes may be taken from the subjects, but they must never be consumed [exploited] in every way.
Musk is to be obtained from deer, yet they are not considered to be slain;
in this same way, everything consists of enjoyment, for that which is a part of it is connected with enjoyment.
One should eat, but one must not kill; killing leads to hell.
Therefore, having become a non-violent person, do not go toward the hells.
"O fisherman, attain heaven; abandon violence and be happy.
Thus instructed, the fisherman bowed to the sages who were in the form of fish.
He begged them for forgiveness for his offense, seeking release from the curse;
this curse was like an arrow discharged by Queen Matsyikā. (65)
"O Sage, my heart is now trembling excessively;
please act in such a way that I may be released from this curse. (66)
Thus you entreated him and begged that again and again;
then, O Badrī, the brāhmaṇa Pipaṭhāyana, having shown compassion, [consented].
He said to me, "By your word, my curse has passed away into a state of powerlessness;
however, having received my word, go to Kuṅkumavāpikā. (68)
Where the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent,
perform your ablutions in the midst of the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake.
Behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as well;
perform His worship with leaves, flowers, and other offerings, and render service unto Him.
Receive from me here this purifying mantra of the Supreme Person:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāyasvāmine svāhā*. (71)
O Badrikā, having heard that counsel and received it from his preceptor, the sage,
that fisherman, together with his wife, undertook the observances (niyamas) and restraints (yamas).

Non-violence, service to the virtuous, non-stealing, living by the forest-dweller's way of life, subsisting on food consisting of bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, and frequenting sacred fords; ||73||
One should always perform devotion with a garland [reciting] "Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," and always perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Mādhavī.
He fully undertook the vow of associating with the virtuous, such as Lomaśa and others, as shown by Pipaṭhāyana,
and of granting fearlessness to all living beings.
Having honored his guru and his learned wife,
as well as all the other brahminical sages, he cast off his net on the riverbank.
Having drunk the water of Bhadrā, and having bowed down to the son of Pipaṭhāyana and received his words of blessing, he returned home together with his wife.
Having taken his son and others along with him, and having abandoned the city of Jvālālaka, Nigaḍabhrama went joyfully to Aśvapaṭṭasara. (78)
He established a sacred ford for the gods, performing their vision, bathing, and worship;
he also observed a fast and beheld Lomaśa.
He then performed the supreme worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
joined with the vision of his true nature, and thereafter offered salutations.
I have accomplished my purpose, O Blessed One, by the sight of your feet;
you, Nārāyaṇa, have bestowed upon me this human form. (8.1)

That which was intended for the sake of dharma has been led by me toward the sake of adharma; now, through attachment to the desire for study, I have attained awakening for the sake of liberation. (82)
I have come here for the sake of liberation from the curse of the fish;
O ocean of compassion, uplift me and set ablaze the mountain of my sins. 83.
"I am a fish-eater, a killer of fish; I have come to you for refuge," having said this, O Badrikā, he fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
His wife also, grasping the feet of Hari, kissed his big toe;
she drank the water from his feet and placed his cooling feet upon her breast. (85)
And she, filled with devotion, placed the dust upon her head; [so did] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [accept] that woman who was bound in chains. 86.
He manifested a divine form that caused even fetters to be mistaken for ornaments,
and out of sheer compassion, he instantly consumed all sins with his splendor.
With divine vision, even while in fetters,
he beheld that Supreme Lord as four-armed, accompanied by Kamalā.
On the bank of the Bhadrā river, amidst a circle of sages, he beheld Hari, the Lord of Śrī, who was Bālakṛṣṇa, sporting and delighting there. ||89||
Then, in the field of the Kuṅkumavāpī, within an abundance of splendor,
he beheld the Lord standing nearby in the presence of that man.
Having thus displayed his own form, he said to him who was deluded by the fetters:
"By means of the method of *pipaṭhāyana*, your suffering caused by Yama has departed. (91)
"By my yoga, go to the delusion of the fetters; [abide] in my imperishable syllable.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the son of Dharma, became silent. 92.
And Nigaḍabhrāmaka said: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self!
Just then, a celestial chariot belonging to the Supreme Lord arrived there.
Divine, attended by his retinue, and adorned entirely with golden ornaments—
both Nigaḍa and Naigaḍī indeed abandoned their material bodies.
Having obtained two other divine bodies, they ascended to Vaikuṇṭha,
the abode of Śrī Hari, and remained there until the end of the kalpa.
Then those two indeed attained the syllable and state of the Supreme Self;
thereafter, their sons and others performed the funeral rites for their parents there.
Having taken refuge in Bālakṛṣṇa, they became supreme Vaiṣṇavas;
those five sons of Hari always performed service for him.
Then, throughout their lives, the three daughters performed service to Hari;
they indeed became virtuous women and virtuous men, the most excellent among the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas). 98.
By name they were the virtuous Puṇḍarīkāsatī, Nirvāṇikāsatī, and the virtuous Ānandaghanikāsādhvī; these three took refuge in Nārāyaṇa. (99)
The five sons were Jñānadarbhi, Prabhādarbhi, Vidarbhika, Viṣṇudarbhi, and Kṛṣṇadarbhi; these were the most excellent among the Bhāgavatas.
There were divine holy men, ascetics, perfected ones, and yogis who, devoted to the service of their Lord, dwelt upon the grounds of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. 101.
O Badrikā, they too, purified by the majesty of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, attained supreme liberation from that place in due course of time.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fishermen's Liberation through Taking Refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and Their Release from the Delusion of the Iron Chain, by means of the Sage Pipaṭhāyana on the Bhadrā River," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Badarī, O Māṇikyā, O dear Mādhavī,
to this story of an ungrateful woman which brings about liberation.
In a city within the region of Saurāṣṭra,
there lived one night a woman named Kuthalī, who was wretched and born of a low caste.
Alone, wretched, young, and indeed helpless, she was afflicted with pain;
from her childhood, her mother, father, kinsmen, and protectors had all died.
Until she reached the age of five, she was a protector of the dead;
then she was nourished and raised in the house by her preceptor among the Sagaras.
Having reached her twelfth year, she recognized her own mother Sāgarī;
because she did not recognize the Brahmin woman, her affection for the Brahmin lady came to an end.
She who is the mother and the bearer of the child is alone the vessel of natural affection;
any other, however, possesses only artificial affection, and in that regard, there is truly no love for a daughter.

The affection a daughter-in-law has for her mother-in-law is not like that which she has for her own mother; nor is the affection one has for one's biological mother like that which one has for the woman who gives her breast milk. (7)
Just as there is affection for one who carries a child in the womb, there is not such affection for her co-wife;
and just as there is affection for a teacher in this world, the affection for a father is even greater than that.
Indeed, affection born of dharma is always secondary to affection born of blood;
however, in times of calamity, that which arises from blood is truly superior to that born of dharma.
Kuthalī, the daughter of Sāgara, through her perception of duality toward the Brahmin women, conducted herself there in service and other duties according to their command. (4.29.10)
For just as she engages in all activities with a deluded mind, she does not perform her household duties, such as fetching water and so forth. (11)

Having risen early in the morning, the Brahmin woman, full of eagerness, performed the sweeping, bathing, the spreading of beds, and the turning of the grinding stone after having eaten what was given [to her].
Devoted to play, she goes to the houses of the Sāgaras;
she is dejected in the house of a Brahmin, yet full of joy in the presence of the Sāgara.
Thus, being exhorted by the women of the Sāgara clan, she became known as Sāgarī.
If she desires to become Sāgarī there, she should quickly marry. || 14 ||
She did not recognize the benefit bestowed upon her by the Guru;
though nurtured from childhood with all manner of gifts, she was never aware of it.
He did not even count those two brahmins as equal to his own parents,
nor did he consider the seven years of nourishment they had provided him.
Whether due to lack of understanding, by her very nature, or because of her childishness, she has become ungrateful, even though she was united with Sāgara. (17)
O Badrikā, the destruction of those who have already attained their gains leads to hell;
likewise, the destruction of those who have performed meritorious deeds is the destruction of merit and leads to the loss of heaven. (18)
The residence of a maiden in the house of her preceptor yields the fruit of ten thousand births;
for one born of another womb, the status of being led by a Brahmin is indeed difficult to attain. (19)
Thus, that [state] became easily attainable for her; nevertheless, impelled by karma, she abandoned her status as a brahmin woman and set her mind upon becoming Sāgarī. (4.29.20)
Then the teacher’s wife instructed his daughter for the sake of peace:
"O daughter, this cycle of karma and worldly existence is nourished by the root of false notions. (21)

It feeds upon sense objects and the like, is watered by the waters of joy and delight, possesses branches such as dharma and adharma, and has leaves and sprouts consisting of craving and the like. ||22||

Richly adorned with the sprouts of desire for enjoyments and yielding the fruits of pleasure and pain, embodied beings are drawn into this [world] by the flowers of passion, hatred, and the like. (23)
The Self, though free from defects, attains the state of being a tree through association;
bound by latent impressions (vāsanā), it becomes a transmigrating being and is therefore said to be subject to suffering.
In childhood, the self is free from defects and stainless, the lord of the senses;
in youth, it becomes the very repository of all defects, defiled, and a slave to the senses. (25)
Whether they be girls or boys, bound by an intense attachment to the taste of the tongue, or young women or even young men, whoever indulges in these impetuous acts at night— (26)
That momentum which has been conquered by which those two become partakers of liberation—
that great liberation is eternal bliss in the abode of the Supreme Lord.
O two maidens, through association with the virtuous and by means of yoga centered on Nārāyaṇa, liberation from saṃsāra occurs; however, hell results from association with others. (28)
The body, matured in the womb and repeatedly refined in childhood, becomes defiled in youth like filth, with the impurities of the senses becoming excessive. (29)
If, through impetuosity, desire, or an exceedingly forceful latent impression, she becomes infatuated with another's body—that is, a human body—she perishes. (4.29.30)
A daughter is considered by the wise to be an object of affection for her parents, just like a son;
she who abandons them and goes to another would be ungrateful in this world. (3.1)
A maiden who is not being given away in marriage ought not to go of her own accord;
having become a bride, she who is sent forth according to dharma goes to her beloved.
Abandoning us, your two Brahmin supporters, you always go to another house;
today is not your time for such conduct, so do not go without our permission.
For young maidens, long residence in another's house is fraught with danger;
through flirtatious gestures and union with men, the destruction of their moral boundaries may occur.
A maiden who is deprived of marriage will undoubtedly suffer ruin.
O Brāhmaṇa, you have been a Sāgarī since birth, even while in the house of a Brāhmaṇa woman. (35)
O maiden, you are indeed a purifier like one who has attained the fruit [of her life], for you are a goddess upon the earth;
your body has become stainless through the act of nourishing the Brahmins.
"O daughter of the ocean, abandon your devotion to the Brahmins and do not go;
if you depart, O daughter, leaving me, a Brahmin woman, behind. (37)
"Having incurred the state of being a betrayer of trust, you will then fall; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus by the Brahmin’s wife, the girl questioned her mother. (38)
"Tell me truly, what are those ungrateful mothers like?
Now, that mother was the wife of a brahmin, and she was indeed named Ātmaśemuṣī. (39)
He said to his daughter: "She who destroys what has been done is indeed ungrateful.
Listen, daughter, for women here, as well as men, become even so. (4.29.40)
On account of that sin, after death, they experience the hells—those girls nurtured by their mothers who do not serve their own mother. (41)
She who is ungrateful is the first [type of] mother; she who causes suffering to her mother is the second.
Furthermore, even a daughter who, though nourished, is perverse and antagonistic [is likewise]. (42)
She who, having performed her duties for the family, speaks of its faults, is ungrateful; she who reveals the household's secrets to outsiders brings suffering thereby. (43)
She is always called ungrateful, a destroyer of the fame of her family members—she who, having reached youth, goes to another's house without permission. (44)
She who, having abandoned the prescribed rite, chooses for herself a *svayaṃvara*, is independent in her own dwelling, ungrateful, and a destroyer of her family. (45)
If she should cause suffering to her parents, being defiled by ingratitude, and having abandoned her domestic duties, she becomes intent upon the affairs of others. (46)
She too protects the household affairs for the sake of her elders;
yet, though she has become a daughter-in-law, that proud woman does not perform service to her husband. 47.
Such a woman who is ungrateful, who causes distress to her mother-in-law, who gives pain to her co-wife, and who is antagonistic toward the household—[is to be avoided]. (48)
Always quarreling with her husband, she brings distress to the household; ungrateful and ever-wakeful, she is indifferent toward domestic duties. (49)

That mother-in-law who never shows affection toward her daughter-in-law or her servant, that aged woman is a source of misery to her daughter-in-law; she is ungrateful and merely a ruler of the household. (4.29.50)
She who shows partiality toward fools, especially regarding food and other such matters, is unrighteous, ungrateful, and devoid of knowledge. (51)
She who disregards a favor received or assistance rendered and transgresses against her benefactor, speaking of faults with hostility—that woman is always considered ungrateful. ||52||
But if, though nourished, satisfied, and protected, she abandons her protector and goes elsewhere like a beast, she is always considered ungrateful. (53)
She who suddenly casts into calamity that man by whom her prosperity was brought about through instruction, food, wealth, and shelter—that woman is ungrateful. (54)
She who casts her teacher, god, protector, father, mother,
or husband into calamities is proclaimed to be ungrateful.
She who speaks of a wrong done to her and never of a favor received—that ungrateful woman, a destroyer of kindness, goes to the hells, O passionate one. (56)
Even for one who is the destroyer of calamity, that [calamity] does not provide assistance when it has occurred;
on the contrary, it always leads to what is undesirable and is considered ungrateful. (57)
The human body has been bestowed by the Supreme Lord for the attainment of liberation;
yet, having utterly forgotten that Supreme Lord, one behaves like an ungrateful person. (58)

She who does not recognize the virtues of either the man by whom a marriage was arranged or the man by whom she was wedded, but instead points out their faults, is a "Kṛtadhnikā" (a woman who ruins what has been done).
Whether she has been taught, instructed, or even initiated by him,
that ungrateful woman, being antagonistic, does not recognize his virtue at all.
A human body exists for the sake of Dharma; she who does not know Dharma at all, but instead meditates on the pursuit of unrighteousness, is indeed ungrateful toward Dharma.
She who is intent on harming those who are considered worthy of providing assistance in the pursuit of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation is always ungrateful.
For the ungrateful, there are indeed hells that always bestow suffering;
even in the world of Yama and in the hereafter, everything belonging to them is destroyed. (63)
The ungrateful one, a mountain of sin, finds no happiness anywhere;
the grateful one attains merit, heaven, happiness, and great festivals. (64)
The maiden, woman, elder, or even man who recognizes a favor done and returns that kindness shall become an inhabitant of heaven.
In this [place], one shines with an extensive lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth;
one prospers with wealth, grain, clothing, riches, gold, and other such assets. (66)
Everything belonging to an ungrateful person indeed goes to destruction along with its very roots;
O daughter, may you not be ungrateful, and may you not go to the hells.
"Having become a source of contentment for me, may she increase my great prosperity, as well as my fame and the growth of my lineage; and thereafter, even in heaven, she shall be superior. (68)
Thus addressed, the maiden Kuthalī Sāgarī, due to the defect of her seed, did not heed her mother’s words—she who perceived no evil [in her own conduct]. (69)
He perceived no fault therein, nor in abandoning it for another refuge; for, due to the influence of his innate flaw, he disregarded those words.
There, her mind being deluded, she gave this reply to her mother:
"O Mother, all forms of ingratitude have been heard by me from your own mouth. (71)
What self-interest do you have here in me, who am like the ocean—a woman of divided loyalties, born of a different caste, and a woman whose conduct and other traits are alien? (72)
"O monk, my livelihood is not in a householder's home, nor am I a female mendicant.
I am of the lineage of Sagara; I shall reach some ocean. (73)
In this matter, there is no better course for me than to serve the Brahmin master;
furthermore, according to dharma, all these young girls who are without protectors must be supported by him. (74)
This principle has been established in every respect by the elders, like the non-returning of a gift:
that which constitutes a benefit for the ignorant is said to be one's duty. (79)
In this matter, there is no ingratitude; the maiden and the wealth are for the sake of another.
O Mother, grant me forgiveness here, for I am departing to my own birthplace. (76)
"O monk, I shall never go to the Brahmin who is surrounded by water.
Having spoken thus, he bowed to his mother and disregarded her words. (77)
On the contrary, having offered criticism, he protected the wife of a Brahmin; for to protect the wife of one who is not a Brahmin while criticizing the wife of a Brahmin is indeed a fault. ||78||
Or rather, a virtuous man should perform a service for others free from the sense of "mine-ness"; yet you have developed this persistent attachment toward me as if I were your own daughter. (79)
"How indeed, O virtuous one, can this humiliation be inflicted upon me, who am worthy of honor—is it in the earth, or in water, or in fire, or in wind? (4.29.80)
They find rest in their own respective essences, and not elsewhere;
likewise, I, the daughter of the ocean, attain peace within the ocean. (81)
"I am going to the ocean; give me my lineage, or do not give me [back]!
Having spoken thus, O Badarī, she bowed to his intellect. (82)
Having completely abandoned Kuthalī, she went of her own accord and took refuge in the house of a virtuous Brahmin, which was like the ocean of the passionate (rājasa) temperament. 83.
She was addressed by the Brahmin woman as "ungrateful one," for she had abandoned her foster-mother and gone elsewhere of her own accord. (84)
Consequently, that maiden incurred the great fault of ingratitude;
nevertheless, she always ate the food provided by divine grace in the house of the Brahmin. (85)
Indeed, through her service such as the worship of the gods, she became possessed of great merit;
by the power of that merit, Kuthalī attained youth. (86)
Then, by the king named Virāmin, that city of Vibhāvarī was handed over to his own servant, Sagara, as she was left without a protector.
She was married by Sagara, whose name was Dharmakara;
she became devoted to the service of the queen, honored, and possessed of excellent enjoyments. (88)
Abiding in the house of the performance of dharma, she rejoiced in the abundance of enjoyments;
for many years, she experienced those pleasures fashioned by her merit. (89)
She had twenty sons and seven daughters;
she was a tree of merit, yet within her was a tree of evil. (4.29.90)
Having attained the state of ingratitude, she was reborn as a Brahmin woman;
once, however, she became afflicted by illness, tormented by cold and fevers. (91)
Afflicted by that, she wept for over a month, being unable to eat; her sons, her husband, and the members of his household performed healing rites for her. (92)
Nevertheless, the fever did not subside, nor did she find comfort;
then consumption (rājayakṣmā) arose in her, bringing about the destruction of everything.
There he remembered his virtuous mother, the Brāhmaṇī who had nourished him;
he recalled her words and that ingratitude, and how its fruit had now come upon him. (94)
That which is to be experienced will be experienced in due time; it does not fail to come to pass.
Yet she [the body] is shunned from afar by sons, daughters, and others out of fear.
Out of fear of consumption (rājayakṣman), no others ever approached her side;
thus she was afflicted by consumption for ten years.
She reaped the fruit of her ingratitude and found no end to it;
fallen upon her bed, she remained there, for she became like a bird in a cage.
Then, her hopes having vanished, she spoke thus to her eldest son:
"Tell me how my liberation may come about, and how my death may occur. (98)
"Act accordingly for my sake to prevent [your] ingratitude;
let her son go quickly toward the hermitage of Lomaśa. (99)
He entreated that most excellent great seer for deliverance,
or rather, that there might arise within him the power of his own self over the disease of the body.
Lomaśa, acting for his welfare, spoke these sin-destroying words out of compassion to his eldest son, who was named Tiraścāyana.
"Take the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and give it to his mother immediately;
likewise, having bathed in the waters of Aśvapaṭṭa, offer the water from that sacred site."
And bestow the auspicious water from the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, which destroys diseases, including the disease of worldly existence. 103.
Having spoken thus, he compassionately bestowed the sin-destroying mantra:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (104)
Having received the mantra and gone to the lake, he bathed and took the auspicious water of the sacred ford;
then, having obtained the water from the feet of the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he held it.
Having received a rosary from Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa for the purpose of chanting "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," he went toward his mother. (106)
The divine water offered to her mother, the mantra, and the sacred ash— by these,
that Kuthalī was instantly cleansed of all her sins at nightfall.
Her affliction was destroyed; however, the consumption (rājayakṣmā) emerged from her body in embodied form, together with that ungrateful woman.
Having laughed, he departed quickly toward the Barburāraṇyaka forest;
Kuthalī, freed from disease, dissolved into meditative absorption (samādhi).
There he beheld the Lord of gods, the Sovereign Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the divine Bālakṛṣṇa standing nearby, the husband of Rādhā and Ramā.
She bowed with a sense of extreme devotion and fell at Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
established in deep meditative absorption, she kissed Kṛṣṇa’s feet many times.
The sin of your ingratitude has been removed by my compassion;
you are now at ease. Devote yourself to Govinda and, at the end of this body, go to the Imperishable.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa departed; she, composed in mind, came outside.
Rising up, she reported the entire account to her sons and others.
Then all those around became devotees of Anādikṛṣṇa;
Kuthalī lived for a hundred thousand years and attained liberation.
Thus, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa brought about the destruction of the sins and the liberation of this ungrateful woman. 1.15.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rearing of Kuthalīsāgarī—whose father and kinsmen had died—by a Brahmin in the city of Vibhāvarī; her becoming the wife of Sāgara due to the fault of ingratitude committed independently; the fruit of ingratitude being consumption (rājayakṣmā); the destruction of that disease through taking refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; and her final liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 29 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the woman Pratāriṇī;
through union with Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, she indeed attained the path of liberation.
In the village of Dhavalāra in Saurāṣṭra, which was crowded with leather-workers,
there lived a woman named Viṣalāṇī, who was devoted to deception.
Though accompanied by sons and grandsons, she is one who has exerted herself in deception;
she is renowned as a knower of all forms of fraud and a deceiver.
Just as there is no other on earth so deceptive and poisonous,
she indeed deceives everyone by means of her artifice and guile.
Every day in the city, all the women were terrified of Viṣalāṇī; she was especially feared whenever she went to anyone's house.
In whatever way possible— through smiles, conversation, speech,
the giving of feigned wealth, and other such means that create the illusion of truth— (6)
By means of various objects, obstructions to vision, deceptive views, delusions, bewildering diversions, transgressions, and likewise by exchanges; (7)
By means of taking and giving back, he constantly deceives;
indeed, many who place their trust therein fall victim to his deception.
For she naturally understands the art known as deception;
