wherever she goes in a house, she deceives the mistress of that house.
Just as a virtuous wife sets out taking her gains in secret,
so too does the mistress of the house suspect her when there is a loss of property or a failure to obtain goods.
"In this way, the object shall be taken from my house by means of deception";
thus was she, intent on trickery, judged by the village folk. (11)
Though she knows only the ways of deception, she captivates all through her cleverness;
yet, being possessed of the fault of deceit, she is indeed a fit object for punishment.
Nevertheless, the king,
with a portion [of his wealth], approved of the performances of wrestlers and actors who assume many forms.
Having entered the midst of the arena, he indeed deceives them as well;
they surely suffer defeat and do not attain victory at all. (14)
Deceiving [her husband] by means of gifts of rewards and the like, she who was thus devoted to deception once went outside the house. (15)
As she went, she beheld a great circle of holy men;
there were a hundred such sages and saintly women who have realized the state of Nirvana.
They established her residence at the edge of the city gate and the edge of the rampart in that village.
Then, all the villagers gathered together for a meal of pure food.
They gave cakes, pearls, milk-puddings, and *prapolikās*;
they gave chickpeas, excellent vegetables, and a most excellent meal.
Having seen that excellent food, all the virtuous ones ate;
but the deceiver, intent on tasting the flavors, thought thus in her heart: (19)
By what means can sweet food be obtained? I shall eat it as well, in such a way that neither the villagers nor the virtuous people may know of it. (4.30.20)
"Having practiced deception here and eaten my fill, I shall go to my own home.
Then she bound her hair into a single mass and made it into a matted lock (jaṭā). 21.
Then he made his own matted hair and body rich with ashes;
having put on saffron-colored robes, he also held a trident in his hand.
Having become a perfected yoginī, she entered the circle of the sādhu-s;
when the sādhu-s had finished eating, she took her place in the row of the sādhu-s. (23)
She sat there in such a way that she could not be seen by others;
having eaten and drunk until she was satisfied, she rose slowly and departed.
Indeed, she was not recognized by the virtuous women as one esteemed for her goodness; nor was this village yoginī questioned or even suspected by anyone. (25)
Deformed by the villagers, she was not perceived as she truly was;
thus, having assumed a deceptive guise, she enjoyed the offering of hospitality. (26)
Having gone home and again assumed her own dress, she slept happily;
in this manner, having eaten for five days, she passed her time daily.
She returns to her own home, yet people do not know her true nature;
for she has partaken of the grace of Kṛṣṇa, which is the very essence of the virtuous man and the virtuous woman. 28.
The water born of his grace is the purifier of all sins and a cleanser;
likewise, food, leaves, or fruit [offered to him] bestows eternal liberation. (29)
There are many evildoers; because of their evil deeds they become hungry ghosts (pretas), and having entered lower wombs, they are born as eaters of carrion.
One who eats only the remnants of offerings (vighasāśī) is always liberated from heaps of sins;
for union with Hari, union with the virtuous, and union with a chaste woman are indeed difficult to attain.
The company of the virtuous is extremely difficult to find; if it should be met, liberation is swift.
Great sins are destroyed by the grace [of the teacher] and by partaking of food [from him]. 32.
Through the grace of Śrī, the precipices of deceit and other evils are consumed;
the self is suddenly purified and becomes fit for liberation. (33)
Śrī Badrī Rāmā said: O Keśava, tell me of that act of deception, whether it be of many kinds or even concealed, by which one comes to dwell in hell. (34)
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; there are indeed many kinds of deceptions by which a person who commits the sin of cheating goes to the hells. (35)
Having obtained a body created by the Supreme Lord, one should perform service to the Supreme Lord with that body; Mādhava was not deceived by him [who does so]. ||36||
Having obtained this body which grants self-liberation and serves as the means for achieving the goal of liberation,
he by whom it has not been utilized has indeed deceived his own self.
If one who is devoted to the crane (Baka) should [attend] the circles and other assemblies of holy men, yogis, and virtuous women, then those holy ones and others have been deceived by him. (38)
That man who teaches the renunciation of wealth, women, and worldly attachments, yet causes others to give up these things only to enjoy them himself—that is a great deception. (39)
Having inspired confidence and displayed various gains, and having created an appearance of affection, he causes [the victim] to act and thus carries off their wealth; such is deception. (4.30.40)
Whether it be a child, a woman, a girl, a youth, a wealthy man, a young woman, or even a mere object—wherever such deception takes place, [it is theft]. (41)
Both types of objects are similar: one of little value and one of great value.
By giving away that of little value and taking back that of great value, one commits deception. //42//
Having caused a task to be completed, he who subsequently neither gives the fruit of his effort nor even acknowledges it, but rather diminishes it—that indeed is deception. (43)
Having obtained gain through action, mind, or speech, he who does not subsequently carry out what ought to be done is a deceiver; indeed, such a person is a "luñcaka. (44)
If one possesses wealth yet does not perform religious duties, does not give, and does not enjoy it oneself—that is indeed a deception regarding wealth that leads to rebirth in hell. (45)
Having become a renunciant, he enjoys the pleasures of householders and gives them away;
he who establishes the lineage of householders is one by whom worldly existence has been deceived. (46)

If one who has inspired faith in the world through devotion should fall under the control of the senses, that devotion—though it brings about liberation—is deceived by him and becomes the cause of hells. 47.
He who, having performed malevolent rites and the like, brings another under his own control, enjoys that which was brought under his power; by him, Dharma has been deceived. (48)
Whatever tasks there may be, however many, and however very firm they may be,
their ordainer is likewise not one who acts with mere superficiality.
One who fails to complete his tasks, one who employs inferior materials, and one who is full of greed for secret gains is a deceiver who follows the path to hell. (4.30.50)
But he who, on an auspicious day, employs oil, water, buttermilk, or milk in place of ghee— being a deceiver— he goes to hell.
One who, having shown a female elephant to an elephant at a certain place, causes it to fall into a pit, is considered a deceiver by virtue of that act. ||52||
Having displayed a beautiful young maiden in the pavilion, he who abandons her and gives another instead is a deceiver who goes to hell. (53)
That swindler who pours water into milk for the sake of selling it as juice, or who puts pebbles into food, dust into flour, or powder into dough, is a deceiver. (54)
In the work of crafts, in artistic works, in the construction of palaces, in bridges, in great gardens, in cities and the like, in mechanical paths, and on great highways; ||55||
Having obtained abundant wealth from a field, a well, a pond, or similar sources, one spends half of it all upon that which is likewise unstable. (56)
Deceit, which is weak and full of treachery, leads to hell;
it is like the nature of crows, jackals, and monkeys.
A person living in this world is indeed full of deceptions regarding their vision, meditation, intellect, attentiveness, and resolve. (58)
He who, having displaced [the wealth] from those [two], takes it away, consumes it, or wins it for himself, or ordains other undesirable things, is a deceiver destined for hell. (59)
The outward appearance should be made like an elephant's tusk;
however, the interior is something else for the purpose of chewing, serving one's own purpose just like the tusk itself. (4.30.60)
Harming others, seeking to injure them, and deceit lead to hell;
indeed, all such acts as these constitute forms of deception.
He who, having become a disciple, does not perform service for his guru with sincerity commits a great sin that leads to hell; indeed, it is a deception. (62)
When she who has become a wife does not perform service for her husband at all, and he who has become a husband does not protect his virtuous wife at all, that is indeed deception. (63)
A servant indeed does not perform the master's work through deception;
those who give poison, set fire, or provide destructive mixtures are truly deceivers.
All those who delight in thievery, who are deceivers, and who go to hell—their deliverance occurs through association with the virtuous. (65)
Having become Indra, he indeed deceived Ahalyā by appearing as Gautama;
likewise, having become Jālandhara in the past, I deceived Vṛndā.
O Badrī, such deception is indeed considered to be a giver of suffering;
from it there may arise a curse, or even misery, or even hell itself. (67)
Although I am the creator of all, the lord of all, the supreme sovereign, faultless, pure, the purifier of *māyā*, and the bestower of liberation upon all; ||68||
For the sake of the work of the gods, for the sake of my devotees, or sometimes even through deception, I act for the purpose of destroying the Daityas; no fault whatsoever exists in me. (69)
In that state, the fault of living beings experiencing their karma arises;
thus has that deception been described, and it perishes through association with the virtuous.
O Badrī, the company of the virtuous is purifying and destructive of sin;
even a venomous serpent becomes free from evil through association with the good. (71)
By eating the remnants of what has been offered to the virtuous, the evil committed by the body is destroyed;
through contact with the virtuous and other such associations, the sin of the senses is destroyed. (72)
Through the devotion of service to the virtuous, the mind's sin is destroyed;
by offering oneself to the virtuous, all the sins of the living being are destroyed. (73)
I am the saintly one, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa Mādhava is the saintly one;
Mādhavīśa himself is the saintly one—the Lord, the Master, and the protector of the virtuous. ||74||
Thus, by means of that food within the assembly of the virtuous, she became free from sin and purified; thereafter, discernment arose within her. (75)
Alas! I am a deceiver and a perpetrator of evil in every way;
for even in that place where all evils are destroyed, I remain intent on deception. (76)
What is the use of this petty act of deception performed for the sake of food?
Today, and for all time thereafter, I shall perform the work of liberation. //77//
Having performed service to the virtuous and service to the chaste, which destroys all offenses,
and having offered salutations to the holy ones, I shall indeed attain liberation and the supreme state.
Having reflected thus, she suddenly obtained wealth and garments and went to the residence of the virtuous; there she gave that wealth and clothing to them.
She gave him food and massaged his feet;
having drunk the water from the feet of the virtuous, she became satisfied and applied the sacred dust [to her head]. (4.30.80)
Resting upon her head, her body, and her chest, Śrī Hari spoke there to the most excellent guru, Bhadrāyana.
O true Guru, act for me in such a way that I may attain liberation, through which the sin of deception is utterly destroyed, and so that there shall be no further rebirth for me. (82)
Having heard this, the virtuous Bhadrāyana, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, spoke:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (83)
O virtuous lady, always recite the mantra while wearing saffron-colored garments, with matted hair and smeared with ashes, being solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (84)
Go by those [paths] to Śrī-kuṅkuma-vāpī, where the Lord Śrī-Kṛṣṇa resides—the Blessed One who shines forth as the manifest Master, the inner witness of all. ||85||

It is the place where the Incarnate Lord, the Master of the Imperishable (Akṣareśa), resides, where the sage Lomaśa dwells, and where the supremely purifying holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara is located. 86.
Where there are sacred fords and numerous great seers,
as well as virtuous women and virtuous men, both the liberated and those striving for liberation.
Śrī, Rādhā, Māṇikī, Kṛṣṇā, Ramā, Bhū, Kamalā, and others—numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions—are the wives of Nārāyaṇa. (88)
O goddesses, O divine ladies, O yoginīs, go there indeed;
there you shall obtain both enjoyment and liberation, as well as the destruction of your sins. (89)
"Even though here, through service to the virtuous, the destruction of your sin has occurred and your purification has been attained, do not give way to grief. (4.30.90)
Nevertheless, having found Kṛṣṇakānta on this earth, become one who rests in happiness;
becoming divine, go to liberation—do not delay, O Viṣalāṇikā! (91)
Having been addressed thus, O Badarī, that Viṣalāṇī immediately set out on foot along the paths and went to Lake Aśvasaras. (92)
Having bathed and gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he prostrated at his feet;
then, having drunk the water from those feet and bowed to the circle of great sages, [he remained there]. ||93||
Having rubbed the dust of the hermitage upon her body and chanting the names of Hari, she went singing to the Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 94.
[He saw] the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the eternal Śrīvallabha, the manifest, peaceful, and formidable form, the beautiful Puruṣottama. ||95||
Upon seeing him, she suddenly fainted; for a moment she became motionless in her form, and absorbed in meditation, she became as if merged into Kṛṣṇa. ||96||
Then, together with her senses and internal organ, she became one with that [consciousness] and possessed of life;
yet she became like a yoginī, devoid of the appearance of a physical body. (97)
O Badarī, if anyone attains even for a single moment an unwavering state of presence within my form in every respect, being purified, they shall attain liberation. 98.
Driven by impatience, she quickly approached the side of Kṛṣṇa;
and full of love, she placed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa on her lap and kissed him. (99)
Hari gave her a kiss, cleansed her, and fully satisfied her;
by his mere touch, she was liberated from the bonds of the ocean of worldly existence.
O Badrikā, she was born with a divine body like Rādhā herself—a young woman endowed with excellent qualities and free from the defects of latent impressions. ||101||
Devoid of all [other] karma, she was born as a woman of the Brahma-order;
possessed of knowledge and divine vision, she [saw] the Lord, the Beloved of Śrī. (102)
The virtuous woman then quickly praised the water from Hari’s feet;
thereupon, by the will of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a divine celestial chariot arrived.
Having ascended by his command, she indeed went to the divine state of imperishable syllables;
thus did the woman Pratāriṇī, the poison-remover for the virtuous, reach Hari. 104.
Having become purified through yoga, he went to the supreme state of liberation;
O Badrikā, by hearing this, the sin of deception is destroyed. (105)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Emergence of Discernment in the Woman named Viṣalāṇī through Her Serving Holy Men Food, Water, and Other Necessities, and Her Liberation by Attaining Anādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at the Sacred Site," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Kaṭakartrī as well;
[it took place] in the village of Kālañjara on the bank of the Ojasvatī, abounding in trees. (1)
There was a Śūdra woman named Gaṅgāñjanī who lived in Kaṭaka;
she, having woven excellent mats and bamboo vessels in Saurāṣṭra, [became prosperous]. (2)
Having fashioned mats, she goes to the city seeking to sell them;
having reached Dharmāṅgadapura, she sells them for their proper price. || 3 ||
Having bowed to Dāmodara in the evening, he departs for his own city,
taking with him whatever wealth, food, clothing, or other acquisitions he has earned.
Having taken it, she went quickly to her own village of Kālāñjara;
having arrived at her home, she placed food, clothing, and other items inside a chest.
Just as she desired, the beautiful woman cooked the food and other provisions;
she had an only daughter, a young girl ten years of age.
Her husband had met his end and her family was no longer there;
she was a virtuous widow, a maker of mats, the daughter of Gaṅgā.
Having eaten at night and holding a rosary in her hand,
the maiden also recites it and sings a song that delights Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s rāsa dance.
The widow, her mind fully absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, listens attentively;
thus, after the song, the mother and daughter take their rest.
Thus they constantly performed the worship of Śrī Hari at night;
once, in the month of Kārttika, the two of them went to the Raivata tīrtha.
They perform supreme service to the virtuous and the holy women, and indeed to the wondrous songs sung of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 11.
Listen with great devotion to the divine wonders of the countless female devotees of the Lord of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Listen to the wonders of Śrī, Ramā, Rādhā, and Kamalā, whose noble deeds are celebrated by the songs of excellent virtuous men and women and the foremost of devotees. 13.
Listen with a spirit of devotion to his wondrous deeds performed for others, as well as to his heroic exploits, such as the uplifting of the poor and the helpless out of compassion. (14)
Hearing this repeatedly on the path of circumambulation in many ways, the daughter Ramāñjanī, filled with joy, questioned her mother. (15)
Even by the thousands, virtuous people sing the praises of the qualities of the Mother of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 16.
Where might He be, or where could the Lord, the husband of Rādhā-Ramā, be found?
My mind runs toward this sacred ford (tīrtha) for the sake of seeing Him.
Or, wherever it may be that I must go—to the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā—then let my sight of you be made meaningful; show yourself to me. (18)
Then his mother, who was like one liberated, having reflected upon the true nature of things,
questioned the virtuous one named Suradevāyana in every way.
Where does the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa reside here? He is sung of by the virtuous men and women, and he is glorified by pilgrims. (4.31.20)
As I listened to his exploits, my heart was captivated by him;
thus, I must go there myself for the sake of embarking upon a journey toward that lord. (21)
Tell me of His greatness: what is that Blessed One truly like?
And how is He praised by the best of virtuous gods at every sacred place?
Leaving aside the Lord of Rādhā, the Master of Kamalā, and the Lord of Māṇikī, how can countless virtuous women and female ascetics even mention [other deities]? (23)
Setting aside Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vāmana, Dattātreya, or Nṛsiṃha,
they cry out for that Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, the beloved Lord.
"I believe there must indeed be some distinction in this matter; explain that to me.
Thus addressed, O Badrikā, the virtuous Suradevāyana spoke to her.
He spoke of the most exalted reality for the sake of accomplishing the worship of Jagad-Ādya;
listen to its majesty, O Gaṅgājani, as I tell it to you. 26.
Here on Mount Raivata, the Lord Dāmodara shines resplendent;
he is Vāmana and Trivikrama, served by King Bali.
The Blessed One exists; therefore, Nara and Nārāyaṇa are superior.
Those two, residing at Badarikāśrama, shone together with Badrī. ||28||
In the Himalayas, those two venerable ascetics dwell on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā, shining for the sake of the welfare of all beings. ||29||
Even more excellent than that is the Blessed One who makes his abode on Śvetadvīpa.
Nārāyaṇa is the beloved of Kamalā, the sovereign lord of the goddess Śrī.
Even beyond that resides the Lord, the most excellent Śeṣanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī who dwells in the Ocean of Milk and is served by the Siddhas. ||31||
Beyond that also dwells the Blessed One, the supreme Lord Viṣṇu, the highest;
he resides in the third realm, Vaikuṇṭha, above the covering of water.
He is the protector of all the cosmic eggs and the destroyer of all the Daityas;
even greater than that is the Lord Mahāviṣṇu.
The aged father of Vairāja is Hari, the sovereign lord of Śrīpura, the husband of Mahālakṣmī, the golden one, the king of kings. ||34||
She who was Mahālakṣmī there is that virtuous Kaṃbharā on earth;
she dwells at Kuṅkumavāpī as the mother of the Supreme Soul. (35)
His father is Mahāviṣṇu, who bears the name Gopālakṛṣṇa;
in his house dwells Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord who has descended as an incarnation. (36)
Beyond Mahāviṣṇu resides the supreme Puruṣa known as Bhūman;
he is the Lord who bestows justice upon the Īśvaras within the auspicious abode of the unmanifest.
Beyond that is the Supreme Lord known as Vāsudeva;
the Master of Ramā shines resplendent in His own abode called Amṛta.
Then, in the most excellent Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord, the Supreme Master, resides as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; and there exists a Saṃhitā named after Him.
This Lord, the husband of Lakṣmī, is eternally present as the Blessed One;
yet even greater than He resides the supreme Lord Rādhākṛṣṇa.
The beloved of countless gopīs, devoted to the service of cows,
holding his flute in Goloka, that Lord is the bestower of welfare upon his devotees.
Thus, twenty other abodes shine there as well.
And there are two other [cities], as well as Sāketa and others, numbering in the tens of millions. ||42||
In each of those places, my incarnations are considered to have made their dwellings;
even beyond that, in the infinite and boundless world of Brahmā known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
In the all-pervading abode, Hari himself, the supreme Lord, the Lord of all, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), shines as the incarnated one within the Supreme Brahman. ||44||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the glorious Supreme Lord; He is the sustainer of all incarnations and is endowed with all sovereign powers. ||45||
He is the Lord of all incarnations, the Master of the Liberated, the Sovereign;
the Lord of the Muktānikās, the Lord of all Śrīs, and the Lord of Māṇikīs. ||46||
The Supreme Brahman is the Lord of all; there is no other equal to Him or superior to Him.
All His incarnations in the divine abodes are the upholders of His command. 47.
He is the Lord of lords, the supreme master among masters;
he is the Blessed One among the blessed, the highest Hari among the Haris. ||48||
The supreme among the dark ones is Kṛṣṇa; the best among the Rāmas is Rāma;
the highest among the lions among men is Narasiṃha; he is the Supreme Lord.
He is the Supreme Self of all selves, the Lord of Lords over the glorious Śivas;
he is the Supreme Self of all those who are the Supreme Selves of the three creations.
He is the Supreme Brahman of the Brahmas, and even of the highest Brahmas;
he is indeed the most exalted King of Brahmas, the glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 51.
His creations are infinite, and his incarnations are likewise infinite;
his powers are infinite, and indeed his wives are beyond counting.
He for whom the entire body— both the insentient and the sentient— is indeed an object of experience,
is the enjoyer, the leader, the lord, and the master of that Imperishable Brahman.
He alone is beyond the syllables, the beloved of the Kārṣṇīs;
the creation of individual souls, the creation of the Lord, and the creation of Brahmā are all brought about by him. (54)
In the twinkling of an eye they come into being, and indeed in a twinkling they dissolve;
these very creations of His abode have their forms subject to His volition.
The incarnations of the Blessed One are his forms manifested by will;
and all his auspicious powers are indeed women who purify.
Indeed, all other sovereignties belong to the virtuous;
such is this Blessed One, the Lord of all the Brahmas. ||57||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the Goddess of Fortune, having become a child in Saurāṣṭra, indeed exists as Bālakṛṣṇa. ||58||
In the house of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, [resides] the son of Śrī Kaṃbhara, from the rays of light emanating from whose eyes all creations arise. (59)
The sun, the moon, fire, and lightning proceed as luminous entities;
by whose breath all embodied beings exist as sustainers of life.
Indeed, by the power of its support, even the spheres of the cosmic eggs remain perpetually established and move within the ether.
When Mahāmāyā, who possesses the three qualities and increases creation, is commanded, she—
fulfilling all and bestowing happiness— proceeds eternally.
By His will the oceans and the clouds give forth water;
by His will the earth is always considered the support of all beings. (63)
He who is the Lord of Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, dwells within the heart as the inner controller (antaryāmī) of all, acting as the witness and observer. ||64||
Hari dwells in the senses, as well as in the internal organs;
that Supreme Person dwells in bodies and in the five elements. (65)
Within the selves, within consciousness itself, within the qualities— within millions of karmas—
and within all meditative realizations, that very Hari, the illustrious Puruṣottama, dwells.
That Lord [dwelt] among women, among groups of men, and among eunuchs;
among maidens, virtuous women, and among both old and young women.
And that Supreme Person dwells within those who possess discernment and those devoid of it—among beasts, birds, trees, and so forth, as well as within the hosts of gods, daityas, and asuras. (68)
He dwells on Mount Raivata, and he is also present among the multitudes of people;
he is in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
He alone remains as the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of millions of billions of powers;
having performed circumambulation there, we shall then depart.
"O Mother, you must come with us and our daughter to the presence of the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (71)
"We shall personally perform the service of beholding the Self-luminous One," thus spoke that daughter of the Bhāgavata, Gaṅgāñjanī, in the presence of the virtuous. (72)
Behaving like a maidservant, she conducted herself like a slave-girl;
and those virtuous ones [remained] after the full moon day of Kārtika.
Virtuous women, multitudes of people, and even hundreds of millions of devotees went to the purifying Akṣarakṣetra at Aśvapaṭṭasara. ||74||
Performing their ritual ablutions, they drank the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, near the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having visited the sacred fords situated along the banks, they went to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
there, having beheld the great seer and having honored the ṛṣis and munis, [they stayed]. (76)
They even found rest in the vast forest ranges;
for indeed, the purifying mantra was bestowed upon them by Lomaśa.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord;
and likewise to the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the female attendants. ||78||
Lomaśa gave the mantra to the men and to the pilgrims;
then the sage gave the mantra to Gaṅgājani and Ramājani.
Then they went from there to the glorious abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; they performed worship, beheld Him, and presented various offerings.
They honored Acyuta with flowers, sandalwood paste, leaves, and other offerings, as well as fruits, garments, ornaments, unbroken grains (akṣata), jewels, gems, and so forth.
Beholding Bālakṛṣṇa, the beautiful Supreme Lord who is higher than the highest, they were then bewildered and became absorbed in meditation. 82.
Women with attached hearts and men with minds fixed upon the Lord attained the fulfillment of their births in Śrī Parameśa. ||83||
Many there, having cast off their bodies and assumed divine forms,
attained eternal heaven by means of celestial chariots.
Others, being liberated, went to the imperishable abode that is higher than the highest;
likewise did the noble women whose hearts were fixed on Kṛṣṇa, now possessing divine forms.
Those who were sixteen years of age or older went to the imperishable abode of Hari; Gaṅgājanī, her body now divine, was freed from her worn-out frame. 86.
Having reached the age of sixteen,
Ramāñjanī’s daughter went to the imperishable abode of the Lord, before Hari, by her mother's command.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, she lived always like a maidservant, conducting herself like a handmaid. ||88||
Thus, O beloved of Badarī, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa indeed displayed his miraculous power at that time, and thousands were led to the imperishable realm.
Indeed, even virtuous women and men are capable of acting in such a way;
so what need is there to speak of Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, the infallible Acyuta?
Where the virtuous and the holy dwell, and where the Lord, the Sovereign of All, resides—
there Māyā has no power, nor does Time, nor even Karma.
Neither power, nor destiny, nor scripture, nor kings and the like; neither gods nor incarnations are capable before Śrī Hari. (92)
Nevertheless, Hari himself is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise;
he is independent, the controller, and the supreme sovereign.
What has been done by him cannot be undone by anyone anywhere;
however, he alone is capable of altering what was done by another. (94)
Having obtained that beloved Anādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her husband, that Ramā-Añjanī thereafter became equal to Ramā, the beloved of Brahmā. ||95||
Divine, enriched with a divine form, and exceedingly beautiful with a divine body;
she is the virtuous lady devoted to wonders, the beloved of Brahmā, and the beloved of Hari. 96.
Thus, in this world dear to Badrī, by virtue of the direct union with Kṛṣṇa, even women who are devoid of purity indeed become eternally pure. 97.
If even his illusory power (māyā) is eternally manifested through his yoga, then what need is there to mention the counting of the illusory bodies of Hari? 98.
Indeed, by the union with light, everything attains the state of light;
indeed, by the union with the dark, everything attains the state of the dark. 99.
The *gopīs*, the cows, the *rāśiyānīs*, the *prācīnīs*, the *paryas*, likewise the *hārītakyas*, the *amaryas*, the *abriktānyas*, and the *uṣṇijās*. (100)
"O Badrī, other innumerable yoginīs have been born as those whose beauty is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa; in this way, they attain divinity, just like Kaṭinī. (101)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Gaṅgāñjanī through her Union with a Holy Man and the Attainment of the State of Ramā by Ramāñjanī," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the account of the potter woman named Sunāriṇī, a devotee residing in Phaṇāgrāma who fashioned water-jars. || 1 ||
That potter woman lived in Phaṇāgrāma on the banks of the Bhadrā;
urged by her husband, she fashioned excellent vessels from clay. (2)
She sells [her goods] in her own home and never goes outside;
her husband, named Raṇastaṃba, carries the vessels on his vehicle.
Having ripened in many ways, he goes at times to another village for the purpose of selling; then, having obtained the price and food, he returns to his own home. || 4 ||
This righteous man always sets aside a tenth part of his income for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and for the sake of virtuous men and women; indeed, he spends it for these purposes. ||5||
He chants the names "Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" and "Śrī Puruṣottama," and with a stylus, he writes "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" upon worthy recipients.
O Badrī, that potter indeed fashioned an image of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in his home and performs its worship every morning.
And his wife, Sunārini, having bathed, performs worship;
she indeed offers cakes and buttermilk as the food offering (naivedya). ||8||
Having offered water, a lamp, mouth-perfume, and betel nut,
and having bowed down, he performs his daily duties immediately thereafter.
At midday as well, having likewise offered him food and other provisions,
the potter himself then always partakes of that which is pleasing.
And with a spirit of devotion, he serves travelers, virtuous ones, excellent yogis, chaste women, and ascetics with food. (11)
By massaging his feet and the like, as well as by providing water for drinking and so forth, and by constantly offering him lodging and serving him again and again. (12)
The desire of those two, who were childless, turned toward seeking a son; meanwhile, they were questioned by virtuous men in the presence of holy sages.
The virtuous men offered blessings to the childless couple, saying, "May you both possess offspring;
may you have a daughter and a son. (14)
The noble-minded ones, being propitiated, were always engaged in service with devotion;
then, after some time, a son was born who delighted the mind. (15)
He is the one whose nature is virtuous, whose conduct is righteous, and who increases all prosperity.
Upon whose neck there was the most beautiful and supreme mark of a garland.
Upon seeing him, the mother, the father, and the other onlookers rejoiced.
And likewise, the virtuous and the truthful, having seen the garland, attained great joy. ||17||
The son, too, was constantly meditative, his speech consisting only of the name "Nārāyaṇa."
Even though not practiced in this body, one is trained therein by virtue of previous habituation. ||18||
With a sweet, low-pitched voice, he uttered the name "Nārāyaṇa," exclaiming, "Oh, what fortune!
Oh, what fortune, that the Lord is present in my home along with Mālikā! (19)
A son devoted to Nārāyaṇa was born through the grace of the virtuous;
that son grew in devotion, in stature, in fame, and in wisdom. (20)

Many virtuous people and numerous seekers of truth come to see the renowned [saint], wondering what kind of garland he possesses; indeed, there are many who have come even for a mere glimpse of his journey.
Men also came, inhabitants of villages and cities, as well as men and women from the countryside and Saurāṣṭra, full of curiosity. (22)
They came to see that charming child adorned with garlands—the child who was Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī. (23)
Having heard, seen, and stood for a moment, and having performed the salutation of the child, he loudly chants the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari. (24)
Considering him to be a great devotee, a portion of a god, or even a portion of Kṛṣṇa himself, one should give him offerings of food, clothing, seals, gold, and fruits. (25)
Vessels made of gems and rubies, purifying by their very form, went forth; the potter’s house became full, born of great prosperity and abundant wealth. 26.
The palace was beautified by the flow of people and by the dwellings of the virtuous;
it was a sacred site renowned for the attainment of sons and enchanting to all.
Then one day, the sage Sārāyaṇa arrived there;
he was served by the two potters and propitiated with meals. (28)
Having been saluted and questioned regarding his son’s garland—how it was that he bore a mark like a garland, and what kind of fortune he possessed—[the sage spoke]. (29)
What is his appearance like? What is his activity? What is his lifespan? And of what nature is he?
Having heard this, the virtuous Sārāyaṇa, seeing the line upon his forehead, [spoke].
Having understood one's fortune in an instant and likewise having observed what was produced in previous births.
He spoke to that potter Raṇastamba, who was intent on his own welfare.
O Raṇastamba, you remain here with your wife as a king among devotees;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself is being served by you.
Likewise, virtuous men are always to be served in the home as if they were the Lord in embodied form;
and virtuous women are indeed to be served by pilgrims as if they were sacred pilgrimage sites themselves.
Indeed, upon all your vessels that are made of clay,
O Kṛṣṇa, Hari is both depicted and remembered by you, O Kṛṣṇa.
Your heart is purifying, and your wife is always a purifier;
she remains a devoted and virtuous woman, just like the saintly Muktānikā. (35)
By virtue of the blessings of the virtuous men and women and the yogis and ascetics, this son has been born in your house; for the moon is indeed the lord of the lunar mansions. (36)
Your virtuous wife, who performs worship here every morning, constantly prays to Hari for a beautiful son as radiant as the moon. (37)
By the grace of Hari, by the blessings of the holy ones, and likewise by yours, this son was born with a garland of stars around his neck. (38)
The deity is the Moon, and this son of yours is a human;
yet he is equal to a god, for by him humans are drawn toward [him]. (39)
Having obtained that son, who is a portion of the Moon, you shall indeed attain the joys of heaven.
In the future, you will hear that he is the great teacher of men. ||40||
He will become a supreme and most excellent Vaiṣṇava, of this there is no doubt;
his name shall become renowned in the world as Candrastamba. ||41||
Having become possessed of sons and wealth, he will then become a virtuous man;
having brought about the liberation of his parents, he will become one who practices renunciation.
Having spoken thus, Sārāyaṇa, the king of sages, departed for Raivata;
meanwhile, having heard of the two potters, [the others] became gracious and joyful in heart.
Knowing their own father to be the Moon, Menā and Himavat considered their fortune to be supreme;
thereafter, they both regarded Candra-stamba as having the form of a god.
A young boy, endowed with good fortune, served by supernatural powers, and divine;
from the time of his birth under the Moon, he remained incessantly in the house of a potter.
Prosperities indeed come together, and manifestations of power come together;
a great feast of food was prepared by that potter. ||46||
There, he constantly enjoys excellent sweet food, like a king of kings over a kingdom, along with more than a thousand men. ||47||
Once, Raṇastamba desired to go on a pilgrimage; he said to his beloved Sunārī, "We shall go to the Akṣara-tīrtha. (48)
Wherever our preceptor Lomaśa is, there also is the illustrious Puruṣottama.
The Supreme Brahman himself, Bālakṛṣṇa, shines forth as the beloved one. ||49||
The son shall attain mastery over mantras, behold Lord Hari and his guru,
and meet with the virtuous who are dear to Brahman and are exponents of the Veda.
Bathing in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and visiting the Devatīrtha and other sacred sites shall result in the fulfillment of one's desire for a son, as well as the fulfillment of all goals. ||51||
Having thus made this resolution, O Badrikā, the son and Sārthaka,
along with Sunāra, Nīra, and Raṇastambha, went to Kuṅkumasthalī.
Accompanied by his parents, as well as by numerous serpents and their offspring, he was provided with garments and countless jewels as bright as the moon.
He likewise departed with carts, carriages, draft animals, horses, bulls, and camels, accompanied by a thousand men and women.
On the full moon day of Māgha, they reached the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and joyfully drank the waters of the holy Śrī Kuṅkumavāpī tīrtha.
Having bathed in the waters of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa at the end of the day,
they then performed the evening ritual of waving lamps for the lake.
Śrī Badarīpriyā said:
O glorious Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, for the welfare of the worlds and for my own sake, please tell me of the supreme fruit of the *ārātrika* rite, which bestows liberation. (57)
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: O Badrikā, for one who performs the *ārārtika* rite with even a single wick soaked in cow’s ghee, the supreme station of Mahendra is attained. (58)
Indeed, with three lines one obtains the unsurpassed footprint of Sūrya;
with five lines, however, it becomes the footprint of Bṛhaspati.
By seven [repetitions] one attains the station of Brahmā; by nine, the abode of Śiva;
by eleven, the sovereignty of Vairāja; and by thirteen, the golden realm.
With fifteen [lines], the supreme state of Mahābhūmi is attained;
then, with fifty-one lines, the abode of Vāsudeva is reached.
With one hundred and one wicks, it shall indeed be Vaikuṇṭha;
with two hundred and one wicks, it is Nirājaka.
He goes to Goloka and joyfully serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa at Badarī,
performing the ritual waving of lights with five hundred and one wicks.
He attains the supreme, imperishable abode; of this there is no doubt.
With one thousand and one wicks, the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) is performed. ||64||
He who performs this indeed goes there to that most excellent imperishable state,
to the two feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having become either a male or female servant, one enjoys eternal bliss;
having attained union with that identity, one enjoys the state of being the master of all.
He attains the authority over all sovereignty, supreme excellence,
and indeed the state of being eternally beloved by Brahmā as well as beloved by Hari.
It is indeed the state of great liberation, and it possesses the quality of being the great liberator.
And he enjoys all desires together with the Supreme Brahman, who is Śrī.
Thus, O Badrikā, such is the auspicious fruit arising from the *ārtrika* rite performed at Aśvapaṭṭa.
In the waters of Aśvapaṭṭa dwell the gods, the ancestors, and tens of millions of *siddhas*. (69)
Saintly sages, the best of yogis, the Gaṇas and Pārṣadas,
those who observe the vow of Brahman, ascetics, and the Mothers all dwell there.
All the goddesses dwell there, and the sacred fords (tīrthas) also reside there;
Rudra, Brahmā, and Hara, as well as the incarnations, dwell there too. ||71||
Then, by performing the *ārātrika* rite, there is the lustration (*nīrājana*) of the three worlds.
That merit becomes accomplished; it arises entirely for the doer. ||72||
Having performed the circumambulation and the evening ritual (sāndhya-vidhi), he then constructed a golden temple for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (73)
They went for the sake of beholding Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self,
who was resplendent upon his divine elephant-throne and attended by gods and goddesses.
He was worshipped by hosts of Siddhas and honored by the beloved wives of Brahmā;
he was venerated by liberated devotees, by Śaktis, by sacred fords, and by twice-born brahmins.
The Supreme Lord was praised by the virtuous and great seers, beheld by them,
and worshipped with offerings such as the tips of their hoods and lotuses.
Thus honored by potters and with ornaments such as jewels and gems,
Śrī Hari was worshipped by Candra-stamba at Badarī.
Then Candra became the radiant moon, whose vehicle is the deer;
he who is the lord of medicinal herbs appeared before the gaze of all the worlds.
He presented a jar of nectar as a gift to the illustrious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as a moonstone gem. (79)
Being pleased, Hari suddenly seized that jewel-jar;
he wore that jewel-jar around his neck and gave it to Śrī.
Then they performed the Nīrājana ceremony for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
And Hari also gave them his own nectar, which was pleasing to the sight. ||81||
Then he caused her to drink that which had arisen from the realm of the imperishable Brahman;
he satisfied them all and offered them due honor.
Having accomplished their purpose, they went to the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa;
there they honored him and offered auspicious fruits and other gifts.
They stayed that night in that vast hermitage, an ocean of bliss;
throughout the night, they performed worship and kīrtana of the glorious Supreme Soul. (84)
And they received the morning mantra from their guru, the sage Śrī Lomaśa:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā. (8)
Then, at the end of the fortnight on the night of the new moon, at the half-point of the night,
the Moon-stump displayed a marvel.
Having himself become the full moon, he released the autumnal radiance,
which made the earth, the sky, and the lake appear as if they were composed of milk.
He made the Kuṃkumavāpikā field white all around;
having remained thus until dawn, he then caused his splendor to vanish.
Having become the son of a potter, he shone among the people;
thus the Lord himself always dwelt in the house of his devotee in Saurāṣṭra. 89.
Having become a human being, he remains for the sake of the welfare of the world;
then, on the final day, there is the instruction of the illustrious Lomaśa.
Having heard this, with the force of dispassion, they all abandoned the householder's stage of life and adopted the stage of renunciation;
both the virtuous women and the virtuous men became ascetics.
He was named Candrastambāyana, for he was indeed a virtuous king.
At that very time, his father Raṇastambāyana was indeed virtuous. ||92||
The virtuous and noble Narayani remained there as a devoted wife,
while others and other men likewise stayed right there with joy for the rest of their lives.
And even the people from the tip of the serpent's hood, through their union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa Hari, attained liberation in due course and went to the great imperishable state. ||94||
Then, in the course of time, Raṇastamba also attained liberation along with Sunāraṇyā in the supreme abode of the Imperishable, the station of Hari. (95)
Then Candrastambāyana also received service from the liberated king;
having cast off his lunar portion in heaven and assumed his liberated form, he remained there.
By the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he became liberated and, having become great, went to the imperishable abode at the feet of the Supreme Self. 97.
O Badrī, how shall I describe here the greatness of Hari, the glorious Kṛṣṇakānta, the Lord of Māṇikī, who is one's very self? (98)
From that, Phaṇāgrāma was born, renowned as Candragrāma;
there, moreover, is the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara water-tīrtha and the Cāndra-tīrtha.
From that time on, O Badrikā, the holy site named Kaumudī has been celebrated;
by reading or hearing of it, one's body becomes radiant with light.
Having attained liberation and achieved it, a man or a woman shall obtain great *mokṣa* and gain the merit of the Great Lustration (*mahānīrājana*).

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Candra through the Devotion of the Woman Sunārī in the House of the Potter named Raṇastamba Residing in Phaṇā Village in Saurāṣṭra, and the Pilgrimage to Kuṅkumavāpī Performed by Candra, Stamba, and Others, as Well as the Liberation and Dwelling of All Therein," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Svarṇakāriṇikā;
it took place in the city of Māṇikya on the banks of the Narmadā in the Middle Country.
Indeed, families of goldsmiths, honored by the king and skilled in the arts of working with gold and silver, resided there.
The sons, daughters, and servants of the goldsmiths all engaged in the business of gold, fashioning various ornaments. || 3 ||
Even though the vessels and the various implements are distinct,
they manifest many different forms and appearances.
Though they undergo various transformations such as sale and so forth, those born of the elements remain as they are;
likewise, kings honored by their kingdoms and subjects honored by their realms [retain their essential nature]. (5)
The lords of subjects and the merchants purchase [it] from the market;
the goldsmiths indeed add a slight amount of gold by the measure of a *kalā*.
Many indeed, having fashioned ornaments from various base metals, create their decorations;
yet some may even offer pure gold for the sake of ornamentation. (7)
Even there, having combined the elements, they extract that [gold];
they perform the mixing especially when the gold is already mixed.
Indeed, having first committed the act of theft, they fashion ornaments;
such are these goldsmiths, who likewise create the ornaments for the kingdom. 9.
And there were mines of ornaments for millions of women;
even those who made them beautiful became wealthy through theft. (4.33.10)
But theft, O Badrikā, never brings benefit to anyone at any time;
indeed, upon reaching the tenth year, it is destroyed along with its very root. (11)
Then once, in that region, there occurred a frequent drought;
the people, afflicted by famine, could not obtain food anywhere at all.
In Mahārāṣṭra, food became inexhaustible due to the occurrence of rains;
it was obtained even without price, and there was no lack of wealth among the subjects.
The subjects, afflicted by the misery of poverty and destitute of food,
became unrestrained and indeed began to engage in plundering.
Indeed, the circles of subjects, resembling armies in battle,
became turbulent and predatory, spreading everywhere throughout the city.
In Rājagṛha, as well as in the residence of the guild-leader and among the goldsmiths—wherever there was wealth consisting of gold, silver, or copper—[it was seized]. (16)
Having plundered all of that, those fierce men went for the sake of food;
having gone to the regions of Mahārāṣṭra, they obtained food. ||17||
The goldsmiths became destitute of wealth and were deprived of their capital;
consequently, being without food, they were tormented by hunger. ||18||
The subjects—the young, girls, and others, as well as sons, grandsons, and their dependents—are afflicted when deprived of you; tormented by hunger, they perish. (19)
At that time, assuming a truly terrifying form, he was seized by the evil age (duṣkāla);
out of fear of death, the subjects performed name-sacrifices (nāmayajña) here and there.
Even though they have gathered in circles in every village and every city,
they perform the kīrtana of Hari’s names with a desire for rain.
The people perform worship with dry leaves and such;
they worship with offerings of their inner disposition, and they even offer praise with cries of distress.
In such a time of calamity as this, sons and kinsmen offer even their own deceased bodies to Hari;
indeed, when such a wicked age has arisen, no one to be sought for refuge is found.
There lived an elderly, devoted, and purifying goldsmith woman named Hemasudhā, who was endowed with the power to fulfill all her intentions.
She who had previously gone to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā with her husband and parents by her own command, [saw] there the venerable sage Lomaśa.
That woman made him her guru and received the mantra from his mouth:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (26)
She constantly recited the mantra one thousand times every day, always chanting "Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (27)
Even in his old age, he repeatedly performed worship with devotion during all his activities, chanting, "Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Beloved of Kṛṣṇa! (28)
In the morning, he indeed performs worship of the image with flowers, water, and other offerings; he also provides food offerings, the waving of lamps, and even the ritual of laying it to rest.
The women gathered together in many ways and celebrated the festival of Hari in that house.
Even while virtuous and truthful people perform [their duties], they come to that house.
He serves virtuous women and holy men with food, water, clothing, and by massaging their feet and other such services; he also delights them with gifts according to their desires.
After bestowing their blessings, those holy men departed for another place;
thus was she meritorious, for her home was a supreme sacred site (tīrtha).
It was always purifying and ever took refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, it was the refuge of spiritual perfection, and even in times of famine, the food remained inexhaustible. (33)
By the power of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, whatever exists in his house flourishes;
divine grains increase, and clarified butter increases in the granary.
Whatever food she might desire in the morning for her offering,
even that— along with vegetables, leaves, and so forth— is obtained from the granary.
Thus she became possessed of supernatural power, such that no others knew her to be so;
nevertheless, seeing her, the suffering people would die. (36)
Devoted to compassion, she was intent on honoring the elderly and excelled in helping others; she likewise provided for young girls, boys, and widows every day. (37)
Indeed, at midday, when they have returned to their own homes, she gives a *roṭaka* to those who are pregnant, the very elderly, and the poor and helpless. (38)
Then, having taken [the food] from a granary situated beside the hearth in her own house, that old woman gives it out of affection; yet, having eaten, they depart overcome by hunger. (39)
This was not known to everyone; therefore, other men and women, being distressed during the time of famine, censured the devotion of that devoted woman. (4.33.40)
Alas! Devotion indeed does not provide a mere crumb in this world;
nor does it ward off famine or the arrival of pestilence. (41)
A cooking pot is not filled by devotion, nor is the mouth or the belly;
through devotion, there is neither the cessation of hunger nor the destruction of thirst.
There is no destruction of time through devotion, nor is there any warding off of death;
indeed, devotion consisting of morsels of food does not arise for the sake of eating alone. //43//
What is the use here of dry devotion, which indeed provides no assistance?
For devotion to the gods is in vain, and devotion to Nārāyaṇa is likewise in vain.
In such a great time (mahākāla), food indeed does not grant devotion;
since there are no morsels of devotion, that [devotion] is therefore false.
Neither Kṛṣṇa nor Viṣṇu provides food during this evil age;
even children and girls die, for he is merciless toward them. (46)
"Let this great old woman see for herself that in this city of Hemasudhātṛ, even one who is devoted does not give food during a time of famine. (47)
Her devotion has become fruitless; how has this famine come to pass?
It appears to us that devotion does not at all ward off Mahākāla. 48.
Fie upon those virtuous men and women there who eat, come, and go while leaving those who live by Hari alone in that time of distress; they do not offer any assistance. 49.
In that way, O Badrikā, ignorant people then indeed utter censure of her,
as well as censure of the devotion of saintly men and women toward Hari.
"Afflicted by hunger, people in this world speak to one another;
this very speech has been heard by me as it grew through the succession of ears. (51)
Then, having understood the time for Camatkāra, that beautiful woman herself set out at that moment to demonstrate the preeminent prowess of Hari.
The elderly woman, beloved of Hari, suddenly desired [to prepare] golden nectar;
in the morning, she took a cooking pot in one hand and a staff in the other.
Having crushed and made it resound, she went out into the city;
like a colorful banner on the great highway, she indeed caused the men to hear her.
"Indeed, those for whom there is food to be expected in my house must come at midday, O people suffering from famine. (55)
Having thus made a public invitation in the city,
she then returned to her own home and there remembered Hari, the Lord of Śrī.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, and Lomaśa came to him in person;
with devotion, they were received with honor and sat down in his house.
Adorned with divine ornaments, endowed with various beautiful forms, with serene countenances, these beloved deities bring about auspiciousness. (58)
They were saluted, honored with devotion, treated with hospitality, and fed;
they were entreated, supplicated, and requested to remain and fulfill [their purpose]. (59)
Under the influence of devotion, they acted toward that old woman in exactly that manner;
and at that time, Viṣṇu became the producer of the *roṭakas* there.
At that time, Lakṣmī was the provider of food there,
and Lomaśa was the donor who was constantly diligent.
At that time, she became a bestower of gold, nectar, and water;
meanwhile, the human beings were indeed wretched, protectorless, and women were beggars.
Men and women, the virtuous and the truthful, as well as others—the wicked and even those who utter insults—are all likewise afflicted by hunger. (63)
Out of curiosity and for the sake of laughter, they came there to watch; yet now they have become old and senseless—why are they so devoid of luster, and is it all in vain?
Is there truth in this? Has devotion been practiced and brought to fruition?
Or is it that she, afflicted by famine, is giving away her food? (65)
"Indeed, he is merely calling out from the cooking pot; it is all in vain, false, and contrary to truth"—thus did thousands of people, overcome by hunger, speak with wonder. (66)
Whether they were endowed with existence or accompanied by non-existence, they arrived;
then the divine Śrī Lomaśa began the act of giving.
Thousands of men, along with all those *roṭakas* that were hurled, traveled through the path of the sky simultaneously, moment after moment. (68)
Then, on that vast surface of the earth, the hungry ones seized the *roṭakas* and did not let them go; having eaten them again and again, they simply departed. (69)
A great crush indeed arose there, yet it caused no distress;
then the preceptor named Lomaśa provided food until evening.
There, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa shine as the presiding deities;
the *roṭakas* are made of wheat, sweetened with sugar and mixed with ghee. (71)
They are obtained and enjoyed, and the eaters indeed attain satisfaction;
in this way, millions of people, having eaten and repeatedly uttered "Victory!", [depart].
They departed for their own homes at evening, and a wonder occurred upon the earth;
for at night, a continuous feast of food, gold, and nectar was provided.
"Men from various districts, villages, and so forth came as mendicants;
they gave food to them from night until dawn, and likewise during the day. (74)
Thus, hundreds of thousands of men and women, burdened by the misery of famine, arrived from all sides after hearing this wonder for seven days. (75)
Day and night, the streams of men, resembling the ocean, surged like overflowing tides, impelled by the wonder of the alms-gathering. (76)
Having eaten that food of faith again and again, those mendicants became auspicious, purified devotees, and they performed the worship of Hari. (77)
O Prabhukṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Śrīkṛṣṇa, Lord of Mādhavī!
By your grace, the hunger of these elderly noble ladies has now been destroyed. (78)
Those who have partaken even once of the grace of the Supreme Self praise Hari and constantly offer hymns of praise, being ever-satisfied. (79)
Month after month, indeed, they experienced no hunger, O Badarī;
such was the wonder those men attained at that time.
Coming again and again, they all received the supreme mantra; the elder indeed caused them to receive that mantra from Lomaśa.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
There, hundreds of thousands of auspicious men became Vaiṣṇavas. ||82||
Requested by Vṛddhā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then caused rain to fall upon the earth, providing satisfaction with cool waters.
Forests, groves, fields, and woods, as well as pleasure gardens and marketplaces, have all become magnificent. (84)
They became enriched with leaves, food, fruits, flowers, and other offerings;
that Hemasudhikā grew old and was worshipped like a deity. (85)
Through her union with Kṛṣṇa, the ascetic goddess who protects the world became known on earth as Annapūrṇā, the bestower of gold, nectar, and food. 86.
Then, having received supreme worship, Lakṣmī, Lomaśa, and Mādhava vanished from that place and went to Kuṅkumakṣetra. ||87||
Possessing a divine body, she was born full of gold, nectar, and food;
for after speaking thus to all, she departed for Kuṅkumavāpikā.
While a hundred thousand embodied beings were looking on, she suddenly vanished and traveled through the sky to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā. 89.
Constantly devoted to the service of Hari’s lotus feet,
she is a divine maiden among the liberated ones, a purifying handmaid.
Possessing a divine form, she remained eternally sixteen years of age before Hari. Then those inhabitants of the Narmada region, who dwelt in Māṇikya—
Hundreds of thousands of men, women, and people came from all directions to the divine field of Kunkumavapika for the great festival of his birth. 92.

On the eighteenth day, during the festival celebrating the birthday of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they arrived for the purpose of beholding him, worshipping him, and likewise for the sake of auspiciousness. ||93||
They all presented gifts and honored Acyuta with jewels, gems, sandalwood, unbroken grains, flowers, and garlands of pearls. 94.
They worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Māṇikī, as well as Lomaśa, Aśvasara, and Lakṣmī. (95)
They performed the rites of the sacred ford and dwelt there for four months;
having performed the ritual bath of Māgha, they became fulfilled in their purpose.
By the power of Bālakṛṣṇa, thousands of men and women, whose latent thoughts and desires had dissolved, went to the imperishable abode of Hari. 97.
At that time, there were virtuous men and virtuous women;
others, all devoted to Viṣṇu, performed the ritual ablution at the holy site and returned home. 98.
Thus, O Badrikā, that goddess Annapūrṇikā, who brings about the welfare of the world, was born as the daughter of a goldsmith. 99.
Then, after some time, they attained the eternal and imperishable state,
which destroys the sins of people belonging to castes such as goldsmiths.
By giving food and other gifts through the grace of Hari, she indeed performed [this act],
and thus she became Nārāyaṇī, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed One, through the devotion of Hemasudhā, the goldsmith of Māṇikyapattana, provided food and liberation during a famine for countless men, and how she herself was led to liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the auspicious story of Viṣṭinārī.
In the most beautiful city named Dhanadhṛk in Saurāṣṭra, [it took place]. || 1 ||
When the teaching of King Devarddhisimha was flourishing, there were many districts consisting of excellent human carriers. || 2 ||
The disciples who are established in the aggregates do not experience even the slightest trembling;
those situated in the palanquin do not perceive any difference between the palanquin and the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Those who have practiced [the art of driving] carry the king, their preceptor,
their mothers, the king’s mothers, the women of the harem, and virtuous ladies.
The carriers of burdens endure their labors with the excellent wealth produced by their carrying;
they serve both the king and his householders like slaves. (5)
They also carry groups of men seeking to travel, excellent married women,
merchants, and likewise royal officials.
In some places they carry virtuous men and chaste women through the heat and other hardships;
furthermore, they serve Vaiṣṇavas, traveling from one sacred ford to another.
During the festivals of the gods, these [vehicles] carry the deities;
indeed, they wander through the city, having gathered together the divine images.
Thus, all those devoted to service, known as *viṣṭis*,
along with groups of servants— both men and women— attend upon the great persons.
In that city of the virtuous, there was a circle with its temple constructed;
there, the Lord Śrī Rādhikāyana was the most excellent among them.
There was a devotee of Hari equal to Rādhā, detached and devoted to Hari;
there were also fifty other saintly disciples who formed his lineage. || 1.1 ||
There were twenty virtuous women, and there was also a beautiful image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
an image of Bāla Kṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor, was present in that temple. (12)
Indeed, eulogies of the laborers are composed with respect by the virtuous,
and truly, beautiful songs are also created for them when they are gathered together.

Even worship and festivals performed during the Viṣṭi [astrological period] become auspicious for those who serve Rādhikā; indeed, such Viṣṭis are as good as a thousand [other favorable times] for them.
Those disciples of Rādhikāyana were indeed supreme Vaiṣṇavas;
they were devoted to their morning baths, intent on meditation, and subsisted on the offering of food (naivedya). || 15 ||
All those men and women, as well as the boys and girls, became devoted to visiting sacred fords and dedicated to the service of the virtuous. (16)
They became exceedingly devoted to Bālakṛṣṇa and followed him without doubt; intent on serving the virtuous, they were dedicated through their bodies, minds, and material resources.
Those virtuous ones who indeed had no doubt whatsoever regarding their duties—
whether in eating, sleeping, bathing, massaging, or being carried on a palanquin.
Whether in a monastery or in divine laughter, in worldly wonders or in the naked state; whether clothed or unclothed, in transformation or in the changeless. ||19||
Whether in pleasure or in delight, on the earth or upon a swing;
whether in walking or running, in singing or even in quarreling.
Since there was no doubt whatsoever in his heart regarding virtuous conduct, such auspicious moments were for him objects of the compassion of the holy ones. 21.
Having received the mantra from the venerable Supreme Soul during the hundredth year of Rādhā,
they all offered themselves and were entirely intent on the surrender of their everything.
They honor the virtuous man as Nārāyaṇa and the virtuous woman as Nārāyaṇī;
through the union of Nārāyaṇa and Nārāyaṇī, the state of Nārāyaṇa is attained.
Hari, even the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, fell under the sway of such tricksters who had come under the power of their own deception. (24)
There, in his eternal abode, he accepts the worship offered by the laborers;
Hari goes from house to house and receives the highest honor.
They perform great worship of the manifest Śrī Hari with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, fragrant oils, and saffron. ||26||
Women worship Him as well with heartfelt emotions, with love, with affection, with the offering of their hearts, with the offering of their bodies, and with the offering of everything.
The young maidens, their minds filled with innocent charm,
bring delight to the laborers upon beholding Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, their beloved, who is beautiful in every limb.
A certain woman, having placed her feet upon the breasts of the Supreme Soul and having placed her hands upon His neck, indeed enjoys eternal happiness. (29)
One woman, having drawn Kṛṣṇa’s face toward her own mouth in every way, skillfully joined her own mouth to his and tasted the essence of the Supreme Soul. (4.34.30)
A certain woman, believing Kṛṣṇa to be her own beloved, lay upon the bed;
clinging to his body in every way, she experienced the bliss of desire. ||3 1||
One woman, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon the seat of her own body, sleeps soundly;
another likewise enjoys the touch of his cheeks, thighs, and shanks.
One woman repeatedly massages and delights her own hips and belly;
another, having taken hold of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, performs a foot-massage for him. Another, placing him upon her own breast, attains a state of identity with him as if through yoga.
One girl kisses Kṛṣṇa, while another remains embracing him. ||34||
The beautiful woman, out of longing, gazed with divine vision at Nārāyaṇa from his nails up to the tip of his crest, and indeed upon his entire body.
Another maiden, having prepared excellent sweet offerings such as the essence of milk and other delicacies for Śrī Hari, feeds Him. 36.
The other girl, having cooked a leaf of *śāka* seasoned with savory flavors, would feed her beloved together with fried cakes (*polikā*). (37)
But the beautiful Śrī holds Lord Hari upon her neck, at her feet, and likewise in her hands; she wears golden ornaments, a crown, and other finery. 38.
Likewise, another woman applies collyrium to her dark eyes,
sandalwood paste to the surface of her forehead, and red lac-dye to her palms.
The passionate woman applies rouge to her lips and anoints her body with oil; another, utterly infatuated, performs the task of adorning her nails. 4.34.40.
Taking exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa, he enjoys great bliss;
he eats curd and rice together from a single vessel, and even places it directly into his mouth. ||41||
She drinks cool water and offers betel leaf as well;
her beloved, out of great affection, enjoys the flavor born of the betel.
Other elderly women, beholding the beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa again and again, indeed experienced inner bliss, meditating with one-pointed minds. 43.
Having seated Nārāyaṇa upon a lion-throne, a comfortable couch, or an auspicious seat,
she herself sat before him and rejoiced for a moment.
With a fan, she gives cool breezes to the Supreme Self;
having woven garlands of flowers, she adorns him in every way. (45)
Others, at that very moment, perform a massage of the body with liquids;
they bathe it with waters scented with perfumes, as well as with the application of unguents and fluids.
Having placed the Lord, who was adorned with ornaments, upon a high couch, other women stood before him and performed the ritual waving of lights (ārātrika). ||47||
They dance and sing songs consisting of mandalas; they perform the *rāsa* dance by lifting up and drawing in their bodies. (48)
Kṛṣṇa indeed fulfills their hearts with great respect; having taken up their intense emotional states, he makes his own being complete through their love in private. 49.
In gardens and the like, in groves, fields, and even in temples;
between trees and pillars, by rivers, on sandbanks, and even in forests. (4.34.50)
In houses, in cow-pens, in pits, and even in mountain caves,
as well as in the inner chambers of homes— wherever she desired, she was there.
Nārāyaṇa, according to his disposition, goes to her and sports with her;
he is the one who fills the minds of his devotees and bestows bliss upon them. 52.
Indeed, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa bestows happiness;
O Badrikā, from children to the elderly, all are eager for Viṣṭisundarī. 53.
They enjoyed Kṛṣṇa intensely with their bodies, senses, souls, and minds;
thus, at that moment, the people of Viṣṭi honored Kṛṣṇa.
The elders honored Mādhava like a sovereign over kings,
while the youths delighted him with excellent service, being full of youthful vigor.
The princes, however, propitiated that friend with playful sports; Hari, in turn, brought about the satisfaction of the people according to their desire. (56)
Indeed, all the households of Viṣṭi were purified by the Wielder of the Discus;
thus, O Badarī, the Lord, moved by devotion, then brought them to purification. 57.
I have described this to you here in brief; it purifies even those who perform it daily.
For such devotees, Kṛṣṇa has indeed attained a state of exclusive devotion.
Neither the restraints (yamas), nor the observances (niyamas), nor the sacred tradition (āmnāya), nor even the teaching (śāsana);
neither the manual (paddhati) nor the conduct (ācāra) operates in the case of Sarvanātha. //59//
Those people who possess devotion and are sought after by the Lord of All are accepted through identity with Him; they do not act in that [worldly] manner toward them.
At that time, the conduct of Kṛṣṇa is Dharma; love for Kṛṣṇa is true honor;
the attainment of Kṛṣṇa is the divine, excellent fruit; and the grace of Kṛṣṇa is the means of accomplishment. (61)
Action for Kṛṣṇa is the great sacrifice; that which aims at Kṛṣṇa is the goal of human endeavor.
The state of being Kṛṣṇa is the great yoga; the vision of Kṛṣṇa is true realization.
The abode of Kṛṣṇa is His bed; liberation is the enjoyment of Kṛṣṇa;
the perfections are found in Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; this is the highest fulfillment.
Life is dwelling by the side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
sport is even in secret in the presence of Hari; renunciation is [finding] peace in Kṛṣṇa. (64)
Activity consists of following the movements of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; and both duty and ritual practice must be performed for the purpose of propitiating Kṛṣṇa. (65)
Delight, joy, resolve, desire, bliss, and celebration—
O Badrikā, all these belong to those who have offered themselves to Hari and are fully satisfied.
The devoted maidservant perceives no separateness from Him there,
nor does she enjoy anything other than Kṛṣṇa, for that [other] is devoid of beauty.
All tastes, all fragrances, and all touches are in Nārāyaṇa;
all Vedic revelations are in Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and the vision of all objects is in Hari. 68.
For those whose food and recreation are all centered on Mādhava, their joys and delights are found in Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. (69)
Emotions, laughter, and amorous pastimes likewise exist in pairs within Hari;
while excellence, lordship, and protection reside in Kṛṣṇa, as does marriage.
For those whose karmic knot is severed by Hari, there is no doubt regarding their liberation;
for those who remain alive, there is the attainment of what is called enjoyment and liberation, along with great bliss in the abode of Hari. (71)
At the end of the body, she resides in the state of the eternal, supreme bliss and the imperishable;
for those possessed of devotion, dwelling in his abode is auspicious in every way. ||72||
O Badrikā, this was created by Kṛṣṇakānta for those who have offered themselves to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
may the devotees who offer themselves be fed here. (73)
All those dwelling in Dhana-dhṛk likewise became Vaiṣṇavas,
in whose houses Kṛṣṇa himself would personally reside and take delight.
In the family of the Viṣṭis there was a virtuous woman named Vidrumiṇī;
she, infatuated by Kṛṣṇa, remained devoted to him during the fourth state of consciousness.
Listen, O Badrikā! Having cast aside shame, having abandoned her husband and home, and having discarded the conduct of human beings, she then became a woman of loose character. (76)
In Kṛṣṇa are the self, mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness; O Janārdana, the body and senses as well are indeed composed of Kṛṣṇa’s essence. (77)
Just as Kṛṣṇa was, so too she became possessed of divine movements;
she caused wonder there among the laborers on all sides. ||78||
Just as a young woman is distracted, or as one who is intoxicated and reveling, or even as a woman who is deluded and filled with passion; ||79||
She remains occupied, chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," and even laughing;
she cries out for her beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and even seeks him out. (4.34.80)
Seeing her in such a state, the people confined her in a prison-house;
yet even when the door was closed, she emerged with a divine form.
Whether cast into a house, thrown into water, or even packed within a chest, they emerge with divine forms in a state of unobstructed being. (82)
Passing from one house to another, she pierces through walls;
thus she becomes invisible to all embodied beings who behold her. (83)
In some places she is a maiden, a young woman, or an old woman; beautiful and auspicious, with a gentle smile and lovely, she sometimes even becomes fierce like Rudrī.
She sings, "O Radiant One! O Kṛṣṇa! O Kṛṣṇa! O Master Kṛṣṇa!
Having led that Master Kṛṣṇa to a secluded spot, she rejoices with him in private. (85)
That beloved woman, her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, intent on meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, her actions devoted to Kṛṣṇa, and her very form being Kṛṣṇa, beheld her beloved lord. ||86||
In some places she is Kṛṣṇa’s form, in some Rādhā’s form, and in some Māṇikī;
in some places she is Priyā, Lalitā, Pārvatī, and Jayā. (87)
Only those possessed of knowledge perceive her as such; they truly realize, "This is indeed a divine assembly of great liberated ones. (88)
Considering Rādhikā to be one whose body was perfected by spiritual attainment and a truly great saintly woman,
the people— both men and women— then performed worship and honor for her.
They drank the water from his feet and, full of eagerness, fed him;
likewise, they accepted his grace in the form of fruits, flowers, and sweet foods.
Touching even that which is illusory, she instantly makes it divine;
she transforms sinful men and sinful women into those endowed with merit. ||9 1||
Having revealed Hari-Kṛṣṇa, he sends forth the Imperishable;
he liberates one from craving and kindles the latent impression (vāsanā). ||92||
It brings about the attainment of Kṛṣṇa, causes one to associate with Acyuta, points out the path to liberation, and leads one to the supreme state. ||93||
Through the power of Vidrumiṇī, thousands of men and women,
as well as even animals and birds, then attained supreme liberation.
Thousands of his disciples became virtuous and saintly women, and hundreds of thousands of people received the two mantras from her mouth. (95)
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Master and my Lord. 96.
"Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama—the Lord—may he always protect us! Thus they offered their praise. (97)
Thus, O Śrī Badrikā, the woman Viṣṭinārī, being virtuous and possessing the luster of coral, was born as the divine Rādhā-samā with that very same body. 98.
She arrived with a hundred thousand people to dwell at the holy site—the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (99)
Having attained union with Bālakṛṣṇa through identity, she disappeared;
thereafter, she dwelt existing within the divine consorts of Brahmā.
Then, men and women dwelt there continuously in many ways; virtuous men and noble women became ascetics, having embraced the stage of renunciation. 10.1.
Having become yoginīs, female ascetics, and likewise male ascetics,
they dwelt on the bank of Lake Aśvasaras in that imperishable, divine abode.
Having taken refuge at the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and having worshipped, served, and propitiated the Supreme Lord; || 103 ||
Hundreds of thousands went to the divine, imperishable abode, as did Viṣaya;
Vidrumiṇī also went to the Lord’s imperishable abode by means of a celestial chariot.
Thus, O beloved of Badarī, that goddess became equal to Rādhikā;
by the mere remembrance of her, Mahāmuktānikā, even the sinner is indeed liberated.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Lakṣādhimāna and Others through Association with the Virtuous Viṣṭinārī Vidrumiṇī Residing in the City of Dhanadhṛk, and Her Own Liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badrī, to the auspicious story of Śavahartrī;
she was always the one who cremated corpses in the village of Mālava in Saurāṣṭra.
There was once a certain outcaste woman who made her dwelling in a cremation ground;
she was accompanied by her husband, sons, daughters, and surrounded by her kinsmen and relatives.
This [fire] constantly performs the cremation of corpses in the cremation ground;
having obtained fuel, it indeed carries out its own inherent function born of its very nature. (3)
Through the constant burning of corpses, auspicious detachment arises;
indeed, it comes from seeing a dead person, whether for a moment or for a long time. (4)
The Mālavas, however, are like dog-cookers;
thus they dwell in a state of detachment, constantly grieving over their own death in the domain of jackals. (5)
