Alas! Children, youths, and the elderly are indeed constantly afflicted by calamities;
and men, too, whether children, youths, or elders, are born only to pass away.
In that same way, I shall meet my death quite unexpectedly; of this there is no doubt.
Both my parents have died, and likewise both my fathers-in-law have died.
The king has grown old and died; embodied beings die incessantly.
Even conquerors have died, and even those who dwell in celestial chariots (vaimānika) must die.
All things go to destruction, and I likewise shall go to destruction;
at the time of death, even a beloved husband, though powerful, cannot then provide assistance.

What need is there to speak of others in that regard? Therefore, Dharma is the one who must be accomplished as a helper; he is the companion in this world and stands by one's side even in the next world.
Happiness originates from Dharma; wherever a living being is born, there Dharma, known as merit and the supreme teacher, follows them equally. (11)
Merit arising from giving, service, and so forth, has the self as its companion;
this includes the gift of cows, the gift of earth, and the gift of clothing, food, and water. (1–2)
The gift of parasols, sandals, and fly-whisks, which subdues pride;
the gift of flowers, leaves, and fruits, along with the offering of various kinds of food and edibles. (13)
The gift of a house, the gift of land, and the gift of utensils;
the gift of one's body, the gift of a son, the gift of a daughter, and the offering of happiness. || 14 ||
The gift of a vow, the gift of oneself, the gift of one's waist-cloth which bestows joy, the gift of wealth, the offering of ornaments and the like, and the gift of a field. ||15||
All such gifts as these, given upon the great path, stand in every way as foremost in the world beyond. (16)
"That which is given is obtained by oneself in the future, but that which is not given is never obtained anywhere.
Therefore, I must indeed give an excellent gift to this dog-eater. (17)
"A worthy recipient is found; I must give to him for my own spiritual welfare.
Having reflected thus, that outcaste woman gathered fruits from the forest. (18)
Having brought jujubes, immortals (amṛta), plantains, and jambu fruits according to the season,
she indeed gave them as offerings for the ritual.
She offers bulbs, leaves, flowers, honey, sweet stalks of sugarcane, and other such pure and suitable things. (4.35.20)
"Indeed, they give gifts to those who have entered the path, to virtuous ascetics;
and the holy ones, having washed them, consume the fruits and other such offerings. (2.1)
Having gathered pieces of wood and even clay images, she gives them away;
in this same way, she likewise makes gifts of tree bark.
He also makes gifts of mats, seats, stones for grinding, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines. (23)
Then, having thus become renowned for her practice of the duty of giving, Mālavānikā became known as Dātrītimālavānikā in the village of Mālava.
Once, by the power of the merit of his generosity, the goddess of Dharma herself appeared in the form of a virtuous woman and went to the hut of the outcaste woman.
The Mālavānī woman remained unwashed, in her menses, and went to the cremation ground;
having performed the half-burning of a corpse, she was already covered in filth by morning. (26)
Early in the morning, a certain virtuous and chaste woman, possessing the nature of renunciation, arrived alone at the house of Malinā by way of the pilgrimage route. (27)
Beholding that virtuous woman, who was self-sacrificing, alone, and exhausted by her toil,
the Caṇḍālī rose up suddenly and quickly bowed at her feet.
She said, "Welcome, O Goddess! Mother, I bow to you with reverence;
I shall perform service at the appropriate time, as it pleases you. (26)
I am a dog-cooker by birth; moreover, I am in my courses, having failed to bathe and remaining in that state after the discharge of impurity.
"I have been cremated with half of a corpse and now dwell in the cremation ground.
What shall I do for the sake of the pure Satī?
Tell me here how, O virtuous lady, I may serve you who have come to this place."
Out of compassion, please inform me of what I may do for the sake of your welcome.
Be gracious toward me, O virtuous lady; command me what is fitting, for I am your devotee, I am filled with devotion, I am your servant, and I shall do your bidding.
"In this matter, service alone is considered appropriate by you; I shall perform that.
Blessed is my fortune, O Mother; today my day is indeed fruitful here. (358)
"O Mother, it will surely happen through even seeing me, and especially through serving me; speak quickly, and I shall do it for you. (35)
When Bhāvaśuddhā had thus made her request, Dharmamati, perceiving her state of mind, was immediately filled with joy. (36)
Then that virtuous and chaste goddess of Dharma said to her:
"Quickly give me your seat, which is always considered pure;
and also give me some Tulasī leaves, if you have them. (37)
"Give me fruits and flowers, if indeed they are available in your house. (38)
"Give me wood and leaves if you have them in your house;
such things as these are never found on the surface of the earth in an impure state. (39)
"Purifying things are always available; give them to me if you have them. If you indeed have sesame seeds, give them; and provide me with rice."
"Having sprinkled [them] thoroughly, I shall indeed always take up these purifiers on earth";
having spoken thus, they, their hearts moved by devotion, went to their own abode. ||41||
Having summoned her, he gave it to the virtuous woman; the virtuous woman, having sprinkled it with water, took it.
She went to the cluster of trees, and having set down the hearth there, she sat upon a seat. ||42||
Having prepared and cooked [the food], he offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation to the gods;
thereafter, he gave an offering to the cow and an offering to the spirits (bhūtas). ||43||
He offered the ancestral oblation (pitṛbali) and also offered the Nārāyaṇa oblation;
then, indeed, he proceeded to eat until the leaf-plate was completely filled.
Just as he was doing so, a certain auspicious guest arrived; having appeared in the form of a dog-eater (caṇḍāla), he requested food. 45.
The virtuous woman gave him food that provided satisfaction; having eaten, he indeed departed. Then another elderly woman arrived there and came forward.
He gave it to that virtuous woman; the chaste lady ate it, which provided her with satisfaction, and having finished eating, she sat down at the foot of the tree, taking refuge in its shade.
Performing her recitation (*japa*) with a rosary, she uttered: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā" (Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā). ||48||
The garland-maker was reciting this while performing her ritual;
having heard it, the virtuous cook then quickly questioned her. (49)
"Who are you, and why do you recite the name of the glorious Nārāyaṇa with your rosary?
What merit or other fruit arises from that? Tell me this.
Then the guest replied: "Listen, O virtuous Pāñcikā!"
By means of this mantra, one shall meet with the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||51||
Even a Cāṇḍālī who cooks dogs is born equal to the twice-born;
by this mantra of the Wielder of the Discus, she becomes a purifier for all castes. (52)

Even those who eat meat, those who drink intoxicants, those who devour raw flesh, and those who consume corpses are purified by the mantra dedicated to Kṛṣṇa as the deity; of this there is no doubt. 53.
He who is the manifest Supreme Self, the Lord of the Abode, the Puruṣottama—by union with whom even the intercalary month became stainless and purifying. (54)
Māyā is always impure, whereas Rādhikā is indeed stainless;
she was born from union with Him, and I recite her mantra. ||55||
O Lord Prabhukṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇa, and Narāyaṇa; O Lord of Māṇikī, Mādhavī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and Ramā! ||56||
Whether toward a dog, a hog, a rogue, a crow, a corpse, an outcaste, Yama, a Rākṣasa, an army, or even a traitor—the Lord behaves in the same way. (57)
Nārāyaṇa dwells in the cow, the deer, the swan, the living being, the twice-born, the preceptor, the deity, the king, the temple, and the friend. (58)
I indeed recite that mantra which is purifying, cleansing, and dark;
through the consumption of his grace and other means, I have become a devotee and purified.
"By name I am Śabalāyoni, a Cāṇḍālī who is always devoted to Viṣṇu.
Having said this, she assumed a divine form and ascended a celestial chariot.
The cook quickly requested the mantra from her;
she too, seated in the celestial chariot, recited the mantra with devotion.
Then the cook quickly took up that supreme mantra;
at that moment, the man who was her former husband appeared there in person.
He too requested that mantra; standing in her celestial chariot, she gave him the mantra, and having bestowed upon him even the name of Kṛṣṇa, she departed for heaven.
"Oh, what great fortune for Śabalā! By giving away wealth dedicated to Dharma, she attained heaven; from her, the deity of Dharma likewise obtained Manu.
Having received him, she swiftly bestowed him there upon the Cāṇḍālī for her ultimate welfare."
Having received that mantra, Cāṇḍālī indeed became composed of divine splendor.
And the man who took the fruit from the hand of Dharmadevī was then a Vaiṣṇava, a human being possessed of a physical form. || 65-66 ||
Manu himself demonstrated the purifying power of Dharmadevī;
she has sixteen syllables and has Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her own deity. (67)
Thus, indeed, compassion there is a purifier, as is the deity of Dharma;
the mantra is a purifier, and likewise, even a Cāṇḍālī woman is a purifier.
Even though she was born from a lowly womb, she was indeed purifying because she was dedicated to Kṛṣṇa;
for by union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, even one born of a base womb [is purified].
Wherever Kṛṣṇa is, that place becomes purifying;
and since he was in the womb of Dharmadeva’s wife, she thereafter became known as Dāsikā.
Having offered herself, Dharmadevī vanished;
and seeing Dharmadevī in such a state, the Caṇḍāla woman quickly [acted]. (7.1)
Once again, she who was exceedingly enchanting performed a hymn of praise there for the sake of a vision:
"Obeisance to the deity of Dharma; obeisance, obeisance to Nārāyaṇī. (72)
Salutations to you who are pleased by the devotion of the Cāṇḍālikā;
salutations to you, and salutations to you whose nature is the womb of the Śabalikā. ||73||
Salutations to you who are the very essence of mantra; salutations to you, the Great Sustainer (Mahādhātrī).
Salutations to you who are the speech of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; salutations to you. ||74||
Salutation to Śakti, to Mahāśakti, and salutation to you, the Purifier; salutation to you, the Bringer of Auspiciousness, and salutation to you, the Divine Mother. ||75||
Salutations to you, the giver of the Mālava melody, the bestower of dharma!
O Mother, grant me your vision once more for my freedom from doubt. (76)
"Having asked this, I shall surely go to the further shore of existence; of this there is no doubt.
When she had thus petitioned, the Goddess of Dharma appeared once more. 77.
Mālavānī bowed down and asked about liberation:
"How may I attain liberation? And how may I reach the further shore? (78)
"Tell me, O beloved, who are you here? Having done what will you depart?
For what purpose have you come? What unsurpassed devotion do you have for me? (79)
"Or how will my fortune unfold? Tell me, O Guru-yoginī!
Thus, O Badrikā, the disciple questioned the deity of Dharma. (4.35.80)
Dharmadevī told her everything exactly as it was: "I have come for the sake of testing you, who are so deeply devoted to your husband. (8.1)
What kind of disposition have you displayed to know her?
O Goddess, I am Dharmadeva, who has come here in this very form. ||82||
Having understood your inner disposition and your devotion to the Dharma, he was exceedingly joyful;
having recognized your welcome devotion and your service, he was exceedingly joyful. (83)
I have prepared this cooked food for you;
it is brought here for your welfare, as well as for the granting of grace and for your satisfaction in this world. (84)
Then I desired to grant you a beautiful mantra;
for mantras of that length composed by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself are purifying. (85)
Having become a sixteen-syllabled man, he has come for the sake of your grace;
though already pure, the mantra is considered even more purifying through its connection with Dharma. (86)
Having thus eaten the alms-food, that Manu then pointed out there the Cāṇḍālī Śabalāyoni, who is Māyā, the heedless one. (87)
This Māyā, which consists of all causes, has come forth as the formless essence of the multitude of all living beings; composed of every womb, it is indeed utterly defiled in every respect. 88.
She too, though pure in form through Dharma, becomes entirely pure through the practice of Kṛṣṇa-yoga; for when offered to Nārāyaṇa, she indeed bestows liberation. 89.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as those born of the lowest castes, and Cāṇḍālas—all these, whatever the wombs of beings may be upon the earth—[are purified]. (4.35.90)
Through union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, all of them attain divinity by means of devotion characterized by total self-surrender; even a Cāṇḍālī woman attains purity.
Having observed everything, you, being devoted, accepted the supreme Manu;
therefore, you have suddenly become a pure and auspicious purifier born from me here.
Through your yoga, there will be the liberation of other Cāṇḍālīs as well;
of this there is no doubt. Today you have become a Nārāyaṇī. (93)
"O Caṇḍālī, you have been purified by devotion; you have been sanctified by me through my grace.
Having been thoroughly purified by the mantra, from this point forward you shall indeed be a Brāhmaṇa. (94)
And you are Mahāmuktānikā, a dweller in the abode of Brahmā;
indeed, your entire family is purifying and belongs to the lineage of Brahmā. 95.
From this day forward, indeed, worship the Lord who is the beloved of Śrī;
abandon actions characterized by tamas and cultivate those characterized by sattva. 96.
Having obtained the beloved Lord Nārāyaṇa as your husband, go to the imperishable state;
proceed to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā together with your family. 97.
"Having attained Bālakṛṣṇa, who is Kṛṣṇa himself in person, go to the supreme state.
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, Dharmadeva vanished from sight. (98)
Having enjoyed the favor of Mālavānī and abandoned her own religious duties, she arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā together with her family. 99.
Having bathed in the water on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he drank the water;
there he beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having quickly beheld with his family the beloved, most beautiful Viṣṇu—four-armed, well-adorned, and Hari of great splendor—[he approached]. 101.
Right there, the Cāṇḍālī Mālavānikā fell into a swoon;
at that moment, a beautiful and auspicious divine chariot arrived there.
Having beheld the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
she, divine and exceedingly beautiful with a celestial body, ascended the celestial chariot together with her family.
Having meditated upon the beginningless Śrī Hari, she went to the supreme imperishable abode;
thus, O beloved of Badrī, the devotees of Mālava are dear to Hari. 104.
Then, together with her family, she became devoted to righteousness and compassion;
she attained the dharma of a great devotee through her husband, the Lord.
Sometimes the dharma to be accomplished is attained even through optional dharma;
from the recitation and hearing of this [text], the bull of merit born of dharma is obtained.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Goddess of Dharma through the Power of Dharma and Service by the Cāṇḍālī Mālavānī; the Vision of the Embodied Sixteen-Syllable Mantra; the Demonstration of the Purification of the Śabalikā Womb; and the Liberation of Mālavānī along with her Family after Her Arrival at Kuṅkumavāpikā," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Rathyāmārjanikā.
There was a virtuous woman named Kārelikā in the village of Śrīkaralāgrāma.
By birth she was a Śūdra woman, devoted to tasks such as sweeping the village streets;
her husband, moreover, performed the sweeping of the royal courtyard.
O King, since his sons indeed served as horse-keepers for the monarch,
the king was also known by the name Grāmaśāstā, though he was called Vidhamankara.
In his kingdom, the brāhmaṇa named Hitāñjali always narrated the discourse known as the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in the evening.
Having gone there, the villagers would listen to her stories in the evening;
so too did Kārelikā, her sons and others, as well as her husband.
Moreover, his daughters always listen with reverence to the most excellent stories.
They have heard it said that for living beings, delusion regarding such stories is the cause of bondage.
I am of the nature of delusion and gross, beautified by name, caste, and so forth; rich with forms, colors, and qualities, I am proud of my childhood and youth.
"This house, field, wealth, and so forth are mine;
today they are mine, tomorrow they will be mine"—such is her own sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā), and through this, delusion (moha) is heard to arise therein.
The abandonment of that [identification] is the emptiness of delusion; it is not the state of being distinct from the body and so forth.
I am the Self whose nature is Brahman; I am the divine one, free from delusion.
I have no eyes, nor do I have ears; forms, sounds, and the rest are not mine.
I have no nose, nor do I have skin; odors, touches, and the rest are not mine. (4.36.10)
I am not the tongue, nor is speech mine; I am not the organ of speech, nor the sound "bhobhava. I am neither the hands nor the feet, nor is grasping mine, nor is movement. || 11 ||
I am not the womb, nor the penis; I have no house, nor do I take delight in it. I am not the anus, nor my vital breaths and so forth, nor even the act of excretion. (12)
I am not the body, nor is the bodily aggregate mine; waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are not mine.
I am not the physical frame, nor is childhood, youth, old age, and so forth, mine.
I am neither woman nor man, nor am I a neuter; I do not exist as such.
I have no illusion, no material essence, and the qualities of passion, darkness, and goodness do not belong to me.
I have no suffering, nor do I have what is to come; I have no merit, nor do I have happiness.
I have no karma, no effort, no enjoyment, and no strife.
I have no field, house, master, wife, sons, daughters, or friends;
I have neither wealth nor the world, nor indeed do I have a family.
Therefore, for me there is neither birth nor joy, nor is there weeping;
all this is indeed fashioned by ignorance, for I am the Self, possessed of knowledge.
I possess pure egoity and a sense of "mineness" toward the Supreme Self;
whatever has been said by me exists entirely within Hari, the Lord of Śrī.
O divine one, my auspicious state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) regarding Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is always free from qualities, free from attachment, and bestows liberation. 1.9.
The vessel, the food, and even the receptacle—these are the Blessed One to me;
bondage and liberation are Hari, who is the refuge for the latent impressions of my contemplation.
Delight and cessation for me is Kṛṣṇa; in Hari, my great bliss;
Kṛṣṇa is my constant satisfaction; and Acyuta is my peace and rest. (21)
Hari is my sphere of experience, manifest even in dream and deep sleep;
within that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, my sense of "I-ness" resides.
My worldly activity is the manifestation within the eternal Śrī Paramātman;
my sleep is the fourth state (turyā) and my deep swoon is within the beloved Inner Self, the Lord. (23)
Thus, O Badarī, this story contained in the Saṃhitā was heard by him;
it was reflected upon and likewise firmly established within his own self. (24)

In the same way, the nectar of the narrative concerning one's own sons, grandsons, and masters is constantly digested at night through reflection, by virtue of association with the virtuous, even within one's own home. (25)
By him, indeed, the entire household was purified by Mārjanī;
it was truly devoid of joy and sorrow, and liberated from the snares of illusion.
It exists, overflowing with the great bliss of the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
there is no delusion, no passion, no ignorance, and no hatred.
Neither fear nor bondage exists for one who delights in the self;
therefore, Kārelikā became free from delusion and attained perfection on earth. (28)
Just as the mother is, so are the sons and daughters; the husband is likewise.
Indeed, that family is free from delusion, consisting solely of the enchantment of Kṛṣṇa.
The sage Hitāñjali, worshipping Nārāyaṇa, causes the worlds to drink the nectar of his discourse and bestows upon them mantras that grant liberation.
Out of reverence for embodied beings who desire liberation, [I offer this] which causes the removal of delusion:
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! ||3 1||
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
one should bear the trident, fish, banner, bow, wheel, and the svastika.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times;
I am Brahman, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||33||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband. (34)
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. Oṃ, I surrender myself to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; Oṃ, obeisances! ||35||
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, and to Śrī. I am called the beloved of Kṛṣṇa; Śrī Hari is my refuge. (36)
The noble Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha Svāmī is my refuge;
the noble Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha Svāmī, Lord Śrī Hari, is my refuge. (37)
Lord Kṛṣṇa, Mālatī-Nārāyaṇa, is my refuge;
thus spoke the sage Hitāñjali with joined palms, reciting many such mantras at Badarī. (38)
He indeed bestows [liberation] upon those seeking release; he makes them free from bondage. Having created the worlds of the great devotees (mahābhāgavatas), he grants them final liberation.
Indeed, many devotees of the Lord on earth—both men and women—became free from delusion through his stories and assemblies. 4.36.40.
Kārelikā, who knew the Self and was devoted to the path of liberation, that virtuous Vaiṣṇavī woman, together with her family, indeed received the mantras. 41.
Free from delusion, steadfast in Hari, a virtuous woman who delighted in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Mahāmuktānikā was born, devoted solely to Kṛṣṇa. 42.
By even the mere mention of her name, other women attained liberation; and living beings who came into contact with her broom likewise did so. (43)
All of them, having been freed from their karmas, attained liberation;
that virtuous woman worshipped the Lord, crying out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! ||44||
Having bathed and worshipped the Lord of Rādhā with ornaments, decorations, and other offerings,
one should likewise present the waving of lights (ārātrika), excellent food offerings (naivedya), fruit, and betel leaf.
Having offered water and a handful of flowers for the grace of Kṛṣṇa’s beloved, that virtuous and highly devoted lady partakes [of the food] together with her family. 46.
And while sweeping on the streets and elsewhere, upon seeing living beings, she would indeed cause them to hear the names: "O Lord Kṛṣṇa! O Hari! (47)
Even for living beings whose death is unknown, liberation may occur wherever the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is heard, O Śrī Badarī, in that sacred place. (48)
There, the karmas are burned, the messengers of Yama do not approach, the latent impressions (vāsanās) go to destruction, and the listeners attain liberation. 49.
Through association with those free from delusion, people attain freedom from delusion—even beasts, birds, living creatures, and even trees. (4.36.50)
Even those who possess only their vital breath attain freedom from delusion;
what then need be said regarding liberation upon meeting with the devotees of Viṣṇu? 51.
Indeed, even the children of Vaiṣṇava women become liberated;
so too do the water, food, house, and clothing of Vaiṣṇava women. (52)
O Badrī, if the grace of the Vaiṣṇavas is obtained even in their absence, it becomes purifying, destructive of sin, and brings about liberation for the living soul. (53)
Indeed, at the time of the departure of the vital breaths, one who has gone to see, touch, or associate with Vaiṣṇavas attains liberation. (54)
Discourses and blessings from Vaiṣṇavas always grant liberation; wherever they reside, that land is the abode of Hari. (55)
O Badrikā, the family of Śrī Hari always resides there:
Vaiṣṇavī, Kamalā, Rādhā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī. (56)
Vaiṣṇavī, Lalitā, Vāṇī, Prajñā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Jayā, Santuṣṭā, Vaiṣṇavī, Brāhmī, Kṛṣṇā, and Nārāyaṇī are thus considered. (57)
By them Kṛṣṇa, the beloved, is sustained; by them Hari is attained;
by them Kṛṣṇa is served; and by them Kṛṣṇa is made manifest. (58)
Except for Kṛṣṇa, they have no delusion, affection, or love for anyone else;
indeed, their dwelling is in the Supreme Brahman, and likewise, Śrī resides within Vaiṣṇavī.
The female deities of Viṣṇu possess eternal identity with Hari; such is their nature. Therefore, the supreme goddess Vaiṣṇavī is indeed the most purifying of women.
She is Kārṣṇī, O Badarī; she is Nārāyaṇī, she is Puruṣottamī;
likewise, she is Vāsudevī, for she is indeed considered Nārāyaṇī of Badarī.
She is the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; she is the essence of the Brahma-lake, resides at Aśvapaṭṭasara, and rules over Kuṅkumavāpikā. 62.
Vaiṣṇavī is in every way the best of sacred fords, the sustainer of all, the bestower of all merit, the giver of liberation, and the shatterer of delusion. ||63||
Thus, having become free from delusion, that virtuous woman became a *kārelikā*;
in the evening, she performs *kīrtana* in the refuge of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then indeed she goes to bed, placing Nārāyaṇa upon her lap;
and in the morning, having thus remembered Hari, the virtuous woman worships him as usual.
Then once, her five very beautiful daughters became eager to gather small badarī fruits during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
They went to all the boundaries, fields, forests, and trees;
there, at the foot of a Badarī tree, was a sage named Badarikāyana.
Then the ascetic, staying in the middle of Badarikāṣaṇḍa, was seen by the five maidens together with the great seer Śaśabindu.
Seeing those maidens, Śaśabindu went to another sacred field;
meanwhile, the seer Badrikāyana, who had been absorbed in meditation, awoke.
He saw five young maidens gathering jujube fruits; having fixed his gaze upon them, he then asked: "Who are you here? (4.36.7)
"How is it that you wander fruitlessly in the grove of Badarīs within the sacred boundary?
The maidens, having witnessed a great marvel, have approached the lord of sages. (7.1)
Seeing the gentle sage, an ascetic with matted hair who appeared emaciated, they bowed slowly and said, "We are Śūdras, sons born of the lineage of Nirmoha. (172)
"We are the daughters of Kārelikā; salutations to you, O Blessed One, here.
Having heard this, he, born of Nirmoha, desired to test them. (73)
He quickly fashioned a form equal to Indra’s, which humbled the pride of Kāma;
it was radiant like the sun, golden-hued, and captivating to the eye;
cool as the moon, and filled with splendor like the beloved of Lakṣmī.
Endowed with all ornaments, fragrance, finery, and the god of love.
It was intended to enchant the maidens, filled with the stirrings of restless senses, and produced extreme delight by means of a gentle, fragrant, and cool breeze. (76)
Indeed, she was sixteen years of age, well-nourished, firm, and endowed with vigor;
she was full of gentle smiles and her gaze was imbued with the sentiment of amorous sidelong glances. (77)
With eyes filled with showers of love and intent on the act of summoning with her lips,
she called him with all her feelings through irreversible gestures.
Possessing a beauty of form beyond compare, endowed with softness and luster, it was filled with wonder, delightful, and captivated the eyes, the mind, and the soul. (7.9)
Even while being abandoned, that renunciation was not seen to have been attained;
rather, it appeared beautiful like Kṛṣṇa, present and fulfilling all desires.
That king of sages indeed assumed such a supreme form.
But those maidens, perceiving him to be a most excellent Great Being, [honored him]. || 8.1 ||
Through the cultivation of the thought of a sentient being and with a sense of pride, they repeatedly bowed;
yet, perceiving the puppet to be illusory, they abandoned their distorted vision.
They experienced neither agitation nor instability toward that puppet.
In this perishable collection of impurities, filled with the hells of the nine gates.
Toward that which exists like one's own body, yet is produced by the transformations of the womb; which is non-self, distinct from the self, insentient, defiled, and artificial— || 8.4 ||
In that place, which was rich with all manner of impurities, foul-smelling, yet bright on the outside, they experienced not even a slight degree of delusion regarding what was beautiful or ugly. (86)
Then, seeing all those maidens free from any sign of agitation,
the sage Badrikāyana spoke these deluding words:
"I offer you a warm welcome here within this forest."
And I am the Ṛṣi who protects young maidens. ||87||
"I am capable here of fulfilling all your desires and have attained success; if you are beloved women who have reached youth and have belonged to no other before,
choose me, O beauties, for by fate this handsome man has come to you."
But a boon that is peerless, worthy of himself, and full of longing [is better]. || 89 ||
Indra, Candra, Ravi, and Śambhu—these deities are my disciples;
choose me as your suitor, for I am a husband who resembles the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Having heard this, O Badrī, those maidens, freed from delusion, said:
"Welcome, O learned one, to Brahmā, the indweller of all. (91)
"O sage who brings about the welfare of others, women are never welcome anywhere;
for young women, Janārdana is their inner self and their protector. (92)
He who is always here in the forest is the protector even of the sage;
for protection does not truly reside in the body, but rather in that which is to be protected.
I shall maintain our equality in every respect, even though she was not protected in her body;
for as long as there is wealth, it serves to fulfill the desires of those who possess longing and craving. (94)
Desires indeed arise for those who are free from longing and have no further requests; however, power and spiritual accomplishments belong to embodied beings who possess contentment.
Successes indeed arise for those possessed of delusion, but they do not exist for those free from delusion.
The individual soul is without prior origin, eternal, and always dear. (96)
The Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, is our most beloved;
He is the most beloved among all selves, and not so the body of a woman. (97)
The human body is foul-smelling, as is the female body;
what loveliness can there be in that which is inherently unpleasant and devoid of passion? (98)
Affection is indeed impermanent and subject to destruction; it is not conducive to one's welfare, like the beautiful exterior of the fruit of the *indravāruṇikā* plant. (99)
It produces a wonder at outward form for those whose eyes are deluded;
but for those who possess the inner eye, it is entirely loathsome and filled with impurity.
Whether it be a woman or a man, that which signifies impurities—namely, the humors such as phlegm and bile—is what is called "beauty" here; what beauty can there be in this? (101)
Youth is indeed rich with the flow of desires, while old age is the expulsion of them;
tranquility is liberation while living, and the bliss of Brahman is absolute liberation.
Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is the supreme; all others are considered inferior.
For one who desires hell, what excellence can there be in that which he craves? (103)
For greed for the womb leads to hell, and a longing for urine is the abode of Yama;
if such is your inclination, O Rajoke-dāraka, then your mind is indeed suited to this place.
At that time, your desire for hell has not ceased at all;
nor does your status as a seer shine forth when you have not realized the Self as Brahman.
Therefore, go from here to another great forest as you please.
For hope is said to be hell, and therein, a woman is even more so.
A man who is devoted to women is indeed far worse than a hell-being;
he is the creator of delusion for hells and likewise the one who casts others into them.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation from Delusion of the Śūdra Woman named Kārelikā through Hearing the Story, the Liberation from Delusion of Her Five Daughters, the Attainment of Enlightenment through the Sage Hitāñjali, and the Examination of Them by the Rishi Badrikāyana," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; having heard those words of the girl, the sage-king Badrikāyana [realized that] the girls were free from delusion. || 1 ||
Having become invisible, he went toward their house;
meanwhile, their brothers were engaged in the work of sweeping the street.
Having gone there, they performed the purification rites, and the sage indeed wept;
seeing him weeping, they then asked him the reason.
The sage, bearing great sorrow and drawing in his breath slightly, said:
"Alas, alas! A great misfortune has occurred in the vicinity of my hermitage."
"What has arisen today, I shall speak of here; there is nothing else worthy of being heard:
five Rākṣasas have arrived near my hut. (5)
The five daughters of Kārelikā chose those wicked men, who were endowed with artificial brilliance and were creators of great delusion.
The Rākṣasas, having quickly led her away, went to their abode at the bottom of the ocean.
"Alas! A supreme misfortune has occurred, causing extreme suffering for this devotee. || 7 ||
"I was unable to endure that; I have come here for the purpose of making this known.
Having heard this, his five brothers, together with their forces, became his companions. (8)
"Therefore, let them bring about the liberation of their sisters, these young maidens;
alas, what delusion it was that these girls became women by taking up a corpse! (9)
Having spoken thus in many ways, the virtuous one lamented in the presence of his brothers;
and those brothers, having observed this, then spoke this reply to the seer.
O Sage, by the sight of you today, our very birth has become fruitful;
for the birth of our sisters has also been made fruitful by their proximity to your hermitage.
Having obtained a vision of you, they have attained the state of being consorts;
and having been beheld by you, they have been purified for the sake of liberation as well.
Even the Rākṣasas, when gazed upon by you, the king of sages, will become great Ṛṣis through your majesty. 12.
There are exactly five maidens born of Dharma who are devoted to Viṣṇu;
they are righteous, purifying, and even grant liberation to sinners.
Through their association with those Rākṣasīs, there will be liberation for them as well;
of this there is no doubt, and no grief should be felt in that regard.
The jewel of a daughter should be given to whoever is a performer of ritual action;
for in this world, husbands and wives are born through the bond of karma.
If Rākṣasa men were inscribed upon their fortunes as their husbands, then what cause for lamentation is there when such husbands have indeed been born? || 17 ||
The maiden’s wealth belonging to another is always considered dependent upon a man; since that [wealth] arises for them at the proper time, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Indeed, all bodies are subject to transformation. || 18 ||
They are indeed composed of the elements; what cause for lamentation is there in that? || 19 ||
Whether it be a man or a woman, the transformation of urine, excrement, and so forth is the same everywhere; what cause for lamentation is there in that? (4.37.20)
If a human being does not worship Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, then even a brāhmaṇa should be known as a rākṣasa; what lamentation can there be in that? 21.
Even a Rākṣasa attains the yoga of Hari and the yoga of devotion;
he alone is a Brāhmaṇa enriched by devotion—what cause for lamentation is there in that? (22)
All gods, humans, and great sages are devoid of devotion;
they are intent on the body and are considered Rākṣasas who merely consume the body. ||23||
But those who know the Self, having renounced the enjoyments of the body and the senses, and being solely devoted to the Inner Self—they alone are considered true sages. ||24||
For those for whom all this is composed of Kṛṣṇa, whose body is Kṛṣṇa,
and who are entirely endowed with Kṛṣṇa, they are indeed said to possess the nature of a divinity.
Those men who possess latent impressions regarding form, taste, flavor, sensual desire, and the body,
and in whom the perception of duality persists— even they are, in this world, nothing but Rākṣasas.
Those maidens are full of devotion and have offered themselves to Him; they are great devotees (mahābhāgavatīs), and those who have entered into their company [attain the same].
Those men among them who were devoted to their welfare, those who were attached to them, and those who had become intent on affection for them—by fate they were not Rākṣasas. ||28||
All the wealth belonging to another may have passed into the hands of another, whether it was suddenly entrusted, or even taken away by force. ||29||
Time has passed like a line drawn in water; what cause for lamentation is there?
Such is the course of saṃsāra: a maiden is given away to another. (4.37.30)
From that, the relative degree of affection between husband and wife is indeed manifested;
when their mutual affection increases, happiness is born for them both. (31)
If affection between the two does not arise or does not increase, then that house of theirs is said to be heaven, fit for the residence of the gods.
Dejection and quarreling, as well as hell, are always present here; such indeed is the condition where the nature of Rākṣasas prevails.
Indeed, for the most part in this creation, beings possess the nature of Rākṣasas;
everything arises in one place and its nourishment is derived from material elements.
But this fruit, daughters, wealth, and so forth, is enjoyed by another; furthermore, the dealings between sisters and maternal uncles have been established here as dependent [on others]. (35)
If that wise maiden chooses a Rākṣasa out of devotion,
no one here would be able to prevent her.
O God, if a maiden is dejected, even if she has been given away, she does not desire the gods;
no one would be able to send her to a *svayaṃvara*. (37)
Wherever the mind has gone and become attached, he alone is her husband;
but where the mind is unattached, there is no ownership at all.
This being the case here in this cycle of existence, what cause for lamentation is there for us?
O Great Seer, you are grieving in vain over a calamity that is as natural as a bull. (39)
The enjoyer surely enjoys the object of enjoyment; the object of enjoyment reaches the enjoyer.
In that state, what grief, what delusion, and even what pain can there be? (4.37.40)
"Welcome to you, O Brahmin; accept this honor, such as food and other offerings.
Having accepted the madhuparka and having purified us here," 41.
O wise one, having bestowed upon us blessings of honeyed sweetness, depart as you came;
O wise one, do not fall into delusion or grief regarding the creation of this natural world.
"We shall do what is appropriate; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
O Badrikā, having been addressed thus by his brothers, the seer was filled with wonder. (43)
All the brothers became free from delusion, and she attained tranquility through her resolve;
then the sage, having approached his mother, spoke to her concerning the maidens. (44)
"Alas! Those sons of mine are merciless and pitiless, acting as enemies to their own sisters, even though the abduction of their sisters was carried out by the Rākṣasas. (45)
Even though they have been awakened by me, they do not come to my aid;
on the contrary, those who possess knowledge even restrain me.
They do not recognize even slightly the worldly nature of being a sister;
with their hearts devoid of affection, they do not hear of your misfortune.
Listen, O Mother, to this great misfortune that has occurred regarding those who have taken refuge at my feet:
the Rākṣasas have forcibly abducted your daughters. (48)
"O Mother, a most undesirable thing has occurred; release your daughters!
It is for their sake that I grieve, having come into your presence. (49)
But without their protection, they would either perish at the hands of the Rākṣasas, or those [demons] would enjoy the young women as if they were their own. (4.37.50)
Or else, these deluded ones will undoubtedly accept you as their own wives;
go quickly for your protection, and I shall follow you shortly after.
Thus addressed, O Badrikā, the mother Kārelikā [spoke] to the lord of sages, who was then lamenting with his head and both hands raised in a whistling gesture. (52)
He said: "O Sage, why indeed do you grieve for the sake of a daughter? She is not yours, nor is there a union with her; no connection exists between you. (53)
You have already crossed over saṃsāra; how is it that you wander in this state of exhaustion?
Remember your own indestructible self, which is free from saṃsāra. 54.
For those like us, even that worldly existence is considered to have some purpose;
however, for those like you, worldly existence is always regarded as being without essence.
Therefore, O King of Sages, why do you contemplate the behavior of women?
Those who are maidens will, in the course of time, become objects of enjoyment. (56)
Others, however, consider human beings, gods, or even Daityas and Rākṣasas to be husbands; indeed, men are regarded as husbands. (57)
Just as it was according to destiny, so it has come to pass, and even now it arises in that very same way;
householders are born with the momentum of their previously accumulated karma. 58.
The very man for whose sake the maiden was created remains as her husband;
indeed, one who was not created [for her] never becomes her master at any time. (59)
If there are Rākṣasa lords who have been created as their husbands, and they have obtained those women, what cause for lamentation is there in that? (4.37.60)
O wise one, by these [means], lead me along the path of Brahman; do not lead me along the path of delusion.
Do not cause me to fall into confusion regarding what belongs to others, or regarding the body, or even that which is beyond the body.
If wealth kept in one's house should belong to another,
that property belonging to another will go to the hands of another according to their destiny.
If one's own wealth has been abandoned by people,
it will surely come back into one's own hand as if it were still one's property.
Clouds born from the ocean, as well as jewels and pearls, descend from the path of the sky into the houses and kingdoms of the fortunate. (64)
Whether they be youths born in the household or maidens who have entered the dharma of ascetics, by the power of destiny they surely go to forests, wildernesses, caves, and the like. (65)
Water grows even within the hidden interior of a coconut fruit;
yet water, though being poured, does not ascend upon a lotus leaf.
Therefore, the yogas performed in previous lives result in [these conditions] for men and women;
likewise they are born as such even among maidens—what cause for lamentation is there in that? (67)
"These maidens created by me are eager for the sake of jujube fruits;
they have undertaken the journey themselves—what cause for lamentation is there on the part of others? (68)
Virginity is not certain, nor is one's mother's home;
the home of another is even less so—what cause for lamentation is there in that? (69)
Vision is not constant, and likewise examination is not constant;
there is no constant examiner. Therefore, what cause for lamentation is there? (4.37.70)
"O learned one, go to your own hut; do not fall into delusion over that [matter].
I shall do, or cause to be done, what is appropriate for the sake of my daughter. (71)
Thus enlightened, the brahmin became filled with great wonder;
his brothers and even his mother were likewise freed from delusion, like young maidens.
Then, having reflected thus with a parched mind, struck down by the outpouring of grief, he spoke to his father who was indeed engaged in his task: 73.
Becoming as if devoid of luster, he went to the father of the maidens;
with both hands, he pressed his cheeks and temples.
He shed many tears and displayed supreme sorrow;
he was then consoled by compassionate words and granted fortitude.
Gently questioned by his father regarding the cause, the Brahmin, accompanied by hiccupping, spoke while shaking his own head. (76)
"Alas, what suffering! Alas, what misery! Alas, how devoid of justice it is!
I have witnessed this pitiless cruelty toward maidens in my presence. (77)
Indeed, in my hermitage, your abduction was swiftly carried out by five powerful rākṣasas through force against those who were defenseless.
O Vibhañjana, come quickly for their protection;
you are their father and their protector, so act swiftly along with me. (79)
The street-sweeper named Vibhañjana said to that sage:
"Welcome, O King of Sages; I offer you my thanks. (4.37.80)
For one who dwells on the path of dispassion, who acts with detachment from passion, who has abandoned attachment to family, and who grieves for the failure to achieve the welfare of others; ||81||
What is lost for you, who are here in vain, fallen into delusion, delighting in yourself, and afflicted by disease, in going with the Rākṣasas to the maidens? (82)
All the Rākṣasas on earth took the hands of maidens, and likewise the Rākṣasa women on earth took the hands of men. (83)
Those who have abandoned shame, dharma, and their duties are considered Rākṣasas;
likewise, husbands and wives who remain naked are always indeed Rākṣasas.
Those who are attached to corpses, greedy for globules of urine, and who, being arrogant, unite with one another in secret—they are indeed Rākṣasas. (85)
This body is called a *rākṣasa*, for it devours the bodies of others;
O sage, depart indeed from the shore of this worldly existence.
O best of Brahmins, exert yourself for the sake of liberation from this state of being a Rākṣasa;
for what distinction is there between you and a Rākṣasa if you are intent on causing distress to others? (87)
Having attained union with karma through action, they undergo separation from those very actions;
in this saṃsāra which consists of the connection with karma, what cause for lamentation is there for you or for me? (88)
Accept this worship, O best of Brahmins, and partake of the food with devotion;
take up residence, find rest, and accept peace—do not grieve. (89)
In this world, everything arises and comes to rest under the power of time;
when that time has passed, it is surely separated from its state and does not remain.
Having received due honor as is fitting, go to your own abode;
since you have abandoned the sense of "I" and "mine," how can sorrow remain within you? (91)
This body is indeed merely an object of enjoyment, the locus of experience for the eternal Self;
the Self experiences it by regarding this body or another body as its own. (92)
Experience is said to be supreme delusion, while non-experience is free from delusion;
for experience is indeed considered to be the direct perception of pleasure and pain alone. (93)
O Sage, let there be no [attachment] for you who are liberated; do not join me to that either.
I am stainless, I am not [a transmigrating being], and I am the shatterer of delusion. (94)
"O maiden, I have no delusion; how then does it exist here? Your deluding power, being unperceivable, makes me suspect it is artificial. (95)
"You display sorrow here; go, O yogin, as you came.
I shall provide the appropriate protection; may there be well-being for you from me in every way. (96)
Having spoken thus, the Śūdra Bhañjana offered them food and other provisions;
meanwhile, those maidens there [offered] ripe badarī fruits.
Having gathered together, they all returned quickly with serene minds;
they were questioned by their brothers, mother, father, and likewise by other people.
When they heard that Badarikāyana had been attacked by Rākṣasas,
and knowing him to be a speaker of falsehoods and likewise fallen from the dharma of a sage, [they departed].
"Since you have made an inquiry into what is impossible, become mute now!
When this was said, the virtuous man became mute through those censures of his speech. (4.37.100)
She mentally prayed for the daughters of Nirmoha;
she also requested her mother, father, and brothers for their consent.
Devoted to compassion, upholders of dharma, and solely dedicated to their beloved Kṛṣṇa,
all those householders rendered the sage speechless.
The sage realized that all were completely free from delusion;
having himself abandoned delusion through his inquiry, he bowed down again and again.
Casting aside pride, he quickly went to offer worship out of fear of punishment;
thus, O beloved of Badrī, O Goddess, [did] the maiden, her brothers, and her father.
Their mother was devoid of delusion and became devoted to Kṛṣṇa; Nirañjana was liberated, free from delusion, and without worldly effort.
And those five brothers of yours are known by name as being without expectation;
they are formless, nameless, without interval, and sinless.
And Nijānandā—these five are their names;
they are all [the daughters] of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
And at the nineteenth Janmajayantī festival, they departed from there,
having obtained Lord Kṛṣṇa as their Lord, with their hopes fulfilled and their desires satisfied.
And by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they became possessed of divine forms.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion and having brought him down within one's own heart.
Having arrived in their celestial chariots at the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
they went swiftly to the supreme imperishable abode by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Thus, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, through devotion to Bālakṛṣṇa, the householder Kārelikā attained union with the path of Badarikā. || 111 ||
Having attained a divine state and reached freedom from delusion,
they all went to the supreme liberation through devotion to the beloved Kṛṣṇa.
From reciting this, from hearing it, from reflecting upon it, and even from listening to it,
both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall indeed come to pass through a mere fragment of the grace of Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Sage Badrikāyana’s Muteness, the Cessation of the Curse, and the Liberation of the Five Maidens, the Five Sons, and the Husband, during the Test of Nirmohitva of the Śūdra Woman Mārjayitrī Kārelikā," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badrī, to the story of Yantrakartrī;
it took place on the bank of the river named Kṛṣṇā, in the city called Dvijavāṭī.
In former times, there was a virtuous woman who was a wife, a householder, possessed of husband and sons, as well as daughters, friends, and kinsmen. || 2 ||
Possessing wealth and grain, her beautiful mansion was filled with prosperity;
she was devoted to Hari, steadfast in dharma, and a true yoginī.
Endowed with all auspiciousness, devoted to the service of the virtuous, free from violence and other such evils, rich in good conduct and righteousness, and established in truth; (4)
She delights in honoring the gods, guests worthy of respect, and the performance of hospitality;
she is devoted to her own spiritual practice, yet remains free from desire for illusion and its products.
She worships the Blessed One, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama;
every day at dawn, having bathed in the Kṛṣṇā river, she performs the auspicious worship of the deity.
Having prepared the food for the elders, having paid homage to them, and having worshipped her husband with devotion,
she took the water from her husband’s feet and applied it to her mouth, head, and body.
Then, placing a *tulasī* leaf from the grace of the deity in her mouth,
the beautiful woman partook of milk for the sake of obtaining sons and other blessings.
By name she was Queen Gomatī, devoted to the service of cows; her husband was named Nayarāja, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu.
Sons, daughters, kinsmen, and all others are indeed the best of Vaiṣṇavas;
they worship the Supreme Self and serve the assembly of holy men.
Having abandoned the binding illusion, they perform what is beneficial for themselves; devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, they abide in the performance of righteous deeds. || 11 ||
But for the sake of their livelihood, they indeed [made] iron implements used for sugarcane juice as well as oil-presses. (12)
They composed other such works according to their style;
they sustained their livelihood with the wealth obtained from the sale of those.
All those highly fortunate people truly proceed [toward liberation] when they employ a furnace for the purpose of melting metallic ores.
Living beings are also burned there, and that becomes a sin; likewise, masses of sugarcane are crushed by machines for the sake of obtaining juice. (15)

Therein, worms and other insects within sugarcane stalks are tormented while mixed with the juice; likewise, [beings] are tormented during the pressing of sesame seeds and the crushing of oilseeds. (16)
Even living beings are crushed in the cotton-pressing machine;
countless insects and other creatures die there. Indeed, that sin consists of such violence.
To those who inflict pain, those who operate machines, those who provide the raw materials, those who construct the machines, and likewise to the owners of the machines. ||18||
For violence arises toward servants as well as toward laborers;
likewise, O Badrī, a share of sin is produced for those who operate the machines.
They are defiled by that sin and go to terrible hells;
yet these are great devotees of the Lord, devoted solely to their birth and their duties.
Even though all of them consist of merit, they nevertheless partake in sin;
for there is constant injury to innumerable insects. (21)
The sin of the makers of machines is always immeasurable;
it surely comes upon them, and thus their liberation remains barred by a bolt.
The great sin of one who attacks with intent to kill is considered to cause the destruction of everything.
But those who manufacture machines are tainted by the sins of those machines, just like an assassin.
Through sins, the destruction of the lineage and the loss of prosperity also occur;
having died, they become ghosts and even afflict their kinsmen. (24)
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, in the course of time, consumption (rājayakṣmaka) afflicted the family of the city's kings and others among the artisans. ||25||
"This disease has taken up residence and has brought people to a state of emaciation. But Gomatī reflected thus: "How can there be sickness among my devotees? (26)
Or how could the affliction of decay and disease prevail against devotion to the Blessed One? How is it that [even] children, the elderly, women, and others are overwhelmed by illness? (27)
"This must be asked of one who knows the Vedas and understands destiny in every respect.
Having reflected thus, he went to the brahmin named Prabhātabodhin.
Then the goddess Gomatī asked him about the cause of his illness;
observing that it was the proper time for questioning, the Brahmin spoke of the fruit arising from the yantra.
The injury to living beings caused by a machine also accrues to the agent; likewise, it transfers to the maker as well as the one who employs it. (4.38.30)
The status of a mistress (svāminī) transfers to the driver, the husband, the one engaged in the action, the observer, and likewise to the supervisor as well. (31)
"O Gomatī, your family is indeed the makers of machines;
therefore, the sin resulting from the injury of insects and other creatures always accrues to them. (32)
A means for his deliverance must be undertaken; otherwise, there will be no doubt that the destruction of the lineage will occur. Do as you wish, O beautiful lady. (33)
Having heard this, O Badrikā, she said to the brāhmaṇa who had awakened at dawn:
"Grant us an expiation by which our deliverance may be achieved. (34)
Prabhātabodha said to her: "First, there must be the restraint of the lower lip;
only then is penance granted, which bears fruit and not otherwise. (35)
Abandoning the construction of mechanical devices and the sale or purchase of clods of earth and the like, he may even dig into the ground for the sake of maintaining his life. (36)
Therefore, by means of this mechanical contrivance, the portion of one's sin is indeed obstructed;
new sin is not produced, and you must perform atonement for that which has already arisen. (37)
Accompanied by your family, perform a pilgrimage indeed to the Godāvarī,
the Narmadā, the Tāpī, and likewise the Sābhramatī.
Then [he visited] Śatruñjayā, Hariṇī, Bhadrā, Gomatī, Svarṇalekhā, Kuṅkumavāpī, and Aśvasarovara. ||39||
Puṣkara, Sārasa-tīrtha, Yamī, the purifying Gaṅgā,
Sarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Brahmaputrā, and likewise Indradyumna.
Having visited the Tāmraparṇī, the Kāverī, Lake Pampā, and the ocean—these sacred fords in due order—become free from sin, O beautiful lady. 41.
"The destruction of evil and the eradication of disease will come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this, the goddess Gomatī then reflected. 42.
For those with hair on their bodies, this [practice] is indeed possible; there is no need for wandering to sacred fords (tīrtha).
Wandering for a long duration, carried out over a great length of time, is difficult to achieve. (43)
Therefore, O wise one, show me another means that destroys sin, by the performance of which the fruit of all sacred fords may also be obtained. (44)
The expiation shall arise as a destroyer of consumption (rājayakṣman);
there shall be happiness for the family, and there shall be no loss of prosperity.
Having heard of this very simple yet highly efficacious atonement, the brahmin declared that service to the virtuous was the appropriate remedy there, acting as a great medicine.
O Gomati, just as you are capable, just as you are intent upon transformation,
and just as you belong to Viṣṇu, even so shall I demonstrate the expiation.
From this day forward, however, may she constantly serve the virtuous, together with her family, full of devotion, endowed with affection, and free from doubt. (48)
May you perform whatever divine service is possible with divine intellect and divine vision, so that the virtuous may become well-disposed toward you. (49)
By means of the body, mind, speech, and even through actions and the senses;
by means of prosperity, wealth, jewels, and the like, as well as by the offering of food and clothing. ||4.38.50||

With the offering of beds and furnishings, as well as with the massaging of feet and other services, both in public and in private, she should serve like a female slave and likewise like a male slave. ||51||
With daughters and sons, with children, the elderly, and family members;
with daughters-in-law, gifts of houses, cows, and even through the offering of one's own self. (52)
Let them perform service toward the virtuous and even toward saintly women in every way;
for through self-surrender and other means, service to the holy is indeed the medicine.
For by daily service and unobstructed devotion performed without doubt, the virtuous indeed become gracious. (54)
Impelled by their grace, the holy ones bestow blessings:
"May you possess wealth, sons, health, and may your prosperity increase. (55)
May you always be possessed of happiness, joy, and every festival;
may obstacles depart far from you, and may your enemies go to their destruction. (56)
May there be the dissolution of your sins; may you also become a mountain of merit.
May it be glorious, full of splendor, highly meritorious, and the destroyer of mental anguish and disease. (57)
May there be for you union with the beloved and the destruction of the disliked;
may you enjoy the divine fruit of serving the virtuous, both in this world and the next.
May you possess eternal devotion toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and may you offer yourselves to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all and the Supreme Master. (59)
May the virtuous dwell in your home, and may the virtuous dwell in your garden; may the virtuous dwell in your heart, and may the virtuous dwell even in your individual soul.
May those virtuous ones who dwell within my body and senses be before me when questioned;
may those virtuous ones always be below, above, or at my side.
May the virtuous ones be present during waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
while traveling, journeying abroad, dwelling, sitting, lying down, and standing still. (62)
May virtuous people be present during yawning, sneezing, rejoicing, and even at festivals; likewise, during ritual acts, play, and sorrow. (63)
May the virtuous be my companions and protectors, and may they be my kinsmen;
may the virtuous remove the suffering of Yama and likewise remove the suffering caused by fate.
May those who destroy [the fruits of] karma bring you happiness;
may the virtuous be the destroyers of afflictions caused by external beings. (65)
May the virtuous ones, devoted to the Blessed One, be protectors of our lives;
may they be performers of worldly journeys here, and also performers of the supreme journey.
May those who perform the great pilgrimage be endowed with all things from every side;
thus shall the virtuous offer this hymn of twelve verses. (67)
By the recitation of this and by these services, protection will be secured;
beginning immediately today, [build] a most beautiful hall for the virtuous.
Have the temple of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa-mūrti constructed;
by that, your obstacles will perish without delay, of this there is no doubt. (69)
Although you are a great devotee and your family is devoted as well, nevertheless,
through service to the holy men (sādhus), it will become preeminent above all.
Neither Indra, nor Rudra, nor Yama, nor the Creator of the Universe;
neither Viṣṇu, nor even Time, nor Dharma, nor religious observance, nor austerity [is its cause]. (71)
Even Nārāyaṇa himself is not able to accomplish that which is so difficult to bear;
yet the virtuous, who are indeed superior to Kṛṣṇa, are truly capable of accomplishing it.
Everything intended by the virtuous should be performed for the sake of the Supreme Self;
that which is intended by Kṛṣṇa is not something merely devised by the virtuous.
Service to the virtuous is meritorious, for association with the virtuous bestows merit;
the sight of the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are indeed mountains of merit. (74)
From the nails to the crest of their hair, these virtuous ones are purifiers with divine forms;
indeed, even a particle of dust from the body of a saint is truly purifying.
Now, [let it be] as toward a husband, as toward a wife, as toward a son, and even as toward wealth; as toward a daughter-in-law, as toward one's parents, as toward a guru, and as toward Hari. (76)
Likewise, affection should always be cultivated toward the virtuous and noble women with sincerity;
service rendered with faith accomplishes all goals. ||77||
The virtuous are indeed to be fed, honored, and satisfied;
the virtuous are to be gladdened, served, and propitiated. (78)
Indeed, the virtuous are to be honored, protected, and gratified;
indeed, the virtuous are to be beheld, touched, and bowed down to. ||79||
The virtuous should always be honored, upheld, and meditated upon;
for through association with the virtuous in this world, one attains heaven and eternal liberation.
The virtuous are exceedingly gracious; they are indeed wish-fulfilling gems, and the virtuous are always like celestial kalpa-trees and inexhaustible vessels. 81.
The cow of desire is indeed virtuous, for those who have Kṛṣṇa as their form are truly virtuous;
association with them is liberation, and the company of the good brings one across the ocean of worldly existence.
Practice that [conduct] which brings about the destruction of disease; may it be well with you, and may you possess freedom from illness and long life. (83)
Having been addressed thus, O Badrikā, Queen Gomatī honored that most excellent brāhmaṇa,
and having returned to her own home, she related everything in its entirety.
Then the husband, the man, and the family members, all with concentrated minds,
separately constructed a single house consisting of excellent halls.
The virtuous come there and serve them with supreme devotion,
offering food, clothing, wealth, and various articles, such as those from the Gomatī river.
Regarding the virtuous as being of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa and as purifiers, the family members and others served them with the prescribed dispositions and actions. (87)
Then, having received the blessings of those virtuous ones, they likewise became purifiers;
gradually, they began to ascend toward the destruction of disease.
In the hearts of the virtuous dwells the Lord, the Master who is without beginning or end;
having recognized their service as the supreme devotion, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself [bestows grace]. 89.
Having become a virtuous man named Kṛṣṇāyana and having made his wife a virtuous woman, he then went to her city and her home.
Having gone to the site of Sādhuśālā, honored by Gomatī and others, Kṛṣṇāyana, having performed worship and received a welcome, took up residence there. ||9 1||
Then, indeed, service was rendered to those two in many ways by the family, with various riches, garments, food, and other forms of worship. (92)
Just as Hari desired, so did they give;
the Blessed One became pleased by the service of the men and women. (93)
The Lord, who was being attended to in every way— whether on her bed, at her meal, or while traveling—
urged that woman to grant him a boon, and she did so at that very moment.
He requested it for the sake of freedom from disease, for the sake of prosperity, for the sake of liberation, for the sake of serving the virtuous, and also for the sake of union with Hari. (95)
Hari said, "So be it; may all this come to pass for you. Indeed, by drinking the water from the big toe of Hari, all shall be purified. (96)
Then, at that moment, the disease of consumption (rājayakṣmā) appeared in embodied form;
by the command of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, it suddenly departed in haste. 97.
Having bowed down, he went to Kailāsa; his family became free from disease, their hearts blossomed, their faces radiant with joy, and they found a source of auspiciousness. 98.
Then Kṛṣṇāyana Kṛṣṇa gave his own mantra to them:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (99)
He gave his own form, consisting of the lineage of Kṛṣṇāyana;
he granted a divine vision of himself as the four-armed Nārāyaṇa.
Having beheld the Lord of Gods, the beloved of Śrī, the Supreme Self, the Infallible One,
the people of Gomatikā became gracious and fulfilled.
Free from sin, masses of merit, divine, and intent upon liberation,
they all bowed down, offered worship, and drank the water from the feet of Hari.
They partook of the prasāda and worshipped Acyuta;
all the women, including the virtuous daughters of Śrī and others, performed the rites of honor.
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, having restored them to health,
that Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa quickly vanished from sight.
Then they too, having gathered together, departed from there for the sake of pilgrimage,
during the twentieth anniversary festival of the victory of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
They arrived at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake during their pilgrimage,
as well as the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the auspicious abode of Lomaśa.
Having bathed and performed the rites prescribed for sacred fords, one should behold and worship Mādhava— the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, dear to Him, known as Kṛṣṇāyana and Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having served the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with devotion,
they then dwelt right there in the realm known as Akṣara for the remainder of their lives.
By taking refuge at the feet of Hari, all those machine-makers became dear to Hari;
they attained divine bodies and became liberated while living, beloved of the Lord. (109)
Always remaining steadfast in the words of Hari-kṛṣṇa, they all then departed for the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma) by Hari’s command, seated upon celestial chariots.
All of them indeed reached the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa by means of celestial chariots;
thus, O Goddess Badrikā, the Blessed Lord delivered them. 11.11.11.1.
From reciting, hearing, and reflecting upon this, there is the destruction of sins;
heaven and liberation shall indeed be swiftly attained through the power of Lord Kṛṣṇa. 1.12

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Śūdra woman named Gomatī, who was a maker of yantras, along with her family, was cured of consumption through service to the virtuous and attained the Lord in a perfected form, thereby achieving liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the liberation of the two rogues;
they were residents of Dhūtārapura and were born of the Cāmaṭha caste.
Devoted to Nārāyaṇa, there was a woman named Kanakāṅgadā;
she possessed a husband and sons, daughters, and brothers with their families.
She lived near the city, dwelling in the shade of a cart, and she was engaged in the buying and selling of bulls and calves. (3)
She was intent on the restoration and repair of worn-out implements;
she was rich in the business of buying and selling, and likewise skilled in managing her household affairs.
Even though she was a devotee of Hari, she remained possessed of the nature of her birth, characterized by roguery;
indeed, she continued to be engaged in falsehood, deceit, untruth, and guile.
Devoted to deception in speech, action, and mind,
they delude others in whatever way possible, even while displaying abundant results.
Having generated trust in many ways, he then practices deception;
whatever wealth, silver, and gold he has obtained through that deception, [he uses]. (7)
Carried swiftly by the mind, she proceeds indeed to another village, along with her cart,
through pleasant regions, fields, and even garden groves.
Karmasandhinī steals food through theft;
even such as she is, she frequents the roads at night where four paths meet.
One passes the time within the boundary by means of the shadow of a cart; if at that time some monk or nun should arrive there— 4.39.10.
Having given him suitable food, she would then eat herself;
thus was she devoted to guests, honoring the mendicant as Kṛṣṇa himself.
Thinking him to be the mendicant Nārāyaṇa, she even offered him hospitality—
massaging his feet at night and attending to his body by day.
Having offered water, flowers, and other such items, she then partakes of her meal;
thus she remains devoted to service, observing the rules for the worship of the mendicant.
Being present before the mendicant, that wise woman, being entirely free from sin, candidly reveals her own deceit for the sake of his innocence. (14)
She, however, knew from her teacher that she must respectfully report her own task to the virtuous one by name, through the propitiation of Carvankara. 15.
One should speak what is true, whether it be secret or public;
whether it be unjust or consistent with justice, sinful or meritorious, or even deceptive. (16)
Deceit, impurity, unwholesomeness, as well as affliction, theft, and plunder—these should always be reported to the venerable Guru. (17)
Whether it be censurable or praiseworthy, whether it is fit to be spoken or unfit to be spoken—all this should be reported to the venerable Guru for the sake of purification. (18)
In this way, the agent attains freedom from sin and purity;
bondage does not arise at all, and the fruit of sin is not produced. (19)
Likewise, from what has been acquired— whether by righteous or unrighteous means— one should always give to the teacher, to a guest, and to a mendicant.
By that, faultlessness arises and one dispels evil;
however, one who eats without having offered [the food] is defiled by sin.
One who eats food that has been offered is not defiled by sin, even when acting as a robber among robbers for the sake of his own belly or for the sake of his family. (22)
Defilement does not arise at all if [the disciple] offers [himself] to the Guru;
having become faultless thereby, the Guru—bestower of liberation—is therefore to be served. (23)
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; the Guru alone is Janārdana;
the Guru alone is the Creator; and the Guru alone is the supreme goal. ||24||
The Guru alone is fire and the sun; the Guru alone is the giver of light.
The Guru alone is supreme merit; the Guru is righteousness, happiness, and wealth. (25)
The Guru is heaven, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is Śambhu, and the Guru is the vow;
the offering to the Guru is the supreme merit; therefore, one should offer everything to the venerable Guru.
Indeed, a sin committed elsewhere is destroyed in the presence of a guru;
one must not commit sin against a guru, for the guru is indeed the supreme refuge. ||27||
Indeed, Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, does not appear even on earth;
rather, it is the Guru, the upholder of truth, who appears upon the surface of the world. (28)
From association with the virtuous, freedom from sin arises; therefore, the virtuous—the glorious gurus—should be served for the sake of purification. (29)
Indeed, saṃsāra is impure, while Hari, the Guru, is pure therein;
through union with the Guru, all bodily impurity is dissolved.
Mental impurity also dissolves through constant devotion to the guru;
and by the remembrance of the guru’s name, the self attains purification. (3.1)
Through the offering of all things to the Guru, there arises purity;
by means of the Guru's yoga, men and women become purified upon this earth. (32)
The form of the Guru is the form of Hari, the purifier of sinners in this world;
therefore, association with the virtuous should be sought by sinners for the destruction of their sins.
She indeed obtained such supreme knowledge from her guru;
therefore, free from hypocrisy, she serves virtuous people. (34)
Indeed, that entire family performed service for the virtuous;
the saint, whose wealth was his beautiful feet, gave her the mantra of Hari.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
He bestowed a divine form and likewise bestowed knowledge consisting of service to the guru. ||36||
Thus, by the command of her guru, Kanakāṅgadā constantly conducts herself;
devoted to the service of her guru, she is daily intent upon the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa. (37)
For the sake of destroying her deceit and sin, she constantly serves Śrī Hari and the Guru with devotion;
yet she also constantly serves hunger and thirst.
Indeed, she never ate water, flowers, fruit, or vegetables without first performing worship to her guru and offering the food to him. (39)
Having thus undertaken this discipline, she remained devoted to her guru;
then one day, for seven days, the guru went into another forest.
Even if some virtuous guest has arrived at her house,
that chaste woman, having first worshipped Hari, gazes longingly toward the garden.
Hungry and thirsty, she gazes at the gatekeeper day and night; though the virtuous man has not come for seven days, even though he has arrived, he has not come.
O Badrikā, that virtuous woman who possesses firm devotion does not eat food obtained through his grace without first giving some to a holy person; what then can be said of others?
Nor did she drink the water without first offering it to the virtuous man;
at that time, he was Ādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, born as Śrī Kṛṣṇa from among the cowherds.
The omniscient Antaryāmī, having become a virtuous man, arrived wearing saffron robes and carrying a neck-garland and a water-pot. ||45||
Carrying a water-pot at his waist and holding a small bag of ashes and other items, he would call out:
"Nārāyaṇa! Hara! Viṣṇu! Kṛṣṇa! Śrī Bhagavān! (46)
The glorious Bālakṛṣṇa cried out loudly, saying, "Victory!
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Padmāvatī, O Master! (47)
"O protector of the righteous, O Lord who protects those who seek refuge!
Reciting this mantra to Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, he arrived at Śakaṭī. 48.
Having placed his seat—a *pāvaṭī* made of *jolī* grass—upon the ground, he said, "Hare! Hare!
and sat down, saying, "May there be victory for the Wielder of the Discus. (49)
May you be happy, O lady of golden limbs, and may your husband also be happy;
may your family, sons, and daughters likewise be happy.
Thus, with an even mind and intent upon offering blessings, he thought: "This virtuous man has come to my house by the turn of fate. (51)
Realizing this, the virtuous woman of golden limbs rose quickly; having bowed down, she then offered him an auspicious seat, pure water, and indeed various fruits.
She gave him fresh food and fanned him with a fan;
she also offered flowers and tulasī leaves with devotion. (53)
"O virtuous one, take your meal and accept the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
receive the bath, the water for rinsing the mouth, and the various kinds of food and drink. (54)
"O holy one, grant me your blessing so that my sin may be destroyed;
by the power of my good fortune, I have encountered one who possesses the very form of Nārāyaṇa. (55)
"O virtuous one, take up residence in my home, accept my service, and receive [this mantra]:
Om, obeisance to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Holy One. (56)
To the yogi, the all-knowing, the protector of devotees, the one who effects the upliftment of the lowly, and the abode of compassion for the poor and the helpless; ||57||
Salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, whose nature is that of the saintly;
salutations to you, the child Gopāla, who is the joy of Kaṃbharā.
Salutation to Him who sports with Rādhā, salutation to the Lord of Kamalā; salutation to the Inner Controller, salutation to the True Being who is devoted to His devotees. 99.
O Inner Self, O Supreme Self, be forever gracious;
service to the virtuous is service to you—O Nārāyaṇa, accept it! 4.39.60
Thus, though distinct in their dispositions, that Kanakāṅgadā gave [her wealth],
and all those sons and daughters gave whatever objects they desired.
Cārvaṅkara also performed service for the virtuous;
with sweet speech, he joyfully massaged their feet. (62)
Thus, at that time, the entire family, including those born of the Cāmaṭha lineage,
became devoted to service, observing a fast for seven days.
Having properly fed the virtuous man and likewise given him water to drink,
and having served him as was appropriate, one should thereafter follow his instructions.
With true devotion, they all indeed accepted the food and water offered as a gift of grace;
moreover, they all attended upon the holy man while he was reclining.
They performed services such as massaging his feet until morning;
then in the morning, the holy man said, "O Āmaṭhas, choose a boon."
