I am pleased by your discipline, devotion, and service to the virtuous;
I am pleased by your inner disposition and do not take your faults into account.
Under the influence of compassion, I destroy all great sins, even the most heinous, as well as various forms of deceit and every kind of deception. (68)
Deceitfulness in every respect, as well as treachery toward those who trust one;
likewise, the sin of theft and the transgression arising from the misappropriation of wealth. (69)
"Under the influence of compassion, I shall destroy all this impurity," he said;
and though appearing in the form of a holy man, he instantly assumed his true physical form.
And for a moment he became four-armed in the form of Nārāyaṇa—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord of Śrī.
The Lord of Śrī Priyā, Mādhavī, Rādhā, and Māṇikī Lalitā, adorned with all divine ornaments, appeared instantly. ||72||
Pervaded by divine splendor and a vessel of divine beauty,
he then quickly manifested his divine and enchanting form.
Then he vanished from that form, and thereafter Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, impelled by compassion, appeared in the form of a virtuous man. ||74||
Then all of them, for a moment, became bewildered, sinless, and possessed of divine vision;
overcome by devotion and under the power of Kṛṣṇa, they spoke with sweet, faltering voices. (75)
Having reached the further shore of existence, they all indeed sought the destruction of suffering;
they sought refuge in Śrī Hari for liberation in the imperishable state. (76)
He entreated him, saying, "Pardon all my sins," and he entreated him, saying, "O Kṛṣṇa, effect my deliverance from the multitude of evils. (77)
Then, O beloved of Badrī, the Lord Śrī Harivallabha himself caused them to drink the water from his feet and indeed granted them divine bodies.
Then a divine celestial chariot belonging to the attendants of Vaikuṇṭha arrived there,
and everyone ascended it with great joy.
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme imperishable abode, they indeed went to the dwelling at the feet of Śrī Hari through their most intense devotion. 4.39.80.
There, Hari, appearing in the form of a holy man, quickly vanished in an instant.
Thus it was, O Śrī Badarī, that Kanakāṅgī and Cāmaṭhī were his devotees. (8–1)
Even though she was a rogue, she attained liberation along with her family, purified by her devotion;
likewise, through hearing and reciting this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.
There shall be the destruction of sin, and even the prosperity of heaven may arise; the fruit of serving the virtuous is realized directly, and even the attainment of Kṛṣṇa may occur. ||83||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of the Lord and Liberation through the Form of a Holy Man by Kanakāṅgadā, a member of the Cāmaṭhī caste, along with her family, through the company of a saint and supreme devotion," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this likewise purifying story concerning a female gambler, a woman named Bhāṇavāṇī.
In ancient times, on the beautiful bank of the Indus river, in the city of Śarkarāpattana,
there lived men and women born of a lineage of experts in the art of gambling.
They know many ways of gambling in the city of Śaṅkāra;
in gambling, women generally achieve victory, there is no doubt. (3)
In the land of Sindhu, the subjects were of such a nature, being devoted to gambling;
the king, the royal courtiers, and the king’s servants were likewise the same.
The subjects were generally skilled in the art of gambling;
both the poor and the wealthy indeed fell into ruin repeatedly through gambling.
The king of the Sindh regions, known by the name Rāyahari,
indeed holds gambling festivals every year with invited kings.
Kings from other kingdoms, experts in gambling, arrive;
they play with many jewels and such, both winning and losing.
They attain abundant gain and acquire kingdoms;
then those kings become lords of the realm, and their subjects are born without enemies within the kingdom.
And those overcome by the practice of gambling are born with perverted dispositions;
at that time, O passionate lady, there will be loud cries of "bhāṇa" among those skilled in gambling.
She was renowned for victory and steadfastness; wherever she stood, there indeed was victory.
For his sake, she sat down at the dice-game as his representative.
His victory indeed occurs through the snares that follow in accordance with him;
at the time of gambling, he brings about the loss of wealth for many. (11)
The lord of Śarkarānagara protected that Bhāṇavāṇī; indeed, that man always kept her in his own residence for the purpose of gambling and playing dice, providing her with palatial dwellings,
food, drink, and the like, as well as garments, ornaments, and decorations.
She was attended by gardeners, carriage drivers, and others, as well as male and female servants.
The king always regarded her with respect, as if she were his own queen,
even though she was born of a lowly family and descended from a humble constellation, yet was by birth a Kṣatriya.
And by virtue of their shared status and his acquisition [of her], he regards her as a queen;
she too, having abandoned pride, behaves toward the king like a maidservant. (15)
The virtuous lady behaves toward the queen like a servant; therefore, that beautiful woman is an object of favor for both the queen and the king. (16)
Even though she has a husband and sons, she occupies the royal bed;
King Rāyahari, having considered her virtue and gain, [did so]. (17)
Thinking her to be his own, he even served his maidservant as if she were a noble lady;
thus, having obtained the king's patronage, she flourished with fame and wealth.
Then, together with his family, he joyfully took up residence in the royal palace;
he accepted the acquisition of the kingdom and enjoyed ever-new pleasures. (19)
Then once, King Rāyahari, the lord of Śrīśarkara,
summoned the auspicious king Hayodara.
In his own residence, for the purpose of gambling at dice, [he summoned] one named Koṭirāya;
and Koṭirāya, having suddenly heard the invitation to the gambling and other activities, [arrived].
He also arrived joyfully at the palace of Rāyahari,
where there was a gambling match in a most splendid assembly.
The king Rāyahari, full of eagerness, made the arrangements;
at that time, Bhāṇavāṇī became the representative of Rāyahari. 23.
Having previously established herself in gambling, that passionate woman seized the dice;
at that time, other kṣatriyas as well as ministers and merchants did the same.
Those observing the gambling took their seats upon great thrones in the assembly hall;
thereupon, a game of dice began, characterized by mutual deception.
Then Koṭirāya said: "This golden necklace, adorned with jewels, is my neck-ornament; it is the wealth staked here in this wager. (26)
"What kind of equivalent payment is there for this? Make a mark on the document.
Rāyahari then said, "Whatever gems I possess are here. (27)
"Take these necklaces and wealth as well; may you be victorious!
Then, in the game of dice, he openly uttered these words.
"O Koṭirāja, this has been won by you"; thus spoke Satyabhāmā with a clear mind.
Then Koṭirāja, right there, [gave her] a necklace beautiful with a thousand gold coins.
He placed the casket down and said, "Conquer my wealth! "A crore has been won by you," replied Bhāṇavāṇī. (4.40.30)
Then, with a serene mind, Koṭirāya deposited one hundred thousand gold coins and ten hundred thousand silver coins. (31)
Bhāṇavāṇī cast forth nooses and declared, "Victory!
Then she [cast] supreme jewels and even supreme pearls. (32)
King Koṭirāja indeed released ten million coins as a stake;
that king also released diamonds worth ten million as his wager.
Having cast aside his speech and his nooses, he declared, "It is won!
Then King Koṭirāja [offered] his own ornaments made of gold.
There he established as stakes jewels set with diamonds, valued at millions, billions, and more,
as well as gems of incalculable worth.
The nooses of Bhāṇavāṇī, cast aside by the gods, turned away from him;
indeed, for the sake of victory over Rāya, they fell [upon him] with supreme joy. (36)
In the assembly, they produced a great and inconceivable wonder:
even Bhāṇavāṇī was defeated, as was Kalāvatī. (37)
King Rāyahari won the most excellent wealth;
he staked all of that as well as everything else he possessed. ||38||
He was defeated and fell into grief for even a moment;
thereafter, he [took] his own jewels, gems, and pearls as well. (39)
Diamonds and golden ornaments, caskets fashioned from jewels,
and a divine golden chariot yoked with four elephants.
Having established the stakes, he said, "Let us play with this [dice];
and having heard this, the son of Kuntī also placed ten million as his wager. ||41||
Then Koṭirāya, having attained victory, released his nooses;
thereafter, Rāyahari gave him there a hundred beautiful female slaves.
Eagerly, Paṇa adorned [them] with the splendor of all ornaments;
having cast down ten million arrows, he declared, "They are conquered! (43)
Then Rāyahari, eager for the wager, adorned a thousand servants there with all kinds of ornaments.
Having stationed hundreds of millions of nooses, he declared, "They are conquered.
Then Rāyahari [stationed] thousands of excellent elephants. 45.
He also gave excellent elephants adorned with golden trappings and mother-of-pearl ornaments, wearing golden garlands,
as well as one thousand female elephants for each [male] elephant.
Having cast down his nooses, Koṭirāya declared, "They are conquered!
Then Rāyahari [bestowed] golden chariots numbering one thousand.
In that gambling hall, he also zealously placed golden chariots yoked to elephants, adorned with gold, jewels, and gems,
as well as golden wheels.
Having cast down his nooses, Koṭirāya declared, "They are conquered!
Then Rāyahari, there, [encountered] horses clad in variegated armor.
Eagerly, he adorned a hundred thousand horses from the Sindhu region as his stake;
having staked crores of wealth and his nooses, he declared, "They are won!
Then Rāyahariṣṭha [staked] even the Naravāhana elephants there.
There were golden palanquins fashioned from gold and diamonds.
He staked a hundred thousand, adorned with parasols and chowries; having laid down ten million as the wager, he declared, "I have won! (52)
Then Rāyahari [sent] ten thousand warriors there,
equipped with weapons and clad in golden armor and attire.
The Lord of the Gods also adorned the dice with all kinds of ornaments; having cast ten million dice, he declared, "They have been won. (54)
Then Rāyahari adorned ten treasuries there, filled with gold coins— the very essence of the kingdom— with ornaments that rendered his own beauty purposeless.
Having cast down his snares, Koṭirāja declared, "They are conquered!
Then Rāyahari [conquered] the royal palaces and great mansions. 56.
Then Koṭirāya, having staked his winnings, adorned the moon-white palaces for the wager and spoke thus: "I have won. (57)
Then Rāyahari adorned his entire kingdom;
"With this kingdom of mine, I shall gamble today with you. (58)
"Tell me quickly, what is being staked by you in this wager?
Thus addressed, Koṭirāya suddenly offered his kingdom as the stake. (59)
Then they released their nooses, and indeed they retreated;
having granted defeat to Koṭiraya, the nooses truly departed.
Having achieved victory, Rāyahari became worthy of praise in the assembly;
he then staked his own wife, Dineśvarī, in that wager.
Koṭirāya spoke likewise: "What stake have you set?
Koṭirāya adorned his own wife, Candreśvarī, as her wager.
Then Bhāṇavāṇī, endowed with her arts, cast forth nooses;
she said, "By means of deceit, the queen Śrīrāya has been conquered here by Hari. (63)
In the assembly hall, a grief as vast as ten million mountains spread abroad;
for he had been deprived of his kingdom here by the voice of Bhāṇa in the final wager.
Then Candreśvarī, devoted to the duty of fidelity to her husband and distressed by the suffering caused by the sin of another's hand, cursed Bhāṇavāṇī.
May you quickly become afflicted with leprosy, mentally deranged, and likewise unfortunate;
may you also suffer from consumption and have a perpetually diseased womb.
"O wicked one, become insane like a sow, always eating excrement;
with this very body, you shall be a Rākṣasī equal to the king."
"Stay forever in the wicked forest together with Rāyahariṇī.
Thus was Bhāṇavāṇikā cursed there in the assembly hall. 68.
King Rāyahariśca also attained that same state;
both of them then repeatedly rose up and suddenly leaped about.
Having become naked and having undertaken a vow of silence, they showed their own teeth;
seeing them thus, the assembly then became overcome with grief.
But even when the kingdom is won, what is achieved if the intellect is defeated?
And even when wealth is won, what is achieved if modesty has vanished? (71)
But even if all were conquered, what was achieved there by not conquering suffering?
And even if women were conquered, what was achieved there by not conquering their words? (72)
"Even if wealth is won, if dharma is not won, what indeed has been accomplished there?
Thus did the assembly speak on their behalf. (73)
The curse of the devoted wife was not overcome here by the power of speech;
the king was conquered, the queen was conquered, and the kingdom, wealth, and home were all conquered. (74)
"The self has not been conquered there; everything else conquered is fruitless.
Then the queen Dineśvarī prayed to Candrikeśvarī.
"O Mother, let the kingdom, all the wealth, and whatever else has been staked here remain yours; let my husband attain well-being. (76)
O Great Queen, may Bhāṇavāṇī be established in a healthy mind and endowed with happiness here; have mercy, for I shall indeed speak to you. (77)
Having spoken thus, she then held his feet and wept for a moment;
Satī said to Candreśvarī, "Listen to this most excellent benefit."
But gambling is its name; its fruit for those who indulge in it is evil, leading to the ruin of either one party or the other, or even the destruction of all. (79)
They destroy both the future and the present; the senses cause destruction in this world, striking down those who are about to die. (4.40.80)
Driven by craving, blinded by intoxication, and lacking the wealth of diligent effort,
kings do not realize what state they will reach in the gamble.
The attainment of the Self is the supreme attainment, and it is the attainment of the Supreme Self;
whereas the acquisition of kingdoms and such is unstable and a source of all suffering. (82)
The speech of one who speaks excessively, the hand of one addicted to gambling, and that which destroys others—these lead to one's own ruin and bring about the destruction of the king. (83)
With dice that are equal to non-dice, she always seizes all one's possessions;
she is the destroyer of one's entire livelihood and the practitioner of great evil. (84)
Today he experiences the fruit of his evil deed; the curse was merely the instrumental cause.
The king as well, being addicted to gambling women, now experiences the fruit born of his own karma.
"My curse shall not be revoked; however, my husband shall gradually perform all the duties of kingship, and your husband's health will be restored. (86)
"Then the kingdom shall belong to you as my lord with half its share;
you are my sister, not a slave. I am pleased; may there be happiness. (87)
Thus addressed, she agreed accordingly; the Goddess, the sovereign of the distressed, bestowed her entire kingdom into the hands of Satī for the sake of her husband’s welfare in every way. (88)
Out of great devotion, Candreśvarī Satī regarded Dineśvarī highly;
likewise, Koṭirāya, the husband of Candreśvarī, held the king in high esteem. (89)
Constantly governing the entire kingdom through his many incarnations,
he always desired that Rāyahari be swift and ever happy.
He then asked the gods for the means by which the removal of the curse and his own well-being might be swiftly achieved; they spoke to him accordingly.
There is no means for warding off suffering equal to service to the virtuous;
indeed, the virtuous should be honored, for they are the removers of calamities. (92)
They are to be propitiated with all kinds of gifts; they are the destroyers of obstacles, the bestowers of all prosperity, and the makers of supreme fortune.
One should always cultivate association with the virtuous, for such association with the holy brings auspiciousness;
it is the divine *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* that exists upon this earth. (94)
Let the recitation of that narrative be arranged here for the duration of a year;
for once they have received the invitation, the virtuous ones will surely come. (95)
Even for virtuous women and yogis who bestow great blessings, everything will become perfectly healthy through even a fraction of their grace. (96)
When the astrologers had spoken thus, King Koṭirāya then caused a most excellent and supreme assembly pavilion to be constructed.
For the sake of obtaining the rewards of the fire-oblation, he had an excellent, most beautiful golden image of Viṣṇu, endowed with Śrī, fashioned upon a raised altar. 98.
At that time, he established halls for alchemy, halls for residence, and halls for storytelling;
he summoned those learned in the *Saṃhitās* from the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, who were knowers of the Saṃhitās, traveled by means of celestial chariots;
they were like purifying fires, being the very embodiment of the holy sites of Saurāṣṭra.
We, possessing celestial vision and traveling in our aerial chariots, descended before the pavilion while uttering cries of victory for the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Soul.
The Saṃhitā named Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, equal to the ocean, consists of a total number of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses. 10.2.
Shining among the verses, she arrived together with the virtuous;
equal to Lakṣmī in her physical form and equal to Sarasvatī in her own nature.
In wisdom she is equal to the Vedas; in wonder, she is like Lakṣmī;
in granting liberation, she is as beautiful as Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself. 104.
She is coolness endowed with radiance; in renunciation she is auspicious, equal to Pārvatī and Īśa;
she is enriched by the splendor of all ornaments and possessed of the goals of human existence.
She arrived by means of a celestial chariot for the welfare of all embodied beings;
O Badrikā, wherever my saints are, there I am, the lover of the virtuous.
There, Lakṣmī, Saṃhitā, Lalitā, Mañjulā, Jayā, Suguṇā, Haṃsikā, and Rādhā shine resplendently; of this there is no doubt. (107)

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Holy Men from the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake," etc., in the section concerning the introduction of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* for the spiritual welfare of King Bhāṇa and King Vāṇīrāya Harin, who had become insane due to the curse of a chaste wife after losing all their possessions in a game of dice between two kings in the Sindhu river region, within the fourth section on the Tiṣya lineage of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 40 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved of Badrī, regarding that excellent city named Śarkarā, which is adorned with a magnificent garden and contains the temple of Rāyahari. || 1 ||
In the place of the hall of discourse, the annual recitation was held;
King Koṭirāya performed this for the sake of attaining the welfare of Rāyahari.
He indeed made the preparations on the eleventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha;
from the very beginning, he summoned virtuous Brahmins through his messengers.
Vyāsas, reciters of the sacred texts, and thousands of chanters arrived from all directions; likewise, virtuous brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇava women came there.
For the Lord, who is self-luminous, was then the primary speaker;
and the sage Lomaśa was there as the preceptor performing the worship.
Others are from the country of Saurāṣṭra, as well as the Ājanābhas and the ancestors; likewise, there are those dwelling in the ancient land of Brahmā and those born in Rāśiyāna.
Furthermore, Brahmins born in Parīpra, as well as those born in Amarīpra, and those originating from regions such as Abrikta, arrived there. || 7 ||
There were also virtuous ones born in the region of Uṣṭraprada, those arisen from Ārārtrika,
and those born on the continents and sub-continents, as well as those born in mountains, forests, jungles, and oceans.
The virtuous ones who knew the essence of the Saṃhitās gathered there; and the noble women, the practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the Muktānikās also arrived.
Sages, ascetics, brahmins, and learned men arrived there;
invited were hundreds of thousands of millions of Vaiṣṇavas from all the worlds.
During the Cāturmāsya vow, as well as during the Pārāyaṇa and especially during the annual rites performed for the sake of the Bull, the best among the knowers of Brahman bestowed long life.
For the sake of all of them, the splendors of the kingdom and the palaces were offered as supreme gifts for the purpose of providing a welcome, happiness, enjoyment, and residence.
Just as the royal splendors are to be enjoyed by kings,
so indeed were they to be enjoyed without distinction by the gods on earth (brahmins) at that time, O beloved of Badarī.
There were thousands of streams of clarified butter, streams of curd, streams of juice mixed with sugar, streams of honey, streams of milk, and streams of syrups.
There, on the banks of the Sindhu river, long corridors were constructed,
and spacious dining halls were established where food was served day and night.
There were hundreds of thousands of female and male servants who provided food and drink,
as well as all the goods that had been staked and won at the gambling match.
Indeed, those [treasures] were offered by both kings specifically for the purpose of the sacrifice;
they were entirely surrendered for expenditure by Koṭirāya.
At that time, King Rāyahari was filled with great joy, like a mad rakshasa; such was his speech. 18.
Everyone saw the king, consumed by a curse and deprived of his senses,
[obsessed with] the sound of the dice, which causes total destruction and is the very belly of the gambling match.
Then people saw her consumed by the curse and driven mad, thinking,
"The complete recitation of these two [hymns] shall arise for their welfare and deliverance."
There, the spectators speak and praise Candrikeśvarī;
they behold and bow down to that chaste and great saintly woman.
At that time, millions of Vaiṣṇavas, intent on great wonders,
were thoroughly gratified with food, drink, lodging, and hospitable greetings.
At the time of dawn on the eleventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha, they went to the assembly ground to the vast pavilion, which was beautifully constructed and adorned with gold.
Beholding another heaven, as if it were the Sudharmā assembly hall,
there stood a most magnificent throne like a celestial chariot.
It was adorned with gold and diamonds, decorated with golden archways,
radiant with canopies like the moon, and filled with many pearls.
Adorned with flower garlands and the like, graced by swans and other birds,
pervaded by small flags and banners, and radiant with necklaces and arched gateways.
Equipped with soft bells, a crescent moon, side-drums, drums, and the like, captivating the mind with mirrors and other ornaments, and adorned with gold, garments, and so forth. (27)
It had pillars made of golden plantain trees and was provided with panels of joined cloth.
It was provided with all the requisites for worship, vessels, and every kind of ritual offering;
it was filled with people adorned with chowries, staffs, and other ornaments.
There, upon the seat of Vyāsa, sat the Brahmin who was devoted to the Self-luminous Reality, honored by virtuous sages with unbroken grains, flowers, garlands, and other offerings.
The primary reciter of the Saṃhitā sat down at an auspicious moment; then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of "Victory! arose.
O Badarī, at that time the Pārameśvarī Saṃhitā was placed upon a tablet, worshipped by Lomaśa, the most excellent among the great liberated ones;
and Goddess Lakṣmī herself appeared visibly within the Saṃhitā.
Divine, with a serene countenance, she was augmented by all splendors. || 33 ||
Richly adorned with the beauty of all ornaments, most captivating,
she holds Nārāyaṇa within her own heart, an ocean of knowledge.
Then, while that speaker was speaking, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa appeared with four arms, absorbed in his own self-luminous nature.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord who creates all beauty, is beloved by Māṇikī, Lalitā, Rādhā, Ramā, and Śrīmādhavī. 36.
At that time, all the auspicious Muktās and Muktānikās stood by her side, holding vessels for worship and other offerings, remaining in her presence. (37)
Brahmins, sages, virtuous ones, holy men, great seers, gods, goddesses, and sacred fords were all present there. || 38 ||
Then, with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, as well as the Śrī Sūkta, the Nārāyaṇa Sūkta, the Devī Sūkta, and other Vedic hymns; || 39 ||
There, Lomaśa performed the worship of the Saṃhitā according to the ritual injunctions with mantras, and Koṭirājaka likewise performed the ārātrika ceremony for Vyāsa.
He performed worship with sandalwood, flowers, unbroken grains, garments, gold, wealth, as well as ritual offerings such as the essence of perfumes and various fruits.
Lomaśa recited auspicious verses preceded by great benedictions and caused them both to perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) for their spiritual welfare. 42.
And at that moment, they stood there absorbed in listening to the discourse;
the assembly became filled with millions upon millions of highly conceited men.
Although the Lord is self-luminous, he, as a disciple of the venerable Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, performed an auspicious rite. (44)
The glorious Lord of the city of Brahman, the Sovereign of the Imperishable, the Master of all incarnations,
whose pair of feet is served by liberated Brahmas, the Lord of the Lord of Rādhā’s abode;
He who dwells within countless Nārāyaṇas, the Lord of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇa himself— [to Him I bow].
May this Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the sacred abode in Saurāṣṭra, be the bestower of happiness. ||45||
He who, wandering upon the earth in ancient times, brought joy through the liberation of kings;
who caused the destruction of the Daityas and supported the arms of the virtuous Arbudasatī;
and who, as the bestower of welfare upon those devoted to him, removed the sins of living beings and women.
He is this Sun of Letters at Kuṅkumavāpikā, the deity of the Śrī-saṃhitā. 46.
Having bowed to that Supreme Self, who is the essence of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
I shall cause this scripture, which consists of the knowledge of Him and bestows liberation, to be heard.
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation and the beloved of His devotees, ever abide in my heart while these narrations unfold. 48.
Having paid homage to the Supreme Brahman, Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and having bowed to Kaṃbharāśrī and Gopāla, one should utter the word "Jaya. (49)
I remember the Supreme Self; I bow to the beloved Lord;
I point toward devotion to Hari; I praise the service of the virtuous. 4.41.50.
Having thus performed this auspicious rite involving the collection of seeds, O Badrikā, he began reciting the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (51)
Then indeed, the gods, humans, and other embodied beings became seekers of meditation upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||52||
Then they became absorbed in meditation upon the form of Kṛṣṇa, who is the very essence of the narrative;
there they drank in the essence of the story, both in brief and in detail.
Every day, at the conclusion of their discourse, they would offer praise to the Supreme Soul:
"O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Bālakṛṣṇa! O Lord Harinārāyaṇa! (54)
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord who bestows liberation!
Thus, all [the devotees], accompanied by musical instruments, performed the congregational chanting of Your names. (55)
With rhythmic clapping, dances, and songs, they performed worship with joy; at the conclusion of the narration, the ārārtika and excellent food offerings were presented. (56)
There itself, the auspicious worship of Vyāsa takes place daily;
and the reciters, the Brahmins, and others triumph over the Supreme Lord. (57)
There, the evening oblation is always performed amidst the radiance of the blazing fire,
and sweet offerings are made here for the guests who have arrived.
The drinking of milk serves as the oblations for the gods,
and for the virtuous Brahmins, the food consisting of the essence of milk and other such items is nectar.
In that state, no sense of difference exists among any embodied beings; what belongs to the gods, the kings, and the sages belongs to all embodied beings alike. (4.41.60)
Every day, at both morning and evening, there always arises conversation regarding similar foods and drinks, such as snacks and meals.
Upon the conclusion of the nightly lamp-offering, there occurs daily worship and other rites;
thus, the nectar of the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa flows incessantly.
Then, every day, there was the bestowing of favors, the offering of food, and the presentation of gifts such as gold. (63)
Thus, O Badrikā, a great festival arose consisting of this compendium;
having drunk the nectar of knowledge by the hundreds of thousands, men became purified. (64)
Having become [devotees] again and again, they indeed become great Bhāgavatas there.
Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! ||65||
The sage Lomaśa also bestowed this mantra upon him;
moreover, many wonderful and diverse marvels occurred during the narration.
Then, the celestial chariots of the gods indeed arrived in the sky for the sake of hearing [the discourse] and remained there, raining down flowers and sandalwood powder.
Having performed [these rites], they constantly go to heaven;
indeed, having arrived in heaven, the sages of the sacred fords and the yogis then become invisible with divine bodies.
Having arrived, having heard [the sound], and remaining in the sky, they take it away to the one who bestows grace;
so too do the musical instruments of the divine worlds and the songs of the Gandharvas. (69)
Then there were the songs of the Apsarases, the dancing of courtesans, the devotion of virtuous women, and the sounds arising from the Vedas of the Brahmins.
At the conclusion of the festival, they are born daily through the service of Vyāsa, the service of gurus, and the honoring of the assembly of the virtuous. ||71||
Welcome to those who have arrived; for those who have departed, there is honor and worship;
for the newcomers, there is the honey-mixture (madhuparka); but for the elders, there are sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
There, food is given daily to the destitute and others as they desire;
the pretas come and listen to the most purifying discourse. (73)
They receive serene faith and from that go to the state of liberation;
indeed, after having related their own accounts, they travel by means of celestial palaces.
O Śrī Badrikā, at that time I shall be the object of enjoyment for those born in Sindh;
there, indeed, the great devotees of the Lord, the saintly Vaiṣṇavas, will shine resplendent. (75)
And there are the narratives of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā;
these stories unfold, endowed with the knowledge of dharma and the divine play (līlā) of Hari. ||76||
Consequently, this place became renowned here as Saṃhitātīrtha;
there, Bhāṇavāṇī and Rāyahari listened to the stories every day.
As those two partook of the prasāda and drank the nectar-like water,
their sins were gradually washed away by the nectar of the sacred narrative.
Through the practice of listening to the sacred narrative, the purification of the self arises;
through receiving the blessings of the virtuous, liberation from curses arises.
Thus, purification was gradually attained, especially during the Cāturmāsya period;
and the householders performed the dedication of the fruits of their vows and gifts.
By that merit, their well-being gradually arose auspiciously;
while the narrative was proceeding, the month of Kārttika arrived. (8.1)
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the kings, the subjects, and the men and women of high standing celebrated the festival of the birth anniversary of Bālakṛṣṇa.
The great seers, as well as the gods, virtuous men,
the Sādhyas, the Brahmins, and those learned in the Vedas, celebrated that great festival.
On the sixth day, King Koṭirāja, accompanied by a limited number of attendants,
received a letter from the sage Lomaśa regarding the bringing of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He traveled by way of the sky to Saurāṣṭra, to the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord. (85)
He arrived by celestial chariot near the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he descended before the temple to behold Bāla-Kṛṣṇa. ||86||
Having performed worship and having offered salutations, he stood before Kṛṣṇa with palms joined in reverence, having received a welcome upon his appearance.
Having attained joy and surrendered his heart to Śrī Hari, he offered everything and requested the cause [of his state]. ||88||
O Blessed One, the auspicious Janmajayantī Ekaviṃśatikā came from the Sindhu regions to the vicinity of Śarkarānagara. 89.
"O Lord, it should be performed by the Blessed One himself in the Saṃhitā pavilion;
out of compassion he has come to lead us there, and going tomorrow is what pleases me. (4.41.90)
On the seventh level, the Śarkarā-bhūmi, you must assemble at midday;
there, an excellent and most grand welcome should be prepared for you. (9.1)
"O Blessed One, you shall become [the savior]; therefore, the Compassionate One must come.
Hari said, "May it be auspicious; 'Om,' I shall come quickly. (92)
The king took rest at night while visiting the sacred fords;
however, by the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he became ready again in the morning. 93.
Then his mother, father, and the virtuous sages became ready;
having divided his own form into two, he indeed ascended the celestial chariot.
All of them, situated in their celestial chariots, were divided into two groups by the Supreme Self;
O Badrikā, the chariot then swiftly ascended into the sky.
The glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa reached the land of Sindh,
while remaining in Kuṅkumavāpikā in his second form.
For the sake of obtaining the festival of his birth, Śrī Hari himself, residing in Kuṅkumavāpikā, came to his own home to satisfy the hearts of those who had arrived. 97.
And having gone to the land of Sindhu for the satisfaction of the minds of those born in Sindhu, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa thus descended to the shore of the Sindhu. 98.
That celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, was first honored by the people;
and Hari, being worshipped with shouts of victory, departed from the chariot.

He was honored with the offering of eyes, with shouts of joy, and with auspicious unbroken grains of rice; he was worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and fully adored with garlands of flowers.
He was honored with parched grain and worshipped with cupped hands;
by people, through their heartfelt feelings and gestures, he was made their own lord.
Hari was fashioned as a shadow-form consisting of thousands of replicas;
Kṛṣṇa was reflected within the very selves of both women and men.
Then Kṛṣṇa went to the palace shown by Koṭirāya;
Lomaśa and the others bowed down to him and honored him with words of welcome and other courtesies.
The great virtuous lady Candreśvarī also gave him water to drink;
she then prepared a *candraka* mark with vermilion, combined with unbroken grains of rice.
Candrikeśvarī placed a garland of flowers around Kṛṣṇa’s neck,
while Dineśvarī performed the washing of Hari’s feet and other services there.
Then, filled with an abundance of devotion, she performed worship and offered him honor;
so too did the other worlds of Śrī Hari, the gods, and the common people.
Then the great seers and the sages offered worship to Hari;
having been asked about their welfare, they all departed for their respective abodes.
There, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa indeed found rest for a moment;
O Badarī, supreme bliss pervaded that place on all sides.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the Welcome Offered to All the Inhabitants of the World on His Birthday (Janmajayantī) at the Commencement of the Saṃhitā Narrative in the City of Śarkarā," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 41 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badrī; then, during that great festival on the seventh lunar day, a vast assembly gathered for the purpose of beholding Śrī Hari.
Kṛṣṇa, whose form is divine, sat down upon a beautiful, celestial elephant-throne that shone with gold, jewels, and other precious things, which was exceedingly high and most lofty.
At that time, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, like the sun, appeared upon the great throne within the range of vision of hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and hundreds of billions of human beings.
Endowed with divine splendor and ambrosia, possessing celestial sovereignty and majesty, he was adorned with boundless, limitless eloquence, generosity, and brilliance. || 4 ||
Adorned with such excellence, sweetness, charm, laughter, and splendor;
filled with the bliss of being drawn by such beauty and loveliness. || 5 ||
He was thus resplendent with the depth, heroism, and strength of youth;
he was thus a showerer of compassion, pity, affection, love, and grace.
Abounding in the exquisite charm of millions of desires and consisting of rhythmic strokes,
it shone forth with the splendor of syllables, producing melodic modulations.
At that time, by his grace, the Blessed One— the Inner Self residing within the hearts of men and women— became visible to the eyes through all his incarnations.
Honored and saluted by all, a welcome ever new was offered by the people and the groups of devotees until evening to the Supreme Soul.
And Hari, being compassionate by nature, indeed instructed [him] in the assembly,
out of grace toward his devotees who have surrendered their entire being for his sake.
"May all embodied beings become happy by the sight of me;
I have come here through my grace for the sake of securing happiness for you. (11)
I am the divine one who originates from the supreme abode, the imperishable world;
I am the sustainer of all incarnations, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, Śrī Puruṣottama.
He is the sovereign controller of all, the Lord who possesses all powers, the master,
and the supreme deity of all perfected beings, sages, ancestors, and gods.
The inner self, the teacher of Time, Māyā, and the Great Puruṣa— I am indeed that very one here, Bālakṛṣṇa, appearing in a form such as yours.
Whosoever have attained union with me, they have gone to my imperishable abode;
for there are countless Vāsudevas and indeed limitless Nārāyaṇas.
The Śrīkṛṣṇas are also innumerable, as are the Viṣṇus of infinite forms;
the Rāmas, the lords of men, and the lords of the Siddhas are likewise exceedingly numerous.
Through my yoga, they are born as fashioned from the bamboo-stalks of you two;
possessing my own nature, being identical with me, they become non-different from me. || 17 ||
Relying upon me, those who possess infinite power indeed accomplish their tasks in all creations by my grace, for they are the supreme lords.
Thus, I am Puruṣottama, the avatāra who sanctifies all creations with the glance of my compassionate side-long look, and I have become an object of perception for you.
For those who here hear or even remember the story of the Saṃhitā,
I shall be their deliverer from the ocean of the worldly existence of Māyā.
Those who indeed worship me as Śrīmat Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—
I, regarding them as my own devotees, shall deliver them from delusion.
Men, women, and eunuchs who shall worship me here, and serve me by surrendering all their possessions, they shall become my abodes. ||22||
I bestow upon all embodied beings a fruit equal to their own karma; such is the law in this world, yet my compassion exceeds it.
In compassion there is no restrictive rule that binds one to the fruits of action;
by my grace I shall uplift the entire world, of this there is no doubt. (24)
Just as everything indeed becomes purified through contact with fire, so too does everything become purified through my yoga. || 25 ||
Just as I am purifying, so too are my forms;
all my virtuous devotees are purifying, and my speech is always purifying.
This composed speech of mine is purifying for all embodied beings;
I am Lakṣmī and Lakṣmī is I—we are a single reality manifested in two ways. (27)
I am Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and Sarasvatī is my Saṃhitā;
by merely hearing her, my imperishable state is attained. (28)
I am the embodiment of sound, the embodiment of the virtuous, and the embodiment of the elements; I am of the nature of intoxication.
I am the threefold embodiment, and my virtuous form is likewise threefold. (29)
I am eternally the sixfold form: the form of devotion, the form of worship, and the form consisting of initiation; I am always present and I manifest myself here and there.
Today, for the sake of your welfare, I have indeed appeared in person upon the shore of the ocean in your monastery, out of compassion, in human form.
Women always worship me in the form of their husbands,
and husbands always worship me in the form of the Creator.
Eunuchs, devoid of fruit, worship me in the form of mental constructs;
whereas kings worship me as the tree that yields sap.
The birds [saw] the sky as their essence, the animals the multitude of medicinal herbs, the gods the nectar, the foremost of the Daityas strength, and living beings moisture. (34)
But those who possess vision worship me according to their own appropriate nature, seeing me as beautiful, though I am utterly devoid of a physical form. (35)

Those with senses [worship] the one with senses; those without senses [worship] me, who am without senses. Those possessing reality [worship] me as endowed with reality; those devoid of reality [worship] me as abandoned by reality.

Those with qualities [worship] me as possessing qualities; those without qualities, me as devoid of qualities; those with affection, me as having an affectionate form; and those without affection, me as the passionless and immutable.
The virtuous worship me, who am Truth, the giver of bliss, and the Lord of the mine of peace; I bestow upon them their fruit according to their fitness.
The embodied ones [perceive] me as possessing a body, while those without bodies perceive me as bodiless;
those seeking their own interests perceive me as destroying the interests of others, while those without self-interest perceive me as having no possessions. (39)
The wise perceive me as self-luminous, while the ignorant perceive me as residing within the elemental self;
those in distress see me as the provider of protection, and those in prosperity see me as the embodiment of their wealth.

The weary approach me as one whose form is exertion; the active, whose form is effort, attend upon me as one who is occupied; and the indolent, full of passion, worship me as one who is at ease and devoid of fruit. (41)
Relying upon their worship, I always grant the desired fruit;
indeed, I am obtainable through compassion and I become obtainable through mantra.
I am to be attained through devotion, attained through affection, and also attained through meditative absorption;
yet I am unattainable and easily attained here by those who recite the Saṃhitā.
"Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, svāhā!
For one who mutters this mantra, I am easily attained at all times. (44)
The fruit of service to the guru is the supreme attainment of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
that this may occur directly in this very life—thus have I obtained this matter here. 45.
Whoever remembers me, bows to me, praises me, meditates upon me, or serves me—in his heart I am always present, and especially before him as well. (46)
He who beholds Śrī in his wife, Nārāyaṇa in his husband,
and my pārṣadas in his offspring— that house is my own imperishable abode.
He who maintains my command in worldly activity, my abiding in renunciation, and identity with me in life—he indeed attains me. (48)
He whose senses, his mind, and even his very self are dedicated solely to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is one who possesses the true goal of human life. 49.
Even if he is of evil conduct in the world, he who takes no other refuge but me and constantly practices devotion to me is a saintly person and a means for attaining liberation.
Even if he were rich in detachment from worldly phenomena, free from possessions, and self-possessed, yet by existing apart from me, his loss would be most grievous. (5.1)
He who does not worship me, his Lord, nor even serves the virtuous, should be considered wicked;
he has utterly lost all that is meaningful.
Even if one has attained the abode of Indra, if he possesses the majesty of Dharmarāja,
or is endowed with the splendor of the Sun, yet is devoid of devotion, he is a denizen of hell.
Even if he were the lord of the elemental principles, the sole treasure-house of perfected powers and sovereignty,
and the ruler of many cosmic eggs, if he were devoid of devotion, he would be a denizen of hell.

Even one who has reached the further shore of the intellect, and even one who has reached the further shore of illusion, and even one who has attained the state of Brahman—is not supreme if he is devoid of devotion. (55)
Even one who is capable of protecting his subjects and is devoted to all proper conduct, if he is devoid of service to the virtuous, has lived this life in vain. (56)
Even one who possesses all vidyās and is endowed with the power of all the teachings, if devoid of service to the virtuous, leads a wretched life in this world. (57)
Even if he has reached ten million gods or attained the status of a great seer,
if he is devoid of compassion for the virtuous, all of that is meaningless for him.
The house of one who possesses the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and the desire-tree (Kalpadruma) in his home, yet lacks virtuous men,
is indeed like the den of a king of jackals.
He whose vision is exceedingly divine and whose inner being is likewise established [in truth], yet who lacks the sight of the virtuous, is forever blind and destined for hell. (60)
Even if honored with worship and shining with fame,
if one is devoid of the sight of the virtuous, he is forever blind and a wretched servant.
Though he may have access to all fourteen worlds, he who is utterly devoid of recourse toward the virtuous is one who has gone to a miserable state— he is a denizen of hell.

Even a forest-dwelling sage who possesses renunciation, detachment, and virtue, if he is devoid of the company of the virtuous and the good, would be nothing more than a wild beast in the forest. (33)
The state of being a bound soul (paśutva) indeed exists for living beings perpetually due to the noose of Māyā;
Māyā should be understood as latent impression (vāsanā), which acts as an obstacle to devotion. (64)
That [impurity] is indeed to be washed away by service to the virtuous and to Hari;
one should offer oneself to Hari, but offer everything to the virtuous as well.
Having entrusted all ritual actions to me, one should here contemplate [the self] as Brahman;
then, having listened to the Saṃhitā, one should thereafter contemplate [it] as being of my nature.
Whoever shall be endowed with devotion to me, I shall uplift them in every way.
May there be well-being for you all, O best of beings, through my direct grace.
Having spoken thus there, O Badrikā, the glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa then ceased; thereafter,
the illustrious Lomaśa caused that supreme mantra to be heard by all and established them as the highest Vaiṣṇavas.
Hari, having become free from all agitation, was worshipped by the people.
For the sake of rest, he went to his own place; there, the king and others performed auspicious *ārārtika* and *naivedya* offerings for Śrī Hari, as well as providing food,
drink, seats, hospitality, and worship for the others.
Then, at the onset of night, the kings and others performed their respective duties;
during the night, the women, men, queens, and kings all attended upon the sage Lomaśa, who was self-luminous and the speaker of that [teaching]. || 71–72 ||
Endowed with divine disposition, they also served the virtuous by massaging their feet and other such acts, pleasing them for the sake of their own spiritual welfare.
There at night, however, there were the songs of the gods and the Gandharvas,
the dances of the Apsarases, and the singing of women.
From that, there arose waves of ancient stories by poets, as well as visions of dramas and the life-stories of Hari. (75)
At that time, there were many magical illusions of those skilled in the arts, as well as the worship of virtuous women and the congregational chanting of the holy. (76)
O Badarī, for those who know yoga, there were indeed various meditative absorptions (samādhis);
however, for those seeking liberation, service to the Self is the highest, as it leads to identity with one's own true nature.
O Badarī, may there be for the intensely devoted that total surrender, and for those who know the Self and those who possess affection, may there be a state of melting away into the Supreme Self.
For the wise, there arose at that time a single-pointedness of cognitions;
for embodied beings, there were states of joy, delight, and supreme bliss. (79)
Then a thrill arose in the fields and sweat appeared on the rivers;
through the union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the purity of the flowing currents was established.
O Badrī, at that time, the manifestation of the virtuous was the delight of the great sages,
while the cultivation of grain became the sustenance for the subjects.
O Badarī, the purity of animals, birds, and even aquatic creatures,
as well as the excellence of life among the Jambū trees, was destined to come about and has indeed now arisen.
At that time, the creepers, shrubs, trees, grass-bearing plants, and tubers on the surface of the earth there became fit for sacrifice. ||83||
Therein, the winds, the fires, and the ether attained their purpose;
likewise, the waters and their transformations attained their purpose through union with Kṛṣṇa. (84)
The beds, temples, and objects constantly frequented by Kṛṣṇa always become purified and possess the supreme quality of bestowing liberation. ||85||
O Badrikā, the story of them has entered the ears of those for whom Bālakṛṣṇa is upon the earth and for whom saintly persons have been seen. (86)
The lords of the gods, having assembled at night and worshipped the Lord Śrīśa, the Master beloved by Śrī, with divine substances, departed after receiving His grace. ||87||
Then all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated on earth and in the sky assembled in secret;
having drunk the water touched by Hari’s feet, they returned to their own abodes. 88.
The Siddhas, dwelling in the mountains, having arrived with their yogic bodies and served Bālakṛṣṇa, departed for their own mountain caves. 89.
Dyau herself, having become a young woman, served Hari, the Lord of the Day;
having accomplished her purpose, she then returned to her own abode in the sky.
The inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa and other realms, as well as the liberated ones and their consorts, those dwelling in the Ocean of Milk and those residing at Badarī, all worshipped Nārāyaṇa.
All the powers, beginning with Rādhā and Ramā, who possess divine forms, served their beloved—the protector of their life—as beloved wives. 92.
Assuming many forms within the night, Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of his wives, accepted the service offered by both men and women. 93.
At the end of the night, for a moment, that Lord took his beloved Yoganidrā as his sleep for just one ghaṭikā; thereafter, he arose.
Rising for a moment, the Lord meditated upon His own primordial form, which is beginningless, consisting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and higher than the highest. ||95||
Then all the incarnations, possessing all the powers of incarnation—the lords and the goddesses—appeared with divine and invisible forms. (96)
There, in secret, they obtained the merit of worshipping Jayantī;
even those liberated ones, established in meditative absorption and residing in the abode of the Abodes, [attained it]. 97.
The attendants of Kṛṣṇa also obtained their share of the offerings;
other attendants and the cowherd women performed worship and service. || 98 ||
Then Gaja, Garuḍa, Śeṣa, and Vājī— the best of steeds—
arrived in invisible forms and performed secret worship of Hari.
O Badrikā, you then obtained the attainment of secret worship together with me, along with Nara, and with the great sages.
Thus, at dawn on the eighth day of the month of Ūrja, the divine goddesses, under the pretext of the Jayantī festival, worshipped the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
They first obtained a gain that was not manifest to others;
then, indeed, half of the Brāhma-muhūrta passed away.
Then Hari awakened by means of the worldly activities [of his attendants], and embodied beings likewise awoke upon hearing the sounds of sweet musical instruments. (10.3)

On the morning of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the goddess Jayantī, having become a divine maiden adorned with all ornaments, appeared in vain [of her former form]. || 104 ||
She arrived with a divine body and worshipped her husband, the Lord of Śrī;
thereafter, that virtuous woman remained invisible to Kṛṣṇa for the entire day.
Thus, when the beloved of Badarī was born, a great festival arose for embodied beings; at that time, people everywhere prepared themselves for the purpose of worship.
Bringing with them all kinds of ritual requisites, comparable to divine wish-fulfilling gems, they went into his presence together to perform worship.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by Śrī Hari in the Evening Assembly at the Pavilion of Śarkarāpattana, the Worship of Hari, the Festivities at Night, and the Secret Worship Performed by the Gods and Others in the Morning," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess, beloved of Badarī, to the great festival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
it occurs on the twenty-first day of his birth, when Kṛṣṇa is in the month of Kārttika. || 1 ||
In the very morning, the queens bathed Hari Janārdana—
the beloved Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of all desires.
With sandalwood and the essence of fragrances, combined with the juices of great medicinal herbs, with waters brought from sacred fords mixed with oil, and with the essences of saffron; || 3 ||
Having thoroughly massaged him and sprinkled him with water, he performed the ritual purification;
then he provided him with garments, ornaments, decorations, flowers, and other such items.
He gave crowns and bracelets made of gold, as well as golden necklaces adorned with gems,
rubies, diamonds, pearls, and crystals.
They applied a tilaka on the neck of Hari and fashioned a decorative mark (candraka);
likewise, they placed a saffron moon-mark upon his forehead and collyrium upon his eyes.
They wore beautiful ear-ornaments as ear-pendants,
a golden girdle upon their waists, and likewise anklets upon their feet.
On his two forearms were bracelets, on his fingers and other limbs rings and the like;
he wore a crest-jewel, earrings, a neck-ornament, and various garlands.
And they wore bracelets and golden sandals;
they wore great jewels whose value was many millions, billions, and trillions.
His radiance, which brought the illusion of midday everywhere,
caused them to apply lac-dye and other substances even to the soles of their feet and the palms of their hands.
They indeed caused the beloved of Śrī Svāmī to have his limbs covered with golden powder while seated upon a golden throne resembling a Saindhava horse.
Then those queens of the kings born of the Sindhu performed the auspicious rites first and worshipped Kṛṣṇa.
Having placed before them offerings consisting of gold, silver, jewels, and pearl necklaces,
they set the queens' feet upon their heads and drank the water used for washing them.
Then the queens performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, augmented with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
He lowered his hands, which had been joined in salutation to dispel suffering, from Kṛṣṇa’s head.
Circumambulating and prostrating like a staff upon the ground, they begged for mercy;
and by the voice of Bhānu, the Sun-goddess brought about the mental confusion of Rāyahari.
Having offered [the oblation], she then prayed for health and eternal happiness;
Hari also spoke to her, saying, "Today your health is indeed excellent."
It shall surely come to pass; do not worry, O Queen, for there will be happiness.
At the end of a moment, even Koṭirāya will become King Rāyahari here.
O Goddess of the Day, having led you here, bring my mind to a state of composure so that I may perform worship; and bring Bhāṇavāṇī before me here. 18.
Having been addressed thus, O Badrikā, Queen Dineśvarī then quickly went to the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, where Bhānu’s speech was rendered senseless.
Kṛṣṇa brought Dineśvarī to his side and touched her head with his hand,
which bore the fish-banner, the trident, and the bow.
In that moment, she became established in her own nature, pure, a yoginī of wisdom, free from affliction and disease, and quickly became like a scholar. (21)
Her mental agitation vanished and perfect wisdom dawned within her;
she then fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed worship, he presented offerings to Śrī Hari, the consort of Ramā;
and having also performed the waving of lights (ārārtika), he drank the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
She requested liberation that destroys all sins;
she sought the complete eradication of the roots of bonds and latent impressions.
She also prayed to the Supreme Self for the destruction of the sin of gambling, the destruction of the sin of sexual misconduct, and her own state as Muktānikā. ||25||
"So be it," Hari replied; at that moment, she attained divinity.
Possessing a celestial body like a goddess, she became endowed with divine sovereignty.
By a mere fragment of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion, Satī became liberated;
she quickly attained liberation while living, freed from the covering of the body. ||27||
Oh, how great is the compassion of Hari, which has arisen even toward this body that is devoid of effort!
For those who possess effort, success indeed follows their prior disposition. (28)
Then, having beheld that great marvel there, thousands of maidens, as well as fortunate women—both those with husbands and widows—[were filled with wonder]. (29)
Both the young girls and the elderly women worshipped the Supreme Lord;
deluded by Him, they uttered the divine-syllabled "Kṛṣṇa" with celestial bodies.
All those [goddesses], endowed with meditative cultivation, became exactly as they had contemplated;
they were divine deities with celestial qualities, celestial bodies, and celestial activities.
Then those women, equal to Rādhā and Ramā, possessed divine vision and divine nature through the touch of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They became beloved of Brahmā and beloved of Hari by the thousands; with the desire to become devotees of Kṛṣṇa, they received the mantra from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Many there became afflicted with disease, and he warded off those ailments. (34)
Kṛṣṇa prevented many women from remaining childless; he also removed the sufferings of others, such as their state of being burdened by distress. ||35||
Likewise, he prevented the poverty and destitution of some others, while through his compassion, he brought about the attainment of husbands for yet others. (36)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of all happiness, bestowed upon others the possession of good fortune and the most excellent state of prosperity. (37)
When the task of worshipping the queens was completed, all the women of the subjects—
women by the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions— all worshipped Hari.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, assuming ten million forms, was born;
standing before each of those women, the Beloved received their worship.
They accepted those blessings, and Hari bestowed auspicious benedictions upon them;
Kṛṣṇa forever established His divine dwelling within the hearts of them all. 40.43.40.
Having thus displayed a great wonder and marvel for the duration of a single ghaṭikā, he then vanished and returned to his singular form. ||41||
Not even a single woman remained among the group of women during the conjunction with Kṛṣṇa;
having shown compassion, Kṛṣṇa, the sustainer of all, accepted their worship.
Then the women, having seen, touched, and worshipped him, attained satisfaction, receiving pleasing food, fruit, flowers, leaves, and water. (43)
With affectionate glances from their eyes, gentle smiles, and gracious minds, those women, possessing both divine and earthly forms, felt that they had achieved all their desires.
Thus Hari, having received the worship of the women and their divine devotion,
as well as their celestial sovereignty, the Infallible One vanished from sight.
Then they all gazed steadfastly upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the Supreme Brahman, the one who is Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī. ||46||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhikā, Hari, the lord of Lalitā, as well as the master and husband of Māṇikyā and Padmāvatī. ||47||
Some beheld Badrikānātha, some likewise Śrībhūpati, and some beheld Kamalānātha, the Lord of Wisdom. 48.
Then they beheld that Lord of Śrī-kuṅkumavāpī;
seeing him thus, they attained great bliss as well as all forms of joy. (49)
Having attained Śrī Hari, the women of Saindhava became radiant;
they became supreme devotees of Viṣṇu, like sacred rivers.
They sang, "To Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmin, the Beloved," and they meditated upon the Śrī Paramātman who dwells both within and without.
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, the supreme worship of women was concluded in the morning;
thereafter, King Koṭirāya arrived.
He went accompanied by many tigers among kings, kṣatriyas who were royal yogins, protectors of kingdoms, protectors of realms, and protectors of armies. ||53||
He worshipped Mādhava with all the royal services,
including a golden crown set with jewels and gems worth ten million.
Earrings inlaid with jewels, necklaces made of gold,
ear-ornaments, bracelets, armlets, and golden chains.
He gave her finger-rings, a girdle set with jewels, necklaces made of gold,
garlands of gems, jeweled bracelets, and gem-studded anklets and foot-ornaments.
Having applied a sandalwood mark on his forehead, he offered it to Hari;
he presented fragrant flowers, garlands, and beautiful wreaths.
Offer ornaments, cosmetics, and garments of great value;
offer beautiful golden vessels and exquisite golden weapons. ||58||
Then he also offered golden balls to Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
along with incense, lamps, unbroken grains, water, food offerings, and the waving of lights.
With golden platters filled with priceless gems and jewels, with utensils richly adorned with gold, and with parasols, chowries, and staffs; ||4.43.60||
Having worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the king gratified him;
he then applied an auspicious tilaka upon Kṛṣṇa’s forehead.
Other kings and nobles, princes and royal ministers, distinguished merchants related to the king, and those holding authority over the kingdom—[all these gathered]. (62)
With the pastes of musk, saffron filaments, gandhasāra, and saffron;
with flowers, unbroken rice grains, clusters of water, leaves, barley, sprouts, and so forth. ||63||
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, bowed down, and drunk the nectar of His feet,
they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and bestowed auspicious blessings.
Then Koṭirāya, full of eagerness, urged Rāyahari— who had attained a state of composure— to go there for the sake of worshipping the Supreme Lord.
Free from ailment, released from the curse, and possessing the awakening of all states of being,
he worshipped his beloved teacher Śrī Kṛṣṇa with supreme devotion.
Then, at the festival celebrating the birth of Kṛṣṇa, all the people,
filled with eagerness, worshipped him who is the Lord of the lords of the lords.
Then the divine form of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shone forth,
residing in the imperishable abode, like that which is higher than the highest.
The sages headed by Lomaśa, as well as the great seers, deities,
Siddhas, Satyas, and Sādhus, all paid homage to the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
The sūtas, māgadhas, and cāraṇas also offered their blessings;
the bards, poets, and learned scholars, possessing auspicious intentions, paid their respects.
Thus, O Badrī, the festival celebrating the birth anniversary continued until the hour of midday;
thereafter, the meals were served.
In the evening, that assembly hall became beautiful, occupied by those possessing a pride exceeding a hundred thousand;
for the Blessed One, self-luminous, indeed taught there.
In this world of mortals, the Supreme Lord indeed regards honor as the highest;
those who have been honored by the Supreme Lord are truly honored, and no others ever are. (73)
The Blessed One, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless and supreme among men, shines here, bestowing honor upon you all. (74)
Kṛṣṇa is honored by you, and therefore you are honored;
for those who receive honor in the presence of Hari, they receive honor everywhere. (75)
In whosever house the Blessed One resides, all those are indeed considered divine;
for even as a householder, he who always establishes Hari in his own home [attains this]. (76)
That householder alone is truly virtuous whose home has Mādhava as its essence;
that woman who performs the worship of Nārāyaṇa is considered a virtuous wife.
Even a king shines where the Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, resides;
he alone is a true king in whose house Śrī Narāyaṇa dwells. (78)
The queen serves the Supreme Lord like a servant free from pride;
she is always virtuous because she has taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa. (79)
Whichever women of the kingdom serve Mādhavīśvara, they should all be considered virtuous, for the Blessed One resides in their homes. (4.43.80)
Those virtuous ones who serve Hari are truly wealthy;
those for whom Nārāyaṇa is their wealth are the saintly, adorned by goodness. (81)
He is indeed Nārāyaṇa; those who in every way hold fast to him at the end cross over themselves and cause others as well to cross over the ocean of existence. ||82||
Those who are peaceful in this cycle of existence accomplish the goals of human life;
those whose activity is for the sake of Kṛṣṇa are indeed the virtuous.
Those whose resolve has Kṛṣṇa as its soul are indeed virtuous;
those ascetics who exert effort toward Hari are declared to be saints.
Those renunciants who are devoted to Hari, intent on liberation, dwelling in the forest and absorbed in Kṛṣṇa—they are considered true saints. ||85||
Those virtuous ones who practice yoga directed toward Kṛṣṇa are indeed yogis;
those ascetics for whom austerity is centered on Kṛṣṇa are truly virtuous.
Those for whom the vow is the Supreme Kṛṣṇa are the virtuous ones and they are the observers of vows;
those for whom the sacrifice is Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa are the virtuous ones and they are the performers of sacrifice.
Those whose very life is Śrī Hari are indeed saintly persons liberated while living;
those who have offered their attachment to Kṛṣṇa, Hari, are indeed saintly persons free from attachment.
Those for whom the objects of the senses are dedicated to Kṛṣṇa are practitioners, and they are indeed saintly persons.
Even those who are virtuous, if they direct their worldly activity toward the Supreme Lord, [attain liberation]. ||89||
Brahman is indeed the Supreme Self; those who move within it for the sake of liberation are called "brahmacaras," and they are truly brahmacārins. (4.43.90)
O sages, those who indeed meditate upon Śrī Hari are truly virtuous;
O seers, those who possess the knowledge of Hari are truly virtuous ṛṣis. (9.1)
Those who possess divine devotion toward Hari are virtuous even as gods;
those for whom every action is directed toward the Supreme are virtuous even as they serve others.
Those whose activities are entirely centered on Kṛṣṇa are virtuous practitioners of meditation;
those who possess absorption in Hari are indeed virtuous ones established in *samādhi*.
Those whose family is for the sake of Kṛṣṇa are the true householders; those for whom all calculations are centered on Hari are considered by the wise to be true followers of Sāṃkhya.
The first birth is from ignorance; thereafter, upon gaining knowledge, comes the second.
These twice-born ones should be understood as virtuous sages who are solely devoted to the knowledge of liberation. 95.
The first birth is from the body, but the second is through initiation (dīkṣā).
Those twice-born who are initiated into Nārāyaṇa are considered virtuous sages (sādhu). ||96||
Saṃsāra is the first birth; liberation is the second birth.
Those virtuous ones who possess the twice-born status of liberation are the saviors of all on earth. (97)
First, there is the practice regarding illusion; thereafter, the practice among the virtuous.
These are the true renunciants, free from all illusion. (98)
Even if she has entered into a union with another, she who has taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa shall become a virtuous wife; she is Nārāyaṇī, the chaste mistress. 99.
She who remains indifferent within the household, who is established in Nārāyaṇa, and who is devoted to the service of the virtuous— that chaste woman shall be a true celibate (brahmacāriṇī).

Those virtuous ones who practice the means for self-realization, who are intent on the means to liberation, who perform ritual actions, and who are devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa—[they alone are true]. 101.
Those for whom purity always resides in Kṛṣṇa are indeed pure and virtuous;
those who always perform the chanting of Kṛṣṇa are indeed virtuous in their Vedic study.
He for whom there is a seat before Hari is one whose seat is always virtuous;
he for whom Hari resides in every breath is indeed one whose breath is a virtuous seat.
He for whom the Blessed One has a preference regarding food is truly considered a virtuous man; he in whom peace toward Hari arises is indeed regarded as a peaceful and holy man. (104)
An embodied practitioner of yoga must be devoted to Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa;
he must endure initial hardships and practice forgiveness toward those who commit offenses.
One should never inflict suffering upon anyone, whether by action,
or even by thought, body, or speech, at any time.
Truth must be maintained and theft must be abandoned by the yogi;
contentment should be protected in every way, and he should remain like a stone. (1.07)
The taste [of the Self] should be grasped in every way by the yogi within the Supreme Self;
delight and love for Hari should be offered by the yogi who is a celibate student.
Even the conduct prescribed by scripture must be maintained toward Hari by a saintly practitioner of yoga who is united with Kṛṣṇa;
such a saint who acts according to the scriptures for the sake of the meaning of the Vedas is the king of yogis.
A virtuous person, acting as a true uniter, should in every way apply their mind to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of mindfulness—whether in childhood, youth, or even old age—to the Supreme Lord. (4.43.11)
Humanity and womanhood must be offered to the Supreme Lord;
these very persons are virtuous because they have placed their means of attainment within the heart of the Lord of Śrī.
Having become truly virtuous here and having made Kṛṣṇa their own husband, let both men and women go indeed to the supreme, imperishable abode of the Lord.
Today is indeed the Jayantī of the birth of the beginningless Supreme Self;
it has been celebrated by you with a truly great festival. (11.3)
May he bring about the supreme prosperity for you, the people of Sindh,
as well as the highest ultimate beatitude and the most excellent welfare.
May he grant eternal great bliss at the feet of Śrī Hari;
[worship] him, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is without beginning or end.
May the virtuous always meditate upon this in their hearts; may they become holy men, and may all kinds of heavenly realms be yours here.
By the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
the supreme Lord Bālakṛṣṇa is pleased here.
May there be well-being for you; may there be prosperity for you; may there always be a great heaven for you.
May there always be for you the expansion of the Vaishnava lineage from a great family.
May there be a virtuous dwelling in your home and field that bestows liberation;
may the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa reside within you as well.
Having spoken these words of blessing, the Lord, who is self-luminous, ceased; then there arose simultaneous shouts of victory.
Victory to the beginningless Lord Bālakṛṣṇa; may he be victorious here!
Victory to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who pervades all; may he be victorious here! (121)
Thus, with the sounds of victory and the blasts of trumpets by the gods and others,
and with salutations and the like, the assembly came to a conclusion.
Hari went to his own abode, and everyone departed for their respective homes;
Koṭirāya, having bowed to Hari, went to the temple of Kṛṣṇa.
He said to the Supreme Soul: "For whatever purpose the Blessed One was summoned here, that liberation of the king has been entirely accomplished."
Liberation from the curse has occurred here, and supreme liberation is also present; for by the mere glance of the Blessed One, it has come into the hands of embodied beings.
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, those two divided the kingdom born in the region of Sindhu into two halves— one for Hāyaudarya and the other for Śārkara.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they attained eternal bliss;
and having partaken of food, drink, and other refreshments at night, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [remained].
He attained supreme rest, and the people indeed attended upon him;
O Badrikā, Śrī Hari entered into a divine sleep. 128.
Thus Hari himself bestowed upon them supreme, divine perfection;
for the grace of Hari grants liberation to the virtuous and bestows all peace.
The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is indeed virtuous, bestowing liberation; it is a science consisting of all perfections and leads to the realization of the Supreme Brahman. 4.43.1-30.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Acceptance of Worship by Men and Women during the Janmajayantī Festival, the Bestowal of Health upon Bhāṇa, Vāṇī, Rāya, and Hari, the Assembly, the Discernment of the Virtuous, and the Rest," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Badrīpriyā Devī said: O Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, there is the festival celebrating the birthday of the Blessed Bālakṛṣṇa. (1)
What was the nature of that second form of the Yogin?
I shall relate to you in brief the story of the glorious Supreme Self.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; at that time, Hari, possessing a divine form, assumed many forms in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The self-effulgent Lord himself, in the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
likewise became Lomaśa, assuming the form of all the great sages.
Then Kṛṣṇa became one whose very nature is self-luminous, who possesses the form of male and female servants, and who assumes the forms of devotees and their wives. || 5 ||
Whosoever went to the Sindhu, for them the Lord assumed their form and attire; indeed, the Lord then became the bearer of all their emblems and implements.
And there, Viśvakarman was summoned by Nārāyaṇa,
as were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Mahendra, Varuṇa, and the others.
The Siddhas, the great ṛṣis, the liberated ones, the Muktānikās, as well as the Īśvaras,
the gods, the goddesses, and the Brahmins were present at the twenty-first festival.
Then, at dawn on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, they arrived for the purpose of performing the worship of Śrī Hari; the brāhmaṇas also arrived.
The Suras, the Surāṇīs, and the gods who are guardians of the world arrived,
as did others dwelling in Saurāṣṭra and those inhabiting other continents on earth.
Then all the goddesses, beloved of Brahmā and beloved of Hari, arrived to celebrate the great festival of the birthday.
With joy, they prepared the amorous attire of the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Consort of Śrī;
following the consecration, they fashioned his costume and the splendor of his ornaments.
On the forehead, he made a *tilaka* and a crescent moon design using saffron, unbroken grains of rice,
and clay, along with saffron filaments, musk, and fragrant, excellent liquid extracts.
Having performed worship with offerings of flowers and lamps for the nightly ritual,
they magnified the Lord of Wisdom, the husband of Mādhavī, with blessings.
They gratified Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and the Supreme Sovereign of Vikuṇṭha,
with various kinds of offerings.
The best of gods, possessing divine knowledge, were struck with supreme wonder;
Hari dwells upon the shore of the ocean, and likewise on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake.

Out of compassion, for the sake of the festival of his own birth-jayanti, Brahmā performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) in two ways, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) likewise performed it. || 17 ||
The brahmins performed the worship of the Supreme Self with mantras and excellent ritual substances;
thus, at dawn, a great festival took place on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake.
There were also meals provided in the evening, and the assembly hall became auspicious;
then Lomaśa, assuming a divine form, performed the duties of the assembly.
He gave instruction in many ways to the people of Saurāṣṭra, as well as to the people from all lands who had come for the festival. (4.44.20)
This Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the benefactor of the world, exists both as one and as many, impelled by compassion for the highest good of all. (2.1)
He dwells today in the land of Sindhu, and he dwells here in Saurāṣṭra;
he dwells in the supreme abode of the Imperishable, and within our hearts.
He dwells in the ocean known as Kṣīra, he resides also on Śvetadvīpa,
he abides at the sacred hermitage of Śrī Badarī, and in the field of Puruṣottama.
He shines likewise in the city of Mūladvāravatī and on Mount Meru;
he dwells in the house of Bhṛgu and also in the temple of Dharmadeva.
She shines in fire, sun, and moon, and in the world of truth (satyaloka);
she dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, in Śrīpura, and in the unmanifest, immortal state.
Hari dwells in Goloka and likewise in the supreme, imperishable state;
in all abodes, that very Hari himself exists as the Lord of all.
Today is the festival of Hari's birth, consisting of twenty-one qualities;
it is celebrated everywhere in all the worlds, in every place.
In this and that place, the Blessed One manifests in various forms;
for the Blessed One, being subject to devotion, attains the state of being devoted to those who worship him. (28)
Whether devoid of virtues or lacking in qualities, the devotee is dear to the Supreme Self; even one of evil conduct or improper behavior, the devotee is dear to the Supreme Self. (29)
