he bestowed gifts of milk, curd, and ghee, as well as offerings for the sacrificial fire.
He indeed gave gifts of woolen blankets and gifts of betel leaves;
he presented gifts of decorative articles for the worship of the image.
He bestowed gifts of vehicles and mounts, the giving of parasols and fly-whisks, and the offering of sandals, turbans, armor, and ornaments. (66)
He likewise gave gifts of beds, gifts of food, and gifts of grain;
he made offerings of gold, silver coins, and the like, and presented precious gems.
He gave to the reciter (vācaka) garments for his attire, a golden pitcher,
all kinds of ornaments, as well as golden robes.
Then his wife Gaṇḍavātā, with a cheerful mind,
gave gold, silver, and ornaments to the wives of the brahmins.
She gave pearls, excellent gems, diamonds, and silken garments; she gave a woman with beautiful curls, a woman with lovely breasts, a woman with fine hair, and a woman wearing a bodice.
He gave her a water-pipe, a gurgling lute, a breast-ornament, and a woolen blanket; as well as a girdle, a hair-braided ornament, a forehead-mark, and an ear-ornament.
He gave signet rings, finger-rings, bracelets, and bangles;
necklaces, armlets, golden garlands, and strings of green gram.
Nara gave her drops of sandalwood paste and golden earrings with chains;
Vātagaṇḍā likewise gave her sweet foods and even water.
Likewise, she gave saffron, unbroken grains, flowers, and ornaments;
her sons and daughters also performed the gift of cows for her.
At that time, they indeed made gifts of horses, gifts of camels, and gifts of bulls;
they performed great acts of giving there for worthy recipients.
They also devotedly gave gifts of food, gifts of palatial mansions, gifts of Tulasī trees, and gifts of sacrificial oblations.
The gift of the Saṃhitā manuscript subsumed all other gifts;
there, all riches, both insentient and sentient, were brought together. (77)
Having recognized the auspicious occasion, they gave gifts out of devotion to Hari;
they bestowed vehicles, mounts, and the gifting of male and female servants.
With their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, they performed what was appropriate for the sake of liberation;
when the fortnight had passed, they were overflowing with the knowledge of the sacred narratives.
Then all those who were of divine nature became possessors of the discus—
servants, maidservants, groups of attendants, kinsmen, and family members.
From children to the elderly, they were all intent upon the path to liberation, being eager to behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||81||
On the evening of the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, after performing the ritual worship and the lustration ceremony (ārātrika),
[the assembly remains] until those skilled in chanting [the praises].
While they were thus performing the chanting of the names, Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, illuminating the sky and the directions with his splendor, descended to the earth. 83.
Accompanied by his beloved Lakṣmī, Hari, from his golden celestial chariot,
then descended outside the chariot and revealed himself.
Hundreds of thousands of people among the listeners—men and women—attained supreme wonder; for a moment they were struck dumb, their vision overwhelmed by those [visions]. (85)
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, they repeatedly beheld that auspicious, beautiful, and charming Lord of the Gopīs, who had withdrawn his excessive radiance. 86.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa became the husband of Mādhavī, she became as infatuated as a cluster of jasmine flowers;
and her daughters likewise became utterly infatuated with the Supreme Soul.
With their mental faculties drawn away by Kṛṣṇa, they became indifferent to all else;
at that very moment, they resolved to offer themselves to Śrī Kṛṣṇa as a gift.
The female servants and the maidens who were young women at that time—all of them, being innocent, then offered themselves as a gift to Nārāyaṇa. (89)
In this way, those men who were servants, sons, slaves, and laborers—
having drawn their souls and bodies toward Kṛṣṇa— chose liberation through Hari.
Having understood their intention, the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa quickly fashioned all of them with divine forms.
Having placed them in their own celestial chariots, he made the liberated men beautiful in form with transformed bodies,
as did the female liberated ones.
Having settled the remaining members of the household—the children, the dependents, the protectors, and the pairs of excellent women—he remained there. ||93||
Having seated them there upon the ground and bestowed auspicious blessings upon them,
he led those men and women worthy of being taken away to his own imperishable abode.
Then, by the very power of that divine body, thousands of men and women, assuming those very forms, went to the imperishable abode of Hari.
Oh, how great is the fortune of those men and women, O Badarī, who offer their all to the Wielder of the Discus and whose leader is Nārāyaṇa! (96)
Oh, how even these material bodies, which are but morsels for Time, have departed together after becoming divine, without falling by the will of Kṛṣṇa! 97.
Indeed, this capacity to act otherwise belongs to the Supreme Self; having transformed the insentient into sentient beings, He sports together with them. (18)
Furthermore, the thousands of other men and women who were then present likewise attained perfection through the hearing of the narrative and by the sight [of him]. (99)
That family of Gaṇḍavātā were descendants of the lineage of Yāska’s doctrine;
those Vaiṣṇavas then departed for their own home at the end of the month.
In their own country, they proclaimed that great wonder everywhere as auspicious:
"The devotees—whether old or middle-aged—have attained liberation through the wielder of the discus. || 10 1 ||
Others likewise prepared a vessel for their own home, O Badrikā;
thus, a great marvel was then proclaimed throughout the earth.
From reading, hearing, and remembering this, there is the destruction of sins;
there shall be enjoyment and liberation, and all desires shall be fulfilled. (10.3)

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa granted liberation to the wielder of the discus (Cakrin) Yāska and his wife Gaṇḍavātā, along with more than a thousand men and women, by listening to their stories," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the woman who reviled [the Lord].
In the city of Bālavana, there lived an atheist who was full of malice. (1)
There was a Śūdra woman well-known by the name Dvirvadantī;
she was childless, the wife of a sick husband, and a reviler of everyone.
If she hears of the preeminence or prosperity of anyone whatsoever, she, being by nature fiery and full of indignation, surely destroys it. (3)
Moreover, she who is full of passion and hatred, unable to endure the dignity of others, indeed reviles the virtuous people, the good men, and likewise the chaste women. (4)
He indeed vainly reviles the Brahmin, the guru, his parents, the elders, his family members, the king, the queen, the virtuous and chaste woman, and the holy men.
Indeed, from such slander, great sin arose for her;
consequently, she remained childless, and likewise her husband became afflicted by disease.
Censure and digging up [the roots] of one's fortune and one's lineage have been declared;
by that sin, the destruction of the lineage subsequently occurs. (7)
Indeed, one who dies without offspring shall dwell in hell;
through censure, there is the destruction of merit, and through censure, even the destruction of dharma.
Fame is lost through censure; indeed, everything is ruined by censure. False accusation comes through censure, and misfortune arises from censure. (9)
An offense through censure consists of the disparagement of the gods, the Dharma, and so forth;
through censure, there arises atheism regarding the scriptures and the neglect of vows, festivals, and other such observances.
Indeed, evils such as these arise from censure;
for a woman whose nature is prone to censure will even revile her own husband. (11)
Indeed, he reviles his mother, father, mother-in-law, and father-in-law, as well as the yogi, the high-souled one, the venerable guru, and the Supreme Lord. (12)
He censures Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Māṇikī, and Lalitā,
as well as the liberated souls, the female liberated ones, and the abodes of Hari.
He reviles temples, those who follow the divine path, and virtuous men; he treats liberating discourse as his own home, and liberation itself as the house of another. (14)
She censures the conduct of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in every way,
and she also reviles his purifying deeds and even the sacred pilgrimage sites.
He censures sacrifices, rituals, and the like, as well as works of charity and public welfare;
such a reviler becomes an object of hatred in every respect. || 16 ||
Therefore, slander is a great evil, resembling a wicked hell;
slander leads to the lower realms and brings about the Mahāraurava hell. 17.
O Badarī, this censure brings about the destruction of one's lineage and the ruin of one's wealth;
thus, the Śūdrī woman, completely enveloped by sin, speaks these double-faced words.
He heard from the mouths of people the greatness that destroys sin,
concerning the Saṃhitā narrative and indeed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Speaking twice, she then addressed her husband with a double roar by name: "The glory of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in Śarkarānagara! (4.50.20)
It is heard that Camatkāra’s direct vision as well as the hearing of this narrative destroys all sins. (21)
Men go there in great crowds for the purpose of pilgrimage;
indeed, I do not consider any such greatness born of a sacred site to be equal to that.
Holy places, vows, sacred stories, pilgrimages, and charity—all these are always in vain for them. What is the use of holy places or sacred stories? Wicked people merely pass their time in vain. (23)
The world follows blindly, acting like a plunderer who seizes only the bait;
indeed, people there vainly sing the praises of Kṛṣṇa’s greatness.
"O Master, how could that be true? I consider it to be a lie;
all of this is merely deceit, a delusion intended for the dull-witted. (25)
Thus addressed, her husband, named Dvirgarjana, said to her:
"Do not say so, do not say so; what you have spoken is indeed the truth, for it is not false."
Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is truth; the story that removes the burden of sin is truth; every wonder is truth; and the Mahālaya of Hari is the eternal reality. 27.
O beloved, pilgrimage, vows, sacred stories, journeys, and charity—all become as if dead;
O beloved, the washing away of sins occurs through pilgrimage and sacred stories.
O wife, the world is not a plunderer, nor does it blindly follow others, provided that one is entirely ignorant of the news of the Blessed Lord. (29)
That great sacrifice lasts for a year; therein they rescue even sinners, except for those who are revilers, atheists, and those who are perpetually sinful and full of evil. (4.50.30)
You imagine only evil and you utter reproaches;
O wicked-speaker, what is gained by you through such censuring of your wife? 3.11
Do not speak thus to me again; for I shall not tolerate your censure.
The fruit of such censure is most terrible: one suffers from childlessness. (32)
"Furthermore, as a result of this censure, you shall go to the abode of Yama.
Thus addressed, she spoke twice over, saying, "The abode of Yama is a falsehood. (33)
Neither Yama nor the abode of Yama exists; that is merely a source of fear for the foolish.
All Yamas are indeed unreal, and the abode of Yama is an abode of falsehood.
Then her husband spoke these beneficial words to her:
"O wicked woman, once you have witnessed the miracle, you will realize that everything is true. (35)
The terrible fruit of sin arising from reviling Kṛṣṇa will surely come to pass;
then you shall truly know that, along with Yama himself, you have reached the abode of Yama.
Having spoken thus, the husband ceased; she too, out of a state of atheism, continued to revile Hari, dharma, the sacred narratives, and the virtuous ones such as Yama.
At that very moment,
having heard the words of her speaking twice over, a messenger of Yama emerged from the sky, and [the others], being prosperous, went to see him.
He appeared exceedingly formidable, with a body as vast as a mountain;
he was terrifying, black as collyrium, and fierce with his jagged fangs.
With hair standing erect, teeth protruding outward, and eyes wide and bloodshot, he brandished a great mallet as a weapon, his tongue lolling out and his body naked. ||4.50.40||
He is nourished by the adamantine hardness [of reality], wears a great garland of skulls, has ears like spikes, possesses two horns, and his hands are endowed with long nooses. ||41||
With a clod of earth and an iron chain upon his shoulders, with an iron girdle bound around his waist, he held an iron staff and a trident in his hands, full of wrath. ||42||
Raising his mallet with speed, he rushed toward her,
roaring in all directions, intent on striking her as she spoke twice over.
Upon merely beholding him, she became terrified and trembled; her bodily frame grew limp, and she fainted, losing control over her excrement and urine. (44)
Having uttered a cry of distress so harsh to hear, she fell there upon the ground;
crying out, "Protect me! Protect me!", she collapsed.
With her hands and feet outstretched, she lay on her back with her mouth wide open;
meanwhile, she became drenched in sweat due to the wrathful Yama-messenger.
Struck with a mallet for the sake of discipline, Dvirvadantikā experienced great agony and quickly became one whose bones were shattered. (47)
Her body reduced to powder, having fallen into great agony and facing death, she became thus;
then the messenger indeed touched her with his hand. (48)
Her body became fully restored, just as it was before,
yet she was struck again with a mace by Vahni for the sake of instruction.
With her backbone broken, her body shattered, and her head crushed, she became overwhelmed;
her frame was pulverized and blood flowed from her on all sides.
Nevertheless, though her life-force remained steady, she experienced great suffering;
again, the messenger touched her all over with his trunk.
Just as she had previously possessed a body,
so too did that follower of Yama violently strike her on the back with an iron staff.
With her back in full bloom [of pain], she, tormented by the Great Māra, let out a great cry of lamentation, beating herself with unrestrained throat. (93)
Having bound her with a noose and stripped her naked, the messenger stood there;
manifesting his true form, he became visible to all embodied beings. (54)
Hearing that great lamentation, the men and women living nearby, looking on, were utterly overwhelmed by great terror. (55)
Remaining far away, they did not approach out of fear;
at the mere sight of the messengers, the powerless ones entered their homes. (56)
Then, while everyone was listening, the messenger, thundering toward the various quarters of the sky, spoke these words that pierce the vitals of that great sinner.
"O slut, you wicked one, evildoer, slanderer, atheist, and villain!
How can you revile dharma, the vow, merit, and the stories of Hari? (58)
"Why do you revile the virtuous, O destroyer of the lineage?
I shall have your tongue cut out, as well as your ears and your nose! (59)
I shall rend your breasts, I shall destroy your head;
I shall cut off your hair and split your body in half.
I shall flay your skin and knock out your teeth; I shall tear open your belly and cast fire into your private parts.
"O wicked woman, I shall pierce your body with an iron spike!
Why do you revile everyone? You boast of lies! (62)
O extreme nihilist, you do not even take account of Yama or the messengers of Yama;
while you are still alive, I shall kill you so that you never act like this again.
Even as he spoke these words to me— who was bound by his noose and under his control—
he repeatedly made me, who was burning with fever, free from fever through his touch.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere in that city;
there was no powerful protector there except for Hari.
Then, suffering extreme agony while being beaten, she who was without refuge, protectorless, and an atheist became a believer for the sake of protecting her own interests. (66)
He remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the protector and the infallible one;
with palms joined in reverence at his heart, he meditated upon the Lord who dwells by Śrī’s side.
Then the messenger, having gathered his own weapons, turned back from the Māras;
at that moment, the wicked one realized the great power of the recollection of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, deeply immersed in distress, she cried out: "Hare Hare!
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmin! Nārāyaṇa Narāyaṇa! (69)
Then the messenger, abandoning the ground, fled and went far away;
having vanished from sight in the sky, Durvadantī departed happily.
Having regained her health, she rose and put on garments upon her body;
yet, with her pride shattered, she was censured and reviled by the people. (71)
Ashamed and with her face cast down, she quickly entered her own home;
there she came to know the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and the greatness of remembering Kṛṣṇa.
She learned the greatness of the names of Kṛṣṇa from the Yamāmāruta;
then, for her own welfare and the removal of sin, she spoke to her husband. (73)
One should go to the Kathāsthāna of the Saṃhitā, which is like a sacred ford (tīrtha);
there, the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) bestows liberation, destroys sins, and is most excellent. (74)
There exists the nectar of the stories of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
for the purpose of drinking that and for the sake of serving the holy ones (sādhus), one must certainly go there. 75.
"In order to destroy the sufferings of Yama, you must go there by all means.
Thus addressed, her husband said, "So be it; do exactly as you say, my dear. (76)
"I too must come there for my own welfare, to that place which bestows liberation"—having thus made this resolve, O Badrikā, that couple [departed]. (77)
They quickly became ready and departed on foot by way of the road;
having reached the stony ground, they then bathed in the waters of the Indus.
Having gone to the two pavilions of the Saṃhitā, they reported their own situation to the high-souled Lomaśa.
At that time, Lomaśa gave him the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s feet,
pure and sweet water, and thereafter he granted him a vow.
Eating only once a day, listening constantly to sacred discourses, serving holy men, eating food offered with grace, and sweeping the assembly hall and other such places. ||81||
He granted them both the vow of service, which includes daily massaging their bodies and other such tasks for the Vaiṣṇavas, as well as a mantra that bestows happiness. (82)
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
O Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa! ||83||
O you who are devoted to the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he thus instructed him to constantly perform *dhūnya* and [chant] the Name. (84)
Then those two, ever-purifying, performed auspicious circumambulations;
their sins destroyed and their afflictions gone, they were sanctified by listening to the sacred narrative. (85)
Through service to the virtuous and other such means, their latent impressions were destroyed;
for the space of a single month, they drank the nectar of the discourse on the complete recitation of the scripture.
Day and night, they performed the service of the virtuous as was appropriate; offering all their possessions, they partook of the food granted by the grace of the holy ones. (87)
They became full of devotion and affection for Nārāyaṇa;
they performed meditation and became deeply immersed in the form of Hari. (88)
All that sin of censure dissolved through service to the virtuous;
his greatness increased among the holy ones and in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (89)
Then, having reached the fullness of their lifespan and being freed from the bonds of saṃsāra,
both Dvirgarjana and Dvirvadantī indeed [attained liberation] at the place of Pārāyaṇa.
In the month of Māgha, on the fifth day of spring following the Vasantotsava festival, they quickly cast off their bodies upon reaching a state of swoon and became divine beings. (91)
With two divine bodies sixteen years of age and endowed with radiant splendor, they were beautiful and auspicious, visible to all the worlds as they moved within their range of perception.
Richly adorned with divine ornaments and garlands, perfumed with divine fragrances, and endowed with divine attire, the two were liberated and became such. (93)
At that moment, a radiant and auspicious celestial chariot made of gold, pervaded by splendor, arrived there and descended from the path of the sky.
There, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari, was present together with Śrī in a celestial chariot, accompanied by Śrīmāṇikyā. ||95||
Adorned with divine garlands, garments, and ornaments, and beautified by divine grace,
he was attended by all the divine Śaktis.
Smiling and bestowing grace upon all embodied beings who beheld him,
he took those two liberated souls in his own celestial chariot and departed for the imperishable abode.
Then shouts of "Victory! and cries of triumph arose on all sides;
thus it was, O Śrī Badrikā, that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Beloved, [was celebrated]. 98.
By the merit of hearing the discourse and by the fruit of serving the virtuous, he, out of compassion, led those two great devotees to his own imperishable abode.
Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa does not take account at all of the faults or offenses of those who have come for refuge and are devoted to Him. (4.50.10)
That compassionate protector of those who seek refuge, having shown mercy, wards off the suffering of calamity and leads one to the supreme, imperishable state. 101.
O Badrī, through the recitation, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this,
enjoyment, heaven, and liberation shall come by the grace of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Compassionate Lord Granted Supreme Liberation to Dvirvadantī and Dviryajana—who were devoted to censuring everyone after seeing the messengers of Yama when they went to hear the *Saṃhitā*—in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the fourth book."
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this story which grants liberation even to the slayer of a guru.
In the city of Khanipura, there was a brahmin named Suraprasādaka.
In their old age, the parents obtained an only son,
who was endowed with intelligence, a worthy recipient of affection, and the supreme object of their love.
With focused minds, they both cherished him properly, protected him abundantly,
and nourished him with food, drink, and other necessities.
They delighted their son with garments, ornaments, and other gifts,
and they also had him instructed in the knowledge of the Brahmins and the Vedic sciences.
Nevertheless, O Badrikā, whatever fortune has arisen from the lines [of one's palm], that very same thing is experienced in due time when it has presented itself for enjoyment. (5)
If merit performed in a previous life is that which bestows a son, then a son is born; he is born for the purpose of discharging one's debts.
If merit were not long-lasting, then even a son born for the sake of one's life would meet with death; for destiny has indeed been fashioned in such a way.
If merit were to grant a lifespan of ten years,
then having remained in the home for only that long, he would depart for the next world.
If the merit acquired by the parents and the son were for the purpose of service, then the son would indeed perform the service of his parents constantly. (9)
If he had not been protected by his parents for the sake of practicing merit, then,
having abandoned his parents, he would have gone to a foreign land and another's house.
Even if he has come into the lap of another, is under the control of another, or has become the son of another, a son does not serve his own parents due to his lack of merit. (11)
Even an adopted son serves his non-biological parents through the power of merit;
for saṃsāra is indeed a bondage of karma, wherein one falls into debt.
O Badrikā, how could even a human being go free from debt, let alone an animal? Whatever is born of the unseen (karma) is indeed far removed.
Whether directly or through a lineage, for that purpose [the seed] approaches him;
thus daughters, cows, elephants, swans, and so forth are born in foreign lands. (14)
They resort to their unseen Lord who dwells in another realm,
offering food, leaves, fruit, flowers, salt, water, and herbs.
The fortunate are born in one place, while others obtain them elsewhere:
heat and cold, water, a seal, fine cloth, ornaments, and diamonds.
Even those born from within the earth attain another birth;
thus indeed, O Badrikā, in this world, beings are joined by the bonds of their karma.
The great wheel turns, bestowing the yoga of the inaccessible; for that purpose the world exerts itself, yet it does not abide for the sake of that world.
That for whose sake one does not strive comes by force and remains;
in such a world as this, indeed, the absence of passion belongs to the wise. (19)
Non-possessiveness, freedom from sorrow, and non-binding; delighting in the self and finding happiness therein, and abiding in the state of the bliss of Brahman. || 4.51.20 ||
They attain the state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), as well as the emptiness of māyā; for those who possess discernment indeed obtain liberation through devotion. ||21||
Otherwise, however, happiness occurs during a favorable conjunction, while suffering occurs during a separation;
for happiness and suffering, as well as union and separation, are bound by karma. (22)
Liberation belongs to one who is empty of karma; for the unfortunate, there is no liberation.
Indeed, all things exist in this world, yet the unfortunate do not obtain them.
Even having sons in old age does not bestow happiness upon one who is unfortunate; likewise, even parents who are exceedingly affectionate do not grant such [happiness] as the grace of the gods.
Eager for their son's education, the two well-wishers sent him to Prabhāsapura, to the house of a learned Brahmin.
Seeking the acquisition of many sciences and other benefits, he went to propitiate the gods;
for indeed, the desire to study higher knowledge is exceedingly powerful. (26)
Having abandoned his mother Devanandinī and his father Devadharman by the power of his desire for knowledge, he went quickly to the house of his guru.
Having bowed to his teacher Bhargacātvālaka, he related the account to him;
the teacher, with a gracious mind, joyfully taught him.
Free from ailment, free from anxiety, constantly engaged in recitation, and devoted to great effort, he lived for many years in the house of his guru. (29)
Through his knowledge of astrology and his realization of the ultimate truth, he acquired the science of the self;
thus the learned man became filled with fame and possessed the power of wisdom.
O Badrikā, although he was endowed with learning, attainment, and merit in every respect,
he lacked the merit of serving his parents and thus did not obtain their service.
Even after having studied, he did not go home at all, being full of pride in his learning;
just as a miser finds no pleasure in his own house, so it was for him.
Therefore, he went neither to serve his parents nor did he obtain that benefit;
for while that benefit was lost to him, it accrued instead to those two elders through their own virtues.
Afflicted by old age and overwhelmed by disease, the two of them, lacking any other support, remembered their only son, who was wise and living far away. (34)
Having studied and not seeing their beloved returned, they abandoned their lives;
crying out, "O son! O son! O our son!", they met their death.
O Badrikā, service to one's parents is obtained only through great merit;
likewise, the sight of a son’s face at the moment of death [is attained only through great merit]. (36)
Through great merit it comes to be, but it would not exist for those devoid of karma;
thus, O Badrikā, sin was born for the son at that time.
Everything performed as service to the ancestors is rendered futile by death through its very breath;
indeed, the wealth of knowledge is not at all superior when in the presence of service to the ancestors and the like. (38)
Service to one's father is most meritorious, supreme, and bestows merit;
it grants liberation, grants heaven, and effects the destruction of all sins. ||39||
O Badrī, you who destroy all calamities and are the most supreme service to the ancestors—if she is not obtained by one's sons, that is the ultimate loss for those born of progeny. (4.51.40)
Everything was destroyed by him, reduced to ashes by the sigh of his father;
even thousands of other blessings are consumed by a father’s curse. (41)
By his grace, O Badrikā, thousands of other curses are destroyed for one who is devoid of merit yet has propitiated the gods. 42.
The sin arising from the neglect of his ancestors resulted in his own ruin;
consequently, the twice-born man began to harbor hatred toward his teacher of sacred knowledge. 43.
Bhargacātvālaka became renowned as a preceptor of learning;
however, being of wicked disposition and excessively proud, he could not endure that fame. (44)
Having attained pride in his learning, he constantly reviles his guru and, having gone elsewhere to assemblies and such places, he disparages the guru’s reputation. (45)
Thus he became especially defiled by sin;
a wicked thought arose within him: "I am a learned man, and no other. (46)
"There is no one equal to my guru; what then can be said of anyone else?
Thus he speaks of his own greatness and thinks in such a manner. (47)
One who utters censure or harbors hatred toward the true guru in thought or word, and even through action, proclaims his own superiority during a ritual; ||48||
O Badrī, one who possesses pride regarding the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and spiritual knowledge, even if he ascends upward, all the merit of that hater of the guru goes to destruction. 49.
Knowledge, fortune, wealth, and fame go to ruin; sin, delusion, mental instability, and madness come to pass. (4.51.50)
But even if he dwells in the teacher’s house accompanied by the fault of pride, if he sees the teacher within his range of vision, he hates him. (51)
The compassionate Guru, who is like a deity, does not expel from his abode a disciple whom he has protected like a son; for affection indeed acts as a restraint. ||52||
Though he was a great scholar, he was like one insane, lacking stability and discernment; his heart was overcome by evil, and his power of discrimination was destroyed by sin. (53)
Once, having approached his sleeping guru at night with an axe in hand,
he severed his head and danced, devoid of consciousness.
Then, having heard the sound of the dancing, the teacher’s wife,
as well as his disciples and others, arrived there in his presence.
Seeing him with an axe in his hand, they were struck with terror;
seeing their preceptor slain, they all wept aloud with unrestrained throats.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the twice-born in the hermitages;
having recognized the extreme wickedness of Vicitta, they then uttered curses.
"Alas! A crime has been committed by this wicked householder, who is like a great outcaste; may he too be slain accordingly! (58)
The murder of a guru is a great murder, equal to the murder of a hundred women;
indeed, the murder of a woman is said to be equal to the murder of a hundred embryos. (59)
The killing of an embryo is said to be equal to the killing of a hundred fish;
the killing of a hundred fish is also equal to the killing of a hundred trees. (4.51.60)
The destruction of a tree is proclaimed to be equal to the loss of a hundred pillars.
The father is the bestower of the seed and is preeminent; the mother is the protector of the embryo. (61)
Indeed, by bestowing knowledge, the Guru is the supreme giver of liberation for those two;
the Guru is Lord Hari, the savior of those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
The true guru grants liberation to living beings and even washes away their sins; like Kṛṣṇa, he provides protection from the noose of Māyā.
He indeed abides as the most excellent, effecting the liberation of countless living beings;
he also bestows the knowledge and intimate acquaintance of Nārāyaṇa.
Moving along, he leads the way for those who follow him, drawing along those who have taken refuge;
he is the witness to righteous deeds and the like, and the one who wards off the sufferings of Yama.
The Guru, who bestows the bliss of Brahman, is the most excellent and supreme;
the four Vedas reside in his mouth, and the virtuous Sarasvatī resides upon his tongue. 66.
The Gāyatrī is on his lips, the Sāvitrī resides in his throat;
the Nirvāṇa of Brahman is in his head, and the station of Rudra is on the forehead of the Guru.
Bhava resides between the eyebrows, while Brahmā is situated in the middle of the brow-knot;
Viṣṇu is in the heart of the Guru, and the Sun and Moon are in his two eyes. (68)
The eternal, imperishable Śabdabrahman resides in the two ears;
Indra and the other gods are in the hands; and the son of the Aśvins is in the nose. (69)
Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha abide in the two breasts of the Guru;
at his rising is the immortal abode, and in his navel is the unmanifest state.
Satyaloka is in the hips, and the teacher’s vow of celibacy is in the private parts;
Hiraṇyagarbha is in the waist, and Meru, the abode of the gods, is in the back.
The great earth is the nature of the two hips, and the Śvetadvīpa and the Ocean of Milk are eternally present in the cavities of the two thighs of the venerable Guru. (72)
The subtle abodes dwell in the knees, the divine powers in the shanks,
and indeed all sacred pilgrimage sites reside in the feet of the venerable Guru.
The ancestors reside in his hair, and the Siddhas dwell upon his skin; all merits abide in his vital breath, while liberation rests in the hand of the Guru.
Through the grace of the Guru, heavens reside in his resolve;
through the Guru’s activity, wish-fulfilling gems and the cows of plenty are established. (75)
In service, he is like a wish-fulfilling tree; in speech, he is like a wish-granting creeper;
in fulfilling desires, he is an inexhaustible vessel; and in affection for the Guru, he is Lord Hari himself.
In the refuge of the Guru is liberation; in the seat of the Guru is the city of Śrī.
The form of the Guru is the Supreme Brahman, Vāsudeva, who resides within the Guru.
O Badrikā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord who fulfills all desires, exists on earth as the venerable True Guru, having attained identity with the Guru. 78.
Without a guru, there is indeed no crossing over the obstacle of the ocean of existence; for embodied beings who lack a guru, there is truly no destination anywhere. (79)
Therefore, one should take refuge in the Guru with devotion through service that offers all one's possessions;
for the slayer of the Guru is the slayer of all knowledge and the destroyer of all the gods and other deities.
One who destroys heaven, liberation, and the attainment of supernatural powers, and who slays himself, is considered a killer of a Brahmin;
he is declared to be the destroyer of all human goals and the obstructer of all power. ||81||
There is no future destination, no stability, and no place for the killer of a guru;
there is no fame and no happiness—cursed in every way be the killer of a guru! 82.
All the sins of the worlds perish in the presence of the Guru;
however, the sin consisting of hatred toward the Guru does not perish even before Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is dependent upon the Guru; Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, as well as all deities possessing the splendor of the *ativāhika* body, are likewise dependent upon the Guru. (84)
The Guru is the unobstructed, divine door for those seeking supreme liberation;
the Guru is the flash of lightning and the great lamp whose radiance shines within.
Upon the destruction of that [sin], the sins of all destroyers arise;
and by serving it, the fruits of all services converge. (86)
When he is pleased, all things become favorable for his devotee;
in gaining the Guru, one gains everything, and in losing the Guru, there is great dissolution. (87)
The form of the Guru is eternally divine, wonderful from the crown of the head to the tips of the nails;
Nārāyaṇa is never separate from the form of the Guru. (88)
Through the worship of the true guru, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is worshipped;
through the feeding of the guru, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa partakes of the meal. (89)
By drinking water for his guru, Kṛṣṇa himself drinks water when satisfied;
through service to the body of the guru, the Supreme Lord is served. || 4.51.90 ||
Indeed, as many services as are lost through the destruction of the guru, so too has that brahmin committed the murder of his guru. (91)
O Bādarī, everything that was considered auspicious for him became ruined;
he became distracted, dull-witted like a fool, insane, and bereft of intelligence. ||92||
Wandering on the path through forests and wilderness, he departed from his teacher’s house;
by the power of fate and due to his past actions, he reached Śarkarānagara.
The learned man went to the place of discourse and stood there for a moment; having heard the story of the *Saṃhitā*, he then attained joy as if drinking the nectar of Hari. (94)
With faith, he partook of food in the great assembly during the sacrifice of sacred discourse, and with joy, he obtained the sight of the virtuous and most excellent great sages. (95)
The sin committed by the murder of his guru gradually subsided;
mental composure arose, and the perception of the body as a solid reality turned away.
His madness subsided, and a state of both mindlessness and perfect mindfulness arose;
thereafter, overcome with grief, he went for refuge to Lomaśa.
He reported all that sin and suffering requiring purification;
then Lomaśa prescribed for him the vow known as Brahmakūrca. 98.
He prepared a decoction of leaves from the *palāśa* tree and other such plants using fire;
having drunk the boiled water of cow-products, he attained purification. ||99||
By hearing this narrative and by serving the virtuous, that brahmin became free from sin; thereafter, Śrī Lomaśa bestowed a mantra upon him.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā!
O Master Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Hari, O Beloved Lord! (10.1)
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lord of Padmāvatī!"—
thus he performed his worship, established in meditation and fixed upon Hari.
Having himself remembered the murder of his preceptor and likewise remembered the abandonment of his father, he was seized by intense agitation and fell into great sorrow.
Day and night he performed worship dedicated to the Supreme Lord;
having attained a state of dispassion, he reached the stage of pratilomya.
Having completely turned back all mental fluctuations and attained supreme withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
he constantly meditated upon the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Great Sovereign.
O Badrī, he meditated within his heart upon Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Ramā, the young cowherd boy;
through samādhi, he very swiftly attained the Lord of Śrī in person.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, having bathed in the morning, he reached the place of discourse while chanting the Name; he remained there, gazing upon Vyāsa.
Accompanied by the mantra, he worshipped Vyāsa and likewise the Saṃhitā;
and while seated in the assembly, he listened at the conclusion of the discourse following the recitation.
Having quickly entered into meditative absorption, his vital breaths were suddenly withdrawn;
indeed, while the virtuous listeners looked on, his body fell to the ground.
A divine, brilliantly radiant celestial chariot descended from the sky;
from it, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa emerged and approached that twice-born man.
Having assumed a divine form and a celestial body,
and having quickly taken him upon a celestial chariot, he went smiling to the imperishable abode.
A supreme wonder has arisen for those who hear this story:
"Oh, how the Lord, the Master, the refuge of all, is the protector even of that brahmin who committed such a grave sin! (11.2)
Having completely shaken off all evil by protecting those who had sought refuge, he, who is affectionate toward embodied beings, led his own devoted brahmin to his own abode. 11.3.
Such is the compassion of that Supreme Soul;
yet living beings are indeed entirely sinful and perpetually engaged in evil deeds.
The Blessed One is compassionate, and the virtuous are merciful;
they grant [their favor] even without an exchange, except for the wicked, who demand a hand-pledge or a debt.
Having purified the wicked and the sinful, He sends them to the imperishable state;
thus indeed, O Badrikā, Kṛṣṇa grants liberation to His devotee.
From reciting, hearing, remembering, or even contemplating this, there will undoubtedly be enjoyment, liberation, auspiciousness, and heaven. 1.17

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Sin and Attainment of Liberation through Hearing the Narrative of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā and Service to the Virtuous," concerning the Brahmin named Suraprasāda—who, though devoid of service to his mother and father and having committed the murder of his preceptor who bestowed knowledge—achieved the destruction of his sins and liberation by hearing the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā and serving the righteous, within the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 51 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Devadrohin. In the city named Vikrama, there was a Kṣatriya named Nāgavikrama. || 1 ||
In accordance with his past karma, even in childhood he was an excellent believer; he always performed the worship of the gods and service to the virtuous with sincere devotion. (2)
Whether through a desire for wealth, a desire for sovereignty, or a desire for a kingdom—wherever there may be virtuous men, whether by means of destiny or human effort—(there they prevail). || 3 ||
In each such instance, he proceeds with desire, seeking to grasp the blessings [of victory];
and in his youth, he should in every way resort to the duty of a warrior by engaging in battle.
He is constantly devoted to that, desiring sovereignty along with his enemies;
wherever he goes for the purpose of battle, seeking victory. (5)
In every instance, he met with defeat and not victory;
consequently, he repeatedly showed disrespect toward the deities.
Even there he obtained fruitlessness rather than victory;
when this was done repeatedly, he subsequently fell into atheism.
The censuring of worship and likewise the censuring of the image of the deity;
the breaking of the Dharmaśāstras and likewise the breaking of the religious duties. || 8 ||
The violation of the virtuous, as well as the breaking of vows, the withholding of gifts, and indeed the obstruction of all meritorious deeds— (9).
The gods act and speak in every way, yet their forms are indeed false; being existent, they are falsely measured, and thus they become false and fruitless.
Valor is indeed real; destiny is merely fruitless. Valor is supreme; destiny is nothing more than a wooden puppet. 11.
Therefore, valor must be exercised, for by it everything is attained;
through valor, kings become enjoyers of their kingdoms.
All the gods in their embodied forms have been fashioned for the purpose of deception;
therein neither the fulfillment of one's desires nor the attainment of the highest gain arises. (1.3)
They do not speak, they do not give, nor do they fulfill what is desired;
therefore, it should be understood that the image is false, being merely fashioned by people. 14.
In that case, the petition made to a stone for the sake of a livelihood would be in vain;
for fruit is indeed obtained from a sentient tree, but not from a wall.
Milk is obtained from cows and the like, but not from stone-cows;
honey is found in the hive of bees, but not from emptiness. (16)
Happiness is obtained through volition, but it is certainly not obtained from a corpse; an offering made to a king indeed bears fruit in many ways, but that which is given to a corpse does not. (17)
Therefore, there is no deity present in an effigy made of wood, stone, or the like, fashioned from cloth; that stone [image] is directly intended only for deception.
A king wearing royal attire is not truly a king anywhere;
a stone image wearing divine attire is never a deity anywhere.
Such a stone image must indeed be shattered in every way;
thus, having fallen into atheism, he reviles the deity.
The Kṣatriya, possessing the prowess of a Nāga, utterly destroys temples, shrines of the deities, and divine dwellings everywhere. (21)
Likewise, in particular, Śaṅkara was always intent on harming the gods, while Viṣṇu was devoted to lust and intent on violence.
Even Indra, Candra, and the others were struck down by the latent tendencies of desire;
how could they bestow auspiciousness when they themselves are filled with faults? (23)
The virtuous are attached to food and devoted to the tasting of flavors; the Brahmins are occupied with marriage rites, possessed of women, and established in the householder stage of life. (24)
Abounding in greed and possessed of faults, they would not lead to spiritual welfare in any way; all these gurus were conceited and filled with a longing for honor. (25)
Thus, how could this creation consisting of craving lead to the highest good here?
Those who cross over and help others cross over never sink down at all.
Those who themselves sink down can by no means deliver others;
therefore, everything in this world is false—the teacher is a mere form and the deity is a fiction. (27)
Valor is the supreme truth whose fruit is immediate;
therefore, people should always practice valor in every way for the sake of their own welfare. (28)
One should be cultivated as a hero and a warrior, never as a eunuch;
for one devoid of prowess, hope placed in destiny is considered the mark of a eunuch.
A fetus is not born from a eunuch, nor is fruit obtained from fate;
even so, O illustrious Badrikā, the prowess of the Nāga is indeed a failure.
Whether standing or moving among the crowds of people, he indeed committed acts of treachery against the gods;
then one day, having reflected thus, he set out for battle itself.
Having assembled twenty excellent and powerful kṣatriyas who resembled himself, equipped with weapons, he went outside the community for the sake of wealth. (35)
That village which is situated at a distance of six yojanas from one's own village is indeed a source of fruitful results;
it remains under the governance of a war-city or a great kingdom.
Having gone there to fight along with all the heroes and their weapons, he,
being eager, sent forth a letter after merely scratching it upon a leaf.
By means of a messenger, the village headman quickly [sent] one named Śārdūlavikrama to the village lord, and Bhaṭeśvara to the lord of Yuddhapura. (35)
Having learned of that formidable event, the great king of Yuddhapura announced his resolve to the one named Nāgavikrama.
He dispatched his army with elephants and celestial chariots;
O Badrī, a righteous battle then quickly broke out there.
With iron arrows, javelins, swords, bhallas, śilīmukhas, shafts, balls, scimitars, bhindipālas, and mallets; ||38||
A battle with both divine and non-divine weapons took place for half a day;
indeed, you were victorious over the army of the great king Yuddharāja. (39)
Some were wounded, some were half-dead, and others had their lives taken;
those such as Nāgaparākrama and the rest were then confined in ten prisons.
Cast down with their feet bound in fetters, they became severely tormented;
afflicted by the pain of wounds, they were further oppressed by disease. ||41||
All those who had committed acts of hostility against the gods came to be in prison, severely tormented by great agony as their bones were crushed by blows to their bodies and limbs. ||42||
Bound by their fetters, they did not obtain even a moment’s peace or sleep;
that was the fruit of their hostility toward the gods and of their fighting out of greed at that time. (43)
O Badrikā, you have been approached swiftly through delusion, pride, force, as well as arrogance, extreme atheism, and the employment of falsehoods. (44)
The entire fruit that was to be obtained on that ground was indeed attained under the pretext of battle;
the king, the lord of Yuddhapura, became a devotee of Narayana.
Recognizing that the wicked Kṣatriya was an offender against the gods, he oppressed him excessively;
he inflicted a most terrible punishment, especially upon those who were hostile to the gods.
Listen, O Badrikā, to the fruit born of his treachery against Nāgaprākrama:
he became mute, crippled, and lame. (47)
He fell into deafness, leprosy, impotence, and blindness;
others too who were his helpers and even those who were warriors [met the same fate]. 48.
They too became mutilated in the prison, with their limbs deficient or redundant;
their pride shattered, they became like miserly men in great distress. (49)
O Badrikā, in this deluded saṃsāra, people are devoid of discrimination;
having attained pride through their own powers, they roar in vain like clouds. 4.52.50.
Driven by the wind of pride, they do not realize at the end of a moment their own destruction and the loss of all their possessions, brought about by time. (51)
Youth does not remain stable, nor does strength ever remain steady;
the body is not indestructible, yet deluded people harbor malice toward it in vain.
Those who commit acts of malice against the powerful invite their own destruction;
for offense against the gods, offense against the powerful, and offense against oneself all lead to ruin. (53)
Due to committing acts of malice against the gods, the deities depart from their bodies;
consequently, they become blind, wolves, lepers, and lame. (54)
Out of a malicious intent toward human beings, they discharge curses;
scorched by these curses, people perish along with their lineages, wealth, and prosperity. (55)
For one who betrays the gods, there may suddenly arise a great and terrible fate—difficult to withstand, irreversible by any means, and bringing an end to life. (56)
Offense against the gods is considered a greater offense than all other offenses; there is no remedy for offenses against others that can equal the remedy for an offense against the gods. (57)
Even one who has reached heaven, an offense against the gods would swiftly cast down;
even one who has reached liberation, an offense against the gods would cause him to fall from that state. (58)
For one who does not harm, there is always peace; for one who harms, there is always fear.
Therefore, having abandoned pride, one should grant peace, and thus there will be no fear.
When fear arises among men, a divine pacification is employed;
even when there is fear of the divine, that same divine pacification is used to turn back the fear.
But in the case of fear arising from an offense against the deity, she is powerless and her efforts are in vain;
for an offense committed in another field is averted by [confessing] it in the field of the deity. (61)
An offense committed against the field of the gods always acts like an adamantine cement;
when the deity is enraged, there is indeed universal destruction—there is no other fruit whatsoever.
Therefore, the gods are always to be propitiated, whether they are present before one's eyes or far away, whether within the range of perception or beyond its reach. (63)
Whether they consist of physical forms, or are embodied as sacred trees, or as sacred sites, or even as spirits—the gods must be propitiated at every moment. (64)
When the gods are pleased, they always bring about happiness and prosperity; when the gods are angered, they inflict wrath and intense suffering. (65)
The household deities, the village deities, the family deities, one's personal deities,
the chosen deities, and the celestial deities are to be propitiated according to the prescribed rites.
The deities of the seasons, the deities of sacrifice, the deities of the earth, the deities of the wind,
and the deities of the sense organs must be propitiated according to the prescribed rules.
The body is a deity, the guru is a deity, cows are deities, and virtuous people are deities;
women are deities and chaste wives are deities—they are to be propitiated according to the prescribed rites. (68)
The deities of the mountains, the deities of the rivers, the deities of the forests, the deities of the roads,
the deities of the lineages, and all the deities are to be propitiated according to the prescribed rules.
The deities of the site, the deities of sacrifice, the celestial deities, and the deities of the palace,
as well as the deities of the mechanical devices, mantras, and tantras, are to be propitiated according to the prescribed ritual.

The deities of the boundaries, the deities of the womb, the deities of the house, the lords of progeny, the deities of the branches and the pavilion, and others— these are to be propitiated according to the prescribed ritual.
The water deities, the fire deities, the Viśvedevas, along with the radiant assembly deities—
all these goddesses of power must be propitiated according to the prescribed ritual.
The Vṛddhadevas, Siddhadevas, Pitṛdevas, Bhikṣukas,
Brāhmadevas, and Pūjyadevas are to be propitiated according to the prescribed ritual.

The household deities— whether characterized by passion (rājasa), darkness (tāmasa), or goodness (sāttvika)— as well as the deities of sorcery (ābhicārika), must be propitiated according to the prescribed injunctions.
The deities of dreams, the deities of the day, and the deities of the night who depend upon them,
as well as the vehicles and servants of the gods and so forth, are to be propitiated according to the prescribed ritual.
The obstructing deities, the cruel deities, and the hostile elemental deities, who are bound by the noose of desire, must especially be propitiated when one is struck down. ||76||
Even the gods and the ancestors likewise place their hopes in such persons; for all those who prance about with expectations are, in truth, beggars. (77)
Therefore, all mendicants should be gratified with gifts desired by them;
when they are pleased, they bring about security, well-being, and prosperity.
All kings desire tribute; all deities desire worship;
all merchants desire honor; and the learned desire respectful treatment. (79)

All beggars always hope for gifts; the ancestors always hope for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha); all mendicants always hope for alms; and the virtuous, beginning with Brahmā, always hope for [the welfare of] others. 4.52.80.

Those with wives always hope for sons; those without wealth always hope for riches; the discerning have no such hopes and are content; and the supreme deities are likewise free from desire and ever satisfied.
Such indeed is this creation; for the deities are to be propitiated.
Propitiation is the abiding in happiness; propitiation is the liberation from thirst.
Supreme satisfaction is heaven; one who is satisfied here is equal to Brahmā.
For the virtuous, contentment is indeed dharma; contentment is the dharma that exists in liberation.
There is constant satisfaction in Hari; such satisfaction is considered the supreme wealth.
When latent impressions (vāsanā) dissolve, satisfaction arises for those whose nature is eternally established in the Self. (84)
That is liberation, that is supreme peace, the highest joy, and the ultimate delight;
for those who are satisfied, it is the eternal flow of the bliss of Brahman held within their hands.
O Badarī, even one who has fallen into suffering turns back if he is not yet satiated;
for him, the suffering is a hardship by which, being distressed, he desists. (86)
Likewise, Nāgaparākrama and others remained by his side until the end, even when he had fallen into extreme suffering, imprisoned and dependent on another. ||87||
They all meditated in their minds upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord, as they had heard him described. 88.
Having meditated upon and remembered Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrīmādhavī, they took refuge in Him within their hearts, the abode of the senses. 89.
They sang out, "O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Nārāyaṇa! And the king of Yuddhapura, perceiving their devotion and worship, [acted accordingly]. (4.52.90)
Having become serene in mind, he then practiced forgiveness for their faults and released all ten of them from prison.
Quickly perceiving the entire supreme and most auspicious majesty of Śrī Hari, they acted for the sake of pacifying the offense and for the total destruction of their sin. (92)
They went to Śarkarāpattana, the pavilion of Pārāyaṇa, and having bowed to the Lord and to their preceptor Lomaśa, the illuminator of Dharma. ||93||
Having bowed to the assembly, they again requested forgiveness from Hari;
Vyāsa, for his part, forgave that act committed by them while he was on the seat of the narrative.
And he caused them to drink the nectar-water of his grace, and then he fed them there with the food of his grace. 95.
Then he gave them the mantra and bestowed upon them the gift of fearlessness:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (96)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O glorious Mādhavī-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O truly all-pervading Lord Lalitā-Kṛṣṇa! 97.
In this manner he gave names to them, and they too performed the recitation;
then, when the month of Māgha had passed, on the full moon day at evening, indeed.
In the moment following that speech, a magnificent celestial chariot arrived from the sky,
wherein the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shone resplendently.
Śrīvallabha quickly descended from there onto the ground;
he touched them with his hand, and they all then became dead.
They possessed divine bodies and remained stationed in celestial chariots;
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led them all to the imperishable state (akṣara-pada). || 10.1 ||
Thus, O Śrī Badrikā, a great marvel occurred there at that time;
while all the worlds were watching, they departed for the supreme state.
Having experienced worldly enjoyment right here, their liberation from that enmity was then brought about by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and by the hearing of this narrative.
Through the chanting of the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, through service to the virtuous,
and through the consumption of his grace-food (prasāda), supreme liberation has been attained.
Through the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s grace, even the destruction of all their enmity occurred;
for them, there was the shattering of the thunderbolt and liberation from which there is no return.
O Badrikā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the cowherd boy,
the son of Śrī Kambharā, grants liberation to all who sing with devotion.
He does not perceive the faults of embodied beings as such, nor does he see their transgressions;
out of pure compassion alone, he grants great liberation to those who seek refuge.
Through reading this, hearing it, remembering it, and reflecting upon it,
one attains enjoyment, liberation, the supreme heaven, and the abode of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Suffering of the Kṣatriya Nāgavikrama—who was hostile to all and an enemy of the gods—along with his companions, such as their mutilation and imprisonment; and thereafter, through hearing the narrative of the *Saṃhitā*, the destruction of sins and liberation of him together with the nine enemies," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; there was a king named Śālamitraka, a Kṣatriya devoted to righteousness and intent upon protecting his subjects. || 1 ||
He was constantly devoted to the virtue of charity, honoring cows, Brahmins, and the virtuous;
in his house there was a perpetual distribution of food, as well as a great distribution of clothing,
and likewise a treasury of wealth that served as a protector for the destitute.
In whose village there are beautifully adorned divine temples, and where there are virtuous Brahmins and noble women devoted to the service of the gods. || 3 ||
In his city, as well as in the kingdoms and villages,
all those who earn their livelihoods subsist on the wealth and means provided by the king.
In every temple, there was a vast field producing crops,
as well as large gardens, wealth in cattle, and male and female servants.
Furthermore, the distribution of food and clothing was performed separately every year, as was the distribution of wealth;
moreover, a livelihood was provided for each household.
Thus, throughout his entire kingdom, there were houses of righteousness;
likewise, there were shades of trees along the roads and gardens within the palace.
At every location, water-wells exist for the sake of flowers for the gods,
as do streams of offerings consisting of sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and saffron for the worship of the deities.
Incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, fruits, and betel leaves are always obtained from the royal treasury for every temple.
Thus, by those of former times, more former, and most former,
these ancient means of livelihood were established in every way for the sake of supporting the gods.
Then King Śālāmitra himself, becoming a devotee, would daily go quickly at the time of worship for the sake of testing him. (11)
Like a mendicant whose eyes are fixed on his alms-round, he goes to each temple and observes that arrangement established by the priests. ||2||
The worshippers do not perform the worship as it was offered by their ancestors;
they do not perform it as it was ordained, nor even the service and the food offering (naivedya). || 13 ||
In some places they do not perform the nightly lamp-offering (ārātrika), in some places there is no prostration;
in some places there is no incense at all, and in some places no lighting of lamps. || 14 ||
In some places there is no sandalwood at all, and in others no tulasī; in some places there is not even bathing water, flowers, garments, and so forth for Mahādeva.
In some places there was no offering of ornaments, garments, or gifts to Hari-Kṛṣṇa; in other places there was no worship, decoration, or libation to the Sun-god or the Goddess.
In some places there is no offering of food (naivedya) to Nara-Nārāyaṇa; in others there is no worship at all, nor does the waving of lights (nīrājana) take place. ||17||
He directly observed calamities among those who worshiped;
men and women devoid of dharma were present within the temples and other such places.

And those who perform worship while devoid of the ritual acts of bathing, as well as those who are impure, dwelling there solely intent on their own interests and merely filling their own bellies. (19)
But in some temples he personally observed that the priests were of corrupt conduct and devoted to liquor. (4.53.20)
Having thus observed the presence of contempt within his own kingdom and in the temples,
the king reflected with an intellect infused by discernment.
Those who were my ancestors gave gifts as their livelihood every day for the sake of Dharma, for the sake of worshipping the gods, and for the sake of divine rites. ||22||
Those who are indeed the male priests and female priestesses in the temples do not perform the worship and the adoration of the deities according to the prescribed rule.
All those eaters of raw flesh who have been abandoned by the Bull (Śiva) consume in vain;
for they have received their livelihood from those very gods whom they ought not to meditate upon.
That which is to be meditated upon does not arise at all, nor does the worship of the deity arise;
those worshippers engage in various vices in every way. (25)
Not even the slightest luster exists in their faces;
indeed, those worshippers in the temples are seen to be devoid of splendor.
Where those who perform worship are of corrupt conduct and fallen from dharma, like miserly soot-stained men, intent only on filling their own bellies. (27)
The gods do not dwell in that place where the worshippers are overcome by calamity, devoid of ritual bathing, and impure within. (28)
Neither gods with soiled garments nor those with soiled bodies dwell there, where the worshippers are indeed those who overcome desire, anger, greed, and deceit. (29)
Gods who are rich in untruth, falsehood, and deceit do not dwell there, nor do those who worship with craving, or who are filled with negligence and laziness. (4.53.30)
Gods who are shameless, devoid of Vedic study, lacking affection for their worshippers, and wicked—abandoning devotion and service—do not dwell there. (31)
Furthermore, gods devoid of reverence for the deity do not dwell there, where the officiants are lacking in vows and possessed of the ostentation of atheism. (32)
Devoid of falsehood and false activities, and lacking festivals for the gods and the like, as well as being empty of modes of worship, the gods do not dwell there. (33)
Where there is no fragrance, no incense, and no lamp;
where there is no lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the gods do not dwell there. //34//
Where there is no purification of the vessels, no purification of the water, and no purification of the food offering, the gods do not dwell there. //35//
There is no purification of the temple, nor purification of the lion-throne;
there is no purification of the divine bed and so forth, for the gods do not dwell there. (36)
There is no sweeping in the temple, nor is there any washing anywhere;
there is no removal of dust, and the gods do not dwell there. (37)
There is no removal of withered offerings, nor the offering of fresh flowers;
there is no new adornment or decoration, and the gods do not dwell there. (38)
There is no offering of new garments, nor any offering of fresh water;
there is no anointing with new sandalwood paste, and the gods do not dwell there. (39)
New grains, unbroken rice, saffron, tulasī, fruits,
sugar, honey, clarified butter, and other such fresh items— where these are not present, the gods do not dwell there.
Where there is no brilliance of furnishings, no brilliance of garments, no brilliance of ornaments, and no brilliance of beautiful forms, there the gods do not dwell. 41.
Where there is darkness, cold, intense heat, and malevolent winds;
where there are afflictions and quarrels—in such a place, the gods do not dwell. (42)
Where the worshipper is a celibate student who is not a cook and devoid of purity, and the reciter is empty of devotion—the gods do not dwell there. (43)
O gods, those men who approach your presence wearing shoes, carrying weapons, and filled with pride—there you gods do not dwell. (44)
Where there is the consumption of liquor and meat, the eating of foul-smelling things, and the drinking of intoxicants and the like, there the gods do not dwell. (45)
Where there is the practice of what is forbidden and likewise the abandonment of what is prescribed,
and where there is no fixed time for worship, the gods do not dwell there.
There are no divine musical instruments, ritual vessels, chowries, and so forth;
where mantras are not found, there the gods do not dwell. //47//
Where men sleep in temples or houses of the gods, there the gods never dwell together with them. 48.
Where the respect due to the gods is not maintained by men, there the gods do not dwell upon the backs of those humans. (49)
Where dogs, pigs, and monkeys roam about in the house, and where those whose lives have fallen away reside, there the gods do not dwell. (4.53.50)
Where the footsteps of sinners tread, where there is the touch of the Divine [by such], and where fallen objects are offered, the gods do not dwell there. 51.
There is no reverence, no cultivation [of virtue], no love, and no affection; nor is there any faith in the worshipper—therefore, the gods do not dwell there. (52)
O gods, where talk of village affairs comes first, where bodily functions take precedence, and where mental impurity stands foremost—in those places you do not dwell. (53)
If the consecration is devoid of ritual rules, if the worship is offered with waterless flowers, and if the entry is without hymns of praise, the gods do not dwell there. 54.
Where the austerity of the worshipper results in the excellence of the worship, and where there is beauty of form, there indeed the gods reside. (55)
Where there are virtuous worshippers devoted to celibacy, or where there are virtuous women who are initiated and firm in their vows, there indeed dwell the deities. (56)
Purity of self, purity of disposition, purity of material, complete purity, purity of worship, and purity of the devotee—indeed, the gods dwell there. (57)
Even though all means of livelihood are available, those men who do not perform worship and festivals—the gods do not dwell there. (58)
If the deities receive no worship, or insufficient worship, or defective worship, they become enraged and indeed uproot the lineages of both the consecrator and the king. (59)
I see in all the temples throughout the kingdom those who perform worship, yet whose worship has fallen away; they bring defilement into the sanctuary. (4.53.60)
Otherwise, a share of the fault would fall upon another—the king and the ruler;
therefore, they must indeed be disciplined by me now through the king's command. (61)
Having reflected thus and established a new rule along with its public proclamation,
he caused it to be heard everywhere for the purpose of daily worship of the gods.
From this day forward, however, those who do not perform the worship of the gods according to the prescribed rule in any way whatsoever, the king shall confiscate their livelihood.
Thus, O Śrī Badrikā, he caused this to be proclaimed in every way throughout his own kingdom; and some men, out of fear of the loss of their livelihood,
began to perform worship according to the prescribed rules with devotion.
Those who were indeed wicked and deceitful, intoxicated by negligence, delusion, and pride; ||65||
Those who hold nihilistic and false views, and who speak falsely regarding the gods and other deities,
do not direct their minds toward the worship and other rites of the Supreme Self.
Then, by the king who was their supervisor, their means of livelihood were confiscated;
some wicked ones were punished, and others were expelled. 67.
Broken images were set upright, livelihoods that had been taken away were restored,
and dilapidated temples were then brought back to life by him.
By doing so, he incurred the sin of seizing the means of subsistence along with its constituent parts.
The sighs and the oaths of the families of the worshippers. 69.
Merit has been acquired bit by bit;
yet a curse destroys it instantly, whereas merit protects for a long time.
In taking away one's livelihood, a sin arises that leads to total destruction;
the livelihood of an aged person must never, under any circumstances, be taken away.
One should perform the restoration of what is decayed, but one must not create a state of emptiness;
for in that case, the fruit of emptiness arises for the doer. //72//
O Badrikā, the sin resulting from that king's seizure of livelihoods and the curse he incurred then swiftly brought about suffering. ||73||
The king was completely overcome by disease— specifically by dropsy,
as well as by the ailments of indigestion and dysentery.
He was overcome by a dull fire dwelling within his stomach;
it did not digest his food, and indeed vomiting occurred. (75)
The dropsy increases and blood swirls within the water;
his flesh withers away, and there is even an emission of blood. (76)
Her belly became like that of a pregnant woman, her feet and hands withered away,
a yellowish-brown hue appeared upon her body, and likewise, there was a loss of strength.
O Badrikā, this incurable great disease ends in death;
yet King Śālamitra caused excellent medicines to be prepared.
Nevertheless, due to the wrath of fate and a curse, she indeed became afflicted with illness;
yet that [illness] was not diminished even slightly, but increased day by day. (79)
Indeed, seizing another's livelihood is a sin greater than all other evils;
it is experienced right here, O Badrī, and therefore one's livelihood must never be taken away. (4.53.80)
The king’s wife, named Jayalakṣmī, likewise became afflicted by disease;
she constantly suffered from a discharge of blood and grew exceedingly weak.
The king was overcome with grief, and medicine was of no avail;
at that very moment, he heard the wonderful news concerning Saṃhitā.
Those people who go to Śarkarāpura for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites indeed recount the story describing the wonders of the Saṃhitā. ||83||
He heard from people the entire description of the supreme majesty [of the Lord], including the liberation of sinners and the direct vision of Hari. (84)
He quickly prepared to depart for the purpose of hearing the Saṃhitā;
accompanied by only a few followers, he went with the queen to hear the discourse. (85)
Having gone quickly to the place of discourse, the king honored the sage reciter with many sacrificial fees and gifts. (86)
Having received the blessings, the king, together with the queen, reverently honored Lomaśa;
and Lomaśa, perceiving that the king was weak, [consoled him].
"O King, may you be free from disease; may your wife be free from disease.
Having both become cleansed of sin, go to the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa. (88)
Indeed, saṃsāra is devoid of essence; its essence is liberation from it.
Life is entirely sinful, whereas merit consists in liberation from saṃsāra. (89)
Thus, by means of these words of blessing, the two were swiftly freed from their misfortunes;
the diseases of their bodies departed right then and there.
Taking embodied form, they spoke, arising from the theft of their livelihood:
"We two are diseases of dysentery, fatal to both of you. (91)
Therefore, there is no remainder of life for you two today;
by the power of Hari, the reciter of Lomaśa’s compendium, you have attained well-being.
Although [the breaths] have departed from your bodies, death is nonetheless certain;
therefore, having given all possible gifts and having obtained the mantra of Hari, [you shall attain liberation]. 93.
"Having offered devotion, you shall surely go to the imperishable abode of the Lord Hari.
Having spoken thus, the king and queen then departed swiftly from their affliction. 94.
Having then entrusted the kingdom to the prince by means of a written document,
he gave all kinds of gifts and further provided them with a livelihood.
Having completely eliminated all cruelty and having received the mantra from Lomaśa,
they both remained for a month near him, practicing devotion while listening to his discourses.
Having purified oneself and one's own soul, and having served the virtuous with devotion, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (97)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Śrīśa Vedīnārāyaṇa, O Lord;
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrīkānta, O True Sovereign! 98.
Thus, with single-minded intent, the two of them, along with their retinue of servants, devoted themselves to the mantra and their spiritual practice, having exhausted all latent predispositions.
Having eaten the prasāda of Hari and having purified their entire bodies,
they became ready to go to the imperishable abode of Hari, which is liberation.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, after the narration [of the story],
at dawn, there appeared a divine golden celestial chariot belonging to the Supreme Self.
Then, while everyone was looking on, O Badrikā, the auspicious Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa descended from the sky and emerged from that [lotus]. 102.
And having suddenly released them from their bodies, making them divine and endowed with celestial forms, the Lord touched them with his hand.
Having placed those two in his own celestial chariot, he departed for his own imperishable abode;
thus, although they were plunderers of their livelihood, they nevertheless became performers of meritorious deeds.
Having purified those who had offered all their possessions for the sake of the Lord,
and having caused them to hear his own story, the Master led them again to his own abode, which bestows liberation.
O Badrikā, then a cry of victory arose everywhere upon the earth;
by the power of the narrative of the Saṃhitā, the king and queen attained liberation.
Tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of people, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, come from all directions to hear the discourse; they obtain their own supreme desire.
O Badrikā, by reading, hearing, or even remembering this,
one attains enjoyment, liberation, the fulfillment of desired goals, heaven, and long life.
There is also the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanās) and the purification of one's own self;
thus, in the imperishable abode, the eternal state and bliss are attained.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation for King Śālamitra and his Queen upon their Arrival There to Hear the Narratives of the Saṃhitā Following the Realization that the King’s Devotion to Life had been destroyed by the theft of his livelihood and the Queen’s life had perished due to severe dysentery," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the slayer of a maiden;
in the great kingdom of Yuddhapura, there was a king named Yuddharāja.
Delighting in the virtue of generosity, performing meritorious deeds, and honoring the virtuous,
he was also a protector of his subjects, yet he remained burdened by pride and arrogance.
In that regard, O Badrī, there was formerly a rumor concerning the daughter's non-violence:
"If the birth of a daughter should occur in the house of a Kṣatriya," (3)
The brother of a maiden might become someone's *śālaka* (brother-in-law), and the father of a maiden might become a *śvaśura* (father-in-law); for that is most undesirable. (4)
A Kṣatriya might not be a Śālaka, nor a father-in-law to his son-in-law;
yet in some cases, he was indeed the father-in-law to his daughter-in-law—such was the renown she attained.
Therefore, a maiden must be slain by a Kṣatriya from birth;
for a proud king of war, a daughter was born of his queen.
Even at the time of the queen’s childbirth, a son was born to a maidservant;
out of affection for the queen and out of fear of the girl’s death, that maidservant [acted]. || 7 ||
Having given his own son, who was exceedingly handsome, to the queen, he took the maiden;
thus the king obtained a son, and auspiciousness spread abroad.
With great joy, the king indeed celebrated an auspicious festival for his son;
the girl and the boy, being well-suited to one another, gradually attained growth.
That maidservant conducted herself with the same pride as a princess,
and the queen likewise conducted herself with the same pride as a princess.
Such was not the case for the prince, for his innate nature was indeed more powerful; even as a youth, he regarded his nurse as his own mother. (11)
Having made her a slave, he lived with her as a servant-girl devoid of human dignity;
then once, the slave-girl, overcome by affection, [spoke] to her own son in private.
