O Bādrī, listen to another great marvel that occurred there in the month of Phālguna: the families of Triśāla were gathered there in large groups.
They had indeed assembled from the city of Mūlatantuka;
Bhavāyana was their leader among those skilled in the arts.
Skilled in both wearing and imitating various costumes,
Bhavāyana himself became their preceptor, providing them with instruction in the arts.
In that beautiful hall of Bhavāyana, which was a center for those skilled in the arts of drama,
there were indeed five hundred disciples who were to be instructed.
Accompanied by all of them, having heard of the majesty of Hari,
he indeed arrived at that place for the purpose of listening to the discourse, as did others.
Having heard this very marvel, in order to examine and behold it, he went to a delightful forest on the shore of the ocean that stood like a pleasure garden. (56)
He made his excellent dwelling within the plumage of the peacock that is the Lord of Existence.
Then, on one occasion, having heard a story at night, they engaged in play.
There they showed it to them; listen, and I shall describe it to you.
In ancient times, a youth born from hunger arose from Brahmā. (58)
Brahmā himself, the creator of the universe, gave him the name Kṣupa;
his friend was the great sage named Dadhīca, the son of Cyavana.
Having spoken thus in the course of deliberating on the superiority between the two,
and having heard that the Brahmin was superior, the king, born of the arms, spoke.
Since the eight guardians of the directions reside within the king,
therefore the Kṣatriya is indeed the most excellent, having the consecrated sovereign as his deity.
Hearing this, Dadhīca became enraged; fearless, he struck the king’s chest with a firm fist formed from his left hand.
The king, in a fit of rage, instantly severed his head with a sword;
thereupon, the terrifying Brahmahatyā (the personified sin of killing a Brahmin) manifested itself.
He suddenly leaped toward the bush and said to him, "I shall kill you!
Or else, O best of Brahmins, revive this man with the Sañjīvanī herb and be happy."
Having heard this, the king remembered Śukrācārya;
he arrived, and that descendant of Bhṛgu performed the reattachment of the head by means of the Sañjīvanī [mantra].
Dadhīca regained his life, and that slaughter vanished; then the Brahmin performed intense penance directed toward Śaṅkara. 66.
Śambhu himself arrived there and granted him two boons:
"O Dadhīca, may invincibility and immunity from being slain be yours forever. (67)
Dadhīca further chose as his third boon the state of having bones as hard as a thunderbolt;
having said, "So be it," Hara vanished from sight.
Therefore, after some time, when a dispute regarding preeminence arose once again between the two friends,
Kṣatriya and Vipra, Dadhīca declared himself to be the superior.
Then the brahmin, blazing with rage, declared his own superiority;
he struck the king firmly on the head with his left foot.
Then the king, having previously obtained the thunderbolt from Indra through his devotion,
struck the brahmin in the chest with it.
Upon touching the vajra, it fell down and did not proceed toward death;
seeing the vajra rendered useless, the king was seized with rage.
Having risen, he went to the house of worship and gratified Viṣṇu;
then, seeing Viṣṇu arrived before his very eyes, the king, seeking a boon, spoke to him. (73)
"O Viṣṇu, grant me your Sudarśana discus, which bestows victory.
Having granted it to him, the infallible Viṣṇu departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the king, filled with rage, released his Sudarśana [discus] at Dadhīca's throat; meanwhile, Dadhīca [uttered] a formidable [mantra].
He produced a hissing sound over the Sudarśana weapon;
then, by that fire of the hissing, all those thousand streams were [extinguished].
Having turned to a liquid state and a state of melting, the wheel was brought to a halt;
the lump of iron fell suddenly to the ground, rendered fruitless.
Then Kṣupa indeed recognized the great power of the Brahmin;
nevertheless, overcome with anger, he once again propitiated Viṣṇu.
King Viṣṇu arrived and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Viṣṇu:
"O Lord, bring about the destruction of Dadhīca, thereby removing his pride. (79)
Viṣṇu replied to him: "O King, the murder of a Brahmin is terrifying;
it must never be committed by one who desires his own welfare."
"But I shall speak with him; do not dispute with the king.
Thus Viṣṇu approached Dadhīca in order to give him this instruction. 8.1.
Having bowed to that Lord, Dadhīca said nothing out of anger;
then Viṣṇu indeed revealed the entire world within his own body.
Then Dadhīca, the king of yogis, showed to Hari the immobile and the mobile, the Rudras, and all that is stable and moving. 83.
Having seen all that is stationary and moving within his own body as Viṣṇu,
the king then said to Viṣṇu, "Show me your illusory power (māyā)."
I am not deluded even by that; a brahmin is always most excellent.
A brahmin is always superior; the kṣatriya is never filled with pride.
O Viṣṇu, by means of these [powers], obtain your own station and take birth again and again;
since you have joined the side of the Kṣatriyas, enjoy the fruit as declared by me. (86)
Your Sudarśana has fallen; regain it just as it was, for the sole purpose of destroying the Daityas, and not for the sake of harming a Brahmin. 87.
Thus was Hari cursed by that high-souled Dadhīca;
thereafter, Mādhava achieved victory over the brāhmaṇa with his arrow.
In all the incarnations, O Daitya, by means of the Sudarśana [discus], Kṣupa then became a devotee, initiated, and a most excellent saint. (89)
Having attained the yoga of renunciation, that supreme and best of Vaiṣṇavas,
the brahmin Dadhīca, then bowed repeatedly to the saint.
Viṣṇu said: "O virtuous one, you are now the most excellent among those who have been forms of Viṣṇu—namely Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Datta, and Vāmana. (91)
And Paraśurāma—all of them were supreme, virtuous Vaiṣṇavas; they were the very embodiment of the Supreme Brahman, stainless gurus of the brahmins. ||92||

Among Brahmins, the virtuous are the best; those born of the lineage of Brahmā are worthy of worship. Among the social orders (varṇas), the Brahmins are the gurus, but for Brahmins, the ascetic (yati) is the guru. (93)
The virtuous are the gurus of all social classes and the most excellent yogis;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa honors the virtuous. (94)
Thus, O beloved of Badarī, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, possessing a divine form, arrived there and worshipped the one in the form of Vyāsa. 95.
Dadhīca also worshipped that virtuous and holy man named Kṣupāyana, who was indeed the very embodiment of Mahāviṣṇu and possessed his own innate radiance. ||96||
Thus, while Hari remained in the virtuous one as the very Hari in the form of the virtuous,
the Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished right there within his own radiance.
Thus, having spoken, they performed the entire drama;
those one hundred thousand disciples of Bhavāyana watched it. (98)
All these spectators—the stainless sages, as well as men and women—were filled with joy upon beholding the drama. (99)
All the peaceful sages, as well as the virtuous women and the virtuous men,
and likewise Lomaśa and Vyāsa, were then filled with joy.
They said to those [gods] for the sake of granting boons: "All of you are granters of boons; therefore, request from the reciter the destruction of sins and liberation. || 10.1 ||
"May this drama, which bestows fame, always exist for us in the world";
thus they also made their request on behalf of those born of their lineage.
"Let it be so," Vyāsa, the author himself, said there;
the sages also spoke likewise, and then there was a cry of victory.
The men and women praised those who had performed pastimes for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—
those dear to the Lord who had fulfilled their purpose by requesting the boon of liberation.
From Śrī Lomaśa, they received the mantra known as Nāmadhunyaka:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā*.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa; Bālakṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Ramāyaṇa. || 106 ||
They performed purification with love and practiced service to the virtuous;
consequently, their sins were destroyed and their latent impressions (vāsanās) went to dissolution.
On the evening of the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, Hari himself,
in his divine form as Bālakṛṣṇa, arrived by means of a celestial chariot.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having likewise made the elders possess divine forms, led them to his own imperishable abode.
The disciples of Bhāvāyana were indeed others in the form of householders; all those men and women were known on earth as the Bhāvāyanas. (11.0)
They became purifiers, delighters of the world, and experts in sports;
all those remaining in Śarkarāpura became Vaiṣṇavas.
At the conclusion of their discourse, they all went to their own city of Mūlatantuka; thereafter, O Badrikā, they all indeed resided at Trigāla.
Those devoted to Nārāyaṇa through devotion shall go to the supreme state;
by reading or hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of How Hari, upon hearing their stories, led Bhaṇḍa named Bhaṇḍaśīla—along with his one hundred and fifty vessels—as well as Bhavāyana, Tri-gālava, Kṣupa, Dadhīca, and Nāṭyakārin together with many others, to the abode of liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the liberation of the wrestlers.
In the city of Śrīkāra, there were wrestlers who were experts in that art of combat. || 1 ||
Fifty excellent men, well-trained and possessing firm bones, as well as other members of the wrestler's clan, likewise became his followers. || 2 ||
Both men and women go there constantly to listen to the stories;
having heard them, they always return home and describe them [to others].
They recounted the divine story heard from householders which brings about liberation, as well as the wonder arising from the celestial chariot that they had witnessed.
"Whosoever attains liberation speaks of that very path.
Then the wrestlers, being pleased and firm in resolve, went to the place of discourse.
Accompanied by many of their own kinsmen, they arrived at the edge of the pavilion; at the conclusion of their conversation, they engaged in a wrestling match that was most wonderful to behold.
Lomaśa, being pleased, joyfully gave them this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (7)
And then he offered worship for the purpose of chanting the Name:
"O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Svāminārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa! (8)
O Anādimādhavī-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Ramāyaṇa!
Those wrestlers, together with their families, indeed performed worship at all times.
They constantly engaged in listening to the discourse,
and with love they performed service to the virtuous and the honoring of the reciter.
With their minds fixed on righteousness, they performed the *ārārtrika* rite for the *Saṃhitā*,
and gave gifts of gold and jewels, ornaments, vessels, and new garments.
They made gifts of rings and cows;
they took refuge in the glorious Supreme Self and listened to the narratives of the Saṃhitās.
Those who have been born are indeed pure, free from sin, and abandoned of latent impressions;
even those women and men who have become aged are fit for liberation.
Their leaders were named Harivarya, Gajakrama,
Śatavāja, Siṃhamarda, Śarabhārda, and Kaseruka.
Drumabhañja, Vaṃśavāra, Śilāda, and Lohapeṣaṇa—
these and others as well, having accomplished their purpose, were free from all expectations.
Even the women and elderly matrons there had their latent impressions (vāsanā) completely burnt away;
they awaited the arrival of Hari upon his celestial chariot for the sake of liberation.
On the new moon day of Caitra, at the conclusion of the discourse, Kṛṣṇa approached those who had performed their worship and were ready to depart, in order to lead them away.
Accompanied by a divine celestial chariot and adorned with divine ornaments,
he was endowed with splendor, fortune, lotus-like grace, delight, and majesty.
Illuminating the quarters, Hari laughed and said to the wrestlers:
"You are indeed worthy of liberation; you shall partake in the merit of liberation."
"Leaving behind their physical bodies, let them ascend to the celestial chariot!"—
thus addressed, those devotees of Malla, prepared to depart for the imperishable state, [ascended].
Those men and women, casting off their bodies and assuming divine forms by the will of Kṛṣṇa, quickly ascended the celestial chariot. ||21||
All the female attendants were liberated; having become divine-souled and handsome, they became servants of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and raised shouts of victory. ||22||
O Queen of Badarī, having led them away, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa went through the sky to His own abode, the Imperishable (Akṣara), while all the virtuous ones looked on.
But other remaining members of the Malla family took their bodies and cremated them, performing the funeral rites for the deceased.
This great wonder spread with extreme velocity through the regions and villages of the wrestlers—a liberation of the self that was superhuman. (25)
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another marvel:
there were usurers and eaters of iguanas who resided in the city of Lūṇī.
At that time, even the householders who sold tooth-sticks heard from people the praises of the Supreme Self. (27)
And the wonder of this narrative, which destroys the sins of the sinful, [bestows] liberation, travel by means of a divine celestial chariot, and the vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (28)
Thereupon, men and women, their curiosity aroused, became attentive and prepared to hear the Saṃhitā, having gathered with the elders. ||29||
Those hundred men—both boys and girls—were led slowly by oxen carrying their own belongings, and they were happy. (4.60.30)
Remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the Vāghgharas departed; they then quickly bathed in the waters of the ocean.
Having consumed their provisions for the journey, they proceeded toward the vicinity of the pavilion;
in the garden, they made their dwelling among a grove of trees.
Then, having brought the auspicious materials for worship in order to hear the story, they, filled with intense devotion, went to Vyāsa’s seat at the place of narration.
With supreme devotion, they worshipped the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, which reveals the true nature of reality; with concentrated minds, they honored it. ||34||
They placed fruits and flowers as offerings before him, laying down gold coins;
likewise, they gave garments, ornaments, garlands, and necklaces of jewels. (35)
They placed before him garlands of guñjā seeds, flower garlands, and unbroken grains,
as well as incense, lamps, food offerings, and saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood paste.
Having offered the waving of lamps (ārātrika), they all prostrated themselves like a staff; then they placed a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of silver coins before him and thereafter related their story.
They listened with devotion and worshipped the sage Lomaśa;
having gone to the hermitages, they performed service to the virtuous day and night.
Thus, all those usurers became free from sin and purified through the performance of the ritual service of the narrative; and from them, Lomaśa [received his reward].
He caused her to hear the mantra and likewise gave her a name-mantra:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā*. (4.60.40)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa-Svāmin, O Lord Mālatī-Nārāyaṇa, victory to You, O All-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa-Lalitā-Nārāyaṇa, Consort of Rādhā! (41)
Having obtained the mantra known as Nāmadhunya, they would always recite it at dawn;
likewise, having heard the discourse in the evening, they would gather together and recite it.
Constantly bringing [materials], they also provided tooth-sticks.
Or [an image] of trees such as the barbur, which possess milky sap and have beautiful branches. ||43||
Having thus gone to the forest at their side, they bring back even the honey— tender, flavorful, and obtainable from within the slender branches.
They offer [these] to virtuous ones and to the great seer, the Vācaka;
they also offer them for the sake of worshiping Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||45||
They bring sacrificial fuel and wood for the purpose of kindling the fire, and they bring earth; there the practitioners of yoga serve [the deity]. (46)
Thus, all the jackal-hunters became devotees of Viṣṇu through their service;
they were purified, freed from sin, and liberated from the cycle of rebirth by hearing the sacred narrative. ||47||
At the end of the month, the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Mādhavīśvara Kṛṣṇa, truly appeared to them in person within a dream, being well-pleased with them. 48.
Four-armed and accompanied by Śrī, endowed with the objects of service and other requisites, smiling and possessing a divine form, he was as radiant as a thousand suns. ||49||
In an instant he vanished; then, having risen early the very next morning and quickly bathed, they went to Lomaśa with joyful hearts.
Having performed worship, they joyfully reported the account of their dream;
and Lomaśa, having heard it, spoke auspicious words to the slayer of the jackal.
Your sin has been destroyed and great merit has arisen;
the sight of Kṛṣṇa, which is difficult for even the gods to obtain, has presented itself before you. (52)
Know for certain that you are all worthy to be led to the state of liberation;
indeed, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa will lead you there in truth. (53)
"Be ready, O elders and others who desire the imperishable state;
Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, will arrive. (54)
Thus addressed, those Vāghgharas became ready for liberation;
both the elderly women and the men awaited his arrival. (55)
At the end of the night of the new moon of the dark fortnight of Caitra, on the first day of the lunar month,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, arrived early in the morning.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself appeared, possessing an exceedingly white and radiant form, brilliant and endowed with splendor.
Adorned with every ornament, entirely serene and sovereign,
he swiftly descended from his celestial chariot onto the ground before the city.
Then a supreme wonder arose and the sky became brilliantly illuminated;
there was the sound of the gods' cries of victory and a rain of flowers from the inhabitants of heaven.
When they had gathered all around there, he spoke to the killers of the jackals:
"Come, for I am well-pleased by your devotion and by listening to this narrative. (4.60.60)
"By serving the virtuous and by chanting my name, you two have become sanctified; come, O celestial chariot that leads to liberation! (61)
O Badrikā, having heard this, those who were ready to go to the supreme state quickly abandoned their physical bodies there. 62.
Having assumed divine bodies, those named Harṣa, Lāla, and others, full of eagerness, ascended the celestial chariot after bowing to the Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
Then, having bowed to Śrī, the men, women, Muktās,
and Muktānikās were led by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and went to the imperishable abode of Brahmā.
While everyone was looking on, O Badarī, they indeed attained supreme liberation through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and by the power of His story. (65)
Now I shall tell you another great wonder that occurred at that time;
listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, for this destroys the sins of those who hear it. (66)
A certain hunter, living with his family in the Sindhuvana forest,
beheld at early dawn a radiant celestial chariot in the sky.
Seeing this suddenly, he rejoiced together with his family;
thereafter, his intellect became pure and directed toward liberation.
Abandoning violence, he went with his family to the place of storytelling for the sake of destroying his sins, and there he worshipped the sage Lomaśa.
He related his own story, which was the cause for the destruction of his sins,
in order to hear the narrative, to receive the mantra, and to go to the supreme state.
Lomaśa spoke this vow to that hunter Kīravaṇa:
"Bathing, worship, wearing garlands, and serving the virtuous. (71)
One should constantly listen to and chant the glories of the Lord of Kamalā:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā! (72)
He gave the mantra of Hari, he gave the nectar of the water from Hari's feet,
he gave the prasāda, the brahmakūrca, and then he gave the vow.
Kīravaṇa and all the others, as members of the household, undertook a vow:
to constantly perform worship, service, listening to the sacred narratives, and recitation. (74)
Thus, when the month had passed, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself came quickly toward Kīravaṇa in the form of a holy man (sādhu). ||75||
He suddenly begged for alms consisting of food such as fruits and flowers,
as well as for the form of a woman— consisting of a bowl, garments, and so forth— to be offered to him.
Having beheld that radiant sage, the delighted Kīravaṇa,
reflecting upon Nārāyaṇa himself, gave him his wife, fruits, and other offerings.
Having undoubtedly tested his own devotee and his female devotee, Mādhava,
Viṣṇu in his four-armed form, appeared in the guise of a holy man.
Having attained the fruit, the Blessed One touched the woman, the man, and the family with his right hand; meanwhile, Kīravaṇa and the others [did likewise].
They quickly became possessed of divine bodies, their forms enriched with celestial beauty;
and Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa [honored] those who had made the gift of all their possessions.
Indeed, by means of a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot, he led those devoted ones who had sought refuge to the world of Brahmā, even as the embodied beings looked on.
O Badrikā, that was indeed the grace of Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
for Kṛṣṇa led even the hunter to His own imperishable abode.
Śrī Badarīpriya said: "O Blessed One, O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Universe, how did this vision of a celestial chariot belonging to a malevolent being come to pass in the sky? (83)
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
In the forest dear to Badrī, he was constantly devoted to the service of holy men, providing them with rest and offerings of fruits, flowers, and other necessities. (84)
Accompanied by his family, he performed services such as massaging the feet of the virtuous; chanting the name of the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, he became a seeker of the company of the saintly. ||85||
By that yoga, O Goddess of Gods, he became pure-souled and highly meritorious;
having abandoned the dharma of hunting, he lived according to the five-fold time-division.
Thus he was meritorious, devoted to the virtuous, and full of deep devotion;
then, at that time, he beheld the vision of this glorious celestial chariot.
O Bādrī, those who are devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) are indeed empowered by Kṛṣṇa;
with divine vision, they behold the divine Kṛṣṇa within his celestial chariot (vimāna).
Those who are sinful, whose bodies are filled with defects, whose nature is defective, and who are wicked; those who are atheists, devoid of devotion, and likewise haters of the virtuous. ||89||
For them there is no deliverance; for them there is no divine vision;
for them there is no auspicious yoga that bestows liberation or even heaven. (4.60.90)
Even those who dwell by the side of the virtuous, if they are atheists, gain no benefit from the company of the virtuous; for them there is neither merit nor liberation.
Even those who dwell far away, if they possess affection for Hari and have hearts characterized by identity with the virtuous, their merit leads to liberation. 92.
O Badrikā, the internal sages must be diligently sought out and met with by those who are good externally; then liberation will be held in the palm of one's hand. 13.
For one devoid of the company of the virtuous, there is no union with the good externally, nor is there internal possession of the objects [of the senses];
for such a person, there is neither heaven nor the supreme goal. 94.
O Badrikā, indeed this entire world is beautiful through the transformations of Māyā;
it is naked within and clothed without, and the state of householdership is even more so.
One whose mind is always fixed on sense objects and who is ever devoted to enjoyment—
though he be well-dressed like a peacock, he is naked and does not attain liberation.
O Badrikā, the saintly are peaceful, their senses conquered, and steadfast in Hari;
though they lack internal objects of sense, they are clad in the directions as their outer garments.
Covered with divine garments possessing the qualities of Brahman, they are adorned;
yet they remain unaltered and free from desire, devoid of the poison of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Devoid of the states of womanhood and manhood, they are considered virtuous and well-attired;
through their union, there is the destruction of sins and the vision of Brahman. 99.
The attainment of divinity by the self, the acquisition of sovereign powers, the attainment of liberation, and the reaching of Hari—all these arise for the virtuous through yoga. (4.60.100)
Through true yoga, there occurs the destruction of time, the destruction of illusion, the dissolution of karma, the destruction of bondage, and the exhaustion of latent impressions. (10.1)
Thus, the hunter in the forest,
devoted to the service of the virtuous and possessing the power of his seed, beheld the celestial chariot of Kṛṣṇa.
From reciting or hearing this, heaven and even liberation may be attained;
for those with desires, there shall be worldly enjoyment, but from the company of the virtuous comes liberation.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation through Hearing the Narratives of the Wrestlers Harivīrya and Others, the Hunters Harṣalāla and Others, and the Fishermen Kīravaṇa and Others," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the serpent Nāgada, a dweller of Līnakṣāra, which destroys both sin and suffering.
In the city of Līnakṣāra, there was indeed a serpent-keeper named Nāgāda who was always a performer of snake-charms and a debater. || 2 ||
There dwells a family of debaters who act as keepers of snakes,
serving as spectators of the natural behaviors and combats between mongooses and serpents.
And he was the protector of wild animals, of reptiles, and the protector of monkeys, bears, and chickens. (4)
Indeed, taking livestock from various kingdoms and neighboring realms,
she makes her livelihood through the play of animals, birds, and reptiles.

"Out of compassion I have come here; I give you the fruit of my story.

Fifty women of the enemy, including men, women, children, and the elderly,

Having fashioned them all with divine bodies, liberated in form, four-armed, and possessing the appearance of gods, he placed as many of them as there were in the celestial chariot.

Now, O beloved of Badarī, listen likewise to another marvel:
having heard the great festival of the narrative from the city known as Ārṣaphala.
Two hundred men skilled in various sports and exercises arrived, as well as women fond of play, lions and other beasts, and elephants. (43)

Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Vādiṭa, named Nāgādana, along with his family, as well as all those residing in the Sārahāsa region, such as Mārtaṇḍamaṇḍala and others, through hearing the sacred narratives, serving the holy ones, devotion, and so forth," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Luñcāda as well. In the city of Lālākhāna, there was a brāhmaṇa who was the chief priest of the royal court.
By name Vilāsadeva, he was a chief minister in the kingdom;
acting under the command of King Śarkara, he was embroiled in a dispute.
He also became an administrator of justice in accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, and together with his family, he held the authority over the sovereignty of the kingdom. || 3 ||
He was skilled in debate for the sake of the subjects, possessed of excellent discernment, and adept at governing the kingdom; yet, he was devoted to greed. (4)
In the dispute between two parties, he indeed examines the hidden evidence;
he justly resolves the appropriate legal matters of both. || 5 ||
When much time had passed in this manner, he attained a firm standing;
indeed, that merchant became a lord of wealth through his abundant earnings from wool.
Even though he was thus born, being full of greed, he did not perform acts of charity or merit;
nor did he visit sacred fords, nor perform sacrifices, nor even give gifts to the virtuous.
She does not honor guests, virtuous women, or the gods; she neither performs festivals nor offers śrāddha rites, nor even causes them to be performed.

O Badrikā, even though he may observe vows or perform some act of devotion, such a twice-born man does not do anything that is truly beneficial for his own self; indeed, he does not practice what is for his own welfare.
Though prosperous, he always remains like a denizen of hell and is like a pauper;
since neither is given away nor enjoyed, he encounters the third destiny.
In this way, the wealth that had been accumulated by this Brahmin named Vilāsadeva became unstable upon the earth.
All the wealth acquired by plucking [the hair] turned into red scorpions;
having assumed the form of scorpions, it emerged from a hole in the ground.
At night, millions of red scorpions emerged from the house;
the wife, the sons, the daughter, and the maidservants were all seized with fear.
Then they all rushed out from the house in haste, utterly distraught;
even the brahmin Vilāsadeva fell into a state of extreme agitation.
Through his insight as a scholar, he understood that the wealth had turned into scorpions;
there he lamented in many ways, making his family members hear him.
"Alas! Our wife, our sons, our daughters, and indeed all our wealth have vanished;
even that which was earned by one so unfortunate goes away like a scorpion. (16)
Behold these copper jars, once filled but now empty;
that wealth which was acquired by me was not employed for virtuous deeds. (17)
Not for her own sake, nor for the sake of the gods, nor for the sake of her family was it employed; always accumulated in a pit, that wealth, having become infatuated with it, has itself gone away.
The wealth of a miser, though it be the goddess Lakṣmī herself, wastes away while devoid of enjoyment;
leaving the one who does not enjoy it, she goes elsewhere like a barren woman. 19.
"I have never at any time obtained a fruit consisting of enjoyment; on the contrary, I have incurred great sin born of plucking [the hair], being a deceiver. (4.62.20)
In the next world, I must experience that fruit of the act of plucking;
the misery in both worlds is manifest before my very eyes. (21)
This was a sin for me as a brahmin, and another sin also occurred while I was intent on the acquisition of wealth: the neglect of my twilight prayers and other such duties. (22)
Truthfulness, purity, forgiveness, tranquility, contentment, observance of vows, worship of the gods, and self-knowledge—these are the innate qualities of a twice-born man. (23)
All that was done by me, a sinner whose nature is greed;
for in this world, greed is said to be the root of all sins. (24)
Greed is the son of unrighteousness; unrighteousness increases from greed.
Fortune, the wife of Hari, has indeed turned away from me who am established in unrighteousness. (25)
Though she was inert, she departed and became a shrine in the form of a scorpion;
for the sake of propitiating her, the practice is the service of Hari. (26)
Without the grace of Lakṣmī, there is indeed no dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha;
therefore, she must be propitiated through the service of Nārāyaṇa. 27.
Thus he lamented, impoverished along with his kinsmen,
having fallen into a state of mental derangement due to that greed for wealth through theft.
Consequently, his family fell into suffering and became devoid of happiness; even that foremost station, known as Kaṣṭa, appeared entirely desolate to him.
Wealth acquired through unjust means has departed, taking its root with it;
therefore, that which is primary—the wickedness consisting of greed, anger, and the like—is what remains.

Indeed, for a Brahmin— and especially for a Brahmin— it is only in a divine rite that his fitness bestows happiness, for such a rite does not destroy heaven, liberation, and so forth, whereas a royal rite certainly does.
The kingdom is always filled with afflictions, and the subjects are ever possessed of sin;
leadership is joined with deceit—how, then, can there be liberation for a Brahmin? (32)
Even at the time of reciting the Gāyatrī, he contemplated matters of state;
even at the time of meditating on Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he endured thoughts of his enemies and the like. ||33||
At the time of worship, performing acts such as grand ceremonies and honoring;
and even at the time of beholding the deity, thinking of thieves, wicked people, and the like. (34)
Even at the time of accomplishing the self, it is the daily accomplishment of illusion;
at the time of accomplishing liberation, it is the intense means of bondage.
At the time of accomplishing merit, the accomplishment of evil is prolonged;
alas, such a state of constant suffering is the very pinnacle of existence! (36)
Therefore, that state of preeminence must be abandoned where there is no pleasant sleep;
indeed, that preeminence must be relinquished where there is no eternal treasury.
The line of destiny indeed spreads out the poverty of a poor man; even the effort of one who strives is rendered weak by that very line. (38)
Just as a powerful birth-line leads one even at the end back to one's own [destiny], so too has my former ascetic state been restored. (39)
Therefore, having abandoned my status as the primary object of affection,
I shall go elsewhere to that happiness which is constantly heard by me from the mouths of virtuous people.
The supreme annual recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā is taking place not far away, indeed in Śarkarāpura. 41.
Brahmins arrived there, as did kings, royal yogis, sages, virtuous men, devotees, and many Vaiṣṇava people. ||42||
The men and women of the merchant guild, numbering more than a hundred thousand, always listen to these divine stories, and they too become purified. (43)
Lakṣmī becomes gracious and Narāyaṇa likewise;
having beheld the faults of sinners, he makes them pure.
Out of compassion alone, Lord Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign,
comes, grants his vision, and leads one even to the imperishable abode.
"I am a Brahmin filled with sin; there is no other auspicious path for me.
Having gone there and heard the discourse, I shall perform the shaking off of my sins. (46)
I shall attain the state of Brahman; may my birth thus bear fruit.
Indeed, this worldly existence is essence-less; even that which has been performed remains as if unperformed.
But having abandoned him through discernment, I shall go to the supreme goal;

Accompanied by my family, I shall now proceed with the narrative;

One should perform one's own duty as well as the duties of the Dharma quickly and with joy;
for the morning time will pass away, and that auspicious moment will not return again. (4.62.50)
Having reflected thus, O Badrikā, that wise Brahmin Vilāsadevaka, being well-prepared and accompanied by his family, became intent on virtuous deliberation. ||51||
Having indeed abandoned that position of preeminence in the presence of the subjects,
and having reached a state of cessation and effected a withdrawal, ||52||
He departed from that city and went to Śarkarāpura;
he established his own residence in a great garden, in the vicinity of the assembly pavilion. ||93||
He set his mind upon attaining the state of the Blessed One for the sake of supreme peace;

Accompanied by his family, the brahmin went to the pavilion for discourses;
O Badrikā, peace arose manifoldly within the heart of that brahmin. (95)
His wife, Muktāgaurī, indeed attained supreme peace;
having visited the pavilion, [he was joined by] five daughters and three sons.
Having beheld Vyāsa, they all desired peace there;
they also beheld the Saṃhitā and had a vision of Lomaśa as well.
Having beheld the virtuous as well as the wicked, and indeed having beheld the Vaiṣṇavas, the sages, and the devotees; ||58||
Thus, by the sight of them, their conceptual constructions dissolved; even their mental dispositions became truly stainless within their hearts. (99)
Agitations have reached dissolution; anxiety has turned away from the mind.
Suffering, disease, mental distress, and all limiting conditions—that everything has gone to dissolution.
Just as there might be the bliss of Brahman, so too was there the bliss of Kṛṣṇa;
or just as there might be the bliss of liberation, so did peace prevail.
Oh, how great is the majesty of this place! The net of illusion has dissolved.
Oh, how great is the majesty of the vision! The impurity of the mind has vanished.
Oh, how great is the majesty of the virtuous! Their latent impressions have been dissolved;
by the mere sight of the brahmin, their afflictions have vanished there.
Having arrived there, he performed an offering before Vyāsa,
as well as the worship of the Saṃhitā and the worship of Lomaśa.
He also performed the worship of the virtuous and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
as well as the offering of incense, lamps, prostrations like a staff, food offerings, and the presentation of fruits.
He placed water, milk, sugar, and auspicious unbroken grains; he also offered garments of fine silk and large bouquets of kunda flowers.
He placed sandalwood and saffron near the collection of scriptures;
he also set down blankets, divine garments, and ornaments made of gold.
He placed before the story beautiful Vedhas and Upaveṣas, as well as bracelets worthy of a king, and likewise divine gifts of jewels.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and bowed to Nārāyaṇa Hari and to Vyāsa,
the twice-born man, accompanied by his family, entered the assembly hall in the pavilion.
Honored by the members of the assembly, he sat down in the place of honor;
his wife, daughters, and sons eagerly worshipped Vyāsa.
Having bowed and held the water of grace upon their faces and over their heads,
they sat indeed in the assembly hall to hear the purifying narrative.
Having heard this, they returned to their own abodes; thus, remaining vigilant, they listened to the sacred narrative and served the holy ones, the foremost among great sages.
From hearing those discourses, detachment arose within them,
and a desire to receive initiation also quickly emerged.
At the end of the month, Śrī Lomaśa indeed gave them this mantra in former times:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (74)
O Lord Nārāyaṇasvāmin, O Lord Mādhavīnārāyaṇa, victory to You, O All-pervading One, O Kṛṣṇa, O Consort of Lalitā and Rādhā! 75.
Thus he joyfully bestowed the worship of His names upon them; thereafter, those Vaiṣṇavas of Śrī Kṛṣṇa performed that worship of His names daily.
Then those householders desired to dwell in the stage of renunciation;
they requested Vyāsa, the expounder whose body is self-luminous, [to serve as their preceptor]. (77)
Vyāsa said, "So be it," and on the eleventh lunar day at the end of the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight, he performed the rite of expiation in the morning. (78)
He performed the ancestral rites with faith for the purification of sins,
as well as the clearing of debts and the appeasement of the planetary influences.
Having performed the ritual for the sacred ford,
he then gave a protective mantra [to him] out of fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, Yama, and malicious hearts.
Having bestowed the protective mantra—characterized by the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika—he then gave him the *prapatti* (surrender). ||81||
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times.
Having thus given this mantra of refuge, he bestowed the Brahma-mantra. (82)
I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (83)
Having bestowed upon her the state of Brahman, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, gave her the offering of self-surrender, saying: "I am indeed your eternal Lord. (84)
May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. Om, salutation to Śrī Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, the mantra against suffering, and to Śrī. (85)
Oṃ, I offer myself to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; Oṃ, obeisance!
Having thus performed this offering, [he should present] the saffron-colored garment and the washed cloth. (86)
He gave him an upper garment, a head-covering, as well as a body-protector and a limb-protector, and also a saffron-colored robe.
Then he gave him a sacred thread, a necklace of tulasī, sandalwood paste, a garland, and an image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (88)
Having thus bestowed [the initiation] upon the men by means of the chanting of the name "Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," he gave the initiation to the women as well.
And having given him the mantras, he gave him a new, auspicious saffron-colored cloth, a saffron water-bag, and a saffron upper garment.
The protection of the saffron-colored loincloth, the saffron-colored tuft of hair on the head, the sacred thread around the neck, and likewise the Tulasī and saffron [marks]. (91)
Then he gave her a garland and the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he also bestowed upon her knowledge in its full extent, consisting of total self-surrender.
The offering of one's body, senses, internal organ, self, qualities, and actions unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is indeed the nature of renunciation (dāna). ||93||
Fasting is the highest austerity; celibacy is the supreme austerity.
Devotion to the service of Kṛṣṇa is considered the highest, bestowing the imperishable. 94.
Indeed, through fasting, that which arises from the transgressions of the body and the senses shall perish;
likewise, there will be purification of internal faults and the exhaustion of defects. (95)
Through celibacy comes the cessation of desires, the destruction of faults, the dissolution of latent impressions, and liberation from rebirth in hell. ||96||
Through the conduct of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, all dispassion (naiṣkarmya) arises;
there is also the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and everything is centered on the purpose of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 97.
Through devotion to Him, one goes to His abode and is seated within His form;
it is said that identity with Kṛṣṇa consists solely in consuming His bliss. (98)
Having thus instructed them, he granted them the nectar of his grace; and those devotees, the most excellent of great Bhāgavatas, [received it]. (99)
Those renunciants, with heartfelt devotion, worshipped the great preceptor Vyāsa;
thus, O beloved of Badrī, even Luñcādana, that bull among the twice-born, [did so].
Born together with his family, the virtuous one abandoned his preeminence;
his name upon initiation became Divyaprakāśakāyana.
The names of the three sons were Suraprakāśakāyana, Muniprakāśāyanaka, and Kṛṣṇaprakāśakāyana. || 102 ||
His virtuous wife bore the name Gaurīmuktāyanī;
likewise, five daughters were given names, such as Mauktikāyanikā.
And Śrīsattāyanikā, likewise Brahmadhāmāyanī, Kṛṣṇakāntāyanī, and Viṣṇukāntāyanī. || 104 ||
Thus they always remained in the hermitage of renunciation at Badarīpriyā;
then, in the course of time, having obtained the grace [of the Lord], they went to the imperishable abode of Hari.
Then, beholding that initiation, thousands of women and men also received the Vaiṣṇava initiation characterized by renunciation on that day.
Many men and women there were initiated as "sick" (ātura-dīkṣita);
some did so on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, and others on the twelfth.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and even on the full moon day, some attained divine bodies; and Śrī Narāyaṇa came to lead them away.
Accompanied by his celestial chariot (vimāna), he arrived there and led [him] to the Imperishable (akṣara). Thus, the path to the abode of the Imperishable was then opened.
O Badrikā, by the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Kānta,
thousands [of souls] went to the imperishable abode of Hari during the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Through reading this, through hearing it, and through the realization of its wondrous power, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, by the grace of the Lord, the Master of Śrī. (111)

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Luñcādana, the Chief Minister of King Vilāsadeva, and his Family Receiving Initiation as Sādhus upon Hearing His Story," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Badrīśvarī, to the story of Sarvādasya.
In the city of Mahīrāya there lived a man named Duritaghoṣa. || 1 ||
The Brahmin who occupies the position of the primary [officiant] is like a person who eats everything;
he is renowned as one who devours all, consumes all, and seizes all. || 2 ||
Devoted to seizing everything, sinful, of wicked conduct, and utterly corrupt,
he takes all things from everywhere, whether by force or by artifice.
There was nothing for him that was not to be taken or not to be eaten by anyone;
through the sin of associating with the wicked, he became like a beast following the ways of the barbarians.
Though formerly one whose actions were virtuous, he later became preeminent in wickedness;
devoid of all righteousness, he became an atheist, a reviler, and a villain.
For royal wealth as well as sin causes a division of the mind;
that wealth, food, taxes, and so forth of the subjects is indeed mixed with sin.
The food of those who carry the staff [the king's officers] is inferior; the wealth of thieves is even lower than that;
the food of murderers and the food of courtesans are as low as the lowest coin.
Through the application of that [vice], the stomach becomes impure and the mind becomes impure;
even the impurity of the intellect is indeed atheism regarding dharma.
The abandonment of virtuous deeds, the pursuit of evil actions, the forsaking of the worship of the gods, and the rejection of the path to liberation and so forth; || 9 ||
Consequently, he develops a craving for forbidden food;
thereafter, even though he is a Brahmin, he becomes an all-consuming eater, just like a Rākṣasa.
Thus, O Badrī, even Duritaghoṣa— though he was a human being,
though he was a brahmin, and though he resided in a celestial mansion— fell into reproach.
Then, having been assembled by all the subjects, he was rejected;
insulted, he was driven out from his own village along with his family.
Then he fell into grief, for the abandonment of dharma is a cause for reproach;
likewise, it always brings contempt from both his subjects and the gods.
Reproached by men, he is not fit for the next world;
he has no auspicious destination, and his fortune is utterly consumed.
His ancestors weep and his family deities become enraged;
Dharma departs and Lakṣmī turns back, planting her feet [to leave]. (15)
"Honor and welcome—these two sons of Fortune have departed to a distance;
indeed, various delightful prosperities dissolve for one who is unrighteous. (1.6)
Obstacles arise in one's undertakings, and there is stumbling at every step; there is defeat in all matters, and fruitlessness in all purposeful actions. (17)
There will be injury to undertakings, and stones shall fall upon those who have begun their work;
there will be famine regarding fruitful things, and the cultivation of that which is fruitless.
Even in his home and among his family circle, strife arises when he occupies that position;
moreover, his life is like that of a dog, being tormented by women, sons, and others. (19)
His conduct in the village is like that of a pig, and he is blind even in the light;
because of the mass of sins within his heart, the fire blazes there every day.
Offenses approach from all sides and afflict him;
they even steal away his devotion to Hari, his service to the virtuous, and his attainment of a guru.
At every moment they obstruct charity, vows, and pilgrimages; they destroy even one's prosperity, supreme welfare, and well-being. (22)
What more need be said, O Badrikā? His human goals vanish;
indeed, all of them become meaningless, and he therefore goes to the lowest state. (23)
Having reflected thus in many ways, he undertook the quest for the path to welfare;
then, from the mouths of people, he heard of the great festival of the Pārāyaṇa.
Together with his family, he heard of the miraculous deeds of Hari, which destroy the sins of sinners, bestow liberation, and grant divine status. (25)
Then, having no other recourse, he resolved to go there;
and quickly, the horses, carts, camels, and mules were made ready.
Taking suitable goods and provisions, he set out in haste with his family, remembering Hari Nārāyaṇa.
Having reached Śarkarānagara, he proceeded to the assembly hall, the Sumaṇḍapa;
then, having performed his ritual ablutions, he took up residence in the great garden.
Having placed his sandals there, he went joyfully with his family to the seat of Vyāsa;
in the evening, he performed the worship of the Saṃhitā and Vyāsa with delight.
Then, having performed worship of Lomaśa and others, and having bowed to the virtuous people,
he sat down in the assembly hall with honor in order to hear [the teachings].
At the conclusion of the discourse, he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with deep devotion;
he drank the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s feet and partook of His grace.
Purified in soul, he was born suddenly and received the mantra from Lomaśa:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (32)
Victory to you, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, glorious Mādhava, Nārāyaṇa; victory to you, O All-pervading Lord, Kṛṣṇa, lover of Lalitā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, husband of Rādhā! ||33||
In this way, he also received the Śrīkṛṣṇadhunī from Lomaśa; he performed the Nāmadhunī daily and served the virtuous every day. (34)
From hearing that discourse, there was also a destruction of his sins;
then, by the instruction of Lomaśa, he performed the Brahmakūrca vow.
At the end of that month, a virtuous aspiration arose in his mind;
a powerful desire to undertake the initiation of renunciation fully took birth within him.
He requested Vyāsadeva, and he then granted him initiation after having caused the funeral rites (śrāddha) to be performed according to the rules following the expiation.
Then, having performed the oblation and other rites, as well as the worship of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
one should then consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and put on the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
He gave the mantras; first, refuge, and then protection;
then the Brahma-mantra, and after that, the self-surrender.
He also gave away his entire possession, including his saffron-colored robes;
he bestowed his whole attire upon the brahmin and likewise upon that woman.
And for his four sons and also for his seven daughters, he gave initiation, as well as a necklace, a garland of *tulasī*, and an image for the purpose of worship. || 4.1 ||
Then he bestowed upon them the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
having received the great initiation, they performed the chanting of His names. ||42||
Victory was theirs, and likewise all other auspicious things occurred there during that initiation, such as the great distribution of gifts and so forth.
Thus they dwelt in the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama), known by the name Saddhoṣaṇāyana;
his wife was named Mahāsatyāyanī, the most excellent of devotees (bhāgavatottamā).
His sons were Vairāgyāyana by name, as well as Śambhvāyana, Yogāyana, and Jñānāyana; thus they came to be.
They had seven virtuous daughters, known by name as Prajñāyanī, Kṛtāyanī, Sevāyanī, Sattvāyanī, and Rāmāyaṇī. ||46||
Bodhāyanī and Pratibhāyanī were the most devoted to Viṣṇu;
they all worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Light. ||47||
In due time, they went to the imperishable abode of the glorious Supreme Self.
O Badarī, such is the supreme narrative of the power of this compendium. 48.
She bestows the dissolution of sins upon the sinful and likewise grants great merit;
at the end, she grants liberation—divine and the giver of eternal bliss. ||49||
It is auspicious, bestowing the attainment of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
it grants heaven and liberation, bestows prosperity, and confers all forms of divine opulence.
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another most purifying story: in a city named Dardura, there lived a very intelligent brahmin who was a minister. (5.1)
Named Dharmabhaṭa, he was always the provider of security and prosperity for the kingdom;
for he had heard from people about his great majesty in abundance. (52)
A desire to hear that story arose within him;
accompanied by his wife, he departed on a single elephant as his vehicle.
Accompanied by a limited retinue, he took gold and silver wealth,
bathed in the waters of the sacred ford, and went to the excellent pavilion for the recitation of the narrative.
He performed worship of the *Saṃhitā* of Vyāsa and of Lomaśa;
he performed worship of the virtuous, the chaste, the holy, and the yogins. (55)
And he deposited there, in the presence of that self-luminous one, gold, silver, jewels, gems, and even the finest pearls. (56)
There, his wife indeed honored the Saṃhitā, the reciter, and the preceptor;
she also worshipped the virtuous women and gave them garments.
They gave wealth, fruits, flowers, and food;
both of them indeed performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
They joyfully placed [the offerings] in a vessel like staffs and sat down in the assembly hall,
honored by the great sages.
They both listened to the divine discourse, which causes the mind to become detached,
generates dispassion, and awakens one to the greatness of serving the virtuous.
Bestowing devotion, instruction, affection for Kṛṣṇa, and the spirit of service,
they joyfully went to the palace in the great garden at the conclusion of the discourse.
Thus, with their hearts perfectly tranquil, they both remained for five days;
meanwhile, they had been serving the virtuous and the chaste in vain.
Those two [sages] were already purifying; they were purified further by service, purified still more by the narrative, and through devotion they were led to a state of divinity. (63)
During the night, while they were asleep, they beheld the Lord of Mādhavī,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the moon-like Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra.
In an instant, Hari became invisible, endowed with divine splendor;
then, early in the morning, those two who were well-acquainted with the greatness of Kṛṣṇa departed swiftly.
Having risen, they joyfully recounted their dream-vision to one another;
both were delighted upon hearing of each other’s supreme vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Dharmabhaṭa indeed considered his own fortune to be blessed, while his wife, Śīlayānī by name, considered her own fortune to be supreme. (67)
Having bathed and worshipped the Lord of Gods, the two of them went to the place of discourse;
there, at the conclusion of the discourse, in the presence of the minister, Śīlayānikā [spoke].
Having gone there and worshipped that Vyāsa, who resembled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was equal to Nārāyaṇa, self-luminous, and most excellent; ||69||
He formed the resolve to sit upon that elephant-throne, which was as radiant as a celestial vehicle and worthy of such a seat;
at that very moment, the king likewise made a similar resolution.
With joy, they formed the intention to behold Vyāsa seated upon an elephant;
full of eagerness, the two of them spoke aloud to Svaprakāśa. || 7.1 ||
At the conclusion of the discourse, Vyāsa then joyfully said to them both, "So be it," as they presented an auspicious elephant adorned with ornaments and accompanied by a golden female elephant.
They brought forth a divine, tawny elephant with long tusks;
then, having seated the venerable Vyāsadeva upon that elephant, they [proceeded]. (73)
Having seated both the sage and Lomaśa there upon the elephant,
Dharmabhaṭa held a golden chowrie over Lomaśa.
Śīlā held a golden fly-whisk over the reciter;
[the assembly was filled] with the sounds of musical instruments, shouts of victory, and the excellent chanting of virtuous men and women. (72)
Having been saluted and honored on the road, and having been offered flowers by the devotees,
the two went to the shore of the ocean on an elephant at the desire of the minister.
Having drunk water and performed other rites, and having bathed, the husband and wife then went to the minister’s residence; there, they both honored their preceptor.
And they performed the nightly lamp-offering, as well as [offered] wealth in golden vessels,
variegated woolen blankets, and silken garments.
Necklaces of precious gems and the like, ornaments enriched with diamonds, various fine decorations, and riches such as fruits and flowers; ||79||

Then the two of them offered worship at his feet with sacred sandalwood paste and other offerings; they performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) with devotion, and offered praise while prostrating like a staff.
Then they both performed prostrations and received the mantra from the reciter:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (81)
Likewise, they both assumed the names Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra and Śrī Mādhavīnārāyaṇa, [saying], "O Lord Nārāyaṇa! O Lord Nārāyaṇa! 82.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, O charming Nārāyaṇa, O Consort of Rādhā, O All-pervading One!
Then they both took up the auspicious water from Your feet, which purifies the world by its very name. 83.
Seated upon their elephants,
Vyāsa and the Guru, resplendent with chowries and accompanied by a great festival, accepted the gift of grace.
They both brought him back again to his place, the Saṃhitā-maṇḍapa;
thus did Vyāsa [attain] the true form of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra day after day.
With devotion to the divine essence, those two, their minds fixed upon Him, served Him;
hear now, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, of the miracle of Hari that followed from this.
Even though other elephants were present, Kṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor, took that very same divine elephant and mounted it. ||87||
Adorned by that very same divine princess Ambālikā, Hari himself went to lead those two, Dharmabhaṭa and Śīlayānī. 88.
The ocean of compassion arrived by way of the sky, making the atmosphere resound with the ringing of his bell and whitening the entire firmament with his splendor. (89)
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, while those with divine vision were looking on,
at the conclusion of the discourse, the Blessed Lord arrived.
Laughing, Dharmabhaṭa said: "Come, [attain] the supreme state!
Practice virtue; come together [with me] to the state of liberation, the supreme state. (9.1)
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, both of them, having cast off the bonds of worldly existence, quickly became ready, taking water in their hands. (92)
Then Dharmabhaṭa and Śīlayānī gave everything, including the gift of elephants and so forth, as well as wealth and other goods, to the venerable Vyāsadeva. (93)
O Badrikā, by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they were born with divine bodies, liberated in form, and captivating to the mind. (94)
Then, while all the worlds looked on, they both mounted an elephant that traveled through the sky, and a rain of flowers fell.
Hari quickly led them both to his own auspicious, imperishable abode;
at that time, shouts of victory resounded repeatedly throughout all the worlds. 96.
Having heard of this marvel, the people were filled with wonder;
the devoted minister went to the imperishable abode, his birth on earth truly blessed. (97)
"Blessed is she, and possessed of virtuous conduct, who has gone to heaven together with her husband"—thus did all the men standing everywhere indeed praise her. 98.
O Badrikā, by listening to this compendium (saṃhitā), liberation from all sins as well as from [the cycle of] births certainly arises for oneself. 99.
From reciting this, hearing it, or even reflecting upon it, there is liberation;
all desired perfections shall be attained, as well as worldly enjoyment and final emancipation.
At whatever moment, whenever, and in whatever place Kṛṣṇa indeed approaches,
one must certainly go along with him, having abandoned the exceedingly binding illusion.
That alone is to be performed which is the liberation from māyā through vows;
by devotion, there is the attainment of the imperishable abode, wherein lies the service of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Duritaghoṣa, the Chief, Receiving the Initiation of Renunciation upon Hearing the Story of His Family, and the Liberation of the Minister named Dharmabhaṭa along with his wife Śīlayānī upon Hearing Their Story," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this story that destroys all sins;
I shall tell you, the presiding judge, this narrative which bestows supreme liberation.
In the city called Prasevanā, there was a twice-born man who was a judge;
by name Mukundasāvitra, he was a presiding officer of dharma and possessed of great intelligence.
Expert in all systems of logic and a pacifier of disputes and controversies, he, seated upon the throne of the court of justice, indeed delivers the final verdict. (3)
He is also the benefactor of all beings; having examined both the proponent and the opponent, he brings about the attainment of both upon reaching a definitive conclusion.
Having demonstrated the pacification of disputes, he indeed renders them free from doubt;
yet, in this way, he has ultimately acquired great wealth through various means of extraction.
Overcome by the disease of hemiplegia caused by his own sin,
he always lies upon a couch, his left side being paralyzed.
For he had been born utterly dependent on others, performing his duties for his wife and servants;
he heard from the circle of his dependents that he experienced suffering in his heart.
Those who attend to this supreme greatness of the narrative—the speech that brings about the destruction of suffering—even if they are diseased, sinful, or unrighteous, [they shall be purified]. (8)
Having heard this story, the pure-souled go to the imperishable abode of Brahmā, which is Hari;
they are born free from disease and become partakers of merit as well.
Having heard this, he spoke to his virtuous wife: "Act on my behalf so that there may indeed be my liberation or the destruction of my disease."
Having heard her husband’s words, that virtuous woman, devoted solely to her husband’s welfare,
sought the consent of the elder subjects.
"How can my husband's disease be destroyed, how can his sin be destroyed, and how can he be liberated?
This must be done by me quickly"—thus she questioned the great men.
Those great men were seekers of virtue, bestowers of justice for the sake of spiritual welfare.
They say that today the hearing of the Saṃhitā is considered the most excellent and auspicious thing.
Ever-new wonders are heard in the place of narration;
there, Hari out of compassion bestows welfare upon embodied beings. (14)
"Lead this upholder of justice to that place of debate;
having heard the discourse, seen the virtuous ones, and bowed to the assembly on all sides. (15)
By worshipping the Supreme Self, that which is desired by you will come to pass; everything desired by your husband will surely be fulfilled, there is no doubt. (16)
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous wife named Gayākṣiṇī departed for the place of Narayana’s discourse, taking with her wealth, servants, and her husband.
Having made Mahodyāna her dwelling place and having bathed, the beautiful woman took her husband in a palanquin and went to the pavilion for storytelling.
Though his husband was overcome by paralysis of the wing, he did not bow to these members of the assembly,
nor to the reciter Saṃhitā, nor to the dark-formed Kṛṣṇa, nor to Lomaśa.
Even while sleeping in his human vehicle, he bowed to the sages and the virtuous;
and even when he found a blade of grass in his mouth, he begged the holy ones for forgiveness for his sin.
The compassionate holy men gave him water for his feet and bestowed their grace upon him;
he too quickly partook of it there.
O Bhadrikā, by that much his strength increased in the body;
his left wing became very powerful and free from dullness.
Indeed, leaving behind the state of emptiness, he became filled with consciousness;
rising suddenly from the midst of the sky, he proceeded toward the assembly hall.
Prostrating like a staff upon the ground, he recognized her supreme majesty;
and by the mere sight of her, his freedom from disease was restored at that very moment.
Then he performed worship with wealth, jewels, and other offerings;
he performed the worship of Vyāsa, the worship of the narrative image (kathāmūrti), and the worship of Lomaśa.
He performed the worship of the *Saṃhitā*, as well as the worship of virtuous men and women,
and the worship of the twice-born and the ṛṣis, accompanied by abundant gifts and sacrificial fees.
He listened to the story and acted accordingly every day;
he also came to understand the greatness of the story in its power to bring about new life.

Through the power of the narrative and the benedictions of the virtuous, he, accompanied by his wife, understood that there would be liberation from the great disease and from the jaws of death. || 28 ||
Likewise, Nyāyākṣiṇī and Nyāyādhiśa constantly and repeatedly practiced the service of the virtuous there in their own residence. (29)
They deliberated on how to protect him from death in this world;
therefore, life must indeed be restored so that Kṛṣṇa may be recovered.
The mind should not go to the home; it should remain in the assembly of the virtuous.
One should listen to the narrative of the Śrīsaṃhitā, which bestows all goals. 31.
The virtuous should be served, the great sages should be propitiated, one's own self should be delivered, and the supreme state should be attained. (32)
For even if justice is established for the worlds in millions or hundreds of thousands of ways,
if justice is not established within oneself, nothing at all has been accomplished by it.
Even those people who delight in disputes and arguments, and who are mostly characterized by strife—even they were satisfied;
yet Kṛṣṇa was not satisfied, and thus everything has been rendered futile. (34)
Those who create strife have been won over, and those people full of deceit have been pacified;
yet if the virtuous have not been won over, then everything has been done in vain. (35)
The wealth earned amounts to ten million, and material riches have increased;
yet the welfare of the self was not achieved—all has been rendered meaningless. (36)
If women and the great, if householders and their dependents have been served, and if holy men have been served, then everything else done is rendered useless. (37)
If those who give wealth are honored, while gluttonous people are fed, and guests are not worshipped, then everything done is rendered useless. (38)
Those who are always quarrelsome are remembered as being constantly engaged in caviling;
if Nārāyaṇa is not invoked, everything done is rendered useless. (39)
One's own body has been nourished and one's hair has always been refined; yet, if the heart is not refined, everything done is in vain. (4.64.40)
You cultivated external consciousness and expanded conceptual constructions;
you did not cultivate dark meditation, and thus everything was rendered useless. (41)
Worldly decisions have been made, existence has been experienced as illusory;
yet liberation for the self has not been secured—everything done has been in vain. (42)
Faith placed in disputes, in falsehoods, or in one's own pride is entirely useless if it is not placed in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (43)
Though he received honor in many ways, a welcome, and was looked upon with favor—if he were not honored by Kṛṣṇa, then every other mark of respect would be meaningless. 44.
The wicked ones—desire and the rest—have been beaten, punished, and cast into prison; no other punishment is necessary. (45)
The worlds were liberated from suffering and calamities were averted;
yet my own destiny in Yama’s realm was not prevented—all that was rendered useless. (46)
Many destinies have been envisioned and other paths have been determined;
yet if the path of Brahman is not embraced, all of it is rendered useless. (47)
That which has been given to many people, but not to the Supreme Self;
that which has been given to devotees, but not to sacrifices—other such giving is useless. (48)
Wealth has been acquired in many ways, as well as fame, renown, and prestige;
yet compassion for the son of Kṛṣṇa has not been acquired—therefore, that which was acquired is useless. (49)
Gold and silver well-guarded in a treasury and within chests, yet Kṛṣṇa not placed within the heart—such protection is useless. (4.64.50)
The vehicles that were mounted and the conveyances that were honored—all became useless, for Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot was not honored. ||51||
The kingdom has been properly protected and the subjects have been duly cared for;
yet if Nārāyaṇa has not been seen, then everything is in vain.
All that has been heard is full of doubt, and all that has been thought is increased by falsehood;
yet the stories of Kṛṣṇa have neither been heard nor thought upon—all else is utterly meaningless. (53)
The poor and the helpless were comforted, and servants and others were taken under his protection;
yet the divine devotees were not comforted—thus his taking refuge and so forth was rendered useless. (94)
The other principles composed of the elements have been explained moment by moment;
yet the principle of Kṛṣṇa has not been told, and thus everything has gone to waste. 55.
The royal footprints have been drawn and the animal arts applied;
yet the Self has not been joined to Kṛṣṇa—such a conjunction is useless. 56.
Even if the oceans were washed and millions of logical arguments churned, and even if latent impressions were not incinerated, all that effort would be entirely in vain. (57)
Even when enemies are fully prepared and one's adversaries are most powerful, victory is meaningless for one who has not conquered their own desires. (58)
Though they may all have studied and constantly recited the scriptures in abundance, if the name of Śrī Hari has not been studied, that chanting is useless. (59)
The letters sent forth, though fixed and joined together, did not reach Kṛṣṇa’s hand; everything else was rendered useless.
Many women have been married, and many sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) have been bestowed;
elephants and swans have been carried along, while the dark Vaiṣṇavas have not been brought [into subjection]. ||61||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Keśava, was not held upon his chest;
at that time, everything carried was indeed a useless burden.
Indeed, beautiful attire has been worn, ornaments have been worn and are well-adorned;
yet the necklace for Kṛṣṇa’s neck was not worn—everything else worn is in vain.
Much was drunk and eaten, and many exquisite flavors were savored;
yet the grace of Hari was not enjoyed. Thus, everything that was consumed resulted only in sin.
All things such as fragrances and the like, when combined for the sake of honor,
but not employed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— all that has been done results in sin.
Other festivals were not performed, nor were divine festivals held;
the great festivals of the virtuous were abandoned by him—all of that was in vain. (66)
If one has constantly observed the anniversaries of one's own birth and even other days, yet the birthday of Kṛṣṇa has not been observed, what has been accomplished by that? (67)
All my life has been exhausted; my body has been subjected to the rigors of karma;
yet passion has not been subdued, hatred has not been subdued—it has all been a futile exertion. (68)
One's own wealth has been divided, and sons and others have been divided;
yet Hari-Kṛṣṇa has not been served—everything else is mere mockery for the devotee.
The entire city was covered, and even the senses were covered;
yet the heart was not covered by Śrī Kṛṣṇa—everything was covered, everything was covered. (4.64.70)
Many have been favored and liberated from the jaws of calamity, yet one's own self has not been liberated at all; therefore, that [liberation of others] is useless.
If one has honored and served one's mother, father, friends, and kinsmen,
as well as the virtuous, then the path to liberation is not difficult for such a person to attain.
The ancestors have been gratified, the poor have been fed, and the gods have been honored;
yet Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has not been worshipped—this indeed is a grievous loss. (73)
The sacred seats have been reached, the beautiful measuring-vessels obtained, and the paths as well have been attained; yet the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa have not been reached.
Nor was a seat obtained for Kṛṣṇa’s feet near the throne;
at last, not even a small space could be found, as if it were empty. (75)
For that embodied being who is devoid of Kṛṣṇa, everything has gone to emptiness;
therefore, Kṛṣṇa must be attained, for everything else is useless. (76)
Right here, for the sake of always obtaining discourse on Kṛṣṇa, an excellent residence is pleasing; therefore, one should dwell here now. (77)
Having thus deliberated with one another regarding their residence there, O Badrikā, the husband and wife, whose souls were dedicated to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, took up their abode.
And then, with joy, the two of them joyfully received the name-mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (79)
Victory to the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Mādhava, the Lord Nārāyaṇa; victory to the all-pervading Lord Kṛṣṇa, the consort of Lalitā, O Lord of Rādhā! 4.64.80.
The self-luminous Lord, having bestowed the mantra and the Tulasī, gave him a necklace for the sake of worship, as well as a rosary and an image. ||8 1 ||
Then, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, the two of them awaited their deliverance;
at the end of the month, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, mounted upon a celestial chariot, appeared.
On the first day of the month of Caitra, Hari arrived to lead them;
he was radiant, dressed in white garments, and adorned with golden ornaments.
He said to the two of them, "My supreme, imperishable abode has arrived. As soon as these words were spoken, that couple began the giving of gifts such as gold and silver.
They both attempted to ascend the celestial chariot by means of the gift of the vehicle; however, as soon as they had taken their steps, they suddenly fainted. (85)
Having cast off their bodies and attained divine forms, O Badrī, they both ascended into a celestial chariot while everyone looked on. (86)
A rain of flowers fell from the path of the sky and shouts of "Victory! arose from the throngs of people;
meanwhile, a celestial chariot appeared there in the air.
He suddenly ascended toward the divine, imperishable abode;
having become distant, he vanished from sight, for that was indeed a great marvel. ||88||
Thus, O Śrī Badrikā, having abandoned all worldly activities out of devotion, the two went to the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through their affectionate devotion. (89)
There, their servants performed the cremation of those two;
thereafter, they too took up devotion to Hari and the name-mantra.
Having destroyed their sins, freed from afflictions, purified, and serving the virtuous, they took refuge in the Lord, the glorious Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 9.1.
Day by day they became objects of compassion, devoted to the sacred stories [of the Lord], possessed by the force of renunciation, and engaged in meditation, worship, and yoga. ||92||
Having become supreme Vaiṣṇavas and having received the highest blessing, they went to their own homes while remembering the Supreme Lord. (93)

Through the ripening of time, all those who associate with the virtuous and possess auspicious intentions—having exhausted their latent impressions and being firmly attached to Śrī Hari—are facing toward liberation. 94.
They were waiting for Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign Nārāyaṇa;
meanwhile, a celestial chariot arrived from heaven for their ultimate welfare.
They too, carried by Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot, went to the abode of Hari; in the city of Prasevana, they all beheld their own chariot.
Divine, enriched with divine splendor and Hari, and perfumed with divine pearls,
the spectators considered their own fortunes to be indeed partakers of liberation.
O Lord, O Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they performed worship for You;
and their sins being exhausted by time, they have gone to the supreme state. 98.
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, the two judges attained liberation through hearing the sacred narrative of Mukunda and Sāvitra, which is an eye for justice. 99.

O Badrī, through the recitation, hearing, remembering, and serving of this [work], as well as by serving the virtuous, there shall be enjoyment and liberation; even one's desired heaven shall be attained.
All divine qualities as well as supreme divine perfections, residence in a divine abode, and union with the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa—[all these are attained]. (101)
By listening to the Śrī-saṃhitā here, divinity shall be attained in every respect;
everything that is to be obtained shall be acquired, for there remains nothing lacking for him.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Brahmin Mukunda Sāvitra, the Formulator of Logic, and His Wife Nyāyākṣiṇī, through Hearing Their Narratives and Other Means," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another purifying narrative;
there was once a scribe who wrote upon palm leaves and wooden tablets.
In the city of Sukarada, there was indeed a Vaiśya named Viśālarekha, who worked with metal plates, wooden planks, and even cloths.
He constantly maintained his livelihood by means of what was produced from writing; being of righteous conduct, he supported his family with contentment. || 3 ||
Once, a dog arrived at his house and entered inside the dwelling; it drank the milk produced by a cow that was contained in a vessel.
Then all that water became impure once it had entered the jar;
the Vaiśya, having gone inside the house, saw the dog drinking it.
In anger, he seized his staff and struck him; the dog, however, fainted, fell to the ground barking, and repeatedly kicked out its legs.
While he was still on his way to death, he was seized by a Vaiśya;
even as he was being thrown into the crossroads, people from the neighboring houses [gathered].
Hearing the outcry, they quickly arrived at that crossroads filled with curiosity,
and there they saw him who had been killed.
The dog had indeed been thrown by the Vaiśya and killed by the Vaiśya;
they insulted that Vaiśya and likewise uttered cries of "Fie! upon him.
"This man is a dog-killer, a doer of cruel deeds, and one who takes water and food from those who should not be approached.
Upon hearing these sinful words, he was then overcome with shame.
Though he was righteous and famous, that Vaiśya, having committed a sin with such haste, fell into a state of unspeakable reproach and grieved intensely in the presence of the people.
