He said to those people standing nearby: "This dog was not struck by me for the sake of causing death; rather, it has been beaten only for the purpose of training. (1-2)
Since he entered the house and drank milk produced from a cow, he rendered it all spoiled;
therefore, indeed, he was struck by me.
Māra was not struck in the vital spot on his side by one who understood;
therefore, Māra suddenly fell upon his own side, right into a vital spot.
"This man is dead; the sin of his slaughter has fallen upon me. I shall perform an expiation.
O learned Brahmins, may you tell me the means of atonement for that. (15)
Thus requested by him, the Brahmins told him of that supreme vow:
the listening to the sacred narrative for one month, as well as the vow of eating only one meal a day.
Association with the virtuous, service to holy men, and charity according to one's wealth;
bathing at sacred fords for a full month, and the constant recitation of a thousand mantras. (17)
The twice-born ones prescribed the chanting of Hari’s names as an atonement;
thus, with broad lines drawn for the removal of his sin, he wandered about.
Śarkarānagara is a sacred ford (tīrtha) and an unsurpassed place of discourse;
for in that location, both the immovable and the movable constitute the sacred ford.
By that rite, he indeed attained the sacred ford born of the ocean;
for he was constantly engaged in listening to the narrative while observing the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Having obtained the mantra as it was taught, he practiced it for only a month;
and that seeker of his own welfare also attended upon virtuous men.
The Vaiśya indeed became one whose sins were destroyed and whose latent impressions were eliminated;
for by serving the virtuous, the evils accumulated in previous births were destroyed.
All karma—both that which has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*) and that which has been accumulated (*sañcita*)—has reached its end;
his lifespan is now complete, and the time of death has arrived. (23)
At the end of the month, on the morning of the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
he bathed and reached the place of the discourse, where he worshipped the eminent Vyāsa.
Having bowed to the Saṃhitā, to Lomaśa, and to the circle of great sages,
he listened to the story of Mālā, preceded by its recitation.
At the conclusion of the discourse and the end of his chanting, yawns occurred repeatedly;
at that moment, Hari Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa arrived from the sky.
While everyone was listening, he said to him, "Come to the celestial chariot.
Hearing this, Viśālarekha, who was destined for liberation, rejoiced.
He quickly fell into a swoon, yet he became possessed of a divine body;
taking him upon his celestial chariot, Hari went to the imperishable abode.
O Badarī, this is the glorious compassion of Kṛṣṇa which bestows liberation;
by means of it, he attained liberation even through the occasion of a penance. (29)
His wife, named Śucikāntā—
a devoted Vaiṣṇavī endowed with good fortune— performed his funeral rites according to the prescribed rules.
Having attained detachment, that auspicious woman, being childless,
constantly practiced devotion to the one named Manu, having received it from Śrī Lomaśa.
She constantly listens to the sacred discourse and serves the assembly of saintly women;
she does so through the force of detachment, as well as through knowledge and service. (32)
She indeed undertook the initiation of renunciation, endowed with all the mantras;
having donned saffron robes, she lived within the circle of virtuous women.
She sent him to Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord and husband of Pārvatī;
O Badrikā, that virtuous woman became independent and destined for the heavenly realms and beyond.
Possessing such meditative concentration, she likewise went even to the assembly of Brahmā;
thereafter, she became known by the name Śucikāntābhavā, the Mistress Beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Then that virtuous woman remained on earth for four yugas,
having caused countless women to perform her worship.
He sent him for the sake of liberation, for the station of Kṛṣṇa is indeed purifying;
he made his residence in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā for four yugas.
Then,
having performed ten thousand rites for her disciples and ten thousand for her female disciples, she attained the imperishable abode.
He wandered through the regions of the earth bestowing awakening upon women;
all those devoted to the truth of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇī took refuge in Nārāyaṇa. || 39 ||
Having established their branches, sub-branches, disciples, and grand-disciples upon the surface of the earth,
they departed for the imperishable abode, the residence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Badrikā, that Vaiśya, the king of devotees, attained liberation through the grace of Kṛṣṇa, by means of devotion, service, and listening [to His glories]. 41.
Now I shall tell you another most wonderful marvel, which, when heard by many scribes, bestows the liberation of wonder. 42.
They arrived from all around the kingdom at the place where the *Saṃhitā* was being recited,
bringing various offerings along with the materials for worship.
Chanting the name of Hari and singing songs of Hari, men and women, children and the elderly, as well as circles of youths [all did so]. (44)
Full of eagerness, they went to the vicinity of Śarkarā, to the great garden;
having made their dwelling in the great garden, they performed their ablutions at the sacred bathing-place.
Carrying begging bowls, they arrived at the assembly hall for the discourse;
they offered shouts of victory and prostrated themselves with palms joined in reverence. (46)
They performed worship of the *Saṃhitā*, of the [divine] image, and of the reciter; and they offered honors to the virtuous ones, the most excellent great sages, and to the chaste women. (47)
They performed worship for the brahmins and yogins, offered the arati lamp,
sat together in the assembly hall, and listened to the nectar of sacred discourse.

They received the mantra from him who was self-luminous, and they took their names from him; then they departed for their own dwellings and remained there for a month, seeking discourse on the meaning [of the teachings].
They performed various kinds of service to the virtuous and engaged in congregational chanting;
they bathed in sacred fords, gave gifts, and offered worship to one another. (4.65.50)
Their sins were removed and their latent impressions of illusion vanished;
thousands of men and women became purified souls. ||5 1||
And on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, O Badrikā, Hari arrived;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa came accompanied by a golden celestial chariot.
Hasan said to all the scribes with compassion and joy:
"Listen with delight as I speak of my stories and serve me, O virtuous ones! (5.3)
And I have come for the sake of the welfare of you who worship Me;
let those who desire to come enter My imperishable abode.
"Be ready quickly and ascend my celestial chariot;
I shall lead you to the imperishable abode, the temple of eternal bliss. (55)
Thus addressed, the five hundred women residing in the body, beginning with Karaṇā, suddenly became ready for liberation.
O Bṛhadbala, the tumultuous shouts of those men, along with the calls for lifting by the thousands, arose on all sides, causing great wonder. (57)
Then five hundred men and women, including those from the young to the old, quickly cast off their physical bodies. (58)
By the waters sprinkled by Kṛṣṇa, they all attained divine bodies;
those auspicious Muktas and Muktānikās were all sixteen years of age.
They ascended the celestial chariot and entered before Hari;
they worshipped him with supreme devotion through embraces, touch, folded hands, and hymns of praise.
Led by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they went to the supreme abode, O Badrikā,
even as they were listening and watching with wonder.
The celestial chariot of all the other worlds entered heaven;
a great wonder arose through the grace of the Lord Hari. (62)
Thereafter, the funeral rites for the deceased were performed by those standing behind;
having heard the discourse, they too became detached and departed from that place.
They practiced devotion to Kṛṣṇa in their respective dwellings,
and in due time, they went to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Soul.
O Badrikā, listen to me as I relate a most wonderful account:
in the city of Trivādana, there was a ruler named Śāhavilāpana.
He possessed abundant wealth, including gardens, fields, houses, and the like;
he also had horses, bulls, gayals, camels, and other livestock.
There were hundreds of cows, goats, buffaloes, and even more servants;
at that time, Khaṇḍarāja was the village headman and Śāhavilāpana.
He indeed maintained the horse-keepers and cowherds with wages;
for that Kṣatriya had heard of a most great festival of stories.
He made up his mind to go there along with the horse-herders;
he quickly prepared himself together with his wife, Śrīsvāminī.
The illustrious Svāminī Satī brought a hundred cows for the purpose of charity and religious duty, as well as for the purpose of drinking their milk.
They set out from their homes and went to Śarkarānagara;
so too did the cowherds, the horse-keepers, and the attendants of the Shah.
Then Śrī Svāminī, as well as her friends and a hundred maidservants,
were adorned with ornaments, equipped with necessary articles, bearing gifts, and possessed of all prosperity.
In the great garden, they each constructed their own dwellings as was appropriate;
having bathed, they set out for the assembly hall with offerings in hand to behold [the sage].
Having heard the discourse, the king, the queen, the wealthy men, as well as the servants and others, then performed worship and the ārātrika ceremony. (74)
They placed ornaments, seals, and garments before Vyāsa,
as well as fruits, flowers, food, delicacies, milk, and dairy products.
The great sages Svaprakāśāyana and Lomaśa also bestowed their blessings upon them, and then they departed for their own dwellings.
Thus, constantly restrained, they listened to the narrative of the Saṃhitā.
One day at night, the king saw his own corpse in a dream; when morning came, [he found it so]. (77)
Rising up in fear, he went to the place of assembly and reported the terrifying account of his dream to Lomaśa.
Then Lomaśa said to the king, whose life was now drawing to a close:
"O King, your task has been completed through your devotion to this narrative. (79)
Receive the mantra and take up even the name of the glorious Supreme Self;
be prepared for the sake of liberation and abandon worldly attachment.
Thus addressed, he quickly indeed took up the mantra and the name:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā. (8.1)
The queen’s female servants as well as the male servants received the supreme mantra:
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā*. (82)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa; Bālakṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Ramāyaṇa. ||83||
Victory to you, O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Mādhava, Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! Victory to you, O All-pervading One, Kṛṣṇa, Lalitā-Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Rādhā! 84.
Having received the mantra, they performed worship together in their own home;
the king and queen gave gifts of elephants and horses. (85)
Having prepared cows, gold, jewels, ornaments, garments, and other riches, the king, accompanied by his queens, awaited [him]. (86)
He properly performs [this rite] to go to the supreme state of liberation;
on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, Hari arrives by means of a celestial chariot.
Having purified the food along with the queen through the service of the virtuous,
and having fashioned a divine body for them, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa made them His own.
Likewise, having endowed other male and female servants with divine bodies and furnished them with all the wealth they desired, he seated them within his own celestial chariot.
While all the worlds were looking on, he was led to his own imperishable abode.
O Badrikā, seeing that great wonder, the other maidservants and attendants—
Having given all their gifts, they were firmly resolved upon the goal of liberation for the sake of the eldest prince, named Bhāskarabhūti. (9.1)
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom [to their son], they became prepared for liberation;
abandoning food, eating, and other such activities, they took refuge in Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa.
At the end of three days, the Blessed Lord Svāmī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa came swiftly out of compassion to lead him to His own imperishable abode.
Having rendered them all unconscious by means of a celestial chariot,
he caused them to relinquish their bodies and bestowed upon them divine forms.
While all embodied beings looked on, he was led to his own imperishable abode;
then Kumāra Bhāskarabhūti performed his funeral rites.
Having become a devotee and having heard the sacred narrative, he considered his good fortune to be supreme and great;
he went to the city of Trivāda and always governed it with justice.
When the time had arrived, that holy man, with a heart free from worldly desires, joyfully entrusted his own burden to his lineage out of devotion. (97)
Driven by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he went to the imperishable abode.
Thus, O beloved of Badarī, a supreme wonder was witnessed by the people. 98.
The bestower of liberation and destroyer of sins, she is the direct union with the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
those who, in the city of Trivāda, heard of that miracle— [99]
They too, enriched by the state of being beyond the senses, took refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
their sins were destroyed, and they became devoted to the service of the virtuous.
Through association with the virtuous and by taking refuge in compassion, they attained the imperishable abode in the end;
by reading or hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.
The horse-herders, the cowherds, and whoever else were at Trivādaka—
they too, having devoted themselves to Kṛṣṇa, went to the supreme imperishable abode.
Even animals of low birth, such as goats and cattle,
attained the imperishable abode of the Lord through the application of offering their milk.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Scribe Viśālarekha along with his wife, many Karaṇas and Kāyasthas, and the Kṣatriya Śāhavilāpana along with his wife, female servants, and male servants, through the hearing of the narrative and other means," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the vulture which bestows liberation;
it concerns the constant consumption of the remnants of the food of the virtuous at the site of Pārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
Having devoured [the corpse] at midday, the vulture attained eternal liberation;
meanwhile, in the grove of banyan trees, there were more than a hundred aged vultures. (2)
Indeed, all of us, from children to the elderly, lived in that grove of banyan trees;
flying up again and again into the sky, we used to search for food.
Having gone far and far away, they would devour whatever was sought;
at the time of their completion, there was always a great festival.
In that Pārāyaṇa-kṣetra, where countless men constantly take their meals upon the grounds intended for food, (5)
Various kinds of food remnants fell, O Badrikā;
fried foods, vegetables, and sweetmeats also fell.
Where there are indeed rows of Vaiṣṇavas day and night,
as well as rows of virtuous women and likewise rows of holy men.
There, virtuous people partake of the food out of grace—
specifically those remnants which have indeed fallen from their plates.
And hundreds of vultures always eat the food left over from the worthy recipients at the end of the row; they all become satisfied every day.
Even in a great heap at the place where food scraps are discarded, birds eat the stale food, vegetables, and other remnants that have been thrown there. (4.66.10)
Listen, O beloved of Badarī: on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, at the auspicious hour of midday, the Lord Vyāsa appeared of his own accord.
Having eaten, he threw the remains, along with his bowl, aside in the field;
then a certain aged vulture flew up from a banyan tree and approached.
He consumed that remnant mixed with the grace of Kṛṣṇa;
at that moment, all his sins were indeed destroyed.
His meritorious soul became instantly purified and his latent karmic impressions were reduced to ashes;
while many looked on, the bird quickly fell to the ground.
Having emerged from the body of the bird, he appeared there in the sky with a divine body and four arms, having become an attendant of Śrī Hari.
All the virtuous ones, as well as the other Vaiṣṇavas, were struck with wonder;
beholding him in the form of an attendant, the virtuous ones questioned him.
"Who are you, who, though in the form of a bird, have assumed the appearance of an attendant? Tell me everything exactly as it is, and satisfy my curiosity."
Having heard this, the attendant, filled with eagerness, spoke to the virtuous ones:
"In a former life, I was a human kaulika on earth. (18)
I was known by the name Daṇḍāraṇi, devoted to violence and theft;
I lived in the city of Khādaka, possessing a very large family.
I, who am old, had an old son; he had ten sons.
From those ten there were hundreds, and from those hundreds there were thousands.
There were likewise maidens, and their lineages numbered a thousand;
the entire city of Khādaka was for the most part inhabited by Kaulikas.
All of us were always householders with good families; for the sake of our livelihood, we constantly performed the work of agriculture.
In times of famine or during the heat of summer, we may commit theft by force, plundering and seizing wealth, food, clothing, and all manner of riches. (23)
We consume the food and other provisions of brahmins, virtuous men, kṣatriyas, and other embodied beings; we wear their garments and so forth. (24)
By that sin, we have indeed become most wicked upon death—whether they be the elderly, children, or youths, and whether they be men or women. (25)
"We are all vultures born here upon this banyan tree, born of this lineage;
having experienced the miseries of Yama, we have indeed become vultures here on this banyan tree. (26)
Among all of them, I was the eldest and became particularly a thief;
having stolen repeatedly from them, I then provided for their maintenance.
Having been released from that great suffering in the realm of Yama, I have attained the state of a vulture here;
I am old, most ancient, and many years of age. (28)
Having obtained the remnants of Vyāsa’s meal, the supreme grace of Hari,
my skin disease was instantly burnt away and my latent tendencies were destroyed right here.
I have reached the state of liberation and am freed from my avian body;
therefore, I shall now depart for the purifying Badarikāśrama.
"I shall go to Śvetadvīpa and thereafter to Vaikuṇṭha;
thus my liberation has been achieved simply by eating this grace. (3.1)
But the greatness of grace cannot be described by me;
even those of great sins and even the lowest are liberated through grace. (32)
Knowing very well the greatness of grace, Brahmā himself, having become a fish, consumed the excellent prasāda. ||33||
The gods always desire grace, and the ancestors even more so;
[it is] a destroyer of sins, a bestower of merit, an increaser of strength, and likewise a giver of liberation. (34)
If the life-breaths of those suffering the pain of death do not depart, then by obtaining his grace, their life-breaths indeed depart swiftly. (35)
The shadow of ghosts, spirits, and demons does not obscure him;
nor do ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and piśācikās afflict him. (36)
For those who partake of the food offered with devotion, their inner selves become stainless;
they proceed toward righteousness, and their darkness and sins are destroyed. (37)
In this world, the body of one who always eats what is not offered with devotion is like a piśāca;
however, the body of one devoted to eating what is offered with devotion is always like a deity. (38)
The gods dwell eternally within the body that partakes of prasāda;
for those who consume prasāda, the divine body is always purifying. (39)
Those who enjoy what has not been offered with faith are indeed consumers of sin; for that which is devoid of faith is the food of ghosts, spirits, and demons.
Compassion for those who constantly subsist on prasāda arises from Kṛṣṇa;
through that compassion, all prosperities are attained, and at the end of the body, the prosperity of liberation is achieved. 41.
Food given with faith is always devoid of [worldly] qualities and free from defects;
even if it is entirely heavy with flavor, it is always considered to be flavorless [to the wise]. (42)
All tastes offered to Kṛṣṇa, even when consumed, do not bind you; nor do those forms which are beautiful, nor those women of lovely appearance. (43)
Even those [objects] possessed of shimmering brilliance and endowed with radiant luster,
when offered to Kṛṣṇa and enjoyed, do not bind at all, for they are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
There are various kinds of fragrances, both high and low, such as those derived from oils and the like,
as well as musk, saffron, camphor, and other essences of scent.
Offered to Kṛṣṇa, those [objects] are devoid of the guṇas; when enjoyed, they do not bind at all.
Beautiful sounds, laden with excellent meaning, captivating, and delightful—[these too, when offered, do not bind]. (46)
Those who possess beautiful voices, who are full of festive joy, and who play captivating stringed instruments—
even if they are devoid of spiritual qualities, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, they do not bind one at all upon being enjoyed.
All musical instruments, songs, melodies, and vocal performances were offered to Kṛṣṇa; they were devoid of qualities and free from bondage. ||48||
Their touches are soft, smooth, gentle, and even cool;
they are warm, accessible, of desirable appearance, bestowing great bliss, and pleasant. (49)
Whether residing in sentient beings or in insentient things, whatever is offered to Kṛṣṇa does not cause bondage;
so too, various types of associations—whether firm or loose—do not bind. (4.66.50)
All liquids whatsoever, as well as those oils that are mutually beneficial, along with insights, poetic compositions, logical reasonings, and likewise intellectual powers. (51)
All kinds of pleasure and pain, all desires and latent predispositions, all hatreds, efforts, and actions, as well as merit, demerit, and so forth—[all these arise from the mind]. (52)
Indeed, all meditations and whatever ritual actions there may be—
whether they be existent states or non-existent states— are always devoid of qualities when offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They do not bind their enjoyer because they are devoid of *māyā*; for *māyā*, *sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*, egoism, possessiveness, and the like [are the causes of bondage]. (54)
Possession, sleep, and lethargy, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, are indeed devoid of qualities;
so too are man, woman, girl, boy, maiden, and youth. (55)
The elderly, those dedicated to the elderly, and even those devoid of merit who have offered themselves to Kṛṣṇa, partake in liberation;
so too do cows, bulls, elephants, camels, horses, goats, and all living beings.
The house with all its utensils and every kind of object of enjoyment, as well as garments, ornaments, riches, vehicles, and even mounts. (57)
Red gems, as well as grains and leaves in every way, and fruits and flowers offered to Kṛṣṇa are indeed without any binding restrictions. 98.
Bathing, meditation, mental retention, worship, service, giving, vows, pilgrimage, merit, desired rites, and the construction of ponds, wells, and tanks—[these are all included]. (59)
Everything is offered to Kṛṣṇa—divine, beyond the material qualities, and free from bondage;
it is a state of exile, the bearing of burdens, servitude, slavery, and active devotion.
Artistry, craftsmanship, and even the supreme skill in the arts dedicated to Kṛṣṇa, as well as the constant manifestation of new [creations], are devoid of [worldly] qualities. (61)
The means for festivals and various kinds of images—whether adorned with ornaments or devoid of qualities—are in every way offered unto Kṛṣṇa. (62)
Cooking, drawing out, carrying, cutting, mowing,
as well as sewing and stitching— all these, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, become devoid of their worldly qualities.
Breathing, looking in a mirror, touch, taste, as well as smelling—
all enjoyment and every fruit thereof, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, becomes free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa).
Shaving, sprinkling, growth, protection,
as well as nourishment and grasping— all this, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, is indeed devoid of [worldly] attributes.
Singing, sneezing, rolling about, tearing [clothes],
laughing, and even sexual pleasure— when offered to Kṛṣṇa, these are indeed beyond the three guṇas.
Abiding, completion, commencement, as well as expansion, contraction, and manifestation—these, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, are devoid of the guṇas. (67)
Yawning, stretching, as well as the closing and opening of the eyes, sleeping, jumping, and falling—all these are offered to Kṛṣṇa and are thus free from the influence of the guṇas. (68)
Running, walking, placing down, steadiness, rising up, and dissolution;
illumination, fame, and glory—may these be offered to Kṛṣṇa and be free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa). 69.
The mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, the broom, the churn,
the bed, and the granary— these, when dedicated to Kṛṣṇa, become free from all worldly qualities.
The head, eyes, ears, chest, throat, hands, belly, and so forth;
likewise the hips, thighs, shanks, knees, calves, feet, and so on. (71)
One who has surrendered the entirety of their body and all possessions to Kṛṣṇa becomes free from the material qualities (nirguṇa) and attains liberation.
Whether there be illness or health, rise or growth, loss or governance—[all these occur]. (72)
Acquisition, trade, and all activities—whether buying, selling, bartering, purchasing, or even taking by force—are rendered free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa) when dedicated to Kṛṣṇa. (73)
Alms-gathering, livelihood, subsistence, income, and likewise expenditure—
all that is good and all that is bad, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, becomes free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa).
The states of female, male, and neuter, as well as the elements and the processes of engagement and withdrawal, when offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, bestow liberation beyond the gunas. (75)
When devoid of attachment, the offerings made to Hara result in all prosperity;
they lead only to liberation and bestow the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
He whose substance is utterly devoid of blackness and likewise lacks qualities,
and whose action is utterly devoid of blackness and likewise lacks existence— (77)
Life is not devoid of Kṛṣṇa, nor are the vital breaths bereft of Kṛṣṇa;
consciousness is not devoid of Kṛṣṇa, nor is color bereft of Kṛṣṇa. ||78||
No hermitage is [true] without Śrī Kṛṣṇa; no renunciation is devoid of Kṛṣṇa;
no initiation is empty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and no death is bereft of Kṛṣṇa. ||79||
All endeavors devoid of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are indeed meritless for him;
everything that has Kṛṣṇa as its purpose is divine, and all of that indeed bestows liberation.
All of that shines forth because it brings about the grace of Kṛṣṇa;
even he becomes a recipient of grace who has offered everything belonging to him to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, that great devotee of the Lord has attained identity with Kṛṣṇa;
he is the ground of ten million auspiciousnesses, and he is the bestower of all auspiciousness.
He would be a remover of unrighteousness; he alone is a partial incarnation (aṃśāvatāra).
He alone is a saintly person, possessed of the wealth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the most excellent liberated soul. ||83||
He who is always devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be known as Brahman itself;
that form is the very temple for the dwelling of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (84)
His body is the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; his mind is the mind of Kṛṣṇa;
his senses are indeed the senses of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not separate from them at all. (85)
Those actions are the actions of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and no others;
He alone is the totality of all things, and His worship is the worship of Kṛṣṇa. (86)
Service to him is service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; he himself is the very form of Kṛṣṇa.
His being pleased is the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa—of this there is no doubt. (87)
His speech is the word of Kṛṣṇa; his blessing is the praise of Kṛṣṇa;
his attainment is the attainment of Kṛṣṇa—there is not even the slightest difference between them. (88)
These very incarnations are said to be the ones who uplift the world on earth;
let them worship that Great King, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (89)
I am departing for Viśālā, subsisting on nothing but the grace [of the Lord].
May it be well with you; [may there be favor] from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord of Śrī.
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, the divine vulture went to Badrīśvara;
having reached me, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, he indeed performed penance. ||9 1 ||
Then he went to the abode of Śvetadvīpa, which is the refuge of Nārāyaṇa;
thereafter, having attained his full desire, he went to Vaikuṇṭha. ||92||
Then, chanting "O Lord Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," he shall depart from that abode of Brahman for the imperishable state.
Thus, O Badrikā, liberation was attained by him through his grace;
therefore, everything that is to be done and everything that is to be performed should be born of his grace. 94.
Then, hundreds of other vultures who had previously been the vulture-attendants of the weaver and had attained the state of vultures took up residence in the banyan tree. (95)
They too constantly enjoyed the favor of the virtuous yogins;
by that means, their karma was exhausted and they became partakers of merit. (96)
Having cast off bodies born of the animal species and having become possessors of divine forms, we both went to the divine hermitage of the Lord of Śrī Badarī. 97.
Having performed austerities there, they went to Śvetālaya, the abode of Hari;
having performed service to Nārāyaṇa there, they went to Vaikuṇṭha. ||98||
Those who recite the *Prajñānārāyaṇa*, the *Padmāśrīnārāyaṇa*, and other [mantras] shall likewise go from there to the supreme, imperishable abode. (99)
Having drunk the purifying dust of Kṛṣṇa, which possesses the grace of Badarī,
and the sanctified water from the feet of the virtuous, they go to the supreme heaven.
Purified by service to the virtuous, they are no longer subject to worldly existence;
for the form of the virtuous is the form of Kṛṣṇa, and their discourse is the auspicious word of Kṛṣṇa. (101)

That which is offered to Kṛṣṇa is indeed Vaiṣṇava; it alone should be consumed and never anything else. Through that, there shall be enjoyment and liberation, and the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shall be perpetual.
By reciting or hearing this, the sin that leads to birth in the animal realm is surely destroyed, and supreme merit is produced; there is no doubt about this.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises, and even among the virtuous, affection is born;
through the disposition of total surrender and so forth, there comes about identification with Him.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Fowler named Daṇḍāraṇi in His Previous Birth through Eating the Remnants of the Grace of the Lord and the Holy Ones, and the Liberation of the Vultures Associated with Him through Eating Their Grace," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this narrative that removes all sins. In a village situated on the bank [of the river], there was one named Govāra. || 1 ||
A cowherd, possessing a wealthy family, was constantly tending five hundred cows within the boundaries, in the fields, and at the watering places. || 2 ||
He constantly leads [the cattle] to grain fields, pastures rich in fodder, and to places where grass grows tall; he lives by the occupation of tending cattle.
The cowherd lives by selling milk, curd, and ghee;
he also performs another task: the herding of cattle for the villagers. (4)
Likewise, he obtains a livelihood by grazing the village cattle everywhere along the boundaries together with his own cows. || 5 ||
In this way he achieves his livelihood; however, being overcome by greed, he milks other cows and sells their milk. (6)
In various places, he indeed commits such theft of milk;
furthermore, there are four hundred cows belonging to the villagers. (7)
He possessed his own hundred cows that yielded milk, and half as many more;
he constantly consumed the milk of five village cows.
Every day, after midday, he steals right at the boundary;
thus he constantly commits the theft of essence even from the virtuous cows.
Indeed, the thread of craving for one's own milch cows is difficult to digest;
through the sin of stealing their milk, he died in the forest after some time.
Deprived of water and food, he has become a cat in the forest;
at dawn, this cat wanders near the city of Śarkarā.
Or else, intent on searching for food during the night,
he comes to the great garden, drawn there by its fragrance.
He approached the heap of discarded food remnants there,
belonging to those virtuous yogis who partook of the food offered as a grace by Kṛṣṇa.
Having obtained the leavings, the wild cat was filled with joy;
he ate them until satisfied and went into the depths of the forest at night. (14)
Thus he constantly ate the sweetest and most excellent food;
consequently, he became indolent, yet at the end of the month his body was well-nourished. || 15 ||
Day and night, he took delight in dwelling fearlessly even upon heaps of grass and clusters of flowers situated by the side of Utkara himself.
Sometimes he sleeps among the thickets after eating;
sometimes he comes outside during the day in a place devoid of dogs and other such animals.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
at a time after midday, he arrived at the *utkaraka* to eat, free from fear.
Having eaten the leavings there, he then fell into a swoon;
deprived of life in an instant, a divine person was born from him. || 19 ||
Then the remover of leavings saw this great wonder: a beautiful, auspicious being with a divine body, radiant and lovely in every limb. ||4.67.20||
They asked that celestial being: "Who are you who have come to the state of a cat?
How did you attain divinity? Salutations to you; tell us about this. (21)
And he said: "In the city situated on that bank, I was formerly known by the name Govāra; I was a cowherd, tending cattle. (22)
I have well tended the milch-cows of the villagers;
however, being tempted by their abundant milk, I have crossed the boundary. (23)
He stole, milked for sale, and sold goods through theft;
he made his livelihood by stealing, and indeed died because of that sin. (24)
Having beheld the agonies consisting of suffering in the city of Yama and having experienced countless miseries, he then attained the state of a cat.
In a place devoid of water and food, tormented by hunger and thirst, and filled with fear of dogs, I wander; may you protect me! 26.
I was searching for food and water if it might be found;
wandering through the forests, I have now arrived at the edge of a river in the woods. (27)
I chose to make my dwelling in a watery region;
night after night, I roam through the villages in search of food. (28)
Driven by fate, I arrived at the grounds of Mahodyāna and then,
during the night, saw a heap consisting mostly of leftovers.
I ate as much as I desired and attained both satisfaction and peace;
thus, I have obtained food here perpetually, day and night. (4.67.30)
Having attained nourishment for my body here, even though I fell into great sloth, being thus indolent, I took up residence upon a heap of straw. ||3 1||
Not far away, I wandered among the clusters of flowers and even the thickets;
having fed there, I would depart, and thus a month passed for me.
I have always eaten the remnants of those holy Vaiṣṇavas who partake of the grace of Kṛṣṇa; by that, my sins have been removed.
Today my sins are destroyed, for I am one who feeds upon the remnants of your grace;
today I have become meritorious and fortunate on this surface of the earth.
I obtained the grace of the holy ones residing at the place of discourse, and having abandoned my feline body, I attained the state of a god. (35)
I, a traveler of the sky, depart for heaven ruled by Mahendra;
having stayed there for a hundred yugas, I shall go to the forest of Badarī.
Then I shall go to Śvetadvīpa, and beyond that to Vaikuṇṭha; thereafter, I shall undoubtedly proceed to the divine abode of the Imperishable (Akṣarapada). ||37||
This is indeed the fruit of enjoying the remnants of the food of the holy ones, granted by the grace of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (38)
"Since I have been born, I shall in every way go to the highest heaven;
may it be well with you, and salutations to you! Having spoken thus, he quickly departed for the celestial realm. (39)
All those who wiped away the remnants attained great wonder, exclaiming: "Oh, the greatness of grace! How it has turned even animals into deities! (4.67.40)
Having understood this, at the conclusion of the discourse, they spoke with great eagerness;
having realized it all, they considered that to be entirely the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of Ṭhaṭṭhola as well.
There was a merchant named Ṭhaṭṭhola who was a rogue and a thief of clothes. (42)
In the city named Hanūda, he was always engaged in the trade of cloth;
from his cloth shop, he constantly purchased various kinds of garments. (43)
He sells those very same items and carries on trade;
here and there, he commits the theft of others' garments from their clothes. (44)
In buying, there is theft; in selling, likewise from the treasuries of others—thus he commits the theft of the knot (granthicaurya), just as no one else knows how. 45.
Through the sin arising from the theft of clothing, poverty came upon him;
he gradually became destitute of food, clothing, and other necessities. (46)
Then, being unable to support his family, he became distraught;
having abandoned his home, he wandered like a madman even through other villages.
Falling under the power of his past actions (prārabdha), he became afflicted by fever;
having died in a desolate place, crows devoured his body.
Due to the sin of stealing clothing, he went to the city of Yama;
having experienced the hells there, he was born as a jackal in the forest. (49)
Overcome by hunger, destitute of clothing, afflicted by cold and heat, and deceitful—endowed with a fraudulent nature—that jackal [entered] Śarkarāpura. (4.67.50)
Driven by the desire to obtain food at night, he himself wandered about and approached the vicinity of the conversation from no great distance. (51)
He reached a heap of food, rich in edibles and containing a collection of leftovers;
there he ate the food that had been discarded as the remnants of a gracious gift.
And he ate with satisfaction the remnants of the grace of the virtuous;
thus, O Badarī, he constantly consumed what had been discarded as refuse.
By that, all his sins—those belonging to previous births as well as those of his current birth, even those pertaining to the state of a beast—were destroyed. (54)
All sins have been destroyed and latent impressions have gone to their end;
the jackal has become pure, for the grace of the virtuous is the medicine. (55)
The grace of Hari, of the virtuous, and of saintly women is the great medicine that removes the disease of rebirth and brings about the destruction of all latent impressions (vāsanās). 56.
For those submerged in the disease of saṃsāra, his grace is the destroyer of that disease;
it bestows the well-being of Brahman and likewise grants the happiness of heaven. (57)
It is the destroyer of the sins of animals, birds, insects, and small-bodied creatures, as well as of trees and species of grass. ||58||
He is the giver of heaven, the giver of merit, and the giver of liberation; he is the bestower of grace, the giver of divine vision, and the giver of divine states, the bestower of grace. ||59||
The food of grace and the water of grace, when eaten and drunk, bestow liberation;
from that, the ancestors, humans, and gods drink and eat.
"May there be the grace of Hari for the sake of liberation, and likewise the grace of the virtuous"—having thus constantly recited, the jackal attained purity. (61)
On the full moon day of Caitra at Badarī, after midday,
he indeed consumed the leavings and instantly fell into a swoon.
Then, from the body of the jackal, a man of divine form appeared,
most celestial and outshining all splendors.
Then, as he was being watched by the officials and others in the sky, he was asked:
"Who are you? How did you, a god, indeed come to be born from a jackal?"
He said: "I am of the merchant caste, a resident of the city of Hanūdarapura.
Formerly, I was known as Saṃṭhaṭṭhola, and I was always engaged in the trade of cloth. (65)
I became intent on stealing clothes from the shops of the trusting, and likewise devoted to stealing the knots [of cloth] from the clothing stores themselves. (66)
And thus, through the great sins of theft, I subsequently fell into poverty;
then, having become insane, I met my death while wandering near a forest.
While crows, vultures, and jackals were devouring my body, the jackal, having experienced the sufferings of Yama, was released by a mere trace of his sin. ||8||
Born here in this forest, overcome by hunger, I wander about;
always naked and miserable, I gather heaps of food here for my sustenance. (69)
Coming here every day, I eat the most excellent food—
the remnants of Hari's grace, the supreme leavings of the virtuous.

Having constantly partaken of that which is purifying and destructive of sin, I am forever freed from evil; being purified and devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), I have become a possessor of merit.
And here, by way of conversation, I obtained a fine meal, by which I became like a deity and ascended to heaven. (72)
"Having dwelt for a very long time on this path, I shall then go to liberation.
Having spoken thus, the Lord then departed for heaven, having become a Badarī.
Then those people, the servants of karma, attained supreme wonder and recognized the greatness of that grace, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
Listen, O beloved of Badarī; thereafter, the minds of the servants of the kitchen became filled with supreme wonder at the eating of food and other delicacies through [your] grace. (75)
And those servants, perceiving that his majesty’s awareness was a grace capable of destroying sin, consumed it while filled with wicked intent.
Indeed, for those servants, their internal senses and so forth became stainless, and their hearts were auspicious.
Free from evil and endowed with the highest discernment,
there then arose in their hearts resolutions for the sake of liberation.
In the receiving of mantras, in the service of the virtuous, and in the chanting and glorification of the names of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul; ||79||
Then those hundred servants, devoted to service,
received the supreme mantra and the chanting of the Name.
They performed japa and chanting through the means of self-luminosity;
having constantly listened to the sacred narratives, they engaged in kīrtana. ||8 1||
Thus, endowed with faith and knowing the majesty of the mantra, they were also aware of the greatness of grace and of service to the virtuous. ||82||
With devotion, they performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa after their meal;
at the end of the month, Kṛṣṇa became pleased with those who were worshipping him. (83)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord of Śrī Kāntā, arrived swiftly from the sky, traveling in a golden celestial chariot. 84.
With a serene mind, divine, and adorned with all ornaments, he was graced by Lakṣmī and attended by Lalitā and Māṇikī. ||85||
He was honored by Rādhā, Japā, and Padmāvatī with wisdom,
as well as by all the men who were active in their duties and devoted to their work.
The beautiful Blessed Lord, the fulfiller of all desires and aims, was beheld by other men as well as by women who were devoted to their duties. (87)
Having been born, he was repeatedly honored with shouts of victory and with unbroken grains and other offerings;
worshipped with flowers from the heart, he descended from his celestial chariot to the earth.
Having surveyed everyone, he spoke to the chief of the servants; then, calling out the name of Hari, he addressed him while all were listening.
"O servant Svarṇāñjana, by my grace you have become pure;
I consider all women and men to be likewise eaters of my grace. (4.67.90)
There are those devoted to the service of sacred discourse, who are purifying and free from sin; they are all indeed fit for liberation, in order to lead everyone to my imperishable state. 91.
"Even though I have arrived, let all come with me to my eternal abode. Thus addressed, O Badrikā, all the male and female servants [responded]. (92)
Ready with shouts of "halahalā," they ran toward the celestial chariot;
these were then sprinkled with droplets of water by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained a swoon and cast off their bodies, they assumed most divine forms;
mounting celestial chariots, these divine beings went to the imperishable abode.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, one hundred men and one hundred women went to the imperishable abode of Hari; they became divine and eternally liberated. 95.
Uttering cries of victory, colored by joy and delight, and making it heard by all the people, they then proceeded with the *kīrtana*. 96.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, O Mālatī-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! Victory to You, O Kṛṣṇa-Lalitā-Nārāyaṇa, O All-pervading Lord, Consort of Rādhā! 97.
Thus, playing cymbals and making joyful cries, they went toward your imperishable abode, calling out to those dwelling upon the earth. 98.
O Badrikā, this grace of Śrī Hari, endowed with compassion, surely bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as whatever else is desired. (99)
For those who indeed worship the Blessed One, nothing remains deficient;
for those who serve the most excellent holy ones, everything proceeds in full perfection.
Indeed, the sins of those who chant the name of Śrī Hari are utterly consumed;
*oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā*. (10.1)
Thus, for those who chant this mantra, millions of merits are born;
and for those who remember Śrī Hari at Badarī, Kṛṣṇa himself appears before them.
And as they offer everything, their refuge is indeed in the imperishable abode;
the glorious Nārāyaṇa himself leads them to his own dwelling.
O Badrī, this bestows liberation upon those who read, hear, or even remember it; it fulfills all desires and grants eternal bliss. (104)

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation through the Graceful Meal and Service-Conversation of Govāra, formerly known as Dhenupāla who had become a cat in a previous birth; of the merchant named Ṭhaṭṭhola who had attained the state of a jackal in a former life; and of the two hundred male and female servants such as Svarṇāñjana and others," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another beneficial narrative. In the village of Gundraka, there lived a supreme devotee named Bharavāṭa.
This very person, named Paramīra, was the protector of a thousand goats;
he subsisted on the milk of only those goats and likewise through the sale of their wool and other such means. (2)
A householder indeed lives by the occupation of selling goats;
he eats the flesh of goats and likewise consumes the young of goats. (3)
Such was this sinful man, who lived perpetually by means of goats and cattle;
he would indeed graze all the goats of men upon the boundaries of fields and other lands.
Even in fields belonging to others, he would graze his cattle at night, even upon the standing crops, fodder, and grass that belonged to them, by means of theft.
Thus, this Bharavāṭa is a source of faults, a storehouse of sin;
devoid of righteous deeds and the like, he has fallen under the power of the noose of Time.
He went to the abode of Yama and was led there by the messengers of Yama into the Raurava hell,
as well as into the Asipatravana, the Kālapāśa, and the Sandaśaka hells.
Cast into the hells of blazing fire and into the realm of those who feed on saliva,
he experienced the sufferings of Yama and was subsequently born as a hawk upon the earth.
Due to the remnants of his evil karma, he was born as a hawk in the forest;
flying from one forest to another, he went to the bank of the Sindhu river.
He reached that stony ground where the story unfolds;
then, at midday, he found rest in the groves of trees.
And here and there,
he saw from afar sparrows standing upon heaps of refuse, searching for food and devouring it.
Seeing the sparrows, their minds fixed on food, quickly devouring the grains of rice left over by the virtuous— which were the very form of Kṛṣṇa’s grace— [the gopīs] indeed [rejoiced].
He quickly leapt from the tree and fell upon the sparrows;
those thousands of sparrows then flew up swiftly out of fear.
One [bird] flew into the sky, clutching an excellent morsel of food;
with its beak, it killed that [other bird], which was the size of a sparrow.
A divine woman, adorned with all ornaments, emerged like a radiant and auspicious goddess of heaven or a celestial maiden. (15)
Holding a garland of flowers in her hand, that beautiful celestial nymph quickly arrived at the pavilion of discourse by way of the sky to perform worship.
Then Śrīprabhā, eager for the Saṃhitā of Badarī, performed its recitation while being observed by all the people present in the pavilion. 17.
Questioned as to who she was, the humble woman replied to the people:
"I am a sparrow; by the grace of eating [only] the sky, I am free from sin. (18)
O people here, today I have become pure and endowed with merit;
having obtained the remnants of the virtuous, I have become a deity for the sake of heaven. (19)
Having attained the status of a preeminent apsarā, I now depart for heaven;
after remaining in the celestial realm for four yugas, I shall experience the merit arising from the worship of the Śrī-saṃhitā.
Having attained merit, I shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, freed from my physical body;
for this Śyena was formerly Bharavāṭa, the Lord of Creatures (Aja-pati).
I was his daughter, born from him, and having died here, I became a sparrow;
held by him even in death, I am now departing for the highest heaven.
Other sparrows also flew swiftly into the sky;
they too became the circle of goats and other animals for Bharavaṭa.
Since all of them will in time become partakers of grace, they shall be freed from sin, become meritorious, and attain the supreme state. ||24||
"By devouring my body, which has indeed been purified by grace, even the hawk will become possessed of meritorious power; of this there is no doubt. (25)
Standing upon a heap of refuse, he will gradually become a consumer of atoms; having become a devotee who eats but a single grain, he shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having spoken thus, O Badrī, the sparrow bowed to and worshipped the nectar-water;
then, drinking the water, she went to heaven while everyone looked on with wonder.
Then, a great wonder arose among those embodied beings as they watched;
O Badrikā, at that moment the hawk devoured the sparrow.
He ate fragrant rice, as well as the remnants of [the king's] faith-offerings;
he partook of other grains of boiled rice, savory and delicious, with great joy. (29)
And the hawk, coming there daily, ate pieces of sweet food that were well-scented and cooked in ghee, which had been placed in a refuse heap. (4.68.30)
Having become pure in soul, he became a hawk; he abandoned the eating of meat.
Possessing the memory of his former births, he thereby desired liberation for his own self.
Likewise, he observed the liberation of sparrows from their previous births;
for a hawk, constantly waiting in a thicket of trees, would await the arrival of the sparrows.
He remains hidden in his lap during the day with his face turned toward the heap of refuse;
and sparrows come there, desiring the remnants of his food out of favor.
With single-minded intent, he continues devouring until the king of birds swoops down; then he seizes either a male sparrow or a female sparrow for his meal.
Even a sparrow dies quickly; then, becoming a god or a deity, it goes to the sky and indeed proceeds joyfully to heaven. (35)
While he was thus constantly performing [his duties], once, while standing upon a tree, he said:
"O sparrows, you were formerly my auspicious goats. (36)
Indeed, your birth here occurs through the power of past action;
for previously, you milked cows for me as a guest. (37)
Once, on the occasion of Śivarātri, they were offered to Nārāyaṇa for the sake of righteous deeds by the virtuous, and for the purpose of bathing Lord Śiva. ||38||
By the power of that merit, you have become sparrows here;
even though born as such, you are eaters of the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s grace. (39)
"O you who seek the divine, become pure and endowed with merit;
remember your former birth today by touching me, Bharavātaka. (4.68.40)
Then, having heard the narrative of the Śrī-saṃhitā and likewise having worshipped the reciter, let them go to heaven, to Vaikuṇṭha, with the self of a hawk. ||41||
"Having worshipped the divine sages who grant liberation, let them go to emancipation"—
thus, O Badarī, did the hawk, remembering his former births, speak to them.
Then all those sparrows, men, and women,
having heard those auspicious words of Śyena, were filled with great wonder.
Then those goats remembered their previous births;
having gained confidence, they bowed to Śyena, their former husband. 44.
The hawk, too, having been honored by them, approached that heap [of grain]; he was greeted with respect by the male sparrows and the female sparrows who had gathered there. (45)
Remembering their past lives, they all recounted their histories to one another;
they considered it a festival there and partook of the divine offerings.
Having undertaken the vow of non-violence, they dwelt together among the trees,
subsisting on leftovers and listening to the nectar of sacred discourse.
While they were dwelling together for a month, death approached them;
all of them, including the sparrows and others, had their karma exhausted and were freed from sin.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, immediately after midday, they ate the remnants of the Lord’s grace along with Śyena. 49.
Having cast off their bodies, they became divine beings;
by the thousands, they were gods and goddesses adorned with every ornament.
Their leader, Bharavaṭa, was also born as Deveśvara;
they all held rosaries in their hands and likewise held flowers.
Having honored the *Saṃhitā* and indeed having quickly honored Vyāsa, he took up the dust of the ground of the narrative, thereby producing the highest wonder. (52)
Uttering shouts of victory, they went by the thousands to heaven;
O Badrikā, at the edge of that celestial realm, they reached the beautiful abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Then those highly fortunate ones, liberated along with their wives, shall go there,
having served Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī through the grace of Hari.
They shall go to Goloka, which is the abode of the grace of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa;
having propitiated Rādhā there, and then indeed having propitiated Kṛṣṇa.
They shall proceed to the imperishable abode, the supreme, eternal bliss.
Thus has this majesty arising from the narrative been told to you. 56.
The greatness of this faith is such that by its recitation or even by hearing it, one may obtain enjoyment, liberation, heaven, or whatever is desired, through a mere fragment of Kṛṣṇa’s grace. (57)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Ajāpāla Bharavāṭa as a Hawk, the Birth of Goats as Sparrows, and the Liberation of Hari and the Holy Men through the attainment of the remnants of His grace and the attainment of sacred stories," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another most purifying story.
Ten groups of ten pigeons arrived through the sky, desiring fresh food. (1)
Having reached the pavilion for discourses, they stood for a moment before the one whose banner bears the elephant;
then, becoming tranquil, they sat down in the pavilion for the purpose of listening to the discourse.
And they were all rememberers of their past births; at the conclusion of their discourse on the twelfth day, specifically after midday in the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha.
In the vicinity of the kitchen, on the floor of the dining hall,
he indeed beheld virtuous Vaiṣṇava men and women who were eating.
Having flown up again and again from what was left over by their intentions,
they remain and sit above the pavilion with longing desire.
Then the virtuous men and women threw the leftovers of sweet rice and other excellent cooked foods onto the heap of refuse.
Ten fearless pigeons quickly arrived for the sake of food;
having suddenly eaten the delicacy and likewise drunk the soup and water, [they departed]. (7)
They became satisfied, contented, and serene, their impurities gone;
purified and rich in blessed fortune, they considered it the highest merit.
Flying up, they settled in a grove of trees and said to one another:
"Oh, how excellent is our fortune! Today there is the grace of Hari toward the virtuous."
Having obtained this supreme remnant and consumed it, which effects the destruction of sin,
we birds have today become purified and fortunate.
We have heard this divine narrative contained in the Saṃhitā which bestows liberation;
oh, how great is the fortune of those humans who constantly listen to this story!
Oh, what fortune for those guests who enjoy your favor!
Oh, what fortune for these insects who eat your leftovers here! 12.
"Oh, what great fortune for these animals who here indeed eat the remnants!
Blessed is this ground, which has become purifying and a bestower of liberation. (1.3)
"Blessed is the Sindhu river; today it exists on earth like an ocean of nectar.
Thus did those pigeons speak, and that was heard by a certain virtuous man. (14)
Named Kṛṣṇavirāma, he was one who could discern the cries of living beings;
by him those pigeons were quickly questioned with affection and a desire for knowledge. (19)
Who are these noble pigeons, who recognize the excellence of Hari’s grace and understand the greatness of the virtuous, appearing like supreme divine beings? (16)
Those pigeons, possessing the memory of their former births, said: "In the past, on this earth, we were inhabitants of a single village, born of the merchant-caste (sārthavāha)."
We were indeed in the city of Mṛttikāpurī, oppressed by the affliction of poverty; then, out of a desire for livelihood, we went to the city named Navakuṭṭa, ten [yojanas] away. || 18 ||
And we went there as well, into the service of a wealthy man's house; indeed, we were employed by that wealthy man on wages for the sake of his own business.
But we were all employed by him in the business of cotton, even in the fetching of cotton from other villages. (4.69.20)
We were employed in both the selling and the buying of cotton;
once, being greedy for wealth, we even became spinners. (21)
Knowing that the property of the merchant Rāmavarcas was buried underground,
they all placed their trust in Rāmavarcas during the night.
Cruelly, they bound me alone with a noose around my neck;
Rāmavarcas met his death, while we escaped by taking the coin. (23)
Indeed, because of that very sin, we departed from the city along the path;
there, we were plundered and likewise killed by many gathered thieves.
Then, corpses cast into pits quickly obtained the fruit [of their actions];
seized by the messengers of Yama with nooses, ten were led to the city of Yama.
Having experienced torments and been cast into pits by the agents of Yama, we emerged from there and were born as bears in this forest. (26)
Then ten monkeys died and were born together;
dying once more, they were born as crows together with them. ||27||
The deceased pigeons were born here as our devourers;
having become eaters of leftovers, they have now become purifiers who remember their former births.
By eating the remnants of your grace, there has occurred today the destruction of sins and the complete cessation of all kinds of evils. (29)
Today we remember everything that was said, including the fruits of the sins we have committed;
today the supreme good shines before us, and the destruction of worldly existence will come to pass.
Hearing this discourse is meritorious; a meal offered with pure faith is meritorious;
the sight of the virtuous is meritorious; and association with the good always bestows liberation. ||3.1||
O holy one, through your grace we have become fearless here;
therefore, grant us immediately that very means for the sake of liberation.
"Having obtained this gain, it shall not be met again; do not delay!"—in this manner, O Badrikā, was he addressed by those pigeons.
Kṛṣṇavirāma stood holding water in his hand and called all those pigeons to seek refuge with him.
Thinking that some auspicious event had arrived, they came quickly;
they fell at his feet, and he too consecrated them with water.
He caused even their names to be heard, saying "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa";
at that moment, those auspicious gods cast off their bird-bodies.
As the virtuous man looked on, the gods became divine and beautiful;
then they said to him, "Give this mantra which grants liberation."
"We do not desire the world of the gods, since from there there is a fall once again.
Having heard this, the virtuous one indeed gave them the mantra of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (38)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Having received this mantra, those pigeons, who were actually gods, quickly vanished from sight. (39)
While the virtuous one was looking on, they became four-armed;
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Padmāvatī, and Lord Nārāyaṇa! (4.69.40)
"Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! To the charming Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Rādhā, the All-pervading One!
As they were thus offering their worship, a celestial chariot appeared there.
Accompanied by Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇasvāmī, he descended from the sky;
and the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose wife is Vallā and who is moved by compassion, spoke to them.
"Let those who have been liberated and have taken refuge in me come indeed to my celestial chariot;
O pigeons, today you shall become excellent birds, attaining perfect liberation. (43)
Having spoken thus and taking them by the hand, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa Mādhava led them to the eternal, imperishable abode while the saintly one looked on.
O Badrikā, they always depart happily from the bond of māyā.
Now I shall tell you another marvel; listen to me. 45.
A flock of one hundred crows arrived there by chance through the path of the sky, near the kitchen. ||46||
Having caught the scent of sweet food and smelled the smoke of clarified butter upon seeing it,
he descended into the grove of trees with a longing for the remnants of the meal.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, at midday, after the meal of those virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, [he arrived]. 48.
Desiring to eat the leavings situated in the refuse heap,
those crows flew higher and higher with joyful minds.
They fell, uttering cries of joy, and partook of the finest delicacies:
milk and the essence of dairy products, as well as *polikās*, *pūrikās*, and other such treats. (4.69.50)
They ate boiled rice as well as soup, chickpeas, and *granthaka* beans;
they consumed cakes and non-cakes, and *kalikā* fruits, leaving behind heaps of refuse.
And all the crows were filled with joy at the sight of that gracious form;
O Badrikā, there too an unexpected and great marvel occurred.
There, all those crows became entirely black-winged,
yet they were beautiful variegated birds with wings enriched by many colors.
For that sinful-souled one had assumed a black form and was hidden among the factions;
then, on another day as well, they ate in that same manner.
Because of that, their fortnights then became predominantly white;
then, on another day, they ate what had been left by those two.
Their wings became entirely white and they took on the appearance of milk;
then, on the following day, they ate that which had been thus left behind.
In every way, those who had the bodies of crows became white in form;
oh, how great is the majesty of grace, the supreme destroyer of sins! (57)
The greatness of the remains of the food of the virtuous destroys all sins;
indeed, sin is considered to be black in color, while merit is always white. ||58||
Those meritorious crows were then born as swans;
thus they enjoyed [their state] eternally, and thereafter they became pure-souled.
The faults characteristic of the crow-nature were destroyed within those whose essence was thus transformed;
they then became wise beings, possessing the memory of their former births, like swans.
Men come there, filled with curiosity, to see them;
and those crows roam about there upon the ground without fear. (61)
They praise the wonderful greatness of the remnants of prasāda:
"Oh, even Hari has obtained the eating of the remnants of the virtuous! (62)
By that merit, our tamasic sins have been destroyed; all our rajasic sins and all evils have been utterly eliminated. (63)
Indeed, those meritorious deeds which are sattvic and bestow heaven have now arisen for us through our service to the virtuous.
For we are indeed sinful crows, eaters of excrement due to our past karma;
yet the virtuous are the doers of good for them, bringing grace to the righteous.
Those who do not partake of the grace of Kṛṣṇa nor that of the virtuous,
even if they are white in color in this world, are nonetheless like ten million crows.
But those who partake of the supreme grace of Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous—they are indeed eternally Kṛṣṇa himself; they are gods, as numerous as ten million swans.
Whiteness is fruitless for those whose food consists of the bodies of the sinful;
blackness is indeed fruitful for those who subsist on the remains of sacrificial offerings (vighasa).
That house is said to be like a place of impurity where the gods do not eat;
that speech is indeed the speech of crows wherein there is no glorification of Kṛṣṇa.
That which was not offered for the sake of Kṛṣṇa is indeed of the nature of leprosy;
that food, that water, that sweet, the vegetable, the leaf, the fruit, and the petal [are likewise so]. (4.69.70)
Whatever clothing, utensils, or other articles have not been dedicated for the sake of Kṛṣṇa—all that is considered here to be like the filth from a crow's mouth, bearing only sin. (71)
There is no fault in animals, nor is there any blame for beasts;
the fault lies with human beings, who, despite knowing [the truth], do not offer [protection].
They do not honor, serve, or take refuge in Hari or the virtuous;
nor do they strive for their own spiritual welfare—such are those who have committed offenses against Hari.
Those who do not perform what ought to be done here are indeed offenders;
they render their humanity futile and do not remember Lord Hari. (74)
Those who have neither served Vaiṣṇavas, nor attained the grace of their guru, nor received the words of blessing from their parents, are certain to go to hell. (75)
Even if your face were like the moon, your speech as sweet as nectar,
and your body like gold— if you were devoid of Kṛṣṇa, they would be nothing to me.
Then those hells should be understood as mines of faults and treasuries of sin;
they are all like the bodies of crows—debased and leading to hell. (77)
Today our word "kāka" has truly become meaningful:
*ka* is happiness, while that which is distinct from it is called *aka*, meaning suffering. (78)
But the suffering we have endured today was contemptible; by resorting to this grace, we are now free from evil and seek only happiness. (79)
What power is said to belong to Brahmā? Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Satī, and Prabhā. By what means do they possess happiness? By what means are we the refuge of happiness? (4.69.80)
What body is there? It is the earth; what happiness exists therein?
Today, indeed, our being called "crows" is consistent with our state of happiness. (8.1)
Thus, O Badrikā, the crows indeed converse with one another;
the people who see them listen to that conversation, filled with laughter. (82)
The people questioned those auspicious white-colored birds: "How is it that you have become crows here? Who were you previously, and who were you after that? (83)
But one crow, who was foremost among them, spoke to the humans: "We shall remain as those of the color of herons; for we were indeed herons in a former birth. (84)
They were plunderers, eating impure food, violators of others' wives, stealers of others' property, and likewise eaters of others' food. ||85||
And those inhabitants of Khadiragrāma, who were devoted to wine and meat, once [gathered] in a forest near the river Pūrvanārā. (86)
Encountering the merchant as he was departing, we carried out a plunder;
the merchant was stripped of a hundred thousand coins. (87)
Just then, fifty other plunderers arrived there by chance; having quickly learned of the situation, those merchants [fled]. (88)
They arrived to plunder us, and then a mutual battle ensued;
all were killed by one another’s weapons and went to the city of Yama. ||89||
Having experienced the fruit born of their deeds performed by all,
those forest-dwelling leopards emerged from the nooses of Yama.
"We were born as killers; after that, we became wolves; then we were born as cats; and now, at present, we have become crows. (91)
Herein is found the remnant of the grace of Hari, as well as that of the virtuous and the Vaiṣṇavas; it is entirely auspicious and the destroyer of all sins. (92)
All our sins have been destroyed by eating the remnants of their meal;
we have now become white and meritorious, like the gods. (93)
If we could obtain here the very water from the hand of the illustrious Vyāsa, we would become gods and swiftly go to heaven, the abode of happiness. (94)
"Let them indeed announce that water of his, which is like nectar;
having heard this, the people will come to Vyāsa’s palace to receive that news. (95)
They spoke to that Lord, whose body is self-luminous, saying:
"Vyāsa has quickly brought the water of grace from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (96)
Having led them all away, he sprinkled them with water while glorifying the Lord, saying, "Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (97)
At that time, O Badrikā, all those gods quickly cast off their bodies after drinking drops of water and touching droplets of water. 98.
Equal to the gods, possessing divine forms and celestial bodies, they were composed of mantra; having thus been taught by Vyāsa, they then worshipped his feet.
Then Vyāsadeva gave him the mantra, the destroyer of [worldly] names:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (4.69.100)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Padmāvatī-Nārāyaṇa!
Victory to You, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lalitā-Śrīkṛṣṇa, O All-pervading Lord, Consort of Rādhā! 10.1
Having received the mantra, having obtained the *dhunī*, and likewise having attained the nectar of his feet,
those gods received his grace and his blessings from Vyāsa.
Having become four-armed and liberated as Vaikuṇṭha-yogins,
they bowed down and suddenly departed by way of the celestial path.
Those traveling in the celestial chariot of Nārāyaṇa reached Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord,
on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, after midday.
Having attained the world of Vaikuṇṭha, they became partakers of the grace of the virtuous;
thus, O Śrī Badrikā, their liberation occurred there at that time.
From reading, hearing, or remembering this, there is the destruction of sins;
there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and the auspicious attainment of Kṛṣṇa shall occur.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation through Compassion and the Eating of Remnants by the Holy Man of the Ten Pigeons born as Caravaners in the Past, as well as the Hundred Crows born as Kaṅka-birds in the Past," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, concerning the hearing of sacred narratives and other matters.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this story that grants liberation;
there, a house-lizard came to rest upon the wall of the pavilion of the sacred narrative.
Formerly, she was a messenger who assisted Bhāṇavāṇī; she was the recipient of the grace of the great queen Dineśvarī and her attendant.
By birth she was a woman of the air-dwelling class, skilled in accomplishing her own ends, devoid of concern for the welfare of others, and as full of deceit as a rogue. (3)
She was like an executor of the queen’s commands, yet she held the orders of others in contempt; she was the queen’s constant companion, yet before the queen she acted as a humble servant.
Then, standing before others like Siṃhikā, she was superior in strength,
invincible to the circle of servants, and altogether resplendent.
Skilled in concealing their own interests, they secretly amass wealth;
they are engaged in the business of buying and selling, as well as in acts of charity and other religious duties.
Deceiving others through theft by means of wealth provided by the queen,
she was constantly skilled in extracting money and possessed a nature of deceit.
Constantly doing this, she would expel those from whom money had been taken and make them her own;
because of that sin, that procuress died with the name Nāṇakinī.
She went there to the city of Yama and was cast into the Kumbhīpāka hell; having been released from there for the sake of rebirth, she indeed became a house-lizard.
In the pavilion of the storytelling, near the lamp,
the devourer of living beings dwelt upon a section of the wall at the archway, free from fear.
Insects constantly devour it, and flies cling to its walls;
even upon its archway, one finds rest day and night with delight.
Then once, having arrived in haste above the pavilion of discourse, she took her place beneath the canopy of the glorious Saṃhitā.
He partakes of the smoke of clarified butter lamps and the finest fragrant incense;
he experiences the coolness of flowers, shoots, and leaves produced by cold water.
The water remaining from the worship, situated upon leaves, flowers, and so forth—consisting of drops in the form of perspiration—he drinks, which bestows perfect satisfaction. (14)
Greedy for flavors, she licks with her tongue the molasses, sugar, and sweet food offered for worship—an enjoyment that provides no satisfaction. (15)
Having thus attained such clarity of mind, she became freed from evil;
she was born with the memory of her past lives, and remembering them again and again, she was filled with sorrow.
Desiring to abandon her body as a female lizard, she became dispassionate and, O Badrī, quickly desired the cause [of death]. || 17 ||
On the morning of the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Lomaśa arrived at the seat of narration for the purpose of worshipping the Saṃhitā. 18.
Dineśvarī, Rāyahari, and others also arrived;
likewise Candreśvarī, Koṭirāya, as well as sages, virtuous men, and brahmins.
And thousands of people, desiring to see and hear him,
arrived at the assembly hall and stood there as was appropriate.
Lomaśa performed the worship, the circumambulation, and the nightly lamp-offering for the book;
he also performed the worship of Vyāsa with leaves, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
Performing the *nīrājana* rite three times with the water from the conch,
Lomaśa also sprinkled that conch-water all around.
In order to bestow a drop of grace upon all, the Sage, repeatedly taking water in his upturned right hand and cupped palm, [sprinkled it]. (23)
Wandering about, he himself threw water in all directions with his own hand;
even that house-lizard became touched by the water on the canopy.
She drank a drop of water cast from Lomaśa’s hand;
instantly she was freed from sin, her latent impressions of evil being burnt away.
Pure in soul and of virtuous conduct, her life having indeed come to an end,
she fell upon the ground in a swoon at the front of the *saṃhitā*.
From the body of the house-lizard emerged a divine maiden;
she became like a celestial nymph, possessing a form consistent with her previous nature.
Though possessing that same form, she was divine in luster, exceedingly beautiful with her celestial golden complexion;
a young girl of sixteen years, like another daughter of the gods.
With her body resplendent with every ornament and beautifully adorned, she,
encircled by a halo of radiance, shone forth within the assembly hall.
Oh, the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and the compassion of Badrikā!
From iron comes gold, from gravel comes diamond, and from the fish comes the pearl.

He makes the jewel [of a soul] a son of the earth through vigor, liberation through consuming the remnants, a god from a living being, and Śiva from a beast, thereby releasing it from the individual soul. 3.1.
O Badrikā, that house-lizard was indeed a beautiful celestial maiden who had died;
she was auspicious, captivating to the eyes, and a magnet for all splendor.
Beholding him there, men and women by the hundreds of thousands were filled with wonder;
for the Lord, manifesting his own light, placed a garland of flowers around his neck.
Lomaśa applied a tilaka mark in the middle of her forehead;
Lomaśa also fashioned a crescent moon with saffron.
Lomaśa indeed questioned her: "Who are you? Were you so in the past, or even now? Are you Kamalā, Satī, Bhakti, or Sāvitrī, O maiden? (35)
Are you a deity or the *saṃhitā*? Or are you the embodied form of the household cow?
Who are you, O lady of auspicious form? Speak, O destroyer of doubt! (36)
Thus questioned, O Badrikā, she spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud before all the virtuous people gathered in the assembly. (37)
Salutations be to you all; salutations be to Vyāsa as well. Salutations again and again to the Goddess Lakṣmī, whose very nature is the Śrī-saṃhitā. ||38||
Salutations here to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, indeed to Kṛṣṇakānta;
and salutations again and again to the preceptor Lomaśa, the bestower of liberation. ||39||
Salutations again and again to all the virtuous sages and the virtuous women;
salutations to the Mother, the Great Queen, and indeed salutations to the Great King.
Oṃ, salutations to all the Vaiṣṇavas and to those who listen to the sacred narrative; salutations, repeated salutations, to the deities of the pavilion and to the goddesses. ||41||
And salutations again and again to all those who have attained liberation and to those who have not;
O Lords, forgive my offenses and forgive my faults.
All you saintly sages, the king and queen who are devotees of Viṣṇu, and my female and male friends—please forgive my offenses. 43.
Formerly, I was a resident of the sky named Nāṇakinī;
I was a companion of the speech of Bhāṇa and a servant of Queen Dineśvarī. (44)
Devoted to my own interests, intent on theft, and a robber of the wealth of dharma—
I, having died, was then led by the messengers of Yama to the city of Yama.
Having thus experienced the fruit of that evil deed, she has come here for the sake of another birth;
