by the power of karma, she has been born as a house-lizard, still experiencing the remainder of her retribution. (46)
My body was touched by the water of worship here, and through the grace of the sage, I died;
by partaking of his food of favor, all my latent tendencies (vāsanās) have been entirely destroyed.
"By hearing this narrative here, I have become possessed of great merit; and through the grace of Lomaśa, I have become a divine goddess. (48)
"I truly desire to go to liberation; I do not even desire heaven.
Grant me the mantra of Hari, which is the destroyer of sins and bestows surrender. (49)
"May this Lomaśa grant me that by which I may go to the Supreme Imperishable;
I bow at his feet, for I am his servant and a devotee. (4.70.50)
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, she prostrated herself on the ground like a staff;
having rubbed the dust upon her own body, she cast it away as a gift of grace.
Rolling her body on the ground, she rolled five times;
then, rising suddenly, the illustrious Lomaśā took up the mantra.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; svāhā!
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, Padmāvatī-Kṛṣṇa, Hari, O Lord! ||13||
"Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! O Lalitāśrīkṛṣṇa! O Lord, Master of Rādhā!
Thus Lomaśa gave him the *dhunyan* (the ritual staff), and she too accepted it.
With a serene heart and peaceful, she became the embodiment of Brahman;
indeed, that Brāhmī Śakti, the power of Hari, became Muktānikā.
"Oṃ, salutations to Kamalā, my mother; salutations again and again to Lakṣmī.
Thus, full of longing, she herself composed this hymn of praise using her own name. (56)
At that moment, a celestial chariot carrying Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa suddenly descended from the sky near the pavilion.
Then the Vaiṣṇavas, engaged in worship, offered victory-salutations to Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa and to Lakṣmī-Kamalā. (58)
"O maiden Nāṇakinī, come!"—thus she was called again and again;
and she too, having paid homage to all, ascended into the celestial chariot and departed.
While everyone was looking on, Hari took her and went to the Imperishable Abode;
thus, O Badarī, even a messenger such as a house-lizard is a deity.
Then, through the power of compassion, Muktānikā attained the imperishable state;
what more can I say here of the many wonders arising from this narrative? (61)
Even flies, stingy insects, moths, and ants—
even such creatures go to the imperishable state if they eat the remnants of [the Lord’s] grace.
Furthermore, O Badrī, I shall relate to you another story, full of wonder—
a supreme, purifying tale that grants liberation to mice.
On the bank of the river Nārā in the village of Bhāgalaka,
there lived a Śūdra named Saṃghavāṭa, who was powerful and a wielder of weapons.
Bearing a bow and bearing a mace, he was skilled in combat and a repository of arts;
renowned in battle and war, he struck fear into his enemies for the sake of victory. (65)
Nevertheless, by his very nature, he commits theft even at night, whether it be of foods, field crops, or in some cases, living beings such as cattle. (66)
Once, having gathered in groups, he went at night to the fields in the long stretches of land to steal rice that was ready for harvest. (67)
While he was still traveling with his wagons laden with heaps of rice,
the lord of the field, accompanied by a multitude of men armed with weapons, arrived.
He arrived for the sake of protecting them, and then a battle took place;
there Saṃghavāṭa was slain by the sharp edge of Khaḍga’s sword.
Having slain one another, some thieves and even their own masters died;
they then went to the city of Yama for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their karma.
Having experienced all manner of sufferings as the consequences of their past deeds,
they were subsequently born as peacocks and then as cocks.
Then they obtained birth as partridges, and after that as owls; thereafter, they obtained birth as mice, which was exceedingly painful.
They were situated near the pavilion for storytelling, in the fields where grain was gathered,
in clusters of flower blossoms, and among the grass and fodder.
Dwelling in holes and subsisting on grass, fodder, and grain-husks,
they remained there on the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, following their discourse.
There were exactly thirty-two mice who fed on the leftovers of his alms;
they were purified by their daily meal and gathered at the site of discourse at the beginning of the night. (75)
After the *ārātrika* ceremony, they arrived at the pavilion by chance and, filled with great eagerness, approached the base of the panel inscribed with the *saṃhitā*.
There were grains of rice, stalks of barley, and even the tender, fresh ears of wheat. (77)
For they had then obtained ancient ears of grain full of flavor,
as well as pieces of sweet food in the form of divine gifts.
Having eaten there and delighting here and there,
they became entirely purified, with all their latent impressions (vāsanās) completely destroyed.
Free from blemish, pure in disposition, and purified in soul like the gods,
they quickly cast off their mouse-bodies within the pavilion.
The gods and goddesses were born like divine beings; they were all beautiful, sixteen years of age, radiant, and full of splendor. ||81||
They praised the Lord Hari, the Supreme Self residing within the *Saṃhitā*:
"Obeisance to the bestower of liberation, the singular focal point for the virtuous. (82)
Salutations to the one who is the object of meditation for the liberated, who descends in all forms;
salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the supreme self and lord of Kṛṣṇa and the others. (83)
To Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved, the lover of all, the protector;
to the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Kamalā, the Lord of Rādhā, the playful one. ||84||
Homage to the abode of the gods, to the inner witness of all;
homage to the one without beginning or end, the compassionate bestower of liberation. ||841||
Salutations also to the illustrious Lomaśa, and repeated salutations to the virtuous ones;
salutations to the divine Vyāsa, who is self-luminous. (86)
Homage to Padmāvatī, Lakṣmī, Prajñā, and Bhūpati;
homage to him who dwells in the heart and who abides in the light! ||87||
Salutations to Prasāda and salutations indeed to the Maṇḍapa;
salutations to the deities of the Maṇḍapa and likewise to the Śravaṇins. ||88||
Salutations again and again to the stars, to the fires, and to the virtuous; salutations again and again to the chaste women, to the faithful wives, and to the devotees of Viṣṇu. ||89||
We, who were sinful, have been uplifted here by your grace and by chance; likewise, through your compassion and by the sight of you, the virtuous, we have attained divinity.
We have become possessors of the memory of our past lives through the power of this place of discourse;
we do not desire rebirth, but rather we desire the eternal, imperishable state.
May the self-luminous Blessed One grant the supreme mantra;
may he bestow the name by which we shall go to the highest state. (92)
"The Imperishable is the supreme abode, ruled by the Supreme Lord"—thus did they pray with longing, O Badrikā. (93)
Then the self-luminous Lord bestowed upon them this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (94)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Padmāvatī-Nārāyaṇa!
Victory to You, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lalitā-Śrīkṛṣṇa, O All-pervading Lord, Consort of Rādhā! (95)
Then he gave them the *dhunyan* (a musical instrument), and they too performed its proclamation;
they became single-mindedly devoted to the beloved Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 96.
At that moment, the illustrious Lord Lalitāsvāmī arrived, accompanied by Badrīnātha, Māṇikya, Padmajā, and Prajñā—the beloved Kṛṣṇa himself. 97.
Accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and seated upon an excellent celestial chariot,
he likewise made all those attendants and the Muktānikās liberated.
Having taken them up into the celestial chariot while all embodied beings looked on, Śrī Hari, accompanied by shouts of victory, led them to the imperishable realm. 99.
Filled with great wonder, they all praised his graciousness;
they extolled the compassion of Hari, as well as the power of the mantra and the merit of chanting its name.
They indeed praised devotion, service, and the sacred narrative that brings liberation;
they also offered words of gratitude to Bhūmi and Maṇḍapa.
The people offered their thanks to all who had attained liberation;
thus, O beloved of Badrī, those mice then attained liberation.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, while they were seated in celestial chariots,
that heavenly realm and its splendors did not become a cause for their bondage.
Compassion alone is the supreme cause for proceeding toward the Imperishable (akṣara), by which Kṛṣṇa himself comes and leads his own people to that very Imperishable.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Nāṇakinī—who in her previous birth was a resident of Khavāsī and later became a house-lizard—by means of hearing the sacred narrative, partaking of the grace-food, and sprinkling with water; and likewise the liberation of the thirty-two Śūdras, such as Saṅghavāṭa and others, who in their previous births were mice," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story that grants liberation to Nakula. Once, while he was hungry upon a heap of grain consisting of the remnants of [my] grace...
A certain Nakula arrived near the pavilion of discourse;
he ate the remnants of that meal, mingled with the grace of the virtuous. || 2 ||
Then, having fainted there, he abandoned his own physical form;
on the fifth day of the month of Vaiśākha, he became manifest in the form of a deity.
Then, during the bright fortnight, that best of gods was seen by all;
when questioned, he recounted the account of his own previous birth.
"Listen, O Vaiṣṇavas, in the city of Acchodara in the past, I was a preeminent knower, Vāruṭa by name, known as Sāgara. (5)
The wise people of the world know me as Sāgaradāna;
having summoned from his own home one who was well-versed in the stories of ancient history, [he spoke thus].
At that time, men cause stories and narratives to be performed and listen to them;
being delighted, they worship and offer wealth and other gifts to me.
Having obtained wealth and being satisfied, I used to go to my own palace;
there, amidst various stories, I would indeed discuss the affairs of the Dānavas with former kings.
I shall speak of discourse on the Dharma, service to cows, service to the ancestors,
service to sacred fords, the observance of vows, the worship of the gods, and religious festivals.
I instruct people in the observances (niyamas) and the restraints (yamas),
and I teach them everything regarding the duties of ritual bathing and so forth in every respect.
I do not protect even the slightest thing in that manner;
I am a speaker of falsehoods, a speaker of sweet words, and one solely intent on achieving my own ends.
I am a wicked soul, a rogue of wealth; I seize riches under the guise of trade.
I practice neither dharma, nor restraint, nor self-control, nor any vow. (12)
Everything was in my speech, but nothing at all in my action;
I was then constantly devoid of proper conduct and a deceiver. (1.3)
O noble ones, I was entirely devoid of service toward cows, my parents, and the gods; moreover, I was one who thundered with false prattle. (14)
Because of that sin, my knowledge became false knowledge; all my explanations resulted in the fruit of deceit and evil. (15)
Those things woven together by verbal quibbles became sources of sin for me;
thus, through the excessive burden of my sins, my life-force was destroyed and I died.
Having gone to the city of Yama, I was cast into a pit of tongs by the servants of Yama;
my tongue was cut away and dragged outside by the Cipīṭakas.
Repeatedly extracted with sharp-edged tongs,
they were pierced, cut, set ablaze, and singed.
My body was torn apart, mangled, and turned to mud;
having endured many hardships there, I have now attained this state as a mongoose.
"I came here out of hunger and ate the remains of a heap of refuse;
by that, even my remaining sins have been destroyed. (4.71.20)
Today I have become one whose soul is purified and who possesses merit, destined for heaven;
today I have become a god and am proceeding to the supreme celestial realm.
Having spoken thus, O Badarī, he did not bow to all those excellent Vaiṣṇavas;
then the sage Lomaśa addressed that deity there.
Listen, O best of gods;
even though you have attained divinity today, death awaits you once more, for there is no immortality among the gods.
Therefore, O virtuous soul, strive for eternal immortality,
known as the state of no-return, the healthy realm of Brahmā.
Having heard this from Lomaśa, he also inquired after his well-being with certainty:
"O Sage, tell me quickly: how may the attainment of the abode of immortality be achieved? (25)
Lomaśa replied to him: "Listen to this story and remain steadfast;
enjoy the grace of Śrī Hari—the food offering presented to Hari."
Observe the vow consisting of service to the virtuous; practice devotion toward the Lord.
Indeed, offer everything as an oblation to the Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa.
Take up this mantra to be recited and become an excellent Vaiṣṇava;
having become a great devotee of the Lord, you shall go to the imperishable abode.
Thus addressed, he who possessed the form of a god vanished there from the assembly of gods in that hall of discourse, his divine form disappearing from view.
He remained steadfast among the hosts of gods to hear the narrative of the Saṃhitā;
by his grace, he undertook a vow of eating only at night for seven days.
A human being performs service for the virtuous in their own form, such as massaging their feet, rubbing their bodies, and offering their sight and so forth. (31)
On the morning of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, after hearing the sacred narrative,
Lomaśa compassionately and swiftly bestowed upon him the secret mantra of Dhunī.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Padmāvatīnārāyaṇa! ||33||
"Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! O Lalitā-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Rādhā, O All-pervading One!
Having obtained the mantra, that god indeed began to chant the Name. (34)
While he remained among the host of deities after partaking of the offering of food,
Śrī Narāyaṇa suddenly arrived at midday.
Mounted upon divine white horses is the Lord of Śrī, the Consort of Kamalā;
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the Lord of Śrī.
The Lord, the son of Kaṃbhā, came upon a winged horse adorned with a parasol to lead him away,
and he called out to that god.
While everyone was looking on, the Lord mounted his horse;
having led him away, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went to the imperishable realm (Akṣara).
This compassion of Śrī Hari is even greater than that of Lomaśa; it leads him from his current state as a celestial being to eternal immortality hereafter. (39)
Nakula and Sakula were also made possessed of the lineage of the Blessed One;
O Badrikā, that supreme story was told there at great length.
Now I shall tell you another marvel of the Lord Hari:
a certain *bhāṭa* arrived at the place of storytelling to hear the tale. (41)
Chanting "Nārāyaṇa, Hara, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa," he composed a verse and offered praise for the *Saṃhitā* in the assembly hall. (42)
This narrative bestows auspiciousness, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the bestower of compassion; therefore, the bard named Kīratāra has approached for the sake of spiritual welfare. 43.
Salutations again and again to Vyāsa and Kṛṣṇa, and salutations repeatedly to the Saṃhitā;
salutations to the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas and salutations repeatedly to Lomaśa. (44)
Salutations repeatedly to the virtuous great seers and salutations repeatedly to the chaste women;
salutations repeatedly here to all the purifying deities. (45)
It is heard that many wicked and evil people have been delivered here through the compassion of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; therefore, deliver Kīratāra as well. 46.
May that Lord who dwells in the heart, who is in Vyāsa, who is in the book, and who is present among the members of the assembly, deliver me. 47.
At the end of many births, I have attained the Supreme Lord; may that Hari, the refuge of all, protect me, his wretched devotee who has sought his shelter. 48.
Today I have obtained gold, jewels, and the nectar of immortality;
having drunk it again and again and become firm, I shall proceed to the supreme state.
The Lord Prabheshvara, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, is my deliverer; having obtained the Mantra-dhunyā and other blessings, I shall go to the supreme abode.
Thus he praised him, offered salutations, and prostrated like a staff;
he surrendered his very self there and rubbed the dust upon his body.
Then the venerable Vyāsadeva, whose lineage is self-luminous,
bestowed upon him the name Manu in the presence of water as a witness.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Padmāvatīnārāyaṇa! ||53||
Victory to Kṛṣṇa! O Lalitā-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, Master of Rādhā!
We know Bāla-Kṛṣṇa; we meditate upon Anādi-Kṛṣṇa. ||54||
He took up the mantra, "May He who dwells in our hearts inspire us," and having attained purity, the Bhāṭa became cleansed of all sin. ||55||
O Badrikā, having eaten that prasāda and drunk the nectar of his feet,
he wore a tulasī garland around his neck and applied the moon-like tilaka mark.
He shook his head while dancing with joy, yet he listened to the discourse as if absorbed;
he constantly drank the essence of Brahman and rendered service to the virtuous. (57)

Having remained thus for exactly one month, worshipping the beloved of Śrīkānta, contemplating the meanings of the stories, and meditating on the Supreme Lord within his heart, [he attained success]. (58)
Bearing the divine son of Kambharā, the delight of the cowherds,
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, he was liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Having heard the story, Kīratāra attained meditative absorption in the pavilion,
just as a celestial chariot adorned with Kṛṣṇa arrived there.
He emitted divine splendors all around, possessing a golden luster; at that time, he of divine form was indeed released from his bonds, becoming as bright as a star.
The attendant of the Supreme Self has four arms and a beautiful form,
adorned with golden earrings, a crown, garlands, head-ornaments, and other decorations.
Summoned by the compassionate one, he ascended that celestial chariot and,
while the members of the assembly looked on, went to the imperishable abode of Hari.
Listen, O beloved of Badarī; here, compassion alone is the cause of Hari’s action.
Mādhava swiftly leads to liberation him who desires it. (64)
Taking refuge is the means for attaining eternal bliss; to the suppliant who says, "I am yours," He grants the supreme state. (65)
The embodied soul indeed becomes divine; his *prārabdha* karma is transformed, and by the grace of Hari, he becomes worthy of dwelling in the temple of Kṛṣṇa. (66)
A man becomes a liberated attendant, and a woman is born as Lakṣmī;
he sports with Kṛṣṇa and enjoys the sublime flavors of Kṛṣṇa.
Nothing is lacking for him; he attains identity with that [divine state] and, seated upon the throne of Kṛṣṇa, enjoys all desires through his Lord and Master.
Embracing Kṛṣṇa, he enjoys all the pleasures of touch, as well as all the pleasures of form, the pleasures of taste, and every kind of flavor experienced by the tongue. (69)
She enjoys all the delights of fragrance, the delights of speech, the joys of every embrace,
and all the pleasures of the bed, through her beloved Kṛṣṇa.
In one place, she serves her own beloved Kṛṣṇa in secret within his abode; in another, having become beautiful flowers, she serves him with their fragrances.
In some places, having herself become the fruit, she serves Kṛṣṇa with its juice; in other places, having become the wish-fulfilling cow, she serves Kṛṣṇa with her milk.
In one place, having become Ramā, she desires Rāma as her garden upon her breast;
in another, having become Śrīmāṇikī, she carries her most excellent beloved.
In one place, becoming a female bee, she partakes of the black fragrance;
in another, having become a friend of Rādhā, she even offers betel-leaf.
Having become Lakṣmī, she partakes of the betel juice from Hari’s lips;
and sometimes, having become a female cook, she prepares his meal.
Having become a female servant, she indeed causes Acyuta to bathe;
having become a male servant, he performs service by massaging his body. (76)
The staff, having become made of gold, finds the touch of his hand;
and the loincloth, having become something else, finds the touch of his face. (77)
Having attained the form of a sandalwood footstool, it receives a kiss upon its feet;
having attained the form of a mirror, it even holds Kṛṣṇa within itself. (78)
Having attained the state of a jujube fruit, it even bears a black back;
having become saffron and sandalwood, it experiences the pleasure of the forehead.
Having become collyrium in some place, it attains contact with the eye;
having become milk or the nectar of milk, it even enters into the stomach.
Having become water, it likewise experiences the sensation of contact with the waist;
having become oil, it experiences the pleasure of contact with the roots of the body hairs. ||81||
Having himself become the mind-born god of love, he experiences the bliss of Kṛṣṇa;
having become Rādhā, she delights with him, and having become his vehicle, she even draws it along. 82.
In one place, having become a lion-throne, he shines while occupied by his Lord;
in another place, having become a woolen rug, he serves Hari on all sides. (83)
Becoming a fragrant breeze, he serves [them] even while remaining cool;
becoming a ring, an armlet, a finger, and the body itself.
The Kaustubha gem, having become a girdle, serves both his chest and his waist;
sometimes becoming a vessel for food, it enjoys all manner of delicacies.
In one place, having become a bathing pool, she bestows touch everywhere; in another, having become a beloved woman, she embraces her lord, the Beloved. 86.
In some places, however, Garuḍa becomes an elephant, a horse, a celestial chariot, or a vehicle such as a human carriage, and thus carries his Lord. (87)
In some places, having become like a noose (pāśavatī), she indeed performs service to all;
and the liberated Muktānikās, out of love, praise the nectar of Hari's birth. ||88||
In the imperishable abode of Badrī, the liberated souls drink that nectar with love;
in Goloka, the cowherd girls and cowherds drink the nectar born of Kṛṣṇa.
In Vaikuṇṭha, the male attendants and female attendants drink that nectar;
likewise in the unmanifest immortal abode, in Śrīpura, and in the forest of Badarī.
In the White Island (Śvetadvīpa) within the Ocean of Milk, the beloveds of Brahmā and the beloveds of Hari, who serve Him, drink His nectar in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā. 9.1.
Jayā, Lalitā, Lakṣmī, Mālatī, and the beloved Māṇikī drink the nectar of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, taking refuge in Rādhā and Ramā. 92.
Padmāvatī, Sukhadāśrī, Nārāyaṇī, Bhārgavī, Tulasī, Padminī, and Padmā—these drink the nectar of Hari. (93)
Badarī, Vikuṇṭhā, Mukti, Śakti, and Sarasvatī—these drink the eternal nectar of the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||94||
The virtuous Sanaka and others, the great sages Nārada and others,
and even Vyāsa and other proclaimers, indeed drink the nectar of the teachings concerning Kṛṣṇa.
The Daityas such as King Bali, the Rākṣasas such as Vibhīṣaṇa, and the lords such as Śaṅkara drink the nectar of Śrī Hari. (96)
The deities beginning with Agni, the Kāśyapas beginning with Garuḍa, and the humans headed by Dhruva drink the nectar of Śrī Hari. (97)
The serpent Śeṣa and others are His enjoyers, while the cows are the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenu; the devotees who offer themselves surrender drink the nectar of Śrī Hari. (98)
O Badrikā, having come for refuge and surrendered in their entirety, these male and female servants and their beloved circles drink the nectar of Śrī Hari. 99.
O Badrī, those who have attained the imperishable abode indeed drink the nectar of the Supreme Brahman constantly, for they take refuge in the grace of the Supreme Brahman.
And through compassion, Sāgara, Kīra, Tāraka, the reciter, the reader, and the listener—these indeed bestow liberation upon one who has attained [this] Saṃhitā. (10.1)

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Sāgaradānavāruṭa and Kīratārabhāṭa through Hearing the Narratives and Serving the Holy Ones," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the story of the astrologer.
In the city of Vikrama, there was a brahmin named Devamatīśvara. || 1 ||
Together with his family and kinsmen, he was devoted to the vows of dharma and other observances; he was intent on the service of the gods and ever mindful of the welfare of his subjects. || 2 ||
He was hospitable to guests, a refuge for others, and a destroyer of the suffering of others;
he was devoted to the duties of a Brahmin and was a scholar of half-competence in the science of astrology.
O Badrikā, one who possesses only partial knowledge regarding all the worlds and all ritual actions does not reach the further shore of certainty; therefore, he becomes a partaker of suffering.
He was thoroughly proficient in all respects regarding medicinal herbs, the knowledge of fortune-telling, astrology, and the arts; he was long-experienced and possessed of great learning.
When the means of accomplishment are favorable, one certainly attains the fruit; however,
even one who has not yet crossed to the further shore may, through effort on a path where destiny is favorable,
suddenly obtain a flower or occasionally obtain a fruit.
For the most part, it does not yield fruit; one always obtains what is fruitless.
One who possesses the pride of wisdom is not stained by the faults of false ostentation;
one should generally remain like something half-burnt, rather than being a source of affliction.

A physician who possesses partial realization is mediocre; one who has committed more than a hundred acts of violence is inferior. However, even one burdened with the sin of a hundred acts of violence attains the highest state.
Likewise, one who possesses only partial supernatural knowledge, a knower of astrology, or a reader of palm lines,
always becomes a sinner among many liars.
By speaking untruths and by displaying doubtful things, they were deprived of certain knowledge and defiled by treachery. || 11 ||
Wandering upon a wrong path, they lead others astray as well;
by that fault, when they die, they are born as animals or as Rākṣasas.
Those who merely offer instruction in this way wander in vain with their words; though they are experts in instructing others, they themselves are devoid of the meaning of what they have spoken. 13.
They enter the wombs of animals and are even born as Rākṣasas, O Badrikā; therefore, [the attainment of] medical skill, scholarship, and the knowledge of the light [of the scriptures]— 14 ||
When joined with truth, they all bestow heaven and even liberation; when joined with untruth, they all lead to a downward state and grant the hellish realms. 15.
O Badrī, he was likewise a half-light ascetic who could foretell the future by observing the planets; he was a predictor of fortune and misfortune, yet at that time he was one of false conduct.
Tainted by that sin, he was known as Devagatīśvara;
he suffered from the disease of goiter as well as the affliction of a throat-tumor.
At that time, he was afflicted by a growth like a crab on his throat;
the root of his tongue was covered with pain, and consequently, his tongue became short.
His speech became indistinct in syllables and gradually turned into muteness;
thus, for him who was overwhelmed by disease, there arose a pain in the head. || 19 ||
An inflammation developed on his cheeks, and he was tormented by that suffering;
a suppuration occurred on his forehead, and there was a discharge of pus from his ears.
Blindness came to his eyes and deafness also arose;
oh, this suffering of prārabdha karma, or perhaps that which was accumulated (sañcita), has now arrived.
Whatever wrong conduct has been committed is experienced here in its entirety;
therefore, one should not act falsely, nor should one ever speak a lie. (22)
One should not practice untruth, nor should falsehood be taught;
that which is unknown should not be taught, and the untrue should not be shown. 23.
One should never speak that which is doubtful or contrary to truth;
nor should one contemplate what is harmful, for such thoughts fall under the influence of the defects of self-interest. (24)
One should not do what is undesirable, nor should anything be caused to be done by anyone;
one should not run along a blind path, nor should others be dragged away.
One should never cause another to fall into a blind pit;
one should speak only what has been seen, and not what has not been seen, provided it is authoritative. (26)
O Bādarī, that which bears fruit should be spoken, and not that which is fruitless, false, or deceptive;
for one should speak what has been heard from a reliable source, and never by means of one's own unreliable hearsay. (27)
Blessings should be bestowed with the desire to offer them unto Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, one should always utter words that are laden with future fruit.
The command must be carried out; the praise, though difficult to endure, brings joy; the drama must be composed so that it is full of aesthetic flavor and causes wonder among the assembly. (29)
Worship, chanting, and singing should be performed for the pleasure of Hari;
indeed, praise of the great should be offered with a sense of reverence.
Description should be performed in every way, a hundredfold or even more than that;
likewise, contemplation should be practiced a thousand times over what has been reasoned out.
However, truth must be spoken when there is illness, when seized by a planet, or in acts of faith;
in worldly dealings, one should likewise speak only what is appropriate as the truth. 32.
"O Badarī, that which is fit for the preservation of life must be spoken by one who knows;
yet this man is but a fortune-teller and a quack, defiled by falsehoods. (33)
Afflicted by many diseases, he found no protector;
and despite spending much, he fell once again into poverty. (34)
"Everything acquired through unjust means has been destroyed by disease";
thus his thought arose after hearing this again and again. (35)
Having praised the discourse in many ways as a destroyer of diseases and likewise a bestower of liberation,
he then went to the place of discourse to protect it through his vows and other observances.
He informed his wife of his intention to depart;
O Badrikā, a living being who experiences suffering resorts to the Lord of Fortune as his master. (37)
A living being, though wise and seeking his own welfare, does not remember this Lord Mādhava, the giver of happiness, during times of prosperity; he remembers Him only in times of calamity. 38.
Human birth has been attained in every respect for the constant purpose of remembering Śrī Hari;
yet, having forgotten that, the wicked spend even a moment in pursuit of wealth and their wives.
They consume what was done in the past and do not acquire anything new;
having abandoned merit, they practice only evil for the sake of hell.
He in whose heart there is untruth, and in whose speech there is falsehood, and in whose actions there is untruth—for him, indeed, these three are hells. 41.
The fruit of that is terrible sin and hell, which bestows further hells;
for one who acts untruthfully, the entire result is the suffering of the infernal realms. (42)
The first hell is proclaimed to be disease within the body; the second hell is the lack of contentment resulting from the acquisition of food and clothing. (43)
The third hell is a wicked wife or a wicked husband;
the fourth hell is servitude, menial labor, and dependence on others.
In the fifth hell, there is indeed constant strife among one's own kinsmen;
in the sixth hell, however, there is an abundance of enemies in the village and the country. (45)
The seventh hell is royal punishment and extreme exhaustion;
the eighth hell is craving and irreversible latent tendencies. 46.
The ninth hell is the loss of one's desired activities as well as humiliation;
the tenth hell is constant poverty, which is the greatest of all.
The eleventh hell, however, is characterized by being half-burnt everywhere;
the twelfth hell is that which is the constant washing away of hell-beings.
The thirteenth hell is indeed the impurities of the nine gates;
the fourteenth hell is the impurity always residing within the stomach.
The body is indeed a vessel of impurity, eternally filled with hell;
its defiled state is like that of a beast in the fifteenth hell.
The sixteenth hell, belonging to Yama, is indeed a thousand leagues in extent;
thus, O Badrikā, do the hells exist in this world. ||51||
A wicked son, a wicked disciple, a wicked king, and a devouring protector; a devouring protector who is also a savior—these indeed lead to the hells.
Adversity, as well as the attainment of the undesired and whatever obstacles there may be—all these are indeed the hells in this world for those of ill fortune. (53)
Dwelling in a prison, as well as dependence on an enemy, living as a beggar during a famine—these indeed become hells. ||54||
Greed, pride, anger, lust, hatred, passion, envy, jealousy, avarice, and agitation—these are, in this world, the hells manifest before one's eyes. (55)
Ignorance, darkness, delusion, theft, deceit, incompleteness, deception, and the betrayal of those who trust—these are the hells. 56.
Insanity, loss of consciousness, and the onset of intense cold and heat;
the state of having limbs that are to be cut or pierced, or being deprived of limbs—these are considered by you to be the hells forever. (57)
All those who harbor excrement and urine are hells embodied in the form of a body;
dwelling in the womb, birth, and death—these are always considered to be hells. (58)
Indeed, as many as there are muds and perspirations, so many are those foul-smelling hells;
ill-repute is a hell, and the fire of grief is a great inferno. (59)
Mental anxieties and physical ailments are the conditions that constitute those hells forever;
O Badrī, for him who possesses contentment, there is unsurpassed heaven.
The bliss of the exhaustion of craving is heaven; the bliss of non-exertion is supreme.
The pig’s station is excrement, and likewise, the Raurava hell is a state of weightiness.
Having abandoned pride and the drinking of intoxicants, one becomes happy through these three [restraints].
For those who do not desire [these], there is the dissolution [of suffering], yet there is no cessation of enjoyments.
There is no emptiness of actions; having abandoned the three, one may become happy.
Indeed, there is no satiety with tastes, and there is no peace for those engaged in action.
There is no cessation for embodied beings, for he who possesses the three qualities is always happy;
he whose day is in the knowledge of the supreme self and whose night is in Nārāyaṇa [is liberated].
Sleep during the contemplation of the Self as Brahman would indeed make one happy in every way;
even the thirst for pleasure causes suffering, so by abandoning it, one shall be forever happy.
The entire body is a hell with nine gates, filled with impurities;
nourished by states consisting of filth, it is essentially a place of torment for the self.
Behold, from the two cavities at the nose of Badarī,
a portion of pus flows out, foul-smelling and smeared upon the lips.
A network of saliva is constantly present in the mouth, and phlegm from the inner regions always flows into the mouth; furthermore, pus appears at the roots of the teeth. (68)
A foul odor arises from the roots of the teeth as putrid pus increases;
indeed, in the morning the mouth is foul-smelling and the breath is filled with stench. (69)
Sweat flows forth from all the pores of the skin everywhere;
it is entirely foul-smelling and alkaline, while fragrance is rare to find therein. (4.72.70)
Even this most excellent limb is thus foul-smelling; what then can be said of other limbs?
This is true for humans, cats, lions, and likewise for rākṣasas.
O Badrikā, the bodies of Piśācas, pigs,
and crows are entirely and eternally filled with foul odors and impurities.
How can this body, which is naturally impure by its very nature, attain purity?
Therefore, practitioners of yoga always and constantly wash their inner selves.
Those who are eager, through meditation, perceive the conscious Self residing within the body;
by means of concentration, they attain this Truth, which is endowed with the nature of reality.
The Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, who is eternally pure—wherever He resides, that seat is pure and of the nature of the Eternal Reality. || 75 ||
The wise always contemplate that true devotee of the Sāttvatas, who is the conscious self, eternal, and whose essence is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (76)
Residing in the heart, that [Self] is resplendent with its Lord;
it is eternally illumined and supported by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Those who are pure in wisdom, free from the notion of a physical body, and have attained detachment through discernment— such holy ones meditate upon the peaceful Reality abiding within the heart.
For therein lies that which is unreal, untrue, trivial, false, and of a deceptive nature.
Even that which is as small as an atom does not exist; the wise meditate upon that which is their own.
Indeed, they reach the further shore of this mire of the physical body;
having cast off all impurities, they go to the Supreme Lord.
Māyā is eternally of the nature of impurity; even there, the quality of rajas prevails, while tamas is eternally defiled, for all impurity is indeed tāmasa.
From that arise the principles of reality, as well as the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego (ahaṃkāra), which are illusory;
the senses, their objects, and the impure elements;
and all derivative material things, which are both impure and defilements.
O Badrikā, because they are true ascetics, they therefore renounce the material world. ||83||
Meditating only upon the eternal, they worship the eternal Hari;
they abide in the state of Brahman and rejoice in the cavern of the Self. (84)
Avoiding that world which is filled with a flood of evils, they strive for the sake of liberation, having taken refuge in a true guru. (85)
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, the Brahmin Devagatīśvara,
having observed the true and false nature of destiny, as well as the planets, [became indifferent].
Everything concerning embodied beings is composed of truth and falsehood and is full of uncertainty regarding the future;
yet it reports to those very beings their own half of sin exactly as it is. (87)
Afflicted by that sin, he sought release along with his wife;
hearing this, his virtuous wife, desiring to do what was pleasing for her husband, [acted]. (88)
Taking her husband upon his shoulder, the virtuous woman went to Śarkarāpura;
there she beheld the sage Vyāsa at the site of discourse and worshipped him.
He reported his master’s suffering to the sage Vyāsa, named Svataḥprakāśa, entreating him for liberation; and Vyāsa, out of compassion, then [acted].
He gave the mantra to the brāhmaṇa and bestowed the vow of Nāmadhunyan:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (91)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Lord Padmāvatī-Nārāyaṇa!
Victory to You, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lalitā-Śrīkṛṣṇa, O All-pervading Lord, Consort of Rādhā! ||92||
The wife also undertook the mantra, the dhunyan, and likewise the vow;
they both drank the auspicious nectar-water from the feet of Hari. 93.
They both ate with relish and listened to the nectar of his discourse;
at the end of the month, the Lord Śrī Hari granted them a vision.
He touched him with the tip of his hand and made the sick man healthy;
he also made his wife divine and likewise rendered her celestial.
Then, entreated by them for the sake of liberation,
Hari placed those two, having endowed them with divine bodies, upon his own celestial chariot.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), he led [them] to his own imperishable abode;
while all the worlds were looking on, Jyotirvit attained liberation.
Together with a virtuous woman, he attained supreme liberation;
O Badrikā, that was a great wonder for all embodied beings. (98)
Within just one month, the Brahmin’s disease was destroyed and he was liberated; the people praised the auspicious and devoted wife of the Brahmin. 99.
Blessed indeed is that housewife in this world who carries out the command of her husband, by whose obedience he has attained liberation. (4.72.100)
Nārāyaṇa is blessed, the refuge, the giver of liberation, and the supreme;
O Badarī, in this world of living beings, affection is the eternally highest heaven. (101)
Service to others arises from affection; service arises from affection.
The quality of bestowing happiness arises from feelings of love, and likewise from faith. (102)
From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, and likewise from practicing it,
there shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and the grace of Kṛṣṇa shall indeed be attained.

Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Brahmin Devagatīśvara—a knower of half-light—who, together with his meritorious wife, attained salvation through the destruction of falsehood, sin, and other evils by listening to the narrative," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this purifying narrative of the bards,
which grants liberation and is filled with praises of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
In the city named Dveṣarāgajaya, there lived a supreme, holy man;
he was a bard named Jayamāna, who was happy.
Living there with his family,
he always sustained himself by making Bandi Suvandana the court bard for kings.
In the village of Dveṣarāgajaya there was a king named Vajravikrama;
he was indeed fond of bards, exceedingly devoted to giving, and most excellent. (4)
Day and night, both by day and at dawn, female and male bards constantly sing songs interspersed with praises in his presence.
Considering him equal to Viṣṇu, equal to Indra, equal to Rudra, radiant as the moon, equal to the sun,
and equal to a universal monarch (cakravartin), men and women [honored him].
They all sing those well-praised stories of his, which have been fashioned [by poets];
and the singer, offering praise, ever sings them anew.
Vajravikrama becomes especially pleased with him,
and he gives him a gold coin as a reward.
Having granted victory while being victorious himself, he bows to that king and, ever joyful, constantly departs for his home and composes new poetry. || 9 ||
And on the second day, having gone there at dawn, he sings in his presence;
thus he always acts in this way and constantly obtains his livelihood.
Then once, while being born, he was so greatly afflicted by fever that he was unable to go before the king, and the king became overwhelmed with distress.
Waiting for him, the king did not obtain a sight of the sage;
rising up, he went on foot to the hermitage of the one who was being victorious.
As he was being born, [the sage] performed the welcoming rites for this king;
he offered him a seat, and the king sat down.
Having inquired after his welfare and seeing that the supreme sage was afflicted with fever, the bards summoned a physician for the sake of pacifying the fever and obtained medicine.
The king caused [the rite] to be performed before him; however, the king remained there. At the end of a muhūrta, the fever vanished, and Jayamānaka became free from disease.
Knowing his mind, he paid homage there to the king, who was fond of bards, saying:
"O King, your name indeed exists in accordance with its true meaning."
You shine like a god in this world; you protect like one who dwells in heaven.
You are resplendent like Kṛṣṇa; equal to Viṣṇu, you bestow prosperity.
O King, you show compassion like Lakṣmī; you look upon all with equanimity like Brahmā; you approach others like a rain cloud; and you listen like the Supreme Self.
O Lord, you impel the people like the sun; you sustain them with righteousness like the earth;
you nourish them like the moon, and you shine forth like the moon. || 19 ||
O King, you serve [them] like a mother; you bring them happiness like the night;
you protect them like a father; you are equal to Śrī upon the earth. (4.73.20)
You appear like another Kubera, a lord of wealth who bestows riches;
you cause gold to flow forth here, being as powerful as Agni.
In this teaching, you shine like a King of Dharma, a lord of the quarters;
O King, wherever you are present, that forest becomes heaven.
The subjects act as if they were in heaven, and heaven itself acts as if it were under the rule of a sovereign.
O King, wherever you abide, that place indeed becomes like Goloka.
That palace where you wander, O fortunate one, acts as Vaikuṇṭha;
and that place where you dwell, even for a moment, acts as liberation itself.
You command even the lords of the earth and the sovereigns of the gods;
all carry out your orders constantly, like servants filled with fear.
"All the scriptures sing of the excellent qualities of Vajravikrama’s valor;
O King, I have heard this today in the city of Śarkarā. (26)
The narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā proceeds, in which the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is glorified. (27)
He is indeed the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign of all sovereigns, the sustainer of all incarnations, and the protector of all the universes. ||28||
He is the sovereign of all sovereigns, the lord of all Lakṣmīs and Ramās, the master of all liberated souls, and the deity of all deities. (29)
The Lord of all powers, the sovereign of all, the sustainer of the cosmic egg, worshipped by all Viṣṇus and Śivas, and saluted by all Brahmās. ||4.73.30||
He is the dweller in all sacred fords, the Lord of Prajñāpadmāvatī;
he is the Sovereign of All, the controller of all embodied beings, and the bestower of liberation upon all. ||31||
Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhā’s victory, is indeed celebrated as Bālakṛṣṇa;
O King, that Blessed One shines forth like a sovereign emperor.
Thus the sovereign emperor shone, peerless on this earth;
"Aha! I consider his fortune supreme, for the king dwells in his home like Kṛṣṇa. (33)
O King, oh what supreme fortune! You always conduct yourself like a virtuous man;
you do not act falsely or deceitfully, but proceed according to the vow of truth.
You speak the truth and you listen to the truth; you find the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
You contemplate the Brahman that is truth; you are established in liberation in every way. (35)
Former kings, being impermanent, have fallen into the jaws of Time;
yet you do not appear so, O King, for you have transcended the noose of Time.
Death, which dwells within all beings, does not exist for you, O Vajravikrama;
nor do old age or the hardships of the southern realm exist for you, O Vajravikrama.
To me, you appear equal to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Oh Kṛṣṇa! Oh Kṛṣṇa! Oh Kṛṣṇa! Hare! Hare! (38)
O King! O King! O King! Hare! Hare!
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Nārāyaṇa! 29.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Ādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Ramāyaṇa!
Oh, O King, oh Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Ramā! ||4.73.40||
"O Viṣṇu! O glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī!
O King Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Hari! Oh, what great fortune is mine! (41)
"Oh, what great fortune for the king! O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Hari!
Oh, our Lord! Oh, our Lord! O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe! (42)
O Yāmin! O Yāmin! O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Light!
O Kṛṣṇa, O Hara, O Master, O Lord of the virtuous Padmāvatī! ||43||
O Lord of the Imperishable, O Master, O Lord of the excellent qualities of Badarī!
O Destroyer of Suffering, O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Rādhā’s beautiful ruby-like gem! ||44||
Victory, O Lord of Mercy, to you who are the master of the swans that are the hosts of liberated souls!
Victory, O beloved of Lalitā, O Lord of Śrī, O Master of all abodes, O Protector! 45.
O Lord of my own liberation, O Lord of the narrative known as the Lakṣmī-saṃhitā, deliver me, O ocean of compassion; deliver Vajravikrama! 46.
Thus, being born as the very self of Brahmā, the worshiper praised the Lord, the son of Gopāla, who is the beloved of Kambharā. 47.
And having heard that the king was one with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through his state of identity, the king named Kṛṣṇa quickly became free from all sin. 48.
Ignorance departed from the king; delusion was then destroyed.
Passion perished, and he became indifferent toward the objects of his own praise. (49)
Through the destruction of his false pride, there arose in him illumination,
as well as a desire to hear the narrative and a desire to behold Hari.
A desire arose in him to destroy time, death, old age, and disease; and a sense of detachment developed toward his body, which is subject to destruction. (51)
Having heard this false praise, the king attained discernment, thinking:
"Aha! This man performs such praise for me even as he is being born. (52)
Not even a fraction of that exists in me; no power resides in me, nor does devotion exist at all, nor the strength of Nārāyaṇa. (53)
I am a fit victim for the noose of Time; I shall die within a moment.
I exist like a mere insect; I have no place in the reckoning of creation.
I am not devoid of death; I am even a morsel for Time. I abide within illusion (māyā) and am by no means established in liberation (mokṣa). ||55||
I do not contemplate myself, nor Brahmā, nor Nārāyaṇa;
I do not protect the truth, for I am devoted to falsehood. (96)
I do not conduct myself like a saintly person, much less like Kṛṣṇa;
nor am I even a regional king, much less a sovereign emperor. //57//
In the absence of [the realization of] the Self, my body does not exist; how much less, then, can there be gods and the like?
I am always possessed of evil qualities; how much less, then, can there be good qualities? (58)
I am a fool, I am a blockhead; I am fond of false fame.
I am bewildered by the net of illusion, like one who is intoxicated or insane. (55)
"Alas! I did not remember Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
I desired to become equal to Nārāyaṇa, though my hearing was false. (4.73.60)
I constantly commit evil, being an evil-souled one like Kṛṣṇa’s enemy;
being a great sinner and an exceedingly wicked soul, I even cause others to perform it while praising it. (61)
I have no betel nut in my hand, yet I desire the status of the Lord of Treasures;
I have no stainless heart, yet I desire the status of the Lord of the Gods.
I consider the body of a wicked person to be entirely impure and far more wretched than even a jackal;
what sort of being am I, a base beast of burden possessed of false pride? (63)
"Truly blessed is this one who is victorious; I am a devotee of the Supreme Self.
He is my liberator, and he is now my guru. (64)
Because of my desire for praise, he certainly instilled harmful knowledge in me; yet that very lack of discernment, which destroyed my false pride, has now brought about my ruin. (65)
All the deities were reminded; the illustrious Narayana was reminded;
and the sin-liberating narrative of the Shri Samhita was recalled.
I shall certainly go to that place of discourse for the sake of destroying my sins;
having attained purifying goodness, I will perform the worship of Hari.
I shall cross the ocean of worldly existence and effect my own liberation;
I shall wash away the sins of falsehood and embrace the path of truth.
Merely by hearing his name, my heart has attained purity;
what supreme welfare might not come to me from hearing his stories? (69)
As I am being born, may my teacher, who bestows discernment, truly be victorious;
may there be such bards as offer praise, and such as show the way to liberation.
May they be removers of ignorance; may they not be mere blowers of conch shells. May they not be speakers of false and harsh words; may they be speakers of truth. (7.1)
Having reflected thus, the king spoke to his bard, who was like a teacher to him, as if he were a disciple:
"Aha! By the gift of your discernment, I have been rescued by you within my own home."
The praise that was uttered by you was heard by me while I was still full of passion; but upon hearing the reply, my passion vanished and my craving came to an end. (73)
The truth and the falsehood that constitute reality have been revealed within my heart by you;
I am your servant, and you are my guru, the one who delivers me from the cycle of worldly existence.
Tell me, where does Hari, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, reside?
And where does the discourse originating from Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa take place? (75)
I have a desire to hear [you] in order to cast off false evil;
I have a desire for liberation, O captive, lead me to where the nectar of your discourse resides. (76)
As the king was speaking thus, a vision of Hari,
the Supreme Self, arose within the light of his own heart.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having swiftly revealed his own form, then vanished from the heart, quickly drawing back the mental fluctuations.
Merely by the sight of the image, the king became subject to another's power;
devoid of bodily consciousness, he danced there in many ways. (79)
He sang of the Lord Hari-Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, with rhythmic clapping and musical instruments, chanting: "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Hari! Hari! (4.73.80)
Even while being born, he engaged in chanting together with him alone;
and filled with joy, he danced together with the king.
"Oh, how great is the grace of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa toward the beloved of Badarī!
Through the praises of Kṛṣṇa in this narrative, Kṛṣṇa himself has appeared. (8.2)
Thus they performed dance and song for just a moment;
then, becoming peaceful and filled with blissful joy, they rested for a while. (83)
And they spoke to one another about their vision of the Supreme Lord, which was great bliss and the supreme good fortune for both of them.
And at that time, other men and women in the house heard [the sound]—those who had arrived, intent on the great wonder, to see the king then. (85)
King Bandī, Bandī’s wife, Bandī’s sons, as well as his daughters, women, and kinsmen, set out toward Śarkarānagara. ||86||
The king, the queen, their sons, the daughters of the queen, as well as the people, the subjects, and even the women and men, became ready to depart. (87)
Thousands of men—the ministers, the chiefs, and the officials—became ready to go toward Śarkarānagara. || 88 ||
Female and male servants, laborers, soldiers, and likewise guards, along with elephant-riders and horsemen, set forth. (89)
They took with them much gold, wealth, and abundant grain,
as well as garments, vessels, ornaments, and blankets suitable for giving.
Many people, full of festive joy and shouting "Halaha!
Halaha!", set out toward Kathāsthali for the purpose of a pilgrimage.
They took their places along the road and arrived at the great garden;
by the thousands, those people gathered in the vicinity of the pavilion for discourse.
Having bathed in the waters of the sacred ford and worshipped the gods, they established their residences in the great garden as was appropriate, proceeding toward the pavilion.
They performed the worship of the Saṃhitā at the conclusion of the discourse;
likewise, they performed the worship of Vyāsa, Lomaśa, and the virtuous ones.
Then they performed the *ārātrika* rite and placed offerings before him;
Vyāsa and the others welcomed him and gave him food as a mark of favor.
Then the king and all the others, eager for their dwelling, departed;
and in the morning, they all assembled once again with Vyāsa and likewise with Lomaśa.
They joyfully took up the mantra, the rosary, and the tulasī;
thus they became Vaiṣṇavas, purified and having sought refuge. || 97 ||
They constantly listened to his discourse and worshipped Vyāsa day after day;
they served the sages, the virtuous, and the chaste women, and they served the Lord Hari. 98.
They took refuge in the Supreme Self, Bālakṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa:
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Nārāyaṇa! (99)
They always made the water pure and turned it into nectar;
all people—the children, the elderly, and the youth—enjoyed it constantly.
Born from him, they were purifiers who had destroyed the accumulated mass of their sins;
they were the supreme Sāttvatas, and at the end of the month, Kṛṣṇa came to them.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, of divine form, seated in his celestial chariot,
descended from the sky to the earth while everyone was looking on.
The cowherd’s son sprinkled water all over them;
they all became possessed of divine vision and beheld Acyuta.
When the Blessed One had spoken, the king and others prepared to go to the imperishable state; thousands of people became ready to travel toward the imperishable.
Having fashioned divine bodies for them and taken them away in celestial chariots,
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa left the remainder behind and went to the imperishable realm (Akṣara).
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Hari led them to the imperishable state.
This great wonder occurred, and it became renowned everywhere.
O Badrikā, those remaining groups were the most excellent of the great Bhāgavatas.
Having heard the discourse, they went to their own city, which was characterized by the conquest of hatred and passion.
Having devoted themselves to Govinda for some time, they too attained the Imperishable.
Through the recitation and hearing of this, one attains enjoyment, liberation, and heaven. (108)

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Vajravikrama and His Subjects through Hearing Their Story and Other Means, Following the Attainment of Dispassion and Discernment by the King via the Hymn of the Bandit-Singer named Jayamāna," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, beloved of Badarī, to this story of Sūta which bestows liberation,
set in the auspicious land of Pañcanada, between the rivers Sindhu and Cīnā.
On the surface of the earth, at the confluence, there was a city named Pañcanādinī;
its king was the excellent Saptābdhisiṃha by name.
Possessing great prowess, renowned for his valor, and the protector of his subjects,
he was the commander of an army consisting of elephants, horses, great vehicles, celestial chariots, and other forces.
The protector of subjects, whose mind was fixed on dharma and who was devoted to the duties of a Brahmin,
had Sukesarī as his charioteer, who drove his own chariot.
He too, being equal to the king in physical prowess, brilliance, mantras, battle, and intellect,
constantly performed the duties of a *sūtaka* and became most dear to the monarch.
Having mounted that excellent chariot urged on by his charioteer,
the king roamed through the vast forest on the riverbank for the sake of hunting.
There, accompanied by his chariot, he went to the riverbank to drink water;
he rested, drank the water, and then the charioteer also drank water.
The exhausted horses, released from the yoke of the chariot for a moment, drank the water;
meanwhile, the king sat beneath the shade of a banyan tree, untroubled by the heat of the sun.
Having obtained a brief slumber, the serpent fell from the banyan tree;
white in color, it quickly bit the king upon his neck.
The charioteer beheld that serpent of long form biting [the wheel];
from afar, the excellent charioteer did not bow, knowing the serpent to be equal to a god.
Salutations to you, white-hued one, who are Śeṣa in form and possess a coiled body;
salutations to you, who have the form of Viṣṇu, as you bite my king. || 11 ||
Salutations to Rudra in the form of Time, to the fierce one who takes away life;
salutations to you, the remover of suffering, the protector—salutations again and again!
"I am the charioteer of this king; here I am his servant and his attendant.
I have no other companion. O compassionate one, protect me! (1.3)
In such a desolate wilderness, while I, your servant, am still alive,
the death of my master is utterly, utterly, and utterly unfitting.
Therefore, O serpent, rescue my master from the fire of poison; bite me instead of him. May it be well with you; salutations to you again and again.
He who gives up his life for the sake of a king, for the sake of a deity, for the sake of a teacher, for the sake of cows, or for the sake of his ancestors, enjoys the divine heaven.
"If the king perishes, my death will certainly follow here;
that sin shall be yours, O serpent, therefore rescue my king."
"O sinful one, you shall have no servants for the rescue of the king;
for when the master has died, the life of a servant is censured on this earth. (18)
Therefore, O Lord of Serpents, show compassion toward me and withdraw your venom quickly, before my life-breaths depart. (19)
"I suspect you are the master dwelling in the forest, residing within the banyan tree; I am here as your guest, O King, and you too are my guest. (4.74.20)
Having become hospitable toward a guest, protect the lord of the earth;
O serpent, offer a welcome to the king by granting him life.
If no evil were incurred here, there would still be a loss of merit for you, when a guest turns back from one's house with his hopes shattered. (22)
Having given his own sin and taken away the merit, that guest departs;
O serpent, those householders who daily honor their guests are truly blessed. (23)
In whosever homes [this is performed] through offerings of worship, food, clothing, and water, there exists no gift superior to that gift, which is equal to the gift of life itself. (24)
The merit produced by all forms of giving belongs to the one who bestows fearlessness;
all evils abide with the one who gives cause for fear—of this there is no doubt. (25)
No embodied being, however subtle, should entertain fear toward anyone;
for there is no doubt that the fruit of one who causes fear will be fear in return. (26)
Therefore, O serpent, you who dwell within the banyan tree, protect the king;
otherwise, know that even your life is in danger from my arrow.
In this world, it is certain that after one, both will meet their end;
having given my life for yours, I shall take my own life and go to the abode of Yama. (28)
"Tell me quickly what must be done; here is an arrow already aimed.
Having said this, O Badrikā, he likewise took up his strung bow along with the arrow. (29)
Having restrained his anger, he waited for a beneficial word;
meanwhile, like a frightened serpent, the other replied with conciliatory words.
Therefore, you ought to hear the truth here from me, who am worthy and deserving;
for if one acts without deliberation, true reality quickly brings about fear.
In former times, at the beginning of creation, Brahmā issued a command to Rudra for the sake of creation; however, that Rudra did not accept it at all.
The peaceful Brahmā himself created various kinds of progeny;
then those beings were born with lifespans lasting until the end of the kalpa.
When they neither increased nor met with destruction, he then,
for the sake of their growth, created offspring from his own body through sexual union.
Hundreds of thousands of thousands of pairs,
and many offspring were produced from those pairs by the hundreds of millions upon millions.
This world was filled by their innumerable lineages;
indeed, the Lord Viṣṇu, the husband of Lakṣmī, provided for their nourishment.
There was no destruction of them when the world was thus crowded with them.
Then Brahmā indeed gave a portion of the destruction of living beings to Rudra. ||37||
Rudra said: "I do not favor violence, for it causes fear;
the fruit of violence is hell, as well as a curse and intense suffering. (38)
O Lord of Creatures, I shall certainly not perform that cruel deed— devoid of compassion, involving violence and the taking of life— which is so full of fault and replete with sin.
Then Brahmā, having reflected, spoke to Rudra at that very moment:
"I shall create Time, Death, Old Age, and Diseases; behold the destroyers! (4.74.40)
They will bring about destruction; O Śiva, let there be no harm to them.
Let the destruction come about through some external cause; you must remain a witness to that. (41)
Thus addressed, the divine Śaṅkara accepted the words of the Brahmin;
Hara assumed the presiding divinity over the acts of dissolution.
Then Brahmā created those mentioned [beings] who are superior to Time, Death, and Old Age;
he also created cruel beings who act as instrumental causes, as well as embodied beings such as ourselves.
The Unborn One created serpents, tigers, and venomous scorpions, as well as embodied beings such as fevers and diseases that weaken strength and bring death.
He gave us an order regarding those for whom death is considered imminent:
"By that very sign, you must indeed afflict them. (45)
Having thus given this command, we were entrusted to Śaṅkara;
we are the destroyers of those whose life-span has ended, and not otherwise. (46)
Impelled by Śaṅkara himself, diseases, times of distress, and incapacities—rich in poison and possessing various forms—arise again and again among living beings. (47)
"O Sūta, we do not examine the lines of destruction nor look for the moment of destruction;
otherwise, the king's life here would have already departed. (48)
"No fault has been seen by me; we are not people who harbor fear.
Whosoever among us are great-souled ones, they likewise become our guests. (49)
I have indeed honored them with hospitality—whatever honor exists in my house—with the offering of poison for their death. (4.74.50)
The king has indeed met his end and will not regain life again;
O charioteer, your life still remains, so take the corpse and depart. (51)
If you take my life with the discharge of arrows,
then by this new deed, you too shall surely lose your life here.
The weapons of mortals have no power against the divine;
I am a serpent, I am the very form of Time. I speak the truth: depart! (53)
Desist from this action and do not destroy your own life;
having reflected upon what is appropriate here, perform that which ought to be done. ||54||
"Here I am, fearless, upon the branch of this banyan tree; take this to heart.
For the perpetrator of such a rash act, tens of millions of sufferings await. (55)
We are the directors of creation, while you, O King, are the one to be directed;
therefore, in this act of violence, the sin is mine alone, and certainly not yours.
If you commit violence against me, you will certainly go to hell; one who desires happiness should not oppose the king, nor should he oppose the people. (57)
There is no conflict with destiny, nor indeed with fortune; whatever may come upon one must be endured, for it has arrived in accordance with one's own past actions. (98)
O Sūta, one who desires happiness must certainly not create opposition with fire, nor should he create opposition with Time. (59)
Not by death, nor by a lord, nor by a teacher, nor even by a woman;
not by a fool, nor by one who is angry, nor even by a bearer of weapons. (4.74.60)
One who is gentle should not engage in opposition with one who is powerful;
neither by means of weapons, nor by supernatural beings, nor by performing magical wonders. (6.1)
One should not oppose the powerful, nor one's mother or father;
one should not oppose a teacher, an ascetic, or a virtuous person.
One who desires well-being and prosperity should not oppose many;
one should never oppose a husband, nor a master of the house. (63)
One should not fight with a piśāca, nor with a rākṣasa or a dānava;
nor with a lion, nor even with an elephant, nor with a serpent or its venom.
One should not fight with one who is wicked, nor with a merciless enemy;
for righteousness truly does not abide in one who is deceitful, wicked, or merciless.
"Withdraw your arrow and perform the funeral rites for the king;
or else, release the arrow quickly at me, so that you may obtain whatever fruit you desire. (66)
One should indeed act with discernment; for one devoid of it is a vessel for calamities. You are a man and you are wise; therefore, perform that which is appropriate.
"O charioteer, this king was not slain by me; he was slain by his own karma.
I shall not meet my death by your arrow, O lion! (68)
On the contrary, this arrow will serve to destroy you;
abandon the delusion of "I" and "mine," and do not cause further delusion.
Where is your king, and where is his charioteer? Indeed, everything is a bond of karma;
the selves are bound by their own actions within these elemental puppets.
For as long as they dwell in the body, they indeed experience the karma created by themselves;
having abandoned that body, they experience further karmas in another body. (71)
If you have no trust in me as a serpent, then release your arrow;
after conducting an investigation, you will abandon your own folly.
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, the serpent ceased from his narration;
the charioteer, having reflected, suddenly cast aside both his bow and his arrow. (73)
"O divine serpent, here I am in your refuge; remove my grief!
You are a god, you are the destroyer of Time, you are Time itself, or you are Śaṅkara. (74)
Whoever you may be, I consider you to be Truth; whatever you have done has been done exactly as it is.
Nevertheless, I offer my salutations so that there may be well-being for me. (75)
O King of Serpents, act here in such a way that, by the decree of fate, your sting shall be rendered fruitless and yet remain beneficial to the king. (76)
Having spoken thus, O Badrī, the charioteer prostrated before him like a staff;
even the serpent, though he was the very form of Death, reflected for a moment upon what would be beneficial.
He said, "O Sūta, leave Bhīma and rise up; summon the king!
I shall remove the poison here today, and let the king live now. (78)
But hold fast to this mantra and cause the king to hear it quickly;
by that merit, I, Kāla, shall take away his life.
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, the serpent Kāla then gave this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (4.74.80)
"Oṃ, let us know Bālakṛṣṇa; let us meditate upon Anādikṛṣṇa;
may that Śrīśa impel us"—thus he indeed gave this mantra. ||81||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa! Bālakṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Ramāyaṇa! ||82||
Then the serpent indeed gave his name to the charioteer, and the charioteer quickly made it heard in the ear of the illustrious king. (83)
At that moment, the king rose up, free from poison and with his body restored to health;
and the serpent said to the king, "Go, O King, to the place of discourse. (84)
Listen to the auspicious narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā; also perform service to the virtuous, and through that, attain the highest welfare. (85)
Then, having learned the particulars of his own history from the charioteer, the king offered words of praise to the charioteer and also to the enjoyer.
Having paid his respects, he quickly returned home in his own chariot;
taking his wife, male servants, and female servants with him, he proceeded to tell the story. (87)
The king worshipped the Supreme Soul, the Lord Kṛṣṇa of beautiful form, and he also worshipped Vyāsa, Lomaśa, and the holy sages. 88.
He gave many gifts, listened to the teaching with devotion, and performed service to the virtuous through the distribution of food. 89.
Reminded by the charioteer, the king indeed performed worship;
the monarch repeatedly received the grace of the water from his feet.
Accompanied by his family, Badripāvana became truly pure;
out of fear of death, he always remained as if merged within the form of Kṛṣṇa. ||9 1||
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, at midday, the Lord Hari—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— mounted his celestial chariot.
He arrived for the sake of his liberation, and the king became prepared;
having paid homage to all the deities, he bestowed all kinds of gifts.
Summoned by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he ascended the celestial chariot,
as did Sūta Sukesarī and Queen Rakṣāvatī.
The sons, daughters, groups of servants, male slaves, and female slaves indeed offered shouts of victory and salutations to the king, who was about to attain liberation. 95.
O Badrikā, while all were looking on, the king named Saptābdhisimha became divine and departed for the imperishable abode of Hari. 96.
Then the queen and others performed the funeral rites for the king;
[so did] Sūta, Sukesarī, Queen Rakṣāvatī, their sons, and the rest. (97)
Having become supreme Vaiṣṇavas and having heard the liberating narrative, they went to the city of Naimiṣa, located in the Saindhava region, which takes five days to reach.
Having worshipped her beloved Lord Kṛṣṇa, the child of the cowherds, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Padmāvatī. (99)
In due time, they all went to the supreme, imperishable abode of Hari.
Thus, O beloved of Badrī, the king who had died was restored to life by means of the mantra.
Having heard this narrative and attained Hari, he went to the imperishable state of Brahman;
indeed, by reciting, hearing, or even contemplating this in every way, [one attains that same goal]. 10.1.
Likewise, liberation from time, illusion, and evil karma may arise;
there shall be excellent enjoyment and liberation, and all desired prosperities may come to pass. || 102 ||
O Badrī, the power of the narrations of Kṛṣṇa is considered superior to all other powers;
greater than that is the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, which accomplishes all goals.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Revival of King Saptābdhisimha, who was bitten by a serpent, through the application of the life-restoring mantra given by his son, and his liberation by hearing the sacred narrative," in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, beloved of Badarī, to the auspicious story of the Māgadha.
At that time, there was indeed a person from Māgadha in the city named Amṛta.
Known by the name Harṣanayana, he possessed knowledge of his own lineage and its branches;
he was one who composed accounts of the deeds and histories of those who preceded him in that lineage and its branches.
He heard from the people, in particular, about the wonder arising from the story concerning the kings of the Five Rivers and those born of the Indus.
The liberation of many kings and subjects is the destroyer of sin;
therefore, having reflected, he went suddenly for the purpose of hearing the story.
He arrived at Śarkarāpurī and entered the pavilion of discourse;
there he paid homage to all of them—to Vyāsa, the venerable Lomaśa, and Hari—and to the Saṃhitā.
He did not hear the sacred narrative from virtuous people, chaste women, saintly Vaiṣṇavas, kings, listeners, or even the queens.
At the conclusion of the discourse, he indeed spoke of the lineages originating from Nārāyaṇa;
filled with devotion, he delighted the people.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord,
is the one who is the cause of millions of divine lords and millions of incarnations.
In the supreme imperishable abode, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) shines;
in his lineage, Kṛṣṇa Vyāsudeva was first born.
From that, Nārāyaṇa was born, and after him Mahāviṣṇu;
from him came Virāṭ, and from Virāṭ were born Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
From Brahmā came Sanaka and the others, as well as the sages such as Mānava and the rest,
in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign; the son of Kaṃbharā and Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the delighter of Gopālā. || 1-2 ||
He is the husband of Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Āramā, Kṛṣṇā, Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, Lalitā, and Kamalā. ||13||

He is the Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of the assembly of the liberated, the Lord of the beloved of Hari, the Lord of all, the Lord of Brahmā, and the Sovereign. 14.
Today, he who is the eternal preeminent one of all lineages exists in the form of a brahmin;
here, Hari is glorified through the stories of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and other such accounts. 15.
May the preeminent among great kings, the king of kings, be victorious here—he who is the ordainer of blessings, the creator of prosperity, and the destroyer of suffering through liberation. (16)
May Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, who protects those who have come for refuge and is a treasure-trove of bliss, be eternally and most pre-eminently victorious! 17.
"The virtuous are victorious, and the Vaiṣṇavas are exceedingly victorious.
Thus, O Śrī Badrikā, with eyes full of joy, [he praised] Hari, the Lord of Śrī. 18.
Having offered praise in the assembly hall, he prostrated himself like a staff,
offering tulasī leaves, flowers, fruits, and likewise sugar.
And having performed worship, he presented betel nut, a golden seal-ring, and auspicious garments to Vyāsa and likewise to the Saṃhitā.
He prostrated and received his grace and the nectar of his feet;
from Vyāsadeva, he received both the mantra and the name-mantra.
He constantly recited mantras and performed the glorification of Dhunī;
he always listened to sacred stories with one-pointed concentration and remained perpetually absorbed in them.
The King of Magadha became purified and his fortune was fulfilled;
on the evening of the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, he was brought under control by devotion. (23)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the divine Hari served by Śrī, arrived mounted upon a celestial chariot to bring him back. 24.
Having transformed Māgadha into a divine form with eyes full of joy,
he placed him in a celestial chariot and led him to his own imperishable abode.
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another purifying narrative:
there, at the site of the Saṃhitā-maṇḍapa, there was an old servant. (26)
He who constantly keeps watch at night and protects [others] always worships Kṛṣṇa and listens to His stories with devotion. ||27||
At the end of the night, he performs circumambulation while maintaining a composed posture; he also daily offers leaves, flowers, and fruits with sincere devotion. (28)
He constantly performs recitation, partakes of the supreme prasāda, drinks water produced from prasāda, and enjoys the grace of the virtuous. (29)
He even performs service for Vyāsa, such as massaging his body and limbs, as well as sweeping the assembly hall and washing his clothes. (4.75.30)
He even bestows desired objects upon the Vaiṣṇavas;
such is the devotee named Yogidāsa. ||3.1||
O Badrikā, Śrī Hari became pleased and arrived;
adorned with all ornaments, Hari came mounted upon a divine swan.
He said to Yogidāsa, "Be prepared for liberation;
I have come here with Haṃsa to lead you toward salvation. (33)
Having heard the words of the Supreme Self, Yogidāsa rejoiced greatly;
he set out toward Śrī Hari, the Swan, for the sake of liberation.
At that moment, he fell into a swoon and his body fell to the ground;
then Yogidāsa, possessing a divine form, became one who has attained the nature of liberation.
Having seated that devotee upon the swan, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa departed for His eternal, supreme abode while all embodied beings looked on. (36)
