Thus, O Badrikā, Yogidāsa, whose mind was fixed on Kṛṣṇa, became liberated through the service of such stories on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha. (37)
Now, O Badrī, I shall tell you another story that grants liberation to devotees:
there was once a betel-preparer named Saurabhasāvitri. (38)
In Śarkarānagara, he became a servant of Badrī, Satā, and Hari;
he remained steadfast in the service of the Vaiṣṇavas every single day. (39)
He joyfully gives thousands of auspicious betel leaves daily, mixed with fragrant juices, powders, and other ingredients. (4.75.40)
Rising daily at dawn and having bathed, he comes to the pavilion;
having arrived at his proper place, [he worships] with leaves, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
He performed worship of the *Kathā-saṃhitā*, as well as of the virtuous ones,
and likewise offered honor to Vyāsadeva and to Lomaśa.
[He performed] the worship of Lālāsana, the worship of Vṛkāyana, the worship of Nīlakaṇa, and the worship of Yavakrīta and the others. ||43||
This is the most excellent divine abode for the Tuṣitas, the Hāritas, those traveling in celestial chariots,
and for yogins such as Eṣāya and Maṅkaṇaka.
Every morning, he constantly performs the worship of virtuous men such as Hemaśālāyana and others, as well as the worship of the gods. ||45||
He indeed offers even fruits— betel nuts, garlands of *tulasī* leaves, and flower wreaths— to Vyāsa and the *Saṃhitās*.
In the worship, he indeed offers according to his capacity mudrās, unbroken grains of wheat, garments, blankets, and fragrant substances and juices. (47)
Thus, through his devotion to Saurabha’s son, Sāvitra became free from all taint;
for even the massaging of the feet and the like, performed by the carriage of the bodies of the virtuous, [is a source of merit]. (48)

Having performed his duties, having eaten, and having drunk the nectar of His feet as a gracious gift, he listened to the stories of the Saṃhitā and became one whose latent impressions were completely burnt away. ||49||
To lead him to the imperishable abode, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
Hari, arrived at the place of discourse, seated upon the white Garuḍa.
With a lotus-face serene, he suddenly descended;
pleased by your service, he spoke words fragrant like the sun. (51)
"Come to my supreme, divine, celestial, and imperishable abode.
Having heard this, Saurabha, accompanied by Savitṛ, leaped up and danced. 52.
Considering the state of liberation to be blessed, he approached Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa;
having bowed down and abandoned his own body, he chanted the mantra acquired in previous lives. (53)
Proclaiming his own name amidst the tumult, he ascended upon Garuḍa;
with his body now liberated and divine, he departed by way of the sky.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, after the narration was concluded, he departed for the supreme state;
having witnessed that supreme wonder, the superhuman beings rejoiced exceedingly.
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to another song of the devotees, the most purifying story of Raṅgakāra that took place there. 56.
There was a dyer named Raṅgila who was always engaged in dyeing;
he was skilled in all the arts of dyeing and in millions of varieties of painting. (57)
In Śarkarānagara, he constantly made his living through theatrical performances;
he was devoted to the service of the gods and was always a devotee of the virtuous. (58)
O Badrikā, he indeed constructed a pavilion for that narrative,
adorning it everywhere with all the various images of the gods and all the various images of the devotees.
Through service and devotion, he performed the painting of the walls and the most beautiful decorations on the cloths in order to attain the favor of the virtuous.
And for the sake of Hari’s grace, he likewise performed service at the temple;
he worshipped the Supreme Soul and constantly chanted the mantra. ||61||
Performing acts such as the chanting of the Lord's names with great devotion,
he also attended upon the Vaiṣṇavas and listened to their sacred discourses.
With devotion, he consumed the food offered as grace, drank the water of the nectar-like feet,
and bore the dust of the feet upon his body.
Thus, having exhausted his sins and thoroughly washed away his latent impressions (vāsanā),
he desired to go to the eternal and imperishable abode of Śrī Hari.
O Badrikā, the all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, the inner controller Śrī Nārāyaṇa, mounted upon his white horse, arrived as the Lord of the lords of lords. 65.
Raṅgila said, "Come, [to] my supreme, imperishable abode.
Eagerly, Raṅgila suddenly abandoned his physical body.
By the glance of Kṛṣṇa, he became possessed of a divine body and mounted the horse;
while everyone looked on, Nārāyaṇa led him to the imperishable realm.
Seeing Raṅgila, the creator of delight, approaching,
the members of the assembly raised cries of victory and bowed toward that direction where Acyuta was.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Raṅgila indeed attained the Imperishable;
O Badrikā, now listen to another story concerning a devotee.
In that city of Śarkarā, there was a virtuous musician named Ḍamarūka; he too was a devotee who fashioned musical instruments and other such things. (4.75.70)
Having secured his livelihood, he maintained himself, served the virtuous, and indeed offered musical instruments with devotion during religious discourses. (71)
Bell-metal vessels, conch shells, kettledrums, and drums—bherīs, ḍiṇḍimas, and gomukhas—as well as mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, murajas, and amarakas. ||72||
He gave mṛdaṅga drums, flutes, lutes, dardura drums, and tortoise-shaped drums; he gave hand-clapping cymbals, ānaka drums, dundubhi kettledrums, and rhythmic clappers.
By that merit, the Blessed One then became pleased with him;
he too, being skilled in the art of instrumental music, performed the playing of musical instruments.
Because of that, O Badrikā, the virtuous became pleased with him;
he constantly performed service for the holy ones and always listened to their discourses.
He constantly maintained his serene devotion, always drank the nectar of [the Lord's] feet, incessantly muttered the mantra, and performed the chanting of the Name. (76)
Thus, devoted to the service of the Vaiṣṇavas and to the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Ḍamarūka became utterly purified, with all his sins destroyed. ||77||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord of Śrī, arrived to lead that Ḍamarūkaṇa to the imperishable abode. 78.

He too, recognizing that moment of liberation and seeing Hari arrived with Hari, did not bow; yet, having prostrated himself before the assembly members, he meditated upon them repeatedly within his heart.
Having cast off his material body and attained a divine form,
he, summoned by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, mounted the elephant.
By the grace of Śrī Hari, O Badarī, he went to the glorious, eternal, and imperishable abode of Nārāyaṇa, from which there is no return. 8.1.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Ḍamarūka went to Akṣara;
listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to that most purifying story. (82)
There, in the city of Śarkarā, there was a man named Bhāvasāra, who was a dealer in clothes and was widely known by the name Cihnarāya. ||83||
The wealthy and happy Vaiṣṇava Cihnarāya, out of devotion, gave a thousand garments for the sake of the pavilion and for the purpose of the place where the discourse was held. (84)
Since he provided woolen carpets, excellent canopies, and most delightful seats for the festival of storytelling. ||85||
He served the virtuous, listened to the stories of Acyuta,
and received from Vyāsadeva the purifying mantra and the practice of kīrtana.
She constantly served him with gifts of clothing and coins;
by that service, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, became pleased. ||87||
Out of grace, Kṛṣṇa, the beloved lord and husband of Śrī, granted a direct vision of himself to the pure Cihnarāya. 88.
He said to him, "I am pleased; come to my imperishable abode. By means of this excellent celestial chariot, I shall lead you to the supreme state. (89)
On the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, at midday, having seen Kṛṣṇa arrive,
he prepared to depart and indeed cast off his physical body.
His body immediately became divine, and he ascended a celestial chariot while chanting the name "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (91)
Together with Śrī Hari, he quickly went to the imperishable realm by means of a celestial chariot;
at that time, there were repeated shouts of victory from the devotees there. (92)
And then, Badrī, at that time in the evening after the narration of the story, a supreme wonder occurred; hear about it from the village priest. (93)
There was a village-priest named Rameśvara who held the Brahmins as his gods;
he would constantly listen to the sacred narratives and perform worship of Vyāsa.
He constantly worships Śrī Hari, daily chants His mantra, and perpetually performs the chanting and glorification of His names with joy. (95)
He constantly received the grace of Śrī Hari and the nectar of His feet;
thus, with his heart purified, the brāhmaṇa lived day after day. 96.
That supreme Vaiṣṇava constantly served the best of holy men;
he made the firm resolve to go to the imperishable, supreme abode of Hari.
At Badrikā, he performed a waterless fast unto death for the sake of attaining liberation; on the third day, Hari arrived there for the purpose of his liberation. 98.
On the new moon day, at the beginning of the night, he arrived by means of a celestial chariot and said to him, "O devotee, come;
this chariot is indeed for your sake."
He too, having quickly become a divine being, ascended that [chariot] and,
accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, went to the imperishable abode, the supreme state.
O Badarī, your wonders spread everywhere upon the earth;
countless humans come for the sake of hearing your stories. 10.1
Those with intense momentum proceed swiftly to the Imperishable after rapid purification;
those with moderate momentum go slowly, and those with sluggish momentum take a long time.
Those who lack affection certainly do not go there, for affection is the cause;
[the means are] clarity, compassion, service, faith, and divine contemplation. (103)
The dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the intensely swift desire to depart [from saṃsāra] occur;
detachment, refuge, and devotion are the causes for liberation. 104.
But those whose [faith] is intense quickly proceed to the supreme state;
from reciting or hearing this, both enjoyment and liberation shall be attained here in this world.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, being pleased by the hearing of stories, service, giving of gifts, and so forth, led Harṣanayana the Māgadha, Yogidāsa the servant, Saurabhasāvitra the betel-preparer, Raṅgila the dyer, Ḍamarūka the musician, Cihnarāya the actor, and Rameśvara the village priest, to the state of liberation," in the Tiṣya lineage within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to this wondrous narrative concerning the liberation of the Vidyādharas, which is supreme and divine.
At that time, there was a Vidyādhara named Svarṇāstaraṇa,
the mind-born son of Brahmā who made his dwelling in the Himalayas.
Desiring to roam through the sky in his own celestial chariot,
he set out by way of the ocean path, beholding the regions situated amidst the forests.
Then, having seen the three sacred sites (tīrthas) beyond Lake Mānasarovara,
he saw Kāśī, Mahā, Pañcanada, and the banks of the Sindhu.
By means of his celestial chariot, he arrived where the great city of Śarkarānagara was located,
and where the pavilion for the recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā stood.
There exists a place resembling heaven, shining with gold by day;
it is vast, where millions of men are settled.
Wherever the discourse proceeds with the resonance of Vyāsa’s throat,
it travels through the sky beyond the clouds and reaches the range of the gods’ hearing.
The fragrant fumes of the oblations, such as clarified butter and other substances, which are exceedingly purifying, proceed from that place toward the world of Vāyu. (8)
Peace proceeds from the surface of the earth upward into the sky;
indeed, for those with tormented hearts, it is from this that the peace of Brahman arises.
At that moment, minds similar to those of the yogins arise even among the people in the sky,
as do the celestial chariots of the subjects for an instant.
Banners, flags, water-pots, the hymns of praise of the virtuous, assemblies of Vaiṣṇavas, and groups of celestial women; 11.
The arrivals and departures of the Vaiṣṇavas in the sky are incessant;
so too are the incarnations of the gods and the sounds of the Vedas uttered by the twice-born.
All of this indeed causes the delusion of Vaikuṇṭha upon the earth; such a great sacrificial session (satra) arises in the form of a narrative. 1.3.

Having observed, reflected upon, discerned, and even ascertained the happiness and the festival, as well as the descent of the celestial chariots of the hosts of gods, sages, and perfected beings; || 14 ||
Beholding his own celestial chariot, he brought it down upon the shore of the ocean,
accompanied by hundreds of Vidyādharīs and hundreds of male and female servants.
Accompanied by hundreds of sons and daughters, he emerged from the celestial chariot;
having stationed the chariot in the courtyard of the great garden, he proceeded to the pavilion.
Having stood and sat there in the pavilion, he listened with a one-pointed mind to the story being recited, and at the conclusion of the narrative, he remained in the presence of Vyāsa.
Accompanied by many attendants and likewise by his family, he arrived for the purpose of worshipping Vyāsa; having bowed to the assembly and the virtuous women, he entered. (18)
Having removed from his head his golden crown and its covering,
he bowed repeatedly to Vyāsa, the Saṃhitā, and Hari.
With sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and other offerings, as well as ornaments of gems and diamonds,
gold, jewels, pearls, and the like, he joyfully performed the worship.
He performed the nightly lamp-offering with a thousand single-wick lamps,
while the Vidyādharīs danced and sang of his weightiness of virtue.
The male and female servants danced, delighted by hearing the narrative;
Lomaśa offered them a welcome and then inquired after their well-being.
He said, "I am a disciple of Lomaśa; I dwell on the Himavat mountain at Mānasāras together with my family."
I came for the purpose of visiting the monastery, but having seen the festival, I descended [from my vehicle].
I have become one who has fulfilled his purpose through listening to the discourse and performing worship. (24)
Peace was born in my heart while I was still in the sky, seeking what is auspicious; therefore, I descended here, for this event has brought me the highest welfare. (25)
The Vidyadhara also made an inquiry to inform Vyasa,
as well as to learn about that preeminent teacher, Lomasha.
Then the virtuous Lālāyana quickly said to the Vidyādhara:
"This is Nārāyaṇa Vyāsa, whose nature is self-luminous. (27)
This supreme narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* belongs to the crown jewel among the disciples of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (28)
He whose disciple you are is this very sage Lomaśa;
I, Lālāyana, am also dwelling here on the Himālaya mountain. (29)
Thus addressed, that Vidyādhara shed tears of affection and quickly fell at the feet of his preceptor, Lomaśa.
The entire family fell at the feet of the sage;
Lomaśa welcomed them and inquired after their welfare and well-being.
The preceptor Lomaśa provided him with lodging in the royal garden, then gave him food,
and out of great honor, he served him as a guest.
At the word of Lomaśa, he dwelt there for a month and daily heard the narrative that liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence.
Together with his family, he constantly enjoyed the grace of Hari;
the male and female servants performed service to their guru and service to the virtuous.
The sons, daughters, and Vidyādharīs performed service to their virtuous guru;
they constantly engaged in kīrtana and chanted his names. (35)
Then Śrī Lomaśa gave them the mantra that bestows liberation:
"Om, I am Brahmā; I become a servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (36)
Having received the mantra, all the Vidyādharas were freed from defilement;
they became liberated in form, with all their latent impressions (vāsanās) extinguished. ||37||
Desirous of liberation and intensely longing for the bliss of Brahman, they made a request to the venerable Guru for the sake of attaining liberation. (38)
Saying "Om," the Guru remembered the Supreme Lord; and as soon as he was remembered by Lomaśa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa arrived. (39)
Seated within every celestial chariot, accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī, his beloveds,
and joined by the male and female liberated attendants of Mādhava, he arrived.
From the celestial chariot of Sūryaprabha, Śrī Hari, with a gracious mind and resplendent with all his ornaments, came outside laughing. (41)
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was honored with offerings of water and nectar by Lomaśa and other virtuous groups of gurus, as well as by saintly women and Vaiṣṇavas. 42.
Out of compassion, he sprinkled the entire host of Vidyādharas with drops of divine nectar for their benefit; consequently, they all became divine. (43)
Having attained transformation, those Vidyādharas, their mortal bodies cast off, were born with divine forms equal to Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā, and Lakṣmī. 44.
All those five hundred, having ascended their excellent celestial chariots and attained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, became eternally liberated. ||45||
Strengthened by the blessings of great sages, holy men, and brahmins, they proclaimed "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa" while clapping their hands. 46.
Roaring through the sky, they raised shouts of victory as Hari suddenly proceeded along the path by way of the Himalayas. 47.
Having led him to Lake Mānasarovara and to the auspicious city of the Vidyādharas, [he gave him] to his grandson named Viśālin, who was young and possessed a golden-colored complexion. 48.
Having given [it], he went by way of the upper sky to his own imperishable Brahman;
Viśālāstaraṇa also indeed practiced devotion to Hari.
Thereafter, he became prosperous and enriched with a lineage of sons, grandsons, and descendants;
and after a long time, through devotion to the Beloved of Kamalā, he attained the imperishable state.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, those Vidyādharas attained liberation at Badarīpriya, reaching the station of the supreme Lord, the imperishable state.
Now, Badrī, listen as I tell you of another marvel:
those auspicious Gandharvas who dwell on the Himavat, such as Citrabarha and others. (52)
They arrived to dwell in the region of Lake Mānasarovara;
they beheld thousands of celestial chariots upon the Himalayas. (53)
They asked Svarṇāstaraṇa, "Where has your father gone?
Svarṇāstaraṇa replied, "My father has gone to the state of liberation. (54)
Indeed, five hundred Vidyādharas went to the imperishable abode of Hari by means of a most divine celestial chariot moved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Merely by hearing this discourse, all attained the state of liberation;
that discourse is currently being propagated in the city of Śarkarā in the land of Sindh. (56)
The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā bestows supreme liberation, wherein the Lord Anādikṛṣṇa shines together with his beloved queen. 57.
He is the embodiment of the deities of the Saṃhitās and the cause of all manifestations;
there resides the sage Śrī Lomaśa, the preceptor of the Vidyādharas and others.
The Blessed Vyāsa is self-luminous, and he is the speaker of that [work] by the mere hearing of which even gods, dānavas, and gandharvas are indeed purified. (59)
Having heard that story, my father and the others departed for heaven;
and upon hearing this wonder, O Badrikā, those who dwell in the Himalayas were struck with amazement.
Citrabarha and others, along with three hundred men and women, also arrived at the place of conversation by means of a celestial chariot, full of eager anticipation.
On the twelfth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, they descended from the sky near the great garden and arrived at the pavilion of discourse.

Indeed, during the bright fortnight, the Gandharvas and Gandharvīs would listen to the Saṃhitā recounting the stories of Hari in the evening, after the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) had been performed.
From Lomaśa they received the mantra and they received the Nāmadhunī;
they accepted his grace and drank the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
In this manner, for fourteen days they listened to that auspicious narrative;
they performed service to the virtuous and daily engaged in dance with joy.
And they performed songs daily that were highly enchanting; they sang with joy before Kṛṣṇa, before the Saṃhitās, and before the virtuous.
Filled with devotion, they indeed performed the congregational chanting of Hari’s names;
by that affection, they quickly became cleansed of all impurity.
With their afflictions exhausted and all habitual tendencies eliminated, they became perfected yogis;
indeed, they all attained [enlightenment] and received the mantra of liberation. || 68 ||
"I am Brahmā, a servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; Om!
Having grasped this mantra, those men and women chanted it with intense devotion. (69)
Pleased with them, Śrī Kṛṣṇa swiftly arrived in a celestial chariot on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha to lead them to His own imperishable abode.
Then Hari cast a handful of water even above all three hundred of them; they were touched by those drops of water at that moment.
All those Gandharvas, possessing divine bodies and having reached the state of liberation, became liberated Gandharvas with celestial forms. ||72||
Summoned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they ascended the celestial chariot,
making it thunder with shouts of victory, after bowing down to the assembly hall where the discourse was held.
Having paid obeisance to their guru and the saintly ones, they meditated upon the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
then, in an instant, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led them away.
Then he led Himādri to his own imperishable abode, Brahmadhāma;
thus, O Śrī Badrikā, they all went to the eternal state.
Listen, O beloved of Badrī, to this divine marvel:
how the Kinnaras and Kimpuruṣas who dwell on the snowy mountain and in the marshy lands [behave].
And having heard of the liberation of the Vidyādharas from that place in the past,
they arrived at the site where the story of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa was told, traveling in celestial chariots.
Five hundred Kinnaras and half as many Kiṃpuruṣas arrived; two hundred Cāraṇas and fifty Siddhas also came together. (78)
Then, celestial chariots descended from the sky into the great garden;
having alighted, they all went to the place of assembly to behold [the Lord].
Honored by Lomaśa and the others, they heard that auspicious narrative;
filled with joy, they accepted his grace and drank the nectar of his feet.
They received from the sage Lomaśa the liberating mantra, which is the destroyer of rebirth,
as well as the worship of Vyāsa, the worship of the sacred narrative, and the constant service of the virtuous.
Those supreme, purifying Vaiṣṇavas, endowed with devotion, performed [the rites];
on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, [appeared].
But at night, Hari appeared directly before all of them, resplendent with all his ornaments and accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī. ||83||
Seated upon his excellent celestial chariot, the Lord, with a serene countenance, said: "Come to my abode, the imperishable and supremely purifying realm."
O Badarī, having been addressed thus, they considered themselves blessed and fortunate; becoming ready, they ascended the celestial chariot adorned with Kṛṣṇa. (85)
By the grace of Śrī Hari, they all became auspicious with divine bodies and beautiful forms; indeed, they ascended into their celestial chariots and traveled about. 86.
O Śrī Badrikā, the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led her from there to the snowy mountain and then to His own abode, the Imperishable Realm (Akṣara-dhāma). ||87||
Having made the Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, Yogins,
and divine liberated souls [his attendants], Hari led them away out of compassion.
Oh, what fortune belongs to the inhabitants of the Himalayas, O illustrious Badarī!
They have attained the celestial chariot of Nārāyaṇa, and they have even attained Nārāyaṇa himself. (89)
Even the attainment of the world of Brahmā results from the practice of listening to the sacred narrative,
from serving the virtuous, and likewise from partaking of the food of grace.
Thus, O Badrī, the attainment of the Avatārī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has ceased;
in this way, there is the constant and auspicious liberation of living beings. 91.
Furthermore, through hearing the sacred narratives, through seeing, and through bowing down to the virtuous, there occurs indeed a union with Hari, the cause of all causes. (92)
The Nāgas, Daityas, Dānavas, Uragas, Yakṣas, and reptiles who came there to Badarī and attained union through yoga; 93.
All of them, their sins exhausted and freed from the material qualities, became yogis of Kṛṣṇa and, time and again, went to the imperishable abode of the glorious Supreme Soul. 94.
Insects, monkeys, wild animals, birds, and even beasts; creatures, creepers, trees, aquatic beings, and even those born from sweat—[all these are included]. (95)
Whosoever died there at the sacrificial session, having been joined by the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, all attained the supreme abode, the imperishable, through the grace of Hari. 96.
Whatever crops, grains, stalks, and clusters there were, as well as trees with fruits, flowers, and leaves, all entered into conversation. (97)
Whether by tradition or directly, through their own limbs and even through fruits and the like, they all attained supreme liberation by virtue of their association with Kṛṣṇa. ||98||
Indeed, everything in this world is easily obtained, but the company of the virtuous is always difficult to find;
through the grace of the virtuous, such company is attained, by which liberation rests in the palm of one's hand.
O Badrikā, by the recitation, hearing, and even reflection upon this, there shall be enjoyment and liberation here; it is the eternal, supreme goal.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Vidyādharas such as Svarṇāstaraṇa, the Gandharvas such as Citrabarha, and the Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Cāraṇas, and Siddhas through Hearing Narratives and Other Means," in the fourth section on the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; as each day passes, hundreds of thousands of people from the world indeed go there while this narrative is being told.
The discourse lasts for only a month, or at most half a month, or even just seven days; knowing this, they come by the hundreds of thousands.
Men and women, children and the elderly, as well as the young, were full of enthusiasm; for the sake of destroying their sins, they longed for a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
And many others, possessed of the desire for liberation, came there constantly, just as [the inhabitants of] Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, or heaven do.
Likewise, the divine land of Śrīśarkarābhūmi indeed shines with its devotees;
there the people worship Vyāsa, the form of Kṛṣṇa, and the Saṃhitā. (5)
To Lomaśa and other gurus, saintly persons, brāhmaṇas, great Vaiṣṇavas, virtuous women, chaste wives, the best of yogis, female ascetics, and female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; || 6 ||
They offered tributes such as jewels, gems, gold, and garments;
they listened [to his teachings], served him, and gave gifts for the sake of liberation.
Having partaken of the prasāda and drunk the water, being filled with devotion,
they departed after having propitiated the holy sages and reached the imperishable abode of Hari.
In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, however, the kings and others from the south,
as well as those dwelling in hot regions and those residing on the land of Prāgjyotiṣa, [should perform the rite].
Those dwelling in the land of Brahmā, those residing in Śyāma and Śambhu,
those living in Prācīna, and also those residing in the kingdom of Śibi.
The kings and men of the Rāśīyas arrived,
as did those dwelling in Ketumāla and those residing in Kiṃpuruṣa.
The Hāritas, along with those dwelling in Parīdeśa, arrived joyfully;
and men and kings from Abrikta also came there.
The subjects of the immortals and the kings arrived by means of celestial chariots;
meanwhile, the men and women dwelling on the earth also arrived.
Men and women emerged from the interior of the earth and from the regions of the entrails,
specifically for the sake of gaining the benefit of hearing the narrative and especially for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa.
They glorify the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhā and the husband of virtuous wives, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who manifests in all incarnations. || 15 ||
Śrī Lomaśa and the others offered them a welcome reception, the madhuparka offering, water, and a residence; Rāyahariścandra provided ten million pieces of gold.
They fashioned celestial happiness according to each individual's fitness;
then they bestowed divine vehicles, food, drink, and worthy dwellings.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, assuming countless forms, gratified them all;
he served his own devotees and became the fulfiller of everyone's desires. || 1 ||
Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Śrī, Bhū, Mādhavī, Māṇikī, Priyā, Maṅgalā, Mañjulā, Revā, Suguṇā, and Sarasvatī. (19)
Gaṅgā is devotion, Satī is liberation, Ekādaśī is delight, and Dayā is Tulasī; Śāntā is the wish-fulfilling cow, Kamalā is Virajā, and Himā is the Himālaya. (4.77.20)
Haṃsā, Mūrti, Gomatī, Kuṅkumavāpī, Annapūrṇikā, Jayā, Durgā, Lalitā, Sāvitrī, Santoṣiṇī, and Kalā. (21)
Badrī, Campā, Mauktikā, Vidyut, Ṣaṣṭhī, and Ṛtambharā;
Śvetā, Raktā, and the Siddhis; then Kṛṣṇā and the Nidhis as well. 22.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, the Śaktis, assuming various forms, performed service to the people in infinite ways according to what was appropriate. 23.
The embodied beings from the fourteen worlds arrived one after another at Śarkarāpurī for the sake of attaining the auspicious story of Kṛṣṇa. (24)
Those men and all those women who had taken refuge in Puruṣottama attained a divine state and became fulfilled in their purpose.
Listen, O Goddess, beloved of Badrī; at that time there was a great festival on the final day of the Āṣāḍha bright fortnight, upon the completion of the Pārāyaṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and the others arrived from Kuṅkumasthala—those who were indeed present there in various forms for the sake of their devotees. (27)
The venerable Gopāla, Kṛṣṇa, and other elder great sages, as well as the wives of Brahmā together with Śrī, Kambharā, and Lakṣmī. ||28||
The attendants headed by Pavana, other gods, great sages,
kings, and even the subjects all assembled at the sacrifice of the narrative.
O reciter, dear to Śrī Badarī, I wish to know by name who has assembled there—whether they be gods, great sages, or likewise gandharvas and apsarases. (4.77.30)
O Lord, cause all those attendants and kings who have arrived at the final stage of the recitation to hear it as they are intent upon the complete study.
At that time, by the mere hearing of the names of the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, the destruction of sin will surely occur, and merit and fortune shall increase. (32)
Blessed are those who have attained union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
by the mere remembrance of whom the bondage of Māyā is destroyed. (33)
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved of Badarī, O Goddess; at the conclusion of the recitation on that leaf, those who have gathered there during the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha—[all of them... 34.
I shall now describe all those who were present there when the eleventh day concluded; listen to these great devotees of the Lord. ||35||
The Ānanda-devas arrived; the Bhuvar-devas assembled together;
likewise, the Bhāva-devas, the Rāmbha-devas, and the Tāpasa-devatās came.
The gods of the Ṛtaveda, the gods of the Ādhvara, the deities of the Pāvaka, the Sāvitra deities, the Havyavāhas, and likewise the Bhūmadevas arrived. ||37||
The Auśikas, the Kauśikas, the gods of Gāndhāra, the Ārṣabhas, the Ṣaḍjanas, and the deities of Mārjālīya likewise arrived. (38)
The Vairājakas, the Mādhyamas, the Niṣādas who have the vital breath as their deity, the Ākūtikas, the Cintakas, and those whose vehicle is the clouds arrived. (39)
The Vijñātikas and Mānasas, the Rāthantara gods, the Sadyojātas, Vāmadevas, the Vīras, and the yellow-clad Kumārakas; 4.77.40.
Satyādyas, Vyāsadevas, Śambhus such as Sutārādyas, and Manus such as Svāyambhuva and others, all arrived at the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). ||41||
All the Vaimānika gods and the thousand-eyed ones arrived;
likewise, the Nārāyaṇas, the Ādityas, and the Prājāpatyas arrived.
The immortal Brahmanical gods, as well as those who endure until the end of the kalpa, the ancestors, and the sages also arrived for the discourse. (43)
Dharma, Ruci, Dakṣa, Marīci, Bhṛgu, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, and Kratu arrived. (44)
Nārada, Ṛbhu, Sanatkumāra, and others arrived; so too did the Gandharvas, Siddhapūrṇa, and Bahvīpūrṇāśa. (45)
Śataguṇa, Brahmacārī, Viśvāvasu, Suparṇaka, Bhānu, Sucandra, Varuṇa, Bhīmasena, and Ugrasena. 46.
Suparṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūryavarcas, Tumburu, Gomān, Subāhu, Prayuta, Patravān, and Arkaparṇaka; ||47||
Bhīma, Citraratha, Śāliśiras, and Parjanya;
also Hāhā, Hūhū, Kali, Haṃsa, and Jyotiṣṭoma as the middle one. ||48||
Ācāra, Dāruṇa, Vareṇya, Varuṇa, as well as Suruci, Sumanas, Vasuruci, and others. ||49||
Then those Gandharvas, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, arrived;
and the Apsarases also came, O Badrikā, as did Urvaśī.
Aruṇā, Vimanuṣyā, Anapāyā, Varāmbarā, Asiparṇā, Miśrakeśī, Śuci, and Kālambuṣā likewise. (51)
Vidyutparṇā, Lakṣmaṇā, Tilottamā, Ārdrikā, Rambhā, Kṣemā, Asitā, Mārīcikā, and likewise Manobhavā. ||52||
Subāhvī, Supriyā, Puṇḍarīkā, and likewise Sudatī;
Surasā, Subhujā, Ājagandhā, Haṃsā, and Sarasvatī. ||53||
Ajayā gave birth to Kamalā, Sumukhī, Haṃsapādikā, Arūpā, Subhagā, Bhāsī, Manuvantī, and Sukeśinī. ||54||
Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇinī, Pūrvacittikā,
Kṛtasthalī, Ghṛtācī, and Pramlocā also arrived there.
Anumlocā, as well as Tanvī, Pūñjikasthalinī, and Uṣā—their daughters and granddaughters arrived by the thousands. (56)
All the maidservants, longing for a vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
likewise assembled there for their recitation.
O Badrikā, the attendants of Bālakṛṣṇa also arrived—Pāvana, Vṛṣabha, Gopa, Vatsala, and Kumāraka. (58)
Siddha, Aruṇa, Hārita, Viśva, Vipra, Kuṇḍala, Sahasrākṣa, Suyoga, Mahīmāna, and Vasantaka. ||99||
Sahasraśiras, Madhvaśna, Urukrama, Vikrama,
Viśvākṣa, Urugāya, Viśvātmā, and Jātavedas.
Ānanda, Ciklīta-deva, Devatrā-vijaya, Jaya, Nanda, Sunanda, Vasuvana, and Jayanta arrived. (61)
Śrutadeva, Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍa, and Sāttvata arrived;
as did Viṣvaksena, Puṣpadanta, Suparṇa, Prabala, and Bala.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, the conscious self Garuḍa, Kaivalyabodha, Haṃsa, Svaprakāśa, and Cinmaya; ||63||
Prapūruṣa, Kalyāṇa, Padmadhara, Sumūrtaka, Prabhoga, Śrīprasāda, Śrīprakāśa, Akṣara, and Naya. ||64||
Santoṣa, Brahmadṛk, Pradhyāna, Citānanda, Ūrjaka, Paramajña, Sunaya, Vinaya, and Prabhañjana. ||65||

Acintya (the inconceivable), Ananta (the infinite), Praśama (the tranquil), Amogha (the unfailing), Dahara (the small), Viśvarūpa (the universal form), Vaikuṇṭha, Prajñāna (pure consciousness), and Oṃkāra. ||66||
Pratattva, Nijabodha, and likewise the excellent Puṇḍarīka;
Uddhava, Śāśvata, Pūrṇabhadra, and Prabhūtaka. ||67||
Ṛṣabha, Subhadra, Nirālamba, Videhaka, Sālambana, Ānanda, Dyukaṇṭha, and Prasattaka. ||68||
Haṃsa, Prahaṃsa, Bhadrākṣa, Mañjula, Pradhanyaka, Prabodha, Sujyotis, Satyeśa, and Savitraka. ||69||
Avyaya, Maṅgala, Tāpasa, Suvrata, Suśīla, Pratūrta, Praviṣṇu, and Varada.
Prajiṣṇu, Vallabha, Prasāda, Pradhana, as well as Avadāta, Amṛta, Prabhava, and Adhvara. ||71||
Utsava, Hiraṇya, Anagha, Viśruta, Nirdeśa, Bhūṣaṇa, Nivṛtta, and Pravardhana also arrived. ||72||
Saṃvṛta, Bṛhadrūpa, Prabhāva, Aśoka, Āyayu, Akāma, Niṣkāma, Śrīgarbha, and Sudarśana. ||73||
Nirvāṇa, Virāma, the vast Dharmayūpa, Purātana, Pramoda, Āmoda, and Supuṇya arrived. (74)
Āditya, Viśuddha, Udbhava, Netrajña, Āyayu, Śrīvāsa, and Kṛṣṇapāda—these attendants arrived. ||75||
The serpents known as Śeṣa and others, who are the foremost among the devotees of Viṣṇu—
Ananta and the rest— arrived at the final festival of the Pārāyaṇa.
O Badrikā, the kings dwelling on the earth also arrived there:
Śāvadīna, Lakṣmaṇa, and King Jummasemla. ||77||
Dakṣaja, Vaṅgara, and Śibideva also arrived; Tharkūṭastha, Vīrajāra, and Śaktyakṣika likewise arrived. (78)
Kālimāśa, Bālakāśa, and Kathaka arrived, as did Pṛthurāja, Uralaketu, and the king of Ur̥ṣṭrāla. ||79||
Tīraṇa and Haṃkāra also arrived at Jayakāṣṭhala;
Alvīnara, Jīnavardhi, and Alpaketu likewise came together.
Jayakṛṣṇavanṛpati, Parīśānanṛpati, Indurāya, Mudrāṇḍa, and Gaṇḍarāja all arrived. ||8 1||
Vṛhacchara, Līnorṇa, and Balalīna arrived, as did King Rāyagānala and King Varasiṃha. (82)
Phenatantunṛpa, Stokahoma, Kolaka, Āyayu, Kāṣṭhayāna, Dinamānārka, and indeed Rāyakinnaṭa [were there]. ||83||
Rāyarokīśvara, Rāyaraṇajīva, Rāyavākakṣaka, and also Rāyamārīśa arrived. (84)
Rāyabaleśvara, King Rāyalambāra, and King Rāyanavārka, as well as King Rāyahuṇḍeśa, arrived. ||85||
And Rāyakūpeśa-bhūpa, Kālīmaṇḍalikeśvara, Vanajeleśa-bhūpa, and King Pārāvārapiba; ||86||
Koṭīśvara, Śrīsatīśa, Tretākarkaśabhūpati, Āṇḍajara, Bālyarajas, and Rāyasomanabhūpati. ||87||
Urugavākṣaka, Parāṅvrata, Īśānapānaka, Rājā, and Rāyapati also arrived at the Pārāyaṇa. ||88||
Svāyambhuva Manu, along with both Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, was there; Yajña arrived, as did Dharma accompanied by throngs of women.
The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ protected that sacrifice;
likewise, the kings beginning with Āgnīdhra, as well as Nābhi and Kiṃpuruṣa.
Ketumāla and others, as well as King Hiraṇya, Ramyaka,
and Kuru— these kings arrived there at the Pārāyaṇa.
Umārāya, Kṣīrapūra, and Nāgavikrama arrived, as did Jayāditya, Vikramārka, and Kṛṣṇadurga of Pāñcāla. ||12||
Prabhālākṣa, Lakṣasena, Amaraśāla, Śrīlaṃbha, Prapatpāla, Prāṇipāta, and Nandibhilla arrived. (93)
Rāyapāra, Indragṛtsa, Gavayendra, Janāstraka, Karṇaputra, Avadhyatejas, Yāgadeva, and Paṭāsana. ||94||
Dārābhāgya, Rājamāna, Mādhava, Brahmapānaka, Śīlahāra, Māṇikābha, and Cittagāṅgeya arrived. (95)
Candranāga, Medakośa, Purukutsa, Upāyayu, Bālasaṃgha, Pārvateśa, and Nāgavijaya arrived. ||96||
Rājabhāru, Mahendrābha, and Madāśana arrived; Śararaṅga, Madhurāja, and Virāmāsa also arrived. ||97||
Trikūṭorkī, Mahāsāra, Cattralāsya, Kālikāñcana, Āpāṇḍa, Ākkalārya, and Vivardhana arrived together. ||98||
Maṇḍalāra, Javalīna, Indradyumna, Māṭharasiṃha, Kuṭidhṛk, Cicintana, and Udaṅprabha approached him. (99)
Śrīnāgari, Dharaṇidhṛk, Mūradhvaja, Rajidhvataja,
Kuṃkumāsyas, and likewise the Khaṇḍarājñas arrived together.
The lords of the continents, the lords of the ocean shores, the lords of battle, the rulers of mountains, and the subordinate princes, accompanied by their subjects, arrived for the Pārāyaṇa.
Whether it be the celestial realm of kings, the celestial assembly of Brahmā, or even the righteous court, or the world of truth—it is Śarkarāpura that truly shines. (102)
O Badrikā, the Nāga kings and the lords of the Daityas, who were devotees, arrived, eager for the complete recitation of the Śrī-saṃhitā. || 103 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Kings and Subjects of the Three Worlds Who Assembled for the Festival Occasioning the Completion of the Pārāyaṇa," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; at the conclusion of the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, there shall be an assembly of infinite number.
In the city of Śarkarā, on the banks of the Sindhu river, there was a vast and great garden extending ten yojanas in width on all sides. || 2 ||
On the ground, which was thick with trees and adorned with fragrant flowers and other offerings,
the Lord provided a welcome meal for the entire assembly.
The attendants, male servants, and female servants performed service for him in his dwellings;
and on the morning of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Hari [appeared].
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and beloved of Śrī,
was bathed by the consorts of Brahmā and adorned with ornaments by His dear wives.
Adorned and arrayed, he was honored by circles of virtuous men;
saluted by bards, genealogists, and others, and bowed to and worshipped by kings.
He was honored by the Vaiṣṇava women, praised by the devotees of the Lord,
gazed upon by throngs of women, and propitiated by his personal attendants.
Magnified by the emblems of the king of kings and by his divine attendants,
having performed acts of worship and other auspicious rites, he caused the sound of musical instruments to resound.
Accompanied by royal insignia, Acyuta arrived at the pavilion of discourse;
seated upon an elephant-throne adorned with golden necklaces of jewels, he shone resplendently.
The blessed Vyāsa, whose form is self-luminous, arrived; honored by the members of the assembly who rose to greet him, he took his own seat.
Honored with offerings of flowers and other gifts, and made to hear the proclamation of victory,
he was graced by hosts of sages led by Lomaśa and by virtuous ones such as Lālāyana.
The powers beginning with Ramā, the jewels such as rubies and the like which are dear to Hari, the goddesses, the deities, the sovereign ladies, and the millions of goddesses. || 1-2 ||
All the brahmins were knowers of the Vedas, devoted to Viṣṇu, purifying, and auspicious;
likewise, O tiger among kings, the subjects—both women and men—were perfected beings.
They arrived at the pavilion where the *saṃhitā* was kept, each according to their rank;
they sat down, and an auspicious commencement of discourse took place.
At the end of a muhūrta, upon the completion of the Saṃhitā as well as that of Śrī Hari’s Nyāsa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and the others performed the worship. ||15||
Koṭirāya, Rāyahari, Agnidhra, and other kings;
all the monarchs, all the gods, and all the virtuous sages.
The subjects and the merchants honored the Śrīsaṃhitā and Vyāsa, who is self-luminous, with leaves, flowers, fruits, and water.
They worshipped with gold and silver coins, diamonds and other gems, excellent pearls, jewels, golden ornaments, sandalwood paste, and unbroken grains of rice.
With excellent garments worthy of a king, with ornaments and other regalia fit for a monarch,
and with priceless crowns and such, they worshipped Vyāsa and Acyuta.
Svāyaṃbhuva likewise [ruled] the kingdom of the earth, as did Priyavrata;
O Hari, Uttānapāda [ruled] the regional kingdom of the earth.
Thus the Agnidhra priest presented [the gifts], while Hiraṇya and others presented [their offerings];
Kimpuruṣa and others presented celestial chariots, and [others] presented elephants and horses.
With joy, they presented golden jars, great lotuses, and tortoises;
they offered countless diamonds, pearls, and other gems, as well as gold.
Even kings presented many male and female servants;
those sovereign rulers of the earth offered their respective territories. (23)
Indra and the other gods presented them with divine garments,
and they bestowed upon them countless nectars of immortality and celestial riches.
And the men offered wealth there according to their means;
whatever was excellent and within their own possession, all that they offered there. (25)
Even the body's own implements are priceless instruments;
there, the three worlds are seen reflected upon couches. (26)
He joyfully offered those to the reciter and likewise to Śrī Hari,
presenting cintāmaṇi jewels, wish-fulfilling creepers, and vessels of plenty.
They presented divine weapons suited for the kalpa, as well as garments appropriate for the kalpa; they then offered all types of bodily ornaments and indeed various vehicles.
Whatever was most excellent on earth, in heaven, and in the netherworld,
all that was brought and offered then by the gods and other inhabitants of those realms.
And a necklace, resplendent with its inseparable brilliance from the Kaustubha gem, was offered by Viṣṇu;
by means of its splendors, which possessed the luster of the sun, he created that divine assembly hall.
And there, the divine umbrella offered by Brahmā, upon which the circle of stars shone,
appeared like another celestial heaven fastened above.
The moon, which dispels the darkness of the world, was offered by Śaṅkara;
and all the goddesses also offered their own respective powers (śaktis). || 32 ||
The most excellent Vyāsa was honored by the virtuous with flower garlands and other offerings,
and he was honored by millions of liberated souls, such as Īśvara and others, with their own splendors.
The guardians of the quarters presented him with victorious chariots drawn by celestial steeds;
the divine Mothers, the mothers of the world, bestowed their blessings. (34)
Eager sacrificers offered the *Saṃhitā* while mounted on elephants as a gift, and the sacrificial fires performed the lustration ceremony (*ārārtrika*) together with the kings. (35)
O Badri, after the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), there arose upon that ground great mountains of offerings consisting of various articles. 36.
Whatever substance each of them possessed was indeed offered there—gems renowned throughout the earth, as well as in heaven and the netherworld. (37)
Whatever is proclaimed as the most excellent in creation, worthy of worship, and worthy of gifts—all that has been offered there by all the inhabitants of every created world. (38)
"It is not the case that such-and-such is absent there"—this was agreed by everyone;
after the waving of lamps, the supreme worship of the virtuous was performed. (39)
Following the worship of the Brahmin-sages, the gods, and likewise of his preceptor Lomaśa,
the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa took place.
There, beautiful showers of flowers and other offerings fell from the sky; showers of sandalwood and celestial nectar also descended from heaven. (41)
The dances of the Apsarases, the songs of the wives of Brahmā, and the names of the rivers became manifest for the devotees on all sides. ||42||
At that time, indeed, poetic compositions and commentaries were produced by learned ones, preceptors of the gods, and poets alike. (43)
O Badrikā, there were gifts of all kinds of jewels, consisting of innumerable objects, given there to the poor, the helpless, and others in need. (44)
At that time, indeed, there were many gifts of food, as well as gifts of gold, and gifts of cows, horses, and elephants. 45.
At that time, there were gifts of maidens and gifts of excellent sons, as well as gifts of wealth consisting of fields, gardens, and houses. (46)
At that moment, O lady radiant as Badarī, gifts of wealth for the sake of sacrifice were being made by kings,
and thus the conversation came to an end.
The divine Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa, Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, and likewise, O Badrī, I am Nara-Nārāyaṇa as well. 48.
Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and likewise Śeṣanārāyaṇa,
bestowed blessings there that grant liberation even to the worlds.
Those who desire to hear the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā shall,
by our grace, attain supreme liberation in the imperishable state.
This compendium is the consort of the Vedas, the most exalted devotee of the Lord, the auspicious Śrī of Viṣṇu, and the pure, sattvic narrative concerning Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 51.
It proceeds as the refuge of all holy fords, the refuge of all dharmas;
it is the refuge of all gifts and the refuge of all knowledge, bestowing complete liberation. //52//
She is the refuge of all merit, the excellent refuge of all virtuous creations, the refuge of all saintly women, the refuge of truth, and she who clings to the body of Kṛṣṇa. ||53||
This narrative is endowed with all Nārāyaṇas, it sustains all incarnations, it consists of all the gods, and it is composed of all worship and meditation. (54)
She consists of all hymns of praise, she consists of the narrative of the seeds of all the Vedas;
she consists of all powers, and she is the ultimate goal of all human aims and the like. ||55||
This narrative bestows all good fortune, fulfills all desires, accomplishes all that is wished for, provides protection from all, and brings about welfare. (56)
Endowed with all sovereignty and the like, attended by all supernatural powers (siddhis), and the remover of all obstacles—this narrative triumphs upon the earth. (57)
Those who hear this chapter shall go to the supreme goal;
and those who satisfy the reciter with water, food, and clothing [shall likewise attain it]. (58)
For they shall go to our imperishable state by means of wealth and other such requisites;
and thereafter, they shall rely upon this primordial creation as the root for their discourses.
Tens of millions of books consisting of primary and secondary narratives will come into being;
likewise, there shall be a single Veda spoken by the Supreme Brahman, as well as a Saṃhitā.
And she who was spoken of as Paranārāyaṇā is indeed the second Vedinī;
having become ever-new in each age, she took recourse in the Veda and the Saṃhitā. 61.
They will write down the stories of the texts and compose commentaries;
therefore, when upheld, remembered, heard, or protected, this [teaching] indeed bestows liberation.
Having spoken thus and recited the victory hymn of the Śrī-saṃhitā, they gathered together;
and having brought the narrative to its conclusion, they likewise performed the dismissal of the assembly.
O Badrikā, whatever the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa was doing for those who had come to worship Him,
the Supreme Lord Himself would rise up and perform all of that.
Out of favor, he indeed restored everything to the donors themselves:
the kingdom, land, houses, fields, gardens, vehicles, and carriages. (65)
Gold, silver, ornaments, and herds of cattle, horses, and steeds—
Mādhava gave all these both to the donors themselves and also to the destitute.
By his very command, he restored their clarity of mind and physical form to those who had bestowed gifts upon him;
furthermore, he gave alms to the twice-born and the classes of the poor according to the prescribed rites.
With hearts full of devotion, they all accepted [the gifts] by the command of Kṛṣṇa;
for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa, and for the sake of dharma, they accepted them. ||68||
Hari gave everything that was required, as well as whatever remained, to the virtuous brahmins and the virtuous women.
There, in her own temple, for the purpose of receiving millions and so forth,
she resides in a golden abode served by Māṇikī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Prajñā, and others.
He offered fields, gardens, wealth, and so forth for the attainment of his livelihood;
then, after everyone had raised a shout of victory, the ritual dismissal was performed.
Then the women, men,
and people in the assembly hall excitedly took up dust from the floor, leaves, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Having fallen down, approached, and risen again, they took the auspicious clay from the Prasāda temple and uttered cries of victory with unrestrained throats.
Having made his departure, Hari went to the sacrificial ground;
Vyāsa, Lomaśa, and other twice-born ones also went to the site of the sacrifice. (74)
The kings also went to the sacrificial ground, which was a yojana in circumference,
where the performance of the sacrificial rites and other ceremonies proceeded through the agency of the brahmins.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, joined by Padmāvatī, together with Prajñā, is the Lord, the Master, the Beloved of Śrī. (76)
He sat down upon a golden sacrificial seat for the performance of the rite;
then Lomaśa, acting as the Brahmā priest, caused him to perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa).
Then follow the expiation (prāyaścitta), the primary ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), the protection of the quarters, the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa), and the adoration of Gaṇeśa. ||78||
Then follows the recitation of the Svasti formula and the proclamation of the Puṇyāha and so forth;
thereafter comes the consecration (abhiṣecana) as well as the worship of the Mātṛkās.

Then he performed the Nāndī-śrāddha, as well as the formal selection of the preceptor and the twice-born priests; he offered the respectful water (arghya), paid obeisance, and presented the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
The installation of the Vardhinī pitcher, the sprinkling of the pavilion, the installation of the Vāstu deity, and the worship of the Vāstu pavilion; ||81||

The installation and worship of the Sarvatobhadra deities, as well as the installation of the deity [in the mandala], followed by the worship and the fire-ritual (agnyuttāraṇa), are performed there. ||82||

He performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍapūjā), and the installation of the fire; then he performed the installation of the house and the worship for the installation of the Yoginīs.

The worship of the altar-bench (mekhalikā) and the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) suitable for the installation of the Field-Protector (Kṣetrapāla), the full adoration of the fire, the honoring of the planets, and the consideration of the ritual fuel-piling (anvādhāna). ||84||
The Creator of the Universe performed the oblations of the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* offerings;
Mādhava performed the oblations for the Vāstu deity, the pavilion, and the gods. (85)
Then he performed the Yoginī-homa, as well as the Pradhāna-homa,
the Vyāhṛti-homa, and the offering of the bali.
Then he performed the raising of the sacrificial post (yūpa) and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana);
he also carried out the worship of the Water-Mothers (Jalamātṛs) and the ritual worship of the waters (jalapūjā). ||87||
He performed worship with conch shells, bells, and other instruments, as well as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) for Kṛṣṇa, and the sixteen-fold worship and others.
Then he performed the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna), as well as the oblations (āhutis) consisting of all the offerings for the gods,
and the great final full-oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti-homa) with streams of clarified butter.
With bilva fruits, various juices, and all kinds of milk-rice and other offerings, as well as with sandalwood, fruits, flowers, and so forth, the Supreme Lord performed [the worship]. (4.78.90)
Hari himself performed the Nīrājana and the great Rātrika ceremony;
he offered a handful of flowers and conducted the consecration of all the sacrificers.
Then Brahmā bestowed auspicious gifts and excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), consisting of abundant gold and jewels; thereafter, he granted his blessings.
The Creator of the Universe caused them to perform a circumambulation and a ritual tasting;
thereafter, their meals consisted of fruits, tubers, and roots.
The auspicious meals consisting of milk-rice and other divine offerings, as well as the food of sages, nectars, vegetables, and milks; ||94||
There, foods appeared for the embodied beings according to their needs; indeed, all people who observed vows were satisfied, each according to their respective requirements.
Then, O Śrī Badarī, the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) took place in the waters of the Indus;
that place became renowned as the great sacred ford (mahātīrtha) known as Avabhṛtha. ||96||
During the great ceremonial bath of the avabhṛtha, many great wonders occurred;
numerous divine golden celestial chariots arrived. (97)
And they were presided over by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and others;
those people who possessed pure dispositions were eligible for liberation. 98.
Then, having abandoned their own bodies, the men and women assumed divine forms,
ascended celestial chariots, and went to the imperishable abode of Hari.
Some went to Goloka, some indeed to Vaikuṇṭha;
others went to the Unmanifest, and some went to the Immortal Realm.
Some devotees went to Śrīpura, others went to Satyaloka,
and still others went to Badrīnātha, Śvetadhāma, and Kṣīradhāma.
Then, according to their purity, they went to Kailāsa and the world of Brahmā;
indeed, O Badrikā, that was a great wonder which bestows liberation. || 10 2 ||
Then those who had performed the recitation went to their respective dwellings;
meanwhile, in the city, there was the procession of the Saṃhitā, its worship, and other ceremonies.
O Badarī, thereafter there was much [of this] in all the lands;
in every house, at every crossroads, in the marketplaces, and even in the temples.
At the palace gate, in the temple, and in every courtyard, worship was performed;
and the auspicious installation of Vyāsa’s Saṃhitā took place. || 105 ||
O Badrikā, offerings of lamps, gifts, acts of worship, presents,
and food oblations arise at every step along the way.
Great musical instruments are sounded and his glories are proclaimed by young maidens, auspicious women, and virtuous ladies. (107)
Thus they are worshipped by the city-dwellers, by queens, and by the wives of householders, both at the royal gate and within the palace in Śarkarānagara. 108.
Having properly completed the establishment of the pavilion,
the bringing forth of the *Saṃhitā* was performed with a great festival.
There was a total crush of elephants, horses, celestial chariots, and other mounts, as well as the finest human vehicles, such that it resembled the heavens.
Beholding him bestows merit, and remembering him indeed bestows merit as well;
reflecting upon him bestows merit, O Badrī, while meditation upon him grants liberation. (111)
Thus, embracing this festival on earth, all the rulers of the land shall perform great sacrifices as well as the most excellent rites of giving.
From reciting or hearing this, liberation shall come; there is no doubt about this.
For those with desires, the attainment of their cherished goals will surely occur; there is no doubt.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship, Presentation of Gifts, Āratī, and Circumambulation of the Saṃhitā, Vyāsa, the Guru, the Holy Men, the Holy Women, the Twice-born, and the Great Sages, Performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, along with the Devas, Kings, Subjects, and All Embodied Beings of Creation, upon the Completion of the Recitation of the Saṃhitā on the Eleventh Day of the Bright Half of the Month of Āṣāḍha," in the Tiṣya Lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Badarīpriya said: O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! What happened after that?
Where and where did he go, and when did the arrival of the Kuṅkumāksara take place?
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, having performed his bath and worship,
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was seated upon His own elephant-throne.
Accompanied by his beloved Padmāvatī,
the sage Lomaśa shone with his own appearance, even though he was self-luminous, as if to bestow his very sight upon them at dawn.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa and others, as well as the Brahmins devoted to their wives,
shone in the assembly in the presence of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Brahmins who were truthful, virtuous, perfected, self-controlled, and stainless shone in the midst of the assembly, radiant as the sun and free from all taint.
Indeed, for the sake of beholding Śrī Hari, the lords of the creations beginning with Svāyambhuva—
Brahmā and the other Blessed Lords, as well as the deities headed by Mahendra— [assembled].
Great sages, kings, queens, groups of goddesses, merchants, and classes of subjects— all were the most excellent and highly devoted followers of the Lord.
Arriving with offerings in their hands, they worshipped the Supreme Lord;
having bowed to Vyāsa, their guru, and Lomaśa, they sat down before them.
Lomaśa offered words of thanks to the venerable Guru and all [the others],
and granted leave to those worthy and excellent ones as was appropriate for each.
It was a provider for the virtuous and the chaste, and for the great seers;
it was also a provider for those of high honor and for guests.
Likewise, he gave [offerings] to the gods, the ancestors, and the Siddhas;
and with joy, he gave to the Gandharvas, the Sūtas, the bards, and his servants.
The sage joyfully bestowed excellent gifts upon the employees;
he gave gold and other items as rewards with great delight.
The sage bestowed upon the Brahmins excellent golden gifts, diamonds, jeweled ornaments, and wealth.
The sage bestowed the means of subsistence upon the goddesses, as well as upon women and maidens, and upon the boys, the celibate students, and the female ascetics.
The sage gave to the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, who were celibate students,
a parting gift as was appropriate, which brought them complete satisfaction.
Golden necklaces, golden ornaments, golden garments, signet rings,
well-fashioned clothes, golden vessels, and even personal articles for the body.
The sage also gave him vessels of celestial design possessing the most excellent forms of beauty, as well as wish-fulfilling cintāmaṇi gems and necklaces of pearls and other jewels.
The venerable preceptor Lomaśa gave vehicles and household furnishings,
and at the conclusion, he respectfully bestowed blessings upon those who had celebrated the great festival.
Vihāya placed flower garlands around the necks of the embodied beings.
Then those kings in the assembly spoke to the sage Lomaśa.
In order to sanctify his own kingdom from his own abode with the scriptures, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and Vyāsa [revealed] the Saṃhitās. (4.79.20)
May Lomaśa, the ancestors, and other deities such as Śrī and Lakṣmī arrive as is appropriate and sanctify our grounds. (21)
May the Blessed Lords come and sanctify our kingdoms, our regions, our subjects, and our temples. (22)
Svāyambhuva Manu, King Priyavrata,
Uttānapāda, and likewise King Āgnīdhra spoke thus.
And at that time, Khaṇḍeśvara, Hiraṇyaka, and the others requested [him] to purify their own dwellings, their subjects, and their lands.
"So be it," Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, granting his word to them;
then Koṭirāya and Rāyahari gave him a great farewell.
O Badrī, like two servants, they performed the dismissal of the assembly for the king and others as was appropriate; thereafter, it was filled with shouts of victory.
There, meals were provided for hundreds of thousands of beings;
preparations were made, and from there, departures took place.
The subjects, with delighted minds, departed for their respective kingdoms and regions; likewise, the local dignitaries and the common people, dismissed by the king, also departed. (28)
Then, on that day, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, the gods and the lords departed;
and Kṛṣṇa, being entreated by the gods, went to the celestial realms and other abodes.
Hari, having resolved to depart at a later time,
released even all the lords who were likewise making their requests.
Having promised to depart at a later time, he released the lords of the quarters;
likewise, having spoken to the ancestors and those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), he dismissed them as well.
Having agreed to depart at a later time, he dismissed them;
on that very day, Hari indeed said "Om" to the kings.
On the very earth, however, that ocean of compassion, at the invitation of Lomaśa, accepted the straw mats as the dwellings for the kings.
Then, on the twelfth day, the entire assembly was indeed dismissed;
the kings alone, having prepared themselves, remained waiting.
Then Kṛṣṇa reflected with a desire for the benefit of all: "Indeed, assuming many forms simultaneously would be the proper measure for all of them. (35)
Then, having reflected thus, O Badrikā, that Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa assumed many similar forms.
The Lord, whose self is the pervasive expansion of self-luminosity, became the soul of Lomaśa;
likewise, the Lord became the soul of his father and the soul of his mother, possessing their respective forms.
The self of the powers such as Rādhā and Ramā, possessing the nature of male and female servants, assumed as many forms as there were excellent kṣatriyas. ||38||
Just as Mādhava ascended into their celestial palaces,
he assumed the forms of all of them, appearing in the likeness of every member of his own retinue.
O Badrikā, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, the aerial chariots belonging to their respective masters indeed became celestial vehicles in the sky after they had abandoned Śarkarānagara.
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Bālakṛṣṇa; obeisance to You, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa! (41)
The worlds, beginning with the deities, offered salutations and increased the offerings of flowers and unbroken grains; they rained down sandalwood paste and other substances.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, the celestial chariots departed from the region of the ocean;
first, one chariot went swiftly toward the abode of Koṭirāya. 43.
The second, however, went toward the palace of Rāyahari;
the third went to the radiant palace of Svāyambhuva.
He went to the divine fourth [world] toward the abode of Priyavrata,
and he went to the divine fifth [world], the palace of Uttānapāda.
The sixth is indeed Āgnīdhra-rājya, while the seventh is Hiraṇyaka;
the eighth is Ketumāla, and the ninth is toward Kuru.
The excellent celestial chariot went toward the tenth king of Kāśī, toward Śāvadīna, Lakṣmaṇa, and King Jummasmla. 47.
He [sent] Dakṣaja against the god Śibi, each separately;
and he sent Tharkūṭastha against King Vīrajāra, who had eyes like spears. 48.
He spoke separately to Kālimāśa, Bālakāśa, and Kathaka;
and to Pṛthurāja, Uralaketu, and the king of Uṣṭrāla.
And at the crossing of the Haṃkāra near Jayakāṣṭhalaka,
Kṛṣṇa’s vehicles proceeded separately, yet they went along together with those very [attendants].
[He sent] Alvīnara, Jīnavarddhi, and Alpaketu, each separately, against King Jayakṛṣṇa and King Parīśāna. ||51||
Indu, Āya, Mudrāṇḍa, and Gaṇḍarāja each separately; and Bṛhacchara, Līnorṇa, and Balalīna each separately. (52)
They went separately to King Varasiṃha of Rājagṛha, to King Phenatantu, to Stokahoma, and toward Kolaka. (53)
They went separately to Kāṣṭhayāna, Dinamānārka, Rāyakinnaṭa, Rāyarokīśvara, and Rāyaraṇajīva. (54)
And also Rāyavākakṣaka toward Rāyamārīśaka;
and Rāyabaleśvara separately toward Rāyalambara. (55)
[He went] toward King Rāyanavārka and toward Rāyahuṇḍeśaka;
[he went] toward King Rāyakūpeśa and toward the provincial governor Kāli. ||56||
And the excellent celestial chariots of Hari went separately toward each of them—toward King Vanajeśa and toward Pārāvārapiba. ||57||
Koṭīśvara, Śrīsatīśa, Tretākarkaśabhūpati, Āṇḍajara, Bālyaraja, and Rāyasomanaka, each separately. ||58||
The *ūrugavākṣaka*, the *parāṅvrata*, the *īśānapānaka*, and the *rājārāyapati*—these various celestial chariots also departed. (59)
To Yajña, Dharma, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ, he assigned them individually;
and to Nābhi, Kimpuruṣa, and another, Ramyaka, he likewise assigned them separately.
At Umārāya, [he visited] Kṣīrapura, Nāgavikramaṇa, Jayāditya, Vikramārka, Kṛṣṇadurga, and Pāñcala. ||61||
They went separately to Prabhālākṣa, Lakṣasena, Āmraśāla, Śrīlambhana, Prapatpāla, Prāṇipāta, and Nandibhilla.
Rāyapāra, Indragṛtsa, Gavayendra, Janāstraka, Karṇaputsa, Avadhyābha, Yāgadeva, and Paṭāsana. ||63||
To Mādhava, who is the lord of wives, who is radiant, who is the drinker of the Brahman,
who is the destroyer of [worldly] conduct, who has the luster of a ruby, and who is the golden ornament upon the heart.
Candranāga, Medakośa, Purukutsa, Bālasaṃgha, Pārvateśa, and Nāgavijayaka each went their separate ways. ||65||
Rājamāru went against Mahendrābha, Madāśana against Nṛpa, Śararaṅga against Madhurāja, and Virāmāsa against [his opponent]; thus they advanced separately. (66)
To King Trikūṭārka, who is of great essence and possesses a variegated dance,
[I offer] Kalikāñcana, who is pale-white, noble in conduct, and a source of prosperity.
[He sent] Maṇḍalāra against King Javalīna Indradyumna, and Māṭharasiṃha against King Kuṭidhara Cicintana, each separately. 68.
To King Udaṅprabha, Śrīnāgāri, Dharaṇidhra, Rajidhvaja, Mūradhvaja, and Kuṅkumāsya, he spoke individually. ||69||
O Badrikā, the celestial palaces of Hari departed separately along with them,
as well as with the regional kings and the lords of the islands dwelling on the shores of the ocean.
Accompanied by the lords of Raṇa, the kings of the mountains, and the subordinate princes, they went forth separately;
having traversed various regions, they proceeded to their respective kingdoms.
They descended upon various royal palaces, gardens, grounds, and other locations; there they caused them to drink water, eat food, and partake of nectar.
Then the rulers of the earth caused [the manuscript] to be paraded through their respective cities;
thereafter, they performed the worship of the Saṃhitā, the worship of Vyāsa, and the worship of the Guru.
Eagerly, they each occupied their own divine and most delightful palaces,
and they presented offerings of jewels, diamonds, and garlands.
Whatever was most excellent in their homes, and whatever was supreme in their kingdoms and realms, those best of kings dedicated all of it to the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They performed the nightly lamp-offering (ārārtrika) and drank the nectar of Hari’s feet;
they partook of the sacred remains (prasāda) from the hand of Śrī Svāmikṛṣṇa.
They served him exceedingly by massaging his feet and other such acts;
they propitiated the husband of Padmāvatī with devotion.
They received the great mantras from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, the embodiment of wisdom:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (78)
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times, from the fear of time, māyā, sinful karma, the enemy, Yama, and the wicked-hearted. (79)
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, svastika, and conch, I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (4.79.80)
I am a divine servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
Om! Oṃ namas śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. ||8 1||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband;
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband. (82)
May He be our father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and nourisher. We know Bālakṛṣṇa; we meditate upon Anādikṛṣṇa;
may that Lord of Śrī inspire us. (83)
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, and Śrī. Oṃ, I offer myself to the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa; Oṃ, salutations! ||84||
I am a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; Śrī Hari is my refuge.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my beloved Lord; Śrī Svāmī is my refuge. (85)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Hari, the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, is my refuge;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Vaiṣṇava teacher, the Master, and the Lord of Padmāvatī. (86)
My eternal beloved is my lord; I am his mistress and beloved.
Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is my refuge. (87)
"Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Full Moon, Nārāyaṇa, is my refuge.
Hari himself, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, gave these mantras. (88)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa!
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Rādhā-Ramāyaṇa! ||89||
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Mādhava, O Śrīnārāyaṇa, O Lord! Victory to You, O Nārāyaṇa, O all-pervading Śrīlalitānārāyaṇa!
"May the Lord and Master, who is fond of Kambharā and Gopāla, protect me!
Thus Hari himself bestowed these name-mantras. 91.
Mādhava also gave them a Tulasī necklace and a forehead mark beautified by the moon, and placed his own feet upon their chests. 92.
They seized Hari’s two auspicious feet, which were reddened by the dye, marked with seals, and beautifully adorned with all the signs of the feet. 93.
They took from the palm of his right hand a beautiful, auspicious ring marked with signs,
which was pleasing for the sake of worship and for the sake of beholding it.
They took a likeness, an image, and a portrait;
having made a painting of Hari, they guarded it in their home every day.
O Badrikā, having stayed in all the dwellings during the night of the twelfth day (dvādaśī), Mādhava then,
in the morning, partook of food with due respect for his service.
Having performed worship for all and being gratified by those who were themselves gratified,
he was surrounded on all sides by the sounds of musical instruments, songs of praise, and shouts of victory.
Having been dispatched, he ascended his own celestial chariot separately;
then all the lords offered their final prayers to the Lord. (98)
O Lord Hare, ocean of mercy, we have been purified by Your grace; likewise, at the time of our end, lead us to Your purifying imperishable syllable. 99.
Always remaining in the center in the form of your physical manifestation, protect us who have taken refuge in you;
and always reveal this divine form of yours within our hearts.
"I am yours" and "I am thine"—protect me always in this way;
thus contemplate that the delusion of Māyā neither comes nor goes. 10.111.
Thus, O Badrikā, they all made this request to the Lord:
"Whatever has come for our worship, let all of that be in the form of His grace. (102)
Overcome by compassion, Hari returned those gifts to the donors;
then, having bestowed auspicious blessings and accepted their prayers, he departed. (10.3)
Having reached this very world of Vidarbha, beholding his devotees such as the king and others,
and looking upon the subjects with love, he caused the celestial chariot to descend.
Suddenly, the black celestial chariots rose up into the sky;
indeed, those chariots, whose essence was Kṛṣṇa, vanished into the space of consciousness.
All having become one, they arrived together in a single celestial chariot at the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, near the Aśvasaras lake in Saurāṣṭra.
The Lord Vyāsadeva, the great sages beginning with Lomaśa, and others descended slowly into the field, illuminating all directions.
The parents, the maidservants, and the servants entered their respective dwellings;
thus, O Śrī Badrikā, was the great festival of this Pārāyaṇa.
That became the foremost of all festivals and indeed the supreme means of reaching the further shore;
thereafter, other excellent devotees of the Lord performed sacrifices.
Likewise, Svārociṣa, Bhūpa, Uttama, Tāmasa,
Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, and Vaivasvata were also their kings.
And these men performed festivals for the complete recitation [of the scripture],
and others as well, the most excellent of great devotees, will perform them.
O Vṛndā, this treatise on liberation yields the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma;
it bestows all that is desired and grants discourse upon the individual self and the supreme self.
Through the recitation, hearing, and contemplation of this festival of stories, the attainment of all desired goals becomes easy, and divine riches become easily obtained. (1.13)
There shall be the attainment of liberation and the fulfillment of all desires;
his intentions will quickly bear fruit like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
There is no doubt that [a man] will become like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in mind;
even a woman, by retaining these stories, will become equal to Lakṣmī. 1.15.
O Badarī, by retaining these stories here, one becomes Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
thus, that complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) triumphs exceedingly over all creation.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, assuming many forms at the request of all the kings, went to the palaces of all the monarchs and their kingdoms in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, accepted worship, purified them, and after vanishing, returned to Aśvapaṭṭasara."
Śrī Badrīpriyā said: O Śrīkānta Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the performer of all auspiciousness! What did he do after that? You ought to tell me his entire life story.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badrī; Svāmī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was invited by King Nāgavikrama to a sacrifice and went there.
Accompanied by his own wife Prabhā of Pāravatī, his beloved and contented sister, and joined by a multitude of male and female servants. || 3 ||
He went to that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in Śarkarāpura regarding that which had been promised by the lord of Yuddhapura for the sake of the sacrifice.
That sacrifice was commenced by him who is known as Nāgavikrama;
there, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went, having been invited.
Mādhava, the beloved of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Śrīśvara, caused the great sacrifice, the Sarvamedha, to be performed.
Nāgavikramarājeśa, the most excellent of great devotees,
while observing the Cāturmāsya vow, performed the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
In the city of Yuddhapura, on the bank of the river Luṇī,
upon a vast expanse of ground five yojanas in extent, he caused a pavilion to be constructed.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, having gathered the necessary materials and urged on by the officiating priests and ritualists,
the lord of the earth commenced the sacrifice.
There arrived hundreds of thousands of virtuous brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas,
as well as men and women, all devoted to the performance of dharma.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself became Brahmā;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇava king named Nāgavikrama was the sacrificer.
In that sacrifice, Gālava and other great sages served as the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
Phālāyana, who was devoted to the Sāmaveda, was the Udgātṛ priest there.
Sārāyaṇa, a knower of the meaning of the Vedas, was the Pratyudgātṛ priest; likewise, Ajāyana, who was well-versed in Vedic rites, was the Āhātṛ priest there.
Daṇḍāyana became the Pratihartṛ, devoted to all ritual actions;
and Bhālāyana, the king of sages, was the Prastotṛ in the sacrifice.
Rasāyana became the Pratiprasthātṛ in the sacrificial rite;
Dhārāyaṇa was the Hotṛ, and Alavāyana was the Pratihotṛ. || 15 ||
The Brahmins of Arbuda were reciters of prayers, the Pauṣkaras were intent on performing fire-sacrifices,
and the Yāmuneya twice-born ones were guardians of the quarters and the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas.
At that sacrifice, the Saurāṣṭrīyas were the worshippers and the twice-born were the attendants;
the Gaurjaras were the cooks and the Marujas were the servers.
The sons of Gaṅgā were the expounders of the Vedic mantras and other texts at the sacrifice;
the sons of Sindhudvīpa were the reciters, while the ancestors served as the members of the assembly.
Those from the south were there for the purpose of offering oblations, and the reciters of prayers were the great seers such as Vasiṣṭha and others, while the preceptors acted as supervisors.
At that time, all were witnesses to those deeds;
there were Vedic Brahmins of renowned names who remained impartial. (4.80.20)
Lomaśa and others, as well as Mārkaṇḍeya and others of divine vision, remained steadfast on the Himalayan mountains in the chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa. ||21||
Thus indeed, O Badrikā, the brahmins were established at the sacrifice;
there were also hundreds of thousands of virtuous people performing acts of devotion.
And the subjects, the regional rājanyas, having been invited, arrived;
at that time, hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of men were present at the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
Then there appeared streams of clarified butter, streams of curd, and streams of nectar;
likewise, there were streams of milk, streams of honey, and mountains of sugar.
