In this Sarvamedha sacrifice, O Badrī, there were mountains of sweet foods, rivers of drinks,
and embankments of edible delicacies.
In that sacrifice, there were great mountains of fruits fit for licking and sucking,
and Meru-like heaps of items suitable for giving as gifts and appropriate for oblations.
In that sacrifice, there were excellent heaps of sacrificial fuel, milk-rice, and milks,
as well as piles of grain-particles and pulses.
Mountains of garments, woolen blankets, and ornaments appeared;
there were also circles of vessels, precious jewels for women, and cows. (28)
And for those desiring bodily requisites as well as household furnishings, there were heaps of riches, including divine treasures. (29)
In that sacrifice, there were heaps of gold and silver, and vessels for the sacrificial seats, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the offerings were filled to the brim. (4.80.30)
O Badrī, they duly performed ten pressings, twelve initiations, and twelve subordinate rites (upasads). || 31 ||
O Badrikā, the sacrifice, lasting thirty-four days and concluding on the full moon of Bhādrapada,
was indeed completed with all its constituent parts in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
The auspicious sacrifices, beginning with the Bṛhaspatisava and ending with the Āptoryāma,
were performed together with all their limbs and sub-limbs, while they remained fully absorbed in Nārāyaṇa.
In the Bṛhaspatisava, there was the gift of thirty-three cows;
likewise, it occurred in the Vaiśyasava, the Viprasava, and the Somasava. || 34 ||
It was likewise so during the Pṛthisava, Gosava, and Odanasava sacrifices, as well as during the Marutstoma, the Agnistuti, and the Mahendra-stavana. || 35 ||
In the Āptoryāma sacrifice, at the Nidhana, and at the Sava, there are the Godāna rites;
likewise, there are separate consecrations and the worship of each respective deity.
The offering of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) also took place according to the ritual;
indeed, the consecration (abhiṣeka) was performed for the sacrificer.
In that sacrifice, the consecration was performed appropriately with water, clarified butter, curd, ghee, and likewise with milk.
Sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), cooked grains (caru), and other oblations were the finest materials; there were also boiled rice, parched grain flour, and auspicious stirred drinks (mantha). || 39 ||
The *rathantara* and other *soma* sacrifices, as well as the ritual terminuses (*saṃsthās*) and the oblations (*havanāni*),
were performed by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow according to their proper requirements.
The incarnations, the lords, the powers, the deities, and the gods appeared in person at Badrī, summoned by Kṛṣṇa to that sacrifice. 41.
And all those gods in the three worlds who were entitled to participate in the sacrifice—
all those deities came within range for the purpose of receiving their sacrificial offerings.
These [offerings] were also made with streams of clarified butter, unsurpassed sacrificial foods,
savory juices, sweet dishes, milk, fruits, and likewise with sacrificial fuel-sticks.
There, offerings of grains, nectar, milk, vegetables,
and tubers are constantly presented, as well as gifts of gold and cows.
Indeed, gifts of food and clothing, as well as gifts of the Dharma that provide satisfaction to the ancestors, were bestowed by the king. (45)
Virtuous men, holy beings, virtuous women, and Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas are honored, as are guests, the helpless, and the wretched—both men and women—with gifts. 46.
By the hundreds of thousands, humans and others enjoy the desired food of *gṛṣṭi*, and they drink the excellent juices that provide nourishment and satisfaction from the *gṛṣṭi*. (47)
There, the fires, acting as the fields of perception, consume [the offerings] with their own hands into their mouths;
the gracious and gentle deities partake of the supreme oblation. 48.
O Bādarī, the ancestors as well as all other deities and the like partake of the supreme prasāda offered from the hand of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 49.
"We are satisfied, we are satisfied, we are satisfied," said those whose faces were like fire.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Bhādra, the sacrifice attained completion.
At the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), Śrī Kṛṣṇa offered into the great fire all the sacrificial foods originating from the three worlds that had been brought there. 5.1.
Sighs of satisfaction arose from those gods, and cries of "No!
No! were uttered by the gods with joy during the final oblation.
The three worlds were gratified by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
the resolve of King Nāgavikrama was brought to fruition. (53)
O Badrikā, there Śrī Hari resides—the soul of the universe, the sustainer of all, the giver, the receiver, the enjoyer, the consumer, eternally satisfied, and identical with the world. ||54||
In that regard, there is no lack of satisfaction because he is himself completely fulfilled;
even King Nāgavikrama, having performed a sacrifice accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), [found no such satisfaction].
O Badrī, that most excellent of great devotees (mahābhāgavatottama) had accomplished his purpose;
he bestowed all manner of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) made of gold and silver upon the sacrifice.
He indeed gave gifts of cattle, ornaments, and daughters;
gifts of land, jewels, and the surrender of his entire wealth.
He bestowed many gifts of knowledge and gifts of the Dharma;
he gave excellent gifts of dwellings and gifts of means of livelihood. ||58||
Then the king, together with the officiating priests, performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), including the worship of the water-mothers and the propitiation of the water-deities. 59.
At the sacred site of Lūṇikā, the king performed all the prescribed rites along with the distribution of gifts, and having done so, he performed his ablutions in the water.
Together with those who possessed excessive pride regarding their fortune, they performed ritual baths and acts of charity;
and there was the queen of King Nāgavikrama, named Arkamālinī.
At the conclusion of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he joyfully bestowed gifts upon the women:
necklaces of diamonds, gems, and the like, as well as golden ornaments and garments.
With great joy, she indeed gave many beautiful garments suited for amorous dalliance, golden vessels, and numerous articles for the body's adornment.

The wives of the brahmins, the maidens, the virtuous women, the truthful ones, and her circle of female friends became joyful in heart, satisfied by the excellent fruit obtained through their gifts. (64)
Thus, O Badrikā, at that time during the avabhṛtha rite, a wondrous marvel occurred instantly; listen as I describe it to you. (65)
Then a great maṇḍala of piśācas arrived;
it fell from the sky into the midst of the water, into the depths of the waters. (66)
Suddenly, those thousands of Piśācas drank the water with great joy; and as soon as they had bathed, they became divine deities.
Adorned with golden earrings, necklaces, and other ornaments, and possessing the brilliance of the sun,
all the gods and goddesses became sixteen years of age and so forth.
With palms joined in reverence, they praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa with heartfelt devotion:
"O Kṛṣṇa, formerly we were merchants engaged in trade. (69)
Departing from the city of Yuddhapura for Śarkarāpura,
Kṛṣṇa set out with his women and children, traveling on camels and great camels as their vehicles.
While they had gone into the midst of the battle, an exceedingly unbearable storm arose, carrying a shower of sand that destroyed the midday [light]. ||7 1||
Indeed, camels, great camels, children, and women on the ground were all killed within a moment by the winds as they remained in their wombs amidst the sands. (72)
Even we who were strong, being struck by a rain of sand,
sat down beneath the sand there, completely covered by the grains.
Indeed, while we were there, we were born as grains of sand;
all of us died while still in the womb and became *piśācas* in the battle. ||74||
O Kṛṣṇa, in the border regions near the city of Yuddhapura, we have continuously been thousands in number, dwelling in the field of battle. (75)
Today, having realized the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) festival of the Sarvamedha sacrifice,
[I have attained] the nectar of the waters from the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having come here to drink and having drunk and bathed in the nectar of his feet, we have become purified and freed from our state as piśācas. (77)
"O Kṛṣṇa, by means of this bath and the acquisition of merit, we have today become endowed with the fitness of the gods; nevertheless, we still possess the nature of deities. (78)
For this reason, O Kṛṣṇa, we do not desire that which consists of return;
rather, we long in every way for the state of non-return.
The Supreme Lord, the Master himself, has now been seen here directly;
here your foot-water has been drunk and bathed in by the waters of your grace.
Therefore, taking refuge in you, we long for that supreme liberation;
grant us your grace and lead us to the eternal nirvana of Brahman. (8.1)
Having heard this, the Blessed One again took water in his hand and,
being of the nature of the offering, uttered his own mantra there.
Having formed a resolution, he cast water upon the gods; instantly, all the gods were released and possessed divine bodies. ||83||
Then all the attendants of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as the attendants of Akṣara, having become divine, bowed to Hari and repeatedly uttered "Victory! (jaya).
Having arrived in their celestial chariots, they went to the imperishable abode of Hari while hundreds of thousands of beings on the bank of the Luni river looked on. ||85||
All the piśācas, endowed with liberation, went to the imperishable abode;
then the people, overcome with wonder, stood as if paralyzed for a moment. (86)
Having thus performed the liberation [of the deceased] and bathed at the conclusion of the avabhṛtha rite, the king and others realized the majesty of Śrī Hari, who possesses a human body. ||87||
Filled with joy, all those Vaiṣṇavas—the gods, goddesses, and holy men—departed for their own abodes together with Śrī Hari. ||88||
Having obtained food, honors, and the favor of the people, the guests—those who were already meritorious—became even more distinguished by their merit. (89)
At night they found rest; the king and queen joyfully served Hari—the beloved noble husband, Bālakṛṣṇa, the excellent lord.
Then, on the first day at dawn, after massaging his feet and other services, the Lord Hari, having bathed and performed worship, remained awake.
He shone upon a divine golden throne presented by the king;
those residing in Yuddhapura arrived there to perform worship for Hari. (92)
Having placed the offerings before Śrī Hari with sandalwood and saffron, with unbroken grains of rice, flowers, garlands, ornaments, garments, and so forth; || 93 ||
They worshipped their Lord, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, with offerings beyond beginning;
those Vaiṣṇava worshippers received His blessings. ||94||
The king bestowed gifts of honor upon them all; having achieved their purpose, they returned to their own countries filled with joy. 95.
Praising the sweetness of the honey-wine, they departed filled with joy;
the citizens of Yuddhapura attended upon Kṛṣṇa in every house.
Having opened their respective dwellings, the women and men attained great joy;
many devotees of Kṛṣṇa, the Vaiṣṇavas, received the mantra.
The people of Yuddhapurī were particularly distressed;
nevertheless, at the persistent request of the queen, he stayed there for three days.
On the fourth day, Śrī Hari became ready to depart for his own abode;
meanwhile, O Badrī, the enemy's army arrived at Yuddhapura. 99.
She quickly dispatched a messenger from the one named Nandibhilla, the king of the Yamunā bank, to Nandibhilla for the sake of battle.
"Give me battle, or give me the kingdom,
or else become a tributary," thus indeed spoke the messenger, having bowed down to Nāgavikrama.
The king also, having honored the messenger, reported that matter to Kṛṣṇa;
and Kṛṣṇa, knowing the pride of Nandibhilla, ordered a battle.
O Badrikā, while the Lord remained present, reports of battle spread everywhere throughout the city of war, instilling fear in all living beings. (103)

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa completed the Sarvamedha sacrifice of King Nāgavikrama of Yuddhapattana," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; the duty of the warrior class (kṣātradharma) is indeed difficult to conquer.
Even while possessing a kingdom, deluded kings desire other realms. || 1 ||
He in whose throat the thread of craving moves about in the form of a noose, even while all objects of enjoyment are present, goes to the jaws of death. (2)
Those whose intellects are blinded by craving do not attain the happiness of prosperity;
those who are driven by passion and hatred do not desire their own welfare. (3)

Even a king who desires the enjoyments of others and covets the wealth and possessions of others is indeed called a paramour; for "paramour-ship" (jāratva) is defined as the state of being an enjoyer of another's property.
When Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the three worlds and the glorious Supreme Lord, has arrived,
those whose thirst for worldly desires is not stilled are indeed like donkeys in this world.
He who possesses knowledge yet lacks tranquility of the senses is indeed a monkey even in human form; such a beast deserves to be taken to the abode of Yama.
He by whom Kṛṣṇa has been worshipped and His image protected in the home, yet He has not been worshipped within the heart—such a person is no protector at all; he is a demon.
Long ago, at the time of the story of Badarī, King Nandibhilla took Śrī Hari by means of a celestial chariot to his own palace and worshipped Him.
That very Lord Acyuta shines here as the Guru;
indeed, at the sacrifice of Nāgavikrama, he was the preceptor of Nandibhilla.
Having heard the fame of King Nāgavikrama’s sacrifice,
Nandibhilla, unable to endure it, set out even though he knew his guru was still present.
Knowing him to be stationed in Yuddhapura, he came for the sake of battle;
know that this delusion was intended for the destruction of Nandibhilla.
He approached to fight where the illustrious Lord resided;
where the Blessed One dwells in person, victory there is certain for him alone.
Although he knew [the truth], the powerful Nandibhilla, the king of Yamunā,
approached for the sake of battle along with hosts of one hundred thousand warriors.
Out of delusion, he dispatched a messenger named Dardurarata to King Nāgavikrama, who was accompanied by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having approached and bowed down to the king, and having prostrated before Śrī Puruṣottama,
he spoke all that had been commanded by his master in words laden with pride.
"Amidst the Ganges, Yamunā, and Sindhu rivers, I am the sovereign emperor;
all others are my tributaries, and you likewise are mine."
Therefore, let Khaṇḍeśa, the tax-payer, quickly pay tribute to me;
otherwise, O King, let him give battle to me, the Nandibhilla.
Let him take the capital city of Nāndibhillī, which surpasses all other kingdoms, as the price for war; let there be no delay, for I am his tributary.
"Since I, out of compassion, have not yet remembered the end of your hand, consider this and remain here with little fame and a small kingdom. || 1.9 ||
But today, having arrived at the sacrifice, he stands upon my head;
how could a sandal remain on the head of one who is a tribute-payer? (4.81.20)
"Either by giving me Yuddhapura in battle, or else let him be my servant;
here I am, present at the boundaries of Yuddhapura. (21)
Rich with inexpressible celestial chariots and accompanied by inexpressible elephants,
he was joined by an army of countless men consisting of camels, horses, mules, and other mounts.
Let him quickly engage in a gamble for his very life, for it is now imminent before him;
or else, having obtained favor, let him rule over an excellent kingdom. (23)
"In this manner, O illustrious one, my king indeed informs you; I am his messenger and relate to you exactly what was said. (24)
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, the messenger ceased speaking and bowed;
showing great respect, he sat down and waited upon Puruṣottama.
The great army of Nandivalli, numbering one hundred thousand men, was stationed on the bank of the Lunī river, fully equipped and eager for battle. 26.
It was joined with hundreds of celestial chariots, beautified by thousands of elephants,
yoked to five thousand camels, and harnessed to ten thousand horses.
Likewise, [he gave] twenty thousand beautiful mahāśvataras, and likewise twenty thousand bulls and so forth. ||28||
Yoked to five thousand chariots and filled with all kinds of weapons and provisions, it was being led by the army commander named Mayūravāhin.
Having quickly learned of such a great army through a secret spy, the lord of Yuddhapura approached Nārāyaṇa.
Having sent the messenger far away, he indeed announced the moment of calamity;
Hari then bestowed a great blessing upon that Vijaya.
Grant me battle, grant me victory, and may you attain the supreme kingdom;
O Indra among kings, I shall remain here every day for the sake of your protection. ||32||
I am the remover of the great pride of the most arrogant, the protector of my devotees, the destroyer of those who act in opposition, and one who is affectionate toward his devotees. 33.
O Badrikā, having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at that time, King Nāgavikrama became satisfied within the lake. 34.
Having summoned a messenger, he commanded him thus: "Inform that king:
'King Nāgavikrama is indeed approaching for the sake of battle. (35)
"O King, be my benefactor today, O Nandibhilla-rāja!
Go ahead; I shall follow behind with my army, according to our strength. (36)
Thus addressed, that messenger, having bowed and quickly received his instructions,
went to Nandibhilla and spoke to him exactly as it was.
Hearing that the army was ready, Nandibhilla quickly commanded his general,
named Indravajra, to set out for battle.
O Badrikā, even the discernment of the world of the wise goes to dissolution for those who are hungry, greedy, thirsty, and full of desire. (39)
Of those most arrogant, those who are conceited, those who are envious,
those of wicked nature, those whose topknots are covered by Time (Death), and those unfortunate sinners.
The intellect of those who have met their end, as well as those of unfortunate people,
of the cursed, of the harmful, and of the angry, perishes.
Discrimination dissolves in battle, O Badrī, for those intoxicated by the madness of war;
just as the perception of those who drink liquor dissolves, so too does it dissolve for those engaged in combat. 42.
The army of Nandibhilla was entirely prepared;
his entire fourfold force awaited the sound [of the approaching host]. 43.
And at that time, indeed, many ill omens appeared within the army;
foremost among them, the banner bearing Indra’s thunderbolt fell from the back of an elephant.
The general’s helmet indeed fell from his own hand;
there were throbbings in his left limbs and the trumpeting and roaring of elephants. (45)
Then the neighing of the horses became harsh upon their ears,
and a wind blew with great force from the front, carrying clouds of dust.
A foul day appeared in the sky above his army;
the mounts began to tremble and turned away of their own accord. (47)
The warriors indeed became somewhat disheartened;
crows, owls, pigeons, hawks, and vultures began to swoop down. (48)
Jackals howl at the tips of banners, at the tops of palanquins, at the front of chariots, and at the heads of warriors;
they even cry out as their feet stumble. 49.
And from its sheath, weapons were produced again and again;
such indeed was the dream of Nandibhilla, consisting of a momentary sleep. (4.81.50)
There he saw a heap of dry wood and the wreckage of a chariot;
the king drank the breast-milk of a courtesan, which was like an untimely explosion from a machine.
There he heard that [the king] had eaten the leftovers while asleep, had thrown himself into a multitude of enemies, and had been cast down into a flood of water. (52)
And in the midst of that, he indeed beheld a forest fire burning his own self,
as well as the mutual combat of his own army against itself.
He beheld his own naked form, as well as his approaching toward the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and the wearing of leather sandals upon his head.
Nandibhillaka saw him embraced by a woman in red garments,
who was pressing against his chest and even striking him with her foot.
Having shaken off his own corpse in the cremation ground after midnight,
the king went there to a great, dilapidated mansion, temple, and other such structures.
He beheld it broken and fallen, inspiring terror;
moreover, a hundred crows alighted upon the head of the king. (57)
The cane fell from the hand of the cane-bearer;
the leader himself fell in the dream due to the fault of tripping at his feet. (58)
Furthermore, she saw in her dream that the paths around were blocked by enemies, and the queen was wailing piteously. (59)
The goddess was named Dilāvarī, after whose name the city came to be known as the city of Dilāvarī,
situated on the bank of the Yamunā.
Indeed, there was a supreme assembly hall there named Nandibhillī,
constructed from gold, crystal, lapis lazuli, diamonds, and other precious materials.
The king indeed beheld that city, which was like a heap of stones,
falling as if it were an army retreating toward the western direction.
The king observed that the queen was in a state of widowhood,
and he beheld the shaving of the queen's own hair upon her head.
The cemetery was seen, and the terrifying messengers of Yama appeared;
seizing even the queen's hair, those powerful ones performed the act of twisting it.
In a dream, the king’s beloved beheld herself overwhelmed by men of black complexion, overcome with suffering, and humiliated. (65)
The queen likewise gazed upon the beautiful maidens who were being threatened and insulted by female slaves and groups of male servants. (66)
Then, indeed, deprived of luster, with soiled faces and overcome by grief,
they abandoned the palace and set out toward the forest.
O Badrikā, upon seeing everything that was unfavorable regarding himself in a mere moment, the king indeed understood it; nevertheless, he did not turn back.
The queen indeed performed the worship of Śaṅkara for the sake of overcoming obstacles;
from Bāṇa, that queen heard: "Your king has been deprived of his fortune."
Do not grieve, O auspicious lady; where Hari himself is present, there is victory.
This king has committed an offense; he shall surely reap the fruit of it swiftly.
Since the Blessed One himself resides there, the king went there to fight; yet, struck down by his own faults and blinded by pride, he did not see at all. (7.1)
Having spoken thus to Dilāvarī at the linga, Śaṅkara ceased;
and at that very moment, Dilāvarī fell into a swoon.
O Badrikā, at that time, the sick woman became utterly hopeless regarding the very earth of King Nāgavikrama.
Omens occurred on all sides that bestowed victory everywhere;
Brahmins arrived, intent on pronouncing blessings and adorned with *tilaka* marks. (74)
The fire moved clockwise, becoming serene and free from smoke;
indeed, a white celestial bull was seen accompanied by cows.
Likewise, maidens rich in gold and jewels, wearing ornaments and fine garments, were seen with cheerful faces [gazing upon] King Nāgavikrama. (76)
Cuckoos, cranes, swans, parrots, and Garuḍas—these birds come into the sky and then depart toward the south, bestowing victory. (77)
A dancing girl, richly adorned with jewel ornaments, was seen by nature to be carrying a golden pitcher. 78.
Divine Vaiṣṇava sages, endowed with topknots and sacred threads, adorned with the *bindu* and *tilaka*, were seen facing toward him as well. (79)
There, the sound of bells arose, awakening the offerings for the gods;
at that time, tremors indeed occurred in the right limbs of the king.
In a momentary dream, he saw himself in a celestial chariot worshipped by the gods;
then, in another moment, he saw himself seated upon an elephant with a golden female elephant beside him.
He saw him on an excellent couch, worshipped by a divine maiden with a lotus garland and attended by many maidens.
It was nurtured by the ancestors with satisfied hearts and serene countenances,
and its abode was made resplendent with great festivals and magnificent ornaments.
He saw himself seated upon a divine throne, surrounded [by his attendants],
and satiated by a meal of milk served upon a lotus leaf.
Remaining in the water, he experienced long-lasting satisfaction in an instant's dream;
thus indeed did the omens of the king arise for victory. 85.
In a dream, that queen had a vision like that of Mahendrāṇī;
during the festival of a great sacrifice, she saw herself as a universal monarch's consort.
Embraced upon his chest by Lakṣmī, the goddess Śrī, who holds a noose and radiates splendor,
she was held fast, adorned with divine lotus necklaces, and joined to his heart.
And she saw her standing in the sky with her husband in a celestial chariot drawn by elephants as white as the moon, while she herself remained there.
Indeed, auspicious omens appeared for the soldiers and warriors as well;
for the king, who possessed the prowess of an elephant, these signs were truly granters of victory.
At that moment, Nandakūbara’s commander struck the right limbs of all the armies on every side.
Then, for the purpose of raising a battle cry within the army, the kettle-drum was indeed struck by him personally;
and at that time, a favorable wind blew from behind.
The army, full of enthusiasm, was indeed like the prowess of a serpent;
all twenty thousand were mobilized in an instant for the sake of battle. (92)
Having secured Yuddhapura, which resembled a great crescent moon, everything was brought together in an instant on the bank of the river Lunī. ||92||
Then, O Bādrī, Queen Arkamālinī, who possessed the prowess of a serpent and was full of splendor, arrived swiftly for the purpose of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 94.
Having worshipped the Supreme Soul, he engaged in a discussion regarding the war—
both its fearful and fearless aspects— in the presence of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Svāminārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa! O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Ramāyaṇa! ||96||
O Lord of Gods, I am your devotee; I do not desire anything illusory.
But, O Kṛṣṇa, for a woman, what is desired is a virtuous state of non-widowhood. (97)
"May it be as you wish for me, like [the granting of] radiance; protect that which is desired by me.
This entire kingdom is indeed yours; I am truly protected and entrusted to you. (98)
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa, do as you wish now that this fear of enemies has arrived," having said this, O Badrī, she fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa. 99.
Kṛṣṇa quickly granted him the gift known as "fearlessness," revealing his own form to Mahākāla, who was terrifying.
He was swiftly devouring all the enemy armies,
while simultaneously bringing to life and protecting his own troops.
Then he showed him the gentle form of Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari;
the Lord in his own gentle form, the bestower of sovereignty.
Having placed her own husband, the smiling Lord of Pārvatī, upon her lap,
she then vanished her own excellent human form.
Hari showed it to her, and she became satisfied;
O Badrikā, Śrī Hari then quickly became eager for battle.
Having prepared himself and mounted his chariot drawn by white horses,
he who was conversant with all weapons and missiles took his position at the front of the battle.
King Nāgavikrama also, standing at the front of the battle in the midst of his chariot,
equipped with all weapons, offered himself to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of King Nandibhilla’s Army from the City of Dilāvarī to Conquer Nāgavikrama, the Departure of Nāgavikrama with His Army for Battle, and the Occurrence of Omens, Ill Omens, Dreams, and so forth," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Badarīpriya said: O Lord, tell me, how many horses, elephants, and other troops did the army of Nāga-vikrama have, and what was the nature of the battle between him and Kṛṣṇa? (1)
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; there were twenty thousand human warriors in the army of Nāgavikrama.
There were a thousand elephants, five thousand horses,
three thousand camels, and twenty celestial chariots.
Likewise, five thousand mules were present in the battle;
all of them were empowered by Kṛṣṇa’s majesty and possessed strength granted by Kṛṣṇa. || 4 ||
The mighty warriors, who were all great chariot-fighters, then became possessed by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and thus acquired bodies as hard as adamant. They became directly visible there to both armies.
The eternal chariot of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Suddenly seeing Nandibhilla at the forefront of the battle, his preceptor,
the sage Agnirāta, although skilled in all weapons and missiles, [was overcome].
Having hesitated regarding victory, he spoke these beneficial words to his disciple:
"O Nandibhilla, behold Kṛṣṇa, who consists of the entire creation."
Janārdana stands before the opposing army, desiring to fight—
he by whose mere resolve the entire universe is born and into whom it also dissolves.
This very Kṛṣṇa, bearing weapons, stands at the head of the army;
by his side stands Jaya, and Vijaya likewise stands there.
Do not indeed exert yourself in vain with the desire for victory;
no one shall conquer Nārāyaṇa, nor will anyone defeat him.
O King, why do you cast away your vast kingdom into the ashes? Enjoy the pleasures, casting aside all envy toward that lord of battle.
Indeed, you sit ten times superior and more excellent than the king of the nagas;
for the downfall of the great occurs when they are provoked by the lowly.
Upon the victory of a base person, fame arises swiftly in a hundred ways;
yet upon the victory of the great, that very same fame remains exactly as it was.
There is no loss of one's own nature nor of one's authority in defeat; having reflected thus, abandon the battle and enjoy your own land. (15)
"Victory does not shine before me today because of these ill omens of yours;
do as I say, O Indra among kings, and do not offer the subjects as oblations into the fire."
Do not sacrifice your happiness, kingdom, and prosperity into the fire,
for while the word of a guru is indeed a giver of bliss, transgressing it brings calamity.
Come, approach, and bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with a spirit of devotion;
having received his auspicious blessings, become fulfilled and happy. 18.
One should not abandon pride in the presence of a guru, nor especially in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
when faced with the destruction of everything, one should sacrifice something in order to preserve the rest.
If you two disciples were both equally humble toward him, then the compassionate Lord Kṛṣṇa would have brought about the welfare of both. (4.82.20)
Pride should be guarded when facing one's equals, but never when facing those who are superior;
even there, pride must not be maintained at all when in the presence of gurus or deities. (21)
For Mādhava is indeed the teacher and preceptor of all former ones, each preceding one;
therefore, one's own body should be offered before the Guru with mind, speech, and action. (22)
Indeed, everything must be offered before the Guru for the sake of attaining all perfections;
the mother is the Guru, the father is the Guru, the elder is the Guru, and the one who bestows knowledge is the Guru. (23)
The Guru is the benefactor and the giver of benefit; the Guru is the destroyer of delusion.
The Guru is the knower of the three periods of time, and the Guru is also considered the one who administers discipline.
All teachers are gurus and protectors in this world and the next;
the words of gurus who are deeply learned should be regarded as divine.
One who desires their own welfare must indeed perform the worship of the Guru at the three junctions of the day;
for he who is the Guru is declared to be Hari, and he who is Hari is considered to be the Guru. (26)
As is Hari, so is Śarva; as is Śarva, so is the Guru.
For the knowledge of Hara is the knowledge of Hari, and the knowledge of the Guru indeed bestows liberation.
Since the Guru consists of all the gods and consists of all powers—whether possessing attributes or devoid of them—one should always uphold his command. (28)
But he who seeks the highest good shall not transgress the teacher’s command even in his mind—whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, singing, or whatever else he may be doing. (29)
Whether in the presence of others or in private, he may obtain the perfections of the self;
yet, in the presence of the Guru or the Deity, he should not sit as he pleases.
Since the Guru is the Lord himself in person, his home is a temple of the Divine;
by serving the Guru with devotion, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of that dharma. (3.1)
Just as gold sheds its impurity through contact with fire, even so does a servant cast off his sin through association with a guru. 32.
Just as a pot of ghee melts when placed near a fire, so too does sin melt in the presence of the Guru and the Divine. 33.
Just as a blazing fire completely consumes refuse and the like,
so too does a teacher, when properly served, utterly burn away all evil.
Brahmā, Hari, Śambhu, the gods, goddesses, and great sages bestow their grace when satisfied; for when the Guru is pleased, they are the givers of happiness. (35)
One should not provoke the anger of the guru through action, mind, or speech;
for by his anger, one's merit, lifespan, knowledge, fortune, and ritual efficacy are consumed. (36)
For those who act with anger toward their guru, sacrifices performed indeed become fruitless;
all riches become fruitless, and the observances and restraints become fruitless. (37)
One should never speak words that oppose the guru;
if one should speak them due to the influence of foolishness, he will certainly go to the Raurava hell. (38)
One should not cause falsehood to be committed toward the Guru, whether in his absence or in his presence, by means of the heart, the mind, wealth, speech, body, or action. (39)
If one is established in vice, a hundredth part of that person's wickedness shall belong to him;
if one is established in virtue, a full share of all that person's goodness shall belong to him. ||4.82.40||
One should always do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru, whether commanded or not;
one should perform service for the guru both in his presence and in his absence. (41)
One should do what is beneficial and pleasing to the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
O King, even if one is falling downward, by doing what is beneficial, one prospers.
O King, that very Guru Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, whom you honored and saluted in your own abode, has now encountered you in this battle.
"O King, I am your preceptor, a Brahmin who has always been your royal preceptor;
considering my words to be auspicious, desist from the field of battle. (44)
Do not contemplate widowhood for Queen Dilāvarī, nor for the city; do not contemplate the loss of sovereignty for the assembly of Nandibhillī. (45)
Do not give way to anger, O Indra among kings; I speak the truth to you:
do not let a kingdom that rests in your own hands fall into the hands of another.
Do not bring about the destruction of heroes by means of those who are more heroic;
one must fight with illusion against illusion, and likewise with a master of illusion.
Nevertheless, one must not fight with Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, in whom everything exists, from whom everything arises, and who shines as the soul of all. 48.
How could one fight in battle against him whom everyone serves for the sake of prosperity?
He who is to be served for the sake of victory must be propitiated for the sake of liberation. (49)

He who inspires clarity, who is to be known for the sake of the goal, who should be praised for the sake of tranquility—he is to be attained by going for refuge; how could a wise man fight against him? (4.82.50)
O King, the earth laughs at you with the froth of the Yamunā's waters as her smiles,
and with the weapons born from her armies as her hands, while the crops and flowers serve as her laughter.
That King Nandibhilla, by means of the sound and foam arising from the flow of the Lūnī river and by his cranes and other birds, invites Death himself.
"O King, I have explained at the proper time the efficacy of the medicine as it truly is. You are independent in your own affairs; act as you see fit. (53)
Having spoken thus to Nandibhillaka, the preceptor Agnīrāta Ṛṣi repeatedly uttered the blessing, "O Badarī, may there be well-being! May there be well-being! (54).
Then, having bowed to his preceptor, Nandibhilla gave his reply,
with his hair held fast by Mahākāla, the personification of death.
"I understand all that has been spoken by you, O Guru;
all of it resides in the state of a virtuous man, yet it is not appropriate for the discourse on kingship. (56)
Whether it be a guru, a father, a brother, a friend, or even a son—
if he has encountered one in battle, he must indeed be fought by the king.
Ascetics and holy men find satisfaction in even a little, as do yogins;
if kings were to find satisfaction with the whole earth, what would remain for the duty of a king? (58)
Jaya and Vijaya— these two servants of power and strength—
are not considered by me to be exclusively attendants at Kṛṣṇa’s side, for they are indeed all-pervading.
Nārāyaṇa is always invincible to all who merely seek liberation;
yet those devotees who seek their own true self conquer Nārāyaṇa again and again.
Agni is Nārāyaṇa himself; even an oblation offered into him bestows liberation.
Yet, for me to engage in combat with the lowly one by means of the great Nārāyaṇa—[this is a contradiction]. (61)
Either my fame shall be great, or I shall attain liberation;
for me, there is no loss whatsoever in being struck by the hand of Kṛṣṇa.
Those seeking liberation offer their happiness, kingdom, and wealth into the fire;
I offer all that into Kṛṣṇa, O Guru, for otherwise my oblation would be in vain.
In this world, the word of the guru is beneficial and leads to a long life;
even in silence, there is victory, O Kṛṣṇa, and residence in the eternal state.
Even upon the destruction of this earthly body, I shall surely attain the eternal gain.
But I have resolved, O Kṛṣṇa, to offer everything with my whole being.
"Success in this world and the next shall be mine through union with Kṛṣṇa;
I shall worship the Lord Hari on the field of battle by means of the duties of a king. (66)
Indeed, that [service] is far better than the black hand of Death;
falling at his feet, I shall perform service to my Guru that is worthy of battle. (67)
Or else, I shall offer weapons, flowers, and consecrated rice upon the head of Hari;
or I shall cast off my impurity quickly and completely through contact with the fire of Hari’s weapons.
If Kṛṣṇa should be pleased by the falling of weapons upon me, then my ancestors would be pleased, as well as the gods and the great sages. (60)
No fault of anger exists in my preceptor Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa;
whether in his absence or in his presence, I shall act according to the duty of a king.
O Guru, since the Lord Hari himself has come to behold me in battle because he is pleased with me, how great indeed must my fortune be! (71)
Even a foolish disciple certainly crosses over in the presence of a guru; there is no doubt about this.
Whether behind his back or in his presence, one should never practice deceitful conduct toward a Kṣatriya.
O brahmin-sage, if I were to go according to the duty of a warrior, my wife Dilāvarī would surely become destitute and unprotected; therefore, dharma would be destroyed. (73)
I wage a battle for the Dharma, with my teacher as the enemy in that conflict; when he comes with his arrows aimed, then that teacher is worthy of worship. (74)
He is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Maheśa; he is Mahāviṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa; he is Yama, Kāla, and Mahākāla; he is the Purāṇa-Puruṣottama. ||75||
Whoever may encounter him, he is indeed worthy of worship with arrows;
for victory belongs to one established in dharma, and never to one established in adharma.
War is the supreme duty of kings; those who stand in battle are within the sphere of slaughter.
These are indeed the duties of the warrior class (*kṣatriya*), and at that time, they were not [violations of] their primary duties.

They possess neither the nature of those worthy of worship, nor the nature of disciples, nor the nature of friends; they possess neither the nature of sons, nor even the nature of family members. (78)
They are neither those who possess their own duty nor those who possess the duty of another;
one must indeed fight alongside them, for that is the eternal duty of a warrior. (79)
If, in battle, I should suffer defeat at the hand of Kṛṣṇa,
that victory would not truly belong to him, nor to the prowess of the Nāga.
If he were to conquer me by abandoning Kṛṣṇa, then I would consider that to be his prowess;
but with Kṛṣṇa joined to him, O Teacher, the entire world appears powerful to me. (8.1)
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer; he is Meru and the Earth;
he is the conqueror, the victor, and the one who brings others to subjection. ||82||
He is the creator, the nourisher, the one who provides sustenance, the protector, and the savior;
having obtained him—who is the refuge, full of compassion, and ever-present before one—[one is saved]. (83)
"Whether in this world or in the next, I shall obtain victory that is not difficult to win;
for when two tasks are encountered, the weaker one is sublated. (84)
The word of the guru is indeed weak compared to the attainment of Kṛṣṇa, which is endowed with power;
upon the attainment of Kṛṣṇa, even the ultimate human goals cease to exist.
One should abandon the village for the sake of the family; one should abandon the family for the sake of oneself;
one should even abandon oneself for the sake of the Guru; and for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, one should abandon everything. ||86||
The Blessed One knows me, and he knows the prowess of the Naga;
the Naga’s stride is full of desire, yet for me there is no desire except for Hari.
In the course of the battle, Hari will lead the disinterested to liberation;
having established the interested in hell in this world, he shall depart.
Just as a Brahmin is a guru, so too is Dharma a true guru;
Dharma always declares that for a Kshatriya, there is battle and no fleeing.
If a person were to have five feet because of having undertaken some action, he would surely become an object of ridicule; indeed, he alone is the destroyer of dharma.
Having deliberated, those undertakings which ought to be commenced must indeed be carried to completion;
whether their fruit be successful or fruitless, it is brought about by the union of human effort and destiny.
Therefore, having offered salutations and holding Hari within the sky of my heart, I shall fight;
O true Guru, I desire your power of yoga there, like a fire that has been kindled.
Having spoken thus, he immediately blew his conch shell for the sake of battle;
at that moment, the war-drums were sounded separately and swiftly.
On all sides, drums, kettledrums, and horns resounded;
the roars of warriors were like voices from the sky, foretelling the coming battle. (94)
Even in the path of the clouds, there arose the thundering of celestial chariots, as well as the trumpeting of elephants for the sake of battle and victory. (95)
In that battle, there arose on all sides the neighing of horses, the trumpeting of bulls, and the braying of camels. (96)
Mahākāla, as well as Rudra, Yama, Viśveśvara, and Hara;
the deities there in the sky, and the great sages who are his attendants. ||97||
Knowing that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was occupied, they arrived;
[they brought] his own Sudarśana discus and the bow that destroys the world. 98.
The Blessed One quickly took up the arrow called Grasana;
indeed, possessing the prowess of a serpent, he held all the weapons.
Nandikubara, the commander of the army, stood at the front mounted upon his chariot;
likewise did Nandibhilla and Senāpindravraja.
Placing their respective chariots in front, they stood with their bows strung, while the armies waited for the signal to discharge their weapons. || 10.1 ||
O Badrī, thus there occurred the preparation for battle at that place, as the great, great sound of conchs arose from each of their respective armies, O Acyuta.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Sounds of the Armies of Both Sides," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, wherein Nandibhilla, considering the instruction of his preceptor Agnirātta— that one must not fight with Kṛṣṇa— to be favorable to his own purpose in battle, sounded his conch shell as a signal for the moment of combat.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O beloved of Badarī, Rudra, Kāla, and Mṛtyu, desiring to serve Śrī Kṛṣṇa, arrived there and offered their salutations.
Suddenly terrified and trembling, they spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, desiring to obtain His favor and wishing to receive the command for service. || 2 ||
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, ocean of mercy, we are indeed Your servants here;
employ us under Your command so that we may quickly achieve perfection.
Having heard this, Hari said to them: "I shall indeed perform the task;
let Mahākāla now enter into me for battle with the prowess of a serpent."
May Rudra enter Nandakubera, and may Maheśvara enter Viśa; may Death enter the arrows, and may the attendants of Death enter the weapons.
May all the imperishable powers quickly enter the armies;
let there be protection in every way for the elephants, the warriors, and the wings of the host.
May the fruit of Nandibhilla’s pride fall upon those who side with him;
for a person reaps what they have done, whether it be war or sacrifice.
For this hunter Nandi fights while consumed by the fault of envy;
therefore, he has committed an offense against the king who possesses the prowess of an elephant.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One blew his conch shell that incites battle;
Indra also blew his own conch shell that incites battle.
Nandakubara blew his own conch, which signaled the commencement of battle;
and then the sounds of kettledrums from the armies rent the sky.
Then, O Badrī, those who incited the battle became terrifying;
their shouts, bestowing valor and strength, were then like the roar of clouds.
Along with the resounding roars, there occurred a mutual showering of arrows between the two armies of Nandakubra and Indravajra.
O Bādrī, in a mere instant, the sky was completely covered by a rain of arrows,
and the entire army was likewise shrouded.
Arrows were seen lodged in the bodies of the warriors,
like the thousand-rayed suns adhering to the forms of the sun.
The bodies of warriors struck by arrows appear like *kiṃśuka* trees;
their limbs are mangled by crescent-headed shafts with sharp points and broad blades. (15)
The pretas are seen divided into two types, appearing as if deformed;
they leap up again and again upon the surface of the earth with a thumping sound.
With their throats severed and their heads cut off, corpses cast forth arrows;
and there in the battle, Rāhus are seen on all sides.
O Bādrī, there Nandibhilla then quickly struck that one of elephant-like prowess with hundreds of sharp-edged arrows.
The elephant also swiftly struck Nandin on all sides with five hundred feathered arrows; that was a great marvel.
Nandī, having severed those arrows, released a thousand of his own arrows with great speed in a mere moment upon the body of the serpent.
The Naga, too, having cut those [arrows] with crescent-headed shafts with extreme agility,
released arrows resembling crescent moons at Nandinī in the battle.
He shattered Nandin’s crown, his bowstring, and even his bow;
Nandin then suddenly seized another, much larger bow.
Then he discharged many arrows capable of taking the life of an elephant;
the elephant, having cut down all of them, struck him back with broad-headed shafts.
With various locks of hair and arrows whose tips and points were shattered,
his bow was lost, then lost again, and likewise the third and the fourth.
Then Nandi seized a great spear, adorned with a hundred bells,
divine, long, possessing great velocity, with a fine point, and filled with poison.
Having pressed down upon the earth with his feet, he released it with great force;
yet even as he did so, she fell into the midst of the chest of the serpent.
Seizing her with his very hand, the Naga lifted her up;
having torn her asunder, he cast her upon the earth and roared.
Beholding this, Nandin became greatly enraged; he seized another, most brilliant spear and suddenly hurled it, which was capable of destroying the neck of the serpent.
But as that spear was falling toward him, the Naga, displaying his agility, swiftly struck it with his own spear; it split in two and fell to the ground. (29)
Just as Nandin was about to seize the third spear,
the powerful king of the Nagas suddenly hurled that spear at Nandin’s chest.
Nandin fell into a swoon, while he, possessing the prowess of a serpent, roared;
the charioteer suddenly carried him, along with Nandin and his chariot, a great distance away.
Then others, the lords of Nandisenā, struck Kṛṣṇa’s chariot excessively with arrows, bhallas, and kunta spears.
With crescent moons, spheres, missiles, and millions of arrows,
that great power stood surrounding the chariot.
She seized all the arrows and various weapons as well;
having repeatedly placed them in her mouth, she swallowed them and even destroyed them. (34)
Hari, however, by means of his own life-force, very swiftly and in every way pierced those millions of arrows that were intended to destroy the elephant armies. (35)
He indeed protects his devotees; the army of the Nāgas is not slain, while the armies of Nandin are destroyed—truly, that was a great marvel.
Then the king, having regained consciousness, arrived at the field of battle on his chariot,
fully equipped with weapons, atop the chariot of Nārāyaṇa.
He hurled sharp weapons, discharged multitudes of arrows,
cast spears in many ways, and indeed released iron shafts.
Hari, having cut through all [the other arrows], then swiftly released a single shaft—one that was impenetrable, undecaying, irreversible, and firm. ||39||
That arrow, having struck Nandin in the chest, fell to the ground;
the charioteer quickly raised him up, placed him in the chariot, and went outside.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose for a moment among the army dispatched by Nandi.
Then Indravajra, the commander of the forces, [attacked] Hari and the elephant Kūbara.
He struck them all with hundreds upon hundreds of sharp-edged arrows;
Hari, however, by the dexterity of his hands, cut down all those shafts.
With his own arrows, Kubera provided protection for his entire army on all sides;
moreover, with ten arrows, he struck Indra’s thunderbolt.
Indra, however, struck Kubara with a hundred arrows;
and Kubara, in turn, struck Vajraka with a hundred arrows.
Indravajra swiftly hurled a life-taking spear;
it fell with great speed and struck Nandakubra in the chest.
As soon as she was touched, held, and quickly bent down by Kubera’s hand, another [woman] arrived there in an instant. (46)
Having seized her as well, the powerful Kubara dragged her along with great force; at that moment, a third spear, most terrifying, arrived.
Rudra, mounted upon his bull, swallowed the spear and likewise digested it;
seeing this great marvel, Indra was indeed struck with fear.
He released that supreme, divine mace, which resembled a great pillar,
was as firm as a mountain peak, and was adorned with a golden band.
Having swiftly arrived through the sky, he fell upon the chariot like a mountain peak;
the chariot of Nandakuvera was crushed and fell to the earth.
Kubara, standing in the middle of the chariot and well-protected by the protection of Rudra,
went forth with his limbs unbroken, like one who has fallen from a palace.
Meanwhile, King Nandibhilla stood firm in the battle before him;
to quickly destroy the elephant, he swiftly released serpent-nooses.
There, Hari indeed dispatched the Garuḍas as devourers;
all the serpents were devoured there by the Garuḍas in an instant. 53.
There, Nandī released the Vidyucchara weapon with the prowess of a serpent;
the serpent released the Tāmra weapon, and thereupon the lightning was extinguished.
Nandī released the fire-weapon (*vahnyastra*), which struck terror into the entire army;
the elephant destroyed those fiery arrows with his own cloud-weapons (*meghāstra*).
Enraged, Nandī released the Brahmā weapon, which cannot be turned back;
Hari suddenly seized that missile with his own Brahmā weapon.
Then Nandī discharged the formidable Pāśupata weapon,
and Mahākāla, mounted upon his serpent, devoured that Pāśupata missile.
Then Nandin discharged the great fiery weapon of withdrawal;
Mahārudra, stationed on Kūbara, brought forth that weapon of withdrawal.
Then Kubara, having raised up the mountain-like Śakti weighing a hundred bhāras and having pressed down upon the earth, hurled it at Vajraka.
O Badrikā, the earth trembled and sank for a moment;
then Indra’s thunderbolt quickly reached and entered her heart.
As Indra’s thunderbolt fell upon the earth, Kūbara released his own vajra;
at that very moment, the great serpent severed that vajra with his own mighty vajras.
Indravajra fell down with his chest shattered and died;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Bhilla army, O Badrikā.
The shouts of victory from Kuvara were heard on all sides;
then, the leader of the Bhilla army named Ghātavajra quickly [advanced]. (6.3)
Standing upon his chariot, he advanced swiftly and with great pride onto the field of battle;
then, a great clamor arose from all sides among the Bhilla army.
Ghātavajra also fought with Nandakuvaraka;
he released ten arrows along with their nocks through a single string.
Kubara, the son of Nanda, swiftly cut down those ten who had approached;
Kubara then released twenty arrows.
Then, having effortlessly and swiftly cut down all those [arrows] with his "thunderbolt-slayer" (ghātavajra),
Kubara released thirty others, which he too cut down.
Kubara released long, broad-headed arrows at Ghātavajra;
Ghātavajra shattered all those broad-headed arrows with his mace-strikes.
He hurled his mace, with all its inherent power, at Kubera;
Kubera swiftly crushed that mace down with his own mace. (69)
He quickly discharged arrows and severed both the bowstring and the bow;
with moon-faced shafts, he cut off his left hand at the forearm.
With one hand brandishing a striking vajra and grasping a sword, he leaped up;
descending from his chariot, filled with rage, he rushed toward Kubara.
But Kubara, seeing him approaching violently with his sword drawn,
warded him off with arrows that flew with great speed.
Nevertheless, though burning with rage, he did not turn back from his running;
then Śrīkubera, swiftly taking up a sword from his chariot, [leaped forth]. (73)
Having descended, he gave battle with a sword brilliant in its whirling;
then the gods in the sky watched the combat between the two generals.
For a moment, those warriors skilled in the art of life-and-death combat remained steady;
then Kubara, with his own sword, split his opponent’s sword in two.
Having quickly fashioned it, he gave a second sword to the warrior;
he too, having seized it, [fought] with various kinds of maneuvers.
He fought there in many ways, displaying various circular maneuvers;
then, in an instant, with his sword, he struck Kūbara on the head. (77)
Just as he struck with his thunderbolt-like blow, Kubera leaped up and dealt a blow with his sword to his [the opponent's] throat, shoulders, chest, and belly. (78)
With a single blow, he brought down both thighs at the hips;
splitting into two, the thunderbolt-like strike fell in the presence of the army.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on all sides within the army of Nandi-bhilla, as it was assailed by the host of Naga-vikrama, who was accompanied by the Śakti-gaṇas.
O Badrī, ten thousand warriors were slain;
such was the slaughter of Nandibhilla’s armies. ||8 1||
Then the third commander indeed arrived, named Haridvajra;
he was a hero wearing golden armor, robust, and youthful, resembling a mountain peak.
Standing on his chariot, he quickly released bhalla arrows toward Kubara;
however, Hara Rudra, standing upon Kubara, swallowed all those bhalla arrows. ||83||
Then Haridvajra quickly released a lethal spear;
however, Hara, stationed on Kūbara, swallowed it entirely and digested it.
Then Haridvaja quickly released the consecrated lion-weapon;
suddenly, thousands of lions appeared in the battle.
In the sky, on the ground, in the armies, in the chariots, and even among the mounts—in a mere instant, armies of lions appeared everywhere. (86)
Mahārudra, stationed on the peak, then commanded his own consort Satī to manifest herself in the form of the entire army. 87.
She quickly became the beautiful Śivā, consisting of an army, bearing all weapons, and manifesting in the form of a woman who embodies all things. ||88||
Seeing that virtuous mother, the lions who were her mounts quickly fell at her feet; then, a great wonder occurred.
The tigers were dissolved by the goddess’s great weapon of yoga;
seeing this, Indra released the weapon of delusion (mohanāstra).
Standing in the midst of the battle, Bālakṛṣṇa swallowed the deluding weapon (mohanāstra);
then, becoming afraid, the yellow-hued one released the poison-weapon (viṣāstra).
With a single arrow, he completely filled the expanse of the sky with poison upon poison;
everything became composed of poisonous air, spreading forth and destroying the eyes. 92.
Then Rudra, stationed at Kubara, who was obstructing the vital breaths and causing death and destruction, removed the poison through yoga.
Indeed, the entire army of Kubara became as if free from poison;
then the illustrious Kubara, seizing his spear, hurled it at Nāśika.
Haridvaja, having shattered that [weapon], released a supreme spear;
Kubara, too, having shattered it, hurled a heavy mace.
Harihaya, seizing his mace, hurled it at Kubera;
Kubera, having become that [mace] in turn, cast it back with great velocity. (96)
He then hurled at her a second spear, and he hurled a third;
that [third] became stuck in the middle of her throat.
Having drawn out the life-breaths, that most terrible [weapon] struck the earth after piercing the chariot;
Haridvajra, along with his chariot, was shattered and died right there.
Cries of "Alas! Alas! arose on all sides from the army of Nandibhilla;
even those skilled in battle fled in fear, with their feet turned backward.
Then, O Badrikā, shouts of victory accompanied by musical instruments arose in the army of Kubara due to the majesty of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (4.83.10)
Nandibhilla once again sounded the war-drum to encourage his retreating troops and to incite them to battle. || 101 ||
Ten thousand warriors of Haridvaja were indeed slain in battle by Śaktinivāsin, who possessed an army with the prowess of serpents.
Another seventy thousand, having reached a mutual agreement,
completely surrounded and pervaded the formation like the horns of a scorpion.
Having resolved to slay all the warriors of Kubara, they, accompanied by the Bhilla army, rushed toward every direction. (04)
O Badrī, all the directions around became terrifying;
then Rudra, stationed at Kūbara, [assailed] his own diseases as well as his attendants.
He caused them to be stationed all around his own army in embodied form;
they possessed unimpeded bodies and were free from the wounds of weapons.
Like difficult mountain passes, they spread across the human army and waged war;
O Badrikā, ten thousand were slain there by their arrows.
The warriors of Nandibhilla, with the exception of Śeṣaśastrin, fled;
at that time, the powerful Senāpati Śailavajra was indeed the fourth.
Having summoned their own armies, they engaged in combat once again;
O Badrikā, various roars arose from both sides.
For the sake of securing victory for both armies, the sounds of conch shells arose in the sky;
and the warriors, ready and filled with fervor, shouted in the battle.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaughter of the Warriors of Nandibhilla—Consisting of Thirty Thousand Soldiers Together with the Three Commanders Indravajra, Ghātavajra, and Haridvajra—in the Battle," in the fourth section, the Tiṣyasantāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 83 ||
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badrī; Śailavajra, the commander of the army, stood at the front, mounted upon his chariot and fully equipped with all weapons and missiles.
In the great army of Nandibhilla, joyful sounds arose:
the blasts of trumpets for the sake of victory, along with the resonant noises of kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments.
In that battle, he discharged hundreds upon hundreds of sharp, piercing arrows at once, shrouding the chariot of Hari.
The Blessed One likewise cut to pieces all the chariots of Kubara and the chariot of the Naga that had arrived and were rushing forward.
With a thousand swift arrows released simultaneously by the Blessed One,
[he struck] even the arrows of Śailavraja and the arrows of Nandibhilla.
Kubara, seizing his bhalla arrows and feathered shafts,
struck the commander of the Bhilla army with hundreds upon hundreds of them all at once.
Then the enemy chariots appeared like mountains shrouded by clouds,
along with Kālavajra and other commanders of the armies.
They completely destroyed the clouds of arrows with many millions of shafts;
then Nandibhilla discharged a sharp, fiery arrow.
The fires produced from that [weapon] set ablaze Kūbara,
as well as his serpent-like stride and his troops on all sides.
There, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, assuming forms in every way, went forth against the entire army fire; indeed, that was a great marvel.
Then Śailavaja discharged arrows charged with mountain-mantras upon the serpent armies; indeed, those mountains appeared in the sky.
The elephant armies fell down and were crushed on all sides;
Kubera released terrible thunderbolts with royal mantras.
Struck by the thunderbolt, those mountains vanished in an instant;
the earth suddenly swallowed all the great mountains on every side.
Then a great wonder arose that caused everyone to stand motionless; Hari restored to health those who had been reduced to powder by his mere glance.
He restored to life the cattle and those situated upon their vehicles, even though they had been joined [to death];
then, O beloved of Badrī, Kubara there, a knower of the Garta-mantra, [acted].
He released the mountain-vajra weapon, a shaft accompanied by a mantra;
beneath the mountain-vajra chariot, that arrow-weapon created a chasm.
But into whose pit the chariot, horses, mountain-hard armor, and weapons descended swiftly—no protection had been provided for him by anyone. (17)
O Badrikā, the Earth swallowed the mountain-thunderbolt within her own womb;
though it died within the womb of the Earth, the Earth once again became as she was before.
Then a great earthquake occurred for both armies;
even the warriors were terrified and fell into a state of confusion for a moment.
"Śailavajra has come here! cried the Nandis and Bhillas;
and those warriors, fighting with the prowess of elephants, raised shouts of victory.
Then there arrived the fifth commander of the army, named Kālavajra;
he was as cruel as Mahākāla and possessed prowess equal to that of Antaka (the God of Death). ||21||
Then musical instruments were sounded rapidly by both armies;
he released a golden weapon empowered by great mantras.
There, stones born of the Himalayas became showers of water in the sky;
stones of extreme cold fell from the heavens, striking down living beings. (23)

Having recognized that the weapon was consecrated with mantras of snow, Kumbhakarṇa quickly released ten million and even hundreds of thousands of solar weapons (saurāstra) capable of destroying the cold.
The Vāḍava weapon was also swiftly activated, which causes the consumption of water;
by it, all the stones, though golden, were indeed dissolved and turned into water.
Then the water quickly attained dissolution in the sky due to the submarine fire (vāḍava);
thereafter, Kubera hurled his supreme thunderbolt at Kālavajra.
Kālavajra released that [weapon], and he destroyed it with his own vajras;
then, for the sake of destroying Kūbara, he dispatched the Bhairava-weapon.
Seeing Śaṅkara upon the Kubara, the fierce and terrifying Bhairava bowed and quickly became hidden; this was indeed a great marvel. ||28||
Kubera discharged his own arrow, enriched with the Sāṃkarṣaṇa weapon,
at Kālavajra— the Time itself upon whom even Death depends for its power to ravage.
The great hero Saṃkarṣaṇa, wielding the great mace and other weapons,
slew the commander of the army, Kālavajra, who was in the form of Bāṇa.
He crushed him along with his chariot into a hundred pieces upon the ground with a single blow;
and when Kālavajra was slain, the Bhilla armies fled.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when Kālavajra was indeed slain;
thereupon, Vahnivajra, the commander of the army, quickly arrived.
At the head of the army, he fought with arrows and gold-feathered bhallas;
like a cloud, he discharged hundreds and thousands of arrows.
From a single [bow], thousands of arrows joined with mantras as weapons issued forth through the path of the sky and fell upon the head of the army.
Showers of arrows fell from all sides with their points turned downward,
and for a moment, the armies, despite the prowess of the Nāgas, were indeed rendered blind and bewildered.
Then Rudra appeared and discharged the space-weapon (vyomāstra);
by Rudra stationed in the southwest, the rain from the sky was brought to an end.
And extremely fierce Rākṣasīs with adamantine bodies were produced, who, having diamond noses, moved through the atmosphere devouring arrows. (37)
Thousands [of arrows] were produced from a single female rākṣasa;
having swallowed that shower of arrows, they indeed fell through the sky into the army.
Then, from all sides, there arose cries of abuse against Nandibhilla:
"Kill him! Devour him! Chew him up! And enter [his body]! ||39||
"Let them tear asunder, let them rend those men belonging to the Bhilla army!"—
saying thus, they swallowed and devoured them.
Furthermore, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere among the Bhilli troops;
there, nothing other than death as their refuge was seen.
Then King Nandibhilla, realizing his calamity was destructive,
went for refuge to his own true guru, the sage Agnirāta.
Then Agni, having made the Rakshasa-slaying mantra his bow, suddenly released an arrow that was the end-maker of the Rakshasas. 43.
From that single arrow, thousands of shafts were produced;
and whomever that arrow touched, she then vanished from sight.
Thus all the rākṣasīs were then restrained by their preceptor;
thereupon Bāṇa discharged the most terrible Vaiṣṇava weapon, which was like a thunderbolt of fire.
Thousands of Viṣṇus, indeed equipped with weapons, arose; having arisen one after another, they suddenly merged into Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||46||
Then, from that fire and thunderbolt, there again arose a supreme wonder:
the vast Nārāyaṇa weapon, which in an instant takes away the lives of all beings.
He released it for the purpose of total destruction, yet even that was absorbed into Śrī Narāyaṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa; indeed, this was a great marvel.
Then, with the fire-vajra, he discharged the great weapon of sleep;
cast by Nārāyaṇa, Sleep dissolved into Kṛṣṇa’s eye. (49)
Thus perceiving his weapons to be futile, he was overcome with anger and released the great weapon Kālakavala, which devours all things.
From the released arrow emerged Mahākāla, terrifying in form,
extending for many yojanas in width and rising for many yojanas in height.
Seeing that Time (Kāla) was about to swallow everything, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa dispatched Mahākāla, who was stationed upon the serpent, for the purpose of its dissolution.
Then Mahākāla, established in the gait of a powerful elephant,
quickly cast off his own form known as Kālakavala.
Seeing that the Kālāstra had become sluggish and that the fear of the fire and thunderbolt from his bow had vanished, he thought:
"Indeed, this great weapon has failed me; I am now weaponless and powerless. (54)
"Nevertheless, I shall fight with a mace, or likewise with a club or a sword.
Having reflected thus, he seized a great spear and released it.
Kubera struck her with his own mace and shattered it;
that mace then fell upon the earth like a crocodile.
And Kubara swiftly hurled a spear at Vahnivajraka;
having pierced Vahnivajraka, it fell to the ground and was split in two. ||57||
Vahnivajra, possessing the strength of a mountain, rose up with his spear;
having risen, he ran toward Śaktilagnita with sword in hand. 98.
But Kubara, the commander of Kubara’s army, suddenly released a second spear at the hollow of the throat in order to render Vyasa lifeless. (59)
He released a third mace at his belly and struck him on the head;
he then loosed sharp crescent-headed arrows at the tips of his feet.
With his feet severed, his throat broken, and his belly ripped open, he fell down;
with his limbs pulverized by the mace and his head split asunder, he died.
O Badrī, Vahnivajra met his death in the thick of battle;
O Badrī, there were thirty thousand troops belonging to Nandibhilla.
The armies of Nāgavikrama met their death at the hands of the Māras in battle.
Then, the seventh commander-in-chief, named Prāleyavajra,
who was carrying out the orders of Nandibhilla, took his position at the head of the army.
He released arrows by the hundreds, roaring in all directions. ||64||
His armies indeed discharged arrows at the elephant hosts,
using bombs, balls, *śataghnīs*, and shafts.

With *bhūśuṇḍī* weapons and fire-missiles, they tormented the fierce warriors there from all sides, from the region of *prāleya* and *vajra*. O Badrikā, they [also struck] the armies of Kubara with balls of fire.
Then, with *śataghnīs* and *bhūśuṇḍīs*, they struck down the army of the Bhillas.
From the bow of Prāleyavajrahasta, hundreds of thousands of arrows issued forth and flew upward over the army.
He cut through Kubara’s bowstring and even the bow itself; then Kubara, taking up another, discharged many arrows.
When Prāleyavajraka quickly destroyed Tarujyā,
Kubara severed his bow and hand with two crescent-headed arrows.
Indeed, Prāleya, whose forearm and hand were empty, discharged a weapon;
he consecrated the Prāleya-weapon with mantras consisting of poisonous heat.
There, the poisonous splendors of twelve suns fell,
quickly causing the army to swoon in a state resembling the dissolution of the universe.
But Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, perceiving that it was the fire of poison, [bestowed] the immortal, nectar-like, imperishable [knowledge] born of Brahman. (73)
He discharged his own innate power, Brāhmī, which destroys all poisons; it became personified in an instant and spread in every direction with the speed of thought.
In that portion of the army within the sky, she who bestows the pacification of poison spread forth;
having drunk the poison, she became like nectar through her gift of immortality to those soldiers.
O Badarī, she nourished her armies in many ways in all directions;
indeed, she withdrew the entire weapon of Prāleya.
Then Kumbhakarṇa, seizing that all-piercing weapon with its excellent wheel,
hurled it— its wheel whirling at the tip of the fruit— like a long arrow.
Having struck that discus, which was joined with arrows and made of frost-like adamant, it fell upon his throat;
and as soon as it did so, it split into two pieces.
An arrow entered his heart and a discus indeed entered his throat;
struck by a thunderbolt-like frost-missile, he was split in two and died upon his chariot.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; Prāleyavajraka was dead.
Even the Bhilla felt grief, and Vahni reported the matter at night.
"O Guru, my seven generals, as well as seventy thousand human warriors who were fierce in battle, have been lost. (8.1)
O Brahmin, this battle continues day and night for two days, and likewise after two nights, there will be a great destruction of the armies. (882)
My human force consists of exactly thirty thousand;
and three generals remain with me, who will grant me victory. (83)
O Guru, becoming the commander of the army, proceed for my immersion;
for defeat in this world invariably leads to hell. (84)
Having heard this, O Badrikā, the Guru spoke to the Bhilla:
"Indraghāta, Haricchaila, Kālāgni, Layavajra," ||5||
Nevertheless, the hope for victory, though heavy with weight, was destroyed along with their forces,
since Nārāyaṇa resided there and Mahākāla was present in the king.
Rudra is seated upon Kubera, and all powers reside within his armies;
therefore, O King, hope for victory is fruitless—cease from battle! (87)
Hearing this, Nandibhilla suddenly became enraged;
with great speed, he then dispatched Raṇavajra, the eighth commander of the army.
Raṇavajra waged war with iron arrows, bhindipāla missiles, shafts, bolts, darts, stone-tipped arrows, and reed-arrows. (89)
With arrows having golden shafts and those with silver shafts, with small swords, knives, crescent-headed arrows, spears, and javelins; indeed, with these [he struck].
In that field of battle, the multitude of arrows, all charged with mantras and increasing in power on every side, completely covered the path of the sky with nets of shafts.
Kubera’s great army was shrouded by showers of excellent arrows;
there the sky could not be seen, nor could the eye move upward.
In an instant, everything became composed of darkness due to his arrows;
that was a marvel there, produced by the deed of Raṇavajra. (93)
Then King Nāgadeva himself took up a weapon called Mahātejas, which reduced all arrows to ashes.
Having pervaded the sky, he reduced the shower of arrows to ashes and discharged a great spear empowered by the Durgā-mantra.
She released the deity Rudra to slay Raṇavajra;
the goddess suddenly went to Raṇavajra’s chest. (96)
It fell just as a thunderbolt might fall upon a mountain;
having pierced his heart, it went to the earth along with his chariot.
Ranavajra was slain there, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; hearing this, even the Bhilla wept and fell unconscious, exclaiming, "Oh, what a tragedy! (98)
Having regained his composure, he then commanded the army commander Yuddhavajra for the sake of victory in battle;
and Yuddhavajra also arrived.
For the sake of destroying even Kumbhakarṇa at the front of the battle, as well as for the destruction of King Śrī Hari,
he likewise advanced to the forefront of the fray.
Having mounted a chariot yoked with women as its drivers, he arrived there,
abandoning righteous combat and placing a woman at the front of his chariot.
That rogue of a warrior arrived, equipped with weapons, missiles, and an army;
yet, where a woman is seen, the discharge of weapons is not permitted.
He descended into the battle, which was indeed created by a woman;
O Badrī, at that time, there arose great laughter among all the troops.

One who has become like a woman, who acts according to a woman's words, who has women as companions, who possesses the nature of a woman, and who is incited by women, surely goes to destruction; there is no doubt in this matter.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇa, seeing the warrior Strīvajraka,
gave the command to Durgā in her female form to fight him.
And at that time, there were infinite Durgās mounted on chariots, riding upon lions,
seated on śarabhas, perched on tigers, mounted on gavayas, and standing upon bulls.
They stood at the forefront there to fight in the presence of the women and the charioteer;
Yuddhavajra was struck with supreme wonder upon beholding them.
Then, facing thousands of difficulties, he fell into doubt regarding his very life;
first, he unleashed a rain of arrows upon the women.
In all directions, they [the demons] swallowed all those arrows from the difficult terrains;
and all of them, with swords in hand, leaping up again and again toward his chariot—
They fell upon the chariot for the purpose of destroying Yuddhavajra;
having entered the chariot, they [attacked] Yuddhavajra, the charioteer, and the woman.
They cut them all into pieces and then destroyed the entire army;
and in that battle, the ninth commander-in-chief, Yuddhavajra, was slain.
Then indeed a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Bhilla armies;
twenty thousand troops were truly slain.
O Badrikā, there, amidst the difficult terrain and the armies endowed with all power and strength,
Nandibhilla then fell into a swoon.
At that time, there was a great festival for the armies of Nāgavikrama.
The teacher of the Bhillas, Vahnirāta, lamented for that most excellent forest.
"In this matter, there is no other supreme means than seeking refuge and protection.
Thus did the true guru begin to instruct the king. (1.15)

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Nandibhilla and the Sixty Thousand Soldiers of the Other Six Commanders in Battle," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; having approached the king, the preceptor Vahnirāta spoke words of benefit for the sake of his remaining life.
O King, the destruction of us, the Nandibhilla chieftains, is occurring;
however, for the armies protected by Kṛṣṇa, there is no destruction, nor does it happen. || 2 ||
By Kubera alone, nine of our generals were slain;
and by ten thousand troops, ninety thousand of us were killed. (3)
Behold his destruction; therefore, either engage in battle or seek refuge.
Do not harbor pride, O Indra among kings, for Mādhava is under the power of the serpent.
Turn back from the destruction of your subjects, especially from the loss of your kingdom, and even more so from your own ruin; turn back and go to your proper place.
Thus enlightened, the exceedingly arrogant Nandibhilla said:
"O Guru, having myself fought and slain all those on every side, I shall [do so] in your presence."
O Lord of the Earth, I shall bring an end to this enmity;
if victorious, I will enjoy the earth, and if dead, I will enjoy the imperishable state.
Out of fear, I shall not turn back from battle under any circumstances;
let the fight continue constantly, for Dharmavajra will be victorious.
Having spoken thus, that ignorant Dharmavajra, impelled by the hope for victory, suddenly issued his command over an army of ten thousand troops.
"By these [mantras], O Great Dharmavajra, slay them all!
First strike down Nārāyaṇa, and thereafter the one with the prowess of a serpent."
"Subsequently, pierce and cut through Nandakubera and then his army;
here I am, having undertaken my vow, standing ready at the fire for the oblation."
"I perform this oblation for the destruction of my enemies; go and slay them!
Having uttered this, the Bhilla quickly entered the fire-chamber.
Having kindled the fire and invoked him, he offered it oblations with his own flesh;
having repeatedly cut off and sliced away the flesh of his arms and the flesh of his thighs, he cast it into the fire.
