"O Fire, be firm! Svāhā! Speaking thus for the sake of destroying his enemies, Nandibhilla then performed the oblation. || 14 ||
The fires, manifest in embodied forms, bearing weapons and capable of burning the creation, indeed leaped forth from the fire and fled with the gait of serpents. || 15 ||
Nārāyaṇa and Kubera rushed toward the armies;
a cry of "Alas! arose among the elephant forces upon seeing the fires.
With their bodies enveloped in flames, they incinerated the enemy forces, reducing the armies, chariots, and mounts to ashes. (17)
Likewise, Mahākāla and Rudra, along with their Śaktis, by the command of Hari,
produced manifest fires that appeared in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Those fires, possessing embodied forms and consisting of great splendor, devoured him excessively; yet, while being consumed by the wielder of the discus, they [were overcome].
Just as they had been devoured by Rudra Mahākāla along with his Śaktis,
they turned back and devoured ten thousand of the Bhilla's troops.
Terrified of Kṛṣṇa, those fires fled far away;
enraged among the Bhilla armies, they acted as forest fires.
Then the Bhilla, his mind distressed, quickly understood from the smoke rising in the sacrificial hall that his own army had indeed been destroyed.
In the battle, out of rage, he struck Vahni with his foot,
[attacking him] with weapons, missiles, arrows, *bhūśuṇḍī*s, clubs, mallets, and swords.
Accompanied by his charioteer, he advanced at the front in battle and slew many;
he struck down the elephant-warriors with a most violent shower of arrows.
Then Dharmavajra assumed the form of a magician;
taking on the form of a serpent, he went toward Nārāyaṇa’s chariot.
Having bowed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his beloved lord, he ascended the chariot;
at that moment, he was struck from the chariot by the goddess Śrī Durgā with her mace.
He quickly fell to the ground; then rising up, the wielder of the mace, sword in hand, rushed forward with the prowess of a serpent to slay him.
At that moment, Mahākāla struck him with a mace;
immediately rising up, he swiftly seized a sword and rushed toward Kūbara.
Rudra, being present there, struck him with a mallet;
from the force of that blow, he fell upon the earth face upwards.
Just as he rose and proceeded toward his own chariot,
at that very moment the charioteer was struck by the pole and the horses were slain by eight arrows.
The chariot of Dharmavaja was indeed burnt by the arrows and fire-tipped shafts of Dharmavrata;
then Dharmavaja quickly descended from the chariot onto a celestial vehicle (vimāna).
And having taken his seat in the sky-path, he struck the Naga armies with fire-weapon arrows, half-golā missiles, and other projectiles, all aimed downwards.
Nandibhilla also suddenly ascended his celestial chariot and rained down a shower of weapons from all sides across the path of the sky.
Other remaining warriors as well, the denizens of celestial chariots (*vaimānika*),
by the command of Nandibhilla, then unleashed a rain of weapons from the sky.
Then, having observed the aerial battle, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa suddenly gave the command from his own celestial chariots for his own [forces] to fight in the sky.
Then, O beloved of Badrī, Nāgavikrama, Nandakūbara,
the commanders of the army, and the warriors also ascended their celestial chariots.
They waged a great battle between the celestial chariots that would bring about universal destruction;
then Hari, having reflected, [invoked] Durgā, who obstructs the path of enemies.
He said: "Bring about the obstruction of the movement of the enemies' aerial chariots;
strike down the enemies' chariots upon the earth on all sides. (38)
Thus addressed, Rodhinī Durgā, whose essence is the inner deity, completely obstructed the movement of Nandi’s Bhilla chariots. (39)
And Garimā, the goddess Durgā, who is herself heavy and the weightiest of all,
swiftly bore a great burden upon those celestial chariots.
The celestial chariots descended and indeed fell upon the earth;
weighed down on all sides by their burden, they were no longer able to move.
Then the groups of warriors belonging to him were slain by weapons and other means;
O Badrī, they then sought refuge with the elephant-riders and those traveling in celestial chariots.
Dharmavajra also took refuge in the Nāga-vikrama [temple],
while Nandibhilla, unable to endure it, seized a long sword.
He rushed forward to slay the naga and ascended his celestial chariot;
meanwhile, however, he was seized by Kālakāla Mahākāla.
With fire upon his head, assuming the prowess and form of a serpent,
he severed the arms of those adorned with swords using his own sword, causing them to fall.
Struck by the mace, he too fell at the forefront of the battle;
with his chest pierced by a great spear, he, desiring death, offered a hymn of praise.
Nandibhilla said: Salutations, salutations to you, the protector of your own; salutations, salutations to you, the destroyer of others.
Salutations, salutations to you, the embodiment of Śiva; salutations, salutations to you, the Lord of all arts (Kalādhinātha). 47.
Salutations, salutations to you, the great deluder; salutations to the excellent teacher of those who are exceedingly arrogant.
Salutations to the Supreme Lord dwelling in the heart; O Anādinārāyaṇa, let there be salutations to you! 48.
Salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable, the supreme and the subordinate; salutations, salutations to You, the cause of all!
Salutations to the infallible One who fills the womb of the reality born from all limbs; let there be salutations to You, O Acyuta! 49.

Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord, who has descended and sustains those who have not yet descended, who is served by infinite liberated souls, and who is eternally dark (Kṛṣṇa) from time without beginning. 4.85.50.
Salutations, salutations to You, the beloved of Śrī, the Lord of Ramā, the sovereign of Rādhā!
Salutations be to You, the protector of the city of Śrī; O Infinite One, salutations to You, the Lord of Lalitā! 51.
Salutations be to you, the Lord of all lords, the sovereign of all sovereigns;
O Acyuta, salutations to you, the Lord of Vairāja, the ruler of the world, and the master of Māyā. 52.
Salutations to you, whose body consists of the ancestors, the celestial sages, and the gods, and who abide within all things moving and unmoving;
salutations to you, the glorious Lord of Māṇikī and Pāśavatī, the sovereign ruler of all. 53.

Salutations again and again to you, the child of the cowherds, whose dwelling is dear to Brahmā and Vāmana, who are praised by Haripriyā and others, and for whom Kuṅkumavāpikā has been made into a sacred ground. ||54||

Obeisance be to You, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, who became the mother Śrī Kaṃbharā; obeisance to You, O Master, whose nature is that of the saintly, who are the essence of sacrifice, and who delight in battle. 55.
O Viṣṇu, O Conqueror, salutations to you, the Supreme Lord who causes the birth, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world];
salutations to Bhava, who is attainable by true devotees, who is subject to compassion, and who is the powerful Time. 56.

Salutations to Rudra, to Bāṇa, to the Charioteer, to the Teacher, to Yama, and to Dharma; salutations to the twice-born, to Prāṇa, to Jīva, to Him who is endowed with those very selves, to the Emptiness, and to the Imperishable. ||57||
O Hara, you who possess the form of a Naga, the destroyer of Madhu, the beloved of the heart, the bestower of Nirvana, and the Sustainer—
quickly take refuge in you, the worthy protector, and lead me to the imperishable state of liberation.

Toward one who has committed an offense, who is filled with great pride, who always blazes upon seeing the prosperity of others, who stands in battle ready to give up his very life—grant him forgiveness and bring about his complete liberation. (59)
O Omniscient One, Lord of All, whose eyes, ears, self, and mind are present everywhere—grant here Your own divine vision and deliver all who have died this day! 4.85.60

O Lord of Śrī, you were insulted out of pride even by me, who was awakened by the enemy of Hara (Śiva); therefore, rescue me who have fallen into the midst of the forest fire of dissatisfaction, and grant me your divine grace. 61.
Whether it be heaven or hell, whatever exists for my sake has been offered here to you, O Kṛṣṇa;
lead the life of this surrendered soul to the imperishable abode in the next world, having destroyed its sin.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
"I am Yours, I am Yours"—O Mādhava, lead me to liberation.
Having spoken thus, Nandibhilla took up silence with palms joined in reverence within his heart; he entered [the state of absorption], remembering and meditating upon the Lord, his Master.
Then, O Badrikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa leaped down from his own chariot and came to grant a vision of himself to Nandibhilla. 65.
Kṛṣṇa, possessing a divine form, came within the range of their vision;
with his hand, he took up water and placed it in the mouth of Nandibhilla.
Then, his sins burnt away after drinking the water of Hari,
Nandibhilla abandoned the earth of Dilāvarī and went to the imperishable realm by means of a celestial chariot.
With a divine body, the servant of Hari shone in the imperishable abode;
likewise, out of compassion for those who had perished or been slain there in battle, [he restored them]. ||68||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa led [them] to liberation in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms;
with the destruction of Nandibhilla, the armies of Hari quickly [followed]. 69.
The remaining men, overwhelmed by fear, sought refuge in him;
meanwhile, Kūbara blew the great conch shell of Vijaya.
Displaying the prowess of a serpent in battle, he raised his banner into the sky;
there, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa blew his conch shell, which bestows victory.
The armies protected by Śrī Kṛṣṇa blew their conch shells,
struck their kettledrums, and likewise held great festivals.
"Victory to the Naga and to Hari! Victory also to Kubera!
There is victory for Kālarudra, Īśa, and Śakti!"—thus they proclaimed.
O Badrikā, they all desisted from the battle on the bank of the Lūnikā;
they rested in their respective places while searching for the corpses.
The soldiers established a distinction between those who were dead and those who were still alive;
by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, those who were living were quickly restored.
Touched simultaneously by his hand, which had assumed its own natural form,
they became free from disease, uninjured, restored to health, and full of vital energy.
Now, as for those corpses that were there—in the river, in pits, in caves, on the surface of the earth, and on the field of battle—for them the funeral rites were performed. ||77||
Then the Naga king held a festival at Yuddhapattana;
having attained the festival of victory, he bestowed gifts in every way.
The subjects presented gifts to the king as tokens of victory;
they performed worship of Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the discus, who bestows victory. (79)
Then, O beloved of Badrī, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
desired to give the city of Dilāvarī to the King of the Nāgas.
Kṛṣṇa spoke thus according to his will to King Nāgavikrama:
"O King, [accept] this auspicious kingdom extending from the snowy mountains to the Vindhya mountains. (81)
I indeed desire to entrust the empire of Nandibhilla to you;
therefore, quickly prepare yourself, fully equipped with the vanguard of the battle army. (82)
"I am going toward the beautiful city of Dilāvarī on the Yamunā;
there, O King, your consecration must be performed by me. (83)
O Badrikā, having received the word of Kṛṣṇa, he who possessed the prowess of a serpent quickly set out with his army and accompanied by Kṛṣṇa toward the city of Dilāvarī.
He went there and summoned the assembly of the Nandibhillī host;
in the presence of the entire gathering, that king spoke aloud: (85)
With Kṛṣṇa as my ally, I obtained Dilāvarī in battle—that city situated in Madhyakhaṇḍa, which resembles the city on the Yamunā. ||86||
The kingdom between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains has been surrendered by me, his devotee, to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; let Kṛṣṇa indeed rule the kingdom in every way. (87)
Thus the Naga king indeed spoke in that assembly of Bhilli women;
then Kṛṣṇa spoke aloud and enlightened him. 88.
"Let all the subjects throughout the kingdom hear: the king brings happiness;
by me, a sacrifice for my devoted Nāga has been auspiciously inaugurated. (89)
Unable to withstand his glory, Nandibhilla engaged in battle;
having been suddenly defeated by the elephant, he then obtained this sovereignty over the Nagas.
"I, Kṛṣṇa, shall consecrate Nāgavikrama as the emperor over the kingdom of Dilāvarīpurī; he is now your sovereign. (9.1)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa placed the imperial crown upon the head of Bhilli at his assembly seat.
O Badrikā, having attained a great empire, even the king of the Nāgas gave gifts to the Brahmins— villages, provinces, and groves.
He gave away houses, fields, cows, horses, elephants, and other such things made of gold and jewels;
he likewise bestowed gifts of maidens, as well as wealth and riches.
For the welfare of those who had died in battle, he performed a śrāddha sacrifice;
thus Mādhava, having hoisted the royal banner over the king’s palace, [departed]. ||95||
Having made King Nāgavikramaṇa the sovereign emperor,
Hari established an excellent order for the kingdom.
The Blessed One gave gifts such as offerings to the army commanders and soldiers; he satisfied all embodied beings with his market stalls.
The Lord indeed made this resolution in the city called Nāga:
"The city shall attain fame by the name 'Nāgāhvayā' (the one called by the name of the Nāgas). ||98||
That city, known by the name Bhillīsabhā and also by the name of the Bhillī woman, shall become Dilāvarī after the name of the virtuous woman Dilāvarī. (99)
That city on the Yamunā shall also be named Dilāvarī after him;
this eternal capital shall endure until the end of the kalpa.
Having thus established everything, O Badrikā, Nārāyaṇa departed by means of his celestial chariot for his own city of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (10.1)
From reciting, hearing, and remembering this, there is the destruction of sins;
likewise, enjoyment, liberation, and peace are attained, culminating in the imperishable state.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seeking of Refuge by the Generals Dharmavajra and Others with Nāgavikrama; the Battle of the Celestial Chariots; the Hymn of Praise at the Time of King Nandibhilla’s Death; the Liberation Granted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; and the Establishment of the Dilāvarī Empire upon Nāgavikrama," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 85 ||

The venerable Vyāsa Śvetāyana said: After thus accomplishing the tasks of his devotees, the Lord, the son of Kṛṣṇa, returned to his own imperishable abode along with Sanaka and the other venerable teachers.
Having thus related this story to Badrī, Nara-Nārāyaṇa ceased speaking; likewise, Badrī ceased [her own discourse] with the remembrance of Hari.
In constant meditation, Badrīpriyā meditated upon her husband Nārāyaṇa;
she became eternally satisfied, for she was filled with the savor of tasting his sacred stories. || 3 ||
Then Hari, having come to Kuṅkumavāpī, dwelt in his own abode;
thereafter, he established an assembly hall that was beloved by all his subjects and filled with devotees.
He related the pleasant account of Vijaya’s victory in detail;
there, the virtuous wife of the Bhilla chief Nandi was indeed named Dilāvarī.
Upon hearing this account, his beloved wife Padmāvatī attained wisdom;
she and her two sisters-in-law became the wives of the true Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having prostrated before their beloved husband, the Lord Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, they both questioned him with humility for the sake of obtaining the favor of all the members of the assembly.
[He meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the infallible Acyuta,
the Master of Kuṅkumavāpikā, who shines as the presiding lord of the assembly.
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said: "O Blessed One, you have stated that Dilāvarī was a virtuous woman (satī). How indeed did Dilāvarī become the wife of Nandi, the Bhilla?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said:
"O two companions, you have asked about what is auspicious; listen.
When the Bhilla Nandi died, the queen remained in Dilāvarī."
At the time of her husband's recitation and worship in the temple of Nārāyaṇa, she, being devoted to him, beheld his victory while contemplating it.
Together with her husband Kṛṣṇa, she was intent on the worship of his embodied form;
then, the [image] adorned with a crown and an umbrella suddenly fell to the ground.
Seeing the sudden falling of her husband’s form, the rapid obstruction [of his movement], and also the falling of the umbrella and the crown, she— 13.
Devoted to her husband's duty, she grieved as she realized her husband had been struck down;
surely Nandibhilla, the lord of Dilāvarī, was dead in battle.
For the sake of which, for the sake of his victory, I have renounced food and water; devoted to the vow of Kṛṣṇa, I am intent on the worship of my husband and engaged in silent recitation.
All that honor shown to me today is certainly not for the protection of my husband;
even truthfulness, though it is indeed true, does not provide protection for my husband here.
"Today the fruit of my worship has not granted assistance for the sake of my husband;
alas, when fate is adverse, everything becomes fruitless. (17)
All efforts are fruitless; even devotion to the gods is fruitless; vows, austerities, and religious observances—all become devoid of result. (18)
Now, the sin of malice toward a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is most powerful;
for one before whom the Lord Himself resides, such malice is terrifying. (19)

In that matter, Nandibhilla did not perform any acts of devotion to the gods that would have provided assistance to the enemy; rather, he committed an act of treachery against the one intent on the sacrifice.
The worship of both the Naga and Hara performed there was in vain for me;
today it has all become fruitless, for my master has been slain in battle. (21)
If this is so, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, Lord of the universe,
Teacher of the world, may true Satī truly ascend me here.
Having spoken thus, she took him by the hand and released water upon the ground;
at that moment, her two feet became smeared with saffron.
When her footprints were impressed upon the ground, Dilāvarī beheld them;
seeing that the vow of the truthful woman was indeed true, she then became a witness to her husband’s death.
Devoted to meditation on Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous woman, intent on thinking of her husband and dedicated to illuminating the welfare of the world, wept for a moment. (25)
Then the daughters, the maidservants, and the groups of attendants arrived;
having understood the true cause of the weeping, they too fainted.
Meanwhile, the messenger, overcome with grief,
descended from his bannerless celestial chariot onto the earth by way of the aerial path.
Having learned from the mouth of a messenger that the king had suffered defeat and death,
the virtuous Dilāvarī produced fire from her foot, in accordance with the truth.
Right there, in the courtyard of the God of Gods, in front of the temple, he blazed forth for the sake of liberation together with Kṛṣṇamūrti and Patimūrti. (29)
All five of those daughters were truly virgins;
they became the daughters who offered the water-libations for the childless Bhillarāja. (4.86.30)
He beheld the golden celestial chariot that had swiftly arrived,
wherein King Nandibhilla was present together with Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The illustrious Satī arrived to take the smiling Dilāvarī;
Dilāvarī was of divine form, moon-faced, and adorned with ornaments.
She sat upon the celestial chariot together with her husband Hari;
she spoke to her five daughters, intending to take Hari as their husband along with them.
Having quickly sprinkled those five daughters with water,
Hari, having endowed them with divine bodies, took them up into his celestial chariot.
Then a great cry of victory arose among the people there;
that city became empty, deprived of its queen. (35)
Then other female slaves, male slaves, subjects, and those born of the kṣatriya and other castes performed for that purpose sacrificial gifts and sacrifices lasting twelve days and so forth.
Even householders, though burdened by ritual duties, attain the imperishable state through devotion;
and even those devoted to desire and worldly dharma reach it if they are solely intent upon the command of Kṛṣṇa. (37)
Those who act contrary to the command of Kṛṣṇa indeed attain great sovereignty, heaven, and likewise the imperishable abode; however, those who oppose it surely go to misery. 38.
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said: "O Blessed One, we have a doubt in this matter; please dispel it in every way.
A householder is joined with a wife, and wives are the very ground of desire. (39)
Desire is a fault rich with latent impressions; indeed, it is more sinful than sin itself.
Since householders possess the nature of desire, how can they attain liberation? (4.86.40)
How indeed can those gods who are subject to the laws of desire, joined with wives and fond of pleasure, be the liberators of others while they themselves remain bound? (41)
O wise one, dispel our doubt, as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmī does; we both ask you for the sake of attaining the welfare of all beings. (42)
In every act of worship, the chosen deities, together with their divine consorts and accompanied by their respective powers and female attendants, are both worshipped and meditated upon. (43)
How can they be givers of liberation while remaining in liberation yet accompanied by women?
How can those joined with illusion cross over illusion, being themselves those who have reached the further shore? ||44||
How indeed can Lords, when joined with their consorts, be givers of liberation?
For those possessed of passion, there is certainly no release; dispel our doubt. (45)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "I shall tell you the truth correctly; listen both of you, my companions!
Having known this, no doubt whatsoever shall ever arise here. (46)
Even doubt shall be dispelled in every way by the constant practice of that which is Ādinārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Śrīkṛṣṇa, and Mādhava. 47.
I issued this command for the sake of creation to the Imperishable Brahman;
that command of mine is the personified power of Śrī Hari, possessing his very own form. 48.
The virtuous Muktānikeśvarī, who is the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Śrī-Muktāśrī of divine form, stood facing her husband. 49.
She is the wife, she is the lawful spouse, she is the Veda, she is the ordainer;
she is Rādhā, Śrī, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Lalitā, and the beloved Mādhavī.
She is Kamalā, Suguṇā, Padmā, Sāvitrī, and Mañjulā;
she is Haṃsā, Saṃjñā, Śivā, Nārāyaṇī, Brāhmī, and Sarasvatī. ||51||
She is the conscious woman, the embodiment of the form of Satī, the personified manifestation of Kṛṣṇa’s will;
she is Līlā, the earth, and divine power (vibhūti), that Great Goddess who is the left side [of the Lord]. 52.

She is Brahmapriyā, Māṇikī, Kārṣṇī, and Kṛṣṇā, the beloved of Hari; she is the one who comes through scripture, the one known by the Vedas, a portion of consciousness, and is filled with the bliss of true yoga. 53.
All of these are indeed the very embodiments of Hari’s commands;
the command is the embodiment of the injunction, the injunction is dharma, and dharma is virtuous action.
Those who abide in the Command are indeed liberated and supreme;
those who do not abide in the Command are bound and are of the nature of hatred. ||55||
All my forms manifest from my command;
they dwell within my heart and vanish within my heart. (96)
O Lord of the Earth, I am eternally united with the Command (Ājñā) along with the Woman (Yoṣit);
therefore, Hari is endowed with the Command and is truly divine, not possessed by passion.
My divine resolve as Nārāyaṇa is ever-present;
my command, which arises from that resolve, is divine and bestows the goals of human existence. (58)
These are the four aims of man: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Dharma is protected by command; command is dharma; and dharma is considered to be the sacred ordinance.
The dharma of the householder, though rich in desires, is performed by command according to the prescribed rule;
it is not intended for passion, nor for bondage, nor for hatred. (4.86.60)

The law of command is not a cause of bondage for the gods, as it is for those subject to desire; however, for human beings, the law of command bestows the highest good when it is in accordance with their own duty.
Obedience and righteousness are prescribed for women, but devotion to her husband is considered supreme;
a woman established in devotion to her husband indeed goes to the world of Brahmā.
And one who stands firm in the vow of devotion to his wife attains the world of Brahmā.
Incarnations, lords, ancestors, humans, and gods [all depend upon him]. 63.
Other embodied beings who remain in a state of ignorance are also partakers of liberation;
for the sake of the subjects, their desire by command is indeed the very goal of human life.
The duty of command and the god of dharma proceed toward a purposeful and auspicious goal,
following the path of the human aim which consists of the perfection of being.
The welfare of sentient beings likewise follows as a concomitant in the subject of desire and conceptualization;
therefore, that conceptualization which is desire is indeed desireless.
That desire which is free from passion and hatred is not composed of latent impressions;
such desire is neither intent upon enjoyment nor intent upon vice.
Desire that exists solely for the purpose of obeying commands bestows dharma; one should indeed approach one's wife during her season, and the husband should approach her after the season has passed.
Thus, the Command is the form of the Dharma; indeed, sexual union is the performance of desire.
That passion, though bestowing bliss, is free from attachment and aversion. (69)
That practice of pleasure, when performed according to the prescribed rule, is then free from bondage; it is devoid of illusion, devoid of sin, and rich in dharma.
Wealth and desire, when accompanied by the dharma of obedience, lead to liberation;
for those who are employed with obedience become one's allies.
All you ladies who are lawful wives are of the very nature of commands;
indeed, all ritual injunctions arise from the very nature of commands.

O ladies, those who are daughters-in-law, wives, and consorts who always abide by their husband's command, they are the very embodiment of the husband's command; indeed, they are the personified forms of the husband's authority.
Women who abide by one's command and provide the enjoyment of desires—even because they are subject to that command—do not lead to bondage at all. (74)
Where there is no bondage at all, there liberation is held in the palm of one's hand;
that very volition (saṃkalpa), the grandson of Dharma and son of Kāma, leads to liberation. //75//
Those women among men who abide in the complete surrender of their entire being through obedience—those alone bestow liberation upon their husbands, who are the heads of their families. (76)
But those who do not abide by the command are indeed bound by the fetters of illusion, for they, being devoid of the prescribed rule, bring about a fall from liberation. //77//
The goddesses are the deities of the gods, born from the various limbs of those respective gods;
they are the embodiments of their respective commands and the presiding deities (adhidevatās) declared by the Vedic injunctions.
Existing thus in the form of women, those beloved of the gods bestow divine enjoyments; they are all entirely free from bondage.
Where there is no command, there is neither bondage, nor passion, nor even hatred;
the command of Kṛṣṇa is virtue beyond the guṇas, for actionlessness does not cause bondage.

The Supreme Brahman is accompanied by women, and the incarnations are joined with their beloveds; the lords are united with their goddesses, and the gods are accompanied by their divine consorts. ||81||
Those men and women who are devoted to the purpose of the Command—for them, this Command of Nārāyaṇa, appearing in many forms, is the impeller. 82.

The command of devotion, the command of sacrifice, the command of marriage accompanied by the daughter, the command of creation, the command of righteous action, and the command of ritual procedure—these always bestow liberation. (83)
That which is the Command (ājñā) is indeed knowledge (vidyā), and knowledge is considered to be the giver of liberation;
that which is non-Command is ignorance (avidyā), and that is considered to be illusion (māyā), the state of bondage.
A woman who is devoted to her husband’s dharma and acts in accordance with her husband’s commands is indeed established in liberation; she is Nārāyaṇī, whose very nature is the sacred revelation.
She is the bestower of liberation, always the embodiment of the Command, and devoted to her husband; she is indeed Prajñā Padmāvatī, and thus she abides in the Command, not out of desire.
For them, desire is not born of passion; therefore, hatred is not possible.
They have no latent tendencies whatsoever, nor is there any defilement or bondage.
Conducting oneself in accordance with the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa leads to liberation;
such conduct bestows the grace of Kṛṣṇa. (88)
There is no doubt that serenity toward Hari bestows liberation;
the self, endowed with serenity, finds and attains liberation. (89)
For this command of the Supreme Soul is not the nature of the individual soul (jīva), nor is it a modification, nor is it illusion (māyā); it belongs to the Lord who assumes a body by His own will.

She who is the wife is Smṛti (Memory), Ājñā (Command), Prajñā (Wisdom), Vidyā (Knowledge), Kalā (Art), Śruti (Revelation), Dhṛti (Fortitude), Niṣṭhā (Devotion), Kriyā (Action), Icchā (Will), Jñapti (Cognition), Jñā (Knowledge), Śakti (Power), and Īśvarī (Sovereign Lady). 91.
That wife is one's own power; she is liberation as declared by the sacred ordinance.
She is neither illusion, nor transformation, nor latent impression, nor bondage. (92)
In ancient times, the eternal command issued from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa emerged;
it is the blessed one whose mouth is the Veda, the bestower of stability upon the worlds. (93)
By entering into that very command, even those with wives become seekers of liberation;
and in reality, there is no difference between the command and its locus. (94)
The Lord Hari himself remains present, having assumed a twofold form;
when he is recognized in this way, people are not bound and become free from doubt. 95.
When the wise one becomes free from attachment by the command of the Supreme Self, then liberation occurs for him in an instant; not otherwise, even through ten million ritual acts.

The sequence of castes and stages of life was established in the world by the venerable Parameṣṭhin for the sake of the increase of living beings; therein, those seeking liberation abide within that sequence. (97)
Those who proceed by means other than the sequence are indeed bound and not for liberation;
through the Command and by grace, liberation occurs in an instant—of this there is no doubt. (98)
Whether staying in the womb, being born, or whether he is a child, a youth, or even an old man, he is indeed liberated, endowed with grace and command. ||99||
Whether born from a sprout, born from an egg, or born from sweat, one who abides by the prescribed rule shall indeed be liberated through the grace of Śrī Hari; there is no doubt in this matter.
This Rādhā stands as the command of Kṛṣṇa; through her, indeed, is liberation in the imperishable realm (akṣara).
She is the embodiment of the command, the very form of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī, and the sovereign lady of men. 101.
She is Gāyatrī, Satī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, and Vaiṣṇavīśvarī; she is all the goddesses who are proclaimed in the Vedas as the presiding deities (adhidevīs). || 102 ||
All of them are indeed of the nature of liberation and bestow liberation when properly worshipped;
even the beloved wife of a living being, when abiding by the command and established in the bull-like master.
Having attained the grace of Kṛṣṇa, she becomes a bestower of liberation;
O wise one, Padmāvatī is always a womanly field of desire.
If that which is immersed in the fulfillment of commands is called the field of liberation, let there be no doubt in you here arising from latent impressions, aversion, or passion. (105)
Having brought the command into the world, Hari proceeds together with his consort;
likewise, the lords, the deities, and the virtuous ones are stainless, being united with their consorts who are the embodiments of that command.
Having attained the state of actionlessness, they are eternally liberated and bestowers of liberation;
established in liberation and free from bondage, they perform the threefold play.
But those base people who do not know the scriptures, who are submerged in darkness, and who are shattered by ignorance— those indeed defile me with their own fabrications.
The wicked ones, acting contrary to my command, will be endowed with power over the gods; behaving like beasts and following their own lusts, they shall disregard my authority.
There were also those who preached dispassion, as well as forest-dwellers,
those immersed in non-possession, and proponents of the emptiness of hatred.
Moreover, there are those who speak words full of passion and hatred regarding the Supreme Lord and his consort, and who commit acts of hostility toward the couple. || 111 ||

And those whose conduct is enveloped by their own imagined hopes, even if they reach that state, remain there with incomplete practice; therefore, being flawed and bound by fetters, they are never liberated.
"Thus, O Mādhavī, I speak: Nārāyaṇa himself is wisdom;
he is the benefactor of the world according to reality, the one whose command is his consort, and who bestows no bondage. (11.3)
Even the chosen deities and the gods worship the self-born ones;
they are the very embodiment of the Command-form, for they are the bestowers of liberation upon those seeking liberation.
Although a woman may be illusion (*māyā*) who is devoid of scriptural injunctions,
since that illusion which is free from [proper] ritual procedure is indeed the command of Nārāyaṇa.
There is no difference between me and Nārāyaṇa, for we two are non-different from Nārāyaṇa and Nārāyaṇī;
I, as Nārāyaṇa, am the giver of liberation, and Nārāyaṇī likewise is the giver of liberation.
For those who abide in the state of realization, illusion (māyā) is forever dispelled;
that very illusion becomes divine, bestowing liberation and destroying bondage.
Through reading and hearing this, atheism is dispelled;
divinity arises in one's vision, in the mind, in the individual soul, and in the Self.
O beloved Mādhavī, for one who is marked by the Command (ājñā), these two—enjoyment and liberation, as well as heaven—will arise; of this there is no doubt. (11.9)

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Chastity of Dilāvarī, the Wife of the Bhilla Chief Nandi; and the Liberation and Bestowal of Liberation upon those who serve the nature of women as being the command of the Supreme Lord, including the incarnations of the Lord of Gods together with their wives," in the *Gṛhagītā* within the fourth section, the *Tiṣyasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said:

"O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, if your command is considered the bestower of liberation, then tell us clearly: what is the distinction between the one who enjoys worldly pleasures and the one who renounces them? (1)
In both the Veda and the world, the stage of renunciation is superior to the householder's stage.
What is the reason for this superiority of the unblemished stage of renunciation?

Is the superiority of the householder's stage of life (gṛhāśrama) truly established in every respect, or not? And is the inferiority of the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama) established anywhere, or not? (3)
What are the faults in the householder’s stage of life, and what are the virtues in the stage of renunciation?
What are the faults in the stage of renunciation, and what are the virtues in the householder’s stage of life? (4)
For whom is there immersion in saṃsāra, even though they abide in their own stage of life (āśrama) and act according to the command? Or is there never any deficiency for them at any time? (5)
How indeed are wives a bondage, and how is a man not a bondage? Or, how could it be that the man is the bondage and the wife is not? || 6 ||
When and for which man or woman will the fruit of liberation come quickly?
For whom—whether a householder or a renunciant—is liberation considered to be attained swiftly? (7)
Is there any similarity between a householder and one who has renounced, or is there not?
O Lord, tell us both how great their difference in practice is, and how great their commonality in practice may be.
Or else, the nature of grasping exists or does not exist for both;
or else, the nature of relinquishing exists or does not exist for both. || 9 ||
What is the object of enjoyment, and who is the enjoyer? Who is the non-enjoyer, the ordinary person?
And what is not an object of enjoyment? O Kṛṣṇa, you who act for our welfare, tell us this truly.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved ones, my companions, for you are the benefactors of all!
I shall explain the entire truth that was asked, by knowing which one becomes a partaker of liberation.
I shall explain in detail according to the truth; listen, O beloved!
One speaker is indeed Badrīkaṇṭaka, and the other is Sarala. (12)
The householder's life is crooked, whereas renunciation is considered straight;
one who is crooked incurs bondage, while for the straight there is no bondage. (13)
The crooked has the nature of a noose, while the straight is devoid of the noose;
even between two things situated on the same level, many kinds of dissimilarities are recognized.
The straightforward person attains depth, while the crooked person does not attain depth;
the crooked speaks of rebirth, but the straightforward speaks of non-rebirth.
The crooked one falls from heaven, while the straight one attains the eternal state;
the crooked one takes the form of a woman, whereas the one who obeys commands does so out of modesty.
The *sarala* exists in human form as both a ruler and a helper;
on the leaf-strips and such, the *sarala* comes first, while the *vakraka* enters later. (17)
Or, if it is curved on the outside, it may be straightened and reach the other side.
O wise Padmāvatī, the stage of a householder is distinct from the stage of renunciation. (18)
One who conforms to the taught Dharma and bestows the bond of excellence,
if he enters crookedly into the practice, does not emerge but sinks down.
A straight arrow, through the application of a pull, surely goes forth and does not sink;
for there are many breaks in a crooked one, but they do not exist at all in a straight one.
The path of renunciation is indeed straight, whereas that which relies on a wife and so forth is crooked;
one who is free from a wife crosses over, but one who is immersed in a wife sinks down.
A wife is indeed a thick wedge for binding, and a chain;
a mace for the destruction of pride, and a wife is the very fear of fear itself.
Wife is the teacher who subdues the mind; wife is the obstructer of independence; wife is the maker of softness toward one's own being; wife is the nature of a confined cave. 23.
A wife is indeed like a thorny creeper; a wife is like the fruit of the gavākṣikā plant.
A wife is like sweet poison; a wife is like a hissing mouse. (24)
A wife is a long delay that creates obstacles for one traveling on a distant path;
moreover, once a wife has entered within and become attached, she certainly does not depart anywhere. (25)
A passionate woman outside the home quickly drives a man mad;
she causes delusion, creates confusion of the directions, and binds him as if in darkness. (26)
Having cast [the person] into the impure cycle of existence, it makes the man defiled;
having made his gaze filled with passion, it surely causes him to forfeit liberation. (27)
Whether in the state of waking or dreaming, regarding that which is to be grasped, retained, or enjoyed, or even in yoga— there,
the wife is a form to be attained before one's eyes, yet she is an obstacle to the realization of Kṛṣṇa’s true form.
O Padmāvati, that wife of a man is in every way the very nature of an obscuration; having abandoned her, those free from passion go to the forest. (29)
For this reason, women who are free from passion depart for the forest, abandoning even a man who is capable of renunciation;
yet whether it be a wife or a son, one who possesses passion is considered bound.
Whether it be a wife or even a son, one who is empty of passion is liberated.
Listen, O two companions: these are the instructions for householders. (3.1)
Those many [women] are not at all protected by householders who are caught in the web of ritual actions;
wretched, they do not honor the gods, nor do they honor guests, virtuous men, or virtuous women. (32)
They do not honor the elderly, nor those of high status, nor sages, nor cows, nor living beings;
they fail to worship their father, their mother, and their children according to dharma. (33)
They do not worship those worthy of worship, nor those deserving of honor, nor their gurus, nor the family deities;
nor the ancestors, nor their mothers, nor those concerned with the inner self, nor those born of sacrifice. (34)
Neither those who have arrived as guests nor those who have come from afar, neither the elders nor the juniors;
neither me, nor my attendants, nor even my powers, nor Vṛṣa, nor Satī.
They do not honor those who have sought their protection, nor Brahmins, nor even mendicants;
they do not properly honor even cattle or birds as is right.
Those householders who are intent solely on their own interests, devoid of service to others, and lacking in [spiritual] command, are always base in every respect. (37)

Those in whose house the feet of the virtuous do not rest, in whose house there is no temple of the gods, and in whose house there is no food offering for Hari—they are dwellers of the cremation ground. (38)
Those in whom there is no offering to Brahman, nor any offering to the virtuous, and in whom there is no devotion to Hari—they are all indeed funeral-ground dwellers. ||39||
Where the kingdom consists of wives, where enjoyments arise from attachment to wives, where meditation is on wives and worship is of wives—you, indeed, are dwellers in hell. (4.87.40)
Thus, one who is addicted to a wife who disregards his commands dwells in hell;
therefore, a wife who neglects her duties toward the household is inferior, and for that reason, renunciation is always supreme. (41)
In the stage of a householder, the debts to the gods, the ancestors, and the seers arise;
these are indeed discharged through worship, progeny, and study, and not otherwise. (42)
The householder’s stage of life is praised for those without offspring as a means to obtain offspring;
if that [stage] is fulfilled yet one remains childless, it leads to hell.

For all embodied beings and for all social classes, the householder's stage of life—characterized by the cultivation of a livelihood and consisting of wife and home—is indeed the provider of sustenance. (44)
The householder’s life is a futile exertion if one is incapable of giving food;
for there is the grinding stone, the mortar, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom. (45)
For those with wives, there are five slaughterhouses that obstruct the way to heaven and cause one to fall:
lust, greed, the relish for flavors, backbiting, and devotion to one's own interests. (46)
Pride, strife, and contempt—these defects dwell in the senses;
as do egoism, delusion, attachment, latent impressions, and passion. (47)
False display, agitation, and faults dwell in the poor; likewise, lack of nobility, hoarding, grasping, and the refusal to let go. 48.
Constant activity, discontent, and faults dwell among the poor; there is also impurity, birth-taint, loss, fear, and frequent exile. (49)
Servitude, dependence on others, and various faults dwell in the poor; likewise, false praise, blame, and the toil of striving for self-mastery [are their lot]. (4.87.50)
In houses, ever-new bonds of hope and various defects dwell;
there is affliction from planets, ancestors, and spirits, as well as suffering arising from ill-omened portents. (51)
Poverty is the suffering caused by disease, hunger, thirst, the loss of strength, and so forth, as well as the failure to obtain the means necessary for enjoyment. (52)

Disrespect toward kings and others, the forcible collection of taxes, indulgence in worldly attachments, festivals, and pleasures, and lack of capability—these constitute the state of being a mendicant [in name only]. (53)
Excellence dwells with those who are near; doubt resides with those who live afar;
separation belongs to those who are distant; and faults dwell among the poor. (54)
Lack of trust among one's own kin, the loss of wealth to others, and the subjection to living in a crowd—these defects dwell in the poor. (55)
Therefore, the householder’s life, with its wife, causes sin and suffering at every step;
it creates doubt regarding heaven and also creates doubt regarding liberation.
Those faults which exist in the stage of a householder generally become virtues for one who has renounced;
therefore, the stage of renunciation is superior, auspicious, and free from the distinctions of social class.
In the stage of the householder, sons and daughters are born as debts;
having paid off that debt, they depart upon the long path and do not return. (58)
In the stage of a householder, the mind intent on renunciation always experiences contraction;
and does the discerning knowledge of the Self ever attain stability or not? (59)
Whether there will be worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa within oneself, or whether liberation will indeed truly come—even these are doubtful in the householder stage of life. (4.87.60)
Then, O wise Padmavati, Narayana, accompanied by Nara, said:
"I shall enter the stage of renunciation, which is free from all bonds."
For householders there is the flavor of illusion; for renunciants, the flavor of the Blessed One.
For the former, it ends with death; for renunciants, there is the eternal flavor.
Indeed, for renunciants who subsist on the bare necessities of life on this earth, there is freedom from anxiety.
The absence of superiority and so forth, and the emptiness of all fear and the like. ||63||
For those who have renounced, the intellect remains equanimous toward both life and death,
as they abide in the Self with equal affection for a clod of earth, a stone, and gold.
Those who always abide in the eternal bliss of the conscious Self, devoted to the bliss of Brahman, contented, renounced, and whose very form is the Self; ||65||
In this state, even those possessing bodies and so forth are devoid of service to the body;
though living, they are immersed in Hari—liberated while living and bodiless.
Those gurus are free from defects and bestow supreme liberation;
they possess the engagement in divine play and are most radiant in their abandonment of *māyā*.
This is indeed the distinction of renunciants over householders, my dear:
if the injunctions for householders are even slightly violated, [the fault is great]. (68)
Therefore, the householder stage of life (gṛhāśrama) is inferior, because one is not capable [of total renunciation] during its protection;
however, the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama) is for the sake of Hari, for the sake of liberation, and is the supreme goal.
The householder's stage of life is for the sake of enjoyment and is intent upon the violation of commands;
therein, living beings are addicted to sensual pleasure, evil drinking, and foul eating.
They proceed naturally and especially beyond all bounds;
indeed, by their command, they cause such beings as humans and others to turn back from that state.
The Vedas and other scriptures are indeed of the nature of injunctions; they are both prescriptive and prohibitive.
Through the medium of injunctions, those which are prohibitive likewise negate according to rule.
"Let them not enjoy the pleasures of the sense-objects"— thus people repeatedly advise them, yet they disregard that advice and fall.

This state of householdership is of such a nature that even one's own command is abandoned therein; therefore, renunciation dedicated to the transcendence of ignorance is superior to the life of the householder. (74)
Listen, O two companions, to the excellence of the householder's stage of life:
whether it be husband and wife, or a man or a woman alone, [this applies] once after each menstrual period. (75)
For the sake of conception, he takes up enjoyment; and after the birth of a child, when the seasonal menses have arrived, he again engages in intercourse for the sake of conception. (76)
The giving of a wife [in marriage] occurs only once in another age-cycle and in another interval;
those two who act in this manner are indeed proclaimed as a virtuous woman and a virtuous man.

A household life accompanied by sons and daughters is always considered excellent; likewise, those established in the vow of celibacy are superior when they are devoted to the practice of Brahman. (78)
For they are contemplators of the inner self, free from faults such as violence and theft;
they are content with whatever gains come their way and are devoted solely to the maintenance of life.
These two excellent stages of life, the householder's and the forest-dweller's, require very few possessions;
they are devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman through leaves, flowers, fruits, and food.

They were devoted to sacrifices to the gods and sacrifices to the ancestors, and they honored guests; they were habituated to serving virtuous men and women, ascetics, and yogis, and to the company of the righteous. ||81||

Devoted to purity, vows, austerity, and contentment, they were free from afflictions; their ritual activities were dedicated to Brahman, and they were engaged in the performance of their duties. ||82||

Constantly contemplating only the command [of the Guru], free from the pursuit of worldly enjoyments, absorbed in the recitation and glorification [of the Lord], and adorned with the ninefold devotion; ||83||

Devoted to the knowledge of the Self and intent on the constant contemplation of the Supreme Self, they were immersed in meditation, with their very lives sustained by the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (84)
In the awakening to the black [state] through all mental activity, they illuminate the black vision;
intent on acquisition, they possess fitness and effort, yet are devoid of attachment. ||85||
Free from passion, free from hatred, and devoid of the qualities of the three states—such a man and such a woman are the most excellent for the life of a householder. (86)
In whose house children, young girls, virtuous women, holy men, mendicants, ascetics, perfected beings, and even the lowliest servants eat; ||87||
The destitute, the lords of the earth, those who have arrived from afar, the devotees of Viṣṇu, guests who have come to him, those on a journey, and forest-dwellers [were all received]. (88)
Kings and their retinues, the classes of subjects—men and women—and the bards, panegyrists, and spies, with the groups of servants as the fourth. ||89||
Beasts, birds, aquatic creatures, and likewise other living beings, indeed enjoy what is given by him; for the householder’s stage of life is the support of all.

In the stage of a householder (dārāśrama), the giving of great gifts is supreme, such as the offering of [liquor] to the gods, and the donation of land, clothing, gold vessels, food, daughters, cows, and houses. (91)
And the gift of all one's possessions is always the most excellent in the householder stage of life, when given to virtuous men, deities, sages, ancestors, and yogis. (92)
Where there is worship and sustenance, the householder’s life with a wife is superior;
for the expansion and continuity of one's lineage proceeds through wives and homes. (93)
O noble lady, virtuous women who attain liberation arise within the lineage;
through their connection, householders are uplifted, and from that, preeminence follows. (94)
Without a lineage, there is indeed no maintenance of creation, for that [lineage] originates from women;
therefore, a woman is the giver of the lineage, and from that comes the excellence of the householder.
For that man whose wife is full of obedience, liberation is held in the palm of his hand;
the stage of household life is always most excellent if one's beloved is a river of commands.
He to whom Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa grants his wife, grants him wealth, and grants him his body, home, and so forth—that is the complete surrender unto Nārāyaṇa. ||97||

The offering of one's accomplishments, the offering of all means of practice, likewise the offering of ritual actions, and the offering of the functions of the senses—all these are to be offered to me, Hari. (98)
The offering of the mind, consciousness, and intellect into me by means of one's own self, as well as the re-offering [of that] to Hari, is likewise the offering of command unto me. (92)

The dedication of sensual delights to Kṛṣṇa and the dedication of sons and daughters to Hari—she whose total dedication is to the Lord of Śrī; indeed, those two are the most excellent wives and stages of life.
Thus, the householder stage of life is the most excellent; I am the fulfiller of all desires, and having fulfilled them, I am the one who brings about their cessation and bestows peace.
I am Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who bestows sovereignty;
and I am Prajñā Padmāvatī, who there bestows the state beyond all qualities (nirguṇatā). || 102 ||
That householder’s life is the best, for it grants both enjoyment and liberation;
those two beloved wives, intent on that same path, go to the supreme imperishable abode.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Inferiority and Superiority of the Householder’s Stage of Life, and the Superiority of the Renunciatory Stage of Life," etc., within the Gṛhagītā of the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, in the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 87 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: O wise Padmāvatī, even within the householder’s life there is indeed liberation;
he who observes celibacy for half of his youth is fully liberated.
Or half of that, or half of that again, one should observe the vow of celibacy;
or for fifty thousand, or five thousand, or a hundred, or even fifty.
One should observe celibacy for twenty-five years, or twelve years, or six years, or even for one year. (3)
One should observe celibacy for either a single season or a month;
for that is declared to be the supreme vow, which bestows liberation according to one's strength.
Thus, this vow for wives is either a giver of heaven or a giver of liberation;
therefore, the gift during the menstrual period is not [recommended], while celibacy is indeed the middle way.
Even by him, indeed, a liberation equal in strength is obtained—
by one who, though ignorant of dharma and adharma, is devoted to the observance of commands.
And even a householder deeply immersed in the service of worldly attachments may attain liberation—
whether he be a man or a woman— if they are devoted solely to the duties of the household life.
Devoted to serving the virtuous wives of the gods, they both attain liberation;
for Kṛṣṇa is Hari on earth, and Rāma is the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Then, through union with that [power], he will swiftly become intent upon manifestation,
by the grace of that compassionate one and also by the grace of His power.
By the grace of the attendants and the devotees, a person is liberated;
for Kṛṣṇa and those who have become one with Kṛṣṇa wander upon the surface of the earth.
Indeed, mendicants in disguised form come to the houses of householders for the sake of alms and for the welfare of the people, their outward marks being unrecognizable.
Then the householder may attain the practice of giving alms and serving;
whether unknown or known, he shall obtain liberation. || 12 ||
Therefore, householders must always give to the mendicant;
for through the gift of liberation, liberation may indeed come to those who follow the householder's path by means of yoga.
The household life with a wife is indeed distinguished as a treasury of honor;
even if one is burdened by many sins, it remains a storehouse for benefiting others.
The householder's life triumphs eternally through service to the virtuous, for it is in such a home that the virtuous come, desiring even a small amount of food. (15)
The state of householdership is distinguished as the ground for the dust from the feet of the virtuous;
it is that wherein there is the nectar of the feet of the virtuous and likewise the food of the virtuous and disciplined.

That house where there is the massaging of the virtuous, where there is a place for liberation, where there is a temple, where there is worship of the gods, and where there is the dwelling of the righteous; || 17 ||
The abodes of Brahmā and Viṣṇu are indeed that very temple of liberation,
where Lakṣmī, Tulasī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī reside.
That very place where Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Narāyaṇa reside is the sacred site (tīrtha) of both the immobile and the mobile; it is the temple of liberation. || 19 ||
Where there are the descent-places of Kṛṣṇa, where there are the abodes of those who practice yoga,
where there are sacred trees and images of the deity— that alone is the temple of liberation.
Thus, in every respect, the excellence of the householder’s stage of life on this earth is supreme;
likewise, its excellence elsewhere has been stated by those who dwell in the home. (21)
O Mādhavī, when one’s life as a householder with a wife is for the sake of helping others, then indeed the state of a householder is the most excellent of all.
O wise one, I shall indeed explain at some point how the stage of renunciation can sometimes be inferior due to a lack of spiritual power or sometimes because of a fault in its manifestation. ||23||
Indeed, that hermitage devoid of supernatural power is incapable of providing assistance;
for one who has renounced, there is neither land, nor house, nor garden, nor son. (24)
The gift of land, the gift of a garden, the gift of a daughter, the offering of a house, the gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and the gift of wealth do not arise [for him]. (25)
No livelihood was provided for others, nor were festivals held;
for the twice-born never eat in the homes of those devoid of wealth. (26)
Neither do the great gods come to his sacrifice, nor do they even depart;
neither the boys nor the girls who frequent it take any delight there. (27)
For the renunciant, the ground, the seat, and the open sky are indeed equal to emptiness;
since everything withers away when one practices renunciation, it brings delight to the mind.
The hearth does not shine anywhere, nor does the fire find satisfaction;
the grinding stone chants the Vedic sound, but never [does it do so] in the realm of Brahmā.
Nor are there granaries of grain, nor even the thought of flour; nor is there any gain from newly harvested crops where hospitality does not exist. (4.88.30)
There was indeed no bed, no dwelling, no mansion, no cow, nor even a field; and there, not even the acquisition of a grain of new harvest existed, even in a dream. (3.1)
Therein, neither the songs of women nor the giving away of wealth exists, nor is there the hearing of the morning chatter of children and the like. (3)
There is no trust in women, nor does activity proceed in a place devoid of women; there is neither prosperity, nor purificatory rites, nor do religious sacrifices take place. 33.
Because of this, the hermitage of constant renunciation always withers, its festivals diminished;
for the animals will not eat anything that has become stale within the hermitage. (34)
Nor do ants and other such creatures eat flour there on the ground;
nor does anything sweet exist where flies do not dwell. (35)
The mice do not scurry about, nor do the pigeons dwell there;
nor do the elders receive water for drinking and other offerings mixed with jaggery. (36)
Where there is no honor for women and no counting of goddesses, and where there is no excellent charity, that hermitage of renunciation is harsh. (37)

In that stage of life where the loincloth, bark garments, ashes, and the mass of knowledge [are present], hunger is not destroyed; therefore, the stage of renunciation is indeed harsher than that. (38)
Where they stand naked yet gathered together, their boundaries appear as if turned downward;
they are submerged in the nectar of the Self, while the external nectar increases.
There dwell ascetics with coarse bodies and emaciated limbs, who endure hardships, wear matted hair, and are adorned with garlands of locks. (4.88.40)
Dwelling in tree-houses, subsisting on the fruits of various trees, using leaves as vessels and gourds as bowls, they were devoted to the destruction of illusion. ||41||
Adorned with various tilakas, they were smeared with clay, ashes, and sandalwood paste; accompanied by smoke and fire, they partook of intoxicating gold.
And where dogs and crows do not constantly obtain the leftovers, while waiting for the arrival of the dwelling place provided with offerings. (43)
One who performs the sacrifice to beings with craving does not attain peace;
for such a person, whose practice of renunciation is harsh, gains no profit in this world. (44)
O wise Padmāvatī, just as renunciation brings fearlessness to those who are already liberated, so too does renunciation bring fearlessness to embodied beings. 45.
In the state of fearlessness, in freedom from craving, and in being devoid of the afflictions of the Kali age—
even when devoid of formal giving and even when harsh— there is a particular excellence in the hermitage of renunciation.
Taking Hari as one's refuge, dwelling in Hari, meditation on Hari, and concentration (dhāraṇā) upon Him;
all actions performed for the sake of Hari—supremacy arises from this through the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama). ||47||
Therein, there is no anxiety regarding house, body, and so forth, nor for wife, children, and the like;
there is no attachment to wealth, fields, and such, and where there is no ritual impurity (sūtaka). ||48||
Where there is no sorrow, no bathing [for purification], no acquisition of wealth, no fatigue, no worldly business, and neither honor nor dishonor— (49)
There is neither debt nor punishment, nor any concern for protection;
there is no delusion, no distraction, and certainly no cleaning of vessels or houses. (4.88.50)
For him there is neither divine nor elemental agitation;
he has nothing that is his own nor anything belonging to another, for he is free from dependence and from violence. //51//
There is no fear of thieves, no fear of Yama, nor fear of death; there is no anxiety regarding disturbances, nor any concern for future acquisitions. (52)
For the yogin who is free from all dependence, there is not even thought of the body or disease;
he has no attachment to life, nor any haste for death. ||53||
There is no desire for nourishment nor for pleasure, nor are there any mental afflictions;
for peace, free from all obstacles, is united with Nārāyaṇa. (54)
Where there is reflection on the purpose of Kṛṣṇa, where there is refuge in Nārāyaṇa,
where there are associations with the virtuous, and where there is the company of yogis.
And where there is service to those devoted to the meditation on Brahman, and where there is the sight [of them], and the hearing from their mouths of the names of Hari again and again. (56)
Indeed, upon seeing renunciation, the mental state of even the masters of illusion attains peace for a moment,
when the mind turns back and enters the Lord within the heart.
But the supreme nectar, the drop of subtle great bliss, shines forth;
therein lies the satisfaction of yogins through drinking the nectar of knowledge and meditation. (58)
Wherein the members of the household are virtuous women and virtuous men, and no other;
and wherein not even the slightest trace of that which is called the world, characterized by latent desires, exists. (59)
Wherein lies the path to liberation, wherein liberation is attained, and where the holy fords, having arrived, are purified by the dust of the virtuous. (4.88.60)
Even divine illusion arises within a hermitage through association with the virtuous;
indeed, the entire world of illusion shines by means of the yoga of the virtuous.
Since one attains the state devoid of qualities (nirguṇya) by resorting to the Brahmanical [stage] and remains transformed therein,
therefore, even in the harsh stage of renunciation, there is indeed preeminence for those seeking wealth and liberation.
In that [work], the divine and virtuous gods are intent upon the fourth goal;
they are the destroyers of all sins, purifiers, and supreme lords. (63)
They rain down the peace of Brahman upon those scorched by the torments of saṃsāra;
they are the deliverers from fearful suffering and likewise the fulfillers of all desires.
Where virtuous men, beloved of Hari, gather in the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama),
that stage of renunciation is the most excellent for the cessation of the weariness of those who have labored.
Just as the shade of those scorched by the sun is the cause of rest,
so too do the virtuous bestow peace upon those tormented by the cycle of existence.
Without Hari, without the service of the virtuous, and without internal devotion;
without the realization of the Self and without meditation, nothing else remains abandoned.
That which is protected must indeed be protected even in the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama) and in the highest stage;
therefore, the stage of renunciation is supreme, as it lies within the range of proximity to liberation.
Lord Hari is manifest, the gods are manifest, and the liberated associates are manifest;
they dwell together with the saintly. Therefore, renunciation is always the highest good.
For in the supreme bliss of the Imperishable, there are indeed festivals of millions of enjoyments;
since the family there is the Infallible One, renunciation is therefore always the highest good.
Dancing for the sake of the Blessed One, activities for the gratification of Kṛṣṇa, and undertakings directed toward liberation—in these, renunciation is always supreme. (71)

Wherein the devotees of the Lord are honored, wherein there is grace from Hari for the virtuous, and wherein agriculture destroys the impurity of illusion—therefore, renunciation is always supreme. (72)
Life is for the sake of self-realization, activity for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa, and departure for the abode of Brahman; therefore, renunciation is always supreme.
He by whom everything has indeed been abandoned is truly abandoned by all things.
Renunciation is the surrender of one's own self to Kṛṣṇa; indeed, the offering of everything leads to liberation. ||74||
Liberation is indeed immersion in the eternal bliss within the imperishable abode;
one who possesses such an experience here is liberated, having abandoned [all else], and is a true Guru. (75)
Whatever objects have become desired, O virtuous Mādhavī, when they are renounced, they are entirely free from stain; O wise one, they are accomplished in every way, like those already perfected.
Therefore, the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama) is the most excellent; it is worthy of worship, worthy of honor, and bestows liberation.
It is the supreme fruit—certainly not the flower, nor the leaf, nor even the blossom-cluster.
Among fruits, the ripe juice is best; among juices, a sweet-sour taste is best.
Among men, Nārāyaṇa is best; therein, an excess of sweetness and sourness is found. (78)
Kṛṣṇa is attained through the possession of affection and devotion, and He is supreme through renunciation;
however, renunciation alone is not the highest good without devotional service.
Renunciation without worship leads to the state of a stone;
renunciation without service and meditation is undoubtedly a transgression. (4.88.80)
Likewise, renunciation without knowledge is in every way a transgression;
so too is renunciation without the guru’s command and without dispassion. (8.1)
He should be known as a transgressor, devoid of attainment, and false regarding the fruit, if he were to abandon saṃsāra in vain without attaining Hari as the Self. (82)

That by which the attainment of Hari is not achieved, and wherein there is the destruction of those things already attained, wherein the goals of human life are fruitless—that is indeed renunciation (tyāga), yet it is truly only a lack of renunciation (āga). //83//
Knowledge, spiritual practice, devotion, divinity, remembrance of Śrī Hari, the state of liberation, virtues, renunciation, goodness, and even emancipation [are found therein]. (84)
But for an embodied being, absolute renunciation is indeed a fault;
even a stone remains exactly as it is when such renunciation is practiced. (85)
Folly, pride, arrogance, as well as dullness, and the desire for fruit regarding objects abandoned along with their inherent nature—these are indeed defects. 86.
If one who has fasted consumes double the amount during the breaking of the fast, then the fasting on the previous day is likewise rendered false by that doubling. (87)
The renunciant later receives a hundredfold reward for his own birth and his ascetic toil;
he attains truth and the world of the Lord—what then is the fruit of renunciation? (88)
But that which was previously non-existent and later becomes impermanent—of these two, the finality lies in destruction; thus, the notion of "abandonment" is overturned. (89)
In the abandonment of faults there is that great delight which consists in supreme passionlessness;
for what has been obtained and what has been abandoned is unstable, and likewise, that which is to be obtained as one's own is also unstable.
The Absolute (Brahman) is certainly not attained by mere renunciation, for there is a threefold defect in such abandonment;
rather, it is through that [discipline] which leads to the attainment of Brahman, whether by means of relinquishing or by means of application. ||9.1||
Whether through service, worship, command, or knowledge, or likewise through renunciation or according to rule—that renunciation is indeed enjoyment itself. ||92||
Since that which bestows Brahman is the most excellent, that very quality is supreme;
the renunciation of one whose desires are subject to the will of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the highest. (93)
The renunciation of that which consists of liberation, stability, and experience is indeed supreme;
without that, renunciation is merely a burden and nothing more. 94.
Listen, O virtuous Mādhavī, O wise one: renunciation is indeed an ornament;
likewise, indifference is a defect, as is the persistence in what has been abandoned. (95)
The renunciation of worldly action is indeed an ornament, whereas the renunciation of Kṛṣṇa is a blemish;
the renunciation of women is an ornament, whereas the renunciation of virtuous deeds is a blemish. ||96||
The abandonment of faults is indeed an ornament, whereas the abandonment of virtues is a defect.
For householders, renunciation is a defect, while the abundance of enjoyments is an ornament.
For those who renounce, enjoyment is a blemish; the avoidance of enjoyment is their ornament.
Devotion to me, service to the virtuous, and the honoring of gods and worthy guests—these are their deities. (98)
A truly righteous marriage, ornaments for the poor, steadfastness in the Self, devotion to Me, and a conduct free from attachment to those things. (99)
Constant devotion and association with the virtuous are indeed the ornaments of renunciants;
forgiveness is the ornament of the righteous, while hospitality is that of householders.
Good character is the ornament of virtuous women; my command is the ornament of my devotees;
charity is the ornament of those who dwell at home; but meditation is the ornament of yogis. (101)
For householders who possess the virtue of renunciation, non-attachment is their true ornament;
for those who have renounced, lack of faith is a fault, as is the identification with the body. (10.2)
Laziness, lack of righteousness, and atheism are indeed defects;
however, the desire to indulge in sense objects is the supreme defect of all. || 10.3 ||
For renunciants, desire for wealth even in the form of a hermitage is always a defect;
for renunciants, the practice of affection toward family members is the ultimate defect.
Poverty indeed causes harm and is a great blemish for householders;
yet for all kings, thirst [for power] is considered an ornament.
Even the thirst for knowledge is always an ornament for the wise, just like renunciation;
even the thirst for devotion is my supreme ornament among my devotees.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Means to Liberation for a Householder, the Austerity and Carefree Happiness in the Renunciatory Stage of Life, True Renunciation and True Faults, and the Nature of Virtues and Vices," in the *Gṛhagītā* within the fourth section, the *Tiṣyasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O virtuous Mādhavī, O wise one, to the state of being submerged in saṃsāra:
a celibate student (brahmacārī) indeed desires his own spiritual advancement first. || 1 ||
By birth, all children are indeed celibate youths;
they contemplate the state of the householder as the highest excellence, prosperity, and advancement.
Study, training in the arts, occupation, means of livelihood, servitude, slavery, or else agriculture, protection, and craftsmanship. (3)
From that [desire] arise volitions endowed with the longing for greatness;
indeed, all those longings are a bond for those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins).
For householders, there arises a constant attachment day after day toward their beloved wives, their masters, their own children and others, as well as toward wealth, home, and prosperity. (5)
That [mind] would be of the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā), and bondage consists of latent impressions;
indeed, for householders who imagine happiness in a corpse, this is worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Bound to one another, they cannot endure separation;
they weep and endure great suffering until some eventually follow in death.
Thus, bound by passion and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
householders are born again as those who turn upon the wheel of rebirth.
Those who possess the desire for worldly existence, the desire for sons, and the desire for wealth,
are indeed submerged in saṃsāra and never cross over from it.
Even for those ascetics who do not desire the dark [intermediate state],
if they desire the worship of the body, passion and attachment are indeed bondage.
Having abandoned home, family, village, wealth, and possessions,
the renunciant [should remain detached] regarding the monastery, the disciples, residence, material goods, and likewise the stages of life (āśramas).
But he, being attached, is undoubtedly submerged in saṃsāra;
having instructed people and deprived them of their wealth and other possessions, he takes that money for himself. (12)
Even one who desires renunciation remains submerged in saṃsāra;
for he who, having become a renunciant, performs service for householders, [remains so]. (1.3)

He alone possesses the activity directed toward his own true welfare; he is submerged in the mire of saṃsāra, yet remaining established in renunciation, he thinks: "Neither honor nor worship is for me."
I have neither fame nor glory; I have no regard for sovereignty, nor for my subjects, nor for honor; even wealth is not dear to me.
I have no palace, nor a vehicle, nor a mount, nor a garden; I have no field, no clothing, no prosperity, and not even a dwelling. || 16 ||
Neither the status of an ācārya nor that of a guru, neither sovereignty nor praise;
neither a field nor a son, nor a servant, nor even cattle or an elephant. (17)
I have no horse, nor do I possess a celestial chariot; there is no festival of eating sweet foods for me, no passion, no charcoal, no house, and no courtyard.
I have no bed, nor a couch; I have no male servant, nor one who performs female service; I have no bard, nor one who performs attendance; I possess neither learning nor refined culture. (19)
Thus drawn in here, one sinks into the bottomless ocean called saṃsāra; once submerged, one never emerges again. (4.89.20)
O Mādhavī, those who, arrogant with desire, act by disregarding the sacred law—those, O wise one, sink deep into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. (2.1)

Having observed the prescribed rite and having fully honored the command of their guru as well as my own command, those who conduct themselves according to my way of life shall never suffer any degradation whatsoever. (22)
A wife who abides by her husband’s command, even if she transgresses it, is never truly degraded; for that command is indeed the very form of dharma.
The ascetic, the saint, the virtuous woman, the renunciant, the yogi, and the detached one—those who abide by my command are free from conventional formalities and worldly customs. ||24||
They were devoid of light and moved contrary to the multitude;
their conduct and behavior were vulgar, and they stood outside the bounds of decorum. ||25||
For those who are ever intent on the supreme state of Brahman are indeed the most excellent;
there is never any descent for those dispassionate ones who abide in Brahman. (26)
For there is no inferiority whatsoever among the gods or the lords;
nor is there any inferiority among the liberated ones, nor likewise among the incarnations. (27)
Nor is there ever any state of degradation for those who have entered [the path], nor is there ever any lowness for virtuous and chaste women. (28)
When obtained through the Command, enjoyments are devoid of the qualities [of the gunas] and do not cause bondage;
for those who are detached, enjoyments attainable through the Command possess the state of being beyond the qualities. ||29||

These do not become bonds for those who renounce, as they are of the nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s grace; the command of Śrī Hari bestows liberation upon the renunciants, whether it possesses attributes or is devoid of them. 4.89.30.
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa’s command is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and thus His action is always devoid of qualities.
Like the world, Hari’s sport—even the sport of renunciation—bestows liberation.
Every activity performed as an offering to Kṛṣṇa attains a state beyond the material qualities (nirguṇatā).
This state, free from deceit, belongs to those who have renounced and is devoid of bondage. 22.
If a wife is a bondage for liberation, provided she creates obstacles to it;
likewise, a man is indeed a bondage, provided he creates obstacles to liberation. (33)
O wise Śrīmādhavī, if those two were mutually bestowers of liberation, there would indeed be no bondage between them; however, listen to the truth regarding that which creates bondage. 34.
If a woman is devoted to her husband and abides in the truth of liberation, that woman is not bound at all; rather, it is the man who is bound by her.
