For that man who is devoted to his wife and who turns away from the path to liberation, that man is indeed not bound; rather, it is the woman who is his bondage.
It is considered that one who is even-minded is not bound by attachment, whereas one who is uneven-minded is bound;
for a man attached to sensual desires, a woman is indeed a constant bond. (37)
For one who is truly detached from that, there is no bondage whatsoever by means of a woman;
likewise, for such a woman, a man is a non-bondage.
Attachment is bondage; craving, passion, and greed are also bondage.
Formative predispositions are bondage, and indeed, latent impressions are bonds as well. (39)
Femininity and masculinity are dependent upon the union with a body;
as long as these flash within the self, so long indeed is it considered bondage.
When the states of womanhood and manhood have vanished through the nature of the Self as Brahman,
then all bondage dissolves within Me, the True Lord.
O Mādhavī, your commentary on the meaning of "you" and "I" is profound;
as long as it is a bondage, so long has that bondage been traversed. 42.
Sins indeed dissolve and heaps of karma are exhausted;
I, the Lord, being gratified by service, truly grant liberation.
When there is freedom from thirst for mere qualities, and affection for me who transcend all qualities,
and when there is total surrender by the woman, there is liberation even for the man.
When delusion has reached dissolution and discernment shines forth, at that very moment when there is an attraction toward Me, there is liberation. 45.
Service to the guru, the scriptures, and the virtuous, as well as devotion to the Supreme Self—when these reach their highest perfection through maturation, then indeed comes liberation. 46.
Through the practice of reality, one's own innate knowledge, imbued with affection for Me, arises;
and upon the exhaustion of the fruits of past actions (prārabdha), liberation is attained as the final result. 47.
"I am the Self alone; I am neither the body, nor illusion, nor latent impressions;
I am neither woman nor man"—for one who possesses such realization, there is liberation.
I am Brahman, and I belong to Brahman; I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Nārāyaṇa abides within me; for one who perceives thus, there is liberation. 49.
When volitions and mental formations directed toward women come to an end, then liberation comes for the man as well; it is never otherwise.

But when the mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) of women regarding the sphere of men perish, and the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) likewise vanish through the exhaustion of false manifestations, then there is liberation. ||51||
"I am feminine," "I am masculine"—as long as such sprouts of qualities exist, the embodied soul remains bound; upon their destruction, its liberation occurs. (52)
Having completed all his duties and withdrawn from all passion, he is as steady as the flame of a lamp in a windless place and free from all waves of agitation. ||53||
When the inner self has formed an attachment to the internal reality, finds delight within it, and attains indifference toward everything else, the self becomes one who has reached liberation. 54.
When a woman’s mind becomes equal to that of Rādhārāmaṇī toward me, then, by the grace of the Supreme Self, she stands established in liberation. 95.
Just as a woman offers her entire being for the sake of her husband,
so too, since she has been offered to me, let there be her liberation through my grace.

Just as a mother’s sense of identity with her only beloved young son consists of meditation upon him, thinking of him, and so forth—if such were my state toward you, then liberation would be attained. (57)
Just as the passion of a corpse-bearer in the cremation ground perishes in an instant, so too for one who is free from passion and the like, liberation occurs swiftly. (58)
Just as a childless woman grieves at the death of her husband, so shall Āvegavatī, O Kṛṣṇa, be released from the bondage of worldly existence. 59.
He who, even for a moment, meditates upon me as his protector when obstructed by great calamities—
meditating thus upon me, Kṛṣṇa, he is swiftly liberated from worldly existence.
If one acts for the sake of oneself or if one acts for the sake of worldly splendor, then liberation is in the palm of one's hand; he enjoys the fruit that has ripened.
Just as swift rivers indeed flow into the oceans, so too, if these women enter me with such speed, they shall attain liberation.
As long as there is even the slightest dependence upon a husband or dependence upon a wife, liberation remains far away; once that dependence is destroyed, it is in the palm of one's hand.
For her whose intellect consists of Brahman, whose vision always consists of Brahman,
and for whom everything touches upon Brahman, there is indeed the bliss of liberation even in this world.
For her whose intellect is free from attachment, who is devoid of cold and heat,
and for whom the relish of illusion has reached dissolution— her fruit here is indeed liberation.
When desires cease— even if they exist— by being focused on Kṛṣṇa and having attained a state free from confusion, then the fruit of liberation is indeed found here in this very life.
In the waking state, Kṛṣṇa is the object; in the dream state, Hari is the object;
in deep sleep, He is the inner self; and in the fourth state (turiya), the Lord abides as the Imperishable.

For whomsoever this [thought] always exists, or for whomsoever those two [exist], they indeed are the ones liberated—just as a thief is in his act of stealing, or as an actor is in his performance. (68)
Just as one's single-minded conduct toward an enemy’s enemy bestows liberation upon me,
so too does the affection of a virtuous woman for a holy man, like that of the cakora bird for the lord of the night.

Just as a moth finds no liberation in a blazing fire, nor a fish in a meal of flour, so does that which grants liberation find no place in a woman for one afflicted by desire; such is its state with me.
Just as there is extreme fainting from a severe blow of a weapon,
or as it occurs in deep sleep or under intoxication, so indeed is [the state] in me, which bestows liberation.
Just as the mind is directed toward one's own life, just as there is an inclination toward one's own self-interest,
and just as there is a perception of qualities in oneself— so indeed is my grace, which bestows liberation.
For a householder, liberation is considered to take a long time, whereas for one who has renounced, it is held to be swift;
a householder who has attained renunciation quickly finds liberation.
If a renunciant follows the conduct of a householder, he delays his liberation for a long time;
whether one is a householder or a renunciant, their similarity is determined by the excellence of their knowledge.
For one to whom sense objects are like poison, there is indeed a similarity between those two;
or for one to whom liberation is like nectar, there is always a similarity between those two.
The world is nectar to one person, while Hari is nectar to another;
if the paths of two are different, then there is a disparity between them. (76)
Whoever they may be— whether they possess the nature of Brahman, have knowledge of Brahman, or are dear to Hari—
when they become virtuous women, they shall then attain liberation.
The state of possessing a wife is the characteristic of a householder, whereas its absence is that of a renunciant;
possession belongs to the householder, while non-possession belongs to the renunciant. ||78||
For one who has attained intense spiritual urgency, liberation will occur swiftly; for a renunciant or a householder of dull faculties, it takes a long time. (79)

Possessing common characteristics is being embodied; the cultivation of selfhood is the absence of such characteristics. Possessing mastery over the intellect is possessing common characteristics; possessing mastery over a woman is the absence of such characteristics. (4.89.80)

Good action is the state of having dharma; freedom from action is the absence of dharma. Attachment to the fruit is the state of having dharma; attachment to the flower is the absence of dharma. (8.1)

Dependence is the state of having a common property; independence is the state of lacking a common property. Seeking [a common property] is the state of having a common property; whereas its deposition is the state of lacking a common property. (82)
When the activity is directed inward, there is the state of having common properties; when the activity is directed outward, there is the state of lacking common properties.
Again, when the will is directed inward, there is the state of having common properties; when the will is eternally [directed] outward, there is the state of lacking common properties.

Gross enjoyment is the state of having attributes (sadharmitva); the enjoyment of wisdom is the state of being without attributes (vidharmitā). Conscious bliss is the state of having attributes; eternal bliss is the state of being without attributes. ||84||
Self-bliss consists in having common attributes, while supreme bliss consists in being devoid of attributes;
thus, for both the householder and the renunciant, that [bliss] is of two kinds respectively for the one who renounces and the one who does not. 85.
Listen, O two wives of the wise one, to the nature of the household duties of both of us:
one indeed comes from the womb, and likewise, one always grows. (86)
Alone does the young man depart, and alone does the old man go to the world beyond;
birth again and death again—indeed, these remain within the house once more. (87)
The womb is the home, the palace is the home, and likewise one's own body is the home;
action is the home, craving is the home—that wherein one is established is the home. (88)
He grasps that which is indeed called a "house" (gṛha) because it is grasped (gṛhyate) by it;
the funeral pyre is the house arising from death, while the womb is the house born of karma. //89//
A mansion is indeed a constructed house; one who possesses such is called a householder.
Whether for one who has renounced or for a householder, that state of maintaining a home exists in both.

Hospitality, self-abidance, dedication to the deity, the observance of vows, giving, bathing, meditation, the propitiation of the beloved [deity], and the chanting and glorification [of the Name]. (9.1)
The performance of fire-sacrifices and the satisfaction of the ancestors—these two constitute the duty of the householder;
for the householder, the wife is considered both the household itself and the home. 92.
But for the renunciant, the form of Hari is always as dear as a wife;
their dwelling together with her is indeed the state of being householders for both. (93)
Listen, Mādhavī and Prajñā, to the nature of renunciation in both of you;
how you two are perfected ones, free from dualities, with your minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa. (94)
Just as I am an ascetic free from dualities and the ultimate refuge for you both,
and just as you two are my wives and I am your husband, even so there is no duality between us.
In cyclic existence there is no such thing as grasping; rather, there exists the nature of renunciation.
For a husband and wife of such a kind, there is always the nature of renunciation. (96)
Just as the union of Śambhu and Pārvatī was intended for the sake of obtaining a son,
so too is the union of such a husband and wife the very essence of domestic life.
If contentment shines forth for the renunciant whether on a seat, in a leaf-hut, under a tree, or within the body, then the state of being a householder is a bond. (98)
For one whose enjoyment is purely mental and whose activity is of both natures, and who finds happiness elsewhere, there is the state of being a householder for the renunciant. (99)
Effort in renunciation, love for Hari, desire for liberation, and stability in the Self; delight in knowledge, ritual action, and recitation, and peace in the Supreme Self. (4.89.100)
For that renunciant who truly possesses [renunciation], his renunciation is the highest;
for the world consisting of the body, senses, intellect, and so forth—which is to be experienced—is composed of Māyā. (101)
The individual self (ātman) is the enjoyer, bound by that [karma], following its actions, and subject to its own power;
however, that which is the supreme self (paramātman), the true self, is the non-enjoyer and is of a distinct nature.
Since everything that possesses consciousness is incapable of being enjoyed and is devoid of modification,
you alone are indeed the direct experiencer of your own pleasure or pain.
He who constantly exists having abandoned worldly enjoyment is the sovereign of the liberated;
he alone, O two virtuous ladies, swiftly attains the Supreme Brahman. 104.
All this has been told; likewise, it should be understood as being for one's welfare.
Having known this and having observed it, nothing remains for the sake of liberation.
The Gṛhagītā, which destroys the bondage of household life, has been spoken by me to you;
by reading or hearing it, enjoyment and liberation shall be in the palm of one's hand.
The attainment of the four aims of human life and supreme peace within oneself—may all anxieties perish through reflection on the meaning of the Gītā while at home. 107.

The cessation of all desires and the attainment of happiness for those with worldly aims, as well as the attainment of liberation while remaining at home through reflecting on the meaning of the Gṛhagītā. || 108 ||
The woman shall become Nārāyaṇī and the man shall become Nārāyaṇa;
O lady of the house, the true nature of this Gītā is composed of the Blessed Lord himself.
For those who understand the meaning of the Gītā while living as householders, there is no taint of sin from their actions;
even in the state of a householder, their stainless equality with renunciants is ever beautiful.
All obstacles are warded off, and even supernatural powers do not hinder those who recite the Gṛhagītā; their latent impressions are no longer impelled toward worldly haste.
For those who recite the songs of the household, there shall be gold, and even immortality; there shall also be divine garments.
Having worshipped me, Kṛṣṇa, according to the prescribed rite, one should then recite the Gṛhagītā;
his desired success will arise swiftly—of this there is no doubt. (113)

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Immersion in Saṃsāra for All Āśramins, the Non-immersion of Those Following the Command of the Injunctions, Bondage and Liberation for Women and Men, Liberation through Service and Other Means, the Dissimilarity and Similarity of those who Abandon Householder Life, and the Purpose of Householder Life," in the Gṛhagītā within the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 89 ||
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, you who are devoted to the liberation of all; O Master, you are indeed the deliverer of those standing in the mire of worldly existence. (1)
For those who possess neither knowledge nor meditation, neither recitation nor a chosen deity, neither a guru nor sacrifice nor dharma, but only sins indeed; || 2 ||
There is no association with the virtuous, no vow, no pilgrimage site, and no feeding of Brahmins; likewise, there is indeed no feeding of the holy and no worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Please tell us that practice which is easy to perform, which grants liberation, destroys evil, and serves as a means for the upliftment of those submerged in saṃsāra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: Listen, O virtuous Mādhavī, O wise one, to this practice of the gift of cows for the liberation of those in saṃsāra and for the destruction of the sins of sinners.
The householder's life is indeed full of sin; however, the gift of a cow is the destroyer of sin, a deliverer from the fear of Yama’s messengers, and a constant protector.
The gift of a cow indeed bestows liberation from the ancestors, grants heaven, perpetuates the lineage,
confers prosperity, and provides both liberation and a virtuous state of existence.
For one who has performed no other merit, the gift of a cow must be made; through the gift of a cow, all desired accomplishments are produced in their entirety. (8)
The gift of a cow is the gift of the earth, for the earth is the very form of a cow;
the gift of a cow is the gift of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the cow is eternally dear to Kṛṣṇa.
The gift of a cow bestows the merit of sacrifices and other virtues; Gaurī herself is the embodiment of the sacrifice.
The gift of a cow is the acquisition of Śrī and Rāmā, for the cow is indeed the very form of Lakṣmī.
The gift of a cow is indeed the gift of all essences, for the cow is the giver of milk;
she is the mother of all worlds, providing nourishment through her milk.
In every way, a milch cow together with her calf should be given as a gift;
she must indeed be bestowed upon a virtuous devotee of Viṣṇu who is one's guru.
She should be given to a Brahmin who performs sacrifices and honors guests;
O lady, the sacrificer, having bathed and performed his salutations, [should receive her].

One should go to a cow-pen, the entrance of a sacrifice, a temple, the monastery of the virtuous, or a sacred ford; indeed, one should perform ablutions with the water of a sacred ford for the sake of purification.
One should perform three sips of water (ācamana), touch the eyes with water, and likewise touch the hands and feet; one should hold auspicious water in the right hand.
One should take note of the place, time, and other factors, and then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited;
the preceptor (*guru*) should then perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the gift and likewise cause it to be performed.
Then, having poured water upon the ground, one should offer salutations to the milch cow together with her calf; thereafter, one should place water back into the hand.
For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as for the happiness of my own relatives and family members, I perform this gift of a cow.
Having spoken thus, one should release that water upon the earth with Varuṇa as witness;
thereafter, one should pay homage to the cow while holding saffron in one's hand.
The sacrificer should speak near the cow for the sake of accomplishing his own desired goal,
for the sake of health, for the sake of prosperity, and for the attainment of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

For the sake of the expansion and happiness of one's lineage, for the sake of happiness as well as fame, for the destruction of the threefold suffering, for the sake of dharma, and for the cause of liberation. ||21||
For the sake of destroying all enemies, for the unimpeded accomplishment of my tasks, for the liberation of the deceased, and for the pacification of all sins and other evils. || 22 ||
For the sake of destroying all afflictions and for the sake of merit, I perform the worship of the cow with saffron and other substances as a constituent part of the gift of a cow. (23)
I apply a drop of vermilion on my forehead with sandalwood and other substances;
for the sake of attaining good fortune, I apply the mark of a cow.
For the sake of the happiness of my family, I perform worship with unbroken grains;
and for the sake of attaining merit, I offer lamps and incense. (25)
I give fodder to the cow for the sake of increasing my prosperity,
and I give water to the cow for the sake of attaining heaven.
For the sake of redeeming my ancestors, I give sweet molasses to the cow;
I also give fresh grains and seeds of cotton.
I give a garment and a beautiful cloak for the back;
I also give garlands, wreaths, flower-garlands, and golden chains. || 28 ||
I give garments and ornaments for the two horns of the cow;
I provide golden horns and silver hooves upon its feet.
I give a milking vessel, a copper bowl, and a chain; I also place around his neck a necklace adorned with golden bells. (4.90.30)
I give a vessel for food, a vessel for drink, and a milking vessel;
and I provide a manger for the purpose of removing the scratching of the cows.
For the sake of pleasing the gods and the preceptor, I offer a sacrificial fee;
I worship the cow with red powder, bīra, saffron, and unbroken grains of rice.
With leaves, flowers, fruits, and likewise with tulasī leaves,
I worship and perform four circumambulations.
I pray for the attainment of happiness as equal to circumambulating the entire earth;
salutations be to those who are the embodiments of Brahman and the mothers of the universe—Oṃ Namaḥ! (34)
Salutations indeed to the Rohiṇīs who dwell in the worlds;
all the gods as well as the lords abide within the limbs of cows. (35)
The incarnations and the Mothers, beginning with Śrī and Ramā, reside there;
Gaṇeśa is in the forehead of the Cow; I bow down to Gaṇeśa. ||36||
I bow to those two, Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha, who dwell in the two horns of the Cow;
I bow to the Sun and the Moon who reside in her two eyes. (37)
Vaiśvānara resides within the mouth of the cow; I bow to Vaiśvānara.
Within the ends of the cow's limbs are all the planets; I bow to all the planets. (38)
I bow to those two Kumāras, the sons of the Aśvins, Gona and Sora;
I prostrate before Nārada and Tumburu, who reside in the lips of the cows. (39)
At Gokarṇa, I bow to those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
at Gojihvā, Śāradā resides, and I bow to Śāradā.
The Praṇava is at Gokaṇṭha; I bow to Oṃkāra.
Brahmā is at the throat and Sāvitrī is at Kambala; I bow to those two. (41)
Śambhu is on the hump [of the bull] and Śivā is on the shoulder; I bow to them both.
Viṣṇu is in the heart and Lakṣmī is in the dung; I bow to them both. (42)
In the urine are the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī; I bow to them. At the tail reside the ancestors; I bow to all the ancestors. (43)
In the spinal column dwell the sages; I bow to all those sages.
In the sides dwell the deities; I bow to those deities. (44)
The perfected ones (siddhas) who dwell upon the hairs are holy; I bow to them. And Śeṣa and Viṣṇu are at the tail, along with Śrī; I prostrate before all of them. ||45||
At the end of the question, I bow to all the holy fords;
in the belly are the guardians of the worlds, and I bow to those guardians of the worlds. ||46||
I bow to the Brahman-nectar, the entire essence of the flood of nectar;
I bow to the sons of Rādhā, in whose breasts all the oceans reside. 47.
On the front of the chest is the Brahma-lake; I bow down to that Brahman.
At the feet are the attendants of Viṣṇu; I bow down to them all.
In their hooves are all sacrifices; I bow to those sacrifices. The cow-pen is the imperishable Brahman, the abode; I bow to the pasture of cows. ||49||
Twilight is a moving sacred ford; I carry its dust upon my head.
There is cow's buttermilk, cow's ghee, cow's milk, and even cow's products.
I offer all this, including fresh butter and even the fivefold nectar of Brahman; may the ancestors and the gods be satisfied.
May the Rohiṇīs, the milch-cows, the sovereigns, and the mothers protect me always.
May cows be before me, and may cows be behind me. (52)
The cows are always upon my head; I dwell in the midst of the cows. The young cow is the form of devotion, and the calf is eternal Dharma.
May Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu, who are dear to one another, always protect me along with my family;
[may they grant] heaven, Satyaloka, Vairāja, Bhauma, and the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (54)
May Śrīpura, Amṛta, the Unmanifest, Goloka, the Imperishable, and the Abode of Brahmā grant me cows and indeed all forms of prosperity. (55)
O Goddess, you are the savior who takes the form of all the gods;
salutations to you, the embodiment of all wish-fulfilling cows. ||56||
O Mother, bestower of all desires, dweller in Goloka, beloved one;
O destroyer of sins, giver of merit, and grantor of liberation—salutations to you, O Mother! (57)
O Lakṣmī, deliver me from this ocean by every means;
O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, bestower of all prosperity, deliver me from the ocean! (58)
Grant me sons, grandsons, and daughters, as well as wealth, grain, and the like;
bestow upon me sovereignty, long life, and health. (59)
O fulfiller of desires, grant me good fortune— good fortune in my husband, good fortune in my wife, and even good fortune in wealth.
Having thus entreated, the patron should offer water into the hand of the preceptor or the twice-born, saying: "This cow has been given by me; please accept it. (61)
One should offer a handful of flowers to a cow, and one should pay homage to a virtuous cow,
to a guru, to a brahmin, and to a holy person who is a worthy recipient.
One should give a cow to a great preceptor, a virtuous teacher, a worthy Brahmin, a fit recipient, and a devotee of Viṣṇu who bears the Śārṅga bow.
It should be given to me, to Kṛṣṇa, to the temple, and to Hara;
likewise, other jewels, grains, and whatever items are to be offered.
One should respectfully give all of those to the worthy recipients;
one should feed the young girls, the boys, the virtuous women, the saintly men, and the twice-born brahmins.
The sacrificer should accept a garland of flowers and the remnants from the cow's mouth;
he should bow down at home to the water used for the worship of the cow and to the sanctifying power of her tail.
One should indeed perform the sprinkling within the house with water purified by cow-dung;
one should also protect the flower-offering, for it destroys obstacles.
There, immediately after the worship of the cows, one should worship the preceptor;
one should also worship the bull and the cow-calf, and perform prostrations and circumambulations.
Having shown due respect, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to his ability—
a tawny cow, a white one, a red one, or even a brindled one.
O two virtuous ladies, by giving her [the cow], one obtains the supreme station of Vairāja as its fruit;
by giving a black, smoke-colored, or tawny cow, one obtains the station of Brahmā (Vedhas) as its fruit.
Whichever milch cow one may give as a gift, the fruit thereof is the station of Indra in heaven;
if one gives a calf, the fruit for him is a divine abode in heaven.
One should give a cow with two faces; its fruit is the supreme state, the imperishable, ultimate liberation, eternal and belonging to the Supreme Person. //72//
One should indeed give a cow that has not recently calved and is a good milker; she is the giver of Goloka.
Then, the donor of the cow should observe the vow pertaining to cows.
Day and night one should observe the vow of eating only once;
one should indeed consume products of the cow and practice service to the cow in every way.
One should observe celibacy for that single day and sleep in a cow-pen;
with a garland, one should chant the names of Śrī Hari, who is I, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (95)
One should give even grass for a month's fodder as equal in merit to the gift of a cow;
one should always give cotton seeds and the like for the cow's consumption. (76)
One should indeed give a living cow; for that is considered the most excellent gift.
In the absence of a cow, one should worship a cow [in an image] and offer its value as the supreme alternative. (77)
A devotee, having bowed repeatedly to the venerable Guru, should give half the price, or half of that, or a small amount, or even a tenth part, according to his wealth. (78)
"I have given according to my ability; please forgive whatever here was incomplete.
One should prostrate before him like a staff and avoid stinginess regarding wealth. (79)
The gift of a cow is excellent when given at a temple; it is even more excellent when given at a shrine for the gods.
It is most excellent when given at a monastery, a virtuous hermitage, during a sacrifice, or in a hall for the recitation of sacred texts.
In a marriage pavilion, at an excellent holy site, or even on the bank of a river; on the day of a vow, on an auspicious day, or during a great festival and a joyful celebration. (8–1)
One should indeed perform the gift of an excellent cow during good health with one's own hand;
that cow which is given as a gift becomes divine after death. (82)
O Goddess, the giver of a cow as a gift goes not to an evil state; for his protector goes ahead and ahead on the path to heaven and the path of dharma.
O beloved, the cow is the deliverer from the river of suffering, the Vaitaraṇī, and she provides food for the deceased spirit as it departs for the next world. (84)
One should give a cow made of gold, and likewise a cow made of silver;
one should give a cow made of grain, and likewise a cow made of cotton.
One who is destitute of daughters on this earth should give a cow consisting of essence, likewise a cow consisting of prosperity,
and a cow consisting of a daughter.
One should construct the pavilion according to the prescribed rules, have the altar and the sacrificial pit prepared,
and likewise deposit all the ritual materials as well as the gems.
Then, having made his own daughter the cow named [after her],
he gave all the garments of a maiden and the ornaments of a maiden.
Having placed a maiden and a cow within the pavilion, one should give them to a twice-born man;
one should cause oblations to be offered there and have musical instruments played.
Then, one should have the proper rite for the giving of a daughter performed in the pavilion;
the fruit of that gift of a daughter becomes equal to that of a giver of cows.
One should indeed give a maiden-cow, a Rohiṇī cow accompanied by a bull, one that is not pregnant, possesses a large calf, and has the appearance of a maiden. ||9 1 ||
By the gift of a great calf, one subsequently becomes possessed of daughters;
thus, the giver of such a gift shall partake of heaven as well as liberation. 92.
He is always born endowed with worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the great liberation;
he is the savior of his ancestors and the savior of his family members. (93)
One who is a worthy recipient of all merit shall become filled with the bliss of Brahman; a giver of a cow who is childless shall indeed have offspring within a year.
One who is childless shall possess a son within a year; of this there is no doubt.
Having obtained an auspicious time and a worthy recipient, one should bestow the gift. (95)
The auspicious time that has passed will never return;
therefore, a householder who is devoid of the goals of dharma and action should perform the gift of a cow.
A cow is the share for that [officiant]; two virtuous women are the shares for those with households numbering one hundred and so forth.
To the giver of the cow, however, the preceptor should offer blessings accompanied by unbroken grains (akṣatas).
O King, may you be wealthy, possessed of sons, endowed with fortune and prosperity;
likewise, may you be healthy, illustrious, and pre-eminent in splendor among men. (98)
May you possess long life, wealth, and the expansion of your lineage;
may you possess heaven, divine prosperity, and, in the end, liberation. (99)
In your lineage, let there arise givers of cows who partake in liberation—righteous, devoted to the gods, and dedicated to the upliftment of their subjects. (4.90.10)
May the women in your lineage be devoted to serving the virtuous, may they be faithful to their husbands, and may they be like Rādhā and Lakṣmī in truthfulness. 101.
May there be well-being for you always in this world, and may it be so for you in the next world as well;
may this cow, standing before you, grant you well-being in every way. || 10.2 ||
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gopati; salutations to the Lord of Rādhā.
Abiding within the very self of the cows, I am the witness Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 103.
"O beloved Padmāvatī, remembering me, you should perform the offering of cows;
having said, 'May this gift be an offering unto Kṛṣṇa,' you should dismiss them."
Thus, O Supriya, this most excellent sādhana has been declared by me to you both;
from reading or hearing it, the fruit of gifting a cow shall be obtained. (105)

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of a Cow (*godāna*) and the Deity of the Cow-pen (*gosthadeva*), as Means for Liberation and Other Goals Even for a Householder Devoid of All Ritual Duties," in the *Gṛhagītā* within the fourth section, the *Tiṣyasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, if the gift of a cow has not been performed, and if there is something else for the sake of liberation, please tell us about it here. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: Service to the virtuous, performed always through body, mind, and action, bestows all prosperity, grants liberation, and destroys sin. (2)
Those who possess neither knowledge of vows nor knowledge of the Dharma,
yet are characterized by poverty and impurity, are devoid of the true ford.
For those virtuous ones, through association with the good, the destruction of sin and liberation arise;
there is no doubt in this matter, for the Blessed Lord resides in the company of the good.
O wife, the assembly of the virtuous occurs in many ways according to the diversity of inclinations;
for whomever it happens, there shall be the destruction of sin and liberation. || 9 ||
The mere act of seeing with the two eyes is association with the virtuous, consisting of that very sight;
massaging with the two hands and the like is association with the virtuous, consisting of the rubbing of the body.
Service, performing one's duty, compliance with commands, the state of a servant, even servitude itself, association with the virtuous, and the offering of one's body [are required]. (7)
The virtuous should always go on foot toward the hermitage;
they should perform circumambulation, seek the company of the good, and offer their feet [in service].
One should bow to a saint with the head; association with the virtuous consists of bowing. One should prostrate before a saint with palms joined; that indeed is association with the virtuous.

One should praise the virtuous with the tongue, for association with the good consists of praising; one should consume the grace of the saintly, for association with the good consists of the sense of taste. 4.91.10
One should listen there to the discourse of the saintly; this is association with the virtuous consisting of hearing.
One should touch the saintly with affection; this is association with the virtuous consisting of touching. (11)
One should grasp the fragrance arising from the flowers of grace belonging to the virtuous;
association with the virtuous consists essentially in smelling the essence of fragrance from the bodies of the good. (1.2)
Association with the virtuous consists of the company of holy men;
it embraces the best of the good, and that association with the virtuous, being like the celestial Nandana grove, brings about grace and joy.
One should offer praise and observe the command; this is association with the virtuous consisting of praise.
One should constantly serve the holy ones; this is association with the virtuous consisting of service. (14)
One should dwell together with the virtuous; association with the good consists of wandering.
One should move about together with the virtuous; association with the good consists of the maṇḍala. || 15 ||
Dwelling together with the virtuous, that association with the good constitutes his home;
regarding the saintly as his father, that association with the good constitutes his son.
One should revere the virtuous Guru; association with the good is the conduct of a disciple.
One should go for refuge to the true saint; association with the good is itself the nature of refuge. (17)
One should give food to the virtuous; association with the good consists of food.
One should give milk, curd, and ghee; association with the good consists of those flavors. (18)
One should give clothing and a woolen blanket; association with the virtuous is of the nature of clothing.
One should give an umbrella and a fly-whisk; association with the virtuous is of the nature of the instruments [of perception].
One should give alms-bowls and a bed; association with the virtuous is the essence of a bed.
One should give a mansion and a palace; association with the virtuous is the essence of a home. (4.91.20)
The gift of a vehicle is a celestial chariot, while association with the virtuous consists of such conveyances;
the gift of food, vegetables, and fruit is the act of satiation that constitutes association with the virtuous. (2.1)
One should offer water and perform anointment; such association with the virtuous is called "bathing.
One should adorn the saint with flowers; such association with the virtuous is of the nature of "ornamentation. (22)

One should invite a saintly person to the village, worship him in the house or the courtyard, and cause him to wander through the midst of the village; such association with the virtuous is the very essence of the festival.
One should uphold the instruction, for association with the virtuous consists of awakening;
one should offer wealth to him, for that association with the virtuous consists of riches. (24)

One should satisfy [the holy ones] with desired gifts, for association with the virtuous consists of such gratification; one receives blessings from the saintly, for that association with the virtuous is the most excellent of things. (25)
One should prescribe medicine and the like for him, for association with the virtuous is free from ailment;
one should offer sacrificial fuel and the like in the sacrifice, for association with the virtuous consists of that very fuel. ||26||
One should indeed teach the virtuous; association with the good consists of teaching.
One should acquire the knowledge of Brahman; association with the good bestows the realization of Brahman.
One should constantly meditate upon me, the Holy One; for association with the virtuous bestows the yoga of meditation.
One should glorify Śrī Hari and the holy ones; for association with the virtuous consists of such glorification. (28)

One should perform all activities for the sake of the virtuous, for association with the good is beyond the material modes; for one to whom Hari himself is the virtuous, there remains no further duty to be done. (29)
O lady, by thus serving the virtuous and through the company of the good, it should be understood that liberation stands within one's grasp; nothing further remains to be done. (4.91.30)
Listen, O virtuous ones, to the meditation upon the Guru as it truly is; I shall describe to you that which has been properly performed according to the prescribed ritual. 3.1.
One should know him as the virtuous, divine, and illusion-free embodiment of Brahman;
the purifier, the embodiment of merit, the untainted Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||32||
The holy dust of the feet of the virtuous is meritorious, and the garment of the virtuous is purifying;
indeed, everything worthy of being served by the virtuous is purifying and free from deceit.
The touch of the virtuous is purifying; indeed, that which is eaten by the virtuous is purifying.
Water, food, fruit, flowers, and so forth—when offered as a favor (prasāda) by the virtuous—are purifying. (34)
Excellent is the seat and the sacred sandals, which are purifying for the virtuous;
and all the various requisites and so forth are in every way purifying for the virtuous. (35)
The teeth, nails, and hair of a virtuous person are purifying and destroyers of sin;
indeed, the embrace of a virtuous person is purifying and the destroyer of all malevolent spells.
The company of a holy person destroys mental and physical afflictions;
the hermitage of a holy person is a great sacred site, and taking refuge in a holy person is purifying. (37)
The divine abode of the virtuous is resplendent as the great Vaikuṇṭha;
the arrival of the virtuous bestows well-being, rains down blessings, and is a source of happiness. (38)
The favor of a holy man is a treasure of virtue obtained through service; the affection of a holy man bestows the attainment of Brahman, while his love grants final liberation. (39)
The company of the virtuous bestows all bliss and is free from fear;
it removes the dread of time, illusion, evil karma, enemies, and Yama.
O virtuous one, at the tip of the crest there is indeed the river Virajā, born of Goloka;
at the root of the crest, the imperishable Brahma-lake shines eternally.
The imperishable abode, Goloka, is at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and it is also at the crown of the head;
Vaikuṇṭha is on the forehead, while Ramāpura is in the middle of the brow.
The two abodes of nectar and the unmanifest are situated at the two ends of the forehead;
while Mahāviṣṇu and Vairāja are both stationed at the two ears.
The sun and moon are in the two eyes, and the two poles (dhruva) are in the two cheeks;
the Marut gods are in the nose, and Nārāyaṇa himself is in the mouth.
Upon the two lips is divine nectar, sweet and filled with bliss;
upon the tongue are all the Vedas, and within the cavity of the mouth resides the deity Agni. 45.
In sound resides Vāṇī, the glory of Śāradā; in form resides Lakṣmī, indeed upon the neck;
in the throat reside all the sciences of Brahman; and in the heart resides the eternal Brahman. (46)
In my consciousness, the Supreme Brahman is the deity; in my volition, Kṛṣṇa is the deity;
in my chest, Dharma is the deity; and on my back, the ancestors are the deities. (47)
On his two sides are Brahmā and Rudra, Viṣṇu stands upon his chest,
Annapūrṇā is in his belly, and in his navel is heaven, the abode of the gods.
On her hips is Śrīgaṇeśa, and in her secret parts are millions of powers of sovereignty;
on her waist is the Earth, and on her two buttocks are the two mountains of sunrise and sunset.
Aniruddha and Pradyumna are both located in the two shoulders;
Saṃkarṣaṇa is in the eyebrows, and Vāsudeva resides between the eyebrows for the virtuous.
The guardians of the directions, the world-protectors, reside in his two arms;
Śrī and Bhū are in his two hands, and his various powers (vibhūtis) are even in his fingers.
The stars are present in his nails; the planets dwell in his joints;
all sacred fords reside in the body of this virtuous one. (52)
In speech they are wish-fulfilling cows; in thought, they are wish-granting gems; in compliance, they are indeed desire-yielding trees; and in friendship, they are wish-granting creepers. (53)
In the channels dwell the sacred rivers and lakes; in the bellies dwell all the Kāśyapas; and in the intestines dwell [the gods] within the body of the virtuous. (54)
Śilāda and Prahlāda were on his two thighs;
Bali and Vāmana were on his two knees; the worlds of the Nāgas were on his two shanks; and Śeṣa and the Tortoise were on his two feet. (55)
The Śaktis reside in all the joints during a righteous war; the attendants abide within the bodily constituents during the honoring of the virtuous. ||56||
In the case of the practitioner, the supernatural powers reside in *dhāraṇā*, while in meditation (*dhyāna*), I am Hari;
I am the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, dwelling in identity with the practitioner.
Indeed, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is present among the virtuous; He is never absent from the virtuous form of the lady of the household in any way whatsoever. (58)
One should thus cultivate the virtuous and likewise always serve them;
for one who offers everything to them, liberation is held in the palm of the hand. (59)
O virtuous woman, having thus meditated, one should worship and serve the virtuous;
at the time of awakening in the morning, one should perform the massaging of the body.
Once she has risen, one should offer her water and present a tooth-stick;
one should also give her a water vessel for the purpose of bodily purification.
One should cause the hands to be washed and have the vessel purified with divine waters as desired, using fragrant water from sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should first cause a bath with sandalwood water mixed with fragrant oils,
and then bathe [the image] with powdered sesame seeds.
One should thoroughly rub the image with powders of *āmalaka* and other fruits,
and then bathe it with milk as well as with pure water.
One should wipe the body with cloths and likewise sprinkle it with fragrant scents;
one should provide garments, ornaments, decoration, and garlands and the like.
Then, with flowers, auspicious powders, saffron, unbroken rice, and sandalwood,
one should offer incense, a lamp, a forehead mark (tilaka), and a moon-mark (candraka).
One should have the colors, forms, and so forth prepared, and should paint the excellent image;
one should apply collyrium to the eyes and oil to the hair as well. (67)
One should offer him a seat, such as a wooden plank, and a lion-throne;
likewise, one should offer the invocation, water for the feet, and water for sipping.
One should offer the *arghya* and the *madhuparka* along with flavorful juices to the illustrious virtuous one;
one should also present the food offering (*naivedya*), water, betel-leaf, fruit, and leaves. (69)
One should give a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), a girdle (mekhalā), and a meditation-band (yogapaṭṭaka);
one should give a woolen blanket (kambala) and a leather mat (naktaka), and place a cluster of flowers (puṣpaguccha) in the hand.
One should offer as an oblation sweet food, fragrant edibles,
and even milk— the essence of milk— which is delicious, along with *pūrikās* and curds.
One should offer buttermilk and water, and likewise offer mouth-fresheners;
one should offer a couch, a mount, a vehicle, sandals, and a parasol.
One should provide a bed and cause him to lie down, and likewise offer him a fan;
one should perform the massaging of his feet and the rubbing of his body, and act as his servant. (73)
Whatever may be required, whether physical or mental,
whether manifest or unmanifest, one should fulfill that which is desired.
In this way, one should perform service to the virtuous, which is purifying and bestows prosperity;
for by him, I myself am directly worshipped, and thus this entire creation is honored. (75)
By him all merit has been performed, and likewise all sacred pilgrimage sites have been visited;
one should drink the divine water from the feet of the virtuous, which purifies even the most holy places.
By that service, every sacred ford, vow, and gift has been performed;
he by whom the holy man is propitiated, by him Kṛṣṇa is propitiated. (77)
He by whom Kṛṣṇa has been propitiated rejoices in the abode of Brahmā;
having become composed of supreme bliss, he enjoys all desires. (78)
For householders on this earth, there exists no other means for the sake of liberation that is more excellent, equal, or as simple as pleasing the virtuous. (79)
Since they are destroyers of all sins, devoted to the character of Hari, dedicated to the vow of Brahman, and because they are great devotees of the Lord; ||4.91.80||
Listen, dear wives, to how a householder should satisfy his wife:
by giving everything to her, he should satisfy his wife. (8.1)
Just as a householder satisfies his son or daughter by granting their desires, so too should he satisfy a virtuous person by fulfilling their wishes. 82.
Just as a householder, having first offered [food] to his brother, father, and master, satisfies a worthy guest, so too should one daily satisfy a virtuous person by giving what is desired. 83.
A householder should make whatever great expenditure he makes solely for the sake of honoring [the virtuous];
if he does so for the sake of the righteous, he shall partake in liberation.
One should place a beautiful floral crown upon the head of the virtuous one, and offer him a flower-made or thread-woven covering-cloth. (89)
One should fasten flower-bracelets on the arms and the forearms;
one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony provided with many wicks.
One should perform circumambulation and joyfully prostrate like a staff;
one should place one's head at [the deity's] feet and cause one's hands to rest upon the crown of the head.
One should enjoy the favor of the virtuous and maintain their auspicious blessings;
one should offer a handful of flowers to the virtuous and bestow gifts according to one's means. (88)
Thus, O beautiful lady, by the service of a saintly person, all sins of householders are destroyed in every way through the power of association with the virtuous. (89)
One may even obtain the merit of the virtuous, which bestows prosperity and grants liberation; one should pray to the virtuous and seek their forgiveness in their presence. (4.91.90)
O ocean of compassion, O ocean of mercy, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge;
O virtuous one, you are indeed the refuge for us, who are among the ranks of the wicked. 9.1
I do not know the means of accomplishment, nor do I perform meritorious deeds; there is no worship that destroys sin, nor is there any practice that bestows liberation. (92)
In this most difficult forest of worldly existence, you are my refuge for those who have no refuge;
you act as a boat, a savior, in the ocean of saṃsāra. (93)
For the sake of destroying all sins, for the sake of liberation, and for the cause of happiness, O virtuous one, you are the very form of Kṛṣṇa; I take refuge in you, the body of Hari. 94.
We have fallen eternally into the terrible mire of saṃsāra;
you are capable of lifting us up by washing us clean—please lift us up! 95.
O Holy One, whatever was deficient in worship or service, or performed out of order, or lacking in respect—forgive that in me who has sought refuge in you. (96)
Oṃ, salutations to the Guru, the God, the holy one, the Supreme Self;
repeated salutations to the one who has the form of our own deity and who is the deliverer. 97.
Having thus entreated him, paid homage, and offered the teacher’s fee, he should dismiss him, saying: "O ascetic, may you always be well-disposed toward us. (98)
Come here always and accept my worship;
grant me worldly enjoyment, liberation, and prosperity—have mercy on me. (99)
One should contemplate the perfected one (sādhū) thus dismissed as having the form of Hari;
in this way, through the vow of a perfected one, liberation stands within the grasp of the two perfected women (sādhvī).
At the time of death, those who are devoted to the holy ones go together with those very holy ones to the supreme, imperishable, divine abode by means of celestial chariots. 101.
A man or a virtuous woman should perform this worship of the Holy One every year or every month; thus they shall attain all their desires. (102)
Wherever the feet of a saintly person are placed, that home is like Goloka;
those who are devotees of the saint are his attendants (pārṣadas), and those women are indeed liberated souls (muktānikās). || 10.3 ||
From reading or hearing this, the fruit of worshipping the virtuous shall arise;
at the end, through devotion, one shall also attain the abode of Brahman—of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Association with Holy and Virtuous Persons is the Supreme Means for Liberation for Householders Devoid of All Religious Duties and Rituals," in the *Gṛhagītā* within the fourth section, the *Tiṣyasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The illustrious Śrī Mādhavī and Prajñā said:
"O Blessed One, O Ocean of Compassion, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
We have become fulfilled by hearing the majesty of the virtuous. (1)
Now, O Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, Mādhava,
we desire to perform all the Jayantīs (festivals) arising from your birth.
"Give us your command, O Lord, O Master; we shall perform a great festival.
By witnessing this unprecedented festival, the liberation of living beings may occur. || 3 ||
The venerable Vyāsa Śvetāyana said:
The sages, beginning with Anādikṛṣṇa, accepted the name of Śrī Nārāyaṇa as their goal;
having received his command, he gave them permission to perform the festival of his own manifestation for them.
In his twenty-second year, on the first half of the dark fortnight of Kārttika,
the eighth lunar day arrived for the successful celebration of his victory festival.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, his father, suddenly prepared an excellent pavilion, auspiciously fashioned from gold and silver.
He also placed a vast tent made of cloth, one yojana in length,
and a golden elephant-throne within the pavilion for Hari.
Lomaśa likewise caused a sacrificial pit to be constructed for the purpose of the oblation;
Lomaśa then prepared all the necessary implements and other requirements.
Brahmapriyā and the other women prepared cooked foods;
likewise, Padmāvatī’s beloveds and other favorites of Hari did the same.
Then, in the pavilion, the venerable elder brother of Hari arranged all the seating places for the assembly.
His brother Śuka was the second who stood there to welcome them;
and the Kumārīs, headed by Santuṣṭā, offered a welcome to the goddesses. || 1 ||

On the morning of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the guardians of the sacrificial hearths arrived from all the worlds in their own celestial chariots for the purpose of bestowing blessings upon Kṛṣṇa.
At the hour of Brahmā, millions of musical instruments resounded,
and the songs of women were heard in the early morning.
The Vedic chants of the Brahmins resounded, centered upon benedictions,
while the songs of the Apsarases accompanied by dance took place all around.
And the songs of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Kiṃpuruṣas, as well as the auspicious praises of the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bards. (19)
At that time, there were excellent poetic compositions by the best of poets,
as well as narrative tales from the Vidyādharas and the Cāraṇas.
During the festival of Jayantī, there were theatrical performances by the learned, hymns of praise by the virtuous, and songs celebrating the names of chaste women.
In the morning, Śrī Hari, the perpetual celibate, having abandoned his yogic sleep and hearing the sounds of divine musical instruments and other noises, bathed in the waters of the lake.
He donned a beautiful attire, ornaments, and articles of adornment.
Adorned with fragrant substances, Hari shone brilliantly with all the auspicious *candrakas*.
His mother, Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī, applied a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) upon her son—
a *candraka* made of saffron and sandalwood paste, combined with *kesara* powder.
The contented sister placed a dot of unhusked rice on the forehead of Hari;
his father placed a garland of gold and jewels around the neck of his son.
Then, thus adorned, Kṛṣṇa approached the pavilion.
Lomaśa arrived there, accompanied by the materials for worship;
saluted by all, he quickly recited the auspicious blessings,
as well as the declaration of a holy day (*puṇyāha*) and prosperity (*svasti*), followed by the worship of Gaṇeśa.

The king of sages then performed the purification of the body, the sprinkling of water, and applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) and the crescent moon-mark (candraka) of Hari upon his forehead; thereafter, he bestowed his blessings.
Lomaśa placed a beautiful garland of flowers around the neck of Kṛṣṇa.
Then the mother, the father, the kinsmen, and the family members [placed it] upon his forehead. || 25 ||
They applied a tilaka-mark with unbroken grains of rice and placed barley sprouts upon their ears;
then they uttered words of blessing, and thereafter Brahmā indeed approached.
Having applied the *tilaka* and placed a necklace upon his neck, he offered praise;
having prostrated, he took his seat, and then Viṣṇu approached him.
[He presented] the necklace, the divine crown, the earrings, and the Kaustubha gem.
Having given [these], he bowed down, and then Śambhu approached Hari.
Having bowed and offered a garland of flowers, he drew a beautiful crescent moon upon his forehead.
Then Indra and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas and the stainless Sādhus, [did likewise].
Sanaka and the others worshipped Śrī Hari with great reverence;
Nārada and the other sages, as well as Sūrya and the others, applied the tilaka. (4.92.30)
The world-protectors, the ancestors, the gandharvas, and likewise the kinnaras; the kiṃpuruṣas, humans, brahmins, the virtuous, and those who dwell in the waters. || 31 ||
The sacred fords, the oceans, the rivers, as well as trees and creepers;
the gods, the Daityas, and the Dānavas; and the devoted Sūtas and Māgadhas. (32)
The Cāraṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, others, Śaivas, the Gaṇas, the Pārṣadas, Apsarases, deities, goddesses, virtuous women, and yogis. || 33 ||
Yoginīs, groups of courtesans, and women who are devotees; men and women of the various castes and stages of life; Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and bards. || 34 ||
The learned Vidyādharas, full of eagerness, worshipped Kṛṣṇa;
as did the Nāgas, the aquatic creatures, and those born from the womb and those born from sweat. || 35 ||
Then the divine ones, possessing celestial bodies, worshipped the Supreme Lord;
the great liberated souls and their wives performed the waving of lights (ārātrika). || 3.6 ||
Then, during that festival, the rivers performed the consecration at his feet,
and all the gods, the most excellent of those worthy of honor, presented him with offerings.
May we both live long, O Kṛṣṇa; may there be well-being and welfare for you.
May health, wealth, and abundant sovereign powers be yours.
May you always possess the quality of being a refuge, compassion, the granting of liberation, the expansion of your lineage, and the sovereignty over the God of Gods. (39)
"May you have every kind of happiness from that treasure-trove of all bliss and joy"—
thus did the gods and others likewise utter words of benediction.
Then Lomaśa offered a welcome, honor, and words of praise;
so too did all the women who were dear to Brahmā and dear to Hari. ||41||
Rādhā, Ramā, Śrī, Kamalā, Vṛndā, Pāśavatī, Priyā, Māṇikī, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, Bhūḥ, Līlā, Bhūti, and Śāradā. ||42||
Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, Saṃjñā, Gāyatrī, and Bhagavatpriyā—these goddesses, as well as the wives of Īśvara and other women who are incarnations [of them]. ||43||
They worshipped the Supreme Soul and applied a tilaka mark upon His forehead;
they respectfully offered a salutation with joined palms and accepted the gesture of the destruction of their suffering.
They placed handfuls of flowers and unbroken rice-grains before Kṛṣṇa and addressed Hari:
"Live long! Be the bestower of bliss upon Satī, Sāvitrī, Śakti, and Īśāna."
"Bestower of prosperity and bestower of liberation, dwell unswervingly within our hearts!"—
thus did they offer this blessing to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
They performed the *ārārtrika* rite and drank water from his feet;
then Hari, having risen, paid homage to the men and women.
Nourished by those of great fortune, I repeatedly bow to the Supreme Lords, my gurus, the elders, the Mothers, the goddesses, and the gods and others. 48.
Out of compassion, I bow here to those who have assembled for my sake;
may all you guardians of the celestial spheres be happy and endowed with prosperity. (49)
And they possess extensive lineages, as well as sovereignty over the abodes of the world;
they are fearless, and their excellence consists in the abundance of the enjoyment of stainless bliss and happiness.
Having spoken thus, O King, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa sat upon his own throne, summoned the assembly of venerable persons, and bestowed many gifts. 5.1.
First, he gave jewels of every kind to all the lords of creation;
thereafter, he bestowed them upon the virtuous, the brahmins, and the bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists.
Monks, girls, boys, yogins, virtuous women, female and male servants, attendants, men, and women—all of them [he addressed]. (53)
Having bowed down again and again, Hari gave them wealth of great value,
as well as appropriate gifts of grace, ornaments, vessels, and garments.
Then Kṛṣṇa quickly gave the order for the dismissal of the assembly;
thereafter, he provided them with various and excellent foods.
The Lord, his father, mother, and kinsmen caused [the rites] to be performed; they gratified Īśa and the other deities with sweet foods and drinks.
By the offering of mouth-fresheners, by the giving of rest-places and seats, by various forms of service, by acts of hospitality, and by appropriate conduct; ||57||
On the eighth day of the twenty-second year, on the anniversary of his birth, the inhabitants of the three worlds desired to become embodied there.
At the time following midday, they prayed to Acyuta Hari to come and purify their own worlds.
"So be it," Hari said, and he dismissed the assembly.
Having received their leave, they all departed for their respective worlds, with the exception of the Unborn One.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā indeed remained there in his abode in happiness;
all the others, with joy, departed for their respective dwellings by means of celestial chariots.
Now, O lords of sages, hear this wonder that occurred there:
the king of the city of Vardhamāna was named Purañjana.
Other kings also arrived for the great festival of his birth, just as they had come;
meanwhile, at night, Purañjana experienced a prolonged dream.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, during the auspicious hour presided over by Brahmā,
the king saw himself fallen into a blazing fire in a dream.
The terrifying messengers of Yama indeed led him to the southern city of Yama,
which is established for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of all one's actions.
Having observed the sins of the king, Dharmarāja assigned him punishment:
"You who have stolen the wealth, children, and wives of others, you shall be the noose of Time (Kālapāśaka)."
"O you who deceive men and women, eat in the terrible hell of Tāmisra," said the Lord Yama; "become one who goes to Andhatāmisra."
Since you cause harm to living beings and are a perpetrator of violence, go to Raurava;
since you merely sustain your own body and are no giver, become a dweller in Mahāraurava.
You, who have taken the lives of beasts, birds, and living beings, go to the Kumbhīpāka hell!
You, who have betrayed your ancestors, Brahmins, and the Veda, go to the Kālasūtra hell! 6.9
"You are indeed a supporter of heretics; enter the forest of sword-leaves. You who inflict punishment upon those who should not be punished, fall into the mouth of a boar! (4.92.70)
Since you cause pain to living beings, may you fall into a blind well;
since you have abandoned the five great sacrifices, may you fall into a pit of worms.
O stealer of gold and jewels, fall into the Sandaśa hell!
O you who have gone to those who should not be approached, indeed, become one who has entered the Tigmaśūrmī [hell]! 72.
You are a supporter of heretics; fall into the Vaitaraṇī river by all means!
Devoid of purity and right conduct, become one who dwells in the mire of pus! 73.
"You are indeed addicted to hunting; go to a place of violent slaughter!
You are a speaker of untruthful words; go headfirst down into the Avīci hell! (74)
O drinker of intoxicants, become one who drinks the fire of blood;
you, the perpetrator of contempt toward the guru, fall into the mire of caustic matter.
"Since you cause universal distress, indeed, become a venomous serpent!
Since you have destroyed the worship of a virtuous guest, become a diamond-beaked bird! (76)
Having spoken thus, Yama addressed the messengers of Yama to lead the king away, saying:
"O messengers of Yama, you have given him suffering through beatings and likewise through mutilations. (77)
By means of killings, burnings with fire, grinding, and likewise cutting; by means of making one drink fire, administering poison, and the application of caustic alkali; ||78||
By means of throat-obstructions, intestinal extractions, repeated blows from vajras, traversing thorns and the like, and being dragged across the ground by weapons; 79.
With copper bands and flames, as well as with hanging nooses,
with the shedding of sword-leaves, and with the pouring forth of pus and blood.
Having experienced such sufferings for a long time in his dream, O King, he was cast out, exiled, and deprived of his inheritance. (8.1)
He indeed returned to his own residence in Vardhamānapura, where he was honored by the people, including the king and the subjects, with great enthusiasm. ||82||
Afterwards, having rested while seated upon the royal throne, he set out on a journey to Kuṅkumavāpī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa on another day.
On the day of his birth anniversary, having celebrated a great festival there, he received his leave; yet he did not even wake from his sleep until that time. 84.
The king grieved in many ways: "What is this terrible dream?
I shall ask the Supreme Soul about everything that was seen. ||85||
King Purañjaya quickly informed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa of the events and grieved for a moment. ||86||
The beginningless Śrī Hari said: "In the past, you were a king who committed sins;
later, you became a devotee here, though formerly you were a great sinner. (87)
The fruit of your sin, which lasted for the duration of a thousand yugas, has indeed all gone to destruction for the sake of your enjoyment in the world of Yama. (88)
O King, by means of my support, whatever portion of food was consumed by you during the dream at night, all of it has indeed been eaten; not even a remnant remains for you.
Now, therefore, receive my mantra with a pure disposition;
having become liberated, go indeed to the imperishable abode, the supreme state.
O King, you have fallen into the fire; no life remains for you.
Go to my imperishable abode in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa gave the mantra to the lord of the earth:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (92)
He gave water; he gave his own water produced from the washing of his feet.
The king drank that water from the feet and indeed became possessed of divine vision.
And through the compassion of Hari, he became one who transcends the conduct of illusion;
indeed, he drew back all the functions of the horses that are the senses.
Quickly established in the state of Brahman, he worshipped the Supreme Lord; filled with supreme devotion, he paid homage to the sages, the virtuous, and the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having given instructions to his own servants,
he arrived there in a body by means of a divine, radiant, and liberated celestial chariot accompanied by auspiciousness.
While all embodied beings were looking on, he quickly went to the imperishable abode;
indeed, having heard of the punishments bestowed by Yama, all his followers [followed him]. 97.
Those groups of servants abandoned their faults and sins;
there was a cry of victory for the king, and then the funeral rites were performed.
All the king’s attendants received the mantra from Acyuta, and they also received the names of the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 99.
"O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Svāmikṛṣṇa, O Ādikṛṣṇa, O Lord, O All-pervading One!
Thus they offered praise and departed toward their own city.
They spoke to the king and attained liberation; thereafter, they went to Lord Hari.
Thus, this circular marvel occurred there, as I have described.
By reading, hearing, or remembering this, one shall become a partaker of liberation;
having abandoned illusion and sins, he went to the world of Brahmā. 102.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival on the Birthday of Śrī Hari, the Twenty-second Incarnation; and King Purañjaya, Lord of Vardhamānapura, Experiencing All the Torments of Hell in a Dream and His Subsequent Swift Liberation in the Presence of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Padmāvatī and Prajñā said:
"O Lord Hari-Kṛṣṇa-Svāmin-Nārāyaṇa, who is dear to his devotees!
Why was Brahmā, the Grandfather, protected here in your presence?"
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: In the city of Śarkarā, I am the great Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; having accepted the prayers of the lords of the gods, the ancestors, the nāgas, and others.
Then, having observed them, the Blessed One spoke to them so that they might go from there to their respective abodes; he himself desired to go to the abode of the Unborn (Ajāspada).
In the month of Kārtika, in order to go to Satyaloka together with Brahmā and for the fulfillment of Brahmā’s mental desire, we indeed took our stand near him.
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Brahmā, having bowed down to me, Hari,
while seated comfortably, asked the cause of his own cessation.
There, I made my announcement and reminded him of that purpose,
together with all those who are dear to Brahmā and dear to Hari, beginning with [the goddesses] Priyā and others.
Having made his request to the Lord of the abode (Ishana) to go to the Creator (Vedhas),
Brahma also obtained his grace and was exceedingly satisfied at that very moment.
There he reported his own beneficial proposal as was appropriate:
"O Blessed One, please cause the Festival of Lamps to be celebrated by me in Satyaloka. (8)
With devotion, I shall offer heaps of food and divine enjoyments;
for there will be the attainment of service to Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī.
There, service shall be rendered to all those who dwell in truth,
and there shall also be a vision of all your women.
"O Blessed Lord, O Master, quickly perform that which is desired;
then, at my pleasure, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa will remove his ignorance. (11)
He fully accepted what was spoken by Brahmā; therefore, remain ready today along with all the women and your satisfied sister.
Together with my maidservants and attendants, the great sages headed by Lomaśa, and my personal associates and groups of servants, I am ready.
The illustrious Vyāsa Śvetāyana said:
Having performed the Ekādaśī vow, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe,
[ascended] a celestial chariot one hundred yojanas in extent, which could move through subtle states of being.
He suddenly expanded in the sky that divine city named Hiraṇyabrahma, which was equal to Vaikuṇṭha and worthy of being the seat for all. 15.
In this celestial chariot, which is enriched with all supernatural powers and all enjoyments and fulfills every desire, dwells the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī.
He sat down quickly, attended by all his male and female servants; then, at the command of Hari, there arose a tumultuous sound for the purpose of the procession.
In the city of Kuṅkumavāpī, there arose on all sides a fragrance rising upward;
likewise, the women were adorned with every kind of fine attire and brought forth ornaments and garments.
Adorned with every ornament, they stood near the vehicle;
he gave them his command, and they quickly ascended the celestial chariot.
Śrī Hari, having bowed down to his two parents in the celestial chariot,
was accompanied by Brahmā and Lomaśa in a second form.
He shone resplendent with his virtuous attendants and all his beloveds; then musical instruments were played, and showers of flowers and sandalwood fell.
From the sky there arose shouts of victory;
then, at the holy Badarikāśrama, [he beheld] Śrī Narāyaṇa at Śrī Badarī.
Having heard the sounds through her divine power, she asked for the story of Śrī Hari;
whereupon Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa told her about his departure.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O beloved of Badarī; after the liberation of Purañjana, Kṛṣṇa performed the twenty-second festival of His own birth, proceeding toward the shore of Satyaloka.
There, everyone, including the servants, became ready to depart;
on the twelfth day, having taken their meals, they boarded the celestial chariot and went to the lake.
Having bowed to the step-well and the fields, and having also bowed to him who is the very embodiment of their own devotion,
men and women, filled with joy, set out through the sky for the sake of the pilgrimage.
The celestial chariot, accompanied by the sounds of victory,
having momentarily released the clouds, moved slowly through the sky as it took the lead.
By the speed of his mind, he reached the earth, heaven, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka in a single moment; for that was indeed a great wonder.
An announcement was made everywhere by all the women, the male and female servants, and the Vegadarśins, that the Blessed One had set out on his journey. ||29||
In an instant, that news spread everywhere throughout all the worlds;
and the yogis, the deities, and those with divine knowledge also learned of it in an instant.
They came from their own abodes to Satyaloka in order to lead Hari away;
Kṛṣṇa, for his part, told them in due order to return as was appropriate.
Then, O virtuous lady, when Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival occurred in Satyaloka, a great joy arose among the inhabitants of Satyaloka. 32.
Welcome, eternal sons of Brahmā residing in Satyaloka, as well as the Siddhas such as Sanatkumāra and others who hold authority in Satya! ||33||
There, the gods performed musical instruments and worship for Hari with offerings such as fruits, unbroken grains, beautiful flowers, parched grain, fragrant substances, and excellent liquids.
Brahmā fashioned the entire city of Brahmā, adorned with ornaments,
with its roads sprinkled with fragrant scents and resplendent with banners and flags.
It was beautiful with golden jars, adorned with necklaces and archways,
and decorated by well-attired celestial women who were embodiments of truth.
It was then resplendent with svastikas and other auspicious symbols placed within its temple-halls,
and beautified by gateways adorned with many branches of plantain pillars.
It was crowded with many celestial chariots, vehicles, and swans,
and it was exceedingly beautiful, resounding with various divine musical instruments.
It was adorned by the gods of truth, goddesses, and celestial nymphs,
and its armies were arrayed in the forms of lions, tigers, swans, elephants, and deer.
It was strewn on all sides with divine flowers and clusters of blossoms,
and it shone with houses and palaces resplendent with auspicious curds.
Welcomed by women holding unbroken grains, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, she was granted peace by the dwellings and crossroads beautified by artificial gardens. (41)
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [established] the true city of Brahmā, which is resplendent with rows of wish-fulfilling trees of desire, by means of the Creator. 42.
Being led forth, strengthened and honored by the gods,
Śrī Hari entered after having circled the vast and true [city] that measured a hundred thousand yojanas.
Having stabilized the celestial chariot, he ascended the swan-vehicle;
Brahmā then led Śrī Parameśvara to the abode of Brahmā.
Brahmā and the sons of Brahmā, the great sages beginning with Sanaka, as well as Ṛbhu, Nārada, and others, worshipped the Supreme Lord. ||45||
Eagerly, they drank the nectar of his feet and performed the ritual circumambulation;
then, having offered necklaces, ornaments, sandalwood paste, and other gifts, they praised him.
O Blessed One, by your grace this world of truth has been purified;
we are not capable of serving you—forgive our lack of ability, O Acyuta. (47)
Brahmā led Śrī Puruṣottama to his divine assembly hall;
there the Blessed One found rest and was fed with nectar and other delicacies. 48.
Then there were women who were Sāvitrīs, Gāyatrīs, and Sarasvatīs;
virtuous wives and perfected beings (siddhas), and even crores of celestial goddesses.
There they worshipped Śrī Hari, as well as Śrī Māṇikī,
Ramā, Lakṣmī, Prajñā, Pāśavatī, Rādhā, and the virtuous Śāradā.
They indeed worshipped the wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and presented various divine offerings produced from them. 51.
Then they performed the ritual waving of lights (ārārtika) and fed the goddesses, all the beloved wives of Brahmā and others, as well as all the male and female servants. || 52 ||
In these rest-houses, the divine ladies provided them with such repose; they, who bestow all things, performed a worship worthy of the Blessed One.
The great sages performed service for the women with offerings from all sides;
Brahmā became fulfilled, and Sāvitrī and the others were filled with joy.
Then the virtuous ones, Sanaka and the others, having achieved their purpose,
remained for a mere moment on the earth, O beloved of Badrī, in the Brahman-satya.
Indeed, for an ordinary human being, it truly extends for ten thousand ages;
but for those who possess yoga and are devoted to the Blessed One, it is not of such a nature.
It is not so for the lords of the world, and even less so for Śrī Hari;
by whom length was created in time, and likewise dwarfhood was brought about. (57)
Since this [world] is dependent upon his will, what room is there for the calculation of time?
O beloved of Badrī, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, having fulfilled the mind of Brahmā, [remained]. 58.
Then she went to the temples of the gods commanded by Brahmā;
previously, she had gone to the palaces of the holy ones, such as Sanaka and others.
And Nārāyaṇa went even to the excellent hermitages of the great-souled Siddhas, who were steadfast in their vows of Brahmanic conduct.
Honored by assemblies of virtuous men, the Blessed One then proceeded from the houses of householders to the temples of the deities presiding over the conclusion of truth.
Honored and saluted by all, fed with food of the same flavor as nectar,
and honored with the waving of lights, he was strengthened and returned once more to the abode of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā and the other gods performed the great worship of Dhanalakṣmī;
on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, they performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
On the occasion of Dīpāvalī, ten million Siddhas, ten million Sādhus, lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhikas), and ten million Brahmakotis performed the great worship of Śāradā-Śrī.
Ṛbhu performed the lustration ceremony, and Brahmā also honored him with joy;
Sāvitrī and other virtuous women performed the worship of Lakṣmī.
They performed the consecration with divine essences such as nectar and the like,
and with all varieties of perfumes and all types of ornaments.
They created for the goddess Lakṣmī a total splendor of attire and beauty,
and a world of truth (Satyaloka) resplendent with tens of millions of rows of Brahma-lamps.
They performed [the rites] on all sides with multitudes of lamps by those of meritorious soul,
along with the great joy of dance and song, nectar and other such sweet foods.
The female attendants produced great majesty and supreme bliss;
Brahmā performed the festival of the mountain of food, abounding in many articles.
He brought forth from Satyaloka multitudes of cooked foods filled with excellent nectar—
every kind of sweet dish as well as salty dishes.
There were savory foods, various kinds of snacks and meals, as well as lickable delicacies rich in flavor and diverse drinks. (7.1)
All kinds of foods to be relished and the finest things to be sucked, as well as those that are bitter, sweet, sour, and pungent, and even those that have been served up. (72)
All the auxiliary ingredients should be coarse and dry;
they should be roasted, prepared, and endowed with divine fragrance and flavor.
Delightful leaves of the *śāka* plant, various vegetables drenched in juices,
all kinds of bulbous roots, and whatever fruits and flowers there may be— 74.
Forms of the most excellent kind, fashioned with every artistic skill, were placed in golden vessels and great platters numbering in the tens of millions and hundreds of billions.
And waters in excellent divine vessels and jars,
as well as fruits, flowers, seeds, and flower-clusters in their very presence.
Having prepared them, they also placed the pods in the presence of Śrī Hari;
there Kṛṣṇa shone upon a golden swan-throne together with Brahma’s beloved consort and the other goddesses.
Commanded by Brahmā and honored by Sāvitrī and the others, the Blessed One—the husband of Śrī, Prajñā, and Mādhavī—enjoyed the praiseworthy foods. (78)
