They fed the Lord of Lords and received the mantra of Hari;
they also gave him leave to depart, and thereafter Hari became ready.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, Kṛṣṇa joyfully went to Mount Lokāloka to sport,
to behold it, and to show its various regions to the women.
Mountains, the paths of the planets, forests,
and groves were traversed with speed by means of circumambulation and travel in celestial chariots.
Then, having gazed upon the Lokāloka mountain and beheld the golden ground,
he returned to Śrī Hari at Kuṅkumavāpikā in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Thus, O Badrikā, the great Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having purified the worlds of the earth by His grace, [purified] their inhabitants as well. (57)
Having become solitary, he observed the Cāturmāsya vow in his own palace; it was the anniversary of his own birth at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The twenty-fifth day of the dark fortnight of this month of Kārtika has arrived;
on that day, his father Gopālakṛṣṇa performed a golden festival.
He constructed a golden pavilion, truly unprecedented and exceedingly beautiful,
bound on all sides with jewels and gems like the imperishable abode itself.
Having bathed and adorned himself, Kṛṣṇa arrived and sat upon a divine elephant-throne; then Lomaśa honored him.
In the morning, musical instruments were played, along with songs and auspicious hymns,
for the gods who had descended in the form of pearls and for the embodied lords.
O Bādari, at that time, the sounds of the Vedas arose everywhere from all the inhabitants of the world, and likewise from the sages on all sides.
The morning fire-sacrifices of the great sages indeed took place in the place of the Imperishable;
thereafter, the worship of Hari proceeded there in due order.
The incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, and the great seers;
likewise the ancestors, the gods, the Daityas, the Dānavas, and the Rākṣasas.
Then there were humans, nāgas, serpents, yakṣas, siddhas, and cāraṇas; as well as sūtas, māgadhas, kiṃpuruṣas, and kinnaras. ||66||
Bandins, Vedic Brahmins, kings, those with the bodies of Vaiśyas, male slaves, female slaves, as well as sacred fords and deities; ||67||
The hosts of Apsarases, as well as the attendants and courtesans,
worshipped the Supreme Soul and presented them with auspicious gifts.
They then applied a forehead mark with saffron, as well as with unbroken grains and sandalwood paste, and thereafter bestowed their blessing, saying, "May you live long! (69)
Then they performed the nightly lamp-offering and indeed gave gifts;
at that time, all the women performed worship.
Then the father gave gifts of jewels and gems,
gifts of cows, and gifts of minerals as well as gold.
Lomaśa also bestowed alms consisting of bowls, ornaments, garments, and other items in numbers such as ten million and a hundred billion, and he granted him supreme blessings.
At the conclusion of the worship, Lakṣmī and the other beloveds of Brahmā fed all the great ones (mahīmānas) and then gave them their leave to depart. ||73||

Whatever has come together and been obtained in all ways throughout all worlds—be it gold, silver, or many other forms of material wealth—is indeed of the nature of a burden during one's wandering. (74)
Diamonds, gems, and various kinds of jewels,
as well as diverse pearls, vessels, and garments.
The father, who was compassionate toward the distressed, gave everything in charity to the brahmins, to the poor, to beggars, and likewise to virtuous women and the righteous. (76)
Then, at that time, he gave sweet food in every way to women, to men, and to the helpless, and indeed to everyone.
He also gave them a parting gift, and from that there was a cessation [of hostilities]. Having taken their leave of Kṛṣṇa, all the gods departed for their own abodes.
All those embodied beings of the cosmic egg went to their own respective worlds;
and the lords, beginning with Virāṭ, prayed to Acyuta.
Hari said, "So be it," to those who were coming from their own worlds;
on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Hari became ready.
O Badrī, Keśava, assuming two forms, set out with all his excellent followers and those lords in a great, divine celestial chariot.
Having become the Blessed One as before, the Supreme Lord set out swiftly through the sky,
proceeding amidst shouts of victory and auspicious sounds.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Wanderings through the Kingdoms of the Sovereigns of the Seven Continents, such as Jambū and Plakṣa, in the Tiṣya Lineage within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, and the Celebration of the Festival for His Twenty-fifth Birth Anniversary at Kuṅkumavāpī. || 98 ||
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
O Badrikā, in a mere moment, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa reached the further shore of Truth and completely transcended even the eight coverings.
Having reached the world of Vairāja by means of that most divine celestial chariot composed of great splendor, Hari dwelt there together with Vairāja.
Honored there in the palace of Vairāja, he dwelt;
and then Vairāja, together with Vairājñī, raised him up.
The subjects of Vairājī also worshipped him with divine offerings;
they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony for Hari and presented great gifts before him.
They propitiated Hari repeatedly with offerings of everything they possessed;
according to the divine manner of the lords, they served Acyuta.
The sons of Vairāja were also Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
there were also eight-faced Brahmās, as well as those with a hundred faces and those with ten thousand faces.
Those with a hundred thousand faces and those with ten million faces likewise served Hari;
as did the three-eyed Śaṅkaras and the Śivas with fifty-one eyes.
They have ninety-nine eyes, or one thousand eyes and so forth;
they have ten thousand eyes and so forth, or excellent vision numbering one hundred thousand and more.
Even those with a single eye on their forehead and the Sadāśivas served them;
likewise, the Brahmāṇīs and the Śivās were also of that same nature.
They served the women of Brahmā and they served Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, there were Viṣṇus with eight arms and even those with hundreds of thousands of arms.
And likewise, millions of crores of Vaiṣṇava women,
endowed with such [powers], served the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with total self-surrender.
In all the Nija worlds during the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa,
and Pauṣa, they brought Kṛṣṇa to the fourteenth star-stations.
They led Hari, Nārāyaṇa, through twenty-eight enclosures and fifty-six grounds, and then through double that number of enclosures.
They welcomed him, performed acts of worship, and presented offerings;
they also fed him with desirable, divine foods.
They caused him to wander through their various kingdoms;
meanwhile, the Blessed One, having received his leave, attained the great abode of Mahāviṣṇu.
The illustrious Supreme Lord went to the auspicious golden abode;
O Badrikā, I shall tell you of the divine wonder that occurred there. 16.
Then Mahāviṣṇu, possessing the glorious form of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
appeared in the form of his own father and vanished from the body of his father.
Likewise, Mahālakṣmī remained within the body of the illustrious Kaṃbharā;
she was seen in the form of Śrīkaṃbharā and then vanished.
The son, Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, was worshipped by his parents with great devotion because he had manifested from them. (19)
Beholding that supreme marvel, Brahmā’s beloved wife and the others then perceived their two forms as both mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Seeing their mother-in-law and father-in-law in embodied form, Padmāvatī’s beloved attained great joy and, as the daughter-in-law’s own children, they both paid homage to them.
For an entire month at a time, Hari dwelt in the house of Mahāviṣṇu,
accompanied by his entire retinue and honored by his father.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa always performed service for his parents, and all [the goddesses], beginning with Brahmapriyā, joyfully served them as well. (23)
Having taken his leave, Kṛṣṇa then went to the divine and enchanting abode of Lalitā Mahālakṣmī, the city of Śrī. 24.
Honored, saluted, served, and propitiated by him, Kṛṣṇa was gratified with the offerings and stayed there for another fortnight.
Then Śrī Lalitā entered the very form of Lalitā; and the other millions of female friends beheld their own beautiful bodies [within her].
Having beheld their own divine nature, and having received worship, food, and even a parting gift, they considered it a marvel. (27)
Having quickly gathered together with Kṛṣṇa,
they ascended the celestial chariot and went to the unmanifest state of the Infinite One.
Then, seeing the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who had arrived,
the Infinite Nārāyaṇa quickly offered him a grand welcome.
Accompanied by his excellent army, he bestowed honors worthy of the supreme sovereign Maheśvara;
and his wives, headed by Ramā, sang songs in praise of Kṛṣṇa.
In the indeterminate, auspicious abode, the palace of the Infinite (Bhūman), he constantly dwelt with Hari;
thus he worshipped Him for one month. ||3.1||
He always fed Kṛṣṇa along with his caravan with nectar and other foods;
then Hari, having received leave to depart, ascended the celestial chariot.
Accompanied by his caravan, he went to the abode of the nectar-like Vāsudeva;
for the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva indeed offered a welcome to Hari.
In the latter half of the month of Phālguna, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resided there in the beautiful temple of Vāsudeva, worshipped by innumerable Vaiṣṇavas.
In the month of Caitra, Kṛṣṇa went quickly to the abode of Aniruddha,
as well as to the palace of Pradyumna and also to the residence of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
He was honored with welcomes and other courtesies by all of them, including their own most divine armies and attendants, and worshiped with the presentation of ritual offerings. ||36||
Having been fed with the enjoyments of nectar and served with heartfelt devotion,
the Blessed One, having received his leave, ascended his own celestial chariot.
In the month of Vaiśākha, he quickly departed for Goloka, the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
there, Parakṛṣṇa was worshipped by Śrī Kṛṣṇa within his own realm. (38)
Hari was honored by all the hosts of Goloka, including the liberated souls (muktas), and the beloveds of Brahmā were served by countless women, beginning with Rādhā. (39)
Honored, fed, saluted, and gladdened, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa dwelt with joy in the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 40.40.
Then, having beheld that supreme wonder and recognized their own forms, Rādhā and the others quickly vanished from their respective appearances. (41)
Then they appeared and attained great bliss;
the wives of Kṛṣṇa served Kṛṣṇeśa for the sake of divine pleasure.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as well as the cowherds and cowherdesses by the hundreds of millions,
propitiated Hari and gratified the Imperishable One.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa also praised his own primordial source, the Supreme Cause,
the Śrī Paramātman who descends through various incarnations.
Since we are your incarnations, existing as distinct from your form, and are the lords of this abode here, homage forever to that Father! 45.
Salutations again and again to that Father, from whom even Rādhā and the others have become the empowered energies (praśaktis) of Your form, and have attained the status of being half of My own body.
And since there are also other incarnations of innumerable forms, salutation to that source of incarnations, the Father who is the Supreme Brahman. 47.
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, be gracious in every way toward Your own forms;
repeated salutations to that Father, whose command we here carry out. 48.
O Father, I shall always perform your worship here in every way;
I ever desire your grace, so that I may be purified and my life made meaningful.
Having thus praised Hari and bowed down to him, and having received his supreme grace,
Kṛṣṇa indeed granted leave of departure to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
In Caitra, however, Hari went by means of a celestial chariot to twenty-three other abodes established for his incarnations.
Through twenty-three incarnations in various abodes, the Lord of Abodes,
the Supreme Brahman, was worshipped, served with devotion, and fully propitiated.
Having been fed, presented with gifts, and praised, Hari was asked for forgiveness;
and having attained knowledge, he beheld that which reaches the limit of the Imperishable.
Having beheld the Fish-form, the Tortoise-form, and the Boar-form of Hari, as well as the Kapila-form and the Vāsudeva-form; ||54||
Having likewise beheld the abode of Pṛthu, and having gazed upon the abode of Dattātreya, and having also seen the abode of Haṃsa, and having beheld the abode of Nṛhari; ||55||
Having beheld the abode of Arṣabha, Vāmana, as well as the residence of Paraśurāma, the sacrificial abode of Rāma, and the abode of Kumāra; ||56||
Having beheld the Hāyagrīva, the Nāradīya, the Rājarājīya, as well as the Vyāsīya, the Kārṣṇa, another [text], and the Buddhist Dhāma; ||57||
Likewise, having beheld countless abodes and met their lords,
and having accepted the honors bestowed by them, he gratified those [lords] who were his own sons.
Having taken leave of all his attendants, he went by means of his own celestial chariot to the world of Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Nārāyaṇa, during the month of Vaiśākha. (59)
There, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by all the hosts of his male attendants and female attendants, offered a warm welcome.
Endowed with all devotion, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the utmost reverence,
[offering] necklaces, armlets, crowns, as well as ornaments such as the Kaustubha gem.
With divine garments, ornaments, and the like, along with unbroken grains, sandalwood paste, and other offerings,
he worshipped the Supreme Self and caused him to dwell in his palace.
All the goddesses of fortune, Śrī, Ramā, and others, served as maidservants;
and all the beloveds of Brahmā, being eager, offered them food.
They served Acyuta by massaging his feet and other such acts;
through hymns of praise and other services, they made Acyuta well-pleased.
They performed the nightly lamp-offering for Nārāyaṇa and for Śrī as well;
then Nārāyaṇa indeed granted a parting gift to Kṛṣṇa.
Hari went to the abode of Prakṛti by means of his own celestial chariot;
Mahāmāyā also performed an offering endowed with all the constituent principles (tattvas).
Then the Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and others worshipped the Lord of the Abode;
they drank the water from his feet and likewise offered him food.
Then Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa bestowed a parting gift upon the eldest [brother],
and he quickly departed by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) for the great abode of Sadāśiva.
There, the Lord Sadāśiva, accompanied by his attendants, offered a welcome to his own chosen deity at the place known as Nityakailāsadhāma. 69.
He worshipped that Hari with supreme affection and served him;
he also presented offerings and rendered Acyuta well-pleased.
Having received his farewell gift, Śrī Hari indeed departed by means of his own celestial chariot to the top of the water-sheath,
at the edge of the luminous sheath.
While [the city] known as Vaikuṇṭha, served by the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and others, remained [there],
Padmeśa arrived there from Akṣara during the month of Āṣāḍha.
Having offered a most excellent welcome, he worshipped him with supreme devotion;
then others, the lords of the enclosures who contemplate the ultimate reality, [did the same].
They worshipped the Supreme Soul with devotion in their respective abodes;
and having beheld those places and received service that bestows knowledge, [they were satisfied].
He arrived by means of his own celestial chariot, dispelling a great, blinding darkness;
he reached Satyaloka in a moment, and the surface of the earth in another moment.
He descended into his own abode in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
having concealed the state of duality, he indeed attained the state of oneness.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign,
revealed Himself in His entirety to his millions of billions of consorts.
And all the abodes of the lords, all the worlds that are illusory, all the kingdoms of kings, as well as all the continents of the earth; ||78||
Through those very means, the omnipresent one bestowed upon everyone their respective gains— oceans, mountains, the sky, and celestial abodes.
O Badrikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was entreated by the great lords,
by the radiant ones, by the Siddhas and Sādhyas, as well as by the sages and the ancestors.
The Lord himself was requested by the world-protectors, the kings, and even the sovereigns of all the worlds to take him to their own abodes under that very pretext.
Accompanied by his entire family, he went and granted them his vision;
at the beginning of creation, he purified the earth through that means. ||82||
By his effortless play, he purified all the netherworlds, the heavens, the abodes of the lords, and even the dwellings of the incarnations.
For this Lord, who is all-pervading, who dwells within all, and whose body is the universe, there is nowhere to go. (84)
Wherever one goes, the supreme Lord remains present before them; yet for others, the thought arises that "this one has gone" or "that one has come. (85)
For this [reality], which is all-pervasive, nothing whatsoever is distant;
and for this, which is established everywhere, there is no cessation whatsoever. (86)
Indeed, for this embodied being, there is nothing whatsoever that is unwholesome;
nor is there anything inaccessible, unbearable, or unattainable. (87)
There is nothing that is not subject to his will, nothing that is unfit, and nothing that cannot be accomplished, for all principles, fields, and abodes belong to him. (88)
He from whom exist emanations both of an insentient nature and of a conscious nature;
by whom time was made long and by whom the moment was shortened. ||89||
By that Kṛṣṇa, the states of existence were fashioned both without a further shore and with a perfect shore; likewise, the infinite sky was fashioned by him as having a limit.
Upon whose will days and other measures of time hang suspended and are shortened;
who assumes the state of primordial nature (prakṛti) within the Imperishable (akṣara), and who likewise assumes the Imperishable even within the body.

In the primordial nature (prakṛti), which consists of illusion (māyā), he sustains all principles; the Imperishable (akṣara) is thus capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise—such is the Lord.
For even He who is the one supreme Lord of all Blessed Ones, being subject to His own divine play, manifested His own glorious forms. (93)
He manifested in every way both the creations of individual souls and the creations of the Lord, as distinct from all his own powers, though they are non-different from himself. (94)
O Badrī, this very delusion appears as duality within non-duality;
having understood it thus, one realizes that which is untainted, actionless, and stainless. (95)

One is immediately liberated from creation by [meditating upon] one's own Lord, the Lord of Compassion, who is the Master of all abodes, worthy of worship, one's own husband, the beloved of Śrī, and the Guru. 96.
Having recognized those women, such as Brahmapriyā and others, who possessed the form of Brahmā,
they attained the supreme state in Hari and realized their own inherent excellence.
Perceiving that all their desires were entirely fulfilled and even surpassed, they attained supreme rest in their own beloved, the Supreme Lord. 98.
Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmī fulfilled their hearts' desires as a secondary consequence of fulfilling the minds of his devotees, through his divine play. 99.
In this world, people with eyes of leather do not know even a fraction of Hari;
they do not understand His intended purpose, which is replete with the four aims of human life.
O Badrikā, the Supreme Lord is served by you, his beloved,
and others while he dwells during the Cāturmāsya in the imperishable sacred field known as Kuṅkuma.
He celebrated his own auspicious twenty-sixth birth-anniversary;
indeed, all the inhabitants of every creation arrived there.

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, having traveled through the worlds of the Vairāja and other Īśvaras and through the abodes of His incarnations and so forth, arrived at Kuṅkumavāpikā along with His retinue," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to [the account] of Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul;
on the twenty-sixth day of His own birth, at the very dawn of the Jayantī festival.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, having performed auspicious rites such as bathing and being adorned with ornaments and fine attire, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama [arrived]. || 2 ||
In that divine golden assembly hall, upon a great elephant-throne,
Hari shone there together with the great seer Lomaśa.
He was honored and magnified with blessings, unbroken grains, and saffron; he was worshipped with sandalwood, flower garlands, and the finest fragrances. || 4 ||
His father placed a crown upon his head and likewise earrings upon his ears; he was adorned with necklaces of jewels and other ornaments upon his neck and chest.
Then, by the liberated ones, by those beginning with Akṣara, by the incarnations, as well as by the Īśvaras, Siddhas, Munis, Pitṛs, Suras, and humans and others; || 6 ||
The Lord was worshipped by kings, yakṣas, kinnaras, sādhyas, as well as cāraṇas, gandharvas, serpents, and those with divine bodies.
Thus the Blessed One shone forth, strengthened by blessings,
and was honored by brahmins, virtuous men, noble women, and yogis.

He was honored with the nīrājana rite in due order, gratified by all manner of offerings, and entertained by songs from throngs of apsarases and by dances performed by those skilled in the art of dancing.
The Blessed One was propitiated and greatly delighted by the dancing girls;
so too were those great beings who had come from the worlds dwelling between the Lokāloka mountain.
The inhabitants of the various abodes were gratified with words of praise by their preceptor Lomaśa,
as well as by their father Gopālayogī.
Honored and respected with gifts of rewards, they were also fed divine foods at the conclusion of the assembly's dismissal. || 12 ||
Satisfied with gifts and honored by all,
they all received their leave and departed for their own great abodes.
When the danger had been averted, the Lord of Beings dwelt happily,
gladdening all his beloveds as he resided in his own abode.
O Badrikā, there men and women, filled with joy, constantly come and return by the thousands for the sake of beholding Hari.
Accompanied by their daughters and sons, adorned by their husbands and kinsmen,
and joined with their wives, families, and others, they indeed come together for the sake of the sacred pilgrimage site.
In some places, gods, ancestors, and sages also arrive,
along with their sons, daughters, and other offspring, as well as women accompanied by their children.
Fortunate and beautiful women, delighting their own sons,
come for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa and depart after having performed their ritual ablution at the sacred ford.
And those devoted women, having placed their sons and daughters upon their hips, rejoice, shine forth with splendor, and even provide them with the drinking of breast milk. (19)
They kiss and touch, they quickly attain pleasures;
they sport with their own children and embrace them, being wholly intent upon that. (4.100.20)
The children call out and invoke "Mother! Father!
and hearing their faltering speech, the mothers rejoice exceedingly. (21)
The pleasures of the touch of wealth and the delights of enjoying prosperity do not equal even a sixteenth part of the joy derived from the touch of one's son.
A mother who has neither sons nor daughters does not shine at all when alone;
childless and fruitless, she does not shine like a plantain tree.
A creeper with offspring and fruit always shines like a doe;
but one without offspring withers, becomes parched, and turns into poison. (24)
A home bereft of offspring, a lap deprived of a child, a festival, and a meal—these never shine at all. (25)
Thus, those dear to Brahmā constantly reflect within themselves, repeatedly beholding mothers who possess offspring and whose forms are identical to their own. (26)

O Badrikā, [I shall dwell] on the surface of the earth together with Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as in the netherworlds (pātālas), the atmospheric realm (bhuvarloka), heaven (svarga), the truth-world (satyaloka), and the world of humanity (janaloka). ||27||
Wherever the wives of Kṛṣṇa went,
there they saw women with their children and made requests for sons.
In the world of Īśa, in the world of the gods, on Mount Meru, and in the seven continents—
wherever they stood in their celestial chariots, they went together with their husbands.
Having observed Brahmapriyā and all the others there, each in their respective places, those women,
who were relishing the joy of having offspring, formed a desire seeking a son.
O Badarī, in this world, a woman without children withers away and falls into grief even in the presence of a woman who has sons and is otherwise equal to her. (3.1)
In this world, barrenness is a reproach, and hell takes on a physical form where there is no place for children and no swing for children to play upon. (32)
There is no house inhabited by ghosts where there is no young child, nor one where there is no pregnant woman, nor one where there is no woman who has recently given birth. (33)
There is no vessel for nursing the breast, and that house is the abode of ḍākinīs;
there the words "mother" and "father" do not exist, nor does the word "son" exist. (34)
Even the word "daughter" does not exist there, for that house is a state of liberation (avadhūtika),
wherein no reflection of one's own nature in the form of a child is found.
But that house which is pervaded by blinding darkness and is always inauspicious—where there is neither a boy nor a daughter—that house is indeed devoid of prosperity. (36)
The life of a householder is like a wilderness, comparable to the den of a jackal king;
it is fruitless for that man who has no child in his lap. (37)
The desire of her who is not pregnant is fruitless;
likewise, ornaments, finery, dress, and the excellence of physical beauty are all in vain. (38)
The state of having a husband is fruitless for her whose arms do not hold a child;
without offspring, one never escapes the debt to the ancestors. (39)
Since the fruit of youth for the foolish is the repayment of debts,
the minerals of that river were rendered fruitless as they were carried away by the current in battle.
Her body is like a battlefield, and her home is like a cremation ground;
her husband is like a stone, and she herself is like a parched ravine.
For those who lack the expansion of their lineage, the next world does not exist;
nor is there any dwelling among the gods in heaven for those bereft of a lineage. 42.
In this world, only those who have no offspring look upon his face, and not others;
yet when he is seen in the morning, it is considered an auspicious omen for oneself.
The fruit of prosperity is enjoyment; the fruit of enjoyments, O children, is progeny;
the fruit of progeny is the lineage, and the lineage brings peace to one's ancestors. (44)
Even cows and cattle, birds and aquatic creatures—whether wild or domestic—are beautiful when joined with their offspring. (45)
Those with offspring deserve honor, while those without offspring deserve contempt;
for the very nature of one's birth lies in having offspring, and therein indeed resides the fulfillment of human purpose.
Therefore, a wife who has sons is a true wife and not otherwise;
we, [the daughters] of Brahmāpriyā and the others, must become mothers of sons.
The beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself will grant us sons;
this is the time for the sake of sons—when will he grant us sons? (48)
"When shall we joyfully behold the images and reflections of our beloved resting upon our own laps?"—thus they entertained such thoughts. (49)
Having understood the true intentions of the virtuous women exactly as they were, Kṛṣṇa then reflected upon seeing the spring season in full bloom.
I shall go to sport in Caitraka, in the great forest of Āmrama, and fulfill the heart's desires of ten million, hundred million, and ten billion consorts.
Having thus resolved, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, he took his own wife with him and went to the mango groves to enjoy himself.
And the forests of Aśoka, Kunda, and Bakula trees;
the forests of Campaka and plantain trees on the Raivata mountain.
And there were forests of karmadāna trees and kṣīrikā trees,
as well as groves of jambū and kiṃśuka trees, and forests of land-lotuses.
The groves of *kadamba* trees and flowering creepers,
as well as the clusters of blossoms on the flowering trees and the slopes of the thickets.
And to the south and likewise to the west of Aśvapaṭṭasara are forests of Madhuka, Amṛta, and Jambīra trees. (56)
There were groves of succulent sugarcane and of bilva trees,
as well as great gardens of śrīvṛkṣa and śrīphala trees.
And there were groves of *aspata* trees and *santara* jujubes, as well as groves of pomegranates, dates, and *khārikā* fruits. (58)
The auspicious grounds where sugarcanes and plantains grow, as well as the groves of grapes, pomegranates, and cardamom. (59)
And forests of betel-nut trees, betel vines, and camphor;
and forests of bamboo, tamarind trees, and *cañjira* trees.
Forests of *cikūra* trees, groves of fresh *raṅga* trees,
magnificent gardens, and delightful forests of *badāma* trees.
There were fields rich with crops of musk-deer musk, chickpeas, wheat, barley, rice, and vegetables. (62)
Forests of *pattriṇa*, *śimbika*, and *uttejaka* trees,
as well as lakes of *kamalī*, *kumuda*, and *sukalma* lotuses.
To behold the various grassy meadows and forest grounds, to wander about, and to show them to his own beloveds. (64)
To sport, to travel, to enjoy happiness, and to fulfill his heart’s desire,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went by celestial chariot to the vicinity of the mountain.
As far as the western ocean, in forests and groves alike, on the banks of the Bhadrā as well as on the banks of the Svarṇarekhā upon the earth. (66)
He likewise went to the Gomati-sāgara on the bank of the Ojasvatī,
and also to the Hariṇī-sāgara in the vicinity of the Śatruñjitā.
Thus, wandering through the tiger forest, the lion forest, and the vicinity of Gokarṇa,
as well as throughout all the regions of Saurāṣṭra, he delighted women.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa delighted their very minds, assuming as many forms as there were women of his own retinue. 69.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa took delight with all the women;
though he was one whose vital seed was drawn up and a celibate student, he took delight while nourishing their virtuous character.
The warbling of cuckoos, the cries of peacocks, the sweet songs of female deer, and the humming of bees; ||71||
Hearing the clear voices of the wild parrots and the stimulating songs of the *ciñcaki* birds,
the lord of women took delight with his beloveds.
Taking various fragrances upon beds of flowers on the ground, tasting the finest flavors, and eating excellent honey. (73)
Tasting the fruits, Kṛṣṇa, eager with longing, took delight with the women;
drinking the nectar of their beloved faces, he gave them the exquisite flavor of betel.
The Blessed One took delight with them in forest after forest upon the faces of his beloveds, eating and feeding on *gundrā* grasses and the pulp of *gundra-panasa* fruits. (75)
Enflaming them with amorous gestures and expressions, he took delight with them in forest after forest,
in bower after bower, at the foot of trees, and in the deep recesses of creepers.
The lotus-eyed one took delight in the midst of a cluster of grass, through embraces, kisses, touches, as well as by means of holding and massaging. (77)
Acyuta took delight with those women through firm and exhilarating desires,
and he caused his beloveds to rejoice with emotions that never faltered.
O Badrikā, she remained there in delight for as long as she desired;
meanwhile, he continued to amuse, satisfy, and gladden Acyuta.

Having observed that the time for their prayer had arrived, and having perceived the inner state of the Supreme Lord— their beloved husband— who was gracious and full of love, those beautiful women [proceeded].
Smiling, prostrating, and embracing him again and again, kissing him on the heart and holding him fast, their beloveds made their request. (8.1)
O beloved, O delighter, O one worshiped by the lords of yogis, O master of yoga, O granter of desires!
O celibate student, O supreme Brahman, O untainted one, O one free from desire! 82.
O effortless one, Lord of all powers, unattached and stainless, you who fulfill all desires, victory to you, the doer of what is dear! 83.
O treasury of bliss, you are victorious with an unshakable nature;
you are immersed in eternal self-bliss, yet you are also the fulfiller of the hopes of your devotees. (84)
O Hari, your vow of moral conduct always revolves around your own form;
we are deluded in this matter, for there is no sowing of seed here. (85)
O Nārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa! O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇeśa, O Lord of Rādhā! O Lakṣmī, who are self-manifested—how may we become possessed of sons? (86)
O Lord of all wombs, O Lord of the cowherd girls, O beloved of Brāhmī, O Lord of Ramā;
O Lord of the Self, O Lord of the Beloved, O Lord of the Beloveds, O Imperishable Lord! 87.
O Lord of the multitude of liberated women, if you do not grant us the seed, how shall we, your wives, come to possess sons and daughters? (88)
O Lord, fulfill the aspirations of us who desire offspring;
act in such a way that we may become mothers of sons and daughters. (89)
The faces of women who have no children are always inauspicious;
neither this world nor the next provides them happiness, for they grant only renunciation. (4.100.90)
People even consider one who is childless to be like a eunuch;
O Kṛṣṇa, the gods do not come to the house of one without offspring, even when it is being worshipped.
Even householders do not come [to you] because of their own inauspiciousness;
therefore, O Blessed One, you are capable of fulfilling the desires of all. (92)
Grant me the fruit of a pair, in the form of a daughter and a son;
and to all [the others], grant one pair each, according to their own individual forms. (93)
For the sake of counting one's place in the world, for the splendor of the householder’s life, and for the accomplishment of expanding the lineage, grant me one separate pair [of children]. (94)
O Kṛṣṇa, each pair of auspicious divine [weapons] is capable, equal to you, possessing the power to deliver one's father, and endowed with the energy of Brahman. 95.
Grant me each one—a daughter and a son—who are the very form of offspring, the object of parental affection, the bond of the mind, and the abode of all auspiciousness. (96)
A son is an assistant to his father, and a daughter is an assistant to her mother;
however, the deficiency of a son cannot be fulfilled by a daughter. (97)
The deficiency caused by a daughter cannot be compensated for by sons;
therefore, one should have one auspicious daughter and one son each. (98)
Grant [this], O glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, noble and true Master; O Lord of all delight, O Lord of the bodiless one, O Lord of the womb, O All-pervading One! 99.
O Lord, sovereign of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; O Lord of the highest good; O Lord of all that is dear; O Lord of the state of being sought—grant me a daughter or a son.
In this manner, all those wives of Kṛṣṇa made their request for a daughter and a son as a twin pair, without partiality.
O Badrikā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, knowing their feelings to be dear to him in love,
sported with them again and again, and they too sported with him out of a desire for a son.
The Lord Hari, whose vital seed is drawn upward, who is a celibate student, and who is the master Śrīvallabha, bestowed upon them the supreme bliss that culminates in a state of rapture.
O Badrikā, having cast off their bodies and becoming intoxicated with the identity of Kṛṣṇa,
all those beloved women became melted in love for Hari.
O Badarī, by remembering these divine sports, even sinful people—
both men and women— become free from sin and attain the supreme goal.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari went during the springtime in the Tiṣya lineage of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā* to the rivers, mountains, forests, oceans, and sandy shores of Saurāṣṭra for the purpose of recreation, and there sported with his wives as they requested him for the sake of sons and daughters. || 100 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Then, O Badarī, the Blessed Lord, perceiving the inclinations of his wives,
spoke these words— which fulfill all desires and purposes— in order to delight them.
I shall grant you whatever you desire: a pair, or several pairs, or even just a multitude of daughters, or just a multitude of sons.
I shall bestow upon you either both a son and a daughter, or one with fewer daughters and more sons,
or one with fewer sons and more daughters, or even many offspring.
"Whatever desire any of you may have, and however much or of whatever kind it may be that would bring satisfaction, I shall grant all those offspring to every one of you. (4)

The creation born of volition (saṃkalpa) is superior, leading to the worlds of Dhāma, Īśvara, and so forth; another creation is that born of vision (darśana), leading to the worlds of the gods, ancestors, and so forth.
The creation of ascetics and yogis, however, is produced from touch;
whereas in the world, the creation of humans, animals, and birds arises from sexual union.
In the Kṛta age, creation arose from mere resolve; in the Tretā, it arose from vision;
in the Dvāpara, it arose from touch alone; and in the Kali age, it arises from sexual union.
Indeed, that creation which arises from the bestowing of seed in the womb and consists of birth-impurity and the like is defiled; such a creation no longer exists on earth today.
Arising merely from physical contact, it is indeed of the nature of conception;
like those [other states], it is impure, not excellent, and accompanied by birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Moreover, creation arises from perception, for it is born from the womb of a woman;
since a wife becomes pregnant by the mere sight of her husband.
Moreover, she who gives birth to a child from a womb is not even considered superior to her;
therefore, you indeed are my wives, if you so desire it in your hearts.
"I grant to each wife divine offspring born of mere resolve, free from impurity and birth-taint, indeed auspicious pairs."
I shall grant here daughters whose forms resemble their mothers and sons who possess my own form, according to your desire; tell me what is requested.
For those fools born of no womb, who have assumed excellent bodies arising from their own volitions,
their state arises in an instant just like the volition of their fathers.
Whether they are newborn, young, adolescents, or even the elderly,
they quickly become exactly as their fathers desire.

The purificatory rites such as the birth-ceremony, as well as the wearing of the sacred thread and so forth, the efforts toward Vedic study, and the vows of studenthood and the like [are all for this purpose]. (16)
For all of them, that which arises from the resolve of their ancestors is produced in an instant;
in that regard, there exists a supreme power bestowed by the ancestors.
For them there is no conception or birth, nor is there any performance of sacramental rites;
they have no regard for time, for their manifestation is purely divine.
All subjects born of his volition are always sovereign lords; they possess all inherent perfections and are free from old age and death. (19)
Free from the defeat of reality and filled with eternal bliss, all those subjects born from his mind were equal to Viṣṇu. ||4.101.20||
In the past, by me in my form as the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa was made the divine Lord of Goloka, the husband of the gopīs, born from my mind.
In my form as the Supreme Brahman, I likewise created Vāsudeva, the Lord of the manifestations,
who is the mind-born master and the sovereign of immortality.
In former times, by me, who am the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa was created as the mental-born lord of Vaikuṇṭha and the husband of Lakṣmī.
In former times, Mahāviṣṇu was created by me in my heart in the form of the Supreme Brahman as Śrīdhāmanātha, the Lord of Mahālakṣmī.
By me, in the form of the Supreme Brahman, the protector of the unmanifest was made;
he is the Infinite (Bhūman), the bestower of justice, and the mental sovereign of lords. ||25||
In my own nature as the Supreme Brahman, I have indeed assumed innumerable incarnations in the past, such as Hari and others, who were born of my mind.
In my form as the Supreme Brahman, I have assumed as the powers of my own form my beloved consorts, Rādhā, Ramā, and others, who are the embodiments of my left side. 27.
All those women, beginning with Māṇikī and Kamalā, are indeed the beloveds of Brahmā; you are my wives here, the beloveds of Hari.
Likewise, there are innumerable Muktānikās born from my mind;
Mahākāla, Mahāmāyā, and Vidyā are also born from my mind. (29)
"Even though pearls produced from my mind exist within my abode, this mental creation of mine—unborn and most excellent—is superior to them. (4.101.30)
Free from the womb and devoid of a physical body, she is indeed not born from a womb;
filled with divine, true consciousness and bliss, she is considered entirely like me. (3.1)
"If you wives desire such excellent offspring, I shall grant it;
let them speak quickly here, and I will give it there without delay. (32)
Aditi performed the milk-vow for a year in order to obtain Vāmana;
there is no need for the milk-vow here in me, who bestows all perfections.
Thus addressed, O Badrī, the wives chose mental offspring;
being united in the same practice of yoga, each one [bore] a pair of auspicious children.

For the sake of simultaneous liberation from debt for one daughter and one son, and for the purpose of removing barrenness and other such conditions, there should be no more and no less than this. (35)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "So be it," and immediately his wives appeared in the forests, adorned with pairs [of male and female forms].
Accompanied by their sons and daughters, and all standing at the feet of their parents,
they quickly stood before each of them there by the will of Prajñākṛṣṇa.
A pair of offspring was born, youthful and adorned, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns, and graced with necklaces and crowns. ||38||

He was resplendent with the virtues, beauty, sovereignty, and noble conduct of his parents; he was accomplished in learning, adorned with every ornament, and had recently undergone the purificatory rites.
Indeed, there were simultaneously pairs of wives numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion;
they were all auspicious and possessed the same form as their husbands.

O Badrikā, within that forest there appeared numbers of gods and millions of Gandharvas who were perfected through the yoga of meditation, numbering in the tens of billions, trillions, and hundreds of billions. 41.
Having perceived Kṛṣṇa’s miraculous power through their divine vision, the Apsarases, Kinnaras, and others quickly descended from the path of the sky to that place. 42.
They rained down a shower of flowers, a shower of sandalwood powder, and likewise a shower of unbroken grains;
they also rained down curds, sprouts, and other offerings, while raising shouts of victory.
And having arrived bringing divine musical instruments, those skilled in playing them played their instruments, filled with great enthusiasm. (44)
The Gandharvas sang, the dancers performed their dances, the women performed auspicious rites, and the lords of the world offered hymns of praise. (45)
Filled with joy, the female attendants sang songs of harmony;
the Siddhas, holy men, and great sages offered their blessings. (46)
The forest goddesses sang auspicious songs and worshipped with reverence;
thus, O Badrikā, were the great festivals for the birth of the offspring celebrated there. (47)
They appeared in many ways in the forest, in the woods, in the village, and in every house;
accompanied by their children, those wives of Kṛṣṇa came together with Śrī Hari. 48.
Accompanied by their respective offspring, they quickly went to their own palaces;
there, Kṛṣṇa was consecrated with the waters of the lotuses from the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
On that account, he indeed felt a great weight of joy there; and Lomaśa performed for him the very rites of birth-consecration.
There, Kṛṣṇa, who is dear to them, gave gifts of gold,
as well as jewels, gems, silver, wealth, food, and garments.
Houses, cattle, horses, ornaments, royal insignia, and household utensils—
these he gave to Brahmins, to ascetics and holy men, and even to the poor and the helpless.
At that time, he indeed gave gifts to women and to young girls;
he then gave well-prepared foods to the mendicants.
The subjects came to Kṛṣṇa’s palace for the sake of seeing his sons and others;
they gazed again and again upon Hari’s sons and daughters, who were in the form of twins.
Having attained great joy and delight, they bestowed their blessings;
and immediately after the birth festival, [the child] quickly attained the fitness for the immediate post-natal sacraments.
Upon seeing those pairs, Śrī Lomaśa then indeed performed supreme consecrations for the sake of accomplishing the flow of their karma.
Lomaśa performed various oblations for those respective purposes,
as well as all the ancestral rites (śrāddha), gifts, and feasts.
The sage Lomaśa performed the rite of naming;
he determined all the divine names from the ancient Purāṇas. (58)
In that regard, O Badarī, I shall tell you the names of the sons and daughters of the principal wives of the eight Kṛṣṇas; listen from the beginning.
The eldest of all was the daughter of Śivasvāmin, born in Kāśī;
she was the foremost of all, the bestower of happiness, Lakṣmī by name, and her son was [known] by name.
Mukundavikrama was the eldest son, and Muktibālā was their daughter;
that couple indeed rejoices eternally in the abode of Hari.
Then the other eight wives were Lakṣmī, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk;
Śrī, the daughter of the Kalpa-tree; and Prabhātmikā, the daughter of the Sun.
Diśāputrī, Pāśavatī, Lalitā, the daughter of Brahmā;
Jayā, the daughter of Sadāśiva, and Māṇikī, born of divine prosperity. (63)
Listen to [the account of] Kamalā, the daughter born from the navel of Vairāja, and her progeny:
Vāsudeva was the son of Lakṣmī, while Divyavāsavī was his daughter.
The son of Śrī was Rāsakṛṣṇa, and his daughter was Rāseśvarī;
likewise, the son of Prabhā was Prabhu, and his daughter was Brahmakānti.
The son of Pāśavatī is Ananta, and her daughter is Bṛhatīśvarī;
likewise, the son of Lalitā is Lāla, and her daughter is Līleśvarī.
Vijaya was the son of Jayā, while Vijayeśī was her daughter;
Kaustubhamaṇi was the son of Māṇikyā, and Maṇīśvarī was her daughter.
Padmanābha was the son of Kamalā, and Nabhovatī was her daughter;
thus, these were the names of the offspring of each pair among the eight wives.
Now hear the names of another hundred wives;
they are indeed one hundred and three—exactly one hundred and three. (69)
The three principal goddesses are known by the names Ramā, Rādhā, and Nārāyaṇī.
The son of Ramā is Rāma, and likewise, her daughter is Rāmāyaṇī.
Rāya was the son of Rādhā; Ṛddhi and Ayā were considered her daughters.
Nara was the son of Nārāyaṇī, and Narottamī was likewise her daughter.
Now listen, O beloved of Badarī, to the names of the hundred consorts:
Brāhmī, Bhāgavatī, Dhāmā, Bhārgavī, and Sarasvatī. (72)
Maṅgalā, Mānasā, Revā, Bhakti, Gaṅgā, Rati, Kṛti, the meritorious Muktir Ekādaśī, and Tulasī are the wish-fulfilling cow. (73)
Satī, Mūrti, Gomatī, Svarṇarekhā, Nandinī, Sāvitrī, Virajā, Durgā, Dolā, Puṣpā, and Kalāvatī. ||74||
Badarī, Mādhavī, Pampā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Prīti, Ṛtadhvajī, Kuśalā, Kāśikā, Cāndrī, Maṇi, Jyotsnā, and Prabhāvatī. (75)
Ārṣī, Surasā, Nandā, Kāñcanī, Hariṇī, Hanū, Viśvā, Vitasti, Rasikā, Suparṇā, and Hiraṇmayī. (76)
Prabhūti, Karīṇī, Padmā, Piṅgalā, Sarojinī, Pūrṇimā, Vallabhā, Kārṣṇī, Joṣṭrī, Jyotsnā, and Padminī. (77)
Sudughā, Yoginī, Vidyotinī, Śānti, Mālatī, Raktā, Urukramā, Vaiśvī, Devatā, Kumudā, and Śivā. (78)
Taralā, Reṇumiśrā, Kānakī, Nalinī, Parī, Sunandā, Kalikā, Sādhvī, Sudhāmbā, Prakṛti, and Śamī. (79)
Śyāmā, Bālā, Mañjulā, Pallavā, Vallavīśvarī, Vedī, Moghavatī, Śvetā, Vaiṣṇavī, Mālinī, and Stavā. (4.101.80)
Amarī, Cāraṇī, Śīlā, and Dugdhā are the names of the hundred-petaled [lotuses].
O Badrikā, hear the names of their pairs of offspring.
In due course, O Brahmarāta, a son was indeed born there from the Brāhmī;
his daughter was named Bṛṃhaṇikā, endowed with the form and qualities of her mother. (82)
Bharga was the son of Bhāgavatī, and the auspicious Bhāgyeśvarī was his daughter.
Ūrjabala was the son of Sudhāmā, and Dhāminī was his daughter.
The son of Bhārgavī was Bahvṛca, and likewise his daughter was Brahmaruci;
the sons of Sarasvatī were Śārṅgadhara and his daughter Kaumudī.
The son of Maṅgalā was Prabhāsaka, and her daughter was Bhāsvarā;
the son of Mānasā was Sammāneśa, and her daughter was Sudhodarī. 85.
The son of Revā was Vārijākṣa, and his daughter was Vāruṇī;
the son of Bhakti was Sarvajña, and his auspicious daughter was Śemuṣikā.
The son of Gaṅgā was Tāraka, and her daughter was Cāturadīkṣikā;
the son of Rati was Mahānanda, and his daughter was the virtuous Santarpiṇī.
From Kṛti was born Sūdyoga, and his daughter was Nayarājati;
from Muktī was born Sunirvāṇa, and his auspicious daughter was Dyushāśvatī. ||88||
The son of Ekādaśī was Puṇyavrata; his daughter was Pativratā.
The son of Puṇyā was Vṛṣavidya, and her daughter was Satīśvarī. (89)
The son of Kāmadughā was Viṣṇu, and his daughter was Surārhaṇā;
the son of Tulasī was Kṛṣṇamāla, and his daughter was Sūryamañjarī.
Satya’s son was Ṛtavārddhi, and his daughter was the auspicious Ṛtaṃbhara;
Mūrti’s son was Aniruddha, and his daughter was Sudarśaneśvarī. ||9.1||
The son of Gomatī was Pāvana, and her daughter was Pīyūṣavarṣiṇī;
the son of Suvarṇarekhā was Śrīvatsa, and his daughter was Projjvalā. 92.
And from Nandinī was born Atoṣa as a son, and Virāmiṇī as a daughter;
from Sāvitrī was born Brahmadyumna as a son, and Girīśvarī as a daughter. (93)
Saṃkarṣaṇa was the son of Virajā, while Ajā-Īśvarī was her daughter.
The leader of the hosts of gods was the son of Durgā, and Kṛṣīśvarī was her daughter. (94)
Svarṇalatikā was the daughter of Dolā, and her son was Torana;
Parāga was indeed the son of Puṣpā, and Saraghā was her daughter. (95)
The son of Kalāvatī was Kāruṇātha, and her daughter was Camatkṛti;
the son of Badarī was Badara, and her auspicious daughter was Patrāvalī. (96)
Mādhavyā’s son was Madhukṛt, and her daughter was the auspicious Madhukī;
Pampā’s daughter was Sārasī, and her son was Vīryasetu. ||97||
The son of Ṣaṣṭhīdevī was Rakṣāvatī, and his son was Rakṣaṇa.
The son of Prīti was Sumelārya, and his auspicious daughter was Pronmīlanī. 98.
The son of Ṛtadhvaja was Śānta; his son was the auspicious Satyavrata.
The son of Kuśalā was Yogīśvara, and his daughter was Suyoginī. (99)
The son of Kāśikā was the wise [Kāśika], while his auspicious daughter was Taijasī;
the son of Cāndrī was Dhavala, and his daughter was Pāyasabhāsurī.
Maṇi’s daughter was Viśvaprabhā, and his son was the auspicious Paridhi;
Jyotsnā’s daughters were [the Viśvadevas], while Viśvajyoti was the auspicious son of Bhūmā.
The daughter of Prabhāvatī was Dṛśyādevī, while Gocara was her son. The daughter of Ārṣī was Gāyatrī, and her son was Praṇavasattama. || 102 ||
Svādavatī was the daughter of Surasā, and Pramāpati was her son;
Nandana was the son of Nandā, while Nandinī was her virtuous daughter.
The son of Kāñcanī was Cāmīkara, and her daughter was Suvarṇinī;
the daughter of Hariṇī was Sampadvatī, and her son was Arthavedana.
The son of Hanvā was Hasinī, and her son was Cibukakesara;
the son of Viśvā was Aśvavāhana, and her daughter was Śruti.
Vitastī’s son was Hastīśvara and her daughter was Prameśvarī;
Rasikā’s son was Premānanda and her daughter was Mahotsavī.
The son of Suparṇā was Śuklavarṇa, and his son was Sulokana;
the daughter of Hiraṇmayī was Piṅgākṣiṇī, and her son was Mauktika.
The son of Prabhūti was Vipañcikā, and her son was Praṇādana.
The daughter of Karīṇī was Svarṇadantā, and her son was Gajānana.
The son of Padmā was Nāla, and her daughter was Rajatapatriṇī;
the son of Piṅgalā was Pitāmbara, and her daughter was Ātmabodhinī.
Sarojinī’s son was Raktagarbha, and her daughter was Sukauśikī;
Pūrṇimā’s son was Sudhākara, and her daughter was Candrakalā.
The son of Vallabhā was Kārṣṇavallabhi; Śalabhā was his daughter.
The son of Kārṣṇī was Kṛśodara; his auspicious daughter was Miṣṭasvarā.
The son of Joṣṭrī was Svaprakāśaka, whose daughter was the discerning Suputrī;
the daughter of Jyotsnā was Anaṅgalatikā, and her son was Sukavi.
The son of Padminī was Salilā, and her son was Mūlakardama. The daughter of Sudughā was Sādhvīvratā, and her son was Payonidhi.
The son of Yoginī was Brahmasamādhi; the son of Muktarājñī was Svargapataṅga; and the daughter of Kṛtinī was Vidyotinī.
The son of Śānti was Virāmarṣi; his auspicious daughter was Nirmohinī.
Mālatī’s son was Tantudhṛk, and his auspicious daughter was Santānikā.
The son of Raktā was Rañjana, and her daughter was the auspicious Smitānanā;
the daughter of Urukramā was Saṃkramā, and her son was Vāmana.
From Vaiśvī was born Viśvāvasu as a son, and Vaiśvadevikā as a daughter;
from Devatā was born Deveśvara as a son, and Divaspadā as a daughter.
The daughter of Kumudā was Pramodinī, and her son was Pramodakṛt;
the son of Śivā was Jāmbūvarṇa, and her daughter was Sukhaṃkarī.
Taralā’s son was Kṣipradhiṣaṇa; Dhīśvara was the son [of Kṣipradhīṣaṇa];
Rājarāja was the son of Reṇumiśrā; and Rāyaṇī was the daughter [of Rājarāja].
The son of Kāñcyā was Bhūṣaṇa, and the virtuous Cūḍāmaṇi was his daughter.
The daughter of Nalinī was Bhrāmarī, and her son was Ṣaḍaṅgavaidyuta.
Parya was the son and Parameśa was the daughter;
Pāravilāsinī was the son of Sunandā, and Nāranivāsinī was her daughter. (1.21)
From Kalikā came the son Vikāsāsya and the daughter Praphullikā;
from Sādhvī came the son Santajana and the auspicious daughter Suvāsinī. 122.
Śaṅkara was the son of Sudhā, and likewise Satī was his daughter;
Ambālikā was the son of Ambā, and Bālikeśī was his daughter.
The son of Prakṛti was Kṛtimān; his daughter was the auspicious Yatneśvarī.
The son of Śamyā was Divyagarbha; his daughter was Viśvarddhisattamā.
The son of Śyāmā was Nīlarāja, and her daughter was Nīlāyanī;
the son of Bālā was known as Bahulārka, and her daughter was Pravālikā.
Mañjūlā’s son was Mātaṅginī, and Maheśvara was the son of Suta;
Pallavā’s daughter was Patrānanā, and Daleśvara was her son. || 126 ||
The son of Vallavā was Bhāravāṭa, and the daughter was Vāgheśvarī;
the son of Vedyā was Makhadharma, and the daughter was Svarṇakeśinī. || 127 ||
The son of Moghavatī was Śārṅgadhara, and the daughter was Talāyanā;
the son of Śvetā was Pāṇḍurakeśī, and her daughter was Himadhruvā. 1.28.
Vaiṣṇavī’s son was Kāṇḍikāputra, whose name was Sarvakrama;
and Mālinī’s son was Jiṣṇudeva, while her daughter was Rohiṇī.
Stavā had a daughter named Astāpahā and a son named Śubha Tapanaka;
Amartya had a son named Amṛta and a daughter named Dhruvaśemuṣī.
Cāraṇyā’s son was Granthavit; the daughter was Brahmarutānanā. Śilā’s son was Vitti, whose son was Rahasyavedana. || 13.1 ||
Dhāriṇī’s daughter was Dugdhā, and Śubhakriya was the son of Dhātā;
these are said to be the offspring of these women, as well as those of other wives.
Thus, their number was calculated to be four hundred;
from those pairs of offspring, beings of auspicious deeds were born.
And from other women, numbering in the hundreds of billions, trillions, and quadrillions, offspring were produced in pairs; their number is beyond reckoning.
And here indeed, the names of the twelve principal women, numbering one hundred, who possessed beautiful offspring, have been declared.
Through hearing and through the manifestation of its meaning, one shall attain divine status and liberation;
indeed, being devoted to the Supreme Lord, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should recite these names,
for him there shall indeed be the destruction of obstacles and the accomplishment of his purpose at every step.

What is the use of saying much more in this regard? For he is indeed Hari, the lineage of Hari; having taken away sins, the infallible Acyuta takes away even the self, leading it to the imperishable state.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Enumeration of the Births of Twin Children on the Third Day of the Bright Fortnight of Caitra for the One Hundred and Twelve Principal Wives of the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as well as for His Twenty-Eight Additional Wives and His Crores, Arbuds, and Padmas of Wives," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the collective names of the others in brief, due to the weight of the expansion of their lineages. || 1 ||
O Badrikā, there were fourteen thousand pairs of children born to Hari from the daughters of Meghanādin.
There were indeed ten million pairs of children born from Koṭidīpāvalī,
and there were ten million offspring of the daughters of Kāmadhenu.
Vasumatī and the other maidens had hundreds of offspring,
while the offspring of Gahvarākanyakā numbered one hundred million.
There were one hundred thousand daughters born of the forest goddesses as well as their offspring,
and likewise two hundred thousand daughters of Dāmanī.
The daughters of Kaṅka and Tālīya had six offspring,
and likewise there were ten thousand pairs of Kaṅkas and Tālas.
The offspring of the sons of Aryaman and the others numbered one hundred thousand;
the children of the maidens of the subterranean realm (Rasātala) numbered five thousand.
Vāsantika indeed had sixteen sons, and Śālamālīya had five hundred daughters who were also children. (8)
There were ten thousand Svastika nāga maidens,
who gave birth to twenty other pairs.
There were one thousand children of the Śāvadīnīya maidens,
and a thousand offspring of the Aindrajālika maidens.
There were pairs of Vidyā and Kanyā daughters, seventy-five young boys,
and two thousand children born of the wives of Lakṣmaṇa’s sons.
Indeed, seventy-two thousand auspicious pairs of children were born as the offspring of the daughters of Vedhas;
and three hundred children were born as the offspring of the daughters of Viśvāvasu.
The offspring of Jummāsemlā were one thousand boys.
The offspring of Sāntapana’s daughter numbered five thousand,
and the offspring of the daughter of Surati were exactly one hundred.
Mahābāleśvarī had three children, and Dākṣajāvaṅgarī also had one hundred children. (15)
There were indeed thousands of pairs of children born of his daughters, and ten thousand sons born of the daughters of his female slaves. (16)
There were twenty pairs born from the daughters of Pitṛ and Kanyā,
and one crore of offspring from the daughters of Parācīna.
There were two pairs of children for Sāntāraṇi, one pair for Lājā, and likewise one child for Krodhanā. (18)
There was one pair of needles made from a single stalk of the ailavīla plant,
and then there were one hundred auspicious pairs of śaibya plants.
There were fifty pairs of maidens from Thārkūṭastha,
and likewise a hundred pairs of maidens from Vairajā.
There were indeed sixty pairs of Śāktyakṣiṇī maidens,
and likewise one hundred pairs of Paiśācinī maidens.
There were two hundred pairs of girls from Kāliṃśīya,
and thirty pairs of both legitimate and adopted daughters.
At that time, there were five pairs of Krāthakīs, and likewise,
there were twenty pairs of Pārthavīs.
There were ten pairs of offspring of the daughters of the king of the Auṣṭrālas;
likewise, there were five of the Haṃkāraṇīs and six of the Tairāṇīs.
There were also five pairs of offspring from the Jayakāṣṭha and Lakanyā women, and likewise five pairs of offspring from the Ālvī and Narīya women.
Furthermore, there were seven pairs of children born to Jīnavardhin,
one pair belonging to Anāthī, and a thousand Prākīrṇakīs.
At that time, there were two hundred pairs of offspring,
as well as seven pairs of offspring belonging to the followers of Alpaketu.
The daughter of Jayakārṣṇī had a pair of children,
and the daughters of Pārīśānīya had twenty-one children.
At that time, there were two pairs of sons born to Aindurāyī;
likewise, there were fifteen offspring named Maudrāṇḍas.
The sons of Gāṇḍī’s daughter were nine pairs;
and there were four pairs of children born to Līnorṇī and her daughters.
There were also eleven yugas of Bārhaccharī maidens,
and forty yugas of Bālalīnīya maidens.
There were five pairs of Nārasiṃhī maidens,
and eight pairs of Rāyagāmalī maidens.
At that time, there were also twins among the daughters of Phenatāntavī;
furthermore, the daughter of Sthaulahomīya had a single offspring who was a twin.
From Kāṣṭhayānī and Kanyakā, one son named Kaulaka was born;
and from Dainamānī and Kanyakā, two children were born.
Rāyakinnarī had fifty-one daughters, and Rāyarokīśvarī had twenty-one children. || 35 ||
There were twenty children of the daughters of Rāyarana-jit, as well as three pairs of children born of the daughters of Rāya-vākākṣikī. (36)
There were also triplets born to Rāyamārī and Śakanyā,
as well as triplets born as twins to the daughters of Rāyabāleśvarī.
The daughters of Rāyalambāra have six offspring as their measure;
the daughters of Rāyanavārkī have seven offspring as their measure. (38)
There were nine pairs of offspring for Rāyahuṇḍeśī and her sons, as well as a pair and a single child for the daughter of Rāyakūpeśa. (39)
There were also four sons of Kālīmaṇḍalin, who were highly esteemed for their cleverness,
as well as ten sons of Vanajeleśī.
And [the mantras] Pārāvāra, Pibīkā, Nyāpatya, Triyama, and Lā;
likewise, the two auspicious Yamalas of Koṭīśvarī and Kanyā. || 41 ||
The three pairs of offspring of the illustrious Satīśī and Bālikā, as well as the seven pairs of offspring of the women of Tretākarkaśikā, [were born]. 42.
Among those born from eggs and those born from wombs, there are four types of offspring; however, for those born from moisture and from sprouts, the offspring are twins or single. 43.
Rāyasomanī had three pairs of twin children; at that time, it was also considered that Urugavākṣī’s two daughters each had a pair of twins. (44)
Two pairs are likewise considered for the *parāṅ* and *vatī* types of *kanyā*;
thus, there are forty-one [varieties] for the *īśāna*, *pānī*, and *bālā* types. 45.
The thirty-three *yamalas* (twins) belong to the *rāja*, *rāya*, and *pati* [categories]; however, the *yamala* of a single offspring belongs to the *rāyapati-svasṛ*. 46.
There were thirteen pairs of daughters of the Dhainupālīs, and ten thousand boys of the Ājanābhīs. (47)
There were also ten thousand daughters and boys of the subjects, as well as twelve children of the female students of Śiva’s school. 48.
The daughters of Dhenupāla had three pairs of offspring;
likewise, the daughters of Kaubera and those of Mahendra also had offspring. (49)
There were also pairs of Yamīs, Vāyavīs, and Vārkṣīs,
as well as pairs of Vaiśvakarmaṇī and Raudrī maidens.
The pairs of Vāhneyī, Śrāvaṇī, and Khānijī gopīs, as well as the pairs of Sāṃvatsarī, Prācīnī, and [other] gopīs. ||5 1||
There were also pairs of children from women of the Piśaṅgī and Rāśiyānī tribes,
as well as pairs of Pāraśī women with hairy bodies.
And pairs of fisherwomen, kinnarīs, and goddesses;
and pairs of fair-complexioned women, dark-complexioned women, and hārītīs. ||52||
And there were the offspring of the women of Pātāla who had been brought forth;
and there were pairs of children born of the celestial apsarases.
The children of the Brahmasarasas, the pairs of Gāndharvīs, and the offspring of the Bhaumīs and Dānavīs in their pairs. || 55 ||
O Badrikā, there were twice as many as two hundred and twenty-five billion [disciples];
the sage Lomaśa performed the naming ceremony for them all.
Then he performed the sacraments, including the feeding with milk-rice and other foods,
the rite of piercing the ears, and also the rite of tonsure.
At the commencement of his studies, Lomaśa performed the investiture with the vow, the bestowal of the sacred thread,
and the purificatory rite of Vedic study.
Lomaśa indeed caused all the couples to study the Vedas and also performed the rite of their formal return home (samāvartana).
O Badrī, at that time, for those wise ones who were ancient yogis, the study of Vedic knowledge was merely a pretext. (4.102.60)
The gods, goddesses, Īśānyas, and Īśvaras were the sons of Hari;
likewise, the Muktās and Muktānikās were his daughters, and the Kṛtaśravas were his sons.
All their sons and daughters became accomplished in the sciences;
they mastered the languages of the Siddhas and became experts in all branches of knowledge. ||62||
Like the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the sons and daughters became knowers of all sciences and masters of all arts.

Remembering their past births, possessing divine awakening, and seeing the truth as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, those sons and daughters became omniscient, just like great sages.
O Badrikā, all those pairs became endowed with the perfection of meditative absorption and possessed eternal conjugal union.
For at the time of the original creation, the birth of pairs occurred in that manner;
therefore, those pairs indeed took the form of husbands and wives.
These were created by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself according to his will;
they are exceedingly affectionate toward one another and possess the purpose of the duties of household life.
Then, having observed that they were indeed fit, Lomaśa, by the command of Hari,
performed the auspicious sacrament known as marriage.
At that festival, the gods, the lords, and their attendants arrived, as did the liberated ones, the ancestors, the perfected beings (siddhas), humans, dānavas, and others. ||69||
And in divine pavilions, the joining of hands of the couples took place,
with the god Agni as witness and in the presence of the great seers.
Having circumambulated the fire, they took the bridegroom’s garland;
having tied the knot consisting of Dharma, they then attained the state of matrimony.
Divine songs were sung, uttered by celestial women;
there were dances of the Apsarases and the sounds of musical instruments at that time. (72)
There were mutual gifts between the two couples;
there was the mutual giving of morsels of food by those joined as pairs. (73)
The presentation of gifts from the hands of the couples, as well as blessings, the ritual dismissal, and likewise the worship of the honored guests. ||74||
Indeed, all divine gifts consisting of cattle, land, and gold occurred, as well as many gifts of jewels and gems. (75)
O Badrī, there were various gifts of alms-bowls, ornaments, and garments,
as well as household utensils, in every house.
Then, meals for the classes of great men were provided for all the embodied beings in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master, fed them;
he granted them leave to depart, and they went to their respective realms. (78)
O Badrī, by the grace of Hari, the expansion of the lineage of the Blessed One brought joy to the mental couples thereafter. (79)
His sons and grandsons were created by his will according to their respective natures;
likewise, there were daughters and the daughters of those daughters, all of whom were stainless deities.
O Badrī, because he was not born from a womb, the marriage of Yamala was entirely unimpeded according to the custom of the Lord of Gods and others. (81)
But in the course of time, by the command of Kṛṣṇa and by the will of Hari, they and those [women] were born upon the lands of their maternal uncles, in various worlds and dwellings.
Having become couples indeed, possessing the duties of husband and wife, they lived there forever in happiness for the sake of residence, due to the great affection of their elders. (83)
Bālakṛṣṇa’s sons possessed four hands; two were principal ones reaching down to their knees, and two auspicious hands were born from their shoulders. (84)
All the maidens likewise became four-armed; two [arms] were primary, reaching down to the knees, while the other two, born from the shoulders, were short. (85)
Lines of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus appeared upon their hands;
their bodies were long, well-nourished, white in color, and possessed of beautiful forms. (86)
There were [sons] for the groups of sons, but those of the women were even more numerous; indeed, their bodies were smaller in size and they were white and red. (87)
Possessing the great sovereign powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, they have forms that are invincible;
they are all-pervading, enriched with all attributes, and their bodies are accomplished by mere volition.
Richly endowed with the power of boundless boundaries, they became happy in every respect;
possessing forms endowed with all virtues, they were radiant with splendor. ||89||
There is no world here within the fourteen tiers of existence where such nocturnal fragrance exists, nor where such supreme glory prevails.
There is no dwelling place, no island, nor even any world or realm where there are not born those of Kṛṣṇa’s lineage, whose very forms are purifying.
Likewise, in the netherworlds, in the heavens, and in all the continents, the abodes of those created by the Four-Armed One came into existence everywhere. (92)
O Badrikā, through the course of time, the mark on his hand has perished;
consequently, only the mark of the sectarian tilaka remains upon his forehead. (93)
That [speech] was lost through the passage of time, and from it there arose mere whiteness;
subsequently, in another period of time, it became the very words of the gods (gīrvāṇa).
Then, after some time, for those embodied as Brahman, there remained only the sacred thread and the yellow garment as their means of sustenance. 95.
That has been lost through the passage of time; form is destroyed and virtues have departed.
Men are indeed equal to beasts, and women are the very ground of hell. 96.
There were various dharmas with diverse modes of conduct, rituals, and dietary practices; through the passage of time, there was a decline of these dharmas among the people as well. (97)
O Badrī, through the performance of dharma, rituals, and other acts, there gradually arose a blending of Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas, resulting in a mixture of all their customs and practices. 98.
Indeed, the dharmas of the Satya age perish and those of the Tretā arise;
thereafter, the dharmas of the Tretā are destroyed and those of the Dvāpara emerge on all sides.
Thereafter, in the Tiṣya age, the dharmas of the Dvāpara age perish;
O Badrī, the men of the Tiṣya age are indeed full of impurity.

Those who partake in afflictions, whose conduct is false, and who are indeed deceitful and wicked, are born with little intelligence, short lifespans, meager contentment, and a fondness for strife. (101)
O Badrī, lords, humans, goddesses, ancestors, deities, and gods—
all these have fallen into the Kali age (Tiṣya-yuga) and have indeed become powerless.
Deprived of vital energy, overcome by hunger, and devoted to thirst and passion—
for that reason, O Badrī, even the spiritual attainments of these yogins perish.
Just as there is a difference in nature between gold and iron, or between moisture and a jewel, so too in the Kali age, deficiency and even decline come into being. 104.
The devotees of Hari are never overcome by the forces of time,
nor are those whose character is that of Brahman overcome by the rapid movements produced by time.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Number of the Lord’s Twin Offspring, Their Sacraments, Their Marriage, Their Progeny, the Strength of the Yuga, and Other Matters," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 102 ||
Śrī Badarīpriyā said: O Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu! How great is the power of Time?
When does it become such, and of what nature is it? And likewise, how is there deliverance from it? || 1 ||
Out of compassion, for the sake of my welfare, please tell me:
what is beneficial, when does it arise, by whom is it produced, or how does it come to be? Speak!
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: In the Satya-yuga, dharmas are indeed mental, having forms created by volition;
they are sustained by truth, accessible to the intellect, spontaneously born, and possessed of physical forms.
All the principles (tattvas) that were intended indeed arise in embodied form for that purpose; at that time, no further effort is required.
The trees showered nectar, and there was honey in every leaf-cup;
all cows were wish-fulfilling, and women were devoted to their husbands.
In that [age], there is no agriculture; the creations are produced by mere volition.
Abundant crops, born from the waters within the earth, remain stable for only half a day.
At midday, the people there are also chirping birds; they possess the supernatural power of irresistible will (prākāmya-siddhi), can travel to all worlds, and live for hundreds of thousands of years.
At that time, the women dwelt in mountain caves, took refuge in the self through meditative absorption, wore flowers as their ornaments, and were free from fickleness.
In the former Kṛta Yuga, neither the seasons nor the seasonal duties existed;
at that time, the manifestation of one pair occurred from another pair.
A pair was born from the mind, joined by the duty of matrimony;
at the beginning of that city, there was no distinction between brother and sister.
At that time, Dharma was born simultaneously with them, like the right and left limbs;
these two are born together with their parents and exist together as well.
And simultaneously, the two vanished from here in the form of a husband and wife;
for all worldly transactions are real, just as they are perceived within the range of direct experience.
Free from the thirst of passion and hatred, he became possessed of eternal contentment;
all [his followers] attained death at their own will and assumed forms according to their desire.
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, all were indeed possessed of the power of creation through mere volition;
then, when the Tretā Yuga arrived, the sense of "I" and "mine" arose within me.
Truth, austerity, sacrifice, and charity—these constitute the fourfold vessel of Dharma.
Through the gradual decline of truth, only three-quarters of Dharma remain. (15)
In the Kṛta age, the dharmas and the spiritual accomplishments were dependent upon truth;
but in the Tretā age, those same fruits of truth became dependent upon austerity.
Volitions have become weak due to the entry of the unreal;
therein, vision is powerful, and the supernatural powers arise from that vision. (17)
It is seen that trees indeed bear fruit; it is seen that righteousness is praised.
When one’s livelihood is sustained by the nurturing of trees, then that becomes one’s means of subsistence. (18)
The success of crops arises from rain; people drink the water of the rains, are nourished by their reliance on material things, and have made trees their dwellings. (19)

O Badrī, at that time the subjects were born with their livelihoods consisting of crops and other produce grown on the portions of land belonging to each individual; there was no fixed rule for the Yuga system.
There was no birth for Yama, and from that time on, he arose as a single being;
at that time, in that age, the giving away of daughters and sons began.
Consequently, protective measures for those of great supernatural power arose for the sake of their livelihood;
furthermore, due to the passage of time, there occurred a decline in ascetic practices throughout the worlds.
All the powers of asceticism were lost, for their life-force was dependent on others; people became reliant on the support of others and lived by means of labor. ||23||
Consequently, people subsist on food obtained through labor, using clothing and other such items;
they also utilize water from wells and similar sources, and their meals consist of food produced by agriculture. (24)
At the end of the Tretā age, the beings will be overcome by material elements; their vehicles will move according to their own whims, and they will have fallen into dissolution.
Furthermore, at the end of the Tretā, the people will be devoid of austerity and bereft of merit.
There, the people were strong through sacrifices and worship, not through other forms of power;
their offspring were born of touch and likewise bound by marriage.
They possess children born from the womb and experience the states of childhood and youth;
they sustain their livelihood by means of the grain that arises from sown crops. (27)

In the Dvāpara age, all those creatures were devoted to occupations for their livelihood; they existed in the state of masters, female slaves, and male slaves, as well as in houses, villages, and dwellings.
Consequently, for those possessed of theft, deceit, thirst, craving, hypocrisy, and the like,
there arises from what has been sown only half the abundance of grain, and never more.
Or it becomes diminished by the pouring of rain and water from wells;
by that [water] do men live, as well as thieves and plunderers. (4.103.30)
Indeed, among the subjects, men were born who were prone to plunder;
for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon them, a king, the wielder of the rod, was requested. ||3.1||
The kingdom, the realm, and all its subjects have become subject to the power of punishment;
likewise, passion, hatred, falsehood, deceit, guile, and trickery prevail. (32)
Consequently, untruth became prevalent, as did afflictions and strife;
at the end of the Dvāpara age, the subjects born from the creation of pairs dwelt in difficult conditions.

Though their nature is happiness, they will be beset by much suffering; though they desire enjoyments, they will be forcibly deprived of them; and even the accomplishments resulting from sacrifices, merit, and other such means will be largely characterized by famine. (34)
They shall also suffer untimely deaths, being devoid of mutual trust;
their lives shall be short, and even their efforts shall yield only half, or even a quarter, of the desired fruit. (35)
At the end of the Dvāpara age, living beings became insatiable, possessed by latent desires, and dominated by hunger; consequently, sacrifices there fell into decline.
O Badrikā, through the force of time, misconduct increased;
people for the most part desired liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse. (37)
"Smoking is also breath-sucking," they said;
thus, protectors and devourers increased in every house. (38)
In the Tiṣya age, when beings had fallen into decay, the king became a paramour;
for in the Tretā age, human beings lived for ten thousand years.
In the Dvāpara age, they lived for over a thousand years; and gradually, in the Kali age, they live for only a hundred years, possessing no greater stability.
