They will suffer much from disease and pain, receiving only half, a quarter, or even an eighth of their expected fruits;
there will be theft in the home, loss in the home, and especially great distress in the home. (41)
In the home, there is constant quarreling between husband and wife, verbal violence,
humiliation by the great, and even concealment within one's own house.
In that moment there is deception; in every moment there is the destruction of moral conduct.
There, speech is always untruthful, and the manner of one's steps is composed of falsehood. (43)
O Badrī, in that Kali age, the world will then be pervaded by documents, burdens of deceit, and extortion; and wealth will be obtained without effort.
They expand the lineage of unrighteousness and destroy the lineage of dharma;
they are corrupt in mind and soul, and they live by the trade of women. (45)
In the Kali age, people will be of one caste, one drink, and one food; they will share the same bed, seat, and vehicle, and eat from the same vessel. (46)

In the Kali age, there is no impurity whatsoever regarding the sharing of beds with one's wife, nor regarding all women belonging to everyone; likewise, there is no impurity in physical touch or in food. 47.
There is no impurity in drink, in bed, in clothing, or even on the body.
Everything intended for the deity is edible; at that time, direct perception is not false.

There are no ritual observances, no birth-impurity, no bathing, no worship, and no sprinkling; there is neither the neglect of those worthy of honor nor the abandonment of the Teacher’s instruction. (49)
In the Kali age, there is no adherence to dharma, no faith, and no lasting conjugal fidelity;
there is the abandonment of giving daughters in marriage and the neglect of hospitality toward guests.
There is atheism toward virtuous gurus; there is no worship of the gods by day or by night;
there is no vision of the deities, no peace, and no pleasant sleep during the middle of the night. (5.1)
There is no satisfaction for anyone in between; people are full of anxiety.
For those who are intent on acquiring wealth, there is no sense of fulfillment even when wealth arrives. (52)
Indeed, even the caste of men and women cannot be discerned by their dress;
they live by the trade of the marketplace, eating food that has been bought and sold. (53)
In the marketplace, they were intent on taking food, and on festival days, they were devoted to drinking; all were fond of the crossroads and gazing at magical illusions. ||54||
Men will be characterized by great expenditures, devoted to affliction, and have a distaste for nakedness,
as all these conditions recur in succession throughout the various ages of Kali.
In the Kali age, young girls will gradually become enjoyers of all pleasures;
and a child in the womb will take recourse to justice under the name of its mother.
At the end of five thousand years, the disappearance of the sacred fords will occur along with their very roots; in the Kali age, even great rivers will flow with water only as deep as a span.
In the fortieth year, there will be eight women with children who shall meet their death;
at that time, the women will be self-chosen brides, devoid of parched grain, and naked of body.
In the Kali age, women lie on the side of every man, are impure with menstrual blood, are afflicted by disease, are intent only on their own self-interest, and are like *ḍākinīs*. (59)
In the Kali age, the rule of staying indoors at night does not apply everywhere to men and women;
the father’s name is no longer used, and the caste name is not known.
Even the motherhood of childhood no longer exists;
moreover, the entire family collective perishes rapidly in the Kali age.
As long as the minds of both husband and wife remain attached to one another, they truly partake in the nature of desire; indeed, true conjugal union does not exist [in that state].
Her limbs are neither covered nor well-guarded; what then can be said of her other members?
Furthermore, there is the wandering of a woman alone, even in foreign lands. (63)
At that time, in the Kali age, the dwelling of women will be in the fields of others, and men will be subject to the dependence of women; such will be the state at the forefront of the female class.
In every age of Kali, there shall be the rule of women and the rule of the low castes;
in the Tiṣya age, there will be the study of ignorance and a predominance of talk about spirits.
In the Kali age, people prefer compositions that are directly perceptible and avoid those that are indirect;
they seek ease without effort and are devoid of their own true spiritual welfare.
The people were then preoccupied with violence, understanding the highest dharma as deceit;
those who ate vomit were considered superior, while others were regarded as utterly inferior. (67)
During Tiṣya, there will be deceit, envy, and even the slaughter of ascetics;
men and women will become dominated by darkness (tamas) and beset by hunger and fear.
Furthermore, as there are repeated upheavals of countries and kingdoms, the authority of the Veda is not established therein; at such times, force is what possesses authority. ||69||

In the Kali age, there will be oppression of the subjects by those who practice malevolent magic, those of wicked conduct, those who perform evil deeds, those who follow false scriptures, and those kings who forcibly seize the hair [of their victims].
The relations between men and women in matters such as sleeping together are according to their own desire;
there, kings and even outcastes oppress those who are truly righteous. (71)
O Prājāvatī, there the killing of a fetus, the killing of a hero, and the killing of a woman are common;
those of low conduct are always esteemed as superior, while the noble are considered base. (72)
The rulers follow the conduct of thieves and act like robbers;
the vow of monogamy no longer exists, and women who go to meet their lovers increase in number. ||73||
In the Kali age, those seated do not rise when seeing virtuous elders worthy of worship;
in the Tiṣya age, sons strike their fathers, grandfathers, and other ancestors.
In the Kali age, those who occupy high seats are lowly, while the foremost and most eminent remain as servants; the best among the lowly always stand at the city gates as attendants.
In the Kali age (Tiṣya), men will serve those of low caste, praise those born of low origins, and there will be many women for each man. 76.
In the Tiṣya age, indeed, there will be an abundance of beasts of prey, the destruction of cattle and other livestock, and the disappearance of the virtuous. (77)
At that time, the clouds will rain in various colors; all will be hypocrites in their mercantile dealings, devoted to immoral conduct, and harsh in speech, age after age in the Kali Yuga.
The people become revilers and fallen; in city after city there are [empty] circles;
the earth has little water, and its fruits are meager or even fruitless. (79)
Upon the passing of ten thousand years, those whose forms were divine go to dissolution everywhere; not even their temples remain.
At the end of fifteen thousand years in the Kali age,
living beings reach old age and death at the age of sixteen.
A maiden of four years is young, while one of twelve years is old;
a child gives birth within six months, and menstruation ceases at ten years.
At that time, during the end of the Tiṣya [era], people will be short, measuring only one span in height, like those living in pits;
indeed, their stature will be no more than two fist-breadths.
In that Kali age, thieves, those who steal from thieves, and even those who steal from the thief—as well as insects, mice, and mongooses—will all prey upon one another. (84)
In the Kali age, people accomplish their goals through futile hardships by killing women, children, and cattle, and even by slaying their own kin. ||85||
At that time, even though charity remains as a partial practice during the Kali age, it indeed becomes a means of salvation;
yet all else goes to destruction, for there is not even talk of giving.

Then, O Badrikā, even those born in the Kali age who are devoid of charity and other virtues, if they have attained refuge in Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal, they cross over [the ocean of existence] by means of Hari. ||87||
In the Kali age, sacrifices, vows, observances, and restraints perish;
in the Kali yuga, people are born devoted to the practices of heretics.
Abounding in suffering, short-lived, possessing little fortitude, and afflicted by disease; the worlds are filled with unrighteousness and are constantly devoted to killing. (8–9)
That same dharma which was accomplished in a hundred years during the Kṛta age was indeed accomplished in a single year during the Tretā;
in the Dvāpara it was to be accomplished in a month, and in the Kali age, it is accomplished in a single day.

O Badrī, by the singular chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the fruit of the religious duties performed throughout one's life is produced; for in the Kali age, Nārāyaṇa is the bestower of liberation.
When all creatures in the Kali age are afflicted by mutual fear, agitated and wandering about, abandoning their wives and their own homes; (92)
Transgressing all bounds and driven to despair, they have abandoned even their home countries;
they now frequent rivers, oceans, wells, and even mountains.
Extremely distressed, they subsist on honey, meat, roots, and fruits;
overcome by old age, disease, and hunger, they remain on the path of others.
In that Kali age, in every house there will be divine paintings depicting naked men seated upon women, or women seated upon the laps of men.
Goddesses, wearing fine garments and appearing mounted upon their consorts, are seen in the courtyard and the house, painted and embracing the Lord. (96)

In the Kali age, even couples standing in places where embracing beyond bounds is forbidden are made objects of public spectacle; and in city after city, there are dances and theatrical performances featuring young girls.
In the courtyards, there shall be the ritual scattering of parched grain for young maidens and young women;
and at weddings, as well as in the home, there shall be an absence of parched grain for the brides.
In that time, no faults are seen in sensual desire; rather, desire is regarded as a great virtue.
In the Kali age, all activities characterized by the quality of passion (rajas) receive the name of "dharma."
In that age, untruth will appear like truth, and deception will be like righteousness;
a maiden will be like a young boy, and in the Kali age, women will be equal to men.
Human legal procedure is indeed of only one kind and not distinct;
for a brother might kill his sister, and a sister might kill her own brother. (101)
In the Kali age, wives will kill their husbands and those two [husband and wife] will kill each other;
led by unjust means of livelihood, such will be the condition of the people in every place.
At that time, all creatures possessed either the nature of Rākṣasas, or the nature of Daityas, or likewise the nature of Piśācas, or the nature of Dānavas. || 103 ||
Likewise, the ways of plunderers and the ways of thieves will prevail in every house;
in the Kali age, there shall be no freedom from exile, and mutual enmity will exist in every home.
Men whose faculties have fallen away become like mice;
O Badarī, they are said to be those who have strayed from the path due to the influence of the Kali age.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Natural Dispositions of Tiṣya Men," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the virtues that effect deliverance even during the Kali age;
by performing them at any moment of the day, the liberation of the people is brought about. (1)
The power of time operates over all things without a doubt;
likewise, the divinity of the gods gradually declines during the Kali age.
The ascetic power of the sages and their sovereign authority even fall into decline;
indeed, the chastity of virtuous women also undergoes diminution during the Kali age.
Even the yogic practice of yogins becomes devoid of power,
and the lordship of lords becomes powerless in the Kali age.
The spiritual luster of the Brahmins dissolves, there is no doubt;
and in the Kali age, the power of the mantras and their moral conduct indeed fall into decay.
In the Kali age, the fruit of burnt offerings and sacrifices perishes;
in the Kali age, the efficacy of recitations and vows dissolves.
The fruitfulness of gifts varies according to the Tiṣya and Yauvana ages;
indeed, the supreme existence of the Yoginīs vanishes in the Kali age.
The perfection of the perfected ones becomes concealed during the time of Tiṣya;
then, in the Kali age, the fruit of worship appears as empty.
The abode of the virtuous becomes like a wretched dwelling, and the peaceful course of dharma then undergoes decline in the Kali age. || 9 ||
Even the fruit of knowledge does not arise for the sake of peace;
indeed, in the Kali age, there occurs everywhere a total disappearance of dispassion.
In the Kali age, the possession of powers leads to the giving of affliction, and pride arises;
furthermore, in the Kali age after Kali age, the moral character of holy places becomes submerged and declines.
The rescue of the stars depends on the crossing [of the ocean], for they are powerless in that task;
the earth is capable of yielding milk, yet water is powerless in providing satisfaction. 12.
In the Kali age, fire is indeed incapable of cooking; the wind does not grant comfort;
Lakṣmī is impure; and all prosperities are accompanied by calamity.
In the Kali age, those who are the refuge [of others] are afflicted by wounds, and there is no weight in what is heavy;
in the Tiṣya [age], respect falls into pits, and consecration is struck down by distress.
In every age of Kali, honor becomes devoid of splendor, action is bereft of meditation, and stability is indeed lacking in trust. 15.
O Badrikā, in the Kali age, all idols and deities everywhere become like corpses; and the heavens shine as if shrouded in darkness.
Hope and craving increase beyond the lifespan of the Kali age;
one possessed of hope dies in the Tiṣya age, but hope itself never dies anywhere.
In the Kali age, on every single day, people are born devoid of faith;
indeed, in every Kali age, religious rites and other such activities become mere objects of formal performance.
In that Kali age, initiation, mendicancy, and training come to an end;
there will be only armpits, mouths, and flanks, while Yakṣas and Rakṣasas provide no protection.
In a garden, there is a tree bearing fruit, while many others are leafy but fruitless; likewise, among men, one who possesses statesmanship is rare, while many follow the path of injustice. 4.104.20

O women, just as a pit filled with water is rare in wells, so too is a leader who acts for the benefit of his masters rare; elsewhere, such leaders are found everywhere, yet they are merely causes of destruction.
In journeys, some are donors while many are consumers; in business, some act for the sake of others, yet in every house, people act for their own sake. (22)
In that age, truthful speech will be rare, while false speech will abound at every step;
during the Kali age, people will laugh in times of calamity and be envious in times of prosperity.
In the Kali age, human beings become nectar-tongued when insulted, fire-eyed when honored, and clappers of their palms when facing calamity. (24)

In the Kali age, men will engage in gambling, jesting, drama, curiosity, and destruction; they will be intent on making peace only when their backs or feet are threatened, and they will turn their backs on virtuous deeds.
In this Kali age, people become rare in their devotion to the Dharma, their vows, their companions, their worship, their awakening, their labor, their discourse, and their service. (26)
In the Kali age, people are for the most part intent on destruction, while those intent on protection are few;
they are rare in their devotion, but in their affliction, they gather in crowds.
During the Tiṣya [asterism], people are not at all inclined toward renunciation;
yet during the eclipse, everyone is intent on killing, and not even one is intent on saving.
Those skilled in throwing [the enemy] down are few, while those who carry him on their heads to rescue him are many;
those who lift him up are empty-handed, but those who submerge him are numerous. (29)
When the rains arrive, they are full of vigor; when they cease, their spirits wither.
During droughts, they abandon their bodies, and in battle, they scatter the pride of their enemies. (30)
In the Kali age (Tiṣya), people will indeed become possessed by the wicked, devoid of respect for the virtuous, and intent on deceiving their disciples. //31//
In the Kali age, villages will be devoid of fortifications, people will be devoid of shame, and marriages will be entirely devoid of the sacred fire. 32.
In the Tiṣya age, knowledge arises everywhere devoid of protection, giving devoid of pride, and song devoid of the deity. //33//
In the Tiṣya age, grasping prevails everywhere, while giving is supreme as emptiness; O one of wise intellect, in the Tiṣya age, the external cause becomes false. //34//
In the Tiṣya age, however, the drink will be flavorful but the food will always be tasteless;
in the Tiṣya age, the breaking of others' affairs is found everywhere.
In the Tiṣya age, food will bring delight to the senses and cause distress to householders; it will consist of many condiments and serve as an ointment for one's constant wandering.
Wealth resides in another's house; a beloved daughter is in another's hand;
one has no mastery over one's own body, and there is dependence in every home. (37)
In the Kali age, sleep is brief, dreams are numerous, quarrels are frequent, peace is scarce, anxiety is great, and the loss of blood is excessive. (38)
In the Kali age, there will be many medical clinics, yet the people will be afflicted by disease;
there will be constant destruction, and their dwellings will be filled with fear.
In the Kali age, ornaments, dogs, children, and the like, as well as the wearing of fine dress, proficiency in the languages of barbarians, and learning—these all arise everywhere. (4.104.40)
Smoking, intoxication, verbal abuse, and the goddess of speech (eloquence) mingling together during a festival constitute dharma in every respect for one who is firm in his vows. //41//
In the Kali age, policy consists of sucking [wealth], gain comes from those who provide financial assistance, and a wife is found everywhere as one who provides sweet food. (42)
In the Kali age, there will be everywhere those who ripen all things yet dwell in the houses of the vulgar;
in every place, they will be the price for a living being in the act of killing. (43)
In the Tiṣya age, men will be devoid of beards yet possessed of matted locks of hair;
in the Tiṣya age, offspring will be born from vessels made of base metals.
In the Kali age, O Badrikā, the animals will be without their calves, the soldiers will be without their own sons,
and the battles will be fought with weapons that lack handles.
O Badrikā, in the Kali age, brothel-houses, small huts, eating halls, and theaters will exist without the need for formal training. (46)
In the Tiṣya age, women will indeed have many husbands, while men will be as beautiful as women; human beings will find joy in artificial dolls.
People with artificial teeth, wearing artificial breasts, satisfied by artificial sights, and sporting with artificial women. ||48||
In the Kali age, there will be those who perform the work of shaving with their own hands, those who massage their own bodies with their own hands,
animals that are milked by machines, and those who cook food using mechanical means.
In the Kali age (Tiṣya), people will have lightning as their vehicle, the worlds will be devoid of living beings and food and drink, and men will subsist by the sale of blood. 4.104.50.
In the Kali age, human beings will be devoted to animal-like affection, men will be intent on animal-like sexual union, and they will follow the conduct and behavior of animals. ||51||

In the Kali age, men become such that some have [virtue] in their hearts, others in their speech, others in their actions, and still others in their results; some possess it in secret, while others possess it in public.
Even when [an offense] is very slight, people who are dominated by darkness (tamas) commit afflictions;
they live for pride and arrogance, and their heroism consists merely in cavil.
In the Kali age, those ever desiring victory will place women at their head;
men will dress in female attire, and women will wear many variegated garments.

In the Kali age, those devoted to Daityas and Mlecchas, who oppose the scriptures and the virtuous, will destroy the eternal Dharma while being intent only on a livelihood based on that [false] dharma. (55)
Deceivers in the service of the gods, usurers in their domestic affairs, they propagate many false traditions and revile one another as well as the gods. (56)
Those who are experts in the mere display of words, devoted to logic and reasoning, doubtful in all their undertakings, and utterly merciless toward their gurus; ||57||

In the Kali age, people indeed become those who nourish their tongues through traditions, those who nourish their genitals through the householder's life, and those who nourish their fame as ascetics. (58)
In the Kali age, a daughter, though cherished like a son, acts like a son; yet a fortunate woman who seeks refuge in another and strives for the sake of others acts like a partisan.

In the Kali age, the twice-born brahmins will generally conduct their business using iron vessels, will offer libations with water from hollow reeds, and will mostly go without the sacred topknot; indeed, such true brahmins will no longer exist.
In the Kali age, deception is considered human effort, logic leads to the plucking [of hair], all wealth is treated like a family member, but dharma is regarded as an enemy. (61)
In every house there were shops and temples;
in every house there were widows and those bereft of husbands, and their unions occurred in every house.
In the Kali age, masters indeed become dependent on their servants, husbands likewise on their wives, and kingdoms on their subjects.

In every age of Kali, there will be kingdoms with vast populations yet devoid of moral boundaries, and regions lacking established order; moreover, there will be a preponderance of merchandise and courtesans.
To drink water while at the place of eating is a form of hospitality;
to smoke while at the place of drinking water is a form of hospitality. (69)
In the Kali age, drinking warm milk and water is the cause of receiving honor;
likewise, honoring the earth, guests, and the virtuous consists merely of words in the Kali age.
In the Kali age, affection is not the cause of hospitality; neither in the eyes nor in the heart is there true feeling. Even outcastes sit upon high seats, while Brahmins occupy lowly places.
O Badrī, in the Kali age, misconduct becomes a hundredfold, false speech a thousandfold, and wasteful expenditure ten thousandfold.
In the Tishya age, rituals are fruitless; in the Kali age, undertakings are devoid of results.
In the Kali age, men are ignoble in all their actions and arts, and are dark-complexioned.
In the Kali age, people are burdened by dust; they possess a veil of deceit upon the earth, on the mountains, and even in the sky, and there is a confusion among all things.
In every age of the Kali, men indeed project faults onto others while regarding their own faults as virtues; they have broken feet and lolling tongues. (71)
In every age of Kali, men indeed have paths of black mud, wear garments touched by indigo, and are filled with turbidity and other such defects.

In every age of Kali, householders—unstable in their station, abandoning [their duties], and possessed of worldly attachments—will become like tigers and lions dwelling on the outskirts of villages, behaving like dogs. (73)
In every crossroads there are jackals, in every house there are jackals;
in every marketplace there are rogues, and at every step there are thieves during the Tiṣya age.
O Badarī, in each and every sacred seat (dhiṣṇya), there are rogues; in each and every group (vṛnda), there are those who form cliques (vṛndalāḥ);
and in each and every group, they forcibly seize the hands [of the faithful].
In the Tiṣya age, human beings will resemble Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas;
they will be like Daityas, dwarfish, short, and hunchbacked.
In the Kali age, the granaries of men are devoid of grain, the water-stations are devoid of water, and the hearts of men toward one another are devoid of affection. (77)
Even for those devoted to exertion day and night, there is no full acquisition of wealth during the Kali age;
therefore, the Kali age is considered harsh.
Nevertheless, O Badrikā, if any meritorious act is performed there, it will indeed yield a thousandfold fruit when done with faith. (79)
Even in the Kali age, which is a repository of all defects, there is a great virtue:
that by the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, a human being attains purity. (4.104.80)
In the Kali age, worship with mere water, glorification by means of the Name alone, and remembrance of the Form alone—these indeed grant liberation from Hari. (81)
Whether they be of such a kind or that kind, those virtuous ones clad in saffron robes have taken refuge [in me], for in the Kali age (Tiṣya), they rest upon the lap of Śrī Kṛṣṇa like stars.
In the Kali age, fire that is smoky, of dull luster, obscured, or resting in impurity; or fire that consumes what is forbidden, is considered pure and virtuous only when it is truly refined. (83)
Having abandoned his own home, field, wealth, wife, and village, the saint remains seated upon the lap of Kṛṣṇa; therefore, his excellence is eternal. (84)
Abandoning his existence, relinquishing dependence, power, and wretchedness, and casting off all punishment, the excellent sage then took refuge [in the Buddha]. (85)
Even in the Kali age, Hari protects him in his heart, takes hold of him on his tongue, and listens to him even in his refuge; therefore, such a sage is superior.
Even one who is intent on improper physical conduct and behavior is a purifier if he delights in devotion;
for such a knower of Brahman is a saintly person who sanctifies the world. 87.
Even if he were prone to infidelity, or intent on deceit and dishonesty, or even possessed by a thirst for wealth—the son of Kṛṣṇa is the excellent sage. (88)

He is seen as the performer of the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, the one who causes it to be performed, the one who has met [with Him], the speaker of Rāma, and the excellent sage who causes [the scripture] to be recited. 89.
Just as one wearing the dress of Kṛṣṇa in a theatrical performance causes others to remember Kṛṣṇa,
and through that remembrance becomes a destroyer of sins, so too is a sage who possesses such excellence.
Seeing his saffron-colored robes, the wicked bow down to that sage who has established the contemplation of the self as Brahman; therefore, such a virtuous man is always superior. 9.1
O Badrikā, by the sight of a saintly person, as well as by touching, serving, massaging, feeding, or drinking water from him, human beings are purified. 92.
By the dust from the feet of a holy man, by partaking even of his gracious food,
and by attaining the true reality through a holy man, human beings are instantly purified.
In the Kali age, human beings are purified through union with one who has received initiation from Kṛṣṇa, by the practice of devotion, and by leading the life of a virtuous person.
In the Kali age, human beings are immediately purified through association with virtuous men and women, by pleasing them, and by carrying out the commands of the virtuous. (95)
By drinking the nectar from the feet of a saintly person, by embracing a saintly person, and through contact with the body of a saintly person, human beings are instantly purified. (96)
By giving their bodies to the virtuous, as well as by surrendering their senses,
by offering their minds, and by giving their very lives, human beings attain liberation.
Furthermore, through identification with the virtuous, by virtue of being joined with non-obstruction, and by virtue of assuming the form of that [virtue], human beings attain liberation. ||98||
By giving away objects as they desire, by bestowing the prosperity of their households,
and by dedicating everything to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, human beings attain liberation.
Through the placement of Kṛṣṇa, through devotion to Kṛṣṇa, through the practice of Kṛṣṇa’s secrets,
and through the conduct of the vows of Kṛṣṇa’s saints, human beings attain liberation.
O Badrikā, during the Tiṣya [asterism], the gods do not purify through their physical forms, nor indeed do sacred fords;
rather, it is the virtuous who purify instantly. (101)
In the Kali age, virtuous people purify men by quickly offering service;
by performing service to the virtuous, men are instantly purified in the Kali age. (102)
Just as the virtuous are won over by the blessings of the good,
so too do men become pure and purifying in the Kali age.
Through association with the virtuous, through taking refuge [in them], and through chanting the praises of the beloved Kṛṣṇa,
women and men become divine by virtue of remembrance and indeed attain liberation.
O Badarī, through the constant service and chanting of the names of the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, embodied beings attain liberation. 10.5.
O Badrī, this simple means for liberation, which consists of total self-surrender, has been clearly and decisively declared by me during the Tiṣya age. (106)
Through service to, recitation of, hearing, and likewise remembering this [work] of the compassionate Lord, the Master Kṛṣṇa, the Yogin; || 107 ||

Through the practice of total surrender and the cultivation of the state of identity [with the Divine], there exists for embodied beings in the Kali age eternal and auspicious enjoyment and liberation. 108.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Faults of the Kali Age, the Qualities of the Means for Liberation, and the Service of the Virtuous," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 104 ||
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to how even King Māyāpāla—
who was devoted to every kind of sin— was liberated through his surrender to the Holy One.
In the eastern region of Kāmarūpa, there was a king named Māyāpāla;
he was a meat-eater, a drinker of liquor, and devoted to the act of sexual intercourse.
One who steals property and one who defiles a maiden—wherever he sees a beautiful woman among the subjects, anywhere at all—he [seizes her]. (3)
Whether she be a young maiden, a girl, a widow, or a married woman,
he forcibly seizes her through the king's messengers and enjoys her.
For the sake of meat, the king constantly causes the slaughter of animals and eats the flesh of birds of every kind. (5)
He was a devourer of aquatic creatures, devoted to wine and liquor,
and he even caused thefts to be committed in foreign kingdoms through his own spies.
Having seized the wealth of Brahmins, widows, or gods who abide by the dharma,
the king may even deposit it in his own treasury.
He was an opponent of sacrifices and righteous deeds, a reviler of charity,
and one intent on the humiliation of the virtuous and faithful women.
He was a causer of suffering for the mendicants, intent on obstructing fire-sacrifices,
a destroyer of temples, and likewise a hinderer of worship.
He does not perceive the deity at all in the image, nor has he faith in the guru;
he does not even regard him as the Lord, much less as the Supreme Lord.
"I myself am the Blessed One, for I am the King, the Supreme Lord.
Let them indeed sacrifice to me, the monarch, the lord of subjects, the Great Lord."
Let the subjects worship me and propitiate me as Hari;
for the king is Lord Hari manifest in the world, and there is no other Hari who is beyond perception.
A woman must always practice devotion to her husband as if he were Hari in the form of a king;
the tribute paid to the king arises solely for the sake of dharma.
The king is the enjoyer of all things, the teacher, the leader, and the protector;
the king is the embodiment of Brahman and should be worshipped by the twice-born in the sacrifice.
The Śrāddha that satisfies desires is not like any other Śrāddha which must be performed as a duty;
the purpose of man is the satisfaction of desires and the gratification of the senses. (15)
In this world, enjoyment brings about the highest good; it is indeed the supreme goal of human life.
Neither heaven nor liberation is superior, for no one remains in the state of a preta forever.
The world of Yama does not exist at all; that very place is my own prison-house. I am Yama, I am Kubera, and I am Nārāyaṇa.
"Let them all worship me; otherwise, they shall indeed be punished by me"—thus did that King Māyāpāla proclaim everywhere, O Badrikā.
He indeed caused a proclamation to be made among the subjects throughout the kingdom:
"The means of livelihood that had been granted by former kings have been seized by him. (19)
By that oppressive ruler, temples were placed under lock and key,
the flow of worship was destroyed, and Brahmins were repeatedly punished.
By that evil-minded one, virtuous women were defiled, the images of Hari were mutilated, and the rites of pilgrimage, charity, and so forth were destroyed.
The wise who were worthy of performing sacrifices were cast into prison;
many virtuous men were struck by him with his own punishments.
Virtuous women were forcibly surrendered by him to men;
thus that king, through his atheism, destroyed what is called a sacred place (tīrtha).
His own wife was made the Great Queen by the name Kāmākṣī;
she alone was proclaimed to be the Goddess, she alone Lakṣmī, and she alone Durgā.
She is proclaimed as the sacred ford, the mother of the gods, and the one to be honored;
he offers her oblations of liquor, meat, and sacrificial food.
Thinking, "The surrender of everything must be made to the king," he does exactly that;
every morning, the king is constantly established upon the throne together with the queen.
The subjects, having arrived daily at dawn in due order according to the royal decree, bow down like gods and worship both of them.
The Brahmins, having proclaimed the virtues of the king to the world, honored them both;
and the subjects constantly fed the monarch and the queen. (28)
In this way, O Badrikā, blindness indeed prevailed at that time when King Māyāpāla ruled over the region of Kāmarūpa. (29)
Thereupon, the wrath of the gods arose, and indeed a great wrath of the subjects also ensued;
famine occurred in the kingdom, and diseases broke out among the people.
Wildfires broke out repeatedly in the forest regions;
indeed, O Badrī, due to the king's fault, afflictions befell the subjects. (3.1)
Since the subjects followed the king and were even atheistic,
they became followers of the king's disposition in every household.
O Badrī, due to that famine, a great cry of "Alas! arose;
indeed, no human being could find either food or water anywhere.
The great river Brahmaputrī became devoid of water;
due to the wrath of the gods, there was no rain upon the Himālaya. ||34||
All the forests and mountain regions in every direction were utterly consumed by forest fires,
and the mountains shone with their ashes.
O Badrikā, at that time the earth appeared as if scorched;
even the beasts, birds, and aquatic creatures all died. (36)
Food was not obtainable in the kingdom, and the people fell into calamity;
there, men became eaters of flesh and, consequently, devourers of human beings.
Like Rākṣasas, they devour one another; men eat each other, as do women and even children, and they consume the flesh of the dead.
Thus indeed, the subjects were struck down by divine wrath and even by disease;
these are the fruits of the sins and extreme wickedness of sinners in this very birth. (39)
They surely come swiftly with great force; there is no doubt.
Even those rich in merit, though moving with speed, are consumed by the fault of association. 40.105.40.
Even that which is dry, situated in the midst of the moist, is indeed consumed by a forest fire;
so too was a king's hundred sons lost, and his hundred daughters by disease. (41)
The king and queen were seized by disease and became afflicted with consumption;
all the male and female servants died, as did even the animals, from the disease. (42)
The mounts were destroyed and the people were indeed afflicted by hunger;
a supreme wrath arose on all sides within the kingdom of Kāmākṣī. ||43||
Then ghosts, spirits, and piśācas roam about the city;
the messengers of Yama beat them, kill them, and lead them away. (44)
Thus the kingdom became like a second abode of Yama;
men were seen on the earth with their feet and hands flailing about.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, they fainted in the courtyards and other places;
naked, unclothed, and shameless, they were tormented by great suffering. Crying out "Water! Water! and "Food! Food! repeatedly upon the ground, [they lay there]. (46)
Though they were plundering, they were unable to rise up, being utterly stupefied. ||47||
Making terrifying, throaty roars, they indeed abandon their lives;
for there is no one who gives them back, nor is there any other who takes them away or grants them peace. (48)
All are in the same state; alas, who would look after whom?
Indeed, the kingdom of this illusory protector is seen to be in a state of dissolution. 49.
Indeed, the entire accumulated fruit of evil has arrived;
a cry of "Alas! Alas! has arisen on all sides, reaching the ears throughout the kingdoms.
In my world as well as in heaven, even that very news has circulated:
indeed, King Māyāpāla is experiencing the fruit of his own sin. (5.1)
It is also directly perceived here in this very birth that [the merit] is enjoyed by the subjects;
and the river Brahmaputrī also related this story in the presence of Brahmā.
Having heard this, the blessed Sanatkumāra became filled with compassion;
he then quickly bowed to his own father along with the daughter of Brahmā.
Driven by compassion, he went to the earth and beheld that condition;
Kāmākṣī and Devikā, bowing with shame, performed a hospitable reception for him.
The divine Sanatkumāra, that son of Brahmā, and his sister the river—
both of them, having been worshipped by Kāmākṣī, sat down in her own abode.
Seeing them seated majestically on auspicious thrones, he asked the reason for their arrival;
the venerable Sanatkumāra spoke to the virtuous Kāmākṣikā.
In this region, indeed, upon the ground where you have established yourself during a famine, many distressed people perish and the subjects go to their destruction. (57)
The sinful king, together with his subjects, reaps the fruit of his evil deeds;
for by that ruler, the gods, their temples, the sacrifices, and the Brahmins have been destroyed.
And since all creatures born are composed of that [Prakṛti], they consequently undergo suffering;
for the celestial sages declare this to be the truth regarding the world of the gods. 99.
Having heard this from the mouth of the daughter of Brahmā, I have come with compassion born within me,
in order to behold her, to rectify her situation, and to console her in her distress.
"If there is compassion for me, I wish to perform protection.
O Badrikā, having heard this from Kāmākṣin, Sanat-muni spoke.
The king is most sinful, and consequently his subjects are likewise;
the king is worthy of punishment, and he is indeed to be punished in every way. (62)
Hearing these words of Kāmākṣiṇī— that the king, though devoted to his teacher and endowed with compassion, was an enemy to the gods— the sage Sanat spoke.
"Let it be so; let the evil-doing king suffer the range of punishment.
Just as she had thought this, Yama’s messenger arrived there.
Terrible, with a gaping mouth, resembling collyrium in hue and like a mountain in splendor,
he descended through the path of the sky into their presence, brandishing a mallet.
Having seized and bound Mārapāla along with his body in the sky,
he led Māra to the abode of Yama, striking him with a mallet.
Precisely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma declared by Citragupta,
he was cast into a great fire to embrace a red-hot iron image.
Then, having been fried in a cauldron filled with intensely heated oil,
he was subsequently devoured by the Raurava spirits in the Mahāraurava hell.
In the Asipatravana hell, the king was shaken and torn apart in many ways;
he was bitten by cats, scorpions, and the like, as well as by snakes and other such creatures. (69)
The king was repeatedly torn apart by living beings in the place of execution,
and the monarch was made to drink the juices of the seven metals again and again.
Struck with clubs and treated with caustic alkaline decoctions such as *yaṣṭīmadhu* and others,
the king was beaten and cast head-first into a pit of fire where he was set ablaze.
Then he was cast upon the copper ground, crushed by mechanical devices,
ground by grinding wheels, roasted, and devoured by the Yamas.
The king’s tongue was pulled out with tweezers and cut off;
molten lead was poured into his ears and also into his mouth.
A red-hot spike was thrust into his eyes and into his throat;
moreover, the king was pierced repeatedly in the chest with a spear.
Having flayed the skin of the king, the Yamas indeed devoured his flesh;
the blood was drunk by the Yamas, and his marrow was tasted by the Yamas.
He was torn apart by wild beasts, cast into the Kumbhīpāka hell,
crushed in an iron machine, and likewise hurled down from a mountain.
He was carried away in the Vaitaraṇī river and his male organ was cut off;
the king was thus rendered neuter and became devoid of testicles.
He was made to possess a thousand vaginas upon his body, enriched by the vulvas of women;
there he was made to drink the urine of women and consume the impurities of animals.
By the placement of the *śaṅku* [mantra], he was tormented at the nose and the anus;
though he was killed by the obstruction of his throat, he was restored to life by the touch of a hand. (79)
Again the king was devoured, and again he was restored to health repeatedly;
in this manner, the king experienced the fruits of his actions with that very body.
By the will of fate, the venerable Sanatkumāra experienced endless sufferings in the abode of Yama through his meditation and concentration.
He indeed beheld all that fruit of sin upon the king at that time;
then, regaining supreme compassion, he spoke to the virtuous Kāmākṣikā.
The subduing of the wicked is the duty [of kings], and that has arisen in the ruler;
however, compassion for the gods is the duty that must now be shown toward the king and others. (83)
The king suffers hardships and even utters cries of reproach:
"Alas, I am ruined! Alas, I am ruined! O Protector, grant me protection! (84)
I shall not practice atheism, nor sexual misconduct, nor violence; nor shall I commit theft or robbery, nor engage in slander or deceit. (85)
I shall not cause the cessation of sacrifices, nor the obstruction of worship;
likewise, I shall not show contempt for holy men or yogins. (86)
"Alas! If there be some protector, whether Nārāyaṇa or even Nara, let them protect me and lead me from here to their own world along with this very body. (87)
I bow to the Supreme Self and I salute Yama, the Dharma;
I bow to Viṣṇu, Hara, and Brahmā, and I prostrate before Janārdana.
I bow to Kāmākṣī, Satī, Durgā, and Lakṣmī, the protectress;
here I prostrate to the sacred fords and I bow to the holy men who are my protectors. (89)
I bow down to all the gods; may they protect me from the abode of Yama.
I shall worship the Supreme Self and honor the virtuous twice-born.
I shall cultivate association with the virtuous; I will perform ritual bathing at sacred fords and celebrate festivals for my gurus.
I shall perform the sacrifice of charity, the sacrifice of Vedic study, and the sacrifice of knowledge.
"I shall perform the sacrifice of recitation, the sacrifice of oblation, and the service of the virtuous.
Speaking and lamenting thus, he bowed repeatedly toward the sky.
Then, by the command of the god, the virtuous sage Sanatkumāra appeared in an instant before the king in the abode of Yama.
His limbs were radiant like the sun; he was a treasury of austerity, beloved by Hari, a worthy recipient of devotion, a protector of the world, a perfected being endowed with compassion. (94)
Seeing him arrive— a tranquil-minded treasure of merit, a perfected yogi, and one supremely devoted to the conduct of Brahman— the messengers of Yama were struck with fear.
Leaving the king, they went quickly toward the assembly hall of Dharmarāja;
they told him the news, and the Lord of Yama was filled with wonder. (96)
Rising up suddenly, the King of Dharma offered a welcome;
he indeed performed hospitality, worship, and praise for the sage. (97)
He asked about another cause and drank the water from the sage's feet;
the sage said to him, "I have come for the sake of releasing the king from his bonds. (98)
The performance of virtuous deeds is praised for the sake of destroying the sins of sinners;
therefore, I too [perform this] for the destruction of his sins and for his liberation from the bonds of worldly existence. 99.
I have arrived, O Indra of Dharma; release him here!
Do not delay, O Indra of Dharma; release the king quickly.
"The infinity of this suffering cannot be perceived by me;
therefore, release the lord of kings, for I shall take him away with his very body. (101)
Having spoken thus, the sage Sanatkumāra suddenly ceased;
Dharma, having reflected upon these words, spoke again to the sage.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of King Māyāpāla’s Atheism and Great Sins, Their Consequences, the Experience of Yama’s Punishment while Still Embodied, and the Arrival of Sanatkumāra for His Protection," in the Tiṣya lineage of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: O Badrikā, Dharmarāja, bearing his own sins, spoke with humility to the sage Sanatkumāra regarding the conduct of the king.
O Sanatkumāra, the king himself must by all means not release Daṇḍapātra,
for he is exceedingly wicked and a perpetrator of great sins.
He has committed the grave act of consuming liquor, meat, and raw flesh;
he has reviled the gods, destroyed their images, and obstructed the sacrificial rites. || 3 ||
He has committed the theft of the property of gods, brahmins, and the wealthy; he has brought about the destruction of gifts and sacrifices, and has practiced violent robbery.
"This man is a destroyer of the virtue of maidens; he has committed sexual misconduct; he is devoted to the wives of others; and he is an eater of beasts and birds. (5)
This one, who considers himself Hari, is exceedingly arrogant and a destroyer of religious duties;
indeed, he has himself consumed the portions belonging to Nārāyaṇa.
He is a devourer of aquatic creatures, a plunderer and a robber; he is a violator of virtuous and chaste women, and a destroyer of sacred bathing places and holy sites.
He was a destroyer of the temples of gods and deities, a reviler of the righteous, and one who spoke of sinful deeds. ||8||

One who causes others to hear evil, an atheist, one who lives unrighteously, a destroyer of livelihoods, a killer of one’s means of subsistence, and one who forcibly ruins another's character. || 9 ||
This man is a slayer of those who have sought refuge, a blocker of the path to heaven,
an adversary to the oblations for the gods, and a destroyer of the worship of the sacred fire.
This destroyer of the virtuous must not be released under any circumstances,
even for thousands of millions of years or even hundreds of billions of years.
Even while experiencing the fruits of his own sins, there is still no deliverance for him here;
such is this most wicked man, who is a constant reviler of the Blessed One.
Seated eternally upon the throne of Kṛṣṇa, he partakes of the food offering for as long as the earth shall endure and as long as the world of Yama exists.
And there is no end even for one who continues to experience his own sins;
thus, this most wicked man must by no means be released.
O virtuous one, the king himself is sinful, for he bestows the results of sin upon his subjects;
since he is always the one who impels his subjects toward paths of wickedness. (15)
Therefore, this evil-souled one, who is the locus for the fruits of the sins of the subjects,
must not be released at any time until the end of Brahmā’s year.
One is liberated from all sins, yet one is not liberated from the offense against the gods,
nor from betraying trust, nor from being treacherous toward a god or a true guru.
Furthermore, there is no atonement whatsoever for one who destroys the Dharma, nor for one who reviles the gods, nor for one who causes the ruin of sacrifices. (18)
"O Sage, there is indeed no atonement anywhere for one who steals an image;
therefore, this man, who bears the sin of destroying a Brahmāṇḍa, must not be released. (19)
Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
It is indeed fitting that Yama, the ruler who wields the rod of punishment, should inflict punishment;
likewise, it is fitting that a compassionate saint should grant liberation from that punishment.
In ancient times, the virtuous were created by Brahmā for the purpose of destroying the sins of sinners;
and I too was created by Brahmā for the destruction of sin and for liberation.
And R̥bhu, as well as Sanaka and the others, were likewise made my brothers;
they are compassionate, destroyers of sin, and givers of liberation to all embodied beings.
The king, indeed, has incurred punishment for his many kinds of misconduct;
furthermore, great suffering exists among the subjects in Kāmarūpa.
I must also deliver those subjects from that which is caused by drought, that which is caused by disease, and that which arises from divine transgression, by means of bringing about rain.
"Release the king quickly; having taken him, I shall depart, for it cannot be otherwise.
May you always have prosperity, O Dharma; uphold the words of the virtuous. (25)
The words of Hari and the words of the virtuous must never be transgressed;
for if the virtuous are displeased, a great loss will surely ensue.
The illustrious Dharmarāja said:
"O sage, you must not give his sins to anyone;
they should be given to the king, and then he will attain liberation. (27)
Indeed, there exists the gift of evil, the gift of suffering, and the gift of the wicked;
one who does not perform the purification of evil is not able to be liberated. 28.
Whether it be a son, a daughter, a sister, a teacher, or a friend—if they take upon themselves all the sin of the king, then he is liberated. || 29 ||
The venerable Sanatkumāra said:
"Wait a moment, O Dharma; his wife is here, and I shall bring her.
Having spoken thus, the sage brought the queen before Yama in a mere instant.
"Speak! Let the king be freed from sin here; take the sin upon yourself, O ruler of the earth!
She replied, "I do not take the sin, because it brings such great suffering. (31)
"I take upon myself the merit of my husband and never his painful sin;
let the king take those sins committed by me. (32)
"By the king's sin, my sons and daughters—by the hundreds—have perished;
the destruction of subjects continues, yet I do not take up the sin for myself. (33)
"I am afflicted and overwhelmed by suffering; how could I commit an evil deed?
May I indeed be a partaker of merit, and never a partaker of sin. (34)
Having spoken thus, that wife ceased and maintained silence;
then, O Badrī, Dharmarāja spoke to Sanatkumāra.
"O Sage, take upon yourself his sins and lead him to your own kingdom.
"So be it," said the compassionate one; he took the sin with the water.
Then the king attained freedom from fault and was released by Yama;
thereafter, the blessed Sanatkumāra was honored by Yama and the others.
And as soon as he had led the king away and was about to depart,
the countless beings in hell raised a violent outcry.
"O virtuous one, we have obtained a great fortune; do not depart, leaving us behind!
By your arrival, we who reside in this pool have likewise been refreshed by your vital breath. (3.9)
O virtuous one, by the mere sight of you, we have attained supreme peace here;
even the sufferings residing within our bodies and the fierce poisons of Yama have vanished.
The fiery flames have perished, even those within;
therefore, O virtuous one, come here and protect us always. (41)
Thus did the hell-beings, full of longing, pray fervently;
then the blessed Sanatkumāra, moved by compassion, spoke once more.
He spoke to the King of Dharma: "O King, by my desire, release these denizens of hell from their great suffering.
For the company of a virtuous person always destroys the suffering of those who are afflicted."
He is the bestower of peace, the destroyer of evil, and the supreme savior. ||44||
O mighty-armed King Yama, show compassion and release me;
otherwise, I shall not go from here, but shall remain right here in your house.
Thus addressed, King Yama replied slowly to the sage:
"O Sage, you are indeed capable, but justice does not prevail. (46)
It is never appropriate for the liberation of sinners from the abode of Yama; they must not be released while remaining in their fetters without first experiencing the consequences of their sins. 47.
If you release the wicked in this manner, the court of justice will become useless;
many virtuous men will come here bringing with them [the wicked]. (48)
They will liberate their own [beings] from hell, as well as others;
thereafter, this current of blind injustice will continue to flow. (49)
Therefore, all these hellish states must indeed be abandoned;
O Sage, take the king and go, and do as you wish upon the earth.
Thus addressed, O Badarī, the holy Sanatkumāra performed the supreme, purifying recitation of the names of the Blessed One while seated. (51)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Hare, O All-pervading One! ||52||
He constantly caused [the teaching] to be heard by wandering throughout that entire city;
and the denizens of hell, having heard it, then became liberated from their bonds.
Upon hearing that name of Hari, the messengers of Yama then departed far away;
and the denizens of hell, having abandoned hell, thereafter went to heaven. (54)
Sanatkumāra wandered constantly for ten cycles,
repeatedly proclaiming [the name] "Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa" in the world of Yama.
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O young cowherd boy; O Acyuta Keśava, son of Kambharā and Śrī Mahālakṣmī! 56.
O Prabhukṛṣṇa, O Supreme Lord, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Acyuta!
O Lord Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Puruṣottama Mādhava! ||57||
Having thus struck the gong, the Sage shook his head toward the abode of Yama;
wandering all around there, he liberated the people.
The denizens of hell, having left the hells and abandoned the fear born of the messengers, emerged with divine bodies and, having become so, went to heaven. (59)
At that time, the sacrificial pits there were mostly empty;
they had become empty through the force of the sage’s drinking. (4.106.60)
Not even a single inhabitant of hell was seen there in the abode of Yama;
thus indeed did Sanatkumāra bestow his grace.
King Māyāpāla also performed supreme worship, addressing the Inner Self with the words: "O Lord Hari, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (6.2)
Having struck the gong, he forcefully shook the Dhunī;
by that, the denizens of hell were made happy and liberated from the abode of Yama.
Likewise, Dharmarāja, his messengers such as Citragupta and others,
and the hosts of Yama’s servants, became divested of their pride.
Not even a single person remained in the world of Yama who was subject to the fault of punishment;
the blessed Sanatkumāra sent them all to heaven.
Yama, filled with wonder, honored that sage:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of this holy man, as supreme as that of Hari! (66)
Hari is indeed capable of acting otherwise, just as a king, having become pleased, [acts] toward those bound in fetters. (67)
In the same way, the Great Sage swiftly liberates [beings] according to his own will;
for in the presence of the power of the capable, all restrictive rules come to an end.
Indeed, the virtuous alone are capable of destroying the sins of sinners;
for the righteous are truly able to effect even a complete reversal of the lines of destiny.
The virtuous ones, capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, who ward off sin and bestow heaps of merit, are evermore powerful. (4.106.70)
Wherever the glory of Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇasvāmī resides in the heart,
all powers indeed dwell there in that virtuous Mādhava.
Having said this, Yama’s lord spoke to him: "I must always be forgiven by you;
even for the sake of prosperity, the householders' faults must be forgiven by the virtuous. (72)
Having thus entreated him, the King of Yama himself offered worship to the sage,
presenting a garland of flowers, sandalwood paste, and the waving of lights, while prostrating like a staff.
The food offering consists of various delicious sweets, the nectar of milk, excellent meals,
auspicious nectar-water, and likewise the finest mouth-freshener.
Having washed the sage’s feet with milk, Dharma himself drank it;
and his wife, Dhūmrorṇā, also drank the water from the sage’s feet. (75)
Citragupta and others, as well as the scribes who are sons of Brahmā,
drank the water from the sage’s feet and thereafter accepted his grace.
All the messengers of Yama, as well as Śravaṇā, the ancestors, and other groups of servants belonging to the family of King Yama. ||77||
They all prostrated themselves like a staff before the sage Sanatkumāra and offered him their leave with loudly proclaimed shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
Sanatkumāra, having bestowed blessings upon them all,
led the king through the path of the sky and went to Kāmākṣiṇī.
Then the queen established both the king and herself in that abode;
for as soon as they beheld those two together in their bodies, all the sufferings of Yama vanished entirely.
Once born, they both became believers in the existence of God and devoted themselves entirely to divine rites;
they then commenced an auspicious sacrifice together with Brahmins and great sages.
In the Viṣṇu sacrifice, those two gave as their sacrificial fee the emptiness of their treasury;
out of devotion, they gave everything they possessed—coins, gold, and silver.
The blessed Sanatkumāra performed the sacrifice;
the clouds rained exceedingly, and diseases were destroyed on all sides.
The king's consumption was indeed destroyed root and branch, and by the grace of the sage, the kingdom became resplendent with abundant harvests. (84)
From the moment he was born, the virtuous one gave to the king a divine and auspicious inexhaustible gourd-bowl filled with sweet food. (85)
Sanatkumāra gave the king and the queen a covered vessel filled with inexhaustible water, as well as a command.
With two gourds that are not empty, filled with food and water, and covered [with a lid], one should give them continuously with the right hand. 87.
That water and food shall remain inexhaustible for the duration of one year;
thereafter, O Tumbikās, you two shall come to me of your own accord. (88)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
He gave this mantra to the king, as well as to the queen and the subjects. (8–9)
Having spoken thus, and having received and then bestowed the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon Tumbikā,
the sage departed by way of the sky to Satyaloka, the abode of bliss.
Then, at the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), the king performed the śrāddha for those who had died;
and those ancestors known as *pretas*, having drunk and eaten [the offerings], [were satisfied]. (91)
Having bathed in the waters of the Brahmaputrī and become liberated, they went to heaven;
Kāmākṣī became exceedingly gracious and the granter of all desires.
Both the king and the queen worshipped her as their mother every day.
He indeed caused all the temples to be constructed once again.
Māyāpāla likewise had the consecration performed once again;
he provided a means of livelihood and appointed the brahmins to their duties.
The king protected non-violence, celibacy, and non-stealing;
the monarch completely renounced meat, liquor, and other such things. (95)
The king indeed caused many festivals of storytelling to be held,
as well as delightful free-food distributions and most beautiful schools of learning.
He caused vast and beautiful hermitages to be built,
as well as provisions for religious duties and the service of virtuous and chaste women.
The king also caused protection to be provided for the destitute and the wretched, and he established sacred circles throughout the kingdom for the purpose of worship. (98)
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, Ādikṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa; O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, Lord of the liberated, whose sole devotion is liberation! ||99||
Thus the subjects performed the ritual purification and engaged in the chanting of mantras;
by the grace of the Supreme Lord, that kingdom indeed became Vaishnava.
O Blessed One, all people have become intent upon the path; with their whole being directed toward the way of liberation, they shall in due time attain final release.
In time, the king also, uplifted by Sanatkumāra,
reached the imperishable abode of Hari, traveling in a celestial chariot together with his wife.
Thus, O beloved of Badarī, if this compassionate one is served, he is a saint who destroys all sins and bestows all merit. (10.3)
It would grant liberation, it would grant heaven, it would destroy calamities, and it would destroy the great evils of the Kali age in a mere moment. (104)
He destroys their shackles and releases them from the bondage of illusion;
he leads his own dependent, who is a vessel of compassion, to the Supreme Self. 102.
Therefore, in the Kali age, the saintly person is indeed the great means that bestows liberation;
he is the divine vessel of the Supreme Lord and the bestower of all goals.
O Badrikā, Hari—the best of holy beings and the destroyer of even the most heinous sins—is to be served by people in the Kali age; He fulfills all desires. 107.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Māyāpāla of Kāmarūpa’s Experience of Torments in the World of Yama with his Physical Body, and His Liberation Effected by the Saint Sanatkumāra," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Badarīpriya said: O Nara-Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, Mādhava!
When half of the Kali age has passed, what kind of duties are to be observed by people? (1)
When material wealth declines, there occurs a decline in virtues and a decline in strength;
when time declines, there occurs a decline in dharma and a decline in faith.
When there is opposition, the desired goal is not achieved; consequently, all forms of decline set in among the masses of people, who are repeatedly incited by atheism.
At that time, what indeed were the purifications, the cleanliness, and the vows?
What was the nature of the worship and other rites, and what were the sacrifices then like?
Proclaim those virtuous conducts that must be observed by me in the Kali age;
for generally, some faithful ones indeed observe them even in the Tiṣya age.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
O Badrikā, during the Kali age (Tiṣya), when the flow of the river is downward, the bulls are considered to be lowly;
listen as I describe all those situated therein in brief.
In the Kali age, bathing with cold water does not exist at all;
rather, bathing with warm water is considered appropriate only here and there.
In the Kali age, the ash-bath is generally for the order of renunciants;
in the Kali age, the morning bath consists merely of washing the hands and the face. (8)
Purification of the mouth is achieved by gargling with ashes or mud;
in some cases it occurs with a wooden stick, and in all cases by the inhalation of smoke.

In the Kali age, the throwing of oil, the cleansing of the head with powder, and the purification of the mouth shall consist of sipping water; at that time, the act of *ācamana* will take the form of drinking sweet water.
In the Kali age, is the worship of the gods performed with water alone, or not? Is the offering of food merely a mental conception, or is it not even that in the Kali age? (11)
The nightly lamp-offering may be performed with a single wick and fire, or with water, or not at all;
the prostration may be performed by lying flat like a staff, or it may be a mere salutation; and there may be the cry of "Victory! or no hymn of praise whatsoever. (12)
The sacrifice consists of pouring drops of oil into the fire of the hearth;
the food offering is a bilva fruit, offered either month by month or year by year.
Likewise, the gift of attire [should be given] to the deities and others every month or year;
the gift of vermilion every year, or the gift of garments and so forth, or even new ones. (14)
Or likewise, the ritual bathing may be performed every month or even every year;
thus, in the Kali age (Tiṣya), the divine procedure is seen to undergo diminution.
In the Kali age, hospitality is performed with water alone or by word alone;
the Vaiśvadeva rite consists merely of placing a morsel of food in one's own mouth.
In the Kali age, evening worship, wandering in groves and gardens, theatrical performances, festivals, and the acquisition of women and wealth exist in every house.
In the Kali age, that bull [the virtuous man] is not defiled by women’s grooming of their hair, the application of auspicious fragrant powders, or cooked food containing grains. (18)
Cooked food that is untouchable is not forbidden for anyone who is a *vṛṣa*;
all kinds of water may be drunk, for pure water is always *vṛṣa*. (1.9)
There is no impurity even in the alms-bowl; the bowl is truly purifying.
Indeed, when washed with the water and grain remaining from the meal, it is always pure.
A vessel wiped with cloth is then pure in every respect;
indeed, in the Kali age, cotton cloth is everywhere pure even when it contains wool.
After the abandonment of impurity, bathing does not exist at all, indeed it does not exist in the Kali age;
purification of the hands is by water alone, and the purification of the private parts is by means of a cloth.
In the Kali age, there is no washing of the feet, nor is there the sweeping of the ground;
in the Kali age, there is no expiation, for royal punishment alone is the purifier.
In the Kali age, purification is by means of wind or by the rays of the sun;
or purification may be through sweeping, but in that age, smearing [with cow dung] is not permitted.
Contact with beasts, birds, and the like does not constitute a defect in foods;
nor indeed is there a defect in what is left over from a meal, nor in that which has stood overnight.
In that age, the fault of touching the bowl or the lips will not exist in every house;
rather, in the Kali age, there will be a confusion of traditions within each household, yet true dharma will indeed remain.
In the case of contact with a corpse, impurity (sūtaka) indeed persists until one bathes;
however, in the Kali age, contact with Rāhu generally does not result in impurity at all. (27)
Impurity due to death lasts as long as the memory of grief persists;
moreover, in the Kali age, the food for the śrāddha rites on the eleventh day and subsequent days is found in every house. (28)
In the Kali age, that meal is understood to be taken even after one day has passed;
as long as the mother's health is not restored, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka) regarding her. 29.
In the Kali age, the impurity of birth (sūtaka) there belongs only to the mother and not to others;
at that time, it is held that for women, the impurity of menstruation (rājasvalya) is no longer considered sūtaka.
In the Kali age, the mere sight of menstrual blood is considered as impure as urine;
likewise, there is no impurity from sexual intercourse for those who are already possessed of sin.
Just as purity is not reckoned in the case of vomiting when it is the discharge of impurity,
so too in the Kali age, those who carry away filth and even outcastes are considered pure in every city.
In the Kali age, even those who eat the flesh of the dead shall be pure in every house;
Yavanas, Śvapacas, and leather-workers shall be servants in every home.
In the Kali age, those who cook and those who serve as cooks in the dwellings of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others incur no fault from touching pigs, donkeys, horses, or camels. (34)
At that time in the Kali age, dwelling in the temples of Mlecchas will indeed be pure;
likewise, there will be great honor for vices and the total abandonment of religious vows.
In the Kali age, eating food that has been prepared for six people is considered a meritorious duty;
in the Tishya age, eating a single meal is reckoned as being equivalent to a full fast.
In the Tiṣya age, one who observes the vow of having only one wife is indeed counted as a perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika);
at that time, even a householder who abandons his duties is reckoned as a renunciant (tyāgin).
In the Kali age, teachers who carry the burden of desire and hatred are counted as givers of liberation;
in the Kali age, gurus who lead others along the path of hatred are givers of liberation. (38)
In the Kali age, even clever cavillers are honored like lords;
a servant who obeys commands is a great guru to a householder. (39)
In the Kali age, even a householder who performs the work of a servant is honored if he is renounced;
and a householder who gives away his wife is honored if he is devoted to compassion and renunciation. ||4.107.40||
He alone is the supreme king of devotees in the Kali age, connected by kinship;
in the Kali age, householders who eat food obtained as alms are truly righteous. ||41||
Those living as householders cause their own state of servitude to be performed for the virtuous;
a virtuous person who performs service for them is the best among those who follow the true dharma of the householder. 42.
In the Kali age, however, the highest duty for teachers and disciples is the sharing of a single wife;
and even for women, being enjoyed by another [as a husband] is for the sake of their bellies. 43.
In every age, in every house, and among every person, the purification of earthen vessels is always performed in every age. 44.
The touch of leather is a defilement, but the touch of feathers is not; likewise, the touch of impurity is a defilement, yet in the Kali age, this applies to all living beings indeed.

In the Kali age, dwelling in a cremation ground is not considered a fault, nor is being grey with the smoke of corpses; even touching a corpse that is lying on its side is not regarded as a defilement.
In the Tiṣya age, people do not consider contact with urine to be a defilement;
in the Kali age, even a garment touched by the impurity of the nose is regarded as pure.
In the Kali age, a clean *dhotī* and a clean loincloth are pure;
even a *ghargharī* is pure in the Kali age, and a loincloth is pure; one with a fine tail-hair [whisk] is always pure. (48)
In the Kali age, the left hand is pure; the nose is pure though possessed of impurities.
In the Kali age, the slender stalk is Kalāvatī; the water-shed is pure, bestowing water. 49.
In the Kali age, a leather case, a well-vessel, a water-pot, the machine of an oil-presser, and the oil-maker himself are indeed pure. (4.107.50)
In the Kali age, liquor shall be pure; in the Kali age, blood shall be pure;
and in the Kali age, all bone shall be pure, resembling the ivory of an elephant. 51.
In that Kali age, the marrow of fish will indeed be pure, the fat of pigs will be pure, and the eggs of chickens and other such birds will certainly be pure. ||52||
In the Kali age, flour-cakes and other such foods cooked in water are pure in every household;
likewise, the barber and his razor are pure, as are the small vessels used for shaving.
In the Kali age, the vessels containing milk, curd, and other such items of a Mleccha are always pure;
likewise, among every person in the Kali age, medicine rich with meat and wine is pure. (54)
In the Kali age, even the falling of a hair into a food vessel makes the food pure;
likewise, a voyage across the ocean and a lock on a palace gate are considered pure.
Onwards from onion and garlic, everything is pure in every house during the Tiṣya [nakṣatra];
likewise, leaf-plates, metal plates, and even mud are pure during the Tiṣya.
Spitting in a corner of the house, against a wall, at a door, or at a city gate, or upon the hearth, in ashes, or beside one's bed—these acts require purification in the Kali age. (97)
In the Kali age, that which is performed after sunrise is considered waking;
even an undertaking made during the middle of the night becomes dharma in the Kali age.
Day and night, the operation, construction, and movement of machines, as well as mutual combat for the sake of petty gain—that is the "bull" (the characteristic strength) in the Kali age. (59)
Even the householder’s stage of life is praised as virtuous for the elderly in the Kali age;
yet in the Kali age, victory through unjust means is considered dharma, though it brings great suffering.
He who, during the Kali age, provides even a slight degree of wisdom to a living being who is otherwise wavering in falsehood, is indeed a teacher of Dharma; he alone is a knower of Dharma.
In the Kali age, those who do not know the scriptures yet shave their heads are indeed the embodiments of dharma;
likewise, a bull is one who spends the hour of Brahmā in sleep or in amorous play.
Failure to remember the gods at evening, the omission of the Gāyatrī during the day, failing to recite the Japa, neglecting the Agnihotra, and likewise studying while among the village folk; || 63 ||

In the Kali age, religious duties consist entirely of gambling, such as the offering of libations to those who have no father, and the making of clear images and dolls; indeed, there is no true spiritual sentiment therein.
Indeed, even in the cutting of nails and hair, impurity is not considered [to apply] in the Kali age;
nor is impurity reckoned there even for one who dwells in a house of excrement. (65)
In that time, the touching of the father-in-law by the daughter-in-law was not considered a corruption;
rather, in the Kali age, connection with another's lineage or one's own lineage and so forth is an ornament.
Marrying a low-born maiden is the highest praised dharma;
the sacred thread around the neck with its moon-shaped ornament is the mark of the divine.
In the Kali age, applying a sectarian mark on the forehead is a blemish; righteousness is like a second moon;
and even while the father is still living, the son undergoes the shaving of his beard and head.
In the Kali age, indeed, dharma is praised as being without the marriage fire, without a Brahmin as a giver, and without the formal bestowal of a maiden—such is the bull of dharma. (69)
In the marketplace, however, the highest bull [of dharma] is the honoring of guests and the giving of food;
in the Kali age, the dharma that requires no ritual refinement and involves no expense is the bull.
In the Tiṣya age, houses will indeed become places of slaughter;
in that Kali age, a bull will be yoked to a cart for the sake of cows.
In that Kali age, the practice of one wife for many husbands is considered dharma;
likewise, there will be the recitation of village leaf-manuscripts in the morning and the ritual of the bull.
In the Tiṣya [age], taking care of widows is the highest service to others;
in the Tiṣya, the acceptance of even sinners is then the most beneficial dharma.
In the Kali age, the drinking of unstrained liquids and juices is a source of virility;
likewise, in the Kali age, even a woman who has not undergone pregnancy attains motherhood through the presence of virility.
In the Kali age, even a young maiden is considered a mother; in the Kali age, even a prostitute is worthy of worship, and even a common actor is regarded as a bull. 75.
In the Kali age, conduct consists largely of silent gestures expressed through verses;
even deceit and mere tradition serve as the primary basis for legal determination.
In the Kali age, all renunciants will be mere traders in every monastery;
in the Kali age, those who merely assume the guise of renunciants will be presiding over circles of many women.
In the Kali age, householders will be neglectful of the worship of the gods through their servants, devoid of devotion, and intent only on the worship of their offspring. (78)
In the Kali age, the bulls of the teachers possess faces on both sides;
in the Kali age, dharma belongs to the householder, who is the enjoyer of the fortune of righteousness.

In the Kali age, the consumption of the institution of Dharma is like a bull being devoured by man; for embodied beings, dharma consists of giving, whether it be small or great, as well as non-taking. (4.107.8)
In the Kali age, miserliness during festivals, the consumption of a daughter's dowry, and the extensive exploitation of the subjects—these are the religious duties practiced at that time. 8.1.
In the Kali age, there is the waging of unjust wars, service for the sake of livelihood, and meager hopes despite abundant gains; thus, dharma is completely obscured.

In the Kali age, there will be the destruction of boundaries, a state of mind characterized by passion (rājasī), falsehood at every step, and the dharma of the bull (vṛṣa) will be overturned on all sides.
In the Kali age, dharma consists in the performance of all types of work by people of all castes, the wearing of all kinds of dress and so forth, and equality among all. (84)

In the Kali age, sons born of the wife (aurasa), those born of the wife’s field (kṣetraja), and the sons of female slaves (dāsīputra) are always equal; they are equal in the division of inheritance, and daughters likewise are equal.

In the Kali age, one who holds authority over the sacred hearths (dhiṣṇya)—whether he be a disciple, a son, or a friend—is established within the community and is considered a great leader of the assembly. 86.
The state of being a Brahmin lasts for only a single body, and at the end of the Tiṣya age, it results in the destruction of the lineage;
the state of being a Kṣatriya brings great power, yet at the end of the Tiṣya age, that power is destroyed.

The status of a Vaiśya and the possession of wealth [prevail] until the end of the Tiṣya age; at the end of the Tiṣya age, there is the loss of wealth, the status of a Śūdra, servitude, and at the end of the Tiṣya age, the disappearance of servitude.
O Badrī, in the Kali age, people indeed possess uniform and identical characteristics;
there, no sin truly resides within people, owing to the power of the Kali age.
At that time, even a very small gift given to a virtuous person bestows heaven and liberation;
indeed, in the Kali age, the mere chanting of Hari's names is the means for attaining liberation.
Recitation on a garland of the name "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" bestows liberation;
