this recitation is the medicine for sins, destructive of evil, and a remover of transgressions in the Kali age.
The washing away of impurities consists of serving the virtuous and the Guru Hare;
the internal remembrance of Viṣṇu is the supreme purifier and sanctifier. 92.
Purity of being is the great purity; in the Tiṣya age, there is no other purity.
In the Kali age, there may be some external purity, but purity of essence exists only rarely.
In the Kali age, there is no purity of action, nor is there purity of merit in any way;
however, in that age, purity of recitation is praised, for it is indeed righteous.
The dedication of everything to Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Guru, the Eternal Lord—this alone is the praised dharma in the Kali age, and therein it is the final means that bestows liberation. (95)
Indifference toward the duties of others, tranquility in one's own duties, and the dedication of all actions to Hari-Kṛṣṇa are the means for liberation in the Kali age. 96.
For all embodied beings in the Kali age (Tiṣya), there are indeed six means for attaining liberation:
service, self-surrender, devotion, meditation, giving, and glorification.
Service to the true guru Kṛṣṇa bestows great blessings;
it is purifying, affectionate, and grants the supreme abode. || 98 ||
The offering of everything to Śrī Hari or to the Guru takes the form of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya);
that actionlessness, when devoid of worldly enjoyment, then bestows purity and liberation. 99.
Devotion with affection, service as a servant, and constant obedience to Hari and the Guru— such service performed out of love then bestows liberation.
Meditation on the form of Śrī Hari should always be held within the heart;
likewise, meditation on the Guru within the heart bestows the state of being absorbed in Him. (101)
Liberation is indeed identity with that [Nārāyaṇa], possessing the very nature of Nārāyaṇa;
and that state which is equal to Nārāyaṇa is the true fruit of meditation.
Therefore, in the Kali age, meditation is always superior to the divine bull;
meditation bestows liberation and is the abode of the limbs of Nārāyaṇa. || 103 ||

One should practice generosity toward Nārāyaṇa, the virtuous, the destitute, the Brahmin, the teacher, the twice-born, the truthful, the chaste woman, sacred knowledge, and those who provide assistance to others.
Indeed, when given to Kṛṣṇa, who is the inner controller of all, a gift bestows liberation;
even a very small gift offered to Hari yields inexhaustible fruit and is eternal.

In the Kali age, all charity given with desire bestows heaven and prosperity; however, when offered with the thought that it is for Kṛṣṇa, it is free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa) and grants liberation.
One should constantly perform the chanting (kīrtana) of the names of Viṣṇu: "O Kṛṣṇa! O Hare! O Lord!
O Nārāyaṇa! O Mahāviṣṇu! O Puruṣottama! O True Sovereign! (1.07)
O Lord, O Anādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Śrīkṛṣṇa Mādhava!
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa who holds Pāśavatī, O Consort of Lakṣmī, O Beloved! || 108 ||
O Badrī, I have thus described to you the practice of the Tiṣya [age], which bestows liberation, destroys evil, and grants great joy. 109.
For at that time, in the Kali age, there will be no expansion of the teachings nor any decline in moral conduct;
rather, in that Kali age, the teachings will be fashioned and made to conform [to the needs of the times]. (4.107.110)
Even a very small amount of Dharma indeed protects one from great fear during the Tiṣya age;
by reciting or hearing this, one established in the Tiṣya age shall become fearless.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "A Concise Description of the Dharmas of the Kali Age and the Exposition that Any One of the Six—Service, Offering, Devotion, Meditation, Giving, and Chanting—is a Means to Liberation," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Badarīpriyā said: O Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe!
At the end of the Kali age, will the dharmas once again become true, or not? (1)
At the end of the final Kali age, at the conclusion of the kalpa, what is the state of affairs?
Does it become empty once more, or does a new, supreme, embodied reality arise? (2)
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; at the end of the Kali age, by the will of Hari, I shall indeed manifest for the sake of establishing the true dharmas.
Then you indeed took the form of a sword, assuming a white appearance;
praised by the gods, you were divine, moving through water, earth, and sky.
You are born as this man with a sharp edge and the form of a horse;
white in appearance, you possess the movement of earth, water, sky, and fire.
When he, who stands at my side and is worshipped by the gods, becomes manifest— then I shall [reveal] him, who is my own form, possessing white horses and a human body.
Having ascended [the chariot], I, the son of Dharma and the son of a brahmin named Viṣṇu,
then beheld you, who were endowed with divine power, in the form of a sword, most beautiful to behold.
O Badrī, having taken hold [of you], I shall wander over the earth, through water, and on land;
then, by my very breath, there shall be the destruction of the sins and impurities of the Kali age.
The destruction of sinners who possess bodies of impurity shall be by my sword;
and the transformation of those undesirable mental states shall occur through meditation upon me.
It increases the lifespan of virtuous men and naturally inclines those whose nature is steadfast in dharma toward it. (4.108.10)
The manifestation of the great sages who have mastered the Dharma, as well as my own assistance from millions of divine teachers, occurred at that time. || 11 ||
It is the source of prosperity for women, maidens, and virtuous wives, as well as for ascetics who are devoted to moral conduct and vows. 12.
In this world, there is generally a harmonious meeting between those who are diligent in action and renunciants who possess divine vision, as well as with children who possess great wisdom. (1.3)
At that time, the power of the divine teachers and gurus who were yogis from birth,
as well as the purity of the transformations of the earth, was brought about by my own power.
The manifestation of previous dharmas and actions that bestow liberation, the perception of virtuous deeds, and the engagement of those whose nature is sacrifice; || 15 ||
And at that time, there was the arrival of the gods upon the earth in my presence, and indeed,
the propagation of the creation of Dharma among every person.
Through contact with my feet, the earth becomes pure, purifying, and auspicious;
through my yoga, the waters also become divine and effective for spiritual practice.
Through my grace, even sacred fords (tīrthas) become empowered, and the sentience of shrines (caityas) likewise arises. (18)
Then mental states possess strength, conceptualization becomes fruitful, embodied beings endure pleasure and pain, and their physical vigor flourishes. (1.9)
Longevity for children, chastity among maidens and others, and even the destruction of the wicked, of barbarians, and of women. (4.108.20)
Indeed, there is no existence for those whose bodies are perfected by the *kalka* [stage];
thus I move with great speed through the sky and upon the earth with my sword. (2.1)
In a mere year, I bring about the transition of the ages for the worlds;
those who are my devotees and have become fit for the Kṛta age remain, and no others.
Cows, medicinal herbs, forests, gardens, and groves shall abound with milk; and they shall become long-lived. (23)
Out of fear of me, the world of thieves shall perish from the surface of the earth,
and their destruction shall be brought about by my armies, who bear divine forms.
Then, by your resolve, hundreds of thousands of white horses with divine forms shall indeed become your sons, serving as mounts for your army.
Then, born from my resolve, the gods in the form of armies destroyed on all sides those wicked Mlecchas and Rākṣasas.
He repeatedly [destroyed] the unrighteous Dānavas and Daityas, as well as those humans who were contrary to dharma;
thus the entire surface of the earth became stainless, auspicious, and untouched by any sin.
But then, O Badrī, at the end of the Kali age, through my refuge, those dharmas which are the very form of truth shall arise; indeed, I shall proclaim them in many ways. (28)
All my subjects were devoted to me, practicing non-violence and truthfulness;
they were dedicated to virtuous conduct and vows, and endowed with mental strength. ||29||
Those who have accomplished their purpose and are devoted to the dharma of peace arise;
they are rare, numbering only a few thousand, and within a single *yojana* there is but one such person. (4.108.30)
Others meet their destruction by my sword of Time, yet through my wandering upon the earth, even the mandalas of the gods [are subdued]. (3.1)
There, even great sages who are beyond the reach of ordinary perception wander upon the earth;
so too do the sacred fords, Dharmadeva, the sons of Dharma, and the Śaktis.
Drawn by my majesty, those Mahānandas wander through the regions previously abandoned, as well as in dwellings and sacred sites (caityabhūmi).
They resume their own dwelling as before,
having been prepared for them through the application of my resolve and by the turning of time.
Through the power of future merit, the transformation of truth among living beings shines forth, manifesting in various places as one who has perfected the self.
And at that time, peace prevails and increases for all embodied beings in the world, when the Moon, the Sun, as well as Puṣya and Jupiter [are in conjunction]. (36)
When they converge in a single zodiacal sign, that is considered the Kṛta Yuga;
when such a conjunction occurs, everything then becomes worthy of being performed as a rite of perfection.
Brahma-sacrifices arise here and there, and Viṣṇu-sacrifices arise at every place;
expiations and pilgrimages to sacred fords arise for embodied beings. (38)
Festivals arise for me in every kingdom and in every home, O Badrī;
likewise, there is purity of being and excellence of being. (39)
Then, like a virtuous person, the purity of all social classes shines forth;
there is constant rain from the clouds and an abundant emergence of flavors.
Then there were many streams of milk and honey, and the increase of prosperity was again and again greater than before. 41.
When that is performed, there arises for embodied beings the vision of the divine, and the actual descent of the gods upon the earth occurs. (42)
When that is performed, there is then a path for men even toward heaven, as well as for women, their chastity, and for ascetics, their state of penance. (43)
At that time, there was tranquility of the senses and the subsiding of forest fires;
there was the calming of fevers and the pacification of anxieties. (44)
At that time, the cultured people were indeed preeminent in their devotion to Brahman;
then the Vedas themselves manifested within the hearts of embodied beings.
Furthermore, in the Kṛta age, the system of castes and stages of life, the establishment of purity and conduct, faith in the afterlife, and truthfulness of behavior arise once again. 46.
At the hour of Brahma, one should perform praise, meditation, bathing, worship,
as well as the propitiation of the gods and the offering and worship for the ancestors.
Saluting the elderly, self-reflection, devotion to the divine, and the performance of the five great sacrifices—these, moreover, arise naturally in one who abides in truth. 48.
In the Kṛta age, dharma, which is the very livelihood, exists among the people through its four feet by virtue of natural reflection. 49.
When the consecration rite of the gods has been performed, mental wonders and even the vision of the gods occur in dreams beforehand.
Then, gradually, there was the appearance [of the gods] in the form of virtuous brahmins;
thereafter, they appeared in person upon the earth. (51)
And for the sake of the virtuous great sages, boys and girls are born endowed with supernatural powers, miraculous wonders, and the attainment of perfections. ||52||
The accomplishments of speech proceed, and even ritual actions become fruitful; furthermore, the abundance of crops shines forth, endowed with every grain. (53)
Devotion to the gods is desired and it prevails among the subjects;
when the Kṛta age arrives, there will be a diminution of defects such as passion and hatred. (54)
The fires shine forth, stainless, bestowing happiness and auspiciousness;
the winds, moreover, are free from disease, pleasant to the touch, and granters of tranquility.
Beings, birds, aquatic creatures, and likewise animals—
those various classes of living beings are born in the Kṛta age, following the course of the Yugas.
Through the power of truth, the bodies of human beings become great;
even animals, birds, and trees possess lofty forms.
Thereafter, his strength was increased a hundredfold, and in the Kṛta age it was multiplied a thousandfold;
likewise, his vigor, knowledge, and heroism were each multiplied a thousandfold in the Kṛta age. (58)
In the Kṛta age, the powers within foods are increased a thousandfold; furthermore, even those whose life-force resides in bones regain their vital breaths in the Kṛta age. (59)
Celestial chariots, temples, and new cities are produced through the creative intellects of artisans when one abides in truth.
In the Kṛta age, the visions of living beings become divine, the truthfulness of virtuous women becomes divine, and the speech of the righteous becomes divine. (61)
Then, for the sake of embodied beings, there arise movements within the depths of the ocean, movements in the sky, and movements upon the upheaval of the earth.
O Badrī, upon the destruction of the Mlecchas,
I shall indeed establish there among the twice-born classes kings who act as protectors.
Thus, when the Dharma is indeed true, its fourfold nature prevails;
truth, austerity, sacrifice, and charity prevail in every place. (64)
Furthermore, at the end of the Satya age, the beautiful dharmas of the Tretā arise; then follow the dharmas of the Dvāpara, and then again those of the Tiṣya (Kali) age.
In this way, the wheel of the Yugas revolves continuously;
it lasts for a thousand Yugas and concludes with the end of the Kalpa.
O Badrikā, at the end of the Kali age, for a hundred years,
a great drought shall arise in the evening that destroys all living beings.
Then those suns heat the earth and indeed parch it;
through the heat of the suns, the earth becomes as dry as charcoal. (68)
Then the entire surface of the earth indeed becomes composed of fire;
clouds born from the steam of that fire rain down for a hundred years.
Indeed, half of the cosmic egg, filled with water as far as heaven, comes into being;
the ten worlds sink into the midst of the waters, reduced to the form of ashes.
When the rivers at the end of the eon become mud,
all those who have been submerged in water come to rest in the netherworld as mud.
In the form of a fish, I, the Blessed One, dwelling in the midst of the waters, protect the seeds in every way for the sake of future creation.
But Kalki, the Blessed One, having himself assumed a subtle form along with his horse, sword, and army,
shall indeed depart from this world while remaining invisible.
At night I take the form of a fish, and at the end of the night, for the sake of the earth,
I indeed exert myself, assuming the form of a boar.
As a fish, I indeed roam in the water at the very break of dawn;
as a boar, I go to the great Kārdama Golaka situated at the base.
Having done so, I, possessed of power, shall carry that globe upon the surface of the water;
then I shall become the Vāḍava fire within the mouth of the mare.
For the sake of the welfare of the eight worlds, I dry up the excess of water;
then, according to necessity, I protect and parch the earth.
With my breaths, I repeatedly create the seven netherworlds;
having scattered seeds everywhere therein, I bring forth all creatures.
Then I, as a fish moving within the waters, shall become invisible;
having made the earth stable and eight-fold, I indeed vanish from sight.
Then, having become Hayagrīva, I shall swiftly bestow upon all subjects the knowledge born of the Vedas during the transition from the Kṛta age.
Then, at the beginning of the Kṛta age, the Lord—the eternal Śrīvallabha Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—assuming a form by His own will, shall manifest upon the earth. (8.1)

Or else, on another bank there in heaven, I shall effect the preservation of the [Vedic] syllables by remaining for one hundred and twenty-five thousand years after having established the practice of worship.
For years upon the surface of the earth, I shall establish the stability of all dharmas;
there, as Hari, I shall everywhere set forth the path to liberation.
And from that, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Master of Lakṣmī, appears in the Ocean of Milk; there indeed I sleep once again. 84.
Then, O Badrikā, after a lapse of time and following the exhaustion of my prosperity,
I shall cause the churning of the ocean for the sake of all the jewels.
Then, while remaining on the mountain, I shall assume the form of a tortoise;
I shall become a beautiful woman, a *mohinī*, who causes delusion to the Daityas. (86)
I cause all the deities to drink that nectar;
then, having become invisible, I again assume the form of a lion for a specific purpose.
I indeed become Hayashirsha for the destruction of the Daityas at certain times;
and for the sake of bestowing knowledge, I become the Swan-souled one and Kapila as well.
I become the dwarf Yajñabhikṣu to bring about the destruction of the Asuras; and for the sake of my devotees, I become Hari, the remover of suffering. ||89||
By virtue of dharma, I become Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Hari;
I become a sovereign emperor, a lord of the earth, for the sake of milking [the world].
I shall become an ascetic of virtuous conduct, one who has bestowed gifts, and likewise a knower of awakening; I shall also become a yogi dwelling in the forest.
Then, at times, I become the wielder of the axe, whose nature is the staff of punishment for the Kṣatriyas;
and I also become the wielder of the discus, the upholder of Dharma, known as Gopa.
I am the sacrifice as well as the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
I become the cultivator of the earth and I am the king of kings.
I become a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and even a servant;
likewise, according to the time, I become a teacher and even Vyāsa.
Whether as a guru, or a woman, or even in the form of a cow, or as a virtuous wife—I am indeed a brahmin known for his devotion to his wife, even here upon this earth. (95)
I am indeed Jiṣṇu in heaven, Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla, Śeṣeśvara in the ocean, and the four-armed Viṣṇu on Mount Meru. ||96||
I am born as a god or even a human, or as a Gandharva; I also become a Cāraṇa, a Vidyādhara, or even a Dakṣa.
O Badrī, I am the Lord who assumes many forms upon the earth; I become a forest-dweller, one engaged in the yoga of renunciation, an ascetic, or one whose conduct is that of Brahman. 98.
In accordance with necessity, in accordance with time, and in whatever form I may appear, it is for the protection of my creations and, in particular, for the sake of liberation. (99)
In some places I become such as one who has been brought under control by devotion;
in other places I become a son who is sought after and who consists of the nature of happiness.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are my three forms; they exist eternally until the dissolution of all beings for the sake of the continuous flow [of creation]. 101.
Thus, O Badrī, I have explained to you the purpose of my manifestation;
having accomplished that purpose and having gladdened those who have taken refuge in me, [I shall depart].
Indeed, by my divine play, I repeatedly manifest and disappear suddenly;
there is no end to my manifestations, nor is there any counting of my births.
There is no limit to my actions, nor to my forms, nor to my conduct;
I am the progenitor of all that is auspicious, and I indeed bring about the welfare of all creatures.
Punishing the wicked, protecting those who are devoted, establishing righteousness, and promoting devotion—these are my duties. (105)
Praised by the gods, I become distinguished and remain inconceivable to them repeatedly; yet when praised by a devotee, I truly become manifest, for I am accessible to anyone who possesses devotion.
I dwell especially in Surāṣṭra, the kingdom of Dharma;
having performed the works of the gods with ease, I then become invisible.
At that time, the people— both men and women—
who came into contact with me were born with divine forms, and thereafter they attained liberation.
Thus, O Badarī, this supreme secret has been told to you by me;
for in whatever form you may exist, you indeed abide accompanied by me.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Expectation at the End of the Tiṣya Age, and His Manifestation at Night and Day during the Kalpa," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrībadrīpriyā said: Whenever you abide on earth, in heaven, in Satyaloka, or in the netherworlds (talātala), I shall be there as well; of this there is no doubt.
In some form, in some symbol, on some side, or in the heart;
wherever she is the executor of my command, there I abide, though situated elsewhere.
In all those places, O Blessed One, those who take refuge in me and rely upon you—being free from desire and having sought the company of the virtuous—attain supreme liberation. (3)
My devotees, having their desires fulfilled, go either to heaven or to a kingdom;
that kingdom is enjoyed by my royal devotees, while in heaven it is enjoyed by the virtuous gods.
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, that great earthly kingdom was [ruled] by the Supreme Soul,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
To which mountain was it given, and who was the king after that?
To whom did he formerly bestow the great kingdom of Haimakhaṇḍa? (6)
Furthermore, what did Kṛṣṇa do thereafter, and how extensive was his lineage?
How much time passed for Kṛṣṇa on this earth after that?
He ought to recount all of this here out of compassion—the enchanting pastimes of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (8)
After that, I wish to hear about those [deities] who are remembered as having been born subsequently;
they indeed bestow liberation and grant supreme bliss and peace. (9)
O Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, cause the noble stories of that Protector to be heard, by the mere remembrance of whom even the torments quickly go to their dissolution.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having created the Vairāja-Puruṣa, the sustainer of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), [proceeded further]. || 11 ||
And through him, having brought forth many ordinances for the creators of the universe,
he gave the procedure for creation to the four-faced one born from the lotus.
Through him, Mahārāja begot Svāyambhuva Manu as king, the lord of the great cosmic egg consisting of fourteen levels;
and Āgnīdhra and others were the sons born of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Those highly heroic ones established kingdoms on various continents by their mere thought.
And Āgnīdhra gave a portion of the Himalaya to Ājanābha;
that great region of Ājanābha extended for ten thousand yojanas.
When King Ajanābha had attained an intense surge of world-weariness and departed for the forest to practice austerities, the Earth became possessed by pride.
At that time, Hari himself bestowed upon Pṛthu, the king of the earth, the abundance of crops, the various kinds of gems, and the flavors, which had been stolen away. 17.
Pṛthu milked the earth and bestowed all the products of that milking upon his subjects; thereafter, he departed for the practice of asceticism.
The Lord bestowed fragmented kingdoms upon his devoted kings,
while Puruṣottama granted divine realms to the gods.
He gave the sovereignty of medicinal herbs and trees,
of sacrifices, vows, austerities, constellations, and the twice-born to Candra.
He gave the kingdom of the waters and the aquatic creatures to Varuṇa;
and he gave the kingdom of wealth, treasuries, and other riches to Kubera.
And he gave the kingdom of the Ravis to Viṣṇu, who possesses twelve forms;
and he gave the kingdom of the Vasus to Agni, the unifier of the elements.
The Lord bestowed the sovereignty of the Prajāpatis upon Dakṣa,
and he indeed gave the kingdom of the Maruts to Śakra, the dweller of heaven.
He gave that [kingdom] to Prahlāda for the sake of the millions of Daityas and Dānavas;
he bestowed the kingdom upon Yama for the ancestors who dwell in the realm of Yama.
Then he indeed bestowed the kingdom of the Piśācas, Rakṣasas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Śivās, as well as that of the mountains, upon Himālaya.
Then he gave the sovereignty over the rivers, such as the Nanda and others, to the Ocean;
and then he gave [the sovereignty] over the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Vidyādharas.
He gave the kingdom of Citraratha to Kiṃpuruṣa, which was auspicious even for men; he gave the kingdom of the Nāgas to Vāsuki, extending as far as Tāmasa.
Then he gave the great sovereignty over serpents to Takṣaka,
and the kingdom over the elephants, the lords of the world-elephants, to Airāvata.
He bestowed sovereignty over winged creatures upon Suparṇa, over horses upon Uccaiḥśravas, lordship over beasts upon the lion, and likewise over cattle upon the bull.
Then he gave [the northern quarter] to Kalpadruma among the lords of the forest (vanaspati),
the eastern direction to Sudharman, and the southern to Śaṅkhapada.
To Ketumān he gave the western region, and to Hiraṇyaromī the northern;
in this manner the Blessed One indeed caused the kingdoms to be bestowed through the agency of Brahmā.
In this region of Ājanābha, on the mountain named Himālaya, when Pṛthu had departed for asceticism, his son Viśvagasta [reigned]. ||32||
Then Nandibhilla ruled the kingdom; he indeed blocked the Yamunā and established a new city named Dilāvarī after the name of his wife.
On the beautiful bank of the Yamunā, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa established the great kingdom of Dilāvarī, which was endowed with formidable fortresses.
Having slain the Bhilla, he gave [the kingdom] to King Nāgavikrama;
when Nandibhikṣu was killed, Nāgavikrama ruled over it.
Endowed with the power of worshipping the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he performed austerities through upāsanā and obtained the Prāleyaka bow. (36)
From the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul,
[he departed] by means of that divine bow and through a celestial chariot in the sky.
Like another Nārāyaṇa, he set out to conquer the earth;
by means of his bow, the kings on all sides were made to pay tribute to him. (38)
He, possessing the prowess of a serpent, made the entire surface of the earth belonging to Viṣṇu his discus,
extending ten thousand yojanas to the edge of the five southern oceans.
Possessing the prowess of a serpent, he indeed obtained the great kingdom of Ājanābha;
by him, the capital city of Dilāvarī was protected at all times.
By him, she was made his own enlightener, known as Nāgapurī;
Hastimālinī was the wife of King Nāgavikrama. (41)
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, a Vaiṣṇavī, a Sāttvatī, and a virtuous woman—after her name, the city on the bank was called Hāstinīpurī. 42.
But King Nāgavikrama, enriched by the force of the detachment he had attained,
set out from his home for the sake of visiting sacred fords, accompanied by Hastimālin.
Then, having bathed in the Yamunā, the Sarayū, the Gaṅgā, the Gogarā, and the Gaṇḍakī,
as well as the Kāñcanagaṅgā, he thereafter proceeded to Brahmapurī.
Having bathed at the Kāpila ocean, he went to the temple of Puruṣottama,
and then to the Mahānadī, the Godāvarī, and the southern Kṛṣṇā.
Having bathed in the ocean, and having bathed in the Śrīmahādri, the Tāpī, and the Narmadā, as well as in the Mahī and the Śatruñjayā, he then went to Somanātha. ||46||
Having visited Mūladvāravatī, Kuśasthalī, and the Gomatī,
and having bathed in the Bhadrā, he went to the great Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake.
Having first bowed to and worshipped Lomaśa at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, which is the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he then [proceeded]. ||48||
Having bathed in the waters of Aśvapaṭṭa, the king set out toward his own chosen deity, the beloved Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, in order to worship him. 49.
Having beheld Hari seated upon a golden elephant throne, opulent and possessing divine eyes, the king then worshipped Him according to the prescribed rites.
Together with his wife and accompanied by his servants, he drank the nectar from the feet [of the Lord];
the queen, filled with devotion, also drank the nectar from the feet of Hari.
Then, having placed various offerings before Kṛṣṇasvāmin,
the queen, accompanied by the king, performed the ārātrika ceremony for Hari.
He praised Hari in many ways and sat down upon the offered seat;
Nārāyaṇa himself then performed a hospitable welcome and honored him.
O Mādhava, they fed the king and the queen according to the prescribed rites;
Śrīgopāla, Kṛṣṇa, and the others extended a royal welcome. ||54||
Then the king, together with his wife and having prepared his dwelling, attained rest; he fell asleep and entered into a state of meditative absorption.
There, he beheld the entire world— including heaven and the realm of truth (Satyaloka)— along with Meru and its inhabitants, all protected by Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu.
That lord of men beheld Īśvara in his various abodes of manifestation,
as well as the Lord residing in the Ocean of Milk and situated in Śvetadvīpa.
The king beheld Nara and Nārāyaṇa residing at Badarī; Hiraṇmaya in the sun; and Vaiśvānara-Nārāyaṇa in the fire. ||58||
The world of the Sadhyas, the world of the Pitris, as well as Yajñanarayana;
the world of Dhruva, the world of Yama, and likewise the realm of Mahendra. ||59||
He beheld the assembly of Brahmā, the world of Viṣṇu, the world of Śiva,
the world of Vairāja, the abode of Lalitā-Śrī, and likewise the unmanifest (Avyākṛta).
He beheld the world of Bhūma known as Amṛta, the abode of Vāsudeva,
Kailāsa of Sadāśiva, and Sāketa.
He beheld the world of Māyā, the world of Mahāviṣṇu, Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the abodes of Sīmā, as well as the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma).
He beheld the supreme abode, the Supreme Brahman, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the sustainer of all incarnations, indeed the Lord of the Imperishable.
He was beautiful, sixteen years of age, known as Mukta, the Supreme Person;
he was worshipped by Muktānikā, pervaded by splendor, and adorned with ornaments.
Wearing divine garlands, as beautiful as ten million celestial Cupids,
he was lovely, youthful, and possessed of a complexion of pure gold from head to toe.
He beheld Lord Badrīśvara-Kṛṣṇa, who is served by Rādhā, Ramā, Priyā, Lakṣmī, and Padmāvatī, as well as Māṇikī.
Filled with the nectar of all loveliness and beauty, he was a supreme embodiment serving as the refuge for love, affection, and joy. (67)
Within a single pore of his hair reside the splendors of millions upon millions of suns,
as well as eternal joys that bestow perpetual contentment and satisfaction.
Then the king beheld Hari, accompanied by his two parents, adorned with the Kaustubha gem and a crown, and decorated with divine ornaments.
And the virtuous queen, out of compassion, indeed beheld everything;
she likewise beheld the divine manifestations and her own auspicious fortunes.
He beheld divine enjoyments, divine yogas, all divine prosperities,
all divine nectars, and divine accomplishments.
He beheld divine abodes and temples, as well as repositories of celestial jewels,
and his own forms composed of divine splendor.
Having attained infinite bliss through Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the two of them have no desire to leave this world and return again.
O Badrī, having indeed attained the state of agelessness and immortality, what person—who has ascended beyond the external world—would wish to go again into that which consists of illusion? (74)
Nevertheless, by the command of Hari, those two returned by force to their own bodies as they resided at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Suddenly rising in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, those two possessed divine majesty;
the senses and inner faculties of both became divine. (76)
At that time, form consisting of illusion did not please them to behold; nor did touch consisting of illusion please them to feel. (77)
Even tastes did not please them to eat, for they possessed most divine bodies; nor did the illusory fragrance please them, as it was like a foul stench to those two. (78)
Therefore, it does not please Śabda to speak of those two as being composed of illusion (māyā);
for to them, everything composed of illusion immediately leads to hell.
Having abandoned food and recreation, with their minds fixed on Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they remain in the presence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Badrikā. (4.109.80)
Indeed, those two, Sukha and Ānanda, partook of the food of Bālakṛṣṇa’s form; at that time, they experienced neither hunger nor even thirst born of illusion. ||81||
Thus, devoted to the enjoyment of such great divine bliss,
those two were liberated while living, liberated even though they appeared as if they possessed bodies.
The priceless value of the essence of Brahman, which has been attained through the form of Kṛṣṇa, cannot possibly stand before the value of the enjoyment of a kingdom. ||83||
At that time, saṃsāra appeared utterly worthless before them; their minds never again found any rest within saṃsāra. (84)
Through meditation upon the Lord Kṛṣṇa Hari, through their meeting, and through their service,
all the veils of those two were destroyed on every side.
In water, on land, in the sky, in a house, against a wall, in fire, or in confinement, their movement is unimpeded, and they are able to cross over and enter [anywhere]. ||86||
The king and queen were born, both renowned for their subtle and great qualities;
such were those two divine beings, devoted to meditation upon Kṛṣṇa. (87)
Devoted solely to the activities of Kṛṣṇa and dedicated to the ritual practices concerning Kṛṣṇa,
they have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, with both their senses and minds withdrawn from worldly objects.
The king and queen, having always surrendered their minds to their own servants and maidservants, remained devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa. (89)
Seeing them in such a state, O Badrī, the male and female servants, as well as the followers,
were deeply distressed and grieved in many ways on their account.
They reasoned thus: "Are these two deprived of their senses, or have they become intoxicated? Or have they been struck down by the wind, or perhaps overcome by the power of incantations? (9.1)
Or perhaps they were acting with indifference, or else possessed by demons; or perhaps they were intent on being haunted by spirits, or utterly overwhelmed by a delusion of mind. (92)
Were their minds unsteady, or were they possessed by some supernatural power, or perhaps were they tormented by the influence of malevolent spirits? (93)
Thus, in many ways, the servants offered various conjectures;
yet they did not reach the true nature of these two, nor did they attain the further shore of their reality.
Then those servants offered this prayer to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Teacher of the World! (95)
We do not even know what the queen or the king’s state of mind may be;
the people and servants are consumed by anxiety over such a kingdom and realm.
"Everything has fallen into a state of agitation because the king's situation cannot be fathomed;
you, Kṛṣṇa, are the one who brings about deliverance, so act indeed as is appropriate. (97)
May the king attain perfect health and his kingdom proceed properly;
having shown compassion in such a manner, please ensure our well-being. (98)
And the queen likewise remains as if unconscious, just like the king;
you know this, O Supreme Soul, so act for our welfare in every way. (99)
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa, perform what is beneficial for the protection of Your devotee"—
thus did the servants and other men of the king entreat Him.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of Kings after the Creation of Brahmā in the Tiṣya Lineage within the Fourth Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning King Nāgavikrama of the capital Dilāvarī, his wandering on a pilgrimage, his arrival at Kuṅkumavāpī, and the attainment of divinity as the fruit of his meditative absorption.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; I shall tell you what occurred after the petition of the servants and others of King Nāgavikrama. || 1 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇārya, Kṛṣṇamādhava,
replied to his servants with auspicious words that were indeed true to the facts.
This king is not intoxicated, nor is he insane, nor is he deranged;
he is neither possessed by spirits or demons, nor is he under the influence of malevolent sorcery.
By my power, that devotee of mine, together with his beloved, beheld me, the King of Kings, within the samādhi in my own imperishable abode.
Having beheld me as divine, my divine abode, all divine prosperities,
and my divine manifestations, he indeed attained divinity.
He now possesses divine vision, divine action, and divine qualities;
he exists as one composed of a divine nature, with divine internal organs and senses.
This world, consisting of illusion and stained with impurity, does not please him;
having attained equanimity, he remains as he beholds this which is subject to decay.
He indeed beholds the entire cosmic egg known as hell,
and he sees his own kingdom, the earth, and everything else as mere mud.
He perceives even the impure and the disfigured as being full of moisture;
like one without a body, he remains as one liberated while living, with his senses conquered.
Having withdrawn his internal organ (mind), he remains like one liberated even while accompanied by his wife;
thereafter, with his latent impressions (vāsanā) removed, he dwells upon the earth like a yogi.
Having ascended to the state of Brahmā, he exists beyond the realm of illusion;
having become free from illusion through my meditative absorption, he has come to possess my own nature.
He dwells like Sanaka and others, equal to Śiva and possessed of dispassion;
therefore, let his followers not grieve for the highly fortunate and divine king.
Due to his divine nature, he has no obstructions whatsoever;
possessing the perfection of the subtle body (aṇusiddhi), he is able to go across the earth, water, and fire.
He is capable of going to heaven, Satyaloka, Vairāja, and Vaikuṇṭha;
neither his kingdom nor his servants here are able to cause him any harm.
Then this master of yogis, the ascetic, proceeds according to the state of a yogi; his wife Satī, who shares his dharma, likewise proceeds as the supreme [consort]. (15)
For the sake of your conviction, I shall urge him to come into your presence, so that he may exert himself to console you. (16)
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, the great lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa urged the king to dispel the grief of his servants and others.
Listen, O King: your servants and others are grieving on your account;
inform them of your own story, as it truly and brilliantly is.
Thus, O Badrikā, King Nāgavikrama was addressed;
he then spoke to his servants and others regarding his own state of detachment.
"Let the groups of servants and others listen, and let them do what I have said;
I speak for the benefit of all, for I have obtained divine wealth. (4.110.20)
"This is indeed the Blessed One himself, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person; the Lord of the Imperishable, the sustainer of all incarnations, has been attained by me here. (21)
Through my yoga and by you as well, Śrīpati-vallabha has been attained—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama). ||22||
By his majesty, I obtained a vast empire;
by his majesty, I have attained divine vision and established stability.
By the power of that supreme, imperishable abode,
I indeed beheld it in meditative absorption, and the divine supernatural powers were witnessed by me.
Since even the prosperities of the lords [the Asuras] are like hell in their ultimate consequence, what then need be said of the far more transient human riches of the gods? (25)
These riches consisting of illusion are indeed nothing but hells;
for these riches do not please me, since they are soiled.
Through union with the divine Hari, I have attained supreme divinity;
may you also, through union with Hari, attain supreme divinity.
May they receive eternal supreme bliss from the beginningless Mādhava, and may they abandon the army of latent impressions, the hellish material home. 28.
The entire kingdom of Hari, as well as that which is beyond all universes—the whole kingdom of Śrī Hari—is indeed his; my own kingdom is not even a fraction of it.
I desire the kingdom of liberation; the kingdom of worldly enjoyment does not please me.
Therefore, may you, my servants and others, take refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the virtuous.
May those who have renounced worldly enjoyments and pleasures find eternal bliss in Keśava; may they not rejoice in the impermanent, but rather rejoice in the Supreme Lord.
For the dead body of a king, there is neither kingdom, nor wealth, nor home;
but for the Self that is liberated, there is the great kingdom of the supreme imperishable.
Reflecting thus, I offer everything to the Supreme Self;
I offer the great kingdom of Dilāvarī to the Highest Self.
I have attained dispassion along with my wife, of this there is no doubt;
having become a virtuous servant of Hari, I shall serve the Guru, Hari, here.
I give the kingdom to Hari, by whom it was formerly given to me;
may he alone protect everything, for I have no desire for the kingdom.
Having spoken thus to his circle of servants, the king, who possessed the prowess of a serpent,
took water in his hand and offered the kingdom to Kṛṣṇa.
While everyone was looking on, he fell at the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
casting off his royal insignia, he swallowed the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
The queen also did likewise; she indeed licked the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s feet with her tongue and likewise the sole of Kṛṣṇa’s foot.
The king’s attendants, including the servants and others, attained supreme wonder;
considering themselves truly fortunate, they then paid homage to Hari.
They praised the king as he set out upon the path to liberation;
and all his servants and others likewise took to the path of renunciation.
Having prostrated before Śrī Hari, they performed their self-surrender just like kings,
for the purpose of renouncing their material nature in the presence of Hari.
Then the illustrious Lord bestowed upon the king a perfect initiation;
the sage Trivikramāyana gave him the name Kṛṣṇa.
The illustrious Kṛṣṇa also gave the queen the name Śrīmālikāyanī;
she was the virtuous Trivikramāyanī, the chaste Śrīmālikāyanī. (43)
O Badrī, all the other thousands of servants worshipped the Supreme Self, Svāmī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as well as their Guru. (44)
Then, remaining in the stage of renunciation, they all received the initiation of a saintly life; having fully embraced renunciation, they took refuge in the Beloved of Śrī. 45.
Those women and female slaves who indeed attained the initiation of the virtuous—there were then a thousand such virtuous women present there. (46)
Possessing divine natures and divine bodies, with all latent impressions abandoned,
they dwelt in that manner in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
The Lord, who is self-luminous, settled them in his own hermitage;
they took refuge in the Supreme Self and served their Lord and Master. 48.
Upon hearing this, all the people on earth were struck with great wonder;
even the kings experienced a marvel concerning such renunciation.
Thus, O Badrikā, King Nāgavikrama entered the hermitage of renunciation there in an instant, accompanied by his wives and his army.
He performed austerities in the sacred field of Hari and worshipped the Lord Śrī Mādhava;
indeed, conducting himself according to the way of Brahman, he served the Lord, the Master.
Then the illustrious Lord said to Trivikramāyana at Badarī:
"Tell me here, to whom should the great kingdom of Dilāvarī be given? (52)
The sage said: "O Hari, sovereignty has been bestowed upon me by you;
let that belong to you, for it is not my kingdom. Grant me instead whatever I desire. (53)
"O Kṛṣṇa, this son of yours shines as a lord equal to you;
by name he is Mukundavikrama, endowed with the qualities of a universal emperor."
On the palm of his right hand, the mark of the wheel shines resplendently;
he is worthy of sovereignty—if you so desire, give it to him indeed. (55)
When this had been said, cries of "Excellent! Excellent! arose on all sides from the men and women there, their voices filled with joy. (56)
Then, for the sake of Mukunda’s valor, the cry of "Victory! arose;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s sons, daughters, and wives likewise spoke thus. (57)
King Mukundavikrama, the son born of the eldest wife, is the eldest of all;
therefore, he deserves the splendid kingdom. (58)
Thus, O Badrī, auspicious words arose from every direction;
and Hari also considered the sage’s thought to be true, saying, "Om."
That news spread quickly throughout the city of Kuṅkumapattana,
and even in every house in Saurāṣṭra, that supreme field of Akṣara.
Likewise, she is firmly established in Ājanābha, in Khaṇḍa, and in other regions;
swiftly she is present in heaven, in Satya, in Pātāla, and in all the worlds.
On this earth, King Nāgavikrama shall be the foremost among givers;
he will become a universal monarch (cakravartin) named Mukundavikrama.
The son of Hari, a portion of Hari, the lord of Dilāvarī,
shall now become the master of the city of Hāstinī in the region of Haimakhaṇḍa.
Muktibāleśvarī, his innate consort born from the Yama [lineage], shall become the sovereign queen, his beloved, the mother of the kingdom, and the most excellent. (64)
Thus, on the ground and everywhere among the people, this great and auspicious news—which causes one to remember Kṛṣṇa—spread from person to person. (65)
And festivals also arose in every house among the people, accompanied by musical instruments, songs, and dances, as well as the elegant dress and ornaments of the women.
Then, at Śrī Badarī, the beginningless Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
beholding Candra directly before him at a most auspicious moment, [spoke].
He gave the command to his sons to go toward Dilāvarī, saying, "Mukundavikrama, the eldest son, shall become the king. (68)
At that festival, let all my wives, as many pairs as there may be, indeed travel in celestial chariots. (69)
Let the male and female slaves, the groups of servants, Dilāvarī, the yogi Lomaśa, and the caravan leader Prakāśakāyana indeed proceed to Dilāvarī.
Trivikramāyana and other virtuous people,
as well as great seers, sages, and ascetics who have mastered the Vedas, [were there].
"Let the diligent Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas indeed proceed to Dilāvarī.
Having thus commanded, the Blessed One sent them forth first. (72)
He also dispatched letters to his attendants on the surface of the earth,
as well as to heaven, the realm of truth (Satyaloka), the netherworld (Pātāla), and throughout all fourteen levels.
He dispatched an auspicious letter of petition to the lords,
the Siddhas and Sādhyas, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
The guardians of the directions and the guardians of the worlds, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras; the kimpuruṣas, cāraṇas, vidyādharas, daityas, and dānavas. ||75||
The Apsarases, the virtuous and chaste women of Brahma’s lake, as well as the Yoginīs, the goddesses Śakti, the deities, and likewise the sovereign goddesses. ||76||
Kṛṣṇa dispatched messengers everywhere with letters of notification to all the lords, including Dhāma, Dhāmādima, Muktā, and Muktānika.
The Blessed One summoned all his devotees, kings, and other lords of various regions by means of saffron letters and other such communications.
Then Hari summoned the lords of the islands and the kings,
as well as his fathers-in-law and his own sons, who were residing in their respective homes and dwellings.
The Blessed One summoned [them] toward the city of Dilāvarī;
then the Blessed One, together with his mother, father, sons, and others—|| 4.110.80 ||
Accompanied by his wife and others, he indeed traveled swiftly by celestial chariot to the auspicious capital of Dilāvarī, situated upon golden ground.
He caused an excellent pavilion ten yojanas in extent to be constructed;
it was made of gold, extending along the Yamunā, and resplendent with divine jewels and other ornaments. ||82||
It was furnished with celestial and non-celestial thrones for the assembly of kings, and adorned with rows of seats for sages, great seers, liberated souls, and others. ||83||
Consisting of all accomplishments, filled with the prosperity of all kings,
and endowed with all visible and invisible weapons, missiles, and effigies.
It was beautified by rows of every kind of ornament, covered with wish-fulfilling creepers and trees,
pervaded by the brilliance of lightning, and adorned with divine mirrors and other such objects.
It was augmented by divine garlands of flowers offered by the deities;
its ground possessed celestial carpets and it shone with divine archways.
It was graced by the playful movements of groups of celestial maidens within its many intermediate courtyards;
it was pervaded by fragrant scents and pleasant perfumes, and possessed a most delightful touch and breeze.

It is fashioned with all kinds of drinks and other offerings, attended by all types of servants and staff, and beautifully adorned with all auspicious symbols such as the lotus and the svastika. ||88||
Adorned with colorful garlands, canopies, and the like, and graced by rows of flower garlands, it was delightful with the sounds of divine musical instruments and gladdened by singers of songs. (89)
It captivated the heart with instrumental music, vocal music, and the arts of song and dance; it was enchanting through all the crafts and skills of Viśvakarman.
It was resplendent with the excellent seats of the deities, such as the fire-pit and others, and was provided with the requisites for consecration and the materials for worship. ||9-1||
It was fully provided with various oblations, gifts, and other means of accomplishment,
as well as the great materials for the royal ritual and appropriate attire.
It was auspicious, provided with the requisites for royal consecration and other items,
along with excellent articles suitable for a king, such as ornaments of gold and jewels.
It was crowded with umbrellas, whisks, staffs, and other items, including footstools and the like,
and it shone with golden jars filled with water from sacred fords.
It was provided with sweet foods, fruits, leaves, and so forth, along with sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass;
it was made fragrant with excellent divine sandalwood and the essence of perfumes. (95)
It was rich with the splendor of a king of kings, bestowing objects that fulfill every wish, and it shone with countless shrines and conscious celestial abodes.
In the center of the western throne of the great lion-throne was a divine pavilion, possessing a splendor like that of the beautiful Vaikuṇṭha. 97.
The Blessed One caused mountains of foods with delicious flavors to be prepared by those skilled in the arts of cooking and confectionery. 98.
He also caused lakes to be constructed for the drinking of milk, nectar, and other such drinks, and he arranged dwellings adorned with comfortable beds and other luxuries. (99)
And there he protected the arrangements for drinks, food, and clothing that were conducive to comfort, as well as those who served as male and female slaves and attendants.
Thus, in every way, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master, then fashioned all that was appropriate and required on every side. (101)
And then, O Badrikā, there was great joy for all living beings;
festivals arose in their hearts, born of natural, supreme bliss.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s Departure for the Capital City of Dilāvarī to Perform the Royal Consecration of His Son Mukundavikrama, and the Construction of the Pavilion and Other Structures," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth book of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī, to the prowess of Mukunda;
Hari caused a fast to be observed on the first day for the sake of purification.
He also caused the consumption of cow products and the performance of the rite of shaving;
likewise, he performed the purification of the body by bathing with the waters of sacred fords.
And on the Akṣayya-tṛtīyā day, at dawn,
the Blessed One caused a consecration festival to be performed with the waters of a thousand sacred fords.
Mādhava also caused the worship of Gaṇeśa, the worship of the family deity, and the worship of Hanumān to be performed.
In the pavilion, the Blessed One, through Lomaśa, caused the worship of the Vāstu deities and the performance of oblations to be carried out according to the rules.
He caused the thorough worship of the fire, the cooking of the sacrificial oblation (caru) in the fire,
and the performance of the Homa sacrifice by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Many instruments were played and songs by women arose;
the great ones dwelling in all the worlds arrived. ||7||
Likewise, the liberated ones, the incarnations, the lords, the perfected ones, the virtuous, the deities of truth, the ancestors, the mothers, the divine beings, and the gods. ||8||
The attendants and other liberated ones, as well as goddesses equal to Lakṣmī, arrived; and the Rudras, Viṣṇus, and the Unborn (Brahmās), who dwell in heaven, came to the pavilion.
The world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, those who dwell on Meru and Mandara,
the sacred fords, the divine trees, and the creepers all arrived.

The principles (tattvas) and the powers (śaktis), which are like wish-fulfilling cows, also arrived; and the great seers (maharṣis), sages (munis), virtuous women (sādhvīs), and faithful wives (satīs) arrived as well. || 11 ||
Soldiers, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins,
as well as male and female dancers, indeed assembled in the pavilion.
The learned ones, the Kiṃpuruṣas, the Kinnaras, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Uragas, the Bhujagas, the Nāgas, the Daityas, and the Dānavas; || 1.3 ||
Beasts, birds of the heavens, and those who remember their past births arrived;
likewise, rivers, mountains, oceans, and the subterranean waters came as well.
The stars, the planets, and the circles of constellations assembled;
men, sages, brahmins, the wretched, and the helpless all gathered together. (15)
Kings and royal retinues, lords of subjects and the common people, as well as millions of Vaiṣṇava merchants and devotees, arrived there. || 16 ||
All the sovereign lords of kings sat upon their respective seats;
the pavilion of all the created beings became magnificent with those emperors. (17)
All the rites prescribed by the Vedas are performed by the twice-born and others;
the sounds of the Vedas arise and resound through the ten directions.
Gopāla had his attendants perform the rites of welcome and so forth;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for his part, granted him honor with water for washing the feet.
And likewise, with offerings of water for the feet and so forth, as well as with honey-mixtures and other honors,
celestial chariots indeed descend from all sides through the sky.
The best of gods, possessing divine forms, arrive at the pavilion;
honored with a welcome, they sit upon their lion-thrones.
Then, O Bādarāyaṇa, the performance of the fire-sacrifice proceeded according to the rules;
there, Mukunda, together with his wife, offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) into the fire.
Endowed with devotion, she offered oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, fruits, and other items;
then Śrī Lomaśa performed the ritual worship there.
And likewise of Suvarṇavarman’s sword, shield,
umbrella, cane-staff, crown, and garment.
There is also the worship of the Śataghnī, as well as the worship of the mace (Gadā), the worship of the discus (Cakra), and likewise the worship of Lakṣmī and Rudrāṇī. ||25||
Then follows the worship of the bow, likewise the worship of the arrow,
and thereafter the worship of all the mantras of weapons and missiles.
He also caused the worship of Rudra, which is worthy of a royal throne,
as well as the worship of Viṣṇu and Brahmā.
Lomaśa also caused the worship of Senādevī, the worship of Kośadeva,
and likewise the worship of Pṛthivī to be performed.
Lomaśa also caused the worship of Vārāha, the worship of his lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the worship of the king’s crown to be performed. ||29||
Lomaśa also caused the worship of Śrī Lakṣmī, the propitiation for gain and auspiciousness,
and likewise the worship of Jayaśrī.
Lomaśa performed the invocation of the guardians of the quarters upon the body of the king;
the preceptor Lomaśa also performed the invocation of the gods.
For the complete attainment of the status of a sovereign, he performed the worship of the Earth;
for the attainment of the status of a lord of subjects, he performed the worship of the Lord of Subjects.
For the sake of attaining the status of Lord of Lakṣmī, he performed the worship of Lakṣmī;
for the sake of attaining the status of Lord of the Staff, he performed the worship of Yama.
For the sake of attaining the status of a lord of wealth, he performed the worship of Kubera;
for the sake of attaining lordship over the rivers and the ocean, he performed the worship of Varuṇa.
He performed the worship of Candra for the attainment of hundreds of grains and medicinal herbs;
he performed the worship of Mahendra for the sake of attaining the achievement of sovereignty.
For the sake of attaining the status of a cook, the sage performed the worship of the Sun;
for the sake of health, he performed the propitiation of Rudra, the Lord of Disease.
Lomaśa performed worship of the fire for the sake of attaining splendor;
Lomaśa worshipped Vāyu, the god who protects life.
He performed the worship of the Mātṛkās for the increase of the kingdom and its subjects, and likewise he performed the worship of all the deities of creation. || 38 ||
Lomaśa performed the worship of the mounts— the peaceful cows, elephants, and horses— as well as the worship of the carriages, mechanical vehicles, and celestial chariots.
Then Śrī Lomaśa offered oblations to all:
to Nirṛti, to the Rākṣasas, to the gods, and to the planets and celestial beings.
And Lomaśa offered oblations for the sake of happiness;
having thus performed the worship according to rule, he performed the propitiatory rite and the ancestral offering (śrāddha) according to the prescribed method.
Then, after Lomaśa had offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the mouth [of the fire],
he applied the mark of grace (prasāda-tilaka) upon the foreheads of the king and the queen.
The king put on the royal attire: the crown, the sacred thread, and the garland;
the lord of the earth then donned the crown and the sprouts of barley.
Mukundavikrama even took up the bearing of weapons and made a vow for sovereignty, which was centered upon the protection of his subjects.
The sages headed by Lomaśa, the elders, the kings and other subjects,
as well as the lords and the liberated Brahmins, performed the ritual waving of lamps.
They also bestowed their blessings: "Live long and protect your subjects!
May you be endowed with sons, grandsons, and the like; remain devoted to the service of your people. (46)
May there be well-being for you at all times, and may auspiciousness always attend you;
may your festivals among your subjects be perpetually joyful. (47)
May your kingdom always be free from obstacles, stable as far as the edge of the ocean, and forever endowed with health, grain, and wealth. //48//
Then those best of the twice-born, having uttered these words,
greatly increased [his prosperity] with excellent unbroken grains and offered handfuls of flowers in succession.
And the sage Trivikramāyana applied a tilaka mark upon him;
he then placed a crown and a garland upon his head and another excellent ornament around his neck.
Other virtuous brahmins also then honored the lord of the earth;
then the venerable Guru Prakāśa gave him a royal edict.
He indeed gave that king a letter of royal authority;
there were shouts of victory, and the kings presented him with gifts. ||52||
They presented the king with gifts, jewels, necklaces made of gems and gold, priceless items, and other supreme, auspicious riches. (53)
One [bore] an umbrella, another likewise a staff and chowries;
one [bore] a crown and earrings, and others bracelets and wealth.
Those born of the royal lineage gave ornaments of gold and silver;
the subjects, the gods, the best of deities, and the divine beings all gave gifts. ||55||
Then, at various times, he presented many priceless offerings;
thereafter, the Blessed Lord Hari applied a tilaka mark upon his forehead.
"O King, may you possess an expansive lineage and become the sovereign lord of the wheel-turning monarchs.
Having spoken thus, he placed his hand upon the head of his son and [placed] a garland [there]. (57)
The Lord spoke in the assembly of all the kings who were listening:
"I have made this man the foremost among you, all you kings. (58)
Mukundavikrama shall be the lord of kings and a sovereign emperor who collects tribute;
indeed, my Sudarśana discus is granted to him for his protection.
"This is indeed for the destruction of those who abide in non-instruction," having said this,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa gave forth His great discus.
He gave him a thousand-spoked, auspicious victory-chariot bearing the banner of the discus, which assumed whatever form was desired and bestowed victory; he also gave him a conch that grants triumph.
Hari himself gave him the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā) and an inexhaustible worthy recipient (sat-pātra);
he placed a handful of flowers upon his neck and then bestowed the garland of life (jīvamālā).
Then, when the worship had thus been performed, King Mukundavikrama shone like Kṛṣṇa himself there upon the royal throne, accompanied by his queen.
He performed salutations to the elders, conducted the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and gave all kinds of gifts, including gold, jewels, and garments. (64)
Elephants, horses, and celestial chariots; houses, gardens, and floors; as well as wealth, riches, divine food, and ornaments.
Even the gift of the cosmic egg, as well as those gifts on the scales, all gifts of cows, and likewise the gifts of daughters; ||66||
At that time, the king also gave gifts of villages, fields, and dwellings;
he provided means of livelihood for temples, the poor, the destitute, and the sick.
The king then released those people who were bound in fetters and severely punished;
he also distributed abundant sweet foods there at that time.
He gave wealth to the charioteers, panegyrists, bards, and wandering minstrels;
indeed, he bestowed great gifts upon the brahmin-sages and the twice-born classes.
Then, on that day in his kingdom, the king distributed food to all from the assembly hall amidst shouts of "Victory! (jayaśabda).
Having quickly bestowed the sacrificial fees and arranged for his safe passage,
he rose up, adorned with royal insignia and saluted by all the kṣatriyas.
Having bowed to and saluted his mother and father, as well as his kinsmen, the king was entreated by those entitled to the foremost positions of the kingdom to undertake his wandering.
Then Vardhamāna, accompanied by his army and surrounded by all his troops, wandered through the royal highways while being kept awake by the people.
Honored, worshipped, and strengthened with blessings, the king,
having gratified the subjects, went to the Yamunā and paid homage to that river.
Having drunk water and worshipped Durgā, he should proceed slowly toward the king’s palace;
afterwards, he should rest for a moment near the auspicious vessels.
He respectfully caused [the rites] to be performed for all the great honors;
he fed everyone and then bestowed gifts upon them. ||76||
The king of chariots caused the victory-hymns of the mechanical instruments to be heard;
at evening, the celestial nymphs performed dances for the delight of the mountain-dweller.
The Gandharvas, as poets, composed songs and poetic works; for their satisfaction, that best of kings bestowed excellent wealth upon them as well. (78)
Then, during the night, the king, his subjects, and all others took rest;
at dawn, they awoke upon hearing auspicious and propitious sounds.
Having enjoyed themselves and partaken of drinks, intent upon bestowing blessings, those great-souled ones returned to their own lands and worlds filled with happiness.
Then the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
[dismissed] his twin sons along with their respective maternal grandfathers and others.
Then she gave her command for them to go together; her fathers-in-law and others likewise departed, being well-honored and highly esteemed.
They departed for their own regions with their respective celestial chariots;
and the subjects, being honored, likewise returned to their own lands.
Then Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, together with his own people,
gave instructions to his son and went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Accompanied by his own wife and others, as well as his family members,
and joined by Lomaśa and the rest, he went to the land of Aśvasaras.
O Badrikā, the son of the Blessed One was consecrated upon the royal throne and ruled over the vast earth extending ten thousand yojanas. (86)
Having made the kings pay tribute and relying upon the power of the Blessed One, he, whose rule was based on righteousness, brought the entire earth under the dominion of Viṣṇu.
In his kingdom, indeed, there shall be no drought, no famine, no oppression by the wicked;
nor shall there be diseases, untimely death, or even widowhood. (88)
There was no deceit, nor backbiting, nor even hypocrisy among the subjects;
there was no violence, nor theft, nor the forcible seizing of property. (89)
At that time, there was no closing of the doors of the dwellings;
indeed, the dwellings always had their door-panels left open. (4.111.90)
There is no deviation regarding the binding of speech, nor is there any breach of one's vow; one should constantly perform salutations to elders and undertake the fifth sacrifice. 9.1.

The practice of the five-fire austerity, the daily ancestral rites (nitya-śrāddha), and other such duties of the virtuous, as well as the chanting of the Vedas by Brahmins in every village and at every sacred spot—[all these were abandoned]. (92)
All cows are wish-fulfilling; women devoted to their husbands are likewise; and the truthful, the virtuous, and the saintly are always so, even when they are householders. (93)
Established on the path of tranquility and devoted to meditation upon Nārāyaṇa, their intellects then bear fruit like the wish-fulfilling vine. ||94||
The weapons, dedicated to Kṛṣṇa and possessing divine forms, then proceed of their own accord to punish the wicked for the sake of justice. 95.
At that time, the rulers in other lands were warriors whose very form was weapons;
consequently, the prisons became utterly useless on all sides. (96)
The fires stationed at its borders protect its excellent kingdom; and the oceans, assuming embodied forms, act as the executors of its fortifications.
At his sacrifices, the gods indeed come in person along with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, together with their liberated attendants and the lords who consume the oblations. 98.
The deities of the villages and the deities of the forests always protect those subjects,
for even the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas have indeed attained a state of virtuous being.
At that time, even those material prosperities that were of a tamasic nature attained a sattvic state;
his subjects became eaters of sacrificial remnants (vighasa), and their homes were adorned with temples of the gods.
O Badrikā, in every way devotion flourished everywhere;
indeed, in the kingdom of Hari’s son, [these] bestow liberation and bring about prosperity. (101)

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Coronation Festival of Mukundavikrama in the Capital City of Dilāvarī," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Goddess beloved of Badarī; King Mukundavikrama [bestowed his daughter] upon the minister, who was the son of Lakṣmī, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk. || 1 ||
Having then commanded Vāsudeva to always bear the burden of the kingdom,
he set out to survey the earth on all sides.
By means of his celestial chariot, he first went to the Snowy Mountains and likewise to the Northern [Kurus],
as well as to Kuru, Kimpuruṣa, Ketumāla, and Ilāvṛta.
Those excellent kings who dwell everywhere— in the eastern regions, the southern, and the western lands— they all [behave] with sincerity.
They offered him honor, the guest-offering (arghya), and a most fitting worship;
and they all paid appropriate tributes to that sovereign of their own lands.
Having beheld the great kingdom of Ekacakra, which extended ten thousand yojanas, he arrived and bathed in the Yamunā; then, having descended into the Dilāvarī, he became steady.
He brought back the jewels numbering ten million times a hundred million that had been given by the king;
having then placed them all at the disposal of Vāsudeva, he departed.
Together with his wife, the king always undertook the vow of self-surrender, which consisted entirely of devotion to the Blessed Lord.
Having caused a beautiful cave to be constructed on the lovely bank of the Yamunā,
he placed there a golden image of his father, the Blessed One, and guarded it well.
The king became devoted to the service of that beautiful and auspicious one, known as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, at all times and in every way.

Wearing matted locks and richly adorned with excellent bark garments, likewise holding a rosary of seeds, he possessed the appearance of a virtuous ascetic, yet his mind was fixed upon the internal state, the form, and meditation.
He was always like the king of yogis at Badarī, having attained liberation;
and every collection of ritual acts was performed by him for the sake of Hari.
The earth-element residing in the body was created solely for the sake of Hari;
likewise, the water-element situated in the body was also created for the sake of Hari.
The fire-element residing in the body was daily dedicated for the sake of Hari;
and the wind-element within the body was likewise made supreme for the sake of Hari.

The element of space (vyomatattva) residing within the body was fashioned as the ether for the sake of Hari; likewise, sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—these were created for the sake of Hari. (15)
Likewise, his two feet were ever joined in circumambulating Śrī Hari,
and his hands were always devoted in every way to the service of Kṛṣṇa.
His speech was employed in the praise of Kṛṣṇa’s glory and in hymns of adoration; his organs of excretion and generation were likewise dedicated to virtuous conduct and self-restraint.
When the eyes are engaged in perceiving forms such as the beginningless black [form of Kṛṣṇa], and when the ears are restrained according to the rules for grasping the sound of Hari; || 18 ||
The skin is eternally established as being in contact with objects belonging to Kṛṣṇa; the tongue moves solely toward the taste of the food offerings (naivedya) of Kṛṣṇa. 1.9.
The nose of Kṛṣṇa was always fashioned for perceiving fragrances;
he whose life was dedicated to the purpose of Kṛṣṇa made all his vital breaths consist of the recitation of His name.
She always fixed her head upon the wheel of Śrī Hari’s feet for bowing,
and she made her throat the source of the qualities arising from the divine voice of the Lord in conversation.
In the presence of Hari, he made a mocking grimace for the sake of Hari;
he feigned a blink of the eye, a sneeze, and the uttering of a name [inappropriately]. || 22 ||
The joining of the lips for tasting the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s grace;
and the turning of the tongue within the mouth in the search for Kṛṣṇa’s favor. (23)
He placed all the colors and positions upon the wheel marked with the name Kṛṣṇa;
he adorned Hari’s neck with garlands and sandalwood paste and other unguents.
Waking is for the sake of objects with distinct forms, sleep for the sake of mental forms, and deep sleep for the state of the Fourth (turya); therefore, it is joined with Kṛṣṇa for His sake.
Scratching, twisting, stretching the body, lying down,
sitting, veiling, and contracting— all these were performed by Hari within the wheel.
He performed for Kṛṣṇa various types of postures, such as the Svastika and others, including lying flat on the ground, lying on one's side, and remaining prone.
With his eyes, hands, feet, mind, head, and chest— these eight parts like staffs— he formed a gesture of reverence with joined palms in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
In the *mālikāvartana* [mudrā], all the fingers are well-joined in a circle;
when the thumb is joined on the palm in a circle for the worship (*arhaṇa*) of Hari, that indeed is it. || 29 ||
He performed actions upon his forearms and likewise upon his elbows;
he performed actions upon his shoulders as he carried out the tasks of Kṛṣṇa.
He performed the activities for the hips, the back, the belly, and the two shanks,
as well as the movement of the winds through the channels, all conjoined with the actions of Kṛṣṇa.
He fashioned the heart as the channel for the activities of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, the very existence of his body hairs and skin folds is entirely for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
The nourishment of his thighs and calves, as well as the formation of his bodily constituents,
his eating, drinking, and tasting— all these occurred through the agency of Kṛṣṇa.
The cleansing of his body, the adorning with ornaments and dress, the grooming,
and the offering of liquid substances— all this is indeed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
The emergence of oiliness on his body hairs as well as the exhilaration of his senses were always present for that king for the sake of delighting and pleasing Kṛṣṇa. (35)
Seizing, going, satisfaction, austerity, restraint, exertion,
laziness, fleeing, and obstruction— all these are for the sake of Hari.
A fist, a birth, and even a hollowed palm with a span of four fingers, as well as the spreading of a hood—all these are for the sake of this Hari. || 37 ||
Cutting his nails, cutting his hair, trembling, dancing, singing, emotional expressions, and running—all these were performed for the sake of Hari. || 38 ||
Restlessness and sagehood, outward movement and inward abiding, belching and hiccuping—these belong to Hari for his own sake, pervading all. || 39 ||
Inactivity and activity, as well as the bodily functions of that person—
all bathing, twilight prayers, recitation, and fire-offerings— are performed for the sake of Hari.
Writing, reciting, holding flowers, leaves, and so forth, as well as obtaining the requisites for worship—all this is for the sake of Hari. ||4.1||
The employment of vehicles and mounts, the union of men and women, and even the procreation of offspring—all these were for the sake of this Hari. ||42||
Consultation, approval regarding action, the occasional observation of the task, completion, or even formal assent—all this is for the sake of Hari. ||43||
The surveying of the land, the undertaking of grand festivals, auspiciousness, and even the manifestation of beauty—all this is for the sake of Hari. ||44||
Royal festivals, military parades, festivals for the gods, as well as festivals for religious vows and acts of charity—all these are performed for the sake of this Hari. ||45||
Sacrifices, services rendered to others, legal punishments, training, prosperity, and riches—all these exist for the sake of this Hari. (46)
For the sake of Hari, his rising and setting are [the divisions of time]; likewise, midday, the hour of gathering (saṃgava), the twilight period, the Brāhma-kāla, and night belong to him. 47.
The seasons, heat, cold, and so forth, as well as rains and sunshades, the wind, and the manifestation of the blazing fire of the summer heat—all these exist for the sake of Hari. (48)
For the sake of Hari, there was hospitality, a welcome, the offering of arghya, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), fragrant scents, honor, and the arrival of great festivities.
Both his income and expenditure are for the sake of Kṛṣṇa; likewise, his treasuries are for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
His male servants, female servants, and the entire class of attendants—all these indeed exist for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Volition, reflection, awakening, contemplation, and satisfaction; likewise meditation, devotion, recognition, remembrance, and fortitude. ||5.1||
Devotion, love, steadfastness, and pride—all these are for the sake of Hari;
as is self-awareness, the enjoyment of the self, and the direct manifestation of one's own nature. (52)
His own bliss and contentment, everything for the sake of this Hari—exclusive service, as well as his very breath, life, and delight. (53)
His eating and fasting, his dwelling in his own body, and likewise his wearing of clothes and so forth—all this is for the sake of Hari. (54)
Even while dwelling in a cave or a house, he speaks for the sake of Hari;
that king perceives the Imperishable One within his own self.
In all things and everywhere, he beheld Mādhava—
the sages, the ascetics, the gods, and the sacred fords— all embodied.
Having come together and beheld that abode, the truthful, the virtuous, the virtuous women, the yoginīs, and likewise the yogins, depart eternally. (57)
Detached from worldly desires, absorbed in Brahman, both the wise and those devoted to meditation stand all around the boundaries of that divine hermitage.
Discourses on Kṛṣṇa proceed there at every moment, as do sacrifices, silent recitations, the chanting of the Vedas, and hymns of praise; these are all carried out in his hermitage.
Consecrations, worship of the gods, offerings, and feasts; sacrificial porridges for the deities and lustration rites performed on all sides. ||4.112.60||
And on all sides of him, the sounds of fine bells and cymbals proceeded forth, along with the blasts of conchs, shouts of victory, and the proclamations, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (61).
Even lions, deer, living beings, birds, and likewise cattle,
as well as insects, worms, and moths, sing the praises of Brahman.
Aquatic creatures dwelling in holes in the earth, those living in the hollows of trees, those residing in your own abode, and those dwelling among leaves— all these proclaim the eternal Brahman.
Even the trees and the creepers remember the eternal Brahman;
and the mountains, the ravines, and even the insentient [elements] roar with echoes. 64.
Thus, O Badrikā, through the influence of the king, all his subjects—both men and women—came to possess constant devotion toward Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (65)
Indeed, divine beings belonging to Viṣṇu were born in every way upon the surface of the earth;
even the ancestors, the deities, and the planetary spirits obtained his grace.
The gods receive worship; Hari is worshipped everywhere.
In every human being, there exists a rosary of beads around his neck.
In every human being there exists the form of Nārāyaṇa;
