By that wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Svarṇāñjana and others were rescued as his servants, and in former times, even Śyena was rescued when he was a mere fledgling. || 131 ||
I bow to that Mādhava by whom sparrows were formerly rescued,
as well as goats, and by whom pigeons were formerly rescued along with merchants.
By him, those crows born of the *kaṅka* species were formerly driven out;
by him, the house-lizard was first expelled from its dwelling in the sky.
By him the mice, formerly Śūdras living in communal huts, were uplifted;
and by him the mongoose, formerly the fisherman Sāgara, was uplifted. (1.34)
I worship him by whom the bard named Kīratāra was uplifted,
and by whom Jyotirvettā Devagatīśvara was rescued.
I bow to him by whom his meritorious wife was rescued;
while the bards were chanting victory, the king, whose prowess is like a thunderbolt, [was restored].
I indeed bow to that venerable master (Śrīsvāmin) by whom the subjects were also uplifted;
his son was Sūta, the lion-king of the seven oceans, whose manes were beautiful.
I bow to him by whom Queen Rakṣāvatī was liberated, and to his servant Harṣanayana Māgadha, who is a devotee of the Yogin. 1.38.
By him was extracted the betel-leaf maker Saurabhasāvitra, as well as Raṅgila the dyer, and Ḍamarūka the musician. || 1.39 ||
I worship him by whom Cihnarāya and Bhāvasāra were uplifted,
and likewise by whom Rameśvara, the village priest, was also uplifted.
By him were rescued Svarṇāstaraṇa, the Vidyādhara Citrabarha and others, as well as the Kinnaras, the Kiṃpuruṣas, and the Cāraṇas.
I bow to you, by whom countless kings were delivered, who slew Nandibhilla and protected Nāgavikrama. 142.
I bow to him who restored the slain army to life;
I bow to him who liberated King Purañjaya. 143.
I bow to that Great Lord by whom many have been liberated—those dwelling in the seven heavens and those dwelling in the seven netherworlds. 144.
I worship that Puruṣottama, the Lord, who granted his vision to the righteous Ishvaras and who is enriched by a multitude of all women and servants. 145.
Salutations to that Śrī Paramātman, who bestowed upon all women, including his own, mind-born pairs of offspring.
I worship that Kṛṣṇa, who honors the virtuous, by whom the great king Māyāpāla—an atheist—was liberated from the realm of Yama. 147.
Then he gave the kingdom of Dīlāvarī to his eldest son and went himself toward the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma) to manifest his wife.
Having led all his own people as well as all the women to his own abode, he granted them residence within his supreme realm in his own form and thus protected them.

Having come to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and having attained renunciation, he who, having taken the initiation of a holy man, conducts himself within the range of the witnesses; ||| 4.120.150 ||
I bow to that Lord, the source of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
salutations to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Yogi.
He who eternally abides as Śrī Hari, possessing a form with seven abodes,
upon whose body Lakṣmī is dissolved, there I dwell, devoted solely to the Sāmaveda.
Wisdom is bound by fetters and remains latent within the Lord, the Sovereign;
yet all His divine sports lead to the ultimate welfare of living beings who possess bodies formed by karma. (153)
To him, the Lord of both the progenitor and the non-progenitor, the supreme Self, the most excellent and highest of all lords, I perpetually offer my salutation. (154)
Homage to the one of distinguished form, who has transcended all sacred fords;
O Blessed One, Lord, for the sake of the sacred ford and for the cause of the world’s welfare. (155)
O Great-Souled One, a longing has arisen within me; please fulfill it.
For throughout countless births, embodied beings have indeed been uplifted by you, O Kṛṣṇa.
O Lord, you have brought about the increase of Dharma in its entirety; furthermore, reflect upon those many people in this world who are devoted to Lakṣmī. 157.
"O Blessed One, having made persistent efforts in the guise of a virtuous man, please liberate those who have taken refuge in me;
thus I entreat you, O Lord, and I shall now desist from my pursuit of you. (158)
Having spoken thus, O Badrikā, Lakṣmī vanished within her mistress;
and whatever person recites this hymn to Lakṣmī with a heart full of devotion, [attains the fruit]. (159)
Like Lakṣmī, she shall attain an eternal place merged within Śrī Hari;
a woman who recites this hymn shall become Lakṣmī herself—of this there is no doubt.
Through this hymn, Lakṣmī became beloved, and Mādhavī became Lakṣmī;
by means of this praise, one shall obtain enjoyment and liberation, as well as the supreme state of the Lord, according to one's desire. 161.
O Śrī Badrikā, whatever belongs entirely to Kṛṣṇa shall belong entirely to that woman who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa and skilled in offering everything to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Self, the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Undertaking the Initiation of a Sādhu Following the Duties of a Vānaprastha, the Hymn of Praise by Lakṣmī, and the Eternal Absorption of Lakṣmī and Others into Their Own Lord," in the Tiṣya lineage within the fourth section of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa said: O Badrikā, thereafter the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Hari,
having internalized Lakṣmī, Prajñā, and Pāśavatī within his own self— || 1 ||
He dwelt in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in one form, while in another form, endowed with Śrī, he resided within.
In the form of a holy man, he traveled to sacred fords with a glorious appearance;
alone, he was beyond the reach of the senses, served by the liberated, and frequented by the gods.

Having drunk the water of the Kuṅkumavāpikā tīrtha, which was as fragrant as the breath of a horse or a crane, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) after bathing in the lake; || 4 ||
Having bowed to and worshipped with devotion both Śrī Gaṇeśa and the Guru, and having also bowed to all the holy fords (tīrthas) and performed the circumambulation of the lake; || 5 ||
He departed from the mango grove for the vast tiger forest;
thereafter he went to the lion forest and then to the auspicious plain of Talaśyāma.
Having bathed, he went to Somanātha and also to Prācīpippala;
then, from Mūladvārāvatī, his own city, he proceeded to Uṣṇapura.
After visiting Gopanātha, he went to Gokarṇa;
having paid homage to Nṛsiṃheśa and Śarabheśa, he departed swiftly through the sky.
He went to the supreme river Nārāyaṇī, which is exceedingly long and most excellent,
as well as to the lake Trināsa and the small lake Rudala.
He went to the Viṣaturīyaka, the Sarastriga, the Gāyana, and the Sarovara lakes, as well as the lake born of Nyāya, and then to the great river Kaṅgū.
Having reached the river Nyāyajarā, he went to the ocean in the middle of the earth;
then he proceeded to the Nīparā, the Dyūnā, the Vātagā, and the Uralā river.
Bālakṛṣṇa went to the lake and the great river Yayaubī; Kṛṣṇa then went to the Āneśī river and the Dvikala lake.
After that, he went to the beautiful Āyurā river and then to the ocean.
And having gone to Bahuliṅgasamudra and the Matkuñcikā river.
Having gone to Gartasrāvasaras, he went to Līnapādasaras;
having gone to Sūparīśasaras, he then went to the river Arkeśā.
Then, having gone to the ocean, he proceeded to the great river Āmañjanī;
having reached the river Pārānasī, he crossed the vast ocean.
Janārdana went to the river Mayūrā at Uṣṭrālaya;
having gone to the river Kāruliṅgī, he proceeded to the Etasa lake.
Having gone by way of the sky from the river Grāsakā to the region of Brahmā,
the Blessed One arrived at Badarī and the great river Menakāṅgī.
The Lord went to the river Śālavīnā and likewise to the river Airāvatī;
he went to the river Śikṣāṅgī, to the river Aṅgaśikṣāṅgā, and to the river Triyājñikā.
Kṛṣṇa then went to the Brahmaputrā, the Gaṅgā, the Godāvarī, and the Narmadā; from there he proceeded to Śatruñjitā and Aśvapaṭṭasāra.
The Blessed One arrived through the sky at his own abode, the field of the Imperishable,
on the auspicious twenty-ninth anniversary of his birth.
Kṛṣṇa, in the guise of a holy man, performed [this] in the temple of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
thus the Blessed Lord fulfilled even the heart's desire of Lakṣmī at Badarī.
He also fulfilled the heart's desire of Padmāvatī’s wisdom;
for whatever holy places there are on earth—rivers, streams, mountains, and oceans [he visited them all]. (22)
To forest lands, mountain caves, wildernesses, villages, islands, and the abodes of the gods—he, whose vehicle is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, went repeatedly to this or that place. (23)
For the welfare, well-being, auspiciousness, and prosperity of embodied beings;
for liberation, release, nirvāṇa, and eternal perfection. ||24||
O Badrikā, Kṛṣṇa has lifted up countless embodied beings from the ocean of worldly existence by His own will, through His grace, playfully, and with His wisdom.
Subject to the devotion of his followers, he travels even to all various regions;
and having performed the upliftment of people, he returns to his own abode. 26.
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā shines, adorned by holy men;
there, hundreds of thousands of *sādhus* and *sādhvīs* dwell day and night. (27)

The thirty-six festivals of Kṛṣṇa, beginning with the one on the first day, which arise from the occasion of his birth, are celebrated by countless devotees, including virtuous men and women, and they bestow great joy. (28)
Through that yoga, countless men are liberated every year;
those couples who are sons of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, even if they reside in foreign lands. ||29||
They too, having arrived and beheld their father, and having served Mādhava,
depart for their own maternal grandfather’s lands, filled with happiness.
O Badrī, countless men and women, Vaiṣṇavas imbued with devotion, constantly come here for the sake of serving the Lord Hari. ||31||
Having served you to their heart's content and attained what was in their minds,
they depart for their own countries and obtain supreme happiness.
Indeed, at the end of the body, they go to the supreme state, the highest abode;
yet Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa remains here upon the earth.
In every way, the Kṛta Yuga indeed prevailed among the subjects;
other ages, however, were not able to exert their influence. ||34||
Just as it was in the Kṛta age, so it was in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages;
likewise in the Kali age, through the yoga of Hari, the stability of the subjects is established as it was in Kṛta.
Then, by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion, the strength for dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation exists for all embodied beings, providing them with happiness according to their true purpose.
O Badrikā, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the beginningless, supreme Lord;
he was repeatedly entreated by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others. (37)
He remained on earth for one hundred thousand years, and twenty-five thousand five hundred years above, moving within the range of all.
At the end of one hundred and twenty-five thousand years,
Hari went to his own supreme abode by means of that very same divine and eternal body.
Then, in the Kuṅkumavāpī and other places, He shines forth in the form of an image,
visible to the physical eyes of all embodied beings.
But for those with divine vision, the divine-souled Lord is always directly perceptible, just as before;
indeed, for Lomaśa and others, the Blessed One is eternally manifest to their perception.
He is the embodiment of goodness for the virtuous and the constant object of perception for the righteous;
He is attainable through meditation by yogis and is the abode within the range of vision of the liberated.
Subjugated by the affection of his devotees, he dwells within their hearts;
that very Supreme Lord exists everywhere as the witness. 43.
O Badrikā, indeed many incarnations of Him arise;
I, as well as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, am truly His incarnation.
And you too are an incarnation of the half-body of that Kṛṣṇa;
worship that Supreme Soul as your beloved, just as I do. (45)
Just as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Maheśa, and the others worship [Him] day and night, and just as the gods, sages, ancestors, and Sādhyas worship [Him] day and night; ||46||
Just as the goddesses Īśā and Īśānikā worship Him day and night after being liberated, so too should you always remember Kṛṣṇa, the beloved who bestows eternal bliss. 47.
Remind others of that Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
O Badrī, cause embodied beings to perform His worship and devotion. 48.
By worshipping him alone, they shall go to the supreme state;
for his worship is such that it bestows liberation. 49.
The hearing of the Saṃhitā bestows liberation and grants eternal joy;
O Badarī, these exploits of Hari have been recited by me for you.
O Badarī, place in your heart that Lord who is charming with His divine play, who bestows liberation upon both devotees and non-devotees, and who is truly full of wonders. (51)
The venerable Vyāsa Śvetāyana said:
"O sages, listen to the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*;
those who hear even a single portion of it shall attain the supreme goal. (52)
Here, Khaṇḍa resides as the first, known by the name Kṛtasantānaka;
and the second indeed remains, known by the name Tretāsantānaka.
The third section of this [work] exists, known as the Dvāpara-santāna;
here, the fourth, named Tiṣya-santāna, is marvelous. (54)
In the first [part], where the lineage was established, there are five hundred and ninety chapters existing in the form of Brahmins. ||55||
The verses, moreover, number fifty-five thousand, five hundred, and twenty-seven. (56)
In the second lineage of the three [lineages], there are thirty-two thousand two hundred and thirty chapters. (57)
Indeed, there are fifty-four verses in the Tīvraka;
in the third, the Dvāpara-santānaka, there are two hundred chapters. (58)
Likewise, there are thirty-seven [chapters] that bestow liberation and possess divine forms;
furthermore, there are twenty-five thousand verses. (59)
In the fourth Tiṣya lineage, there are indeed one hundred and sixty-two chapters that bestow liberation and devotion; furthermore, there are one hundred chapters as well.
There are also twenty-three [chapters] that bestow the abode of Brahman;
there are thirteen thousand verses, and more besides. (6.1)
All thirty-eight [Tantras] are supreme, directly bestowing liberation;
they belong entirely to the Saṃhitā that takes the form of the four lineages.
There are one thousand chapters, and beyond that there are also hundreds;
furthermore, there are fifty [chapters], all of which in every way bring about liberation.
The verses of this complete compendium number one hundred thousand, and furthermore, twenty-five thousand more. (64)
Indeed, there are nine hundred and eighty-one verses beyond that; furthermore, there exist seven additional verses as well. (65)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the Beloved of Śrī,
dwelt upon the earth for a hundred thousand years, and thereafter the sages remained there.
Twenty-five thousand and five hundred [people] were there who performed wonders, and they were beyond even the scope of calculation. (67)
All those deeds performed by Kṛṣṇa in the form of a saint have indeed been written with reverence by the saints in the Sādhusaṃhitā.
But by Sanatkumāra and others who are devoted to liberation,
throughout every verse here, the yoga of Hari for embodied beings has been taught.
The grace of Kṛṣṇa, which is attained through the desire for liberation and is indeed difficult to obtain, is the very embodiment of compassion; therefore, this Saṃhitā bestows liberation.
This compendium is identical in form to Lakṣmī; this compendium is the very embodiment of Śrī.
As is Lakṣmī, so is this; as is this, so is Ramā. (71)
She is the beloved wife of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation, the purifier of all worlds, and the mother of those who attain emancipation. (72)
This nourisher of those belonging to this world, bestowing prosperity upon those who possess desire—this Goddess has manifested from the throat of Kṛṣṇa in a divine form. (73)
Therefore, she is of the nature of the Veda; like the Veda, she is indeed the knower.
When worshipped, recited, or heard, she bestows the fruit of the Vedas.
This [goddess] is always the bringer of peace, the one who causes joy like a forest of liberation;
like Rādhā, she is the possessor of prosperity and supernatural powers, the bestower of all prosperity and supernatural powers. || 75 ||
She is Nārāyaṇī in embodied form, the awakener of Nārāyaṇa;
when worshipped, recited, or heard, she brings about the attainment of Nārāyaṇa. (73)
She is the personified form of Vaiṣṇavī, the delighter of the Vaiṣṇavas,
the Yoginī of the news of the ages, and the Brahma-yoginī who brings awakening.
She who assumes the form of Brahman for the listener, the speaker, and likewise the worshiper—this Svāhā, whose essence is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. (78)
This wisdom is born from the beloved form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
it bestows the further shore of Brahman and takes the form of the final purificatory bath of a sacrifice.
Sarasvatī, the consort of Brahmā, is this eternal speech of Hari; she, in the form of a blessing for the virtuous, was manifested by Lomaśa. (4.121.80)
Well-nourished by her disciples Śveta, Prabhāti, Sanaka, and others, the divine sky became the means of sustaining the lives of millions of gods. 81.
This divine goddess is considered a great virtuous woman, immortal, the Gaṅgā who destroys sins, and the bearer of Viṣṇu. (82)
This auspicious one is the giver of well-being, the bestower of prosperity, and the constant grantor of bliss;
this solar Gāyatrī is known as the giver of honor and the supreme protector. (83)
This Kaumudī night, belonging to the moon, is the rightful portion for all the ancestors and bestows welfare upon the deceased; it grants the taste of nectar and is as delightful as a lotus pond. 84.
This Padmā is Padmikā, like the bearer of the lotus, the performer of the imperishable;
she is Annapūrṇā, bestowing the bliss of enjoyment through the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa. ||85||
The Gāṇeśī [form] destroys all obstacles and bestows security and gain;
the Hānumatī is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), while the Śīlinī is the Brahmavaṛculā. ||86||
The tortoise-shaped, hooded spear that performs the lifting of the earth—this is the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā, the plaything of Nārāyaṇa. (87)
This Badarī on the Golden Mountain is an ascetic woman who destroys all affliction;
this Yamunā is my sister, who blocks the path to the realm of Yama. (88)
This Gomatī is the very essence of the radiance of the rays of the Supreme Brahman;
she is the wish-fulfilling cow who bestows the fragrance of Kṛṣṇa upon those who serve her. 89.
When served with milk-rice, she fulfills all desires;
she is nectar to her attendants, bestowing the great immortality.
This eternal Kalpavallī tree fulfills the desires of the mind;
this is an inexhaustible vessel, endowed with the imperishable stories of Kṛṣṇa.
This compendium has the nature of the wish-fulfilling tree, raining down the essence of all goals;
it is the wish-granting gem for all, contemplating upon Kṛṣṇa.
This [Vrata] is always like a wish-fulfilling jewel that shatters the mountain of latent impressions (vāsanā);
it is a great hall for all vows, and when practiced, it bestows the fruit. 93.
This [goddess] embodies all sacred fords and awakens all sacred fords;
she is the sovereign of all, the Great Goddess who causes the lords to remember.
She is righteous, the protector of Dharma, and the upholder of Dharma;
she is eternal prosperity and the incarnate form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 95 ||
This transition is accompanied by the yoga of the Kṛṣṇa-saṃkrānti;
it is always a great festival, bringing joy to both the listener and the speaker. 96.
Formless yet having sound as her form, this tongue of Kṛṣṇa is laden with flavors;
she is the source of Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of bliss upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (97)
The celestial chariot of liberation is most excellent, a very tender path to the divine abode;
it is divine, consisting of Kṛṣṇa’s bed, and bestows the side of Kṛṣṇa. || 98 ||
She is the very embodiment of the face of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a consumer of Kṛṣṇa’s betel;
she is indeed the self-form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 99.
What need is there for much? This garland of *tulasī* is virtuous, bestowing the four goals of human life; it is indeed a virtuous initiation.
And this Kaṇṭhī-saṃhitā is always a great renunciation;
it is eternally filled with truth and constantly enhances the quality of goodness. || 101 ||
She is the goddess of the subtle body, this imperishable supreme knowledge;
she is the ritual power of the scriptures, and likewise the embodiment of devotion.
This Śrī, the destroyer of suffering, is eternally beloved by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
when read or heard, she bestows the fruit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. 103.
She is auspicious, bestowing merit and liberation for a hundred thousand Viṣṇu-sacrifices;
likewise, she grants the fruit of all kinds of austerities and bestows peace.
She is the bestower of merit upon all vows and all sacred fords,
and she yields the supreme fruit of giving ten million cows, elephants, and horses.
She bestows the fruit of the gift of the entire universe, grants fearlessness to all living beings,
yields the merit of giving away ten million maidens in marriage, and is equal to the gift of ten million goddesses of fortune.
The Upaniṣad is personified, bringing one into the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
it is indeed the knowledge of the Self for those free from desire, and the bestower of desired objects for those with desire. 107.
She is the giver of wealth, the giver of sons, the giver of daughters, and the giver of health and fame;
she is the giver of sovereignty, the giver of nourishment, the giver of women, and the giver of a desired husband.
Bestowing heaven, bestowing the divine abode, bestowing liberation, and providing a residence at the feet of Kṛṣṇa—
this Saṃhitā always grants all things and daily bestows welfare.
As a housewife among householders, she nourishes the stability of the home;
as the Yoginī of Hari, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, she dwells in the hearts of the virtuous.
This [goddess] bestows all good fortune and grants supreme excellence;
she showers the bliss of sovereignty known as the abode of infinite bliss. 111.
And this *Mahāmuktānikā* Saṃhitā exists upon the earth;
its lineages are indeed the sons of Nārāyaṇa, equal to Nārāyaṇa himself in liberation, strength, fame, and prosperity. (112)
Just as [the ritual] was performed for all dharmas, so it was performed in its entirety at the sacrifice.
Dvīta was peerless in all forms of giving; Tiṣya was incomparable in all forms of recitation;
Kṛta was endowed with great power; and Tretā possessed divine conduct. (1.14)
In the Dvāpara age, he is Tiṣya, rich in divine pastimes and the savior who provides refuge;
in the Tretā age, he is Satya, who rescues his own self through the strength of his own soul by taking recourse to the gods and others.
Due to the wonder of Kṛṣṇa, Dvīta became Tiṣya through his meeting with the saintly; this Tiṣya, the descendant of Kṛṣṇa, remained alone, devoted to and reciting the scriptures.
He who is heard of, and also made to be heard of, who is honored, protected in the home,
remembered for his virtues, and embraced— such a one swiftly delivers those who have taken refuge in him.
Having fashioned an auspicious golden, excellent image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, he established this lineage of Tiṣya.
One should give with devotion as a gift to a learned man who expounds the Veda,
especially to a Vaiṣṇava, and also to an Ācārya or a Guru.
To a Brahmin who is a teacher and habitually recites sacred narratives,
one should give a cow accompanied by ten thousand calves and provided with all necessary utensils and equipment.
He who offers a fully furnished and soft bed, as well as alms-bowls, and gives jewels, grain, clothing, and so forth, shall indeed attain liberation. 121.
Having attained heaven with his desires fulfilled and a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā,
he enjoys all pleasures and, by virtue of the gift of the Saṃhitā, proceeds indeed to the Imperishable.
This lineage of Tiṣya is the sustainer of the existence of the virtuous;
it generates affection for the good and likewise bestows the awakening to the dharma of service.
He is the washer away of all sins, the bestower of liberation upon the wicked,
and the blissful one who grants the abode of Brahman to living beings who have sought refuge in him.
Even a sinner may become a recipient of the grace of the virtuous Hari;
whether born as an animal, from sweat, from an egg, or from a womb, such a one is fully liberated.
Whoever, with a concentrated mind, recites even a single chapter of the Tiṣya in his home,
quickly obtains the fruit of reciting the entire Tiṣya lineage.
For the sages who recite the Tiṣya-pāṭha, the force of Tiṣya does not afflict them;
the defects of Tiṣya do not arise, and Yama goes far away from them.
Desirous of hearing the discourse on Tiṣya, he is indeed a vessel for my compassion;
for by resorting to holy men who grant liberation from everything, he attains the imperishable state.
For one whose practice consists of charity, austerity, and ritual recitation, but lacks moral discipline,
there is liberation through taking refuge in Tiṣya and through the support of virtuous women.

Having fashioned a golden celestial chariot and established it upon a fragment of the Tiṣya constellation, the donor, after worshipping it, should offer it to a worthy recipient; such a giver shall travel in that celestial chariot to the imperishable realm.
Together with his entire family, he rejoices in the abode of Hari;
he attains both worldly enjoyment and eternal liberation—of this there is no doubt. || 131 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Visits to All Holy Places on Earth by the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Sage and His Other Divine Form for the Purpose of Fulfilling the Desires of Śrī Manu; the Return to Kuṅkumavāpikā; the Specification of the Number of Chapters and Verses in the Tiṣya-Santāna and the Entire Saṃhitā; and the Greatness of Giving and Other Virtues Pertaining to the Entire Saṃhitā and the Tiṣya-Santāna," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 121.1.
The venerable Śvetāyana Vyāsa said: Listen to the supreme *puraścaraṇa* of the Śrī-saṃhitā;
it must be performed by one who desires prosperity for every single *saṃhitā*.
One should recite it oneself or cause it to be recited by one hundred and eight twice-born Vaiṣṇavas, virtuous men and women, who are devoted to the character of Brahman.
One should have a beautiful and spacious pavilion constructed for the sacrificial pit,
and one should place gentle seats made of wool around it.
Furthermore, one should place each individual book upon wooden seats and the like, each on its own excellent seat, and then perform worship. || 4 ||
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering (ārārtrika) and then have the recitations performed;
every day, one should feed [the devotees] with purikās, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Whatever is required, one should give it all or cause it to be given;
furthermore, a month-long recitation of the entire text (pārāyaṇa) constitutes the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this.
Or one should have it performed for two months, which grants the attainment of the four aims of human life;
or one should have it performed for six months, or have it recited annually.
One should always feed virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, the poor, and the helpless;
one should also feed Brahmins, virtuous women, girls, and boys.
Likewise, one should cause gifts of vessels made of gold and silver to be given; one should also cause gifts of wealth, garments, grains, and food to be performed.
One should perform the worship daily of the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī, and likewise one should carry out the fire sacrifice (havana).
One should worship the Supreme Self, Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, together with Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Prajñāvatī, and Śrīmāṇikī.
One should regularly perform the *daśāṃśahoma* (the oblation of one-tenth the number of recitations) with ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
as well as with fuel-sticks from sacred trees, fruits, flowers, juices, and so forth.
During the monthly *pārāyaṇa*, the observer of the vow should regularly have the chapters recited.
In two months, however, there are exactly forty-two [days], and in half of that [time], half of those. || 13 ||

The observer of the vow should recite six [verses] daily for six months, and three [verses] each for a full year; or, having divided them as appropriate, he may recite more or less according to the circumstances.
One should constantly perform oblations of ghee in proportion to the number of verses;
one should give various kinds of pleasant sacrificial fees to the reciters. 15.
Having wrapped the book in a new cloth and worshipped it,
one should carry it around the city, mounted upon a golden elephant and attended with chowries.
Then one should bestow gifts upon the excellent reciter who is worthy of them:
the gift of an umbrella, the gift of sandals, and the gift of garments and so forth. (17)
One should indeed give ornaments, cows, land, gold, and so forth to a preeminent virtuous person, to a teacher of eloquent speech, to a guru, to a teacher of knowledge, and to a yogin. (18)
One should especially give with devotion to a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa;
one should also feed the best of brāhmaṇas, as well as virtuous men, virtuous women, and children.
One should feed all the Vaiṣṇava devotees and then dismiss them;
by performing the *puraścaraṇa* in this manner, one shall attain one's desired goals. (4.122.20)
I shall proclaim the great gift worthy of an emperor; learn it from me.
In ancient times, the universal monarch, the great king Āgnīdhra, bestowed it.
Svāyambhuva Manu also bestowed [it] on the bank of the Gomatī,
and Kubera bestowed it upon Viśālā in the Himalayas.
Koṭirāya also gave [gifts] on the bank of the Indus near the ocean;
in this manner, others likewise gave according to the time and according to their wealth.
Listen as I describe that great universal gift (sārvabhauma-mahādāna);
here are the gods who have been glorified, and the goddesses who are devoted and destined for liberation. 24.
Having collected all the names and having had images made from gold, one should give them all by the millions as a gift at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Wherein even a single deity of the *saṃhitā* is not exceeded,
one should indeed offer all the deities in the gift, preceded by the gift of a cow.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should give to virtuous Brahmins and to all who are worthy recipients; for such a person, there is no end to their merit.
Only he by whom everything has been offered for the sake of the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari is truly capable of performing a great gift in its true sense. ||28||
Indeed, by the power of his great gift, he shall deliver the entire world;
for Hari is ever present in the vicinity of one who bestows such a great gift. (29)
And Lakṣmī shall always be within his reach; of this there is no doubt—for him who performs and promotes the sacrifice of the narrative of the Saṃhitā.
All his supernatural powers shall become inexhaustible and ever-increasing;
by making a gift on this day in the month of Kārttika, he becomes Brahmā, the creator of the universe.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, the giver of this [text] becomes Nārāyaṇa;
in Pauṣa, the giver of the Saṃhitā becomes Rudra Śaṅkara. (32)
In the month of Māgha, the giver of this Saṃhitā is indeed born as Viṣṇu;
but in Phālguna, the giver of it is born as the immovable Dhanada.
In the month of Caitra, the donor of this [gift] indeed becomes one whose deity is the Sun;
in Vaiśākha, the excellent donor becomes a steadfast Vaiṣṇava.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the giver shall become Virāṭ; in Āṣāḍha, the giver shall be Sadāśiva;
and in Śrāvaṇa, the giver shall undoubtedly be Mahāviṣṇu. ||35||
In the month of Bhādrapada, Mahendra shall be the giver; in Āśvina, however, Bṛhaspati;
and in the intercalary month (adhimāsa), Vāsudeva becomes the giver. ||36||
Thus has the supreme fruit of giving been proclaimed, arising from my grace;
the woman who gives becomes Rādhā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Mādhavī. (37)
All forms of poverty are destroyed by the giving of this;
all three kinds of suffering are destroyed by the giving of this. (38)
Having placed this entire Saṃhitā upon the head of an elephant, or alternatively, having placed the golden Saṃhitā upon a golden elephant; ||39||
He who gives [this] shall possess sovereignty over the fourteen worlds;
even one who gives a fragment becomes a Manu, while Hari is the giver of the whole.
For the speaker of this verse, there shall never be an unfortunate rebirth; moreover, by the recitation of this [verse], one obtains the fruit of all the duties of the castes and stages of life. 41.
The wise person who, having committed this Saṃhitā to memory, shall recite it, will indeed, by that very body and through a divine state, [attain liberation] in every respect. (42)
Having attained the supreme state by means of a celestial chariot granted by Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
he shall depart for the imperishable realm, praised and honored by the gods and those who have attained liberation.
He who holds the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in his heart shall become the lord of the abode of Vaikuṇṭha in another creation. (44)
A woman shall always be the sovereign Lakṣmī, the mistress of Vaikuṇṭha;
one possessed of desire obtains what is desired, and one with specific wishes attains their fulfillment.
A man who is free from desire and seeks liberation shall become Nārāyaṇa;
and a woman shall become Nārāyaṇī by constantly maintaining the retention of this Saṃhitā. 46.
One who desires eternal prosperity should always perform these four:
the worship of Lakṣmī, meditation on Hari, giving gifts, and listening to her stories. (47)
One who desires eternal liberation should always practice these four:
service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, remembrance of His divine play, and dedication to Him. (48)
One who desires eternal peace should always practice these four: non-undertaking of actions, cessation from worldly life, the recitation of mantras, and discernment within the self. (49)
Whoever here should be possessed of wisdom and desire eternal bliss, as well as the state of being the supreme lord of the three worlds and the lordship over all lords; [he should practice this].
Moreover, may he constantly drink the nectars arising from the Śrī-saṃhitā, which consist of supreme liberation and the nature of incarnation. 4.122.50.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the *Puraścaraṇa* of this Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, the Procedure for the Great Universal Gift (*Sārvabhauma-Mahādāna*), and the Fruit of Retaining the Saṃhitā," in the fourth section, the Tiṣya lineage, of the glorious Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Naranārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Śrī Badarī, O Nārāyaṇī, O Supreme Sovereign;
I shall remind you in brief of the matters concerning the lineage of Tiṣya.
In the fourth chapter, concerning the lineage of Tiṣya, the manifestation of my own form as Nara-Nārāyaṇa at the sacred Badarī has been narrated to you.
The narrative of the royal sage named Badara and of Himācala is told,
as well as the casting into a pit of the Asura Hemānala.
The glorious Māṇikyā has proclaimed the nature of Badarīśī and others;
furthermore, the liberation of the deceased Brahmin Śrīśīla has been described.
The testing and liberation of the king named Dārābhāgya, as well as the account of the lineage of the Brahmin Brahmadeva, are narrated. (5)
By Badarī, the youthful Yoginī, the Gītā was spoken, which bestows the state of Brahman,
as well as servitude, the status of a Bhāgavata, the status of a Vaiṣṇava, and the state of a Yogin.
And the description of the essence of love for the Supreme Brahman is proclaimed;
through service to the virtuous, liberation is said to be attained by Nāgnajitī in the forest. (7)
Through the devotion of Vinodinī toward her beloved, Nārāyaṇa appeared;
and that she was composed of the nature of a deity—all this has been declared. (8)
Furthermore, devotion to Līlāvatī is illustrated by way of abundance;
likewise, the seventeenth [chapter] is proclaimed as the festival for the birth of Anādikṛṣṇa.

Liberation is said to be attained through service to the Māliya and Mallika flowers; likewise, the essence of Brahman, which is obtainable through knowledge, is declared to be reached through meditative worship (upāsanā). 4.123.10.
The description of the great yoga of the supreme dharmas that bestow rasa, and [the account of] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with the young yoginīs. 1.1.1.
He caused the marriage to take place, and this story was then told;
thereafter follows the liberation of the true devotee Nikāmadeva.
And the form consisting of the yoga of its own nature is enjoined in the Supreme Brahman;
therefore, Hari is declared to be the self of the non-duality of the distinguished Brahman. 1.3.
The discourse on fearless yoga and likewise the hymn of praise were thus proclaimed;
furthermore, for the one who offers praise, there is the vision of the abode of all through that very hymn.
Then, their divine liberation while still in their physical bodies was proclaimed, as well as the release of the fishermen who had been wandering in fetters. 15.
Then, O Badrikā, it was indeed said by means of the method of recitation that Ekalā and Kuśalīsāgarī suffered from royal consumption (rājayakṣman). || 16 ||
O Badarī, it was indeed stated there that protection and liberation were attained by Viṣalāṇī through the food given as a favor by the virtuous.
From that, liberation is declared; thus, liberation is proclaimed as being produced from Gaṅgā.
And from Ramā, the state of Ramā is produced; thus, liberation is fully proclaimed as being produced from Ramā.
Through service to a virtuous person, the Moon attained the state of being the son of Raṇastambakumbhakāra’s wife; from that, liberation was proclaimed. (19)
Then there was the wonder of the goldsmithess named Devasudhā:
during a famine, she provided food for countless living beings and likewise brought about their liberation.
The divine state of the noble Viṣṭinī, daughter of Vidruminī, through association with the virtuous;
and the vision of Dharma by Cāṇḍālī, the daughter of Mālava, through service. 21.
The vision of the embodied mantra and liberation have also been proclaimed; and the state of being free from delusion has been illustrated by the examples of Kārelikā and the Śūdrī. ||22||
The muteness of the saint Badrikāyana and his release from the curse, as well as the prevention of consumption disease by Yantrakartrī Gomatī. ||23||
The liberation of Kanakāṅgadā was accomplished through service to the virtuous;
likewise, for the sake of the liberation of the two intoxicated ones, Rāya and Haribhāṇuvāṇi.
The recitation of the narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā and the eighteenth great festival of Hari’s birth have been described. (25)
The liberation of those residing at the Nārāyaṇa lake from King Ruccha, as well as the sanctity of Vidyotā and her liberation, has thus been declared. (26)
The liberation of the potter’s family, as well as that of the goldsmith’s wife, of the smelter of minerals, of the actor, and even of the miser.
The liberation of the subjects of King Kṣīroda and his queen was proclaimed; thereafter, the liberation of Somika and the other courtesans was declared. (28)
The destruction of suffering and liberation were bestowed by Hari upon the wine-drinker;
it is said that many followers of the Cakrin-Yāska doctrine attained liberation. (29)
For the two revilers, Dvivadan and Dvigarjana, there was a vision of the messengers of Yama, and from that, liberation was proclaimed. (4.123.30)
O Badarī, it has been stated that liberation comes from hearing the story of the Brahmin Suraprasāda, who killed his preceptor, through service to the virtuous. (3.1)
The protection and liberation of those fallen into imprisonment, those who have committed offenses against the gods, and those such as Nāgavikrama and others are proclaimed [in this work]. (32)
The destruction of the lifespan of King Śālamitra and his queen was declared to have been averted through the hearing of the narrative of the Saṃhitā. (33)
For one who fights in battle, for one who administers poison, and regarding daughters and the like,
there is the arrival of the messengers of Yama, death, and protection performed by the virtuous.
For the woman Anaṅgavallarī, who was promiscuous and a destroyer of embryos, the destruction of her sins and her liberation have been declared through recourse to this narrative. (35)

The liberation of eunuchs and others through hearing the discourse on Ṣaṇḍhavajra and the rest is proclaimed for those who are neuter, as well as for others, by means of the manifestation of male and female characteristics. (36)
Liberation has been proclaimed for the slayer named Yavasandhya;
there is also the release of the one called Bhaṇḍaśīla and of Bhavāyana. (37)
O Badrī, the liberation of wrestlers such as Harṣavīrya and others, of hunters, and of usurers has been proclaimed through the hearing of this narrative. (28)
Through the occasion of a virtuous conversation concerning Nāgārjuna, Vādirāja, Sāraha, and the playful [siddhas], liberation was then proclaimed. ||39||
Then the initiation of the brahmin Vilāsadeva and of Luñcāda is described,
followed by the initiation of the one known as Duritaghoṣa.
Through Śīlā, there was the liberation of her husband Dharmabhaṭa;
and through Nyāyākṣiṇī, there was the liberation of her husband Nyāyādhiśa. ||41||
The liberation of the scribe Viśālarekhaka and others has been described;
thereafter, the liberation of the Kṣatriya Śāhavilāpana is told.
The liberation of Daṇḍāraṇika from his birth as a vulture is told, as is the release of Govāra from his birth as a cat. (43)
For one born as a jackal, liberation is said to come from the merchant Ṭhaṭṭhola;
for those who resemble gold and collyrium, release is declared to be through service. (44)
Liberation was also declared for the goat-herd who had been born as a hawk, and thereafter,
the liberation of goats born as sparrows was likewise proclaimed.
Likewise, there was formerly the liberation of the pigeon caravan-leaders,
and formerly the liberation of the Kaṅka-birds and the crow-birds.
The liberation of Nāṇakī, who was born as a house-lizard while dwelling in the sky, and the liberation of the Śūdras of Saṃghavāṭa and others, who were born as rats; [these are told]. 47.
Of Sāgara, Dānava, Āruṭakīra, Tāra, and Bhāṭa;
of Puṇyavatī and her husband Devagatīśvara. ||48||
O Badrikā, the liberation of King Vajravikrama from the bards who were chanting his victory was proclaimed by him upon hearing their story. 49.
The liberation of King Siṃha, who was bitten by a serpent after seven years;
and also the liberation of Harṣanayana-saṃjña, the ruler of Magadha.
Then, O Badarī, the liberation of Yogidāsa was told, as well as the liberation of Saurabhasāvitra by name and of Tāmcūlin. (51)
Thereafter, the liberation of the maker of the stage known as Ragila was declared, and the liberation of the maker of the musical instrument called the ḍamarūka was also proclaimed. 5.2.
The liberation of the one named Cihnarāja, whose essence was devotion, has been told;
as well as the release of the Vidyādharas, including those upon golden carpets and others. || 5.3 ||
Then follows the liberation of the supreme gandharvas, such as Citrabarha and others;
thereafter, the liberation of the kinnaras, the cāraṇas, and the siddhas.
Upon the conclusion of the recitation of the Saṃhitā, there shall be worship and other rites,
as well as a procession of the Lord through the city and throughout all the kingdoms and realms.
Then follows the journey of Śrī Hari to Kuṃkumavāpikā;
thereafter, the Sarvamedha sacrifice of King Nāgavikrama is described.
Then followed the battle between the lord of Dilāvarī, Nandibhilla,
and King Nāgavikrama, involving the armies of both sides.
Then, O Badrikā, the victory through the prowess of Nāga, the destruction of the Bhilla Nandi, and the chastity of Dilāvarī were narrated. (58)
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, however, spoke the auspicious Gṛhagītā for his own wives, which is the means of liberation for householders. (99)
Liberation has been declared even for householders who possess knowledge of the meaning of the injunctions;
thus is described the twenty-second festival, the Janmāṣṭamī of Śrī Hari.
The experience of hell by King Purañjaya in a dream, as well as his liberation, was narrated; furthermore, Hari went to Satyaloka.
Having traveled through the seven worlds, the Blessed One went to Aśvasāra;
even after traveling through the subterranean realms beginning with Atala, Hari reached his own birthday.
He celebrated the twenty-fourth festival at Kuṅkumavāpī as narrated in the story;
having traveled to the seven continents, he celebrated his own festival as the twenty-fifth.
And the Supreme Lord, moving upwards through the worlds and abodes beginning with Vairāja, established [his presence] at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Then Hari, having shown his abodes to his wives, departed for the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the lands of Siṃhāraṇya and other regions.
The Lord wandered for the sake of recreation together with his wives;
there, at that time, all of Hari's beloved offspring were present.
There he gave to all of them pairs of children who were divine and mind-born, O Badarī, not born from a womb.
Thereafter, the ritual procedures for those [deities] were declared, followed by the description of the nature of Tiṣya and the praise of the qualities of Tiṣya. ||68||
The protection of King Māyāpāla from the rod of Yama was provided by the sage Sanatkumāra, and his liberation from that state was likewise accomplished by him.
In the Kali age, the means for liberation manifest from Hari;
likewise, there is the pilgrimage of King Nāgavikrama and his divine nature.
Śrī Hari indeed performed the consecration of his own son, Mukundavikrama, in the capital city of Dilāvarī.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa went by means of ten million celestial chariots and fulfilled the desire of his wives to behold him even for a moment. ||72||
The wives attained the state of being liberated from their female forms, as did the immersion in the Brahma-lake, the sight of Mount Koṭiśṛṅga, and the beholding of the dance pavilion. ||73||
Beholding the circle of the *rāsa* dance, beholding the circle of the monastery;
beholding the circle of the kingdom, and beholding the city of the abode of the Imperishable. ||74||
The vision of the great hall of Brahmā and the observation of the abode of the incarnations—all this has been described; beyond that lies the supreme realm. (75)
The journey, the discernment of the *Rahasyopaniṣad* and other texts, the description of the eight difficult terrains, and [the description] of the city of the Supreme Brahman. (76)

The description of the abodes of those liberated from the Supreme Brahman and others; the secret of the tens of millions of liberated ones; and also the state of being twofold and the state of oneness. (77)
Then, the vision of the sixteen Maholās is described,
along with the gaze of liberation characterized by identity with the Primordial One who resides within the womb of the forms.
The offering of one's own wives in their entirety as being identical with [the deity] and liberated is declared to be the collective form of the seven abodes of Śrī Hari. (79)
The arrival of Śrī Hari at Kuṅkumavāpī has been described, as well as the gifts of his own countless opulences that were bestowed. (4.123.80)

Following the forest-dweller's stage of life, the initiation of the virtuous and the glorification of Hari are recounted; then follows the hymn composed by Lakṣmī, and thereafter the pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Furthermore, the return of Hari together with Lakṣmī to Kuṅkumavāpikā is described,
as well as that of tens of millions of Śrī-Svāminīs.
The number of chapters in the Saṃhitā and the number of verses have indeed been declared;
likewise, the greatness of receiving the Saṃhitā and the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) have also been described. ||83||
Thereafter, the procedure for the great gift of the universal monarch was proclaimed;
furthermore, O Badrikā, the recollection of the stories was also recounted to you. 84.
Thus, O Badrī, all these objects have been described by me;
by hearing of them and by remembering them, an embodied being attains liberation. (85)
O Badrikā, the objects of the senses have been described for each section at its respective end; therefore, they should be understood from those respective conclusions. ||86||
The greatness of each respective section has been established at its conclusion;
through recitation, hearing, and meditation upon it, both worldly enjoyment and liberation will surely be attained. 87.
O Badrī, I shall now rest for a moment upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
you too, O Sunandā, go to find rest in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
"Come, come! Let us both become one with the ocean of great bliss;
let us enjoy the bliss born of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa as much as we desire. (89)
Śrī Vyāsa, the son of Śveta and Kṛṣṇā, said:
While the conversation was thus proceeding, Badrikā spoke:
"I am blessed; I am an ascetic woman, and I am endowed with great fortune."
I am that power, the half-form whose nature is the Supreme Person; I know myself as Māṇikī and Mādhavī, who consist of valid cognition.
I know myself to be Lakṣmī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇī herself;
my Lord and beloved, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, is my husband. (92)
I recognize him as the Supreme Lord who has descended in his entirety;
he is the venerable Nārāyaṇa of Badarī, accompanied by Nara. (93)
I am that Nārāyaṇī-Badrī, the Sovereign of All, the Supreme Person;
O Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa, [I attained this] through association with the virtuous and by hearing Your sacred narratives. 94.
"Through me as a cause, the supreme welfare of the worlds shall come to pass;
blessed is this entire earth, and blessed are these human beings. (95)
Blessed are those women of every kind whose husband is Nārāyaṇa—the sustainer, the supporter, the creator, and the eternal protector—in whom the auspicious grace of Hari always resides. (96)
Indeed, the compassion of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) toward all is especially directed toward the six;
and that of Him in the form of Kṛṣṇa is toward Rādhā, as is that of Nārāyaṇa toward Lakṣmī. 97.
In the case of Prajñā who possesses the noose, and also in the case of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Nārāyaṇī-Śrī, who possess the form of Puruṣottama. ||98||
Even for Nara-Nārāyaṇa at Badarī, there is eternal [residence] with me;
here, Nārāyaṇa recited the Kṛta-khaṇḍaka for the sake of Lakṣmī.
The Strī-khaṇḍa was narrated by Him in the form of Kṛṣṇa to Rādhā; likewise, it was narrated in the form of Puruṣottama to Nārāyaṇī Śrī.
You have informed me of the final lineage of the Dvāpara age,
as well as the Gṛhagītā and other works uttered for the sake of wisdom and the liberation from the bonds of worldly existence.
O Blessed One, here I am, fallen at your feet; having absorbed me within your form, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, [be gracious].
"O Lord, grant me a moment's rest; I shall meditate upon that Hari.
Having spoken thus, Badarī quickly became absorbed in meditation.
At that moment, there suddenly arose a great wonder and a great marvel;
a pervasive, cool, sweet, and blissful great splendor appeared.
There, the resounding and enchanting tinkling of small bells was heard,
as they rested upon their ornaments on the feet, hands, waist, and chest.
The sweet, pleasure-inducing tinkling of small bells was heard;
there, amidst that splendor, a single most beautiful maiden appeared.
With her body possessing the luster of the moon at the peak of its rising youth,
she holds four books in her four beautiful hands.
Smiling with a gentle laugh, she was adorned with all ornaments;
she shone with divine golden bracelets and other jewels, as well as a celestial crown.
Richly perfumed with divine fragrances, beautifully adorned with celestial garments,
she was exceedingly beautiful and enchanting to all the women.
She was well-nourished, beautiful in all her limbs, and endowed with strength that filled her to the brim;
in her four hands, which were joined together, she held excellent garlands.
The four [consorts] are Dhṛtimatī, Prasannavadanekṣaṇā, Lakṣmī, and either Rādhikā, Māṇikī, or Badrī Pramāthavā. (111)
Nārāyaṇa then composed the Mādhavī-saṃhitā;
and knowing Badarī to be incarnate, he likewise composed this Lakṣmī-saṃhitā.
They did not inquire after her welfare, yet they both offered her a welcome;
Nārāyaṇa presented her with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and an auspicious seat.
Questioned as to who she was, from where, and how, she related her own story:
"I am the Śrī Puruṣottamī, the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (1.14)
I myself have manifested from the body of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, possessing a divine form and bearing the very nature of Rādhā-Lakṣmī.
She is the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇī and Śrī, having the form of Badrī and consisting of light;
she takes the form of Padmāvatī and always possesses four hands.
She is the bearer of the four books, her form consisting of the four lineages;
she is the mother born from the four Vedas and possesses the nature of the four abodes.
The speech of Nārāyaṇa consists of four [aspects] and exists throughout the four yugas;
it is intended for the four stages of life and the four social classes, and is endowed with the four means of accomplishment.
I possess four feet and am supported by the four Nārāyaṇas;
I am the embodiment of the four Nārāyaṇas, having the four liberations as my excellent form.
O Blessed One, possessing four forms and bearing four garlands,
I am now truly complete today, consisting of the essence of the four Nārāyaṇas.
I desire to worship that Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, the beloved of the noble one, who dwells in Badarī.
Having spoken thus, she approached Śrī Narāyaṇa with her four arms of equal length in order to worship him; at that very moment, the Blessed Lord, the Master, arrived before her.
Kṛṣṇa appeared with Rādhā, possessing two arms and holding a flute;
Nārāyaṇa appeared with Lakṣmī, bearing four arms.
Endowed with the splendor of Nārāyaṇī, he became Śrī Puruṣottama;
and Badrīnārāyaṇa also appeared in the place before him.
Lord Prajñā-Badarikāsvāmī is clearly perceived in all four [forms]; Hari is present there to receive worship, to show compassion, and to bestow blessings. (125)
Seeing him to be such a person, he offered him four lotus garlands and applied unbroken grains, saffron, and sandalwood paste as a mark upon his forehead.

Having performed the rites and offered worship to the couples, she praised them with her mind fixed upon them; though her desires were already fulfilled, she was overwhelmed, her heart full of affection, and deeply composed.
Hari, the Supreme Person and Lord of the beloved, who is served in manifold ways, dwells in the transcendent, imperishable abode that is his own;
he is accompanied by his attendants, the Amās, who possess forms identical to his own.
May he alone be my supreme refuge, the fulfiller of all excellent boons.
And he who sports here together with Rādhā, served by many kinds of gopīs, that Lord Kṛṣṇa stands before us to completely fill the hearts of his own people.
May he fulfill my heart's desire here.
The Lord who repeatedly expands Himself in countless forms within His abode is indeed the Lord of Kamalā, assuming the form of Nārāyaṇa; for He,
the mine of great compassion, has here become clearly manifest before my very eyes.
May he dispel whatever is in my heart that is detrimental to my entire body.
For the sake of bringing about the state of ultimate bliss for beings of various dispositions, he has indeed constantly withered even his most beautiful form through asceticism;
may that sage Badarīśa, the bestower of immeasurable awakening, be mine in this world.
And may he grant me that which is the object of my husband's desire to the highest degree. || 131 ||
Bowing down again and again here, I have repeatedly placed myself at the soles of the feet of Hari, who bears the fourfold forms;
for, though possessing an odd number of limbs, I am intent on attaining the state of being a pair.
To whom shall I go, she who delights in the four [objects of sense] and consists of manifest speech? 1.32.
Thus the goddess Sahitā praised the four lords;
then, bowing with modesty, the passionate woman set forth, observing silence.
The four Haras bestowed boons upon her, saying:
"O auspicious goddess, this [Veda] has issued forth from our mouths. (134)
Since You abide in Rādhā, in Śrī, in Badrī, and in Lakṣmī, You shine forth eternally; therefore, You are the eternal one who assumes our very form.
You abide as the true progenitor of the Vedas, containing our very intention within you;
indeed, you are the most excellent vessel for ten thousand boons.
O you who possess the forms of the fourfold nature, we grant boons to you;
from this day forward, you shall be the eternal consort of the four.
Just as Catuṣpatnī is equal [to them] and Prajñāpāśavatī is equal [to them], and just as those goddesses are givers of liberation, so too are you always a giver of liberation. (138)
The supreme goddess of all abodes, the Great One, the Highest of Persons, O divine lady, dwell forever within our homes and sanctuaries. 1.39
By your second form, O Speech, you dwell as the bestower of liberation upon those who have taken refuge in you, your worshippers, and your listeners, according to your compendium.
Likewise, may there be supreme welfare in the abode for those habituated to recitation;
may there be dharma for those desiring dharma, and prosperity for those desiring prosperity. (141)
May there be fulfillment of desires for those who desire them, and may there be liberation for those who long for liberation;
may no misfortune ever befall those who serve [you], and may there always be well-being for them.
May there be progeny for those who desire progeny, and may there be fame for those who desire fame;
indeed, the protection of the royal throne consists primarily in the welfare of the subjects.
May their prosperity be vast, and may their well-being be higher than the highest;
may they possess valor, splendor, and strength, and may they always be free from fear. (144)
May there be health, beauty, possession of virtues, great respect, freedom from bondage, liberation from all calamities, and sons and grandsons. (145)
May the lineages, the kingdom of heaven, sovereignty, lordship over the gods, mastery, the capacity for enjoyment, and all supernatural powers (ṛddhi) be yours forever. (146)
Whatever state one is intent upon, let that very thing be desired;
let there be both scholarship and knowledge of the arts, as well as future prosperity. (147)
May there be recollection of past lives, omniscience, and indeed freedom from all obscurations;
may there be the state of a yogi, proficiency, and even mastery of the Gandharva arts. (148)
Perfection, asceticism, and even the states of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa belong to her;
the woman who serves the *Saṃhitā* is Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and indeed the Sovereign Goddess herself.
"Let there be Nara and Nārāyaṇa; we grant you these excellent boons.
You shall attain fame in the world as the *Saṃhitā*, the upholder of the Vedas. (4.123.150)
"You are the very essence of the Vedas' establishment, you are the womb of the Vedas, and you are the Vedic one.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and the others took their leave. 151.
Then Rādhikā and the others, with serene faces, said at that time:
"May you possess unbroken good fortune and be the certain bestower of liberation. (152)
Having spoken thus, they vanished and took the wife, who was the personified Saṃhitā, away;
they protected her on earth in the form of Vāṇī for eternal years.
May she, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is the eternal support in the world of the Lord and the world of Brahmā, be victorious in this world. 154.
Worshipped indeed by all as the Mother of All and the Supreme Sovereign, she dwells even within the households of the Vaiṣṇavas. || 155 ||
He shall dwell forever among the Vyāsas, the virtuous, the holy, those possessed of true being, and the devoted; he shall attain victory over those who are devoted.
Victory to the Saṃhitā, who is the nature of the creeper of one's own self like all the wish-fulfilling trees, the excellent vessel for the essence of the Vedas, the bestower of union with Brahman,
the mistress of the resonance of refuge, and the maker of liberation!
May he lead us, who are enriched by our own virtues, to the syllable that is his own name.
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all, be victorious;
may his mother be Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī, and his father Gopāla Kṛṣṇa. (158)
Victory to Kuṅkumavāpī and to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake!
May the region of Saurāṣṭra be ever victorious, and may the sage Lomaśa be triumphant! 159.
May self-luminous consciousness be victorious; may eternal Lakṣmī be victorious;
may liberation be victorious; and may devotion, which swiftly bestows happiness, be victorious.
May there be victory, may there be auspiciousness, may there be well-being, happiness, and prosperity; and may there always be auspiciousness and devotion to the Supreme Brahman.
Thus remembering the Supreme Beloved, we indeed offer words of blessing:
Om, obeisance to the beginningless Teacher, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Om. (162)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Subjects of the Tiṣya Lineage; the Manifestation of the Saṃhitā in the Form of a Virgin Girl in the Presence of Badrikā-Nārāyaṇa; the Manifestation of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama-Nārāyaṇa, and Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa along with Their Respective Śaktis at that Very Place; the Bestowal of Boons upon the Saṃhitā; and the Fruit of Hearing the Narratives," in the Tiṣya Lineage within the fourth section of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Thus ends the section on the lineage of Śrī Tiṣya.
This complete Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, consisting of four sections, stands triumphant.
